definition: A word, saying, or message that expresses a thought or idea, often the content of what someone says or teaches.
article: At its core λόγος is a word that carries meaning—not just a name but an expressed thought, statement, or message. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 331 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "word" in 84% of cases, "message" in 14%, and "speaking" in about 1%. In the Septuagint it appears 961 times and most often stands in for the Hebrew דָּבָר ("word, matter"), used 698 times. The everyday papyri show its lively sense of speech in progress—one letter even urges a man to tell his wife "in my words" to look after the pigs.
caution: Strong's notes a special use in John for "the Divine Expression" (Christ), but the measured renderings here cover only the ordinary senses of word, message, and speaking.

definition: Love—deep affection, goodwill, and esteem directed toward God or other people.
article: ἀγάπη means love in the fullest sense: warm affection, goodwill, and esteem, whether between people, toward God, or God's love toward humanity. It is overwhelmingly consistent, rendered "love" in 112 of its 116 New Testament occurrences (99%), and in its 15 Septuagint appearances it always translates the Hebrew אַהֲבָה. The most striking detail is its rarity outside the Bible: Moulton-Milligan note only three supposed instances in non-biblical Greek, two now read differently and the third doubtful, making this almost a distinctively biblical term.

definition: Forethought or careful planning, including the provision and attention one arranges in advance for something or someone.
article: πρόνοια means forethought—the careful planning or provision one makes ahead of time. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Acts 24:3, where Tertullus credits a governor's foresight, and in Romans 13:14, where Paul warns against making provision for the desires of the flesh. Moulton-Milligan notes that while later Greek used the word for divine "providence" (first appearing in that sense in the Greek Bible at Wisdom 14:3), the New Testament never uses it that way—it always means practical forethought or care, a usage echoed in everyday papyri where someone is thanked for their pronoia (their attentive care).
caution: The two NT occurrences are too few to map a clear range, and the automated sense labels here are garbled and should not be trusted.

definition: To bring or lead someone or something down, including the nautical sense of bringing a ship to land.
article: κατάγω means to bring or lead down, whether moving a person from a higher place to a lower one or escorting someone somewhere. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "brought down" in 57% of cases, with 3 instances simply absorbed into surrounding phrasing. It also carried a specific nautical sense of bringing a vessel to land, and the everyday papyri show it frequently used of bringing down corn and goods to the sea coast or a harbor.

definition: Someone who shares jointly in something or someone with whom you partner together.
senseLabels: one who shares jointly in something
article: This word combines "with" (σύν) and "sharer/partner" (κοινωνός) to describe a person who participates jointly in something alongside others. Its range is narrow but flexible: it can take a thing being shared (Romans 11:17, 1 Corinthians 9:23) or a person you share with (Philippians 1:7). The Majority Bible renders it "share" twice and "partners" once, and a papyrus from A.D. 110 shows it used in an ordinary letter's greeting, confirming it was everyday Koine vocabulary.
caution: With only 3 Byzantine occurrences (4 in the critical text), the evidence base is thin and the renderings vary between "share" and "partners."

definition: Describing something extremely costly, precious, and of great value.
article: πολύτιμος combines πολύς (much) and τιμή (price or honor) to describe something of great value—the word the Gospels use for the expensive perfume Mary poured on Jesus' feet and the costly pearl in Jesus' parable. The Byzantine NT has it twice, and translators handle it as part of a larger phrase about costliness rather than a single English word. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 295 describes 'very costly clothes,' confirming this was ordinary commercial language for high-priced goods. Older lexicons also note a rarer secondary sense, 'much revered,' seen in Menander's phrase 'highly honored gods,' though that meaning does not appear in the measured NT data.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two Byzantine occurrences, both absorbed into surrounding phrasing, so the measured rendering data is limited.

definition: Zebedee, a Galilean fisherman who was the father of the apostles James and John.
article: Ζεβεδαῖος is simply the personal name Zebedee, borne by the father of the apostles James and John. It appears 12 times across 4 books in the Byzantine New Testament, and translators render it either as the bare name "Zebedee" (50%) or within the phrase "son of Zebedee" (25%). The name comes from Hebrew (compare זְבַדְיָה), and Abbott-Smith notes the Septuagint spells related forms variously as Ζαβδειά, Ζαβαδαῖας, and Ζαβαδαῖος.

definition: A grammatical form of the verb "to be" — used to say that something exists, happens, or is present.
article: This is the subjunctive form of εἰμί ("to be"), the basic Greek verb for existence and identity. Like the English "to be," it covers a wide range: that someone or something exists ("in the beginning was the Word," John 1:1), that an event takes place, or that something is present in a place. As a subjunctive specifically, it shows up in conditional and purpose constructions, often paired with particles like εἰ ("if"). There are no measured senses for this exact form in the digest, since the Byzantine New Testament data records no separate occurrences under this entry.
caution: The digest reports zero Byzantine occurrences and no measured senses for this specific form, so its meaning is described entirely from grammatical and lexicon evidence rather than from corpus translation data.

definition: Deep compassion or pity, the heartfelt tenderness one feels toward someone in need.
article: οἰκτιρμός refers to compassion or pity—the warm inner tenderness that moves a person to care for someone suffering. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 5 times, and the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "compassion" (40%), while it pairs naturally with words for the inner organs, as in "a heart of compassion" (Col 3:12) and "compassion and mercy" (Php 2:1). The most telling background is the Septuagint, where it appears 26 times—usually in the plural—and chiefly translates the Hebrew רָ֫חַם, a term for womb-deep mercy, which is why it so often describes God as "the Father of compassion."
caution: The word occurs only 5 times in the New Testament, so its range rests heavily on Septuagint usage; some of the listed renderings ("beloved compassion," "rejected of mercy") reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word's core meaning.

definition: A preposition or conjunction marking a limit reached—"until" a point in time, "as far as" a place, or "to the point of" a degree.
article: μέχρι marks the boundary or end-point of something—most often "until" in time, but it can also mean "as far as" a place or even "to the point of" a degree. In the Byzantine NT it appears 17 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "until" in 7 of those cases (70%), while in another 7 it disappears into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: phrases like "up to the present time" and "the interest up to date" use μέχρι exactly the way the NT does.
caution: Strong's distinguishes μέχρι (denoting the terminus) from the closely related ἄχρι (the intervening time or space), but the two overlap heavily and this fine distinction is not firmly measurable from usage.

definition: A person devoted to wisdom and learning—a philosopher.
article: φιλόσοφος literally means "lover of wisdom" and refers to a philosopher. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 17:18, where the Majority Standard Bible's surrounding context renders it among the Epicurean and Stoic thinkers Paul encountered in Athens. The papyri and inscriptions show the word's range nicely: it could be a formal title (one official document lists tax-exempt philosophers of the Museum) or a warm personal description, as in an inscription praising a woman who "loving her husband and sober-minded, a lover of wisdom, lived modestly." In the Septuagint it once stands in for the Hebrew אַשָּׁף, a term for wise men or enchanters.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on a single passage and outside evidence.

definition: Born first; the firstborn child, or figuratively the one holding the rank and privileges of a firstborn.
article: πρωτότοκος means "firstborn" — literally the first child a mother bears, as in Luke 2:7. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "firstborn" in 7 of its occurrences, and it appears heavily in the Septuagint (128×), almost always translating the Hebrew בְּכוֹר. Beyond birth order, the New Testament stretches it to express rank and priority, applying it to Christ (Colossians 1:15; Romans 8:29); intriguingly, a pagan grave inscription cited by Moulton-Milligan calls someone "a priest of the firstborn," hinting that firstborn status carried special privilege.

definition: Describing something that cannot be denied or argued against because it is plainly true.
article: This word describes a fact so clear that no one can reasonably dispute it — "undeniable" or "beyond contradiction." It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 19:36), where the city clerk uses it to call a truth beyond question and urge the crowd to stay calm. Outside the Bible it shows up in everyday Koine: an inscription from Pergamon (2nd–1st century BC) uses it to mean "beyond possibility of dispute," matching the New Testament sense exactly.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range is inferred mainly from outside documents rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: To cry out or shout loudly, often in a tense or excited crowd, calling, demanding, or protesting at the top of one's voice.
article: κραυγάζω means to shout or cry out loudly, used of people raising their voices in urgent appeal, demand, or protest. Though the digest splits the renderings into several fragments, they all point to one core idea — loud shouting — as seen when Jesus cried out to Lazarus with a loud voice (John 11:43) and when crowds shouted before Pilate (John 18:40; 19:6, 15). Abbott-Smith notes it equals κράζω and could even describe animals baying or croaking, but in the New Testament it always refers to human shouting; its single Septuagint appearance translates a Hebrew word tied to crying or weeping.
caution: The measured sense fragments look garbled and the Hebrew counterpart is reported inconsistently (בֶּכִי versus רוּעַ), so treat the breakdown loosely.

definition: To wither, fade, or waste away, like a flower or plant losing its life and vigor in the heat.
article: μαραίνω originally described a fire dying out, then broadened to cover many kinds of decay and enfeeblement; by the New Testament era it was used of flowers and grass wilting. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at James 1:11, where a rich person "fades away" like a scorched flower, and twice in the Septuagint, including Job's imagery of withering. Tellingly, the papyri and inscriptions show it frequently on grave epitaphs, as when one mourner says Hades "snatched away and withered" the deceased's prime of life.
caution: Evidence is thin (one Byzantine occurrence) and the digest's measured rendering label "midst" appears to be a tagging artifact rather than the word's actual meaning of withering or fading.

definition: A filling up to the point of fullness or satisfaction, especially the gratifying or indulging of physical desires.
senseLabels: satisfying or indulging of the flesh
article: πλησμονή describes being filled up to satisfaction or satiety, and in its single New Testament appearance (Colossians 2:23) it points to gratifying the flesh. The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 23 times across 13 books, usually translating Hebrew words built on the root for 'fullness' or 'being satisfied.' Moulton-Milligan note it often carries a negative flavor — overindulgence rather than healthy fullness — and quote Euripides to that effect; the lexicon Abbott-Smith records that scholars even disagree over whether the Colossians phrase means 'against the indulgence of the flesh' or 'for the full satisfaction of the flesh.'
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering 'appearance' does not match the lexicons' core meaning of 'filling/satiety,' so the translation here is genuinely disputed.

definition: The territory or district within certain boundaries; a region marked off by its borders.
article: In the New Testament ὅριον always appears in the plural and refers to a territory or district — the area lying within a set of boundaries. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "region" in 56% of its 11 occurrences and "left region" (in phrases about leaving an area) in another 33%, with two cases absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The word's literal sense of "boundary-line" shows up vividly in everyday papyri: a document from 139 B.C. lists the ὅρια (boundaries) of land, and another marks distance "as far as the boundaries of the farmstead." In the Septuagint it occurs 276 times, overwhelmingly translating Hebrew גְּבוּל ("border"), 232 times.

definition: To stain, soil, or defile something, used both literally for physical marks and figuratively for moral corruption.
article: σπιλόω means to stain, spot, or defile, and it shows up only twice in the New Testament (James 3:6 and Jude 23), both times figuratively for moral corruption rather than literal dirt. The word comes from σπίλος, a spot or stain, and turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary vocabulary. A vivid parallel comes from the Testament of Asher, which says the greedy person "stains his soul" while making his body shine — a neat picture of inward defilement hidden by outward polish.
caution: Confidence is low: only two NT occurrences, and the measured renderings ("fire" in James, "stained clothing" in Jude) reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word's own core meaning of staining.

definition: A full twenty-four-hour span covering one night and one day together.
article: This word combines the Greek words for "night" (νύξ) and "day" (ἡμέρα) to mean a complete twenty-four-hour period. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 11:25, where Paul says he spent a night and a day adrift at sea; in that one place it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, including a related form νυκτῆμαρ in a fourth-century Christian letter describing people who "go about and walk night and day."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is rare overall, so its precise force rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To put someone in prison or hand them over into custody.
article: φυλακίζω means to imprison or lock someone up, and it comes from φύλαξ, meaning a guard. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 22:19, where it is rendered "imprisoned," and the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles agree on that translation 100% of the time. Outside the New Testament it shows up in the Septuagint just once, at Wisdom 18:4, so the overall body of evidence is quite thin.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: Pontus, a region of Asia Minor along the southern shore of the Black Sea.
article: Πόντος is a place name: Pontus, a district in northern Asia Minor bordering the Black Sea (the πόντος Εὔξεινος). It appears only twice in the New Testament, in Acts 2:9 and 1 Peter 1:1, both times naming the region where Jews or Christians lived. Abbott-Smith notes it took its name from the adjacent sea, and Strong's records that the underlying word can simply mean "a sea."
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both proper-name references to the same region, the entry rests on very thin evidence; the "Cappadocia" label in the measured data reflects a list of neighboring regions in Acts 2:9 rather than a separate meaning.

definition: The number six hundred, used to count people, objects, or measured distances.
article: This is simply the cardinal number six hundred, formed from the words for six and hundred. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, both in Revelation (13:18 and 14:20), where it functions as part of a larger numerical phrase rather than standing as its own English word. It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 65 times across 11 books and usually renders the Hebrew word for six (שֵׁשׁ, 57 times).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into larger number phrases, the New Testament evidence is thin, though the meaning itself is not in doubt.

definition: To forget something, or to neglect or overlook it by letting it slip from your mind.
article: This middle-voice verb means to forget—to lose something out of mind—and by extension to neglect what you should keep in view. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 8 times, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "forgotten" or "forgetting" (each twice), with two more occurrences absorbed into the phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 105 times and almost always stands for the Hebrew שָׁכַח (shakhach), "to forget," and everyday papyri attest the same word, including a charming first-century BC letter that asks, "how can I forget you?"
caution: With only 8 New Testament occurrences and two absorbed into phrasing, the measured English picture is thin, though the sources agree on the core meaning.

definition: Deceit or trickery — the use of cunning, fraud, or treachery to mislead someone.
article: δόλος means deceit, the deliberate use of cunning or fraud to fool others. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "deceit" in 40% of cases, with closely related terms like "trickery" and "guile" filling out the rest — so its range is tightly clustered around dishonest scheming. In the Septuagint it appears 34 times, most often translating the Hebrew מִרְמָה ("deceit," 14×). A striking detail comes from the classical evidence: the word originally meant a "bait" in Homer, then a "snare," before settling into the abstract sense of craft or deceit found throughout the New Testament.

definition: A Parthian, a person from Parthia, the region beyond the eastern edge of the Roman Empire between the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf.
article: Πάρθος simply names an inhabitant of Parthia, a land lying east of the Roman Empire between the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf. It appears only once in the New Testament, in the list of nationalities present at Pentecost in Acts 2:9, where it is named alongside Medes and Elamites. The word is probably of foreign origin, which fits its use as a geographic label for a distant people.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: Food or provisions needed to sustain people or animals, especially fodder and basic sustenance.
article: χόρτασμα means food or provisions, the basic sustenance needed to keep people and animals alive. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:11, where it describes the sustenance the patriarchs could not find during a famine. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for fodder (מִסְפּוֹא, 6 times), and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one third-century document speaks of preparing supplies and χορτάσματα for travel, and another of animals having free fodder.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests mostly on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: With difficulty; describing how hard something is to accomplish.
article: This adverb means "with difficulty" or "hardly," describing how hard an action is to carry out. In all three of its New Testament appearances (Matthew 19:23, Mark 10:23, Luke 18:24) it occurs in Jesus' parallel saying about how hard it is for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. The Majority Standard Bible and the Berea Standard Bible both render it as "hard" in 100% of cases, matching the older lexicons' "with difficulty, hardly." It is an adverb formed from the adjective δύσκολος.
caution: Evidence is thin — only three closely parallel occurrences — though the lexicons and measured renderings agree fully.

definition: A comparison word meaning "as if" or "as it were," softening a statement by marking it as a likeness rather than a literal claim.
article: ὡσπερεί is a connecting word that flags a comparison, roughly "just as if" or "as it were." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 15:8, where Paul says Christ appeared to him "as to one untimely born" — which is why the measured renderings cluster around "birth" (the word itself isn't "birth" but sits next to that image in the verse). Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, with a related form ὡσπεροῦν found in a 6th-century document.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range here rests on a single verse plus the broader sense given by lexica.

definition: A royal treasury or store of valuable possessions, originally a Persian term for treasure.
article: γάζα is a borrowed Persian word meaning treasure or the royal treasury, and the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) consistently gloss it as "treasure." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 8:27), where it describes the Ethiopian eunuch as official over the queen's treasury. In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times, translating several Hebrew words including גִּנְזֵי ("treasures," 3×) and גִּזְבָּר ("treasurer"); a 3rd-century BC inscription from the Red Sea coast even uses it of treasure carried back to Egypt after the Persian conquests.
caution: The measured rendering label here reads "Ethiopians," which reflects the surrounding context of Acts 8:27 rather than the word's actual meaning of "treasure," so treat that data point with care.

definition: Slowness or delay in acting, especially being later than expected to do something.
article: βραδύτης refers to slowness or delay in taking action, and in the New Testament it appears just once, in 2 Peter 3:9, where it is rendered "slow." The word comes from βραδύς (slow) and was ordinary, everyday Koine vocabulary, showing up in the papyri and inscriptions of the period. Classical lexica note it could describe both physical slowness (as far back as Homer) and slowness of mind (as in Plato), though the single biblical use simply means delay.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on that single verse plus general Koine usage.

definition: To look at something closely and learn from it by careful observation or consideration.
article: καταμανθάνω means to study something attentively—to look closely and take in what you see. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Matthew 6:28, where Jesus tells his hearers to "consider" the lilies of the field; the verb is built from κατά (an intensifier) plus μανθάνω ("to learn"), so the sense is learning thoroughly through observation. The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: one document asks Nicanor to "look at" a dress pattern, and another asks someone to inspect an olive-yard because it is overgrown.
caution: This word appears just once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence supported by Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: The comparative form meaning smaller, less, younger, or inferior in size, quantity, age, rank, or quality.
article: ἐλάσσων is the comparative of "little" (related to μικρός), so it covers a range of "less": smaller in size, fewer in quantity, younger in age, or poorer in quality. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 4 times, and in just 1 of those does it get its own English word, rendered "fine" (more literally "poorer") at John 2:10; the other 3 are folded into surrounding phrasing. It shows up far more in the Septuagint (19 times), most often translating the Hebrew word מָעַט ("few, little," 8×), and everyday papyri use it for things like a "smaller assessment" of tax.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and just one rendered by a distinct English word, the measured picture is thin and leans on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: To go or come down from a higher place to a lower one, whether descending a road, stepping off a boat, or coming down from heaven.
article: καταβαίνω is the ordinary Greek word for movement downward, and the New Testament uses it 80 times in a very physical way — people walking down from a hill, stepping out of a boat, or the Spirit descending from heaven. The translations cluster tightly around "come down," "down," and "went down," which together cover three-quarters of its uses, so its meaning is stable and concrete. In the Septuagint it appears a remarkable 321 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew יָרַד ("go down"), and the everyday papyri show the same plain sense — one document records an oracle telling a man "not to go down until the 25th."

definition: To fall on or onto someone or something, whether physically, in affectionate embrace, or as fear or the Spirit coming over a person.
article: At its core ἐπιπίπτω means literally to fall upon something, but its range stretches widely depending on what does the falling. People fall on someone's neck to embrace them (Luke 15:20), fear or reproaches fall on people, and the Holy Spirit falls upon believers in Acts. The everyday papyri preserve a harsher edge: one document from 246 BC describes a man who 'fell upon' another and struck him on the neck, showing the word could carry real hostility and violence.
caution: In 5 of its 13 New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into English phrasing rather than rendered as a distinct word, so its precise force often depends on context.

definition: An adverb meaning something happens a single time, often with the sense that it is done completely and never needs repeating.
article: ἐφάπαξ appears 5 times in the New Testament and carries two related shades: a plain "once" or "at once" (as in the 1 Corinthians 15:6 report of Jesus appearing to over 500 people at one time), and the stronger "once for all" — a single decisive event that need never be repeated, used in Hebrews for Christ's sacrifice. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "once" 3 times and ties it to a once-for-all sacrifice in Hebrews 9:12 and 10:10, where the labels reflect surrounding words about offering. It's a compound of ἐπί ("upon") and ἅπαξ ("once"), and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, including a document from A.D. 616.
caution: With only 5 occurrences, the line between "at once" and "once for all" depends on context, and the measured labels for Hebrews fold in nearby words about sacrifice rather than the adverb alone.

definition: The high point, ledge, or turret-like projection of the Jerusalem temple complex.
article: πτερύγιον literally means "a little wing" (it's a diminutive of πτέρυξ, "wing"), and by extension it refers to anything that juts out like a wing — a gable, turret, parapet, or pinnacle. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both times for the high point of the temple where the devil sets Jesus (Matthew 4:5 and Luke 4:9), which English Bibles render as "pinnacle." In the Septuagint the same word is far more common (18 times), usually translating the Hebrew כָּנָף, "wing" or "edge," showing its underlying sense of an extremity or far corner.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same scene, the precise architectural feature meant by "pinnacle" remains uncertain.

definition: An adverb pointing to a location away from the speaker, meaning "there" or "in that place," and sometimes "to that place."
article: ἐκεῖ is a common location-pointing adverb meaning "there" or "in that place," appearing 103 times in the Byzantine New Testament. Because it functions as a small connecting word, in 93 of those 103 cases it gets absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own; where it does surface, translators render it as "where," "place," or "went." The lexica note it can also carry a sense of motion ("to that place," thither), as in classical Greek. In the Septuagint it shows up 715 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew שָׁם ("there"), and the papyri preserve it in ordinary instructions like "stay there till you have watered the olive-yard."

definition: Describing someone who loves pleasure, especially more than they love God.
article: φιλήδονος combines φίλος (loving) and ἡδονή (pleasure) to describe a person devoted to pleasure. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:4, where it lists pleasure-lovers among people in the last days. A close parallel comes from Philo, who contrasts being φιλήδονος (pleasure-loving) with being φιλάρετος (virtue-loving) and φιλόθεον (God-loving) — exactly the kind of contrast Paul draws.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A clear, convincing piece of evidence that establishes something as certain.
article: τεκμήριον means a sure sign or positive proof — evidence solid enough to settle a matter beyond doubt. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 1:3), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "proofs," the same word the KJV strengthens to "infallible proof." The strength of the word is confirmed in everyday Koine: an Ephesian inscription (c. A.D. 160) calls a month named after Artemis the "greatest τεκμήριον" of the honor paid her, and papyri pair it with words like "strongest" and "greatest."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests on a single passage backed by outside Greek usage.

definition: Something given to another person — a gift or present.
senseLabels: a gift credited to one's account
article: δόμα simply means a gift or present, formed from the verb meaning "to give." In its 4 New Testament appearances the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gifts" 3 times and once (Philippians 4:17) as a gift "credited to an account" — both reflect the same core idea, just applied in a financial setting. The word is heavily attested in the Septuagint (38 times in 17 books), where it usually translates the Hebrew מַתָּנָה ("gift," 11×), and it also turns up in everyday papyri, where one document from 255 BC uses it for a supply or allotment given to workers.

definition: A specific thing asked for — a request or petition put before someone in authority or before God.
article: αἴτημα is the concrete thing you ask for — the actual petition or demand, rather than the act of asking. The New Testament uses it only 3 times, and in two of those (Philippians 4:6 and 1 John 5:15) it refers to requests brought before God, while elsewhere it can describe a demand made to authorities. In the Septuagint it appears 11 times and most often translates the Hebrew שְׁאֵלָה ("request"); Moulton-Milligan note it is fairly common in everyday papyri and inscriptions, where it could even mean a billeting demand for lodging.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and the two measured senses each resting on a single verse, the evidence here is thin.

definition: Heat — the warmth given off by a fire.
article: θέρμη means heat or warmth, and in the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 28:3, where the heat of a fire drives a snake out of the brushwood Paul has gathered. The word is well attested in everyday Koine, especially in connection with public baths — papyri from Oxyrhynchus mention superintending repairs to 'the baths of Hadrian.' In the Septuagint it likewise refers to natural warmth, as in Job, Psalms, and Ecclesiastes (where two people lying together 'have heat').
caution: This entry's measured-sense data is mislabeled 'bundle' and conflicts with every lexicon, which uniformly give 'heat'; the word also occurs only once in the New Testament, so confidence is low.

definition: The edible fruit of the fig tree, eaten fresh or dried.
article: σῦκον simply means a fig, the fruit of the fig tree, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "figs" in 3 of its 4 New Testament occurrences. The one remaining case (Mark 11:13) describes Jesus looking for figs on a leafy tree, the same fruit just seen in context. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for figs (תְּאֵנִים, 6×), and everyday Koine papyri confirm the ordinary sense—shopping lists mention "2,000 figs," "400 summer figs," and a basket of dessert holding 100 figs.
caution: The word occurs only 4 times in the New Testament, but the meaning is consistent and well attested in the Septuagint, papyri, and lexica.

definition: The starting point of something in time or order, or a person or power holding rule and authority.
article: ἀρχή carries a double meaning that traces back to its two related verbs: it can mean the "beginning" of something (its sense in 31 of 57 New Testament uses, about 70%) or, concretely, those who hold "rule" — rulers, magistrates, and powers (5×, 11%). In the Septuagint it appears 179 times and most often translates Hebrew רֹאשׁ ("head," 28×) and words for "first" or "beginning." One striking detail: a second-century Oxyrhynchus papyrus has been cited to help untangle the famously difficult phrase in John 8:25, showing the word was at home in everyday Koine speech.
caution: In about 13 of 57 occurrences the word is absorbed into English phrasing and gets no word of its own, so its precise force there depends on context.

definition: To pour something out, whether liquid like wine or blood, or figuratively to bestow something generously.
article: ἐκχέω is the basic verb for pouring something out — wine from a wineskin, water from a bowl, or blood that is spilled ("shed"). The Byzantine NT uses it 28 times, and just over half of those are rendered "poured out," often of Christ's blood at the Last Supper. In the Septuagint it appears 119 times and almost always translates the Hebrew שָׁפַך ("to pour, spill"), so its core meaning is well anchored; everyday papyri even use a related noun for the "emptying" of a bath-house. Beyond the literal, it stretches figuratively to the pouring out of the Spirit and the bestowing of God's love.

definition: Open to sight or plainly evident, so that something is visible, clear, or made known publicly rather than hidden.
article: φανερός describes something that is out in the open — visible to the eye, obvious to the mind, or publicly known rather than concealed. Across its 20 Byzantine occurrences the translation work is fairly spread out: the Majority Standard renders it as "what" twice (15%) and "clear" twice (15%), while 7 of 20 times it simply gets absorbed into the surrounding English phrasing, which fits its frequent role in set expressions like "become known" or "make known." The everyday papyri confirm this practical sense beautifully: a writer says φανερόν σοι ποιῶ, "I inform you," using the word in routine business notices to mean making a matter plain to someone.
caution: Because the word so often dissolves into phrases (7 of 20 times) and its measured renderings each cover only 15%, no single English equivalent captures it cleanly.

definition: To resemble or be like something else, as in a comparison.
article: This verb means to resemble or be like something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 2 times, both in James, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "like" in 100% of cases (James 1:6 and 1:23). Lexicons note it as an obsolete present form connected to the perfect ἔοικα, and the Septuagint uses it only twice, where it translates two different Hebrew words.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences (none in the critical SBLGNT text) and a single sense — so confidence is low and the form itself is treated as obsolete by lexicographers.

definition: To lose heart or become discouraged and despondent, losing the inner spirit to keep going.
article: ἀθυμέω literally means to be "without heart" (from a negative particle plus θυμός, "spirit"), and describes someone who has lost their inner drive and grown despondent. The word appears just once in the New Testament, at Colossians 3:21, where children should not be discouraged to the point of losing heart; the Septuagint uses it 6 times, translating Hebrew words like חָרָה (to burn with anger). The everyday papyri capture its flavor vividly: one ancient letter simply pleads μὴ ἀθύμει — "don't be discouraged."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the Majority Bible's rendering as "provoke" frames it differently from the lexicons' "lose heart, be disheartened."

definition: A starting point or opening that gives someone the chance, incentive, or pretext to do something.
article: ἀφορμή literally means a "starting point," and in military language it described a base of operations from which a campaign was launched. In the New Testament's 7 uses, all by Paul, it always carries the figurative sense of an opening, occasion, or opportunity—sometimes a foothold that sin or critics exploit, sometimes a legitimate chance to act. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this range: one edict of an Eparch of Egypt (A.D. 127) speaks of people "seeking an occasion (ἀφορμή) for wrongdoing," almost exactly the negative nuance Paul gives it.
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the line between "opportunity" and "pretext" depends heavily on context rather than the word itself.

definition: Aaron, the brother of Moses and Israel's first high priest, used as a personal name.
article: Ἀαρών is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Aaron (אַהֲרוֹן), Moses' brother and the first high priest. It appears 5 times in the New Testament and is rendered "Aaron" in every case the Bible translates as a word, with one instance absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The name is overwhelmingly common in the Septuagint—357 times across 13 books, almost always for the Hebrew Aaron (333×), though it occasionally renders other Hebrew words like Moses (4×).
caution: As an indeclinable foreign name, its meaning is fixed and uncontroversial, though it occurs only 5 times in the New Testament.

definition: A hidden or enclosed space such as a cellar or vault, where something can be tucked away out of sight.
article: κρύπτη refers to a concealed space — a cellar, vault, or hidden spot where an object can be put away. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:33, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "cellar" (100% of occurrences), and the Berean Standard Bible agrees. The word is well attested in everyday Koine: a third-century B.C. papyrus (PSI V.547) lists it among parts of a building alongside doors and windows, describing "the cellar similarly plastered" — concrete evidence that it named a real architectural feature.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the entry rests on a single verse, though the papyri confirm the "cellar" sense.

definition: Zerah, an ancestor of Jesus, the son of Judah and Tamar named in Matthew's genealogy.
senseLabels: Zerah, son of Judah and Tamar
article: Ζαρά is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Zerah, appearing once in the New Testament (Matthew 1:3) where he is listed in Jesus' genealogy as a son of Judah and Tamar. It is an indeclinable proper name borrowed from Hebrew (זֶרַח). In the Septuagint the same Greek form shows up 14 times across 4 books, mostly rendering the Hebrew name זָ֫רַח, though once it stands in for a different Hebrew name (אָזְנִי).
caution: This is a proper name with only a single New Testament occurrence, so its 'meaning' is simply the person it names.

definition: To throw, fling, or toss something or someone, often quickly or carelessly, including casting things away or down.
article: ῥίπτω means to throw, fling, or toss—anything from money (Matthew 27:5) to cargo thrown overboard (Acts 27:19) to a person flung to the ground (Luke 4:35). Strong's notes it implies a quick toss, contrasting with the more deliberate hurl of βάλλω. Everyday papyri show the same flavor: one Tebtunis document describes a man who "threw away his garment and took to flight," matching the sense of casting off in haste.
caution: Two passages are unsettled: the "large" rendering in Matthew 15:30 isn't really a measured meaning of this verb, and scholars dispute whether Acts 22:23 means to throw off garments or to shake/toss them about.

definition: A sharing or partnership between two parties, the kind of common ground they hold together.
article: μετοχή refers to having a share in something with someone else — a partnership or common ground. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:14, where Paul asks what μετοχή righteousness can have with lawlessness; the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase "unequally" (as in "unequally yoked"), though the underlying noun means "partnership" or "fellowship." Everyday Koine papyri use the word concretely: one document speaks of someone being left "completely without any share" of an inheritance, showing its sense of holding a portion in common.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range rests on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: Salt, the common mineral used to season and preserve food, and figuratively for wise or gracious speech.
article: ἅλας simply means salt, the everyday mineral for seasoning and preserving food, and it appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The two measured "senses" are really the same word—most occurrences cluster in the saying about salt losing its flavor (Matthew 5:13, Mark 9:50, Luke 14:34). It commonly stands for the Hebrew word for salt (מֶלַח) in the Septuagint, and the everyday papyri show it in plain shopping lists, like "oil, salt, wood." Lexicons also note a figurative use for wit, wisdom, or grace in speech, as in Colossians 4:6.
caution: The two listed senses are not truly distinct meanings but the same word counted within and outside the "salt loses its flavor" saying.

definition: To shoot someone down or kill them with an arrow.
article: κατατοξεύω means to strike someone down or kill them using an arrow, combining the preposition κατά with a word derived from τόξον, meaning "bow." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up 6 times across 4 books of the Septuagint, where it translates several different Hebrew words. Notably, in Exodus 19:13 it renders the Hebrew verb meaning "to throw" or "shoot," describing how anyone touching Mount Sinai was to be killed; Abbott-Smith notes that some editions read it in Hebrews 12:20 quoting this passage, though leading critical editions omit it there.
caution: This word never appears in the Byzantine New Testament, its supposed New Testament occurrence in Hebrews 12:20 is disputed and omitted by major critical editions, and the listed Hebrew counterparts vary across sources.

definition: To send someone along together with another person or thing.
article: Συμπέμπω combines "with" (σύν) and "send" (πέμπω) to mean dispatching someone in the company of another. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 8 (verses 18 and 22), where Paul describes sending trusted companions along with Titus. The everyday papyri confirm this plain sense — one document from AD 186 uses it of sending something "along with the letter" — and a few examples even carry the nuance of sending help to someone.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though the meaning is consistent and well supported by the papyri.

definition: Clever scheming used to deceive or manipulate others; craftiness or cunning.
article: πανουργία describes the kind of shrewdness that gets used for deception — cunning, trickery, or sly maneuvering. In the New Testament it appears 5 times and almost always carries a bad sense; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "cunning" in two-thirds of cases (as in 2 Corinthians 11:3 and Ephesians 4:14), and elsewhere folds it into phrasing like Jesus seeing through their craftiness in Luke 20:23. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it more neutrally — translating Hebrew עָרְמָה ("shrewdness") in places like Proverbs, where it can mean simple cleverness, and Moulton-Milligan documents the negative "knavery" sense in an everyday papyrus warning people off swindling their creditors.
caution: Sources differ on tone: the Septuagint uses the word in good or neutral senses, while New Testament and classical usage lean strongly negative.

definition: A wave or surge of the sea, especially a swelling, breaking, or toppling wave.
article: κῦμα means a wave of the sea, typically one that swells up and breaks or crashes—Strong's captures this as "a billow." All five Byzantine New Testament occurrences refer to literal sea waves battering boats, though Jude 13 uses it figuratively ("wild waves of the sea"). In the Septuagint it appears 17 times and most often translates the Hebrew גָּל (gal, "wave"), 7 times; everyday Koine papyri likewise speak of being tossed "by the waves of the sea."

definition: A room or hall where an audience gathers to listen, such as a place for hearing legal cases.
article: This word names a room set aside for listening — an audience chamber where formal hearings or court cases took place. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 25:23, where Paul is brought before Agrippa and Festus. The classical lexicons (Abbott-Smith citing Plutarch) and Strong's agree on the 'audience-room' meaning, though the measured rendering oddly shows 'pomp,' which likely reflects a translation artifact rather than the word's actual sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ('pomp') conflicts with the lexicons' clear 'audience-room' meaning, so treat the measured data with caution.

definition: Relating to the Levites, the Israelite tribe that handled priestly duties.
article: This adjective means "Levitical" — having to do with the tribe of Levi and its priestly system. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 7:11, where it describes the Levitical priesthood, and shows up in the Septuagint as the title of the book of Leviticus. The single measured rendering here happens to be "basis," which reflects the phrasing of that one verse rather than the word's own meaning, which is simply "Levitical."
caution: With just one New Testament occurrence, the evidence is thin, and the measured rendering "basis" reflects its sentence context rather than the word's actual sense.

definition: To speak out plainly and declare something, often in a weighty or solemn pronouncement.
article: This verb means to speak forth or declare plainly, and it appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Acts. The measured renderings in our data are scrambled (showing fragments like "enabled," "Judea," and "answered am sobriety"), but the underlying word consistently describes solemn, emphatic speech — the Spirit-enabled utterance at Pentecost (Acts 2:4, 14) and Paul's declaration before Festus (Acts 26:25). An intriguing detail: in the astrologer Vettius Valens the word carries a darker, oracular sense (rendered "to prophesy" or rave), suggesting it could describe inspired or ecstatic utterance.
caution: Evidence is thin — only three NT occurrences — and the measured rendering data is garbled, so the precise sense rests largely on the lexica.

definition: To wrap a cloth or garment tightly around oneself or someone else, like fastening a towel at the waist.
article: Διαζώννυμι means to tie or wrap something snugly around the body, such as a towel or outer garment. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in John's Gospel (13:4, 13:5, and 21:7), where it describes Jesus girding himself with a towel and Peter wrapping his outer garment around himself. Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including one describing a wooden ladder wrapped with silver serpents, showing it was ordinary vocabulary for binding things tightly.
caution: With only 3 occurrences, all in one book, the measured range is narrow, so the two listed senses really reflect a single basic meaning of wrapping cloth around the body.

definition: An adverbial phrase meaning "by name" or "named," used to introduce a person's name.
article: This is a compressed form of τὸ ὄνομα ("the name"), squeezed together by crasis into a single word that functions as "by name" or "named." It appears just once in the New Testament, at Matthew 27:57, where it introduces Joseph of Arimathea. Abbott-Smith notes it works as an accusative absolute — a fixed grammatical tag for attaching a name to a person.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: To brag or show off, drawing attention to oneself in a vain, self-promoting way.
article: This verb means to play the braggart — to talk yourself up and vaunt your own importance. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 13:4, where love is described by what it does NOT do, so the Majority Standard Bible renders the whole phrase as "love is kind" rather than translating the word directly. The lexicons agree it means "boast": Moulton-Milligan note that elsewhere it pairs with a word for playing the toady, and Basil defined it as taking on anything not for need but for showy decoration.
caution: This is a rare word appearing only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "kind" reflects the negated phrasing rather than the word's own meaning of "boast."

definition: A person responsible for guarding prisoners and keeping a prison secure.
article: This word names a jailer — the official who guarded prisoners and kept the prison locked. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the story of Paul and Silas at Philippi (Acts 16:23, 27, 36), and is built straightforwardly from the words for "bond/chain" and "guard." It was ordinary everyday vocabulary: third-century BC papyri use it the same way, describing prisoners handed over to a named jailer, and the Septuagint uses it once to translate a Hebrew word for prison.
caution: The two listed senses are really one meaning — "jailer" — split only because translators rendered surrounding words differently in Acts 16:36.

definition: To slip or creep into a place secretly, sneaking one's way in.
article: This verb describes the act of slipping or sneaking into somewhere, used just once in the New Testament at 2 Timothy 3:6, where it pictures people who 'creep into' households. The lexicons connect it closely with ἐνδύω, which more often means to clothe or put on; ἐνδύνω carries the related idea of entering or pressing into. It shows up in everyday Koine papyri, including a third-century magical text, confirming it was ordinary working vocabulary.
caution: The digest's measured rendering 'worm' appears to be a tagging error, so the single occurrence gives thin evidence and the sense rests mainly on the lexicons.

definition: To surround something completely on every side, as an army encircles a city under siege.
article: περικυκλόω means to encircle or hem in something on all sides, built from περί ('around') and κυκλόω ('to circle'). In the New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 19:43, where Jesus foretells enemies who will surround Jerusalem; the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'barricade' there, and the BSB agrees. The Septuagint uses it 15 times, most often for the Hebrew סָבַב ('to surround'), and one charming fourth-century papyrus letter from a deacon to a bishop stretches it figuratively, saying the bishop's good reputation 'encircled the whole world.'
caution: The New Testament gives only a single occurrence, so the measured 'barricade' sense rests on one verse, though the broader 'surround' meaning is well supported by the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: Describing something as different or varied, and by extension as superior or more excellent than another.
article: διάφορος comes from the verb διαφέρω ("to differ") and basically points to something that stands apart. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, and where it gets its own English word the Majority Standard Bible renders it "excellent" both times (Hebrews 1:4 and 8:6), using the comparative form to say one thing surpasses another. The lexicons, however, document a wider range: the plain sense "different" or "various" shows up in everyday Koine papyri, such as an Oxyrhynchus document referring to "various persons," and the same word in its neuter form could even mean "money."
caution: With only 4 occurrences and two of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured "excellent" sense reflects narrow data, while the lexicons list a broader "different/various" sense not captured in the rendered counts.

definition: A correlative word meaning "what sort of" or "what kind of," pointing to the quality or nature of something.
article: ὁποῖος asks or points to the quality or nature of something — "what sort of" thing it is. It appears just 5 times in the New Testament, and translations vary: in Acts 26:29 and 1 Thessalonians 1:9 it comes through as "what," in 1 Corinthians 3:13 it stresses the "quality" of one's work, and in Galatians 2:6 and James 1:24 it shades into "what manner of" or "what kind." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that although this word was very common in classical Greek, it was already fading out in later Koine — yet it still turns up in everyday papyri, as in an Oxyrhynchus letter telling someone "you know what hospitality requires."
caution: With only 5 occurrences and the renderings spread across four different English choices, the precise force in any single verse depends heavily on context.

definition: To sell something, offering goods or property in exchange for money.
article: πωλέω means to sell — to put goods or property up for exchange, usually for money. The New Testament uses it consistently this way, whether for sparrows sold cheaply (Matthew 10:29) or someone selling all they own (Mark 10:21); the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sold" 11 times and "selling" 5 times out of 22 occurrences. In the Septuagint it almost always translates the Hebrew word מָכַר ("to sell"), and the everyday papyri confirm the same plain sense, one even echoing Mark 10:21 with a man who "sold all his property."
caution: Older lexicons note an original sense of "barter" or "put up for sale," but Moulton-Milligan notes only the simple meaning "sell" appears in the New Testament.

definition: To use something fully or to the utmost, often implying using it up completely rather than holding back.
senseLabels: use up or depend on fully
article: This compound of κατά and χράομαι carries an intensive force: not just "use" but "use to the full" or "use up." It appears only twice in the New Testament (both in 1 Corinthians), once for those who deal with the world without being absorbed in it (7:31) and once for Paul's full use of his rights (9:18). A striking parallel comes from an Egyptian papyrus (P Oxy II.281), where a woman complains that her husband Sarapion "squandered my dowry as he pleased" — showing the word's everyday sense of spending or using something up completely.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a broad classical range, the precise nuance in each verse is uncertain, and Strong's even suggests a negative shade ("misuse, abuse") not reflected in the measured renderings.

definition: Fair Havens, a harbor or bay on the south coast of the island of Crete.
article: Καλοὶ Λιμένες is a place name meaning literally "Good Harbors," referring to Fair Havens, a bay on the island of Crete. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:8, during the account of Paul's sea voyage. The name combines καλός ("good, fair") and λιμήν ("harbor"), and the two-word form here is plural.
caution: This is a proper place name appearing only once in Acts 27:8, with no occurrences in the Byzantine NT counted in the digest, so its usage range cannot be measured.

definition: To choose someone in advance for a task or role; to appoint, designate, or select beforehand.
article: This verb means to pick someone out ahead of time for a particular purpose, and in its 3 New Testament occurrences (all in Acts) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "appointed" twice. The everyday Greek of the papyri confirms this strongly: documents speak of "appointed collectors" of taxes and officials "appointed" to receive and transmit records, showing it was an ordinary administrative word for designating someone to a job. Built from "before" (pró) and a derivative of "hand" (cheír), it literally suggests taking something into one's hand in advance, which Strong's and Abbott-Smith connect to the figurative sense of purposing or choosing.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences, all in Acts) and the rendering data and lexicons divide it differently, so the exact shading is uncertain.

definition: To separate one thing or group from another, often to set someone or something apart for a special purpose.
article: ἀφορίζω literally means to mark something off by a boundary, then to separate or set it apart. In the Byzantine New Testament's 10 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "separate" 4 times (44%) and "set apart" 3 times (33%), with the BSB independently agreeing 100% on both. The papyri preserve a vivid technical use: a Greek land record speaks of acreage "set apart" so its produce could be reserved for Alexandria, the same boundary-marking idea applied to property. In the Septuagint it appears 85 times, often translating Hebrew words for closing off, pasture land, or offerings lifted up and dedicated.

definition: The first-person pronoun "I" or "me" in its emphatic dative form, marking the speaker as the one to whom something is given, done, or directed.
article: This is simply the emphatic dative form of the personal pronoun ἐγώ ("I"), meaning "to me" or "for me." It appears 236 times across 30 books of the Septuagint, though it does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament. According to Abbott-Smith, the full forms like ἐμοί are the emphatic counterparts to the lighter enclitic forms (μοι), used when the speaker is being stressed; one striking pattern is that it often renders the Hebrew "here I am" expression (הִנֵּנִי) and the simple "I am" (אֲנִי) in declarations.
caution: The digest reports zero New Testament occurrences and assigns no confidence tier, so the description here rests on Septuagint frequency and the grammatical notes rather than measured New Testament senses.

definition: To dream, or to see visions in one's sleep.
article: This verb means to dream or to experience visions while sleeping. In the New Testament it appears only twice—in Acts 2:17, where it describes old men dreaming dreams (quoting Joel), and in Jude 1:8, where it labels certain people as 'dreamers.' The word was at home in everyday Koine: Egyptian papyri even mention an ἐνυπνιοκριτής, a professional dream-interpreter at the Serapeum, showing how seriously dreams were taken. In the Septuagint it occurs 15 times and almost always translates the Hebrew חָלַם (to dream), 11 of those times.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured range is very thin, though the Septuagint and papyri evidence strongly agree on the basic meaning.

definition: Describing someone who actively shows mercy and compassion toward those in need.
article: ἐλεήμων describes a person who is full of pity and actively compassionate, related to the verb ἐλεέω ("to show mercy"). It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice—of those who will receive mercy in Matthew 5:7 and of Christ as a "merciful" high priest in Hebrews 2:17. In the Septuagint it occurs 18 times and chiefly renders the Hebrew חַנּוּן ("gracious"), where Moulton-Milligan notes it is frequently used of God but only rarely of human beings.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences this word's range is thinly attested, though the sense is consistent and the sources agree.

definition: A judgment or verdict—the decision reached in a judicial process, often the sentence God or a court passes on faults.
article: Κρίμα is the outcome of a judging process—a legal decision or verdict, which in many New Testament passages refers specifically to God's judgment. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "judgment" 10 times (45%) and "condemnation" twice, with 6 of its 28 occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing without a word of their own. The everyday legal flavor is clear in the papyri, where third-century BC documents use κρίμα for an official "legal decision" about taxes; in the Septuagint it appears 197 times, mostly translating Hebrew מִשְׁפָּט ("justice, judgment").
caution: Lexicons note an additional sense of "a lawsuit" or "case at law" that the measured New Testament renderings do not clearly show.

definition: In many ways or in various manners and forms.
article: This adverb describes doing something in many different ways or by varied methods and forms. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 1:1, where it pairs with a similar-sounding word to describe how God spoke. The related adjective πολύτροπος literally meant "much turning" or "manifold," and interestingly it survives in Modern Greek with a positive sense of "adroit" or resourceful.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: A personal name in Romans 16:7 for a believer greeted by Paul, which may be either male (Junias) or female (Junia).
article: Ἰουνιᾶς is a proper name of Latin origin appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 16:7, where Paul greets this person alongside Andronicus. The form has not been found anywhere else, and Moulton-Milligan suggest it is probably a contracted form of the Latin name Iunianus, common in inscriptions. Notably the sources disagree on the person's gender: some treat it as a man's name (Junias), while Souter and Moulton read it as the feminine Junia, as in the older Authorized Version.
caution: This name occurs only once, is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, has no parallels elsewhere, and the sources genuinely disagree over whether it is masculine (Junias) or feminine (Junia).

definition: The condition of being equal or balanced between parties, and by extension fair, even-handed treatment.
article: ἰσότης points to equality—an even balance between people or shares—and from there shades into the sense of fairness or fair dealing. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, twice in 2 Corinthians 8 about balancing material need and supply, and once in Colossians 4:1 where masters owe slaves what is "just and equal," the sense Abbott-Smith labels equity. Everyday Koine confirms the fairness sense: Moulton-Milligan cites the maxim of Menander, "honor equality and take advantage of no one."
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint—and the measured rendering labels here track surrounding phrases rather than crisply isolating the word's own meaning.

definition: Cumin, a small plant whose seeds were used as a spice and could be tithed.
article: Cumin (κύμινον) is a garden herb whose seeds served as a common spice, and in the New Testament it appears once, in Matthew 23:23, among the small things some carefully tithed. The word is of foreign, likely Phoenician, origin, and in the Septuagint it shows up three times in Isaiah, translating the Hebrew word for cumin. It was clearly an everyday commodity: Moulton-Milligan cite account papyri that simply list measures of cumin alongside oil, the way a shopping ledger would.
caution: The Majority Standard rendering "matters" in Matthew 23:23 reflects the surrounding phrase rather than the plant itself, which all lexicons agree means cumin; with only one NT occurrence, evidence is thin.

definition: A firm sense of confidence, trust, or reliance placed in someone or something.
article: This noun simply means confidence or trust — the settled assurance you place in a person or situation. Across its 6 New Testament occurrences (all in Paul's letters) it is consistently rendered with words like "confidence," and the four measured renderings ("confident," "confidence," "such confidence") are really just one underlying sense shaped by context. One curious detail: ancient Atticist grammarians actually condemned this word as substandard Greek, yet it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and once in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew בִּטָּחוֹן ("trust, security").
caution: The word appears only 6 times, all in Paul, plus a single Septuagint occurrence, so its measured range rests on thin evidence.

definition: A professional public speaker, and especially a legal advocate who argues a case in court.
article: In the New Testament ῥήτωρ refers to a forensic advocate—a lawyer who pleads a case before a judge. It appears just once (Acts 24:1), where it names the man who argued against Paul, and both the Majority Standard Bible and BSB render it as a lawyer. While the older lexicons stress the broader sense of "orator" or public speaker, the everyday Koine papyri back up the courtroom meaning: documents like a lawsuit report from AD 49 introduce counsel for the plaintiff with this exact word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range here rests on a single verse plus outside documentary evidence.

definition: The stomach, the digestive organ; in earlier Greek it referred to the throat or an opening of the body.
article: The single New Testament use of στόμαχος is in 1 Timothy 5:23, where it plainly means the stomach. The word literally derives from στόμα ("mouth"), and early Greek writers used it for the throat or an opening before it came to mean the stomach in later authors like Aristotle and Plutarch. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show a metaphorical streak: one document (P Oxy III. 533) uses στόμαχος to mean vexation or annoyance, and another source uses it for anger.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there is very narrow.

definition: A place near the Sea of Galilee where Jesus and his disciples traveled by boat, its exact location now unknown.
article: Dalmanutha is a place name appearing just once in the New Testament, at Mark 8:10, where Jesus comes there by boat. Every version surveyed treats it the same way, simply naming the region of Dalmanutha. Its precise location is no longer known, though Abbott-Smith places it near the Sea of Galilee and notes the parallel name Magadan; the word is probably of Chaldee (Aramaic) origin.
caution: This is a single-occurrence place name whose location remains unidentified, so the evidence is thin.

definition: A departure or loosing, used as a gentle metaphor for leaving this life through death.
article: This word literally means a loosing or releasing — like a ship being untied from its moorings or animals being unyoked — and from there it comes to mean a departure. In the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 4:6, where it serves as a calm metaphor for death, the writer's coming departure from life. The vivid background image, noted in the lexicons, is the unfastening of something for the journey home.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single passage.

definition: A passing through or by; in the New Testament it appears only in the phrase meaning 'in passing' or briefly.
article: πάροδος literally means a passing, a passage, or a way through, built from παρά ('alongside') and ὁδός ('road'). In the New Testament it occurs only once, in 1 Corinthians 16:7, where Paul says he does not want to see the Corinthians merely 'in passing' (ἐν παρόδῳ). The Septuagint and everyday papyri use it more broadly, including for a 'passer-by' or traveller; one Imperial-era epigram even pictures an old man telling 'each passer-by' to drink while he still can.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax appearing only once, so its measured range in the NT rests on a single verse.

definition: An adverb meaning far away or at a distance, sometimes used in its comparative form to mean farther on.
article: πόῤῥω is an adverb meaning "far off" or "at a distance." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times: three times simply as "far" (as when Jesus says people honor God with their lips but their heart is far from him), and once in the comparative form meaning "farther" (Luke 24:28). It's the later Attic spelling of the older πρόσω, and the Septuagint uses it 13 times, most often to translate the Hebrew רָחַק ("to be far")—and Moulton-Milligan notes it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: The evidence base is thin—only 4 New Testament occurrences—and the second sense is just the comparative form, not a genuinely separate meaning.

definition: A tunic — the basic garment worn next to the skin, beneath an outer cloak.
senseLabels: a tunic worn next the skin
article: A χιτών is the inner garment worn against the skin, distinct from the outer cloak (ἱμάτιον), and shows up 11 times in the New Testament. The translation "tunic" and "second tunic" each cover about a third of occurrences, the latter in passages where Jesus tells his followers not to take a spare. The word appears throughout everyday Koine papyri, where shopping lists and price records pair the χιτών with the ἱμάτιον just as the New Testament does; in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew kuttoneth 23 times.

definition: To boast about great things or talk arrogantly, vaunting oneself.
article: μεγαλαυχέω is a compound verb meaning to boast or brag about great things, often carrying the sense of arrogant, big-talking pride. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (James 3:5) and three times in the Septuagint, where it once renders the Hebrew גָּבַהּ ('to be high, haughty') in Ezekiel 16:50. Interestingly, the critical text (SBLGNT) doesn't read this single word here at all but splits it into two words, μεγάλα αὐχεῖ ('boasts great things'), and Moulton-Milligan notes this division yields a neat parallel to the preceding 'small member' in James, suggesting the sense 'has great things to boast about' rather than mere empty bragging.
caution: Evidence is thin: just one disputed New Testament occurrence, and scholars disagree on whether it is even a single word or two separate words with a slightly different sense.

definition: A Samaritan, a person from the city or region of Samaria.
article: Σαμαρείτης simply means a Samaritan—someone from the city or region of Samaria. The Byzantine NT uses it 9 times across 4 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Samaritans" in every clear case (the few odd renderings are just phrase-splitting noise). It points to the people rather than the place, and in John 8:48 it appears as an insult thrown at Jesus, showing how the term could carry contempt; the word also turns up in the Septuagint translating the Hebrew shomroni and in everyday Koine papyri.

definition: To gather or collect things together, such as crops, weeds, fruit, or people, into one place.
article: Συλλέγω means to bring things together into one place — gathering up crops, pulling weeds, picking fruit, or collecting people. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across just 2 books, often in farming images like gathering weeds for burning or picking grapes and figs. The Septuagint uses it 40 times, mostly to translate Hebrew לָקַט ("to glean or pick up," 32 times), and the everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth sense: one document has a man dispatched "to collect them all" (meaning rents), and another describes gathering chaff from everywhere for a hot winter bath.
caution: In 4 of its 8 New Testament uses the word blends into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English equivalent, so translations vary.

definition: A market where meat and other provisions were bought and sold.
article: Μάκελλον refers to a meat market or provision shop, the kind of place where ordinary people bought their food. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 10:25, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "meat market" in that single occurrence. The word is a borrowing from Latin (macellum) and shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; one inscription describes selling "every kind of goods in the macellum," confirming it meant a general provision market, not just a butcher's stall.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Describing something that is straight, upright, or in a direct line, used both physically and figuratively.
article: ὀρθός describes something straight—whether standing upright in height (as a person rising to their feet) or running straight in line, including figuratively of a path made straight. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, at Hebrews 12:13, where it has the figurative sense of straight, direct paths (drawing on the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew יָשָׁר, "upright/straight," 9 times). The everyday papyri show its concrete edge nicely: it describes standing hay still upright in the field and columns still erect as opposed to those fallen on the ground.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine NT, so its measured New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: Describes someone or something that cannot be moved or shaken—firmly settled and unwavering in position or commitment.
article: This adjective means "immovable" or "firm," built from a negative prefix and a verb meaning "to move away." It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:58, where Paul urges believers to be "steadfast, immovable." Moulton-Milligan note that the related adjective ἀκίνητος shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so this family of words was at home in ordinary legal and practical language, not just religious writing.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A grapevine — the climbing plant that produces grapes, whether a literal plant or a figure for a person.
article: ἄμπελος is the ordinary word for a grapevine, used 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible splits its renderings between "fruit vine" (3×, often in Jesus' words about not drinking again of the fruit of the vine) and plain "vine" (3×), but both point to the same plant — Strong's notes the name pictures it coiling about a support. The word turns up frequently in everyday Koine papyri describing land "planted with vines," and in some of those documents it carries a collective sense equivalent to a whole vineyard.
caution: With only 9 occurrences and the two measured senses pointing to the same plant, the "fruit vine" versus "vine" split reflects translation phrasing rather than a real difference in meaning.

definition: To give someone or something a name, or to mention or address them by name.
article: ὀνομάζω comes from the noun ὄνομα ("name") and means to name, call, or mention by name. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "named" in half of those cases and absorbing it into surrounding phrasing in 4 of 10. The everyday flavor of the word shows up clearly in the papyri: in a second-century Egyptian petition (P Oxy X.1272) it is used for a man giving the names of associates to be summoned before a judge, exactly the plain "naming" sense.

definition: To die, whether by natural causes, violence, or in a spiritual sense of being dead to something.
article: ἀποθνήσκω is the ordinary Koine verb for dying, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 111 times across 15 books, almost always rendered "died" (80×, 85%) or "dies" (9×, 10%). Its range covers natural death, violent death (as the passive counterpart of "kill"), and a figurative spiritual death, as in being dead to sin or to the law. In the Septuagint it appears a striking 485 times, mostly translating the Hebrew verb מוּת ("to die") 403 times, showing how thoroughly it served as the standard word for death.

definition: Hungry and without food, describing people who have gone without eating, sometimes for an extended time.
article: νῆστις describes someone who has not eaten and is therefore hungry or faint. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times when Jesus refuses to send a crowd home νῆστις ('hungry,' 'faint') lest they collapse on the way (Matthew 15:32; Mark 8:3). The word lived on in everyday Koine: medical and dietary texts use the related form for giving a patient medicine or food while 'fasting' (on an empty stomach), and Modern Greek νηστικός still means 'hungry.'
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the measured evidence is thin, though the sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: To press hard against someone from every side, as in a crowd squeezing in on a person.
article: ἀποθλίβω describes the action of a crowd squeezing in hard on someone from all sides. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 8:45, where the crowds 'press against' Jesus, and once in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew לָחַץ in Numbers 22:25 — the scene of Balaam's donkey crushing his foot against a wall. Moulton-Milligan find the word in everyday Koine papyri, including a 116 BC document about people being 'pressed' or hard-pressed, confirming its use beyond the Bible.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: Something that keeps a person or act in memory—a lasting remembrance, memorial, or commemorative offering.
article: μνημόσυνον is something that preserves the memory of a person or deed, ranging from "memory" (used twice in the Byzantine NT, 67%) to "memorial" (once, in Acts 10:4). It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 46 times across 12 books, most often translating the Hebrew words for "remembrance" (זִכָּרוֹן, 18×; זֵכֶר, 7×). A striking parallel comes from a third-century inscription where a father sets up a tomb for his daughter as "an immortal memory, a memorial tear"—showing the word's everyday use for commemorating the dead.
