caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine NT (zero in the SBLGNT critical text), the measured sense reflects phrasing rather than the word's own meaning, and editions disagree over the spelling σφυρόν versus σφυδρόν.

definition: A flight of stairs or steps, especially the staircase leading up from the temple area in Jerusalem.
article: ἀναβαθμός means a set of steps or a stairway, built from the verb ἀναβαίνω ("to go up"). Both New Testament occurrences are in Acts 21, describing the stairs where Paul was carried because of the crowd's violence (21:35) and where he stood to address the people (21:40). The word is far more common in the Septuagint, appearing 27 times and almost always translating the Hebrew מַעֲלָה (26×); notably, it forms the title "Song of the steps" (ascents) for Psalms 120–134.
caution: The two New Testament uses are both in a single passage and treated as one sense ("steps"); the apparent split between senses reflects context, not different meanings.

definition: Good, kind, or pleasant—describing things that are agreeable or people, especially God, who are gracious and benevolent.
article: χρηστός covers a range from "useful" or "pleasant" when describing things to "kind" and "gracious" when describing people, especially God. In the New Testament it appears 7 times across 6 books, rendered "good" twice (40%), and in single cases as describing wine that is "better," as "kind" (Ephesians 4:32), and of God in 1 Peter 2:3. In the Septuagint it shows up 28 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew word for "good" and often applied to God, and the everyday Koine papyri confirm its warm sense—one inscription praises a man "on account of his excellent character."
caution: With only 7 occurrences, the English renderings vary widely (from "good" to "better" to "kind"), so context determines whether the word leans toward usefulness, pleasantness, or moral kindness.

definition: A gnat or mosquito, used proverbially as an example of something tiny.
article: κώνωψ refers to a gnat or mosquito, a small stinging insect. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 23:24, where Jesus describes straining out a gnat while swallowing a camel — a vivid contrast of something tiny against something huge. The classical historian Herodotus also used the word, and its Latin equivalent is culex.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A cymbal, a hollow metal percussion instrument that makes a loud ringing or clashing sound.
article: A κύμβαλον is a cymbal — a metal percussion instrument named from κύμβη, a cup, reflecting its hollow shape. The word appears just once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 13:1) but is common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 16 times across 6 books, mostly translating the Hebrew word for cymbals (12 times) used in temple worship. A papyrus from about 245 B.C. lists cymbals alongside a tabret and rattles being gathered for a household festival, showing the instrument was part of ordinary everyday celebrations, not just religious ceremonies.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning here rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: To hang or suspend something or someone, including hanging a person on a tree or cross.
article: κρεμάννυμι means to hang or suspend, whether it's a millstone tied around a neck, a person executed on a tree, or something held up. In the New Testament it appears 7 times across 4 books, and in passive or middle forms (κρέμαμαι) it shifts to the intransitive sense of "being hung" or "hanging." One striking metaphorical use is in Matthew 22:40, where all the Law and Prophets are said to "hang" on the two great commandments. The word is well attested in everyday Koine, showing up in inscriptions describing suspended crowns and bodies, and it most often translates the Hebrew תָּלָה ("to hang") in the Septuagint, where it occurs 30 times.
caution: Two of the listed sense entries ("land although Him" and "hanging Although") appear to be garbled data artifacts rather than genuine distinct meanings, so the word effectively carries the single core sense of hanging or suspending.

definition: A means of atonement or propitiation; in the Greek Old Testament, the cover of the Ark of the Covenant where atoning blood was sprinkled.
article: ἱλαστήριον is a rare term that appears only twice in the New Testament, but it shows up 27 times in the Septuagint, where it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew kapporeth (17×), the cover or 'mercy seat' of the Ark sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement. The word carries two related strands: a physical place of atonement (the Ark's cover) and, more abstractly, a means of propitiation, as in Romans 3:25. Notably, Deissmann argued from everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions that the word in Romans should be read as 'a means of propitiation' rather than narrowly as the Ark's lid, treating it like votive-offering words such as σωτήριον.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament (only 2 occurrences, one absorbed into phrasing) and scholars genuinely disagree over whether Romans 3:25 means the 'mercy seat' or a broader 'means of propitiation.'

definition: A bitter-tasting plant (wormwood), used in Revelation as both a name and an image of bitterness.
article: Ἄψινθος refers to wormwood, a notoriously bitter plant, and it appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Revelation 8:11. There it works as a proper name for a fallen star and as an image of the bitter, undrinkable water that results. The lexica note related forms (ἀψίνθιον, ἀψινθία), and Abbott-Smith specifically flags its use as a proper name in this passage.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice, both in a single verse, and its derivation is uncertain.

definition: The Roman province of Achaia, covering southern Greece and governed by a proconsul.
article: Ἀχαΐα is the name of the Roman province of Achaia, which covered roughly southern Greece and was administered by a proconsul. It appears 11 times across 5 books in the Byzantine NT and is rendered "Achaia" in 8 of those cases (73%), with the few odd renderings like "resolved Achaia" coming from how surrounding words got grouped. Abbott-Smith notes its consistent use for the Roman province specifically, appearing in passages like Acts 18:12 and 1 Corinthians 16:15.
caution: The word's derivation is uncertain, but its meaning as the province name is well attested and agreed upon.

definition: Lebbaeus, an alternate name for Thaddaeus, one of Jesus' twelve apostles.
article: Lebbaeus is a personal name appearing in some manuscripts of the apostle lists, where it identifies one of the twelve—the disciple elsewhere called Thaddaeus. It occurs just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 10:3) and is rendered "Lebbaeus," though it drops out of the critical (SBLGNT) text entirely. The interesting wrinkle is the textual disagreement: some witnesses read Lebbaeus and others Thaddaeus at the same spot, and Dodson treats Lebbaeus as a pet-name for Thaddaeus whose full form is unknown.
caution: Evidence is thin and disputed: the name appears once in the Byzantine text but not in the critical text, its origin is uncertain, and the sources differ on whether the apostle is called Lebbaeus or Thaddaeus.

definition: Gennesaret, a fertile plain and lake on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.
article: Gennesaret is a proper name for a fertile plain on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee, and the adjacent lake was sometimes called the Lake of Gennesaret. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, always rendered "Gennesaret" (Matthew 14:34, Mark 6:53, Luke 5:1), where the land is meant in Matthew and Mark and the lake in Luke. The name comes from Hebrew, related to Kinnereth (יָם כִּנֶּרֶת, the Sea of Chinnereth in Numbers 34:11), and the Greek form also turns up as Γεννησάρ in 1 Maccabees 11:67.
caution: This is a place name with only 3 occurrences, so its range is narrow and the spelling varies across manuscripts.

definition: To see clearly again, regaining full or unobstructed vision after something has blocked it.
article: This verb combines "through" (διά) with "to look" (βλέπω) and describes seeing clearly or recovering full vision. In the two Byzantine occurrences (Matthew 7:5 and Luke 6:42), it appears in the same image: once the plank is removed from your own eye, you will "see clearly" to remove the speck from another's eye. Abbott-Smith notes an older sense of looking straight ahead, and points to the related noun διάβλεψις used by Aquila in Isaiah 61:1.
caution: Evidence is thin, with only two Byzantine occurrences and the renderings split between two nearly identical phrasings.

definition: A person who travels abroad together with someone else as a companion on a journey.
article: Συνέκδημος literally describes someone who is away from home alongside another person — a travel companion. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 19:29 and 2 Corinthians 8:19), and in one of those the Berean Standard Bible folds it into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendering it with its own English word. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; one inscription (OGIS 494) treats συνέγδημος as the equivalent of the Latin comes, and another describes private individuals who voluntarily accompanied an official delegation to Samothrace.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the precise nuance rests largely on outside inscriptions and papyri rather than biblical usage.

definition: Made of ivory; describing an object crafted from elephant tusk.
article: This adjective means "made of ivory," derived from the word for elephant. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:12, where it describes luxury goods—and shows up 10 times in the Septuagint, several times translating the Hebrew word for "tooth" or "horn" (שֵׁן). The everyday papyri and inscriptions confirm the meaning, with one third-century BC papyrus even using the related noun for the actual hunting of elephants.
caution: The digest lists the measured rendering as "wood," which appears to be a tagging slip—every glossary and the underlying evidence point to "ivory."

definition: The completing or fulfilling of something, such as a set period of time reaching its end.
article: This noun names the bringing of something to completion or its full term. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:26, where it refers to the fulfillment of a period of days; the corpus shows it absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. Outside the New Testament it shows up in 2 Maccabees 6:14 in the Septuagint, and it derives from the verb ἐκπληρόω, meaning to fill up or complete.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and almost no other attestation, the range of this word is hard to pin down.

definition: A heavy device, often iron, lowered from a ship to grip the seabed and hold the vessel in place.
article: ἄγκυρα is simply an anchor — the four New Testament uses all refer to the device that holds a ship steady, and every translation surveyed renders it that way 100% of the time. Three of those uses describe a real ship in danger (Acts 27), while Hebrews 6:19 uses it figuratively, calling hope an anchor for the soul. Everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions confirm the literal sense, mentioning iron anchors with their teeth, and one inscription even echoes the figurative use found in Hebrews by speaking of an 'anchor of old age.'

definition: A person who leads others along a way, used literally for a guide or figuratively for a teacher or instructor.
article: ὁδηγός is someone who shows others the path, whether literally pointing the way or figuratively instructing and leading. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "guides" in 4 of those cases, with the remaining instance (Matthew 23:16) being part of the same phrase. The word is built from ὁδός ("road, way") and ἡγέομαι ("to lead"), and several New Testament uses are figurative, such as calling someone a guide of the blind in Romans 2:19.
caution: The Septuagint data is thin (just one cited occurrence), and the listed Hebrew counterpart appears to be a labeling artifact rather than a true translation equivalent.

definition: Describing a fire that cannot be put out and keeps burning continuously.
article: ἄσβεστος literally means "not extinguished," formed from a negative prefix plus a word for quenching, and by implication points to a fire that burns on without stopping. In all 4 of its Byzantine New Testament appearances it describes fire and is rendered "unquenchable," a usage echoed across the standard glosses. Interestingly, the Septuagint shows the word only weakly: in Job 20:26 one manuscript tradition has ἄσβεστος while others read ἄκαυστον ("unburnt"), where it stands in for a Hebrew phrase meaning "not blown" or fanned.
caution: The Septuagint evidence is thin and disputed, with manuscripts splitting between ἄσβεστος and ἄκαυστον in the single Job passage.

definition: A thought or idea that someone has reasoned through in their mind.
article: This word refers to a thought or notion that the mind has worked through. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:17, where it is consistently rendered "thoughts" (100% of the time, with the BSB agreeing). In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times across 4 books, translating several different Hebrew words including ones for "stumbling block" and "height," which suggests its Greek meaning could be stretched to cover a range of underlying ideas.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just six in the Septuagint translating a mix of unrelated Hebrew words, the evidence for this word's range is thin.

definition: To wear out or become old through use and time, or to declare something outdated and no longer in force.
article: This verb describes things growing old—either physically wearing out, like clothing or a temple wall, or becoming outdated and no longer valid. In the New Testament it appears just 4 times, rendered "wear out" in two-thirds of cases (Luke 12:33, Hebrews 1:11) and "obsolete" once (Hebrews 8:13). In the Septuagint it shows up 22 times, most often translating the Hebrew בָּלָה ("wear out"), and the papyri confirm the everyday sense: a document from 69 B.C. uses it of a temple building that had become old.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the "declare obsolete/abrogate" sense rests on thin evidence, and some translators have understood Hebrews 8:13 transitively rather than passively.

definition: A negative particle expressing 'not' or 'do not,' used especially in commands, conditions, questions, and wishes rather than flat denials of fact.
article: μή is Greek's qualified or subjective negative, the partner to οὐ: where οὐ flatly denies a fact, μή denies in the realm of will, thought, and possibility — so it dominates commands, conditions, and purpose clauses. Across 1,029 Byzantine occurrences it is rendered most simply as 'not' (240×, 40%) and 'do not' (119×, 20%), but it appears in dozens of small combinations and is absorbed into English phrasing 426 times with no word of its own. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew negatives, most often לֹא ('not', 632×) and אַל (the prohibitive 'do not', 556×), neatly matching its command-and-prohibition role.
caution: The many one- and two-word renderings reflect English grammar packaging the same particle rather than distinct meanings, so the sense list should be read as patterns of usage, not separate definitions.

definition: A footprint or track left by walking, used figuratively to mean the path or example someone leaves for others to follow.
article: ἴχνος means a footprint or track — the mark a foot leaves behind. In the New Testament all 3 occurrences are figurative, picturing someone walking in another's footsteps as a model to imitate (Romans 4:12; 2 Corinthians 12:18; 1 Peter 2:21). Everyday papyri keep the literal sense alive, including a tax called ἴχνους ἐρημοφυλακία that paid for desert police guarding caravan tracks, and an inscription that closely parallels the figurative wording of Romans 4:12 and 1 Peter 2:21.
caution: The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, so its measured range there is narrow even though wider literal and figurative uses are well attested elsewhere.

definition: Job, the man whose endurance through suffering is celebrated in the Old Testament book bearing his name.
article: Ἰώβ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Job (אִיּוֹב), the central figure of the Old Testament book named after him. It appears just once in the New Testament, in James 5:11, where his patient endurance is held up as an example, and 63 times in the Septuagint. Interestingly, while it mostly renders the Hebrew name Job (59 times), the Septuagint digest also links it a handful of times to unrelated Hebrew words like 'firstborn' and 'to escape,' which likely reflects quirks of translation alignment rather than alternate meanings of the name.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests entirely on its single James reference and Septuagint usage.

definition: A woman's name, Chloe, mentioned once in the New Testament as someone whose household reported divisions in the Corinthian church.
article: Χλόη is a personal name, borne by a woman whose people informed Paul about quarrels among the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 1:11), its only appearance in the New Testament. The name literally suggests "tender foliage" or "green growth," and Strong's notes the underlying sense "green." The most interesting clue comes from Moulton-Milligan: "the Verdant" was an epithet of the goddess Demeter, and the name turns up commonly among the freedman class, leading some scholars to suggest Chloe herself may have been a freedwoman with business connections in Corinth or Ephesus.
caution: With only a single occurrence as a proper name, nothing can be said about its range, and the social background of this particular Chloe is scholarly conjecture, not established fact.

definition: To sprout or spring up out of the ground, as a seed germinating in soil.
article: This verb describes plants quickly springing up from the ground, used both times in the New Testament for seed sprouting in shallow soil (Matthew 13:5 and Mark 4:5). In the Septuagint it appears 5 times, mostly translating the Hebrew צָמַח, meaning to sprout or cause to grow. Interestingly, the lexicons note it can be used either intransitively (the plant springs up) or, in the Septuagint, transitively (to cause something to spring up), though the New Testament uses only the springing-up sense.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences and 5 in the Septuagint — and the Hebrew counterparts listed are not fully consistent across sources, so confidence is low.

definition: A hundred times as much or as many; a hundredfold increase.
article: This word means "a hundred times as much," and in the New Testament it always describes an abundant return on what someone gives up for God's sake. It appears just 3 times, all rendered "hundredfold" by the Majority Standard Bible (the "fail a hundredfold" reading in Mark 10:30 reflects a particular phrasing rather than a separate meaning). The word is at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan finds it in ordinary papyri and inscriptions, and the classical historian Xenophon already used it for "a hundred times as much."
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament uses—and the two listed "senses" really describe the same meaning in different phrases.

definition: To keep something safe from ruin, protect a person, or hold a memory closely in one's heart.
article: συντηρέω is an intensified form of τηρέω ("to keep"), carrying the sense of keeping something safe and whole against loss or harm. In the Byzantine NT its 4 uses split three ways: preserving things like wine in wineskins (2×), protecting a person (Mark 6:20), and Mary "keeping" sayings in her heart (Luke 2:19). The everyday papyri make this concrete — one second-century letter begs someone to "do everything possible to protect my wife until I arrive," using exactly this word.
caution: With only 4 NT occurrences spread across distinct shades of meaning, each sense rests on very few examples.

definition: Harsh mistreatment or suffering inflicted on someone, especially oppression and affliction endured by a group of people.
article: κάκωσις refers to mistreatment, oppression, or the misery that results from being treated badly. It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 7:34), in a quotation from the Septuagint where it describes the affliction of God's people in Egypt; in the Greek Old Testament it shows up 12 times across 7 books, translating Hebrew words for pain, poverty, and haste. One striking detail: an everyday Koine papyrus uses the word for physical harm to the body predicted by an astrological conjunction, showing it could describe bodily affliction as well as social oppression.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into a Septuagint quotation, so its independent range there cannot be measured.

definition: A man who is getting married, the groom in a wedding.
article: νυμφίος means "bridegroom"—the man being married—and that single sense covers all 16 New Testament occurrences, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "bridegroom" 13 times (87%) and the rest absorbed into phrasing. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew חָתָן ("son-in-law" or "bridegroom") 9 of 11 times, confirming the same core meaning. Notably, the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a touching grave inscription mourning a young bridegroom who died untimely.

definition: The genitive form of the relative pronoun "whoever/whatever," found in the New Testament only inside the phrase "until" (heōs hotou), marking the time something continues.
article: ὅτου is a case form of ὅστις ("whoever, whatever") that in the New Testament appears only inside the set phrase ἕως ὅτου, meaning "until" or "while." Because it works as part of a time expression rather than a standalone word, the measured renderings vary widely — "it," "still," "again" — and in 1 of its 6 occurrences it gets absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own. The most telling detail is that critical texts like SBLGNT show zero occurrences, so it survives in the Byzantine tradition but drops out of the standard scholarly editions.
caution: The translation data is thin and scattered, and the word does not appear in the critical text at all, so the labeled "senses" reflect phrase rendering rather than distinct meanings of the word itself.

definition: A person who belongs to a particular city or community as one of its citizens or fellow citizens.
article: πολίτης means a citizen — someone who belongs to a city or community. It can point either to a citizen of a specific place (as in Luke 15:15 and Acts 21:39) or to a fellow citizen sharing a common community (Luke 19:14, Heb 8:11). The word was thoroughly ordinary in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite a papyrus order to deliver up an arrested man "being a citizen," showing how routinely the term appeared in legal and civic life.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into broader phrasing, the split between "citizen" and "fellow citizen" rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To stand against someone or something in opposition; as a participle, it names the people who do the opposing — one's adversaries.
article: ἀντίκειμαι literally means "to lie opposite to," and from that physical image it came to mean actively opposing, resisting, or withstanding someone. In the New Testament's 8 occurrences it splits between describing the act of opposing (43%) and, as a participle, naming the opponents themselves — "the adversaries" (29%). Built from ἀντί ("against") and κεῖμαι ("to lie"), it shows up in everyday Koine too: a papyrus from around 153 BC uses it of someone simply being "opposed to us."
caution: The Septuagint connects it to several different Hebrew words (including ones for "enemy" and "adversary"), so its exact force varies somewhat with context.

definition: To press someone into a tight space; figuratively, to feel cramped, hemmed in, or restricted by pressure.
article: στενοχωρέω literally means to keep someone in a tight place, built from words for "narrow" and "space." In the New Testament its three occurrences are all figurative: in 2 Corinthians 4:8 it describes being under pressure yet not crushed ("hard pressed"), and in 6:12 it points to emotional restriction or being closed off. The everyday flavor shows in the papyri, where one B.C. 241 letter uses it to mean simply being short of billets or cramped for space.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament uses (all figurative and absent from the critical text), so the measured senses rest on a very small sample.

definition: A strong desire or appetite, used in the New Testament for a powerful sexual craving.
article: Ὄρεξις is the most general word in Greek for any kind of desire, longing, or appetite, formed from the verb ὀρέγομαι ("to reach out for"). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:27, where it carries a clearly negative sense of inflamed lust. Interestingly, the word itself is neutral elsewhere: Moulton-Milligan notes that in Stoic philosophy (for example in Epictetus) ὄρεξις simply means desire, with no bad connotation, and it also turns up in the Septuagint and in everyday papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single passage.

definition: Describing a woman who watches over and stays at home, a keeper of the household.
article: This adjective combines "house" (οἶκος) with the idea of guarding or keeping, describing someone who looks after the home. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Titus 2:5) and not at all in the SBL critical text, where editors prefer the closely related οἰκουργός ("house-worker"). The textual situation is the most interesting detail: ancient manuscripts split between the two spellings, and the medical writer Soranus of Ephesus uses οἰκουργός in a phrase about leading a sedentary, stay-at-home life, where either form would fit.
caution: This word occurs only once and competes with the variant οἰκουργός in the manuscripts, so its exact form and reading are genuinely disputed.

definition: To break something into pieces, especially breaking bread or loaves into portions.
article: κατακλάω means to break something up or break it into pieces, formed from κατά ("down") plus κλάω ("break"). In the New Testament it appears just twice, both describing Jesus breaking the loaves before feeding the crowd (Mark 6:41; Luke 9:16), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "broke" in every case. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine could use the word figuratively, as in the Letter of Aristeas where it describes a person's character "degenerating" or breaking down into a worse condition.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin and confidence is low.

definition: The state of being free rather than enslaved or bound, especially the freedom believers enjoy in Christ.
article: ἐλευθερία means freedom or liberty — the condition of one who is not a slave. In its 11 New Testament appearances it is rendered "freedom" 9 times (82%), and Paul especially uses it for the spiritual liberty believers have in Christ, as in Romans 8:21 and Galatians 2:4. One vivid detail: the same phrase "for freedom" (ἐπ᾽ ἐλευθερίᾳ) that Paul uses in Galatians 5:13 appears in an old Delphi inscription about purchasing a woman's release from slavery, so readers would have heard the real-world ring of being set free.

definition: To search carefully for someone, especially a person who is hard to find.
article: ἀναζητέω means to look for someone with effort, carrying the sense that the search is difficult. Both of its appearances in the Byzantine New Testament involve hunting for a person — Mary and Joseph searching for the boy Jesus (Luke 2:44) and Barnabas going to find Saul (Acts 11:25). The everyday papyri confirm this nuance vividly: one document urges making "every effort to search for" runaway slaves, showing the word's natural fit for tracking down people who are hard to locate.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, so the entry rests heavily on supporting papyri and lexicon notes.

definition: To listen to someone and respond favorably, especially to hear and answer a prayer.
article: ἐπακούω means to listen to someone with favor — not just to hear sound, but to heed and respond, most often to a prayer or plea. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:2, where it quotes Isaiah 49:8 from the Septuagint. The word is far more common in the Septuagint (93 times), where it usually translates Hebrew verbs for answering or hearing (עָנָה, שָׁמַע), and the everyday papyri confirm this prayer-answering sense: one inscription appeals to the goddess Isis with "hear me, have mercy."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests almost entirely on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: To lift oneself up over others, becoming arrogant or setting oneself above all that is honored.
article: This middle-voice verb literally means to raise oneself over something or someone, and in the New Testament it always carries the figurative sense of becoming haughty or self-exalting. It appears only 3 times across 2 books, and the renderings vary: in 2 Corinthians 12:7 the Majority Standard Bible reads it as 'torment' (within a difficult phrase), while in 2 Thessalonians 2:4 it describes one who 'exalts himself above' all that is called God. The everyday papyri preserve a non-arrogant sense too: in a legal plea a plaintiff 'does not press his claim beyond' two talents, and a tax record speaks of priests who 'exceeded' their fixed number.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and the renderings split evenly between 'torment' and 'exalt,' the New Testament evidence is thin and the sense in 2 Corinthians 12:7 is genuinely uncertain.

definition: To go or enter into a place together with someone else.
article: This verb is a compound of "with" (σύν) and "enter" (εἰσέρχομαι), so it literally means going into a place in someone's company. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in John (6:22 and 18:15), where translators fold it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. Everyday Koine papyri show the same ordinary use — one second-century document describes officials "entering together" into a house — confirming this was plain, non-technical language.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament uses and 3 in the Septuagint, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: A shadow, or the dark shape cast by something blocking light.
article: ἀποσκίασμα refers to a shadow — the obscuring or darkening produced when something casts shade. It appears only once in the New Testament, in James 1:17, where God is described without 'shadow of turning,' and is rendered 'shadow' in every counted occurrence. Interestingly, the noun in this exact -μα form is otherwise unknown (a hapax in Greek literature), though closely related words turn up elsewhere, such as ἀποσκιασμός in Plutarch describing shadows thrown across a sundial.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the noun form itself is otherwise unattested, so its precise nuance rests on related words rather than direct parallels.

definition: A blue precious stone, the sapphire (possibly lapis lazuli), used among the foundation gems of the New Jerusalem.
article: σάπφειρος names a blue precious stone, usually rendered "sapphire," though some lexicographers think it actually meant lapis lazuli. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Revelation 21:19, where it is one of the jeweled foundations of the New Jerusalem; oddly, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "emerald" there. The word is a Semitic loanword (from Hebrew סַפִּיר) and the Septuagint uses it 12 times, mostly to translate that same Hebrew term. The papyri show the word living on in everyday lists of colors and goods, including a "sapphire Dalmatian vest" in a third-century document.
caution: Evidence is thin (only one New Testament occurrence) and the gem's exact identity is uncertain, with lexicons split between true sapphire and lapis lazuli.

definition: Describing something that pleases or satisfies someone, meeting their approval or expectations.
article: ἀρεστός describes whatever is pleasing, agreeable, or satisfactory to someone — in the New Testament usually what pleases God. It appears only 4 times, but its range is consistent: something meets approval or fails to (as in Acts 6:2, where neglecting the word of God is 'not pleasing'). The everyday Koine papyri make the flavor vivid: buyers accepted goods only 'if satisfactory,' and one document promises wine that will 'keep and be satisfactory' until a set date — the word of ordinary commercial approval.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the listed senses simply reflect different phrasings of one basic meaning rather than truly distinct uses.

definition: A fish, the aquatic animal caught for food.
article: This is simply the ordinary Greek word for a fish, and the New Testament uses it that way in all 20 occurrences—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fish" 79% of the time, with the rest being food-related phrasings like "only fish." The Septuagint uses it 25 times across 15 books, mostly translating the Hebrew words for fish (דָּגָה and דָּאג). It was equally at home in everyday life: papyri show people shipping fish to town and merchants selling it, and one document even uses the word collectively to mean a catch of fish.

definition: To depart by ship; to sail away from a harbor or place.
article: ἐκπλέω is a straightforward nautical verb meaning to sail away or set out from a place by ship. All 3 New Testament occurrences are in Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sailed" in 2 cases (67%) and "sailed" with a later rejoining sense in 1 case (Acts 20:6). The everyday flavor of the word shows in the papyri: one memorial tablet (OGIS 69.5) was set up by someone thankful for having "sailed safely out" of great dangers on the Red Sea.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence is thin, though the basic meaning is well supported.

definition: Simplicity or sincerity of heart — an unpretentious, single-minded attitude.
article: ἀφελότης describes plainness or simplicity of disposition, an uncomplicated and sincere frame of mind. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:46, where it characterizes how the early believers shared meals "with sincerity of heart." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan shows the word in everyday Koine papyri and in the astrological writer Vettius Valens, who describes a cultured man "betrayed by simplicity and lack of practical capacity" — proving Luke's word choice was at home in ordinary, non-biblical Greek.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one occurrence, so its precise range cannot be measured from the biblical corpus alone.

definition: A man's name in Jesus' family tree, listed as an ancestor in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ἐλμωδάμ is a personal name appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 3:28, where it names an ancestor of Jesus. The name is indeclinable and of Hebrew origin, perhaps connected to H0486. Notably, the spelling varies across manuscripts: the form Ἐλμαδάμ (Elmadam) is the reading in some critical editions, and the name drops out of the SBLGNT critical text entirely.
caution: This is a single-occurrence proper name with disputed spelling (Ἐλμωδάμ vs. Ἐλμαδάμ) and uncertain Hebrew background, so its form is not firmly settled.

definition: To place someone in a position of authority or responsibility, appointing or making them something.
article: καθίστημι is about putting someone or something into a settled position — most often appointing a person to a role or office. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 21 times, with the meaning splitting fairly evenly between "put in charge" (6×, 40%), "appointed" (5×, 33%), and "made" (3×, 20%), while 6 of 21 occurrences get absorbed into the surrounding phrasing without a word of their own. Everyday Koine papyri show the same official sense: one document from 239 BC reads "I have appointed Isocrates as scribe," and another names guardians for a minor until he comes of age — exactly the administrative usage we see in the New Testament. In the Septuagint it appears 142 times and renders several Hebrew verbs, most often פָּקַד ("appoint, oversee," 13×).

definition: One's parents — the father and mother who gave you birth, usually referred to together.
article: γονεύς is a kinship term for a parent, and in the New Testament it almost always shows up in the plural meaning "parents." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "parents" in 16 of 19 occurrences (89%), and the BSB agrees 100% of the time, so its range is narrow and stable. The word was common in everyday life: Oxyrhynchus papyri use it in such phrases as a woman dying "childless in her parents' lifetime" and a son performing "what is owing from children to parents."

definition: Lack of strength, whether bodily illness or a broader frailty of body, mind, or will.
article: ἀσθένεια covers a spectrum from physical sickness to general feebleness and frailty. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "weakness" in 12 of 24 occurrences (67%), with the BSB independently agreeing 92% of the time, while 6 occurrences get absorbed into surrounding phrasing without their own English word. Everyday Koine papyri show the same range: one man cites "my weakness" as the reason he had someone else write his signature, and another asks an oracle whether he will recover from the ἀσθένεια afflicting him.
caution: Standard lexicons spread the meaning across "weakness," "frailty," "sickness," and "illness," so context decides whether bodily disease or general feebleness is meant.

definition: Sweet new wine or fresh grape juice, fresh from the press, which could still ferment and intoxicate.
article: γλεῦκος refers to must — the sweet, freshly pressed juice of grapes — and by extension the new wine made from it. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 2:13, where mockers accuse the disciples of being filled with it; the Majority Standard Bible renders the sense there as "drunk," reflecting that this fresh wine could still intoxicate. The word is well attested in everyday Koine papyri (for example, a 105 B.C. document speaks of "sweet wine," and a 277 B.C. one of pouring out the must), and it is related to γλυκύς, "sweet."
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one occurrence, and the lexica vary on whether it means unfermented juice or fermented wine, so its precise range is uncertain.

definition: An Aramaic command meaning "get up!" or "arise!", spoken to someone lying down.
article: Κοῦμι is an Aramaic word, not native Greek, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament — in Mark 5:41, where Jesus tells a dead girl "talitha koumi," meaning "little girl, arise." In that single instance it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word. Abbott-Smith notes it functions as a masculine imperative used like an interjection, corresponding to the Hebrew root קוּם ("to rise"), and observes that some editions read κούμ rather than κοῦμι.
caution: This word occurs only once, is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, and its exact spelling (κοῦμι vs. κούμ) varies between editions.

definition: A call inviting or urging others to come, often paired with another verb to launch a shared action.
article: δεῦτε is an exclamatory call meaning "come!" or "come here!"—functioning like the plural of δεῦρο. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times, rendered simply "Come" in 7 cases (58%) and "Come let" in 3 (25%), the latter when it pairs with another verb to summon people into joint action, as in the parable vineyard schemes (Matthew 21:38, Mark 12:7, Luke 20:14). It often combines with prepositions—"come after me" in Matthew 4:19, "come to me" in Matthew 11:28—and in the Septuagint, where it occurs 40 times, it chiefly renders the Hebrew imperative לְכוּ ("go!" or "come!").

definition: To laugh at someone scornfully, mocking or ridiculing them with contempt.
article: καταγελάω means to laugh someone down — to deride or mock with scorn, always aimed at a person (in the New Testament it takes the genitive of the person being ridiculed). It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, all in the same scene: the crowd jeering at Jesus when He says the dead girl is only sleeping (Matthew 9:24, Mark 5:40, Luke 8:53). A papyrus letter (BGU III.814) shows the same flavor in everyday life, where a soldier complains to his mother that 'everyone is laughing at me' because his father visited but brought no gifts. In the Septuagint it occurs 16 times, most often translating the Hebrew words לָעַג and שָׂחַק.
caution: The two MSB renderings reflect one underlying sense of scornful laughter; the digest's second 'sense' is a phrasing artifact, and overall evidence is thin (low confidence).

definition: Abel, the second son of Adam and Eve, whom Cain killed; the first righteous person murdered in the Bible.
article: Ἄβελ is the proper name Abel, the son of Adam and Eve killed by his brother Cain. It is an indeclinable name borrowed from Hebrew (הֶבֶל) and appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 3 books, always referring to the same person; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Abel" in 3 of those 4 places. In the Septuagint the underlying Hebrew הָ֫בֶל also carries the everyday meaning "breath" or "vapor," which is why the same form turns up far more often there (13 times), sometimes for unrelated words.
caution: The second "measured sense" listed ("Abel killed sanctuary") is a digest artifact from a longer phrase in Luke 11:51, not a separate meaning of the name.

definition: To take a long time, linger, or delay in coming or acting.
senseLabels: to be a long time coming
article: χρονίζω is built from χρόνος ("time") and means to spend or take time — to tarry, linger, or be delayed. Across its 5 New Testament uses it consistently carries this single idea of delay, whether a master who "takes a long time" to return or Zechariah lingering in the temple. In the Septuagint it appears 16 times, most often (9×) rendering the Hebrew אָחַר, "to delay," and the everyday Koine papyri show it both for general delay and, interestingly, for the specific sense of dating a letter or document.

definition: A likeness or representation of something, such as a portrait, statue, or the figure stamped on a coin.
article: εἰκών means an image or likeness — a derived representation that points back to an original, like the head on a coin or a parental likeness in a child. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "image" in 15 of 23 occurrences (75%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing, and the BSB agrees 100%. In everyday Koine, Moulton-Milligan shows it was the standard word for the physical description of individuals in official documents like bills of sale and registrations; in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew צֶ֫לֶם ("image"), 15 times.

definition: The number eighty.
article: This is simply the cardinal number eighty. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both rendered "eighty" (the prophetess Anna in Luke 2:37 and a debtor's account in Luke 16:7), and it shows up far more often in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew word for eighty 29 times. One nice detail: the everyday papyri preserve spelling variants like ὀγδοιήκοντα and even ὀδώκοντα, showing how ordinary Greek-speakers wrote the number in daily documents.

definition: A Latin loanword for a soldier who carried out executions on a ruler's orders.
article: σπεκουλάτωρ is a Latin loanword (from speculator) that originally meant a scout or courier, but in the New Testament it refers to a soldier acting as an executioner. It appears only once, in Mark 6:27, where Herod sends one to behead John the Baptist. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri too — for example, in a list of accounts from A.D. 191/192 and in an order addressed to a village police chief — confirming it was a real, recognized job title in the Roman world.
caution: The translation data oddly labels its single occurrence as "delay," which conflicts with every lexicon's "executioner" — treat the measured sense as unreliable here, and note this word appears only once.

definition: A person who devises or comes up with something, used in Romans 1:30 specifically of those who invent evil.
article: This word means an inventor, contriver, or discoverer — someone who thinks up or devises something new. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 1:30, where it describes people as inventors of evil; the Majority Standard Bible renders that occurrence loosely as "haters." The same construction shows up in 2 Maccabees 7:31 (κακίας εὑρετής, "contriver of evil"), and the underlying word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary vocabulary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the literal sense "inventor/contriver" differs from the looser "haters" rendering counted in the data, so the measured sense should be read with care.

definition: The territory surrounding a town or landmark; sometimes, by extension, the people living in that area.
article: περίχωρος literally means "around the land" (from περί, "around," and χώρα, "land"), and in the New Testament it functions as a noun—"the region round about"—with γῆ ("land") understood. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "surrounding region" in 3 of 10 occurrences and, in a couple of places, as part of phrases describing news spreading through that region. By a natural extension it can stand for the people who live in that area rather than the territory itself, and in the Septuagint it renders several different Hebrew words, most often כִּכָּר (the Jordan plain) 4 times and פֶּלֶך 7 times.

definition: A phrase meaning "except perhaps" or "unless," introducing a tentative or qualified exception to what was just stated.
article: This is a compound expression built from εἰ μή ("if not, except") plus the neuter of τις ("some, any"), giving a softened sense like "except perhaps" or "unless somehow." The KJV renders the broader family simply as "except." It does not appear at all in the Byzantine New Testament, so its meaning here rests on the parts that compose it rather than on measured usage.
caution: This phrase has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so any sense given is reconstructed from its components rather than from attested use.

definition: The accusative plural masculine form of the demonstrative "this/these," pointing to specific male persons or things as the object of a verb or preposition.
article: τούτους is simply a grammatical form of the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος ("this, these"), here in the masculine plural and accusative case—so it means "these (men/things)" when they receive the action of a verb or follow a preposition. The base word works like Latin hic ("this here," the nearer thing) as opposed to ἐκεῖνος ("that there"), and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew demonstratives זֶה and זֹאת. It can stand alone as a noun ("this one, these ones"), and in classical usage it could even carry a dismissive, contemptuous tone, as in Gospel passages where people sneer "isn't this the carpenter's son?"
caution: This particular form has zero measured occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament corpus and no computed sense data, so the description rests entirely on the grammar and lexicon entries for its parent word οὗτος.

definition: An emphasis particle meaning "surely" or "of course," strengthening a statement as something the speaker and reader both recognize.
article: δήπου is an emphasis particle that adds the sense of "surely" or "of course" to a statement, presenting it as something acknowledged and beyond dispute. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 2:16, where both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it "surely." Abbott-Smith notes it carries the flavor of "we know," appealing to shared understanding, and it is built from the particles δή and πού.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: To choose or prefer something for oneself, picking it out over other options.
article: αἱρέομαι is the middle-voice form meaning to choose or prefer something for yourself, and this is the only form found in the New Testament's three occurrences. Two of those (67%) are simply rendered "choose," as in Philippians 1:22 and Hebrews 11:25, while the one instance in 2 Thessalonians 2:13 carries the sense of being chosen by God. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times, most often translating the Hebrew bāḥar ("to choose," 4×), and the everyday papyri show the same sense, as when one document tells someone to "write to me about whatever you choose."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin evidence, so the apparent split between ordinary "choose" and divine "chosen" reflects context more than a firmly distinct sense.

definition: To scatter or disperse something or someone, like a wolf driving sheep apart or people fleeing in different directions.
article: σκορπίζω means to scatter or disperse, whether driving a flock apart or sending people fleeing in different directions. In the New Testament's 5 uses it stays close to this physical sense — a wolf scattering sheep (John 10:12) or disciples being scattered (John 16:32). The everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth range: one document even tells a worker to "scatter the manure" across the fields, while another describes plums strewn about a plot. Lexicons note an extended sense of one who freely "disperses" blessings or gives alms (2 Corinthians 9:9, drawn from the Septuagint), though that broader figurative use sits at the edges of the measured data.
caution: With only 5 occurrences, the generous "distribute alms" sense rests on a single quoted-from-Scripture verse rather than broad New Testament usage.

definition: A frog, the small amphibian that lives in or near water.
article: Βάτραχος simply means "frog," and its meaning is stable across every source. It appears only once in the New Testament (Revelation 16:13), but the Septuagint uses it 14 times in 2 books, mostly to translate the Hebrew word for frog (צְפַרְדֵּעַ, 12×) — notably in the Exodus plague accounts. One curious detail: a 4th-century magical charm on papyrus lists "frog's tongue" (γλῶττα βατράχου) as an ingredient, showing the word in ordinary everyday Koine, and an Ionic spelling (βάθρακος) even survives in Modern Greek.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, but its meaning is not in doubt since all sources agree it means "frog."

definition: A loosening or letting-up that brings relief, ease, or rest, especially as the opposite of pressure or distress.
article: At its root ἄνεσις means a "loosening" or relaxation, and across its 5 New Testament occurrences it conveys relief or ease — though translators render it variously, with the Majority Standard Bible using "allow," "peace," and "when" once each and absorbing it into broader phrasing twice. Except for Acts 24:23, every New Testament use is Paul's, and he consistently sets it against θλῖψις (pressure or affliction), so the relief is felt as the easing of distress. Outside the Bible the word lived an everyday life: papyri and inscriptions use it for being "remiss" and even for relief from taxation, showing how concrete its sense of letting-up could be.
caution: With only 5 occurrences rendered three different ways, the precise English word varies a lot by context even though the underlying sense of relief is stable.

definition: An accursed thing or object placed under a divine ban or curse.
article: κατανάθεμα refers to something cursed — an object or person on which a ban has been laid. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (and the form drops out of the critical text entirely, which reads κατάθεμα instead). Moulton-Milligan note it seems to be a stronger form of the more common ἀνάθεμα, and that in Revelation it refers to the very object the curse falls upon.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word whose form is disputed — the critical text and sources favor κατάθεμα, and no clear classical examples are cited.

definition: Small in number, amount, size, degree, or duration—few or little.
article: ὀλίγος is a flexible everyday adjective meaning "few" or "little," covering small number, quantity, size, degree, and even short duration. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 42 times: most often "few" (15×, 56%) or "little" (8×, 30%), with the rest tucked into phrasing that needs no separate English word. Greek papyri show the same range, from "a short time" (a soldier's letter urging courage because "your time is short") to "no small" quantity of olives, while in the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew מְעָט, also meaning "few" or "little."

definition: Barabbas, the prisoner whom the crowd chose to release instead of Jesus at his trial before Pilate.
article: Barabbas is the personal name of the prisoner released in place of Jesus, appearing 11 times across 4 books, all referring to the same man. The name comes from Aramaic meaning "son of a father," which Jerome took to mean "son of a teacher." Standard translations consistently render it "Barabbas" (10 of 11 occurrences, 91%), and notably some manuscripts at Matthew 27:16 even read "Jesus Barabbas."

definition: Phanuel, the personal name of the father of the prophetess Anna in Luke's Gospel.
article: Phanuel is a Hebrew personal name carried over into Greek, appearing just once in the New Testament (Luke 2:36) as the father of the prophetess Anna. It is the same name as the Hebrew Penuel (פְּנוּאֵל), which the Septuagint uses 10 times across 3 books. A nice detail: Philo records the Hebrew name Phanuel and explains it as meaning "the turning away of God," while treating Greek as his own native tongue.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence (a hapax) used only as a proper name, so its range cannot be measured.

definition: A deep groan or sigh expressing pain, distress, or longing.
article: στεναγμός refers to a heartfelt groan or sigh, the kind that escapes someone in pain or deep longing. It appears only twice in the New Testament, where it is rendered "groaning" in every case (100%)—once of Israel's cries under oppression in Egypt (Acts 7:34) and once of the inexpressible groanings the Spirit makes on our behalf (Romans 8:26). The Septuagint uses it 22 times, most often translating Hebrew words for a sigh or distressed cry, and everyday papyri pair it with words for pain and grief, confirming its plain emotional sense.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, this entry rests on thin biblical evidence, though the Septuagint and papyri agree on the meaning.

definition: A servant who lives and works within a household, often a domestic slave belonging to a master.
article: Οἰκέτης refers to a servant attached to a household—someone who lives in and works for the family, often a domestic slave. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible mostly renders it simply as "servant," each occurrence tied to the idea of belonging to a master. The everyday papyri back this up: one third-century BC document uses οἰκέτης for someone else's slave in a legal dispute, while Abbott-Smith notes that in classical writers like Plato and Herodotus the plural could cover the whole household (the Latin familia), not just servants.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the range here is thin, and the classical sources note a broader "whole household" sense not measured in the New Testament data.

definition: To rise up against someone in rebellion or attack, turning on them as an enemy.
article: This verb means to rise up against a person, usually in hostility or rebellion. In both of its New Testament appearances (Matthew 10:21 and Mark 13:12) it describes children rising up against their parents to have them put to death, always taking a direct object with 'against.' The Septuagint uses it 36 times, most often for the Hebrew קוּם ('to rise'), and the word survived into Modern Greek as ἐπανάστασι, meaning 'revolution' or 'insurrection' — capturing the sense of violent uprising.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the measured 'rise' rendering is brief, but the lexica consistently confirm the fuller sense of rising up against an enemy.

definition: To make someone lie down or recline, or to recline oneself, especially at a meal in the ancient manner.
senseLabels: have someone lie down or recline
article: ἀνακλίνω comes from ἀνά and κλίνω ("to lean"), and its basic idea is causing someone to lie back or recline. In its 8 Byzantine occurrences it covers two related actions: directing people to sit down (as when Jesus has the crowds recline before feeding them, MAT 14:19, MAR 6:39) and reclining at a meal table in the customary ancient posture. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that the New Testament writers favored this word for "reclining at table" instead of the classical alternatives, suggesting it was characteristic of everyday common speech.
caution: The word appears only 8 times and is twice absorbed into surrounding phrasing without its own English word, so its precise force in each verse can be hard to pin down.

definition: To throw, lay, or put something upon another thing, often used for grabbing or arresting a person by laying hands on them.
article: At its core ἐπιβάλλω means to throw or lay one thing upon another, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 18 times across 6 books. The most common situation is physical: laying hands on someone to seize or arrest them (5 of its measured uses combine 'seize' and 'seized/arrested'), though it also covers literally putting one thing over another, like throwing garments over a colt or waves breaking over a boat. The everyday Koine flavor shows in the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan record it for pouring oil onto lamps and even letting sheep loose onto a neighbor's crop. In the Septuagint it appears 54 times, frequently rendering Hebrew words for sending, setting, or stretching out the hand.
caution: In 7 of 18 occurrences the verb is absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own, and Abbott-Smith notes a disputed reflexive sense ('when he thought thereon') in Mark 14:72.

definition: Speechless or struck dumb, especially the kind of stunned silence that comes from amazement or shock.
article: ἐννεός describes someone left dumbstruck — unable to speak, typically out of astonishment, as with Paul's companions in Acts 9:7. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all point to the same idea: silent from amazement. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew word for muteness in Isaiah 56:10, and the construction 'to make speechless' appears in Proverbs 17:28.
caution: It appears only once in the Byzantine NT and is absent from the SBL critical text, and our measured data renders it 'traveling' (likely from the surrounding phrase), which clashes with every lexicon's 'speechless' — so treat the measured sense with caution.

definition: Describing something that has been in a particular state for four days, used in the New Testament of a body four days dead.
article: This adjective means "of or on the fourth day," and in its single New Testament appearance (John 11:39) it describes Lazarus as having been dead four days—which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase as "stinks." The word's range was broader in everyday Koine: papyri preserve healing charms that use it of a "quartan" fever, one recurring every fourth day. The Septuagint shows it once (2 Kingdoms 3:4 in one manuscript), corresponding to a Hebrew word meaning "fourth."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single occurrence, and the rendering "stinks" reflects the surrounding context rather than the word itself, which simply means "on the fourth day."

definition: The command "be!" — telling one person to be, exist, remain, or stay in a certain state or condition.
article: This is simply the singular command form of the verb "to be" (εἰμί), addressed to one person: "be thou" or "stay." Like the English verb "to be," the parent verb covers a huge range — existing, being present in a place, things happening, and serving as a linking word between subject and description. The form ἴσθι itself does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament, so its force here is drawn from the imperative meaning of its parent verb rather than from measured New Testament usage.
caution: There are zero occurrences of this exact form in the Byzantine New Testament, so its sense is inferred entirely from the parent verb εἰμί rather than from direct attestation.

definition: The hanging curtain or veil in the Jewish temple, especially the one separating the Holy of Holies from the rest of the sanctuary.
article: This word names the temple curtain or veil—literally something that hangs down. In all 6 New Testament uses it refers to the temple's veil, most famously the one torn in two when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51, Mark 15:38, Luke 23:45), and Hebrews even speaks figuratively of Christ's flesh as this veil (Hebrews 10:20). In the Septuagint it appears 35 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for the inner veil of the Holy of Holies, and Moulton-Milligan note it wasn't purely a Biblical word: an inscription from Samos dated 346 BC lists a 'katapetasma' meaning a table-cover.

definition: A span of two years, used to mark how long a period of time lasted.
article: Διετία simply means "a period of two years," and the New Testament uses it that way both times it appears (Acts 24:27 and 28:30), where it marks how long a situation continued. Dodson notes that by ancient reckoning the term could cover any stretch between one and two years, so it need not always mean a precise 24 months. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary, non-technical use: a lease from Oxyrhynchus speaks of paying rent "for the remaining two years," showing the word at home in business and legal documents.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in the New Testament and Abbott-Smith noting limited Septuagint attestation, the precise boundary of the time span (one-to-two years versus a full two) cannot be pinned down.

definition: The sun, the bright star that gives light and heat to the earth and marks day and night.
article: ἥλιος simply means the sun, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: all 27 times it is rendered with an English word, it comes out as "sun" (100%), with another 5 instances absorbed into phrasing like "sunrise" or "sunset." In the Septuagint it appears 173 times, mostly standing in for the Hebrew word for sun (שֶׁמֶשׁ, 126×). Everyday Koine papyri show the same down-to-earth use — one calendar text from around 300 BC describes "the courses of the sun" dividing night from day and winter from summer, and another marks the time as "at sunset."

definition: A person who is imprisoned or held captive alongside someone else, a fellow prisoner.
article: This word describes someone sharing captivity with another person—a "fellow prisoner." It appears only 3 times in the New Testament (Romans 16:7, Colossians 4:10, Philemon 23), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fellow prisoner" every time, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing fully. Properly the term refers to a fellow prisoner of war, and Moulton-Milligan notes it as one of Paul's many compounds beginning with σύν- ("with"), also attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: With only 3 occurrences, this word's range is narrow, though all sources agree firmly on the "fellow prisoner" meaning.

definition: A temple or shrine dedicated to a pagan idol.
article: This word names a temple built to house and honor a pagan idol. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 8:10, where Paul speaks of eating in such a place; the Septuagint uses it a handful of times, including in Daniel where it renders a Hebrew phrase for a god's treasury. Moulton-Milligan note that while it hasn't yet turned up in non-biblical Greek, it parallels everyday Koine names for shrines like the Isieion and Anoubieion, temples of Isis and Anubis.
caution: The single NT occurrence is rendered "informed" in the digest, which clearly mismatches the dictionary sense "idol's temple"—the measured-sense label appears to be a tagging error, so rely on the consistent classical and Septuagint evidence.

definition: Morally pure, innocent, and undefiled — clean in heart and conduct, whether ethically or in a state fit for worship.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament ἁγνός appears 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "pure" in 6 of those 8 cases (75%), with the rest scattered as "godly" or "Christ pure"; the BSB agrees with "pure" 100% of the time. It describes both persons and things as morally clean, chaste, and innocent. The classical and lexical tradition adds a fuller range: the word originally meant free from ceremonial defilement, in a condition fit for worship, and the papyri show this vividly — an inscription from Assos (A.D. 37) calls Athena "the pure Virgin," and other documents apply it to holy places one is permitted to enter.
caution: The corpus measured only the single sense "pure," but the lexica describe a broader ceremonial and ritual range that the limited New Testament data does not fully display.

definition: To be insane or out of one's mind, raving like a madman.
article: μαίνομαι describes a person being insane, raving, or out of their right mind. Across its 5 New Testament uses the meaning is consistent — whether someone is dismissed as crazy (as Festus says of Paul in Acts 26:24-25) or thought to be possessed and insane (John 10:20). The word turns up in everyday Koine too: a papyrus records an emperor saying he is used to bringing 'those who are mad or beside themselves' back to their senses, the very situation Paul faced before Festus.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and a couple of Septuagint uses, the evidence is thin but the sources agree closely on the core meaning.

definition: Disobedience, understood as the refusal to heed or obey what has been said.
article: In the New Testament παρακοή consistently means disobedience, appearing 3 times across 3 books, and is rendered "disobedience" in every case. The word's literal root sense is a failure to hear or a hearing amiss, and disobedience develops from that idea of inattention to what one is told — fittingly, in Romans 5:19 it stands opposed to ὑπακοή (obedience). Beyond the New Testament it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where Moulton-Milligan note two Byzantine examples of the noun.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a confidence tier of low, the range rests on thin evidence, though sources agree on the meaning.

definition: Made of dust or earth; belonging to the physical, earthbound order of things.
article: χοϊκός describes something formed from dust or soil — earthy, belonging to the ground rather than to heaven. All 4 New Testament occurrences sit in one passage (1 Corinthians 15:47-49), where Paul contrasts the dust-made first man with the heavenly one; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "dust" once and "earthly" once, with the word folded into the phrasing the other two times. It derives from χόος ("dust, soil"), and the Greek rhetoricians use the same word vividly of "the weight of the dust" — the burden of our earthbound nature.
caution: All four occurrences come from a single passage, so its full range outside that context is poorly attested.

definition: The physical body of a person or animal, whether living or dead, and by extension a unified whole made of many parts.
senseLabels: a lesser part of the body
article: σῶμα is overwhelmingly straightforward: in 129 of 146 New Testament occurrences (94%) it simply means "body," the physical body of a living person or, as in Matthew 27:58–59, a corpse. The remaining handful of "measured senses" are really the same word seen through Paul's imagery of a single body with many interconnected parts (1 Corinthians 12, Ephesians 4). The everyday flavor of the word shows up vividly in the papyri, where σῶμα appears in standard letter greetings hoping the recipient is well "in body," a routine wish for good health.
caution: Strong's and KJV note a rare sense of "slave," but no New Testament occurrence in this digest is measured that way, so treat that meaning as outside the biblical evidence here.

definition: To play or amuse oneself, especially through singing and dancing in festive, sometimes morally loose, revelry.
article: At its root παίζω means to play like a child, but it broadened to cover any kind of merrymaking, including singing and dancing. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Corinthians 10:7), where it describes the festive revelry around the golden calf, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "indulge revelry" every time. In the Septuagint it shows up 23 times, usually translating the Hebrew שָׂחַק ("to laugh, sport," 11×), and a sepulchral inscription captures its lighter sense vividly: "play, indulge, live—you must die."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise New Testament shade rests heavily on the Old Testament quotation it appears in.

definition: To block, close, or stop something up, used figuratively for silencing a mouth or stopping an argument.
article: At its root φράσσω means to fence in or block up, but in the New Testament it always appears figuratively for silencing. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "silenced" in 2 of its 3 occurrences (with the third absorbed into surrounding phrasing), as when every mouth is stopped before God (Rom 3:19) or the boasting that cannot be shut up (2Co 11:10). The literal sense shows up vividly in everyday Koine: an Oxyrhynchus papyrus from A.D. 190 reports robbers breaking through a door that had been "blocked up with bricks," and in the Septuagint it can mean fencing off a path (translating Hebrew שׂוּך in Hosea).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin.

definition: A Greek personal name, "Didymus," meaning "twin," used as the surname of the apostle Thomas.
article: In the New Testament, Δίδυμος appears only 3 times, always in John's Gospel (11:16; 20:24; 21:2), and always as the Greek surname of the apostle Thomas, meaning "twin." Every translation renders it the same way — simply transliterating it as "Didymus" — so there's no real range of meaning to debate here. As an ordinary Greek word the term meant "double" or "twin," and the papyri make this vivid: it shows up in the lengthy correspondence about the "Serapeum Twins," two women named Thaues and Taous who petitioned the king and described themselves as δίδυμαι, "twins."
caution: With only 3 occurrences, all the same proper-name use, the corpus evidence is thin, hence the low confidence tier.

definition: To be lacking, missing, or short of something needed.
article: In the New Testament λείπω usually means to lack or fall short of something needed, as when Jesus tells the rich ruler he still lacks one thing (Luke 18:22). The measured renderings—"lack" (3×), plus phrases meaning "everything" or "without"—all cluster around the same idea of being short of what is required. The classical lexicons preserve an older transitive sense, "to leave behind," and Moulton-Milligan notes that everyday Greek epitaphs carefully kept the active form for "to leave life" (i.e., to die), distinct from the passive.

definition: Rehoboam, the son of Solomon who reigned as king after him.
article: Ῥοβοάμ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Rehoboam, the son of Solomon and a king of Israel. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:7), where the Majority Standard Bible always renders it "Rehoboam." In the Septuagint it shows up 61 times and most often translates the Hebrew רְחַבְעָם, though the digest also lists it alongside other Hebrew words like לָחַם, likely reflecting similar-looking forms rather than the name itself.
caution: This is a proper name with only two New Testament occurrences, so the evidence is thin even though every source agrees on the meaning.

definition: A law-court or tribunal — the place or panel where legal cases are decided.
article: κριτήριον refers to a court of justice or tribunal where disputes are settled, and by extension the legal case being tried. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the translators rendered it as a word of its own ("judge") just once, folding it into surrounding phrasing the other two times. The word is well attested in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite papyri where people "shall be tried before the appointed tribunal," confirming this courtroom sense in ordinary legal documents.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 NT occurrences, two absorbed into phrasing), and the lexica list a broader range — "criterion" or "means of judging" — that the measured data does not confirm.

definition: In a way that shows no favoritism, judging everyone fairly without regard to social status or appearance.
article: This adverb describes acting "without respect of persons" — that is, impartially, showing no favoritism toward anyone based on who they are. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 1 Peter 1:17, where every translation surveyed renders it "impartially." Moulton-Milligan note that the word grew out of the Jewish technical phrase "to receive a face" (πρόσωπον λαμβάνειν), a literal translation idiom for showing partiality, which the negating prefix here reverses.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: Describing something made of or resembling brimstone (sulfur), with its characteristic yellow color.
article: θειώδης is a rare adjective meaning "sulfurous" or "like brimstone," built from θεῖον (sulfur/brimstone). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 9:17, where it describes the breastplates of the apocalyptic horsemen. Interestingly, the measured rendering in the Majority Standard Bible reads "riders" rather than a word for sulfur, while the classical lexica (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) uniformly define it as "of brimstone, sulphureous" — a clear disagreement between the corpus translation data and the dictionary definitions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured translation ("riders") conflicts with the lexica's "sulfurous," so the sense should be treated as uncertain.

definition: To make dark or to be darkened, whether literally as in physical darkness or figuratively of a clouded mind.
article: σκοτόω means to darken or be darkened, built from the noun σκότος ("darkness"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, in Revelation 16:10, where a kingdom is plunged into darkness; the lexicons note it can also apply figuratively to a darkened mind, as in Ephesians 4:18. A vivid everyday glimpse comes from a Greek papyrus where the writer says new wine "has already blinded" some people, showing the word's reach beyond purely physical darkness.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one Byzantine occurrence and five in the Septuagint, so the confidence tier is low.

definition: To agree with, approve of, or consent to something that someone else is doing or proposing.
article: συνευδοκέω means to join with someone in approving or agreeing to something, whether you approve of an act, consent to a plan, or are willing to go along with a course of action. It appears 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and the English renderings vary by context: it can describe consenting to others' deeds (Luke 11:48, Romans 1:32) or being willing to do something (1 Corinthians 7:12–13, where it describes a believer willing to stay married to an unbelieving spouse). Moulton-Milligan notes it was a common everyday Koine word, found in papyri as early as 103 BC in legal contexts—for example, witnesses "agreeing to" the terms written above in a contract.
caution: The various English renderings reflect different grammatical constructions rather than distinct meanings, so the word's core sense of "agree/consent" stays consistent throughout.

definition: At no time at all; never.
article: μηδέποτε is an emphatic way of saying "never" — "not even ever" — built from μηδέ ("not even") and ποτέ ("at any time"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:7, where it describes people "always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth," and every translation surveyed renders it "never." Moulton-Milligan show it was at home in everyday Koine: a Tebtunis papyrus from 114 B.C. uses it of people "when they had never made this payment."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests mainly on the single passage plus everyday papyri usage.

definition: Azotus, the Greek name for the Philistine city of Ashdod on the coast of Palestine.
article: Ἄζωτος is simply the Greek name for the Philistine coastal city of Ashdod, which appears once in the New Testament (Acts 8:40) when Philip is found there. The word is a place name, not a common noun, so it has no real range of meaning. The Septuagint uses it 16 times across 8 books, where it overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew אַשְׁדּוֹד (Ashdod, 10 times) but also stands in for nearby towns like Ashkelon (2×) and Jabneh (2×).
caution: The listed measured sense "appeared" reflects how the verse was rendered rather than the meaning of this proper noun, so treat that label with care.

definition: To give help or relief to someone in need, providing the support their situation requires.
article: This verb means to come to someone's aid, supplying the relief or support they need — it always takes a person as its object. Although the Majority Standard Bible's renderings break into two surface labels at 1 Timothy 5:16, both occurrences really point to the same idea of helping the needy, and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully with "help need." Built from ἐπί and ἀρκέω, it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, including a touching line where a Jewish speaker says "this was my delight, to give help if anyone was in want." Classical lexica record a wider range — "to be strong enough for" and even "to ward off" — that the New Testament does not display.
