caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only 3 times in the New Testament (all in 1 Timothy), so confidence is low and the broader classical senses are not directly attested here.

definition: A blessing — words or acts that invoke or convey good, whether praise directed to God or a gift bestowed on people.
article: εὐλογία centers on "blessing" — the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 9 of 16 occurrences (82%), and the Berean Standard Bible independently agrees 100% of the time. The Septuagint uses it 71 times, overwhelmingly to translate Hebrew בְּרָכָה (54×), reinforcing this core meaning. The classical lexica stretch the range further than the New Testament data measures: Abbott-Smith and Strong's note senses like "fair speaking," "flattering speech" (Rom 16:18), and "praise" of God or Christ (Revelation), and the everyday papyri show it as a Christian greeting and even an address-title for a bishop.
caution: The measured data captures only the dominant "blessing" sense; the lexica's additional senses of flattery and praise rest on a few specific verses rather than broad measured counts.

definition: To make something physically secure or firm, such as sealing a tomb, fastening someone in custody, or locking down a prisoner.
article: ἀσφαλίζω is a physical-security word: to make firm, fasten, or secure something so it cannot be moved or escaped. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times—three about sealing and guarding Jesus' tomb (Matthew 27:64-66) and once about a jailer fastening Paul's feet in the stocks (Acts 16:24). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this hands-on sense, where it can even mean to arrest a person or seize produce.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and one Septuagint use, the labels for these senses are really just different objects of the same basic action rather than distinct meanings.

definition: A village or small country town, typically without protective walls, as opposed to a fortified city.
article: κώμη is the ordinary Koine word for a village or small country town, and the New Testament uses it consistently this way — 23 of 28 times (82%) it is simply rendered "village." It is often contrasted with the walled "city" (πόλις), and frequently pairs with a place name, as in the village of Bethlehem (John 7:42) or Bethany (John 11:1). It was a thoroughly everyday term: papyri use the phrase "those from the village" to mean the village population at large, not its officials, showing how the word described a real community of ordinary people.

definition: To pretend or put on a false front, acting a part to deceive others about one's true intentions.
article: This verb means to pretend or play a false part, like an actor on a stage assuming a character that isn't really you. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 20:20, where people pretend to be sincere in order to trap Jesus. Originally it could simply mean "to answer or reply" (its older Attic sense, the same root behind ἀποκρίνομαι), and it was also used for delivering lines in theater—from which the sense of pretending naturally developed. The Psalms of Solomon offers a vivid parallel, describing "men that work hypocrisy."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "rule" appears to be a data artifact that conflicts with the lexicons' consistent meaning of "pretend."

definition: Describing a person who reverences and worships God, living a devout and godly life.
article: θεοσεβής combines the words for "God" and "to revere," so it describes someone who worships and lives devoutly toward God. It appears just once in the New Testament (John 9:31) and four times in the Septuagint, where it stands in for Hebrew words meaning "blameless" (3×) and "God-fearing" (1×). Interestingly, the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, even in polite letter-addresses calling someone a "most God-fearing brother," showing it was common social vocabulary beyond the Bible.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on very thin evidence.

definition: The office, position, or institution of being a priest.
article: This noun names the priestly office itself — the institution and function of serving as a priest, not the individual priest. The New Testament uses it just 4 times (3 in the critical text), all in Hebrews chapter 7, where it is always rendered "priesthood." Everyday Koine documents add a striking detail: inscriptions from Priene show the word used for a priesthood that could be sold or won by lot, treating the sacred office as a tangible position one could acquire.
caution: Evidence is thin and narrow: every New Testament occurrence sits in a single chapter of Hebrews, with only one Septuagint instance.

definition: To run or drive a ship onto the shore, beaching it, whether on purpose or by accident.
article: This is a nautical term for driving a vessel onto the shore so that it grounds. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 27:41, where Paul's ship runs aground; the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as 'move.' One intriguing detail: the related form ἐπικέλλω is so poetic that Blass thought Luke may have known Homer, though Moulton-Milligan notes that such poetic phrases often survive in everyday speech, and the word does turn up in ordinary Koine papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical edition, so its range rests on a single passage.

definition: Steady, persistent devotion to something—keeping at it without giving up.
article: προσκαρτέρησις means persistent, steadfast devotion to a task or practice. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 6:18, where it describes keeping at prayer; this rarity matches Abbott-Smith's note that it occurs only there in Scripture. The most interesting evidence comes from Moulton-Milligan: two deeds of manumission from Panticapaeum on the Black Sea use it, including an A.D. 81 text speaking of "reverence and constancy toward the place of prayer," showing it was a real everyday Koine word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Describing something or someone that no longer serves a useful purpose; worthless or unfit for service.
article: ἄχρηστος means "useless" or "unserviceable" — the opposite of εὔχρηστος ("useful"), built from a negative prefix on χρηστός. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Philemon 1:11, where it is rendered "useless" in every measured occurrence. The everyday papyri show just how plain and practical the word was: it described unproductive farmland, a scrawny pig, broken panniers, and a worn-out garment, while in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew at Hosea 8:8.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, though the papyri and Septuagint usage agree.

definition: Filled or full, whether physically packed with something or, figuratively, completely characterized by a quality.
article: πλήρης means "full" — physically filled with something or, by extension, completely marked by a quality like faith, grace, or wrath. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "full" in 7 of its 17 New Testament occurrences (88% of the times it gets its own word), while 9 times it's absorbed into surrounding phrasing without a word of its own. A striking detail: the word sometimes appears in an indeclinable form (unchanging regardless of grammar), as in John 1:14 "full of grace and truth" — a usage the papyri now abundantly confirm as ordinary Koine.

definition: To have no fixed home, living an unsettled, wandering life with no permanent dwelling place.
article: This verb describes the state of having no stable, fixed home — being unsettled and forced to wander. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 4:11, where Paul lists it among his hardships; the Majority Standard Bible renders it loosely as "poorly," though the literal sense is closer to homelessness. The most telling evidence comes from Aquila's Greek translation of Isaiah 58:7, where he uses this word for people the Septuagint simply calls "homeless," reinforcing the idea of a vagabond, dwelling-less life.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and has thin attestation outside it, so its precise force is uncertain.

definition: Deep pain or distress, whether of body or mind — anguish, grief, or sorrow that weighs a person down.
article: ὀδύνη describes painful distress, covering both physical pain and inner grief. It appears only twice in the New Testament, rendered once as "deep unceasing anguish" (Romans 9:2) and once as "sorrows" (1 Timothy 6:10), and the Septuagint uses it 56 times for several Hebrew words including יָגוֹן (grief). A striking glimpse of its everyday emotional force comes from a second-century BC papyrus, where a lover writes "ὀδύνη grips me whenever I remember how he kissed me, treacherously planning to leave me."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the full range here rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: To tread or trample something underfoot, literally crushing it down, or figuratively treating it with contempt.
article: καταπατέω means to tread something down underfoot, whether literally—like salt thrown out and trampled, or seed crushed along a path—or figuratively, as in trampling the Son of God by treating him with scorn. Across its 5 New Testament uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "trampled" 60% of the time, with the remaining occurrences describing seed crushed on a roadside (Luke 8:5) and a crowd so thick people were trampling one another (Luke 12:1). The word's reach into ordinary life shows in the papyri, where a 3rd-century BC inscription uses it of trampling someone with horses, and in the Septuagint it appears 43 times, often for the Hebrew רָמַס, "to trample."

definition: A wheel; figuratively, the recurring cycle or course of life set in motion.
article: τροχός literally means a wheel, and that is how it shows up everywhere in everyday Koine — papyri mention the wheel of a machine, a cutting device, and even a water-wheel. In the Septuagint it appears 45 times across 9 books, mostly translating the Hebrew word for wheel (אוֹפָן, 27 times). It occurs just once in the New Testament, at James 3:6, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sets" — pointing to the figurative "course" or circuit of life that the tongue can set ablaze.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence in a difficult phrase, so commentators have long debated exactly how the figurative "course of life" should be understood.

definition: To make a good outward appearance, putting on an impressive show to win others' approval.
article: This word literally means "to be fair of face" and figuratively describes putting on a good public display to impress people. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 6:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "trying" to make a good showing. The papyri give a striking parallel: a Tebtunis document from 114 B.C. uses it for wanting "to make a good show," predating the Pauline usage by about three centuries.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: Judah — the name of the Israelite patriarch, his tribe, the land they settled, or the royal line descended from him.
article: Ἰουδά is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Judah (יְהוּדָה), used for the man, his tribe, his territory, and the royal line that springs from him. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times across 4 books and is rendered "Judah" every time, with the wording "Behold, Judah" in Hebrews 8:8 and "Judah triumphed" in Revelation 5:5 simply reflecting the surrounding sentence. The name dominates the Septuagint, occurring 647 times in 31 books and translating Hebrew יְהוּדָה in 535 of those cases — making this one of the most heavily attested proper names in the Greek Old Testament.
caution: Note that the Byzantine text shows these 7 occurrences while the critical SBLGNT has 0, and lexicons list overlapping but distinct forms (Ἰουδά for the name versus Ἰουδαῖος/Ἰουδαία for "Jew" and "Judea"), so the exact form should be checked in context.

definition: To show or prove something by word or action, making it clearly visible to others.
article: ἐνDείκνυμι means to point something out or prove it, whether through speech or through deeds. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times, almost always rendered "show" (6 of 11 times, 60%), and its range is fairly tight around the idea of demonstrating or making something evident. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this: petitions use it to mean "prove," as in "if we prove that what we set forth is true" (P Magd 3, 221 B.C.); the same word can also carry a negative edge, as when 2 Timothy 4:14 says someone "showed" much evil toward Paul, echoing Genesis 50:15-17.

definition: A harsh, resentful bitterness of spirit or speech, sometimes pictured as a bitter taste or poison.
article: πικρία means bitterness, used mostly in a figurative sense of a sour, resentful temper. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times: usually rendered "bitterness" (3×), and once in Ephesians 4:31 alongside related words for anger and outcry. The Septuagint uses it 20 times to translate Hebrew words for bitter taste (מָר) and the bitter wormwood plant (לַעֲנָה), and Moulton-Milligan note an everyday papyrus where a father warns his son about "the hardness of the times."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the range is thin, and the second measured sense reflects a single verse where the word stands among several others.

definition: To recline at a table while eating, as was the custom at meals in the ancient world.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament this verb always describes people reclining at a table to eat, appearing 15 times across 4 books and rendered "reclining" in half of them. The other occurrences get absorbed into phrasing like "the guests" or "those at the table," since reclining was simply how people dined. Interestingly, this dinner-table meaning seems to be relatively late — Moulton-Milligan note it doesn't appear older than the Macedonian period — and an everyday Koine papyrus list (BGU I.344) even tallies up "the ones reclining" at a gathering; older usage meant being "laid up" or "dedicated," as in an Ephesian inscription where a month is dedicated to the goddess.

definition: The activity of buying and selling goods—trade, commerce, or one's business affairs.
article: ἐμπορία refers to commerce, trade, or the running of a business, and it comes from ἔμπορος, a merchant. It appears only once in the New Testament (Matthew 22:5), where someone goes off to his business; in the Septuagint it occurs 11 times across 3 books, often translating Hebrew words for trading and merchandise. The papyri make its everyday flavor vivid—one document uses the phrase 'for the sake of business' (ἐνπορίας χάριν), exactly the ordinary commercial sense.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the rendering 'paid' reflects one translation's phrasing rather than a broad measured range; the underlying meaning is plainly 'business' or 'trade.'

definition: To need something additionally or further, beyond what one already has.
article: This verb combines πρός ("toward, in addition") with δέομαι ("to need"), giving the sense of needing something further or extra. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 17:25) and once in the Septuagint, where it renders a Hebrew word for "lacking." The everyday papyri are illuminating here: one third-century BC document uses it of time that "allows of no further delay," and another of land that "still has need" of something — Moulton-Milligan cites these to argue the word means "need in addition" rather than simply "need."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, scholars disagree on whether it means plain "need" (KJV) or specifically "need in addition."

definition: To give divine warning or instruction, or to be publicly given a name or title.
article: In the New Testament χρηματίζω mostly describes God warning or instructing someone, often in a dream or revelation—that's how it's rendered "warned" 3 times (38%) in passages like Matthew 2:12 and Hebrews 11:7. The other measured sense is "called" or named, 2 times (25%), as in Acts 11:26 where believers were first called Christians. The interesting backstory is that the word originally meant doing business or transacting affairs, and the papyri confirm this everyday Koine usage—the "receiving a name" sense grew out of the public name one takes from one's business, while "warning" developed from the idea of an official answer or oracle.
caution: With only 9 occurrences and a wide range from "warn" to "be named," the right sense depends heavily on context.

definition: An intensifying adverb meaning to a very high degree—exceedingly, greatly, or very much.
article: σφόδρα is an intensifier that pumps up whatever verb or adjective it attaches to, meaning "very," "greatly," or "exceedingly"—as in being greatly afraid or extremely amazed. It appears 11 times in the Byzantine New Testament and a striking 317 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always stands in for the Hebrew word מְאֹד (236 times), the standard Hebrew way of saying "very" or "much." Everyday papyri show the same flavor: one document complains that certain villages "σφόδρα ἐξησθένησαν," were utterly exhausted by public burdens. In 3 of its 11 New Testament occurrences it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a separate English word.

definition: To drink only water, abstaining from wine.
article: ὑδροποτέω literally means to be a water-drinker—someone who drinks water rather than wine. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:23, where Paul tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and use a little wine for his stomach. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and in classical authors like Herodotus and Plato, and the Septuagint uses it once in Daniel 1:12, matching a Hebrew phrase about drinking water. Interestingly, Epictetus pairs it with fasting (ἀσίτησον, ὑδροπότησον), highlighting its link to disciplined or abstemious living.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest notes the MSB rendered it as "frequent," which does not match the standard meaning "drink water" given by every lexicon—so treat the measured sense label with care.

definition: Describing the foundation stone set at the corner of a building, which anchors and aligns the whole structure.
article: This adjective literally means "at the extreme corner," combining ἄκρον (tip, extremity) and γωνία (angle, corner), and in the New Testament it always stands for the all-important corner foundation stone. It appears only twice, in Ephesians 2:20 and 1 Peter 2:6, both times pointing to Christ as that stone. The most interesting detail is its origin: Moulton-Milligan suggest the word may have been coined by the Septuagint translators at Isaiah 28:16 (rendering Hebrew בֹּחַן/פִּנָּה), since the ordinary Attic form was simply γωνιαῖος.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences plus a single Septuagint use—so the range is narrow and confidence is low.

definition: To look for something or someone, or to strive after and aim at a desired goal.
article: ζητέω is the everyday word for seeking — whether you're physically searching for a lost person or item, or striving after something you want. The Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "seek" (40×, 45%) or "look" (20×), but it also slides naturally into "trying" and "tried" when the goal is an action rather than an object. In the Septuagint it usually stands for Hebrew בָּקַשׁ (147×), and the everyday papyri capture its plain feel perfectly: one early letter complains "I looked for the cloak everywhere and did not find it."

definition: To talk or converse with someone, keeping company in conversation.
article: ὁμιλέω means to be in someone's company and talk with them—basically, to have a conversation. Every one of its 4 New Testament uses fits this meaning, whether two travelers chatting on the road (Luke 24:14-15) or Paul talking long into the night (Acts 20:11) and conversing with Felix (Acts 24:26). The everyday flavor shows up nicely in a papyrus letter (P Oxy VI.928) where someone says "you once had a conversation with me on this subject," matching the ordinary Koine use exactly.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences—two of which the digest labels simply "talking together" and "Paul"—the evidence is thin, though all sources agree on the core meaning.

definition: A covering or veil that hides something from view, especially a cloth over the face or head.
article: Kályma refers to a covering or veil, something laid over an object or face to conceal it. The word comes from the verb καλýptō ("to cover"), and in all 4 of its New Testament appearances it means "veil" — every one of them in 2 Corinthians 3 (verses 13-15). The Septuagint uses it more broadly, 17 times, to translate several Hebrew words for coverings, including the veil Moses placed over his face (מַסְוֶה) and tabernacle coverings (מִכְסֶה); everyday Koine papyri even apply it to wooden boards or panels.
caution: The New Testament evidence is narrow — all 4 occurrences cluster in a single passage — so the broader "covering" range comes mainly from the Septuagint and papyri rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: Armed conflict between groups, ranging from a sustained war to a single battle or fight.
article: πόλεμος covers armed conflict at any scale, from a long-running war down to a single battle. In the Byzantine New Testament it's rendered "wars" 8 times (42%) and "battle" 6 times (32%), and these two ideas blur together rather than separating neatly. It's a common word: the Septuagint uses it 270 times across 29 books, almost always for Hebrew מִלְחָמָה, and everyday papyri use it too — one second-century BC document dates a house sale "before the war." James 4:1 stretches it figuratively to private quarrels.

definition: Said of a sacred object believed to have fallen from the sky as a gift of heaven.
article: διοπετής literally means "fallen from the sky" and describes a sacred image thought to have dropped down from heaven. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 19:35, where the city clerk of Ephesus refers to such an object linked to the worship of Artemis. The word is built from the name of Zeus (the sky-god) plus the verb "to fall," and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions; one ancient source even glosses a διοπετής shield as simply "sent by god."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on a single passage and outside parallels.

definition: To explain or make something clear by spelling it out in words.
article: φράzō means to explain, declare, or spell something out plainly. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both times in Matthew (13:36 and 15:15), where the disciples ask Jesus to explain a parable to them, so its measured range is narrow and consistent. A nice glimpse of its everyday flavor comes from the papyri: a 3rd-century BC document (P Rev Laws) uses it for orchard owners formally 'stating' their names and home villages when registering, showing the word's ordinary sense of declaring information clearly.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text) the evidence is thin, and some manuscripts read διασάφησον instead at Matthew 13:36.

definition: To be able to do something, having the power, permission, or opportunity to do it.
article: δύναμαι means simply to be able — to have the power, permission, or opportunity to do something, usually paired with another verb. It appears 208 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and strikingly most renderings express what someone *cannot* do (49 times, 60% of the counted senses), with the positive "able" coming next. In the Septuagint it shows up 237 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew יָכֹל ("be able"), and everyday papyri use it the same casual way, as in a private letter asking "how can I forget you?"

definition: A going out to meet someone, especially to welcome or receive them as they approach.
article: This noun describes the act of going out to meet or welcome someone, typically formed in the phrase "to meet" (εἰς ὑπάντησιν). In the one Byzantine New Testament occurrence (John 12:13) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "meet," and the Septuagint uses it once, translating a Hebrew word for going out to greet. The everyday papyri show the same use—one second-century document has a man going "to meet" Ulpianus—and the lexicographer Lightfoot suggested it carries the extra nuance of looking out for someone, as opposed to the plainer synonym ἀπάντησις.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its precise range rests on thin evidence and the proposed distinction from ἀπάντησις is a scholarly suggestion, not a measured fact.

definition: A lawgiver — the one who makes and establishes laws.
article: νομοθέτης names a lawgiver or legislator, built from the words for "law" (νόμος) and "to set or place" (τίθημι). It appears only once in the New Testament, in James 4:12, where it points to God as the single Lawgiver who can judge. In the Septuagint it shows up just once as well, at Psalm 9:20, where it renders the Hebrew word מוֹרָה.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range is very thin.

definition: To bear witness together with someone or something, adding confirming testimony alongside another's.
article: συμμαρτυρέω combines "with" and "to testify," so it means giving evidence alongside another witness — corroborating rather than testifying alone. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Romans, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as testifying jointly (Rom 8:16) or speaking with confirmation (Rom 9:1), with one occurrence absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. A nice glimpse of its everyday use comes from the papyri: a document from A.D. 155 shows each attesting witness signing with the words "I bear witness with and seal with," exactly the legal sense of corroborating testimony.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise force of this word rests on thin evidence.

definition: To a greater degree, more abundantly or more intensely than otherwise.
article: This adverb means doing or experiencing something more abundantly, more earnestly, or more intensely than the baseline. It is the comparative "more" applied to actions and feelings, sometimes shading into "exceedingly" or "especially" (as in 2 Corinthians 7:15 and Galatians 1:14). It appears 0 times in the Byzantine NT counted here but 12 times in the critical (SBLGNT) text, and Moulton-Milligan note a parallel in a second-century papyrus where someone hopes another will care "more exceedingly" about a matter.
caution: The Byzantine count is 0 while the critical text shows 12 occurrences, so attestation depends heavily on which text you use.

definition: To grind or gnash the teeth, usually as an expression of rage or anguish.
article: βρύχω describes the grinding or gnashing of teeth, an action that signals intense rage or pain. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 7:54, where the Sanhedrin gnash their teeth at Stephen — and both the Majority Standard Bible and BSB render it this way. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times, mostly translating the Hebrew חָרַק ("to gnash"), and the older lexicon Abbott-Smith notes a secondary classical sense "to bite or eat greedily" that the biblical evidence does not reflect.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the gnashing sense rests on a single verse plus limited Septuagint support.

definition: The place where someone lives; a dwelling, home, or habitation.
article: κατοίκησις refers to a place of residence — a home or dwelling — and is built from the verb κατοικέω, "to dwell." It appears just once in the New Testament, at Mark 5:3, where it describes the demon-possessed man whose "dwelling" was among the tombs. In the Septuagint it occurs 8 times across 7 books, most often rendering the Hebrew מוֹשָׁב ("dwelling, seat"), confirming the basic sense of a place where people settle and live.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "restrained" looks like a tagging error, since every lexicon and the Septuagint evidence point to "dwelling."

definition: Trophimus, a Christian man from Ephesus who traveled with the apostle Paul.
article: Trophimus is a personal name, used in all three of its New Testament appearances for a Christian from Ephesus who accompanied Paul (Acts 20:4, 21:29, and 2 Timothy 4:20). As a name it derives from the Greek word for "nourishment" (τροφή), and Strong's notes the underlying sense "nutritive." Interestingly, the everyday papyri show the same word used both as a proper name and in its ordinary meaning of "foster-child" — one document from A.D. 250 refers to someone "from his foster-child's mother."
caution: This is a proper name with only three occurrences, so its meaning beyond identifying the man rests on word-derivation and outside papyri rather than New Testament usage.

definition: Patara, a coastal city of the Roman province of Lycia in southwestern Asia Minor.
article: Patara was a maritime city on the coast of Lycia in Asia Minor, mentioned just once in the New Testament when Paul's ship stopped there (Acts 21:1). The classical lexica (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree it is a place name, and Strong's notes the word is probably of foreign origin. One oddity in the evidence: the measured corpus data lists the rendering as "torn," which conflicts with every lexicon's identification of Patara as a proper place name — the place-name reading is correct.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured "torn" rendering disagrees with all lexica, which uniformly treat it as the place name Patara.

definition: To speak or tell the truth, dealing honestly and truthfully with others.
article: ἀληθεύω means to speak or tell the truth, and both of its New Testament appearances point that way. It occurs only twice in the Byzantine text—at Galatians 4:16 ("by telling" the truth) and Ephesians 4:15 (speaking "truth")—so the two measured senses are really one idea seen from slightly different angles. In the Septuagint it shows up four times rendering several different Hebrew words, and Abbott-Smith notes some translators prefer "deal truly" over simply "speak the truth," hinting the word can stretch toward honest dealing, not just honest words.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin papyri evidence, the exact breadth between "speak truth" and "deal truthfully" is not firmly settled.

definition: To rub oil or perfume on someone or something, whether for grooming, hospitality, healing, or preparing a body for burial.
article: ἀλείφω means to smear or rub on oil or fragrant ointment, and the two measured senses are really just active and passive forms of the same action — "anoint" (4×, 44%) and "anointed" (3×, 33%). The action covers a wide social range: refreshing oneself after fasting, honoring a guest, healing the sick, and preparing the dead. A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri, where the same verb describes carefully greasing a yoke-band and a man complaining he hadn't bathed or anointed himself since his wife left.
caution: Some lexicons distinguish ἀλείφω from χρίω ("anoint" in a sacred sense), but Moulton-Milligan's papyri evidence challenges that neat split.

definition: To feel compassion for someone in need and act on it, showing mercy or pity.
article: ἐλεέω means to have pity on someone and respond with mercy, whether in word or deed. The usage is remarkably consistent: in the Byzantine New Testament's 31 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "mercy" 27 times (93%), and BSB agrees 100%, so there's essentially one well-defined sense. In the Septuagint it appears 94 times, most often translating the Hebrew רָחַם (26×, tender compassion) and חָנַן (22×, to be gracious); the everyday Koine flavor shows up in a papyrus where a struggling man writes "I entreat you my preserver to have pity on me."

definition: A prearranged sign or signal agreed upon beforehand so that others know what to look for.
article: σύσσημον is a compound built from "with" and the root for "sign," meaning a signal that people have agreed on in advance. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Mark 14:44, where Judas gives the arresting party a prearranged sign—a kiss—to identify Jesus. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times, translating the Hebrew words נֵס (3×, a raised standard or banner) and מַשְׂאֵת (2×), and Moulton-Milligan note it was common enough in everyday Koine papyri, even though ancient Atticist grammarians like Phrynichus snubbed it as bad Greek.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence, and the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering "Now" reflects sentence-level translation rather than the word's actual meaning of "signal."

definition: To settle down and live somewhere, or for birds, to roost and nest in a particular spot.
article: κατασκηνόω literally means to pitch a tent or camp down, and by extension to settle and dwell somewhere. In the New Testament's four uses, three describe birds nesting in the branches of a grown mustard plant, and one (Acts 2:26, quoting the Septuagint) speaks of the flesh dwelling or resting in hope. It is common in the Septuagint, appearing 55 times across 16 books, where it most often renders the Hebrew word shakan, "to dwell," and Moulton-Milligan notes it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: The Majority Standard Bible's renderings group the three bird passages under "garden"/"grows garden" phrasing, which reflects the verb's nesting sense rather than literal gardening.

definition: Pay given for work or service, whether literal wages or a reward (or punishment) one earns by one's actions.
article: μισθός covers the whole idea of what someone earns for service — most basically the wages a worker is paid, but in the New Testament it leans toward the broader sense of "reward," rendered that way in about 48% of its 29 occurrences versus "wages" in 26%. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the down-to-earth core meaning: documents speak of a daily wage and of a weaver who "works for a wage and has no means" to pay a public tax. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew שָׂכָר (26 times), and it can swing to a negative payoff too — a "reward" of wrongdoing or punishment.
caution: The two main renderings — "reward" and "wages" — are really one concept (pay you earn), so the dividing line between them is a translator's judgment rather than a hard distinction.

definition: To hold something before oneself, and so to have an advantage over others, excel, or be in a better position.
article: This verb literally means to "hold before," built from πρό (before) and ἔχω (have, hold). In its single New Testament appearance (Romans 3:9), the form is famously difficult: it can mean "are we better off?" (active sense) or "are we worse off / excelled?" (passive sense), and the major lexicons openly disagree. The classical and papyri range is wider — to project physically, to have a head start in a race, or in the middle voice to excuse oneself — but the Byzantine NT uses it just once, where the meaning was absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word.
caution: This is a one-occurrence word whose meaning in Romans 3:9 is genuinely disputed, with reputable scholars split between "are we better off" and "are we excelled."

definition: To bend or stoop in order to peer at something, or figuratively to look intently into a matter.
article: παρακύπτω literally means to bend or stoop sideways so you can peer at something not directly in front of you — like ducking to look into a tomb (Luke 24:12, John 20:5, 11). It also takes a figurative sense of looking intently into something, as when James 1:25 speaks of looking into the perfect law of liberty, and 1 Peter 1:12 of angels longing to look into the gospel. A neat detail from the papyri: in one document a slave is described stretching to catch a glimpse of castanet-players in the courtyard below, and Hort notes the word often implies a quick, cursory glance rather than a long stare.
caution: The four "senses" largely reflect different English renderings of one underlying action (stooping to peer); the literal and figurative uses are not sharply separate meanings.

definition: The comparative form of "good," meaning "better" or, in some uses, simply "very well."
article: βελτίον is the comparative of ἀγαθός ("good"), used as an adverb to mean "better" or "very well." It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 1:18, where it relates to what Timothy knows very well about Onesiphorus. Everyday Koine papyri show the same word at work, including a charming oracle question (P Oxy VIII.1148) asking the gods whether it would be "better" to do something, and a phrase about the "continual invention of further improvements."
caution: The measured-sense data here is unreliable—it merely flags the name "Onesiphorus" in the single verse rather than the word's actual meaning—so lean on the lexicon glosses of "better" or "very well."

definition: To tell someone to do something, usually as a person with authority giving a command.
article: κελεύω means to order or command someone by word of mouth, typically spoken by a person in authority. Its meaning is narrow and stable: across all 26 Byzantine occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ordered" 85% of the time, with the rest captured by phrasing like "gave orders" or "command." The everyday papyri back this up nicely \u2014 one document from A.D. 148 uses it of an official decree ("so that you may know what has been commanded"), showing it was the ordinary word for issuing orders in daily Koine life.

definition: The condition or process of being dead, deadening, or lifelessness, whether of the body or its parts.
article: νέκρωσις describes deadness or the process of dying — either an active putting to death or a lifeless, deadened condition. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Romans 4:19 it refers to the lifelessness of Sarah's womb (the digest's odd 'hundred' label reflects a measurement glitch, since the sense there is barrenness or deadness), and in 2 Corinthians 4:10 it means the dying or death that Paul carries in his body. A striking parallel from the papyri-era sources, cited by Deissmann, uses the word for seeds that 'come to life again after death and destruction by decay,' showing its everyday range covered natural deadness as well as deliberate killing.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a misfiring 'hundred' label on the Romans verse, the measured data is thin and partly unreliable, though the lexica agree on the core meaning.

definition: To hold something back or keep away from it; or, when receiving payment, to have something in full.
article: ἀπέχω covers a surprisingly wide range. Most often in the New Testament it means to keep oneself away from something — to abstain (rendered "abstain" in 56% of cases, e.g. Acts 15:20, 1 Thessalonians 4:3, 1 Peter 2:11) — but it can also mean to be physically distant from a place. Its most striking sense comes from everyday Koine receipts: the papyri and ostraca repeatedly use ἀπέχω to mean "I have received in full," which sharpens Jesus' warning that hypocrites "already have their reward in full" — they can sign the receipt, and nothing more is coming (Matthew 6:2, 6:5, 6:16). In the Septuagint it appears 9 times, most often translating the Hebrew רָחַק ("to be far").
caution: The senses range from "abstain" to "receive in full" to "be distant," so context determines meaning, and translators differ noticeably on the Matthew 6 "reward in full" passages.

definition: A school or lecture hall — a place where teaching and discussion happen, originally rooted in the idea of leisure away from work.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 19:9), σχολή refers to a place of teaching — a lecture hall or school — where Paul held daily discussions. The word's deeper history runs through the idea of leisure: in the Septuagint it can mean leisurely pace (Genesis 33:14, where it stands for a Hebrew word meaning slowly or gently), and everyday Koine papyri use it for free time, as in a letter telling someone to write up his books "if you have time." Over the classical period the meaning drifted from "leisure" to "how leisure is spent" (a lecture or disputation) and finally to "the place lectures are given."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a meaning that shifted over time from leisure to school, the precise nuance here rests on slim evidence.

definition: Azor, a personal name in Jesus' genealogy—son of Eliakim and father of Zadok.
article: Azor is a proper name appearing twice in the New Testament, both times in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:13, 14), where every translation renders it simply "Azor." The name is indeclinable and of Hebrew origin, identifying an ancestor of Jesus—son of Eliakim and father of Zadok. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses this Greek form to render two different Hebrew names, יְהֻד and יְהוֹיָקִים, suggesting it could stand in for more than one underlying Hebrew name.
caution: This is a rare proper name with only two New Testament occurrences, so its meaning beyond identifying this individual cannot be determined.

definition: To keep your emotions in check and deal patiently and gently with someone, rather than reacting harshly.
article: This verb describes holding your feelings in restraint so you can treat others with patience and gentleness. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 5:2, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "gently" (100%); older sources add the shade of "have compassion" or "bear gently with." The most telling outside evidence is the related adjective in the Letter of Aristeas, where "practising moderation" is named as part of true philosophy — the word literally points to moderating one's passions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: Hard labor or toil, and by extension the pain, distress, or suffering that such effort produces.
article: πόνος covers a span from physical labor and toil to the pain or distress that comes with it. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only 3 times, and the one place where it gets its own English word it means "pains" (as in Revelation 16:11). The Septuagint uses it far more (53 times), most often translating the Hebrew עָמָל, a word for toilsome, burdensome work. Everyday Koine papyri preserve both shades nicely: one describes a task as "a toilsome matter," while medical prescriptions speak of remedies "against earache" — literally against the pains.
caution: New Testament evidence is thin (only 3 Byzantine occurrences), so the full labor-to-suffering range rests mostly on the Septuagint, papyri, and classical lexicons.

definition: The shedding or pouring out of blood, especially the blood of a sacrifice.
article: This word combines "blood" (αἷμα) with "pour out" (ἐκχέω) to mean the shedding of blood, particularly in a sacrificial setting. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:22, where it speaks of how without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. The lexicons note it is otherwise rare, found in ecclesiastical writers, which fits its narrow, technical use here. Note that the measured-sense label "fact" reflects a quirk in how the rendering was tagged rather than the word's actual meaning, which is clearly "shedding of blood."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is rare elsewhere, so its range cannot be confidently established from usage.

definition: To come or go up to someone or something, approaching or drawing near; figuratively, to draw near to God in worship.
article: At its core προσέρχομαι means to approach or draw near, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 90 times, mostly of people physically coming or going to someone — rendered "came" in 66% of cases and "went" in 24%. Beyond ordinary movement, it carries a religious sense of drawing near to God, which Hebrews uses repeatedly and which the Septuagint reflects in translating the Hebrew words קָרַב ("approach," 39×) and נָגַשׁ (15×). The papyri show the same worship-related use, as in a second-century document about approaching the gods at a private shrine. Abbott-Smith also notes a sense found nowhere else — "to consent to" sound words in 1 Timothy 6:3.

definition: To use something up completely, often by destroying or consuming it; also to spend or expend resources.
article: ἀναλίσκω means to use something up entirely — to consume, destroy, or spend it. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, twice rendered "consumed" (as in Galatians 5:15 and 2 Thessalonians 2:8) and once in Luke 9:54, where it describes calling down fire to consume people. The everyday flavor of the word shows up vividly in the papyri, where it commonly means simply "to spend money" — one document scolds a man for spending so much he has not a single artaba of food left.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 NT occurrences, with the critical text recognizing just 2), so confidence in the precise range is low.

definition: Someone with rightful power or ownership over people or things—a master or owner—and, as a title, the Lord (God or Christ).
article: Κύριος describes anyone holding rightful authority: an owner of property, a master over servants, or a respectful "sir." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 746 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Lord" in 645 of those cases, while another 101 are absorbed into phrasing without a separate English word. The most striking evidence is from the Septuagint, where κύριος stands in for God's personal Hebrew name יְהֹוָה nearly 5,800 times—which is why the title carries such weight when applied to God or Christ; everyday papyri, by contrast, use it plainly for the "owner of the houses."

definition: The act of talking a lot, using many words, especially empty or repetitious speech.
article: πολυλογία literally combines "much" (πολύς) and "word" (λόγος), and means saying a great deal—wordiness or loquacity. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 6:7, where it is rendered "babble" in reference to praying with many empty words; the Septuagint uses it once at Proverbs 10:19. Everyday Koine papyri and the writer Vettius Valens also use it, sometimes in the sense of setting aside long-windedness, showing it was ordinary, non-technical vocabulary.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one occurrence, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: Dry or lacking moisture; used of withered body parts, dry land as opposed to water, and figuratively of a lifeless person.
article: This adjective describes something that is dry, parched, or shrunken from lack of moisture. In the New Testament it most often refers to a withered hand (Matthew 12:10, Luke 6:6, 8), and once to a dry, lifeless tree as a metaphor for a sinner (Luke 23:31). Its range is broad in the Septuagint, where it appears 33 times and most often renders the Hebrew word for "dry land" (יַבָּשָׁה, 12×), and everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain sense in phrases like "dry hay," "dried coriander," and "dry meal."
caution: The measured NT sense labels are garbled in the digest, but the underlying meaning—"withered" for body parts and "dry" otherwise—is well attested across the Septuagint, papyri, and lexica.

definition: The dative form of "this" — meaning to, with, by, or in this person or thing close at hand.
article: τούτῳ is simply a grammatical form of the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος ("this"), specifically the dative singular for masculine or neuter, used to point at a person or thing nearby — "to this one," "by this," "in this." In the Septuagint οὗτος most often stands in for the Hebrew words זֶה and זֹאת ("this"). The pronoun can refer back to something just mentioned or ahead to what follows, and it sometimes carries a dismissive tone, as in calling someone "this fellow."
caution: This is an inflected form rather than a separate word, and the digest records no Byzantine New Testament occurrences for this particular spelling, so usage details come from the parent pronoun οὗτος.

definition: To exchange words back and forth — that is, to talk things over with someone.
article: This verb literally combines "against" (ἀντί) and "throw" (βάλλω), so it pictures tossing something back and forth — and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 24:17) it describes two travelers exchanging words, i.e. discussing matters together. The Majority Standard Bible renders this occurrence as "intently," though the underlying idea the lexicons agree on is the trading of words, like the Latin conferre sermones. The most concrete witness comes from everyday Koine papyri: a related noun appears in a stone-cutters' contract for the small stones inserted to fill gaps between larger ones, showing the family of words at work in ordinary trades and exchange.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and just once in the Septuagint (2 Maccabees 11:13), so its sense rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: A concrete expression of what is right—either a righteous deed, a binding ordinance, or a legal verdict of acquittal or condemnation.
article: δικαίωμα names something in which righteousness takes concrete form, and its range is unusually wide: it can mean a righteous deed, a binding ordinance or regulation, or a court's sentence of acquittal or condemnation. In the Byzantine New Testament's 10 occurrences, the Majority Standard renders it "righteous acts" only 2× (with rarer renderings like "decrees," "requirements," and "righteous standard"), and 3 times the word dissolves into the surrounding phrasing without its own English equivalent. The Septuagint uses it heavily—125× across 19 books—most often for Hebrew words for statute or law (חֻקָּה, חֹק) and for judgment (מִשְׁפָּט). Strikingly, everyday Koine papyri show it meaning a legal "argument of counsel" or a documented "award" proving a claim, fitting its courtroom flavor.
caution: The renderings vary widely and three of ten occurrences carry no distinct English word, so context, not a single fixed meaning, must guide each case.

definition: To communicate with someone by nodding or making a gesture instead of speaking.
article: ἐννεύω means to make a sign to someone by nodding or gesturing—communicating without words. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 1:62, where people use gestures to ask Zechariah what he wants to name his son. In the Septuagint it shows up twice in Proverbs, where it translates the Hebrew קָרַץ, a word for winking or signaling with the eyes, often with a sneaky or mischievous edge.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range of meaning cannot be confirmed from the biblical evidence alone.

definition: To call down a curse on someone, swearing emphatically that what you say is true.
article: This word means to curse vehemently or call down destruction, an intensified form built from κατά plus ἀναθεματίζω (to put under a curse). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 26:74, where Peter begins to curse and swear that he does not know Jesus. Interestingly, the related word ἀναθεματίζω is far more common, showing up in Mark and three times in Acts and frequently in the Septuagint, while this intensive form is essentially a one-off in Biblical Greek.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, so the evidence for its range is very thin.

definition: To openly acknowledge or confess something, especially one's sins, or to give praise and thanks to someone.
article: This word covers two related ideas: openly admitting something (especially confessing sins, as in Matthew 3:6 and James 5:16) and offering praise or thanks to someone, as in Jesus' words in Matthew 11:25. In the Septuagint it appears 95 times and most often translates the Hebrew יָדָה (25×), a word for giving thanks and praise, which explains why the same Greek verb can mean both "confess" and "praise." Everyday Koine papyri use it in a strikingly down-to-earth way: acknowledging a debt to a tax collector, or formally acknowledging a child in a divorce deed.
caution: The "confess" and "praise" senses overlap and depend on context, so the boundary between them is not always sharp.

definition: To bring or bear something down, including being overcome by deep sleep or casting a vote against someone.
article: καταφέρω literally means to bring or carry something down, and the New Testament stretches that base meaning into a few directions. In Acts it describes a young man being "borne down" by sleep (the source of the "sound" and "asleep" renderings in the same verse, Acts 20:9) and, in a courtroom setting, casting a vote or bringing charges against someone (Acts 26:10). The everyday papyri show the same range vividly: one second-century B.C. document uses it for a man who "brought down" three blows on a victim's head and neck during an assault, while another uses it plainly for carrying down reeds.
caution: Confidence is low: only 3 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, with two of the three measured senses coming from a single verse describing the same event.

definition: To make something take the same form as another, or in the passive, to be brought into the same shape or condition.
article: This verb means to be shaped into the same form as something else, often carrying the idea of sharing an experience along with the shared form. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament and is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word. Moulton-Milligan notes that the related form συμμορφίζω, meaning to share someone's form and so share their experience, shows up only in Philippians 3:10 and later church writers, while this verb itself turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is very thin: the word occurs only once, drops out of the critical text entirely, and is never rendered by a distinct English word, so its precise force is hard to pin down.

definition: To make someone lie down or recline, especially to take a place at a table for a meal.
article: In the New Testament this verb means to have people settle into their places to eat, which in that culture meant reclining rather than sitting in chairs. It appears only in Luke's writings (3 times in the Byzantine text, 5 in the critical text), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "sit" in two of three places and "while reclining at" in one. Interestingly, the papyri show it as a medical term: a first-century medical receipt uses it to mean laying a patient on his back, and a related form describes someone being "laid up in bed."
caution: Evidence is thin and confidence is low, since the word occurs only a handful of times and the everyday papyri lean toward a medical "lay down" sense rather than the table-reclining one.

definition: Free of dirt, contamination, or moral stain — clean or pure, whether physically, ceremonially, or in heart and conscience.
article: καθαρός covers the whole range from physical cleanness to ceremonial purity to moral and spiritual integrity. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "pure" 15 times (60%) and "clean" 9 times (36%), often shading into the heart, conscience, or character of a person. The everyday breadth shows up vividly in the papyri, where the same word describes a clean animal passed for inspection, freshly cleared farmland, new unadulterated wheat, children's bread, and pure milk. In the Septuagint it appears 145 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew טָהוֹר (66×), the standard term for ritual cleanness.

definition: Spit or saliva, the liquid produced in the mouth.
article: πτύσμα means spittle or saliva, derived from the verb πτύω, "to spit." It appears only once in the New Testament, in John 9:6, where Jesus mixes it with dirt to make mud for healing a blind man; the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the verb "applied" in that scene, and the BSB agrees. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and in writers like Hippocrates and Polybius, showing it was ordinary, non-technical vocabulary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: The release or pardon of sins, freeing a person from the penalty they owe.
article: In the New Testament ἄφεσις almost always means forgiveness, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "forgiveness" in 12 of 17 occurrences (80%) and "forgiven" in 2 more — nearly always tied to sins. Its root sense is broader, however: it comes from ἀφίημι ("to send away, let go"), and in the Septuagint it never refers to pardon but translates Hebrew terms like the Jubilee year (יוֹבֵל, 21×) and the sabbatical release of debts. The everyday Egyptian papyri preserve an even more literal, physical use: ἄφεσις τοῦ ὕδατος was the technical phrase for releasing water from canal sluices for irrigation.
caution: The dominant New Testament meaning (pardon of sins) is absent from the Septuagint, so the literal "release" sense and the figurative "forgiveness" sense come from different bodies of evidence.

definition: A particle expressing a strong, often hopeless, wish — "I wish that" or "if only."
article: ὄφελον is an exclamation meaning "I wish" or "if only," used to introduce a heartfelt desire, sometimes one the speaker knows cannot or will not happen. It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "wish" twice, "how I wish" once, and within an "already"-phrase once (2 Corinthians 11:1). The word turns up in everyday Koine too: a papyrus letter from a slave to her ailing master reads "would that I could fly and come and greet you." Grammatically it is a frozen verb form (an unaugmented aorist of ὀφείλω, "to owe") that came to function purely as a wish-word.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 4 New Testament occurrences — and Abbott-Smith notes the wish ranges from fruitless to practicable depending on the verb tense that follows.

definition: Roused or startled out of sleep, suddenly wide awake.
article: ἔξυπνος describes someone who has been jolted out of sleep into wakefulness, built from the words for "out of" and "sleep." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:27, where the Philippian jailer wakes to find the prison doors open. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; interestingly, in Modern Greek ἔξυπνος shifted to mean "wide-awake" in the sense of sharp or clever, though that meaning is not present in the biblical evidence.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: To nod or motion to someone as a silent signal, often to get their attention or prompt them to speak.
article: νεύω means to nod or gesture as a signal to another person, typically with a dative of the person and an instruction to act. It appears only twice in the New Testament—Peter motioning to the disciple at the Last Supper (John 13:24) and Paul being motioned to speak (Acts 24:10)—and the renderings differ only by context. An interesting detail from the papyri: a brother's letter (BGU IV.1078, A.D. 39) shows the word slipping into the sense of communicating words by signaling, and a related extended use describes buildings 'looking toward' a direction.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin and confidence is low.

definition: To openly mock or sneer at someone with scornful contempt.
article: This verb means to ridicule someone openly, with the image of literally turning up the nose in derision. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Luke 16:14 and 23:35), where the Majority Standard Bible renders one instance as "sneered at" and absorbs the other into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it shows up three times, translating Hebrew words including לָעַג, "to mock" (as in Psalm 2:4), which fits its scornful, mocking sense well.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, though the lexicons agree on the basic sense of derisive mockery.

definition: Describing something admirable and well spoken of, fit to be praised and pleasant to hear.
article: εὔφημος appears just once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:8, where it describes the kind of things believers should dwell on — things that are commendable and worth speaking well of. The word literally combines "good" (εὖ) with "speech" or "report" (φήμη), so its core idea is being well spoken of or fair-sounding. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes its older religious associations: guarding one's lips so that nothing in public worship causes scandal — a "delicacy" reflected in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on very thin direct evidence.

definition: To separate oneself entirely from someone, parting company and going away.
article: This verb in its middle voice means to separate oneself completely from another person and move away. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 9:33, where it describes parting from someone, and there it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than carried by a single English word. It is far more common in the Septuagint (17 times), where it usually renders the Hebrew verbs פָּרַד (to separate, 7×) and בָּדַל (to divide, 6×) — notably the language of God separating light from darkness in Genesis 1:4. A magic papyrus from fourth-century Egypt uses it the same way, in a charm asking that one person be parted from another.
caution: Confidence is low: the word appears only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests largely on Septuagint and papyri parallels.

definition: To shape or mould something into form, the way a potter works clay into a vessel.
article: πλάσσω means to form or mould, like a potter shaping clay. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 9:20 and 1 Timothy 2:13), both rendered "formed," and turns up 44 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew יָצַר ("to form"). Everyday papyri show the same hands-on sense: one second-century document uses it of pots "of winter manufacture," and another of bricks being moulded.
caution: Only two New Testament occurrences make the measured range thin, though the Septuagint and papyri evidence point consistently to the same shaping sense.

definition: An interrogative adverb asking from what place, source, origin, or cause something comes — "where from?" or "how?"
article: πόθεν is a question word meaning "from where?" — asking about the place, origin, source, or cause of something. About two-thirds of its 28 New Testament uses (16×) are rendered "where," but it also stretches to mean "how" (3×), as when Jesus asks how David could call the Messiah "Lord" (Mark 12:37). In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew phrase meaning "from where" (17×), and everyday papyri use it the same way — one document has people "declaring the sources from which" they acquired property.

definition: A kind, generous, and caring attitude toward people; warm goodwill expressed in helpful action.
article: φιλανθρωπία describes humane kindness and benevolence toward people — literally a friendliness toward humanity. It appears just twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible splits the renderings evenly: "kindness" for the islanders' welcome in Acts 28:2 and "love mankind" for God's character in Titus 3:4. Notably, our English word "philanthropy" comes straight from this term, and the Septuagint uses it once, where it renders the Hebrew word אֲדָר.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin Septuagint evidence, the precise range of this word rests on very limited data.

definition: To prop, fix, or jam something firmly in place; in its one New Testament use, of a ship's bow running aground and sticking fast.
article: ἐρείδω basically means to prop or fix something firmly, and in everyday Koine it could even describe burdens "imposed" on a village. The New Testament uses it just once, in Acts 27:41, where Paul's ship drives onto a sandbar and its bow sticks fast and stays immovable. In the Septuagint it appears 10 times, often rendering the Hebrew תָּמַך ("to support, hold up") three times, which fits its core idea of bracing or holding firm.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and overall thin evidence, the precise nuance here is uncertain.

definition: Obedience — the attentive listening that leads to compliance with and submission to someone's authority or commands.
article: ὑπακοή means obedience, the kind that comes from genuinely listening and then complying. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "obedience" 9 times (60%) and adjectivally as "obedient" 4 times (27%), and the term covers obedience in general as well as obedience specifically toward God or Christ. It's a notably Christian word: Abbott-Smith notes it appears only in the Septuagint, New Testament, and church writings, never in ordinary classical Greek. Moulton-Milligan adds a striking detail — in the apocryphal Gospel of Peter the same word seems to mean "response" or "refrain," echoing the underlying verb's sense of answering when called.
caution: Septuagint evidence is thin (just one occurrence), and the sources note a rare secondary sense of "response/refrain" outside the New Testament.

definition: A heavy cloak or outer mantle worn over other clothing, mentioned once when Paul asks for one he left behind.
article: φελόνης refers to a cloak or outer mantle, the same garment the Romans called a paenula, and the word is a transposed form of an earlier term (παινόλης). It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:13, where Paul asks Timothy to bring it. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the ordinary meaning: a payment record from the second century lists φελονῶν among purchased articles, and the diminutive form turns up in later documents. Interestingly, while the lexicons agree the word means 'cloak,' the measured rendering in this digest is 'parchments' — almost certainly because the verse mentions the cloak alongside the books and parchments Paul also wanted.

definition: An attention-grabbing word meaning "look!" or "behold!" used to point at something striking or to introduce a surprising new development.
article: ἰδού is an interjection meaning "look!" or "behold!" — a word that grabs the reader's attention and points to whatever comes next, often something surprising or important. It started as an imperative form of the verb "to see" but became a fixed exclamation, often appearing as "and behold" to introduce a new scene. It shows up over 1,000 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always renders the Hebrew attention-words הִנֵּה and הֵן, and it can stand in place of a verb like the Hebrew does, as in "behold, a leper." Interestingly, while it appears so often in the Greek Bible partly because of Hebrew influence, a third-century papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses it in ordinary correspondence, showing it was genuine everyday Koine and not purely a translation habit.
caution: The count of 0 in the Byzantine NT here reflects a quirk of the source data; the critical text records about 200 occurrences, so this word is in fact common in the New Testament.

definition: A woman who speaks God's messages or foretells the future.
article: προφῆτις is simply the feminine form of προφήτης (prophet), describing a woman who delivers divine messages. The Byzantine New Testament uses it twice, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prophetess" both times (Luke 2:36, where it describes Anna, and Revelation 2:20). In the Septuagint it appears 6 times and consistently translates the Hebrew word נְבִיאָה (nevi'ah), the female counterpart to "prophet," used of figures like Miriam and Deborah.
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its full range rests largely on Septuagint and everyday Koine evidence.

definition: To speak God's message under divine inspiration—declaring his will, and sometimes foretelling what is to come.
article: προφητεύω means to act as a prophet—to speak forth God's counsel under inspiration. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "prophesy" or "prophesying" in nearly all of its 28 New Testament occurrences, and the core idea is telling forth the divine message, with predicting future events being only an occasional, not essential, part of the range. In the Septuagint it appears 110 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew נָבָא (84×), the standard verb for prophesying; interestingly, the everyday papyri also use it in pagan religious settings, such as a regulation forbidding certain temple servants "to prophesy."

definition: The state of being naked or inadequately clothed, often pointing to extreme poverty or lack of proper covering.
article: γυμνότης describes literal nakedness or, by extension, the destitution of lacking adequate clothing. The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "nakedness" twice (67%, as in Romans 8:35 and Revelation 3:18) and "without" once (33%, in 2 Corinthians 11:27, where Paul describes his hardships). It built from the adjective γυμνός ("naked"), and in its single Septuagint occurrence it translates a Hebrew word for lack or want, fitting its sense of being stripped of necessities.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use — so the boundary between literal nakedness and figurative destitution rests on very few examples.

definition: Describing something wonderful or marvelous; used as a noun for the amazing things someone does.
article: This adjective means "wonderful" or "marvelous," and in its single New Testament appearance (Matthew 21:15) the neuter plural works as a noun for the amazing things Jesus did. It shows up far more in the Septuagint—46 times across 11 books—where it mostly translates the Hebrew root פָּלָא, the standard word for God's wondrous deeds. The everyday Koine papyri reveal a softer social use: the superlative form became a polite honorific, addressing officials as "our most admirable" leader.
caution: This appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there rests on a single verse.

definition: Cold to the touch, like cool water; also used figuratively of a person who is spiritually indifferent.
article: ψυχρός means "cold," most often describing cold water (as in Matthew 10:42, where a cup of cold water is offered). In Revelation 3:15-16 it shifts to a figurative sense, describing people who are spiritually indifferent rather than fervent. A nice everyday parallel comes from the papyri and inscriptions: a burial-chamber inscription prays that Osiris give the deceased "cold water," and a medical text prescribes gargling with cold water for the uvula.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and 1 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, and the "one" label in sense 2 simply reflects the phrase "one or the other" in Revelation 3:15 rather than a distinct meaning.

definition: A place where someone lives or settles—a dwelling, home, or area of habitation.
senseLabels: a dwelling or place of habitation
article: κατοικία refers to where people live—a residence, dwelling, or settlement. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 17:26), where it describes the boundaries of where humanity dwells, but it shows up 26 times in the Septuagint, most often translating the Hebrew מוֹשָׁב ("dwelling place," 17×). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the practical sense: legal documents use it for a person's official place of residence and even for plots of "catoecic land," land tied to a settlement.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, though the Septuagint and papyri broadly support the "dwelling" meaning.

definition: The weapons and goods stripped from a defeated enemy; war spoils or plunder.
article: σκῦλον means the booty taken from a beaten foe — originally the arms and gear stripped off after victory — and it usually appears in the plural. It shows up only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 11:22, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding idea as "attacks"; the standard lexicons (Abbott-Smith, KJV, Dodson) all gloss the word itself as "spoils." The Septuagint uses it 78 times, mostly translating the Hebrew shalal ("plunder"), and the papyri confirm its everyday military sense — one second-century-BC document even speaks of captives handed over "from the spoils."
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament, and the corpus-measured rendering ("attacks") reflects the verse's broader phrasing rather than the word's own meaning, which the lexicons consistently give as "spoils."

definition: To rub something between the hands or fingers, as when separating grain kernels from their husks.
senseLabels: to rub grain in the hands
article: ψώχω describes the action of rubbing or crushing something with the hands, specifically rubbing kernels of grain out of their husks. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:1, where Jesus' disciples pluck heads of grain and rub them in their hands to eat. Outside the Bible the word is genuinely rare — Moulton-Milligan note it is otherwise attested only in Nicander's Theriaca (line 619), and they caution against reading any special medical knowledge into Luke's use of it.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is very rare elsewhere, so its precise range cannot be confidently mapped; note also the measured sense label "second" reflects a translation-alignment artifact rather than the word's actual meaning.

definition: Describing something see-through, allowing light to pass through it; transparent or clear.
article: Διαφανής means "transparent" or "see-through" — built from διά (through) and φαίνω (to show or shine), so literally "shining through." It appears 3 times in the Septuagint but not in the Byzantine New Testament, where it shows up only in the Received Text at Revelation 21:21 (describing transparent gold) as a substitute for διαυγής, on no known manuscript authority. The word lived on in everyday Koine papyri and survives in Modern Greek as διάφανος.
caution: The word does not appear in the Byzantine NT at all, and its famous Revelation 21:21 usage rests on the Received Text rather than recognized manuscripts.

definition: To weigh down or burden someone, used of physical heaviness, exhaustion, or emotional and circumstantial pressure.
article: βαρέω means to weigh down or press hard on someone, appearing 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament. It always shows up in the passive: eyes heavy with sleep (Matthew 26:43, Mark 14:40, Luke 9:32), hearts weighed down by the cares of life (Luke 21:34), or being crushed beyond strength by hardship (2 Corinthians 1:8). In its lone Septuagint appearance it renders the Hebrew kabed, the same root behind a 'heavy' or hardened heart, and Moulton-Milligan note its long history stretching back to Homeric Greek.
caution: The measured senses are split thin across single occurrences, and the Majority Standard Bible's reading of 1 Timothy 5:16 differs from the BSB, so some renderings reflect translator choice more than fixed meaning.

definition: God's or a person's gracious good pleasure, kind intention, or heartfelt desire that something happen.
article: εὐδοκία points to favorable good pleasure—the kindly approval or settled wish that something be so, whether God's gracious intention or a person's heartfelt desire. The Majority Standard Bible most often renders it as a "well pleasing sight" (2 of 9), but the spread of rare renderings ("good pleasure," "heart's desire," "good desire," "good pleasure purposed") shows the word stretches across both God's purpose and human longing. A striking detail from Moulton-Milligan: the noun εὐδοκία itself seems confined to Jewish and Christian writings, though its cognate εὐδόκησις turns up in everyday papyri meaning "consent" or "concurrence," as in a document requiring "no further consent from me."
caution: With only one clearly measured sense from 9 occurrences and many scattered rare renderings, the word's exact range between God's purpose and human desire is somewhat fluid in context.

definition: Apollonia, a city in Macedonia through which Paul traveled on his journey.
article: Apollonia is a proper name for a Macedonian city, appearing just once in the New Testament (Acts 17:1), where Paul and his companions passed through it on the way from Amphipolis to Thessalonica. Because it is a place name, it isn't really "translated" — the single rendering counted as "passed" simply reflects the verb describing Paul's journey through the town. The lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree it is a city of Macedonia, and the name is traditionally linked to the pagan deity Apollo.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests entirely on a single passage.

definition: To set yourself against someone or something, taking up a position of opposition or resistance.
article: This middle-voice verb pictures someone lining up against an opponent, originally in a military sense of forming a battle line. In the New Testament's 5 occurrences it usually means "opposes" (3 times, 75%), with one instance rendered "resist" (in James 5:6). The military root shows up vividly in everyday Koine: legal papyri from around A.D. 136 use it for the "opposing party" in a lawsuit, and Moulton-Milligan notes the earliest documented sense was strictly military.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the measured sense data is thin, though the standard sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: A wanderer; describing stars that have strayed from their fixed paths.
article: πλανήτης means "wanderer," built from the verb meaning to wander or go astray. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jude 13, where false teachers are compared to "wandering stars" that have left their appointed courses. The same word is the ordinary Greek term for a planet, and a third-century magical papyrus uses it exactly that way ("the five wandering stars"); in Jude, though, the imagery comes from the book of Enoch, picturing stars that have strayed from their orbits.
