Its only Septuagint appearance, in Hosea 9:17, renders a Hebrew word meaning "to wander."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: An adverb meaning "not yet," indicating that something has not happened up to a given point in time.
article: μήπω is a negative adverb meaning "not yet," formed from μή ("not") and the particle -πω ("yet"). It appears only twice in the New Testament — in Romans 9:11 (with a participle) and Hebrews 9:8 (with an accusative and infinitive) — describing something that had not happened at a particular moment. The same word turns up in everyday Koine papyri: one second-century letter uses it for goods someone "has not yet bought," showing it was ordinary, practical language for things still pending.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the measured sense data is thin, though the meaning "not yet" is well supported by papyri and lexicons.

definition: To rob a temple or steal sacred things, an act treated as serious sacrilege.
article: This verb means to plunder a temple or steal what has been dedicated to a god — temple-robbery as a specific crime. It appears only once in the New Testament (Romans 2:22) and once in the Septuagint (2 Maccabees 9:2), so its biblical footprint is tiny. Everyday Koine inscriptions confirm the literal meaning: a third-century-BC inscription from Delphi uses it of people who stole part of a sacred offering and were prosecuted for it.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall attestation, this entry rests on limited evidence.

definition: To increase or multiply something in number, or to grow more numerous.
article: πληθύνω means to increase or multiply, used both for actively making something grow in number and for something growing more numerous on its own. In the New Testament the Byzantine text has it 12 times across 7 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "multiply" in 40% of cases (4×), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing or handled with words like "grow." It shows up massively in the Septuagint—163 times—where it most often translates the Hebrew רָבָה (114×), the same root behind God's command to "be fruitful and multiply."

definition: To hear something beforehand or in advance, having learned of it earlier.
article: This compound joins the prefix πρό ('before') with ἀκούω ('to hear'), so it literally means 'to hear in advance.' It appears only once in the New Testament, at Colossians 1:5, where it describes the hope the readers had already heard about earlier through the gospel. Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence as 'proceeding,' which reflects how translators handle the sentence rather than the word's basic 'hear beforehand' meaning given by the lexicons.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured, and the rendering 'proceeding' reflects sentence structure rather than the lexical sense 'hear beforehand.'

definition: To be away from a place or person; to be absent rather than physically present.
article: ἄπειμι simply means "to be away" or "absent," formed from ἀπό ("away") plus the verb "to be." In all 7 Byzantine uses it carries this single idea, almost always paired with its opposite, being present — Paul repeatedly contrasts being absent in body with how he acts when present (e.g. 2 Corinthians 10:11; Colossians 2:5). The everyday Koine papyri show the very same usage: one letter from 153 B.C. has a man writing "though I was absent, I took thought for you," and another speaks of acting in someone's name "during my absence" exactly as if present.
caution: Evidence is fairly thin (only 7 NT occurrences, 4 of which are absorbed into phrasing with no distinct English word), so the measured senses rest on just 3 clearly rendered cases.

definition: A connecting word meaning "according to what," "to the extent that," or "in proportion as."
article: καθό is a compound adverb (from κατά plus the relative ὅς) that links one thing to another by measure or proportion — "according to what," "to the extent that." The Byzantine New Testament uses it 4 times across 3 books, and in 2 Corinthians 8:12 it appears twice in a single verse, governing a gift "according to what a person has." Everyday Koine papyri show the same proportional sense: one document speaks of acting "according to traditional custom," confirming this was ordinary, practical language rather than a specialized term.
caution: The label "overjoyed" reflects how a translation smooths the phrase in 1 Peter 4:13, not a separate meaning of the word itself, which consistently signals proportion or correspondence.

definition: To raise or lift something up—such as the eyes, hands, or voice—whether physically or, figuratively, in pride.
article: ἐπαίρω means to lift or raise something up, and in the New Testament it almost always pairs with a specific body part or object: lifting the eyes (to look up), raising the hands in prayer, raising the voice to speak, or even a ship's sail being hoisted. Used 19 times in the Byzantine NT, its renderings cluster tightly around this physical act of raising—the four most common translations all express "up" or "lifted up." It also carries a figurative sense of being "lifted up" with pride (as in 2 Corinthians 10:5), and the everyday Koine papyri show the same range, including walls "built to a greater height" and a door "lifted."

definition: An adverb meaning surely or by all means, used to strengthen a statement, and in negatives to make the denial complete.
article: πάντως is an adverb built from πᾶς ("all"), and it works to intensify whatever it modifies — "surely," "certainly," or "by all means." It appears 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament, but in 3 of those cases it dissolves into the phrasing without its own English word, which is why translators render it so flexibly. With a negative it sharpens the denial into a complete one (Romans 3:9). The everyday flavor shows up nicely in the papyri, where one writer urges, "Be sure, Aphrodisius, to send me the loaves and the relish."
caution: The measured renderings split evenly between "surely" and "all," and a third of occurrences carry no English word of their own, so the exact force depends heavily on context.

definition: An official verdict or sentence handed down by an authority, used figuratively for a final judgment one feels has been passed.
article: This noun comes from the verb ἀποκρίνομαι in its older sense of judging, and it points to an official decision or sentence. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 1:9, where Paul speaks of having within himself the "sentence" of death — the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase with "felt" in all of its single occurrence. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: papyri and inscriptions use ἀπόκριμα for official rulings, including, in an inscription from Rhodes dated A.D. 51, the favorable "decisions" of the Emperor Claudius, very close in time to Paul's letter. Note that scholars are split — Abbott-Smith lists both a judicial sentence and a simple "answer" as possible meanings here.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the lexica disagree on whether it means a judicial sentence or merely an answer, so its precise force is uncertain.

definition: To go or come out from somewhere, or to proceed forth from a source.
article: ἐκπορεύομαι is a movement word built from ἐκ ("out of") and πορεύομαι ("to go"), and it consistently means to come or go out from a place or source. Across its 32 Byzantine occurrences the renderings cluster tightly around "come," "come out," and "proceed," with no surprising shifts in meaning. In the Septuagint it appears 153 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew יָצָא ("to go out") 113 times, confirming this core sense. The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: one letter even uses it of messengers "going out" to carry correspondence, and another of leaving the city while "many friends were departing."

definition: The bringing in of something additional or in place of what came before.
article: ἐπεισαγωγή describes the act of introducing something extra or in addition to what already exists. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 7:19, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "introduced" (its sole measured sense). The most interesting evidence comes from the papyri: while the noun itself was hard to find, Moulton-Milligan note that the related verb appears in marriage contracts as a technical term forbidding a man to bring another woman into his house alongside his wife.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage and rests largely on outside evidence.

definition: To act in an ungodly way — to live wickedly or behave with contempt toward what is sacred.
article: This verb describes living or acting in an ungodly, impious way. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as "ungodly" (2 Peter 2:6) and once in the phrase about the harsh deeds the ungodly have committed (Jude 1:15). The Septuagint uses it 28 times, most often translating the Hebrew פָּשַׁע (to rebel or transgress, 10×) and רָשַׁע (to be wicked, 6×), and Greek inscriptions repeatedly pair it with acting impiously toward a temple or the divine.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise range here rests mostly on Septuagint and inscriptional evidence.

definition: A state of madness or frenzy, when someone seems out of their mind or irrational.
article: μανία means madness or frenzy — being out of one's right mind. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:24, where Festus tells Paul his great learning has driven him to "madness," contrasted with the "words of truth and reason" Paul claims in the next verse. An everyday papyrus from the second century BC uses it the same weakened way: "you seem to have gone mad, for you pay no regard to yourself." In the Septuagint it shows up three times, twice rendering the Hebrew word for hostility or enmity.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests on a single passage.

definition: The Aramaic name of a Christian woman in Joppa, also known by the Greek name Dorcas, meaning "gazelle."
article: Tabitha is a personal name, the Aramaic equivalent of the Greek name Dorcas, both of which mean something like "gazelle" or "antelope." It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 9:36 and 9:40, referring to a Christian woman at Joppa. Interestingly, the name shows up in everyday Koine documents too — Moulton-Milligan cite a papyrus from around A.D. 706–7 mentioning a "Tabitha daughter of David."
caution: This is a proper name occurring only twice, so its meaning rests on the name's Aramaic root rather than measured usage.

definition: To have the means or resources to do something, especially to be financially able.
article: εὐπορέω describes having the resources or means to act, often in the sense of being financially well off. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 11:29, where it refers to each disciple giving "according to his ability" — and notably it does not appear at all in the critical SBLGNT text. The papyri show the word in vivid everyday use beyond money: one third-century letter from Oxyrhynchus uses it to mean "finding no boat available," so the core idea is simply being well-supplied with whatever is needed.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text and is absent from the critical text, so the New Testament evidence is very thin.

definition: Describing something morally evil, wrong, or simply bad and harmful, as opposed to what is good.
article: κακός is a broad word for what is bad—covering moral evil (rendered "evil" 70% of the time), things that are wrong or unjust ("wrong," 16%), and what is simply bad or harmful ("bad," 9%). In the Septuagint it appears 295 times, most often translating the Hebrew רָע ("bad, evil," 145×), confirming this wide range. Everyday Koine papyri show the same flexibility: one document calls Metrodoros "the cause of all the troubles," and another refers to a "false entry" (κακῆς παραγραφῆς) in records. Strong's notes a distinction from πονηρός—κακός points to something inherently worthless or injurious rather than to its harmful effects.

definition: An Aramaic-Hebrew word meaning "why," spoken by Jesus on the cross in the cry "why have you forsaken me?"
article: λαμά is a transliterated Hebrew/Aramaic word meaning "why," appearing only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in Jesus' cry from the cross (Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34). It comes from the Hebrew מָה with a prepositional prefix, and it is not really a Greek word at all but a preserved fragment of Jesus' actual spoken language. Interestingly, the manuscripts vary in spelling: Mark tends toward the Hebrew form λαμά while Matthew shifts toward the Aramaic λεμά, and the critical (SBLGNT) text reads it zero times, preferring the alternate spelling.
caution: Evidence is thin and the spelling is genuinely disputed across manuscripts (λαμά vs. λεμά), with the critical text not using this form at all.

definition: To go without food for a period of time as a religious or spiritual practice.
article: νηστεύω means to abstain from food for religious reasons, and the meaning is remarkably stable: 16 of 21 New Testament occurrences (76%) are simply rendered "fast," with the BSB independently agreeing 94% of the time. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew צוּם ("to fast") 19 of 23 times, reinforcing the same sense. One striking find comes from the papyri: an early saying attributed to Jesus (P. Oxy. I.1) reads "unless you fast the world, you will not find the kingdom of God" — using the verb with an unusual object.

definition: To wash or rinse something off, especially fishing nets after use.
article: ἀποπλύνω means to wash or rinse something off, built from ἀπό (off) plus πλύνω (to wash). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament—at Luke 5:2, describing fishermen washing their nets—and notably it drops out of the critical text entirely. In the Septuagint it shows up 3 times and renders different Hebrew words, with Abbott-Smith noting it most often stands in for the Hebrew verb for washing clothes (כָּבַס).
caution: Evidence is thin: only one Byzantine occurrence, none in the critical text, and Abbott-Smith treats the reading as a textual variant for plain πλύνω.

definition: Melea, a man listed as one of the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.
article: Melea is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Jesus at Luke 3:31. It is not really a word with a meaning but a proper name, which is why translations render it consistently as part of the family line (the Berean translations connect it with "son" 100% of the time as the genealogy lists who descended from whom). Abbott-Smith links it to a Hebrew form (מְלֵאָה) and treats it as indeclinable, while Strong's notes its origin is uncertain.
caution: This name occurs only once in the Byzantine NT (and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text), and sources call its origin uncertain, so little can be said with confidence.

definition: To make something different, transform it, or exchange one thing for another.
article: ἀλλάσσω means to make something different — to change, transform, or swap one thing for another. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 6 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "changed" in all 5 cases that get their own English word, though the lexicons spread the range wider into "transform" (as in 1 Corinthians 15:51-52, the changing of believers) and "exchange." In the Septuagint it appears 32 times, most often for the Hebrew חָלַף, and the everyday papyri show it as a plain commercial term — one document from AD 137 uses it for swapping or selling livestock.
caution: The single measured sense "change" understates the lexicons' broader range of "transform" and "exchange," which the NT also attests.

definition: Military service or warfare, used in the New Testament figuratively for the spiritual struggle of Christian living.
article: στρατεία means military service or a campaign, and the New Testament uses it just twice—both times figuratively, for the believer's spiritual battle (2 Corinthians 10:4 and 1 Timothy 1:18). The two translation choices, "warfare" and "fight," really reflect the same underlying idea of an ongoing military effort. Everyday papyri confirm the down-to-earth, literal sense: one document records a man "discharged from military service" (P Fay 91, A.D. 99), showing this was the ordinary word for soldiering before the New Testament applied it to spiritual struggle.
caution: With only two occurrences, both metaphorical, the evidence base is thin, and the word is easily confused with the near-identical στρατιά (army).

definition: Describing someone who does not love money or crave wealth, free from greed.
article: This adjective describes a person who is free from the love of money — not greedy or avaricious. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Timothy 3:3 and Hebrews 13:5), in both cases as a quality expected of believers or leaders. Though Grimm-Thayer once suggested the word was unique to the New Testament, Moulton-Milligan shows it (and its adverb form) turning up in everyday Koine inscriptions and papyri, some dating to the second century B.C.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured sense rests on thin evidence, though the lexicons agree closely on its meaning.

definition: Patiently putting up with mistreatment or evil without retaliating; bearing wrongs with calm endurance.
article: ἀνεξίκακος describes someone who endures ill-treatment patiently instead of striking back—built from the verb "to bear with" (G430) and the word for "evil" (G2556). It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:24, where the Lord's servant is told to be forbearing rather than quarrelsome. The word also turns up in everyday Koine: a medical papyrus fragment from the late second century A.D. uses it of a person who has "general endurance" but cannot bear thirst, showing it described practical staying-power, not only moral patience.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical use alone.

definition: The right or power to act, decide, or rule—whether granted, possessed, or exercised over others.
article: ἐξουσία is one of the New Testament's key words for legitimate power, appearing 103 times. Most often (70%) it means "authority," but it also shades into raw "power" (10%) and the personal "right" or freedom to do something (10%), as when John 1:12 speaks of the right to become children of God. Its everyday roots show clearly in the papyri: legal documents like wills and contracts use it for the claim, right, or control one holds over property, which fits its derivation from a word meaning "it is permitted."

definition: To translate a word or name from one language into another, giving its meaning.
article: This verb means to translate something from one language into another and explain what it means; in the New Testament it almost always introduces the meaning of a Hebrew or Aramaic word, as in 'Immanuel, which means God with us.' Its measured uses are essentially one idea — the two labels both reduce to 'means,' with the second simply attached to the name Jesus. Strikingly, the papyri show the same word at work in ordinary life: documents from as early as the late second century B.C. use it for the official translation of Egyptian (demotic) legal contracts into Greek.
caution: The two measured senses really reflect a single meaning ('means'), so the split is about surrounding phrasing rather than a genuine difference in sense.

definition: A person who guides someone helpless, especially a blind person, by leading them with the hand.
senseLabels: one who leads by the hand
article: χειραγωγός literally combines "hand" and "lead," meaning a guide who takes a helpless or blind person by the hand. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:11, where the blinded sorcerer Elymas seeks people to lead him around. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) agree closely on this sense, and Moulton-Milligan confirm the word and its relatives turn up in everyday Koine papyri, including a London papyrus pairing it with words for gentleness.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "mist" appears to be a tagging error rather than the word's actual meaning of "hand-guide."

definition: A military camp, an army drawn up for battle, or the fortified barracks where soldiers were quartered.
article: παρεμβολή is a military term that covers a camp, an army arrayed for battle, and the barracks where troops were stationed. In the Byzantine New Testament's 10 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "barracks" 5 times (often the fortress at Jerusalem where Paul was held) and "camp" 3 times, the meanings used in Hebrews and Revelation. The word's reach is wide because it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew מַחֲנֶה ("camp") in the Septuagint, appearing there 218 of 243 times, and Moulton-Milligan finds the same camp sense in everyday papyri describing soldiers going off to enlist.
caution: The lexica note the word originally meant "insertion" before becoming a military term, and some classify it as a regional Macedonian usage, so its earlier non-military sense does not appear in the New Testament data.

definition: Strength or might, especially the power to rule or act decisively; often used in worship to ascribe dominion to God.
article: κράτος means strength or might, and in the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "power" in 6 of its 12 occurrences, with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. The word stretches from physical strength to dominion and even "a mighty deed," and it shows up especially in doxologies that ascribe power to God. The everyday Koine flavor is clear in the papyri: a petition to Ptolemy (181–145 B.C.) prays the gods would grant the rulers "health, victory, power (κράτος), strength, and lordship," pairing it with related words for might and rule.

definition: To speak against something or someone—to contradict, oppose, or argue back.
article: Built from ἀντί ("against") plus λέγω ("say"), ἀντιλέγω means to speak in opposition—to contradict, dispute, or push back against a claim. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as plain "say" twice and as "contradict" twice across its 12 New Testament uses, with the rest absorbed into varied phrasing; the underlying force is consistently one of verbal resistance rather than mere speech. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this opposing sense vividly: one document advises a man "not to agree now with his father, but to oppose him (ἀντιλέγειν) and make no contract."
caution: With only 12 occurrences and English renderings split between neutral "say" and stronger "contradict," the intended force can depend on context.

definition: An army or organized host; in the New Testament, the heavenly host of angels or the stars of the sky.
article: στρατιά basically means an army or organized host, and in everyday Koine it shows up in papyri referring to actual military forces. In the New Testament's two occurrences it carries this military image into the heavens: the multitude of angels praising God at Jesus' birth (Luke 2:13) and the "host of heaven"—the stars—that Israel wrongly worshiped (Acts 7:42). The Septuagint uses it 29 times, most often translating the Hebrew צָבָא ("army, host"), which underlies the familiar phrase "the LORD of hosts."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, note also that Abbott-Smith flags 2 Cor 10:4, where some editions read στρατεία ("warfare") instead of στρατιά.

definition: To face something head-on; of a ship, to head into the wind and hold its course against it.
article: Literally this verb means "to set your eye against" something — to look it straight in the face. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just once, in Acts 27:15, as a sailing term: Paul's ship could not face the wind and so was caught and driven along. Beyond that single nautical use, the word carries a broader range in other sources — the Septuagint (Wisdom 12:14) uses it of a ruler who cannot look God in the face, and Polybius and Koine papyri use it metaphorically for resisting or withstanding (even resisting with money).
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests entirely on that single occurrence.

definition: The filth scraped off something dirty, used figuratively for a despised, worthless outcast.
article: περίψωμα is a vivid word for the muck wiped or scraped off a dirty vessel, applied figuratively to people treated as the lowest scum of society. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Corinthians 4:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it in the sense of being treated as 'slandered' refuse), and the SBLGNT critical text does not include it. The most intriguing evidence comes from Moulton-Milligan: the Greek phrase 'become our περίψημα' was reportedly pronounced over a criminal thrown into the sea at Athens as a propitiatory offering, which is why some take the word to mean 'ransom' in its other ancient appearance, Tobit 5:18.
caution: This word is extremely rare (just one Byzantine occurrence, absent from the critical text), and sources genuinely disagree over whether it means 'offscouring' or 'ransom.'

definition: A spear or lance — a thrusting weapon with a sharp metal head used to pierce.
article: λόγχη refers to a spear or its metal head, a piercing weapon. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 19:34, where a soldier uses one to pierce Jesus' side. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for spear (רֹמַח, 4 times). One vivid bit of evidence comes from an ancient healing inscription at Epidaurus, where a man named Euippos carried a spear-point lodged in his jaw for six years until, in a dream, the god removed it.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be confirmed.

definition: The supreme Jewish high court (the Sanhedrin), or by extension any council or local tribunal that meets to judge.
article: In the New Testament συνέδριον almost always names the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish court — the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 18 of 22 occurrences. More broadly the word simply means a council or assembly that sits together to deliberate or judge, and Abbott-Smith notes it can describe a local Jewish tribunal (Matthew 10:17, Mark 13:9) as well as the meeting itself or its meeting place. The everyday breadth shows up in the papyri, where a judicial document from 120 B.C. uses it of being summoned 'to the council' (eis to synedrion).
caution: In the Septuagint it translates several different Hebrew words (such as סוֹד and מָדוֹן), so its sense there is looser than the fixed 'Sanhedrin' meaning of the New Testament.

definition: To act as an umpire or arbiter—to decide, govern, or rule over something the way a referee controls a contest.
article: βραβεύω comes from the world of athletic contests, where it meant to act as an umpire deciding a match, and from there it broadened to mean arbitrate, decide, or govern. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Colossians 3:15, where the call is for something (peace) to 'rule' or arbitrate in the heart. The everyday Koine papyri are especially telling here: documents from the second century B.C. use it for things being 'administered reasonably' or managed 'in the best way,' confirming the practical sense of overseeing and directing.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering 'thankful' reflects translation choices in the surrounding verse rather than the verb's own meaning, which the lexica consistently give as 'rule' or 'arbitrate.'

definition: To go away from a place or situation, often to escape danger or to seek seclusion.
article: ἀναχωρέω means to withdraw or depart, and in the New Testament it most often carries the sense of pulling back from danger — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "withdrew" in 6 of 14 occurrences (46%) and "gone" in another 2. Several of the Matthew passages describe people leaving precisely to avoid threat, which matches the lexicons' note that it frequently means avoiding danger. A neat detail from the papyri: the same verb was used for the Nile receding (P Magd 11, 221 BC), and the related noun could describe a person being away from home, even absent without leave.
caution: The lexicons distinguish a basic sense "go back" from "withdraw," and even disagree (Abbott-Smith vs. Thayer) on how to read Matthew 2:12, so the exact nuance can be uncertain.

definition: To go away, depart, or leave from one place toward another.
article: This common verb, built from "from" (ἀπό) plus "come/go" (ἔρχομαι), simply means to leave a place and head somewhere else; over half its 119 New Testament uses are rendered "went" and another fifth "went away." It often comes with a destination or direction, and in a special construction (with ὀπίσω) it means to "go after" or follow someone. In the Septuagint it appears 191 times, usually translating the Hebrew verb meaning "to walk" or "go" (114× for יָלַך), and the papyri show a touching everyday sense where a Christian epitaph uses it for someone who "departed" into a bright land.
caution: Many of the listed "senses" (such as "Jesus" or "men") simply reflect the surrounding subject in translation rather than distinct meanings of the verb itself.

definition: The process of growing or increasing, especially the natural growth of a living body.
article: αὔξησις refers to growth or increase, the noun form built from the verb αὐξάνω ("to grow"). It is rare, appearing only twice in the New Testament (Ephesians 4:16 and Colossians 2:19), and once in the Septuagint at 2 Maccabees 5:16. Interestingly, the standard lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all define it as "growth" or "increase," yet in both NT verses the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ligament" — reflecting the body-imagery context where parts are joined and grow together. An inscription from 57 BC uses it of a temple "being brought to growth," showing its ordinary Koine sense of expansion or development.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the NT, and the measured "ligament" rendering reflects an interpretive choice in body-imagery passages that differs from the lexicons' core sense of "growth."

definition: The number one hundred.
article: ἑκατόν is simply the cardinal number "hundred," an indeclinable word that stays the same in every grammatical setting. It appears 17 times in the Byzantine New Testament and a hefty 206 times in the Septuagint, often as part of larger numbers or phrases — in fact 10 of its 17 New Testament uses get absorbed into the surrounding wording with no English word of its own. The everyday Koine flavor shows up in the papyri, where a document from A.D. 194 mentions a fee of "a hundred denarii," and the word survives in Modern Greek as ἑκατό.

definition: In a natural, instinctive way, as animals act by instinct rather than by reason or learning.
article: This adverb describes acting by nature or instinct, the way creatures behave without reasoning. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:10, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berea Standard Bible both render it "instinctively" (100% agreement). Older sources like the KJV translate it "naturally," and it derives from the adjective φυσικός, meaning natural or inborn.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from multiple uses.

definition: A person belonging to another nation or race; a foreigner, especially one outside the Jewish people.
article: ἀλλογενής literally means "of another race" (from ἄλλος, "other," and γένος, "race"), and in practice means a foreigner — someone not part of the Jewish people. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 17:18, where Jesus calls the grateful Samaritan leper a foreigner, but it shows up 30 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew words for "stranger" (זוּר, 16×) and "foreign" (נֵכָר, 9×). The most striking evidence is an inscription from the Jerusalem Temple barrier (OGIS 598) warning "let no foreigner enter within the screen and enclosure surrounding the sanctuary," which uses this exact word.
caution: It occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To make someone or something clean, either through religious ceremony or by moral and spiritual purifying.
article: ἁγνίζω means to cleanse from defilement, and it spans both ceremonial purification (as in the temple rites of Acts and John) and inner moral cleansing (as in James 4:8 and 1 Peter 1:22). The Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times, and the Septuagint employs it 29 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew קָדַשׁ ("to make holy," 19 times). Notably, the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a magical text describing a pit dug in a "purified place," showing it was common ritual vocabulary outside the Bible.
caution: Abbott-Smith notes that in the Septuagint the word is always ceremonial, while the New Testament splits between ceremonial and moral senses, so the range depends on context.

definition: A year, or a full cycle of time measured as one annual period.
article: ἐνιαυτός means a year, understood as a complete cycle of time. The New Testament uses it consistently this way—11 of 14 occurrences (79%) are simply rendered "year," as in Luke 4:19 and John 11:49. Abbott-Smith notes its root sense as "a cycle of time," and the everyday papyri confirm this concrete meaning: one document defines it as the 360 days making up a year. In the Septuagint it appears 129 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for "years" (89×), but also rendering "jubilee" (10×).

definition: A price paid to free or buy back someone, like a ransom given in exchange for another.
article: ἀντίλυτρον means a ransom — a price paid in exchange to set someone free. It's built from ἀντί ("in place of") plus λύτρον ("ransom price"), which sharpens the sense of one thing given in the place of another. The word appears only once in the entire New Testament, at 1 Timothy 2:6, where every source agrees it means "ransom"; Abbott-Smith also notes a single appearance in a Greek version of Psalm 49:9.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage.

definition: To hide something completely or keep oneself entirely out of sight.
article: περικρύπτω means to conceal entirely, built from περί ("around") plus κρύπτω ("hide"), so the picture is of wrapping something up out of view. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 1:24, where Elizabeth, having conceived, kept herself in seclusion for five months. Moulton-Milligan confirms the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and they note the form used in Luke (περιέκρυβεν) comes from a late variant present tense περικρύβω that the New Testament doesn't otherwise use.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in biblical usage cannot be measured from that single instance.

definition: To live and conduct oneself in a particular way, especially as a responsible member of a community.
article: This verb literally means to live as a citizen, and in the New Testament it carries the broader sense of conducting your whole life in a certain way. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "conducted myself" in Acts 23:1 and "conduct" in Philippians 1:27. Everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions preserve its more official flavor — one inscription from 188 B.C. speaks of living "according to your laws" — and Abbott-Smith notes the New Testament uses it metaphorically of behavior shaped by citizenship.
caution: With only two occurrences and a computed low confidence tier, this word's full range in the New Testament rests on thin evidence.

definition: Something solid and firmly set—used for steadfastness or stability, and in the Greek Old Testament for the solid dome of the sky.
article: στερέωμα is built on the idea of something solid and established. In its single New Testament appearance (Colossians 2:5) it describes the firm "condition" or steadfastness of the readers' faith, and translators agree fully on this rendering. The most striking evidence comes from the Septuagint, where it appears 23 times and usually translates the Hebrew רָקִיעַ—the solid "firmament" or dome of the sky, as in Genesis 1:6; a magical papyrus from the third century AD likewise calls God the master of "the heavenly firmaments."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the firmness sense rests on slim direct evidence, though the Septuagint usage is plentiful.

definition: To stay on alongside others, remaining present and continuing with them.
article: This verb describes staying together with people, built from σύν ("with") and παραμένω ("remain"). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Philippians 1:25, where it is rendered "continue" — and notably it shows up only one time in the Septuagint, there standing in for the Hebrew word for "trust" or "confidence." Worth knowing: in the critical (SBLGNT) text it drops out entirely, since Abbott-Smith notes it is a received-text reading where other editions simply have παραμένω.
caution: Evidence is very thin — a single Byzantine occurrence that the critical text replaces with the simpler verb παραμένω, so confidence is low.

definition: A first-person past form of the verb "to be," meaning "I was" or "I existed."
article: This is simply a first-person singular past form of the verb "to be" — "I was" or "I existed" — described as a lengthened form of ἦν. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up only once in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew word רִיב. Moulton-Milligan note that a similarly spelled form (ἦ μήν, an emphatic oath particle, "truly") turns up in everyday Koine papyri and is common in the LXX, though that is a different word that can be confused with this one in spelling.
caution: Evidence is very thin — zero New Testament occurrences and only a single Septuagint instance — and the papyri citation actually concerns the look-alike oath particle ἦ μήν rather than this verb form.

definition: Rachel, the younger wife of the patriarch Jacob, named in a New Testament quotation of Old Testament grief.
article: Ῥαχήλ is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Rachel, Jacob's younger wife, and it stays unchanged regardless of grammatical case. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 2:18, where Rachel is pictured weeping for her children—a quotation drawn from the Old Testament. In the Septuagint the name turns up 50 times across 4 books, almost always rendering the Hebrew רָחֵל (46 times), though in a few places it stands in for other names like בִּלְהָה.
caution: The measured sense here is mislabeled as "lamentation"; the word is actually a personal name, Rachel, drawn from the surrounding quotation rather than a meaning of the word itself.

definition: Describing someone who has gone abroad, away from home and traveling in another country.
article: ἀπόδημος describes a person who has left home to travel abroad, literally "away from the people." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 13:34, where it pictures a man leaving on a journey, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in its single occurrence (with the KJV's "taking a far journey"). Moulton-Milligan documents the word in everyday Koine inscriptions, including one that contrasts those at home (ἐνδάμους) with those away (ἀποδάμους), showing this was ordinary travel vocabulary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: Describing something or someone that is welcomed, accepted, or looked on with favor.
article: δεκτός is a verbal adjective from δέχομαι ("to receive"), so it describes what gets a warm reception — something acceptable, welcome, or favored. In the New Testament it appears just 5 times across 4 books, covering the "year of the Lord's favor" (Luke 4:19), a prophet not being "accepted" in his hometown (Luke 4:24), and God welcoming the person who fears Him (Acts 10:35). The most telling background is sacrificial: it is very common in the Septuagint (31×), usually rendering Hebrew רָצוֹן ("favor, acceptance," 23×), and Moulton-Milligan notes a Lycian inscription describing a sacrifice as accepted or rejected by the god.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and two of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the sense divisions rest on thin data.

definition: A coincidence or chance happening, used in the phrase "by chance" for something that occurs without prior planning.
article: συγκυρία means a coincidence or chance occurrence, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 10:31, in the phrase κατὰ συγκυρίαν ("by chance")—describing how a priest happened to come down the same road in the parable of the Good Samaritan. The word turns up more often in later Greek writers and in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, where the related verb συγκυρέω was commonly used for the "appurtenances" belonging to a house. Symmachus used it once in the Septuagint at 1 Kings 6:9, matching the Hebrew word for "chance" or "happening."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse plus comparative evidence from papyri and late writers.

definition: To gain or keep something for oneself, whether by acquiring it, taking possession, or preserving it alive.
article: This middle-voice verb covers two related ideas: securing something as your own (acquiring, gaining possession) and keeping or preserving something safe for yourself. The Byzantine New Testament has it only twice — once meaning to keep (Acts 20:28) and once meaning to acquire (1 Timothy 3:13). It's well attested in everyday Koine papyri, where one document (c. 119 BC) speaks of someone "acquiring great authority for himself," and another of officials "gaining more for the king," matching the sense in 1 Timothy exactly.
caution: The New Testament evidence is very thin (only 2–3 occurrences), so the measured split between the two senses rests on single examples each.

definition: A conditional particle meaning "if indeed" or "seeing that," introducing an assumption the speaker often treats as true.
article: εἴγε is a strengthened form of the simple "if" particle εἰ, combined with the emphatic γέ, so it leans toward "if indeed" or "seeing that." It appears just 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and notably is absent from the SBL critical text. Each of its occurrences is rendered slightly differently in the Majority Standard Bible—ranging from "surely" to "if you"—reflecting how the surrounding context shapes whether the condition feels assumed-true or genuinely open.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 5 occurrences with no two rendered the same way, and the word is missing entirely from the critical text, so its exact force is hard to pin down.

definition: The origin, birth, or line of descent of a person, especially the record of one's ancestry.
article: γένεσις points to where something or someone comes from — origin, birth, or genealogical line. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times in the Byzantine text, with the Majority Standard Bible giving it the sense of a genealogical record in passages like Matthew 1:1, while the other 2 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it 40 times, mostly translating the Hebrew תּוֹלְדוֹת ("generations" or "descendants," 24×), and everyday papyri are striking: the word commonly meant "nativity" in astrological horoscopes, as in a London horoscope papyrus referring to the "lord of the nativity."
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 NT occurrences with just one rendered by a distinct English word — and the lexica list broader senses (birth, nature) that the measured data does not confirm.

definition: An egg, the kind laid by a bird and eaten as food.
article: ὠόν simply means an egg, and its meaning is stable across every source. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:12, and six times in the Septuagint, where it consistently translates the Hebrew word for egg (בֵּיצָה). It was an ordinary word in everyday life: one papyrus from AD 327 records an egg-seller's pledge to sell his eggs only in the public market, and other documents list eggs by the hundred in household accounts.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, but its meaning is well attested and undisputed across the Septuagint and everyday papyri.

definition: To give something freely as a gift, granting or bestowing it without charge.
article: δωρέομαι means to bestow something freely as a gift, and in the Byzantine New Testament every occurrence is rendered "given" (2 of 3 times, with the third absorbed into the phrasing). It comes from δῶρον, "gift," and the everyday Koine papyri show its plain use—one first-century letter describes wrist-bands that "your brother Pausanias gave you." In the Septuagint it appears only 4 times, translating several different Hebrew words, suggesting no fixed Hebrew counterpart.
caution: This is rare—only 3 New Testament occurrences and 4 in the Septuagint—so the evidence base is thin and confidence is low.

definition: Having or showing wisdom—skilled, learned, or sound in practical judgment.
article: σοφός describes someone who is wise—a meaning that covers everything from practical good sense to learned skill and intellectual depth. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "wise" in 20 of 22 occurrences (95%), and the word's range is broad enough to cover skilled craftsmen, learned scholars, Jewish teachers, and even God himself. In the Septuagint it appears about 150 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew חָכָם (107×), the standard word for a wise person; everyday Koine papyri use it too, including one that calls a man "wise" simply because he expounds the whole truth.

definition: To live or settle somewhere as if pitching a tent — to take up residence among others.
article: σκηνόω literally means "to pitch a tent" and so to take up residence, often with the sense of dwelling among people. It appears 5 times in the New Testament — famously in John 1:14, where the Word "became His dwelling" among us, and four times in Revelation. The everyday papyri are illuminating: one document speaks of someone "living in the house of Aristobulus," and the term often carries the flavor of a temporary, tent-like dwelling rather than a permanent one. In the Septuagint it appears only 4 times, translating several different Hebrew words.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and varied Septuagint counterparts, the precise force — temporary versus settled dwelling — is hard to pin down from usage alone.

definition: The founding or establishing of something, used in the New Testament almost entirely in the phrase "foundation of the world."
article: In the New Testament καταβολή means the founding or establishing of the world, appearing 11 times across 7 books and rendered "foundation" in 60% of cases and "since the foundation" in another 20%, nearly always within the set phrase "foundation of the world." The word's literal root sense is a "laying down," and Hebrews 11:11 uses it differently for the "laying down of seed" (i.e. conceiving), which is why older glosses like the KJV include "conceive." The most striking outside evidence comes from everyday papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show καταβολή frequently meant a "payment" or financial installment paid through a banker — a commercial sense entirely absent from the biblical "foundation" usage.
caution: The everyday papyri sense of "payment" and the Hebrews 11:11 sense of "conception" both fall outside the dominant biblical "foundation" meaning, so context determines the sense.

definition: To allow someone or something to go farther forward; to permit further progress.
article: This rare verb describes letting someone proceed onward, formed from "toward" (πρός) plus "to permit" (ἐάω). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:7, where the wind "did not permit" the ship to hold its straight course any farther; the Majority Standard Bible there renders the passage as "arrived," capturing the overall sense of the sailing narrative. Moulton-Milligan note it is one of the few New Testament words for which Grimm's old judgment held true: "Not found elsewhere" — though they themselves chronicle it in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A Hebrew personal name, Simeon (also rendered Simon), borne by several different people in the Bible.
article: Συμεών is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Shimon, applied in the New Testament to several distinct people. The Byzantine New Testament has it 7 times across 4 books, and translators usually render it "Simeon" (5×) but sometimes "Simon" (2×), since the Greek Σίμων was an alternative form of the same name. In the Septuagint it appears 56 times, almost always for Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן, especially the son of Jacob and his tribe. One intriguing detail: Deissmann suggested that the solemn form Συμεών for Peter in Acts 15:14 may reflect the formal tone of James's speech.
caution: The three "senses" here are really one name applied to different individuals, and whether some references read Συμεών or Σίμων varies between manuscripts and editions.

definition: A time word meaning "when" or "whenever," marking the moment at which something happens.
article: ἡνίκα is a relative adverb of time meaning "at which time" or "when," and before ἄν it shades into "whenever." It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice—both in 2 Corinthians 3 (verses 15 and 16)—but it was common everyday Koine, attested 103 times in the Septuagint and well documented in papyri. The papyri show its range nicely: it can take the indicative for a definite past time ("when I was about to sleep") or the subjunctive without ἄν for ongoing time, as in one document meaning "in her lifetime."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured senses rest on very thin evidence and lean heavily on the broader Septuagint and papyri record.

definition: To extort money or property by intimidation or false accusation, or more broadly to defraud and cheat someone.
article: This verb describes squeezing money out of people unfairly — whether by threats, false charges, or outright cheating. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke: once when John the Baptist tells soldiers not to extort money by force (Luke 3:14), and once when Zacchaeus admits he has cheated people (Luke 19:8). It is far more common in the Septuagint (8 times), often standing in for Hebrew words about oppression and false dealing, and a papyrus from 156 BC even shows an official warning subordinates against people "making unfair claims" against ordinary folk.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and translators choosing different words ("force" versus "cheated") for each, the precise force of the term is uncertain.

definition: To roar or howl, the deep menacing cry of a wild beast such as a lion.
senseLabels: roars or prowls like a beast
article: This verb describes the roaring or howling of an animal, especially a lion, and it can also be used of people making loud cries. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 5:8, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prowls" and the devil is pictured as a roaring lion. In the Septuagint it shows up 10 times across 7 books, most often translating the Hebrew shāʾag ("to roar," 6 times), and Moulton-Milligan notes that the Peter passage likely echoes the roaring, ravening lion of Psalm 22:14.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise force here is uncertain — the MSB's "prowls" softens what the lexicons consistently define as "roar" or "howl."

definition: To consider someone deserving or fit for something, judging them worthy of a privilege, honor, or experience.
article: καταξιόω means to count or deem someone worthy—it judges a person fit for something rather than making them so, as Moulton-Milligan notes by contrasting it with words for 'make.' In the New Testament it appears only 4 times (3 in the critical text), and all three measured renderings revolve around the same core idea of being judged worthy: worthy to escape coming dangers (Luke 21:36), worthy to suffer for the Name (Acts 5:41), and worthy of a share in the resurrection age (Luke 20:35). The everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, including a request that someone be 'deemed worthy of equal letters' (BGU IV.1080), showing it was ordinary polite usage for granting favor or recognition.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and a handful of Septuagint appearances, the evidence is thin, though the measured senses and the lexica agree closely.

definition: To flash or blaze with light all around someone, like a sudden burst of lightning.
article: This verb describes light suddenly flashing all around a person, enveloping them in brightness. Both of its New Testament appearances (Acts 9:3 and 22:6) describe the light that surrounded Saul on the road to Damascus, and the renderings agree closely on the picture of light flashing around him. It is a rare word built from 'around' (περί) and 'flash like lightning' (ἀστράπτω); outside the New Testament it appears in 4 Maccabees 4:10, where angels are described 'flashing around' the crowds.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences, both describing the same event, so the word's full range is hard to map.

definition: At that very moment; instantly, with no delay between an action and its result.
article: This adverb describes something happening on the spot, the instant it occurs—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "immediately" in 10 of its 18 New Testament appearances (71%) and "once" in another 4 (29%), with the rest folded silently into the phrasing. The two measured senses are really the same idea, and the lexicons agree completely: Abbott-Smith gives "on the spot, forthwith, instantly." Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri show it was a stock phrase in money dealings, as in P Fay 92 (A.D. 126) παραχρῆμα διὰ χιρός, "directly from hand to hand"—though one papyrus even pairs it with a month's delay, showing "immediately" could be a legal formality.

definition: The act of condemning someone or pronouncing a sentence against them.
article: κατάκρισις means condemnation—the act of pronouncing a sentence against someone. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians (3:9 and 7:3), and translations consistently render it as condemnation. Though once thought to be absent from non-biblical Greek, the word actually turns up in everyday Koine documents; Moulton-Milligan cites examples including the phrase "condemnations for envy."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured evidence for this word is thin.

definition: Alphaeus, a Jewish personal name borne by the father of the apostle James and (probably) the father of Levi.
article: Alphaeus is a proper name appearing 5 times across 4 New Testament books, always rendered "son of Alphaeus" or in connection with someone's father by that name. Abbott-Smith and Dodson note it likely refers to two different men: the father of Levi (Mark 2:14) and the father of the apostle James. The name traces back to an Aramaic/Hebrew original (חַלְפַּי), reflecting its Jewish origin.
caution: It is uncertain whether the father of Levi and the father of James are the same Alphaeus, since the sources note these as apparently two persons.

definition: Fear or dread of something threatening; also, by extension, the reverence or awe inspired by something overwhelming.
article: φόβος is the standard New Testament word for fear, dread, or alarm, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "fear" in 28 of its 47 occurrences (68%). It also stretches toward "awe"—the reverential response to God's power, as when amazement and awe seized the crowds after a healing. In the Septuagint it shows up 130 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for the "fear" of God (יִרְאָה, 24 times) alongside several words for sheer terror, and the everyday papyri use it in very ordinary ways, like fear of incurring a legal penalty.
caution: Earlier classical usage (Homer) carried the sense of "flight," which is no longer present in the New Testament range.

definition: To guard or keep watch over someone or something, like a military sentinel, whether to confine, protect, or hold securely.
article: φρουρέω comes from the world of soldiers and sentries — to mount guard, watch over, or keep something under control. The New Testament uses it only 4 times, and the sense shifts with context: a governor's guards watch the city gates to capture Paul (2CO 11:32), the law "locks up" or holds people in custody (GAL 3:23), and God's power "shields" or guards believers (1PE 1:5). Moulton-Milligan finds the literal military meaning all over everyday papyri, where φρουροῦντες are simply paid guards posted at a town like Socnopaei Nesus.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and renderings that span confining, imprisoning, and protecting, the exact shade in any given verse depends heavily on context.

definition: A conjunction combining "if" with "and/also," meaning roughly "even if" or "although."
article: This is a compound particle built from εἰ ("if") and καί ("and, also, even"), and it carries the sense "if also," "even if," or "though." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament corpus measured here (0 occurrences), so its sense range cannot be confirmed from that evidence. The component εἰ is itself a common conditional particle used in conditions and indirect questions, which gives the compound its conditional flavor.
caution: There are no measured occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so this entry rests only on the derivation and glosses rather than corpus evidence.

definition: Julia, the personal name of a Christian woman greeted by Paul in Romans.
article: Ἰουλία is the Roman name Julia, borne by a Christian woman whom Paul greets in Romans 16:15 — its only appearance in the New Testament. The name was extremely common among the slaves and freed members of the Imperial household, which fits the suggestion that this Julia may have belonged to that setting. Moulton-Milligan note inscriptional examples of the name among such household slaves, lending background color to Paul's greeting.
caution: This is a personal name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its sense is fixed but the woman's identity and background remain a matter of inference.

definition: A person who lives nearby; a neighbor in the sense of someone whose home is around yours.
article: περίοικος literally means "dwelling around," and it works as a noun for the people who live in the surrounding area — your neighbors. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:58, where Elizabeth's neighbors rejoice with her, and every translation in the digest renders it the same way. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times across 5 books and translates several different Hebrew words, including one tied to a place name, suggesting its meaning could shade toward "those round about" a location as well as personal neighbors.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To torture someone to death by beating, originally connected to a drum-like instrument of torture.
article: In the New Testament τυμπανίζω appears just once, in Hebrews 11:35, where it describes faithful people who were tortured to death rather than accept release. The word comes from τύμπανον, a drum, and the older meaning literally was 'to beat a drum'; from there it shifted to the violent sense of beating someone to death on an instrument of torture. The everyday Koine papyri preserve a related form: a Paris papyrus from 157 B.C. uses it of people fearing they would be 'tortured by beating,' showing the brutal meaning was current in ordinary documents.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament use and one Septuagint occurrence, so the precise range of meaning rests largely on outside sources.

definition: A small wooden or wax board used for writing notes.
article: πινακίδιον is a small writing tablet, the everyday tool someone would use to jot a quick note. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:63, where Zechariah asks for a tablet and writes that his son's name is John. The word is a diminutive of πίναξ (a board or plate), and Moulton-Milligan show it was common in ordinary Koine documents — one papyrus even records someone buying a tablet and another complaining, 'I lost a writing tablet.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical evidence alone.

definition: Describing the eye as clear, sound, or healthy, picturing a whole and undivided inner condition.
article: In the New Testament ἁπλοῦς appears just twice, both times describing the eye (Matthew 6:22, Luke 11:34), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "good" in 100% of cases. The literal idea is "single" or "folded together into one" — hence clear, sound, or undivided — and lexicons note a moral sense as well. The papyri are the most telling piece of evidence: a marriage contract uses ἁπλῆν of repaying the dowry "pure and simple," which shows the word carried plain everyday meanings, not only the moral sense some lexicons claimed.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin and the precise shade between "good," "single," and "sound" is hard to pin down.

definition: To dash or break violently against something, the way floodwaters smash against a building.
article: This verb describes something striking forcefully against an object, like waves or a flood crashing against a wall. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke 6:48-49, where a river bursts against two houses—one founded on rock, one without a foundation. A nice parallel comes from Marcus Aurelius, who pictures a promontory "whereon the waves break unceasingly," using this same word, and Abbott-Smith notes it can also be used transitively, as when something is dashed against rocks.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a single sense, the New Testament evidence for this word is thin.

definition: A mother-in-law — specifically, the mother of one's wife or husband.
article: πενθερά means "mother-in-law" in every New Testament instance; it is the feminine of πενθερός. The two "measured senses" the digest reports actually reflect the same meaning, since the "law" entries simply come from the phrase "mother in law" being counted by its word "law" — both halves point to a wife's or husband's mother. The Septuagint backs this up, using the word 13 times mostly for the Hebrew חֲמוֹת (11×), and an everyday papyrus letter shows the same ordinary use: someone "sent a message to your mother-in-law about the farm."
caution: The two listed senses are an artifact of counting the phrase "mother in law," not a genuine semantic split; the word consistently means mother-in-law.

definition: A personal name, Berechiah, identified as the father of the Zechariah mentioned by Jesus in Matthew 23:35.
article: Βαραχίας is a Hebrew personal name, rendered "Berechiah," that appears just once in the New Testament (Matthew 23:35) as the father of a murdered Zechariah. It comes from the Hebrew בֶּרֶכְיָה, which the Septuagint renders 11 times across five books. Interestingly, who this particular Berechiah was remains uncertain—one suggestion connects his son to the Zechariah killed during the last Jewish War.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the identity of the person named is genuinely uncertain.

definition: To burn something completely, consuming it down to nothing by fire.
article: κατακαίω means to burn something up completely, with the prefix κατά adding the sense of total consumption to the simple verb "burn" (καίω). The Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "burned" (5×, 50%) and frequently pairs it with "up" (3×, 30%), reflecting that complete destruction. It appears 90 times in the Septuagint, chiefly translating the Hebrew שָׂרַף ("to burn"), and the everyday Koine papyri use it both literally and even for the scorching, parching power of a hot south wind on plants.

definition: A freedman — someone who was once a slave but has been formally set free by their master.
article: This word describes a person who has been released from slavery through legal manumission, distinct from someone born free. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 7:22, where Paul calls the called slave "the Lord's freedman." Moulton-Milligan notes the word is very common in everyday papyri and inscriptions, often in the official title "freedman of the Emperor" (ἀπελεύθερος Καίσαρος), which lends color to Paul's phrasing about belonging to the Lord.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests almost entirely on outside papyri and lexicon evidence.

definition: An indefinite time-word meaning "at some time," used either of the past ("formerly," "once") or, after a negative or question, "ever."
article: ποτέ is a small, unstressed particle that points vaguely at a moment in time rather than naming one — "at some time," "once," "formerly." Most of its measured renderings cluster around describing what people or things used to be ("were," "once were," "formerly"), and after a negative or in a question it shifts to mean "ever." Because it leans on surrounding words, it often disappears into the English phrasing entirely — 7 of its 29 Byzantine occurrences carry no separate English word. The papyri show the same flavor: P Fay 110 calls a man "the former president" (τόν ποτε ἡγούμενον).
caution: Its meaning depends heavily on context, so the many overlapping renderings ("were," "once," "formerly") reflect translation choices rather than sharply distinct senses.

definition: To split something into parts—either by handing portions out among people or by breaking a group into opposing factions.
article: διαμερίζω covers two related ideas of splitting: physically parting something out (like soldiers dividing Jesus' clothes among themselves) and dividing a group into hostile factions (a kingdom or household "divided against" itself). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times, rendered "divided" 3 times and "divided against" 3 times. The Septuagint uses it 18 times, most often for the Hebrew חָלַק ("to divide or apportion"), and Moulton-Milligan finds it in everyday papyri—one document even uses the same "divide among themselves" construction seen in Luke 22:17.

definition: To come near or approach someone or something, often physically walking up to a person.
article: προσπορεύομαι means to approach or come near to someone, built from πρός ("toward") and πορεύομαι ("to go"). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, where the sense is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word, but it shows up 16 times in the Septuagint, four times rendering the Hebrew נָגַשׁ ("draw near"). Notably, the everyday Koine papyri use it the same plain way: one document from 159 B.C. records a man saying "I saw Apollonios, he approaches me." Strong's wrongly glosses it as "go before" and KJV similar — but that confuses it with a different word (προπορεύομαι); the measured and classical evidence agree it means coming near.
caution: With only one New Testament use (where it carries no English word of its own), the meaning here rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence, and Strong's/KJV "go before" appears to be a confusion with a similar word.

definition: A set phrase meaning "but if not" or "otherwise," introducing what would happen if a stated condition were not met.
article: This is a fixed Greek expression built from "if" (εἰ), "but" (δέ), and "not" (μή), sometimes with the particle γε added for emphasis. It works like English "otherwise" or "or else," pointing to the alternative outcome if a condition is not met — and in the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across 3 books. Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes it follows both positive statements (Matthew 6:1, Luke 10:6) and negative ones (Matthew 9:17, Luke 5:36), so it can signal the flip side either way. The translation data shows it is most often rendered as part of a "will" clause (5 of 8 times), reflecting how English phrases the consequence rather than a one-word gloss.
caution: It does not appear in the SBLGNT critical text and functions as a multi-word particle phrase, so its rendering depends heavily on the surrounding sentence rather than a fixed meaning.

definition: To draw a dividing line that sets people apart into separate groups or factions.
article: This rare verb means to mark off or set apart, drawing a boundary that splits people into factions. It appears only once in the entire New Testament, in Jude 1:19, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as those who "cause" divisions. The word is built from elements meaning "off," "through," and "boundary" (horos), and Moulton-Milligan note the related simplex διορίζω in everyday Koine documents, including a leaden curse tablet from Carthage where it describes God who "set a boundary to the earth and divided the sea."
caution: This is a one-time word in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To lack a suitable opportunity or right moment to do something.
article: This verb describes having no fitting occasion or chance to act, the opposite of εὐκαιρέω ("to have a good opportunity"). It is built from a negative particle plus καιρός ("opportune time"), so literally it means being out of season or without the right moment. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Philippians 4:10, where the BSB and MSB render the idea as the Philippians being "concerned" for Paul but lacking the opportunity to show it; the older glosses like the KJV's "lack opportunity" stay closer to the word's literal sense.

definition: Acting hastily and without thought, or being impulsive and reckless in behavior.
article: Literally meaning "falling forward" or "headlong," προπετής pictures someone who rushes ahead without caution. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: describing rash action in Acts 19:36 and reckless people in 2 Timothy 3:4. The two measured renderings ("rash" and "lovers") simply reflect how the surrounding phrase was translated, since both classical lexica and everyday Koine papyri agree the word itself means impulsive or reckless—Moulton-Milligan even cites a second-century epitaph using "reckless fate."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a computed low-confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, though the lexica and papyri agree on the core meaning.

definition: A jar or earthenware container, originally for storing wine but used for holding many things.
article: στάμνος is an earthenware jar, originally the kind used for racking off wine but extended to hold all sorts of contents. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Hebrews 9:4, referring to the golden jar that held the manna inside the ark. Everyday Koine papyri richly attest the word: jars holding copper coins (one containing 1600 drachmae), wine, milk, and figs, showing it was an ordinary household container. In the Septuagint it shows up 4 times, including Exodus 16:33 where it translates the Hebrew word for the manna jar.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests almost entirely on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: The unseen realm where the dead reside, the place of departed spirits.
article: In the New Testament ᾅδης refers to Hades, the abode of departed spirits — translators render it that way in 10 of its 11 Byzantine occurrences (91%). The Septuagint uses it 73 times, most often (47×) for the Hebrew שְׁאוֹל (Sheol), the place of the dead, which shaped its biblical meaning. Originally in Homer the word named Hades the god of the underworld before coming to mean the underworld itself; the KJV's older renderings 'grave' and 'hell' reflect this broad range, though modern translations simply transliterate it as 'Hades.'

definition: A projectile weapon such as an arrow, dart, or javelin shot or thrown at an enemy.
article: βέλος means a missile weapon — an arrow, dart, or javelin — meant to be launched at a target. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 6:16, where it pictures the "flaming darts" warded off by the shield of faith. The Septuagint uses it 35 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for arrow (חֵץ, 15 times), and inscriptions show it referring both to arrows stockpiled with catapults and to a spear, confirming its everyday military range.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade there rests on Septuagint and inscriptional evidence rather than direct New Testament usage.

definition: To have dealings or social contact with someone; to associate together with others.
article: This verb literally means "to use jointly with," and in the New Testament it describes having social dealings or associating with people. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 4:9, where it explains that Jews do not associate with Samaritans. The everyday Koine papyri show its more concrete side: one document from the third century B.C. uses it of jointly using forty donkeys in preparations for an official's visit, so the word ranges from sharing physical resources to sharing human company.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: To be sick with a fever; to be feverish.
article: πυρέσσω means to be ill with a fever, derived from a root tied to fire (πυρά). It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 8:14 and Mark 1:30), both describing Peter's mother-in-law lying sick. The word was common in everyday Koine, and Moulton-Milligan note its appearance in papyri and in writers like Diogenes Laertius, who quotes a remark that doctors stay with the sick yet do not themselves catch fever.
caution: The measured-sense labels here ("Peter's" and "bed") reflect surrounding translation choices rather than the word's actual meaning, which all sources agree is simply "to have a fever"; with only two occurrences the evidence is thin.

definition: Made of barley; describing bread or grain produced from the barley plant.
article: κρίθινος is an adjective meaning "made of barley," derived from the noun κριθή (barley). In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in John 6 (verses 9 and 13), describing the loaves used in the feeding of the crowd; the two measured senses ("barley" and "barley loaves") are really the same idea applied to bread. The word was ordinary everyday Koine: papyri use it of barley grain and even "barley chaff" packed in wicker baskets, and the Septuagint uses it six times where it matches Hebrew words including שְׂעֹרִים (barley).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same passage, the evidence base is thin, so the entry rests largely on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: A river or stream of flowing water, including the rushing torrents that swell suddenly after heavy rain.
article: ποταμός is the ordinary Koine word for a river or stream of running water, used 16 times in the Byzantine New Testament. In about three-quarters of cases it means a literal river, but a quarter of the time (4×) it refers to the sudden rushing torrents that batter a house in Jesus' parable. In the Septuagint it appears over 200 times and most often translates the Hebrew נָהָר; interestingly, the papyri show it could even name an artificially constructed canal, like the Agathos Daimon canal in an inscription from AD 80.

definition: An adverb meaning "no longer" or "no more," marking that an action or state should stop or not continue.
article: μηκέτι is built from μή ("not") and ἔτι ("still, yet"), so it literally means "not anymore" — it tells you something has ceased or should cease. Translators render it flexibly: "longer" in 39% of its 21 New Testament occurrences, with smaller shares going to "again," "no," and "stop," and three times it simply blends into the surrounding phrasing. It pairs with various verb forms — subjunctives, imperatives, even an optative and infinitives. Moulton-Milligan note a nice everyday papyrus parallel (P Oxy III.528) using "ἵνα μηκέτι" exactly as Paul does, and they caution that the word doesn't strictly demand "stop doing" — the underlying "yet" simply means "any longer."

definition: Belonging to the Lord; in the New Testament, set apart as the Lord's (Christ's).
article: This adjective simply means "belonging to the Lord," and in the New Testament's two uses it points to Christ — the "Lord's supper" (1 Cor 11:20) and the "Lord's day" (Rev 1:10). The most striking evidence is how ordinary this word was outside the Bible: the everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions use it to mean "imperial," belonging to the emperor or his service, such as a camel provided "for Imperial service" on the caravans. So the same word that named the emperor's property was used by Christians to mark what belongs to Jesus as Lord.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in the New Testament, the range of meaning rests heavily on outside papyri and inscriptions rather than biblical usage.

definition: Describing a person who speaks falsely or tells lies.
article: ψευδολόγος combines the words for "false" (ψευδής) and "speak" (λέγω), so it literally means someone who speaks lies. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 4:2, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "liars" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees completely. Beyond Scripture, the word and its relatives turn up in everyday Koine documents — Moulton-Milligan cite a fourth-century papyrus describing "replies full of false statements" (ψευδολογίας).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range can't be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To cover or decorate something with gold, gilding it for splendor.
article: This verb means to gild or overlay an object with gold, making it gleam with ornament.
