In both of its New Testament appearances (Revelation 17:4 and 18:16) it describes a figure decked out in gold, and the Septuagint uses it eight times, most often to translate the Hebrew צָפָה ("to overlay"). Everyday papyri confirm the same practical meaning: one document from Oxyrhynchus refers to a "gilded wooden" object, and an inscription mentions a "gilded key."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured senses here are essentially identical and the range is narrow.

definition: Wheat flour or finely ground meal, used for making bread.
article: ἄλευρον means flour or ground meal—the milled wheat from which bread is made. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the parable where a woman mixes leaven into three measures of flour (Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21). The Septuagint uses it 14 times, almost always for the Hebrew word qemach ("meal"), and everyday papyri mention practical things like a "sack of flour," confirming it was a common household term.
caution: The two Byzantine occurrences fall in the same parable, so the New Testament evidence for its range is very thin.

definition: A trough or vat, especially the one in which grapes were trodden to make wine.
article: ληνός refers to the trough or vat used for treading grapes and collecting their juice—a winepress. In the Byzantine New Testament all 5 occurrences carry this sense, rendered "winepress" in 4 of them, with the fifth absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it 22 times to translate several Hebrew words for wine and oil vats, and everyday papyri confirm its ordinary commercial meaning: one lease from AD 137 instructs tenants to deliver "the wine at the vat, new and unadulterated."
caution: In Revelation 14:19 the word appears with a mismatched masculine adjective, which Abbott-Smith notes may be an inadvertent grammatical slip.

definition: A straying from what is true or right—error, deception, or being led astray in belief or behavior.
article: πλάνη literally means "a wandering," but in the New Testament it always carries a moral or religious sense, describing a straying from truth into error or deception. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "error" in 3 of its 10 occurrences (33%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing or translated variously. An interesting detail comes from the papyri: Moulton-Milligan cite a first-century BC letter where πλάνη carries the active sense of "deceit," describing the trickery of a named person—matching the KJV's older glosses like "deceit" and "delusion."
caution: The measured data only firmly supports "error," while lexicons and papyri also document an active "deceit" sense, so the word's range may be broader than the New Testament renderings alone show.

definition: To feel and express intense joy, often by leaping or shouting—to rejoice greatly or be exceedingly glad.
article: ἀγαλλιάω describes joy at full strength—not quiet contentment but exultation, the kind that bursts out in celebration. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, rendered "rejoiced" in about 44% of cases and "glad" in 33%, all clustering around the same core idea of overflowing happiness. The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 67 times—mostly in the Psalms—and chiefly translates the Hebrew גִּיל (15×) and רָנַן (6×), both words for shouting or ringing out with joy. Strong's traces the sense back to the idea of jumping for joy, which fits its derivation from "much" plus the verb "to leap."

definition: To live in self-indulgent luxury, enjoying comfort and pleasure to excess.
article: τρυφάω describes living a soft, indulgent, luxurious life — faring sumptuously and pampering oneself. It appears just once in the New Testament (James 5:5), where it is rendered "luxury," and the Septuagint, classical lexicons, and KJV all agree on this self-indulgent sense. A striking parallel comes from a second/third-century tombstone epitaph that strings the word together with others in a carpe-diem motto: "Play, live luxuriously, live — for you must die."
caution: This verb occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A surname of the apostle Peter meaning "son of Jonah," identifying him by his father's name.
article: Βαριωνᾶς is the surname Jesus uses for Simon Peter, built from an Aramaic phrase meaning "son of Jonah." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 16:17, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "son of Jonah" in that single verse. The word is plainly a personal designation rather than an ordinary noun, formed from the Aramaic bar ("son") plus the name Jonah.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text, so the evidence is very thin.

definition: Darkness, whether literal nighttime gloom or figurative spiritual and moral darkness, often contrasted with light.
senseLabels: being dark or in the dark
article: σκοτία means darkness, and the Byzantine NT uses it both literally (the dark of night, as when Mary comes to the tomb in John 20:1) and figuratively for spiritual darkness opposed to light, as in 1 John 1:5. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "darkness" in 10 of 16 occurrences (63%) and "dark" in 3 more (19%). Abbott-Smith notes it's a later-writer equivalent of σκότος, the parent word it derives from, and also flags a sense of secrecy or hiddenness — what is whispered "in the dark" versus proclaimed in the light (Matthew 10:27, Luke 12:3).
caution: With only 3 Septuagint occurrences translating three different Hebrew words, its non-NT usage range is thinly attested.

definition: To mix or blend liquids together, especially diluting wine with water, or to pour out such a drink.
senseLabels: to mix or pour a drink
article: This verb means to mix two things so they blend into one—most often wine diluted with water for drinking. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all in Revelation, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "back" twice (in the image of pouring back a double portion, REV 18:6) and "undiluted" once. That last use (REV 14:10) is a deliberate oxymoron: "mixed unmixed," wine prepared yet at full strength. In the Septuagint it consistently translates the Hebrew מָסַך ("to mix"), and everyday Koine papyri use it of mixing wine and even medical drinks of raisin wine, honey, and pine-cones.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences, all in Revelation, so the measured "back" sense reflects how a poured-out drink is described rather than a separate meaning of the verb.

definition: To be impossible, or (of a person) to be unable to do something.
article: In the New Testament ἀδυνατέω appears just twice, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "impossible" both times (once absorbed into the surrounding phrasing), as in Matthew 17:20. This "impossible" sense is the one that shows up in the Septuagint (11× across 8 books, often translating Hebrew פָּלָא, "to be too hard"), but the older classical and everyday usage points the other way: the papyri use it of persons being unable or incapable, as in petitions about people who cannot farm. So the word sits between two related ideas — a thing being impossible versus a person being unable — and the lexicons note both.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT occurrences), and sources split on whether the sense is "be impossible" or "be unable," notably affecting how Luke 1:37 is translated.

definition: The Greek definite article, marking a noun as specific or known, much like English "the," though often left untranslated in English idiom.
article: This is the Greek definite article, by far the most common word in the New Testament, appearing 20,263 times across all 27 books. About 84% of the time it simply means "the," but it also blends into possessives, relative phrases ("who," "of the"), and over half its occurrences (10,388) are absorbed into English phrasing without any word of their own. Interestingly, the lexica note it originated as a demonstrative pronoun ("he, she, it"), a usage that survives in the New Testament chiefly in constructions like "the one… the other," and the papyri confirm this older demonstrative force lingered in everyday Koine.

definition: To be arrogant or proud, thinking too highly of oneself.
article: This compound verb, built from words for "high" and "mind," literally means to be lofty in thought — that is, conceited or proud. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (critical texts have it just once), and where translators render it with its own word, they consistently choose "arrogant" (100%). Notably, in 1 Timothy 6:17 some manuscripts split the compound into the separate words "think lofty things," which is why the critical text counts only one occurrence.
caution: Evidence is very thin — only two occurrences, one absorbed into surrounding phrasing, and a textual variant affecting whether it counts as one word at all.

definition: Severe distress or hardship that leaves a person feeling cramped and with no way out.
article: στενοχωρία literally means "narrowness of space" or lack of room, and the New Testament uses it figuratively for the crushing distress that comes from having no way to turn. It appears 4 times, always paired or grouped with θλῖψις ("trouble"), and translators render it as "distress," "anguish," or "hardships." The everyday Koine papyri preserve the same phrasing: a sixth-century document speaks of "the troubles and distresses (θλίψεις καὶ στενοχωρίας) which I endured," showing this was ordinary language for real-life hardship.

definition: To insult someone, treating them with open contempt or outrageous disrespect.
article: This verb means to insult or outrage someone, treating them with contempt. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 10:29, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "severely" in describing how a person treats the Spirit of grace. The papyri show the same force in ordinary life: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 186 uses it of a woman who "continues her outrageous behaviour and insulting conduct towards me."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there cannot be confirmed from internal usage alone.

definition: A person who guards a door or gate, controlling who may enter a house or property.
article: θυρωρός is the person stationed at a door or gate to control entry — what older translations called a "porter." The word appears 4 times in the New Testament and is rendered "doorkeeper" twice and "gatekeeper" once, with the meaning essentially the same in each case. Notably, in John 18 it refers to a woman (the Greek allows both male and female), and Moulton-Milligan show the word was common in everyday life, appearing in papyri naming actual doorkeepers as early as 163 B.C.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the split between "doorkeeper" and "gatekeeper" reflects translation style rather than a genuine difference in meaning.

definition: Compassionate and tenderhearted, having warm sympathy toward others.
article: εὔσπλαγχνος describes someone who is tenderhearted and full of compassion, built from εὖ ("well") and σπλάγχνον (the inward organs the Greeks saw as the seat of emotion). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "tenderhearted" in both of its two New Testament appearances (Ephesians 4:32 and 1 Peter 3:8). Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes the word began as a medical term in Hippocrates referring literally to the internal organs, before taking on this metaphorical "compassionate" sense in the New Testament.
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Having no recorded family line or pedigree, so that one's ancestry cannot be traced.
article: This word describes someone whose descent is not on record — no traceable genealogy or family tree. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 7:3, where it is rendered "without" (genealogy). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes it is found nowhere in classical authors and looks like a word an author simply coined for a specific purpose, though it does turn up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This is a rare word appearing only once in the New Testament, so its full range of meaning cannot be confidently mapped from such thin evidence.

definition: To have too little or fall short of what is needed, lacking a full amount.
article: This verb describes coming up short or having less than enough of something. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 8:15, where Paul quotes the Septuagint of Exodus 16:18 about the gathering of manna — the one who gathered little 'had no lack.' In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 8 times in 4 books, usually translating the Hebrew word ḥāsēr ('to lack'), and the Moulton-Milligan papyri evidence confirms it was genuine everyday Koine, found in documents as early as 217 B.C.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and entirely within an Old Testament quotation, so its New Testament range can't be measured independently.

definition: Describing someone who refuses to be persuaded and will not obey.
article: ἀπειθής describes a person who won't be convinced or won't comply — stubbornly unwilling to obey. The translation is remarkably consistent: of its 6 New Testament occurrences, 5 are rendered "disobedient" (the sixth being absorbed into surrounding phrasing), and the BSB agrees fully. Its makeup says it all — the negative prefix joined to πείθω ("persuade"), so literally "unpersuadable"; in the Septuagint it stands behind Hebrew words for rebellion and stubbornness like סָרַר and מָרָה.

definition: A personal name, Tryphaena, borne by a Christian woman in Rome whom Paul greets.
article: Tryphaena is a woman's proper name, appearing just once in the New Testament when Paul greets her as a Christian in Rome (Romans 16:12). The name derives from the Greek word for luxury or daintiness (tryphē), but as a name it simply identifies a specific person rather than describing her. Moulton-Milligan note it was a common everyday name in Koine documents, turning up in a first-century list of names from Crocodilopolis and of three different people in Alexandrian papyri from the age of Augustus.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so there is no measurable range of meaning beyond identifying the individual.

definition: God's saving act or deliverance—often pictured concretely as the salvation God provides.
article: σωτήριον is the neuter form of the adjective "saving" used as a noun, pointing to God's salvation or the means by which it comes. In the New Testament it appears 5 times and always carries a spiritual sense, rendered "salvation" in three of those cases and once in the phrase about all humanity seeing God's salvation (Luke 3:6). The Septuagint shows a broader background: it occurs 128 times and most often translates the Hebrew word for a peace or fellowship offering (שֶׁלֶם, 72×), while everyday papyri use the related word for a thank-offering or gift made to secure deliverance.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and one rendered loosely, the precise force in any single verse is hard to pin down.

definition: A small connecting particle that links sentences, usually signaling a mild contrast ("but") or simply moving the narrative forward ("and," "now").
article: δέ is one of the most common words in the Greek New Testament, appearing 2,866 times in the Byzantine text, yet it carries very little weight of its own. About 84% of the time the Majority Standard Bible renders it "but," but it just as often signals nothing stronger than "and" or "now" as a story moves to its next step — in fact it was absorbed into the phrasing with no English word at all in 1,955 of its occurrences. Notably, it almost always sits second in its clause rather than first, and the surrounding senses like "they," "he," and "a" simply reflect the small words English adds when translating the clauses δέ introduces.
caution: Many of the measured "senses" are really artifacts of translation phrasing, not distinct meanings, since δέ so often vanishes into English wording.

definition: A female child or, more broadly in biblical usage, any female descendant or even a female inhabitant of a place.
article: θυγάτηρ is the everyday word for "daughter," and that is how it is rendered 27 of 29 times (96%) in the Byzantine New Testament. Its range stretches well beyond a literal child, though: following Hebrew idiom it can mean a distant female descendant ("daughter of Abraham"), a tender form of address ("Daughter, your faith has healed you"), or even the people of a city, as in "daughter of Zion." In the Septuagint it appears 554 times, almost always translating Hebrew בַּת. One nice papyrus detail: inscriptions use the phrase "by daughter-adoption" (κατὰ θυγατροποΐαν) for adopting females, paralleling the term for adopting sons.

definition: To move away or withdraw from someone or something, whether physically leaving or, in a deeper sense, abandoning one's loyalty or faith.
article: At its root ἀφίστημι combines "from" and "to stand," so it pictures standing back, withdrawing, or departing. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times across 6 books and is most often rendered "left" (4×) or, in a spiritual sense, "turn away" (2×), as when Hebrews warns against falling away from God. The everyday Koine papyri show a striking concrete use: in contracts of sale the seller promises to "repel" or fend off anyone who tries to claim or trespass on the property. In the Septuagint it occurs 165 times, usually translating the Hebrew סוּר, "to turn aside."
caution: About a fifth of its occurrences get absorbed into surrounding phrasing without a distinct English word, so the rendering counts understate how widely it is used.

definition: The neck, the part of the body joining head and shoulders, also used in phrases about embracing or risking one's life.
article: τράχηλος is simply the neck, the body part where the head meets the shoulders, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "neck" in 4 of its 7 New Testament occurrences (67%). The other appearances are part of vivid phrases: "falling on someone's neck" to embrace them (Luke 15:20, Acts 20:37) and figuratively "laying down one's neck" to risk one's life. In the Septuagint it shows up 62 times, mostly translating the Hebrew צַוָּר ("neck," 30×) and עֹרֶף (the back of the neck, 11×); everyday papyri use it plainly, as in physical descriptions noting a scar "on the neck."

definition: A crowd quickly rushing or running together, especially an excited or riotous gathering of people.
article: συνδρομή describes people running together into a sudden crowd, often with the sense of a riotous or tumultuous mob. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:30, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as the people having "rushed" together. The word also shows up in the Septuagint (Judith 10:18, 3 Maccabees 3:8) and in everyday Koine papyri; interestingly, ancient medical writers used it for a "concourse" of symptoms appearing together.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: A cultivated field or piece of farmland that someone works and tends.
article: γεώργιον refers to a tilled field or farmland — land that is worked and cultivated. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 3:9, where Paul calls the believers God's field; the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way 100% of the time. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the down-to-earth sense: a land survey from 114 BC uses it for cultivated fields where the crop was found stunted and unharvested.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on that single verse.

definition: To scatter people, animals, or things widely apart; figuratively, to squander or waste resources.
article: διασκορπίζω means to spread something out so it's no longer together — sheep that flee, people who are dispersed, or grain being winnowed. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "scattered" in 7 of those, with 2 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. It can also shade into "squander" or "waste," as Abbott-Smith notes for the property in Luke 15:13 and 16:1, and the Greek Old Testament uses it 48 times, most often for the Hebrew פּוּץ ("scatter," 15×). One striking detail: the early Christian Didache uses it of broken Eucharist bread once "scattered upon the mountains" and then gathered into one.

definition: In a way that is open and public, or that can be seen or understood clearly.
article: This adverb means doing something openly or in plain sight, as opposed to secretly. It can also shade toward "clearly," describing something perceived without doubt, as in the angel Cornelius saw "clearly" in Acts 10:3. The contrast is sharpest in John 7:10, where Jesus goes up to the festival not openly (φανερῶς) but in secret (ἐν κρυπτῷ) — and everyday papyri show the same pairing, with one document distinguishing "neither secretly nor openly."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint instance, the evidence is thin, though the standard lexicons agree on the meaning.

definition: A scribe—a Jewish expert in the Law and religious teacher—or, more broadly, a secretary or official clerk.
article: In the New Testament γραμματεύς almost always means a scribe: a learned expert in the Jewish Law who taught and interpreted it, rendered "scribes" in 57 of 67 occurrences (88%). But the word's range is wider than the Gospels suggest—Dodson notes it can mean the town-clerk or city secretary (as at Ephesus), and the papyri and Septuagint show it used of military officials who kept the army's register, reflecting an Egyptian Greek clerical usage. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words, most often סָפַר ("scribe/counter," 26×) and שֹׁטֵר ("officer," 18×), confirming that "clerk/official" was its older, more general sense.
caution: The three measured "scribes alongside Jesus" senses simply reflect surrounding phrasing, not distinct meanings of the word itself.

definition: A female slave or servant, a woman bound to serve her master or lord.
article: δούλη is the feminine form of δοῦλος and means a female slave or servant, a woman wholly bound to serve someone. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, rendered "servant" twice (as when Mary calls herself the Lord's servant) and once alongside menservants. It's far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 39 times and most often translates the Hebrew words אָמָה (21×) and שִׁפְחָה (15×), both terms for a maidservant or bondwoman.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this word's range rests largely on Septuagint evidence.

definition: To make an official ruling or pronounce a formal decision, such as granting a request or passing sentence.
senseLabels: to decree or grant a demand
article: This is a legal and administrative term meaning to give an official decision or pronounce judgment. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 23:24, where Pilate "decreed" that the crowd's demand be carried out — the Majority Standard Bible renders it as granting their "demand," while older versions like the KJV say he "gave sentence." The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where this word was very common for the official examination of men called up for military service, showing it belonged to the language of bureaucratic decisions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and just twice in the Septuagint, so its precise force rests on limited biblical evidence.

definition: To communicate with someone by sending a letter, conveying instructions or a message in writing.
article: In the New Testament ἐπιστέλλω always means to write or send word by letter, appearing 3 times and rendered "written" in every case (Acts 15:20; 21:25; Heb 13:22). The verb is built from ἐπί plus στέλλω, and the everyday Koine papyri confirm a slightly broader range: it can mean simply "to send" or "send to," as in a second-century BC document ordering someone brought "under guard." Abbott-Smith likewise lists both "to send to" and "to send a message by letter," with the Septuagint using it for the Hebrew שָׁלַח ("to send").
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the broader "send to" sense seen in papyri and the Septuagint sits alongside the measured "write" sense, so the full range is thinly attested in the NT itself.

definition: To sternly rebuke, scold, or warn someone, often commanding them to stop or stay silent.
article: This verb means to speak sharply to someone — rebuking, scolding, or firmly warning them, frequently with a command to stop or be quiet. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 29 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "rebuked" or "Jesus rebuked" in 75% of cases, with a smaller group (7%) carrying the sense of a stern warning. In everyday Koine papyri the word could even mean to lay someone under a penalty or fine, and in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew גָּעַר ("to rebuke"), as in Zechariah 3:2.

definition: A personal name, Philologus, borne by a Christian whom Paul greets in Rome.
article: In the New Testament Φιλόλογος is simply a personal name, that of a Christian Paul greets in Romans 16:15 — its single occurrence. Though the name literally combines "fond of" (φίλος) and "word" (λόγος), and classical writers used the adjective to mean "fond of speaking" or "fond of learning," the New Testament uses it only as a name. Interestingly, the papyri and inscriptions show this was a common slave name, and one document (P Lond 256) lists a Philologus as a consignee of grain shipped from inland Egypt to the coast.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament, so its use there rests on a single verse.

definition: To wait for or expect something or someone to happen or arrive, whether in hope, watchfulness, or fear.
article: προσδοκάω covers the whole range of waiting in expectation, from watching for a person to arrive to anticipating a future event. In the Byzantine New Testament's 16 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "look" (4×), "expecting" (3×), "waiting" (2×), and "anticipate" (2×), and these shades blur together more than they separate. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one third-century letter says "many times in the day we expect you to come to us," capturing the warm, watchful sense of awaiting someone you long to see.

definition: To bring or carry something to someone, and especially to present offerings, gifts, or sacrifices to God.
article: προσφέρω is built from πρός ("toward") and φέρω ("carry"), so its core idea is bringing something to someone. In the Byzantine New Testament's 48 occurrences it splits fairly evenly between simply "bringing" people or things (37%) and the religious sense of "offering" sacrifices and gifts to God (about 54% across "offered" and "offer"). The Septuagint reinforces the worship sense, using it 138 times, most often to translate the Hebrew קָרַב ("to bring near," 95×), and everyday papyri show the same mundane meaning of presenting accounts or handing over documents to people.

definition: Describing a person or thing that is useful, serviceable, and worth putting to good use.
article: εὔχρηστος describes someone or something that is genuinely useful or serviceable, the opposite of being useless. In all 3 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "useful," and the BSB agrees 100%; in Philemon 11 it is set directly against ἄχρηστος ("useless"). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense vividly: one letter describes a man named Petous as εὔχρηστον — "of great value" — to the people of his district, the same construction with the dative of person seen in 2 Timothy 2:21.
caution: The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range is narrow.

definition: A member of the people of Israel, a descendant of Israel often called by this name as one of God's chosen people.
article: Ἰσραηλίτης names a descendant of the nation of Israel, used 9 times in the New Testament. Translators render it as "Israel" in 4 occurrences (44%) and as "Israelite" in 3 (33%), so the meaning is consistent even when the English form shifts. Abbott-Smith notes the word carries a sense of theocratic privilege, and a curious detail from the manuscripts is that Codex Sinaiticus spells it ΙΣΔΡΑΗΛΕΙΤΗΣ in eight of its nine New Testament appearances.

definition: To announce or proclaim something publicly and with authority, especially a message about God or Christ.
article: καταγγέλλω means to announce something openly and with authority, and in the New Testament it almost always describes proclaiming God's word, the gospel, or Christ himself. The Byzantine text uses it 18 times, and the Berean Standard Bible renders it as "proclaim/proclaimed" in 14 of those (about 93%), with the remaining 3 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. A vivid window into its everyday force comes from a third-century AD papyrus (P Oxy X.1274), where a widow uses the word for the "lamentable news announced" to her about her husband's death — showing the sense of a formal, authoritative announcement. Classical lexica also note a secondary sense "to denounce" (in Xenophon), which does not appear in the measured biblical data.

definition: To make an earnest request, whether begging a person for help or praying to God for something needed.
article: δέομαι covers asking from a position of need, and the translations cluster tightly around that: "beg" (30%), "ask," "pray," and "prayed" each at 15%. It runs along a spectrum from urgently pleading with a fellow person (Luke 5:12, Acts 21:39) to praying to God (Luke 21:36, Acts 4:31), with the line between them set mostly by context. As the middle voice of δέω ("to bind"), Strong's pictures the petitioner as binding himself to the request, and Moulton-Milligan notes it was very common in everyday papyri for both having a need and voicing it.

definition: To carry something around from place to place; in the passive, to be swept or driven back and forth.
article: περιφέρω is a compound of περί ('around') and φέρω ('carry'), and it means just that — to carry something about from one place to another. The Majority Standard Bible renders both clear New Testament uses as 'carry around' (100%), as in 2 Corinthians 4:10, while the passive can mean being driven to and fro, as in Ephesians 4:14. A nice everyday parallel turns up in the papyri: an Oxyrhynchus letter (3rd century AD) says 'our whole youth carries you in their hearts,' showing the same verb used warmly for keeping someone in mind.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (one of which is absorbed into phrasing), so confidence in the full range is limited.

definition: To go beyond the usual limit; to exceed, surpass, or transcend something in degree or measure.
article: ὑπερβάλλω literally means to throw past the mark, and in the New Testament it always works figuratively: something so great it goes beyond what came before. Every one of its 5 occurrences is rendered with the idea of surpassing or exceeding, whether Christ's surpassing glory, God's surpassing power, or the surpassing riches of His grace. The everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—Aristeas speaks of a generosity "beyond all precedent," and an inscription praises a man "excellent in knowledge."
caution: With only 5 occurrences, all clustered in 2 Corinthians and Ephesians and all translated similarly, the measured range is narrow though consistent.

definition: A respectful or affectionate way to address a woman, like "lady" or "dear lady."
article: Κυρία is the feminine form of κύριος ("lord"), used as a courteous term for a woman. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in 2 John (verses 1 and 5), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lady" and "dear lady." The most interesting evidence comes from everyday papyri: Moulton-Milligan cites a letter from 1 B.C. addressed "to my dear Berous," suggesting κυρία was simply an affectionate form of address, which has fueled debate over whether 2 John's "lady" is a real friend, a church, or a dignified woman. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for "mistress" or female head of a household.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the confidence tier rated low, scholars genuinely disagree about whether the "lady" in 2 John is an individual woman or a symbol for a church.

definition: To surround or grip someone (as with amazement), or to contain something, especially what a written document says.
article: This verb literally means to hold something all around, and its three New Testament uses each point in a slightly different direction: it grips Peter's companions with astonishment (Luke 5:9), it introduces what a letter contains (Acts 23:25), and it describes what a passage of Scripture says or 'stands' (1 Peter 2:6). That last, intransitive use—'as it stands' or 'as it is contained'—is well attested in everyday papyri, where wills and leases are described with the same phrase, διαθήκη ὡς περιέχει, 'as the will contains.' In the Septuagint it appears 23 times across 8 books, often rendering Hebrew words for watching or surrounding.
caution: Each New Testament sense rests on a single occurrence and the overall evidence is thin, so the precise force in any given verse is somewhat uncertain.

definition: The use of something; in the New Testament, specifically sexual relations.
article: At its root χρῆσις simply means "use" — how something is employed or put into service. Both of its New Testament appearances are in Romans 1:26-27, where Paul uses it in a sexual sense, the "natural use" of women. Everyday papyri show the broader range nicely: wine bought "for use" (i.e. present consumption) and a will granting a woman the "right of using" a house for her lifetime, a meaning that shades toward "loan."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (both in one passage) and a single Septuagint use, the word's broader range comes mainly from papyri rather than biblical evidence.

definition: Nahum, the personal name of a man listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ναούμ is a Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Nahum, borne here by one of Jesus' ancestors in Luke 3:25, the only place it appears in the New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as part of the phrase identifying him as a "son" in the genealogy, but the word itself is simply the proper name. In the Septuagint the same Greek form shows up twice, translating the Hebrew names נַחוּם (Nahum) and רַעַמְיָה, confirming it functions purely as a name.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament and refers to an otherwise unknown ancestor, so there is little to define beyond its identity as a personal name.

definition: Costing nothing; offered free of charge, without expense to the one who receives it.
article: ἀδάπανος describes something that costs nothing — built from the negative prefix and δαπάνη ("expense"), it literally means "without expense." In the New Testament it appears only once, in 1 Corinthians 9:18, where Paul speaks of offering the gospel free of charge. The word also turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions and papyri, including a second-century BC text from Teos about maintaining a group "without expense," which shows it was ordinary, practical vocabulary rather than a specially religious term.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A man who has been castrated, or a court official such as a royal chamberlain; figuratively, a man who abstains from marriage.
article: In the New Testament εὐνοῦχος refers to a castrated man, rendered "eunuch" in 5 of 8 occurrences (63%). The word covers a range: a literally emasculated man, a court official like the chamberlain in Acts 8:27, and figuratively a man who chooses not to marry (Matthew 19:12). In the Septuagint it appears 34 times, almost always translating the Hebrew סָרִיס (28×), a term that, as Abbott-Smith notes, did not always mean a literal eunuch but could simply mean a court officer.
caution: The word's exact force varies between literal castration, court office, and voluntary celibacy, and the underlying Hebrew סָרִיס was itself not always literal.

definition: To be fiery red, used of the sky glowing red at sunrise or sunset.
article: This verb describes something glowing a fiery or reddish color. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Matthew 16:2-3, where it always refers to a red sky used to forecast the weather. A closely related form, πυρρίζω, shows up in the Septuagint (Leviticus 13-14) for the reddish color of skin sores, translating the Hebrew word for "reddish."
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in a single passage, the evidence for this word's full range is thin.

definition: In a complete or perfect way; fully and without wavering.
article: This adverb means doing something completely or perfectly, with the action carried all the way through. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 1:13, where it describes setting your hope "fully" on coming grace; commentator Hort took the related phrase to mean a perfect sobriety that enters into all one's thoughts and ways. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, including a sixth-century deed of divorce describing a couple completely settling their separation, which shows it was ordinary, practical language.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shading there rests on a single passage.

definition: Firmness or steadfastness; a stable, settled condition that keeps one from being shaken.
article: στηριγμός describes being firmly set or stable, and figuratively a person's steadfastness. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 3:17, where believers are warned not to fall from their own steadfastness. Interestingly, the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including an astronomical text from A.D. 138 that uses it for the fixed 'station' of a planet, showing its root sense of being set in place.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: To run ahead of others, getting somewhere first by outrunning them or running on in advance.
article: προτρέχω combines πρό (before) and τρέχω (run) to mean running ahead or outstripping others. It appears only twice in the New Testament: Zacchaeus runs ahead to climb a tree in Luke 19:4, and in John 20:4 the other disciple outruns Peter and reaches the tomb first. Abbott-Smith notes it also surfaces in the Septuagint, once translating a Hebrew word, though the digest's broader citation list and the Moulton-Milligan papyri note actually discuss the look-alike word προτρέπω (to urge forward), so that papyri evidence should be treated with care.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a Moulton-Milligan excerpt that actually concerns a different word (προτρέπω), the supporting evidence beyond the NT is thin and partly mismatched.

definition: Describing a calm, undisturbed, peaceful state, especially an inner tranquility or a settled, quiet way of life.
article: ἡσύχιος describes someone or something that is calm, tranquil, and peaceful. In both of its two New Testament appearances the Majority Standard Bible renders it "quiet" (100%), whether describing the peaceful life believers pray to lead (1 Timothy 2:2) or the inner "gentle and quiet spirit" prized in 1 Peter 3:4. The word turns up in everyday Koine: a sixth-century Oxyrhynchus papyrus has a father wanting his daughter to lead "a peaceful and quiet life," and Abbott-Smith notes that, unlike a synonym suggesting calm imposed from outside, ἡσύχιος points to tranquility coming from within.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence, so the confidence tier is low.

definition: A shallow, flat bowl used for pouring out liquids, such as libations or offerings.
article: A φιάλη is a broad, shallow bowl—essentially a flat dish—used for pouring out liquids like libations. All 12 New Testament occurrences fall in Revelation, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "bowls" (50%) or, in the dramatic judgment scenes, the "angel bowl" poured out (33%). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain meaning: shipping records mention sending "three pairs of bowls" and pairing φιάλας with cups, and in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew מִזְרָק (23 of 33 times), a vessel for sprinkling or pouring.
caution: The word is restricted to Revelation in the New Testament, so its full range there is inferred from a single book.

definition: To put, place, or lay something down, often physically, but also figuratively to appoint, establish, or set in position.
article: τίθημι is a common, versatile verb meaning to put, place, or lay something down, appearing 97 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 16 books. Its core sense is physical—setting an object in a spot, laying the dead to rest, kneeling down, or laying aside garments—but it stretches into figurative uses like appointing people (6×) or laying down one's life. The Septuagint is striking for its sheer volume, using τίθημι 482 times to render the Hebrew שׂוּם ("to set, place") 221 times, and the everyday papyri show the same plain meaning, as when one letter asks "where did you put the notice of payment for the hay?"

definition: The ordinal number eleventh, marking something as eleven in a sequence or order.
article: This is simply the ordinal number "eleventh," built from the word for "eleven" (ἕνδεκα). All three New Testament uses point to the same meaning: the eleventh hour in Jesus' parable of the laborers (Matthew 20:6, 9) and the eleventh foundation stone in Revelation 21:20. The everyday papyri show it doing the same plain work — dating documents to "the eleventh of the month" or recording "the eleventh hour of the day" — and in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew expression for eleven (עַשְׁתֵּי) twelve times.
caution: The three measured "senses" reflect surrounding words in the translation, not real differences in meaning; the word always simply means "eleventh."

definition: A member of a governing council, used in the New Testament for members of the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem.
article: βουλευτής means a councillor or member of a governing body, and in both of its two New Testament appearances it refers to a member of the Jewish council (the Sanhedrin), describing Joseph of Arimathea in Mark 15:43 and Luke 23:50. Though the digest lists two measured renderings, both point to the same single sense — the variation is just wording in surrounding phrases, not a difference in meaning. One intriguing note from Moulton-Milligan: this word was common in everyday Koine for ordinary city councillors, and the Gospel writers seem to have used it precisely because their Gentile readers would understand it, since Jews did not normally use βουλευτής as a technical Sanhedrin term.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences and confidence is rated low — so the apparent two senses really reflect one meaning rendered with different surrounding words.

definition: The mental ability to grasp how things fit together — understanding, insight, or practical discernment.
article: σύνεσις is the capacity to put ideas together in the mind and grasp how things connect, ranging from general understanding to sharper insight. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, rendered "understanding" in 67% of cases and "insight" in the remaining 33%. The word was common in everyday Koine: a 2nd-century BC inscription pairs it with education ("advancing in σύνεσις and learning"), and one Greek inscription even uses it to mean a formal "decree." In the Septuagint it shows up 76 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for understanding, בִּינָה.
caution: Lexicons distinguish σύνεσις (grasping how principles apply) from σοφία (wisdom), but the two senses measured here overlap heavily and the boundary between them is soft.

definition: Made by human hands; describing something built or fashioned by people rather than by God.
article: χειροποίητος literally means "made by hands" and describes things constructed by human effort. In the New Testament it appears 6 times, mostly of physical temples (as in Mark 14:58 and Acts 7:48), and once of circumcision performed by people (Ephesians 2:11). What's striking is the shift in usage: in the Septuagint (12 times) the word is applied only to idols, often translating the Hebrew אֱלִיל, while a travel-letter papyrus from the 1st–2nd century AD uses it simply for "works of art made by hands" along the Nile.
caution: The three measured sense labels reflect minor wording differences rather than truly distinct meanings; all point to the same core idea of "made by hands."

definition: A state of being at a loss, with no way out — bewilderment or anxious uncertainty about what to do.
article: ἀπορία describes the feeling of being stuck with no solution in sight — perplexity, anxiety, and doubt rolled together. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 21:25, where it describes the dismay of nations facing the upheaval of sea and waves. In everyday Koine papyri the word could even shade toward 'poverty' or 'lack of resources,' as in an inscription where people abandoned a city 'because of the ἀπορία.'
caution: The standard lexicons render this 'perplexity,' but the digest records the single NT occurrence translated as 'roaring,' which does not match the dictionary sense — treat the precise nuance in Luke 21:25 with care.

definition: A Hebrew personal name borne by several different men in the New Testament, and also the name of the patriarch Judah and his tribe.
article: Ἰούδας is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Yehudah (יְהוּדָה), and it covers a surprising number of distinct people: in the Byzantine New Testament it appears 38 times, rendered "Judas" about 81% of the time. The same name also points back to the patriarch Judah and his tribe, which is why it sometimes shows up as "Judah" in genealogies and tribal references. The word's reach is wide — Abbott-Smith counts at least eight different individuals named Judas, from Judas Iscariot to the Lord's brother to Judas the Galilean. The name was ordinary enough in daily life that it turns up in a first-century tombstone inscription reading "Judas son of Judas, about thirty years old."
caution: Because the same name labels at least eight different men, the right English form and identity depend entirely on context rather than on the word itself.

definition: To sneer at or mock someone, literally by turning up the nose in contempt.
article: μυκτηρίζω comes from the word for nose and literally means to turn up the nose at someone — to sneer, ridicule, or treat with contempt. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Galatians 6:7 ("God is not mocked"), where it is woven into the phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word; in the Septuagint it shows up 14 times across 9 books, most often translating the Hebrew לָעַג ("to scorn," 4×). One intriguing wrinkle: Moulton-Milligan suggests that in Galatians the sense may shade toward "outwitted" or "deceived," since someone who is outsmarted ends up looking ridiculous.
caution: The word appears only once in the New Testament and is rare outside the Septuagint, and scholars differ on whether Galatians 6:7 means "mocked" or "outwitted."

definition: The Kidron, a seasonal brook (and its valley) running just east of Jerusalem, which Jesus crossed on the night of his arrest.
article: Κεδρών is a place name—the Kidron, a winter stream (χείμαρρος) and valley on the east side of Jerusalem. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 18:1, where Jesus crosses it, and it shows up 14 times in the Septuagint, mostly rendering the Hebrew קִדְרוֹן. The most interesting wrinkle is a textual one: many manuscripts read τῶν Κέδρων ("of the cedars"), which Moulton-Milligan and others judge to be a popular misreading of the indeclinable Semitic name Κεδρών, said to mean "dark"—a fitting label for the brook's turbid waters.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament and the manuscripts disagree over whether to read "Kidron" or "of the cedars," so the form is genuinely uncertain.

definition: Describing something of great worth—either costly and valuable, or held in high honor and esteem.
article: τίμιος describes something prized, whether in literal money value or in the regard people hold for it. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 14 times and is rendered "precious" in 11 of them (92%), covering everything from costly stones to a farmer's valued crop in James 5:7. The Septuagint mostly uses it for the Hebrew יָקָר (21 times), and the everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth range—one writer asks for corn to be sent so he won't have to buy it at a high price (τίμιον). Alongside the dominant "precious" sense, the lexica note a related meaning of "honored" or "esteemed," as in Hebrews 13:4 where marriage is to be held in honor.
caution: The corpus overwhelmingly renders it "precious," but the lexica document a genuine secondary sense of "honored/esteemed" that the measured data barely registers.

definition: A selfish drive to push your own interests or build your own faction, putting personal gain ahead of others.
article: ἐριθεία describes a self-centered ambition — the drive to advance yourself or gather your own following at others' expense. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "selfish ambition" in 4 of 7 occurrences (80%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 75% of the time; the remaining cases shade toward "self-seeking." Interestingly, the word's roots lie in ordinary working life: Moulton-Milligan trace it to a verb meaning "work for hire," connected to ἔριθος, a wool-weaver attested in Koine papyri, before it developed the sense of scheming for personal advantage.
caution: The word appears only 7 times and 2 of those were absorbed into surrounding phrasing, so its precise range is somewhat thin and the older glosses (KJV's "strife, contention") reflect a different emphasis than the measured "selfish ambition."

definition: A person who eats too much; a glutton.
article: φάγος describes someone who overeats — a glutton. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times as an accusation thrown at Jesus (Matthew 11:19 and Luke 7:34), where it is paired with οἰνοπότης, "drunkard." The lexicons (Strong's, Abbott-Smith, Dodson) all define it as "glutton," and Moulton-Milligan confirms the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Although the lexicons consistently gloss it "glutton," the Majority Standard Bible renders both of its only two occurrences as "drunkard," so translation choice and lexical sense diverge here.

definition: A question word asking in what way or by what means something happens or could happen.
article: πῶς is the everyday interrogative adverb for asking "how" or "in what way," and it dominates: in 82 of its uses (92%) the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it "how." Beyond plain questions, it can introduce a question someone asks or push back on a claim ("how can you say...?"), and it sometimes works in indirect speech meaning roughly "that" or "how." It can also carry an exclamatory force—"how much!"—which a papyrus comedy fragment captures vividly: "oh, how thoroughly wicked is human nature!"

definition: The restoration of a broken relationship, bringing two estranged parties back into peace and favor with each other.
article: In the New Testament καταλλαγή always means reconciliation—the restoring of a relationship that had been broken, used by Paul of how God brings people back into his favor. It appears only 4 times, all rendered "reconciliation" by the Majority Standard Bible (the lone variation in Romans 5:11 simply reflects the surrounding phrase about rejoicing). Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri preserve an older, more concrete sense: in a business account from 267 BC the word means "exchange," the literal idea behind the figurative "restoration to favor."
caution: This is a rare word with only 4 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, so its measured range rests on thin evidence.

definition: An adverb meaning at a great distance, used of physical space or figuratively of being far from something.
article: μακράν means "far" or "a long way off," describing distance either literally or figuratively. It's grammatically the feminine accusative of the adjective μακρός ("long"), with the word for "road" (ὁδός) implied — so it originally meant something like "a long way." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "far" 67% of the time and "distance" 22%, and it can also stretch metaphorically, as when Jesus tells a scribe he is "not far from the kingdom" (Mark 12:34). It's solidly attested in everyday Koine papyri, where one third-century document uses it of a smith being "a long way from us."

definition: What someone wills or wishes — a purpose, intention, or desire, often referring to God's purpose.
article: θέλημα refers to a person's will — both the act of willing and the thing that is willed. In the New Testament it appears 64 times, very often about God's will: roughly 43% of the time the Majority Standard Bible renders it in phrases like 'thy will be done,' and in fact about 50 of those 64 occurrences are absorbed into English phrasing rather than translated as a single word. A striking detail is that Moulton-Milligan note the word is 'almost unknown outside biblical and church writings,' appearing in a fourth-century Christian charm that prays for things to be done 'in accordance with thy will.' In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew chephets, meaning delight or desire (16 times).
caution: The senses (willed thing, God's will, desire) shade into one another, and the bulk of occurrences are blended into phrasing rather than rendered by a distinct word.

definition: A person who watches over and is responsible for a group, especially a leader entrusted with caring for a church community.
article: ἐπίσκοπος literally means "one who watches over," combining the ideas of supervision and care. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, most often (60%) for a church "overseer" (often translated "bishop"), once paired with deacons in Philippians 1:1, and once in 1 Peter 2:25 picturing Christ as the guardian of straying souls. The most striking evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions: Deissmann showed the word was a common civil and religious title long before Christians used it, including a council of five ἐπίσκοποι in Rhodes and an ἐπίσκοπος among temple officials of Apollo.
caution: With only 5 occurrences, the "sense" counted in 1 Peter 2:25 reflects how a whole phrase was translated rather than a distinct meaning of the word itself.

definition: The act of going into a place, or the entrance through which one goes in.
article: εἴσοδος combines "into" (εἰς) with "road, way" (ὁδός) and covers both the act of entering and, sometimes, the place where you enter. In the New Testament it appears 5 times across 4 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it three measurable ways — a welcome, a visit, and entering a place — though two of its five occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday papyri are the most telling evidence: there εἴσοδος is constantly used for the entrance of a temple or house, as in a document securing the "entrances and exits" of a building.
caution: Sources disagree on whether some New Testament uses mean the act of entering or the physical place of entrance, as Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan both note.

definition: Describing someone who loves God, devoted to him rather than to pleasure.
article: φιλόθεος combines the words for "loving" (φίλος) and "God" (θεός), so it literally means "loving God" or "God-loving." It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:4, where it stands in contrast to those who are "lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God." The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Aristotle used it too, so it was at home in ordinary Greek as well as Scripture.

definition: To think something over in one's mind, or to talk it over with others, often weighing or reasoning toward a conclusion.
article: This verb covers both private mental reasoning and back-and-forth discussion with other people, with the dividing line often being whether someone is thinking "in their heart" or talking "with one another." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 16 times across 4 books; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "thinking" 4 times (29%) and "discussing among" 2 times (14%), with the rest scattered across many phrasings. A striking detail from the papyri: Moulton-Milligan note that the word and its noun were standard terms in Egyptian documents for the conventus, the Roman governor's traveling judicial circuit, showing its everyday administrative weight beyond mere private musing.
caution: The English renderings are highly varied and split between "thinking" and "discussing," so context, not the word alone, decides whether silent reflection or open debate is meant.

definition: Showing tender compassion or mercy toward others, especially as a quality of God's character.
article: This adjective describes someone full of compassion and mercy. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice rendered "merciful" and once shifted to the noun "mercy" (James 5:11). In the Septuagint it shows up 15 times and most often translates the Hebrew word רַחוּם (8×), a term tied to deep, tender compassion. Abbott-Smith notes it was originally a poetic word in classical Greek, used in place of the more common ἐλεήμων.

definition: To sit or be seated, and by extension to stay settled or dwell in a place.
article: κάθημαι basically means to sit or be seated, and the corpus bears this out: about 79% of its 89 Byzantine occurrences are rendered "sitting" or "seated." The word can stretch from a literal posture to the idea of remaining or dwelling somewhere, which is why the King James glosses include "dwell" alongside "sit." In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew יָשַׁב (95 of 157 times), a verb that itself carries both "sit" and "dwell," and everyday papyri use it the same way—one document even complains that a man should not have to "sit idle."

definition: Outside, or apart from — pointing to what lies beyond, or excluding, a person or thing.
article: ἐκτός basically means "outside" — the exterior, as opposed to the inside (ἐντός). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times, but only 2 of those (67% of the rendered cases) actually become an English word like "outside"; in the other 6 it dissolves into the surrounding phrasing. The classical lexicons stretch it further than the New Testament does — used as a preposition it can mean "apart from," "except," "free from," or even "beyond hope" (ἐκτὸς ἐλπίδος in Sophocles), and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri as well.
caution: The word is rare and slippery — most New Testament occurrences carry no English word of their own, so the lexicons' broader "except/apart from" range rests more on classical and Septuagint usage than on the measured New Testament data.

definition: A person who tends and guards a flock of sheep, also used figuratively of one who leads and protects a group of people.
article: ποιμήν means a shepherd, the person who feeds, guards, and leads sheep. In the New Testament it appears 18 times and is rendered "shepherd" in 15 of them (88%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing; the word also stretches figuratively to those who lead and protect people, as when it describes Christ or Christian pastors. In the Septuagint it shows up 78 times, most often translating the Hebrew רָעָה (52×). Everyday papyri use it freely too — sometimes not flatteringly, as in one complaint about shepherds behaving lawlessly and another where a shepherd is even a lessee of sheep.

definition: A small island or islet.
article: νησίον is a diminutive of νῆσος ("island"), so it literally means a little island or islet. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:16, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as the place name "Clauda" rather than the generic "small island" found in lexicons like Abbott-Smith and Dodson. The classical lexica (citing Herodotus and Thucydides) treat it simply as a smaller version of νῆσος, equivalent to νησίς.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering as a proper name ("Clauda") reflects the specific context of Acts 27:16 rather than the word's general meaning.

definition: Enjoying a deep, fortunate state of well-being and divine favor; truly happy or blessed.
article: μακάριος describes someone who is genuinely well-off in the deepest sense—blessed, fortunate, to be envied. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "blessed" in 43 of 50 occurrences (90%), and in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew אַשְׁרֵי (16×), the word behind those famous "Oh, the happiness of...!" sayings in the Psalms. Moulton-Milligan notes it points to a state of true well-being in Hebrew thought, which is why Jesus' Beatitudes use it (Matthew 5:3); interestingly, it is also applied directly to God himself in passages like 1 Timothy 1:11 and 6:15.

definition: Quirinius, the Roman official whose governorship of Syria Luke ties to the census at Jesus' birth.
article: Κυρήνιος is a proper name of Latin origin (Quirinius, sometimes spelled Cyrenius), referring to a Roman official linked to the census in Luke 2:2, its only appearance in the New Testament. Because it names a real person, it has no range of meaning beyond that identification. Interestingly, inscriptions discovered in the early twentieth century have been used to study Quirinius's governorship of Syria and the date of the Nativity, with one scholar dating it to roughly 8 BC.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the manuscripts preserve several different spellings of the name.

definition: To walk about among people—pictured as God moving and living in the midst of his people.
article: This compound stacks "in" and "walk about" to mean moving around in a place or living among people. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:16, which itself quotes the Greek Old Testament, and shows up 7 times across 6 Septuagint books. The most telling evidence is its Hebrew background: it usually renders הָלַך ("walk"), as in Leviticus 26:12, where God promises to walk among his people—the exact phrasing Paul borrows.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence (a direct Old Testament quotation), the word's range in the New Testament rests almost entirely on Septuagint usage.

definition: Describing someone who has mastery over themselves, exercising self-control over their appetites and conduct.
article: This word literally means having power or mastery over something, and from there it came to describe a person who is master of themselves—self-controlled. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:8, where it lists a quality required of an elder. Interestingly, everyday papyri show the more literal sense: one document from 114 B.C. describes attackers who had "gained power over" their victims, and others speak of someone becoming legally "in possession of" deeds or property. The lexicon Abbott-Smith traces this same range from "strong, powerful" to "master of" to "self-controlled."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense there rests on a single verse, even though wider Koine usage is well attested.

definition: A connecting word meaning "then" or "next," marking the next step in a sequence of time, events, or items in a list.
senseLabels: next step in time or sequence
article: εἶτα is a small connecting particle that signals "then" or "next," whether marking the next stage in time, the next event, or the next item in an enumeration. Its meaning is so structural that in 8 of its 16 New Testament occurrences it simply gets absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own. A nice everyday touch: Moulton-Milligan note that grammarians praised εἶτα as proper Greek over the "barbarous" εἶτεν, and it shows up frequently in ordinary papyri — including one where a robbery victim describes what happened "afterwards."
caution: The measured renderings ("all," "appeared") reflect how surrounding phrasing was translated rather than the word's own meaning, so the lexicons' "then/next" sense is the more reliable guide here.

definition: A clay roof tile, or by extension the tiled roof made of such tiles.
article: In the New Testament κέραμος appears just once, in Luke 5:19, where friends lower a paralyzed man through the tiles of a roof—and every translation surveyed renders it "tiles." The word's broader range covers fired clay more generally: the lexica list potter's clay and earthenware vessels, and in a papyrus from around 245 B.C. it means a clay jar. Everyday Koine documents support the "tiling" sense seen in Luke; building accounts for a temple at Delos (279 B.C.) list "timber and tile" together.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, though the sources agree on the roofing-tile meaning here.

definition: To use up or destroy something completely, especially by burning.
article: καταναλίσκω means to use up entirely or consume completely, a forceful compound built from κατά and ἀναλίσκω. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 12:29, where God is described as a "consuming" fire, and the Septuagint uses it 14 times, chiefly to translate the Hebrew verb "to eat" or devour. A papyrus letter from the fourth century AD shows the everyday force of the word: a wife complains that her husband "used up" the family's property, while an inscription speaks of interest money being spent on teachers.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense here rests mostly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than broad biblical usage.

definition: A collective term for clothes or clothing, often the fine or costly kind worn as outward attire.
article: ἱματισμός is a collective word for clothing or apparel, appearing 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament. Across all its uses it simply means "clothes," though Abbott-Smith notes it usually points to sumptuous or fine attire — fitting for passages like Luke 7:25 about those in soft, splendid dress. The everyday papyri confirm this ordinary sense: one document (c. B.C. 245) urges that a person "wear as fine clothes as possible," while contracts list it alongside food, household goods, and poll-tax as a basic provision. In the Septuagint it occurs 25 times, rendering several Hebrew words for garments, including שִׂמְלָה (3×).

definition: Nereus, the personal name of a Christian greeted by Paul in his letter to the Romans.
article: Nereus is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:15, where Paul greets a Christian by this name. Moulton-Milligan note that the name was not limited to Rome but turns up in inscriptions from Athens and from Ancyra in Galatia, showing it was a common Koine name. In Greek mythology the same name belonged to a sea-god (the father of the Nereids), and the word may derive from a root meaning "wet," but in the New Testament it is simply the name of a person.
caution: The translation data show "Julia" rendered for this verse, which looks like a digest mismatch, but the lexical sources agree the word is the personal name Nereus.

definition: The sea or any large body of water, including inland lakes like the Sea of Galilee, as opposed to dry land.
senseLabels: the sea or a large lake
article: θάλασσα means the sea, used 91 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "sea" in 98% of cases. Its range is broad: it covers the open Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and inland freshwater lakes such as the Sea of Galilee, since Greek used the same word where Hebrew used יָם—which it translates 306 times in the Septuagint. An everyday papyrus letter even thanks the god Serapis for rescue when the writer was "in danger at sea," and another asks someone to buy fish "from the sea," showing how ordinary the word was in daily Koine.

definition: To coat a surface with lime or plaster, giving it a white finish.
article: κονιάω means to whitewash or plaster a surface, literally coating it with lime to make it white. In the New Testament it appears only twice and is rendered "whitewashed" both times—once of decorated tombs (Matthew 23:27) and once figuratively of a hypocrite, a "whitewashed wall" (Acts 23:3). The everyday, non-theological nature of the word shows up clearly in the papyri, where it turns up in temple building accounts from Delos describing the plastering of an altar, and the related noun κονιατής simply means "plasterer."
caution: With only two New Testament uses and three in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on the meaning.

definition: An adverb meaning that something happens many times or on frequent, repeated occasions.
article: πολλάκις is a straightforward adverb built from πολύς ("much, many") that means "often" or "many times." Its range is narrow and consistent: in the Byzantine New Testament's 18 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "often" in every case where it gets its own English word (8 times, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100%), while in 5 of 18 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The everyday papyri show the same plain sense, as in an Oxyrhynchus letter saying "the man about whom you write to me so often."

definition: The eyebrow, and by extension the jutting edge or brow of a hill.
senseLabels: brow or edge of a hill
article: Literally ὀφρῦς means the eyebrow, but the New Testament uses it figuratively for the edge or brow of a hill. It appears only once in the Byzantine NT, at Luke 4:29, where the crowd takes Jesus to the brow of the hill to throw him down. The everyday papyri make its literal meaning vivid: personal descriptions of people regularly note things like "a scar on his left eyebrow," and the Septuagint uses it once in Leviticus 14:9 for the Hebrew גָּב in describing the eyebrow.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in biblical usage cannot be firmly measured.

definition: To be overwhelmed with amazement, or (more rarely) to be driven out of one's mind.
article: This verb literally means to put or stand something out of its place, and in the New Testament it almost always describes people being knocked off balance emotionally — utterly amazed. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "astounded" in 12 of its 17 occurrences (71%), and the BSB agrees in every case. The classical lexica note a stronger secondary use: to drive someone out of their senses, or to be "beside oneself," even mad (as in Mark 3:21 and 2 Corinthians 5:13). One striking detail from everyday papyri: the same word was the standard legal term for resigning or handing over property, as when a woman "resigns" her inheritance share to another party.
caution: The measured data captures only the "amazed" sense; the "out of one's mind" meaning is well attested in the lexica but not reflected in the dominant renderings here.

definition: Phoenicia, a coastal region in the Roman province of Syria, north of Palestine.
article: Φοινίκη is a place name for Phoenicia, a strip of coastline in the Roman province of Syria north of Palestine. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts (11:19, 15:3, 21:2), where every occurrence is rendered "Phoenicia." Interestingly, the name derives from G5404 (φοῖνιξ, the palm tree), which is why older sources like Strong's call it the "palm-country."
caution: The Septuagint Hebrew counterparts listed (מָן, מָסַס, עֲבוּר, סָחַר) don't correspond to a place name, suggesting these may reflect a different word or textual quirk rather than the proper noun.

definition: The number twenty, used to count people, objects, or measurements.
article: εἴκοσι is simply the cardinal number "twenty," appearing 11 times in the Byzantine New Testament. It's an indeclinable word, meaning its form never changes regardless of grammatical role, and it shows up heavily in the Septuagint (260 times), where it almost always renders the Hebrew word for twenty. A nice detail from the papyri: scribes consistently spelled it εἴκοσι rather than εἴκοσιν, even before a vowel — Moulton-Milligan found only one exception in everyday documents.
caution: The measured sense "twenty down" simply reflects passages (mostly in Revelation) where twenty is part of a larger count like the twenty-four elders, not a separate meaning.

definition: The day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday, the Sabbath-eve.
article: Προσάββατον combines πρό ("before") and σάββατον ("Sabbath") to mean simply the day before the Sabbath. In its single New Testament appearance (Mark 15:42), it serves as an explanation of the word παρασκευή for non-Jewish readers. It is rare overall, turning up only here, in Judith 8:6, and in the titles of two Psalms in the Septuagint, where it once renders a Hebrew word for "song."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and is sparsely attested elsewhere, so its range cannot be measured broadly.

definition: Frankincense, the fragrant resin (or the tree producing it) used as incense and a valued trade item.
article: λίβανος refers to frankincense, an aromatic resin used as incense; in classical Greek it could also mean the tree itself, though the New Testament uses it for the substance. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament—once as a gift to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11) and once among the luxury cargo of Babylon (Revelation 18:13). The word is of Semitic origin and renders Hebrew לְבוֹנָה 17 of 18 times in the Septuagint, and everyday papyri confirm it as a common item in spice and sacrifice lists, including one writer asking a friend to mail him some incense.
caution: The two measured 'senses' both simply mean frankincense, differing only by context (gift versus trade good), so this is essentially one meaning attested in just two New Testament verses.

definition: The quality of being morally pure, clean, and blameless in one's conduct.
article: ἁγνότης names the state of being pure or morally clean, often carrying the sense of blamelessness or chastity. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in the critical SBLGNT), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "purity" every time, as in 2 Corinthians 6:6. Interestingly, the word also turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions: an Argos inscription pairs it with δικαιοσύνης ("righteousness"), showing it described real-world moral reputation, not just religious devotion.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only once (or twice in the critical text), so its full range cannot be measured confidently.

definition: To go or come into a place, person, or situation — to enter.
article: εἰσέρχομαι simply means to go in or enter, whether a house, a city, or a situation. It's one of the most common motion verbs in the New Testament, appearing 196 times, and translators render it flexibly — "enter," "entered," "went," or "come" — depending on context, since English needs different words for the same Greek action. The word stretches naturally beyond physical doorways: it describes demons taking possession of a person, food going into the mouth, thoughts entering the mind, and even entering into temptation. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly stands in for the Hebrew בּוֹא ("come/go"), used 512 of 620 times, and everyday papyri show it for ordinary acts like coming in from the field or even "entering upon" a lawsuit.

definition: A person who teaches or trains others, and by extension one who corrects or disciplines.
article: παιδευτής describes someone who instructs and trains, coming from the verb παιδεύω. It appears only twice in the New Testament: once rendered "instructor" (Romans 2:20), and once absorbed into the phrasing rather than a single English word. The lexicons stretch the range a bit wider than the measured data: Abbott-Smith and Dodson note a second sense, "a corrector" or "one who disciplines" (as in Hebrews 12:9), and the word's only Septuagint use translates a Hebrew word tied to discipline. The papyri show it as an ordinary term for a paid teacher, as in an inscription about wages owed to teachers.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the disciplinary sense rests on the lexicons rather than the measured renderings, so treat the range as tentative.

definition: To become a parent — for a man, to father a child; for a woman, to give birth — and figuratively, to produce or bring something about.
article: γεννάω covers the whole act of bringing a child into the world: said of the father it means "to beget" and of the mother "to give birth," with the passive meaning "to be born." In the Byzantine New Testament these two ideas dominate — "father" 39 times (46%) and "born" 37 times (44%) — with rarer renderings clustering around the same family relationships. It can also stretch metaphorically, as when Paul says he "fathered" a convert (1 Corinthians 4:15) or warns that arguments "breed" quarrels (2 Timothy 2:23). The everyday papyri confirm this plain sense: birth registrations use it in fixed formulas like "we register the son who was born to us."

definition: The quality of being old or outdated, especially something belonging to a former, superseded order.
article: παλαιότης means "oldness" — the state of being old, antiquated, or obsolete. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 7:6, where it describes the "oldness of the letter," and the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on this sense. It is built from the adjective παλαιός ("old"), turning that quality into a noun. Notably, the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase loosely as "way," but the underlying word itself simply means "oldness."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single context.

definition: An urging word meaning "come here!" used to summon someone, and occasionally a time-word meaning "up to now."
article: At its core δεῦρο is a one-word command—"come!" or "come here!"—used with someone you're calling to yourself, as when Jesus says "come, follow Me" (Matthew 19:21) or calls out "Lazarus, come forth!" (John 11:43). In the Byzantine New Testament the MSB renders it "come" in 3 of 9 cases, while the other occurrences get folded into the surrounding phrasing. It also carries a temporal sense, "up to now," and the papyri nicely confirm this: documents from around A.D. 150–346 use phrases like "up to the present" (μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο), strikingly close to Paul's own wording.
