caution: With only 9 occurrences and just 3 directly rendered "come," the measured data is thin, and the lexicons add a temporal sense ("now, hitherto") that the Byzantine count barely captures.

definition: To lead someone by the hand, especially guiding a person who cannot see for themselves.
article: χειραγωγέω means to take someone by the hand and guide them along. In the New Testament both of its 2 occurrences (Acts 9:8 and 22:11) describe Paul, blinded after his encounter on the Damascus road, being led by the hand. Everyday Koine papyri use it more figuratively too: one document from 164 B.C. speaks of even an inexperienced person being "guided by the facts themselves," and the Septuagint uses it once in Tobit 11:16 (with a Hebrew counterpart in Judges 16:26 in some manuscripts).
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences, both describing the same situation, so the broader figurative range rests mainly on outside sources.

definition: Foolish or unbelievable talk; nonsense that seems like an empty, made-up story.
article: λῆρος means silly talk or nonsense — the kind of unbelievable story you'd dismiss out of hand. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 24:11, where the apostles treated the women's report of the resurrection as an "idle tale." The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri: one document from around AD 100 uses the related verb to mean "don't talk nonsense about your threshing," and it also turns up in 4 Maccabees 5:10 in the Septuagint.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range can't be measured; the digest's lone measured rendering ("seemed") reflects how Luke 24:11 is phrased rather than the word's core meaning of "nonsense."

definition: A matter being debated or investigated, especially a disputed question or point of controversy.
article: ζήτημα refers to a question, dispute, or subject under inquiry—the kind of contested point people argue or investigate. It comes from the verb ζητέω ("to seek"), and fittingly it shows up only in Acts in the New Testament, always describing matters being debated (it appears 5 times). The English renderings in the digest ("question," "own," "since") mostly reflect how translators reshape the surrounding phrase rather than four distinct meanings, so the core sense stays unified. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one Oxyrhynchus document speaks of being held accountable "in any inquiry concerning unknown facts," and it could even mean a legal "claim."
caution: The four "measured senses" mostly reflect different English phrasings rather than genuinely separate meanings—the word consistently denotes a question or disputed matter.

definition: An adverb meaning "to that place" or simply "there," pointing toward a location.
article: This adverb means "thither" or "there" — directing attention to a particular place. Its range is narrow, and in everyday Koine papyri it often simply means "there" (equivalent to ἐκεῖ) rather than indicating motion toward a place. In its lone Septuagint appearance (Job 39:29) it renders the Hebrew word for "there," and in one of its two New Testament uses (Acts 22:5) it is folded into the surrounding phrasing so it gets no English word of its own.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: The deep part of the sea, especially its bottom or open waters far from shore.
article: βυθός refers to the deep sea — either the very bottom or the open, deep water away from land. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:25, where Paul says he spent a night and a day adrift in the deep after a shipwreck. The Septuagint uses it six times, often translating the Hebrew מְצוּלָה ("depths"), and the everyday papyri attest the word too, including a magic formula at Oxyrhynchus that calls upon "the gods in the deep."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from that single use.

definition: Er, a man's name in the genealogy of Jesus, listed as an ancestor in Luke's record.
article: Ἤρ is simply the personal name Er, appearing once in the New Testament (Luke 3:28) as one of Jesus' ancestors. The word is indeclinable in Greek, borrowed directly from the Hebrew name עֵר, which the Septuagint renders eight times. Interestingly, in the Septuagint the same Greek spelling also stands in for two other Hebrew words (צְפוֹן twice and אֶשֶׁד once), showing how a short name-form could overlap with unrelated terms.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single passage.

definition: Sharing in another person's feelings, especially their suffering; sympathetic and compassionate toward others.
article: συμπαθής describes a person who feels alongside others, sharing in their experiences and especially their suffering — the root literally combines "with" and "suffer/feel." It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:8, where believers are urged to be of one mind and sympathetic toward one another. Everyday Koine inscriptions use it the same way: one decree praises the Roman senate for treating a city "most sympathetically" (συμπαθέστατα), showing this was warm, practical language outside the Bible too. Classical lexicons note a second flavor — "exciting sympathy" — seen in Job 29:25, but the New Testament use is straightforwardly "feeling with others."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse, and the "Finally" rendering simply reflects the opening of that sentence rather than the word's own meaning.

definition: The tossing or rolling surge of the sea, especially in a storm, used figuratively for turmoil and dismay.
article: σάλος names the heaving, restless tossing of the sea in rough weather, and by extension the agitation or dismay that such turmoil evokes. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 21:25, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "dismay" — the sea's roaring and surging stand for human anxiety. The classical lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) stress the literal "rolling swell of the sea," so there is a slight gap between the measured figurative sense and the dictionaries' more concrete picture; the Septuagint uses it seven times across four books, translating several different Hebrew words like מוֹצָא and זַעַף.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense range there rests on a single verse, and the measured "dismay" leans more figurative than the lexicons' literal "sea-tossing."

definition: The act of using something up completely, until it is consumed or destroyed.
article: ἀπόχρησις describes the using-up or consuming of something through its intended use. It appears only once in the Greek Bible, at Colossians 2:22, where it refers to rules about things that are destined to perish as they are used. The word comes from the verb ἀποχράομαι (to use to the full), and the papyri show a sharper edge: an edict from A.D. 49 (OGIS 665.16) uses the related verb for officials who greedily abuse their authority, so the term can carry a sense of misuse, not just neutral consumption.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lexicons split between neutral 'using up' (Strong's, Moulton-Milligan) and negative 'abuse, misuse' (Abbott-Smith, Dodson), so its exact shade is uncertain.

definition: An adverb meaning from above (from a higher place or from heaven), or from the start, or over again.
article: ἄνωθεν is an adverb built on ἄνω ("up"), and its core idea is "from above" — whether from a higher physical place or from heaven, as in James 1:17, 3:15, and 3:17. The wider New Testament range stretches further than the measured data shows: lexicons also list "from the beginning" (Luke 1:3, Acts 26:5) and "anew/again" (John 3:3, 7), the latter sense being famously debated. The everyday papyri make the spatial sense vivid: a postal record from around 255 B.C. uses ἄνωθεν for goods delivered "from the upper country," paired with κάτωθεν, "from the lower country."
caution: Only one sense ("above") was measurable here, and lexicons disagree over whether the John 3 uses mean "again" or "from above."

definition: Thessalonica, an important city in the Roman province of Macedonia in Asia Minor.
article: Θεσσαλονίκη is simply the proper name of Thessalonica, a major city of Macedonia (modern Saloniki). It appears 5 times across 3 New Testament books, and the lexicons agree completely on its meaning. Strong's notes the name derives from a Thessalian element plus νίκη ("victory").

definition: Hard to understand or grasp mentally; difficult to comprehend.
article: δυσνόητος describes something that is difficult to understand or mentally grasp, built from the prefix meaning "hard" plus a root tied to perceiving or thinking. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 3:16, where it refers to certain things in Paul's letters that are hard to comprehend. Notably, the Majority Standard Bible's rendering at that verse landed on the word "parts," reflecting the phrase "some things hard to understand," while the classical and lexical sources (Strong's, KJV, Abbott-Smith) consistently define the word itself as "hard to be understood."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from multiple uses.

definition: An adverb meaning "here" or "in this place," pointing to a specific spot.
article: This little word means "here" or "in this place"—it marks a specific location. Though it looks like a form of αὐτός ("he/it"), it functions as an adverb of place, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "here" in its one measured occurrence (Matthew 26:36, Jesus telling his disciples to wait while he prayed). Notably, 3 of its 4 Byzantine appearances get absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, and in the Septuagint it pairs with Hebrew terms like פֹּה ("here").
caution: Evidence is thin—only 4 occurrences, with several appearing only in alternate manuscript readings, so the picture is limited.

definition: To sail toward shore and land, bringing a boat in to a destination by water.
senseLabels: to sail to shore and land
article: καταπλέω describes sailing in from open water to land at a place, as when Jesus and the disciples "sailed to the region of the Gerasenes" in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 8:26). The most telling detail comes from the papyri: this was the standard word for sailing down the Nile to Alexandria, with everyday letters using it for arriving in a city or port by boat. The Majority Standard Bible renders its one occurrence simply with "lake," though the verb itself carries the fuller idea of sailing in and putting ashore.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse, with most of its breadth drawn from outside papyri evidence.

definition: A person from Damascus; a resident of the city of Damascus.
article: Δαμασκηνός is the adjective meaning "of Damascus" or "Damascene," used to describe people from that city. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:32, where Paul mentions the Damascenes during his escape from the city. The word is built directly from Δαμασκός, the name of Damascus itself, and the standard lexicons agree it simply identifies someone connected to that place.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: To swim, or properly to dive or plunge into water.
senseLabels: to swim or dive in water
article: This verb properly means "to dive" or "plunge into water," but in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 27:43) it means "swim," describing shipwreck survivors heading for shore. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and the medical writer Galen used it for invalids exercising in a swimming-bath. Note that the measured rendering label here shows "thwarted," which does not match the word's actual meaning and appears to be a data artifact rather than a genuine sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering label ("thwarted") is inconsistent with the lexical evidence, so treat the corpus data with care.

definition: A complete, settled inner certainty or full assurance—or, in one case, simply fullness or completeness.
article: πληροφορία describes the state of being fully convinced or completely assured, the kind of inner confidence that leaves no room for doubt. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, paired with things like understanding (Colossians 2:2), hope (Hebrews 6:11), and faith (Hebrews 10:22), where most translations render it as 'full assurance.' Notably, this word never shows up in classical Greek writers or the Septuagint, and Moulton-Milligan could find just one instance in the papyri (P Giss I.87)—and that one is damaged—so it seems to have developed mainly within early Christian Greek.
caution: Sources note the sense may shade toward objective 'fullness' rather than subjective 'assurance' in Hebrews 6:11, so the precise range is somewhat disputed.

definition: To carefully think over or weigh something in your mind, considering it attentively.
article: This verb means to consider something carefully, almost like reckoning up or balancing accounts in your mind. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 12:3, where readers are urged to think over Jesus' endurance. Moulton-Milligan note its oldest sense across the word-group was arithmetical—'reckoned up' or 'told off,' as in a B.C. 116 papyrus—and suggest that calculating metaphor was still felt when the word came to mean broader contemplation.
caution: The measured-sense label 'hostility' looks like a tagging artifact; the actual evidence and lexicons all point to 'consider attentively,' and with only one NT occurrence the data is thin.

definition: Decay, ruin, or corruption — the process by which something breaks down, rots, or perishes, whether physically or morally.
article: φθορά names the breakdown of something into ruin — physical decay, rottenness, and destruction, and by extension moral corruption. Its range is fairly wide: it can mean the perishable state of bodies (set against eternal life in Galatians, and contrasted with imperishability in 1 Corinthians) as well as moral decay (2 Peter). The everyday papyri are a nice window here: the word shows up in a land lease meaning simple 'loss' and in another document tallying the death of cattle, so ordinary Koine used it for plain material loss before any theological weight.
caution: The measured rendering data is thin — in 6 of 9 New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into English phrasing rather than translated as a single word, so the sense breakdown rests mainly on the lexicons.

definition: To leap or jump up physically, or figuratively of water to spring up and gush forth.
article: This verb covers literal jumping—a lame man leaping to his feet (Acts 3:8; 14:10)—and the vivid image of water springing up like a fountain (John 4:14). Though it appears only 3 times in the New Testament, each occurrence shows a different shade of meaning, splitting evenly across leaping and gushing. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document describes a thief who had "sprung into" a farmstead under cover of night, the same energetic sense of a sudden upward or inward movement.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences spread across three distinct renderings, the precise force in any one passage rests on thin evidence.

definition: A sharp point that pierces — the sting of an insect, the spike of a goad, or, figuratively, what makes death painful.
article: κέντρον names a sharp piercing point: literally the sting of a creature (Revelation 9:10) or the spike of a driving-goad, and figuratively the painful sting of death (1 Corinthians 15:55–56). The Byzantine New Testament uses it 4 times, rendered "sting" in two-thirds of cases. Abbott-Smith notes a further sense, "goad," used in Acts 26:14, and Moulton-Milligan adds a striking touch from a Byzantine tomb inscription where the word means "desire" — the ceaseless sting of love for a departed soul.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and a Septuagint pattern that translates several different Hebrew words, the exact range is thin and partly drawn from sources outside the measured senses.

definition: To look at something carefully and deliberately, to behold or watch closely with attention.
article: θεάομαι means to look at something with careful, deliberate attention — more than a casual glance. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "seen" in 21 of 24 occurrences (91%), and in the New Testament Abbott-Smith notes it always carries a literal, physical sense of vision that interprets its object. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from a 2nd-century BC papyrus from the temple of Serapis at Memphis, where someone who received a vision writes that he "beheld" it, hinting at the deeper, contemplative weight the word can carry.

definition: Scarlet or crimson, a bright red color produced from a dye made from the kermes insect.
article: Κόκκινος describes the bright red color scarlet, and the Byzantine New Testament renders it that way in all 6 occurrences, often referring to dyed clothing or fabric. The word comes from κόκκος, the "berry"-like body of the kermes insect from which the dye was made. The Septuagint uses it 43 times, most often translating the Hebrew שָׁנִי (26×), and everyday papyri confirm its ordinary use—one second-century pawnshop account even lists a "scarlet shirt" (κιτὼν κόκκινος), and another papyrus pairs it with purple just as Revelation 17:4 does.

definition: A particle of strong affirmation used to say "yes" or to confirm and agree with something stated.
article: ναί is a simple, emphatic "yes" — the natural Koine way to affirm a statement or answer a question positively. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 34 times across 11 books and is rendered "Yes" in 70% of cases, with another 13% as "Yes" in the sense of answering. It ranges from plain affirmation to solemn confirmation, and can be doubled for emphasis (ναὶ ναί, "yes, yes") as in James 5:12. Notably, the word was so much a part of everyday speech that it shows up in ordinary papyri — including the record of a Senate proceeding where a clerk simply says "ναί" — and it even survives in Modern Greek.

definition: A person owned as a slave or bound servant, lower in status than free people and masters.
article: δοῦλον is a form of the noun δοῦλος, meaning a slave or servant—someone owned as property or otherwise bound to serve another. Abbott-Smith notes the word can also be used figuratively, in a bad sense for moral or spiritual bondage and in a good sense for a devoted minister, though those usages come from the wider δοῦλος evidence rather than this specific form. This particular form is very rare in the surveyed corpus, appearing 0 times in the Byzantine New Testament and only once in the Septuagint.
caution: Evidence for this exact form is extremely thin—no Byzantine NT occurrences and just one Septuagint use—so its meaning is inferred from the parent word δοῦλος.

definition: Describing someone or something foreign, unfamiliar, or strange; as a noun, an outsider, guest, or host bound by hospitality.
article: ξένος covers the idea of being foreign or unfamiliar—whether a person from elsewhere or a teaching that sounds strange. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "strangers" in 5 of its 14 occurrences (56%), with the other half folded into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. Beyond "stranger," the word stretches both ways within hospitality: it can mean the guest or, surprisingly, the host (Romans 16:23). Everyday papyri show the same flavor of being away from home—one writer reassures his family, "do not be anxious about me because I am away from home... I am not a stranger to those here."
caution: While "foreigner/stranger" is well attested, the secondary senses (host, or something "strange/novel") rest on only a handful of passages, so context decides the meaning.

definition: A state of peace—whether freedom from war, harmony between people, or the inner well-being and security of a person.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament εἰρήνη appears 92 times, and translators render it "peace" in 89 of them (99%)—a strikingly stable word. But that single English word covers a wide range: freedom from war between nations, concord between people, and a deeper sense of security and total well-being. That last shade comes straight from its Hebrew background: in the Septuagint it most often translates שָׁלוֹם (162 times), which is why greetings like "go in peace" carry the rich meaning of a person's whole welfare, not just calm.

definition: Relating to everyday life and its ordinary, practical affairs—the concerns of daily living in the present world.
article: βιωτικός describes things that belong to ordinary, everyday existence—the practical business and concerns of daily life. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament across 2 books, and in 2 of those cases the translators fold it into a phrase rather than rendering it with a single English word. The papyri make its everyday flavor especially clear: documents speak of βιωτικὰ σύμβολα ("business documents") and of someone leaving home βιωτικῶν χάριν ("on business concerning his livelihood"), the very ordinary affairs of common life.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and most absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To give up hope, or alternatively to hope for something in return.
article: This rare verb, built from ἀπό ('from, back') plus ἐλπίζω ('to hope'), appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 6:35, where the Majority Standard Bible takes it to mean expecting something back. But its meaning is genuinely disputed: the classical lexica and Septuagint usage (where it appears twice, including Esther 4:17) point to 'give up in despair,' while a second tradition reads it as 'hope to receive in return.' A vivid papyrus inscription from the 2nd century AD uses the passive form to describe a sick man who had been 'given up' by everyone before a miraculous recovery.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and the lexica split between 'despair of' and 'hope to receive in return,' the precise sense here is uncertain.

definition: To be drunk or intoxicated from drinking too much alcohol.
article: μεθύω means to be drunk or intoxicated, and all of its New Testament uses point to that single core idea, whether describing someone who is drunk (4 of 6 times, 67%), people who are drunkards, or someone who gets drunk. It appears far more often in the Septuagint, where it shows up 41 times across 16 books and most commonly translates Hebrew words for drinking and being drunk (שָׁכַר 11×, שִׁכּוֹר 8×). One vivid piece of evidence comes from the papyri: a temple inscription at Abydos records a man named Nikanor scrawling that he arrived 'drunk,' showing how ordinary the word was in everyday Koine.
caution: Abbott-Smith notes the word can also be used figuratively (as in Revelation 17:2, 6), so context determines whether literal drunkenness is meant.

definition: Bread, the baked food made from grain, whether spoken of as a substance or counted as individual loaves.
article: ἄρτος is the ordinary Koine word for bread, and the New Testament uses it that way 75% of the time, with another 21% referring to countable loaves. It appears 98 times across 9 books and is hugely common in the Septuagint (275×), where it almost always translates the Hebrew לָ֫חֶם (218×). Everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth usage—one private account from around the first century A.D. mentions "pure bread for the children, ½ obol"—and the lexica note it can extend to food in general or, in fixed phrases, to the temple shewbread.

definition: To see or notice something beforehand, whether in place or in time; in the middle voice, to keep something steadily before oneself.
article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to see" (ὁράω), and it ranges over both seeing ahead in time and noticing something in advance physically. In the New Testament the Byzantine text has it 3 times across 2 books, where translators render it as either foreseeing or seeing before, and one occurrence is absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Notably, the everyday Koine papyri use the middle voice to mean "pay regard to" — one document describes people "paying no regard to religious scruple," which lines up with the David quotation in Acts 2:25 where he keeps the Lord always before him.
caution: The evidence is thin — only 3 Byzantine occurrences and a low confidence tier — so the boundary between "foresee" and "keep in view" rests on very few examples.

definition: Cos, an island in the Aegean Sea, south-west of Asia Minor, mentioned as a stop on Paul's sea voyage.
article: Κῶς is a proper name for Cos, an island in the Aegean Sea off the south-west coast of Asia Minor. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:1, where it marks a stopping point on Paul's voyage. The island had a notable documentary history of its own — Moulton-Milligan point to a whole published collection of inscriptions from Cos, and the Septuagint's two uses of the same spelling actually render unrelated Hebrew words, reflecting how the form crops up in different contexts.
caution: This is a place name attested only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond identifying the island.

definition: Coming late in the season, especially the late spring rains that ripen crops before harvest.
article: ὄψιμος means "late" or "latter," describing something that comes late in the agricultural cycle. In its single New Testament appearance (James 5:7) it refers to the late rain a farmer waits for, with the word for "rain" left understood. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times and mostly translates the Hebrew מַלְקוֹשׁ (6×), the term for the latter or spring rain, and everyday papyri use it of crops or seasons being late.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "how" reflects the surrounding clause rather than the word's actual meaning of "late."

definition: A lightning flash, or by extension the bright, dazzling shine of a light source.
article: ἀστραπή means lightning — the sudden flash in the sky — and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in all 9 New Testament occurrences, whether as "lightning," "lightning flashes," or bundled with rumblings and peals in Revelation's storm imagery. By extension it can describe the dazzling brightness of a lamp, as Abbott-Smith notes for Luke 11:36. In the Septuagint it appears 17 times and most often translates the Hebrew בָּרָק (10×), the ordinary word for lightning.

definition: To bite, gnaw, or chew something, often from pain or distress.
senseLabels: to gnaw or bite in pain
article: This verb means to bite, gnaw, or chew, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Revelation 16:10, where people in agony gnaw their tongues. The Majority Standard Bible renders that occurrence as "plunged" 100% of the time, but the lexical sources (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all define it as chewing or gnawing. A nice glimpse of its everyday use comes from a magical papyrus (P. Lond. 46, 4th century AD) describing fish "gnawing with their mouths," and in the Septuagint it renders a Hebrew word at Job 30:4.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the translation "plunged" sits oddly against the lexicons' agreed meaning of "chew/gnaw," so treat the rendering with care.

definition: A hard struggle or contest, like the strenuous effort of an athlete in competition.
article: ἄθλησις is an athletic word: it names a contest or combat of the kind athletes endure, and the New Testament uses it figuratively for a tough struggle. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 10:32, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as a 'conflict.' The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the inscriptions and papyri Moulton-Milligan cites, including one that pairs it with Olympian Zeus and the games themselves, confirming its roots in real athletic competition.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Of high or noble birth, belonging to a respected family, or by extension noble-minded in character.
article: εὐγενής literally means "well born" — someone of high rank or good family. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "noble" in 2 of those (one further use is folded into the phrasing). Both Strong's and the lexicons note a figurative stretch toward "noble-minded" character (Abbott-Smith ties this to the comparative form in Acts 17:11), and the everyday papyri confirm the everyday social sense: one Oxyrhynchus document (A.D. 335) insists an adopted son not be enslaved "because he is well born and from noble free parents."
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use — so the line between "high birth" and "noble character" rests on limited data.

definition: To verbally attack someone with insults, reproaches, or taunts, often shaming them publicly.
article: ὀνειδίζω means to revile, taunt, or heap reproach on someone, whether by mocking insults or serious accusation. The Byzantine NT uses it 10 times, and though the measured renderings here are messy (the word often gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing, as in 'even' at MAT 27:44 and MAR 15:32), the consistent thread across lexicons is reproach and insult. In the Septuagint it appears 44 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew חָרַף (24×), 'to reproach'; everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, including one document charging a man with insulting a woman's fortune.
caution: The measured renderings are unusually scattered because the verb is frequently swallowed into English phrasing, so the corpus data understates its core sense of insulting or reproaching.

definition: Describing something that cannot be changed or altered—fixed, permanent, and settled for good.
article: This adjective means "unchangeable" or "fixed," and as a neuter noun (τὸ ἀμετάθετον) it means "unchangeability" itself. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews 6:17–18, where it describes the permanence of God's purpose and promise; the Septuagint uses it only twice as well, in 3 Maccabees. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions: an inscription of King Attalus II orders his decree placed in temples so it would remain "unmoved and unchangeable for all time," showing the word was everyday language for official, legally binding permanence.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament uses, both folded into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word.

definition: The act of doing good or living virtuously.
article: This noun refers to the practice of doing good — virtuous, upright action. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 4:19, where Peter urges suffering believers to keep entrusting themselves to God while continuing to do good. The standard lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on the sense "well-doing," though the measured rendering data here oddly shows "Creator," reflecting the surrounding phrase about the faithful Creator rather than the word itself.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ("Creator") conflicts with every lexicon's gloss of "well-doing," so confidence is low.

definition: To kill a person unlawfully; to commit murder.
article: φονεύω means to kill a human being unlawfully — to murder. It appears 12 times in the Byzantine New Testament, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "murder" in 7 cases (70%) and "murdered" in 2 more, often quoting the commandment "You shall not murder" (Matthew 5:21, Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20). In the Septuagint it occurs 46 times and most often translates the Hebrew רָצַח (25×), the same verb behind that commandment, and everyday Koine papyri use it plainly for real killings, as in one document describing a son who murdered his own father and fled into the wilderness.

definition: Describing something firm, secure, and reliable—able to be trusted because it stands solid and will not give way.
article: βέβαιος describes something solid and dependable, whether a literal anchor (Hebrews 6:19) or, more often, things you can count on—a promise, a hope, a covenant, or God's spoken word. In the New Testament it appears 9 times across 4 books, though in 5 of those it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. The most interesting evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri: Deissmann showed it was a legal term for property or leases that were 'guaranteed' and secure, which adds force to passages where a promise or covenant is called βέβαιος.
caution: Septuagint evidence is very thin—just one occurrence linked to Hebrew בָּזַז—so the picture rests mainly on the New Testament and papyri.

definition: A forum or marketplace—here part of the place name Forum of Appius, a station along the Appian road.
article: Φόρον is a Latin loanword (Latin "forum") meaning a marketplace or public square. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 28:15, and only as part of the place name "Forum of Appius," a station on the Appian Way; the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding phrase about Paul being "traveled" to or met at that spot. Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine documents, including a sixth-century papyrus referring to the "forum of the Thebaid," which the editors flagged as a fresh expression.
caution: This is a single-occurrence Latin loanword used only within a proper place name, so its independent meaning in the New Testament is barely attested.

definition: To remind someone of something, calling it back to their memory; in the passive, to remember or recall.
article: This verb means to bring something back to someone's mind — to remind, prompt, or call to memory. Across its 7 New Testament occurrences it consistently carries this single core meaning, with the various 'measured senses' really just reflecting differences in what is being recalled (Jesus reminding of 'everything' in John 14:26, or Paul reminding 'of these things' in 2 Timothy 2:14). The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cites letters like a 3rd-century BC papyrus saying 'remind him that he is to receive the fine olives,' showing it was the ordinary word for jogging someone's memory in daily correspondence.
caution: The five labeled senses are essentially one meaning ('remind') with different grammatical objects, not genuinely distinct senses, and the Septuagint evidence is very thin.

definition: A precious gemstone listed among the foundation stones of the heavenly city, traditionally identified as topaz or a similar bright stone.
article: τοπάζιον names a prized gemstone that appears only once in the New Testament, in the description of the New Jerusalem's foundations (Revelation 21:20). The Septuagint uses it five times, where it translates the Hebrew פִּטְדָה (3×) and also stands in for words for fine gold. Notably, ancient sources describe it as a green stone rather than what we now call topaz: Moulton-Milligan cite Pliny calling it a 'green kind,' even as the standard English translations render it 'beryl' or 'topaz.'
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and there is genuine disagreement about which stone it names—translations say 'beryl' or 'topaz' while ancient writers describe a green stone.

definition: To struggle or fight hard for something, putting up an earnest, sustained effort on its behalf.
article: This verb means to struggle or contend earnestly for something, and it appears only once in the New Testament, where Jude urges his readers to "contend" for the faith (Jude 1:3). It is built from the preposition ἐπί ("upon, for") added to ἀγωνίζομαι ("to struggle, compete"), giving the sense of throwing oneself into a fight on behalf of a cause. Abbott-Smith notes it can mean either "contend with" (in Plutarch) or "contend for," and the everyday papyri are striking: one inscription describes someone who "vied in good will towards the city," showing the word used for energetic public devotion, not just combat.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence, confidence is low and the word's full range rests mostly on outside sources like papyri and classical authors.

definition: Honey, the sweet substance made by bees, valued as food.
article: μέλι simply means honey, the sweet bee-produced food, and that single meaning runs through the whole word's range. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, twice paired with the word for "wild" to describe the wild honey John the Baptist ate (Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6), and twice in Revelation 10:9-10, where a scroll tastes as sweet as honey in the mouth. The word is ancient and widespread, attested from Homer onward and turning up in everyday Koine papyri, including a medical prescription that directs the reader to "add honey and rose-extract."
caution: The separate measured senses "eat honey" and "angel's it honey" reflect how surrounding words were rendered in particular verses, not distinct meanings of μέλι itself, which consistently means honey.

definition: Set or fixed by arrangement, especially of an appointed day or agreed-upon time.
article: τακτός describes something arranged or set in advance, most often a fixed day or time. It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 12:21) and once in the Septuagint, where it shows up in Job. The everyday papyri give the clearest picture of its range: it was common in business and legal contracts for things like a "fixed rent" or "fixed days" — practical, contractual language for what has been settled beforehand.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the biblical evidence is thin, though the papyri confirm its ordinary meaning.

definition: A contemptuous insult for someone who picks up scraps of others' ideas and repeats them like an idle babbler.
article: σπερμολόγος is a vivid term of mockery, used just once in the New Testament, when Athenian philosophers dismiss Paul in Acts 17:18. The word originally described birds pecking up seeds, then in Athenian slang became an insult for an adventurer who scraps a living in the marketplace, and from there for anyone who collects bits of information and rattles them off without depth. Interestingly, although the Berean translations render it as referring to Paul amid the "Stoic" setting, the older lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all point to "babbler" or "idle gossip" as the actual meaning, so the measured rendering and the classical sources describe different things.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ("Stoic") reflects the surrounding context rather than the word's actual meaning, which the lexicons agree is "babbler."

definition: A lake, a body of standing fresh water of any size.
article: λίμνη means a lake, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it that way every time it appears, rendered "lake" in 10 of its 11 occurrences (91%). It refers to real bodies of water such as the Lake of Gennesaret (the Sea of Galilee), but Revelation also applies it to the "lake of fire." The word turns up frequently in everyday Koine papyri, including a second-century instruction to deliver wheat to "farmers of the lake," showing it was ordinary, practical vocabulary.

definition: To be completely baffled or at a loss, unsure what to make of something puzzling.
article: διαπορέω describes being thoroughly stumped — at a complete loss over something you can't explain. All 5 Byzantine occurrences (4 in the critical text) point to a single idea of deep perplexity, whether someone is mystified by reports they hear or struggling to grasp a vision's meaning. It's a strengthened form built from ἀπορέω ("to be at a loss") with the prefix διά intensifying it, and Abbott-Smith notes it shows up only twice in the Septuagint, at Psalm 77:5 and Daniel 2:1.
caution: With just 5 occurrences and renderings that vary in the surface wording, the measured "senses" really reflect one underlying meaning.

definition: To speak insultingly or impiously, especially against God, but also to slander or revile other people.
article: βλασφημέω covers a spectrum of abusive speech, from impiously mocking God to simply slandering or reviling other people. In the New Testament it appears 35 times, most often rendered "blasphemed" (about 47%), though in 20 of 35 cases it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. The Septuagint uses it to translate Hebrew words like גָּדַף (to revile or insult), notably in Sennacherib's taunts against God in 4 Kingdoms 19; Abbott-Smith likewise splits its range into speaking profanely of sacred things and plainly reviling or slandering people.

definition: To risk or expose oneself to danger, or (in one reading) to disregard one's own safety.
article: This rare word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Philippians 2:30, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "disregarding" — describing someone who set aside concern for his own life. There's a textual wrinkle: many editions read the closely related form παραβολεύομαι, which means "to expose oneself to danger" or "hazard one's life." The most telling evidence comes from an Olbian inscription of the second century AD, cited by Deissmann, where this very word describes a man who "risked" dangers for friendship's sake all the way to the ends of the earth — proof it was ordinary Koine, not a coinage of the NT author.
caution: Evidence is thin and the sources disagree: this is a once-occurring word with a disputed spelling, and "disregard" versus "risk oneself" hinge on which textual form is read.

definition: An adverb meaning tomorrow or the following day, the time just after today.
article: αὔριον is a straightforward time word meaning "tomorrow," rendered that way in 9 of 15 New Testament occurrences (64%) and as "the next day" in 3 more (21%). It can stand alone or pair with "day" (Greek ἡμέρα), which is understood even when not written. In everyday Koine it was a common word: one papyrus letter records a boy complaining that a beer-seller told him daily "today, tomorrow" (you'll get it) but never delivered. In the Septuagint it appears 58 times, mostly translating the Hebrew מָחָר ("tomorrow"), so its meaning is well anchored.

definition: Sardis, the chief city of the region of Lydia in Asia Minor, and one of the seven churches addressed in Revelation.
article: Σάρδεις is simply the name of Sardis, the leading city of Lydia in Asia Minor, appearing 3 times in the New Testament, all in Revelation (1:11; 3:1, 4). Every source agrees it is a place name and nothing more. The two "measured senses" are an artifact of how the translation broke up phrases — the second one ("Sardis soiled," at Rev 3:4) just reflects nearby words in that verse, not a separate meaning of the name itself.
caution: The apparent second sense is a digest artifact, not a real distinct meaning; the word is consistently just the city name.

definition: Help or assistance given to someone in need; also, in a nautical context, supportive measures like ropes used to brace a ship.
article: βοήθεια means help or assistance, and that primary sense covers nearly all its uses. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and notably its two occurrences point in two directions: Hebrews 4:16 uses it for divine help in time of need, while Acts 27:17 uses it as a nautical technical term for measures taken to brace a storm-tossed ship. In the Septuagint it occurs 42 times, most often rendering Hebrew words for help such as עֶזְרָה, and the everyday papyri show it constantly at the close of petitions, where someone pleads to obtain 'help' from a patron or official.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the unusual nautical sense in Acts resting on technical interpretation, the word's full range here is thinly attested.

definition: All, the whole, every one — a strengthened form of the ordinary word for "all," covering everyone or everything in a group.
article: ἅπας is an emphatic version of the common word πᾶς ("all"), meaning all, the whole, or every single one. Across its 39 Byzantine New Testament occurrences it is rendered "all" 22 times (69%) and "everything" 9 times (28%), with the BSB independently agreeing in every case. One nice detail from the papyri: scholars note that the choice between ἅπας and πᾶς was often just a matter of euphony — in Ptolemaic documents ἅπας almost always follows a consonant, smoothing the sound. It turns up most frequently in Luke and Acts.

definition: To cover something up completely or conceal it entirely.
article: συγκαλύπτω means to veil or cover something thoroughly, combining σύν ('together/completely') with καλύπτω ('to cover'). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 12:2, where it is rendered 'disclosed' — but note that the Greek word itself means 'covered up,' so this reflects the verse's negation ('nothing is covered up that will not be revealed'). In the Septuagint it occurs 17 times in 9 books, mostly translating the Hebrew כָּסָה ('to cover'), and a papyrus inscription uses it of covering one's head in a temple ritual.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the lone measured rendering 'disclosed' reflects the verse's negation rather than the word's own meaning, which the lexica agree is 'to cover completely.'

definition: The act of healing or curing someone, restoring them to health.
article: ἴασις refers to the act of healing or curing, naming the process of restoring someone to health. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Luke and Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "healing" twice (67%) and "miraculously healed over" once (33%) — the second simply describing a healing miracle rather than marking a distinct meaning. In the Septuagint it shows up 18 times and most often translates the Hebrew word מַרְפֵּא, "a healing" or "cure"; interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that the same phrase Luke uses in 13:32 ("I perform healings") also turns up in everyday Greek writers in a more figurative sense.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence is thin, though all sources agree on the core meaning.

definition: A punishment or penalty imposed as discipline on someone who has done wrong.
article: In the New Testament this word appears just once (2 Corinthians 2:6), where it refers to a punishment or penalty the community has imposed on an offender. Interestingly, the word originally meant something quite different — "citizenship" or "franchise" — and that older sense still turns up in a third-century rescript of Severus among the papyri. The penalty meaning, by contrast, is paralleled in everyday legal documents (for example, papyri threatening triple penalties) and matches the related word ἐπιτίμιον, plus its one appearance in the Septuagint at Wisdom 3:10.
caution: This is a hapax in the New Testament with only one Septuagint parallel, and lexicons split it between two very different senses (citizenship versus penalty), so confidence in its precise range is low.

definition: To make something living, especially to bring the dead to life or give life to what had none.
article: ζωοποιέω means to give life or make alive, formed from the words for "living creature" and "to make." The various Majority Standard Bible renderings — "gives life," "gives," "life," and "made" — are really just different ways of phrasing the same core idea across its 12 New Testament occurrences. In classical Greek it could mean to produce something alive, but in the Septuagint and New Testament it consistently means to make alive or revive; in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew חָיָה ("to live"). Interestingly, the related adjective ζωοποιός shows up often in later papyri as a title for the Trinity.

definition: To make someone sufficient or fit for a task, equipping or qualifying them to do it.
article: ἱκανόω means to make someone adequate or fit for something — to qualify or equip them. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, and both times the Majority Standard Bible and BSB render it "qualified" (2 Corinthians 3:6; Colossians 1:12). The Septuagint uses it 14 times and most often translates the Hebrew רָב, while the everyday papyri stretch it toward the idea of granting authority — one document tells someone they "have full powers" until the writer returns.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A person who legally guarantees that an obligation will be met; a surety or pledge backing an agreement.
article: ἔγγυος refers to a guarantor or surety — someone who legally vouches that a commitment will be honored. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 7:22, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "guarantee" (with the BSB agreeing 100%). The most telling evidence is from everyday business papyri, where the word is common in legal documents about loans and payments — for example, one papyrus speaks of borrowers being "sureties for one another" to repay a loan, and another uses "on my security" — showing it was ordinary commercial language for someone who stood behind a financial obligation.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its biblical range rests almost entirely on outside papyri and Septuagint evidence.

definition: A reddish precious stone, identified as carnelian or sard, used in describing radiant or jeweled appearances.
article: σάρδιος refers to a red gemstone, a variety of sard that we'd call carnelian today. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in Revelation (4:3 and 21:20), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "carnelian" every time. The Septuagint uses it seven times for several Hebrew stone names, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions — one inscription from around 180 BC mentions a gold ring set with a sard.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences (none in the critical text), and the exact stone meant is uncertain, with sources suggesting either sard or carnelian.

definition: To beat someone severely with a whip or lash, usually as a formal punishment.
article: μαστιγόω means to scourge or flog—to beat someone with a whip, often as a legal punishment, as when Jesus was flogged in John 19:1. The Majority Standard Bible renders all seven New Testament uses with "flog" in various phrasings, and the word can also be used figuratively for chastisement, as in Hebrews 12:6. Moulton-Milligan note it was the standard everyday term for judicial scourging, citing a papyrus where a prefect declares a man "deserving to be scourged" before releasing him to please the crowd—strikingly close to the Gospel scenes.
caution: Abbott-Smith reports the Hebrew counterpart as נָכָה while the digest's measured data lists קָלָה and others, so the Septuagint pairings are not fully settled.

definition: To bury someone together with another, used by Paul as a picture of believers being buried with Christ.
article: συνθάπτω literally means to bury one person along with another, formed from σύν ('with') and θάπτω ('to bury'). In the New Testament it appears only twice, both times in Paul (Romans 6:4 and Colossians 2:12), where it describes believers being symbolically buried with Christ through baptism. Everyday Koine papyri use the word in its plain sense, including a will from 285 BC that obligates heirs to help bury the deceased — showing the literal burial meaning behind Paul's figurative use.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical SBLGNT, both occurrences being figurative.

definition: To stay on in a place or remain with someone, often with the sense of holding fast or persisting in something.
senseLabels: to stay on, continue in a place
article: προσμένω is built from πρός ("toward") and μένω ("remain"), and it means to stay on, continue, or remain — sometimes physically with a person, sometimes figuratively by holding fast to a person, cause, or practice. The measured senses span this range: remaining with a crowd (Matthew 15:32, Mark 8:2), staying loyal (Acts 11:23, "abide"), continuing in a place (1 Timothy 1:3), and persisting in prayer (1 Timothy 5:5). The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, where a 168 BC letter uses it of someone advised not to "remain" stuck until they can come up with funds.
caution: The corpus is small (6 occurrences) and some renderings register as "nothing" or "all" because the word is absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated by a single English word.

definition: Cenchrea, the eastern harbor town that served the city of Corinth on the Saronic Gulf.
article: Κεγχρεαί is a place name: Cenchrea, one of the seaport towns serving the city of Corinth. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 18:18 and Romans 16:1), and every translation surveyed renders it consistently as "Cenchrea." The name probably derives from the word kegchros, meaning "millet."
caution: This name occurs only twice in the New Testament, so the evidence is thin, though its meaning as a place name is not in doubt.

definition: To cause sores or ulcers on the body; in the passive, to be covered with open sores.
article: This verb describes the condition of being afflicted with open sores or ulcers, derived from the noun ἕλκος (a sore or wound). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 16:20, where the beggar Lazarus is described as covered with sores; older lexica also note a broader sense of "to wound." The single measured rendering counts the word as "lay" because the translators grouped it with the surrounding clause, but the lexical force is clearly about being ulcerated, as the KJV's "full of sores" reflects.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a measured rendering ("lay") that reflects sentence structure rather than the word's own meaning, the evidence here is thin.

definition: To speak out or declare something aloud, especially to proclaim what has been hidden.
article: This rare verb appears just once in the New Testament, in Matthew 13:35, where it means to utter or declare aloud — there it introduces things hidden since the foundation of the world. Its literal sense is striking: it originally meant to belch or spit out, and in classical Greek it described oxen bellowing or roaring (Homer), which softened over time into simply 'to speak out loudly.' In the Septuagint it appears 5 times, mostly translating the Hebrew שָׁאַג ('to roar'), preserving that forceful, vocal flavor. One vivid bit of evidence: a Callimachus fragment from the Oxyrhynchus papyri uses a related form to mean 'blurt out' a secret tale.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and rests on thin evidence, so its precise force there is hard to pin down.

definition: At once and without warning, all of a sudden.
article: This adverb describes something happening abruptly and without warning. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "suddenly" in 3 of 5 New Testament occurrences (75%), as when a host of angels suddenly appears in Luke 2:13 or a light suddenly flashes around Paul in Acts 9:3; the other rendering, "otherwise" in Mark 13:36, reflects the same idea of being caught off guard by an unexpected arrival. In the Septuagint it appears 9 times, most often translating the Hebrew word פִּתְאוֹם ("suddenly"). It was ordinary, everyday Koine: the papyri show a man writing "and suddenly I open my eyes" (P Par 51, 160 BC).
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and some textual variation in spelling, the evidence base is modest, though the sources agree closely on its meaning.

definition: A Latin proper name borne by two different Romans mentioned in Acts: an emperor and a military officer.
article: Κλαύδιος is a Latin personal name that appears 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts, and the translators render it "Claudius" every single time (100%). It refers to two different men: the Roman emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28; 18:2) and a military tribune named Claudius Lysias (Acts 23:26). The name comes from Latin, and the dictionaries note the same two-person split that the text itself shows.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences in one book), so this entry rests on a small sample, though the sources fully agree.

definition: To keep on doing something continuously, persisting in an action over a stretch of time.
article: διατελέω literally means to accomplish thoroughly, but in practice it works as a verb of persistence — to keep on doing something continuously. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:33, where Paul notes that his companions have continued without eating; here the Majority Standard Bible's rendering is tagged "daybreak," reflecting the surrounding clause rather than the verb's core meaning. The everyday Koine papyri capture its flavor nicely: one writer says he has "long administered the revenues with regularity," and another that he is "continually praying to the gods."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a measured-sense label ("daybreak") that reflects the context rather than the verb itself, confidence is low and the rendering data should be read cautiously.

definition: To give an authoritative order or command to someone, directing them to do something.
article: ἐπιτάσσω means to command or give an authoritative order, built from ἐπί ("upon") and τάσσω ("arrange"), so literally something like "arrange upon" — to lay a directive on someone. It appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often with the person commanded in the dative and the thing commanded as an object or infinitive. The everyday papyri show this same plain force: one Oxyrhynchus letter from A.D. 32 has a worker reassuring his employer, "I did not neglect your instructions," showing the word used for ordinary commands given and obeyed.
caution: The Septuagint Hebrew counterparts in the digest (חָתַם "seal," אַף "anger/nostril," גָּוַע "expire") don't obviously match "command," so the LXX evidence here is murky and may reflect alignment noise rather than real sense range.

definition: A surname distinguishing the apostle Judas (and his father Simon), probably marking him as a man from the place Kerioth.
article: Ἰσκαριώτης is not really a word with a meaning so much as a name—the surname attached to Judas the betrayer, and in two places to his father Simon (John 6:71; 13:26). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Iscariot" in 45% of cases and "Iscariot son" in 18%, the difference reflecting which person is being identified rather than any shift in meaning. The most interesting detail is its likely Hebrew root: scholars connect it to "man of Kerioth" (קִרְיָא אִישׁ), suggesting Iscariot points to Judas's hometown, though Mark uses a slightly different indeclinable form, Ἰσκαριώθ.
caution: The exact Hebrew background is offered only as probable by the sources, and some readings (e.g. Mark 14:43) are textually disputed.

definition: To complete or finish something fully, such as a journey, bringing it all the way through to its end.
article: This verb means to carry something through to completion, built from the prefix διά ("through") plus a root meaning "to effect." It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 21:7), where it is woven into the phrasing rather than translated as its own English word, and it shows up once in the Septuagint (2 Maccabees 12:17). Lexicons note a possible second sense, "to continue," in some later writers, and Moulton-Milligan finds the word in everyday Koine papyri where it takes a direct object, as in "I completed the labors."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and sources differing over whether it means "finish" or "continue," the precise sense is uncertain.

definition: A Sabbath rest — the state of resting, as one does on the Sabbath day.
article: σαββατισμός means a keeping of the Sabbath, or the rest that comes with it. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 4:9, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Sabbath" (100%) and the BSB agrees. The verb behind it (σαββατίζω, "to keep the Sabbath") shows up in the Septuagint at Exodus 16:30, and Moulton-Milligan notes the noun is so rare that the author of Hebrews may have coined it himself, with only a disputed possible parallel in Plutarch.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament and may have been newly coined by the author of Hebrews, so its precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: To meet up with or get to someone, especially after making one's way through obstacles.
senseLabels: to meet with or reach someone
article: συντυγχάνω means to meet with or fall in with someone, often joining them or managing to reach them. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 8:19, where Jesus' mother and brothers could not 'reach' him because of the crowd. The everyday papyri confirm this ordinary sense: documents repeatedly use it for arranging to meet a person, as in an Oxyrhynchus letter telling the reader 'whom you will meet.'
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint instance, the range of meaning rests mainly on the papyri and lexicons rather than biblical usage.

definition: The mouth, the bodily opening used for eating and speaking, and by extension speech itself or the cutting edge of a sword.
article: στόμα overwhelmingly means the physical mouth — 50 of 79 New Testament occurrences (86%) — whether of people or animals. From there it stretches naturally into related senses: "lips" (3×) and the act of speaking (3×), since the mouth is the organ of speech. The Septuagint uses it nearly 400 times, mostly for the Hebrew word for mouth (פֶּה, 273×), and the lexicons note vivid extended uses like "the edge of the sword" and the "mouth" of a river — papyri even use it for the mouths of canals on the Rosetta Stone.

definition: A small connecting word meaning "or," used to link alternatives, and after comparisons to mean "than."
article: ἤ is a tiny but extremely common particle that mostly means "or," linking two options or alternatives — it does this in 216 of 354 Byzantine occurrences (82%). Its other main job is comparative: after a comparison it means "than," as in "more than." Many of the measured "senses" here (like "it or," "or it," "is") are really just the surrounding English words bundled in by the translation engine, not separate meanings of ἤ itself; in fact it was absorbed into phrasing with no English word of its own 92 times. In the Septuagint it appears 788 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew word for "or" (אַו, 272×).
caution: Several listed "senses" reflect neighboring English words captured by the measurement, not distinct meanings — the genuine range is just "or" and "than."

definition: To make something a habit or established practice; in its one New Testament use, what the law had made customary.
article: ἐθίζω means to accustom or make habitual, and it comes from ἔθος, meaning custom. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 2:27, where the passive participle τὸ εἰθισμένον refers to "the established custom" of the law. The everyday papyri confirm this practical, routine sense: documents speak of "the customary oath" and "the customary reports," showing the word belonged to ordinary administrative life describing standard, expected procedures.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on a single passage supported by outside papyri evidence.

definition: A leaning toward one side, meaning favoritism or partiality that shows unfair preference for one person over another.
article: πρόσκλισις describes an inclination or leaning toward someone, used in the sense of partiality or playing favorites. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 5:21, where Paul charges Timothy to act without it; the Majority Standard Bible renders this single occurrence with the broader idea of impartial "principles," while the older lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, KJV) all settle on "partiality." Worth noting: it is easily confused with the near-identical word πρόσκλησις ("a judicial summons"), which some manuscripts actually read at this verse, and Moulton-Milligan note our word also turns up three times in early Christian writer Clement of Rome.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and manuscripts disagree between πρόσκλισις (partiality) and the look-alike πρόσκλησις (summons), so confidence is low.

definition: To give someone a firm order or instruction, often warning them strictly to do or not do something.
article: In the New Testament this middle-voice verb consistently means to charge or strictly order someone—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "commanded" in 2 of its 8 occurrences (29%), with related orderings and warnings elsewhere. Beyond "command," the older sense was to separate or distinguish: in the Septuagint (51× across 21 books) it most often translates Hebrew בָּדַל, "to set apart" (18×), and זָהַר, "to warn" (7×). The everyday Koine papyri confirm the commanding sense vividly—one letter from 232 BC uses it to mean "give instructions to Ptolemaeus."
caution: With only 8 New Testament occurrences and most renderings varying widely, the precise force shades between "command," "warn," and "charge" depending on context.

definition: A concession or allowance granted because of circumstances, rather than a strict command.
article: συγγνώμη appears only once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 7:6), where it means a concession—Paul granting something as an allowance rather than issuing a command. The everyday Koine papyri broaden its range considerably: it often slides into the sense of "pardon" or "forgiveness," as in a letter from 257 B.C. asking someone to "have συγγνώμη" with the writer. Abbott-Smith additionally lists "confession" and "fellow feeling," and the LXX uses it in Sirach and 2 Maccabees 14:20, showing a wider spread than the single NT verse suggests.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured "concession" sense rests on a single verse, while the lexica and papyri point to a broader range including pardon and confession.

definition: A governor or subordinate ruler set over a district or people, ranking below a king.
article: An ἐθνάρχης is a governor or subordinate ruler placed over a region or ethnic group—not a king, but an appointed official. The word combines ἔθνος ("people, nation") with ἀρχή ("rule"), and Moulton-Milligan note it appears in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions as a technical title for a deputy governor. It shows up only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 11:32, where it describes the official guarding Damascus under King Aretas; the Septuagint uses it a few times in 1 Maccabees.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense rests largely on outside evidence from inscriptions, papyri, and 1 Maccabees.

definition: To take firm hold of something or fasten onto it, often with the sense of latching on or attacking.
article: καθάπτω describes grabbing hold of or fastening onto something, sometimes with a hostile edge like an attack. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:3, where a viper "sticks" to (fastens on) Paul's hand—and notably this single occurrence takes a genitive object (χειρός, "hand"). The lexica also record a gentler sense, "to put upon" or "fasten on," and Moulton-Milligan cites a parallel from Epictetus of someone gripping by the neck, showing the word was at home in everyday Koine.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the word's full range rests mainly on outside sources rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: An adverb meaning 'from somewhere else' or 'by another way,' describing entry from a different direction than the proper one.
article: ἀλλαχόθεn is a rare adverb meaning 'from another place' or 'by some other way,' equivalent to the more common ἀλλοθεν. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 10:1, where it describes someone climbing into the sheepfold by a route other than the door. The word also turns up in 4 Maccabees 1:7 and is documented in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, showing it was ordinary spoken Greek.
caution: The measured rendering 'sheepfold' reflects the surrounding noun in John 10:1, not the adverb itself, which actually means 'from another place'; with only one New Testament occurrence the evidence is thin.

definition: To sail straight to a destination, taking a direct course across the water.
article: This nautical verb describes a ship running a straight course to where it's headed, without detours. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in Acts (16:11 and 21:1), and in both places the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it "sailed." The word is built from the parts meaning "straight" (εὐθύς) and "course" or "running" (δρόμος), and Abbott-Smith notes it was used of ships and is also attested in the writer Philo.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice, both in Acts, so its full range cannot be measured from the New Testament alone.

definition: To stir up or incite a crowd of people, urging them toward agitation or action.
article: In the New Testament ἀνασείω appears just twice (Mark 15:11 and Luke 23:5), and in both places it means to stir up or incite a crowd — the chief priests rousing the mob, and the charge that Jesus was agitating the people. The literal root sense is to shake back and forth, which you can see in an ancient inscription describing someone shaking a bronze water-jar; the figurative "incite" meaning belongs to later Koine writers. A papyrus from around 114 B.C. uses a related form to mean being positively "incited" to do one's duty more easily, a striking contrast to the stirring-up-trouble sense found in the Gospels.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences, both rendered identically, so the word's fuller range is known mainly from outside sources.

definition: To formally confirm or make something valid and binding, like ratifying an agreement or a decision.
article: κυρόω means to give something official force — to confirm, ratify, or make it binding. It appears only twice in the New Testament, where it covers both reaffirming love toward someone (2 Corinthians 2:8) and the validity of a settled human agreement (Galatians 3:15). The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where the word is common in legal documents: in one deed, a buyer promises that once the sale is "confirmed" (κυρωθεῖσα) he will pay into the government bank — showing its solid commercial, contractual flavor.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and three in the Septuagint, the measured sense range is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: A small, low-value Roman copper coin, worth a fraction of a day's wage.
article: Both of the word's two New Testament appearances refer to a tiny, nearly worthless Roman coin, rendered "penny" in modern translations (Matthew 10:29; Luke 12:6). The word is borrowed from Latin (the as), and Abbott-Smith places its value at one-tenth of a drachma, while Moulton-Milligan reckons it at one-sixteenth of a denarius. Everyday papyri and inscriptions confirm its ordinary use: one Smyrna decree mentions a ferry fare reduced to two assaria, showing just how small a sum it named.
caution: Both occurrences carry the same sense, but the sources give slightly different values for the coin, so its exact worth is uncertain.

definition: Service or active work done for others, especially religious ministry and the exercise of duties within the Christian community.
article: διακονία covers the whole range of serving others, from waiting at a table to the formal work of ministry in the church. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 34 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ministry" in two-thirds of cases (19×), with "service" (5×) and "serve" (3×) filling out the rest. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that this word is almost absent from everyday papyri before the sixth century A.D., suggesting it was somewhat literary or reserved for an almost technical use until it entered common speech.

definition: To look upon someone, often with attention, favor, or concern for their need.
article: At its core ἐπιβλέπω means to direct one's gaze toward someone, and in both the New Testament and the Septuagint it usually carries the warmer sense of looking with favor or compassion. The three New Testament uses all involve God or people turning their attention to someone — God regarding Mary's lowliness (Luke 1:48), a father begging Jesus to look at his son (Luke 9:38), and showing partiality to a well-dressed visitor (James 2:3). A striking parallel comes from an everyday Koine papyrus where someone prays 'look upon my birth,' an appeal for divine regard and help that echoes Luke's wording.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and the measured 'sense' labels reflecting messy phrase-level renderings rather than distinct meanings, treat these as one underlying sense of favorable looking.

definition: A puffed-up, swollen sense of one's own importance; arrogant pride.
article: φυσίωσις describes the kind of inflated self-importance that puffs a person up with pride. It comes from the verb φυσιόω (to inflate or puff up), and the imagery of swelling carries straight into the meaning — the older KJV even rendered it literally as "swelling." The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:20, where the Majority Standard Bible translates it "arrogance."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from broader usage.

definition: To go toward someone and meet them, often coming out to encounter a person who is approaching.
article: ὑπαντάω means to go and meet someone, usually taking the dative of the person met. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 5 times (the critical text has 10), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "met" in 4 of 5 cases, with the remaining instance being "entered met" in John 11:30 — essentially the same act of meeting. The word was ordinary Koine: papyri use it for one person meeting another and even for "presenting oneself" at monthly statements, while Abbott-Smith notes it can describe meeting in battle (Luke 14:31).
caution: The Byzantine and critical texts differ sharply in count (5 versus 10), and the Septuagint evidence rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Stephen, an early Christian named in Acts as one of the first seven deacons and the first martyr.
article: Στέφανος is the personal name of Stephen, the man appointed among the first seven deacons in Jerusalem and remembered as the church's first martyr. All 7 Byzantine occurrences are simply this name, rendered "Stephen" 5 times and twice expanded with a connecting word ("Now Stephen," "While Stephen") that reflects the surrounding sentence rather than any different meaning. The name was common in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan note it in ordinary papyri, including a 4th-century Christian letter addressed to "Stephen, beloved son, a deacon."
caution: The three measured "senses" are really one name; the variants just carry English connecting words, not distinct meanings.

definition: Lydia, a woman from Thyatira who sold purple cloth and became a believer at Philippi.
article: Lydia is a proper name—a specific woman, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira who heard Paul at Philippi and was baptized. She appears just twice in the New Testament, both times in Acts 16 (verses 14 and 40), and the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) agree she is the same person. Moulton-Milligan note that some have read the name as a nickname meaning 'the Lydian woman,' but the addition of 'by name' in Acts 16:14 marks it clearly as her actual personal name.
caution: The measured senses ('respond' and 'city') reflect surrounding translation choices, not the word itself, which simply names the woman Lydia—evidence here is thin.

definition: A preposition meaning "beside" or "near," whose exact sense shifts with grammar—often "from" (a source), "with" (alongside someone), or "by" (an agent).
article: παρά is one of Greek's hardest-working prepositions, built on the core idea of "beside" or "near," but its English rendering depends heavily on the grammar and context. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 200 times, most often translated "from" (34%) when marking a source or origin, and "with" (20%) when describing being alongside a person; remarkably, 87 of those 200 occurrences carry no English word of their own and are simply absorbed into the phrasing. One striking detail: in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew word for "sign" (אוֹת) 97 times, the most frequent of its Hebrew counterparts, showing how loosely a preposition can map across languages.
caution: Because παρά changes meaning with the case it governs and is often swallowed into English phrasing, no single gloss captures it—readers should weigh each context separately.

definition: A downcast, gloomy state of dejection, shown in a face cast down out of shame or sorrow.
article: Κατήφεια describes deep dejection or gloom, the kind of sorrow that shows on a downcast face. It appears only once in the New Testament, at James 4:9, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Study Bible both render it "gloom" (100%). The word literally points to eyes cast down, and Moulton-Milligan note a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (2nd century AD) using the related adjective for someone with eyes cast down out of shame, suggesting James intends visible gloominess rather than the older "heaviness" of the KJV.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured.

definition: To be angry or filled with rage at someone.
article: χολάω means to be angry with someone, and in its single New Testament appearance (John 7:23) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "angry" every time, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing completely. The word derives from χολή, "bile," reflecting the old idea that anger comes from bodily fluids — which also gives us the English word "choleric." An interesting twist: in its original sense, seen in the playwright Menander, the word actually meant "to be mad" or mentally deranged, before settling into the meaning of plain anger.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To wait for someone or something, staying around in expectation until it arrives.
article: περιμένω means to wait for someone or something, sticking around in anticipation.
