It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:4, where the apostles are told to wait for what the Father promised; the Septuagint uses it once too, at Genesis 49:18, to render the Hebrew קָוָה ("wait, hope for"). Everyday papyri confirm this plain sense beautifully—one letter from Hadrian's time reads "I received your letter gladly, and I am waiting for you." Note that the measured "gift" rendering reflects how the surrounding phrase was translated, not the word itself, which consistently means "wait for."
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range rests mostly on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: To get something ready ahead of time; to arrange or complete a preparation in advance.
article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to make ready" (καταρτίζω), so it means to prepare or arrange something beforehand. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:5, where Paul sends people ahead to get the promised collection ready in advance. The lexicons agree on "make ready beforehand," though notice the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding phrase with "gift" — that reflects the object being prepared rather than the verb's own meaning of advance preparation.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on a single passage.

definition: A long, flowing robe worn as a mark of dignity, status, or for special occasions.
article: στολή refers to a long robe, the kind of fine flowing garment associated with high status and ceremony. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times and is rendered "robes" in 6 of them (75%), as when scribes parade about in long robes (Mark 12:38) or the returning son is dressed in the finest robe (Luke 15:22). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain, concrete meaning: one document describes a trunk holding "as much as ten robes," and another records a man buying a robe for someone left naked.
caution: The classical lexica note an older sense of "equipment" or "armament," but this never appears in the New Testament evidence.

definition: A combination meaning "if somehow" or "if by any means," expressing a tentative hope that something might possibly happen.
article: εἴ πως pairs the conditional particle "if" (εἰ) with the indefinite adverb "somehow" (-πως), producing the sense "if by any means" or "if somehow" — used when a speaker hopes for an outcome without certainty. The digest records no occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so this entry rests entirely on its component parts and the Strong's gloss "if somehow." The most useful evidence is the long Abbott-Smith treatment of εἰ, which shows how flexibly "if" functions across conditions and indirect questions, the framework into which εἴ πως fits.
caution: The digest reports zero Byzantine New Testament occurrences and no measured senses, so this definition is inferred from the word's parts and a brief gloss rather than corpus evidence.

definition: Enosh, a biblical patriarch — the son of Seth and grandson of Adam.
article: Ἐνώς is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Enosh, a personal name with only one meaning: it always refers to the patriarch who was Seth's son. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:38), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Enosh" 100% of the time. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times in 2 books, every instance translating the same Hebrew name אֱנוֹשׁ, first introduced in Genesis 4:26.
caution: This is a proper name with a single fixed referent, so there is no real range of meaning to debate despite the low confidence tier.

definition: To play a stringed instrument such as a lyre or harp, by plucking or strumming its strings.
article: This verb means to play a lyre or harp, and it appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 14:7 and Revelation 14:2). The two measured renderings—"instruments" and "strumming"—really describe the same activity from slightly different angles rather than two distinct meanings. It shows up in the Septuagint just once (Isaiah 23:16), where it translates the Hebrew verb נָגַן, and an inscription from Teos shows it was a normal part of everyday Koine, listing harp-playing among the skills boys were taught before joining the ephebes.
caution: With only two New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence, the evidence is thin, though the sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: The act of speaking badly about someone — slander, defamation, or being spoken of with a bad reputation.
article: δυσφημία means evil-speaking or defamation — having a bad reputation spread about you. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:8, where Paul pairs it with its opposite, εὐφημία (good report), to describe being viewed through both bad and good reputation. The word is built from the prefix δυσ- (bad) and φήμη (report or rumor), and it shows up in the Septuagint and in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a first-century inscription referring to public complaints or bad press about marketplace projects.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on a single passage.

definition: To use or make use of something, or to deal with and treat a person in a particular way.
senseLabels: to use or make use of
article: χράομαi basically means to put something to use — to employ a tool, an opportunity, or a circumstance. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times across 4 books, and half the time the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it "use" (e.g. 1 Corinthians 7:31, 1 Timothy 1:8). The word stretches naturally to mean dealing with or treating people: Abbott-Smith notes it can mean "to deal sharply" (2 Corinthians 13:10) or "to treat, deal with" a person. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical range — one document from 221 B.C. uses it of no longer being able to use the ship's sails.
caution: In 3 of its 11 occurrences the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own, so its precise force there depends on context.

definition: The Greek verb "to be" in the form meaning "you (plural) are" — stating that a group exists, is present, or has some quality.
article: This is simply the second-person plural present form of εἰμί, "to be" — it means "you are" when addressing more than one person. Like the English verb "to be," the parent word εἰμί covers a wide range: existing ("in him we live and move and have our being"), happening or taking place, being present in a place, or linking a subject to a description. Abbott-Smith notes its flexibility, including impersonal uses like "there is" or "there was."
caution: The digest reports zero occurrences of this exact form in the Byzantine NT and assigns no confidence tier, so the description rests on the general behavior of the parent verb εἰμί rather than measured data for ἐστέ itself.

definition: A person from Athens, the famous Greek city; an Athenian.
article: Ἀθηναῖος simply means "Athenian" — a person belonging to the city of Athens. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 17 during Paul's visit to that city. The word is built from Ἀθῆναι ("Athens"), and the two measured renderings ("Athenians" and "Athens") really reflect the same underlying meaning, since translators sometimes rephrase "the Athenians" as "the men of Athens" depending on the sentence.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice, and the split between "Athenians" and "Athens" reflects translation phrasing rather than two distinct meanings.

definition: A good reputation or favorable report — speaking well of someone, the opposite of slander.
article: εὐφημία means a good reputation or the praise people speak about someone, and it stands as the opposite of slander (δυσφημία). It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:8, where the Majority Standard Bible actually renders the pairing in terms of "slander," while the lexicons and the word's own derivation point to its positive sense of "good report." A nice piece of everyday evidence comes from a fourth-century papyrus letter to a bishop praising him: "your good reputation, father, has encircled the whole world" — showing how naturally the word carried the idea of widespread good repute.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ("slander") reflects its contrast with the surrounding phrase rather than the word's own positive meaning of "good report" found in the lexicons.

definition: Snow, the white frozen precipitation, often used as an image of brilliant whiteness.
article: χιών means "snow" in every one of its 3 New Testament appearances, where it consistently describes dazzling whiteness — the angel's clothing at the tomb (Matthew 28:3), Jesus' garments at the transfiguration (Mark 9:3), and the white hair of the exalted Christ (Revelation 1:14). In the Septuagint it shows up 18 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew word for snow (שֶׁלֶג, 13×). Interestingly, the word also surfaces in everyday Koine sources: the magical papyri include phrases like "become snow" and a reference to "the lord of the snows."
caution: This entry is rated low confidence simply because the word is rare in the New Testament, though its single meaning is clear and the sources agree fully.

definition: A preposition meaning "with" or "together with," stressing close association, companionship, or being joined to someone or something.
article: σύn is a preposition that expresses close togetherness — companionship, association, or addition — and is rendered "with" in 89 of its 126 Byzantine occurrences (86%). It covers a tight range, with the variations ("along with," "also with") all pointing back to the same core idea of being joined together. One striking detail: the lexicons note this was once the elegant, "aristocratic" preposition of Attic Greek, but by New Testament times it was steadily giving way to μετά, surviving mostly in Luke and Paul. Strong's stresses that σύn implies a closer union than either μετά or παρά.

definition: A person, usually a young woman, who has not had sexual relations; a virgin.
article: παρθένος refers to a virgin — overwhelmingly a young unmarried woman, though the New Testament also applies it to chaste men (Revelation 14:4). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "virgin" in 10 of 14 occurrences (77%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time, so its core meaning is well settled. In the Septuagint it usually translates Hebrew בְּתוּלָה (40×) but occasionally renders עַלְמָה, the word behind the famous "virgin" of Isaiah 7:14. The everyday papyri are revealing: a man calls his daughter "my virgin daughter," and one inscription even uses παρθένος of a five-year-old child, showing the word could simply mark youth and unmarried status.
caution: In a handful of contexts (notably 1 Corinthians 7) the word shades toward "unmarried," so the exact emphasis can depend on setting.

definition: A word meaning inside, within, or inner—pointing to what is in the interior, whether something stays there or moves into it.
article: ἔσω marks what is on the inside or interior, and the New Testament uses it in two closely related ways: as a plain adverb meaning "inside" (Acts 5:23, 1 Corinthians 5:12) and as an adjective meaning "inner," especially in the phrase "the inner man" (Romans 7:22, Ephesians 3:16). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "inside" 2 times and "inner" 2 times across its 8 Byzantine occurrences, while one occurrence is simply absorbed into the phrasing. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word פְּנִימָה ("inward, within"), and everyday papyri show the same ordinary meaning—one document from 160 B.C. describes a man "sitting inside" a chamber.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and varied renderings, the precise nuance—rest "within" versus motion "into"—depends on the accompanying verb rather than the word itself.

definition: A messenger sent to deliver news or carry out instructions, most often a heavenly being who serves God.
article: In the New Testament this word overwhelmingly means "angel": the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 171 of its occurrences (100% of those translated), and the BSB independently agrees. But the core idea is simply a "messenger," and that plain sense survives in places like Matthew 11:10. The everyday roots show clearly in the papyri and inscriptions, where ἄγγελοι are named human envoys and the word can mean an intermediary; in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew מַלְאָך ("messenger") 218 times.
caution: In Revelation 1:20–2:1 the "angel" of each church is read variously as a heavenly being, a human messenger or leader, or a symbol of the church itself, and sources do not settle the matter.

definition: To smolder—to burn slowly and give off smoke without bursting into flame.
article: τύφω describes something that smokes or burns slowly without flaming up, used in the passive to mean "smoldering." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 12:20, where the image is of a faintly smoking wick that will not be quenched. Notably, the same passage in the Septuagint uses a different word for the idea, καπνιζόμενον ("smoking"), so Matthew's choice of τύφω is his own way of capturing that picture.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range here rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To turn around or turn something in a new direction, whether physically pivoting one's body or figuratively changing course.
article: στρέφω is the everyday verb for turning—most often someone pivoting their body to face a different way, as when Jesus "turned" to address his disciples. The two measured senses are really one idea in different grammatical dress: the participle "turned" (9×, 47%) and the plain "turn" (7×, 37%), with the Berean Standard Bible matching independently 100% and 86% of the time. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew הָפַך ("overturn, change") most often, 13 of 36 times, and a charming everyday papyrus describes a constellation "that turns the axis"—the same word used of the sky's rotation.
caution: Lexicons list a figurative "change" or "convert" sense (Matt 18:3; Rev 11:6), but this shows up only in rare renderings, so the metaphorical range is real yet thinly attested in the measured data.

definition: To arrive, come, or appear on the scene at a particular place.
article: παραγίνομαι is a movement verb meaning to arrive, come, or show up somewhere, and across its 37 Byzantine occurrences the renderings cluster tightly around "came" (12×) and "arrived" (10×), with a few framed as "when" someone arrived and a few as "went." It works as a near-synonym for the ordinary verb "to come" (ἔρχομαι), and Moulton-Milligan notes a scholar overstated things by calling it a "choicer" word than the plain alternative. In the Septuagint it appears 124 times, most often translating the Hebrew בּוֹא ("to come/go," 14×), and the older lexicons preserve an additional sense "to stand by, support someone" (as in 2 Timothy 4:16) that the measured New Testament renderings don't otherwise capture.
caution: The classical lexica list a "stand by, support" sense not reflected in the measured renderings, so its full range is slightly broader than the corpus data alone suggests.

definition: A personal name (Semein), listed as one of the human ancestors in the genealogy of Jesus.
senseLabels: a man's name in the genealogy
article: Σεμεΐ is a proper name, transliterated from the Hebrew name Shimei, and appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 3:26 within Jesus' genealogy. The Septuagint uses it far more often—46 times across 8 books—where it most commonly renders Hebrew שִׁמְעִי (41 of those times), though it occasionally stands in for other Hebrew names. As a name it carries no separate meaning to translate; English versions simply spell it out.
caution: This is a personal name with only one New Testament occurrence (none in the critical text), and the Greek spelling varies between Σεμεΐ and Σεμεείν across sources.

definition: The basic verb meaning "is"—the third person singular form used to say that someone or something exists, happens, or is present.
article: This is simply the "is" form of the verb "to be," covering the same wide range as the English verb. It can state that something exists ("in the beginning was the Word"), that an event takes place, or that someone is present in a place. Because it is such a common little word, translators render it dozens of ways depending on context, which is why the KJV uses everything from "are" and "be" to "meaneth," "profit," and "remaineth."
caution: The digest reports zero occurrences of this exact form in the Byzantine NT and assigns no confidence tier, so the listed uses come from the broader description of the verb rather than measured data for this spelling.

definition: Belonging to or following the natural order; in-born, instinctive, or the way nature designed something to be.
article: φυσικός describes what comes from nature itself — the inborn or instinctive way things are. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament: twice in Romans 1:26-27, where Paul contrasts the "natural" with what is "against nature" (para physin), and once in 2 Peter 2:12, where it describes creatures "born of mere instinct." A vivid touch from the papyri: a 4th-century adoption deed uses the word for a "true and natural son" (huios gnesios kai physikos), showing how everyday Greek used it for something genuine and by-birth rather than acquired.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences) and the precise force in 2 Peter 2:12 — "mere animals" versus "creatures of instinct" — is genuinely disputed among translators.

definition: To bring something to its intended completion—whether finishing a task, fulfilling a purpose, or making a person or thing perfect and fully mature.
article: τελειόω covers a span from finishing a job to making someone spiritually complete. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 24 times, and translators most often reach for "made perfect" (8×) or "perfected" (6×), with "finish" and "accomplished" filling out the rest; the core idea is bringing something all the way to its goal. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: in legal papyri the word means to "execute" a deed or formally complete a contract by adding date and signatures—so its ordinary sense was finishing paperwork properly, not abstract perfection.
caution: In the Septuagint it renders several different Hebrew words (including one for "consecrate" the priests' hands), and scholars dispute its exact force in passages like Hebrews 2:10.

definition: A meal—originally a morning or midday one, but in the New Testament simply a dinner or feast to which guests are invited.
article: In classical Greek ἄριστον meant breakfast, but by New Testament times it had shifted to mean an ordinary meal or dinner—Abbott-Smith notes it had come to stand for the older word δεῖπνον. It appears just 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, twice clearly meaning "dinner" (Matthew 22:4; Luke 14:12) and twice in scenes of Jesus eating. The everyday papyri are revealing: one Oxyrhynchus account lists an ἄριστον costing so little it was probably a light snack, while another mentions leeks bought for a weaver's breakfast, showing the word covered everything from a quick bite to a fuller meal.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and a meaning that shifted over time from "breakfast" to "dinner," the exact sense in any verse depends on context, and the measured senses for Luke 11:38 and 14:15 reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To push someone or something away from yourself, and so to reject, refuse, or thrust aside.
article: This verb literally means to shove or push something away, and in the New Testament it always carries the figurative sense of rejecting or refusing a person. Across its 6 Byzantine occurrences it consistently describes turning away from people—whether Israel rejecting Moses, Paul asking if God has rejected His people, or hearers being thrust aside. The literal physical force still shows in the everyday papyri, where one document (2nd century AD) uses it for being "illegally ousted," and a related compound describes someone being shoved into prison.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and some rendering variation (one instance translated "abusing" where the BSB disagrees), the precise force in a few verses is a matter of interpretation.

definition: An idiom meaning "one by one" or "each in turn," describing people or things taken individually rather than all together.
article: This is a fixed phrase built from εἷς ("one") repeated with κατά ("by" or "according to") wedged between the two words, producing the sense "one by one" or "each in turn." Lexicons gloss it as "severally, one by one, single person, united," and the older glosses settle on "one by one" as the core meaning. It is an idiomatic construction rather than a single dictionary word, which is why it shows up as a phrase rather than a standard inflected term.
caution: There are no measured occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament and the phrase is absent from the critical text used here, so the meaning rests entirely on lexicon glosses rather than corpus evidence.

definition: To cut short or bring something to a swift, decisive completion, used of executing a decree quickly and fully.
article: Literally this verb means to cut down or cut in pieces, but in the New Testament it appears only figuratively, describing an action that is cut short and brought to swift completion. It shows up just twice in the Byzantine text (once in the critical text), both within the same quotation in Romans 9:28, where it refers to the Lord carrying out his decisive word on the earth. Notably, the Septuagint uses it four times, three of which translate the Hebrew חָרַץ (to decide or determine), and Moulton-Milligan finds the same metaphorical sense of "cut short" in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences in a single quoted passage, and the rendering "sentence" versus "decisively cut short" reflects how the same verse is parsed rather than two clearly distinct meanings.

definition: To confront someone with their wrongdoing—rebuking, correcting, or bringing hidden faults into the open so the truth is exposed.
article: ἐλέγχω is about confronting wrong: it ranges from rebuking and disciplining a person (its most common use, rendered "rebuke" 5 times) to exposing hidden deeds to the light ("exposed," 3 times) and proving someone guilty ("convicted," 2 times). The core idea ties these together—bringing the true character of a person or action out into the open, as in John's Gospel. Everyday papyri confirm this legal flavor: one document from around 157 BC uses it of someone "convicted" of acting improperly against the revenues. In the Septuagint it appears 49 times, mostly translating the Hebrew יָכַח, "to argue or reprove."
caution: Translators differ on individual verses—the same Greek word is rendered "rebuke," "exposed," or "convicted" depending on context, and lexicons note the senses shade into one another.

definition: A large beam or plank of timber, like the long wooden joists used in building.
article: δοκός is a sturdy beam or plank of timber. Though the Majority Standard Bible most often renders the word "speck" in its six New Testament occurrences, that reflects the surrounding eye-contrast saying rather than the word itself, which the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith, KJV) uniformly define as a beam — Jesus' famous image of the beam in one's own eye against the speck in another's. The everyday building sense is confirmed by the papyri, where δοκός shows up alongside "timber" (τὰ ξύλα) in a steward's account and among supports and braces for an olive-press.
caution: The measured rendering "speck" actually belongs to the contrasting word in the saying, not to δοκός, which the lexicons consistently define as a beam.

definition: Salt, the common mineral used to season and preserve food.
article: This is the older Greek word for salt, and it appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Mark 9:49), where it sits behind the rendering "salted." It is actually a variant form of the more usual word ἅλας, and the critical text (SBLGNT) reads zero occurrences here, preferring the alternative. The Septuagint uses it 14 times across 9 books, almost always translating the Hebrew word for salt (מֶלַח, 11 times).
caution: Evidence is thin: this form occurs only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical text, where it is treated as a variant of ἅλας.

definition: To chase someone away, drive them out, or persecute them relentlessly.
article: This compound of ἐκ ("out") and διώκω ("pursue") means to hound someone out — to drive away or persecute without letup. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only 2 times in the Byzantine text and just once in the critical text (1 Thessalonians 2:15, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "drove"). The Septuagint uses it 11 times, and Moulton-Milligan note it turns up in everyday Koine documents, including a sixth-century papyrus describing soldiers being expelled.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one or two New Testament uses — so the precise force (mere expulsion versus relentless persecution) is hard to pin down from usage alone.

definition: In a sharp, severe, or stern manner — dealing with someone harshly rather than gently.
article: This adverb describes acting toward someone in a sharp, severe, or stern way. It appears only twice in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 13:10 and Titus 1:13), once rendered "severe" and once "sternly," so its range is essentially a single idea seen from two angles. The word traces back to the notion of "cutting off," and the classical evidence preserves that literal edge: an inscription from Pamphylia uses the related adjective for the genuinely sharp iron weapons handed to gladiators, replacing the blunt ones the crowd found too dull.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and thin attestation overall, the precise force of the word rests on a very small sample.

definition: A suspicious thought or guess about someone's hidden motives, often unfounded and corrosive to relationships.
article: ὑπόνοια describes a suspicion or distrustful guess about what someone is really up to. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:4, where it sits in a list of harmful attitudes; the Majority Standard Bible there renders it as part of "interest," though the underlying word means suspicion. Everyday Koine papyri illustrate this sense vividly—one petition from around A.D. 130 mentions someone who "had not the least suspicion" (P Oxy III.472), showing the word was common in ordinary life.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on thin evidence, and the digest's measured rendering "interest" sits oddly against the standard sense of "suspicion."

definition: A piece of cloth used to patch or cover a garment, especially a patch sewn onto worn clothing.
article: In the New Testament ἐπίβλημα always refers to a patch — a piece of cloth put on a garment to mend it — appearing in all three Synoptic versions of Jesus' saying about sewing new cloth onto an old garment. The word literally means something "thrown over" or put on, and the older lexicons note a wider range outside the Gospels: a cover, a tapestry, or embroidery. Its single Septuagint appearance translates a Hebrew word in Isaiah 3:22 for a piece of clothing, and an early inscription (around 420 BC) lists it alongside bedding and a garment, showing it was an everyday term for cloth coverings.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use — so the broader senses of "cover" or "tapestry" come from the lexicons rather than the measured biblical data.

definition: A person hired to work for wages, especially a paid laborer or servant who works for money rather than personal loyalty.
article: μισθωτός is simply a wage-worker — someone paid to do a job. The four New Testament uses cluster in two places: Mark 1:20, where Zebedee's hired men work alongside his sons, and John 10:12-13, where Jesus contrasts the hireling, who flees when wolves come, with the shepherd who owns and cares for the sheep. In the Septuagint it appears 16 times, most often translating the Hebrew שָׂכִיר ('hired man'), and the everyday papyri show the related word μισθωτής used for tenants and lessees, confirming this was ordinary commercial vocabulary.
caution: The four 'measured senses' here are really one meaning — a hired worker — split across phrases like 'hired away' and 'man away' that just reflect surrounding words, not distinct senses.

definition: To be sober and clear-headed—both literally free from drunkenness and figuratively alert, calm, and self-controlled in mind.
article: νήφω literally means to abstain from wine and stay sober, but in the New Testament it is used figuratively for moral alertness—keeping a calm, clear, self-controlled mind. It appears 6 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "sober minded" (2×), with related phrasings like "let us remain," "be sober," and being clear-minded in the rest. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: in an inscription from around 100 BC the word pairs with ἁγνεύω (being pure) to describe the proper readiness of worshippers, and the figurative sense shows up in Aristeas, where staying sober "for the greater part of one's life" is named a quality of a good ruler.
caution: The MSB renderings vary because the verb is embedded in different grammatical constructions, so the apparent "five senses" are mostly translation variants of one core meaning rather than distinct definitions.

definition: Describes something small in extent—a short span of time, a little distance, or a small amount or number.
article: βραχύς is a flexible adjective meaning "short" or "little," stretching across time, distance, quantity, and number. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, but in 5 of those it gets absorbed into the surrounding English phrasing rather than translated as its own word; the two measured renderings are "short time" (Acts 5:34) and "briefly" (Hebrews 13:22, literally "in few words"). The everyday Koine papyri show the same breadth—it describes a man's short stature, a "trifling" gift, and even, in one inscription, a man who is "not of small account." In the Septuagint it appears 13 times, most often rendering the Hebrew word for "few" or "little" (מְעָט).
caution: With only 7 occurrences and most absorbed into phrasing, the measured senses capture just a fraction of the wider range the lexica document (time, distance, quantity, and number).

definition: To sleep or be asleep; sometimes used figuratively for death or spiritual carelessness.
article: καθεύδω simply means to sleep or be asleep, and that literal meaning covers nearly all of its 22 New Testament uses, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sleeping" (52%) or "asleep" (29%). The word is everyday Koine—papyri use it for ordinary nightly sleep, and one inscription regulating a shrine even instructs men and women to sleep separately in the sleeping quarters. Beyond the plain sense, the lexicons note two figurative extensions: sleep as a euphemism for death (as in Jairus's daughter "not dead but sleeping") and sleep as a picture of moral or spiritual dullness, as in Ephesians 5:14. In the Septuagint it usually translates Hebrew shakab, "to lie down."

definition: To lie around something, whether wrapped around it, hung about it, or worn like a covering—often used figuratively for being surrounded or burdened.
article: Períkeimai literally describes something lying all around an object—a great millstone hung or thrown about someone's neck (Mark 9:42, Luke 17:2), or a cloud of witnesses surrounding believers (Heb 12:1). In Acts 28:20 it shifts to the sense of having something around oneself, where Paul is bound with a chain; the Majority Standard Bible renders this as 'called,' but the BSB disagrees entirely, reflecting the 'wear/carry' meaning that Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan confirm. A vivid piece of evidence comes from an illiterate fourth-century papyrus letter where a woman named Valeria writes that she is 'afflicted with' (períkeimai) a grievous shortness of breath, showing how the word stretched to mean being encompassed by sickness.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and the Majority Standard Bible's 'called' in Acts 28:20 contradicting both the BSB and the lexica, the rendering of that one verse is genuinely disputed.

definition: Troas, a harbor city in the region of Mysia in Asia Minor, near the Hellespont.
article: Τρωάς is simply the name of Troas, a port city in Mysia (northwest Asia Minor) near the ancient site of Troy. It appears 6 times across 3 New Testament books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "Troas" every time; the lone variant rendering "went Troas" in Acts 16:8 just reflects the surrounding travel narrative, not a different meaning. Strong's notes the name connects to the Troad, the plain of Troy, which is why the city sits in that famous region.

definition: To refuse to obey or believe, rejecting an authority's command or message through willful resistance.
article: ἀπειθέω covers a spectrum from outright disobedience to refusing belief, and the Byzantine NT shows this blend: of 16 occurrences, translators split it evenly between "rejects," "disobedient," and "disobeyed," with 6 cases absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The classical lexica (Abbott-Smith, Moulton-Milligan) lean firmly toward "disobey," matched by everyday papyri where the word describes people who defy royal orders—one document calls out a man "who has continued to disobey your orders." In the Septuagint it appears 34 times, most often rendering the Hebrew מָרָה (8×) and סָרַר (6×), both carrying the sense of rebellion against authority.
caution: Translators disagree on whether to stress disobedience or unbelief, and 6 of 16 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing rather than given a clear English word.

definition: To stand or to make something stand—to place, set up, or establish someone or something in a fixed position.
article: ἵστημι is one of the most common verbs in the Greek Bible, appearing 154 times in the Byzantine New Testament and over 600 times in the Septuagint. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "standing" in 99% of cases, but its full range is wider: when used transitively it means to place, set up, establish, or appoint someone or something. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew עָמַד ("to stand," 334×) and קוּם ("to rise/establish"), and a fascinating detail from everyday papyri shows it used in financial deals to mean "fix" or "agree upon" a price—as in a receipt for "the 46 drachmas agreed upon."
caution: In about 30 of its 154 occurrences the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word, so its exact contribution can be hard to pin down.

definition: A young domestic ox — a calf, bullock, or heifer — often raised for food or animal sacrifice.
article: μόσχος means a young ox — a calf, bullock, or heifer — and in the New Testament it always carries this sense, whether the fattened calf killed for the prodigal's homecoming (Luke 15) or the calves whose blood was used in sacrifice (Hebrews 9). The word is common in the Septuagint, appearing 233 times and standing in for several Hebrew words for cattle, most often פָּר ("bull," 122 times). Everyday papyri confirm the same plain meaning: one farming letter from A.D. 38 urges the reader to "take care of the calf," and another mentions asking a tanner for the hide of a sacrificed calf.
caution: Older lexicons note an original sense of "young shoot or twig," but no New Testament occurrence uses anything other than the "calf" meaning.

definition: A huge sea creature or sea-monster, such as a great fish or whale.
article: κῆτος refers to an enormous sea creature — a great fish, sea-monster, or whale. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Matthew 12:40, where Jesus recalls Jonah being in the belly of the great fish; the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in all its occurrences, and the BSB agrees 100%. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times across 4 books, standing in for several different Hebrew words including the great fish that swallowed Jonah and even Leviathan (לִוְיָתָן), showing the term covered a range of large sea beasts rather than one specific animal.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its exact range there rests on a single verse and its Septuagint background.

definition: Healthy or sound in body, restored to health; also used of things that are intact or, figuratively, of speech that is wholesome.
article: ὑγιής describes being physically sound and healthy, and most often appears in healing stories—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "well" 4 times (40%) and "healed" twice (20%), while in 4 of its 14 occurrences it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The word ranges beyond bodies: classical and papyri usage apply it to intact objects, and Titus 2:8 uses it figuratively of wholesome speech. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this concrete range vividly—one document describes a rented mill as "safe and uninjured" (ὑγιῆ καὶ ἀσινῆ), another speaks of "whole wine-jars."
caution: The Septuagint Hebrew counterparts listed (such as לָבָן "white" and צָרָ֫עַת "leprosy") don't match the core "healthy/sound" sense, suggesting the digest's LXX pairings may be unreliable.

definition: To treat someone with violent insolence — insulting, abusing, or shamefully mistreating them.
article: This verb covers the overlap between insult and abuse: treating a person with arrogant contempt that often spills into physical mistreatment. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, always aimed at people, and the Septuagint uses it only 4 times for a handful of different Hebrew words. The everyday papyri make the sense vivid — one complaint describes a man being 'grossly insulted,' and a wife reports a husband who 'continually ill-treated and insulted me, using violence towards me.'
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and several distinct Hebrew counterparts in the Septuagint, the measured 'senses' largely reflect translation context rather than truly separate meanings.

definition: A companion or comrade, often used in direct address as "friend," sometimes with a pointed or reproachful edge.
article: ἑταῖρος means a companion or comrade, and in the New Testament it appears only in Matthew, all four times. Three of those uses are Jesus addressing someone directly as "friend" — and in each case the tone carries a sting, since the person being called "friend" is in the wrong. In the Septuagint it shows up 19 times and translates Hebrew words for companion or associate like רֵעַ and חָבֵר; Moulton-Milligan note it is absent from the papyri but common in inscriptions, where it pairs with words for foster-brothers and fellow members of a group.
caution: Evidence is thin: it occurs only 4 times (3 in the critical text), all in Matthew, and one instance (Matthew 11:16) reflects a disputed reading where some manuscripts have ἑτέροις ("others") instead.

definition: Persistent, irritating arguments or wrangling that produce friction rather than truth.
article: This rare word describes ongoing, fruitless disputes that breed mutual irritation, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Timothy 6:5). The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "constant," describing the endless friction stirred up by quarrelsome people, and older sources cast it as "useless wrangling" or "perverse disputing." Notably, the critical text reads a slightly different form (διαπαρατριβαί), which Field connects to the idea of "mutual irritations," comparing the simpler word παρατριβαί used by Polybius for tensions between Carthaginians and Romans.
caution: This word rests on thin evidence, appearing only once and only in some minuscule manuscripts, with the critical text preferring a different spelling, so its exact form and force are disputed.

definition: A medicinal salve or ointment, shaped like a small roll, applied to soothe and heal the eyes.
article: κολλούριον is a healing ointment, often rolled into the shape of a small bread cake (the word is a diminutive of a coarse bread roll), used here for treating the eyes. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 3:18, where the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles both render it as an eye salve to anoint with. The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri: it shows up frequently in medical prescriptions, including a yellow salve prescribed for discharges, wounds, bruises, and weals.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense there rests on a single passage supported by outside medical evidence.

definition: The act of spending the winter somewhere, or a place suitable for staying through the winter season.
senseLabels: a place to spend the winter
article: παραχειμασία refers to wintering — staying somewhere over the winter — and by extension a place fit for doing so. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "harbor," describing a port unsuitable for spending the winter. The lexica (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) consistently define it as "a wintering," and an inscription from A.D. 48 (Syll 762) uses it the same way, of someone's wintering, confirming it was ordinary Koine vocabulary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range is hard to map, and the measured rendering "harbor" reflects the context more than the word's core sense of "wintering" given in the lexica.

definition: Something that covers or protects, especially clothing or shelter for the body.
article: σκέπασμα refers to a covering, and the lexicons consistently point to clothing in particular — the word comes from σκεπάζω, "to cover." There's an interesting tension in the evidence: the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, KJV "raiment") all read it as clothing, but the one place it appears in the New Testament (1 Timothy 6:8) is rendered "food" 100% of the time in the measured translations. Moulton-Milligan ties it to everyday Koine usage and cites a parallel phrase "meat and drink and raiment," suggesting the broader sense of basic bodily necessities like shelter and clothing.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ("food") flatly disagrees with the lexicons ("clothing"), so its precise meaning here is genuinely uncertain.

definition: To close the eyes, used figuratively of people who shut their eyes so they will not see or understand.
article: καμμύω literally means to close or shut the eyes. In both New Testament occurrences (Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27) it appears in a quotation from Isaiah 6:10, describing people who have deliberately shut their eyes — which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it as 'callous' in both places, treating the shut eyes as a picture of a hardened, unresponsive heart. The word is a shortened (syncopated) form of καταμύω that ordinary Koine writers used, and it even shows up in a third-century magical papyrus, where someone 'having closed his eyes and looked up' sees a shadow standing before him.
caution: With only two New Testament uses, both echoing the same Isaiah quotation, the rendering 'callous' reflects the figurative context rather than the word's plain literal meaning of closing the eyes.

definition: A piece of land surrounded by water; an island.
article: νῆσος simply means an island, a body of land surrounded by water. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 9 times, and it is consistently rendered "island" in 8 of its 9 occurrences (89%), as in Paul's shipwreck on Malta (Acts 28:1) and John's exile on Patmos (Rev 1:9). In the Septuagint it appears 32 times, usually translating the Hebrew אִי (23×); intriguingly, the everyday Koine papyri also used it for land flooded by the Nile and cut up by canals, contrasted with ἤπειρος, the high mainland.

definition: The state of being laid waste or made desolate—a place stripped bare and left in ruins.
article: ἐρήμωσις names the condition of devastation, a place emptied out and ruined. All 3 of its New Testament appearances render as "desolation" (100%), and they cluster in one striking phrase: the "abomination of desolation" (βδέλυγμα ἐρημώσεως) in Matthew 24:15, Mark 13:14, and Luke 21:20. In the Septuagint it shows up 18 times and most often translates the Hebrew שִׁקּוּץ (5×), a word for something detestable, alongside terms for being made desolate (שָׁמֵם).
caution: This word appears only 3 times in the New Testament and the confidence tier is low, though all sources agree on its meaning.

definition: Describing a person whose loyalty or purpose is split, wavering between two minds instead of being settled and single-hearted.
article: δίψυχος literally combines "two" and "soul," picturing someone torn between two intentions and unable to commit. Both New Testament uses come from James (1:8 and 4:8), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "double minded" once and "double" once, with BSB agreeing fully in each case. The most striking detail is that this word seems to have been coined here: Moulton-Milligan notes it is first found in James and then rapidly caught on among early Christian writers like Clement of Rome, Barnabas, and especially Hermas.
caution: Confidence is low: the word appears only twice, both in James, so its full range cannot be measured beyond this single author.

definition: To overlook something and choose not to act on it, especially to pass over wrongdoing without punishing it.
article: This verb means to look past or take no notice of something—in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 17:30) it describes God having "overlooked" times of ignorance. The sense is not mere failure to see but a deliberate passing-over, which is why older translations rendered it "wink at." In the Septuagint it shows up just twice, where it stands in for Hebrew words connected to guilt and transgression, fitting the idea of disregarding offenses.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and twice in the Septuagint, and the listed Hebrew counterparts vary between sources.

definition: Describing speech that is swollen and arrogant—boastful, pompous words that overstate and impress.
article: Literally ὑπέρογκος means "of excessive size," built from ὑπέρ ("over") and ὄγκος ("bulk, mass"), and it gets stretched figuratively to describe speech that is overblown—big, swollen, arrogant talk. In the New Testament it appears just twice, in 2 Peter 2:18 and Jude 1:16, both times of arrogant boasting, and the MSB and BSB render it the same way 100% of the time. Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and that Jude's usage echoes the Assumption of Moses 7:9, where mouths "speak enormous things."
caution: With only 2 NT occurrences and a computed low-confidence tier, the sense rests on a thin sample, though the sources agree.

definition: To pile or heap things up, used literally for stacking objects and figuratively for loading someone down with something.
article: σωρεύω means to heap or pile things up, whether literally or figuratively. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the two measured renderings reflect very different sentence contexts: in Romans 12:20 it describes heaping coals, while in 2 Timothy 3:6 it pictures people "loaded down" or overwhelmed with sins (here the "women" label simply reflects the surrounding phrase, not the verb's meaning). The related noun σωρός, "a heap," turns up commonly in the papyri and ostraca, often for piles of grain.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and the "women" sense label reflects sentence context rather than the verb itself.

definition: The intense, eager anticipation of someone watching closely for something they expect to happen.
article: This word describes a keen, straining anticipation—literally the picture of watching with the head stretched forward toward what you expect. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Romans 8:19 and Philippians 1:20), once as a noun and once rendered adverbially, and both the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB agree fully on the sense of eager expectation. The most vivid evidence comes from a sixth-century Egyptian papyrus where oppressed peasants describe awaiting an official's arrival like those in Hades watching eagerly for the coming of Christ—showing the word's flavor of longing for someone's arrival.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and limited supporting attestation, this is a low-confidence, rarely used word.

definition: To step on, walk over, or trample something underfoot, whether literally or figuratively.
article: πατέω covers the whole range of putting your feet on something — from simply walking over a place to violently trampling it down. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, used for treading on serpents (Luke 10:19), enemies trampling Jerusalem underfoot (Luke 21:24, Revelation 11:2), and treading the winepress of God's wrath (Revelation 14:20, 19:15). A vivid extra-biblical example comes from an early papyrus gospel fragment, where a Pharisee challenges Jesus for daring to "walk" in the temple's place of purification without first washing.
caution: With only 5 occurrences spread evenly across senses, several of the listed sense labels reflect awkward word-by-word alignment rather than clear distinct meanings.

definition: To know or be aware of something or someone, often as the settled result of having seen or perceived it.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament this verb almost always means "know" — 280 of 318 times (99%), with a handful of cases (3×, 1%) shading into "understand." The form you actually meet (οἶδα) is a perfect tense doing present-tense duty: literally "to have seen," hence "to know." The everyday flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where a wall-scratching reads simply "Andronikos saw and marveled," and Strong's notes the word borrows its other tenses from related verbs meaning "to see."
caution: The lexicons frame this as fundamentally "to see," while the measured New Testament data overwhelmingly renders it "know," so the seeing sense lives mostly in the word's history rather than its actual usage.

definition: Describing something that comes from or resembles demons, used to characterize a destructive kind of so-called wisdom.
article: δαιμονιώδης means "demon-like" — having the character or origin of demons. It appears only once in the New Testament, at James 3:15, where it describes a counterfeit "wisdom" that James contrasts with wisdom from above. The word is built from δαιμόνιον (demon) and a root meaning "form" or "kind," and Abbott-Smith notes it also turns up in the Greek of Psalm 90(91):6, making it a rare term overall.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is very rare elsewhere, so its precise range cannot be measured with confidence.

definition: A relative adverb meaning "as often as" or "whenever," marking how frequently an action is repeated.
article: This little adverb means "as often as" or "as many times as," pointing to a repeated action without fixing a count. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, twice in Paul's words about the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:25-26) and once in Revelation 11:6, and it normally pairs with ἐάν ("whenever"). The everyday papyri make the meaning vivid: one writer says "as often as I find an opportunity, I write to you," showing the word was ordinary Koine for routine, recurring events.
caution: With only 3 occurrences, the second "measured sense" simply reflects the following word ("Lord's") and is not a distinct meaning—the word's sense is uniformly "as often as."

definition: To present or display someone publicly, often to demonstrate, prove, or officially declare them as something.
article: This verb covers a range from simply showing something off to demonstrating or proving a point, and in its strongest sense, publicly proclaiming someone into an office or role. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the renderings vary: in Acts 2:22 Jesus is "certified" by God's works, while in 2 Thessalonians 2:4 it describes someone proclaiming himself to be God. The papyri make its administrative flavor vivid — it commonly meant to appoint or nominate someone, as in a will declaring a son as heir, or proclaiming an appointment to public office.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and meanings shaped heavily by context, the precise force in any one verse can be debated.

definition: The comparative form meaning "less" or "worse" — describing something inferior, weaker, or to a lesser degree.
article: This is a comparative word meaning "less" or "worse," the neuter form used adverbially. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: in 2 Corinthians 12:15 it means "less" (Paul loving more while being loved less), and in 1 Corinthians 11:17 it appears in the phrase "for the worse" (the opposite of "for the better"). In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times across 3 books, translating four different Hebrew words, which reflects how flexibly a general comparative like "less" can be applied.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences (one absorbed into phrasing with no English word of its own), so the measured range is narrow.

definition: Describing something remarkable and splendid, deserving notice — glorious, renowned, or strikingly conspicuous.
article: ἐπιφανής describes something that stands out as splendid, renowned, or notable — built from the verb meaning "to appear or shine forth." In the New Testament it occurs just once, in Acts 2:20, where it describes the "glorious" day of the Lord (quoting the Septuagint, where the word shows up 10 times across 8 books). The most striking outside evidence is the Rosetta Stone (196 BC), where ἐπιφανής is a royal title for King Ptolemy V, suggesting an air of majestic, almost divine, splendor.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a quoted Septuagint context, the precise shade of meaning rests on thin evidence.

definition: Something shameful, disgraceful, or improper to do or say.
article: αἰσχρόν is the neuter form of the adjective αἰσχρός, built on αἶσχος meaning "shame" or "disgrace," and it points to something base or improper. The digest records no occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, though the related adjective appears in passages like 1 Corinthians 11:6 and 14:35, Ephesians 5:12, and Titus 1:11. One notable detail is its Septuagint use in Genesis 41 (where Pharaoh's dream features "bad" or ugly cattle), translating Hebrew words for badness, רַע and רֹעַ.
caution: The evidence here is thin: there are zero measured New Testament occurrences for this exact form, so the sense rests mainly on lexicon notes and Septuagint parallels.

definition: A sudden rush of amazement or astonishment, often mixed with awe or fear, at something unexpected.
article: θάμβος names a jolt of astonishment — the stunned reaction people have when confronted with something startling, frequently shading into awe or even terror (Dodson). It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all in Luke and Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it both as being overcome with amazement (Luke 4:36) and as wonder at an event (Acts 3:10). Moulton-Milligan note it began as a poetic word but turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and that in the New Testament Luke treats it as a neuter noun.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences split evenly between two senses — so the apparent distinction may reflect translation choices more than a real difference in meaning.

definition: An enclitic particle that adds emphasis or force to the word it attaches to, meaning something like "indeed" or "by far."
article: "Per" is a small enclitic particle that never stands alone — it always attaches to another word to strengthen or sharpen it, adding a sense of "indeed" or "by far." You meet it embedded in familiar compounds like "hosper" and "kathaper" ("just as"), "kaiper" ("although"), and "eiper" ("if indeed"). Abbott-Smith notes it is akin to "peri" and in the New Testament is always affixed to a preceding word rather than used independently.
caution: There are no measured senses because the particle never appears on its own in the Byzantine New Testament — it survives only inside compound words.

definition: To give someone or something a name or title, or to call them by that name.
article: This verb means to name something or call it by a particular title, often in the passive sense of being given a name. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Romans 2:17), where someone calls themselves by a name, and the critical SBLGNT text omits it entirely. In the Septuagint it shows up 36 times across 9 books, chiefly translating the common Hebrew verb קָרָא ("to call"), and Moulton-Milligan note a vivid everyday example from a 88 BC parchment where a vineyard is described as "the one called Dadbakanras."
caution: Confidence is low: this word appears only once in the Byzantine NT and is absent from the critical text, so its New Testament range rests on thin evidence.

definition: A wrongful act against God or others — a moral lapse, offense, or trespass.
article: παράπτωμα is the New Testament word for a moral failing — an offense or trespass against God or another person. The Byzantine NT renders it "trespasses" in 20 of 23 occurrences (91%), and the meaning is stable across the corpus, as in Jesus' teaching on forgiving others' trespasses (Matthew 6:14, Mark 11:25). Interestingly, the everyday papyri use a much milder sense: a royal tax ordinance (P Tebt I.5, 118 BC) uses it for measurement "errors" allowed to revenue officers — closer to a slip or unintentional lapse than willful sin.
caution: The classical and papyri sense leans toward an accidental "slip" or "blunder," while the biblical usage carries a stronger ethical weight of deliberate wrongdoing.

definition: A time word meaning "when" — marking the point or moment at which something happens.
article: ὅτε is a common temporal particle that points to the time at which an event occurs, rendered "when" in the overwhelming majority of cases (67×, 89% in the Byzantine NT). A few times it shades into "after" or "once" (4×) when one event follows another. Note that the listed renderings "Jesus," "came," and "these" aren't meanings of ὅτε itself — they come from neighboring words in the sentence, and the word is absorbed into the phrasing without its own English equivalent 30 times out of 105. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, including an amusing letter where a man writes his estranged wife counting the days "from when" they last bathed together.
caution: The "Jesus," "came," and "these" renderings reflect translation phrasing of surrounding words, not separate meanings of ὅτε.

definition: A lie or falsehood — something untrue that is told or fabricated.
article: ψεῦσμα names a lie or falsehood, the untrue thing itself. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 3:7, where every translation surveyed renders it "falsehood" or "lie" with full agreement. The Greek translators Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus used it in passages of Job and Proverbs, and it also turns up in classical writers like Plato and Plutarch, so the meaning is steady across sources.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: Describing something that brings death or proves fatal, like a deadly poison.
article: θανατήφορος combines the words for "death" and "to bear/bring," so it literally means "death-bearing" or fatal. It appears just once in the New Testament, in James 3:8, where the tongue is called full of "deadly poison." Everyday Koine documents back this up: the astrologer Vettius Valens uses it of "deadly" or "dangerous" circumstances, and the Septuagint applies it in passages like Numbers 18:22 and Job 33:23.
caution: The single corpus-measured rendering here is "unruly," which clashes with every lexicon's "deadly"; the lexical evidence strongly favors "death-bringing," so treat the measured label with caution.

definition: To corrupt or tamper with something pure—like watering down wine—so as to deceive others.
article: δολόω means to adulterate or tamper with something, much as a dishonest merchant might dilute wine or fake precious metal. Its single New Testament appearance, in 2 Corinthians 4:2, applies this image to handling "the word of God," which the Majority Standard Bible renders as "renounced" (a paraphrase of refusing to corrupt it). The everyday Koine papyri make the metaphor vivid: one document checks whether tin "has been adulterated" (δεδόλωται) before melting it down—exactly the sense of falsifying something genuine.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single rendering measured, the precise force here rests heavily on context and external evidence rather than repeated biblical usage.

definition: An adverb meaning at every moment or on every occasion; always.
article: πάντοτε is a simple adverb of time built from "all" and "when," meaning "always" or "at all times." Its range is narrow and consistent: of 42 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "always" 33 times (83%), with the rest being phrasings like "all times" or "time" that carry the same meaning. The word turns up in everyday Koine letters too — one papyrus has a slave writing to her master, "I always pray for your health" (εὔχομαι πάντοτε περὶ τῆς ὑγιείας σου), showing it was common, ordinary language.

definition: A thick clot or large drop, used in the New Testament for clots of blood falling like heavy sweat.
article: θρόμβος means a lump or clot — something thickened, fittingly traced to a root meaning "to thicken." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:44, describing Jesus' sweat falling like "clots of blood" (θρόμβοι αἵματος); the Majority Standard Bible renders the word as "sweat" in its single occurrence. Notably, Hobart showed that this exact phrase, θρόμβοι αἵματος, was common in ancient medical writing, which fits Luke's traditional association with medicine.
caution: The word occurs only once and in a passage some manuscripts omit (Luke 22:43-44 is bracketed in critical editions), so the evidence is thin.

definition: To come or arrive somewhere, often used of something—a calamity, an enemy, or the Holy Spirit—coming upon a person.
article: ἐπέρχομαι combines "upon" (ἐπί) with "come" (ἔρχομαι), and means simply to come or arrive, frequently with the sense of something coming upon someone. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times, where translators render it "come" about a third of the time and "upon" in another fifth; it often describes calamities or an enemy bearing down, but also the Holy Spirit coming on a person, as in Luke 1:35. An interesting twist comes from everyday Koine papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show it commonly meant to proceed or make a legal claim against someone—language drawn from contracts and lawsuits.

definition: A small Roman copper coin, the quadrans, worth a quarter of an as — the smallest coin people handled.
article: κοδράντης is a Greek spelling of the Latin coin name quadrans, the fourth part of an as, and it appears just twice in the New Testament (Matthew 5:26 and Mark 12:42). It refers to one specific tiny coin, so its range is narrow — the King James Version simply calls it a "farthing." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that Luke, who tended to avoid Latin and Aramaic words, replaced it with λεπτόν (a coin worth half a quadrans) in his parallel passage, while Mark even pairs the two coins together.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence is thin, though the sources agree that it names a single small coin.

definition: To throw one's arms completely around someone in an embrace.
article: This verb is built from pieces meaning "with," "around," and "take," so it literally pictures taking someone fully into your arms. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 20:10, where Paul embraces the young man Eutychus. Outside the Bible the word shows up in everyday land-surveys meaning "included" or "taken up" — for instance, describing how much land a shrine of Isis occupied — which fits its core idea of enclosing or encompassing something.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the sense rests on thin evidence, and the digest's lone rendering label "threw" is misleading for what is really an embrace.

definition: A false Messiah—someone who pretends to be the Christ but is not.
article: This word combines "false" (ψευδής) and "Christ" (Χριστός) to describe a counterfeit Messiah, a pretender to the role God promised. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in parallel warnings by Jesus that such figures will arise and try to deceive even the elect (Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22). Abbott-Smith helpfully points readers to the related term ἀντίχριστος ("antichrist") for comparison.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in parallel passages, the evidence for this word's range is very thin.

definition: To turn your attention away from everything else and fix your gaze steadily on one thing.
senseLabels: to look steadfastly at one thing
article: This verb literally means to look away from all else and fix your eyes intently on a single object. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 11:26, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "valued" — capturing Moses' steady focus on his reward rather than a literal act of seeing. A nice parallel comes from an Ephesus inscription (2nd century AD), where someone "looks to" both the piety of the goddess and the honor of the city, showing the same sense of fixed, purposeful attention in everyday Koine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning "little girl" or "maiden," spoken by Jesus to a child.
article: Talitha is not really a Greek word at all but an Aramaic term meaning "little girl" or "maiden," preserved untranslated in the New Testament. It appears only once, in Mark 5:41, where Jesus addresses a dead child with the phrase "Talitha cumi." The word reflects the underlying Aramaic טְלִיתָא, and the Gospel writer keeps Jesus' original words before translating them for readers.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is a foreign term carried over from Aramaic, so its range cannot be measured from Greek usage.

definition: Born outside lawful marriage, such as the child of a slave or concubine; illegitimate rather than a true, recognized heir.
article: νόθος describes someone born outside a lawful marriage—an illegitimate child who lacks the standing of a true, recognized son. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 12:8, where being without discipline marks one as illegitimate rather than a genuine child. The everyday Koine papyri make the contrast vivid: one tax document from A.D. 71/72 lists νόθοι (bastards) from the temple over against the νόμιμοι, the legitimate priests, showing this was a real legal and social category.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range in Scripture rests on a single verse; the lone tabulated rendering ‘experience’ reflects how the verse was phrased rather than the word's core meaning, which the lexica consistently give as ‘illegitimate.’

definition: To bend, bow, or lean something; or to turn aside, decline, or cause an enemy to give way.
senseLabels: to bow or lower (the head, face)
article: κλίνω is a flexible verb built on the idea of slanting or tilting—bowing the head, leaning down to rest, or causing something to give way. In the New Testament it appears just 7 times, and the Majority Standard Bible only renders it with a distinct English word in about 3 of those, since it often gets absorbed into phrasing like "bowing His head" (John 19:30) or "turned to flight" enemy armies (Heb 11:34). Its breadth shows up clearly in the Septuagint, where it occurs 52 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew נָטָה ("to stretch out, bend") 12 times; the papyri even use it of a ship listing to one side and sinking, and of vigor that has declined.
caution: With only 7 NT occurrences and 4 of those absorbed into phrasing, the measured English senses rest on single examples each, so the lexicons (covering reclining and day-declining uses too) show a wider range than the count suggests.

definition: To fall, drop, or collapse downward — whether a person, object, or someone bowing to the ground in worship or submission.
article: πίπτω means to fall in nearly every sense: things dropping, people collapsing, or someone falling prostrate before another in worship or supplication. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "fell" in 80 of its 90 New Testament occurrences (98%), and the lexicons agree this covers both literal descent and figurative falling, such as falling under judgment. A nice detail from the everyday papyri: the form πέπτωκεν was common business shorthand meaning "paid," as in money that has "fallen" onto a bank's table.

definition: To regard something as utterly disgusting and turn away from it in loathing.
article: This verb means to find something so foul that you recoil from it—to loathe or abhor it. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: in Romans 2:22, where it describes detesting idols, and in Revelation 21:8, where its passive form describes people who have become detestable. The Septuagint uses it far more often, 37 times across 13 books, most frequently rendering the Hebrew תָּעַב (12×), which carries the same sense of treating something as an abomination. Abbott-Smith notes its root literally evokes a stink, and Moulton-Milligan shows ancient grammarians prized it as good Attic Greek even though it was common in everyday writing.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the measured rendering for Revelation 21:8 listed oddly, the English data here is thin and should be weighed against the much richer Septuagint usage.

definition: To make something resemble or be like another thing; in the passive, to be made like or resemble.
article: This verb means to make one thing closely resemble another, built from the prefix meaning "from" plus the verb "to make like." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 7:3, where Melchizedek is described as being "made like" the Son of God. The measured rendering label here reads "mother," which appears to be a data artifact rather than the word's actual meaning — the genuine sense is "made like" or "resembling." Outside the New Testament it shows up a handful of times in the Septuagint (Wisdom 13:14 and the Letter of Jeremiah), used of fashioning or comparing images.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured sense label appears garbled, so lean on the classical and lexical evidence.

definition: A mass of clouds; used figuratively for a dense crowd or great gathering of people.
article: νέφος literally means a mass of clouds, much like the related word νεφέλη. In its single New Testament appearance (Hebrews 12:1), it is used metaphorically for a dense throng—the "great cloud of witnesses" surrounding believers. This figurative sense of a crowd is well attested in classical authors like Homer and Herodotus, and the Septuagint uses νέφος 25 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for cloud (עָב, 9×).
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its sole measured sense rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To run out or fall short, so that something is not enough for what is needed.
article: This verb describes time, resources, or opportunity giving out before the task is finished. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:32, where the writer says time would fail him if he tried to recount every faithful person — rendered "more shall not" in the standard translation counted here. The everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one inscription speaks of "leaving out no effort" in handling requests, showing it could mean coming up short or being lacking.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, this entry rests on very thin biblical evidence and depends heavily on outside papyri and lexicon data.

definition: A preposition meaning in front of or in the sight of someone, used to show being in their presence.
article: ἐναντίον works as a preposition meaning "before" or "in the presence of" someone, often carrying the sense of being in their sight or view. The measured New Testament renderings cluster tightly around this one idea, with the translation differences ("his," "before," "before His") simply reflecting the surrounding words. The Septuagint shows just how common this was, appearing 387 times and most often standing in for the Hebrew פָּנִים ("face," 159×), which fits the literal picture of being "in front of someone's face."
caution: It is the neuter form of the adjective ἐναντίος ("opposite, hostile"), so context decides whether "before" or "contrary" is meant; the New Testament uses it only as the preposition.

definition: To twist or distort something from its right state, especially to morally corrupt people or to mislead and turn them away.
article: At its root διαστρέφω means to twist or distort, and in the New Testament it works almost entirely in a moral sense: a "perverse" generation, a man "subverting" the nation, leaders who draw disciples "away" after them. It appears 7 times across 4 books, often in the participle διεστραμμένος ("twisted, perverse"), and the Septuagint uses it 29 times, frequently for Hebrew עָקַשׁ ("crooked"). One vivid touch from the papyri: a related noun appears in a sixth-century Oxyrhynchus letter where farmers had been "put to such straits" (διαστροφῇ), showing how the idea of being twisted bled into everyday hardship.
caution: With only 7 occurrences spread thinly across four senses, the boundaries between them rest on just one or two examples each.

definition: To flee somewhere for safety or protection, especially to take refuge with someone who can help.
article: καταφεύγω means to flee to a place or person for safety, with the sense that the refuge is actually reached. It appears just twice in the New Testament, once literally of people escaping danger (Acts 14:6) and once figuratively of those who "have fled for refuge" to lay hold of hope (Heb 6:18). The papyri make the picture vivid: it was almost a technical term for petitioners and suppliants appealing to a ruler or authority for help, as in a plea "I flee to you, O king, that I may obtain justice."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the measured range is thin, though the Septuagint and papyri evidence strongly supports the "flee for refuge" sense.

definition: A liquid measure of capacity, roughly nine gallons (about 39 liters) per unit.
article: μετρητής names a standard unit for measuring liquids like wine and oil, equal to about 9 gallons (roughly 39 liters). It appears only once in the New Testament (John 2:6), describing how much the stone water jars held, and three times in the Septuagint, where it renders Hebrew terms for measures such as the seah and the bath. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical commercial use—one document from 210 BC estimates a grape harvest at "six metretae of wine." Note that the literal Greek root means "measurer," and classical writers like Plato used it that way, though in the Bible it always refers to the unit of volume.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and three in the Septuagint, the exact size given (about 9 gallons) reflects scholarly estimate rather than precise certainty.

definition: A specimen or sample put on display, used in Scripture as a warning example of what others should avoid.
article: At its root δεῖγμα means a thing shown — a specimen or sample — and the everyday papyri confirm this, where it names a sample of corn to be sealed or weighed (P Hib I. 39) and even a plan or sketch (P Giss I. 15). In the New Testament it appears only once, in Jude 7, where Sodom and Gomorrah are set out as a δεῖγμα — a public 'specimen' that functions as a warning example. The Majority Standard Bible renders that single occurrence as 'immorality,' but the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) treat the word as 'example' or 'warning,' so the meaning is the displayed example itself rather than the sin on display.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering 'immorality' differs from the lexicons' 'example/warning,' so its precise force here is uncertain.

definition: To loosen, slacken, or let go of something, including leaving someone unsupported or giving up a harsh behavior.
article: ἀνίημι covers a spread of related ideas built on the sense of releasing tension: physically loosening or unfastening something (the prisoners' chains in Acts 16:26 came loose), leaving or abandoning someone (Hebrews 13:5, "I will never leave you"), and figuratively giving up a behavior—in Ephesians 6:9 masters are told to stop threatening. The Majority Standard Bible's four uses split into three senses, matching the broad range that Abbott-Smith and the Septuagint (35 times, often for Hebrew רָפָה, "to relax" or "let drop") confirm. The everyday papyri are vivid here: one third-century document uses it for a man "permitted to remain in arrears," and an inscription describes schoolboys being "let off" from their lessons.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences spread across three distinct senses, each meaning rests on very thin measured evidence.

definition: A state of stillness and calm, especially the sea becoming quiet after being stormy.
article: γαλήνη means calm or stillness, and in the New Testament it always describes the sea growing quiet—every one of its 3 occurrences comes from the same scene of Jesus stilling a storm (Matthew 8:26, Mark 4:39, Luke 8:24). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "calm" two-thirds of the time and "perfectly calm" once. A nice glimpse of its everyday range comes from the papyri and inscriptions: the related adjective appears in a third-century inscription describing people "leading a quiet and serene life," and in later documents γαληνότης ("serenity") served as an honorific title.
caution: This word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the same storm-calming episode, so its full range rests on outside evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: A precious gemstone combining the red of sard and the white of onyx, listed among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem.
article: Sardonyx is a banded gemstone whose name combines 'sard' (a reddish stone) and 'onyx,' producing layers of red over white.
