It appears just once in the New Testament, among the twelve foundation stones of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:20. Notably, the Majority Standard Bible renders this single occurrence as 'amethyst' (100%), which differs from the standard lexical identification as sardonyx — the Roman writer Pliny describes it as white set upon red, 'like a human fingernail laid over flesh.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured translation ('amethyst') conflicts with the lexicons, which identify it as sardonyx.

definition: An upright stake or post, especially the wooden cross used by the Romans to execute people by crucifixion.
article: σταυρός refers to an upright stake or pole, but in the New Testament it overwhelmingly means the Roman cross used for execution—rendered "cross" in 23 of its 28 occurrences (82%). It also appears in phrases about crucifying someone ("let cross," 2×), and Jesus uses it figuratively in the famous saying about taking up one's cross daily. A striking parallel comes from a 4th–5th century Christian prayer on papyrus that addresses "O God of the crosses that are laid upon us," treating crosses as the trials God both sends and eases. The lexica note that the earliest Greek writers used the word for a plain stake, with the crucifixion sense emerging only in later authors.

definition: A guard or sentry posted to watch over and protect something, especially prisoners or a place.
article: φύλαξ is a person assigned to watch and protect, like a sentry standing duty over prisoners or property. It comes from the verb φυλάσσω ("to guard"), and all three New Testament uses appear in Acts, describing the guards watching apostles in custody. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense vividly: one document speaks of sending a guard to protect ripening fruit at harvest time.
caution: The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts, so the measured range is narrow.

definition: Not bending or wavering; standing firm and unyielding, used figuratively of holding steady.
article: ἀκλινής literally means "unbending" and is used figuratively for being firm or resolute. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 10:23, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Let us resolutely" hold fast our confession; it also shows up a handful of times in 4 Maccabees. Outside the Bible, Moulton-Milligan note it in an everyday papyrus petition, where it describes the "impartial" (literally unbending) ears of an official.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: The act of giving or establishing law, especially God's giving of the Law of Moses to Israel.
article: νομοθεσία means the giving or establishing of law, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Romans 9:4, where it refers to Israel's reception of the Mosaic Law as one of their privileges. The translation tables list its rendering as part of the phrase 'theirs is the giving of the law,' which is why the measured sense shows up simply as 'Theirs.' Beyond the Bible it was a common word in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite a royal petition from around A.D. 375 that speaks of 'your divine and benevolent legislation,' showing it was ordinary administrative vocabulary, not a purely religious term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests almost entirely on outside evidence rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: The condition of being empty, pointless, or unable to reach any true purpose.
article: ματαιότης describes emptiness or futility—a state of having no real purpose or of failing to reach one. In the New Testament it appears only three times (Romans 8:20, Ephesians 4:17, 2 Peter 2:18), where it is rendered "futility" each time it gets its own English word. The most telling evidence comes from the Septuagint, where it appears 54 times and translates the Hebrew word הֶבֶל ("vapor, breath") 30 times—the famous "vanity" of Ecclesiastes—anchoring the sense in fleeting emptiness.
caution: Confidence is low: the word is rare outside the Bible (found in almost no secular authors), so its full range rests largely on its biblical and Septuagint use.

definition: A back-and-forth discussion or sharp dispute, where people question and argue with one another.
article: συζήτησις describes people questioning and arguing back and forth — a discussion that can shade into heated dispute. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 15:7 and 28:29), rendered once simply as the setting "among" people and once as "disputing sharply among." Notably, the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and even in Cicero, who borrowed the Greek term to describe daily intellectual discussion with a friend.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences, and Acts 28:29 is omitted in some critical texts), so the exact force of the word is uncertain.

definition: To read something written, often aloud to others, and so to take in and understand its contents.
article: In the New Testament ἀναγινώσκω overwhelmingly means "to read" — 23 of 32 times (74%), plus another 3 times where someone reads in reply to a question. The word literally combines "again" with "to know," and older lexicons like Dodson and Strong's preserve the broader idea of "recognize" or "know certainly," but the measured New Testament data shows it settled firmly on "read." A nice detail from the everyday papyri: the word regularly meant reading aloud — petitions, wills, and official dispatches "being read" before a gathered group — which fits New Testament scenes of public Scripture reading.

definition: An adverb meaning "on the whole" or "at all," used with a negative to mean "not at all" or "in no way whatsoever."
article: καθόλου built from κατά and ὅλος ("according to the whole") and basically means "on the whole" or "in general." In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 4:18) it comes with a negative to mean "not at all" — the authorities tell the apostles not to speak or teach in Jesus' name whatsoever. The everyday papyri confirm this absolute, sweeping force: one document from A.D. 36 uses it to say nothing "at all" was added to a sum of drachmas. Note that the measured rendering labels this occurrence "again," but the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) and the papyri all point to "at all / not at all" as the actual meaning.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "again" conflicts with the lexicons and papyri, which uniformly support "not at all"—the negated sense in Acts 4:18.

definition: A strong fermented or intoxicating drink, distinct from ordinary wine.
article: σίκερα refers to fermented, intoxicating liquor — what English Bibles call "strong drink." It appears just once in the New Testament (Luke 1:15), where John the Baptist is to drink neither wine nor σίκερα, but it shows up 16 times in the Septuagint, always translating the Hebrew word shekar. The word itself is an indeclinable borrowing from Aramaic, and Moulton-Milligan note it turns up in everyday Koine papyri, where one document may even reference a special jar for drinking it.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise range of σίκερα rests mainly on its Septuagint and everyday Koine usage rather than New Testament evidence.

definition: A serious, honorable quality of character that commands respect; dignity in how one lives and conducts oneself.
article: σεμνότης describes a person's dignity — the grave, honorable seriousness that earns others' respect. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the Pastoral Epistles, and the Majority Standard Bible renders every instance "dignity" (100%). The word was at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription where a doctor is praised for it, and the Latin Vulgate even translated it "chastity" in some verses, though "seriousness, dignity" fits better.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a single measured sense, the evidence is thin, and translators have ranged from "gravity" to "chastity."

definition: A name meaning "the Destroyer," used in Revelation for the king of the abyss.
article: Ἀπολλύων is the Greek name given to the angel of the abyss in Revelation 9:11, where it stands as the translation of the Hebrew name Abaddon. It is literally the active participle of the verb ἀπόλλυμι ("to destroy"), so it functions as a title meaning "the Destroying One." It appears just once in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Abaddon" in that single verse, matching the Hebrew name it explains.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests entirely on that single passage.

definition: To throw something off or away, and by extension to lose or let go of what you have.
article: ἀποβάλλω literally means to throw something off or away, as when blind Bartimaeus throws off his cloak before coming to Jesus (Mark 10:50). It extends figuratively to losing or letting go of something, as in the warning not to cast away one's confidence (Hebrews 10:35). The word appears just 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where one inscription uses it of a city that has 'lost' a good citizen.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin evidence, and one rendering ('up die incomplete' at Revelation 3:2) reflects a translation fragment rather than a clear measured sense.

definition: Made of stone; describing an object formed or carved from stone.
article: λίθινος simply means "made of stone," an adjective built from the noun λίθος ("stone"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, describing things like stone water jars (John 2:6) and stone idols (Revelation 9:20), and all sources agree on its plain meaning. The everyday Koine papyri show the same usage in ordinary contexts—stone troughs, stone presses, a stone bowl, even a small necklace of stone beads—confirming this was a routine descriptive word, not a specialized one. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for tablet (לוּחַ, 14×), as in the stone tablets of the law.
caution: The two listed senses are really the same meaning ("of stone") split only by translation wording, so do not read any difference into them.

definition: To sit on something, or to set or place someone on top of something.
article: This verb is built from "epi" (on/upon) plus "kathizō" (to sit), and it means to sit on something or to set someone upon it. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 21:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as Jesus sitting. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times across 6 books, often translating Hebrew words tied to riding (rākab) and to a mule (pirdâ), fitting its connection to mounting or seating someone on an animal.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense there rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A quality of inner sincerity and openness that, in giving, becomes wholehearted generosity.
article: ἁπλότης describes an undivided heart — being sincere, straightforward, and without hidden motives — and in several passages this open-handedness shifts into the sense of generous giving. Of its 8 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "generosity" 3 times (mostly in 2 Corinthians' discussion of giving) and "leading" or simplicity-related ideas elsewhere, while older glosses like KJV add "bountifulness," "liberality," and "singleness." In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew words for integrity and uprightness (תֹּם and יֹשֶׁר), and a Roman inscription noted by Moulton-Milligan praises a man who "practiced ἁπλότης" toward his friends — showing it was valued as plain-dealing sincerity in everyday Koine.
caution: The word's range genuinely splits between "sincerity" and "generosity," and the rendering of any given verse can be disputed.

definition: Describes someone who treats others with mildness, gentleness, and kindness rather than harshness.
article: ἤπιος describes a gentle, mild manner shown toward other people. It appears just twice in the New Testament (1 Thessalonians 2:7 and 2 Timothy 2:24), and in both cases the English translations fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than rendering it with a single word. A nice glimpse of its everyday flavor comes from a late Roman sepulchral inscription cited by Moulton-Milligan, which praises a man named Sarapion as 'mild and gentle to all people' — capturing exactly the idea of kindness toward others.
caution: Evidence is thin (only two NT occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing), and at 1 Thessalonians 2:7 manuscripts disagree between ἤπιος and νήπιος ('infant').

definition: Relating to a king — royal in nature, belonging to a king, or a person in royal service.
article: βασιλικός is an adjective meaning "royal" or "belonging to a king," and it stretches naturally to cover anything connected with a king — a king's land, a king's clothing, or a man in royal service. In the New Testament's 5 occurrences it shows this range: it modifies things ("royal" 2×), names a courtier ("royal official" 1×, John 4:49), and in James 2:8 describes a law as supremely "royal." The everyday Koine flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where the phrase "the royal road" (βασιλική ὁδός) appears as early as 240 BC and matches the Septuagint's wording in Numbers 20:17.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences, the senses rest on thin data, and some manuscripts read βασιλίσκος instead in John 4:46, 49.

definition: To come or go down, moving from a higher place to a lower one, such as from hills to the coast or by ship to port.
article: This verb describes movement downward—from high ground to low, from inland toward the coast, or from the open sea into harbor. It combines κατά ("down") with ἔρχομαι ("come/go"), and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 13 times, rendered "came down" (31%), "went down" (23%), or simply "came" (15%); Abbott-Smith notes it can also mean coming into port by ship and, figuratively in James 3:15, of "wisdom" not coming down from God. It was a favorite word of Luke and shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where one letter writer apologizes that he "was unable to come down" (P Fay 123).

definition: An adverb meaning very, exceedingly, or to a great degree, intensifying whatever word it modifies.
article: λίαν is an intensifying adverb meaning "very" or "exceedingly," used to strengthen an adjacent word. Its meaning is straightforward, though it often disappears into the phrasing of English translations — in fact, 7 of its 14 Byzantine occurrences leave no separate English word of their own. The everyday papyri show a charming pattern: the letter-formula "ἐχάρην λίαν" ("I rejoiced greatly"), as in 2 and 3 John, appears almost word-for-word in personal letters of the era expressing joy at hearing a friend is well. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew מְאֹד, meaning "very" or "exceedingly."
caution: Because λίαN intensifies nearby words, translations frequently absorb it into phrasing rather than rendering it as a distinct word, so measured English glosses understate its consistent meaning.

definition: To behead someone by cutting off their head with an axe.
article: This verb means to cut off someone's head with an axe, a specific form of execution. It appears just once in the New Testament (Revelation 20:4) and the same single time in the critical text, where translations fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. Everyday Koine papyri use the related noun πέλεκυς for an ordinary axe — one document lists 'ten axes' for woodcutting — and the historian Polybius uses the verb of executing people 'according to their custom.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests largely on outside evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: To wave or motion with the hand as a signal, especially to get attention or call for silence.
article: This verb literally means to shake something down, but in the New Testament it always refers to motioning or waving the hand as a signal, appearing 4 times, all in Acts. In 3 of 4 cases it simply means "motioned" (often to a crowd), while in Acts 19:33 it specifically means motioning for silence. Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri preserve the same word in a magical text where someone waves toward a lamp while reciting an incantation, showing the gesture sense was common outside Scripture too.

definition: To become rusted or corroded, with metal eaten away and tarnished by oxidation.
article: This verb describes metal that has become rusted or eaten away by corrosion, intensifying a simpler word for "to rust." It appears just once in the New Testament, in James 5:3, where rich people's gold and silver are pictured as corroded. The word also turns up once in the Septuagint, at Sirach 12:11, so its attestation is thin overall.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence base for this word is very limited.

definition: To eat a meal — originally breakfast, later any main meal — sharing food with others.
senseLabels: to dine or eat a meal
article: This verb means to eat a meal, and in classical Greek it specifically meant to breakfast, though by later Greek it broadened to taking any main meal. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and Abbott-Smith notes the morning sense survives in John 21:12, 15 while Luke 11:37 reflects the wider 'dine' meaning. One quirk: although the digest lists two measured senses, the second ('know') reflects a translation choice in John 21:15 rather than a genuine separate meaning of the word, which everywhere concerns eating.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences — and the listed 'know' sense is a rendering artifact, not a real second meaning, so treat the sense breakdown with care.

definition: Grass or green plants, especially the vegetation that grows in fields and serves as fodder for animals.
article: In the New Testament χόρτος consistently means grass or field vegetation, rendered "grass" in 7 of its 15 occurrences (78%), with the remaining cases absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 43 times, most often translating the Hebrew עֵ֫שֶׂב (14×) and חָצִיר (6×), both common words for green growth. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the practical sense: one document from A.D. 30 describes someone carrying off "five hundred bundles of my hay," and another mentions "rotten hay," showing the word covered both growing grass and harvested fodder.
caution: Classical and lexical sources note an older sense of "enclosure" or "feeding place" (Homer), but this meaning does not appear in the measured biblical data.

definition: Free from worry or anxious care; untroubled, with nothing weighing on the mind.
article: This adjective describes someone who is free from anxiety or care, built from a negative prefix joined to the word for "worry" (μέριμνα). It appears only twice in the New Testament: Paul wants the unmarried person to be "free from concern" so they can focus on the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:32), and in Matthew 28:14 the soldiers are promised they will be kept out of trouble. The everyday papyri make the flavor vivid — one letter says "have no more anxiety about your household than you would if you were present," showing it was common, practical language for putting someone's mind at ease.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a wide range from "anxiety-free" to "out of trouble," the precise shade depends heavily on context.

definition: A rising from the dead; a coming back to life after death.
article: This noun comes from the verb ἐγείρω ("to raise") and appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 27:53, where every translation surveyed renders it "resurrection." Outside the Bible it had a wider range, meaning a "rousing" or "waking"—Abbott-Smith notes this older sense in Plato, and the Letter of Aristeas contrasts it with going to sleep. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan point to a magic spell in an everyday papyrus headed ἔγερσις σώματος νεκροῦ, "raising of a dead body," matching the exact sense found in Matthew.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured biblical range rests on a single verse.

definition: A word for a huge, countless number, or more precisely the number ten thousand.
article: This word points to a very large quantity—either the specific figure ten thousand or, more loosely, an uncountable multitude. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, rendered "ten thousand" twice (as in the servant who owed ten thousand talents in Matthew 18:24) and once as part of a larger number in 1 Corinthians 14:19. The lexicons split on emphasis: Abbott-Smith treats the countless, infinite sense as primary, while Moulton-Milligan cites everyday papyri using it literally for 10,000, as in an order for "10,000 bundles."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and the sources disagreeing over whether the core sense is "ten thousand" or "countless," the exact force in any verse can be uncertain.

definition: A tiny stroke or hook that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from a similar one, used to mean the smallest possible detail.
article: κεραία literally means a "little horn," and it refers to the small mark or point that tells apart similar-looking Hebrew letters. In the New Testament it appears only twice (Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17), both times paired with the idea that not even the tiniest detail of the Law will pass away. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "single stroke of a pen" once and simply "pen" once, while the KJV famously translates it "tittle."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise nuance rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A basin or washbowl used for washing, especially the hands or feet.
article: This word names a basin used for washing, related to the verb νίπτω ("to wash"). It appears only once in the New Testament, in John 13:5, where Jesus pours water into one to wash the disciples' feet, and in that single occurrence it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. The lexicons describe it variously as a basin, a ewer, or a vessel for washing the hands or feet.
caution: This is a hapax in the New Testament with only one occurrence, so its precise shape and use cannot be pinned down from the biblical evidence alone.

definition: An Aramaic surname Jesus gave to the apostles James and John, explained in the text as "sons of thunder."
article: Boanerges is a nickname Jesus gave to the brothers James and John, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Mark 3:17. The Gospel itself supplies the meaning, which Dodson gives as "sons of thunder," while Strong's offers "sons of commotion." The word comes from Aramaic (Chaldee) roots, and Abbott-Smith notes it is indeclinable and that scholars still debate exactly how the name was formed.

definition: The act of burning, or being burned up by fire.
article: καῦσις means "burning" — the act of setting something on fire or being consumed by it, formed from the verb καίω ("to burn"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 6:8, where unfruitful ground is said to end in burning; note that the Majority Standard Bible's rendering there is counted as "land," which reflects the surrounding phrase rather than the word's own core meaning. Everyday papyri use it in very concrete settings — for instance, the "burning of lamps" (καύσεως λύχνων) in temple offerings and contracts.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range in biblical usage is very thin.

definition: A lion, the large wild cat, sometimes used as an image of a dangerous or powerful threat.
article: λέων simply means "lion," and every one of its 9 New Testament occurrences is translated that way. It shows up both literally—as in the lions whose mouths were shut in Hebrews 11:33—and figuratively, picturing a deadly enemy, as when 1 Peter 5:8 likens the devil to a prowling lion. The word was common in everyday Koine: a first-century papyrus even uses it in a saying, "a lion he was who took it, a fool who lost it," and in the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew words for lion, most often אֲרִי (68 times).

definition: Shared by everyone in common, or—in religious contexts—ordinary in a way that makes something ritually unclean or unholy.
article: Κοινός has two faces in the New Testament. Its basic meaning is "shared," as when the early believers held everything "common" (Acts 2:44; 4:32), a usage echoed in everyday papyri where it describes a shared courtyard, a joint decision, or a husband and wife's "common" life. But in religious settings it flips to mean "ordinary" in the sense of ritually unclean or unhallowed—the food Peter refuses to eat (Acts 10:14) or what cannot enter the holy city (Rev 21:27). One striking detail: of its 13 Byzantine occurrences, 3 are simply absorbed into the surrounding phrasing and get no English word of their own.
caution: The "unclean/profane" sense is a Hebraistic development rather than the word's classical core, so the two senses sit some distance apart and context must decide which is meant.

definition: To give birth to a child; also used figuratively of the earth producing plants or of something bringing forth a result.
article: τίκτω is the ordinary Greek word for giving birth, and that is how the New Testament uses it nearly every time — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gave birth" in 10 of 19 occurrences and "born" in another 3. The Septuagint shows the same focus, using it 237 times, overwhelmingly to translate the Hebrew verb יָלַד ("to bear, beget"), 223 of those times. Beyond literal childbirth the word can stretch figuratively: Abbott-Smith notes it used of the earth bringing forth plants and even of lust "giving birth" to sin. Everyday papyri confirm the plain sense, as in a first-century BC letter wishing a woman luck "if you bear children."

definition: Slow or sluggish, whether physically delaying an action or being slow to grasp and believe something.
article: Βραδύς describes being slow, and the New Testament uses it in two related ways: slow to do something, as in being "slow to speak" (James 1:19), and slow in the mind, as when Jesus calls the disciples "slow of heart" to believe (Luke 24:25). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, often in document signatures describing people who wrote "slowly" because they were unskilled at writing. So the range runs from literal slowness to a figurative dullness of understanding.
caution: Only 3 occurrences in the New Testament, so this profile rests on thin evidence.

definition: The word by which a person or thing is called; a name, which can also stand for someone's reputation, character, or authority.
article: ὄνομα is simply a "name" — the word by which a person or thing is called — and it carries this single meaning with remarkable consistency: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "name" in 214 of its 232 New Testament uses (the other 18 are absorbed into surrounding phrasing). In the Septuagint it appears 896 times, almost always translating the Hebrew שֵׁם ("name," 702×). Beyond the bare label, the lexicons note it can extend to a person's character, fame, or reputation, and the everyday papyri show the same plain usage — one traveler even wrote of carving "the names of my friends on the sanctuaries for perpetual remembrance."

definition: Having great wealth or possessions; used of people who are rich, and figuratively of being abundantly supplied with something.
article: πλούσιος means "rich" or "wealthy," and the New Testament evidence is remarkably consistent: it is rendered "rich" in 73% of its 28 occurrences and "rich man" in another 19%, with the Berean Study Bible agreeing 100% on those choices. The two senses are really the same idea — sometimes the word stands alone as a noun meaning "a rich man" (as in the camel-through-a-needle's-eye sayings). In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew עָשִׁיר ("rich") 15 times, and the everyday Koine papyri show the same plain meaning — one even calls a young man a "handsome and rich stripling." The lexica also note a figurative use, "abounding in," applied to God being rich in mercy, though that nuance is not separated out in the measured data here.

definition: To bring something upon someone, especially something harmful like punishment, accusation, or disaster.
article: In the New Testament ἐπάγω appears only 3 times across 2 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "bringing" in 2 of those cases (the third is absorbed into surrounding phrasing). The word carries the sense of laying or inflicting something on a person — in 2 Peter 2:1 and 2:5 it is destruction or a flood, and in Acts 5:28 it is the bringing of someone's blood upon others. A striking piece of evidence comes from the papyri: a document from A.D. 38 uses the very same verb for someone who "had the audacity to bring baseless accusations" against another, matching the New Testament's pattern of bringing harm or charges upon people. In the Septuagint it appears 119 times, frequently translating the Hebrew word for "evil" or "calamity."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured evidence is thin, so this entry is low confidence.

definition: A person who proclaims the good news of the gospel; a preacher or bearer of glad tidings.
article: An εὐαγγελιστής is someone who announces good news—in the New Testament specifically a preacher of the gospel. The word appears only 3 times across 3 books (Acts 21:8, Ephesians 4:11, 2 Timothy 4:5), and despite the varied surface renderings in the data, every instance points to the same role. It comes from εὐαγγελίζω ("to bring good news"), and one intriguing piece of evidence is a disputed inscription from Rhodes where the word may describe a chief priest as a "proclaimer" of oracular announcements—though scholars read that text differently. Abbott-Smith notes that only later, in church usage, did the word come to mean a writer of a gospel.
caution: With just 3 occurrences and confidence rated low, the evidence is thin, and the cited Rhodes inscription is itself textually disputed.

definition: The state of being away or not present.
article: ἀπουσία means "absence"—the state of not being present—and that is exactly how it is rendered in its single New Testament appearance in Philippians 2:12. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense, including one early second-century letter pleading "not to forget me in my long absence." Lexicons like Abbott-Smith and Dodson also note a secondary sense of "deficiency" or "waste" found in business documents, but that meaning never appears in the New Testament.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be confirmed from biblical usage alone.

definition: The wing of a bird or other winged creature, used both literally and in imagery of shelter and flight.
article: πτέρυξ simply means a wing, whether of a real bird or of the visionary creatures in Revelation, and the two measured senses both come down to that one idea. Its range is narrow and stable: 4 of 5 New Testament uses are plainly "wings," with the remaining instance (Revelation 12:14) describing wings given for flight. In the Septuagint it appears 76 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew kanaph ("wing"), and an interesting papyrus note records it in a fourth- or third-century B.C. oracle reading bird flight for omens, marking left and right wings.

definition: To make something or someone unclean, polluting them in a moral, physical, or ritual sense.
article: μιαίνω means to stain, taint, or contaminate—to make something unclean. In the New Testament it appears 5 times and usually points to moral or ritual defilement, as in the ritual concern about entering the governor's palace in John 18:28 or the corrupted conscience in Titus 1:15. The Septuagint uses it heavily, 113 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew word for "unclean" (טָמֵא), and a vivid papyrus from the Serapeum dream-vision warns that women, once defiled, "shall never at all be pure."
caution: Several of the measured senses simply reflect different surrounding words in single verses rather than truly distinct meanings, so the core sense is consistently "defile."

definition: Earnest intensity or wholehearted zeal in pursuing or serving something.
article: This noun describes earnestness, intentness, or zealous effort — putting your whole self into something. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 26:7), where Paul speaks of the twelve tribes earnestly serving God; the everyday papyri use it the same way, as in a letter (164 BC) urging someone to act "using every effort and taking every precaution." Notably, the word was unknown to classical Attic Greek and surfaces in the Septuagint and Koine documents, where it carries this ethical sense of devoted intensity.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured "promise" rendering conflicts with the lexicons, which agree on "earnestness/zeal."

definition: The act of remembering or keeping something in mind; in its key phrase, recalling or making mention of something.
article: μνήμη means memory or remembrance, and it appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 1:15, where Peter wants to ensure his readers can recall his teaching after he is gone. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times across 3 books, mostly translating Hebrew words for remembrance or memorial. The most interesting detail is the phrase μνήμην ποιεῖσθαι: in everyday papyri and classical Greek it usually means 'to make mention' rather than 'to remember' — a dying emperor's letter uses it of giving an accurate account — so 2 Peter 1:15 could carry either nuance.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lexica note its key phrase may mean 'make mention' rather than 'remember,' so its precise sense there is genuinely disputed.

definition: To raise something to a higher position, or figuratively to lift a person up in honor or status.
article: ὑψόω means to lift or raise up, either literally (something physically elevated) or figuratively (someone raised in honor). In the Byzantine New Testament it splits between exaltation language ("exalted," "exalt") at about 60% and physical lifting ("lifted up") at 33%, and it often stands opposite ταπεινόω, "to humble." The Septuagint uses it heavily—161 times—most often for the Hebrew רוּם (48×), "to be high," and an everyday papyrus even describes the earth heaving up and being "lifted high" when a serpent appeared.

definition: To trouble, disturb, or harass someone, often by crowding in or causing tumult.
article: This verb, built from the word for "crowd" (ὄχλος), carries the idea of pressing in on someone and so troubling, harassing, or annoying them. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Hebrews 12:15), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "cause," though the wider sense across sources is "trouble" or "annoy." Everyday papyri confirm this ordinary use vividly—one document has a widowed woman petitioning that tax collectors not be allowed to harass her since she is without a husband or help.
caution: With only one Byzantine occurrence and thin New Testament evidence, the single "cause" rendering reflects context more than the word's core meaning, which the lexica give as "trouble."

definition: Lacking formal education or literacy; without schooling or training in letters.
article: This word describes someone who has no formal schooling or training in letters, appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 4:13, where it characterizes the apostles. The most telling evidence comes from everyday papyri: ἀγράμματος shows up constantly in the standard legal formula 'I wrote on behalf of so-and-so, who cannot write,' used when an illiterate person needed someone else to sign a document for them. Because the term so regularly meant simply 'unable to read and write' in daily Koine, the description in Acts 4:13 likely pictures the apostles as plainly illiterate, though Dodson notes it could carry the narrower sense of being untrained in rabbinic teaching.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there—plain illiteracy versus lack of rabbinic schooling—rests on outside evidence.

definition: To carry or bring someone or something inward, into a place or situation.
article: εἰσφέρω simply means to carry inward—bringing a person or thing into some place, formed from εἰς ("into") and φέρω ("carry"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, rendered mostly as "bring" (4×), with the rest split among "lead" and "into," including the famous "lead us not into temptation" of Matthew 6:13. It's a common everyday word: it shows up 87 times in the Septuagint and turns up in ordinary papyri, including one where men carry the writer by force into an official's office.
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences, several measured senses rest on a single instance and reflect English phrasing more than distinct meanings.

definition: A cloud—a distinct, visible mass of water vapor in the sky.
article: νεφέλη means a cloud, and it's remarkably consistent: in the Byzantine New Testament it's rendered "cloud" in 24 of 26 occurrences (92%), and the Septuagint uses it 117 times, mostly translating the Hebrew עָנָן (73×). Ancient lexicographers distinguish it as a single, specific cloud, as opposed to νέφος, a vast indefinite mass of vapor. One striking detail: in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 clouds are pictured as the vehicle carrying believers to meet the returning Lord, and the papyri note that later Jews called the Messiah the "Son of the Cloud."

definition: A pause or rest from work, bringing relief and refreshment before resuming labor.
article: ἀνάπαυσις means rest in the sense of a cessation from labor that brings refreshment, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it this way every time it carries its own English word (4 of 5 occurrences, with the fifth absorbed into the phrasing). In the Septuagint it appears 43 times and often translates Hebrew words tied to Sabbath and settling down, including שַׁבָּתוֹן (10×) and מְנוּחָה (7×). The everyday papyri are especially telling: one document has a seventy-year-old man pleading for relief from public duties, and another grants veterans a five-year period of rest after military discharge, capturing the word's core idea of a respite that prepares you for future toil.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured range is narrow, though it agrees well with the Septuagint and lexicons.

definition: Milk, used both literally and figuratively for basic teaching suited to spiritual beginners.
article: γάλα simply means milk, the everyday drink, and that literal sense covers 4 of its 5 New Testament uses (80%). The fifth use, in Hebrews 5:12, applies it figuratively to elementary Christian teaching contrasted with solid food — the kind suited to those still spiritually immature. It is well attested in ordinary Koine: one papyrus account from around A.D. 1 lists "milk for the children" at half an obol, and in the Septuagint it translates Hebrew חָלָב 39 of 44 times.

definition: Belonging to or located on the earth, as opposed to heaven or the sky.
article: ἐπίγειος literally means "of the earth" (from ἐπί, "on," and γῆ, "earth"), and in the New Testament it consistently describes things that belong to the earthly realm rather than the heavenly one. Across its 7 occurrences it is rendered "earthly" most often (4×, 67%), with a couple of cases pointing to "earthly things" or "earthly splendor." A striking piece of evidence is a third-century magical papyrus that lists "heavenly, airy, earthly, or underground" beings in almost the same arrangement as Philippians 2:10 — not a quotation of Paul, but proof that both drew on the same familiar categories of everyday Koine.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and the senses largely overlapping, the distinctions between "earthly," "earthly things," and "earthly splendor" reflect context rather than separate meanings.

definition: The act of worship or sacred service offered to God.
article: λατρεία refers to worship, specifically the religious service rendered to God, and in the New Testament it always carries this sacred sense. In the Septuagint it appears 5 times and consistently translates the Hebrew עֲבֹדָה, the word for the service performed in connection with God's sanctuary. Classical Greek originally used it for ordinary hired service, but by New Testament times the divine, worshipful sense dominates; the word still survives in Modern Greek meaning adoration or worship. The Majority Standard Bible's renderings cluster tightly around "worship" and "service," with all readings confirmed by the BSB.
caution: With only 5 occurrences, the distinction between "worship" and "service" rests on a thin sample, though all sources agree on the overall religious meaning.

definition: A Roman pound, a unit of weight equal to about twelve ounces.
article: λίτρα is a unit of weight borrowed from the Latin libra, appearing only twice in the New Testament (John 12:3 and 19:39), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "about" a pound in both cases. The word is well documented in everyday Koine papyri, where it measures all sorts of goods — one fourth-century papyrus even uses it for beer, and another records pounds of chaff supplied to marching soldiers. Lexicons note that λίτρα could also name a Sicilian silver coin, but in the New Testament it always refers to weight.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences this is thin evidence, and the coin sense noted by lexicons does not appear in the biblical text.

definition: A seal or signet that stamps an impression to mark something as genuine, owned, protected, or closed.
article: σφραγίς refers both to the physical seal or signet ring and to the impression it leaves, which served to authenticate documents, mark ownership, or keep something private and closed. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 16 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it plainly as "seal" 63% of the time and as the Lamb's seals on the scroll in Revelation 31% of the time. Everyday Koine papyri show how concrete the word was: one second-century letter asks someone to buy "a silver seal," and another mentions cloth tied up and sealed "with my seal." In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew חוֹתָם (6×), the word for a signet or seal.

definition: To put a boat out from shore onto the water, or, used by itself, to go back or return.
senseLabels: put a boat out to sea
article: This is a small, practical word with two everyday uses: in fishing scenes it means to push a boat out from the shore (Luke 5:3-4), while standing alone it can mean simply to return, as when Jesus heads back to the city (Matthew 21:18). It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, splitting evenly between these uses. The papyri show it doing other work entirely — in one 164 B.C. document it means to render acknowledgments to Zeus, and elsewhere to apply doubtful cases to a rule — so its general range in everyday Koine was wider than its narrow biblical footprint suggests.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, the evidence is thin and the measured senses are tied to single verses.

definition: To become empty or foolish in one's thinking, ending up in worthless and pointless reasoning.
senseLabels: become foolish or empty in thinking
article: ματαιόω describes the process of being made or becoming empty, foolish, and worthless—especially in how one thinks. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 1:21, where people's reasoning becomes futile, and the single measured rendering ("neither") reflects an awkward fit with the surrounding sentence rather than the verb's core meaning. The most telling evidence comes from the Septuagint, where it occurs 6 times and translates two vivid Hebrew words: סָכַל ("to be foolish," 3×) and הָבַל ("to be vain or empty," the word behind Ecclesiastes' famous "vanity," 3×).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single odd measured rendering, lean on the Septuagint and lexicon evidence for the verb's real sense.

definition: A tax, especially a per-person poll-tax collected by Roman authorities.
article: Κῆνσος is a Latin loanword (from census) that came into everyday Greek, and in the New Testament it always refers to a tax — specifically a per-head or poll-tax owed to Rome. It appears just 4 times, rendered "taxes" three times and "pay taxes" once, all in tense scenes about whether to pay Caesar. Moulton-Milligan note the word in ordinary papyri and inscriptions, including a first-century B.C. inscription and later documents where it carries the related sense of "census" — the enrollment that the tax was based on.
caution: With only 4 occurrences the range is narrow, and the underlying Latin term could mean either the census-enrollment or the resulting tax.

definition: A deliberate turning away from or rebellion against an established loyalty, belief, or practice.
senseLabels: a religious rebellion or falling away
article: ἀποστασία describes a defection or revolt—a turning away from something one was committed to. In the New Testament it appears only twice, once for forsaking the law of Moses (Acts 21:21) and once for a coming "rebellion" or falling away (2 Thessalonians 2:3), and both lexicons note the NT use is always religious. Interestingly, in the Septuagint and in everyday papyri the related vocabulary often carries a political sense of revolt: documents from the 2nd century B.C. describe Egyptian rebels (ἀποστάται) burning title-deeds and crowds being put down by force.
caution: With only two NT occurrences and a measured sense ("forsake") that overlaps the abstract noun's range, the precise scope here is thin and the evidence tier is low.

definition: To make something disappear—by destroying it, hiding it, marring its appearance, or letting it fade away.
article: This verb covers a range from making something vanish to destroying, disfiguring, or marring it. In the Septuagint it appears 80 times across 23 books, most often rendering the Hebrew words שָׁמֵם (16×) and שָׁמַד (14×), which carry ideas of devastation and destruction. The everyday papyri are vivid here: one third-century document complains that "the hippopotamus destroyed nothing," and another reports that gazelles were spoiling a writer's crops—the same word used for animals ruining a field. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 5 times, where the lexica spread the meaning across destroying treasure (Matthew 6:19-20), disfiguring a face (Matthew 6:16), and life vanishing like vapor (James 4:14).
caution: The corpus measured only one clear English sense ("fade away"), since four of the five New Testament occurrences were absorbed into phrasing, so the fuller range of "destroy" and "disfigure" rests on the lexica and Septuagint rather than measured renderings.

definition: Hermes—either the Greek messenger god or a Christian man bearing that name.
article: Ἑρμῆς is a proper name appearing only twice in the New Testament, split evenly between two uses. In Acts 14:12 it refers to the Greek messenger god (the Romans called him Mercury), the title the crowd gave Paul because he was the chief speaker; in Romans 16:14 it is the name of a Christian Paul greets. Outside the New Testament the name turns up in everyday Koine documents, including a third-century magical formula on papyrus that ties Hermes to the goddess Isis searching for Osiris.
caution: With only two occurrences and one of each sense, the evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To mutter complaints in low-level, simmering discontent, often quietly among yourselves rather than openly.
article: γογγύζω means to mutter or murmur with smoldering discontent — the kind of low, ongoing grumbling people do under their breath, sometimes secretly (it's even rendered "whispering" once). It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament and 14 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew לוּן, the word for Israel's complaining in the wilderness. The everyday flavor shows up vividly in the papyri: one document from 241 BC has a work-gang "murmuring" that they were being wronged, and another records a crowd grumbling at the Emperor.

definition: An adverb meaning quickly, soon, or hastily — describing something done with speed or sometimes too rashly.
article: Ταχέως is a plain adverb meaning "quickly" or "soon," describing the speed at which something happens. It appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "quickly" in 3 cases and "how quickly" in 2 more, with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Abbott-Smith notes that in some passages, like Galatians 1:6 and 1 Timothy 5:22, it carries a hint of rashness or acting too hastily, and the everyday Koine papyri confirm this urgent flavor — one letter pleads, "come back quickly, for it is pressing." In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew מְהֵרָה ("speedily"), 5 of its 11 occurrences.

definition: A great flood or deluge—an overwhelming inundation of water, especially the flood of Noah's day.
article: κατακλυσμός means a flood or deluge—a massive overwhelming of water. All four New Testament occurrences refer to the flood of Noah's time (Matthew 24:38-39, Luke 17:27, 2 Peter 2:5), and the renderings all reduce to the single sense "flood." In the Septuagint it appears 15 times, most often (12×) translating the Hebrew מַבּוּל, the word specifically used for Noah's flood, and the term still survives in Modern Greek meaning inundation.

definition: Jairus, the personal name of a synagogue leader whose daughter Jesus restored to life.
article: Ἰάειρος is simply a personal name, Jairus, borne by a Jewish synagogue ruler in two Gospel scenes (Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41). It comes from the Hebrew name יָאִיר (Jair), already used in the Greek Old Testament, where Esther 2:5 mentions Mordecai as "son of Jair." Beyond the Bible, Moulton-Milligan note a similar form in an everyday papyrus letter from Ptolemaic Thebes, showing the name was in ordinary circulation.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only twice in the Byzantine text and absent from the SBLGNT critical text, so the evidence is thin.

definition: To prepare a dead body for burial, including the customary wrapping and applying of spices and ointments.
article: This verb covers the whole process of readying a corpse for burial — anointing, wrapping in cloth, and laying it to rest according to local custom. It appears only twice in the New Testament: once when Jesus says a woman's perfume prepares him for burial (Matthew 26:12), and once describing how Joseph and Nicodemus wrapped his body in Jewish fashion (John 19:40). The most striking evidence is the related noun ἐνταφιαστής, which in everyday Koine papyri named professional embalmers — even trained physicians who examined the dead — and which the Septuagint uses (Genesis 50:2) for the Egyptian physicians who embalmed Jacob, translating the Hebrew word חָנַט.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, so the two measured renderings reflect specific contexts rather than firmly distinct senses.

definition: Friendship or close affection, the bond of fondness shared between people or directed toward something.
article: φιλία means friendship—the warm bond of fondness between people, or affection directed toward an object. It appears only once in the New Testament (James 4:4), where it speaks of friendship "toward" the world, but it shows up nine times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew word for love. Everyday papyri confirm the social sense vividly: one document sets φιλία against ἔχθρα ("enmity"), and an erotic fragment calls love "the stablisher of friendship."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To leave a port by ship and sail away on a sea voyage.
article: This verb means to set sail or sail away from a place, picturing a ship departing on a voyage. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in Acts (13:4; 14:26; 20:15; 27:1), where it describes the sea travels of Paul and his companions. In half of those cases the translators fold it into the broader phrasing rather than giving it its own English word, but where it surfaces it is rendered simply "sailed" or "sailing." It is built from ἀπό ("away from") plus πλέω ("sail"), so the "away" sense is baked right into the word.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, all in Acts, the evidence base is small though the meaning is consistent.

definition: A combination of two Greek negatives used in questions, asking in effect "is it not really the case that...?"
article: This is the pairing of two negative particles, μή and οὐ, used together in questions where the speaker expects or assumes a positive answer — roughly "is it not that...?" The first particle, μή, is the "subjective" negative used where one supposes a thing is not, as opposed to οὐ, which denies a fact absolutely; here they combine in interrogative force. There are no occurrences of this combined form in the Byzantine New Testament, so the entry rests entirely on how the individual particles behave and on lexicon notes rather than measured usage.
caution: This combination has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament and no measured senses, so its meaning is inferred from the two particles rather than from attested data.

definition: Banned from the synagogue; expelled from the Jewish religious community as a form of excommunication.
article: This adjective describes someone who has been put out of the synagogue, cut off from the gathered Jewish community. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, all in John's Gospel (John 9:22, 12:42, 16:2), and every occurrence carries this same meaning of being excommunicated. Notably, the word is not found in classical Greek authors and was likely coined specifically for use within the Jewish community to name this kind of expulsion.
caution: With only 3 occurrences, all in one book, and no attestation in classical authors, the evidence base is narrow.

definition: A guard or detachment of soldiers assigned to watch over something, borrowed from the Latin word for custody.
article: κουστωδία is a Latin loanword (from custodia) meaning a guard or watch—in the New Testament, the Roman soldiers posted to secure Jesus' tomb. It appears just 3 times, all in Matthew (27:65-66; 28:11), and translators consistently render it as a 'guard' or 'guards' in every case. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri too: a document from A.D. 128 mentions 'public clothing for the guards,' confirming this was ordinary administrative vocabulary, not a specialized religious term.
caution: With only 3 occurrences—all in one book and one scene—the evidence base is thin, though the sources fully agree on its meaning.

definition: A lowly or humble condition — being brought low in status, circumstances, or spirit.
article: ταπείνωσις describes a state of being low — whether in social rank, outward circumstances, or inner spirit. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, and in every case it is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. In the Septuagint it shows up 30 times across 13 books, most often (12×) translating the Hebrew עֹנִי, "affliction" or "misery," which colors it toward hardship as much as humility; everyday papyri even use it concretely, as in a text describing the "lowering" of the sun.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, all absorbed into phrasing, the precise shade between "affliction" and "humility" depends heavily on context.

definition: To send someone or something out or forth, dispatching them to a destination or task.
article: ἐκπέμπω means to send someone forth or dispatch them, built from the preposition ἐκ ('out') plus πέμπω ('send'). It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 13:4 and 17:10), where it is rendered 'sent' in both cases. The everyday papyri are especially vivid here: the verb is common in legal documents for sending people up to trial or ordering arrests, as in a first-century papyrus reading 'send out Galates and his wife.'
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single measured sense, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Smooth, pleasant-sounding speech used to win people over, here with a deceptive or manipulative purpose.
article: χρηστολογία combines the words for "good/kind" and "to speak," so literally it means fair or pleasant speaking. In its single New Testament appearance (Romans 16:18) it carries a negative edge: smooth talk meant to deceive, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it "smooth." One commentator's tag captures the flavor perfectly—someone "who spoke well but acted badly"—and church writers later used the same word in a genuinely good sense.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its negative "deceptive" coloring comes from that single context rather than a broad measured range.

definition: Eaten or destroyed by moths, describing clothing or material that has rotted away through neglect.
article: σητόβρωτος literally means "moth-eaten," built from the words for "moth" (σής) and "to eat" (βιβρώσκω). It appears just once in the New Testament, at James 5:2, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "rotted" to describe garments destroyed through hoarding. The word is rare overall: in the Greek Bible it occurs only here and in Job 13:28, and Moulton-Milligan note that outside the Bible it had been found only once in secular Greek, describing wooden idol-images that moths had gnawed.
caution: This is a very rare word with only one New Testament occurrence and minimal attestation elsewhere, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: The throat as the organ of speech, often pictured as the source of a person's words.
article: λάρυγξ literally means the throat or larynx, the bodily passage through which speech comes. In the Septuagint it appears 16 times in 3 books, most often translating the Hebrew word for palate or roof of the mouth (7×) and once for throat, and it readily stands in figuratively for what a person says. Its single New Testament appearance, in Romans 3:13, uses it this way: the throat as the source of harmful words, which the Majority Standard Bible renders with the metaphor of "practice" ("their throats are open graves").
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence rendered metaphorically, the literal sense "throat" rests entirely on Septuagint and lexicon evidence rather than measured New Testament usage.

definition: To give something to someone before they have given anything in return; to give first.
article: προδίδωμι combines the prefix "before" (πρό) with "give" (δίδωμι) to mean giving first, before the other party has given anything back. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Romans 11:35, where the Majority Standard Bible's rendering centers on God as the one to whom no one has given first. Everyday Koine papyri use the word in the same plain financial sense — one document from around A.D. 146 speaks of a dowry "previously given" to a daughter. Some lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) also record a second sense, "to betray," though that meaning shows up in 4 Maccabees rather than the New Testament.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin attestation, the measured sense rests on a single verse, and the lexicons add a "betray" meaning not found in the NT data.

definition: "We are" — the first-person plural present of the verb "to be," used to state that a group exists, is present, or has a certain quality.
article: This is simply the "we are" form of the common Greek verb εἰμί, "to be." Like the English verb, it covers a wide range: stating that people or things exist, that something is present, or linking a subject to a description. The parent verb εἰμί does heavy lifting across the New Testament — from "In the beginning was the Word" to impersonal phrases like "there is."
caution: The digest reports zero occurrences of this exact form in the Byzantine NT and no measured senses, so this entry rests entirely on the general lexicon for the parent verb εἰμί.

definition: To exercise authority or control over someone, taking authoritative action on one's own initiative.
article: This rare verb means to take authoritative action over another person, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 2:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "exercise." Its precise force is debated: older sources like the KJV lean toward a negative "usurp authority," while others give a more neutral "govern" or "have mastery over." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that the related noun αὐθέντης carried two very different histories — one meaning "murderer" and one meaning "master" — and they cite research clearing up this tangle and confirming the word was at home in everyday Koine papyri, not just biblical Greek.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a long-standing dispute over whether it implies neutral or domineering authority, the precise range here is genuinely uncertain.

definition: A proconsul, the Roman governor in charge of a senatorial province.
article: This is the precise title for a proconsul, the official who administered a senatorial province of the Roman Empire, ruling in place of a consul. In the New Testament it appears only in Acts, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "proconsul" 75% of the time and "what proconsul" once. Moulton-Milligan notes a nice real-world detail: the word turns up in everyday inscriptions and papyri everywhere except Egypt, since Egypt was ruled by a prefect rather than a proconsul, so no proconsuls appear there.
caution: The second "sense" is just the same word with a question word attached, not a distinct meaning.

definition: A surname meaning "Zealot," identifying Simon the apostle as a member of, or sympathizer with, a zealous party.
article: This word appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 10:4 and Mark 3:18), both times as a surname for Simon the apostle, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Zealot" in both cases (100%). Despite the look-alike spelling, it does not mean "Canaanite"—the KJV's "Canaanite" reflects an old mistake of confusing it with a derivative of Χαναάν (G5477). The evidence points instead to a Semitic root meaning "zealous" (compare Luke 6:15, where Simon is simply called "the Zealot"), and Moulton-Milligan note that scholars like Dalman traced the original form back to a word for "a zealot."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice, appears in the Byzantine but not the critical text, and the sources spell it variously (Κανανίτης / Καναναῖος) while older glosses mistakenly read it as "Canaanite."

definition: Nicanor, the personal name of one of the seven men chosen to serve the early church in Jerusalem.
article: Νικάνωρ is a proper name belonging to one of the seven men appointed in Acts 6:5, the only place it appears in the New Testament. The name was common in everyday Koine, showing up in inscriptions and even casual wall-scratchings — one playful graffito reads "Nicanor, I have arrived... drunk." It likely derives from the verb νικάω ("to conquer"), giving it the sense "victorious," though in context it functions simply as someone's name.
caution: The label "proposal" in the measured data is a tagging artifact; this word is purely a personal name appearing only once.

definition: A hidden rock or reef in the sea over which waves break; figuratively, a hidden danger among people.
article: This word appears only once in the New Testament, at Jude 1:12, where it describes ungodly people lurking at love-feasts. In classical poetry σπιλάς meant a rock or reef over which the sea dashes (used by Polybius and Josephus), and applied to people it pictures a hidden danger that wrecks others. The translation is genuinely disputed: some read it as 'reef/hidden danger,' while others take it as equal to σπίλος meaning 'spot, stain' (the parallel passage 2 Peter 2:13 uses that word), and the KJV's 'spot' reflects that confusion; the Majority Standard Bible renders the sense as 'shamelessly.'
caution: This is a single-occurrence word with low confidence, and the sources openly disagree over whether it means 'hidden reef/danger' or 'spot, stain.'

definition: A negative word meaning no one, nothing, or not any, used in commands, requests, and other non-factual statements.
article: μηδείς is the negative pronoun for "no one, nothing, not any," the counterpart to οὐδείς but used in commands, wishes, and other non-factual settings. Its renderings spread widely because English handles the negation differently each time—"anyone" appears 18× (23%), "no" 16×, "nothing" 15×, and it dissolves into the phrasing entirely 14 times out of 91. A neat detail: it often piles onto another negative for emphasis, as in "no longer let anyone eat fruit" (Mark 11:14), where two negatives strengthen rather than cancel the denial.
caution: The word's English rendering shifts heavily with context, and an alternate Hellenistic spelling (μηθείς) appears once at Acts 27:33, so individual translations vary.

definition: Capernaum, a town in Galilee on the shore where Jesus based much of his ministry.
article: Καπερναούμ is simply the place name Capernaum, a town in Galilee, appearing 16 times across four books in the Byzantine text. Every source agrees on this single meaning; the so-called extra senses like "Jesus Capernaum" are just artifacts of how the rendering software counted surrounding words. The most interesting detail is the name's Hebrew background: Abbott-Smith traces it to כָּפָר נַחוּם, meaning "Nahum's village."

definition: An authoritative order or command, especially one issued by someone with the standing to require obedience.
article: ἐπιταγή means a command or order given by someone with the authority to issue it, appearing 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The renderings cluster tightly around "command" (5×, or 71%), with the remaining occurrences in Titus describing a command delivered with full authority. Notably, dedicatory inscriptions used the phrase κατ᾽ ἐπιταγήν to mean "by divine command" — an altar set up because a god ordered it in a dream or oracle — which matches Paul's use of the word for God's commands.
caution: The two single-occurrence senses in Titus reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings, and the underlying sense is consistently "command."

definition: A bird; a flying creature, often appearing in the phrase "birds of the air."
article: πετεινόν simply means a bird or flying creature, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 14 times this way. The two measured senses differ only in phrasing: 64% of the time translators render the fuller "birds of the air" and 36% just "birds," so this is one meaning with two stylistic shades rather than two distinct senses. In the Septuagint it appears 48 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word עוֹף ("flying things," 26×), and Moulton-Milligan shows it was the ordinary Koine term for a bird in everyday papyri.

definition: To find fault with someone or something, blaming or criticizing them for a shortcoming.
article: μέμφομαι means to blame, criticize, or find fault, and all three of its New Testament uses point to that single core idea even though the translations are worded differently ("found fault," "God find fault," "fault"). It's a common everyday word in the papyri: one letter complains "I blame you greatly for the loss of two pigs," and another says "I blame the person who told you," showing how ordinary the term was. In the Septuagint it appears only a handful of times (Sirach 11:7, 41:7, and 2 Maccabees 2:7).
caution: This word is rare, appearing only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament (2 in the critical text), so its measured range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To make something wet, or to cause rain to fall.
article: βρέχω covers two related ideas: making something wet directly, and the falling or sending of rain. In the New Testament it appears 7 times, split fairly evenly — about half the cases mean "rain," while the others describe wetting something, as when a woman wets Jesus' feet with her tears (Luke 7:38, 44). The everyday Koine papyri show the word constantly used for the irrigation of farmland by the flooding of the Nile, with one notice complaining that a village was abandoned "because for a long time there has been no inundation there." In the Septuagint it appears 15 times, most often rendering the Hebrew מָטַר ("to rain").
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences spread thinly across senses, the exact boundary between "rain" and "wet" rests on limited data.

definition: An old man; a man advanced in years.
article: πρεσβύτης refers to an old man, and the New Testament uses it just three times, where it consistently points to a man advanced in years (Luke 1:18; Titus 2:2; Philemon 9). In the Septuagint it appears 33 times, most often translating the Hebrew word zaqen, "old." An interesting wrinkle: because πρεσβύτης looks almost identical to πρεσβευτής ("ambassador"), Dodson and some scholars suggest the sense "ambassador" in Philemon 9, and the Septuagint even spells it this way for "envoy" in a few places — but the measured renderings always treat it simply as "man."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and the close overlap with πρεσβευτής ("ambassador"), the sense in Philemon 9 is genuinely disputed between "old man" and "ambassador."

definition: Something shaped or molded, like an object formed by a craftsman from clay.
article: πλάσμα refers to something that has been molded or fashioned, derived from the verb πλάσσω ("to form"). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 9:20, where Paul uses the image of a molded clay object questioning its maker; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "talk" there, while older sources like Strong's and Abbott-Smith give the more literal "thing formed." Interestingly, in everyday Koine it shows up in a magical papyrus (P London 46) describing a molded figure of Hermes wearing a cloak, confirming its concrete sense of a crafted image.
caution: Evidence is thin (one NT occurrence) and the measured rendering "talk" reflects a loose translation that differs from the literal "thing formed" given by the classical lexica.

definition: To lend money or goods, usually expecting repayment; in the middle voice, to borrow.
article: This verb covers the two sides of a loan: in its active form it means to lend, and in the middle voice it flips to mean borrow, which is why Matthew 5:42 is about borrowing while Luke 6:34-35 is about lending. The Septuagint uses it 16 times, most often for the Hebrew לָוָה (9×), and the everyday Koine papyri are full of it in loan contracts—one even mentions lending 7½ artabae of wheat. Strong's notes the lending was often done on interest, and Abbott-Smith contrasts it with κίχρημι, which means to lend simply as a friend.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, all four 'measured senses' are really just the lend/borrow distinction described differently.

definition: The ordinal number fifteenth, used to mark the fifteenth in a sequence such as a year of a reign.
article: πεντεκαιδέκατος is simply the ordinal number "fifteenth," built straightforwardly from the words for "five," "and," and "tenth." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 3:1, dating John the Baptist's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's reign, which is why the rendering shows up as "reign" in that context. It was ordinary everyday vocabulary: a second-century papyrus uses it for a calendar date, where a writer hopes to sail home "after the fifteenth."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single dating formula.

definition: Putting on a false front—pretending to be something you are not, like an actor playing a part.
article: In the New Testament ὑπόκρισις always carries its figurative meaning: pretending, putting on a mask, acting a part you don't really mean. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "hypocrisy" in 5 of 7 occurrences (and as "through their hypocrisy" once), and the word appears in everyday Koine papyri as well. The most interesting detail is the original sense behind it: Greek writers used the word literally for play-acting on stage—Marcus Aurelius even lists it alongside dancing—so the metaphor pictures a hypocrite as a stage actor performing a role.
caution: One of the seven counted occurrences (James 5:12) shows a garbled rendering in the data, so treat that single data point as unreliable.

definition: A person who works alongside another toward a shared goal; a partner, helper, or colleague in a task.
article: Συνεργός describes someone who labors together with another, a co-worker or partner in a common task. The word is remarkably consistent: across all 13 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fellow workers" 12 times (92%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100%, often used with a genitive naming the person one works alongside. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary sense \u2014 a Fayum document from around 103 B.C. uses it of taking on a confederate, and another describes a woman who "became his fellow worker."

definition: To be stored away or kept in reserve, especially something set aside and awaiting a person in the future.
article: At its root ἀπόκειμαι means something is put away and kept safe, like the servant's coin literally 'laid up' in a cloth (Luke 19:20). From there it stretches naturally into the figurative sense of something reserved for someone — a hope stored up in heaven (Col 1:5) or the appointment that awaits all people. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this reach: one second-century B.C. text says divine wrath 'is laid up' for those who refuse to live rightly, and a royal inscription speaks of favor 'reserved' from gods and heroes for piety.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the senses rest on thin evidence, and the three measured 'senses' are really parts of single phrases rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To boil or be hot, used figuratively of someone burning with energy, zeal, or earnestness.
article: At root ζέω means to boil or be hot, the way liquids bubble over a fire—a sense well documented in everyday Koine papyri, including a recipe that tells you to boil an egg and another to boil cypress fruit. In the New Testament both of its 2 occurrences are figurative, describing a person fervent or burning in spirit (Acts 18:25; Romans 12:11). The two measured senses here really reflect the same idea—the Majority Standard Bible renders one as "fervent" and the other within "spiritual," but the BSB only agrees with the first—and the lexica confirm the metaphorical use for anger, love, and zeal. In the Septuagint it appears 3 times, translating a Hebrew word for boiling or raging.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the two measured renderings overlapping in meaning, the labeled "senses" reflect translation choices rather than genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: Describing someone of honorable social standing or wealth, or something that looks proper, fitting, and presentable.
article: εὐσχήμων covers two related ideas: outwardly proper and graceful, and socially prominent or influential. In its 5 New Testament appearances the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prominent" (2×), "men" of standing (1×), and "parts" of the body (1×), with one occurrence absorbed into phrasing. The papyri offer a striking detail: there was an Egyptian official actually called the εὐσχήμων, a kind of guardian of public morals or local magistrate (BGU III.926, P Ryl II.236), which matches the word's "honorable estate" sense.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the sense range rests on thin evidence, and the "presentable" versus "prominent" meanings depend heavily on context.

definition: To close or shut something such as a door, gate, or prison, used both literally and figuratively.
article: κλείω means to close or shut, whether a door, a gate, a prison, or even something figurative like heaven or one's heart. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times, rendered "shut" in 8 cases (57%) and "locked" in 3 (21%), as when the disciples gathered behind shut doors in John 20:19. The verb was utterly ordinary in everyday life — papyri use it for shutting a temple door, sealing storerooms, and closing up shops — and in the Septuagint it usually stands for the Hebrew סָגַר.

definition: A scorpion, the small venomous creature whose painful sting was widely feared.
article: σκορπίος simply means a scorpion, the stinging desert creature. The three measured "senses" all refer to the same animal — the differences are just translation phrasing in the Majority Standard Bible, such as "Behold scorpions" in Luke 10:19 or the rendering in Revelation 9:5 where scorpions describe the locusts' stinging power. In the Septuagint it consistently translates the Hebrew עַקְרָב (6 of 7 times), and everyday papyri make the sting vivid: an Egyptian mummy tablet records that a man named Apollonius "died from a scorpion," and the word also named the zodiac sign Scorpio.
caution: The three listed senses are not distinct meanings but variations in English phrasing for the same animal.

definition: To wait for or expect someone or something, looking ahead to their arrival or to a coming event.
article: In the New Testament ἐκδέχομαι means to wait for or expect, whether a person (as Paul waiting for his companions) or a thing (the coming of an event). Of its 7 Byzantine occurrences, 4 are absorbed into English phrasing without a single word of their own, and the rest split between "waiting" (67%) and "expecting" (33%). Interestingly, the classical lexica note that the word's original meaning was "to take or receive from" — a sense confirmed by the everyday papyri, where it is used for receiving money or being received with honor — while the New Testament uses only the rarer "await" sense.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and over half absorbed into phrasing, the measured data is thin, and the classical "receive" sense does not appear in the New Testament.

definition: To flee from or escape something, especially to get away from moral corruption or harmful influences.
article: This verb combines "away" (ἀπό) with "flee" (φεύγω), giving the strong sense of fleeing from or escaping something. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in 2 Peter, where it consistently describes escaping corruption or the defilements of the world. It shows up in everyday Koine documents too: a papyrus from A.D. 192 uses it for a man trying to dodge the burden of a public office.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences—all in a single book—the evidence base is thin, so this entry rests on limited data.
