definition: The act of buying someone back or setting them free, as in paying a ransom to release a captive or debtor.
article: λύτρωσις names a ransoming or release — paying a price to free someone, whether from slavery, debt, or misfortune. The Byzantine NT uses it just 3 times, rendered "redemption" twice (including the work of Christ in Hebrews 9:12) and "redeemed" once (Luke 1:68). The everyday papyri make the literal sense vivid: one tax account from the first century BC records 4 drachmas "for the redemption of cups," and another lists money paid for the redemption of goats — ordinary buy-back transactions, not yet a religious term.
caution: This is a low-confidence entry: the word appears only 3 times in the NT, so its full range rests largely on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: Something that corresponds to an original pattern—either a copy of an archetype or the reality that an earlier symbol pointed toward.
article: ἀντίτυπον describes one thing matching another, like an impression made by a seal answering to its archetype. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the two uses pull in opposite directions: in Hebrews 9:24 it labels the earthly sanctuary as a copy of the true one, while in 1 Peter 3:21 it points to the reality (baptism) that an earlier symbol foreshadowed. The most interesting detail is Polybius's military use, where ἀντίτυποι describes auxiliary infantry "posted opposite" the cavalry—showing the basic idea of one thing set to correspond with another.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, confidence is low, and the word's direction (copy of the original, or the reality itself) shifts between its two appearances.

definition: A command form of the verb "to be," meaning "let it be" or "let him/her/it be."
article: ἔστω is simply a command form of the ordinary Greek verb "to be" (εἰμί), expressing "let it be" or "let him/her/it be." Since it comes from the verb "to be," its meaning follows that verb's wide range — existence, presence, happening, or identity — but cast as an instruction or wish. The digest records zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament used here, so no measured senses could be drawn for this specific form.
caution: The evidence shows zero attestations of this form in the measured corpus, so any meaning is inferred only from the parent verb εἰμί rather than directly observed.

definition: To go, go away, or depart, often used as a command to leave or set off.
article: In the New Testament ὑπάγω overwhelmingly just means "go" or "go away" — it is rendered "go" in 66 of 81 occurrences (90%), and as "going away" twice. It is a word of everyday speech, well documented in ordinary Koine papyri, where it carries the plain sense "go off" or "go back" (one papyrus even uses it for someone leaving the next day). Interestingly, the older classical lexicons note a transitive sense "to lead under" or "subdue," and its one Septuagint appearance fits this older usage, but the New Testament evidence shows only the intransitive "depart" meaning.
caution: The older classical "lead under, subdue" sense and the single Septuagint use diverge from the consistent New Testament meaning of simply "go away."

definition: Jacob, the Hebrew patriarch son of Isaac and ancestor of Israel; also the name of Joseph's father in Matthew's genealogy.
article: Ἰακώβ is the indeclinable Greek spelling of the Hebrew name יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿaqov), used 27 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "Jacob" 24 of those times (96%). It usually points to the patriarch, son of Isaac, but in Matthew's genealogy (1:15-16) it also names the father of Joseph, Mary's husband. A striking detail from the papyri: the appeal to "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (compare Mark 12:26) shows up frequently in magical incantations, where the Hebrew names were deliberately left untranslated to preserve their supposed power.

definition: Completely clear and obvious to everyone, leaving no room for doubt.
article: ἔκδηλος is a strengthened form of δῆλος ("clear"), meaning something is fully visible or unmistakable to onlookers. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:9, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "further" in the phrase about folly being made plain to all. Everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions use it the same way—an Egyptian decree (OGIS 665) speaks of making official acts "clear to everyone," and it also turns up twice in 3 Maccabees.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force here rests on outside Koine evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: A linking adverb meaning "then" or "afterward," marking the next item in a sequence of events or a list.
article: ἔπειτα is a sequencing word that points to what comes next, whether in time ("afterward") or in an ordered list ("then, second..."). The Byzantine NT uses it 16 times, and in 10 of those it gets absorbed into the English phrasing without a word of its own, which tells you it mainly oils the joints of a sentence rather than carrying weight by itself. It often teams up with "first" (πρῶτον...ἔπειτα), and the everyday papyri show the same pattern—one writer opens "first greeting you, then praying to all the gods."
caution: Septuagint evidence is very thin (just one occurrence), but the NT and papyri usage agree closely.

definition: A person who does physical labor, especially a farm worker, or more broadly anyone who works at a job or task.
article: ἐργάτης means a worker—originally a field hand or farm laborer, but extending to workmen of any kind. It appears 16 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "workers" in 11 of those, with 4 more absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where laborers (ἐργάται) are recorded being paid 9 obols a man and a man hiring "two workers"; the classical lexica also note a figurative stretch to "a worker of" something, as in "workers of iniquity" (Luke 13:27).

definition: To take away something that surrounds or covers, including casting off ropes, removing a veil, or stripping away hope and sins.
article: περιαιρέω literally means to take away what surrounds something, and its uses spread across both physical and figurative removal. In the New Testament it covers casting off a ship's anchors (Acts 27:40), the removal of a veil (2 Corinthians 3:16), the loss of all hope (Acts 27:20), and the taking away of sins (Hebrews 10:11). The Septuagint uses it 52 times, most often for the Hebrew סוּר ("turn aside, remove"), and everyday papyri show it for stripping wool off an animal or striking a dead priest's name off a list.
caution: With only 4 Byzantine occurrences, each rendered differently, the measured senses rest on single examples rather than a broad pattern.

definition: Simon, a personal name borne by at least nine different men in the New Testament.
article: Σίμων is simply the personal name "Simon," rendered that way in 60 of its 76 Byzantine appearances (83%); the other counted "senses" are just cases where the name sits beside Jesus in the surrounding phrasing rather than carrying any different meaning. The name itself covers at least nine distinct men, including Simon Peter, Simon the Zealot, Simon of Cyrene, Simon the Pharisee, and Simon Magus. Interestingly, it is a Greek name adopted as a stand-in for the Hebrew Simeon (from H8095) because the two sound alike, and Moulton-Milligan note it appears commonly in everyday papyri without necessarily referring to Jews.
caution: It is a proper name, so the "senses" reflect English word order around Jesus rather than real differences in meaning.

definition: To make someone feel shame, or—in the middle/passive—to feel respect or regard toward a person.
article: This verb carries two related shades: actively it means to put someone to shame, while in the middle or passive voice it means to feel respect or reverence toward a person. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 7 books, and where the Majority Standard Bible gives it a clear English word, "respect" wins (LUK 18:4; 20:13). The everyday Koine flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where one writer says "but for the fact that I am a little ashamed, you would never have seen my face"—the "shame" sense that still survives in modern Greek.
caution: Only one English sense ("respect") could be cleanly measured from the renderings, and 2 of 9 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing, so the "put to shame" sense rests mainly on the lexica rather than the corpus counts.

definition: Describing a person who is either skilled and polished in speaking or well-educated and learned.
article: λόγιος comes from λόγος ("word") and describes someone gifted with words — either eloquent in speech or learned in knowledge. The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:24, describing Apollos. Interestingly, the sources disagree on its exact force: classical Greek used it to mean "learned," while later Koine commonly meant "eloquent" — and Moulton, citing the grammarian Phrynichus and the popular usage of the multitude, preferred "eloquent" over "learned." The word also turns up in everyday papyri and inscriptions, showing it was in common circulation.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources genuinely split between "learned" (classical) and "eloquent" (later Koine).

definition: A sponge, the soft porous sea creature's skeleton used to soak up and hold liquids.
article: Σπόγγος simply means a sponge — the absorbent object used to hold liquid. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the same scene: a sponge soaked in sour wine offered to Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:48, Mark 15:36, John 19:29). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, including a third-century B.C. document referring to "rough sponges," which fits its ordinary practical use.
caution: The two listed senses are really one meaning — "brought a sponge" just reflects how one verse was phrased — so this is essentially a single-sense word.

definition: To touch, take hold of, or come into physical contact with someone or something.
article: This verb covers physical contact across a wide range—from Jesus touching a leper to people reaching out to touch his clothing. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 36 times, almost always rendered "touch" or "touched" (80% of cases combined), and the BSB agrees with these readings 94–100% of the time. In the Septuagint it shows up 113 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew נָגַע ("to touch," 95×). Beyond simple contact, the older lexicons note related senses the NT data here barely reflects: to kindle or set a fire, to "touch a woman" as a phrase for marriage or intimacy (as in 1 Corinthians 7:1), and even to harm (1 John 5:18).
caution: The two cases rendered "Now" reflect English sentence flow rather than a distinct meaning, and the lexicons list extended senses (kindle, harm, marry) that the measured NT renderings rarely capture.

definition: A deadly epidemic disease or plague; figuratively, a troublesome person who spreads harm like a contagion.
article: λοιμός most often means a pestilence — a widespread deadly disease — and appears in lists of disasters in the Gospels (Matthew 24:7, Luke 21:11). It also carries a vivid figurative sense: a dangerous, troublemaking person, as when Paul is called a "pest" in Acts 24:5, a usage the lexica trace back to classical Greek and the Septuagint. A neat detail is the everyday papyrus letter (P. Oxy. XIV.1666) where a writer says "I heard that there has been plague in your neighbourhood," showing the word's ordinary, real-world use. In the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew words, including those for a worthless or arrogant scoffer, matching its human "pest" sense.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences (2 in the critical text), the measured data is thin, so the sense breakdown rests on limited evidence.

definition: The first-person plural pronoun "we" or "us," used especially when the speakers are emphasized.
article: This is simply the word "we" — the plural form of the pronoun "I" (ἐγώ). Because Greek verbs already show who is acting, this standalone form is often used when the speakers want to stress "we ourselves." It appears 133 times across 24 books of the Septuagint, where it regularly renders the Hebrew word for "we" (אֲנַחְנוּ, 88 times).
caution: The digest reports zero Byzantine New Testament occurrences, so the count here reflects only the Septuagint evidence.

definition: A large earthenware jar used to hold water for a household's needs.
article: A ὑδρία is a clay water-pot or jar for storing a family's water supply, and all three New Testament uses keep this plain meaning — the stone jars at the Cana wedding (John 2:6, 7) and the jar the Samaritan woman leaves behind at the well (John 4:28). In the Septuagint it appears 22 times, always translating the Hebrew word kad, which is likewise a water jar. The everyday papyri show the word stretching well beyond water: it could mean a jar or pot for almost anything, including pomegranates, loaves of bread, or even coins and money.
caution: Only three New Testament occurrences, all the same scene-type, so the measured senses are really one meaning split across passages rather than distinct uses.

definition: Barley, a common grain cheaper than wheat, used for food and measured by quantity.
article: κριθή means barley, the everyday grain that was cheaper and more common than wheat. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 6:6, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within a measure of grain ("three quarts of barley for a denarius"); in the Septuagint it shows up 34 times and almost always translates the Hebrew word for barley, שְׂעֹרִים (27 of those times). The everyday papyri confirm how ordinary the word was, with merchants and farmers writing about preparing barley, shipments of barley, and barley ruined by hail.
caution: The single New Testament occurrence is rendered "quart," reflecting the measured quantity in context rather than the plain meaning "barley," so the lone NT data point can mislead.

definition: A person who falsely claims to be a fellow believer or member of the community.
article: This word combines "false" with "brother" to describe someone who pretends to belong to the Christian community while not genuinely being part of it. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times from Paul, in 2 Corinthians 11:26 and Galatians 2:4, and translators consistently render it "false brothers." Abbott-Smith and the other lexicons agree that it specifically refers to professing Christians who are not what they claim to be.
caution: With only two occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though all sources agree on its meaning.

definition: To throw stones at someone, especially to kill them by stoning as a form of execution.
article: This verb means to pelt or kill someone with stones, a deliberate act of execution rather than casual throwing. It built from the words for "stone" (λίθος) and "throw" (βάλλω), and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 9 times across 6 books, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it with "stones" in 7 of those occurrences. In the Septuagint it appears 27 times, usually translating the Hebrew verbs רָגַם (14×) and סָקַל (10×), both of which describe the legal practice of stoning.
caution: Moulton-Milligan notes this compound is rare outside biblical Greek, so its everyday usage is thinly attested.

definition: The people you are related to by blood — your extended family, relatives, or kindred.
article: συγγένεια refers to your blood relations as a group — the wider family network of relatives and kin. It can also carry the abstract sense of kinship itself, the relationship that ties people together, before standing concretely for the relatives themselves. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, but it was a common everyday word: a second-century papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses it of a child who had no relatives (συγγένεια) on either the father's or mother's side to serve as guardian. In the Septuagint it shows up 40 times, most often translating the Hebrew מִשְׁפָּחָה ("family/clan").
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a computed low-confidence tier, the measured senses rest on thin evidence.

definition: Provisions or food supplies, especially what travelers gather or carry to eat.
article: This word means food or provisions — the supplies people need to feed themselves. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 9:12, where the crowd needs to find lodging and food. Across the Septuagint it shows up 13 times in 6 books, usually translating the Hebrew word for travel provisions (צֵידָה, 11 times), and the papyri show it in ordinary use for feeding people, sometimes alongside livestock.
caution: The lemma appears just once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ('neared') reflects how it sits in its verse rather than the word's own meaning, so lean on the consistent Septuagint and lexicon evidence for 'provisions.'

definition: To teach someone by word of mouth, instructing or informing them, often about the things of the faith.
article: κατηχέω means to teach or instruct someone by spoken word, and by extension to inform or notify a person of something. It appears 8 times across 5 New Testament books, and in 5 of those 8 cases the translators folded it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a single English word. Literally the word combines "down" with "sound" (it can mean "to resound"), and a papyrus from A.D. 250 shows it used in a legal setting, where an advocate says someone never "informed" or convinced him.
caution: Because it is absorbed into broader phrasing in 5 of 8 occurrences, its exact force in any given verse depends heavily on context.

definition: Unable to be seen; not perceptible to human eyes.
article: ἀόρατος means simply "invisible" — something that cannot be seen with the eyes. All five New Testament occurrences carry this single sense, and the Majority Standard Bible, BSB, Strong's, Dodson, and the KJV all agree on "invisible"; the three measured "senses" are really the same meaning in different phrases (the invisible Son in Colossians 1:15, the eternal invisible God in 1 Timothy 1:17). The word also lived in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan finds it among divine epithets in the magical papyri and even describing fire, and a Milesian epitaph uses it of the "unseen path" of life. In the Septuagint it twice renders Hebrew words for emptiness or hiddenness, including the formless "void" of Genesis 1:2.

definition: To lie close at hand or be present, ready and available to someone.
article: παράκειμαι literally means to lie beside something, hence to be near, present, or ready at hand. It shows up only twice in the New Testament, both in Romans 7 (verses 18 and 21), where translators render it differently — once as something being 'present' or available ('discover'), and once as a 'principle' that is always close by. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same down-to-earth way: one son writes to his mother that if more money 'had been at hand' he would have sent it (P Oxy III.530).
caution: Confidence is low: with only two New Testament uses, both in the same chapter, the word's full range is thinly attested and translators handle the two cases quite differently.

definition: The trough or pit dug beneath a winepress to catch the juice as it ran down from the press above.
article: This word names the lower receptacle or pit set beneath a winepress (the ληνός) to collect the juice that flowed down into it. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just once, in Jesus' parable of the vineyard owner in Mark 12:1, where translations render it "vat" or "pit for the winepress." Beyond the Bible it shows up in everyday Koine documents—Moulton-Milligan cite a fourth-century AD account from Oxyrhynchus listing ὑπολήνια—and in the Septuagint it appears 4 times, mostly translating the Hebrew yeqeb, "winepress."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense rests largely on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: Hymenaeus, the personal name of a man condemned in the New Testament for abandoning the Christian faith.
article: Ὑμεναῖος is simply a man's name, Hymenaeus, appearing twice in the New Testament (1 Timothy 1:20 and 2 Timothy 2:17), each time identifying someone who turned away from the faith. The name itself derives from Hymen, the god of weddings, and the related adjective shows up in ordinary Koine papyri and inscriptions — including a tomb inscription mourning someone who never reached the marriage bed. As a proper name it carries no separate meaning beyond identifying the individual.
caution: This is a personal name attested only twice in the New Testament, so its sense is fixed but the evidence base is very thin.

definition: Belonging to the people or the state — public, or in its adverbial form, openly and in public.
article: δημόσιος describes something belonging to the people or the community — public property, public officials, or actions done in the open. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times, all in Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "public" twice, "publicly" once, and as part of "anything helpful publicly" once; the feminine dative form works as an adverb meaning "in public." The papyri make the everyday flavor vivid: it was an extremely common label for public officials (δημόσιοι) and public taxes or roads (ὁδὸς δημοσία), showing it was ordinary civic vocabulary.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and three closely related shades of meaning, the line between "public" and "publicly" depends on grammar more than a sharp difference in sense.

definition: To make something larger or greater, or to praise and exalt someone or something as great.
article: μεγαλύνω covers two related ideas: literally making something bigger (like enlarging the borders of garments in Matthew 23:5) and figuratively praising or exalting someone as great (as when Mary's soul "magnifies" the Lord). It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament and far more often—70 times—in the Septuagint, where it usually translates the Hebrew גָּדַל ("to be great," 38 times). A lovely glimpse of its everyday use comes from a Christian letter on papyrus (3rd–4th century AD), where a woman tells her father she "was greatly exalted" and rejoiced to receive his message, matching the "get glory and praise" sense found in Philippians 1:20.
caution: In 5 of its 8 New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word, so its exact force can be hard to pin down in translation.

definition: A person who saw or heard something and can testify to it, especially in a legal setting or about Christ.
article: μάρτυς is straightforward: it means a witness, someone who can vouch for what they saw or heard. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "witnesses" in 31 of 34 occurrences (91%), and it covers both courtroom witnesses (Matthew 18:16, Mark 14:63) and those who testify about Christ (Luke 24:48). Everyday Koine papyri show the same usage vividly, listing the names of "witnesses" to contracts and legal documents, including phrasing close to Matthew 18:16's requirement of at least two witnesses. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates Hebrew עֵד (40 of 55 times).
caution: Although Strong's and the KJV note a later "martyr" sense (one who witnesses by death), this meaning belongs to later Christian literature and is not among the measured senses here.

definition: To agree with someone, to be in harmony, or to settle on terms such as a price.
senseLabels: to agree on what is done
article: συμφωνέω literally means "to sound together," hence to be in harmony, and by extension to come to an agreement—whether agreeing about a matter, settling on a price, or matching things together. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 6 times, all rendered with some form of "agree," including the bargain over a day's wage in Matthew 20:2 and 20:13. The most telling evidence is from everyday papyri: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 59 speaks of "what was agreed upon between me and Antiphanes," echoing the contractual sense seen in Acts 5:9.

definition: An adverb meaning traveling on foot, or by land as opposed to going by boat.
article: πεζῇ is an adverb describing how someone travels: on foot, by land, rather than by boat. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Matthew 14:13 and Mark 6:33), and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "on foot." The contrast with sea travel is well documented in everyday Koine: a papyrus from A.D. 133 pairs it with sailing ("neither sailing nor going by foot"), and lexicographers note the same boat-versus-land contrast in Mark's account itself.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, sources note the sense can shade between "on foot" and the broader "by land," and editions disagree on which fits Matthew 14:13.

definition: Describing a wind as violent and stormy, like a hurricane or whirlwind.
article: This adjective describes a wind that is fierce and tempestuous, the kind that whips up like a hurricane. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:14, where the Majority Standard Bible and Berea Standard Bible both render it as the wind of a "cyclone" that strikes Paul's ship. The word traces back to Typhon, who in Greek magical papyri (like a fourth-century AD text from Oslo) was the malignant storm-demon invoked in spells, which gives the storm imagery its menacing punch.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Having enough — either an outward sufficiency of resources or an inner attitude of being satisfied with what one has.
article: αὐτάρκεια appears just twice in the New Testament, and the two uses pull in slightly different directions. In 2 Corinthians 9:8 it points to a concrete sufficiency — having all you need — while in 1 Timothy 6:6 it describes an inner contentment. The everyday papyri back the concrete sense strongly: one document from A.D. 137 uses αὐτάρκεια simply to mean "the necessary amount" of pigeon guano, and Moulton-Milligan conclude the word there is "only concrete, a sufficiency."
caution: With only two occurrences split evenly between two senses, and the papyri leaning entirely toward the concrete "sufficiency" meaning, the exact range here is uncertain.

definition: A fortress or stronghold; figuratively, any defended position or argument in which someone places confidence.
article: ὀχύρωμα literally means a fortified place — a castle, fortress, or stronghold — and the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri, where it can also mean a prison (a wall guarding people in). In the Septuagint it appears 36 times across 17 books, most often translating the Hebrew מִבְצָר, "fortified place" (11×), and both the Greek Old Testament and Proverbs already use it figuratively for whatever one trusts in. Its single New Testament appearance, in 2 Corinthians 10:4, takes this metaphorical step, picturing strongholds to be torn down.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, and Moulton-Milligan note they cannot illustrate its metaphorical sense from the papyri, so the figurative meaning rests on Septuagint usage rather than direct documentary parallels.

definition: A correlative word meaning "of what sort" or "such as," pointing to the kind or quality of something.
article: οἷος is a qualitative relative pronoun that compares or describes the kind of thing being talked about — "such as," "of what sort," or simply "as." It appears 15 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often classically paired with τοιοῦτος ("such") but in the NT usually standing alone, as in Matthew 24:21 ("tribulation such as has not been seen"). An everyday papyrus from AD 17 uses it the same way, requiring a servant to return a mill "in the condition in which (οἷον) he received it," showing how ordinary this comparative usage was in common Koine.
caution: In about a quarter of its occurrences (4 of 15) the word is absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own, so its force is often grammatical rather than independently translatable.

definition: The unlawful killing of a human being—murder or deadly slaughter.
article: φόνος means murder or the deadly slaughter of a person, and the New Testament use is remarkably consistent: of its 10 Byzantine occurrences, 7 (88%) are rendered "murder," with the rest absorbed into phrasing. The lexicons agree, adding "slaughter" and "killing" as near synonyms, including the phrase φόνος μαχαίρης ("slaughter by the sword") in Hebrews 11:37. A nice glimpse into everyday Koine comes from the papyri: an amnesty decree by Ptolemy and Cleopatra (118 BC) pardons all subjects "except those guilty of wilful murder or sacrilege"—showing the word's place in ordinary legal language, sometimes shading toward manslaughter rather than premeditated killing.

definition: Describes a person who is not married, whether never wed, divorced, or widowed.
article: ἄγαμος simply means "unmarried" — a person not currently in a state of wedlock. All four New Testament occurrences fall in a single chapter, 1 Corinthians 7, where Paul discusses marriage and singleness, and the Majority Standard Bible renders every one the same basic way. The word built straightforwardly from the negative prefix and the noun for "marriage" (γάμος), and it shows up in everyday Koine documents, including a marriage contract and even a gravestone bearing the word ἄγαμε.

definition: A lack of good sense or sound judgment; foolish thinking or behavior.
article: ἀφροσύνη names senselessness — the absence of wisdom or sound judgment, whether in a person's words or conduct. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, and the translation splits between calling someone or something a "fool" (2×) and naming "foolishness" as a quality (2×), as in Mark 7:22 where it sits among the evils that defile a person. In the Septuagint it shows up far more often (31× in 9 books), usually rendering Hebrew words for folly such as נְבָלָה and סִכְלוּת, and some lexicons stretch its range toward "impiety" or "wickedness."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the boundary between simple "foolishness" and the stronger moral sense of "impiety/wickedness" listed by some lexicons rests largely on Septuagint usage.

definition: To do, practice, or carry out an action, often repeated behavior and frequently used of doing wrong.
article: This common verb means to do, practice, or accomplish something, and it shows up 38 times across the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible most often renders it simply "done" (7×, 44%), but in 22 of 38 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own, which tells you how flexible it is. Older lexicons stress that πράσσω suggests the action of a moral, responsible person—like Latin agere—and is often used for committing wrong deeds, in contrast to ποιέω; Moulton-Milligan note the same word turns up in everyday papyri for transacting business and collecting payments.
caution: With most occurrences absorbed into phrasing and lexicons noting its overlap with ποιέω cannot always be maintained, the precise shade of meaning in any given verse is somewhat uncertain.

definition: To heed or submit to a command or authority; to obey.
article: ὑπακούω means to listen attentively and then comply — to obey or submit to someone's authority. In the Byzantine New Testament this single sense dominates: across all 21 occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it with some form of "obey" (50% as "obey," plus variants like "even obey" and "obeyed"). Its literal makeup is "to hear under," and the everyday papyri preserve an older, more concrete sense: one document even uses it for answering a knock at the door (compare Acts 12:13), reflecting how the word moved from listening to heeding.

definition: A wrong or injury done to someone, especially one serious enough to count as a crime or legal offense.
article: ἀδίκημα is the concrete noun built from ἀδικέω ("to do wrong"), pointing to an actual wrong deed rather than wrongdoing in the abstract. In the New Testament's three uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "crime" both times it gets its own English word, fitting its appearances in legal settings like Acts 18:14 and 24:20. The Septuagint uses it more broadly (16 times) for Hebrew words like פֶּשַׁע (transgression) and עָווֹן (iniquity), and the papyri show it as everyday legal language—for example a marriage contract describing a wrong done to a wife.
caution: Evidence is thin: only three New Testament occurrences with one absorbed into phrasing, so the confidence tier is low.

definition: To make a loud ringing or roaring sound, as a struck object resounds or the sea roars.
article: ἠχέω describes producing a loud, resonant sound — the clang of a struck instrument or the roar of the sea. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice in the Byzantine text (just once in the SBLGNT critical text), and in both cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding English phrasing rather than translated as a single word. The Septuagint uses it more freely, 17 times, most often rendering the Hebrew הָמָה (5×), a word for roaring, murmuring, or tumultuous sound, which fits the verb's sense of noisy reverberation.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is very thin — only two occurrences, both blended into phrasing — so the precise nuance leans heavily on Septuagint and lexicon usage.

definition: The ear, the organ of hearing on the side of the head.
article: ὠτίον is the everyday word for an ear, used in all five New Testament occurrences for the ear of the high priest's servant struck during Jesus' arrest. Although it is technically a diminutive of οὖς ("ear"), the measured renderings treat it simply as "ear," and the various phrasings in the data ("cutting off ear," "off ear," "more man's ear") just reflect the surrounding narrative rather than separate meanings. In the Septuagint it appears 14 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for ear (אֹזֶן, 9×). One nice detail: the related form ὠτάριον shows up in everyday papyri meaning the "handle" of a jar, since handles look like little ears.
caution: The four measured "senses" are really one meaning (ear) split by narrative wording, so do not read distinct senses into them.

definition: The birth or being born of a person, the event of coming into the world.
article: γέννησις refers to a person's birth or being born, and appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament—at Matthew 1:18 (Jesus' birth) and Luke 1:14 (the birth of John). Note that it does not appear at all in the critical text (SBLGNT), where related forms are read instead, so its presence depends on the manuscript tradition you follow. Moulton-Milligan show it was a normal everyday Koine word, found in papyri and inscriptions; Abbott-Smith adds that beyond plain "birth" it could also mean "begetting," and in the Septuagint it once renders a Hebrew word for "family" (1 Chronicles 4:8).
caution: Evidence is thin: only two Byzantine occurrences, none in the critical text, and the readings at both verses are textually disputed.

definition: The warm welcome and care shown toward strangers and guests; hospitality.
article: This word means love of strangers — the active practice of welcoming and caring for guests. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Romans 12:13 and Hebrews 13:2), where it's rendered "practice hospitality" and "hospitality," and both the lexicons and everyday Koine papyri agree on this single meaning. One charming example comes from a fourth-century letter (P Lond 1917) where a writer hopes his correspondent will read his note "with joy and with hospitality of long-suffering," showing how the word carried a warm, generous tone in ordinary life.
caution: Confidence is rated low because the word occurs only twice and is absent from the critical text (SBLGNT).

definition: A snake or serpent, sometimes used as an image of cunning or as a name for Satan.
article: This is the ordinary Greek word for a snake or serpent, and the New Testament uses it just that way — "snakes" 8 times (62%) and "serpent" 4 times (31%), with the BSB agreeing fully on every rendering. In the Septuagint it appears 35 times, mostly translating the Hebrew נָחָשׁ (28×), the standard word for snake. Beyond the literal reptile, the lexicons note it could picture wisdom and cunning, and in Revelation it names Satan; everyday Koine papyri even preserve a spell "to kill a serpent," showing how common the word was.

definition: A two-word phrase meaning "if anyone" or "if anything," introducing a conditional that applies to any person or thing.
article: This is not really a single word but a combination of two common Greek words: εἰ ("if") and τις ("anyone, anything"). Together they mean "if any man," "if anyone," or "if anything," and the King James translators rendered it flexibly as "he that," "whether any," or "whosoever." The digest records no measured senses and zero occurrences as a separate entry, which is expected since it is a phrase rather than a true lexical unit.
caution: There are no measured corpus senses for this entry because it is a word-combination rather than a single word, so its meaning depends on how εἰ and τις function in each specific verse.

definition: A tower or fortified structure, including a watchtower built to guard a vineyard.
article: Πύργος means a tower — a tall, often fortified structure. In the New Testament it appears 4 times, twice for an ordinary tower (as in Luke 13:4 and 14:28) and twice for the watchtower a landowner builds in his vineyard (Matthew 21:33, Mark 12:1). The Septuagint uses it 60 times, almost always for the Hebrew migdāl, and everyday Koine papyri confirm its plain sense: one document even describes a sleeping-chamber up on a tower, and another reports tools being stolen from one.

definition: To lead someone in a triumphal procession, displaying them publicly as a conquered captive.
article: This verb comes from the imagery of the Roman triumph, the grand victory parade in which a conquering general displayed his captives. The New Testament uses it just twice: in 2 Corinthians 2:14, where God 'leads' people in His triumphal procession, and in Colossians 2:15, where defeated powers are made a 'public' spectacle. A fascinating piece of evidence comes from a related verb in a Koine papyrus from 14 B.C. (BGU IV.1061), where it means to have an affair 'noised abroad' or made public, and the ancient scholar Photius likewise glossed the word as 'made public.'
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences) and the lexicons disagree on whether Colossians 2:15 means 'triumph over' or 'make a spectacle of.'

definition: The Greek numeral 666, written with three letter-symbols, given as the number of the Beast in Revelation.
article: This isn't really a word but a number: the Greek letters chi (600), xi (60), and stigma (6) combined to write 666. In the Byzantine text it stands in for the spelled-out phrase "six hundred and sixty-six" (hexakosioi hexēkonta hex). It appears at Revelation 13:18 as the number of the Beast, and notably some manuscripts read 616 instead of 666 (noted in margins).
caution: This is a numeral, not a vocabulary word, and it occurs only in this single disputed passage where manuscripts differ between 666 and 616.

definition: The stern, the rear part of a ship.
article: πρύμνα is the back end of a boat—the stern—as opposed to the πρῷρα, the prow at the front. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in nautical scenes: Jesus sleeping in the stern of the boat (Mark 4:38) and sailors managing a ship in Acts 27. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where a 257 BC document measures a boat as 'two and a half cubits broad at the narrow end round the stern,' and a later text describes a vessel 'from prow to stern.'
caution: This entry rests on only 3 New Testament occurrences (low confidence tier), though all sources agree the meaning is simply 'stern.'

definition: To act as if about to do something, making a show or pretense of an intention.
article: προσποιέομαι is the middle form of a verb that literally means "to make over to" or "add to oneself," but in practice it came to mean putting on an appearance or pretending an intention. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and in both cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than mapping to a single English word — the standard example is Luke 24:28, where Jesus "made as though" he would travel further. The everyday Koine papyri show the same ambiguity scholars debate: in P Oxy I.121 the editors first read it as "make over" property but suggest "don't make any pretence," and in the Septuagint it renders two unrelated Hebrew words.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing) and even the papyri editors waver between "make over" and "pretend."

definition: An adverb meaning on each occasion, every time, or always.
article: This adverb means "each time" or "always," describing something that happens on every occasion. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 1:15, where it's absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. Though unknown to the Septuagint, the everyday papyri confirm its place in ordinary Koine speech — one letter writer (P Gen I.31, A.D. 145–6) apologizes for "bothering you every time" he visits.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests largely on outside papyri evidence.

definition: To make something powerless or inactive—to cancel, abolish, do away with, or set aside its effect.
article: This is a favorite Pauline verb meaning to render something idle, ineffective, or void—stripping it of its force so it no longer operates. It covers a wide range, from nullifying a promise or law to things that simply fade and pass away, and with people it can mean being released or severed from something (as in Romans 7:2-6, Galatians 5:4). The everyday Koine flavor shows up in the papyri, where a man complains that something "hinders me in my handicraft," and elsewhere it describes an animal or tool being put out of use. In the Septuagint it appears only 4 times, all in one book, translating the Hebrew word for stopping or making to cease.
caution: The measured renderings here are heavily shaped by surrounding phrasing—11 of 27 occurrences carry no English word of their own, so labels like "came" and "away" reflect translation context rather than the verb's core meaning of nullifying or rendering inactive.

definition: A person from Crete, the large island in the Mediterranean Sea.
article: Κρής simply means a Cretan, someone who lives on or comes from the island of Crete. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the plural "Cretans" — once among the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:11) and once in Titus 1:12. The word is derived directly from Κρήτη, the name of the island itself.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the New Testament, so its measured range is very limited.

definition: Having a sound, disciplined mind that keeps one's desires and behavior under control.
article: σώφρων describes someone with a sound, level-headed mind who keeps their passions and impulses in check. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, always rendered "self-controlled," listed among the qualities expected of church leaders and mature believers (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:8; 2:2). Interestingly, ancient inscriptions collected by Deissmann use this same word as an ideal of womanhood — describing wives who were "soberminded" and devoted to husband and children — which lines up with the way Titus 2:5 uses it.
caution: The word appears only 4 times in the New Testament, so its measured range is narrow even though lexicons note a broader sense of being "sound of mind."

definition: A false apostle—someone who falsely claims to be a genuine apostle of Christ.
article: This word combines "false" (ψευδής) with "apostle" (ἀπόστολος) to describe someone who pretends to hold apostolic authority they do not actually have. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:13, where Paul brands certain opponents as "false apostles, deceitful workers." The lexicons agree closely, glossing it as a spurious or pretended apostle.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range of meaning cannot be measured across multiple contexts.

definition: To hesitate or hold back from doing something, and so to delay or be slow to act.
article: This verb describes shrinking back from an action — hesitating, being reluctant, and so putting something off. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 9:38, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "delay" (100%), and the classical lexica add the underlying sense of hesitation or being loath to act. The everyday papyri preserve a charming detail: it became an epistolary formula, with writers urging "do not hesitate to write to us" (μὴ ὀκνῶν γράφειν).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured data is thin, though the papyri and Septuagint usage confirm the meaning.

definition: To charge something to someone's account or hold them responsible for it, like an entry in a financial ledger.
article: This is a bookkeeping word: it means to enter something onto someone's account, whether a debt or a charge. The New Testament uses it just twice, and in both places the Majority Standard Bible renders it "account" (Romans 5:13, where sin is not charged against people, and Philemon 1:18, where Paul offers to cover a debt). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this, including a letter from two women instructing their steward to "charge to my account" whatever he spends.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, confidence is low, though the financial sense is well supported by the papyri.

definition: Antipatris, a town in Palestine on the road between Caesarea and Jerusalem.
article: Antipatris is a place name, a town located between Joppa and Caesarea on the route from Jerusalem to Caesarea. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:31, where soldiers bring Paul there overnight. The name derives from the same root as Antipas (G493).
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering 'followed their orders' reflects the surrounding sentence rather than the place name itself.

definition: Spain, the region of Europe roughly matching the modern country of the same name.
article: Σπανία is simply the place name Spain, the country in western Europe, which Paul mentions as the destination he hoped to reach (Romans 15:24, 28). It appears just twice in the New Testament, both times in that single passage, and translators render it consistently as "Spain." Abbott-Smith notes that earlier Greek writers called this region Ἑσπερία or Ἰβηρία, while later authors adopted the Roman-style names Ἱσπανία or Σπανία, as used here.
caution: This is a proper noun appearing only twice, both in one passage, so its range is naturally limited to a single place name.

definition: News or a report about someone that spreads from person to person through a region.
article: φήμη refers to a report or rumor that circulates and spreads, the kind of talk that travels through a region about a notable person or event. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 9:26 and Luke 4:14), both describing how news about Jesus spread, and the translations are consistent and straightforward. Moulton-Milligan note that the word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it was ordinary, common-life vocabulary rather than a specialized term.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, though the meaning is clear and the sources agree.

definition: To be at a loss or mentally stuck, not knowing what to do or think about a situation.
article: ἀπορέω describes the feeling of being mentally cornered — literally having "no way out" of a puzzle, so you don't know what to think or do. In the Byzantine New Testament's 4 occurrences, the Berean Standard Bible renders it "perplexed" 3 times (75%) and once as "how" (Acts 25:20), where someone is unsure how to handle an inquiry. The everyday Koine papyri capture the same flavor vividly: one writer says he is "at his wit's end" after being ruined by creditors, and another confesses he is "at a loss how to write more" about a sick woman.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 4 Byzantine occurrences), and the sources differ slightly on which verses count, so the precise range is somewhat uncertain.

definition: A load or burden, especially the cargo carried by a ship.
article: φόρτος refers to something carried — a load or burden — and in practice especially the cargo of a ship. It comes from the verb φέρω, "to carry," and is well attested from Homer and Herodotus onward into later prose. The word does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament text; Abbott-Smith notes it at Acts 27:10 only in the Received Text (a textual variant rather than the standard reading).
caution: This word does not occur in the Byzantine NT and appears at Acts 27:10 only as a Received Text variant, so its New Testament basis is uncertain.

definition: Worthy of praise and blessing — a title of honor applied to God, declaring him deserving of grateful acclaim.
article: εὐλογητός describes someone as deserving to be blessed or praised, and in the New Testament it is used almost exclusively of God. Across its 8 Byzantine occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Blessed" 3 times (43%) and "worthy praise" twice (29%), with BSB agreeing 100% each time. The Septuagint uses it 51 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew בָּרַך ("to bless," 26 times), and Abbott-Smith notes that while it can describe people in the Old Testament, in the New Testament it points to God as the one entitled to receive blessing.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the split between "blessed" and "worthy of praise" reflects translators' word choices rather than two sharply distinct meanings.

definition: On the right side, or the right hand—the side opposite the left, often marking a place of honor or power.
article: δεξιός simply means "right" as opposed to left, used either of the right hand specifically (about 59% of its 54 New Testament uses) or of the right side more generally (about 39%). The two senses really differ only in what noun is in view, since the word often stands alone for "the right hand" with "hand" understood. In the Septuagint it appears 183 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew word for "right hand" (יָמִין), and the everyday papyri use it the same way—one document even shows someone appointed "by your propitious right hand," while others use the right hand (δεξιά) to mean a pledge or handshake of friendship.

definition: The inner moral awareness that judges one's own conduct as right or wrong, and the consciousness of having acted well or badly.
article: συνείδησις literally means "co-knowledge"—an inner awareness that judges your own actions. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "conscience" 22 of 32 times (76%) and "clear conscience" in 6 more (21%), while Abbott-Smith notes an earlier, broader sense of simple "consciousness" or awareness of something (as in Hebrews 10:2). A vivid everyday parallel comes from a 2nd-century papyrus where a woman is described as "oppressed by the consciousness of what she had appropriated," showing the same guilty self-awareness the New Testament associates with the word.

definition: To shake, unsettle, or disturb someone; originally used of a dog wagging its tail and, by extension, fawning or beguiling.
article: σαίνω appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Thessalonians 3:3), where it is rendered "shaken" — Paul's concern that the Thessalonians not be unsettled amid their afflictions. The word's literal sense, attested from Homer onward, is a dog wagging its tail, which then developed figuratively into "fawn upon, flatter, beguile." Moulton-Milligan notes this fawning/alluring sense fits the verse well, suggesting Paul feared the believers might be drawn aside by hardship, though English translations settle on the broader idea of being disturbed.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical SBLGNT; the text and exact meaning here are disputed, with some sources proposing emendations.

definition: To be at home or present in a place, living among one's own people rather than away.
senseLabels: to be at home or present
article: This verb means to be at home or settled in a place, as opposed to being away (its natural opposite is ἀποδημέω, "to be abroad"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in 2 Corinthians 5, where Paul contrasts being "at home" in the body with being "at home" with the Lord. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri and inscriptions: one Oxyrhynchus document (A.D. 211) orders a royal scribe "not to be at home," and an inscription speaks of resident foreigners (ξένοι) currently living in a town.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 occurrences, two of which are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word.

definition: To shout or call out loudly toward someone or something, often as a crowd voicing approval, condemnation, or a demand.
article: ἐπιφωνέω means to call out or shout at someone, built from ἐπί ("at, toward") and φωνέω ("to make a sound, call"). Across its few New Testament uses it covers crowds shouting condemnation (Luke 23:21), acclaiming a ruler (Acts 12:22), and clamoring a demand (Acts 22:24), so the tone ranges from hostile to celebratory. The everyday Koine papyri match this nicely: one document from A.D. 192 has bystanders shouting "Let Achilles be crowned!", and an inscription records the crowd crying "Well said, Philocles!"
caution: With only 3 Byzantine occurrences (each rendered differently) and thin Septuagint evidence, the precise range is hard to pin down, so this entry sits at low confidence.

definition: Money, riches, or worldly wealth, often pictured as a rival master competing with God for a person's loyalty.
article: Mammon is a loanword from Aramaic meaning riches, money, or possessions, appearing 4 times across 2 books in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "worldly wealth" where it stands alone (as in Luke 16:9), while in the other 3 instances it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. Strong's notably frames it as "avarice (deified)" — wealth treated as a personified master — though one suggested derivation traces it instead to a word meaning something "deposited" or entrusted; Moulton-Milligan confirms the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: It does not appear in the SBLGNT critical text, and the lexicons offer competing derivations, so its exact background is uncertain.

definition: Citizenship or membership in a community, including the rights and status that go with belonging to a city or state.
article: πολιτεία refers to belonging to a political community — either citizenship as a personal status (as when Paul's tribune mentions the high price he paid for Roman citizenship in Acts 22:28) or the commonwealth itself, the body people belong to (Ephesians 2:12). It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the second occurrence is hard to pin down: the measured rendering reads it loosely ("remember"), while older lexicons take it as "commonwealth." Everyday Koine documents back the broad range nicely — an Oxyrhynchus papyrus from A.D. 254 uses it for the ancestral usages of "our constitution," and other Egyptian examples treat it as practically equivalent to "city."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the digest's measured rendering of Ephesians 2:12 disagreeing with the lexicons' "commonwealth," the precise sense in that verse is uncertain.

definition: In a way that is either physically secure and safe, or mentally certain and beyond doubt.
article: The adverb ἀσφαλῶς covers two related ideas: keeping something physically safe or secure, and knowing something with firm certainty. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 3 times, rendered "securely" twice (as when guards hold a prisoner) and "with certainty" once, in Acts 2:36's call to know assuredly. Abbott-Smith notes its Septuagint use, including Genesis 34:25, where it translates a Hebrew word for security or safety (בֶּטַח).
caution: This entry rests on only 3 New Testament occurrences and is rated low confidence, though the measured senses and classical lexica agree closely.

definition: Not known or recognized; describing something or someone whose identity has not been made known.
article: This adjective combines the negative prefix with the word for "known," so it simply means "unknown." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:23, where Paul refers to an Athenian altar inscribed "to an unknown god." A striking parallel turned up in 1909 at Pergamon, where archaeologists found an altar inscription that probably read "to unknown gods," dedicated by a torchbearer named Capito — confirming that this kind of dedication was a real practice in the Greek world. The word also shows up in the Septuagint and in everyday papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from that single use.

definition: Syntyche, the personal name of a Christian woman in the church at Philippi.
article: Syntyche is a woman's name, appearing just once in the New Testament at Philippians 4:2, where Paul urges her and Euodia to agree with each other. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as a proper name in its single occurrence, and it isn't really a word with a meaning so much as a label for a specific person. Interestingly, the name turns up in everyday Greek inscriptions (such as CIG II), and Moulton-Milligan notes a masculine Latin form, Sintichus, plus a tradition speculating she might be the Lydia of Acts.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single passage.

definition: To catch or trap, literally by hunting or fishing, and figuratively to ensnare someone in their words.
article: ἀγρεύω means to catch by hunting or fishing, and its single New Testament use is figurative: in Mark 12:13 opponents try to "catch" Jesus in his words, like trapping prey. The Septuagint uses it five times, mostly translating the Hebrew verb צוּד ("to hunt"), keeping the hunting imagery. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain meaning beautifully — one third/fourth-century letter complains, "we cannot catch a single animal."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its figurative "entrap" sense rests on a single verse.

definition: To run together toward something or rush along with others, whether literally crowding to a place or figuratively joining in a course of action.
article: συντρέχω combines "with/together" and "run," and at its core means to run together—people converging on a spot or running alongside one another. It appears just 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible only renders it as an explicit word ("ran") once, as at Acts 3:11; the other two times it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same practical way, as in a document describing cultivators who "ran off" together after their suspicions were aroused, and Abbott-Smith notes a figurative sense at 1 Peter 4:4 of rushing along with others into a way of life.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences with just one given a distinct English word—so the confidence tier is low.

definition: A firm support or foundation that holds something steady, used figuratively as a base or bulwark.
article: ἑδραίωμα refers to a firm support, foundation, or bulwark — something that holds another thing steady. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Timothy 3:15) and is derived from the adjective ἑδραῖος (steadfast). The lexica agree on "support, stay, bulwark," and the scholar Hort, following the near-universal Latin rendering firmamentum, argued strongly for "stay" or "bulwark."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured-sense label "delayed" conflicts with every lexicon, which uniformly gives "support" or "foundation" — trust the lexica here.

definition: To turn aside or veer away from something, whether leaving the right path or actively avoiding people and evil.
article: ἐκκλίνω literally means "to bend away," and in the New Testament it covers two related ideas: people who have turned away from the right path (Romans 3:12) and the deliberate choice to avoid evil or troublesome people (1 Peter 3:11; Romans 16:17). It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament but is very common in the Septuagint, occurring 141 times where it usually renders the Hebrew סוּר (51×, "turn aside") and נָטָה (39×, "stretch out" or "bend"). The everyday Koine papyri add a striking nuance: in a decree of Ptolemy Philometor the verb is used for shrinking back from danger or hardship, and elsewhere it carries the sense of "to fail" or fall short.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin biblical data, so the fuller range comes mainly from the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: That which fills or completes something — the full amount, full measure, or fullness of a thing.
article: πλήρωμα is the noun built from the verb πληρόω ("to fill"), so it points to whatever fills something up or to the resulting fullness. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "fullness" in 7 of 17 occurrences (58%), with another 2 in the phrase about the Lord's fullness of the earth (1 Corinthians 10:26, 28); notably, 5 of the 17 cases are absorbed into surrounding phrasing and get no English word of their own. The Septuagint uses it 15 times, mostly for Hebrew מְלֹא ("fullness, that which fills"), and the everyday papyri offer a striking concrete use — a labor "gang" or full company of workers not to be withdrawn before finishing a job.
caution: The lexicons note the word swings between a passive sense ("that which is filled/the fullness") and an active sense ("that which fills up"), so the precise nuance can be debated in individual passages.

definition: To make something known to others, or to come to know or recognize something.
article: γνωρίζω most often means to make something known, to declare or reveal it — that's how the Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 of 24 times (52%). But it also runs in the other direction, meaning to come to know or recognize something, which is the classical lexicon's primary listing. Everyday papyri show a sharp practical use: a γνωστήρ was a witness who could vouch for someone's identity, and the verb appears in legal contexts about recognizing a person "at your own risk." In the Septuagint it appears 43 times and most often translates the Hebrew yadaʿ, "to know."
caution: The two directions of meaning — "make known" versus "come to know" — can blur, and the Majority Bible and the classical lexicon weight them differently, so context decides which applies.

definition: In a way that shows self-control and sound judgment in how one lives.
article: σωφρόνως is an adverb describing living with a clear, disciplined mind — soberly, prudently, with self-control. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Titus 2:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "upright," though the older lexica (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all stress the sense of "soberly" or "with moderation." Its only Septuagint appearance is in Wisdom 9:11, so the evidence base is very thin.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, and the single measured rendering ("upright") differs in emphasis from the classical lexica's "soberly/prudently," so confidence is low.

definition: A deep-seated bad character that twists things toward malice, reading the worst into people and acting with ill will.
article: κακοήθεια describes a settled malicious streak in a person's character — not just an occasional bad mood but an ingrained bent toward malevolence. The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Paul's vice list at Romans 1:29, and shows up a handful of times in the Septuagint (Esther, 3 Maccabees, 4 Maccabees), where in one case it stands for the Hebrew אֲדָר. The most telling evidence is its everyday Koine use: a papyrus from A.D. 581 lists it alongside words for deceit and fear in a legal disclaimer, confirming it meant real-world bad faith and mischief, not an abstract theological term.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests largely on Septuagint and papyri parallels rather than New Testament usage.

definition: The earth as a whole, or a particular stretch of land, ground, or region.
article: γῆ is one of the most common words in the Greek Bible, covering everything from the entire planet down to a patch of soil. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 250 times, rendered "earth" in 80% of cases and "land" in 19%, with the meaning ranging across the globe, dry ground (as opposed to sea), cultivated soil, and named regions like "the land of Israel." In the Septuagint it shows up an enormous 2,784 times, mostly translating Hebrew אֶרֶץ (2,083×), and the papyri preserve the same word in ordinary documents, including rare plural forms ("lands") used in property deeds from the second century BC.

definition: A merged form of "and I," used to mean "I," "I also," or "I too," depending on context.
article: κἀγώ is a crasis—two words fused into one—built from καί ("and/also") and ἐγώ ("I"). In practice it mostly just means "I": the Majority Standard Bible renders it as plain "I" or "I am" in 65% of its 71 Byzantine occurrences, while the "also/too" sense (carrying over the force of καί) accounts for about 15%. This crasis was common in everyday Koine—a third-century BC papyrus letter uses it casually ("so that I also may know"), showing it belonged to ordinary correspondence, not just literary Greek.
caution: In the Septuagint the form occasionally lines up with unrelated Hebrew words like עַקְרָב ("scorpion," 3×), reflecting textual or alignment quirks rather than the word's actual meaning.

definition: Artemis, a goddess worshipped especially at Ephesus, whom the city's silversmiths and crowds defended against Paul's preaching.
article: Ἄρτεμις is simply the name of the goddess Artemis, appearing 5 times in the New Testament, all in the riot scene at Ephesus in Acts 19. Every occurrence refers to the same deity, and the apparent extra senses in the data ("began Artemis," "began is Artemis") just reflect surrounding words, not different meanings. Notably, the lexicons stress that this Asiatic Artemis—linked to fertility and worshipped at Ephesus—should be distinguished from the Greek maiden huntress of the same name, even though the KJV translated her as "Diana."
caution: Although she is one figure, older translations call her "Diana," so readers should not confuse this Ephesian goddess with the classical Greek Artemis.

definition: The number eight; in combinations it also forms larger numbers such as eighteen (ten plus eight).
article: ὀκτώ is the plain cardinal number "eight," an indeclinable word that stays the same in every grammatical setting. When paired with "ten" it helps express "eighteen," which is how the Majority Standard Bible renders it twice in Luke 13. It is common everyday Greek: Moulton-Milligan cite business papyri counting things like eight artabas of grain, and in the Septuagint it appears 68 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for eight (59 of those times).

definition: To overlook, neglect, or pass over someone or something, failing to give it the attention it deserves.
article: παραθεωρέω means to look past someone and fail to attend to them properly. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:1, where the Hellenist widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food — though the Majority Standard Bible renders the verse with "grumble" (describing the resulting complaint), the word itself denotes the neglect being complained about. The lexica note a fuller range: literally "to examine side by side" or compare, then "to overlook, neglect," and a papyrus inscription about temple asylum uses it the same way, warning that the divine should not be "overlooked."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard rendering ("grumble") reflects the surrounding action rather than the verb's core sense of "overlook," so its exact force here rests on thin evidence.

definition: To come on or arise, used especially of a wind springing up or of time passing or events following after.
article: This verb means "to come on" or "arise," and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 28:13) it describes a south wind springing up to carry Paul's ship along. The translation tables show the word landing on "Rhegium" in that one verse, which simply reflects the surrounding place-name in the sentence rather than the verb's actual meaning. The most useful evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show it commonly used of time elapsing — "further periods having passed" — and even of lambs "born afterward," pointing to a core idea of something coming along after or in addition.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured sense label reflects an adjacent place-name rather than the verb's meaning, so lean on the papyri and lexicon evidence here.

definition: The interest or profit earned on money that has been lent out.
article: In the New Testament τόκος means the interest or return paid on borrowed money, appearing just twice (Matthew 25:27 and Luke 19:23) where both the Majority Standard and the BSB render it consistently as "interest." The word literally comes from τίκτω, "to give birth," so its original sense is a bringing forth or offspring; the financial meaning pictures money "breeding" more money. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, most often translating the Hebrew nešek (10×), the word for lending at interest, and it is well attested in everyday Koine: a third-century BC papyrus speaks of depositing "the silver and the interest" at the royal bank.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin biblical evidence, though Septuagint and papyri usage strongly confirm the financial sense.

definition: Dionysius, the personal name of an Athenian who became a believer after Paul's speech at the Areopagus.
article: Dionysius is a man's name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Acts 17:34) as an Athenian and member of the Areopagus council who believed after hearing Paul. The Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it as the name 100% of the time, with all the standard sources agreeing. Moulton-Milligan note that this name was extremely common in the Hellenistic period—it derives from the god Dionysus (Bacchus)—and its frequency is worth weighing when picturing the religious world Paul worked in.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single passage.

definition: To weaken or disable the body, especially through paralysis that leaves a person unable to move.
article: παραλύω literally means to "loosen beside," but in the New Testament it consistently describes the body being weakened or enfeebled, usually by paralysis. All 5 Byzantine occurrences cluster around this medical sense, and in Luke 5:24 the rendering "mat" simply names the bed belonging to the paralyzed man. The everyday Koine papyri preserve the older, broader meaning: one document uses the related verb to speak of being "set free" from a task and another of a city being released from interest payments, showing how a word for "loosing" narrowed into a term for a loosened, disabled body.
caution: This word does not appear in the critical (SBLGNT) text at all, and the measured "mat" and "shrieks possessed paralyzed" labels reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To long for or yearn after someone or something with deep affection and desire.
article: This verb expresses a strong, affectionate yearning — to long deeply for someone or something. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (in the Textus Receptus of 1 Thessalonians 2:8, where the critical text reads a different form, ὁμείρομαι) and only once in the Septuagint, at Job 3:21, where it renders the Hebrew word for hidden treasure (מַטְמוֹן). One nice touch from everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite the poet Bacchylides, who pairs the verb with both rich and poor — "the rich man yearns for great things, as the poorer for less."
caution: Evidence is very thin — only one disputed New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use — and the sources disagree on whether the correct form is ἱμείρομαι or ὁμείρομαι.

definition: Describes someone who has been born, used in the phrase "born of women" to mean human beings.
article: γεννητός means "born" or "begotten," an adjective formed from the verb γεννάω ("to give birth"). In all 2 of its New Testament occurrences (Matthew 11:11 and Luke 7:28) it appears in the set phrase "those born of women," a way of saying "mankind" or "human beings." The same idiom shows up in the Septuagint's translation of Job, which renders the Hebrew yelud ishah ("born of woman") in passages like Job 14:1.
caution: The word occurs only twice in the New Testament, always inside the fixed phrase "born of women," so its independent range is hard to measure; the BSB rendering "than" reflects surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself.

definition: A dividing wall or partition that separates two areas, used figuratively for a barrier between groups.
article: This word names a middle or partition wall that physically separates spaces. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 2:14, where it pictures a barrier between people. Interestingly, although it shows up nowhere else in the Bible, Moulton-Milligan found a close parallel in everyday papyri romracracts regarding house-property sales at Hermopolis, where the related form refers to literal partition walls between properties.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon (occurring just once in the New Testament), so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A person from Alexandria, the major city in Egypt.
article: Ἀλεξανδρεύς simply means someone who comes from Alexandria, the great city in Egypt. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 6:9 and 18:24), and the word's meaning is straightforward and undisputed across the lexicons. Interestingly, in one of its two occurrences the term gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word, while the other is rendered simply as part of describing certain men.
caution: The word occurs only twice in the New Testament, so the evidence base is thin, though its meaning is not in doubt.

definition: A drachma, a Greek silver coin roughly equal in value to a Roman denarius and a typical day's wage.
article: A δραχμή was a Greek silver coin worth about the same as a Roman denarius, the kind of money handled in everyday transactions. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Luke 15:8-9, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "coins" in the parable of the lost coin. The papyri show just how ordinary it was: it turns up in wills and pay records, and in Tobit 5:15 Raphael agrees to work for one drachma a day plus expenses.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in a single Lukan passage.

definition: A person who runs an inn or lodging house, taking in travelers for the night.
article: πανδοχεύς is the keeper of an inn or lodging house — the one who receives and cares for travelers. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:35, where the Good Samaritan hands the wounded man over to the innkeeper for ongoing care. Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a charming epitaph greeting 'Decomia Syriska, the good hostess (πανδόκια), farewell.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: The prize or award given to the winner of a contest, used figuratively for the reward awaiting faithful believers.
article: βραβεῖον is the trophy or prize handed to the victor in athletic games, derived from the word for an umpire (βραβεύς) who judges the contest. It appears just twice in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 9:24 and Philippians 3:14), and both times the runner pictures the Christian's pursuit of a heavenly reward. Everyday Koine inscriptions confirm this athletic sense—one from Priene (1st century BC) speaks of prizes given to winners, and another describes someone honored with a 'golden prize.'
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, this word's range rests largely on outside inscriptions and lexicons, though those agree firmly on the meaning.

definition: A person passionately devoted to a cause, person, or thing — eagerly committed and ready to defend it.
article: ζηλωτής describes someone burning with eager devotion, whether to God, the law, ancestral traditions, or spiritual gifts. In the New Testament it appears 7 times and is most often rendered simply "zealous" (3×, 60%), though twice it dissolves into the surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it carries striking weight, six times translating the Hebrew קַנָּא to describe God himself as a "jealous" God (Exodus 20:5, Deuteronomy 4:24); everyday Koine inscriptions likewise use it for people who are "zealous for the noblest things."
caution: With only 7 occurrences and two cases absorbed into phrasing, the sense range is thin; note also that some classical and Lukan uses point to a fixed title ("Zealot," the political party) not measured here.

definition: A transliteration of the Hebrew/Aramaic title meaning the Anointed One, equivalent to the Greek word Christ.
article: Μεσσίας is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew word Mashiach (the Anointed One), which translates directly into the Greek title Christ. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in John (1:41 and 4:25), and each time the writer immediately explains or translates it for readers who would not recognize the Hebrew term. Beyond the Bible, Moulton-Milligan note that the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, showing it was a recognized name in the wider Greek-speaking world.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in a single book, the evidence base for this word is very thin.

definition: The end of physical life, whether by natural causes or violence; also used figuratively for spiritual death.
