article: θάνατος means death, and that single sense covers nearly all its uses — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "death" in 107 of its occurrences (99%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% of the time. The word stretches from the death of the body to the death of Christ, to death personified, and figuratively to spiritual death, but English almost always lands on the same word. One telling detail: in the Septuagint it translates not only the Hebrew words for "death" and "to die" but also דֶּבֶר, "plague" or "pestilence," 31 times — the deadly epidemic itself standing in for death. It was an ordinary, everyday Koine word, well documented in the papyri, including legal phrases about what happens to property "after death."

definition: To cry out or shout loudly, whether in fear, anger, urgent appeal, or public proclamation.
article: κράζω means to cry out loudly—the kind of raw, unrestrained shout that breaks from a crowd or an individual in fear, anger, or urgent pleading. The measured senses (cried out, shouting, shouted) all cluster tightly around this single idea of loud vocal outcry, so the word's range is narrow but vivid. Strong's notes the word's origin as imitating the croak of a raven, and everyday papyri confirm its ordinary use: a first-century petition has a man "crying out" his complaints, and another describes a farmer literally shouting that manure must not be ruined by water.

definition: A leopard, the large spotted wild cat known for its fierce, predatory nature.
article: πάρδαλις refers to the leopard (or panther), a spotted big cat. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 13:2, where the beast resembles one; note that the measured rendering here reads "bear," which conflicts with the standard lexical meaning of "leopard" given by Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith. In the Septuagint it appears 7 times, always translating the Hebrew נָמֵר ("leopard"), and the everyday papyri list it among real animals like the lion, weasel, and shrewmouse, with one source even noting it as a byword for roguery.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ("bear") clashes with every lexicon, which consistently defines it as "leopard."

definition: A piece of clothing, usually the outer cloak or mantle worn over the tunic, or in the plural one's clothes in general.
article: ἱμάτιον refers to clothing, and in the New Testament it splits almost evenly between two uses: the plural means "garments" or "clothes" generally (22×, 54%), while the singular usually means the specific outer "cloak" or mantle thrown over the tunic (19×, 46%). The lexica stress that, apart from the plural, it nearly always denotes that outer garment, often paired against the χιτών or undergarment, as in Matthew 5:40 and Luke 6:29. Everyday Koine papyri confirm both uses — a marriage contract from A.D. 66 lists robes and mantles together, while a third-century B.C. robbery account distinguishes the ἱμάτιον from the inner χιτών. In the Septuagint it appears 200× and chiefly translates Hebrew בֶּ֫גֶד (137×).

definition: A place or supply of grazing for animals, and figuratively the spreading of a sore through the body.
article: νομή basically means pasture — the grazing land or feeding that animals depend on. In its only two New Testament uses, the translators rendered it "pasture" once (John 10:9) and folded it into the phrasing the other time (2 Timothy 2:17), where it describes how unhealthy teaching "spreads" like a gangrenous sore eating its way through flesh. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the literal sense vividly: one document from around 245 BC complains of people who had used up the pastures, and a lease grants a renter "the pastures and secondary pastures."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the metaphorical "spreading sore" sense rests on thin evidence.

definition: A high-ranking official in the Roman province of Asia who funded and presided over its public games and festivals.
article: An Asiarch was one of the leading officials of the Roman province of Asia, elected by its cities and responsible for paying for and overseeing public games and festivals; ancient sources connect the role with the worship of Rome and the Emperor. The word combines "Asia" with "ruler" and appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 19:31, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "officials." Beyond Scripture, the term turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions and papyri, which is where scholars have learned the most about what these men actually did.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense rests largely on outside inscriptions rather than biblical usage.

definition: An Aramaic term of contempt meaning roughly "empty-headed" or "worthless," hurled as an insult at another person.
article: Rhaka is a borrowed Aramaic insult, transliterated rather than translated, that Jesus condemns in His teaching at Matthew 5:22 — its only appearance in the New Testament. It comes from an Aramaic word meaning "empty," used to call someone worthless or empty-headed, and Moulton-Milligan note it turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions too. Interestingly, an early commentator (Lightfoot) judged it a milder insult than the word "fool" (moros) that follows it in the same verse, marking degrees of contemptuous speech.
caution: This word appears only once and is a transliterated Aramaic term, so its precise force is reconstructed rather than directly measured; the corpus rendering label here is unreliable.

definition: A small word introducing a condition ("if") or an indirect question ("whether"), setting up something supposed, tested, or asked about.
article: εἰ is one of the most common little connecting words in the Greek New Testament, appearing 502 times and most often meaning "if" (270×, about 70% of the time). It chiefly introduces conditions, but it can also flag an indirect question ("whether") or, paired with a negative, mean "except." In the Septuagint it shows up 646 times, usually standing in for the Hebrew word אם ("if"), 305 times. One interesting wrinkle from everyday Koine papyri: writers increasingly blurred the line between εἰ and the related word ἐάν, even occasionally pairing εἰ with verb forms it traditionally avoided.
caution: Because εἰ is a grammatical particle rather than a content word, 116 of its 502 occurrences are absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, so the many short "sense" labels reflect translation patterns rather than distinct meanings.

definition: The Jordan, the major river of Palestine that formed the eastern boundary of Galilee, Samaria, and Judea.
article: Ἰορδάνης is simply the proper name of the Jordan River, the great waterway of Palestine where John baptized and Jesus was baptized. The measured renderings all point to the same place, though the phrasing varies: about 43% just name "Jordan," while another 29% describe the territory "beyond Jordan" (the region across the river). The name comes straight from the Hebrew יַרְדֵּן, which the Septuagint renders with Ἰορδάνης 190 times out of its 211 occurrences.

definition: To perform religious service or ministry, especially the public duties of priests, but also broader acts of service rendered to others.
article: λειτουργέω means to render service, and in the New Testament's three uses it describes religious ministry—priests serving at the altar (Hebrews 10:11), believers serving one another (Romans 15:27), and worshippers ministering to the Lord (Acts 13:2). The Majority Standard Bible's second listed "sense" ("While they were" in Acts 13:2) is just part of the surrounding sentence rather than a distinct meaning, so the word really carries one core idea: to minister or serve. The most striking evidence is its journey through the language: in classical Athens it meant funding public offices at one's own expense, but by the Koine period the papyri show it narrowing to personal and religious service—an inscription even uses it of temple servants at the great Serapeum near Memphis.
caution: With only three New Testament occurrences and one "measured sense" that is actually a sentence fragment rather than a real meaning, this entry rests on thin corpus data.

definition: To feel shame or be disgraced, especially in front of others; in the passive, to be put to shame.
article: This verb describes the feeling of shame or being put to shame, often in the eyes of others. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times and is rendered "ashamed" in 4 of them, with one negated case (1 John 2:28) where believers are urged not to be ashamed at Christ's coming. It translates the Septuagint over 75 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew בּוּשׁ ("to be ashamed"), and one papyrus letter touchingly shows a man who "no longer comes to me, being ashamed" — the same social embarrassment we feel today.
caution: The two measured senses are really one idea, since the "confident unashamed" reading at 1 John 2:28 simply reflects the negated verb in context.

definition: Belonging to someone else rather than yourself, or coming from outside one's own family, people, or nation.
article: ἀλλότριος basically means "someone else's" — not your own — and by extension "foreign" or "strange," the opposite of what's familiar or akin. Built from ἄλλος ("another"), it covers everything from another person's property to alien peoples; the lexica split it into "belonging to another" (as in Romans 14:4 or 1 Timothy 5:22) and "foreign/strange" (as in Matthew 17:25 or John 10:5). It was common everyday vocabulary: a third-century papyrus letter uses it bluntly of "a strange woman," and the Septuagint employs it 127 times, often for the Hebrew נָכְרִי ("foreigner," 38×) and זוּר ("stranger," 23×).
caution: In the Byzantine New Testament only 3 of 14 occurrences land on a clear measured English word ("others"), with 5 absorbed into phrasing, so the corpus data is thinner than the lexicons' fuller picture.

definition: To revel or indulge in something with great pleasure, often suggesting luxurious or wanton enjoyment.
article: ἐντρυφάω means to take delight in or revel in something, built from ἐν ("in") and τρυφάω ("to live luxuriously"). It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:13, where it carries a somewhat stronger, more wanton sense. In the Septuagint it shows up four times, often translating the Hebrew עָנַג, which carries the idea of taking pleasure or delight; the everyday papyri also attest the word, where it can simply mean "take delight in" a person.
caution: The measured-sense data here is unreliable—the single NT occurrence is tagged "daylight," which reflects context rather than this verb's actual meaning of "revel in," so lean on the lexical sources.

definition: To pull a plant up by the roots, or figuratively to remove something completely so it cannot grow back.
article: ἐκριζόω means to tear something out by the roots, built from ἐκ ("out") and ῥιζόω ("to root"). In the Byzantine New Testament it occurs 4 times, and where it gets its own English word it is always rendered "uprooted," as in Luke 17:6 (a tree obeying faith) and Jude 1:12; in the other 2 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it for several Hebrew words of removal and destruction, including נָתַשׁ in Jeremiah 1:10 and עָקַר, and Moulton-Milligan note it in an everyday inscription where someone is threatened with being "uprooted, whole family and all."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and half of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured sense rests on a thin sample.

definition: Describing something that belongs to or happens in the morning, especially the early dawn.
article: πρωϊνός means "belonging to the morning" or "early," derived from the word for early morning (πρωΐ) and standing in contrast to ἑσπερινός, "belonging to the evening." In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Revelation, describing the "morning" star (Rev 2:28; 22:16). In the Septuagint it occurs 10 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew word for morning, בֹּקֶר.
caution: The second "measured sense" ("give am Offspring") is a data artifact, not a real meaning, and with only two NT occurrences the evidence is thin.

definition: To carry something through or about, or to be different from or worth more than something else.
article: This verb literally means to carry something through or around, but in the New Testament it usually shifts to figurative senses: being different from something, or surpassing it in value. Of its 13 occurrences, the measured renderings cluster around worth and value ("more valuable than," "more than") and around making a difference ("What" in questions like Galatians 4:1), with 3 instances absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own. The everyday Koine papyri show the same range vividly: one petition uses it for goods that were physically "carried off," while another uses it to mean services that "differ" from one another.
caution: The English renderings vary widely and 3 of 13 uses dissolve into phrasing, so the exact force often depends on context rather than a fixed meaning.

definition: Describes a quality that is even-handed and free of favoritism or wavering uncertainty toward others.
article: This adjective appears just once in the New Testament, at James 3:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "accommodating" (BSB agrees 100%). The word's exact force is genuinely disputed: built from a negative prefix plus a form of διακρίνω ("to distinguish, judge"), it can mean "impartial, without favoritism" (so KJV's "without partiality") or "without uncertainty, undivided." A papyrus from A.D. 131 (P. Oxy. IV.715) uses the adverb in a property registration, with one editor taking it as "jointly, equally" and Wilcken preferring "without investigation" — a divergence that mirrors the debate over James 3:17 itself.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with low confidence, and the lexicons openly disagree on whether it means "impartial" or "without uncertainty."

definition: To be cheerful and in good spirits, or to keep up one's courage and stay encouraged.
senseLabels: be cheerful or in good spirits
article: This verb covers a small but warm range: it means to be in good spirits, whether that shows up as keeping your courage in a crisis or simply being cheerful. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament — twice in Acts 27, where Paul urges his shipmates to take courage during the storm, and once in James 5:13, where it describes someone who is cheerful. Everyday Koine letters in the papyri use it constantly: one early second-century note tells a friend "don't be anxious about the young barley," and the verb regularly pairs with "be healthy" as a standard letter-writing well-wish.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise shade between "courage" and "cheerfulness" depends heavily on context.

definition: Empty—either literally containing nothing, or figuratively pointless, fruitless, and without real substance or effect.
article: κενός basically means "empty," and the New Testament stretches that from physical emptiness to a figurative sense of efforts, words, and beliefs that come to nothing. In the Byzantine NT it appears 18 times: rendered "vain" in 47% of cases, "empty" in 20%, and "empty-handed" twice (when people are sent away with nothing, as in Luke 20:10-11). The everyday Koine sense shows up vividly in the papyri, where an inscription distinguishes camels that are κεναί (unladen) from those that are laden, and a complaint describes a thief throwing an emptied box into someone's house. Lexicographers note it differs slightly from its synonym μάταιος: μάταιος stresses the failed aim or effect of an action, while κενός points to its hollow quality.

definition: A unit of Roman soldiers, a cohort or smaller detachment, sent to keep order or make arrests.
article: In the New Testament σπεῖρα always means a body of Roman soldiers — a cohort or smaller detachment — and the seven occurrences are rendered with words like "regiment," "band," or "company" depending on context. The word originally meant a coil or anything wound up, and the military sense grew out of that older meaning; the papyri confirm the soldierly use, as in an Oxyrhynchus document referring to the "first cohort of the Damascenes." The Septuagint uses it only once, in a passage where it renders a Hebrew word, showing how rare it is outside the soldiering context.
caution: The differing English renderings (regiment, band, company) all point to the same single military sense, so the variety reflects translators' style rather than genuine differences in meaning.

definition: Gethsemane, the garden place near Jerusalem where Jesus prayed before his arrest.
article: Gethsemane is a proper name for a specific spot near Jerusalem, between the brook Kidron and the Mount of Olives, and every one of its 2 New Testament occurrences refers to that place. The name comes from a Hebrew/Aramaic phrase meaning "oil-press," which fits its location near the Mount of Olives. Interestingly, the word appears by name only in Matthew 26:36 and Mark 14:32; John 18:1 describes the same site simply as a "garden" (κῆπος) without naming it.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences, none in the critical SBLGNT text) and the spelling varies across manuscripts (Γεθσημανῆ / Γεθσημανεῖ / Γεθσημασεί).

definition: Tiberius, the Roman emperor whose reign provides the date-marker for the start of John the Baptist's ministry.
article: Τιβέριος is the name of the Roman emperor Tiberius, used just once in the New Testament, at Luke 3:1, where his fifteenth year dates the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry. The word is Latin in origin and was probably linked to the river Tiber. Notably, the papyri preserve everyday uses of his name, including a petition addressed to a priest of Tiberius Caesar Augustus—what the editors call the first mention of such a priest in the papyri.
caution: The English label "tetrarch" in the measured data reflects the surrounding context of Luke 3:1, not the word's actual meaning, which is the personal name Tiberius; the evidence base is a single occurrence.

definition: To fight with wild beasts, used figuratively for facing fierce human hostility and danger.
article: This rare verb literally means to battle wild animals, as a beast-fighter would in a gladiatorial show, but Paul uses it figuratively in 1 Corinthians 15:32 for the deadly opposition he endured. It appears only once in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it "fought." Strikingly, Ignatius later used the very same word when describing his journey "from Syria to Rome" as a kind of fighting with beasts, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it was real common-language vocabulary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and scholars still debate whether Paul meant literal beasts or figurative human enemies.

definition: An adverb meaning "still" or "yet," marking that something continues, remains, or is added—whether in time or in degree.
article: ἔτι is a small but busy adverb that marks continuation: something is "still" going on, there's "more" to add, or "any longer" with a negative. Its range splits between time ("still, yet, while still") and degree ("even more, further"), and in the Byzantine NT the most common rendering is plain "still" at 22 of 92 occurrences (33%). It's so woven into clauses that 25 times it gets absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own—and a papyrus letter from 168 B.C. captures the everyday feel exactly: "while you were still at home, I went short altogether." In the Septuagint it appears a massive 452 times, overwhelmingly translating Hebrew עוֹד ("still, yet, again") 317 times.

definition: To place or arrange under someone's authority, or to willingly put oneself under another's control and obey.
article: ὑποτάσσω started as a military term meaning to rank soldiers under a commander, and that core idea of ordered placement underneath runs through all its uses. In the New Testament it splits between an active force (to subject or put something under, 53% rendered "submit" plus another 22% as "subject" or "subjected") and a middle/passive sense where a person voluntarily submits or obeys, often with the dative of the person obeyed. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the parallel in the Stoic Epictetus, who speaks of being "subordinated to God" much as James 4:7 commands, and observes that submission to God specifically appears only in James 4:7 and Hebrews 12:9.
caution: About 8 of 40 occurrences carry no distinct English word of their own, since the meaning gets folded into surrounding phrasing.

definition: A person with a serious, scaly skin disease, traditionally called a leper.
article: λεπρός describes someone suffering from a scaly, diseased skin condition, and in the New Testament it almost always works as a noun — "a leper" — appearing 9 times and rendered "lepers" in 7 of them (78%). The Septuagint uses it 13 times, every single one translating the Hebrew word צָרַע (tsara), the term for ritual skin affliction. Interestingly, classical Greek used the word more literally to mean "scaly" or "rough," but the biblical writers apply it specifically to people with the disease, including "Simon the leper" who had presumably been healed.

definition: The practice of dice-playing, used figuratively for trickery or deceptive scheming meant to mislead people.
article: Literally κυβεία means dice-playing or gaming, but in its single New Testament appearance (Ephesians 4:14) it carries the figurative sense of trickery or sleight, the kind of manipulation that tosses people around. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as part of the imagery of being "tossed" by deceit. Interestingly, the everyday papyri attest the related verb in its literal gaming sense—a magic text from third-century A.D. London prays for help to win at dice—while writers like Epictetus use the word group for the derived meaning of cheating.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its figurative range rests on a single passage plus outside sources.

definition: To become furious or enraged; in the New Testament it appears only in the passive, meaning to be filled with anger.
article: θυμόω describes being roused to intense anger, and in the New Testament it shows up only once, in Matthew 2:16, where Herod is "filled" with rage. The Septuagint uses it far more often—59 times across 20 books—most frequently translating the Hebrew חָרָה ("to burn with anger," 31×). Notably, the lexicons point out that the active form does not occur in Attic Greek; the word is normally used in the passive or middle, meaning "to be very angry" rather than "to anger someone else."
caution: This word appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text), so its New Testament range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To force or pressure someone into doing something, whether by physical compulsion, authority, or strong persuasion.
article: This verb covers a spectrum of pressure, from outright force to firm persuasion that won't take no for an answer. In the Byzantine NT it appears 9 times across 6 books; the Berean Standard Bible most often renders it "made" (3×) or "compel" (2×). A nice detail from the everyday papyri is its weakened sense: one document asks someone to "have the manure banked up," which lexicographers connect to Luke 14:23's "compel them to come in" — the constraint of insistent hospitality rather than violence.
caution: With only 9 occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is moderate, and the line between "force" and gentler "urging" depends heavily on context.

definition: A gift or sacrifice presented to God, or more generally the act of bringing something forward as an offering.
article: In the New Testament προσφορά consistently means a sacrificial offering presented to God, rendered "offering" in 5 of its 9 occurrences (63%). The underlying idea is "a bringing to" or "presentation," and the classical lexica note this older, broader sense of simply offering something. The everyday papyri show the word stretching well beyond worship: it could mean a dowry or wedding gift, as when a mother gives a house to her daughter at her marriage, and it even appears in a medical text for the worsening of symptoms.
caution: With only 9 New Testament uses and a handful of Septuagint instances, the religious sense is well attested, but the wider papyri range shows the word was not exclusively about sacrifice.

definition: To supply or provide something abundantly, furnishing what is needed.
article: χορηγέω means to furnish or supply something generously, used in the New Testament for God supplying seed to the sower (2 Corinthians 9:10) and for the strength God provides for service (1 Peter 4:11). Though it appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, the lexicons agree on the meaning and trace a vivid backstory: the word originally meant to lead or fund a chorus (from χορός, a dance/chorus, and ἄγω, to lead) before broadening in later Greek to mean lavish provision of any kind. Everyday papyri confirm this practical sense, such as a marriage contract from the time of Augustus where a man agrees to supply his wife with all that she needs.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, this is a thinly attested word, though the surviving evidence and the lexicons agree closely on its meaning.

definition: A gracious, gentle fairness in dealing with others—treating people with kindness, moderation, and reasonableness rather than harsh severity.
article: ἐπιείκεια describes a kind, reasonable, and gentle way of treating people—what Matthew Arnold famously called "sweet reasonableness." It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 24:4 and 2 Corinthians 10:1, where it stands alongside πραΰτης, "meekness"), and the lexicons consistently point to fairness, mildness, and clemency. A vivid everyday example survives in the Abinnaeus papyri (c. A.D. 346), where an official urges a commander to mount a guard "with all ἐπιείκεια"—showing the word's practical, courteous flavor in ordinary Koine.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and one rendered oddly as "when," the measured data is thin and the second sense label should be read cautiously.

definition: Making a judgment about someone before knowing the facts; deciding for or against a person out of partiality.
article: πρόκριμα means prejudging someone, deciding in their favor or against them before the facts are clear. It appears only once in the Greek Bible, in 1 Timothy 5:21, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "bias" (100% of occurrences), and the BSB agrees. The same phrase used there, χωρὶς προκρίματος ("without prejudgment"), turns up three times in an everyday legal papyrus from A.D. 172, showing this was ordinary Koine used in disputes to mean acting without bias.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Greek Bible, so its range rests on a single verse plus outside papyri evidence.

definition: A person who looks down on or scoffs at something, treating it with contempt.
article: This word names someone who holds another person or thing in contempt — a scoffer or despiser. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:41, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "scoffers" (matched by the Berean Standard Bible). It comes from the verb καταφρονέω ("to look down on"), and in the Septuagint it translates Hebrew words for treachery and faithlessness; the term also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary working vocabulary.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one measured occurrence, so its full range in Scripture cannot be confirmed from usage alone.

definition: To twist, weave, or braid materials together into a single shape, as when forming a crown out of thorns.
article: πλέκω means to plait, weave, or twist things together into one form. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, and every occurrence describes the soldiers twisting together a crown of thorns for Jesus (Matthew 27:29; Mark 15:27; John 19:2). The everyday Koine flavor is clear in the papyri, where related forms describe "plaited fish-baskets" and even rope, while one source cites ivy "intertwined with acanthus" — showing the word's basic sense of binding strands into a single object.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, all in the same crown-of-thorns scene, the measured range of this word is narrow.

definition: The early part of the day; morning, especially the hours soon after dawn.
article: πρωΐα refers simply to the morning, the early hours of the day soon after dawn. Although the renderings split it into three samples ("morning as was," "morning conspired," "Early morning"), these are really one and the same sense — the differences come from surrounding words, not from πρωΐα itself. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain time-of-day meaning: one document from 28 B.C. dates an event to "the morning," and another spans the working day "from morning until evening."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences (and just 2 in the critical text), all reflecting the same basic sense, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Having full command or mastery over something, getting it under control.
article: This word means to get something firmly under your control or to master it. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:16, where sailors struggle to "secure" (gain control of) the ship's lifeboat during a storm. A telling parallel comes from an everyday papyrus (around A.D. 150) that uses the phrase "in order that you may easily master the business," showing the word's ordinary practical sense; it also turns up in the Greek version of Susanna 39.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured sense is mislabeled "island" rather than the actual meaning of mastering or controlling something.

definition: The skin or hide of an animal, especially one used as clothing or material.
senseLabels: the skin or hide of an animal
article: δέρμα means the skin or hide of a beast, the kind of material used for clothing or sold as a farm commodity. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:37, where faithful people wandered about "in sheepskins and goatskins." The everyday Koine papyri back this up nicely: farm accounts list "sheepskins" as a line item, and one record describes thieves who "carried off four goatskins." In the Greek Old Testament it occurs 77 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew word for skin or hide (73 of 77 times).
caution: The word is a once-only term in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse, though the Septuagint and papyri confirm the meaning.

definition: A ruler over the world, used in the New Testament of the spiritual powers governing this present age of darkness.
article: κοσμοκράτωρ combines the words for "world" (κόσμος) and "to rule" (κρατέω), literally a "world-ruler." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 6:12, where it names the dark spiritual powers Christians struggle against; the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase with "against" 100% of the time, with the BSB agreeing. Tellingly, the same title was applied to ordinary earthly rulers too — Moulton-Milligan note an Egyptian inscription where the Emperor Caracalla is given the title.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To strongly urge or persuade someone by insistent pleading until they give in.
article: παραβιάζομαι describes pressing someone hard with entreaties until they yield, and in both of its New Testament appearances it has this sense of insistent persuasion — as when the disciples 'urged' Jesus to stay with them in Luke 24:29. The Septuagint uses it 7 times, most often translating the Hebrew פָּצַר (3×), a verb for nagging or pressing someone. Interestingly, the classical lexica preserve an older, literal meaning — to force something against nature or law, as in Polybius — which the biblical usage softens into compelling by request rather than by violence.
caution: Evidence is thin, with only 2 New Testament occurrences (one absorbed into phrasing), so confidence is low.

definition: A lump or mass made by mixing and kneading, most often a batch of bread dough.
article: φύραμα is a kneaded lump, the kind of swollen mass you get when liquid is worked into a solid — in the New Testament always a batch of bread dough, appearing 5 times across 3 books. The two measured senses are really one image ("batch" and "batch dough"), and Abbott-Smith notes it can also stretch to a lump of clay (Rom. 9:21). The everyday flavor of the word shows up nicely in the papyri: a first-century beer-seller's account lists a quantity of φύραμα priced in drachmas, confirming this was ordinary commercial vocabulary, not a specialized term.
caution: The two measured senses are essentially the same dough image, and the broader "lump of clay" meaning rests only on the lexica rather than the counted renderings.

definition: Athens, the famous city in Greece and intellectual center of the ancient world.
article: Ἀθῆναι is simply the place-name Athens, used 4 times in the New Testament and always rendered "Athens." Notably the Greek form is plural (literally something like "the Athenses"), because the city was made up of several distinct parts joined together. The name derives from the goddess of wisdom said to have founded the city, and the Bible associates it with Paul's visit recorded in Acts 17.

definition: To go forward or move ahead, often going on before others or arriving somewhere ahead of them.
article: This compound of πρό ("before") and ἔρχομαι ("come/go") basically means to move forward or go on ahead, whether in place or in time. The five Byzantine occurrences cluster around three closely related ideas: going ahead to prepare something, leading the way before people, and arriving somewhere first (as the crowds did in Mark 6:33). The everyday Koine papyri show a softer sense too — "to come forward," as when one writer says he was "forced to come forward" to make a request because someone kept pressing him.
caution: With only five Byzantine occurrences, the three measured senses are really shades of one core idea of "going ahead" rather than sharply distinct meanings.

definition: A bridal chamber or wedding hall; in a set phrase, the friends or attendants of the bridegroom.
article: νυμφών literally means the bridal chamber, but in all three New Testament occurrences it appears in the phrase "sons of the bridechamber" (οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος), which refers to the bridegroom's friends or guests who attend the wedding. The word is rare in everyday Greek, but a London papyrus from the 2nd–3rd century A.D. uses it in a letter about preparations for a wedding feast, matching its plain sense. In the Greek Old Testament it shows up only in Tobit, and it corresponds to the Hebrew word for a wedding canopy.

definition: An inseparable prefix meaning hard, difficult, bad, or wrong, marking something done with trouble or opposition.
article: This is not a standalone word but an inseparable prefix attached to the front of other words, much like the English "un-" or "mis-" in "unrest" or "mischance." It is the opposite of the Greek prefix εὖ ("good, well"), and it adds the idea of difficulty, opposition, or harm to whatever it joins. It never appears on its own in the Byzantine New Testament, which is expected since by nature it only lives in composition.
caution: Because δυσ- occurs only as a prefix and never independently in the New Testament, its meaning is described by lexicons rather than measured from standalone usage.

definition: The second-person pronoun "you," referring to the person being addressed.
article: σύ is simply the Greek word for "you" (singular), one of the most common words in the New Testament with 2,961 occurrences across all 27 books. Its many "measured senses" aren't really different meanings but just reflect how it gets bundled with other pronouns in English translation—rendered straightforwardly as "you" 69% of the time and "your" 18%. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew אַתְּ ("you," 591 times), and lexicographers note its nominative form often carries emphasis or contrast, as in Jesus' loaded reply σὺ εἶπας, "you say it."

definition: To bend the body forward or lower the head, stooping down toward the ground.
article: κύπτω describes the physical act of bending forward or stooping, whether to write on the ground or to lower oneself before someone. It appears just 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament: John the Baptist says he is unworthy to stoop down and untie Jesus' sandal (Mark 1:7), and Jesus twice bends down to write on the ground (John 8:6, 8). In the Septuagint it shows up 16 times and most often translates the Hebrew קָדַד (11×), a verb for bowing the head, which fits its core meaning of a deliberate downward bend.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (just 1 in the critical text) — though the LXX usage and lexicons agree closely.

definition: To look upon someone or something with attention, whether to help and bless or to take notice for judgment.
article: This verb (a second-aorist form, with no present tense in use) basically means to fix your gaze on someone or something. In its 2 New Testament uses the range splits evenly: in Luke 1:25 God 'looks upon' Elizabeth to show favor and remove her disgrace, while in Acts 4:29 the believers ask the Lord to 'consider' the threats against them. The everyday papyri confirm this plain sense of observing closely — one writer (P Tebt II.286) speaks of something he saw 'of my own personal observation.'
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the MSB and BSB disagreeing on how to render Acts 4:29, the precise force in each context is uncertain.

definition: The state of being exposed as worthless or discredited, leading to loss of reputation or contempt.
article: This rare word describes the danger of something being shown up as worthless and so falling into disrepute. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 19:27), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "discredited." The word is an easy derivative from ἀπελέγχω ("to refute, repudiate"), built on the same pattern as the Septuagint's ἐλεγμός from ἐλέγχω, and Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A down payment or deposit given in advance that guarantees the full amount will follow later.
article: ἀῤῥαβών is a commercial term for a first installment handed over as security that the rest of a payment will come — what older Bibles called an "earnest." The Majority Standard Bible renders all 3 New Testament occurrences as "pledge," and the BSB agrees fully. The word is Semitic in origin, mirroring the Hebrew עֲרָבוֹן, and shows up in everyday business papyri — one document records a woman receiving 1,000 drachmae as a deposit for a cow; remarkably, in Modern Greek the word came to mean an engagement ring.
caution: Confidence is rated low because the word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all rendered the same single way.

definition: A public message or announcement that is proclaimed aloud, especially the content of what is preached.
article: κήρυγμα is what a herald cries out—the message itself, as distinct from the act of announcing it. The word appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where translators most often render it "preaching," though they also use "message" and "proclamation." One striking detail comes from the papyri and inscriptions: Moulton-Milligan cite an Egyptian tomb inscription where a man calls himself "a most great κήρυγμα" (a great proclamation) of his brother, showing the word's everyday use for public announcements far beyond religious preaching.
caution: With only 8 New Testament uses and translators splitting between "preaching," "message," and "proclamation," the precise emphasis in any given verse can vary.

definition: The feminine form of the number "one," used for grammatically feminine nouns.
article: μία is simply the feminine version of the Greek word for "one" (εἷς), used when the noun being counted is grammatically feminine. Like its root, it covers a wide range: one as opposed to many, a single thing to the exclusion of others, and metaphorical uses of unity or oneness. The most useful thing to know is that this is not a separate word at all — to understand its full range, look up εἷς, which it follows in every meaning.
caution: This form has no occurrences recorded in the Byzantine corpus digest, so all sense information comes from the parent word εἷς rather than direct measurement.

definition: A tiny crumb or morsel of food, especially a bit that falls from the table.
article: Psichíon is a diminutive meaning a little crumb or morsel of food, the small bits that fall from a table. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all carrying the same basic sense of "crumbs" — the variations the translators give ("crumbs," "even crumbs") just reflect English phrasing of one idea. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that this word isn't found in classical Greek authors but does turn up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and it even survives in Modern Greek as ψίχα.
caution: With only 3 occurrences (none in the critical text) and no classical attestation, the evidence is thin, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: To harden or make insensitive, used figuratively of hearts and minds that become stubborn or unresponsive.
article: πωρόω literally means to petrify or form a callus, but in the New Testament it's always used figuratively for hearts or minds that have grown hard and unresponsive. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "hardened" in 2 of its 5 occurrences, while the other 3 are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. The word comes from πῶρος, a kind of stone, and Marcus Aurelius even called marble nothing but "nodules of earth" (πῶροι γῆς) — a vivid reminder of the literal stoniness behind the metaphor.

definition: To create or bring something into existence, used in the New Testament of God making the world and people.
article: In the New Testament κτίζω consistently means to create, and it is used almost exclusively of God's creative work — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "created" in 55% of its 14 occurrences and "created things" in another 18%. The Septuagint uses it 30 times, most often (11×) to translate the Hebrew בָּרָא, the very word for God's creating in Genesis. Interestingly, classical Greek used κτίζω more broadly for founding a city or colony, and the papyri preserve this sense; one inscription even speaks of love as the "establisher" of friendship, a usage that edges toward the biblical idea of creating or forming.

definition: The act of gathering or being brought together into one assembly or group.
article: ἐπισυναγωγή refers to the act of bringing or coming together into one assembly. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "together" — once for believers meeting (Hebrews 10:25) and once for being gathered to Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:1). The word was once thought unknown outside the Bible, but Deissmann found it on a pre-100 BC inscription from the island of Syme, where it meant the "collection" of a sum of money to cover expenses.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and very thin attestation, confidence in the full range of this word is low.

definition: A dulling of mind or senses, a stupor or deep insensibility that leaves a person unresponsive.
article: κατάνυξις describes a kind of mental numbness or stupor — a deadened, unresponsive state, almost like the body part that has "fallen asleep." It appears only once in the New Testament (Romans 11:8, quoting the Septuagint), where it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word, and twice more in the Greek Old Testament, rendering Hebrew words for deep sleep and reeling. Interestingly, one later Koine source cited by Moulton-Milligan uses it with the opposite-seeming sense of "incitement" or "stimulus," showing how its underlying "pricking" root could pull in unexpected directions.
caution: Evidence is thin and the sources disagree: the literal root means "a pricking," yet the measured biblical sense is "stupor," possibly through confusion with a similar-sounding word for drowsiness.

definition: An adverb meaning in the same way or likewise, pointing back to something just described and applying it to another case.
article: ὡσαύτως is a connecting adverb that says "the same goes here too" — it links one situation to another it resembles. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "same way" 7 times (41%), "likewise" 5 times (29%), and "same" twice (12%), with the BSB independently agreeing 100% of the time on each; all the lexica cluster tightly around "in like manner, likewise." It shows up in ordinary Koine paperwork too: a third-century BC papyrus uses it for shipping instructions — "likewise, too, 100 ropes, but if you have plenty, 200" — showing it was plain everyday vocabulary, not a literary flourish.

definition: To think out or rehearse something in advance, especially preparing what you will say beforehand.
article: Προμελετάω means to work something out ahead of time, particularly rehearsing words before you need them. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 21:14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with 'mind' in the sense of preparing one's defense in advance. The word combines πρό ('before') with μελετάω ('to practice' or 'meditate'), and Abbott-Smith notes the same 'practice beforehand' usage in the classical historian Xenophon.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: To announce something widely and openly, spreading news or making a message known to others.
article: This verb means to announce or publish something far and wide, building on the idea of a messenger (ἄγγελος) carrying news "through" (διά) to many people. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and in two of those occurrences the Majority Standard Bible absorbs it into surrounding phrasing rather than rendering it with its own English word, so the one clear example is the command to "proclaim" the kingdom of God in Luke 9:60. In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times across 4 books, translating several different Hebrew words including סָפַר (to recount or tell).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and just one given its own English word, the measured evidence for this word is thin.

definition: To pile up or accumulate more and more of something, used figuratively of gathering a large number.
article: This verb means to pile something up in growing quantity, combining the idea of 'heaping' with the prefix meaning 'upon' or 'in addition.' It appears just once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 4:3), where it describes people gathering teachers for themselves; the corpus shows it absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. Everyday Koine papyri attest the same sense, and Epictetus uses it of someone who 'has gone on adding to his heap ever since' — a vivid picture of relentless accumulation.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on thin evidence.

definition: Kept from stumbling or falling; secure and sure-footed, used figuratively of being preserved from spiritual fall.
article: ἄπταιστος literally means "without stumbling" or "sure-footed," built from a negative prefix on the verb πταίω ("to stumble"). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:24, where it describes God's power to keep believers from falling, and once in the Septuagint at 3 Maccabees 6:39. Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in Marcus Aurelius, who uses it for "the security and happy course of all things" — showing the word carried a broader everyday sense of stability and safe-keeping in ordinary Koine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and very rarely elsewhere, so its precise figurative range rests on thin evidence.

definition: A span of four months, used as a unit of time.
article: This word means "four months" — literally a compound of "four" and "month," used as a noun for that length of time. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (John 4:35, "are there not four months until the harvest?") and shows up in the Septuagint twice in Judges. The everyday Koine papyri make its ordinary nature clear: one document from the second century AD uses "μετὰ τετράμηνον" to mean simply "after four months," exactly as a modern person would mark off a stretch of the calendar.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (and none in the critical SBLGNT text), the sense rests on limited biblical evidence, though the meaning is consistent across the Septuagint, papyri, and lexica.

definition: To dip or immerse someone or something, and especially to baptize as a religious washing rite.
article: βαπτίζω basically means to dip or immerse, and in the New Testament it appears overwhelmingly in its religious sense, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "baptized" in 70 of 80 occurrences (97%). Beyond ceremonial use, the word carried a plain physical meaning of submerging or sinking — a fourth-century magic papyrus uses it of a sunken boat, and classical writers apply it to soldiers wading breast-deep or ships going under. The Septuagint uses it just twice, once translating Hebrew טָבַל ("to dip," as when Naaman dipped in the Jordan).

definition: The dative form of the Greek pronoun "I," meaning "to me," "for me," or "me."
article: This is simply the enclitic dative form of the first-person pronoun ἐγώ ("I"), meaning "to me" or "for me." It doesn't appear in the Byzantine New Testament as a separate listing, but it shows up 823 times across 35 books of the Septuagint, where it frequently turns up in speech contexts — its top Hebrew counterparts are verbs like אָמַר ("to say," 44×) and נָגַד ("to tell," 42×), reflecting phrases like "tell me" or "say to me." The unemphatic enclitic forms like this one attach quietly to verbs, nouns, and prepositions, while the fuller form ἐμοί carries more weight when emphasis is needed.
caution: This is a grammatical pronoun form with no distinct measured senses, so it carries meaning only in combination with the words around it.

definition: To control or hold something back as if guiding it with a bridle, used figuratively of restraining the tongue or body.
article: χαλιναγωγέω literally means to lead with a bridle, like steering a horse, and the New Testament uses it figuratively for keeping yourself under control. It appears just twice, both in James, once of bridling the tongue (1:26) and once of restraining the whole body (3:2). Moulton-Milligan note that no examples of the word have been found earlier than James, though it does show up in everyday Koine papyri and in Lucian, who uses it of holding back the cravings of pleasures.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice, both in one book, and was absorbed into surrounding phrasing both times rather than translated by a single English word.

definition: A woman from Samaria, the feminine form of the word for a Samaritan.
article: This word simply names a female inhabitant of Samaria, the feminine counterpart to the masculine term for a Samaritan. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in John chapter 4, in the account of the woman Jesus meets at the well, and in both cases it is woven into the phrasing rather than translated by a single English word. Interestingly, the lexicon Abbott-Smith notes that in the historian Josephus the same word can also mean the region of Samaria itself, not just a woman from it.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice, both in one passage, and does not appear at all in the SBL critical text.

definition: A two-word phrase meaning "so that...not" or "lest," used to introduce a clause stating something to be avoided or prevented.
article: This is a compound expression formed from ἵνα ("so that, in order that") and μή ("not"), together meaning "so that...not" or "lest." It marks a negative purpose or result — the thing a person acts to prevent. The digest records no occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament and lists no measured senses, so the meaning here rests on its parts and Strong's gloss rather than on counted usage.
caution: The digest shows zero occurrences and no measured senses, so this entry relies entirely on the phrase's components and a brief gloss rather than corpus evidence.

definition: Zion, a hill of Jerusalem, used to stand for the city itself, its people, or the heavenly dwelling of God.
article: Σιών is a place name borrowed from Hebrew צִיּוֹן, originally a hill in Jerusalem but stretched to mean the city, its inhabitants ("daughter of Zion"), the whole people of Israel, or even heaven itself. The New Testament uses it 7 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "Zion" in 6 of those and "Instead you Zion" once in Hebrews 12:22, where it points to a heavenly Jerusalem rather than the earthly one. The word is overwhelmingly a Septuagint term, appearing 166 times and almost always translating צִיּוֹן (113×); interestingly, it also turns up in everyday papyri as a personal name.
caution: The two "senses" the data lists are really one place name; the second simply reflects a wording choice in a single verse, not a distinct meaning.

definition: Favor or kindness freely shown to someone, especially God's generous goodwill toward people, often given without being earned.
article: χάρις centers on favor and kindness—either the goodwill someone shows or, especially in the New Testament, God's free and generous grace toward people. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "grace" in 123 of 156 occurrences, with the remaining 33 absorbed into phrasing that has no single English word. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew חֵן (58×), the word for "favor." Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one inscription speaks of "works of one's own grace," and the classical lexica also note a sense of physical gracefulness or charm of speech, which the measured biblical data folds into the single "grace" sense.
caution: The classical lexica list a wider range (gracefulness, gratitude, a specific favor) than the measured biblical data, which collapses almost everything into "grace"; the 33 absorbed cases mean the word's full flexibility isn't visible in the rendering counts.

definition: To sail along close to a coastline, keeping the shore nearby as you go.
article: παραλέγομαι is a nautical term meaning to sail past or coast along, hugging the shoreline as a ship makes its way. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 27 (verses 8 and 13), and in both cases the Berean Standard Bible renders it "along [the] coast." Interestingly, the same word shows up in everyday Koine papyri with a quite different sense: in one first-century document (BGU II.665) it seems to mean casual, incidental speaking, reflecting its roots in παρά ("alongside") and λέγω.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the New Testament, and the papyri attest a separate, unrelated sense of casual speech, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: A hole or pit dug in the ground, such as a ditch or cistern that an animal or person might fall into.
article: βόθυνος refers simply to a hole in the ground — a pit, ditch, or cistern. All three New Testament uses share this single meaning; the differing labels just reflect the surrounding situations, like lifting an animal out of a pit or two blind men tumbling into one together. The everyday, practical sense is confirmed by Koine papyri: one document from 14 B.C. mentions a plant growing "on the pit," and the word appears alongside digging a trench, showing it was ordinary vocabulary for excavated ground. In the Septuagint it appears 12 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew word פַּחַת ("pit").
caution: Confidence is rated low because the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament, though its meaning is consistent and well-supported.

definition: Philip, a personal name borne by several distinct men in the New Testament.
article: Philip is a Greek personal name, derived from words meaning "fond of horses," that the New Testament applies to several different men: the apostle, the tetrarch, the husband of Herodias, and the deacon-evangelist. It is rendered "Philip" 28 times (78%) and "Philip's" 3 times in the Byzantine text. The two cases counted as "people" (Matthew 16:13, Mark 8:27) actually refer to Caesarea Philippi, the district named after Philip the tetrarch. Outside the Bible it was an extremely common name, and an inscription cited by Moulton-Milligan shows a church at Hierapolis dedicated to St. Philip the Apostle.

definition: To lead someone away from the truth into error, or in the passive, to be led astray and wander off.
article: ἀποπλανάω means to draw someone away from truth into error; it appears just twice in the New Testament, once for each shade of meaning. In active form it describes deceiving people (Mark 13:22, where false prophets try to mislead), while in passive form it describes those who have wandered away themselves (1 Timothy 6:10, of people led astray by love of money). In the Septuagint it shows up three times, where it translates the Hebrew נָדַח, a word for being driven or pushed off course.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences—one per sense—the evidence is thin, and the BSB renders the 1 Timothy passage ('wandered') differently from the Majority Standard reading.

definition: The plural form meaning "they are," the basic word for existing, being, or being present.
article: εἰσί is simply the third-person plural present form of the verb "to be" (εἰμί), meaning "they are." Like the English verb "to be," it covers a wide range: stating that people or things exist, that events happen, or that someone is present in a place. Abbott-Smith notes the parent verb can even function impersonally to mean "there is" or "there was," much like the French "il y a."
caution: This exact form does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament corpus measured here, so no usage senses could be counted; the description rests on the lexicon entry for the parent verb.

definition: To make something firm and certain—to confirm, establish, or guarantee that it is reliable and will hold.
article: βεβαιόω means to make something solid and secure, whether a spoken message, a promise, or a person's standing. In the New Testament it splits evenly between active 'confirming' (29%) and passive 'confirmed' (29%), used of God confirming his promises and of teaching being confirmed among believers. The most striking evidence comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show it was an everyday legal term for guaranteeing a sale—a seller would promise to 'guarantee with every guarantee' that the buyer's title was valid.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the data set is small, though the measured senses and the lexica agree well.

definition: To scatter seed on the ground for planting, and by extension to spread something that produces a later result.
article: σπείρω is the everyday word for sowing seed, and that literal farming sense dominates: across 53 New Testament occurrences it is rendered with "sow" or "seed" in nearly every form, most often simply "sows" (18×, 35%). The word also carries a well-established figurative use—you reap what you sow—seen in passages like Galatians and 2 Corinthians, where sowing stands for actions that bring later consequences. The papyri confirm how ordinary it was: agricultural documents pair it with reaping and harvesting (e.g. an Oxyrhynchus contract about sowing wheat), and in the Septuagint it almost always translates the Hebrew זָרַע, "to sow," used 42 of 57 times.

definition: The ordered world — the universe, the earth, or the people who live in it.
article: In the New Testament, κόσμος almost always means "world" — rendered that way in 179 of 186 occurrences (99%), covering the universe, the earth, or its human inhabitants depending on context. The word's root sense is actually "order" or "arrangement," and from that comes a much earlier meaning of "adornment" (still visible in 1 Peter 3:3, the source of our word "cosmetic"). One striking piece of evidence: an inscription from about 9 BC calls the birthday of Augustus the beginning of good news "to the world" (κόσμος), showing the word in everyday imperial usage.

definition: Cain, the firstborn son of Adam and Eve, who killed his brother Abel.
article: Κάϊν is simply the Greek spelling of the personal name Cain, the son of Adam who murdered his brother Abel. All three New Testament uses (Hebrews 11:4, 1 John 3:12, Jude 11) refer to this same figure, and every translation surveyed renders it "Cain." The name comes straight from the Hebrew קַיִן, which the Septuagint carries over 16 times in Genesis; the word is indeclinable in Greek, meaning its form never changes regardless of grammatical role.

definition: To find someone or something by actively searching for them, to track down or discover after seeking.
article: This verb combines ἀνά with εὑρίσκω ("to find") to mean finding something specifically as the result of a search, not by chance. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Luke 2:16, where the shepherds find Mary, Joseph, and the baby after looking, and in Acts 21:4, where Paul's companions seek out the disciples at Tyre. Moulton-Milligan shows the word was at home in ordinary Koine, appearing in everyday papyri and inscriptions as far back as the 4th century B.C.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the standard translations splitting between "found" and "sought," the precise emphasis is hard to pin down.

definition: James, a Greek form of the Hebrew name Jacob, borne by several men in the New Testament.
article: Ἰάκωβος is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jacob, and it's rendered "James" in 40 of its 42 New Testament occurrences (98%). Though only one English meaning is measured, the name belongs to several distinct men: the son of Zebedee, the son of Alphaeus, the Lord's brother, and the father of the apostle Judas. The everyday reality of the name shows up in the papyri, where a slightly different spelling (Ἰάκουβος) names a Jewish steersman on a cargo-boat in an Egyptian document from A.D. 77.
caution: The single English rendering hides the fact that the name refers to multiple different individuals, and identifying which James is meant in a given passage can be uncertain.

definition: To rouse or stir people up, especially to incite them into hostility or opposition against someone.
article: This verb combines "upon" (epí) with "to raise" (egeírō), giving the sense of rousing something up against a target. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Acts, where opponents stir up persecution and turn people's minds against Paul and Barnabas. Abbott-Smith notes it takes a direct object — a "persecution" in Acts 13:50 and "souls" (minds) in Acts 14:2 — and the same word shows up in an inscription describing enemies rousing themselves against a city.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both in Acts and both about inciting hostility, the measured range is very thin.

definition: A word meaning much or many, describing a large amount, number, size, or degree of something.
article: πολύς is the basic Greek word for largeness of any kind—it can describe a big number ("many"), a big quantity ("much"), a big degree ("great"), or a comparison ("more"). It is extremely common, appearing 423 times in the Byzantine New Testament, with "many" alone covering about 65% of uses, and it can even stand alone to mean "the people" or a crowd. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew רָב and its related forms, and the papyri show it was an everyday word, especially in letter greetings like "much thanks to the gods if you are well."

definition: The olive tree or its fruit; in the Gospels often part of the name for the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem.
article: The basic meaning of ἐλαία is the olive tree and its fruit, a familiar part of everyday Mediterranean life. In the New Testament, though, the standout use is in the name "the Mount of Olives" (literally "the mount of the olives"), which accounts for over half its occurrences in the Gospels; the rest refer to actual olive trees, as in Romans 11, or to the fruit, as in James 3:12. The everyday flavor shows in the papyri, where olive branches feature in a third-century spell for casting out demons, and the word appears in trade records for shipping and storing olives.

definition: The measured height or elevation of something, and by extension the heights above — heaven, or a person's high standing.
article: ὕψος names physical height or elevation, and from there reaches up to mean "the heights" — heaven itself — or figuratively a person's lofty position. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 6 times across 4 books, and in phrases like "from on high" (Luke 1:78, 24:49) it points to heaven; James 1:9 uses it for the high standing of a lowly believer. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, where the same word measures dykes and temples "raised to the ordained height," sometimes given precisely in cubits.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and 2 of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured English sense breakdown rests on very few examples.

definition: An adverb meaning "not yet," marking that something has not happened up to the present moment.
article: οὔπω is a time adverb meaning "not yet" — it tells you something hasn't happened so far, though it may still be coming. The meaning is remarkably stable: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "yet" in 18 of 23 occurrences (86%), and the standard lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, KJV) all agree on "not yet." An everyday papyrus from A.D. 22 shows the same force, where an anxious man writes that he is "not yet" even anointing himself until he hears news from his brother.

definition: To stay constantly beside something, attending to it regularly like a servant on duty.
article: This rare verb pictures someone sitting close by and tending to a task without leaving, like a servant on permanent duty. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical SBLGNT), where it describes those who attend at the altar; in that one instance it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. Notably, the critical text reads the closely related verb παρεδρεύω here instead, so editions differ on which form Paul actually wrote.
caution: Evidence is very thin: just one Byzantine occurrence, zero in the critical text (which substitutes παρεδρεύω), so the reading itself is disputed.

definition: To get something ready in advance, preparing or arranging it beforehand for a future purpose.
article: προετοιμάζω combines πρό (before) with ἑτοιμάζω (to prepare), so it means to make something ready ahead of time. It appears just twice in the New Testament, once describing vessels prepared beforehand for glory (Rom 9:23) and once for good works God prepared in advance (Eph 2:10). It surfaces only once in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew word שָׂדַד; the dictionaries add the stronger nuance of appointing or predestining beforehand, though the measured renderings simply emphasize advance preparation.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and sources differ on whether it carries a sense of predestination beyond plain advance preparation.

definition: To strip off clothing from someone, or to take off a garment yourself.
article: ἐκδύω means to strip the clothes off a person or to take off a garment, and in one New Testament case it is used figuratively of being "unclothed" of the body (2 Corinthians 5:4). It appears only 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and in 4 of those the translators folded it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. The everyday Koine papyri use it just as starkly — one document (P Fay 12) describes robbers who "stripped off the cloak I was wearing," and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew פָּשַׁט (20 of 26 times).
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and a single measured rendering, the sense range here leans heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: To build something again, rebuilding what has fallen or been torn down.
article: This verb combines "again" with "to build," giving the sense of rebuilding or restoring something that has collapsed or been razed. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both quoting the same passage (Acts 15:16) about rebuilding David's fallen tent; the Septuagint uses it much more broadly, 20 times across 12 books for Hebrew words like גָּדַר. Everyday papyri show the plain construction sense too — one third-century B.C. complaint involves a neighbor who "built" a staircase in a shared courtyard.
caution: With only two NT occurrences (both the same quotation), the measured English data is very thin, though the wider Septuagint and papyri evidence is consistent.

definition: Suffering or treated in a way that is unfair and undeserved, against what is right.
article: ἀδίκως is an adverb meaning to do or endure something unfairly or undeservedly. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 2:19, where it describes someone bearing up under suffering they did not deserve. It's far more common in the Septuagint (20 times across 6 books), where it renders several Hebrew words including חִנָּם, meaning 'without cause' or 'for nothing' — a fitting match for the idea of being wronged undeservedly.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: To breathe one's last and die, expire.
article: This rare verb means to expire or breathe one's last — simply, to die. All three New Testament occurrences are in Acts (5:5, 5:10, 12:23), where it describes sudden death, and the three measured renderings ("came... died down," "died," "died down") are really just stylistic variations of the same single sense. Moulton-Milligan notes the word is confined in the NT to Luke and appears in medical writers, and points to a vivid line in Herodas where the verb conveys a gasping, dying effect.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 NT occurrences plus 2 in the Septuagint, so confidence is low even though the meaning is consistent.

definition: A governing body of elders—either the Jewish Sanhedrin or the assembled leaders of a Christian congregation.
article: πρεσβυτέριον is a collective noun built from πρεσβύτερος ("elder"), naming a body of elders rather than a single person. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament and refers in two cases to the Jewish ruling council, the Sanhedrin (Luke 22:66; Acts 22:5), and once to the assembled Christian elders who laid hands on Timothy (1 Timothy 4:14). Abbott-Smith notes it appears in the Septuagint only in the Theodotion version of Susanna 1:50, where it likewise means a body of elders.
caution: With only 3 occurrences the evidence is thin, and the translation "spoken over at" reflects a rephrased rendering of 1 Timothy 4:14 rather than a distinct meaning of the word itself.

definition: Supporters of Herod, a group who backed the Herodian rulers in first-century Judea.
article: The word is a proper-name group label meaning the Herodians—people who supported Herod's dynasty. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, in Matthew 22:16, Mark 3:6, and Mark 12:13, always rendered "Herodians." One nice detail: Abbott-Smith notes the historian Josephus uses a parallel phrase, "those who favored Herod," matching exactly the partisan sense the lexicons assign here.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 occurrences—and the second "measured sense" ("began Herodians") is just a rendering artifact, not a genuinely distinct meaning.

definition: Zacchaeus, the wealthy chief tax collector of Jericho who climbed a tree to see Jesus.
article: Zacchaeus is a personal name, that of a chief tax collector in Jericho who appears only in Luke 19, where the word occurs all 3 times in the New Testament. The name comes from the Hebrew זַכַּי (Zaccai), which the Septuagint also spells Ζακχού, and it shows up in everyday Koine documents too — Moulton-Milligan note it restored in a Coptic ostracon. The seemingly different "senses" in the data ("Zacchaeus," "looked Zacchaeus stay," "Zacchaeus up") are just fragments of surrounding text, not distinct meanings: it is one name throughout.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only 3 times, all in one Luke passage, so the listed "senses" are artifacts of phrasing rather than real distinctions in meaning.

definition: In a pure, sincere way—acting from honest motives without hidden agendas.
article: This adverb describes doing something with genuinely pure motives, honestly and sincerely. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 1:16-17, where it describes preaching Christ from sincere intentions. The classical lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on the sense "purely" or "sincerely," and it is built directly from the adjective ἁγνός, meaning pure or holy.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lone measured rendering of "former" seems to reflect surrounding verse content rather than the word's actual meaning, which the lexicons consistently give as "sincerely."

definition: To hide or conceal something, whether by covering it physically or keeping it secret from view or knowledge.
article: κρύπτω means to hide or conceal—covering something up so it can't be seen or known. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 17 times and is almost always rendered "hidden" (10 of 17, or 67%), and it stretches from literal hiding (a city on a hill cannot be hidden) to figurative concealment (truths hidden from the wise). It's the workhorse word for hiding in the Septuagint, where it translates four different Hebrew verbs over 122 times, and an everyday papyrus shows a wife complaining that her husband "again hid the keys from me."

definition: To violently shake or throw someone into convulsions, as when a spirit seizes and racks a person's body.
article: In the New Testament σπαράσσω consistently describes a violent physical seizure—an unclean spirit throwing a person into convulsions, appearing 4 times across 2 books, always in scenes of demonic affliction. The older lexicons preserve a broader original range: Abbott-Smith and the KJV note it could also mean to tear, rend, or mangle, and Herodas uses it to mean "maul," while a vivid metaphorical example from Teles has Socrates joke that Xanthippe's nagging "racks" them with heartburn. So the measured biblical sense (convulse) is narrower than the word's full classical reach.
caution: With only 4 NT occurrences and a single damaged papyrus citation, the evidence is thin, and the gap between the NT "convulse" sense and the classical "tear/mangle" sense should be kept in mind.

definition: Caiaphas, the Jewish high priest who served during the ministry and trial of Jesus.
article: Caiaphas is the personal name of the Jewish high priest who appears at key moments in the Gospels and Acts, notably during Jesus' trial. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Caiaphas" in 8 of its 9 occurrences (89%), with the remaining case folded into a phrase like "whose name was." An interesting wrinkle is the spelling: the name appears in two Greek forms (Καιάφας and Καΐφας), and scholars like Burkitt traced how the Syriac transliteration handled it differently from the similar-sounding name Cephas (Κηφᾶς).

definition: The form of "we" meaning "to us," "for us," or "with us" — the dative plural of the pronoun "I."
article: ἡμῖν is simply a grammatical form of the first-person pronoun, the dative plural meaning "to us," "for us," or "with us." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament as catalogued here, but it shows up 328 times across 29 books of the Septuagint, where it frequently renders Hebrew question words and phrases like מָה ("what," 27×) and מִי ("who," 9×) inside expressions involving "us." The pronoun is everyday Koine, well attested in ordinary papyri, and carries no special emphasis on its own — emphasis usually falls on the nominative forms instead.

definition: To converse or talk together with someone.
article: συνομιλέω means to talk or converse mutually with another person, built from σύν ("with") and ὁμιλέω ("to speak"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 10:27, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "talked." Moulton-Milligan note that the word shows up in everyday Koine documents — including a papyrus letter using the very form συνομειλῶν μετὰ ("conversing with") — confirming it was ordinary, conversational language rather than a specialized term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there cannot be tested against multiple contexts.

definition: To look away from where you are toward something else, hence to see or perceive how things stand.
article: ἀπείδω is the aorist form (literally "I looked away to") that serves as the past tense for ἀφοράω, "to look away toward." The basic idea is turning your eyes from one thing in order to fix them on another, and so to perceive or make something out. It does not appear at all in the Byzantine New Testament, and Abbott-Smith notes it has no present tense in actual use, surviving only as a second aorist alongside εἶδον.
caution: This word has zero New Testament occurrences and only thin grammatical evidence, so its meaning here rests on its relationship to ἀφοράω rather than measured usage.

definition: To take someone or something along with yourself, or to receive what has been handed down to you.
article: παραλαμβάνω covers two main ideas: physically taking a person or thing along with you (60% of its 49 uses, like Joseph taking the child in Matthew 2:13), and receiving something passed down to you, such as a teaching or tradition (19%, as in 1 Corinthians 15:1). A small subset means taking someone aside privately. A nice detail from the everyday Koine papyri is that this verb was the standard word for receiving anything except money, where a different verb was used, and it regularly pairs with παραδίδωμι ('to hand over')—the giving-and-receiving relationship you see in the New Testament too.

definition: The cost or expense of something, the money needed to complete a project.
article: δαπάνη means the cost or expense of carrying something out — the money you must spend.
