It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 14:28, where it describes counting the cost before building a tower, and the Septuagint uses it just twice more. The word was extremely common in everyday Koine: papyri use it constantly for ordinary expenses, including one writer warning a correspondent that he will be held liable for the costs of stale drugs.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: To cause something to take root and become firmly fixed, used figuratively of being solidly established or grounded.
article: ῥιζόω comes from the noun for "root" (ῥίζα) and literally means to cause something to take root, then figuratively to fix firmly or establish. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in a spiritual sense — being "rooted" in love (Eph. 3:17) and in Christ (Col. 2:7). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the word was used in everyday Koine of founding cities and even building a bridge ("αἰώνιος ἐρρίζωται," rooted forever), which helps explain why Colossians can shift so smoothly from rooting to building imagery.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (and none in the critical SBLGNT text), the measured range is thin and rests heavily on metaphorical usage.

definition: To clean something up — either by pruning a plant of its dead parts or by clearing away the burden of guilt.
article: καθαίρω is the everyday verb for cleaning or clearing, and its two New Testament appearances pull in different directions: in John 15:2 it describes a gardener pruning a vine, while in Hebrews 10:2 it refers to clearing away guilt. The papyri show just how ordinary the word was — one document has a farmer agreeing to "measure out and winnow the produce" for the State, the same earthy sense of cleaning grain or land. In the Septuagint it appears only twice, translating Hebrew words tied to threshing and winnowing, which fits its hands-on agricultural background.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text) and 2 in the Septuagint, so the full range is hard to map confidently.

definition: To look at something carefully and think it over, so as to perceive or understand it fully.
article: κατανοέω is built from κατά and the verb for "perceive," giving it the sense of looking closely and taking full note of something. In the Byzantine New Testament its 14 uses split evenly between "consider" (33%) and "look" (33%), with the remaining occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing—reflecting how it can point either to careful thinking or attentive looking. In the Septuagint it appears 23 times and most often renders the Hebrew בִּין, "to understand or discern," which fits its core idea of perceptive observation; everyday Koine papyri likewise use it for perceiving or understanding a fact.

definition: A lily or similar showy wild flower, named in Jesus's lesson about how God clothes the plants of the field.
article: Κρίνον means a lily — a bright wild flower of the field. The two New Testament uses both come from the same teaching of Jesus (Matthew 6:28 and Luke 12:27), where translators render the surrounding phrase as 'consider how the lilies grow; they do not spin.' The Septuagint uses it 20 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew shoshan (lily, 9×), and the word also turns up in everyday Koine: an epitaph wishes that violets and lilies might sprout from the dead person's bones, while related forms describe lily-scented myrrh and oil.
caution: Both NT occurrences are part of one saying, and lexicons note the exact flower is uncertain — possibly a lily, red anemone, or sword lily.

definition: New, fresh, or recent — describing something newly made or recently come into being.
article: πρόσφατος means "new, fresh, recent." Though it appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 10:20, of the "new" way opened for us), it occurs four times in the Septuagint and is well attested in everyday Koine. The most interesting detail is its origin: the word literally meant "freshly slain," combining πρό with the root behind σφάζω (slaughter), but as Moulton-Milligan note, that violent second element died out early — a medical papyrus even uses it for pounding "fresh" hellebore.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise nuance here rests on broader Septuagint and papyri usage rather than New Testament evidence.

definition: To put clothing on someone or oneself, or to be dressed in something — used both literally and figuratively for taking on a quality or person.
article: ἐνδύω is the ordinary Koine word for getting dressed or dressing someone, and the New Testament stretches it figuratively to mean taking on something like a person, power, or quality — "clothing" yourself with the new self or with Christ. Of its 28 occurrences, the most common rendering is "clothed" (8×, 42%), with the rest spread across "put," "dressed," "put clothes," and "wear." In the Septuagint it appears 93 times and almost always translates Hebrew לָבַשׁ (74×), "to wear or put on." An everyday papyrus letter (c. A.D. 50) uses it for a man's linen tunic being torn off him, showing how concrete the word's basic meaning was.

definition: Secundus, a Christian man from Thessalonica who traveled with the apostle Paul.
article: Σεκοῦνδος is a personal name of Latin origin (meaning "second"), borne by a Thessalonian believer who accompanied Paul, mentioned just once in the New Testament at Acts 20:4. The name was common in the region: it appears in a list of Thessalonian politarchs on a triumphal arch and again in a memorial inscription from A.D. 15 found in the city's Jewish quarter, confirming it as an ordinary everyday name there. The single measured rendering, "accompanied," reflects the surrounding narrative rather than the meaning of the name itself.
caution: This is a personal name appearing only once in the New Testament, so beyond identifying the man little can be said about its usage.

definition: To agree together with others, settling on a shared plan, decision, or arrangement.
article: In its middle voice, συντίθεμαι is about people coming to a mutual understanding — they consent, agree, or settle on a course of action together. The literal idea behind it is "placing things together," and the everyday papyri show that plain sense: one document from AD 280 uses the related verb for putting wine jars away in a shed. In the New Testament's four occurrences the meaning has shifted to social agreement, whether the chief priests gladly agreeing to pay Judas (Luke 22:5) or the Jewish leaders deciding to expel anyone confessing Christ (John 9:22).
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences spread across three slightly different shades of "agree," the precise nuance in each verse leans on context rather than a firmly fixed range.

definition: Free from spots or stains, hence pure and undefiled, whether physically or morally.
article: This word describes something unblemished — literally without a spot or stain, and by extension morally pure. In its 4 New Testament appearances it ranges from the literal (a lamb "without spot" in 1 Peter 1:19) to the figurative (keeping oneself unstained in James 1:27 and 2 Peter 3:14), and the two measured renderings ("without...spot" and "spotless") amount to the same idea. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan notes it is older than once thought: an Eleusis inscription from around 300 B.C. uses it of "sound, white, unspotted" stones, showing its everyday literal sense.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and 2 absorbed into phrasing, the split between the two labels reflects translation wording rather than two genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: Separately or apart from someone or something; commonly used to mean "without" the presence, help, or involvement of a thing.
article: χωρίς marks separation, most often working as a preposition meaning "without" (rendered that way 21 of 39 times, 66%) or "apart from" (6×, 19%). It can describe being physically separate, as in the cloth lying "by itself" in John 20:7, or being functionally cut off, as in "apart from Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). Everyday Koine papyri confirm both uses; one early first-century medical recipe even tells you to work each ingredient up "separately" with water.

definition: To blow a trumpet or sound a trumpet blast, whether literally or figuratively.
article: σαλπίζω simply means to blow a trumpet and sound a blast. In the New Testament it appears 12 times, heavily concentrated in Revelation where angels sound their trumpets, plus a striking figurative use in Matthew 6:2 where Jesus warns against "sounding a trumpet" to advertise your giving. The Septuagint uses it 58 times across 17 books, mostly translating the Hebrew תָּקַע (48 times), the verb for blowing a horn; some scholars debate whether Matthew 6:2 is purely metaphorical or alludes to the literal sounding of the ram's horn (shofar) on public fast days.

definition: To hit someone repeatedly, striking or beating them with the hand or an object.
article: τύπτω means to strike or beat someone, usually with repeated blows. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 14 times and is rendered almost evenly as "struck" (7×) and "beat" (6×), covering everything from soldiers hitting Jesus on the head to a wicked servant beating his fellow servants. Strong's notes it properly suggests pummeling with a stick or repeated blows, distinguishing it from words for a single hand-blow; in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew נָכָה ("to strike," 15×). The everyday papyri confirm this plain, physical sense, recording complaints of people being struck and abused.

definition: To throw stones at someone, especially to kill them as a form of execution or attack.
article: λιθάζω means to pelt or kill someone by throwing stones, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it this way in all 8 of its occurrences, rendered "stoned" half the time. The word derives from λίθος ("stone"), and Abbott-Smith notes an older sense of simply throwing stones, distinct from the execution-style stoning that dominates biblical usage. In the Septuagint it appears twice, once translating the Hebrew סָקַל (to stone) — the same verb used for the prescribed penalty in the law.
caution: Evidence is moderate; the word appears only 8 times in the NT and just twice in the Septuagint, so its range is narrow but well attested.

definition: Describing someone who is strong or capable, or describing a thing that is possible or able to be done.
senseLabels: able to do what is promised
article: δυνατός runs along two related tracks: applied to people it means strong, mighty, or capable, and applied to things it means possible or doable. In the Byzantine NT the "possible" sense (often as the neuter δυνατόν, sometimes in the phrase "if possible") is the most common, while "able" and "powerful" cover the personal uses. A nice everyday parallel comes from the papyri: a Greek land-lease from 221 BC distinguishes the field "possible to be sown" from the part "not possible to be sown," exactly mirroring the able-to construction in 2 Timothy 1:12.
caution: In about a third of its occurrences (12 of 36) the word is absorbed into English phrasing without a distinct rendering, so individual translation choices vary; in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew gibbor, "mighty man."

definition: To sit down or be seated, and in its causal use, to make someone sit, set, or appoint them to a position.
article: καθίζω covers both sitting yourself down and causing someone else to sit—the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "sit" or "sat down" in 92% of its 48 New Testament appearances. The causal sense ("to set, appoint") is well attested too: a Greek papyrus from A.D. 298 uses it for an overseer who "set" the local inhabitants to work on dykes, matching its New Testament use in passages like Ephesians 1:20. In the Septuagint it appears 200 times, almost always translating the Hebrew verb יָשַׁב, "to sit" or "dwell."

definition: To receive something as one's own, especially as a possession or birthright handed down to you.
article: κληρονομέω means to inherit—to come into possession of something as your rightful share, whether literal property or a promised blessing. In the Byzantine New Testament it's rendered "inherit" in 14 of 18 places (88%), and the BSB agrees 100% of the time. The word lived in everyday legal language too: a second-century papyrus petition uses it for a woman inheriting her grandmother's belongings, and another cites Imperial law on those who have "inherited nothing" from the deceased. In the Septuagint it appears 154 times, most often translating the Hebrew verb יָרַשׁ ("to take possession of"), which is why it can stretch from inheriting land to inheriting the kingdom or eternal life.

definition: To bring someone safely through danger, sickness, or disaster to a place of safety; to rescue or recover.
article: διασώζω means to carry someone safely through some threat — a storm, an illness, an enemy — and deliver them to safety. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible most often captures it simply with "safely" (3 times, half the occurrences), as when Paul is brought safely through shipwreck and journey in Acts. The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor vividly: one letter rejoices that grain "made it through" safely, and another reports being "brought safely through great dangers," the very sense the word carries in Scripture. In the Septuagint it appears 57 times, frequently rendering the Hebrew מָלַט, "to escape" or "slip away to safety."
caution: Of the 8 occurrences, only 3 produce a distinct English word and 2 are absorbed into phrasing, so the measured sense rests on a fairly small base.

definition: A goat, especially a young goat or kid.
article: ἔριφος refers to a goat, often specifically a young goat or kid. It appears only twice in the New Testament, where it is rendered "goats" both times (Matthew 25:32 and Luke 15:29). In the Septuagint it shows up 28 times and most often translates the Hebrew word for a kid (גֶּ֫דִי, 17×), with the rest covering the broader word for goat (עֵז, 6×) and a few others.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the precise distinction between a full-grown goat and a young kid rests mainly on Septuagint and lexicon evidence.

definition: An adverb meaning up, upward, or above, often pointing to a higher place or to heavenly realities.
article: ἄνω is a simple adverb of direction and location meaning "up" or "above," the natural opposite of κάτω ("below"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "above" in 43% of cases, with about 3 of 10 occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing without their own English word; it can point literally upward ("up to the brim" at John 2:7) or refer to "the things above" and heavenly realities (John 8:23, Gal 4:26). The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where phrases like εἰς τοὺς ἄνω τόπους ("to the upper regions") describe ordinary places, and in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew מַ֫עַל ("above") 10 times.

definition: To move along or past a place, or to go away; figuratively, to be passing away or fading.
article: In the New Testament παράγω is used intransitively to describe someone moving along or passing by — Jesus passing by, or walking beside something. The Byzantine NT has it 10 times, and where it gets its own English word the Majority Standard Bible renders it "passing" in 3 of those cases, with the BSB agreeing entirely; in 3 of 10 occurrences it simply blends into the surrounding phrasing. Interestingly, papyri show a transitive sense "bring forward" that the NT never uses — one document (BGU IV.1139) even uses it of compelling a man to produce his daughter. It also carries a figurative edge of "passing away" or "fading" (as in 1 Cor 7:31 and 1 John 2:8), and in the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew verb meaning "to pass over."
caution: Only one measured sense surfaced clearly, but the lexica list a broader transitive range absent from the NT, so the figurative "passing away" usage rests on relatively few attestations.

definition: A common preposition placing something on, upon, over, or against a person, place, or thing.
article: ἐπί is one of the most flexible Greek prepositions, basically meaning placement "on" or "upon" but stretching to "in," "over," and "against" depending on context and grammatical case. It is hugely common — 900 times in the Byzantine New Testament — and renders "on" in 293 cases (67%); notably, in 461 of those 900 occurrences it gets absorbed into surrounding English phrasing without a word of its own. The clearest signal of its core meaning is in the Septuagint, where it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew עַל ("on, upon"), 3,830 times out of 6,083 uses.
caution: Many of the measured "senses" are really translation artifacts of English phrasing (e.g. "will," "was," "a") rather than distinct meanings, and the word's actual force depends heavily on which case follows it.

definition: To strive eagerly or make it one's ambition to do something.
article: In the New Testament's three uses (Romans 15:20, 2 Corinthians 5:9, 1 Thessalonians 4:11), this verb means to aspire to or strive eagerly toward something, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "aspire" in all 3 cases. The word literally combines "love" (φίλος) and "honor" (τιμή), originally meaning to be ambitious or eager for honor, but Moulton-Milligan note that in these passages it has largely lost that competitive edge and means little more than "am zealous, strive eagerly." Everyday Koine papyri confirm this softer sense — one third-century BC letter uses it simply to say "you were eager for me to come to you."
caution: This word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and sources note its older "ambitious" sense has faded, so its precise force can be debated.

definition: To get away by fleeing, to escape, especially from danger or punishment.
article: This verb combines "through" with "flee," giving the idea of escaping by getting away or slipping through danger. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:42, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "swim" in the context of prisoners who might escape from the shipwreck by swimming to land—though the underlying word simply means "escape." The Septuagint uses it ten times, often translating Hebrew words for a "survivor" or "fugitive" (פָּלִיט, שָׂרִיד), and the papyri show the same everyday sense, as in a contract hoping a wrongdoer "may not escape unpunished."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, note that the "swim" rendering reflects the Acts context rather than the word's core meaning of escaping by flight.

definition: Encouragement, comfort, or consolation given to strengthen and uplift someone, sometimes also an appeal or urgent request.
article: This word covers a cluster of closely related meanings centered on coming alongside someone to strengthen them—whether through encouragement, comfort, or consolation. In the Byzantine New Testament, the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'encouragement' 7 times (29%) and 'comfort' 6 times (25%), with the rest shading between these, so the two ideas blend together rather than splitting apart. The Septuagint shows the comfort side clearly, where it 4 times translates the Hebrew tanchumim ('consolations'); the everyday papyri, however, often carry the more transactional sense of an 'appeal' or 'entreaty,' as in a documented request to let soldiers travel.
caution: The classical lexica list a fourth sense—'appeal' or 'entreaty'—that barely surfaces in the measured New Testament data, so its full range is broader than the rendered senses alone suggest.

definition: Happening suddenly and without warning, catching people unprepared.
article: αἰφνίδιος describes something that arrives suddenly and unexpectedly, leaving no time to prepare. It appears only twice in the New Testament—in Luke 21:34 and 1 Thessalonians 5:3—and both occurrences carry the same core meaning of 'suddenly,' so the two measured senses are really one idea phrased slightly differently. The word was at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite it in an uneducated personal letter from a papyrus (around A.D. 100) and in inscriptions describing 'a sudden calamity' and an enemy 'falling upon them suddenly.'
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a handful of Septuagint and papyri attestations, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: To harvest crops by cutting them, and figuratively to gather the results of what one has done.
article: θερίζω means to reap or harvest a crop, the action of cutting and gathering what has grown. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "reap" in 12 of 21 occurrences (63%), and the New Testament freely uses it figuratively—you reap what you sow (Galatians 6:7), reaping life or destruction. In the Septuagint it almost always translates the Hebrew קָצַר ("reap," 19 of 24 times), and a Magdola papyrus from 217 B.C. shows a real farmer petitioning that his landlords not be allowed to reap his crops until a legal dispute was settled.

definition: To pass on an authoritative instruction—to command, order, or charge someone to do something.
article: παραγγέλλω means to hand down an authoritative instruction, ranging from a firm command to a solemn charge; the Majority Standard Bible spreads its 30 occurrences across "instructed" (5×), "command" (5×), "ordered" (3×), and "give" (2×), with 11 more absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Built from παρά plus the root of ἄγγελος ("messenger"), its core idea is transmitting a message that carries weight. Moulton-Milligan shows the most telling background: in Ptolemaic papyri the word commonly describes an official court summons—calling someone to appear before authority—which matches its consistently authoritative tone in the New Testament.
caution: The senses cluster tightly around "command/order," but with no single dominant rendering and a third of occurrences blended into phrasing, exact shades depend heavily on context.

definition: To join others in rising up against someone, acting together to assault or oppose them.
article: This compound verb literally means to stand up together, and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 16:22) it describes a crowd joining together to attack Paul and Silas. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "attack" in that one verse, and the BSB agrees completely. Interestingly, classical Greek used the word more broadly — Abbott-Smith notes that in Thucydides it could mean simply "to stand over," while the New Testament sense of rising up against someone is the hostile, joint-action meaning.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: To cut or hew something out of rock, especially carving a chamber or tomb from solid stone.
article: λατομέω means to carve or hew something out of stone, the work of a quarryman cutting rock. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both times for Joseph of Arimathea's tomb cut into the rock (Matthew 27:60; Mark 15:46), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "cut" every time. The everyday flavor of the word shows up vividly in the papyri: a 255 BC letter from quarrymen to an architect uses it to report they had already quarried out the rocks but were now idle for lack of workers to clear the sand. In the Septuagint it occurs 10 times, most often translating the Hebrew חָצַב ("to hew"), 7 of those times.
caution: The New Testament evidence is thin—only 2 occurrences, both describing the same kind of rock-cut tomb.

definition: A cord, chain, or binding rope; in the Septuagint it can also mean a braided lock of hair.
article: σειρά is a physical word for something that binds or holds — a cord or chain. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only once, in a phrase where it carries no separate English word of its own, and the standard glosses point to 'chain.' Interestingly, when the Septuagint uses it (5 times across 2 books), it three times renders a Hebrew word for braided locks of hair (in the Samson story of Judges 16), so its range stretches from chains to plaited strands; an inscription from around 180 B.C. likewise uses it of something 'hung from a cord.'
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence (absorbed into phrasing) and a handful of Septuagint uses — so the precise sense in any given passage is hard to pin down.

definition: Reu, an ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ῥαγαῦ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Reu (רְעוּ), a patriarch who appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. It occurs just once in the New Testament (Luke 3:35), always rendered simply as the personal name. The Septuagint uses it five times across two books, consistently standing in for the same Hebrew name, which is where the Greek form comes from.
caution: This is a personal name appearing only once in the New Testament, so there is no real range of meaning to weigh.

definition: To ask back or demand the return of something, especially what is owed or due.
senseLabels: to ask back what is yours
article: This verb combines "from" (ἀπό) with "ask" (αἰτέω) to mean asking something back or demanding its return. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke—once about not demanding back what someone takes from you (Luke 6:30), and once when God says a man's life will be "required" of him (Luke 12:20). Everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: tax collectors "demanding" payments, sometimes specifically payments that were in arrears, which fits its core sense of asking back what is owed.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, confidence is low, and the papyri themselves leave it unclear whether the word implies a payment already overdue or just a general demand.

definition: In the same way, likewise — marking that one thing matches or follows the pattern of another.
article: ὁμοίως is an adverb meaning "likewise" or "in the same way," built from the adjective ὅμοιος ("similar"). It points back to something already said and tags a new item as matching that pattern, so translators render it variously as "same" (7×, 29%), "same way" (5×), "Likewise" (4×), or even "others" (2×) — and in 8 of its 32 New Testament occurrences it gets absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own. A vivid everyday example comes from a 2nd-century BC papyrus where a frustrated writer swears "all things are false, and your gods likewise."

definition: In the Greek language; the adverb describing speaking or writing in Greek.
article: Ἑλληνιστί is an adverb meaning "in Greek" — describing the language something is spoken or written in. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Greek" both times (John 19:20, where the inscription on the cross was written in Greek, and Acts 21:37, where Paul is asked if he knows Greek). The same word turns up in everyday Koine papyri: legal documents from the second century B.C. note Egyptian texts "translated into Greek" (Ἑλληνιστί), showing it was the ordinary way to flag the language of a document.
caution: With only 2 occurrences the measured range is thin, though the single sense is consistent across all sources.

definition: Sharing the same human nature, feelings, and weaknesses as someone else.
article: ὁμοιοπαθής combines "like" (ὅμοιος) with the root of "suffer/experience" (πάσχω), describing someone who is made of the same stuff as another person — subject to the same feelings, passions, and frailties. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 14:15 and James 5:17), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "like" in both, a reading the Berean Standard Bible matches 100%. The word also turns up in the Septuagint (Wisdom 7:3, 4 Maccabees 12:13) and in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, where Moulton-Milligan note it carries the sense "of like nature."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin evidence, though the lexica agree closely on its meaning.

definition: To thoroughly frighten or terrify someone.
article: This verb combines the preposition ἐκ ("out") with φοβέω ("to frighten"), giving the sense of frightening someone utterly. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 10:9, where Paul says he does not want to seem to be trying to terrify the Corinthians by his letters. The Septuagint uses it 9 times, most often for the Hebrew חָרַד ("to tremble"), and Moulton-Milligan finds it in everyday papyri—one document from A.D. 185 describes people who "became invisible" out of fright.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense here rests on very thin evidence.

definition: An adverb meaning terribly or severely, describing how badly someone suffers or how fiercely others act.
article: This adverb describes intensity gone bad — either suffering terribly or behaving fiercely. In its only two New Testament appearances it covers both ranges: a servant lying "terribly" tormented in Matthew 8:6, and scribes pressing Jesus "vehemently" in Luke 11:53. The everyday Koine papyri back the first sense vividly, with one fourth-century letter where a sick woman writes that she is "terribly ill" (deinōs echō), too weak to rise from her bed.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the rendering "things" in the digest reflecting a fuller phrase rather than the adverb itself, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Beneath or under something, indicating a position lower than or below another thing.
article: ὑποκάτω is a straightforward word meaning "under" or "beneath," built from ὑπό ("under") and κάτω ("down"). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "under" in 6 of its occurrences (67%), and it functions as a preposition taking the genitive. It shows up 81 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always translates the Hebrew תָּ֫חַת ("under"), and it was common in everyday life too—papyri use it for things like a mare that died "under" (belonging to) an official, or land lying "below" a wall.

definition: A small bed or portable couch, especially a mat or litter used to carry a sick person.
article: κλινίδιον is a diminutive of κλίνη ("couch"), so it points to a small bed or pallet — the kind of light mat or litter on which someone could be carried. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke 5 (verses 19 and 24), where the Berean Standard Bible renders it once as "mat" and once as the bed a paralyzed man picks up. Interestingly, this word and the related κλινάριον are peculiar to Luke; one scholar even cited it as evidence for the medical character of Luke's vocabulary, though that thesis has been questioned.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in a single passage, the evidence is thin and the precise nuance (plain mat versus sick-bed litter) cannot be firmly distinguished.

definition: A warm goodness of heart toward others, shown as kindness, gentleness, and generous goodwill.
article: χρηστότης means kindness or goodness of heart, and in the New Testament that is overwhelmingly how it works: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "kindness" in 9 of its 10 occurrences (the tenth is absorbed into surrounding phrasing). The word appears only in Paul's letters, in passages like Romans 2:4, 2 Corinthians 6:6, and Galatians 5:22. The older lexicons note a slightly broader range — Abbott-Smith lists "goodness, excellence, uprightness" alongside "kindness of heart" — and the everyday papyri show a charming extra use: like our "your Grace," people addressed superiors as "your χρηστότης."
caution: Lexicons list a wider range (goodness, uprightness) than the measured NT data, where "kindness" accounts for all renderings.

definition: A bored hole or opening, used in the New Testament for the eye of a sewing needle.
article: τρύπημα refers to a hole made by boring, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Matthew 19:24, for the eye of a needle through which Jesus says a camel cannot pass. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and even in medical writers, where it describes physical openings—one papyrus fragment uses it for holes in the sacrum bone. It belongs to a small family of near-synonyms (τρῆμα, τρυμαλιά) that all mean an opening, and many manuscripts actually read τρῆμα instead at Matthew 19:24.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the manuscripts disagree on whether the original reading is τρύπημα or the synonym τρῆμα.

definition: An adverb meaning "once," either a single occurrence in time or something done once and for all, never to be repeated.
article: ἅπαξ is an adverb meaning "once." In the Byzantine New Testament it most often marks a single occurrence (8 of 14 times, 67%), but in places like Hebrews 10:2 and 1 Peter 3:18 it carries the stronger sense of "once for all"—something done a single time that needs no repeating. It can also pair with another word to mean "once and again," that is, repeatedly, as Abbott-Smith notes for Philippians 4:16 and 1 Thessalonians 2:18. The everyday papyri show the same range: one document pleads, "pardon him this once," while another stresses "not once alone," and in the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew word for "time" or "occurrence" (פַּעַם, 32 times).

definition: A person who decides legal cases or settles disputes, including officially appointed magistrates and rulers.
article: κριτής means a judge — someone who hears cases and renders a verdict — and it is rendered "judge" in 16 of its 17 Byzantine New Testament occurrences (94%). The range stretches from a courtroom official to God or Christ as the final judge, and in the older Israelite sense it can mean a ruler who led the people (as in Acts 13:20). The everyday Koine papyri sharpen the picture: documents from A.D. 135 use κριτής for someone formally appointed to the office of judge by the Prefect, confirming its concrete official sense.

definition: A preposition meaning "for the sake of," "because of," or "on account of," showing the reason or purpose behind something.
senseLabels: because of, for the sake of
article: χάριν began as the accusative form of the noun χάρις ("grace, favor") but functions as a preposition meaning "because of" or "for the sake of." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 7 books, and the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it simply "for" (4 of 9 times). A nice detail from the papyri: in everyday documents like a 2 BC Oxyrhynchus papyrus it shows up in phrases like "for the rents," and Moulton-Milligan notes that in classical Greek and the New Testament it normally follows its noun, while in the Septuagint and the papyri it usually comes first.
caution: With only 9 occurrences and one dominant rendering, the measured data captures just part of the range that lexicons attach to this word ("for the sake of," "in order to").

definition: In vain, to no purpose, without achieving any result.
article: κενῶς is an adverb built from the adjective κενός ("empty"), and it means doing something pointlessly or without effect. It appears just once in the New Testament, at James 4:5, and once in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew word רִיק at Isaiah 49:4. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on "in vain, to no purpose," and an everyday papyrus from A.D. 139 pairs it with "useless" (κενῶς καὶ ἀνωφελῶς), confirming this was ordinary Koine.
caution: The measured rendering label "Spirit" reflects the surrounding text of James 4:5 rather than the actual meaning of this adverb, which the lexicons consistently define as "in vain"; with only one New Testament occurrence, confidence is low.

definition: Cheerful, in good spirits, or filled with courage and confidence.
article: εὔθυμος describes someone who is cheerful, of good cheer, or feeling encouraged. Built from εὖ ("well") and θυμός ("spirit, mood"), it literally points to being in good spirits, and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri — one fourth-century letter uses the comparative form in the phrase "that I may make you more cheerful." Abbott-Smith notes an older sense "kind" in Homer, but in the New Testament's two uses the meaning is consistently about cheerfulness or encouragement.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin evidence, the range is narrow and the older "kind" sense noted by lexica does not appear in the biblical text.

definition: The third floor or story of a building.
senseLabels: the third story of a building
article: This compound word (from "three" and "roof/story") names the third floor of a multi-story building. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:9, and the lexicons agree it means "the third story"—the Septuagint uses it in Genesis 6:16 and Ezekiel 42:6. Everyday papyri confirm the ordinary meaning: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 55 describes inheriting half of a "three-storeyed house."
caution: The Majority Standard Bible's rendering "sinking" reflects the action in the verse rather than the word itself, which all lexicons define as "third story"; with only one New Testament occurrence, evidence is thin.

definition: Being satisfied and self-sufficient, finding what you already have to be enough whatever your circumstances.
senseLabels: content, satisfied with what one has
article: In the New Testament αὐτάρκης appears only once, in Philippians 4:11, where Paul says he has learned to be "content" in any situation. The word is built from "self" and "to be enough," and in classical and philosophical usage it carried the fuller idea of being self-sufficient and independent. The everyday papyri show a more practical, down-to-earth flavor: people simply meant "enough" or "sufficient" — a sufficient number of jars, enough seeds, adequate sailors — so the term ranged from a personal attitude of contentment to a plain measure of having enough.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: To take unfair advantage of someone, cheating or exploiting them for your own gain.
article: In the New Testament this verb always means to exploit or defraud someone for personal gain, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "exploit" in every clear case (3 of 5 occurrences, the other 2 absorbed into surrounding phrasing). All five occurrences are in Paul's letters. A nice everyday parallel comes from a papyrus of A.D. 184, where a man complains that a "self-willed" person "takes all sorts of advantages over me" regarding their shared property — exactly the bullying, grasping sense Paul has in mind.
caution: Classical Greek also used this word intransitively to simply "have more" or "have an advantage," but that neutral sense does not appear in the New Testament usage.

definition: The act of putting ornaments around oneself, such as wearing jewelry as adornment.
article: This noun describes the act of putting something around or on oneself—specifically the wearing of decorative items like jewelry. It comes from the verb περιτίθημι ("to put around"), and it appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 3:3, where the Berean Standard Bible renders it "beauty" in reference to outward adornment. Notably, the lexicons also point to Symmachus' version of Psalm 32:9 as one of the very few other places the word surfaces.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be confidently mapped from biblical usage alone.

definition: To inspect closely or spy on something, especially secretly to gather information for hostile purposes.
article: κατασκοπέω means to look something over carefully, with the strong sense of spying or inspecting for hostile ends. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Galatians 2:4, where false brothers slipped in to "spy out" the freedom of believers. The Septuagint uses it 13 times across 6 books, most often to render Hebrew רָגַל (10×), the word for sending out scouts or spies, and Moulton-Milligan notes it in everyday Koine papyri, including a temple-list examination in an Oxyrhynchus document.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise nuance rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: A sparkling yellow gemstone used in adornment, traditionally identified as chrysolite or yellow jasper.
article: χρυσόλιθος literally combines the words for "gold" and "stone," naming a bright yellow gem. It appears only once in the New Testament, where Revelation 21:20 lists it among the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sardonyx" here, though Strong's, the KJV, and Dodson favor "chrysolite" or "topaz." Interestingly, the word turns up in a list of painters' colors in a second-century papyrus (P Lond 928), showing it was an everyday term for a pigment as well as a precious stone.
caution: The exact gem is genuinely uncertain—sources disagree, ranging from chrysolite to topaz to yellow jasper, and the MSB's "sardonyx" differs from the traditional glosses.

definition: To mock, scoff, or jeer at someone or something with contempt.
article: This verb means to ridicule or sneer at someone, treating them with open contempt. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament and just once in the critical text, both times woven into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. It also shows up in everyday Koine papyri — for instance a Byzantine document where someone complains, "now I have been mocked by him" — and a related noun appears in a petition from an old man who suffered a broken contract and mockery.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word is nearly a New Testament hapax with both senses absorbed into phrasing, so its precise force rests mainly on outside papyri and lexicons.

definition: To summon someone to come to you, calling them near for instruction, sending, or a decision.
article: προσκαλέομαι means to call someone toward yourself—to summon them so they come near. In the New Testament it always appears in the middle voice, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "called" in 20 of its 31 occurrences (91%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing or rendered "invited." The everyday papyri confirm this same usage: documents from before 100 B.C. use it for summoning named individuals, and it even shows up in a legal context for summoning someone from a public office.

definition: To frighten someone into handing over money or goods; to extort or intimidate by force or threats.
article: Literally this verb means "to shake thoroughly," but in everyday Koine it took on the figurative sense of shaking someone down — intimidating them to extort money. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:14, where John the Baptist tells soldiers not to do this to people. The papyri confirm the meaning vividly: a document from around 120 BC (P Par 15) uses it for harassing people "in order to extort from them and bring them to harm."

definition: To lay a matter before someone in order to explain it and seek their counsel or advice.
article: In the middle voice, ἀνατίθεμαι means to set forth or explain a matter to another person, usually with a view to consulting them about it. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 25:14 and Galatians 2:2), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "before" in both cases, and the literal sense is "to lay upon" or "set up." The everyday papyri confirm this consulting nuance: one document (P Par 69, A.D. 233) uses it of laying a matter before someone untouched, matching its New Testament use.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single measured sense, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: Publius, the leading Roman official on the island of Malta who hosted Paul.
article: Πόπλιος is a proper name, the Greek form of the Latin praenomen Publius. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 28 (verses 7 and 8), where it names the chief man of Malta who welcomed and lodged Paul. Interestingly, the scholar Ramsay noted that it is unusual for an official to be called by just his praenomen, suggesting Publius may have been so well known among the local peasantry that Luke simply adopted their familiar way of naming him.
caution: Evidence is thin: the name occurs only twice, in adjacent verses describing the same person.

definition: To be furiously enraged against someone, raging like a madman.
article: This verb describes being violently, madly angry at someone — a fury so intense it resembles insanity. It is built from the prefix ἐν- plus μαίνομαι ("to be mad" or "rave"), and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:11, where Paul describes his rage against Christians. Moulton-Milligan note a related form in the playwright Menander, describing someone "rushing in like a madman," which captures the wild, frenzied edge of the word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured; note also that the digest's measured rendering "frequently" reflects the wider verse rather than the verb's own raging-against meaning given by the lexicons.

definition: Salem, a place name in the Bible traditionally linked with the city later known as Jerusalem.
article: Σαλήμ is a proper name appearing 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where it is rendered "Salem." It refers to a place in Palestine, traditionally identified with Jerusalem, associated with Melchizedek the king. In Hebrews 7:2 the name is glossed by interpreting its meaning, which the Majority Standard Bible captures with phrasing about the name being given, while Abbott-Smith ties the word to the Hebrew שָׁלֵם in Genesis 14:18.
caution: This is a rarely-occurring proper name (only 3 times) with low confidence, and the supposed identification with Jerusalem is traditional rather than proven by the evidence here.

definition: Bethesda, the name of a pool in Jerusalem mentioned in John's Gospel.
article: Bethesda is the proper name of a pool in Jerusalem, appearing just once in the New Testament, at John 5:2. Strong's links the name to a meaning like "house of kindness," from a Chaldee origin, but Abbott-Smith notes the derivation is uncertain. The most interesting wrinkle is in the manuscripts themselves: while the received text reads Bethesda, the major critical editions print Bethzatha, with Bethsaida noted in the margin — the very name of the place is disputed.
caution: This word occurs only once and its spelling and meaning are uncertain, with manuscripts and editions disagreeing on the name itself.

definition: Describing something hard, solid, and unshakable, used both physically and figuratively for steadfast faith.
article: Στερεός describes things that are hard, solid, and stable — and it carries that sense both literally and figuratively. In its 4 New Testament occurrences it covers a firm foundation (2 Timothy 2:19), solid food as opposed to milk (Hebrews 5:12), and being steadfast in faith (1 Peter 5:9). The everyday Koine papyri show its concrete edge nicely: it was the standard word for 'hard' or ripe grain, as in receipts for hard wheat unmixed with barley.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences spread thinly, the figurative range rests on single examples per sense, and Abbott-Smith notes the classical word could also mean 'hard' in the negative sense of cruel.

definition: A fish-hook, the bent metal device used on a line to catch fish.
article: ἄγκιστρον is a fish-hook, named for its bent shape. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 17:27, where Jesus tells Peter to cast a hook and catch a fish. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times, most often translating the Hebrew חַכָּה ("hook," 3×), confirming the basic fishing-tackle meaning across both Testaments.
caution: The digest's measured sense lists "four" at 100%, which contradicts every lexicon's "fish-hook" — this looks like a tagging error, so treat the rendering data with caution.

definition: To mix leaven into dough so that the whole batch ferments and rises; figuratively, to spread influence throughout something.
article: ζυμόω means to leaven—to add yeast so a small amount permeates and transforms an entire batch of dough. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 4 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "works through" where it gives the word its own English, capturing the figurative idea of a little influence spreading through the whole (as in 1 Corinthians 5:6 and Galatians 5:9). In the Septuagint it appears 4 times, translating both the Hebrew word for dough (בָּצֵק) and the word for leavened or soured (חָמֵץ), tying it directly to bread-making.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and half of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than given their own English word, the measured sense rests on a thin sample.

definition: To go unnoticed or hidden, or to fail to realize or pay attention to something.
article: λανθάνω is about something slipping past unseen — staying hidden or escaping a person's attention. It appears 6 times in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "escape notice" (twice), "notice," "knowing," and "let escape notice." In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 12 times, most often translating the Hebrew עָלַם ("to be hidden" or "concealed"), and the everyday papyri preserve the same flavor, as in a 2nd-century letter saying οὐκ ἔλαθέ με, "it did not escape my notice." One striking idiom appears in Hebrews 13:2, where the verb pairs with another word to mean doing something unawares — entertaining angels without knowing it.
caution: With only 6 occurrences, several senses rest on a single instance, so the measured range is thin.

definition: A pointing word meaning "that" or "that one," referring to a person or thing set apart from the speaker, often someone or something already mentioned.
article: ἐκεῖνος is a demonstrative pronoun that points to a person or thing as "that one" — often something more remote or already named, as opposed to οὗτος ("this"). Its single core meaning shows up in many grammatical shapes: translators rendered it as "that" 67 times (33%) and as an emphatic "he" 39 times (19%), with many small combinations like "that he" or "will that" reflecting how it joins surrounding words; in fact 49 of 253 occurrences are absorbed so fully into the phrasing that they get no English word of their own. In the Septuagint it appears 611 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew word הוּא ("he/that"), which appears 410 times — showing how naturally it does double duty as both a pointer and a plain pronoun.
caution: The many measured "senses" are really one demonstrative word taking different English forms depending on grammar, not distinct meanings.

definition: An Aramaic phrase meaning "you have forsaken me," spoken by Jesus from the cross.
article: This is not really a Greek word at all but an Aramaic phrase written out in Greek letters, meaning "you have forsaken me." It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in Jesus' cry from the cross (Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34), where it is left untranslated as part of the spoken phrase. Most interestingly, this echoes Psalm 22:2, where the underlying Hebrew uses the verb עָזַב ("to forsake, abandon"); manuscripts even preserve a variant spelling (ζαφθανεί) that some think was an attempt to reproduce the Hebrew rather than the Aramaic form.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both absorbed into a quoted phrase, and competing manuscript spellings, the evidence is thin and the confidence tier is low.

definition: To crush, break in pieces, or shatter something; figuratively, to break a person down through oppression.
article: θραύω means to crush, shatter, or break something to pieces, and it can be used figuratively of breaking a person down. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 4:18, where the broken-down or oppressed are set free; the Septuagint uses it 17 times, often translating the Hebrew רָצַץ (to crush). A striking witness comes from the papyri and inscriptions: an inscription on the left leg of the Memnon statue records that Cambyses 'broke' (ἔθραυσε) the stone, showing the word's plain everyday sense of physical shattering.
caution: The single NT occurrence is a quotation from the Septuagint, so the measured 'liberty' rendering reflects the larger phrase in Luke 4:18 rather than the verb's core meaning of crushing.

definition: To destroy, ruin, or corrupt something or someone, whether physically spoiling it or morally depraving it.
article: φθείρω covers a spread from outright destroying or ruining to morally corrupting or leading astray, and the New Testament uses it for both physical and moral spoiling. In the Byzantine text it appears 7 times, most often in Paul — destroying God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:17), corrupting hearts (2 Corinthians 7:2), and being corrupted by deceitful desires (Ephesians 4:22). The everyday Koine flavor shows up vividly in the papyri: marriage contracts forbade a wife from 'ruining' (φθείρειν) the shared household, and nursing contracts guarded against a nurse 'spoiling' her milk. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, chiefly rendering the Hebrew shachat (to destroy or spoil).
caution: The renderings range widely from concrete destruction to moral corruption, and two of the seven occurrences are absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word.

definition: Worthy reception or approval—the warm acceptance given to something or someone judged trustworthy and deserving.
article: ἀποδοχή means acceptance or approval, the welcome you give to something you fully receive as worthy. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Timothy (1:15 and 4:9), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "acceptance" 100% of the time, and both times it forms the phrase "worthy of full acceptance." The Moulton-Milligan evidence is especially telling: inscriptions from Magnesia and Ephesus show that "worthy of acceptance" (ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος) was a stock honorific formula in everyday Koine, used to praise distinguished public figures.
caution: With only 2 occurrences—both in the same fixed phrase in one book—the measured range is thin, so the fuller shades of "reception, welcome" listed by Dodson are not directly witnessed in the New Testament data.

definition: Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea who presided over Jesus' trial.
article: Πιλᾶτος is the personal name of Pontius Pilate, the Roman official who appears 55 times across 6 New Testament books, almost always in the trial narratives of the Gospels (e.g. Matthew 27:2, Mark 15:1, Luke 3:1). The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "Pilate" in 87% of cases, with the remaining variations just reflecting surrounding phrasing. The name is of Latin origin, and Strong's connects it to a root meaning "close-pressed" or "firm"; interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that the same spelling shows up later in everyday Koine papyri, used as an ordinary personal name for a scribe as late as A.D. 553.

definition: A person who holds authority over others — a ruler, official, or leader at any level of power.
article: ἄρχων points to someone in a position of power, and the New Testament uses it across a wide range — national rulers, local magistrates, synagogue leaders, members of the Sanhedrin, and even the devil as "prince of demons." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "rulers" most often (16×, 48%), then "leader" (5×) and "prince" (3×). It shows up heavily in the Greek Old Testament (565×), where it most commonly stands in for the Hebrew שָׂר (220×) and נָשִׂיא (102×), confirming its core meaning of a chief or appointed official.

definition: To carry something out completely, or to convince someone fully so they are entirely persuaded.
article: This verb literally combines "full" with "carry," and it pulls in two directions: completing a task all the way and persuading a person all the way. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, split evenly across "fully persuaded" (Rom 4:21), "fully" (Rom 14:5), and "fully proclaimed" (2 Ti 4:17), with two more uses absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Notably, the everyday Koine papyri use it for settling or finishing off legal matters "in order that I may finish off the matter," which fits the "accomplish completely" side rather than the "convince" side.
caution: With only 5 occurrences spread evenly across three different rendered senses, and Abbott-Smith dividing the range differently than the measured data, the word's exact emphasis in any given verse can be debated.

definition: A report or piece of information passed to someone, especially news brought to officials about a crime or disturbance.
article: φάσις means a report, news, or information delivered to someone, and in its single New Testament use (Acts 21:31) it is word brought to the Roman commander that the whole city of Jerusalem was in an uproar. Abbott-Smith notes it often carries the sense of information laid against fraud or another crime, fitting its legal-sounding context. Everyday papyri show how common and plain the word was: one letter from A.D. 22 has a man saying he won't even anoint himself "until I hear word (φάσιν) from you on each point."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests on a single occurrence supported by outside Koine evidence.

definition: Farther on, at a greater distance; the comparative form meaning 'more distant' or 'beyond'.
article: This is the comparative adverb of πόῤῥω ('far off'), meaning 'farther' or 'onwards, beyond' — describing a greater distance. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree closely on this 'farther/beyond' range. Notably, the word does not appear at all in the Byzantine New Testament, so there are no measured senses from that corpus to refine the dictionary glosses.
caution: With zero New Testament occurrences and no measured-sense data, this entry rests entirely on lexicon glosses rather than corpus evidence.

definition: A theater building used for public shows or assemblies, or figuratively a spectacle put on display for others to watch.
senseLabels: a theater building or assembly place
article: θέατρον refers to a theater—in the ancient world a semicircular stone structure often open to the sky—but it could also serve as a general meeting place for public assemblies. In two of its three New Testament appearances (Acts 19:29, 31) it names the actual theater at Ephesus, and the rendering of these as a place of public assembly is neatly confirmed by inscriptions and papyri that show crowds gathering 'into the theater' for an assembly. In its third use (1 Corinthians 4:9) it shifts to the figurative sense of a spectacle or show, picturing the apostles as something put on public display.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the figurative 'spectacle' sense rests on a single passage.

definition: A journey or the act of traveling, also used figuratively for the course someone is pursuing in life.
article: πορεία means a journey or the act of traveling somewhere, and it appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 13:22 it describes Jesus literally journeying toward Jerusalem, while in James 1:11 it is used figuratively for the rich man's "course" — Hort's clever suggestion being that he perishes while still on the move, before reaching the restful enjoyment he keeps expecting. In the Septuagint it shows up 18 times across 10 books, mostly rendering Hebrew words for going or marching, and an inscription even uses it for the orbiting "course" of the sun and moon.
caution: Both New Testament occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word, and the figurative sense in James rests on a single interpretive suggestion.

definition: To look ahead and provide or arrange something in advance for someone's benefit.
article: This is a rare compound of πρό ("before") and βλέπω ("see"), so its literal sense is "look ahead"—but in practice it shifts toward providing or furnishing something in advance. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Hebrews 11:40), where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word, and the standard versions render it "provide." Its single Septuagint use (Psalm 37:13) instead carries the plainer sense "foresee," and a sepulchral inscription shows a man "providing" a tomb for himself and his family, neatly bridging the two ideas of foreseeing and making provision.
caution: Evidence is very thin (one NT and one LXX occurrence), and the sources split between "foresee" and "provide," so the precise force is uncertain.

definition: A basket, probably woven from wicker, of the kind Jews carried for food.
article: A κόφινος is a basket—likely wickerwork—used to carry provisions, and in the New Testament it always appears in the accounts of feeding the crowds, where leftover food filled several of them. It occurs 6 times in the Byzantine text, and apart from one place where the translation reads 'pieces' (John 6:13, describing what filled the baskets), every rendering points to baskets full of gathered food. An interesting detail from everyday Koine: a military account in the papyri (P Oxy I.43, A.D. 295) mentions κόφινοι each holding 40 pounds, and Dr. Hort argued the difference between this word and σπυρίς is one of material rather than size.
caution: The single 'pieces' rendering reflects the surrounding phrase rather than a distinct sense of the word, so the basket meaning is essentially uniform.

definition: To solemnly affirm something as if calling witnesses, or to earnestly urge and charge someone to act.
article: This middle-voice verb, built from the noun for "witness," originally meant to summon someone as a witness. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, rendered "testify" in 3 of those (75%) and as urging or charging once (25%), with one occurrence absorbed into the phrasing. The everyday Koine papyri show the same range vividly: one document has people "calling to witness" those about to seal an affidavit, and another has people swearing "by your Fortune" — a natural slide from formally summoning witnesses to solemnly affirming or pleading.
caution: With only 5 occurrences split across two senses, the line between solemn affirmation and earnest exhortation can blur in individual verses.

definition: Obed, a man's name in the Old Testament genealogies, listed as the son of Boaz and father of Jesse, an ancestor of David and Jesus.
article: Ὠβήδ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Obed (עוֹבֵד), appearing in the genealogy of Jesus as the son of Boaz and grandfather of David. It is an indeclinable proper name and carries no meaning beyond identifying this individual. The Septuagint uses it 14 times across 4 books, where it usually renders Hebrew עוֹבֵד but occasionally stands in for other Hebrew names, suggesting some variation in how the name was applied.
caution: The three measured "senses" reflect tagging artifacts within genealogy verses rather than real meanings, and the manuscript spelling itself varies (Ἰωβήδ in some editions), so the underlying name is simply Obed.

definition: Describing something that goes on without stopping, constant and unremitting.
article: ἀδιάλειπτος means "unceasing" or "incessant" — something that keeps going without a break. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 9:2 and 2 Timothy 1:3), and in both cases English translations fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own word. Built from a negative prefix plus a form of "to leave off," it was a common everyday Koine word: papyri use the adverb for unflagging zeal, ongoing public service, and even a persistent cough.
caution: Only two New Testament occurrences, and in both the word is absorbed into the phrasing, so its precise force rests largely on outside Koine evidence.

definition: A person of the same age as oneself; a contemporary or peer in years.
article: This word means a contemporary — someone who belongs to your own age group. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Galatians 1:14, where Paul says he advanced in Judaism beyond his peers, and in that one verse it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word. Moulton-Milligan confirms the same meaning in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, citing a Greek inscription where it likewise denotes a contemporary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the biblical text alone.

definition: Describing something inanimate or lifeless, like an object or instrument that has no soul or breath of its own.
article: ἄψυχος is built from the negative prefix "a-" and ψυχή ("soul, life"), so it literally means "without a soul" — that is, lifeless or inanimate. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 14:7, where Paul speaks of "lifeless" musical instruments like the flute or harp; in that verse the word gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than taking its own English word. The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri: Moulton-Milligan cite a third-century magical text mentioning someone living on "lifeless" (plant-based) food, and the term survives into Modern Greek still meaning "lifeless."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from the biblical evidence alone.

definition: To dare or have the courage to do something, sometimes implying the boldness to presume beyond what is proper.
article: τολμάω means to venture or have the courage to act, and in all 16 New Testament uses it carries this core idea of daring. The renderings range from neutral courage ("dare," 47%, as when no one "dared" to question Jesus) to a more negative shade of overstepping bounds ("presume," 20%, as in Romans 15:18 or Jude 9). The everyday Koine papyri sharpen this darker edge nicely: one document (P Ryl II. 144) uses it for someone who "had the audacity" to bring baseless accusations.

definition: To give birth to someone again, used for spiritual rebirth into a new life.
article: This verb means to beget or give birth again, and in the New Testament it always describes spiritual rebirth into a new life. It appears only twice, both in 1 Peter (1:3 and 1:23), and in one of those the translation folds it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a single English word. Interestingly, the same idea and word turn up in the Hermetic religious writings, where someone marvels at being 'born again' from a mysterious womb, showing the rebirth image circulated more widely in everyday Koine.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the New Testament, so its full range is hard to pin down.

definition: To eat the main meal of the day, to dine or have supper.
article: δειπνέω means to take the chief meal of the day — to dine or sup — built on the noun δεῖπνον. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 4 times, mostly of the Lord's Supper (Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25), with a figurative use in Revelation 3:20 where Christ promises to share a meal with the one who opens the door. The most colorful evidence comes from everyday papyri: an Oxyrhynchus dinner invitation asks the recipient to dine at the table of the lord Sarapis at 9 o'clock the next day, showing the word's ordinary social use.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the sense distinctions rest on thin evidence.

definition: The quality of being great, glorious, or majestic, especially the splendor and grandeur belonging to God or a powerful figure.
article: This word points to overwhelming greatness and splendor, the kind of grandeur that inspires awe. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, rendered "majesty" twice (Acts 19:27, 2 Peter 1:16) and "greatness" once (Luke 9:43). Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions used it as a ceremonial title for officials—one Greek inscription even renders the Latin phrase for "the majesty of the Roman people"—showing it carried real-world weight as a term of honor.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, so its exact range is hard to pin down.

definition: In a disorderly, undisciplined way—living irregularly without proper order or self-control.
article: This adverb describes behaving in a disorderly or irregular manner, used by Paul in both its New Testament appearances to describe believers living without discipline (2 Thessalonians 3:6, 3:11). The Majority Standard Bible renders both occurrences with the sense of leading an undisciplined life, and the BSB agrees fully. Its root carries a moral sense of irregularity, though Abbott-Smith notes Symmachus used it in 4 Kings 9:20 in a more neutral way, simply describing irregular movement.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both in one book, the evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: Aeneas, the name of a paralyzed man in Lydda whom Peter healed.
article: Αἰνέας is simply a man's name, appearing only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 9 (verses 33 and 34), where he is a bedridden man in Lydda whom Peter heals. The two measured "senses" reflect the surrounding narrative phrasing rather than any difference in meaning—the word is just a personal name. The lexicons themselves disagree on his background: Strong's calls him an Israelite while Dodson describes him simply as a citizen of Lydda, and the name's derivation is listed as uncertain.
caution: Both occurrences are confined to a single passage and the sources disagree on whether Aeneas was an Israelite, so background details are uncertain.

definition: To go back to where one came from; to return.
article: ὑποστρέφω simply means to turn back or return, and in the New Testament it is used intransitively almost without exception — someone goes back to a place they had left. The measured renderings cluster tightly: "returned" (69%), "return" (20%), and "back" (6%), all of which BSB confirms 100%. It's a favorite word of Luke, and everyday Koine papyri show the same plain sense, as in a 3rd-century document with "E. went back" and an official order that "all should return to their own homelands." In the Septuagint it chiefly translates the common Hebrew verb שׁוּב ("to turn/return").

definition: A person who lends money to others and is owed repayment.
article: δανειστής is the everyday Koine word for someone who lends money and is owed it back — a moneylender or creditor. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 7:41), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "moneylender" every time. The Septuagint uses it three times, translating Hebrew words tied to lending and debt, and Moulton-Milligan show it was common in ordinary business papyri, including a first-century letter complaining "we have many creditors."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (and none in the critical text), this entry rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: To ask for or demand someone to be handed over to you, often successfully obtaining the request.
senseLabels: to demand someone be handed over
article: This verb in its middle voice means to ask for someone or something for yourself, and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 22:31) it carries the sense of demanding that a person be given up to you. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "asked all" there, while scholars like Field argue it implies success — Satan having actually obtained the disciples by his asking, as the RV margin notes. The everyday papyri back this up: one inscription uses the same form for people who "obtained by asking" specific named individuals, suggesting a successful requisition rather than a mere request.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and its precise force — whether a simple request or a successful demand — is genuinely debated among the sources.

definition: A high-ranking military officer, especially a Roman tribune commanding about a thousand soldiers.
article: χιλίαρχος literally means "ruler of a thousand" and refers to a senior military officer—in the New Testament usually a Roman tribune commanding a cohort. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "commander" in 17 of 21 occurrences (81%), with the rest also being "commander" tied to specific contexts like Paul's arrest. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for "thousand" (אָלֶף, 17 times), and the word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including one reading "commander of a legion."

definition: A personal name, Hermas, belonging to a Christian greeted by Paul in his letter to the Romans.
article: Ἑρμᾶς is the name of a Christian whom Paul greets in Romans 16:14, and it appears just once in the New Testament. The name is a Doric form of Ἑρμῆς (Hermes) and was, according to Moulton-Milligan, widely used in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. One small wrinkle in the evidence: the Majority Standard Bible's rendering is tagged as "Phlegon" in the digest, though the standard lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) all identify the word as the name Hermas.
caution: This is a personal name occurring only once, and the measured rendering label ("Phlegon") does not match the lexicons' identification as "Hermas," so treat the tagging cautiously.

definition: To arrange something in proper order, especially to decorate or beautify it; sometimes simply to set in place.
article: κοσμέω covers a range from practical arranging—putting a house in order (Matthew 12:44; Luke 11:25)—to decorating and beautifying, whether a bride, a building's foundations, or a person's character. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "adorn" in over half its occurrences, while the rest mean simply to put or set in proper order. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew עָדָה ("to adorn," 3×), and a striking parallel appears in an inscription where Augustus is praised for having "adorned" public life, the same metaphorical use found in Titus 2:10.

definition: A Greek person, or more broadly any Greek-speaking non-Jew, often standing opposite to Jews.
article: Ἕλλην literally means a Greek—someone from Hellas—but in the New Testament it usually widens to mean any Greek-speaking non-Jew, the standard counterpart to "Jew." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Greeks" 85% of the time and "Greeks alike" (paired with Jews) the remaining 15%. A telling parallel comes from a 118 BC papyrus decree, where Ἕλληνας covers all non-Egyptian soldiers regardless of actual nationality—mirroring how the word came to mark the broad Jew-versus-Greek divide. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew name Yavan (Greece) four times.

definition: Something that can be eaten; fit for food.
article: βρώσιμος means simply "edible" or "fit to eat," describing food rather than the act of eating. It appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 24:41), where the risen Jesus asks whether the disciples have anything to eat, and three times in the Septuagint (Leviticus 19:23, Nehemiah 9:25, Ezekiel 47:12). The word turns up in everyday Koine sources too, including a fourth- or fifth-century love-spell papyrus and an inscription referring to "the edible meats."
caution: The digest's measured sense is mislabeled "disbelief," but every supporting source (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith, papyri) agrees the word means "eatable"; treat the label as a data error.

definition: An exclamation of surprise, fear, or indignation, roughly "ah!" or "ha!", that interrupts speech with strong feeling.
article: ἔα is an interjection — a burst of emotion rather than a word with meaning — expressing surprise, fear, or indignation, something like "ah!" or "ha!". It appears just 2 times in the Byzantine New Testament and only once in the critical text, at the demon's cry in Mark 1:24 and Luke 4:34. Note a sharp disagreement in the evidence: the measured data shows translators rendering it as "us" in both places (likely because the surrounding phrase blends the cry into the sentence), while the classical lexica treat it as a standalone exclamation of alarm; Abbott-Smith notes it is chiefly poetic in classical Greek.
caution: The evidence is thin and conflicting — the word is nearly a hapax, and the measured rendering "us" clashes with lexicons that call it an interjection, so its exact force here is uncertain.

definition: To stir someone up emotionally—either to anger and irritation, or in a positive sense to spur them on enthusiastically.
article: ἐρεθίζω means to rouse or stir someone up, and its tone depends entirely on context. The New Testament uses it both ways: negatively in Colossians 3:21, where fathers are warned not to provoke their children, and positively in 2 Corinthians 9:2, where Paul says the Corinthians' eagerness has stirred up others to give. In the Septuagint it appears 5 times, often rendering the Hebrew גָּרָה ("to stir up strife"), and Moulton-Milligan note the related noun shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing with no single English equivalent, so the precise force in each case leans heavily on context.

definition: Describing something that extends far down or is profound, and—when used of time—the deep, early part of dawn.
article: βαθύς basically means "deep," whether literally (a deep well in John 4:11) or figuratively ("the deep things of Satan" in Revelation 2:24). It also has a special time-related use: paired with "dawn" it means the deep, very early part of morning, as in Luke 24:1, and with "sleep" it describes a deep sleep in Acts 20:9. The everyday papyri confirm this range nicely—one document uses it for "very late evening," another wishes a couple to reach "deep old age," and one even applies it to a deeper shade of purple dye. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for "deep" (עָמֹק).
caution: The labels "certain women" and "certain deep" come from how surrounding phrases were rendered rather than from βαθύς itself, which consistently means "deep" or "early"; with only 4 New Testament occurrences the evidence is limited.

definition: To lie or rest on something, or figuratively to press hard, bear down on, or be imposed upon someone.
article: ἐπίκειμαι literally means to lie or rest on top of something — a stone laid across a tomb's entrance (John 11:38), bread set on coals, or a crowd physically pressing in on a person. From this physical base it stretches to figurative pressures: a storm bearing down (Acts 27:20), the crowd pressing Jesus with their demands (Luke 23:23), or a necessity laid on someone like an obligation (1 Corinthians 9:16). The everyday Koine papyri capture the concrete sense vividly — one document from 113 BC describes the Nile's water 'covering' the land at its annual rise, and another notes seals 'still in their place' on a document.
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences and 3 of those absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word, the measured sense divisions reflect very thin per-sense evidence.
