definition: A person who owes a debt to someone else.
article: χρεωφειλέτης is simply a person who owes money or a debt, formed by combining the words for "debt" and "one who owes." It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in Luke's parables (Luke 7:41 and 16:5), and the two measured renderings are really just one meaning expressed in slightly different contexts. The word also shows up in everyday Koine documents: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription (c. 85 BC) recording that creditors "released the debtors," confirming this was ordinary commercial language.
caution: The evidence is thin (only 2 NT uses, both in Luke, and absent from the critical SBLGNT text), and sources note spelling variations like χρεοφιλέτης.

definition: A particle meaning "lest," "otherwise," or "so that…not," warning against an undesirable outcome, sometimes softened to "perhaps."
article: μήποτε is a negative particle that mostly flags a danger to be avoided — "otherwise" or "lest it happen." It appears 25 times in the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "otherwise" in 57% of cases and a simple "not" in 29%, though in 11 of 25 places it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no word of its own. In the Septuagint it shows up 79 times and most often translates the Hebrew פֶּן ("lest," 43×). An everyday papyrus letter captures the flavor nicely: someone decides to grab a document "lest haply we should come to grief at the audit."
caution: In a few later contexts the word weakens to "perhaps" (as some read Matthew 25:9), and the lexica also note a debated "never" sense in Hebrews 9:17 that depends on the manuscript text.

definition: The personal name of a Christian from the Roman province of Asia who, along with others, deserted the apostle Paul.
article: Phygelus is a proper name, mentioned just once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 1:15), where he is named alongside Hermogenes as one of those in Asia who turned away from Paul. The name itself probably derives from the Greek verb meaning "to flee" (pheugō), which is why some sources gloss it as "fugitive." Notably, Moulton-Milligan finds the related name form in everyday Koine inscriptions, and a similar name (Phygelios) appears in an ancient inscription catalogue, showing it was a real-world personal name; the spelling itself is debated, with editors preferring Phygelos (one 'l') over Phygellos.
caution: This is a one-time-only name with thin evidence, and the sources disagree over its exact spelling (Phygelos versus Phygellos).

definition: A son — a male child, descendant, or someone figuratively counted as belonging to a person, group, or category.
article: υἱός means a son: it covers an immediate male child, a more distant descendant, and figurative uses where someone is called a 'son' of a person or group. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 377 times, and translators render it 'Son' in essentially every case it carries its own word (351×), though 26 times it disappears into the phrasing rather than getting an English equivalent. The Septuagint uses it a staggering 4689 times, almost always for the Hebrew בֵּן ('son'), and everyday papyri show the same stretched usage — one letter addresses a man as 'son' where the context makes clear he was not a son by blood.

definition: The hand; also used figuratively for a person's power, action, or agency.
article: χείρ is the ordinary Greek word for the hand, and that is overwhelmingly how it works in the New Testament—rendered "hand" in 143 of 174 occurrences (99%). The remaining cases are mostly absorbed into English phrasing (29×), and Greek often uses "hand" in idioms where it stands for someone's power or activity, as Strong's and Abbott-Smith note. The Septuagint detail is striking: across 1,689 uses it chiefly translates the Hebrew word יָד ("hand"), 1,327 times, so the Bible's frequent figurative talk of someone's "hand" reflects this underlying Hebrew idiom.

definition: Group dancing accompanied by music, the festive celebration of singing and dancing at a joyful occasion.
article: χορός refers to dancing, especially the group dancing and music that marks a celebration. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 15:25, where the older son hears "music and dancing" as the family celebrates the prodigal's return. In the Septuagint it shows up 17 times, usually translating the Hebrew words for dance (מָחוֹל and מְחֹלָה). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes a Christian gravestone inscription where the word means a "choir" or band of singers — the "choir" of angels — showing how the term could shift toward singing rather than dancing.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and uncertain derivation, the word's precise range (dancing versus a singing choir) rests on slim direct evidence.

definition: A wedding, the celebration or feast that goes with it, or marriage as the married state itself.
article: γάμος covers the whole world of weddings: the ceremony, the festive banquet that follows, and marriage as an ongoing relationship. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 16 times, most often meaning a wedding (5×) or a wedding banquet (4×), with only 2 uses pointing to marriage itself (Hebrews 13:4, Revelation 19:7). The everyday flavor of the word shows up vividly in the papyri, where a marriage contract from 92 BC is labeled a "γάμου" agreement, and an invitation survives asking someone to dine "at the weddings of her children."

definition: To make someone proud or arrogant, literally to puff or inflate them like air filling a bellows.
article: φυσιόω literally means to puff up or inflate, like air blown into a bellows, and the New Testament uses it figuratively for being swollen with pride or arrogance. All 7 occurrences sit in Paul's letters, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it with words like "arrogant," "puffs up," and "proud" — though some counts simply absorb it into surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word. The related form φυσάω turns up in everyday Greek writing, as in Herodas where people are described "priding themselves on their birth," which nicely captures the inflated-with-self-importance flavor.
caution: The measured "senses" here are really translation fragments of one underlying meaning (puffed up with pride), not genuinely distinct senses.

definition: A person from Colossae, a city in ancient Asia Minor.
article: Κολοσσαεύς simply means an inhabitant of Colossae, the city addressed in Paul's letter to the Colossians. The word is derived from the place-name Κολοσσαί (G2857), and it appears only in the title and subscription of that letter rather than within the New Testament text itself. Notably, Abbott-Smith records spelling variation between Κολασσαεύς and the Received Text's Κολοσσαεύς, reflecting differences among the manuscript traditions.
caution: This word does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament text or the critical text, appearing only in a letter's title, so there is no measured usage to draw on.

definition: To call out to someone or address them, whether shouting a summons or giving a formal speech.
article: προσφωνέω means to direct your voice toward someone — to call out, summon, or address them. Its range is fairly tight, covering everything from children calling to playmates in a marketplace (Matthew 11:16) to Paul formally addressing a crowd (Acts 21:40), and once to Jesus summoning his disciples by name to choose the twelve (Luke 6:13). It appears 7 times in the New Testament, and the everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one document even says "not a word has been uttered from you," showing how it edged toward the official sense of reporting or making a formal statement.
caution: The corpus is small (7 occurrences) and a couple of the measured sense labels look garbled, so treat the fine distinctions between "calling," "summoning," and "addressing" as one connected range rather than sharp categories.

definition: Dirt or filth, the grime that clings to something and needs to be washed away.
article: ῥύπος means literally dirt or filth — the kind of grime that gets washed off. It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Peter 3:21), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as 'removal' (of filth); other lexicons like the KJV and Dodson give straightforward glosses such as 'filth,' 'dirt,' and 'squalor.' One vivid detail: in everyday Koine papyri the word could mean 'wax,' as in a medical recipe calling for the ear-wax of a female mule.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on thin evidence, and the MSB 'removal' reflects context rather than the word's core meaning of 'filth.'

definition: Describing someone whose courage or spirit is small, leaving them discouraged, faint-hearted, and easily downcast.
article: ὀλιγόψυχος literally combines "little" with "spirit" or "soul," describing a person of small courage who is faint-hearted or easily discouraged. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Thessalonians 5:14) and six times in the Septuagint, where it renders several different Hebrew words. The everyday Koine flavor is captured in a papyrus letter (P Oxy X.1294) that uses the related verb: "do not lose heart about the rent, for you will get it once for all."
caution: The measured rendering "unruly" sharply disagrees with every lexicon here (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith, KJV), which all point to "faint-hearted"; with only one NT occurrence, treat the measured label with caution.

definition: Nathanael, an early disciple of Jesus from Cana in Galilee, possibly the same person as Bartholomew.
article: Ναθαναήλ is simply a personal name, appearing 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament — all in the Gospel of John, where he is introduced as an early follower of Jesus. The name comes from the Hebrew נְתַנְאֵל, which the Septuagint renders 13 times across 5 books. The three measured "senses" here ("Nathanael," "anything Nathanael," "Nathanael approaching true") simply reflect surrounding words caught alongside the name in the rendering data, not different meanings; it always names the same man.
caution: The supplied digest's separate "senses" are artifacts of phrasing, not real distinct meanings; both Dodson and Abbott-Smith only tentatively identify Nathanael with Bartholomew.

definition: To sing, especially songs of praise to God.
article: ᾄδω simply means to sing, and in the New Testament it always points to songs of praise directed to God. It can be used on its own with a dative (as in Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16, "sing to the Lord") or take a direct object naming the song sung (as in Revelation 5:9, 14:3, and 15:3). In the Septuagint it appears 72 times and most often translates the Hebrew שִׁיר ("to sing," 42 times); papyri even show it used in the passive, with hymns "being sung" in a foreign tongue.
caution: The five New Testament uses are split across slightly different phrasings, but they all reflect the single core meaning "to sing."

definition: To suffer or be mistreated beforehand, at an earlier time.
article: προπάσχω combines the prefix πρό ("before") with πάσχω ("to suffer"), meaning to undergo hardship or mistreatment at an earlier point. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:2, where Paul recalls suffering before arriving in Thessalonica. Classical writers like Herodotus, Thucydides, and Xenophon used it similarly, and Moulton-Milligan note a closely related compound, προσπάσχω, in a fourth-century letter possibly penned by Athanasius himself.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: An Aramaic command meaning "be opened!" spoken by Jesus when healing a deaf man.
article: This is an Aramaic word, transliterated into Greek, that means "be opened!" It appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 7:34, where Jesus speaks it while healing a man who was deaf and could barely talk. Mark records the foreign word and then translates it for his readers, and the lexicons trace it back to an Aramaic form (אֶתְפְּתח) behind the Greek spelling.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured; note also that the digest's lone "sighed" rendering reflects the surrounding verse rather than the meaning of the word itself, which means "be opened."

definition: The point where roads lead out of a city, especially where streets fork or meet—a busy crossing or thoroughfare.
article: διέξοδος literally means a "way out through"—the spot where roads diverge as they head out of a city into the country, which is why translations land on "crossroads" or "partings of the highways." It appears only once in the New Testament (Matthew 22:9), but turns up 30 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew word for "borders" or "outgoings" (תּוֹצָאוֹת, 22 times). Interestingly, the everyday papyri show a quite different use: in a document from 217 B.C. the word means the conclusion of a trial, prompting some scholars to picture Matthew's phrase as the places where streets "issue out" of town.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and reference works offering varied pictures—crossroads, highways, or city exits—the precise nuance in Matthew 22:9 is uncertain.

definition: An Arab, a person from Arabia.
article: Ἄραψ simply means an Arab, someone from Arabia. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 2:11, where Arabs are listed among the peoples present at Pentecost. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times across 4 books, usually translating the Hebrew word for Arabian (6 of those times).
caution: The measured rendering labels this occurrence as "Judaism," which conflicts with every lexicon (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) defining it as "an Arabian" — the standard lexical meaning should be trusted here, and the single occurrence makes the corpus data thin.

definition: To dip something into a liquid, sometimes to dye or stain it by dipping.
article: βάπτω basically means to dip something into a liquid, and by extension to dye or stain it through dipping. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times (4 in the critical text), always rendered with "dip" — dipping a fingertip in water (Luke 16:24), dipping a morsel (John 13:26), and a robe dipped in blood (Rev 19:13). In the Septuagint it shows up 16 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word ṭāḇal ("to dip"). The everyday Koine papyri are especially telling: tax records from Egypt mention fullers and dyers and even "coloured garments," showing the word's strong link to the dyeing trade.
caution: With only 3-4 New Testament occurrences this is thin evidence, and the "dye" sense in Rev 19:13 depends on a disputed reading where some manuscripts have a different word entirely.

definition: To compete as an athlete in a contest, following the established rules of the games.
article: ἀθλέω means to compete or contend like an athlete in a public contest. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice—both in 2 Timothy 2:5—where Paul pictures an athlete who must compete "according to the rules" to win the crown. The classical lexica connect it to ἆθλος, a contest staged in war or sport, with related senses of wrestling and combat.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only twice, both in the same verse, and the measured renderings ("Likewise," "competes according") reflect phrase divisions rather than distinct meanings.

definition: A person from Tarsus; a native or citizen of that city.
article: Ταρσεύς simply means someone who comes from Tarsus, the city in Cilicia. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 9:11 and 21:39), both times describing Paul, and the standard translations agree it points to Tarsus. An interesting trace of the city's reputation shows up in the papyri: a related adjective ταρσικοϋφικός describes a loom for weaving 'Tarsian cloths,' recorded in a sale document from A.D. 298.
caution: The word occurs only twice and one of the two measured renderings ('ask man from') reflects surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself, so the data is thin.

definition: To determine the size or amount of something by a fixed standard, or to give out a quantity by measure.
article: μετρέω means to measure something—by space, number, or value—and by extension to give out an amount by measure. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times across 5 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "measure" in 10 of those (91%). The word was thoroughly ordinary in daily Koine: papyri use it for measuring out grain or making up a deficiency "from one's private means," and the Septuagint uses it for Hebrew מָדַד (to measure) and related terms. Note the proverbial saying behind Matthew 7:2, Mark 4:24, and Luke 6:38—"with the measure you use, it will be measured to you."

definition: A cousin — a relative descended from one's aunt or uncle, on either the father's or mother's side.
article: ἀνεψιός means "cousin," the child of one's aunt or uncle. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Colossians 4:10, where Mark is identified as the cousin of Barnabas; the Septuagint uses it once as well, at Numbers 36:11. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the precise meaning: documents specify a cousin "on the father's side" or "on the mother's side," showing the word covered cousins from either parent.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests largely on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: To be frightened or alarmed, especially by news or some unsettling event.
article: In the New Testament θροέω always appears in the passive and means to be troubled or alarmed, typically in warnings not to panic over reports of wars or end-times rumors. All 3 Byzantine occurrences (Matthew 24:6, Mark 13:7, 2 Thessalonians 2:2) are rendered "alarmed," and the Berean Study Bible agrees in 67% of cases. Interestingly, classical Greek used the active voice quite differently — to cry aloud or make an outcry — a sense that has dropped away by the time of the New Testament, where only the "be troubled" meaning survives.
caution: The word is rare — only 3 Byzantine occurrences and a single Septuagint instance — and the modern "alarmed" sense diverges from the classical "cry aloud," so the evidence base is thin.

definition: The deep, open sea—the vast main waters away from shore.
article: πέλαγος refers to the deep or open sea, the wide expanse of water far from land. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Acts 27:5, where it plainly means the sea, and in Matthew 18:6, in the phrase "the depth of the sea" (literally the πέλαγος of the θάλασσα). The papyri make its everyday flavor vivid—an inscription from the third century B.C. records a Jewish man named Theodotos giving thanks for being "saved from the open sea" (ἐκ πελάγους).
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the range is thinly attested, and the two renderings ("depths" vs. "sea") reflect different phrasings rather than firmly distinct senses.

definition: A person who is paralyzed, unable to move part or all of the body.
article: παραλυτικός simply describes someone afflicted with paralysis, and every one of its 10 New Testament occurrences points to that single idea. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "paralytic" or "paralytic son" in the clearest cases, with the rest folded into surrounding phrasing about the men carried on mats. Although it appears only in the Gospels here, Moulton-Milligan note it as a rare word also found in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it was real medical vocabulary of the time.

definition: Pisidia, a region in the south of Asia Minor (modern Turkey) within the Roman province of Galatia.
article: Pisidia is a place name for a mountainous region in southern Asia Minor, mentioned twice in the New Testament (Acts 13:14 and 14:24). The two occurrences split evenly between referring to the region itself ("Pisidia") and describing "Pisidian Antioch" as inland. Notably, Moulton-Milligan and the scholar Ramsay point out that Pisidian Antioch was actually near Pisidia rather than strictly within it, which is why the city carried the regional label.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a computed low-confidence tier, the precise geographic scope is thin and the "Pisidian Antioch" reference lies near rather than inside the region proper.

definition: A standing above others—whether in skill, rank, or status—used for excellence, eloquence, or a position of authority.
article: ὑπεροχή literally means a projection or eminence, like the peak of a mountain, and figuratively points to standing above others in skill, rank, or character. In its two New Testament uses it splits evenly: once for excellence of speech ("eloquence" in 1 Corinthians 2:1) and once for those in positions of authority (1 Timothy 2:2). That second use is nicely illuminated by an inscription from Pergamum (after 133 BC) and a papyrus where the phrase "those in eminence" refers to persons of consequence—exactly the New Testament sense.
caution: With only 2 occurrences spread across two distinct senses, the evidence base is thin and confidence is low.

definition: The Adriatic Sea, a name sailors extended to the broad waters between Greece, Italy, Malta, and Crete.
article: Ἀδρίας is the name of a sea, appearing just once in the New Testament (Acts 27:27), in Paul's storm-tossed voyage. Though the name properly belonged to the Adriatic, ancient sailors stretched it to cover the open Mediterranean southeast of Italy — the waters between Greece, Italy, Malta, and Crete. The lexicons note this widened usage in later Greek, which fits the shipwreck setting where the vessel was driven across that southern stretch of sea.
caution: This proper name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its exact geographic range here rests on broader Greek usage rather than repeated biblical evidence.

definition: To plow, breaking up soil with a plow in preparation for planting.
article: ἀροτριόω is a farming word meaning to plow the ground, a later form of the older verb ἀρόω. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 17:7 and 1 Corinthians 9:10), always about literal field work, and shows up in everyday Koine papyri describing oxen plowing along a public road. In the Greek Old Testament it translates several Hebrew farming terms, mostly חָרַשׁ ('to plow'), and one striking note is that in Sirach 7:12 it carries the figurative sense 'to devise' (plotting like one plowing up a scheme).
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences (none in the critical SBL text), and the digest's third measured sense 'thresher' likely reflects a neighboring word in 1 Corinthians 9:10 rather than this verb.

definition: To be tossed back and forth by waves, used figuratively of being unsettled or swept around by shifting ideas.
article: This vivid sea-image word means "to be tossed about by waves," and the New Testament uses it figuratively in its single occurrence (Ephesians 4:14) for people swept this way and that by shifting teachings. The lexicons agree on the wave-tossed picture, and a real-world papyrus parallel from Vettius Valens applies it to a helmsman tossed about and losing his bearings while battling the sea. In the Septuagint it appears once, at Isaiah 57:20, describing the restless tossing of the sea.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its figurative range rests on thin evidence; note also that the digest's measured rendering label ("clever") looks like a tagging artifact rather than the word's actual meaning.

definition: A dwelling-place or habitation — a place where someone or something lives.
article: Κατοικητήριον means simply a dwelling-place or habitation, built from the verb κατοικέω, "to dwell." It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice (Ephesians 2:22 and Revelation 18:2), and in both cases it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word. It shows up far more often in the Septuagint, 18 times across 7 books, where it usually renders the Hebrew מָכוֹן (7×), a word for a fixed or established place.
caution: The two New Testament occurrences are both absorbed into phrasing, so its precise force rests largely on Septuagint usage and the lexicons.

definition: A sheet of paper made from the papyrus plant, used for writing letters and documents.
article: χάρτης is a sheet of paper made from strips of the papyrus plant, the standard everyday writing material of the ancient world. It appears only once in the New Testament (2 John 12), where the writer says he has more to say but does not want to use "paper and ink." The word is common in surviving Koine papyri and inscriptions; in the Septuagint it stands behind the Hebrew word for "scroll" (megillah) in passages like Jeremiah 36.
caution: The lexica plainly mean "paper/papyrus sheet," but the measured corpus data labels its single occurrence as "face," which looks like a data error rather than a real sense.

definition: To ward off an attack or threat, defending oneself or coming to someone's aid against an aggressor.
article: This verb, used in the middle voice, means to ward off danger—either defending yourself or stepping in to protect someone else. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (at Acts 7:24, where Moses defends a mistreated Israelite), and it's woven into the phrasing rather than translated as a single word. It shows up 8 times in the Septuagint, where it can also carry the sense of requiting or repaying an enemy.
caution: Evidence is thin—just one New Testament occurrence and few elsewhere—and Moulton-Milligan notes the word seems to have nearly dropped out of everyday Koine speech.

definition: A fellow person regarded as one's neighbor; as an adverb, near or close by.
article: In the New Testament πλησίον overwhelmingly means "neighbor," the person beside you whom you are called to love—it's rendered that way in 14 of 16 Byzantine occurrences (93%). Underneath, the word literally means "near" or "close by": it began as an adverb (as in John 4:5) and is still used that way in everyday Koine papyri, where one document mentions an estate "near Murmux." In the Septuagint it appears 168 times and mostly translates the Hebrew word רֵעַ (rēaʿ, "friend, fellow"), used 103 times, which is exactly the background of the famous command to love your neighbor as yourself.

definition: Foam or froth, especially the bubbly saliva produced at the mouth during a convulsion or fit.
senseLabels: foam or froth at the mouth
article: ἀφρός means foam or froth — the bubbly substance seen here as saliva at the mouth during a seizure. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 9:39, where a spirit makes a boy convulse and foam at the mouth. Classical writers used it more broadly for the foam of the sea or of an angry lion, and Moulton-Milligan notes its presence in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; the medical writers' use of the word, documented by Hobart, fits Luke's well-known interest in clinical detail.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single passage, though the broader meaning 'foam, froth' is well attested in classical sources.

definition: A spot or stain that mars something, used figuratively for a moral blemish or disgrace.
article: σπίλος refers to a spot or stain, and in the New Testament's two occurrences it always carries the figurative sense of a moral blemish (rendered "blemish" 100% of the time). Interestingly, in earlier Greek the word originally meant a rock or cliff; only in later writers did it come to mean a spot or stain, matching the Attic word κηλίς. In 2 Peter 2:13 it is even applied to people themselves — a usage paralleled in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who calls disreputable persons "the dregs of humanity" driven from the city.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and uncertain derivation, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on the meaning.

definition: A reason or cause for something, or in legal settings a formal accusation or charge against someone.
article: αἰτία covers two related ideas: a general "reason" or "cause" for something, and a legal "accusation" or formal charge brought against a person. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 20 times across 8 books, with the legal sense prominent—it's the word for the "charge against" Jesus posted on the cross (Matthew 27:37, Mark 15:26). The everyday papyri confirm this courtroom flavor: one third-century BC document uses it of a man sent to Alexandria "to meet a charge against him and make his defense," and Moulton-Milligan note it was a standard legal formula.
caution: In 6 of 20 occurrences the word is absorbed into English phrasing without a distinct rendering, so the sense split is somewhat approximate.

definition: To call something to mind, recall, or keep someone in your thoughts; in the passive, to be remembered.
article: This verb covers the whole act of remembering—calling a fact, person, or event back to mind. In the Byzantine New Testament its 23 uses split almost evenly between active remembering and being remembered, with a couple of instances of "recalling." In the Septuagint it appears 72 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew זָכַר ("to remember," 54×), and the everyday papyri show the same range—one second-century letter has a writer saying it is necessary to keep someone's good character in mind. Note too that one form, the perfect μέμνημαι, carries a present-tense sense of "bear in mind," and when used with a negative about sins it shades into "forgive."
caution: The critical (SBLGNT) text contains zero occurrences against the Byzantine text's 23, so the precise word-counts depend on which Greek edition you follow.

definition: A paid worker hired for wages, contrasted with a slave who serves without pay.
article: Místhios describes a wage-earner — a laborer who works for pay rather than a slave bound to a household. The word is built from the noun for "wage" (misthós), and in the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the parable of the prodigal son in Luke 15, where the wayward son thinks even his father's hired servants are better off than he is. Interestingly, this is not a peculiarly biblical term: the papyri show it in ordinary contracts, such as one from A.D. 162–163 that names a "místhios" alongside a "partner," and in the Septuagint it consistently renders the Hebrew word for a hired laborer (śākîr).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured sense range is thin, though the papyri and Septuagint agree on the basic meaning.

definition: The act of deceiving someone, or the misleading quality of something that lures people away from the truth.
article: ἀπάτη means deception or the deceitful pull of something, appearing 7 times in the New Testament. About half the occurrences (3×) are rendered "deception," while the rest describe the deceitful quality of something else, often attached to a noun—"the deceitfulness of riches" (Matthew 13:22, Mark 4:19), "the deceitfulness of sin" (Hebrews 3:13). The everyday papyri confirm a concrete legal edge: one Oxyrhynchus document uses ἀπάτη for a lawsuit over fraud, so the word could mean outright trickery, not just abstract delusion.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and several tied to following nouns, the line between active "deception" and the passive "deceitfulness" of something is somewhat fluid.

definition: To place, set, or lay something on a person or thing, often in the formal gesture of laying hands on someone.
article: At its core ἐπιτίθημι means to set or lay one thing upon another, built from ἐπί ("on") and τίθημι ("put"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 41 times, rendered "place" in 12 (55%) and "laid" in 8 (36%), though in 19 of those it dissolves into the surrounding English phrasing with no word of its own. A frequent special use is the laying on of hands — for blessing, healing, or commissioning, as when Jesus places his hands on the blind or sick. Strong's notes it can carry either a friendly or hostile sense ("impose"), and the Septuagint uses it heavily, 239 times across 26 books, often for the Hebrew śûm ("set," 28×) and sāmak ("lean, lay on," 24×).

definition: To leap or jump for joy, used of a sudden bound of excitement—including the movement of an unborn child.
article: σκιρτάω means to leap, jump, or bound, and in the New Testament it always carries the sense of joyful movement. It appears only 3 times, all in Luke—twice describing John the Baptist leaping inside Elizabeth's womb (Luke 1:41, 44) and once urging the persecuted to leap for joy (Luke 6:23). It was an ordinary word in everyday Koine: a tomb inscription pairs it with delight ("I leap and rejoice"), and a related noun appears in a Christian hymn meaning "dancing," set against sorrow. In the Septuagint it even renders the unborn twins' struggling inside Rebekah (Genesis 25:22).
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament uses, all in Luke—so the measured "senses" are really one core meaning (leaping for joy) shown in three different settings.

definition: An adverb meaning "nearer" or "closer," used of moving in close along a coast.
article: This is a rare adverb meaning "nearer" or "close in," the comparative form of a word for "near." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:13, where it describes a ship sailing close in along the coast of Crete; lexicons render it "close" or "nearer." Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible's automated tally records it here as "opportunity"—almost certainly because the rendering captured surrounding words about seizing a chance to sail, not the adverb itself, which the standard lexica agree means "nearer."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured "opportunity" rendering disagrees with every lexicon, which uniformly give "nearer/close," so treat the corpus tally with care.

definition: To notice or grasp something through perception or understanding.
article: αἰσθάνομαι means to perceive, notice, or come to understand something. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 9:45, where it describes how the disciples failed to grasp Jesus' meaning. Although Moulton-Milligan notes a scholar once claimed the word was absent from the papyri, they correct this with everyday examples — including one that simply means 'noticed anything' — showing it was ordinary Koine vocabulary.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, and the BSB rendering 'veiled' actually reflects the broader sentence rather than this verb's own core meaning of 'perceive.'

definition: Belonging to or living in the sea; used of marine creatures.
article: ἐνάλιος describes things that live in the sea, and in the New Testament it appears as the plural noun phrase "sea creatures." It shows up just once, in James 3:7, where it is part of a list of animal types humans have tamed. The word is built from ἐν ("in") and ἅλς ("the sea"), so it literally means "in the sea."
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: Poor or destitute, lacking material resources; sometimes used figuratively of those who are spiritually needy or humble before God.
article: πτωχός describes someone who is poor — and in its earliest classical sense, specifically a beggar who crouches or cowers. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "poor" in 30 of 33 occurrences (100% of the times it gets its own English word), covering both literal poverty and figurative uses like "poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). Moulton-Milligan note a fascinating detail: in everyday Koine papyri the word "was always used in a bad sense until it was ennobled by the Gospels." In the Septuagint it appears 92 times, most often translating the Hebrew words דָּל (18×) and עָנִי (17×), both meaning the lowly or afflicted poor.

definition: To shine or give light, to light something up, or figuratively to enlighten someone's mind or bring hidden things into the open.
article: φωτίζω comes from φῶς ("light") and covers a spread from literal shining to figurative enlightenment. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times across 7 books, rendered "illuminated" 4×, "light" 2×, and "enlightened" 2×, the last often describing spiritual understanding being opened up. The lexicons add a further nuance — "to bring to light, make known" — and a magical papyrus (3rd century AD) captures the elemental sense beautifully, naming God as the one "who lights up and darkens the world."

definition: To soil, stain, or pollute something so that it becomes morally or ritually unclean.
article: μολύνω literally means to soil or stain, but in the New Testament's three occurrences it is always used figuratively for moral or spiritual defilement (1 Corinthians 8:7; Revelation 3:4; 14:4). The Septuagint uses it about 10 times across 7 books, rendering several Hebrew words including גָּאַל and טָבַל. A striking parallel comes from an early papyrus fragment (P Oxy V. 840), which speaks of someone 'polluted' walking in a temple that is meant to be pure—echoing the same figurative sense of staining what should be clean.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 NT occurrences—and the digest's sense breakdown mixes phrase fragments rather than clearly distinct meanings, so treat the single 'defile' sense as the reliable one.

definition: To place something underneath, used figuratively for risking one's own life or for suggesting and advising someone.
article: This verb literally means "to place under," but in the New Testament's two occurrences it appears only in figurative uses. In Romans 16:4 it describes Priscilla and Aquila laying down—risking—their own necks for Paul, while in 1 Timothy 4:6 the middle voice means to suggest or advise. Moulton-Milligan cites a private letter from the first or second century AD supporting the idea that in 1 Timothy 4:6 the word means simply suggesting or advising rather than reminding someone of what they already knew.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the rendered senses ("grateful," "pointing") differing sharply from the lexicon glosses, the practical meaning here rests on thin evidence.

definition: The act of moving something from one place to another, or changing something that was previously established.
article: μετάθεσις means moving or transferring something, and by extension changing something already in place. The translation data captures only one of its three New Testament uses as 'removal' (Hebrews 12:27), while the other two get absorbed into surrounding phrasing — yet the lexicons split the range into two clear ideas: physical removal (as when Enoch was 'taken' in Hebrews 11:5) and a change of an established order (the change of the law in Hebrews 7:12). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the concrete sense, with one third-century BC document using it for 'the removal of a stair' during house repairs.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and just 1 yielding a measured English word, the sense data is thin, though the lexicons agree on the basic range.

definition: Wealth or abundance, whether literal money and possessions or a figurative fullness of something valuable.
article: πλοῦτος means riches or wealth, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "riches" in 16 of its 22 New Testament occurrences (84%). The word covers both literal money and possessions and a figurative, abundant fullness of good things. One interesting detail: in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew עֹ֫שֶׁר (34×), and Paul tends to use it figuratively, even shifting it from masculine to neuter declension eight times in Hellenistic style. Everyday Koine papyri use it literally too, as in a phrase about someone "made proud by wealth."

definition: Describing a garment that reaches down to the feet — a long, ankle-length robe.
article: ποδήρης describes clothing that hangs all the way down to the feet, built from the word for "foot" (πούς). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Revelation 1:13, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Study Bible both render it "long" (a long robe). In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times across 3 books, where it translates several different Hebrew words for priestly and ceremonial garments — including the robe (מְעִיל) and other temple vestments — and the Letter of Aristeas even pictures golden bells around the border of such a long robe.
caution: Confidence is rated low: this word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: An act of willing or wishing — what someone wants or chooses to do.
senseLabels: an act of will or wish
article: θέλησις names the act of willing — what a person wants, chooses, or determines to do, formed from the verb θέλω ("to will, wish"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 2:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gifts" in describing how God distributed gifts according to his will. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times across 5 books, translating Hebrew words for favor or delight (רָצוֹן in Proverbs 8:35) and for what one takes pleasure in (חֵפֶץ in Ezekiel 18:23), which fits the lexicons' core meaning of "will" or "willing."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall evidence, the precise force here is uncertain, and the standard "will" of the lexicons sits behind the contextual rendering "gifts."

definition: An adverb meaning 'more' or 'to a greater degree,' often used to mark what is preferred or chosen instead of something else.
article: μᾶλλον is a comparative adverb that fundamentally signals 'more' or a greater degree, and it appears 82 times across 17 New Testament books. Its range stretches from simple comparison ('more,' 20×) to expressing preference or substitution ('rather than,' 'instead'), and it often pairs with qualifiers to mean 'how much more' or 'all the more.' Notably, in about 11 of its 82 occurrences it carries no English word of its own — it just shapes the phrasing — and the everyday Koine papyri show the same flexible use, as in an Oxyrhynchus document reading 'in defiance of rather than in obedience to the proclamations.'

definition: A handwritten document, especially a signed record of debt or a legal bond.
article: χειρόγραφον literally means something written by hand, but in everyday usage it had narrowed to a specific legal sense: a signed IOU or bond recording a debt. The papyri make this concrete — one document (P Oxy IV.745) speaks of a buyer drawing up a χειρόγραφον for a wine purchase, and another asks someone to press a debtor to settle his bond. It appears just once in the New Testament (Colossians 2:14), where it is used figuratively, and the Septuagint examples in Tobit likewise refer to a written record.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and was absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word, so its precise force there is debated.

definition: To direct or command someone to do something, giving them instructions to carry out.
article: In the New Testament, συντάσσω means to instruct or command, and it always appears with a person who is being given the order — as when the disciples did "as Jesus directed them." In the Byzantine New Testament it occurs only twice (three times in the critical text), and in both cases it is woven into the phrasing rather than translated as a single standalone word. It is far more common in the Septuagint (110 times), where it chiefly renders the Hebrew verb צָוָה ("to command"), and the everyday papyri confirm this practical sense, as in a letter where "the King has been bidding me sow a second crop on the land."
caution: New Testament evidence is thin (only 2–3 occurrences, all absorbed into phrasing), so the sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: Manaen, a man in the Antioch church who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch.
article: Manaen is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:1, where he is listed among the prophets and teachers at Antioch. It is a Greek form of a Jewish name (the Hebrew מְנַחֵם, Menahem), given a Greek look by the -ην ending, and the same name turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. Dodson notes he was probably connected to Herod Antipas' court.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once in the New Testament, so there is no real semantic range to map; note the measured-sense label oddly shows "Niger," which appears to be a data mismatch.

definition: A person who kills or violently strikes his own mother.
article: This rare word combines "mother" with a root meaning "to smite or thresh," yielding either "matricide" or, more literally, "a striker of one's mother." It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:9, in a list of the lawless and ungodly. Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering here shows "father" rather than "mother" — a likely tagging artifact, since the word's components and the classical lexica (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) clearly point to the mother. Abbott-Smith notes the alternative "smiter of his mother," comparing Exodus 21:15, and Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: The single measured rendering reads "father," which conflicts with the word's components and all the cited lexica that point to the mother; treat the measured sense as unreliable here.

definition: An untranslated Aramaic phrase meaning roughly "our Lord, come!" or "our Lord has come," used as an early Christian exclamation.
article: This is actually an Aramaic phrase carried over untranslated into Greek, appearing only in 1 Corinthians 16:22 (2 occurrences in the Byzantine text but absent from the SBLGNT critical text). Scholars divide and read it two ways: "maran atha" (our Lord has come) or "marana tha" (our Lord, come!), and the sources genuinely disagree on which is right. One striking parallel comes from the early Christian manual called the Didache, where the same word appears in a eucharistic prayer alongside "Amen," showing it functioned as a familiar Christian watchword.
caution: The measured "senses" here are just fragments of a single Aramaic phrase, not real meanings, and authorities disagree on whether it means "our Lord has come" or "our Lord, come!"

definition: Picked out or chosen, often describing people whom God has selected; in the New Testament usually His elect.
article: ἐκλεκτός means picked out or selected, and across its 24 Byzantine uses it almost always describes people chosen by God — rendered "elect" about 46% of the time and "chosen" 38%. The word carries a basic everyday sense too: papyri use it for a "choice" lodging being rented and for baskets "selected" as better quality than the rest, and Paul applies that flavor of "choice" or eminent to Rufus in Romans 16:13. In the Septuagint it appears 84 times, translating several Hebrew words including בְּחִיר ("chosen") and מִבְחָר ("choicest"), the background for its strong Israel-as-chosen-people association.

definition: Lacking experience or skill in something, especially through having had no practice or training in it.
article: This word describes someone who lacks experience or familiarity with a thing, usually paired with a genitive naming what they're unskilled in. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 5:13, where a person who only takes spiritual milk is called "inexperienced" in the word of righteousness, and every English version measured renders it that way. The everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: a Giss document describes a man as ἄπειρος of certain places, meaning unfamiliar with them, though in older Attic inscriptions the closely related form ἀπείρων could mean "endless" instead.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: Going without food, usually as a deliberate religious practice, though sometimes the hunger is forced by circumstances.
article: Νηστεία means abstaining from food, most often the voluntary, religious kind tied to prayer and devotion. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "fasting" in half its 8 New Testament appearances, with two more folded into the phrase "except by fasting"; in two cases it gets no English word of its own. The Septuagint uses it 27 times, mostly for the Hebrew צוֹם (17×), and in Acts 27:9 it points specifically to the fast of the Day of Atonement. Abbott-Smith notes it can also describe involuntary going-hungry, as in 2 Corinthians 6:5 and 11:27.
caution: The two phrase occurrences (Matthew 17:21, Mark 9:29) are absent from many critical texts, so the evidence base is thinner than the eight Byzantine occurrences suggest.

definition: To go along with someone, following or accompanying them as a companion.
article: συνακολουθέω means to follow along with someone, that is, to accompany or go together with them. It's built from σύν ("with") and ἀκολουθέω ("follow"), so the "together" sense is baked right in, and it always takes the person being followed in the dative or after μετά. In the everyday papyri the word turns up in ordinary contexts, including an instruction to "go along with him to the house" — a plain, practical sense of accompanying someone on a journey or errand.
caution: This word appears only 2 times in the Byzantine New Testament (3 in the critical text), so its range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To eat or consume food, including the food itself in some uses.
article: This verb means simply to eat or take in food, and that literal sense dominates: 84 of 96 Byzantine occurrences (91%) are rendered "eat." In a few places the focus shifts slightly toward what is eaten — "something to eat" (5×) or even "food" itself (2×, as in John 4:33 and 1 Corinthians 9:4). It's actually the future and aorist forms of the more common verb ἐσθίω, and in the Septuagint it shows up 315 times, almost always translating the Hebrew אָכַל ("to eat").

definition: A violent shaking of the ground or sea, most often an earthquake but sometimes a sudden storm.
article: σεισμός comes from the verb σείω, "to shake," and describes a sudden, violent commotion — usually an earthquake, but it can also mean a tempest. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "earthquake" in 8 of those (73%); the one striking exception is Matthew 8:24, where it describes a storm shaking the sea rather than the ground. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew רַעַשׁ (10×), and everyday papyri use it both literally — an inscription mentions monuments that "fell in the earthquake" — and metaphorically for extortion or upheaval.

definition: To look down on someone or treat them with contempt, refusing to take them seriously.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Titus 2:15), περιφρονέω means to despise or look down on someone, and both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it that way 100% of the time. Built from περί ('around') and φρονέω ('to think'), it could literally mean 'to think beyond' — and Abbott-Smith notes an older sense, 'to examine on all sides, consider carefully' (Aristophanes), alongside the later sense 'to despise.' The everyday Koine usage backs the 'despise' reading: a papyrus from A.D. 303 (P Oxy I.71) records a widow complaining that two overseers, 'despising my inability,' had mismanaged her affairs.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests on a single verse plus outside sources, and the classical lexica record an older 'consider carefully' sense not seen in the biblical text.

definition: In a generous, openhearted way—giving freely without holding back or finding fault.
article: This adverb appears only once in the New Testament, in James 1:5, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berea Standard Bible both render it "generously"—God gives wisdom freely to all who ask. The word comes from a root meaning "single" or "simple," and older lexicons capture a wide range: simply, sincerely, graciously, or bountifully. Interestingly, in everyday Koine papyri the word shows up most often in legal documents, where it added emphasis to a statement—for example, "any other single act of injustice" in a second-century Oxyrhynchus contract.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a broad spread of older glosses (from "simply" to "sincerely" to "generously"), the precise shade of meaning in James 1:5 rests on thin evidence.

definition: An adverb meaning well, rightly, or as an exclamation of approval, "Well done!"
article: εὖ is a small adverb that mostly means "well" or "rightly" (used in 3 of its 6 New Testament occurrences), but it also serves as an exclamation of praise, "Well done!", as a master commends his servants in Matthew 25:21, 23. In the Septuagint it appears 40 times and usually renders the Hebrew yatav (25×), "to do well" or "to make good," often in set phrases like "to do good to" someone. Notably, Moulton-Milligan observe that εὖ became rare in everyday papyri, where καλῶς largely replaced it, though it lingered in polite letter-writing phrases like "please" and "farewell."
caution: With only 6 occurrences, the line between the plain adverb "well," the exclamation "Well done!", and the phrase "do good to" depends on context, and Abbott-Smith notes some manuscripts read εὖγε or εὐποιεῖν instead.

definition: Describing someone who is guiltless, free from blame for a wrong or offense.
article: ἀναίτιος means "innocent" or "guiltless," built from the negative prefix and a root for "cause" or "blame" — literally "not the cause." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Matthew 12 (verses 5 and 7), where Jesus calls his disciples guiltless. In the Septuagint it shows up 4 times, always rendering the Hebrew נָקִי and consistently paired with "blood" (innocent blood), and Moulton-Milligan note an inscription echoing this very LXX phrase "the innocent blood" in a Jewish prayer for vengeance.
caution: The two listed "senses" are really one meaning (innocent) shown across two verses, and with only 2 New Testament uses the evidence base is thin.

definition: The process or state of being made holy and set apart for God, also called sanctification or consecration.
article: ἁγιασμός describes either the ongoing process of becoming holy or the resulting state of holiness, which is why translators render it both "holiness" and "sanctification." Across its 10 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible uses "holiness" most often (4×), with two cases stressing the idea of "leading holiness" (Romans 6:19, 22). As a verbal noun ending in -μός, it properly points to the action of making holy rather than the finished condition, though grammarians note that in places like 1 Timothy 2:15 it may lean toward the resultant state.
caution: Scholars disagree on whether the word names the process of sanctification or the resulting state of holiness, and this can shift from verse to verse.

definition: Devout and morally pure in a way that pleases God, said of holy people, God himself, and the promised Messiah.
article: ὅσιος describes someone who is religiously right and pure—pious, devout, set apart for God. In the New Testament it covers a striking range: it labels ordinary holy people (Titus 1:8), describes God himself (Revelation 16:5), and twice serves as a title for the Messiah, "your Holy One," in Acts 2:27 and 13:35. In the Septuagint it appears 42 times and most often translates the Hebrew חָסִיד (godly, faithful), used 7 times, and the papyri show the word was common in everyday religious inscriptions, including a leaden plate from Cnidus invoking ὅσια on people who keep a trust.
caution: With only 7 occurrences in the Byzantine text, several measured "senses" reflect rendering quirks rather than distinct meanings, so the labels for single uses should be read loosely.

definition: An exclamatory word placed before someone you are addressing, signaling either solemn address or strong emotion like surprise or rebuke.
article: ὦ is a small interjection used when speaking directly to a person, often translated "O" (9 of 17 times in the Byzantine NT, 53%) or "O you." It carries two flavors: simple address, as in Acts 1:1, and emotional outburst expressing surprise or reproof, as in Matthew 15:28 or Luke 24:25. In the Septuagint (41× across 15 books) it most often renders the Hebrew הוֹי (10×), a cry of woe or warning, and Moulton notes that this word was used less and less in everyday Greek than in earlier classical writing.

definition: Loose dirt or dust — soil thrown or poured out, the kind people shook off their feet or threw on their heads.
article: Χόος refers to loose earth or dust, the kind that can be poured out, scattered, or thrown. Across the Greek Old Testament it appears 43 times in 19 books, most often standing in for the Hebrew עָפָר ('dust'), 31 times. In the Byzantine New Testament it occurs only twice: the dust disciples shake from their feet (Mark 6:11) and the dust mourners throw on their heads (Revelation 18:19). Abbott-Smith notes that the basic classical meaning is 'earth, soil,' and that the narrower sense 'dust' belongs to later writers like the Septuagint, so both meanings are well attested.
caution: It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so the New Testament evidence is thin.

definition: To sleep, and very often as a gentle figure of speech meaning to die.
article: κοιμάω covers ordinary sleeping but in the New Testament it overwhelmingly carries the figurative sense of dying, gently described as "falling asleep." In the Byzantine text it appears 18 times, with about 47% rendered "fallen asleep" and the remaining occurrences as "asleep" or "sleep," while the literal and figurative senses blend together. It is extremely common in the Septuagint, appearing 188 times and most often translating the Hebrew shakab ("to lie down"), and the papyri show its everyday use—one woman writes that she "went to bed" without eating from anxiety over her absent husband.

definition: A person who deceives others by misleading their minds; a deceiver or seducer.
article: φρεναπάτης combines the words for "mind" (φρήν) and "deceit" (ἀπάτη), describing someone who leads other people's thinking astray. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:10, and the standard lexicons agree on the sense "deceiver" or "seducer." One striking piece of evidence comes from the papyri: a second-century B.C. document (P Grenf I.1) has a woman calling her former lover "the deceiver," confirming the everyday meaning was deceiving others rather than the alternative "one who deceives his own mind" (i.e. conceited) that some scholars proposed.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and scholars have debated whether it means "deceiver of others" or "one self-deceived," though the papyri favor the former.

definition: Describing something wild or untamed, growing naturally in the fields, and by extension fierce or savage.
article: This adjective comes from the word for "field" (ἀγρός) and basically means "wild" — untamed and naturally occurring, like the wild honey John the Baptist ate (Matthew 3:4, Mark 1:6). It can also carry a fiercer, more savage sense, as in Jude 1:13, where it pictures raging waves. Interestingly, everyday papyri and inscriptions use the word for a malignant or angry sore, showing how naturally it shaded from "wild" into "violent."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, all rendered "wild," the fiercer sense rests on limited evidence from outside sources and a single passage.

definition: To go or come out of a place, to leave or depart from where one was.
article: This common verb means to go or come out from somewhere — to leave, depart, or exit. Built from ἐκ ("out of") and ἔρχομαι ("come"), it shows up 223 times in the Byzantine New Testament, with renderings clustering around "went out," "out," "left," "went," "came out," and "came." In the Septuagint it appears 617 times, overwhelmingly translating Hebrew יָצָא ("go out"), and a complaint from an Oxyrhynchus papyrus (A.D. 30–35) uses it in the same everyday sense: "finally she left the house." It also covers special uses like demons being driven out of a person and prisoners being released.
caution: Several minor sense labels ("Jesus," "out come," "left go") reflect quirks of how renderings were counted rather than distinct meanings, so treat them as the same basic idea of going out.

definition: Too wonderful to put into words; impossible to express in speech.
article: ἀνεκλάλητος describes something so overwhelming that ordinary speech cannot capture it. It is built from a negative prefix plus a form meaning "to speak out," so it literally means "not able to be spoken out." The word appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 1:8, where joy is described as "unspeakable" — and in that single use it gets folded into the surrounding phrase rather than standing as its own English word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range of meaning cannot be measured and rests on that single passage.

definition: A cluster of ripe grapes, or the grapes themselves growing on the vine.
article: σταφυλή means a bunch or cluster of ripe grapes, and it shows up only 3 times in the New Testament. In the Septuagint it appears 22 times across 11 books, most often translating the Hebrew word for grapes (17 times). According to Swete, it specifically describes the ripe grape-cluster (as opposed to an unripe one) and emphasizes the grapes themselves rather than the woody cluster they grow on; the everyday papyri back this up, mentioning things like "a box of exceedingly good grapes."
caution: The measured sense "thornbushes" reflects how one occurrence (Luke 6:44) was rendered in context, not a separate meaning of the word itself, which consistently denotes grapes.

definition: An impersonal verb meaning that something is possible, allowable, or fitting to happen.
article: ἐνδέχεται is an impersonal form (literally "it admits") that means something is possible or acceptable, typically followed by an infinitive. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 13:33, where it describes what is fitting or possible. The everyday papyri confirm this ordinary sense: a document from 246 B.C. uses the phrase ὡς ἐνδέχεται, "as far as it is possible," exactly the way Koine speakers used it in daily life. Abbott-Smith notes a broader range elsewhere, including "to admit, approve" in the Septuagint.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse plus outside evidence.

definition: To be physically sick or to be weak in body, strength, faith, or moral capacity.
article: This verb covers two closely related ideas: being physically ill and being weak or feeble in a broader sense. In the Byzantine New Testament it's almost evenly split — rendered "sick" 15 times (52%) and "weak" 13 times (45%), with the Majority Standard Bible and BSB agreeing fully on both. In the Septuagint it shows up 58 times and most often translates the Hebrew כָּשַׁל, "to stumble," and the everyday papyri preserve a touchingly blunt note where a writer squeezes in the single word "I'm sick" between household details and his closing greetings.

definition: A spoken curse or invocation calling down evil on someone.
article: ἀρά means a curse — words spoken to call down evil or harm on someone. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 3:14, where it's rendered "cursing," though the broader critical text counts many more uses. Interestingly, Strong's notes the word properly meant a prayer (something lifted up to heaven), and that older sense shades into the negative meaning of an imprecation; in the Septuagint it appears 28 times, most often translating the Hebrew אָלָה, an oath or curse.
caution: With only one Byzantine occurrence and an overall low confidence tier, the New Testament evidence is thin, and lexicons note an older neutral sense ("prayer") alongside the measured meaning.

definition: To endure mistreatment or hardship together with others, sharing in their suffering.
article: This verb describes choosing to endure adversity alongside other people rather than escaping it. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:25, where Moses chose to suffer with God's people instead of enjoying fleeting pleasures. The word combines "with" (σύν) and "to mistreat" (κακουχέω), and Abbott-Smith notes it is found nowhere else; Moulton-Milligan adds that a closely related form turns up in an everyday Egyptian papyrus from A.D. 194.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and, according to the lexicons, essentially nowhere else, so its meaning rests on a single passage.

definition: The rough, surging water of a storm-tossed sea — choppy, churning waves rather than a single wave.
article: κλύδων describes turbulent, rough water — the heaving, churning surface of a sea whipped up by a storm. The careful sense, as Hort noted, is "rough water" generally rather than a single wave (contrast κῦμα, "a wave"); the word appears only twice in the New Testament (Luke 8:24 and James 1:6) and four times in the Septuagint, where it renders Hebrew words for stilling, tossing, or storm. The two NT renderings differ in surface wording — one English version reads "arose," the other "wind" — but both point to the same picture of storm-driven water.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 NT occurrences, and translators render it differently each time, so the precise English wording is uncertain even though the core meaning is clear.

definition: To fill someone completely with food or other things until they are fully satisfied or even glutted.
article: κορέννυμι means to fill up completely or satisfy to the point of having more than enough, used both literally of food and figuratively of spiritual abundance. It appears only twice in the New Testament: literally in Acts 27:38 (eating their fill before lightening the ship) and metaphorically in 1 Corinthians 4:8 (where Paul says the Corinthians are already filled or sated). An interesting witness comes from a third-century AD inscription cited by Moulton-Milligan, which uses the word for an appetite that, even when filled, was never truly satisfied.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the measured evidence is thin, and one of those uses was absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a distinct English word.

definition: To fall away from faith, abandoning the belief one once held.
article: In the New Testament παραπίπτω appears only once, in Hebrews 6:6, where it describes people who have fallen away from the faith. The wider Greek range is much broader: classical authors and the Septuagint use it for things that merely 'befall' or happen by chance, as well as for failing or going astray, and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew מָעַל ('to act unfaithfully,' 4 times). A papyrus from AD 129 uses it of a contract whose terms are 'broken' or rendered invalid, which nicely supports the serious, negative sense it carries in Hebrews.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there leans heavily on outside evidence rather than internal usage.

definition: A riddle or obscure saying; something seen indirectly, unclearly, or imperfectly understood.
article: αἴνιγμα refers to a riddle or dark, puzzling saying — something perceived only obscurely rather than plainly. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 13:12, where Paul speaks of seeing indirectly, as though in a dim reflection; the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles both render this idea of seeing imperfectly. In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times, almost always translating the Hebrew חִידָה ("riddle"), as in Numbers 12:8 where God speaks to Moses plainly rather than in riddles.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse and is supplemented mainly by Septuagint and lexicon evidence.

definition: A name, meaning destruction, used in Revelation for the angel ruling the Abyss.
article: Ἀβαδδών is a Hebrew name carried over into Greek, where it appears just once in the New Testament (Revelation 9:11) as the name of the angel of the Abyss. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Apollyon" in all of its single occurrence, matching the Greek word for "Destroyer" given alongside it in the text. Interestingly, in the Septuagint the underlying Hebrew word אֲבַדּוֹן ("destruction") is translated ἀπώλεια and refers to a place — the realm of the ruined dead — rather than a personal being, appearing in passages like Job 26:6 and Proverbs 15:11.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, and the Septuagint treating it as a place rather than a person, the word's range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To take control over others and dominate them, often by force or heavy-handed authority.
article: κατακυριεύω means to gain or exercise dominion over someone, usually with a negative edge of domineering or overpowering them. The New Testament uses it just 4 times, and in two of those cases (Matthew 20:25, 1 Peter 5:3) it describes the kind of heavy-handed rule that leaders are warned against. In the Septuagint it appears 14 times and most often renders the Hebrew כָּבַשׁ ('to subdue'), notably in Genesis 1:28 where humanity is told to subdue the earth.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and two of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured sense range is narrow.

definition: Tyre, an ancient coastal city and major commercial port of Phoenicia.
article: Τύρος is the name of Tyre, a maritime city of Phoenicia, and it means just that in all 11 New Testament occurrences — rendered "Tyre" 100% of the time. The name comes from the Hebrew צֹר (Tsor), which the Septuagint translates 23 times across its 35 uses of the word. In the Gospels it usually appears paired with Sidon, the neighboring coastal city, as a stock reference to the Phoenician region.

definition: Worthy or deserving — having the weight, value, or fitness that matches a particular reward, treatment, or response.
article: ἄξιος is overwhelmingly about being "worthy" — rendered that way in 31 of its 41 New Testament appearances (84%), with another 2 cases shading toward "deserve." The core idea, rooted in weighing, is that something or someone carries enough value to balance a corresponding reward, punishment, or honor, so it works equally for praise ("the laborer is worthy of his wages") and for judgment ("they deserve it"). Everyday Koine papyri show the same range: one document from 14 B.C. has a man saying he doesn't think he is "worthy" to be mistreated, and another describes someone as a worthy man who is also in need.

definition: Damascus, an ancient city of Syria named throughout the New Testament.
article: Δαμασκός is simply the name of Damascus, a major city in Syria, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in all 15 New Testament occurrences (87% directly, with the rest being parsing artifacts). It appears in the dramatic accounts of Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus, as well as in his own letters (2 Corinthians 11:32, Galatians 1:17). The name comes from the Hebrew דַּמֶּשֶׂק and shows up 42 times across the Septuagint, confirming its long history as a well-known place name.

definition: A particle used in oaths to affirm something strongly, meaning "by" or "as surely as" followed by whatever is invoked.
article: νή is a small particle used to swear or affirm something emphatically, placed before the person or thing invoked, much like our "I swear by." It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:31, where Paul affirms "by" his pride or boasting in his readers. The everyday papyri make this vivid: people wrote oaths like "by the gods" (νὴ τοὺς θεούς) and even "by your safety" in private letters, showing how ordinary the expression was. Note that the digest's translation data lists "face" for the single occurrence, which conflicts with every lexicon that defines it as an oath particle.
caution: The measured rendering "face" disagrees sharply with all the lexica, which uniformly treat νή as an oath particle, and the New Testament evidence is just one occurrence.

definition: Golgotha, the place outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, a name meaning "place of the skull."
article: Golgotha is a proper name for the site of Jesus' crucifixion, appearing 3 times across Matthew, Mark, and John. The Gospel writers themselves explain that the name means "the place of the skull," and the word comes from an Aramaic term tied to the Hebrew word for "skull" (gulgoleth), which the Septuagint renders as kranion ("skull") in passages like Judges 9:53 and 2 Kings 9:35. Although the corpus tally splits the three occurrences into separate "senses," all three point to the same single place.
caution: This is a low-confidence entry only because of the tiny sample of 3 occurrences, and the surface variations (including the "Carrying own which" fragment from John 19:17) reflect surrounding phrasing rather than distinct meanings.

definition: Good in a way others can see and recognize—fitting, excellent, fine, or beautiful, whether in appearance, quality, or moral character.
article: καλός covers goodness that shows—something fine, fitting, or beautiful that's recognized as good by those who see it. In the Byzantine New Testament it's overwhelmingly rendered "good" (63×, 91%), with occasional "right" (3×) and "better" (2×), and it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing 32 of 101 times. The classical lexica add a nuance the raw counts don't capture: καλός is often contrasted with ἀγαθός, where ἀγαθός denotes goodness by its results and καλός denotes goodness that is at once seen to be good—hence its use of beautiful or fine objects, like the "goodly stones" of the temple in Luke 21:5. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew טוֹב ("good," 95×) but also יָפֶה ("beautiful," 30×), confirming this blend of moral worth and outward attractiveness.

definition: To treat someone with contempt by insulting, shaming, or dishonoring them.
article: This verb means to dishonor or insult someone, treating them with contempt or shame. Though the digest lists six separate renderings, they all cluster tightly around a single idea of dishonoring, and every occurrence is rendered consistently — the variation is mostly grammatical (active versus passive, 'dishonor' versus 'dishonored'). A vivid glimpse comes from a third-century BC papyrus that captures the everyday force of the word: 'for it is a dreadful thing to be insulted before a crowd.'

definition: To live by Jewish customs and religious practices, or to adopt a Jewish way of life.
article: This verb means to follow Jewish customs and religious practice—to live as a Jew does. It is extremely rare, appearing just once in the New Testament (Galatians 2:14) and once in the Greek Old Testament, where it translates a Hebrew word meaning to become a Jew (Esther 8:17). The lexicons agree it describes conforming to Jewish ways of life, especially ceremonially.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence base for this word is very thin.

definition: Jannai, a man named only as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ἰαννά (also spelled Ἰανναί) is a personal name appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 3:24, where it sits in Jesus' genealogy. According to Dodson, Jannai was the son of Joseph and the father of Melchi—so the word does nothing but identify a link in that ancestral chain. It is probably of Hebrew origin, and notably the SBL critical text does not include the form at all, reflecting the variation between the spellings Ἰαννά and Ἰανναί.
caution: This is a name occurring only once, with thin evidence and disagreement among sources over both its spelling and its inclusion in the critical text.

definition: A Roman army officer commanding about a hundred soldiers.
article: κεντυρίων is a Roman officer who commanded roughly a hundred soldiers, and all 3 New Testament occurrences appear in a single passage of Mark (15:39, 44-45). The word is actually a borrowed Latin term (centurio), and Matthew and Luke prefer the Greek equivalent ἑκατόνταρχος instead. The three 'measured senses' here are just one meaning split across phrases of the same Mark scene, so they all point to the identical office. Tellingly, this Latinism turns up in everyday Koine documents too: a soldier named Apion, writing home to his father from Italy, signs off noting the century unit he was enrolled in.
caution: Confidence is rated low because all evidence comes from a single Markan passage, though the meaning itself is not in doubt.

definition: Gehenna, the place of final punishment, named after a valley outside Jerusalem that became a symbol of fiery judgment.
article: γέεννα refers to the place of final, fiery punishment, almost always rendered "hell" in English Bibles; it appears 12 times in the New Testament across 4 books. The word comes from Hebrew Ge-Hinnom, the "valley of Hinnom" south and west of Jerusalem, which became infamous for fire-worship, was desecrated by King Josiah, and reportedly served as the city's rubbish dump—imagery later attached to the place of future punishment. Although the digest separates the renderings into three "senses," phrases like "causes sin than" and "than hell" are really fragments of surrounding sentences rather than distinct meanings of the word, which consistently denotes hell.
caution: The listed "senses" beyond "hell" reflect how surrounding words were captured rather than genuinely different meanings, so γέεννα effectively carries a single sense.

definition: A person who works aboard a ship; a sailor or seaman.
article: Ναύτης simply means a sailor or seaman, someone who works on a ship, and that meaning holds steady across all 3 New Testament occurrences. The two "measured senses" are really the same idea—the only difference is that in Acts 27:27 the context is the open sea, so the rendering becomes "sea sailors." Though the word is fairly rare in Greek prose, everyday Koine papyri show it in ordinary contexts—one document even worries that if the sailors scatter, it won't be easy to gather them again.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: To treat someone badly, mistreating or tormenting them, especially through physical hardship or abuse.
article: κακουχέω means to treat someone badly — to mistreat, hurt, or torment them. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Hebrews (11:37 and 13:3), and both times the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mistreated." The most vivid evidence comes from everyday papyri: it shows up regularly in marriage contracts, where a husband promises not to "mistreat" his wife, and in divorce complaints accusing a husband of constant abuse — so the word carried a very practical, real-life sense of ill-treatment.
