caution: With only 2 occurrences in the New Testament (and none in the critical SBLGNT text), the biblical sample is thin, though the papyri evidence strongly supports the meaning.

definition: Describing something sweet or fresh in taste, the opposite of bitter, salty, or brackish.
article: γλυκύς describes a pleasant taste — water that is fresh rather than salty, or anything sweet as opposed to bitter. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times, evenly split: twice for fresh water (James 3:11-12, set against bitter and salt water) and twice for sweetness (Revelation 10:9-10). In the Septuagint it shows up 13 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "sweet" (מָתוֹק, 9 times), and everyday Koine papyri use the neuter form γλυκύ for sweet wines like raisin wine and pomegranate wine.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the "fresh" versus "sweet" split reflects context (water versus honey-taste) rather than two truly distinct meanings.

definition: To send someone out on a mission, or to send a person away or dismiss them.
article: ἐξαποστέλλω means to send a person forth, usually on a commission or task, but it can also mean to send someone away or dismiss them. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it 'sent' (36%), 'sent away' (27%), and simply 'away' (18%). It is hugely common in the Septuagint—255 times—where it mostly translates the Hebrew שָׁלַח (208×), and Moulton-Milligan show it carrying the sense 'commission, send forth' even in official Koine documents like the Rosetta Stone.

definition: To pull or draw something up and out, as in hauling an animal out of a pit or lifting an object back up.
article: ἀνασπάω is a physical verb meaning to drag, pull, or draw something up and out. It appears only twice in the New Testament: Jesus asks who wouldn't pull a son or ox out of a well on the Sabbath (Luke 14:5), and Peter describes a sheet being drawn back up into heaven (Acts 11:10). The everyday Koine flavor shows up clearly in the papyri, where the word is used for pulling up barley and wheat from the fields.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 3 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, and the sources disagree on which Hebrew words it translates.

definition: To provide, supply, offer, or cause something for someone, whether a physical thing or an action like trouble or kindness.
article: παρέχω literally means to "hold near" and so to present, furnish, or supply something to someone — ranging from physical things to actions like causing trouble, showing kindness, or offering a cheek to be struck. It appears 16 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 8 books, and in 12 of those it dissolves into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word, which is why translators handle it with verbs as varied as bring, give, show, offer, and minister. A nice glimpse of its everyday flavor comes from the papyri: a marriage contract from 311 BC uses it for a husband providing his wife "all things that are fitting," and another for supplying "wine that will keep."
caution: Because the word so often blends into English phrasing rather than mapping to a single word, the measured renderings capture only a thin slice of its real range.

definition: Copper or bronze metal, and by extension the coins made from it — small change or money.
senseLabels: copper money carried in a purse
article: χαλκός literally means copper or bronze, the metal itself, but it easily came to stand for the coins made from it — everyday small change. In the Byzantine New Testament all 5 occurrences lean toward the 'money' sense, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it 'money' or 'money in' (as in the offering box of Mark 12:41); the basic metal sense shows up elsewhere in passages like 1 Corinthians 13:1 and Revelation 18:12. The everyday papyri confirm this beautifully: letters say things like 'send me the money (χαλκόν), since I am coming.' In the Septuagint it appears 34 times across 15 books, mostly translating the Hebrew word for bronze/copper, נְחֹשֶׁת.
caution: The handful of New Testament uses all point to money, so the underlying 'metal' sense rests on outside evidence rather than the measured occurrences here.

definition: A word meaning either "about" (with numbers and amounts) or "like, as if" (in comparisons).
article: ὡσεί does two jobs depending on context: with figures it means roughly "about," softening a count (16× in the Byzantine NT, 53%), and in comparisons it means "like" or "as if" (13×, 43%). The Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles agree on these renderings 100% of the time, and the classical lexicons line up neatly with the measured data, splitting the same two ways. The everyday Koine papyri show both uses too — one farmer's letter has it meaning "as it were turned coward," while a contract uses it for "about one cubit."

definition: To pull out a weapon, especially to draw a sword from its sheath.
article: σπάω means to draw or pull out, and in the New Testament both of its two occurrences refer specifically to drawing a sword (Mark 14:47 and Acts 16:27). It is far more common in the Septuagint, appearing 30 times across 9 books and most often translating the Hebrew שָׁלַף ('to draw out,' 22×). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this same usage, with one document (c. 113 BC) describing people who 'drew their swords' (σπασαμένων τὰς μαχαίρας).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences—both meaning to draw a sword—the measured sense range is narrow, though the Septuagint and papyri support this reading confidently.

definition: At a fitting or convenient time; when a good opportunity arises.
article: This adverb describes doing something at the right or convenient moment, and it appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it once as finding an "opportunity" (Mark 14:11) and once as being ready "in season" (2 Timothy 4:2), with the BSB agreeing both times. It was a common everyday word in Koine, turning up in papyri such as a third-century B.C. document with the phrase "if you have a convenient moment."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one Septuagint use (Sirach 18:22), the evidence is thin, hence the low confidence tier.

definition: The remaining people or things in a group; also used adverbially to mean "finally" or "from now on."
article: At its core, λοιποί points to whatever or whoever is left over in a group — "the others" (40%) or "the rest" (33%). The same word, in its neuter form, shifts into an adverb meaning "finally" or "for the rest" (13%, as when Paul wraps up a letter in 2 Corinthians 13:11 or Philippians 3:1). In the Septuagint it most often renders Hebrew יֶ֫תֶר ("remainder, what is left"), appearing 41 of its 64 times that way, which fits its basic "leftover" idea nicely.

definition: To fill something up completely, or to complete a period of time so that it fully arrives.
article: This verb literally means to fill something up completely — Luke uses it for a boat filling with water in a storm. But its more striking use is with time: when a set period is fully accomplished, as when the day of Pentecost 'came' in Acts 2:1. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this time sense, using the same word for a span of years reaching completion, and in the Septuagint it once renders a Hebrew word in Jeremiah.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, and two of the three are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a distinct English word.

definition: The rite of baptism, the religious washing or immersion ritual; also used figuratively for an overwhelming experience of suffering.
article: βάπτισμα refers to the rite of baptism, which the Majority Standard Bible renders "baptism" in 16 of 22 occurrences (73%). It covers both John's baptism and Christian baptism, but it also appears figuratively for affliction, as when Jesus speaks of a "baptism" he must undergo (Mark 10:38, Luke 12:50). Abbott-Smith notes the word denotes the result of the act of immersing, in contrast to βαπτισμός which names the act itself; Moulton-Milligan adds that the noun is essentially peculiar to the New Testament and church writers, even surfacing in a fourth-century papyrus fragment asking about a "new baptism."

definition: A person sent out as an official representative, especially one of those commissioned by Jesus Christ to spread his message.
article: In the New Testament, ἀπόστολος almost always means an apostle—someone officially sent and authorized to act for another—and translators render it "apostles" in 77 of 81 Byzantine occurrences (97%). The word can also carry the plainer sense of "messenger" or "envoy," which the lexica trace back to Herodotus and to one Septuagint passage (3 Kingdoms 14:6) where it describes a man sent with hard news. It's a well-attested everyday Koine word, documented in papyri and inscriptions, formed from the verb ἀποστέλλω, "to send out."

definition: A preposition used with numbers to mean "each" or "apiece," or in fixed phrases meaning "among" or "in turn."
article: In the New Testament ἀνά is one of the rarest prepositions, appearing 15 times in the Byzantine text, and its most common standalone use is distributive—pairing with a number to mean "each" or "apiece" (rendered "each" 4 of those times, as in Matthew 20:10 and John 2:6). The rest of the time (9 of 15) it disappears into fixed phrases like ἀνὰ μέσον ("among, between") and ἀνὰ μέρος ("in turn") rather than standing as its own English word. The phrase ἀνὰ μέσον is striking because it shows up constantly in everyday Greek papyri and inscriptions—from a 221 B.C. document describing something "between" two walls to one noting a scar "between the eyebrows"—and in the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew בֵּין ("between"), used 318 of its 351 occurrences.
caution: Most New Testament occurrences are part of fixed phrases rather than independent meanings, so the single measured "each" sense covers only part of how the word actually functions.

definition: Jannes, the name of one of the men who opposed Moses before Pharaoh, mentioned alongside Jambres.
article: Jannes is a personal name, appearing only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:8, where he and Jambres are cited as men who opposed Moses. The lexicons agree it is a proper name of Egyptian origin, traditionally understood as one of Pharaoh's sorcerers. Because the word occurs just once and is simply a name, there is little range to measure beyond the single reference.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests entirely on that single verse and traditional identification rather than measured usage.

definition: Describing someone who is subject to suffering or destined to suffer.
article: παθητός is a verbal adjective from the same root as πάθημα (suffering), and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:23, where it describes the Christ as one destined to suffer. The Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence in the phrase "suffer rise," agreeing fully with the Berean Standard Bible. Notably, Moulton-Milligan points out that this is the only verbal adjective ending in -τός in the whole New Testament, and Abbott-Smith records two possible nuances: "one who has suffered" or "subject to suffering."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources differ on whether it means "having suffered," "capable of suffering," or "destined to suffer."

definition: To be present, on hand, or arrived—whether speaking of a person, a thing, or a moment in time.
article: πάρειμι combines παρά ("beside") and εἰμί ("to be"), and means to be present or to have arrived. It applies both to people who are physically here and to things like time or circumstances—Abbott-Smith notes its participle covers "the present time" and even "present" possessions. The Byzantine NT uses it 24 times, but in 11 of those it dissolves into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word, which is why the measured renderings ("here," "now come," "come") cover only the clearer cases. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, as when a writer recalls something said to a correspondent "in your presence."

definition: Comfort or consolation, especially encouraging words offered to someone in distress.
article: παρηγορία means comfort or consolation, and in its single New Testament appearance (Colossians 4:11) it describes the encouragement Paul received from his fellow workers. The word's root sense involves addressing or speaking alongside someone, which the older lexicon Abbott-Smith captures with a separate sense "an address, exhortation" found in the Greek of 4 Maccabees. The most striking evidence comes from ancient tomb inscriptions, where παρηγορία appears as the consolation a grieving person finds even in the dead—showing how naturally Koine speakers reached for this word in their letters of sympathy.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single verse.

definition: A young bird, especially a nestling not yet grown — used in the New Testament for young pigeons offered in sacrifice.
article: νεοσσός means a young bird or nestling. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 2:24), where it describes the young pigeons offered at Jesus' presentation in the temple, quoting Old Testament sacrificial law. It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 20 times across 7 books, often rendering the Hebrew word for turtledove (9×) and for young birds (3×); the everyday papyri even attest a related term for a seller of young birds.
caution: The evidence is thin in the New Testament — a single occurrence that is itself a Septuagint quotation — so its sense rests mainly on Greek Old Testament usage.

definition: An object that people worship or treat as sacred, such as a god, altar, or shrine.
article: σέβασμα refers to anything people venerate as holy—a god, an altar, a sacred image. It appears only twice in the New Testament: Paul points to Athens' many objects of worship in Acts 17:23, and warns of one who exalts himself over everything called god or worshiped in 2 Thessalonians 2:4. Both the measured Bible renderings and the classical lexicons agree on this single meaning, and Moulton-Milligan confirms the word was at home in everyday Koine, citing a similar use in Aristides describing the worship-objects of the Chaldeans and Greeks.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the New Testament, so its range is narrow and based on thin evidence, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: The act of being taken up, used in the New Testament for Jesus being taken up to heaven.
article: ἀνάληψις refers to a taking up or lifting up, and it appears just once in the New Testament (Luke 9:51), where it points to the time of Jesus being received up. The Majority Standard Bible renders it within the phrase about the days being 'set' for this event, and Strong's connects it to the ascension. The everyday papyri give the word a much more ordinary range: one document from A.D. 123 uses it for the receipt of money, and a third-century inscription uses it for hospitality or entertainment given to guests, showing how broadly 'taking up' or 'receiving' could be applied in common Koine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its New Testament sense rests on a single passage.

definition: The equipment or gear of something, especially a ship's tackle and rigging.
article: σκευή refers to equipment or gear — in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 27:19), it specifically means a ship's tackle, which the sailors threw overboard during a storm. Everyday Koine papyri show the word's wider reach: one document uses it of a woman's ornaments and jewelry, and another of household goods or furnishings. So while the Bible uses it narrowly for ship's equipment, the word could cover any kind of gear or belongings.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To shout out loudly or cry aloud, raising one's voice to call out.
article: This verb combines "up" (ἀνά) with "shout" (βοάω) to mean crying out loudly or raising the voice. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where it's rendered "cried out" in two-thirds of cases, as when Jesus cried out on the cross (Matthew 27:46). It's far more common in the Septuagint (35 times), where it usually translates Hebrew words for crying out or shouting (צָעַק and זָעַק, 9 times each), and Moulton-Milligan note one striking papyrus where a condemned criminal shouted out in the middle of Rome to summon onlookers as he was led to death.
caution: Confidence is low: the New Testament evidence is very thin, and editors dispute whether the word even belongs in Matthew 27:46, where the critical text reads a different verb.

definition: A part or portion that belongs to someone—their share, allotment, or stake in something.
article: μερίς is fundamentally about a portion or share that falls to someone, whether a literal allotment or a stake in a larger whole. In the Byzantine NT it appears only 5 times and is rendered "share" most often, while in Luke 10:42 Mary has chosen the good "portion" that won't be taken away. The Septuagint uses it heavily (124×), most often translating the Hebrew chelek, "portion" or "allotment." Interestingly, the papyri reveal a secondary geographical sense—"district" or administrative division—as in Acts 16:12, a usage scholar Hort once doubted but everyday Koine documents have since confirmed.
caution: The geographical "district" sense (Acts 16:12) is well-attested in papyri but was historically disputed, and the NT sample here is small at only 5 occurrences.

definition: In a way that is unworthy of something, doing it improperly or without proper reverence.
article: This adverb describes doing something in a way that fails to match what it deserves — improperly or without due reverence. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in 1 Corinthians 11 (verses 27 and 29), where Paul warns against eating the Lord's bread or drinking the cup in an unworthy manner. Outside the New Testament it shows up just once in the Septuagint, at 2 Maccabees 14:42, so the overall evidence is quite thin.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is small and the precise force is hard to pin down.

definition: To go and see someone in order to help them, to look after those in need, or to inspect and examine something.
article: At its core ἐπισκέπτομαι means going to see someone — but in the New Testament that visiting almost always carries the warm sense of coming to help, care for, or look after a person, whether God caring for His people (Luke 1:68) or believers attending to orphans and widows (James 1:27). The word's range stretches from this caring visit to a more neutral 'inspect' or 'examine,' which is the dominant meaning in everyday Koine papyri, where it appears in administrative complaints sent off to be examined. In the Septuagint it occurs 146 times and most often renders the Hebrew פָּקַד (109×), a verb that itself spans visiting with help and even visiting with punishment.
caution: The English renderings split fairly evenly across 'visit,' 'visited,' and 'care,' so the exact shade depends heavily on context.

definition: To fill up or complete something, whether fulfilling a prophecy, taking up a place, completing a requirement, or supplying what is lacking.
article: ἀναπληρόω means to fill something up to completion, and the New Testament spreads it across a wide range: a prophecy being fulfilled (Matthew 13:14), someone occupying a place (1 Corinthians 14:16), perfectly keeping the law (Galatians 6:2), and supplying what was missing (Philippians 2:30). The MSB renders all six occurrences differently, but they all circle the same core idea of bringing something to full measure. Notably, everyday Koine papyri use this very word for completing business contracts and even for filling out (intercalating) the calendar, which matches its sense of supplying or making up what is lacking.
caution: With only six New Testament occurrences each rendered differently, the senses overlap heavily and the divisions between them are more about context than truly distinct meanings.

definition: To say something beforehand, whether warning in advance, foretelling, or stating openly what was said earlier.
article: προέπω covers anything said ahead of time: a prior warning, a prophecy, or simply repeating something already stated. Its range stretches from foretelling future events (as in prophecy contexts) to the plain bookkeeping sense seen in the papyri, where a fourth-century Oxyrhynchus document uses it for "as aforesaid." Strikingly, a Christian slave's letter about his mistress's illness uses the same word for "as I said before," showing how ordinary the term was in everyday Koine. The classical lexica add a secondary sense of proclaiming publicly or declaring openly.
caution: This verb does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament, so its meaning here rests on Septuagint, papyri, and lexicon evidence rather than measured NT usage.

definition: The farthest point or tip of something — an end, edge, or topmost extremity.
article: ἄκρον is the neuter of an adjective meaning "highest" or "extreme," used as a noun for the outermost point of anything — an end, edge, or tip. In the New Testament's 6 occurrences it ranges from the cosmic "ends of the earth" or "far end of heaven" (Matthew 24:31, Mark 13:27) to the small scale of a fingertip dipped in water (Luke 16:24). The everyday Greek papyri show the same flexibility: a scar at the tip of an eyebrow, the top of a sundial's shadow, even a cook's bill listing two trotters. In the Septuagint it appears 82 times, most often rendering Hebrew קָצֶה ("end," 23×) and בֹּהֶן ("thumb/big toe," 22×).

definition: To chase after someone or something, whether harassing enemies as a persecutor or eagerly striving toward a goal.
article: At its core διώκω means to chase after, and the New Testament leans heavily on the hostile end of that range: in the Byzantine text it is rendered "persecute" 25 of 44 times (66%) and "pursue" 7 times (18%). The pursuit can be neutral or even positive, as when believers "pursue" peace, love, or righteousness. The everyday Koine papyri preserve a strikingly practical use: a first-century Egyptian letter urges the reader to "hasten" or "carry forward" the irrigation and digging of olive-yards, showing how the word covered ordinary pressing-on as well as chasing enemies.

definition: To grow or increase beyond the ordinary measure, far more than usual.
article: This verb combines the prefix ὑπέρ ("over, beyond") with αὐξάνω ("to grow"), giving the sense of growth that exceeds the normal degree. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Thessalonians 1:3, where Paul says the Thessalonians' faith was growing exceedingly. Moulton-Milligan note that such ὑπέρ-compounds are a marked feature of Paul's vocabulary, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was real working language and not a coinage.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the biblical corpus alone.

definition: A Greek dry measure of grain, slightly less than a quart, roughly a day's food ration for one person.
article: Χοῖνιξ is a standard Koine unit of dry measure equal to about 1.92 pints—a little under a quart—typically used for grain. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in Revelation 6:6, where it measures out quantities of wheat and barley at famine prices. The word turns up in everyday papyri too: one document from A.D. 40 even uses it of "two boxes," suggesting the term could attach to a container as well as the amount it held.
caution: One of the two measured senses is rendered "saying," which clearly belongs to a neighboring word in the same verse rather than to χοῖνιξ itself, so treat the grain-measure sense as the real one.

definition: The quality of being firm, safe, or certain — reliability that gives confidence or protection.
article: ἀσφάλεια covers a small but flexible range, from firmness and certainty to physical safety. Its three New Testament uses each land in a different spot: the "certainty" of what Luke taught (Luke 1:4), a prison locked "securely" (Acts 5:23), and the false "security" people feel before sudden disaster (1 Thessalonians 5:3). The most telling evidence comes from everyday papyri, where the word served as a legal term meaning a "written security" or "proof" submitted in a case, and from inscriptions where it pairs with words for safety and exemption.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences — one per sense — the boundaries between these meanings rest on very thin evidence.

definition: Describing an only child, or someone or something that is the one and only of its kind.
article: μονογενής describes a child who is the only one a parent has, and by extension someone or something utterly unique. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "only" in 5 of its 9 New Testament occurrences (56%), and the Berean Standard Bible agrees with that rendering 100% of the time. There's a notable scholarly point in the evidence: Moulton-Milligan argue from everyday Koine papyri that the word literally means "one of a kind, only, unique" rather than "only-begotten" (which would be a different Greek word), even though older sources like Strong's and the KJV preserve the "begotten" wording.
caution: Sources disagree on nuance: traditional lexica gloss it "only-begotten," while Moulton-Milligan insist on "only/unique," so the precise force is contested.

definition: To be terrified or struck with panic, especially the sudden fright caused by alarming news or a startling sight.
article: πτοέω means to be terrified or seized with panic, and in the New Testament it always appears in the passive — describing people who are frightened rather than the thing that scares them. It shows up only twice, both in Luke: once for people alarmed by rumors of wars (Luke 21:9) and once for the disciples startled at the sight of the risen Jesus (Luke 24:37). The Septuagint uses it far more often (32 times), most frequently to render the Hebrew חָתַת, "to be shattered or dismayed," and a fascinating papyrus charm even has demons who "are terrified" merely on hearing a divine name.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin (only 2 occurrences, both in Luke, and none in the critical SBLGNT text), so the picture leans heavily on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: The comparative form of "bad," meaning worse, more severe, or in a more aggravated condition than before.
article: χείρων is simply the comparative of κακός ("bad"), so it means "worse" — describing a situation, person, or condition that has become more severe than it was. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times, and translators render it "worse" or "worse than" in every case, so its range is narrow and stable. It was ordinary everyday Greek: a papyrus from A.D. 186 (P Oxy II. 237) uses it in the line "it is worse to take away a wife from her husband," showing the word at home in real legal and domestic disputes.

definition: To spit something out, used figuratively to mean rejecting or treating with disgust and contempt.
article: ἐκπτύω literally means "to spit out," built from ἐκ ("out") plus πτύω ("to spit"), and figuratively came to mean spurning or loathing something. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Galatians 4:14, where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes a scholarly dispute: some take the Galatians use literally, alluding to the ancient custom of spitting as a protective gesture at the sight of the sick (especially epileptics), while most read it metaphorically as "reject with contempt."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and sources disagree on whether its single use is literal spitting or a figurative expression of disgust.

definition: The festival of the new moon, marking the first day of a month in the Jewish calendar.
article: Νουμηνία refers to the new moon and specifically the Jewish festival held on the first day of each lunar month. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:16, where it sits alongside other observances like Sabbaths. The Septuagint uses it 23 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew word חֹדֶשׁ ("new moon/month"), and the everyday papyri confirm its ordinary calendar meaning — for instance a document from A.D. 166 dates an event "on the first of the month Pachon."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To give false testimony, especially lying about someone when serving as a witness.
article: This verb means to lie while acting as a witness, giving false testimony against someone. Across its 5 New Testament occurrences it is rendered "bear false witness" 3 times, and the other two renderings ("false" and "men testified falsely") describe the same act, so the word's range is essentially unified. In the Septuagint it appears in Exodus 20:16 and Deuteronomy 5:20 as the word behind the commandment against false witness, and Moulton-Milligan note a related compound, ψευδογραφέω ("make a false statement"), in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: With only 5 occurrences, all pointing to a single core meaning, the evidence is limited but consistent across sources.

definition: Jericho, an ancient city located a little north of the Dead Sea in Palestine.
article: Ἱεριχώ is simply the place-name Jericho, a city north of the Dead Sea. The word is indeclinable and appears 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament, always referring to the same location—the apparent multiple "senses" in the data just reflect surrounding words the translators carried along. It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 57 times and renders the Hebrew name יְרֵחוֹ in 53 of those cases.

definition: A broken piece or fragment, especially of bread broken off and left over after a meal.
article: κλάσμα refers to a fragment or piece broken off from something larger, and in the New Testament it almost always means the leftover bits of bread gathered after Jesus fed the crowds. Built from the verb κλάω ("to break"), it appears 9 times, rendered as "pieces" or "broken pieces left." Interestingly, the everyday papyri and temple inventories from Delos use it more broadly for broken-off bits of objects, like fragments of an ivy wreath, and the early Christian Didache uses it for the broken bread of the Eucharist.

definition: To go away from a place; to depart or leave.
article: This verb means simply to leave or go away, formed from the preposition ἀπό ("away from") combined with a verb meaning "to go." It is very rare, appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament (at Acts 17:10) and once in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew נָבַט. In its single New Testament use the word is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a distinct English word, which is why it leaves little visible trace in translations.
caution: Evidence is very thin — only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use — so its full range cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: An adverb meaning either without good reason or to no purpose, depending on the context.
article: This adverb covers two related ideas: doing something without a good reason or cause, and doing something that produces no result — in vain. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times across 5 books, and translators rendered it as 'without' twice, 'vain' once, and 'otherwise vain' once, while folding it silently into the phrasing 3 times. Its only Septuagint appearance is in Proverbs 28:25, and lexicons trace it to a root tied to the idea of failure or yielding.
caution: With only a handful of occurrences and translators often absorbing it into the phrasing, the boundary between 'without cause' and 'in vain' is set by context rather than the word itself.

definition: To divide something up and hand out the portions to different people.
article: This verb means to split something into parts and assign those parts to particular people — to apportion or distribute. The Septuagint uses it 35 times for Hebrew words like חָצָה ("divide," 12×) and חָלַק ("apportion," 10×), and everyday papyri use it for dividing up land between heirs or parties. In the New Testament it appears only twice: once in 1 Corinthians 12:11, where the Spirit "apportions" gifts to each person, and once in Luke 15:12, where it is absorbed into the phrasing of dividing an inheritance.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (one not even rendered by its own English word), confidence in the measured range is low.

definition: The act of watching carefully or looking for visible signs that something is happening.
article: παρατήρησις means a careful watching or observation, especially looking out for visible signs. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 17:20, where Jesus says the kingdom of God does not come with παρατήρησις—rendered "observable signs"—meaning it cannot be detected by watching for outward indicators. Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Hobart even claimed it as a medical term for clinical observation.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force in Luke 17:20 rests on a single example.

definition: A preposition meaning "before" or "in the presence of," placing someone or something face-to-face with another.
article: ἔναντι is a preposition (taking the genitive) meaning "before" or "in the presence of" — picturing one party standing face-to-face with another. It is rare in the New Testament but extremely common in the Septuagint, appearing 227 times, where it most often renders the Hebrew word for "face" (פָּנִים, 53×), which fits its sense of being in someone's presence. Moulton-Milligan note its appearance in everyday papyri and inscriptions — including a 170 BC translation of a Roman senatorial decree — proving the word was ordinary Koine and not confined to biblical Greek.
caution: The word appears only once with its own force in the Byzantine NT, and editions disagree on its readings (some print the related ἐναντίον), so its NT distribution is uncertain.

definition: To decide or mark out something in advance, settling beforehand what will happen.
article: προορίζω combines πρό ("before") with ὁρίζω ("to set a boundary, appoint"), so it literally means to fix or determine something ahead of time. In the New Testament it appears 6 times and consistently carries the sense of God deciding beforehand, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it "predestined" in 3 of the occurrences. The "also" rendering counted once (Rom 8:29) reflects English phrasing rather than a separate meaning, and in fact 2 of the 6 uses get absorbed into the surrounding wording with no English word of their own. Abbott-Smith notes its flexible grammar, taking a direct object, an infinitive, or a phrase with εἰς.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and 2 of them absorbed into phrasing, the lone "also" rendering reflects translation style, not a genuine second meaning.

definition: Describing speech or a person that insults, slanders, or shows irreverence toward people or God.
article: βλάσφημος describes abusive, slanderous, or irreverent speech, and can also label the person who speaks that way—a slanderer or blasphemer, as in 1 Timothy 1:13. The word appears only 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the digest's measured renderings ('against', 'blasphemies against', 'yet') largely reflect how it sits inside larger phrases rather than a tidy gloss list. Notably, Moulton-Milligan stress that the special sense of irreverence toward God was not built into the word itself but acquired over time; everyday papyri and writers like Vettius Valens show it used broadly for insulting both people and the gods.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 5 NT occurrences (one absorbed into phrasing) and a single Septuagint use—so the measured 'senses' largely reflect surrounding phrasing rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To feel courage and confidence, to be of good cheer or boldly assured.
article: θαῤῥέω means to have courage or confidence, whether facing a situation calmly ("of good cheer") or speaking and acting boldly toward others. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only 6 times and only in Paul and Hebrews; in half of those cases (3 of 6) it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. Interestingly, it is simply the later spelling of θαρσέω, and the everyday Koine papyri show the same sense of "having confidence"—one Oxyrhynchus document (A.D. 186) speaks of a man who "has confidence in the proofs of his accusation."
caution: With only 6 occurrences split evenly across three rendered shades of meaning, the sense divisions reflect very thin data rather than sharply distinct meanings.

definition: The state of placing oneself under another's authority — submission, obedience, or subordination.
article: ὑποταγή describes putting oneself under someone's authority — submission or obedience. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 3 books, and in two of those the translation absorbs it into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendering it as a single word, as in 2 Corinthians 9:13. The word comes from ὑποτάσσω (to subordinate), and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document describes a man as being 'in subjection,' and another equates it with servitus, slavery or servitude.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and half of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured sense data is thin and rests heavily on the consistent classical and papyri glosses.

definition: With a rushing, roaring sound, like the whistling of an arrow or the crackle of racing flames.
article: This adverb describes something happening with a loud rushing or crackling noise. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 3:10, where the heavens are said to pass away with this kind of roar. Abbott-Smith traces it back to ῥοῖζος, the whistling of an arrow, and the lexicons agree it points to the sound of roaring flames or a rushing crash; Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence, this word's range cannot be measured beyond that one verse.

definition: The act of interpreting or translating something so its meaning becomes clear to others.
article: ἑρμηνεία means interpretation or translation—making the meaning of something understandable. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Paul's discussion of spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:10 and 14:26), where it consistently refers to the interpretation of tongues. The everyday Koine papyri give a concrete flavor: one document is literally headed "Translation of a will" (Ἑρμηνία διαθήκης) for a Latin will rendered into Greek, showing the word's plain practical use for translating one language into another.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the full range is hard to pin down.

definition: Loud weeping or crying, the outward expression of deep grief or distress.
article: κλαυθμός means weeping or crying out loud, the audible sound of someone overcome with grief. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "weeping" in 8 of its 9 New Testament occurrences, and it often appears in the vivid phrase "weeping and gnashing of teeth" (Matthew 8:12, Luke 13:28). In the Septuagint it shows up 31 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew בְּכִי (15×), the ordinary word for weeping, while everyday papyri confirm it was common Koine vocabulary.

definition: To an extreme degree; violently or exceedingly.
article: σφοδρῶς is an adverb meaning "exceedingly" or "violently," formed from the same root as σφόδρα. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:18, where a ship caught in a storm is being battered so badly that the crew begins throwing cargo overboard — which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding action as "jettison." The classical lexica (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on the basic force of "exceedingly" or "vehemently," describing the intensity of the storm rather than the act of throwing things out.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single context, and the "jettison" label reflects the surrounding action rather than the adverb's own meaning of "exceedingly."

definition: Describing someone clever enough to do anything—usually in a bad way, meaning crafty or cunning.
article: πανοῦργος literally combines "all" and "work," describing a person ready to do anything to get a result—hence shrewd, clever, or (most often) crafty. In Greek literature and its single New Testament appearance (2 Corinthians 12:16) the negative sense dominates, but the Septuagint shows it can be neutral or even positive, where it usually renders the Hebrew עָרוּם ("shrewd," 7 times) and twice appears favorably in Proverbs. A vivid bit of evidence: a fourth-century papyrus spell mentions a "crafty stick" (πανουργικὸν ξύλον) used for catching a thief.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the digest's reported rendering as "burden" does not match the cunning/crafty sense found in every lexicon, so the measured data here is unreliable.

definition: Describing a dark blue or purple color, like that of the hyacinth flower or smoky blue flame.
article: This adjective describes a deep blue or purple color, named after the hyacinth flower. In its single New Testament appearance (Revelation 9:17), it pictures the dusky, smoky blue of sulphurous flame, fitting the fiery context. The Septuagint uses it 24 times, mostly to render the Hebrew word tachash (15×), a material used in the tabernacle, and tekeleth (4×), a blue dye; everyday papyri also use it for blue gemstones.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the listed translation "riders" reflects a rendering glitch rather than the word's actual color meaning.

definition: To rub or smear something onto a surface, especially to apply ointment or salve to the eyes.
article: ἐγχρίω means to rub in or smear something on, built from ἐν ("in/on") plus χρίω ("anoint"). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Revelation 3:18, where the eyes are to be anointed with salve so a person can see. Tellingly, the same verb shows up in magical papyri giving practical instructions to smear ointment on the right eye, which fits the eye-salve image in Revelation exactly. The Majority Standard Bible's rendering as "counsel" reflects the surrounding sentence rather than the verb itself, which the classical lexica consistently define as "rub in, anoint."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone; the lexicons agree it means "anoint," which differs from the contextual "counsel" rendering counted in the data.

definition: Jeconiah, a king of Judah listed as an ancestor of Jesus in Matthew's genealogy.
article: Ἰεχονίας is simply the Greek form of the personal name of Jeconiah (Hebrew Jehoiakin), a king in the line of David who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew 1, once as the man living at the time of the exile to Babylon and once as the father of Salathiel. In the Septuagint it shows up 11 times across five books and renders several related Hebrew spellings of the name, including יְכָנְיָה and יְהוֹיָכִין, reflecting how this same king's name was written in different ways.
caution: This is a proper name with only two New Testament occurrences, so its sense range is fixed rather than nuanced.

definition: Saying one thing to one person and something different to another; two-faced or insincere in speech.
article: δίλογος appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:8, where deacons are told not to be "double-tongued"—that is, not to tell different stories to different people. Built from δίς ("twice") and λόγος ("word"), the term is rare enough that Moulton-Milligan note it can't be illustrated from everyday papyri, and the related words διλογία and διλογεῖν actually mean "repetition" rather than insincerity. Abbott-Smith suggests the New Testament sense compares to διγλωσσος ("double-tongued") found in Proverbs 11:13 and Sirach 5:9, pointing to deceitful speech rather than mere repetitiousness.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with thin outside evidence, and the sources disagree—classical usage points to "repetition" while the Pauline meaning of "double-tongued" is unsupported in the papyri.

definition: A place where prisoners are held, or the act, persons, or nighttime period involved in keeping guard.
article: At its root φυλακή is about guarding (it comes from the verb φυλάσσω, "to guard"), and the meaning spreads across the whole idea: the act of guarding, the people who guard, the place where prisoners are kept, and even a division of the night. In the Byzantine New Testament the concrete sense "prison" dominates, covering 24 of 47 occurrences (63%), with "jail" adding a few more, while "watch" (a nighttime period) appears 3 times. The Septuagint uses it 109 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew מִשְׁמֶרֶת and related words for "keeping" or "guard duty," and everyday papyri show it meaning simply something given "into safekeeping."
caution: Several of the listed "senses" like "Even" and "prison even" are artifacts of surrounding phrasing rather than distinct meanings of the word itself.

definition: A spreading, flesh-eating sore that destroys living tissue if left unchecked.
article: γάγγραινα is a medical term for gangrene — an ulcer or eating sore that spreads and destroys tissue. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 2:17, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render it "gangrene" 100% of the time. The word derives from a root meaning "to gnaw," which fits the image of a sore that eats away at flesh; the older King James Version rendered it "canker."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests on a single passage.

definition: Midian, a region of Arabia where Moses lived in exile, and the Arabian people associated with it.
article: Μαδιάν is the Greek form of the Hebrew place-name Midian (מִדְיָן), an Arabian region where Moses fled and lived as a foreigner. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 7:29, referring to the land Moses escaped to. The name is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 94 times and almost always renders Hebrew מִדְיָן; the lexicons note it can refer to a son of Abraham, the Arabian tribe descended from him, or the land itself.
caution: The single measured NT rendering is labeled "remark," which appears to be a data error, since all sources agree the word names the region or people of Midian.

definition: A crawling or creeping animal, such as a reptile or snake, that moves along the ground.
article: ἑρπετόν refers to creeping or crawling creatures—reptiles and similar small animals that move along the ground. All four New Testament uses point to the same single sense, and the Majority Standard Bible and BSB agree completely on rendering it as reptiles or creeping animals. In the Septuagint it appears 40 times, mostly translating Hebrew רֶ֫מֶשׂ and שָׁ֫רֶץ, broad terms for swarming or creeping things. A striking detail comes from an everyday papyrus amulet that prays for a house to be freed "from every evil reptile," showing the word's ordinary use beyond the Bible.

definition: The faculty of smell — the bodily sense by which a person perceives odors.
article: ὄσφρησις refers to the sense of smell, the bodily ability to perceive odors. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 12:17, where Paul lists the senses while describing the body and its parts. Interestingly, the word turns up in everyday Koine documents too: an astrological papyrus (P Ryl II.63) groups "the tongue, smell, and hearing" together as belonging to Mercury.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there cannot be measured from multiple uses.

definition: Belonging to one's fathers or ancestors; inherited or handed down from past generations.
article: πατρικός means "of the fathers" — something passed down from one's ancestors, whether traditions, property, or longstanding ties. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Galatians 1:14, where Paul speaks of his zeal for his ancestral customs; the Septuagint uses it 9 times across 5 books. Everyday papyri show how concrete the word could be: one document from 163 B.C. uses it for a family inheritance ("patrimony"), and another from 99 B.C. speaks of a "hereditary friendship" handed down of old.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall data, the precise nuance in any given passage should be confirmed from context.

definition: The correct proportion or ratio between things, the measure by which one thing matches another.
article: ἀναλογία means proportion—the right measure or ratio between two things. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Romans 12:6, and every translation surveyed (Majority Standard, BSB, KJV, Strong's, Dodson) renders it "proportion." The everyday Koine papyri back this up nicely: a third-century document uses κατ' ἀναλογίαν to mean "proportionately," and a tax record speaks of a "proportionate allowance" of rent, showing the word's plain commercial sense of matching one quantity to another.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense there rests on a single passage.

definition: Belonging to or characterized by the flesh — either physical and material, or driven by human appetites and worldly impulses.
article: σαρκικός comes from σάρξ ("flesh") and describes whatever belongs to or takes its character from the flesh. The measured senses split fairly evenly: about 30% point to flesh itself, 20% to physical or material things (as in Romans 15:27 and 1 Corinthians 9:11, where it contrasts material support with spiritual gifts), and 20% to a moral "worldly" quality describing behavior ruled by human impulses. Abbott-Smith notes a related word, σάρκινος, that more strictly means "made of flesh," but Moulton-Milligan and the papyri caution that in everyday Koine the distinction between the two forms should not be pressed too hard.
caution: The word's range stretches from neutral "material" to a negative "worldly" sense, so context decides the meaning in each verse.

definition: A person given to physical violence — someone who hits or attacks others.
article: πλήκτης describes someone quick to strike or brawl, built from the verb πλήσσω ("to strike"). It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in lists of qualities a church overseer must not have (1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 1:7). The measured data shows it rendered "violent" once and "money" once, but the "money" reading reflects the surrounding phrase rather than this word itself, since every lexicon — Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith — agrees the word means a striker or brawler. Abbott-Smith notes its only Septuagint-related appearance is in Symmachus at Psalm 35:15.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences) and one measured rendering as "money" conflicts with all the lexicons, which uniformly define it as a striker.

definition: Lazarus, a personal name borne by two different men in the Gospels.
article: Lazarus is a proper name used for two distinct individuals in the New Testament: the brother of Martha and Mary in Bethany whom Jesus raised (John 11), and the poor beggar in Jesus' parable (Luke 16). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Lazarus" in 12 of its 15 occurrences (80%), with the rest being phrase fragments rather than alternative meanings. The name is a contracted, colloquial form of the Hebrew Eleazar, and Moulton-Milligan note it survived into Modern Greek, appearing in a folk tale about a cobbler named Lazarus.

definition: To declare someone guilty and deserving of punishment; to pass sentence against a person.
article: κατακρίνω means to give judgment against someone — to condemn them or sentence them to punishment. It built from κατά ("against") and κρίνω ("judge"), and the New Testament uses it 17 times, most often in the sense of being "condemned" (8×) or to "condemn" (5×). A striking detail is its use in everyday legal life: a 230 BC papyrus uses it for a case being "decided against" someone, and an Egyptian trial record warns that an offender will "not only be condemned but also flogged."
caution: The third measured sense ("condemn one," 3×) reflects the metaphorical idea of someone condemning others by a good example, and the BSB renders these differently 100% of the time, so this grouping is partly a rendering artifact rather than a clearly distinct meaning.

definition: To hand something over or pass it to someone, putting it directly into their possession.
senseLabels: hand over or give to someone
article: This compound of ἐπί and δίδωμι means to hand something over or pass it to someone, and in the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "give" in 9 of 11 cases (90%). The picture is concrete—putting an object directly into another's hands, as when a father gives his child bread or a fish (Matthew 7:9, Luke 11:11). The classical lexica add a couple of nuances the NT data barely shows: Abbott-Smith notes a rarer intransitive sense "give way" (used of a ship driven by wind in Acts 27:15), and Moulton-Milligan reports that in everyday papyri it was the standard word for formally submitting a report or document to an official.

definition: To bind something or someone—either tying objects together into a bundle or putting a person in chains.
article: δεσμεύω covers two related kinds of binding: chaining up a prisoner (Luke 8:29; Acts 22:4) and tying things together, as when heavy burdens are bound up into loads (Matt 23:4). The Septuagint uses it seven times, including Joseph's dream where sheaves are bound in the field (Genesis 37:7), and it shows up often in everyday farm accounts in the papyri—workers being paid for bundling armfuls of hay or grain. Notably, in both Byzantine New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word.
caution: Evidence is rated low confidence, with only 2 Byzantine occurrences (3 in the critical text) and both absorbed into phrasing rather than standing as a distinct English word.

definition: A street or open roadway through a town or village, especially where roads meet.
article: In the New Testament ἄμφοδον appears just once, in Mark 11:4, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "street" — describing where the colt was tied. The word literally combines "around" and "road," which gives rise to older glosses like "a fork in the road" or "where two ways meet," but the measured usage simply points to a public street. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri of the Roman period, where the word is common and Grenfell and Hunt translate it "quarter" or "vicus" — that is, a neighborhood or block defined by its streets, as in tax records listing people "from the quarter of Hermouthias."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the lexicons differ on its precise force ("fork in the road" versus "open street"), so confidence is low.

definition: An official order or edict issued by someone in authority, such as a ruler or magistrate.
article: διάταγμα refers to an authoritative edict or decree handed down by someone with power to command. It appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 11:23) and twice in the Septuagint, where it once renders a Hebrew word. In Roman times it was the technical term for an imperial edict, and the papyri show it used for the decrees of emperors and prefects \u2014 one document even applies it to a testamentary disposition.
caution: The Byzantine NT rendering recorded here as "parents" looks like a data error, since every lexicon and the papyri agree the word means an edict or decree.

definition: To use force—either forcing one's own way forward or being forcibly treated by others.
article: βιάζω carries the idea of force, but the direction of that force is famously hard to pin down. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 11:12 and Luke 16:16), and in both cases it's woven into the phrasing rather than translated as a single English word, which is why scholars still debate whether the kingdom 'suffers violence' (passive) or people 'force their way' into it (middle). In the Septuagint it shows up 11 times across 6 books, translating several different Hebrew words including פָּצַר (to press/urge) and פָּרַץ (to break through), and the everyday Koine papyri confirm the verb was common—one Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 22 has a writer saying he is 'forced by friends,' a clearly passive use.
caution: The two New Testament uses are genuinely disputed: ancient versions and major lexicons disagree on whether the force is suffered (passive) or self-directed (middle), and on whether the sense is positive or hostile.

definition: To bring someone to life together with another person, used spiritually of being made alive along with Christ.
article: This compound verb joins "with" (σύν) to "make alive" (ζωοποιέω), so it literally means bringing dead people to life alongside someone else. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:5 and Colossians 2:13), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "made," with the BSB agreeing 100%. In both cases the lexicons note it is used metaphorically of spiritual life — being made alive together with Christ.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in similar contexts, the evidence for this word is thin.

definition: To grow or increase, whether of plants, people, or movements, either growing larger oneself or making something else grow.
article: αὐξάνω covers growth and increase across a wide range—plants growing, infants maturing, crowds multiplying, and even the gospel spreading. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "grow" in 12 of 23 occurrences (52%), "increase" 4×, and "continued spread" twice (notably of God's word in Acts 12:24 and 19:20). In the Septuagint it appears 36 times, most often translating Hebrew פָּרָה ("be fruitful," 20×), echoing the language of being fruitful and multiplying. Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes the intransitive "grow" meaning (something growing on its own) is a later Greek development found nowhere in the Septuagint.

definition: A person who brags loudly and arrogantly, putting on airs to impress others.
article: This word describes a swaggering braggart—someone who shows off with loud, empty self-promotion. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both times in lists of vices (Romans 1:30 and 2 Timothy 3:2), where it's rendered as a mix of "arrogant" and "boastful." Interestingly, Abbott-Smith traces its root to a word for wandering, suggesting the original picture was a roving impostor or charlatan, and in the Septuagint it translates Hebrew terms for the proud and the haughty.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise shading of this word rests on thin evidence.

definition: A cushion or pillow used to rest or support the head, as on a couch or seat.
article: Proskephálaion literally means "something for the head," formed from prós ("toward") and kephalḗ ("head"), and refers to a cushion or pillow. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Mark 4:38, where Jesus is asleep on one in the boat. The word turns up regularly in everyday Koine papyri "a couch and the cushions" in a sale document and even in Theophrastus, where a flatterer grabs cushions to spread on a theater seat, showing it was a common household item.

definition: To carve or stamp letters or images into a hard surface, leaving a permanent impression.
article: This rare word means to engrave or imprint something so that it leaves a lasting mark, the way letters were cut into stone. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 3:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "engraved" 100% of the time—a reading other lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, KJV) share. The Greek translation of Exodus 39:30 uses it for the Hebrew term for engraving, and an ancient letter (Aristeas 67) describes crystal and electron being "inlaid" into a table, showing the same idea of setting a permanent design into a surface.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise nuance rests on limited evidence, though all sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: A proper name for a pagan god or idol, referring to the deity associated with the planet Saturn.
article: Ῥεμφάν is a proper name appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 7:43, where it names a pagan god whose images Israel carried. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "idols" in that single occurrence, while reference works identify it more specifically as the Egyptian or Assyrian name for the deity linked to the planet Saturn (also called Chiun or Kijun). The most interesting detail is that the name itself is a transliteration of the Hebrew סִכּוּת in Amos 5:26, the Septuagint passage Acts quotes—and the spelling varies widely across manuscripts (Ῥομφά, Ῥεφάν, Ῥεμφάν).
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once, the manuscripts disagree sharply on its spelling, and it arose as an imperfect transliteration of a Hebrew name, so its exact form and identity are uncertain.

definition: To engage in conflict, whether physical fighting or verbal quarreling, arguing, and disputing with others.
article: This verb covers a spectrum from literal fighting to heated verbal conflict. In the New Testament's 4 occurrences it leans toward arguing and quarreling—people disputing with one another (John 6:52) or breaking into strife—though Acts 7:26 describes actual fighting. The Septuagint uses it 21 times, most often for the Hebrew word רִיב (rîb, 6×), which means to bring a legal dispute or contend; everyday papyri also use it figuratively, as in a fourth-century letter urging a man not to 'fight stubbornly against fate.'
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, each rendered differently, the boundary between physical fighting and verbal quarreling depends heavily on context.

definition: An attitude of arrogant pride that looks down on others with contempt.
article: ὑπερηφανία means haughtiness or arrogance — the kind of pride that disdains other people. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Mark 7:22, where the MSB and BSB both render it within a list of vices, and it shows up 26 times in the Greek Old Testament, most often translating the Hebrew גָּאוֹן ("pride" or "majesty"). Everyday Koine papyri use the related verb the same way, as when a document describes someone "puffed up by wealth" treating his friends arrogantly, though one third-century letter uses it in a softened, almost playful sense of "you couldn't be bothered with us."
caution: Appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests on a single occurrence supported by wider Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: To hold an opinion or suppose something, or to seem or be regarded a certain way by others.
article: δοκέω covers both what goes on inside your head—"I think," "I suppose"—and how things look from the outside—"it seems," "is reputed to be." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 61 times, and the dominant measured sense is "think," rendered that way in 89% of the counted cases; notably, 26 of the 61 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing without their own English word. The lexicons add a well-attested second sense, "to seem" or "be reputed," as in Paul's phrase "those of repute" (Gal 2:2), and the everyday papyri show a polite idiom "if your fortune sees fit" used in formal requests.
caution: The measured data captures mainly the "think" sense, while the classical lexicons document a robust "seem/be reputed" sense that the corpus rendering counts underrepresent.

definition: To trouble, bother, or distress someone, often by imposing on their time or effort.
article: In the New Testament σκύλλω means to trouble, bother, or distress people, and all 4 of its occurrences carry this metaphorical sense. That's a notable shift: the classical lexica (Abbott-Smith, Aeschylus) record an original physical meaning of "to skin, flay, or rend," and Moulton-Milligan confirms it kept this concrete sense in the papyri—one document (163 BC) even uses it for plundering a temple. By the New Testament era the word had become almost entirely figurative, ranging in force much like the English "distress," from being deeply harassed (Matthew 9:36) to the polite "don't trouble yourself" (Luke 7:6).
caution: With only 4 occurrences and the three measured senses overlapping heavily, the apparent variety reflects different translation phrasing rather than genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: A case or holder for keeping something, especially the sheath that holds a sword.
article: θήκη comes from the verb τίθημι ("to put" or "place"), so at root it means a place where you put something — a receptacle, case, or chest. In its single New Testament appearance (John 18:11), Jesus tells Peter to put his sword back into its θήκη, its sheath, and every translation surveyed agrees on this rendering. The everyday Koine papyri show its broader range nicely: it labels everything from a sword's scabbard to a "store of anise" and wooden boxes in temple inventories.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its sole biblical sense rests on a single verse.

definition: Sidon, a major coastal city of Phoenicia, mentioned alongside Tyre in the New Testament.
article: Σιδών is the proper name of Sidon, an ancient maritime city of Phoenicia on the Mediterranean coast, rendered "Sidon" in 10 of its 11 Byzantine New Testament occurrences (91%). It appears 24 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always translates the Hebrew name צִידוֹן (Tsidon). Interestingly, in Mark 7:31 some scholars (such as Wellhausen) have suggested reading "to Bethsaida" instead of "through Sidon," reflecting a textual question about that one verse.

definition: A Hebrew-derived exclamation of worship meaning "praise the LORD," shouted in joyful adoration of God.
article: This is the worship cry "Hallelujah," borrowed straight from Hebrew ("praise" plus the short name "Jah" for the LORD) and left untranslated. It appears 4 times in the New Testament, all clustered in Revelation 19, where heavenly voices shout it. The Septuagint uses it 21 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew word Jah, and it sits as a heading or closing word on certain Psalms; intriguingly, the everyday papyri show it surviving in liturgical fragments and even on a protective amulet from the 5th–6th century.

definition: A court officer responsible for enforcing judicial sentences, especially collecting payments or fines from those who owe.
article: πράκτωρ refers to an official who carries out a judge's ruling, particularly by extracting what is owed—the ancient equivalent of a bailiff or debt collector. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke 12:58, where the Majority Standard Bible splits its two occurrences between rendering it as the "officer" himself and the "effort" of payment he exacts. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan note the word is very common as a title for a collector of revenue—handling fines in Ptolemaic times and ordinary taxes under Roman rule.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the New Testament (both in one verse) and once in the Septuagint, so confidence is low.

definition: Many times more; an amount multiplied over and over compared to what was given up.
article: πολλαπλασίων is an expressive compound built from "much" (πολύς) and a root meaning "to fold," so it literally suggests something "folded many times over" — a return multiplied again and again. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 18:30, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as receiving "many more," and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully. Moulton-Milligan note the word's everyday currency in the papyri, comparing a related form in a husband's letter to his wife, and Abbott-Smith records that some manuscripts read "sevenfold" (ἑπταπλασίων) here instead.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text, the evidence is thin, and manuscripts disagree on whether the reading is "many times more" or "sevenfold."

definition: To fill someone completely with food so they are satisfied, or figuratively to satisfy a deep longing.
article: χορτάζω means to feed someone until they are full and satisfied, used most often in the Gospel feeding stories where crowds are "satisfied" (5×, 42%) or "filled" (3×, 25%). The word originally described feeding or fattening animals, but in everyday Koine it was extended to people — a colloquial usage that, according to one scholar, makes its appearance in Philippians 4:12 one of the few vulgarisms Paul allows himself. It can also turn figurative, as in Matthew 5:6, where those who hunger for righteousness will be "filled."

definition: An older or aged woman.
article: πρεσβῦτις is the feminine form of πρεσβύτης (an old man) and simply means an aged or older woman. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Titus 2:3, and shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, as well as once in the Septuagint (4 Maccabees 16:14). Moulton-Milligan note that some have wondered whether the older women of Titus 2:3 form an organized or priestly class, given the temple-like language that follows, but conclude the word need only describe ordinary older women carrying themselves with dignity.
caution: The measured sense reads "addicted," which reflects how the surrounding clause in Titus 2:3 was translated rather than the word itself; the lexica uniformly define it simply as "an aged woman," and the corpus evidence is thin (one NT occurrence).

definition: Describing something made from or belonging to a goat, especially goatskin.
article: This adjective simply means "of a goat" — used in the New Testament for goatskins worn by persecuted believers (Hebrews 11:37), its only occurrence there. In the Septuagint it appears 4 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word עֵז ("goat"). Everyday papyri confirm the ordinary sense: one document from A.D. 133 complains of four stolen goat skins, and recipes mention goat blood and bile, showing this was plain commercial vocabulary.
caution: The measured sense label "put" reflects an indexing quirk from the verse phrasing, not the word's actual meaning, which is clearly "of a goat."

definition: To clean a floor or surface by sweeping it with a broom.
article: Σαρόω means simply to sweep, the way you'd clean a house with a broom. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, always describing a swept space \house clean (Matthew 12:44, Luke 11:25) or a woman sweeping to find her lost coin (Luke 15:8) \u2014 and in every case English translations fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a standalone word. The papyri confirm this was ordinary everyday Koine: one document from A.D. 118 uses it for sweeping out a district, and another mentions a "sweeping of leaves."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, though the meaning itself is clear and consistent.

definition: A bunch of leafy branches or rushes cut and spread out, used to carpet a path or make a bed.
senseLabels: leafy branches spread on a road
article: This word appears just once in the New Testament, in Mark 11:8, where people spread leafy branches on the road before Jesus. The basic idea is a litter or layer of cut foliage, reeds, or rushes laid out flat — and in everyday Koine papyri the related form στιβάς even shifts to mean a mattress, with one sale document from A.D. 143 listing three of them. The Greek translator Aquila used it at Ezekiel 46:23 for a Hebrew term, and the spelling varies between στοιβάς and στιβάς across manuscripts.
caution: This is a single occurrence with variant spelling, and the standard critical text (SBLGNT) does not include it at all, so the evidence is thin.

definition: To have happened earlier or taken place beforehand, referring to something already done in the past.
article: This verb means something occurred or came about at an earlier time, used in the New Testament only as a perfect passive participle. It appears just once in the entire Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 3:25, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "presented" though the underlying sense is "having happened before." Everyday papyri confirm this past-time meaning vividly: one document from A.D. 259 uses it for two town-bathhouse dressing-rooms that "formerly belonged" to a deceased father.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on a single verse and outside evidence.

definition: Visible or openly shown, describing something made plainly evident rather than hidden.
article: ἐμφανής describes something brought into plain view—visible, manifest, out in the open. It appears only twice in the New Testament, split evenly between describing God making the risen Jesus visible (Acts 10:40) and God revealing himself openly to those who did not seek him (Romans 10:20, quoting Isaiah). The everyday Koine papyri sharpen this sense nicely: a legal contract uses the phrase "ἐν τῷ ἐμφανεῖ" to require producing a man "openly, outside a temple or any other shelter," showing the word carried a concrete, almost legal force of being out where everyone can see.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a thin evidence base, the picture of this word's range rests largely on Septuagint and papyri usage rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: A person who treats people unequally, favoring some over others based on outward status rather than fairness.
article: προσωπολήπτης describes someone who plays favorites, judging people by appearance or social standing rather than treating everyone alike. It is built from the words for "face" (πρόσωπον) and "to receive" (λαμβάνω), literally meaning "a receiver of faces." The word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 10:34, where Peter declares that God is not one. Moulton-Milligan note that this word group also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was familiar language, not just a religious term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text and is absent from the critical SBLGNT, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: A dispute over words rather than substance—a pointless quarrel about terms or trivialities.
article: λογομαχία describes verbal wrangling—arguments centered on words and trivialities rather than anything genuinely useful. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:4, where it is listed among the unhealthy results of false teaching. The classical and lexical sources agree closely here: Strong's calls it 'disputation about trifles,' Abbott-Smith 'a strife of words,' and Dodson 'an unprofitable controversy,' all pointing to the same idea of fruitless debate.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be confirmed from biblical usage alone.

definition: To gather ripe fruit, especially grapes at harvest time.
article: τρυγάω means to gather in ripe produce, most often grapes at vintage time, though it can also cover other crops like olives. In the New Testament's three uses, it always involves grapes — either the fruit itself (Luke 6:44) or the act of harvesting it (Revelation 14:18-19). The everyday papyri are especially vivid: one third-century BC letter announces "take notice that I shall have my vintage on the 9th of Payni," showing the word as ordinary farmer's vocabulary for harvest scheduling.
caution: Only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, so the measured range rests on thin evidence supplemented by Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: Describing someone who has no reason to feel ashamed of their work or conduct.
article: This adjective combines a negative prefix with the idea of being put to shame, so it describes a person who acts in a way that gives them nothing to be embarrassed about. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 2:15, where Paul urges Timothy to be a workman who has no cause for shame because he handles God's word rightly. Interestingly, the historian Josephus uses the same word, and Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary language rather than a special coinage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range of meaning cannot be measured from the biblical text alone.

definition: Zebulun, one of Jacob's sons and the Israelite tribe descended from him, also used for the tribe's territory in Palestine.
article: Ζαβουλών is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Zebulun, Jacob's tenth son, used both for the man, the tribe descended from him, and the region they settled. In the New Testament it appears only as the proper name "Zebulun" — 2 times in the Byzantine text and 3 in the critical text — always rendered the same way. The Septuagint uses it far more often, 57 times, and interestingly it almost always translates the Hebrew זְבוּלוּן but in a handful of places stands in for other Hebrew names like Issachar (twice), showing occasional copying or textual slippage.
caution: This is an indeclinable proper name with very few New Testament occurrences, so its range rests mainly on Septuagint usage.

definition: Describing someone who is poor or needy, lacking material resources.
article: πενιχρός describes a person who is poor or in need, essentially a synonym of the more common πένης from which it derives. It appears just once in the New Testament, where Jesus notices a poor widow putting two small coins into the temple treasury (Luke 21:2). Everyday papyri confirm the same plain meaning: a court document from the late fourth century AD describes an old woman as 'poor and aged' (πενιχρὰ καὶ πρεσβύτης), and the Septuagint uses it for the needy in Exodus and Proverbs.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri parallels.

definition: To harm or injure someone, causing physical or other damage.
article: βλάπτω means to harm or injure, and in both of its New Testament appearances (Mark 16:18 and Luke 4:35) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "harm" every time, with the Berean Standard Bible fully agreeing. Strong's notes a more literal sense of "to hinder" that shades into "injure," but the measured biblical usage points squarely to causing harm.
