An interesting detail from everyday papyri: the word is repeatedly used for damage to the eyes ("injured in the right eye," "injured in both eyes"), and it was also a common legal term for property damage.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 1 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin and rated low confidence.

definition: Timon, the personal name of one of the seven men chosen to serve the early church in Jerusalem.
article: Τίμων is a proper name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Acts 6:5), where Timon is listed among the seven men selected to help care for the Jerusalem church. The name comes from τιμή ("honor"), and it was an ordinary Greek name in everyday life — though Moulton-Milligan note that even in the wider Koine record they found only two examples, including a wall-scratching that reads "Aspidas son of Heraklios, the lord Timon." Beyond this single verse, the New Testament tells us nothing further about him.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so the evidence for it is very thin.

definition: Welcoming and generous toward guests and strangers, ready to open one's home to others.
article: φιλόξενος describes someone who loves welcoming guests and strangers — literally a blend of "loving" (φίλος) and "stranger/guest" (ξένος). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice rendered "hospitable" (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:8) and once as "show hospitality" (1 Peter 4:9), and the lexicons agree on this single sense. The word was at home in everyday Koine, with Moulton-Milligan noting it in ordinary papyri and inscriptions, and an early Christian writer (Hermas) using it of overseers who gladly received God's servants into their homes.
caution: With only 3 occurrences this word is thinly attested, though all the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: Of low birth or social standing; regarded as common, unimportant, or beneath notice.
article: ἀγενής describes someone or something of no family standing — lowly, common, or held in low esteem. It is the opposite of εὐγενής ("well-born, noble"), and the New Testament uses it just once, in 1 Corinthians 1:28, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "lowly despised things." A vivid example from everyday Koine survives in a papyrus (P Oxy I.33), where a condemned man's appeal to his nobility prompts the Emperor to snap back, "So you're saying that we are ignoble?" — showing how charged the word's social sense could be.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on a single occurrence supported by outside Koine and classical usage.

definition: Without a witness or proof; lacking evidence to testify to something.
article: ἀμάρτυρος is built from a negative prefix plus a form of the word for "witness" (μάρτυς), so it literally means "without a witness." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 14:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it in the sense of testimony — God did not leave himself "without witness." The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri (for example, a document from around A.D. 225–241 uses it in the phrase "so that it may not be without witness"), and even in the poet Callimachus, confirming it was ordinary, well-attested Greek.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: The state or period of being young; one's early years of life.
senseLabels: youth, the time of being young
article: νεότης refers to youth or youthfulness — the early stage of a person's life. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, rendered "youth" in all 4 cases where it gets its own English word, often in the phrase "from my youth" (ἐκ νεότητος), a set expression found as far back as Homer and common in everyday papyri. In the Septuagint it occurs 49 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for one's youth (נְעוּרִים, 28 times), and Moulton-Milligan note that "youth" here can stretch to cover even fairly mature age, as in 1 Timothy 4:12.

definition: To toss or fling something about, as with garments thrown into the air.
article: This is a strengthened form of ῥίπτω ("to throw, cast, hurl"), appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 22:23, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "tossing" — and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100%. The interesting wrinkle is that lexicographers disagree about which shade of meaning fits that single verse: some read it as the crowd "throwing off" their garments (as the KJV's "cast off"), while others, like Abbott-Smith, take it as the related sense "to shake, toss, throw about." In the Septuagint the underlying verb chiefly translates the Hebrew shalak ("to cast").
caution: This form occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources openly disagree on whether it means "throw off" or "toss about" in that lone verse.

definition: To be full of something or filled with it, often used of containers, places, or things brimming with their contents.
article: γέμω means to be full of or filled with something, used 11 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "full" in 8 of those (73%) and "covered" in the remaining 3 (27%), the latter all in Revelation. The classical lexica trace it from a literal sense of a ship being loaded down (Xenophon) to a general sense of being full of things; one papyrus from the 4th century AD reads πυρὸς γέμι, "full of fire," and a modern Greek echo, "I am full of possessions," shows the same construction found in Revelation 17:3.

definition: Herodias, a woman of the Herodian royal family in the New Testament.
article: Ἡρωδιάς is simply the name Herodias, a member of the Herodian dynasty, appearing 6 times across 3 books. According to Dodson she was the granddaughter of Herod the Great, married first to her uncle Herod and later to his half-brother Herod Antipas; the name itself derives from Ἡρώδης (Herod). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Herodias" in 5 of 6 cases, with the one outlier (Matthew 14:3) being a phrasing artifact ("arrested account Herodias") rather than a separate meaning.
caution: This is a proper name with a single referent, so the one differing rendering reflects sentence phrasing, not an actual second sense.

definition: To overturn or knock something down, used figuratively for upsetting, undermining, or ruining people's faith or households.
article: ἀνατρέπω literally means to overturn or knock something down, but in the New Testament's 2 occurrences it always works figuratively—either upsetting people's faith (2 Timothy 2:18) or ruining whole households (Titus 1:11). The papyri show both meanings vividly: one second-century BC document describes a family home "utterly overturned" through reckless living, while another from AD 190 uses it literally for breaking down a door onto a public street. In the Septuagint it appears 4 times, translating several different Hebrew words, which fits its broad range from physical demolition to social and spiritual ruin.
caution: With only 2 New Testament uses and varied Hebrew sources behind it, the precise figurative force in each case rests on thin evidence.

definition: A bird, especially a wild or flying bird such as those gathering to feed.
article: ὄρνεον simply means "bird," and although it's technically a diminutive form (suggesting "little bird"), the evidence shows it is translated plainly as "bird" in all three of its New Testament appearances, all in Revelation. The Septuagint uses it 23 times across 9 books, most often rendering the Hebrew word צִפּוֹר (12×), the common term for a small bird. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary usage, including a third-century B.C. document referring to "hunters of wild birds."
caution: The two listed senses are really one meaning ("bird"); the second is just a phrase from one verse, and the word appears only 3 times in the New Testament.

definition: A preposition meaning out of or from, marking the source, origin, or starting point of motion, separation, or cause.
article: This common preposition points to where something comes from — its source, origin, or the place it moves out of, and it always takes the genitive. It's overwhelmingly rendered "of" (46%) or "from" (30%), with a long tail of mixed and rare renderings, and in 231 of its 906 appearances it gets absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own. The Septuagint uses it 3,151 times, most often for Hebrew מִן ("from"), and the everyday papyri show it marking departure ("departed from Memphis") or even weakened to "belonging to," as in people connected with the Serapeum.
caution: The many overlapping rendering categories reflect how flexibly translators handle this preposition rather than sharply distinct meanings, so the sense divisions are softer than the numbers suggest.

definition: A bedroom or sleeping chamber; in one expression, the official set over the royal bedroom—a chamberlain.
article: κοιτών means a bed-chamber, a room for sleeping. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 12:20, where the phrase "the one over the bedroom" (ho epi tou koitōnos) names a king's chamberlain—the trusted official in charge of the royal sleeping quarters. The Septuagint uses it 10 times, mostly translating the Hebrew cheder ("chamber"), and everyday papyri confirm it as the ordinary Koine word for a bedroom, even though the strict Atticist Phrynichus condemned it as substandard.
caution: The Majority Standard Bible's recorded rendering for the single NT occurrence reads as "dispute," which conflicts with the dictionaries' clear sense of "bedroom/chamberlain"—likely a tagging artifact, so treat the measured sense with care.

definition: To make peace, bringing things into harmony or reconciliation.
article: This verb means to actively bring about peace—to reconcile parties or harmonize what was at odds. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Colossians 1:20, and just once in the Septuagint (Proverbs 10:10), where it renders the Hebrew word lābaṭ. Strong's frames it figuratively as harmonizing, while the simpler glosses ('make peace,' 'reconcile') capture the core idea well.
caution: Evidence is very thin—just one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use—so the word's full range cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: To come near or approach something or someone, drawing physically close.
article: προσεγγίζω means to draw near or approach, built from πρός ("toward") plus ἐγγίζω ("to come near"). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Mark 2:4), where it is folded into the phrasing and has no separate English word of its own; notably, the critical text reads a different verb (προσενέγκαι) there instead. It shows up more clearly in the Septuagint, occurring 15 times across 11 books, most often rendering the Hebrew נָגַשׁ (9 times), which itself means to come near. Abbott-Smith notes a rare transitive use "to bring near," but the New Testament and most Septuagint usage is intransitive—simply approaching.
caution: Evidence is thin and confidence is low: the word occurs only once in the Byzantine NT, is absent from the critical text, and the relevant verse is textually disputed.

definition: Describing something set apart as sacred or belonging to the deity, as in the "sacred writings" of Scripture.
article: ἱερός means "sacred" or "set apart for God," and in the Byzantine New Testament it shows up just twice, where it describes the holy "Scriptures" (as in 2 Timothy 3:15). Its broader Greek range is much wider than the New Testament's narrow use: classical writers and the Septuagint apply it to temples, sacred rites, and offerings, and the related noun τὸ ἱερόν regularly names the Jerusalem temple precincts. The everyday papyri and inscriptions confirm this temple-centered flavor—it commonly labels heathen temples, sacred revenues, and ritual things, and there's even a parallel where "sacred laws" protected the temple of Jupiter at Magnesia.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in the Byzantine text—just one carrying a measured English sense—the corpus evidence here is very thin, so the rich classical and Septuagint range rests mostly on outside sources.

definition: Israel, the name given to Jacob, used for both the man and the nation or people descended from him.
article: Ἰσραήλ is the name Jacob received, and in the New Testament it almost always points to the nation or people that descended from him—rendered simply "Israel" 84% of its 68 occurrences, with the rest spelled out as "Israelites" or "people of Israel." The word stretches naturally between the political nation, the geographic land, and the people of God, and writers use it in set phrases like "house of Israel," "tribes of Israel," and "king of Israel." The most striking detail is its sheer weight in the Septuagint, where it appears 2,662 times across 35 books, nearly always translating the Hebrew name יִשְׂרָאֵל.

definition: To lift something up, pick it up and carry it, or take it away and remove it entirely.
article: αἴρω covers a tight cluster of physical actions: lifting something up, picking it up to carry, and taking it away or removing it altogether. The measured senses show this clearly — about 30% mean simple lifting "up," 29% mean "took," and another 14% slide into "take away," so the same verb spans gentle raising and forceful removal. It appears 102 times in the Byzantine NT and a striking 251 times in the Septuagint, where it usually renders Hebrew נָשָׂא ("to lift, carry, bear"), 165 times. A nice everyday parallel survives in a second-century inscription where a woman "raises her hands" (αἴρει τὰς χεῖρας) in prayer, the same gesture seen in Revelation 10:5.
caution: The verb is so flexible that 23 of its 102 occurrences carry no distinct English word of their own, so the exact shade often depends on context rather than the word itself.

definition: An adverb meaning that something is real, genuine, or actually true, often emphasizing that a person or thing is truly what it claims to be.
article: ὄντως is an emphatic adverb stressing that something is genuinely so — "truly" or "really." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "truly" in 4 of its 10 New Testament occurrences (40%), with the rest scattered across phrases like "indeed" and "certainly," and the Berean Study Bible independently agrees on "truly" 75% of the time. A striking feature is that it can function almost like an adjective when paired with the article and a noun, as in "the truly widow" (the genuine widow) in 1 Timothy 5:3 — a usage Moulton-Milligan confirms from everyday Koine papyri. Built from the participle of "to be," it also survives in Modern Greek as τόντις.

definition: To buy or purchase something, especially in a market.
article: ἀγοράζω simply means to buy or purchase, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: in all 22 occurrences where it gets its own English word, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "buy" (100%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing every time. Built from ἀγορά (the marketplace), it originally meant to frequent the market, then settled into the everyday sense of purchasing; Moulton-Milligan note it is extremely common in papyri deeds of sale, including the purchase of slaves. In the Septuagint it appears 16 times, most often for the Hebrew שָׁבַר (9×), and the New Testament also stretches it figuratively to people being "bought with a price" (1 Corinthians 6:20; 7:23).

definition: To groan or sigh, expressing inner grief, longing, or displeasure that is felt deeply but often left unspoken.
article: στενάζω describes a heartfelt groan or sigh that comes from inner feeling — grief, longing, or frustration — that is usually internal and unexpressed. Across its 6 New Testament uses the Majority Standard Bible renders it mostly as "groan" (40%), but also "complain" in James 5:9 and the deep "groan inwardly" of Romans 8:23. In the Septuagint it appears 20 times, most often translating the Hebrew אָנַח, "to sigh," and the everyday papyri even show it used of the gods groaning at a woman's death.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences spread thinly across four renderings, the boundary between an audible "groan" and a verbal "complain" rests on individual contexts rather than a firmly measured range.

definition: A word meaning no one, none, or nothing—a strong negation denying any person or thing.
article: οὐδείς is the all-purpose Greek negative that wipes out any person or thing, rendered "no one," "none," or "nothing" depending on context. It is extremely common, appearing 235 times across 19 New Testament books, and the data show its three main jobs clearly: standing alone for a person (44%), pairing with a noun as "no" (28%), and the neuter "nothing" (23%). In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew מְאוּמָה ("anything/nothing," 22×) and even תֹּהוּ, the formless emptiness of Genesis 1, and everyday papyri use it the same way—one letter reassures a friend that "nothing vexatious may happen to you."

definition: To overflow or abound exceedingly, far beyond what is ordinary or expected.
article: This intensified verb means to be present in extreme abundance — it pairs the prefix ὑπέρ ('over, beyond') with περισσεύω ('to abound'), literally stacking 'super' onto 'abound.' It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Romans 5:20, where grace abounds all the more, and in 2 Corinthians 7:4, where Paul's joy overflows. In the 2 Corinthians passage the verb takes the middle voice with a dative, and translators render it as 'overflows,' which Abbott-Smith confirms as the same intensified sense.
caution: With only two occurrences split across two different shades of meaning, the evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: To be inside something; the plural participle means "the things that are within" — the contents of a container.
article: This verb literally means "to be in" or "within," and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 11:41, as a plural participle (τὰ ἐνόντα) meaning "the things inside" — Jesus telling people to give the contents of their cup and dish as alms. Everyday papyri confirm this concrete sense beautifully: one document speaks of "the little basket with its contents," and another of "a bag which contained it." Abbott-Smith notes a secondary possibility, "to be possible," listed in a margin for the same verse, but the measured rendering and the papyri both favor the "contents" meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and even there scholars have debated whether it means "the contents" or "what is possible."

definition: To foam up like a turbulent wave, used figuratively of people who throw off their own shameful deeds.
article: This rare verb pictures the sea foaming up and casting its refuse onto the crest of the waves, applied figuratively to people who 'foam out' their own shame. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Jude 1:13, where wicked men are compared to wild ocean waves. The lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on the vivid image of foam and surf-borne debris, though the Majority Standard Bible's single rendering here is 'wandering,' which reflects the surrounding imagery of the verse rather than the verb's core sense of foaming.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering ('wandering') does not match the lexicons' 'foam out,' so the precise force is uncertain.

definition: To wash a part of the body, such as the hands, feet, or face, with water.
article: νίπτω means to wash, almost always referring to a specific part of the body rather than the whole — the hands, feet, or face. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 17 times, rendered "wash" or "washed" in over 80% of cases, with strong agreement across translations and lexicons. In the Septuagint it usually stands in for the Hebrew רָחַץ (18 of 25 times), and an early apocryphal text vividly contrasts the Jewish leaders, none of whom "washed their hands," with the scrupulous Gentile procurator who did.

definition: The kidneys, used figuratively for a person's innermost feelings, will, and desires.
article: Literally νεφρός means "kidney," but in the Bible it is used figuratively for the deepest part of a person — their hidden desires, emotions, and will. It appears only once in the New Testament (Revelation 2:23), where it is paired with "hearts" to describe what God searches out within people, and the older King James Bible rendered it "reins." In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 28 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for kidneys (24 of those times), and everyday papyri confirm its plain physical meaning — one cook's monthly meat bill simply lists "1 tongue, 2 kidneys."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the New Testament, and even there it is folded into a phrase rather than translated as its own English word.

definition: To wake someone fully from sleep, or rouse something like the sea into stirring, motion, or action.
article: διεγείρω means to arouse completely — most often waking a sleeping person, as when the disciples wake Jesus in the storm (Mark 4:38; Luke 8:24). The same verb stretches to the sea being whipped up by wind in John 6:18, showing it covers stirring things into motion, not just waking people. A striking trace of its everyday Koine life comes from a papyrus magical spell (2nd–3rd century AD) that uses the word to command a dead body to rise, illustrating how broadly Greek speakers applied this idea of rousing.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and 2 of them absorbed into phrasing without their own English word, the measured sense breakdown rests on thin data.

definition: To fight as a boxer, throwing punches with the fists in a contest.
article: This verb means to box—to fight with the fists like a competitor at the games. It appears just once in the New Testament, where Paul says he does not box "aimlessly" (1 Corinthians 9:26), using the image of disciplined athletic training. The everyday reach of the word shows up in the papyri and inscriptions: a tomb epitaph praises a man who "boxed often in the stadiums," and game accounts mention payments to a boxer (πύκτης), including one nicknamed "the tall boxer."
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical text), so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: To meet or encounter someone, and figuratively, of events, to happen or befall a person.
article: At its core συναντάω means simply to meet or encounter someone, and that is how it works 5 out of 6 times in the New Testament (about 83%). The remaining occurrence (Acts 20:22) stretches it figuratively to events that will 'befall' or happen to a person—rendered 'compelled' in the Majority Standard Bible. The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine, showing up in papyri like a third-century B.C. letter describing people who 'met me outside the village,' and in the Septuagint it appears 51 times, often standing in for the Hebrew פָּגַע (11×) and פָּגַשׁ (7×).
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and the figurative 'befall' sense resting on a single verse, the evidence for that secondary meaning is thin.

definition: An adverb meaning from far away or at a distance, describing how something is seen or positioned.
article: πόῤῥωθεν is an adverb meaning "from afar" or "at a distance," built from πόῤῥω ("far") with an ending that signals source. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Luke 17:12 and Hebrews 11:13), and in both the sense is simply distance. In the Septuagint it shows up 15 times, most often translating the Hebrew רָחוֹק ("far," 8×) and its related form מֶרְחָק (5×); Moulton-Milligan note it also occurs in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, sometimes carrying the plain sense of "at a distance" rather than strictly "from a distance."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base for this word is thin.

definition: To pay back fully, giving someone the equivalent of what they did — whether reward for good or punishment for evil.
article: This verb means to give back a complete, matching return for what someone has done. It works in both directions: rewarding good deeds (as in Luke 14:14, Romans 11:35, and 1 Thessalonians 3:9) and paying back wrongdoing (as in Romans 12:19, 2 Thessalonians 1:6, and Hebrews 10:30). It's heavily used in the Septuagint, appearing 66 times and rendering Hebrew words like גָּמַל and שָׁלַם, and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday papyri where it simply means paying people back what they're owed.
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences, the many separate "senses" listed are really one core meaning split by translation wording rather than genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: Causing no burden or financial strain to someone, especially by not demanding their support.
article: ἀβαρής literally means "weightless," but in everyday Koine it was used figuratively to mean "not burdensome"—often about not imposing a cost or obligation on someone. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 11:9, where Paul says he kept himself from being a burden to the Corinthians. The everyday papyri show the same polite usage: one second-century letter (BGU I.248) writes "if it is not a burden to you, lend me a little donkey," capturing exactly the social courtesy the word carried.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in biblical usage cannot be measured from that alone.

definition: Bartimaeus, the blind beggar near Jericho whom Jesus healed, named in Mark's Gospel.
article: Bartimaeus is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament, in Mark 10:46, where it identifies the blind beggar Jesus healed near Jericho. Strong's and Abbott-Smith explain the name as Aramaic for "son of Timaeus," which Mark himself spells out in the same verse. The lexicons note some uncertainty in the exact Aramaic form behind the Greek.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single passage.

definition: To grumble or mutter complaints among themselves, as a crowd voicing shared displeasure.
article: διαγογγύζω describes a group muttering and complaining together — the prefix δια- adds the sense of the grumbling spreading throughout a crowd. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both in Luke (15:2 and 19:7), where people grumble at Jesus, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as some form of "began to grumble." The Septuagint uses it nine times across four books, most often translating the Hebrew לוּן (six times), the same verb used for Israel's complaining in the wilderness, as in Exodus 16:2.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured range is narrow, though the Septuagint and lexicons agree closely on its meaning.

definition: To lead, bring, or carry a person or thing somewhere; sometimes to go, or to spend and keep a day.
article: ἄγω is a common, everyday verb meaning to lead, bring, or carry someone or something from one place to another, appearing 76 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The largest share is rendered "brought" (40×, 63%) and "led" (11×, 17%), with the rest covering departures and being "led away" to trial or judgment. The standard lexicons add ranges the raw counts don't fully highlight: it can mean to spend or keep a day (as in Luke 24:21, Acts 19:38) and an intransitive "let us go" (ἄγωμεν). It frequently renders the Hebrew נָהַג (14×) and בּוֹא (5×) in the Septuagint, and Moulton-Milligan note its forms turn up constantly in ordinary, even uneducated, papyri.

definition: The back, the rear part of the body of a person or animal.
article: This word simply means "the back" — the rear part of a human or animal body. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 11:10, where Paul quotes the Septuagint of Psalm 69:23 about backs being bent down forever. In the Septuagint it shows up 43 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for "shoulder" (18×) and also "neck" (5×); papyri use it in vivid expressions like "do not give your back to anyone," meaning "do not run away."
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament and is borrowed straight from the Septuagint, so its New Testament range cannot be measured independently.

definition: A conditional particle meaning "if indeed" or "if in fact," introducing a condition the speaker often treats as true.
article: Εἴ περ is the conditional particle εἰ strengthened by περ, giving the sense "if indeed" or "if it is really so." It appears only 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and not at all in the critical (SBLGNT) text. In practice the particle is so woven into its clause that translators usually render it through the surrounding verb — "are," "however are controlled," "we are also" — rather than as a standalone "if," and in one of the 6 cases it gets no English word of its own. Moulton-Milligan confirms it was at home in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 6 Byzantine occurrences and none in the critical text — and the word is so absorbed into its clauses that the "measured senses" reflect English phrasing more than distinct meanings.

definition: To sprinkle something with a liquid, often as part of a ceremonial act of purification or cleansing.
article: This verb means to sprinkle or besprinkle, almost always in the context of ceremonial cleansing. All four New Testament uses appear in Hebrews, where it describes sprinkling blood for purification (e.g. Hebrews 9:13, 19, 21; 10:22), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sprinkle" every time. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew nazah, "to sprinkle"; Moulton-Milligan note it is a newer Koine word that replaced the older classical form rhainō, and a third-century BC papyrus uses the related rhantos to describe "spotted" birds.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, all confined to Hebrews, the measured range rests on a narrow base.

definition: An adjective meaning made of, or colored like, an emerald—a bright green gemstone.
article: σμαράγδινος describes something that has the look or color of an emerald, a green gemstone. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 4:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'gleamed' (with the BSB agreeing) to describe a rainbow around the throne. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show the same word used for an emerald-green garment worn by a woman (CPR I.27, A.D. 190) and an emerald-green belt (P Hamb I.10), confirming it was a normal color-word in daily Koine speech.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense there—'made of emerald' versus simply 'emerald-green'—rests on outside evidence rather than internal usage.

definition: In the Lycaonian language, the native speech of the region around Lystra.
article: This adverb means "in Lycaonian," referring to the local language spoken in the inland region of Asia Minor. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 14:11, where the crowd at Lystra shouts in their native tongue after a healing. Moulton-Milligan notes how naturally that local Lycaonian speech would have sprung to the lips of an excited city crowd, a vivid detail that fits the scene exactly.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from usage.

definition: An adverb meaning seventy times, used in the phrase "seventy times seven" to express a vast or unlimited number of repetitions.
article: This word is an adverb built from the number seventy (G1440), and it appears just once in the New Testament, in Jesus' answer to Peter about how often to forgive in Matthew 18:22. There it joins with "seven" in a phrase that translators render either as "seventy times seven" or "seventy-seven times" — the difference hinges on how the Greek combines the two numbers. The most telling clue comes from the Septuagint, where the same word appears once in Genesis 4:24 translating a Hebrew expression; because the Greek drops the connecting "and," it stays unclear whether 70 + 7 or 70 × 7 is meant.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, and sources disagree on whether the phrase means "seventy-seven" or "seventy times seven."

definition: A young or small donkey, used as a riding animal.
article: ὀνάριον is a diminutive form of ὄνος (donkey), meaning a young or small donkey. It appears just once in the New Testament, in John 12:14, where it is rendered "young donkey" in every measured occurrence. The word was everyday conversational Koine: a third-century papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses it for a donkey requisitioned from the local police chiefs, and another papyrus even has the double diminutive ὀναρίδιον, "a small donkey."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: At no time at all; expressing that something has never happened or will never happen.
article: οὐδέποτε is a strong negative adverb meaning "never" or "not even at any time," built from "not even" (οὐδέ) plus "at some time" (ποτέ). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "never" in 10 of its 16 New Testament appearances, with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing or slight variations, and all sources agree on this single meaning. It also turns up in everyday Koine documents — a papyrus from around 244 BC has someone complaining "you have never listened to me" — though Moulton-Milligan note the word is fairly rare in those sources.

definition: Made of gold or overlaid with gold; used to describe objects and ornaments.
article: χρύσεος simply means "golden" — made of or overlaid with gold. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 19 times, and translators render it "golden" in 88% of cases and "gold" in the remaining 12%, with the difference being only whether English treats it as an adjective or noun. In the Septuagint it appears 179 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew word for gold (זָהָב), and everyday papyri use it for concrete items like a golden earring or a golden crescent ornament.

definition: To choke, throttle, or strangle someone, or grip them by the throat; in the passive, to drown.
article: πνίγω means to choke, throttle, or strangle, and in the passive can describe drowning. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only twice, and in its one measured rendering it is translated 'grabbed'—as when the unforgiving servant seizes a fellow servant by the throat in Matthew 18:28. The word lived in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite a child's writing exercise on papyrus reading 'I will choke myself, for it is cold,' showing how ordinary the term was.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 Byzantine occurrences with a single measured rendering—so confidence is low, and the lexicons note related uses (choking plants, drowning) not captured in the measured data.

definition: The act of fleeing or running away to escape danger.
article: φυγή means a flight or escape — the act of running away from danger. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament (and only once in the critical text), both times in Jesus' warning about the urgency of fleeing in the end times (Matthew 24:20, Mark 13:18). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain sense vividly: one document describes a man who "threw away his garment and took to flight," while others mention people fleeing to evade payment of a debt. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew מָנוֹס and related forms, meaning a place or means of escape.
caution: This word is rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice (once in the critical text), so its measured range rests on thin biblical evidence supplemented by papyri.

definition: A reflexive pronoun meaning himself, herself, itself, themselves, or yourselves — pointing the action back to the subject doing it.
article: This is the standard Greek reflexive pronoun, used when an action loops back onto its own subject — "he hurt himself," "they said among themselves." Its 331 New Testament appearances stretch across an enormous English range, from "himself" and "themselves" to a possessive "own," and in fully 108 cases (about a third) it's absorbed into the phrasing without a separate English word of its own. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that although the word is technically third-person, illiterate papyri show it spilling over into first- and second-person uses ("my own," "your own"), and the Bible reflects this too with renderings like "yourselves" (19×, 9%).
caution: The wide spread of renderings reflects the demands of English grammar rather than separate meanings, and the personal reference shifts with context, so the form alone rarely fixes who is meant.

definition: To flog or whip someone with a scourge as a public, official punishment.
article: φραγελλόω means to scourge—to whip someone severely as a formal public punishment. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both describing the flogging of Jesus ordered by Pilate (Matthew 27:26 and Mark 15:15), and the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles agree completely on rendering it as "flogged." Notably, the word is borrowed straight from the Latin flagello, and Moulton-Milligan confirm it turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, showing it was familiar street vocabulary, not just a literary term.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in parallel accounts of the same event, so its measured range is very narrow.

definition: To suffer or be caused sharp pain or distress, whether bodily torment or deep emotional anguish.
article: This verb covers acute suffering of body or mind — from a parent's worried distress to the torment of someone in flames to deep grief at parting. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times, all in Luke's writings (the Gospel and Acts), always in the passive or middle voice meaning "to be pained" rather than to inflict pain on others. A nice everyday touch: it shows up in a second-century BC Alexandrian love poem, where a lover complains "these things wrong me, these things pain me," showing the word's use for ordinary heartache as well.
caution: The four New Testament uses are split evenly across distinct shades of meaning, so each sense rests on a single occurrence; sources also lean toward a single broad sense ("suffer pain/distress") rather than sharply separate ones.

definition: To praise, commend, or applaud someone for what they have done.
article: ἐπαινέω means to praise, commend, or applaud — built from αἰνέω (praise) with an intensifying prefix. It's a fairly stable word: across all 6 New Testament occurrences the sense is consistently "praise" or "commend," whether of a person or an action, and the modern Berean Standard Bible agrees with the Majority Standard rendering every time. One nice detail from everyday Koine: an inscription has a city formally voting that "the people praised and crowned him," showing the word's natural home in public honors and official commendation.
caution: With only 6 occurrences the apparent variety of English renderings (praise, extol, commend) reflects translators' style rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To explain something by telling it in full, narrating or reporting what happened.
article: This verb means to lay something out in words — to narrate, report, or fully explain an event or experience. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times across 3 books, and all measured uses cluster around the same idea of recounting what took place, as when people tell how an event unfolded (Acts 10:8; 15:12; 15:14). The everyday Koine papyri show the same plain usage: one document from 27 B.C. describes a man who 'recounted' a matter clearly to the writer, so this was ordinary reporting language, not specialized religious vocabulary.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and half of them absorbed into broader phrasing, the three labeled senses are really one closely related meaning rather than sharply distinct uses.

definition: A concrete sinful act—a specific wrongdoing or violation of divine law, rather than sinfulness in the abstract.
article: ἁμάρτημα refers to a sin as a concrete act—a particular wrong done, derived from the verb ἁμαρτάνω ("to sin"). The Byzantine NT uses it 4 times (5 in critical texts), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it mostly as "sins," including sins people speak (Mark 3:28) and sexual sin against one's own body (1 Cor 6:18). In the Septuagint it appears 19 times, usually translating the Hebrew words for "sin" (חַטָּאָה, חֵטְא); notably, an Oxyrhynchus papyrus uses the same word for legal violations punishable by the state, showing it was at home in ordinary Koine.
caution: With only 4–5 New Testament occurrences, the apparent distinctions between "sins spoken" and "sexual sin" reflect specific contexts rather than separate established meanings of the word itself.

definition: The community of fellow believers regarded as a family, or the brotherly affection that binds them together.
article: ἀδελφότης is built from the word for "brother" (ἀδελφός) and refers to the family of believers taken as a whole — the Christian "brotherhood." It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Peter (2:17 and 5:9), and Abbott-Smith notes it can carry either an abstract sense (brotherly affection) or a concrete one (the community itself). The papyri show it was ordinary Koine: in P Oxy I.158 a writer addresses someone as his "true and illustrious brother (ἀδελφότης)," and a likely third-century Christian tomb inscription reads "peace to all the brotherhood."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the measured renderings ("treat," "knowledge") reflecting surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself, the evidence here is thin and the labels should be read cautiously.

definition: A silver coin, the stater, equal in value to four drachmas and matching the Jewish shekel.
article: A στατήρ was a silver coin worth four drachmas, equivalent to the Jewish shekel, used by later Greek writers as a name for the tetradrachm. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Matthew 17:27, where Jesus tells Peter he will find one in a fish's mouth to pay the temple tax. The word turns up regularly in everyday Koine papyri tracking sums of money — one document even uses it in an alphabetical acrostic noting an item bought for ten staters.
caution: The measured sense labeled "hook" almost certainly reflects a tagging glitch, since every lexicon and the actual verse make clear this word means a silver coin.

definition: Legal possession or holding of property, especially land received and held as one's own.
article: κατάσχεσις refers to taking and holding something as a possession, and in the New Testament both of its 2 occurrences concern property — the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "land" in Acts 7:5. The word is far more common in the Septuagint, appearing 66 times across 11 books, where it nearly always (53×) translates the Hebrew אֲחֻזָּה, a term for held or inherited property. While classical lexica note an older sense of "a holding back," the measured biblical usage consistently points to "possession" or "holding fast."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (one absorbed into surrounding phrasing) the evidence is thin, so confidence in its full New Testament range is low.

definition: The dark shape made when something blocks light, or by extension a faint outline or foreshadowing of a greater reality.
article: σκιά is the ordinary word for a shadow or shade — the dark patch where light is blocked, as when a passing person's shadow falls on someone (Acts 5:15) or birds nest in the shade of branches (Mark 4:32). It stretches metaphorically in two directions: the somber phrase "shadow of death" for ignorance and error (Matthew 4:16, Luke 1:79), and the idea of a mere outline or foreshadowing set against the real thing, as in Colossians 2:17 and Hebrews 8:5. The everyday flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where σκιά names the moving shadow on a sundial and the instruction to dry a medical preparation "in the shade." In the Septuagint it appears 48 times, most often rendering Hebrew tsel (shadow), but also the dramatic tsalmaveth ("shadow of death") nine times.
caution: The corpus shows only 7 New Testament occurrences, and some measured "senses" reflect awkward word-alignment fragments rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: A warm, willing goodwill or kindness toward someone, served with genuine eagerness rather than mere obligation.
article: εὔνοια describes heartfelt goodwill—the kind of willing, eager kindness you show someone you genuinely care about. In the New Testament it appears only twice: once of slaves serving with sincere goodwill (Ephesians 6:7), and once in the context of conjugal duty (1 Corinthians 7:3), where some translations read it as the affection partners owe each other. The papyri show the same warm flavor: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 156 records a man freeing slaves "out of goodwill and affection" (kat' eunoian kai philostorgian).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and disagreement over whether 1 Corinthians 7:3 means "goodwill" or "conjugal duty," the precise range here is uncertain.

definition: A period of three years.
article: This word names a span of three years, built from the words for "three" (τρεῖς) and "year" (ἔτος). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:31, where Paul recalls the three-year stretch he spent warning the Ephesian church. Everyday Koine documents back this up nicely: Moulton-Milligan cite several papyri using τριετία for ordinary contracts and accounts, such as one phrase meaning "for the remaining period of three years."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: The skill of guiding or directing others, like a helmsman steering a ship—used of leadership in the church.
article: κυβέρνησις literally means steering or piloting a ship, and figuratively refers to guiding or governing—it shows up just once in the New Testament, in Paul's list of gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:28. In the Septuagint it appears 3 times, always rendering the Hebrew word for wise counsel or guidance (תַּחְבֻּלוֹת). The everyday Koine evidence is telling: the related verb describes a woman piloting herself and her child safely through a crisis, capturing the hands-on sense of steering through danger.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise meaning there rests on thin evidence and the underlying steering metaphor.

definition: The mint plant, a fragrant garden herb used as seasoning.
article: ἡδύοσμον is the common Koine name for the mint plant, and the New Testament uses it that way in both of its appearances (Matthew 23:23 and Luke 11:42), where Jesus notes that the Pharisees carefully tithed even this small herb. The word literally combines "sweet" and "smell," so it names the plant by its pleasant fragrance. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes it survives in Modern Greek as δυόσμος, now meaning jasmine, and that ἡδύοσμον was simply the popular everyday term for what was technically called μίνθη.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence is thin, though all sources agree the meaning is simply "mint."

definition: To know something or someone beforehand, or to know in advance—used both of ordinary prior knowledge and of God's foreknowledge.
article: This compound verb joins "before" (πρό) with "to know" (γινώσκω), giving the straightforward sense of knowing something or someone ahead of time. It appears only 5 times in the New Testament, split between ordinary human knowledge (the Jews having known Paul "from the first," Acts 26:5) and God's foreknowledge of people (Romans 8:29, 11:2; 1 Peter 1:20). The word was at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite a 14 B.C. papyrus where a man speaks of having "known beforehand" about some rings.
caution: On 1 Peter 1:20 the scholar Hort argued the sense is closer to "designate beforehand" rather than simply "foreknow," so the precise meaning there is debated.

definition: A connecting word meaning "just as" or "according as," introducing something done in keeping with a command or pattern.
article: καθά is a linking adverb meaning "just as" or "according as," pointing to something done in agreement with what was said or commanded. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 27:10, in a quotation), but it is common elsewhere: the Septuagint uses it 96 times across 14 books, most often translating the Hebrew for "command" (26×). The papyri confirm its everyday use, as in a contract reading "according as we have received," and Moulton-Milligan note it is a late form of καθάπερ first found in the writer Polybius.
caution: The New Testament evidence is extremely thin — a single occurrence inside an Old Testament quotation — so its measured sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: To stretch someone out and tie them in a tense position, here to prepare them for a beating.
article: προτείνω appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 22:25, where Paul is stretched out with thongs in preparation for whipping. Older translations like the KJV took it as simply "bind," but Moulton-Milligan and Field argue it means stretching the body forward into a tense posture to receive blows, rather than merely tying. A papyrus from the second or third century AD uses it of "stretching forward" a fist, and the verb could also carry the everyday sense "put forward, propose."
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence with low confidence, and the sources disagree over whether it means "tie" or "stretch out."

definition: To train or correct someone, ranging from teaching and bringing up a child to disciplining or punishing them.
article: παιδεύω covers a spectrum from gentle instruction to firm correction, all rooted in raising and shaping a person. In the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "disciplined" 5 times (71%) and "punish" twice (29%), with another 6 of its 13 occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The classical lexicons add a milder educational side—Abbott-Smith notes the "train, teach, instruct" sense in passages like Acts 7:22—while the everyday papyri show both: one prodigal's appeal to his mother reads "chastened I have been as I deserve," and another describes someone "educated in every kind of learning." In the Septuagint it appears 58 times, most often translating the Hebrew יָסַר ("to discipline"), 30 times.
caution: The measured New Testament data shows only the "discipline" and "punish" senses, while the lexicons also list a milder "teach/instruct" sense not captured in these counts.

definition: To thoroughly rob or plunder someone's possessions, carrying off their goods by force.
article: διαρπάζω means to plunder or rob someone completely, stripping them of their belongings by force. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times across two books, all in Jesus' picture of a strong man's house being looted once he is bound (Matthew 12:29, Mark 3:27) — translators split evenly between rendering it "steal" and "plunder." The Septuagint uses it 32 times to translate several Hebrew words for seizing and looting, and an ancient papyrus from 161 BC even complains of temple revenues being "plundered" by officials, showing this was everyday Koine language for theft and confiscation.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, all in the same parable, the measured range rests on very limited evidence.

definition: To place or put something around someone or something, including putting on clothing, and figuratively to bestow or confer.
article: At its core περιτίθημι means to put something around — like a hedge around a vineyard (Matthew 21:33, Mark 12:1) or a sponge placed on a reed (John 19:29). The Majority Standard Bible renders all 6 of its rendered uses as 'put,' with two further occurrences absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. Beyond the New Testament its range widens: in the Septuagint it appears 40 times and is used for putting on garments and ornaments, and a papyrus from the first century BC even uses it of a man placing gold jewelry on a woman, while a metaphorical sense 'to bestow or confer' shows up in 1 Corinthians 12:23.
caution: The figurative 'bestow' sense is noted by the lexica and Septuagint but is not separately reflected in the measured New Testament renderings here.

definition: A small emphasizing particle attached to a word to highlight it, often too subtle to translate into English.
article: γέ is an enclitic particle that gives extra prominence to whatever word it follows, marking it as either the least or the most important thing in view. Its force is usually so subtle that English leaves it untranslated — in the Byzantine NT 2 of its 15 occurrences are absorbed into the phrasing with no word of their own, and when it is rendered it shows up as "even" (2×) or gets folded into "will" (2×). It very often pairs with other particles (ἀλλά γε, ἄρα γε, εἴ γε, εἰ δὲ μήγε), and in the Septuagint it stands 128 of 162 times for the Hebrew גַּם ("also, even"). A papyrus from 168 BC nicely captures the emphasis: "now at last on your return I should obtain some relief."
caution: The renderings here are scattered and inconsistent because γέ rarely maps to any single English word, so the "measured senses" reflect translation choices more than distinct meanings.

definition: A step or stair, used figuratively for a standing, rank, or position someone attains.
article: Literally a βαθμός is a step or stair, but in its single New Testament appearance (1 Timothy 3:13) it carries the figurative sense of a standing or rank one achieves. The Septuagint uses it six times, including for the steps of a sundial in 2 Kings 20, and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. One inscription from Mytilene uses the related form for someone who proved worthy of an honorable office, which fits the idea of gaining good standing in 1 Timothy.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the evidence base is thin, so its exact shade of meaning is somewhat uncertain.

definition: To wake someone out of sleep, or to rouse them from sleep.
article: This verb means to awaken someone out of sleep, used in the New Testament with a direct object (the person being woken). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 11:11, where Jesus speaks of going to wake Lazarus. The word is a Hellenistic (later Koine) form replacing the older ἀφυπνίζω, and the Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew יָקַץ ("to awake") three times, including in the Samson story of Judges 16; Moulton-Milligan also note it surviving into Modern Greek as ξυπνῶ.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse plus a handful of Septuagint examples.

definition: The inherent character, makeup, or natural condition of a person or thing, or the regular order of the natural world.
article: φύσις refers to the inborn character or essential makeup of a person or thing, and by extension to the regular order of the natural world. Across its 14 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "nature" half the time and "natural" in another 17%, with the remaining uses absorbed into phrases like "against nature" or "according to nature." A nice detail from everyday Koine: an Oxyrhynchus papyrus uses the very phrase "by birth and not by adoption" (φύσει... καὶ μὴ θέσει), confirming the secondary sense of physical origin or descent that lexicons list.
caution: Lexicons note a "birth/origin" sense (Gal 2:15, Rom 2:27) that the measured renderings register only as a rare reading, so weigh that meaning by context.

definition: Balak, the Moabite king who hired Balaam to curse Israel.
article: Βαλάκ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Balak, the king of Moab known for hiring Balaam to curse Israel. It appears only once in the New Testament (Revelation 2:14), always rendered "Balak," and shows up 54 times in the Septuagint. Interestingly, while the Greek spelling mostly translates the Hebrew name בָּלָק (44 times), the Septuagint also used it for a few other Hebrew words, including one meaning a place name and one related to being "satisfied."
caution: This is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, so its sense is fixed and not a matter of translation range.

definition: The temple treasury—a room or set of collection chests where worshipers' money offerings were stored.
article: This word always refers to the treasury of the Jerusalem temple, whether the room itself or the trumpet-shaped chests where offerings were dropped in. The measured renderings in the Byzantine text fragment the five occurrences into several phrases (like "Jesus than treasury"), but these are artifacts of the surrounding sentences—the underlying meaning is a single, consistent idea of "treasury." In the Septuagint it appears 12 times and mostly translates the Hebrew word for a temple "chamber" (לִשְׁכָּה), and a third-century BC inscription even uses it for a military treasury, showing it was ordinary Koine vocabulary for a strongroom.
caution: The measured "senses" mostly reflect phrasing in context rather than distinct meanings; the word's actual range is narrow and stable.

definition: To declare something solemnly and earnestly, giving weighty testimony or a serious warning to others.
article: This verb is an intensified form of the simpler "to testify" (μαρτύρομαι), and the extra force comes through clearly: it means to bear witness or urge something with great seriousness, sometimes close to a formal protest or solemn charge. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times, mostly in Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "testifying" or "testified" about half the time, with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The most interesting detail is its Septuagint background: it translates the Hebrew עוּד ("to warn, admonish, call to witness") 19 times, which explains the warning, hortatory edge that Moulton-Milligan notes appears especially in Paul's usage.
caution: Sources disagree on emphasis—classical Greek leans toward "to testify/protest," while Hellenistic usage adds a "warn, admonish" sense, and 5 of 15 occurrences are absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word.

definition: A descendant, especially a grandchild or other child born from one's own children.
article: This word names someone descended from you — a child, grandchild, or further offspring. It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Timothy 5:4), paired with "children" to describe family members who should care for aging parents; the KJV famously rendered it "nephews," using an old sense of that word meaning "grandchildren." It is much more common in the Septuagint (28 times across 5 books), where it translates several different Hebrew words, including one (בָּ֫טֶן) literally meaning "womb" or "offspring." Interestingly, the everyday Koine evidence shows real flexibility: on the Rosetta Stone it was read as "son," while elsewhere Wilcken understood it as "great-grandchild."
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use, where it is folded into a phrase rather than translated as its own word, and the sources stretch the meaning from "son" to "great-grandchild."

definition: Rotten or spoiled, and so worthless or bad — used of trees, fruit, fish, or, figuratively, harmful speech.
article: σαπρός describes something decayed and therefore good for nothing — the kind of fruit or fish you throw away rather than eat. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "bad" in 6 of those cases (75%), usually paired against "good" (καλός, ἀγαθός) when contrasting good and bad trees or fruit. It also stretches to a moral sense, as in Ephesians 4:29's warning against "bad" speech. The everyday papyri make the literal meaning vivid: one document from A.D. 256 lists "rotten figs" (συκαρίων σαπρῶν), and another applies the word to stale, low-quality drugs.
caution: The word's original classical sense was specifically "decayed," but Moulton-Milligan note that in Hellenistic Greek this faded and it broadened toward "bad" or "shameful," so the precise force can vary by context.

definition: A woman whose husband has died and who therefore lacks his support and protection.
article: χήρα simply means a widow — a woman left without a husband — and the meaning is remarkably stable, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "widow(s)" in essentially every one of its 27 New Testament occurrences. In the Septuagint it appears 56 times and almost always stands for the Hebrew אַלְמָנָה (46×). The everyday papyri bring the word to life: petitions written by widows describe themselves as "a feeble widow woman" appealing for protection, showing how vulnerable such women were in ordinary Koine society. Abbott-Smith also notes a rare figurative use in Revelation 18:7, where a forsaken city is pictured as a widow.

definition: A book, scroll, or written volume, often carrying a sense of sacredness or special importance.
article: βίβλος refers to a book or scroll — every measured New Testament occurrence (8 of 9, with one absorbed into the surrounding phrasing) is rendered "book." The word's range is narrow and stable, but the interesting detail is its tone: Moulton-Milligan and Abbott-Smith note a consistent "connotation of sacredness and veneration," and a papyrus from A.D. 138 uses it for the old wise books handed down from ancient Chaldean sages. In the Septuagint it usually stands for Hebrew sēper ("book" or "scroll"), and it derives from the inner bark of the papyrus plant used to make writing material.
caution: The evidence base is modest — only 9 New Testament occurrences and 12 in the Septuagint — so the suggested aura of sacredness rests largely on lexicographers' observations rather than the measured renderings.

definition: To break something into pieces, used in the New Testament especially of breaking bread.
article: κλάω means simply to break or break in pieces, and in the New Testament it is used almost entirely of breaking bread—at Jesus' feedings of crowds, the Last Supper, and shared meals. Across all 15 Byzantine occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "broke" 67% of the time, with the remaining cases being the same action described as Jesus spoke and broke the bread. The everyday Koine reach of the word shows up vividly in the papyri, where one document complains of being mercilessly beaten and "broken," and where a related form even describes someone as curly-haired.

definition: A secret agreement among people to commit a harmful act; a plot or conspiracy.
article: This word names a group's secret pact to carry out a wicked plan—literally a "swearing together," built from σύν (together) and ὀμνύω (to swear). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:13, where more than forty men bind themselves to kill Paul. The everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions confirm the same meaning: one inscription from around 300–280 BC pledges to report any conspiracy that arises to the authorities.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Stubbornness or hardness of heart — an unyielding, obstinate inner attitude.
article: σκληρότης literally means "hardness," and in the New Testament it is used figuratively for a stubborn, unrepentant attitude. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 2:5, where it describes a hard and unrepentant heart. The Septuagint uses it four times, including Deuteronomy 9:27 where it renders the Hebrew word for "stubbornness," matching the New Testament's metaphorical sense; Moulton-Milligan also notes the word turning up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: The measured-sense label "righteous" reflects a tagging glitch in the rendering data and contradicts every lexicon, which agree the word means hardness or stubbornness; with only one New Testament occurrence, confidence is low.

definition: Judea, the region of Palestine south of Samaria whose capital was Jerusalem, sometimes standing for its inhabitants.
article: Ἰουδαία names the southern region of Palestine, with Jerusalem as its center, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Judea" in 39 of 43 occurrences (91%). Its range is narrow and stable: it can mean the strict southern district, occasionally all of Palestine in a wider sense, and by metonymy the people who live there. A nicely concrete touch comes from the papyri: a poorly spelled army-supply receipt from A.D. 128 (P Ryl II.189) mentions cloaks for the soldiers "serving in Judaea," showing the word in plain everyday use. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Judah).

definition: An adverb meaning quickly, soon, or without delay.
article: ταχύ is the neuter form of ταχύς used as an adverb, meaning "quickly" or "soon." The Byzantine NT uses it 12 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "quickly" or as part of phrases like "I am coming soon" (Revelation 22:7, 12). It was a common word in everyday Koine: a papyrus letter from 2 B.C. urges that "it is well for him to come quickly, for he will instruct you," and the Septuagint uses it 23 times, mostly to translate Hebrew words meaning to hurry or hasten.

definition: To be at full ripeness or prime, the point at which fruit is ready to be harvested.
article: ἀκμάζω describes something reaching its peak or prime, most concretely when fruit on the vine is fully ripe and ready to be gathered. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Revelation 14:18, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as the grapes being ready to "gather," and the BSB agrees. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri: a magical text speaks of "all the fruits that are ripe," while an inscription has Nero wishing he could have freed Greece "while it was at its prime."
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one measured occurrence, so its full range here rests largely on outside Koine and classical evidence.

definition: To spread news, a report, or someone's fame widely, broadcasting it to many people.
article: διαφημίζω means to broadcast news, a report, or someone's reputation far and wide. It is rare, appearing only 3 times in the New Testament, and translators render it mostly as "spread news" (2×, 67%), with one case at Matthew 28:15 where the Majority Standard Bible reads it differently as "guards." Abbott-Smith notes it pairs with the Greek for "the matter" (Greek λόγον, standing in for the Hebrew dāḇār), and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday Koine papyri and three times in the astrologer Vettius Valens, where people are "talked about" for their noble deeds.
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only 3 times, the lexica describe just one sense ("spread abroad"), and the measured "guards" rendering at Matthew 28:15 likely reflects the verse's wider phrasing rather than the verb itself.

definition: The act of restoring something to its former or proper condition.
article: This noun means restoration or putting something back into its proper state. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 3:21, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render it "restoration." The everyday Koine evidence is striking: the papyri and inscriptions use it for very ordinary matters, including the repair and renewal of temple buildings—one inscription speaks of "the restoration of the temple" of Artemis at Magnesia.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise scope there rests on a single passage.

definition: A personal name belonging to a man whose wife, Mary, stood by Jesus' cross.
article: Κλωπᾶς (Clopas) is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, at John 19:25, where Mary the wife of Clopas is named among the women at the cross. The name is of Aramaic origin, and the KJV renders it "Cleophas." Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and point readers to compare the related name Κλεόπας.
caution: This is a personal name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: Describing a person who is irreverent and disregards what is sacred or holy.
article: This adjective means "unholy" or "profane" — it labels someone who shows contempt for sacred things. It's built from a negative prefix plus the word for "holy" (ὅσιος), and the New Testament uses it only twice, both times in lists of wicked people (1 Timothy 1:9 and 2 Timothy 3:2). The everyday Koine papyri are striking here: the word was repeatedly hurled at Jews during the Jewish war in Egypt (around A.D. 115), showing it carried a charged, accusatory force in ordinary speech.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the entry rests on limited data.

definition: To stick faithfully and steadily to a person, place, or activity, keeping at it without giving up.
article: προσκαρτερέω describes persistent, steadfast commitment—whether sticking close to a person, attending faithfully to a duty, or continuing in a practice like prayer. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times across 4 books, rendered mostly as "continued" or "devoted," and 2 of those 10 are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word. Tellingly, the same word turns up in everyday Koine papyri: a Strategus swears in his oath of office to keep at his post "unceasingly," showing this was the ordinary language of sticking dutifully to a job.

definition: Someone who watches or oversees something firsthand, an eyewitness or spectator of events.
article: ἐπόπτης describes a person who looks on and sees something directly — an eyewitness or spectator. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (2 Peter 1:16), where the writers claim to have been eyewitnesses of Christ's majesty, and the word's force gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. In both the Septuagint (where it translates Hebrew נֹ֫כַח) and in everyday inscriptions, the term was applied to God or to powerful rulers as an "overseer"; one inscription from Cyzicus even calls Pompey the Great the ἐπόπτης of land and sea.
caution: This is a rare word with only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, so its precise range in biblical usage rests on thin evidence.

definition: Esli, a man listed as one of the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ἐσλί is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Luke 3:25), where it names one of the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy. Although the translation data counts it as "son" 100% of the time, that simply reflects its place in the chain of fathers and sons; it is really just a proper name. According to Dodson it identifies the son of Naggai and father of Nahum, and the name is of Hebrew origin, probably linked to H0454.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its background rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To rouse someone fully — either to stir them into action and purpose, or to raise them up from the dead.
article: ἐξεγείρω means to fully rouse or raise someone up, built from ἐκ ('out') and ἐγείρω ('to wake, raise'). In the New Testament it appears only twice, split evenly between two senses: in Romans 9:17 God 'raises up' Pharaoh for a proclaimed purpose, and in 1 Corinthians 6:14 it refers to raising the dead. The word was at home in everyday Koine — Moulton-Milligan cite a third-century BC inscription where a healed man at a temple of Asclepius is described as 'roused up' to full health. In the Septuagint it appears 78 times, most often translating the Hebrew עוּר ('to wake, stir up'), 38 times.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, each illustrating a different sense, the measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A person who reaps and gathers a crop at harvest time.
article: θεριστής is the worker who brings in the harvest, a straightforward agricultural term built from the verb θερίζω ("to reap"). Both of its New Testament appearances are in the same parable (Matthew 13:30, 39), where Jesus identifies the harvesters as angels gathering at the end of the age. The word was everyday Koine vocabulary: papyri show harvesters being levied for fieldwork by official list, and it even survives in Modern Greek.

definition: To renew or restore something to a fresh state, bringing it back to a former condition.
article: ἀνακαινίζω means to make something fresh again or restore it, built from the parts "again" and "new." It appears just once in the New Testament (Hebrews 6:6), where it speaks of renewing fallen people to repentance, and four times in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew word for "renew" (חָדַשׁ) among others. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) and the everyday-Koine papyri all agree on this "renew/restore" sense, even though the single NT verse appears in a context of being "fallen."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured range is very thin, so the fuller sense rests on the Septuagint and lexical evidence.

definition: Asher, one of Jacob's sons and the Israelite tribe that descended from him.
article: Ἀσήρ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Asher, both a son of Jacob and the tribe descended from him. The New Testament uses it just twice—Luke 2:36 (the prophetess Anna's tribe) and Revelation 7:6—and translators render it "Asher" 100% of the time. In the Septuagint it appears far more often (50 times across 9 books), almost always translating the Hebrew אָשֵׁר, though a few times it stands in for other Hebrew names like Manasseh.

definition: To serve or worship God (or false gods) through devoted religious service and homage.
article: This verb describes religious service rendered to God—or, occasionally, to idols. In the Byzantine New Testament it is translated "serve" 12 times (63%) and "worship" 5 times (26%), and the two ideas blend together, since the serving in view is always sacred. It carries this religious sense throughout the New Testament; in everyday papyri the word root traces back to a hired servant, but in the Septuagint, where it appears 96 times, it almost always renders Hebrew עָבַד ("serve," 83 times) and consistently means the worship of God or of pagan deities.

definition: The number three hundred.
article: τριακόσιοι is simply the number "three hundred," formed from the words for "three" and "hundred." It appears just twice in the New Testament (Mark 14:5 and John 12:5), both times in reference to the three hundred denarii that the expensive perfume could have been sold for. It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 71 times across 13 books, usually translating the Hebrew word for "three" (40 times) in counting contexts.
caution: The two NT renderings recorded here ("three" and "wasn't three hundred") reflect fragments of longer phrases rather than separate meanings, so treat them as a single sense; the word straightforwardly means "three hundred."

definition: To have free time or a good opportunity to do something.
article: εὐκαιρέω means to have leisure or a convenient opening to do something, built from εὔκαιρος ("well-timed"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the renderings vary by context: not having time to eat (Mark 6:31), spending time on novelties (Acts 17:21), and finding a favorable opportunity (1 Corinthians 16:12). The everyday flavor shows up clearly in the papyri, where one letter writer says he will come at once "as soon as I have the opportunity" (P Par 46).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise shade in each verse depends heavily on context.

definition: A flower or blossom, the bloom of a plant that quickly fades.
article: ἄnthos means simply a flower or blossom. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 4 times, rendered "flower" in 3 of them and "field flowers" once, always in passages about how quickly human glory withers like a fading bloom. It is far more common in the Septuagint (20 times across 8 books), where it usually translates the Hebrew צִיץ; notably both New Testament uses are essentially quoting Isaiah 40:6-7, and the word still survives in Modern Greek. Everyday papyri and inscriptions also use it, including a rule forbidding anyone to carry flowers into a temple.
caution: The "flower" and "field flowers" labels reflect translation choices on the same kind of image rather than two genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: To refresh or revive someone, giving them relief from distress or hardship.
article: This verb means to refresh or revive a person, originally carrying the literal idea of cooling off and figuratively the sense of giving relief. It appears just once in the New Testament, where Paul says Onesiphorus often "refreshed" him (2 Timothy 1:16), and five times in the Septuagint, often for the Hebrew נָפַשׁ in the sense of reviving oneself. A striking everyday example comes from a 168 BC papyrus letter, where a wife writes to her recluse husband that she hopes to obtain "some relief" (ἀναψυχῆς) on his return — showing how naturally Koine speakers used this word for emotional and physical comfort.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, though Septuagint and papyri usage agree on the meaning.

definition: Showing mercy and favor rather than anger; used of God being gracious, or in a fixed phrase meaning "may it never happen."
article: ἵλεως describes a disposition of mercy and favor, especially God being gracious toward people. In the New Testament's two occurrences, it shows up in two quite different ways: once in the fixed exclamation "Far be it!" (Matthew 16:22, where it likely implies "may God be gracious to you" = may this never happen), and once meaning God's merciful forgiveness of wrongs (Hebrews 8:12). The Septuagint uses it 26 times, most often (15×) for the Hebrew סָלַח, "to forgive," and the papyri preserve the same flavor — one prayer reads "come to me, goddess of goddesses, becoming gracious, hear me."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences split between two very different uses, and the Matthew sense resting on an implied phrase, the measured range is thin.

definition: To promise or announce something in advance, ahead of the time it is fulfilled or delivered.
article: This compound verb literally stacks "before" (πρό) onto "announce/promise" (ἐπαγγέλλω), giving the sense of promising something ahead of time. It appears just once in the Byzantine NT (twice in the critical text), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gospel promised beforehand" in Romans 1:2, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing entirely. The word also turns up in everyday Koine: a Priene inscription from 84 B.C. uses it for festivities "promised in advance" to the people by a man named Zosimus, showing it was ordinary public language, not a specialized religious term.
