caution: Evidence is thin — only one Byzantine occurrence — so the measured sense rests on a single verse, though papyri and lexica consistently confirm the "promise beforehand" meaning.

definition: A word or spoken expression, appearing only in the phrase meaning "so to speak."
article: ἔπος means a word—specifically the articulated expression of a thought, as distinguished from λόγος (reasoned speech) and ῥῆμα (a mere utterance). In the New Testament it appears just once, in Hebrews 7:9, and only inside the set phrase ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, "so to speak," used to soften a strong claim. The same literary phrase shows up in an Oxyrhynchus papyrus from a property dispute (A.D. 338), confirming it was a recognized turn of speech in everyday Greek as well as literature.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and just twice in the Septuagint, always in fixed or literary usage.

definition: To tell or relate something in full detail, recounting it thoroughly.
article: This verb means to narrate something fully, telling the whole story in detail. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts, and four times in the Septuagint, where it translates several different Hebrew words including one meaning 'to relate' and another 'to be astonished.' Note that one Byzantine occurrence (Acts 13:41) was rendered 'perish' in the measured data, but this clashes with the lexicons and the BSB's own 'declare/recount' reading, so the genuine sense throughout is 'tell in detail.'
caution: Evidence is thin—only two NT uses—and the measured 'perish' rendering at Acts 13:41 conflicts with every lexicon, suggesting a tagging or context artifact rather than a real sense.

definition: Galilee, the northern region of Palestine where Jesus carried out much of his ministry.
article: Γαλιλαία is the place-name for Galilee, the northern district of Palestine in New Testament times, and it shows up 63 times in the Byzantine text across five books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "Galilee" in 83% of cases, with the remaining occurrences still referring to the same region as the setting of Jesus' activity. The name comes from the Hebrew גָּלִיל, meaning "circle" or "district" — which the Septuagint translators carried over in passages like Matthew 4:15, where Galilee is called "Galilee of the Gentiles."

definition: To take hold of someone or something in order to help, support, or partake in it.
article: This middle-voice verb pictures taking hold of someone or something—either to help and support a person, or to partake of and benefit from a thing. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, split evenly: God helping Israel (Luke 1:54), supporting the weak (Acts 20:35), and partaking of a benefit (1 Timothy 6:2). It is far more common in the Septuagint, where its 39 occurrences translate Hebrew words for supporting and holding fast, such as סָמַך and חָזַק; the everyday papyri use it for taking up a duty or office.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, the sense range here rests mostly on the much broader Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: The benefit, profit, or usefulness that something produces; what good a thing actually does.
article: ὄφελος refers to the practical advantage or benefit that something yields — the "good" it does or the profit it brings. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice in James (2:14, 2:16) asking what good faith is without works, and once in 1 Corinthians 15:32 asking what use Paul's struggle would be if the dead are not raised. Notably, it shows up in everyday Koine papyri with exactly this sense, as in an Oxyrhynchus letter saying it is "of no use" if someone arrives too late to help.
caution: This word is rare, with only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint appearance, so its measured range is thin.

definition: Describing a person who is self-controlled and clear-headed, free from the influence or excess of wine.
article: This adjective describes someone who is temperate and clear-headed, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it just 3 times, all in pastoral lists of qualities for leaders and older believers (1 Timothy 3:2; 3:11; Titus 2:2). Originally, as Abbott-Smith notes, classical Greek used it of drink "not mixed with wine," and only later writers like Plutarch applied it to people meaning sober or temperate. A striking trace of the literal sense survives in an inscription where "three νηφάλιοι altars" may mean altars for wineless offerings, showing the word's roots in the idea of being free from wine.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences, none in the critical SBLGNT text) and the spelling νηφάλεος is a late variant, so confidence is low.

definition: To threaten someone, warning them of harm or punishment if they don't comply.
article: ἀπειλέω means to threaten or menace someone, often as a warning to stop a certain behavior. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and the two occurrences are rendered differently: "warn" in Acts 4:17 (where the council threatens the apostles) and "abuse" in 1 Peter 2:23 (describing how Christ, when suffering, did not retaliate). In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words, including גָּעַר ("rebuke") twice; one papyrus letter even has a child playfully "making threats" to a relative, and Moulton-Milligan suggests the word was actually fading out of everyday speech.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the two standard Bibles disagreeing on how to render 1 Peter 2:23, the precise range here is uncertain.

definition: The act of taking, receiving, or sharing in something—in its one New Testament use, the receiving of food.
article: μετάλημψις means the taking in or sharing of something, and the lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) gloss it as participation, receiving, or sharing in. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 4:3, where it refers to receiving food that God created to be shared with thanksgiving. The Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering as "prohibit" reflects the wider sentence (forbidding people from eating) rather than the noun itself, which centers on the act of receiving. One nice everyday touch: the papyri use the same word in a marriage contract for the "concurrence" or consent of the other party (P Oxy X. 1273).
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lone measured rendering reflects the surrounding sentence rather than the noun's own meaning of receiving or sharing.

definition: Arabia, the geographical region lying to the south and east of Palestine.
article: Ἀραβία is simply the place name Arabia, a region southeast of Palestine. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Galatians (1:17 and 4:25), and the renderings are functionally identical — just the proper noun. One curious detail from the papyri: the same name was also used for an Egyptian administrative district (nome) on the east side of the Nile, so in everyday Koine documents "Arabia" did not always point to the same place.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences — and the Septuagint and papyri show the name attached to more than one location.

definition: To bring back word about something, announcing or reporting it to others by message.
article: This verb covers the whole act of relaying information—telling, reporting, announcing, or bringing back word from one place to another. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 44 times and the Majority Standard Bible renders it most often as "tell" (12×, 29%) and "reported" (6×, 14%), with a cluster of closely related shades like "proclaim," "informed," and "announced." Its background is heavily a messenger's word: in the Septuagint it appears 221 times and translates the Hebrew נָגַד ("to make known") 188 of those times, and Moulton-Milligan finds it in everyday papyri letters where someone "reported" news brought by a letter-carrier.

definition: Small in size, amount, importance, or duration—covering everything from physical littleness to a brief span of time.
article: μικρός is a basic, everyday Greek word for "small" that stretches across several dimensions: physical size, quantity, social rank, and even time. In the New Testament it appears 45 times, most often meaning simply "little" (15×), but it also marks a short span as "a little while" (7×) and can describe someone of low standing—the "little ones" or the "least." In the Septuagint it shows up 133 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew קָטָן (small, 53×) and מְעָט (few, 34×); interestingly, papyri suggest it was sometimes used to mean "junior" by age rather than short in stature, though the evidence there is mixed.

definition: A Scythian, a person from the region north of the Black Sea, used by Greeks as the very image of a wild, uncivilized people.
article: Σκύθης names an inhabitant of Scythia (roughly modern Russia and Siberia) and was, to Greek speakers, shorthand for the wildest of barbarians. It appears only once in the New Testament (Colossians 3:11), and there it is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word. Interestingly, the papyri show it was also simply a personal name in everyday Koine, as in a letter where a man named Σκύθης greets Ptolemy (P Hib I.55, about 250 B.C.).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall evidence, the sense rests largely on lexicon descriptions rather than measured usage.

definition: A person who lives in Jerusalem; an inhabitant of the city.
article: This word simply means someone who lives in Jerusalem, derived from the Greek name for the city (Ἱεροσόλυμα). It appears only twice in the New Testament — once in Mark 1:5, where it refers collectively to the people coming out from Jerusalem, and once in John 7:25, referring to the city's residents. It also shows up a handful of times in the Septuagint, including Sirach 50:27 and several places in 2 Maccabees, where it likewise names inhabitants of the city.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though the meaning is consistent across all sources.

definition: A narrow street, lane, or alley within a town or city.
senseLabels: a street where the needy are
article: In the New Testament, ῥύμη always means a narrow street, lane, or alley in a town or city, appearing 4 times across 3 books. All four measured renderings—"needy on streets," "alleys," "the street called Straight," and the city street where Peter walked—point to the same basic sense of an urban passageway. Interestingly, classical Greek used this word quite differently, for the force or rush of a moving body, especially a charge of soldiers; the "street" meaning is a later Koine development, well attested in everyday papyri, including one that describes a "blind alley."
caution: The everyday "street" sense in the New Testament differs sharply from the classical "rush of a moving body," so don't read the older meaning into the biblical text.

definition: To be together with someone, present in their company at a given time.
article: σύνειμι is a simple compound of σύν ("with") and εἰμί ("to be"), meaning to be in someone's company or present alongside them. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (the critical text has three), once describing Jesus' disciples being with him while he prayed (Luke 9:18) and once Paul's companions (Acts 22:11). Everyday Koine papyri use the word so often of "coming together in wedlock" that phrases like "her present husband" or "my present wife" become a standard idiom — a vivid window into its ordinary social range.
caution: With only two Byzantine occurrences and a noted textual variant at Luke 9:18 (some witnesses read συνήντησαν), the New Testament evidence is thin.

definition: Vomit — food or matter thrown up from the stomach.
article: This noun simply means vomit, the matter disgorged from the stomach. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:22, which echoes Proverbs 26:11 (where the Septuagint uses a related word, ἔμετον). Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including an inscription describing a cure at a temple of Asclepius where a related verb describes vomiting up "all the evils," and the related verb survives in Modern Greek (ξερνῶ, to vomit).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be tested from biblical usage alone.

definition: Clothing or a garment, especially the visible attire someone is wearing.
article: ἔσθησις means clothing or a garment, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 1:10, describing the white garments of the two men who stood by the disciples. It's a fairly rare word, related to ἐσθής (clothing), and shows up only twice in the Septuagint (2 Maccabees 3:33 and 3 Maccabees 1:16). A striking everyday example comes from a papyrus (BGU I.16, A.D. 159–160) where a priest is reported for wearing woollen garments (ἐρεαῖς ἐσθήσεσι) and letting his hair grow too long.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and is rare overall, and the KJV gloss "government" does not match the clothing sense given by other sources.

definition: To call something or someone to mind; to remember, keep in memory, or sometimes to mention.
article: μνημονεύω means to hold something in your memory or call it to mind, and it's the standard New Testament word for 'remember,' rendered that way in 12 of 21 occurrences (86%) with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100%. Its range stretches slightly toward 'making mention of' someone or something, as Abbott-Smith notes for passages in Hebrews. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri: a third-century BC letter writes 'you would do well to remember us' (μνημονεύων ἡμῶν), and a fourth-century AD Christian letter pleads, 'remember me in your holy prayers.' In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew זָכַר, the common verb for remembering.

definition: A bridle or bit—the strap-and-mouthpiece gear used to control and steer a horse.
article: χαλινός is the gear used to control a horse: the bit placed in its mouth and the bridle that steers it. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament—James 3:3 (the bits put in horses' mouths) and Revelation 14:20 (blood rising as high as the horses' bridles). In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times, most often rendering the Hebrew מֶ֫תֶג, and everyday papyri even mention a 'bridle of silver' (PSI V.543, third century BC).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the second tagged as 'rose' rather than a bridle term, the measured data is thin and the lexica (which agree on 'bridle/bit') should be weighted more heavily.

definition: A Phoenician town near Sidon, called Zarephath, where the prophet Elijah was sent during a famine.
article: Σάρεπτα is the Greek name for Zarephath, a town in the district of Sidon in Phoenicia, mentioned just once in the New Testament (Luke 4:26). It is a place name, not a common word, and every translation renders it the same way. The Greek form comes directly from the Hebrew צָרְפַת, which appears 3 times in the Septuagint, including the prophet Obadiah's reference (Obadiah 20).
caution: This is a rare proper noun appearing only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be tested across varied contexts.

definition: A person who plays the flute, especially as a musician at festivals, funerals, or other gatherings.
article: αὐλητής means a flute-player, a musician who performs on the flute. The word appears only twice in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as "flute" (Matthew 9:23) and once as "flute players" (Revelation 18:22). Everyday Koine documents confirm this ordinary sense: a papyrus from around 245 BC requests that a flute-player named Petous be sent for a festival, and a later papyrus mentions the head of a company of flute-players and musicians hired for a five-day village celebration.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence is thin, though the sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: It is permitted or allowed by law, custom, or rule; something one is free to do.
article: This impersonal verb means "it is permitted" or "it is lawful," usually pointing to what rules, law, or custom allow. The Byzantine NT uses it 31 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lawful" in 64% of cases and "unlawful" (with a negative) in another 27%; nine times it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary legal sense — for example, a second-century document reads "this was not permissible" (P Ryl II. 77), showing the word was common contract and legal language, not just a religious term.

definition: A love of money or greedy craving for wealth.
article: φιλαργυρία literally combines the ideas of "loving" and "silver," describing an intense craving for money or avarice. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "craving." In the Greek translation of 4 Maccabees this same vice is named alongside other passions, and an ancient Jewish text quoted by Moulton-Milligan warns that φιλαργυρία "leads to idolatry."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the corpus alone.

definition: To perceive or grasp something mentally, becoming aware or understanding it, sometimes with the sense of sharing private knowledge.
article: συνείδω is an irregular aorist form (related to συνοράω) meaning to "see together" and so, of mental vision, to comprehend or become aware of something. The Byzantine NT has it 4 times, though the critical text drops it to zero. In the Septuagint it shows up only 3 times across 3 books, translating three different Hebrew verbs once each, which suggests it had no single fixed Hebrew counterpart and was used loosely. Note that the listed sense "wife's" reflects the surrounding phrasing in Acts 5:2 rather than the verb's own meaning, which is really about awareness or shared knowledge.
caution: Evidence is thin and partly muddled: the critical text omits it entirely, one of the three measured "senses" is just absorbed phrasing, and the LXX uses are scattered, so treat the range cautiously.

definition: To grasp or comprehend something with the mind, especially to understand a teaching, sign, or meaning.
article: In the New Testament συνίημι means to understand or perceive—to put pieces together mentally. The Byzantine NT uses it 26 times, and translators render it "understand" in roughly 83% of cases, with the rest being slight variations of the same idea. While Strong's notes a literal sense "to put together" and even "to act piously," the everyday Koine evidence backs the mental sense: a third-century BC papyrus uses συνίημι exactly where another closely parallel text uses ἐπίσταμαι ("I know"). In the Septuagint it appears 84 times, most often translating the Hebrew בִּין (30×) and שָׂכַל (17×), both words about discernment and insight.

definition: The soft tissue of a body, and by extension the physical body itself or human nature.
article: σάρξ literally means the soft, fleshy substance of an animal or human body, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it that way 81% of the time across 150 occurrences. In about 17% of cases the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "body," treating the flesh as a stand-in for the whole physical person, as in Acts 2:26. In the Septuagint it appears 160 times and almost always translates the Hebrew בָּשָׂר (126×), the same broad word for flesh, body, and kindred, which strongly shaped its New Testament range.
caution: The lexicons note theological extensions like "human nature" with its frailties, but those broader uses are interpretive and were not isolated as measured senses in this digest.

definition: A pair of animals or things joined or counted together, such as two oxen yoked for work or two birds.
article: Coming from the verb "to yoke," ζεῦγος means a pair or team of things bound or counted together. In the New Testament's two uses, it covers both a yoke of oxen (Luke 14:19) and a pair of birds (Luke 2:24), and the Septuagint uses it 15 times, mostly for the Hebrew צֶמֶד. Everyday Koine papyri show just how ordinary the word was: it counts pairs of loaves, single pairs of gold earrings, and silver bracelets in shopping and inventory lists.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (one of them absorbed into the phrasing), the confidence tier is low, though the wider Septuagint and papyri evidence is consistent.

definition: An item of clothing or a garment, especially an outer robe worn over other clothes.
article: ἔνδυμα refers to clothing or a garment, and the word is built from the verb ἐνδύω, "to put on." It appears 8 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "clothes" in the clear cases, with the Septuagint using it mainly for the Hebrew word לְבוּשׁ (clothing). Everyday Koine papyri give it a sharper edge: in one document a man stripped of his cloak and sent out naked is resupplied by friends with an ἔνδυμα, evidently an outer garment, matching Strong's note that it especially means the outer robe.

definition: To go away from a place or person, leaving or withdrawing.
article: ἀποχωρέω means simply to go away, depart, or withdraw, built from ἀπό ("away from") and χωρέω ("to move"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and although the translations look varied — "depart" in Matthew 7:23 and Luke 9:39, and a reference to "companions" parting in Acts 13:13 — they all express the same basic idea of leaving. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain sense: one document uses it of a man who "had returned to his own country," and another illiterate letter says "if I leave I will send to you to greet you."
caution: With only 3 New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence, the evidence base is thin, so the three "senses" really reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To make something known officially, especially by presenting a formal report or case to authorities; in some contexts, to reveal or show oneself.
article: In the New Testament, ἐμφανίζω most often carries a legal or official sense — bringing charges, presenting a case, or filing a formal report to the authorities, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "case" or "presented their case" in most of its 10 occurrences. The word also has a broader range meaning "to make visible" or "to show oneself," as the older lexicons note (e.g. revealing oneself or appearing). The papyri confirm this courtroom flavor beautifully: a 221 BC petition uses the very same word for lodging an official complaint with the local magistrates, showing it was standard bureaucratic Koine.
caution: With only 10 occurrences and 3 of them absorbed into phrasing without an English word of their own, the measured data reflects a narrow legal slice of a word whose wider "reveal/appear" sense rests mainly on the lexicons.

definition: To be well-disposed or friendly toward someone, and so come to terms or make peace with them.
article: εὐνοέω means to be kindly disposed toward another person, and by extension to settle a quarrel and come to friendly terms. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Matthew 5:25, where Jesus urges someone to make peace with an adversary while still on the way to court. The everyday papyri make the friendly sense vivid: in one document a woman solemnly promises εὐνοεῖν, to be well-disposed toward her husband, and other letters use it of showing goodwill and faithfulness to family.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just two in the Septuagint, the word's range in biblical Greek rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To secure justice for someone who has been wronged, either by defending them in court or by punishing the offender.
article: ἐκδικέω covers the full sweep from defending a wronged person to actively avenging them, depending on who acts and on whom. In the Gospels it leans toward securing justice for a victim (Luke 18:3, 5), while in Romans, Revelation and elsewhere it shades into vengeance and punishment. It's heavily used in the Septuagint—68 times—where it most often renders the Hebrew נָקַם ("avenge"), and Moulton-Milligan finds it in everyday papyri, including a guild's pledge to "answer the claims" made against its members.
caution: With only six New Testament occurrences split across justice and vengeance senses, the exact force depends on context in each passage.

definition: To shine out brightly or blaze forth with light.
article: This verb describes light beaming out brightly, built from the prefix ἐκ ("out") and λάμπω ("shine"). In the New Testament it appears just once, in Matthew 13:43, where the righteous will "shine forth" like the sun — rendered "shine" in every counted occurrence. It also turns up twice in the Septuagint, translating Hebrew words for brightness and light, and even shows up in everyday Koine: a horoscope papyrus from the first or second century A.D. uses the same word.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just two in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: The personal name Felix, the Roman governor (procurator) of Judea before whom Paul appeared.
article: Φῆλιξ is the Latin name Felix, borne by Marcus Antonius Felix, the Roman procurator of Judea who heard Paul's case. It appears 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament and is rendered "Felix" in 8 of them (89%), with the Berean Standard Bible independently agreeing 88%. The name was common in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan note a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (c. A.D. 153) where Felix is the name of a prefect.

definition: A difference or variety, where things vary in kind while sharing a common source.
article: This noun points to differences or distributions — the idea that things can vary in kind while still belonging together. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all clustered in 1 Corinthians 12, where Paul speaks of varieties of gifts, ministries, and workings that come from the same Spirit. In the Septuagint it shows up 32 times, most often (22×) rendering the Hebrew word for a 'division' or 'allotment,' and the everyday papyri use it concretely for dividing up land or wheat among farmers.
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament, all in a single passage, so its NT range is narrow.

definition: A fragrant spice or perfume, especially the aromatic substances used to anoint or prepare a body for burial.
article: ἄρωμα refers to aromatic spices or perfumes, and in the New Testament it appears only in connection with preparing a body for burial. All four occurrences cluster around Jesus' burial and resurrection (Mark 16:1, Luke 23:56, 24:1, John 19:40), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "spices" every time; the so-called second sense ("spices rested") simply reflects the surrounding sentence in Luke 23:56. Outside the Bible it was a common everyday word: the papyri and inscriptions list it among items used in sacrifices and temple rites, such as an Oxyrhynchus papyrus mentioning "every spice except frankincense." In the Greek Old Testament it most often translates the Hebrew word for balsam or sweet spices.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, all in burial scenes, the measured range here is narrow, though the wider Septuagint and papyri evidence confirms a broader sense of fragrant spices.

definition: Aquila, the Greek form of a Latin man's name, borne by a Jewish Christian who, with his wife Priscilla, worked alongside Paul.
article: Aquila is a personal name, the Greek spelling of the Latin name Aquila (which means "eagle"). It appears 6 times in the New Testament, always referring to the same man—a Jew from Pontus who, together with his wife Priscilla, partnered with Paul in ministry and tentmaking. The papyri confirm the name was in everyday use, showing up in documents from around A.D. 101 onward, which settled an old scholarly doubt about whether its genitive form even existed.

definition: Openness or frankness in speaking, and the inner confidence or boldness that goes with it.
article: At root παῤῥησία is about speaking freely and openly—saying things plainly, in public, without holding back. From that core it readily extends to the inner attitude behind such speech: confidence and boldness, which is actually how the Majority Standard Bible renders it most often (9 of 31 times, 36%). The Septuagint shows the same flexibility, once using it for the Hebrew קוֹמְמִיּוּת in Leviticus 26:13 (walking "upright" or with heads held high), and Moulton-Milligan find the word in everyday papyri, including a phrase "with boldness" that echoes Acts 28:31.
caution: The word's range is genuinely wide—spanning open speech, public visibility, and inner confidence—so 6 of 31 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no single English word.

definition: Food or nourishment — what people or animals eat to stay alive and grow strong.
article: τροφή means food or nourishment, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "food" in 11 of 16 occurrences, with the Berean Study Bible agreeing 100% of the time. It can also be used figuratively, as in Hebrews 5:12–14, where it contrasts solid food with milk to picture spiritual maturity. The everyday papyri make the basic sense vivid — one document mentions buying "rye for the food of calves," and another laments having no food even for one's cattle, showing the word covered animal feed just as naturally as human meals.

definition: Tychicus, a Christian from the Roman province of Asia who traveled with and carried letters for the apostle Paul.
article: Τυχικός is simply the personal name Tychicus, a Christian companion of Paul mentioned 5 times across 5 New Testament books (Acts 20:4, Ephesians 6:21, Colossians 4:7, 2 Timothy 4:12, Titus 3:12). Every translation reviewed renders it the same way; the three "measured senses" the data lists are just the name picked up alongside neighboring words like "tell news" and "however," not separate meanings. The name derives from a word related to τυγχάνω and carries the sense "fortunate," though one interesting detail is that Moulton-Milligan notes the name does not appear in Preisigke's index of papyri names.
caution: This is a proper name with a single referent, so the three listed "senses" reflect rendering artifacts rather than genuine variation in meaning.

definition: Gentle, mild, and humble in attitude—an alternate spelling of the more common word πραΰς (meek).
article: πρᾷος is a variant spelling of πραΰς, both meaning gentle, mild, meek, or kind. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all, and Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint almost always uses the -ΰς form, with this -ᾷος spelling showing up only once, in 2 Maccabees 15:12. In the Greek Old Testament the word group stands behind the Hebrew terms for the poor or humble (עָנָו, עָנִי).
caution: This form is unattested in the Byzantine New Testament and rare even in the Septuagint, so its meaning rests on its more common variant πραΰς rather than direct measured usage.

definition: The mind or understanding — the seat of thinking and intellect.
article: φrḗn refers to the mind, intellect, or thinking faculty. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing just twice and both times in 1 Corinthians 14:20, where Paul urges readers not to be "infants in thinking." Originally the word named the physical area around the heart or midriff, and from there came to mean the mind itself — a shift visible in everyday Koine papyri, including magical texts that speak of binding or tormenting someone's φρένες (mind). In the Septuagint it appears 8 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "lacking" (חָסֵר, 7×).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (both in one verse) and notes that one use is absorbed into phrasing, the evidence here is thin.

definition: To engage in business or trading, putting money or resources to productive use.
article: This verb means to busy oneself with practical affairs, especially commerce and trading. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:13, where a master tells his servants to do business with the money entrusted to them; the related word διαπραγματεύομαι covers the same idea. The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where the word repeatedly describes government officials and tax-farmers conducting State business, showing its strong link to managing money and official affairs.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint use, the measured evidence is thin, so the range rests mainly on the papyri and lexica.

definition: Grown together with something so as to be closely united or joined to it.
article: σύμφυτος describes things that have grown together and are now closely united, the way two plants might be intergrown. In its single New Testament appearance (Romans 6:5) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "united," and the Berea Standard Bible agrees fully. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: the papyri repeatedly use it of farmland that is "planted" or "under cultivation" — leased land described as planted and flourishing — which is also where the KJV's gloss "planted together" comes from. Abbott-Smith adds that classical and 3 Maccabees usage carries a further sense of "innate" or "congenital," something inborn rather than joined later.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise force in Romans 6:5 is uncertain, and the sources span meanings from "planted" to "innate" to "united."

definition: To fit or join parts closely together into a coordinated, unified whole, as with the pieces of a building or a body.
article: This verb describes parts being carefully fitted and joined into a single, well-coordinated structure. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Ephesians—once for the stones of a building rising into a temple (Eph 2:21) and once for the members of a body growing together (Eph 4:16). Moulton-Milligan note it belongs to everyday Koine, citing a closely related word in an inscription about fitting stones tightly against one another, which captures the same image of compact, precise joinery.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only twice in the New Testament (both in Ephesians) and zero times in the critical SBLGNT text.

definition: A person who translates or explains a message so others can understand it, especially someone tongues into intelligible speech.
article: This noun refers to an interpreter — someone who explains or translates a message for others. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 14:28, where Paul addresses the orderly use of tongues in worship and says a speaker should stay silent if no interpreter is present. Moulton-Milligan note that the word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, though some early manuscripts (B and DFG) read differently here.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and some early manuscripts dissent from the reading, so the evidence is thin.

definition: The end or final completion of something, especially the closing point of an age or era.
article: In the New Testament, συντέλεια always points to an ending or final completion, occurring 6 times and rendered "end" in every case—most often in the phrase "the end of the age." The Septuagint uses it far more broadly (62 times), most often translating the Hebrew words כָּלָה (completion, 14×) and קֵץ (end, 11×). Interestingly, the classical lexicon notes an older, very different meaning—a joint payment or shared contribution for public service—and the everyday papyri confirm the temporal sense, as in an Oxyrhynchus document using it for "down to the end of the 21st year."
caution: The biblical sense is consistent, but the word's classical meaning (a joint financial contribution) is entirely absent from the New Testament usage.

definition: To make someone rich, whether with literal wealth or, more often in the New Testament, with spiritual abundance.
article: πλουτίζω means to make wealthy or enrich, built from the noun πλοῦτος ("riches"). In all 3 New Testament occurrences it is used metaphorically of spiritual rather than material riches—being enriched in speech (1 Corinthians 1:5), making many rich (2 Corinthians 6:10), and being enriched in every way (2 Corinthians 9:11). In the Septuagint it appears 8 times and almost always translates the Hebrew עָשַׁר ("to be rich"), 7 of those 8 times, anchoring its core meaning in literal wealth.
caution: With only 3 New Testament uses, the three "senses" are really one meaning (to enrich) applied in slightly different phrasings, so the split is thin.

definition: An adverb meaning "in Latin" or "in the Latin language."
article: Ῥωμαϊστί is an adverb describing something written or spoken in Latin, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at John 19:20, where Pilate's notice on the cross was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. The word is built from the name for Rome (Ῥώμη) and follows the common Greek pattern for "in such-and-such a language." Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine documents and quote the philosopher Epictetus using it the same way, showing it was ordinary usage and not a biblical coinage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, though outside evidence confirms the single meaning.

definition: To lose heart, become discouraged, or grow weary and give up, especially when facing hardship or delay.
senseLabels: not grow weary in doing good
article: This verb describes growing faint-hearted or weary and being tempted to give up, almost always used in the New Testament with a negative—encouraging believers NOT to lose heart amid hardship, delay, or suffering. Across all 6 Byzantine occurrences the Berean Standard Bible independently agrees 100% with the renderings, clustering tightly around the idea of losing heart or growing weary. One striking detail: this verb is rare even in ordinary Greek, with Moulton-Milligan noting the 'poverty of the profane attestation,' citing one uncertain papyrus and Polybius, where it means to fail to act through cowardice.
caution: The fragmented sense labels (e.g. 'lose', 'give', 'well') are artifacts of phrase-splitting rather than distinct meanings, and the form is spelled ἐνκακέω in critical texts, which drop it entirely from the SBLGNT.

definition: To separate or part from someone or something, whether splitting away from a companion or being torn apart.
article: This compound verb joins ἀπό ("from") with χωρίζω ("separate"), and it covers both people splitting up and things being torn apart. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: once of Paul and Barnabas sharply parting company (Acts 15:39), and once in the passive of the sky being "swept aside" or split apart (Revelation 6:14). Notably, in its single Septuagint appearance (Ezekiel 43:21) it translates the Hebrew מִפְקָד, an appointed or designated place.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences (and zero in the SBL critical text) — so the full range of meaning is hard to pin down.

definition: To make light of something or treat it with too little concern, as if it didn't matter much.
article: This verb means to treat something carelessly or think little of it. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 12:5, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "forgotten" (you have "forgotten" the exhortation), though the lexicons consistently define it more strongly as "esteem lightly" or "make light of." That Hebrews quotation comes straight from the Septuagint of Proverbs 3:11, and everyday Koine papyri use the word the same way — one letter from 257 BC pleads against being charged with any "neglect."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the standard translation "forgotten" is softer than the lexicons' "make light of," so the exact force is uncertain.

definition: To wage war or campaign against someone, used figuratively of an opposing force fighting within a person.
article: This verb describes making war or campaigning against someone, built from ἀντί ("against") and στρατεύομαι ("to wage war"). It appears only once in the entire New Testament, at Romans 7:23, where Paul pictures a law within him "warring against" the law of his mind. Abbott-Smith notes it takes the dative case, and Strong's adds a figurative shade of attacking or destroying, fitting the imagery of inner conflict.
caution: This word is a hapax, occurring only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: To receive something from a predecessor and carry it on, taking one's turn in a succession.
article: This verb describes taking over something passed down by others — receiving it in your turn rather than from scratch. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 7:45), where the meaning is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word; modern versions translate it 'in their turn.' Everyday Koine papyri use the word in its ordinary sense of succeeding someone: one document from A.D. 146 has a writer carrying on duties while an official is away in Egypt.
caution: Evidence is thin — just one New Testament occurrence and four in the Septuagint — so confidence is low.

definition: The plural "you" — the word used when speaking directly to more than one person.
article: This is simply the plural form of "you," used when addressing a group rather than a single person, and it works as the subject of a verb ("you all do" rather than "to you all"). It appears as an irregular plural of the singular σύ. In the Septuagint it shows up 317 times across 30 books, regularly standing in for the Hebrew second-person pronoun אַתְּ (242 times). It often carries emphasis, drawing a contrast or pointing pointedly at the people being addressed.
caution: The digest reports zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament and provides no measured senses, so its New Testament range here rests on Septuagint and lexical evidence rather than direct corpus counts.

definition: To feed or pasture animals, the work of a herdsman; in the passive, of livestock grazing.
article: βόσκω is the herdsman's word for feeding or pasturing livestock; in the passive it describes the animals themselves grazing. The measured senses in the Byzantine NT mostly come from the Gospel scenes of swine being fed (the "pigs" rendering simply reflects translating the herd that is grazing). It appears 28 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always stands in for the Hebrew רָעָה ("to pasture"), and everyday Koine papyri use it of both sheep and a herd of swine — one rough document from A.D. 12 speaks of the "swine cattle they feed," matching the Gospel usage exactly.
caution: The measured NT data only captures the literal feeding sense; lexicons note a metaphorical "pastoral care" use (John 21:15, 17) that falls outside the counted occurrences.

definition: To stay awake and watchful, often for the sake of prayer, alertness, or vigilant care over others.
article: This verb literally means to be sleepless or wakeful — its roots combine "not" and "sleep." In the New Testament's 4 occurrences it always carries the figurative sense of spiritual alertness: staying watchful in prayer (Ephesians 6:18) or keeping vigilant care over others (Hebrews 13:17). The everyday papyri preserve the plain physical meaning, including a touching letter describing someone "continually sleepless night and day" (P. Giss I.19), and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew שָׁקַד, "to watch."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences spread evenly across distinct renderings, the boundaries between these senses are soft rather than sharp.

definition: To treat something sacred as common—to violate or desecrate it, stripping away its holiness.
article: βεβηλόω means to defile or profane something holy, treating it as ordinary. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice—once of priests "profaning" the Sabbath (Matthew 12:5) and once of an alleged attempt to desecrate the temple (Acts 24:6). The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 69 times across 12 books and almost always renders the Hebrew חָלַל (57 times), the standard word for treating the sacred as common.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured senses rest on very thin evidence, though the Septuagint and classical lexica agree on the core meaning.

definition: To turn something down—to refuse, decline, or ask to be let off from an obligation or invitation.
senseLabels: reject or have nothing to do with
article: παραιτέομαι covers a range of polite-to-firm declining: refusing a request (4×, 36%), rejecting something outright (3×, 27%), or asking to be excused (2×, 18%). The measured New Testament uses match the classical lexica well, which trace it from "beg off, ask to be excused" (as in Luke 14:18-19, where dinner guests make their excuses) to the stronger "refuse, decline." Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical flavor—one document has tax-collectors literally begging off from their duties.

definition: A moth, especially the clothes moth whose larvae destroy fabric and stored goods.
article: σής means a moth, the insect (and its larvae) that eats and ruins clothing and other stored treasures. The meaning is narrow and stable: in all 3 New Testament occurrences it simply means "moth," usually paired with rust as agents of decay (about 67% of the time), as in Jesus' warning not to store up earthly treasures. The Septuagint uses it 5 times, mostly translating the Hebrew עָשׁ (moth), and Moulton-Milligan notes a striking parallel in Pindar, who said neither moth nor weevil devours gold.
caution: Although the word is rare in the New Testament (only 3 times), its single meaning is well attested across the Septuagint, papyri, and classical sources, so the sense is secure despite the low confidence tier.

definition: To go away from a place or crowd, retiring or withdrawing quietly to somewhere else.
article: This verb describes pulling back or retiring, usually to a quieter place — in both New Testament occurrences (Luke 5:16 and Luke 9:10) it refers to Jesus withdrawing. Although the translation data splits it into two phrasings, both really point to one core idea: withdrawing. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show a more legal flavor, where the related noun and verb describe formally ceding or making over property to someone in a dispute.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, so the measured sense range is limited.

definition: A person held in custody as a captive or prisoner.
article: δεσμώτης simply means a prisoner — someone held in bonds or custody. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the same chapter (Acts 27:1 and 27:42), where it describes captives being transported by ship, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prisoners" in 100% of cases. The word was at home in everyday Koine: a papyrus from 258 BC speaks of prisoners being delivered by an administrator named Apollonios and the need for more room to hold them.

definition: Manna, the food God miraculously provided to feed the Israelites during their journey through the wilderness.
article: Manna is the bread-like food that God supernaturally supplied to the Israelites in the desert, a word borrowed straight from Hebrew מָן. In the New Testament it appears 5 times across 3 books, mostly in John 6 where Jesus contrasts the manna the ancestors ate with himself as the true bread, and once symbolically in Revelation 2:17 as "hidden manna." The Septuagint uses it 9 times, rendering the Hebrew word 8 of those. Interestingly, a first-century medical papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses μάννα for a natural gum-like substance in a recipe to stop nosebleeds, showing the word had an everyday medical sense alongside the biblical one.
caution: The various measured "senses" mostly reflect surrounding wording rather than distinct meanings of the word, which consistently refers to manna itself.

definition: To invite someone back in return for an earlier invitation they gave you.
article: This verb describes returning a social favor — inviting back the people who once invited you. It combines the prefix ἀντί ('in return') with καλέω ('to call, invite'), so the 'in return' sense is built right into the word. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 14:12, where Jesus warns against inviting friends merely so they will invite you back; the lexicographers Dodson, Strong's, and Abbott-Smith all agree on this 'invite in turn' meaning, with Abbott-Smith noting its earlier use by the historian Xenophon.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage.

definition: Joseph, a Hebrew personal name borne by several men in the Bible.
article: Ἰωσήφ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Joseph (יוֹסֵף), used for several different men in Scripture, including Mary's husband, Joseph of Arimathea, and the Old Testament patriarch. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Joseph" in 29 of its 35 New Testament appearances (94%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than given a separate English word. An interesting detail: everyday Koine papyri show a Greek-styled variant of the name, Ἰώσηπος, as in a document where a man named Joseph reports the death of his son who shared his grandfather's name.

definition: Without raising any objection or argument; doing something readily and without resistance.
article: This adverb describes acting without putting up any argument or pushback. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 10:29, where Peter says he came when sent for without raising objections; in that verse it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word. The lexicons cluster around two shades — 'without contradiction' (Abbott-Smith) and 'promptly/without hesitation' (Strong's, Dodson) — which both fit the idea of compliance offered freely.
caution: Evidence is thin: this word occurs only once in the New Testament and no Septuagint or papyri data is supplied, so its exact emphasis (unprotesting versus prompt) rests on a single verse.

definition: An evil supernatural spirit, a demon, hostile to people and recognizing Jesus' authority.
article: In the New Testament δαίμων means an evil supernatural spirit, a demon, and is treated as identical in meaning to its more common relative δαιμόνιον. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine text (just once in the critical SBLGNT) and is consistently rendered "demon." The most striking evidence is from everyday papyri, where the word kept its older, neutral sense: a notice of Nero's accession from A.D. 54 calls the emperor the "good δαίμων of the world" — a divine guardian spirit, the Greek equivalent of the Latin Genius. The single Septuagint occurrence translates the Hebrew גַּד.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 4 NT occurrences), and the everyday papyri show a much broader, even positive, range than the uniformly negative biblical use.

definition: Mnason, a man's personal name—an early Christian from Cyprus who hosted Paul on his journey toward Jerusalem.
article: Mnason is a proper name, not an ordinary Greek word, and it appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 21:16), where he is described as an early disciple from Cyprus who provided lodging. The name was common among Greeks, and Moulton-Milligan point to a papyrus from around 261 B.C. that mentions a 'Mnason the controller' being sent under guard—showing it was an everyday name in Koine. Its origin is uncertain, and as a name it carries no independent meaning to translate.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and is a personal name of uncertain origin, so there is little linguistic evidence to weigh.

definition: The act of drinking, or by extension the drink itself that is consumed.
article: πόσις basically means "drinking"—the act of taking liquid in—but it can also shift to mean the drink itself, the way "a bite to eat" can mean the food. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament: twice rendered "drink" (John 6:55, Colossians 2:16) and once in a phrase about drinking (Romans 14:17). A nice everyday glimpse comes from the papyri, where a second-century ostracon mentions "the drinking of beer" at a temple festival, showing the word in ordinary use.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint instance, the evidence is thin, and translators differ on whether some uses mean the act of drinking or the beverage itself.

definition: To exchange one thing for another, swapping it out or trading it away.
article: μεταλλάσσω means to exchange or swap one thing for another. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Romans (1:25 and 1:26), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "exchanged" 100% of the time — describing swapping the truth for a lie and natural relations for unnatural ones. The everyday Koine papyri reveal a striking secondary use: the phrase μεταλλάσσω τὸν βίον, literally "to exchange life," was a common way of saying "to die," and the verb alone often carried that same sense.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament occurrences plus a couple in the Septuagint, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: A young child, from a newborn infant to a half-grown boy or girl.
article: παιδίον is a diminutive of παῖς and refers to a young child, ranging from a nursing infant to an older boy or girl. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 51 times, rendered "child" in 68% of cases and "little children" or "little child" in most of the rest. The everyday Koine flavor is striking: the papyri show it used for a child "at the breast," while it also functioned as an affectionate address (like "lads"), as in John 21:5 and 1 John 2:18.

definition: Archelaus, the son of Herod the Great who ruled Judea, Samaria, and Idumea after his father's death.
article: Ἀρχέλαος is simply the personal name Archelaus, used once in the New Testament at Matthew 2:22, where it is rendered "Archelaus" in every occurrence. According to the lexicons, he was a son and successor of Herod the Great who reigned over Judea (with Samaria and Idumea) from 4 B.C. to A.D. 6. The name itself is built from the Greek words for "to rule" and "people," fitting for a man identified as a ruler.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests entirely on that single passage and the historical notes in the lexicons.

definition: A young female slave or servant girl; sometimes simply a young woman or maidservant.
article: παιδίσκη is the feminine diminutive of παῖς ("child") and most often means a female slave or servant girl, the sense in about 42% of its 13 New Testament occurrences, with another 17% rendered simply "girl." In Galatians 4 it appears twice as "woman," referring to Hagar the slave woman, and the Septuagint uses it 76 times to translate the Hebrew words for maidservant (שִׁפְחָה 35×, אָמָה 29×). Moulton-Milligan note that the word originally meant just a young woman but came in later Koine to denote a female slave, a shift confirmed by everyday papyri where παιδίσκη is bought and sold like property.

definition: Foul, shameful talk — obscene or abusive speech that should not come out of a person's mouth.
article: This word combines "shameful" (αἰσχρός) and "word" (λόγος) to mean dirty or disgraceful talk. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Colossians 3:8, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "filthy." Interestingly, the sources tilt two directions: Abbott-Smith and one ancient papyrus (where a man hurled "many αἰσχρολογίας" in someone's face) lean toward "abusive language," while Moulton-Milligan notes that in Colossians the sense is generally taken as foul or filthy speech rather than mere abuse.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources disagree over whether it means obscene speech or abusive insult.

definition: Comparative form meaning lower or situated below something else.
article: κατώτερος is the comparative of κάτω ("down"), meaning simply "lower" or "situated below." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Ephesians 4:9, where it describes the "lower parts" of the earth, and once in the Septuagint, where it renders Hebrew words for "lower" or "lowest." Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions use it too—including as an astrological term paired with its opposite ἀνώτερος ("higher")—showing it was ordinary, practical vocabulary, not specialized religious language.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, this is a thin sample, and the exact sense of "lower parts of the earth" in Ephesians 4:9 is debated.

definition: To suffer from a continuous flow of blood, as in a chronic hemorrhage.
senseLabels: suffered from a flow of blood
article: This word describes someone losing blood over an extended time — a chronic hemorrhage. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 9:20, describing the woman who had bled for years, where the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it "suffered" (and the Berean Standard Bible agrees). Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it once at Leviticus 15:33 to translate the Hebrew word for a woman who is menstruating or ailing, and Moulton-Milligan note that a related noun shows up in an everyday Koine magical text alongside a healing spell.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament (and not at all in the critical text), so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: The natural movement of air, the wind, sometimes used for the directions or quarters from which winds blow.
article: ἄνεμος is the ordinary Koine word for wind, and that's overwhelmingly how it's used — translated "wind" in 25 of its 31 New Testament occurrences (89%). In the plural it can shade into meaning the four compass directions, as in "the four winds of the earth," and the papyri confirm this everyday usage: an Egyptian document from A.D. 268 lists neighbors "from the four winds," simply meaning the four cardinal points. In the Septuagint it usually renders Hebrew רוּחַ (24×), the same word that can mean breath or spirit.
caution: A couple of measured occurrences show garbled rendering data ("disciples were wind"), but this reflects phrasing artifacts rather than any real ambiguity in the word's meaning.

definition: A person who gives false testimony, deliberately bearing untrue witness against someone.
article: This word names someone who bears untrue testimony — literally a "false witness." It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 2 books, and the critical text (SBLGNT) doesn't include it at all. One striking detail is the use in 1 Corinthians 15:15, where it takes an object in the genitive: Paul says he would be found a false witness of God if the resurrection were not true. In the Septuagint it shows up in the story of Susanna, again describing those who give lying testimony.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences, none in the critical text — and in one of those the word is absorbed into broader phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word.

definition: In a correct or proper way; rightly, accurately, as something should be done.
article: ὀρθῶς is an adverb meaning to do or say something rightly, correctly, or as it ought to be. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "correctly" in most cases — for example when Jesus tells someone they have answered or judged rightly (Luke 7:43; 10:28; 20:21). In Mark 7:35 it describes a healed man speaking "plainly," showing the word can also mean clearly or properly functioning. The everyday Koine flavor shows up in the papyri, where an official swears to manage public works "uprightly and justly" (ὀρθῶς καὶ δικαίως).

definition: Drunkenness — the state of being intoxicated from drinking too much.
article: μέθη is a straightforward word meaning drunkenness, and the New Testament uses it consistently this way across all 3 occurrences (Luke 21:34; Romans 13:13; Galatians 5:21). The slight variation in translation — "drunkenness" versus "drunkenness practice" — reflects the plural form used in Romans and Galatians, which points to repeated or habitual drinking bouts rather than a single state. The everyday flavor of the word shows up nicely in a papyrus invitation celebrating Hadrian's accession (A.D. 117), which speaks of "laughter and drunken revels," and in the Septuagint it regularly renders Hebrew words for strong drink and intoxication.
caution: Confidence is rated low because the word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, though all sources agree on its meaning.

definition: Esau, the elder son of Isaac and twin brother of Jacob, ancestor of the Edomites.
article: Ἠσαῦ is simply the Greek spelling of the personal name Esau, the firstborn twin of Isaac who sold his birthright and became the forefather of the Edomites. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament (Romans 9:13, Hebrews 11:20, 12:16), always naming the same individual; the two "measured senses" only reflect that one verse speaks of him in a future-oriented blessing. In the Septuagint it occurs 104 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew name עֵשָׂו, though a handful of times it stands in for other words like בְּכֹרָה ("birthright"), likely through translation choices in the Esau narratives.
caution: This is a proper name with few New Testament occurrences, and its overall confidence tier is rated low.

definition: In a way marked by pleasure or eagerness; willingly and with enjoyment.
article: This adverb describes doing something with pleasure or eagerness — it's the manner-word behind "gladly" or "willingly." It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice describing how people loved listening to a speaker (Mark 6:20; 12:37) and once in Paul's pointed remark that the Corinthians "gladly" put up with fools (2 Cor 11:19). Built from the root meaning "sweet," it shows up in ordinary Koine documents too: the Emperor Claudius used it in a letter to say he "gladly received" a golden victory crown.
caution: Confidence is low: only 3 New Testament occurrences, so the measured range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To set something on fire or get a flame going, whether a literal blaze or a kindled fire.
senseLabels: to kindle or set on fire
article: ἀνάπτω means to kindle or light a fire. It appears just 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and in 2 of those the Majority Standard Bible renders it "kindled" (as at Luke 12:49 and Acts 28:2), with the third instance absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The word turns up far more in the Septuagint—19 times across 9 books, most often translating the Hebrew verb יָצַת ("to set on fire")—and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday papyri, including one text about kindling altars for sacrifice.
caution: New Testament evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences, 2 in critical texts), so the confidence tier is low.

definition: Erastus, the personal name of one or more Christians associated with the apostle Paul.
article: Ἔραστος is simply the proper name "Erastus," borne by Christians connected with Paul, and it appears 3 times across 3 New Testament books. Abbott-Smith distinguishes possibly two people: a companion of Paul (Acts 19:22 and probably 2 Timothy 4:20) and the city treasurer of Corinth (Romans 16:23). The name was common in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan points to an inscription from A.D. 129 mentioning an Erastus who was a shipowner of Ephesus.
caution: Because this is a personal name, the apparent second "sense" in the data is just surrounding words; whether the references point to one man or two is uncertain.

definition: Describing a surface that is smooth, level, or even, the opposite of rough or rugged.
article: λεῖος describes something smooth or level, the opposite of rough (τραχύς). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 3:5, in a quotation from Isaiah about rough ways being made smooth—which is why the Berean translations render it "made" there, capturing the sense of being smoothed out. In the Septuagint it shows up five times across three books, translating Hebrew words for smooth skin and smooth stones, and the everyday papyri use it of unengraved or unchased silver, a sense that even matches its Latin cousin lēvis.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall data, the entry rests on a small evidence base.

definition: A wrongdoing done out of ignorance rather than deliberate rebellion—an unintentional sin or error.
article: This word refers to a sin or offense done out of ignorance rather than open defiance, and it appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 9:7). It derives from ἀγνοέω, "to be ignorant," so the wrongdoing is tied to not knowing rather than willful rebellion. A fascinating detail comes from the papyri: a royal amnesty decree from 118 B.C. lists ἀγνοήματα alongside ἁμαρτήματα, with the editors distinguishing them as "errors" versus "crimes"—showing the word marked the milder, less culpable category of offense in everyday legal language. In the Septuagint it appears once translating the Hebrew word for an unintentional mistake.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on a single instance plus outside evidence.

definition: An orderly written account or narrative that sets out events in some fullness.
article: διήγησις means a narrative — an account that lays out events in order and with some fullness, as opposed to a brief summary. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:1, where Luke notes that many had undertaken to compose such an account; the Septuagint uses it just three times. The papyri are revealing here: a rhetorical treatise (PSI I.85) contrasts a διήγησις with the concise χρεία, showing that the word implies a developed, fuller telling rather than a clipped report.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a thin handful of Septuagint uses, the precise range rests largely on outside sources like the papyri and lexica.

definition: A fragrant ointment or perfumed oil, often costly, used to anoint people for honor, hospitality, or burial.
article: μύρον refers to a scented ointment or perfumed oil, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "perfume" in 13 of its 14 New Testament uses (the remaining one is absorbed into surrounding phrasing). The range is narrow and consistent: it is the costly oil poured on Jesus and the spices prepared for burial. A telling piece of evidence comes from the papyri, where a private account of about A.D. 1 lists "perfume for the dispatch of the mummy" of a man's daughter—exactly the burial-anointing use seen in the Gospels. The word is a Semitic loanword, and the Septuagint pairs it most often with Hebrew terms for fragrant ointment or oil.

definition: A tense waiting for something still to come; an expectation.
article: In the New Testament ἐκδοχή means "expectation" — a waiting for something that lies ahead. It occurs only once, in Hebrews 10:27, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "expectation" (100%). Interestingly, in classical Greek and in everyday papyri the word usually meant something different: in a papyrus from 164 B.C. it carries the sense "interpretation" (of a decree), and Abbott-Smith notes its classical meanings of "a receiving from" or "succession" — none of which match the New Testament use, where it instead equals προσδοκία.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence whose "expectation" sense differs from its usual classical and papyri meanings, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: Fire — the burning, flaming heat used for cooking, destruction, light, or as an image of judgment and testing.
article: πῦρ is the ordinary Greek word for fire, and the evidence is overwhelmingly consistent: in 65 of 75 Byzantine NT occurrences (98%) it is simply rendered "fire," with the BSB independently agreeing 97% of the time. The Septuagint uses it 405 times, almost always to translate the Hebrew אֵשׁ ("fire," 317×), occasionally for נֵר ("lamp," 8×). Beyond literal flames, the older lexicons note figurative reaches — the heat of the sun, lightning, trials, and the "eternal fire" — and a striking everyday papyrus from AD 292 even reports an actual house fire breaking out in hay-scraps during a heatwave.

definition: Describing a place that is poorly situated or unsuitable for a given purpose, such as a harbor not fit to spend the winter in.
article: This adjective describes something that is badly positioned or not fit for its intended use. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:12, where a harbor is judged unsuitable for wintering a ship. The word is built from a negative prefix on εὔθετος ("well placed, fit"), and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary language even if Luke may have been among the first to coin this negative form.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from biblical usage.

definition: A Hebrew-derived name for Satan, the adversary or devil.
article: Σατᾶν is a Hebrew-derived name for Satan, meaning "adversary" or "enemy," used as a title for the devil. It is extremely rare, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the SBL critical text, with the Septuagint using it just twice (where it translates the Hebrew name Hadad). One quirk worth noting: the single measured rendering in the Majority Standard Bible reads "conceited" at 2 Corinthians 12:7, which clashes with the standard lexical sense of Satan given by Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith.
caution: Evidence is very thin (one disputed New Testament occurrence absent from the critical text), and the measured rendering "conceited" conflicts sharply with the lexicons' consistent definition of "Satan."

definition: An effect or result produced by something at work — an activity or operation carried out through power.
article: ἐνέργημα refers to the effect or operation produced when a power is at work, derived from the verb ἐνεργέω (to work or be active). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Corinthians 12 (verses 6 and 10), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as the various ways God works in people and once as a "working." The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and in Vettius Valens it describes the workings or activities of the soul, showing it was ordinary vocabulary for produced effects.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in a single chapter, the evidence for its precise range is thin.

definition: To expel saliva from the mouth — to spit.
article: πτύω simply means "to spit," expelling saliva from the mouth. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in healing accounts where Jesus uses spittle (Mark 7:33; 8:33; John 9:6), and the various measured renderings ("man's," "spit man's," "spit") reflect the surrounding phrasing rather than different meanings. The word is onomatopoetic, echoing the sound of spitting, and shows up in everyday Koine papyri — even in a colloquial phrase "before you can spit" in Menander; in the Septuagint it once renders the Hebrew יָרַק ("spit") in Numbers 12:14.
caution: Only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, but every source agrees the meaning is simply "to spit."

definition: A grandmother, the mother of one's parent.
article: μάμμη means grandmother, the mother of one of your parents. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 1:5, where in this corpus it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by its own English word. The everyday Koine evidence is rich: papyri preserve warm family letters, including one (P Rein 49) mentioning "my mother and my grandmother Aurelia," and an ancient note even has Epicurus hoping a child and "your grandmother" are in good health. Interestingly, classical lexicographers note that in older Greek this was a child's pet name for mother, with the "grandmother" sense developing only in later Greek.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament (a single occurrence) and the word shifted meaning from "mother" in classical Greek to "grandmother" in later usage.

definition: A Hebrew—an Israelite or Jew, especially one of Hebrew or Aramaic speech and pure Jewish descent.
article: Ἑβραῖος names a Hebrew, that is, a Jew, appearing 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "Hebrews" in every case it carries its own English word (3×). In the Septuagint it occurs 28 times, almost always translating the Hebrew עִבְרִי, distinguishing Israelites from people of other races. By New Testament times the term had narrowed: lexicons note it specifically marked a Jew of Semitic (Hebrew or Aramaic) speech, set against the Greek-speaking "Hellenist," which is why Paul stacks it up in Philippians 3:5 ("a Hebrew of Hebrews") to stress his unmixed Jewish pedigree.
caution: The evidence is thin (only 4 NT occurrences), and lexicons note the term's exact force—linguistic versus ethnic—is debated.

definition: A grasping desire to have more, especially money or possessions, often at others' expense.
article: πλεονεξία describes a greedy craving for more — money, possessions, or advantage — and the grasping conduct that flows from it. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times across 8 books, and translators render it "greed" in 6 of those (67%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing or rare wordings. The everyday papyri show the same edge: in one inscription it pairs with "grasping ambition," and in another it travels alongside "injustice," capturing the aggressive self-seeking the lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) also note. In the Septuagint it appears 6 times, usually translating the Hebrew בֶּצַע, a word for unjust gain or plunder.

definition: To gather separate things into a single whole, summing them up or bringing them together under one head.
article: This verb means to take many things and pull them together into a unified whole — to sum them up. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: Paul says the commandments are "summed up" in loving your neighbor (Romans 13:9), and that God's plan is to "bring together" all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10). The word is built from the common noun κεφάλαιον ("sum, total"), so Moulton-Milligan notes that even though it belongs to more cultivated speech and isn't found in everyday papyri, its meaning would have been obvious to ordinary readers.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and zero in the critical SBLGNT text, the evidence base is thin, so this entry rests on very limited usage.

definition: An adverb meaning on the inside or from within, describing what lies internally rather than on the surface.
article: ἔσωθεν is an adverb that points to the inside of something, whether describing where something is (within) or where it comes from (from within). Across its 13 New Testament occurrences it is rendered "inside" 5 times (45%) and "within" 4 times (36%), with the rest absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri: an Oxyrhynchus inventory describes a silver lamp "the interior being of wood" (ἔσωθεν), showing the same plain spatial sense used in ordinary documents.

definition: The jawbone or cheek—the side of the face below the eye.
article: σιαγών refers to the cheek or jawbone, the side of the face. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the saying about turning the other cheek (Matthew 5:39 and Luke 6:29), and is found 29 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew word לֶ֫חִי ("jaw, cheek"). Everyday Koine papyri confirm its ordinary, non-technical use: one document records a camel "branded T.A. on its right cheek (σιαγών)," showing the word belonged to common speech, not learned vocabulary.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences—and one of those absorbed into phrasing rather than rendered as a standalone word—the measured evidence is thin.

definition: Bartholomew, the personal name of one of the twelve apostles of Jesus.
article: Bartholomew is simply the name of one of Jesus' twelve apostles, appearing 4 times across 4 books and always rendered "Bartholomew" in every translation surveyed. The name comes from Aramaic meaning "son of Tolmai," so it is really a patronymic — identifying him by his father rather than a given name. Abbott-Smith notes he may be the same person called Nathanael elsewhere in the Gospels.
caution: The proposed identification of Bartholomew with Nathanael is a traditional association, not something the name itself establishes.

definition: Crispus, the personal name of a synagogue leader in Corinth who became a believer.
article: Κρίσπος is a personal name, not a common word, appearing only twice in the New Testament (Acts 18:8 and 1 Corinthians 1:14), both times referring to the same man — a synagogue ruler in Corinth who came to faith and was baptized by Paul. The name is Latin in origin, where it means 'curly.' Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Lightfoot cites other examples of Jews bearing this Roman name, which fits a synagogue leader living in a Roman colony like Corinth.
caution: This is a proper name with only two occurrences, so its 'meaning' is simply the person it identifies rather than a translatable sense.

definition: An authoritative order or instruction, especially one of God's commandments that people are expected to obey.
article: ἐντολή is an authoritative directive — an order, injunction, or commandment. Of its 71 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "commandment" 53 times (82%) and "command" or "commanded" in nearly all the rest, so the meaning is remarkably stable. While the New Testament usually applies it to God's commandments, the broader range covers any authoritative instruction: everyday Koine papyri use it for a royal ordinance of a Ptolemaic king, and in the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew מִצְוָה ("commandment," 128 times). The word is built on the verb ἐντέλλομαι ("to command").

definition: The forced removal of a people from their homeland into exile, especially the deportation of Judah to Babylon.
article: μετοικεσία literally means a change of dwelling place, but in the New Testament it consistently carries the heavier sense of forced removal: all 4 of its occurrences refer to the Babylonian exile, and the Majority Standard Bible renders every one as "exile." In the Septuagint it appears 8 times and most often translates the Hebrew word גּוֹלָה (3×), which itself means exile or captivity. A striking detail is that the related verb μετοικέω turns up in a fourth-century Phrygian epitaph describing someone "removed" from earth into heaven, showing the word's everyday range from ordinary relocation to weighty departure.
