caution: The word appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in a single genealogy, so its New Testament range is narrow even though wider Koine usage covers ordinary migration.

definition: A connecting word meaning "so that" or "in order that," used to introduce a purpose or to report what someone asks or urges.
article: ὅπως is a little connecting word that almost never gets translated as a standalone English word — in 56 of its 57 New Testament appearances it disappears into the phrasing, doing its work as part of a clause. Its core job is to introduce purpose ("in order that," "so that"), and it also follows verbs of asking or urging to report a request. The Septuagint uses it 170 times, most often to render the Hebrew מַ֫עַן ("for the sake of, so that") 83 times, which lines up neatly with its purpose-driven meaning; everyday Koine papyri show the same range, including one document where it functions almost like "so let it be given."
caution: Older lexicons note a rarer use of ὅπως meaning "how" or "as" (as in Luke 24:20), so the word's range is slightly broader than its dominant purpose sense suggests.

definition: Conceited and boastful, craving empty praise or status one has not actually earned.
article: κενόδοξος describes someone who is full of empty self-importance — literally combining κενός (empty) and δόξα (glory). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Galatians 5:26, and is part of everyday Koine, showing up in papyri and inscriptions as well as once in Epictetus with the same "vainglorious" sense. Because it occurs only a single time in Scripture, all the lexicons agree on its meaning rather than mapping a wide range.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: Naked, without clothing — or scantily and poorly clad, lacking proper outer garments.
senseLabels: lacking clothes, needing to be clothed
article: γυμνός describes someone naked or, just as often in everyday Greek, someone scantily clad — wearing only an undergarment after being stripped of an outer cloak. In the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "naked" 60% of the time, with two cases (in Matthew 25) tied to clothing the unclothed. The papyri make the range vivid: in two complaints a robbery victim describes being stripped of his ἱμάτιον (cloak), showing that "naked" could mean simply lacking one's outer garment. In the Septuagint it appears 32 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for naked, עָרֹם.
caution: The word's exact force varies between fully naked and merely poorly clothed, so context decides which is meant.

definition: A word meaning the inside of something, or being in the midst of or among a group of people.
article: ἐντός is a small word built from ἐν ("in") that points to what is inside or within. In its two New Testament appearances it does double duty: in Matthew 23:26 it refers to the inside of a cup, while in Luke 17:21 it describes the kingdom of God being "within" or "among" you—a phrase that has been long disputed. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the very same phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν appears in an early non-biblical saying attributed to Jesus (P Oxy IV. 654), where the surrounding context favors the translation "within you."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a famously disputed sense in Luke 17:21 (translators split between "within you" and "among you"), this word's exact range is uncertain.

definition: A time adverb meaning that something has already happened or is happening by now, often stressing that the moment has finally arrived.
article: ἤδη is a time word that marks something as already true or true by now. In the Byzantine New Testament it means "already" most often (30 of 59 times, 67%) and "now" in another 18%, with a couple of cases ("already late") that simply combine the time-sense with context; notably, about 14 times it disappears into the English phrasing without a word of its own. One striking detail from the papyri: the word turns up in magical incantations paired for urgency, as in "now, now, already!" — showing its sense of immediate, pressing action. In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew כְּבָר ("already," 8×).

definition: To be next to or share a boundary with something, especially a neighboring building or property.
senseLabels: borders on, is next door to
article: This verb describes one thing sitting right beside another, like two buildings sharing a wall. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:7, where a house "borders on" the synagogue. The plain form of the word (ὁμορέω) shows up in everyday papyri describing neighboring plots of land, which fits its very ordinary meaning of physical adjacency.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To carry or bring something out from a place, including carrying out the dead for burial or producing crops.
article: At its core ἐκφέρω simply means to carry or bring something out, combining ἐκ ("out") with φέρω ("carry"). In the Byzantine NT it appears 7 times, most often rendered "carried out" (4×, 67%), notably for carrying out the dead for burial (Acts 5:6, 9). The Septuagint uses it 77 times, chiefly for the Hebrew יָצָא; the classical lexica add a sense the NT also shows in Hebrews 6:8 — the ground "bringing forth" or producing crops. Moulton-Milligan note it is less common in everyday papyri than expected, though it does appear in petitions and inscriptions.
caution: With only 7 NT occurrences, the measured senses rest on thin data, though the corpus and lexica broadly agree on the range.

definition: To declare or treat someone as righteous, innocent, or in the right; to acquit or vindicate them.
article: δικαιόω is a legal-sounding word meaning to pronounce or regard someone as righteous or innocent, and it appears 38 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "justified" in 26 of those cases (79%), with smaller groups translated "vindicated" or "since been justified," so its range stays fairly narrow. In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew צָדַק (18×), and the everyday papyri show the same flexibility — in one document a man says he "did not think it right" to buy a defective girdle, while a court record uses it of a judge deciding a verdict.

definition: Describing something that inspires fear or dread because it is formidable and terrible.
article: φοβερός describes something dreadful or formidable — something that makes people afraid. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times (all in Hebrews), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fearful" in the two cases where it gets its own English word. The Septuagint uses it about 30 times, often translating the Hebrew word יָרֵא (related to fear), and classical lexica note it can run in two directions: actively "causing fear" or passively "feeling fear, timid" — though the New Testament uses only the active sense. Notably, the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and even on a Christian protective amulet, paired with φρικτός ("shuddering"), describing God's awesome name.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences, and the passive "timid" sense noted by lexica does not appear in the measured biblical data.

definition: To bring something to rest or stop, or to rest oneself, especially ceasing from work.
article: καταπαύω covers both causing something to cease or rest and resting oneself, with the New Testament uses (all 4 in Hebrews 4) centered on the idea of resting from work. The transitive side can mean to restrain or stop people, as in Acts 14:18 where it describes holding a crowd back. The Septuagint uses it 56 times across 19 books, most often translating the Hebrew נוּחַ ("to rest," 18×) and שָׁבַת ("to cease," 12×), tying it closely to Sabbath and rest themes. Moulton-Milligan note it appears in everyday Koine papyri, and one inscription even uses a related form for a musical "pause."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences (all in Hebrews 4), the measured senses rest on a narrow sample, though the Septuagint and lexicons broadly agree on its range.

definition: To press or crowd someone, and figuratively to oppress, distress, or afflict them with hardship.
article: θλίβω literally means to press or crowd—Mark uses it of a boat kept ready so the crowd wouldn't crush Jesus, and Matthew speaks of a "compressed" narrow way. From that physical squeezing it readily shifts to the figurative sense of oppressing or afflicting someone, which is how the New Testament mostly uses it. The everyday papyri show the same range: one petitioner of A.D. 123 complains an opponent was "using every means of oppressing me," exactly the pressured, hard-pressed feeling the word carries. In the Septuagint it appears 85 times across 19 books, often rendering Hebrew words for distress or constriction like צָר and לָחַץ.
caution: Although the Majority Standard Bible only renders θλίβω with a distinct English word twice (both "afflicted"), absorbing it into phrasing 6 of 10 times, the lexicons agree on its core range of pressing and afflicting.

definition: A gate or doorway, especially the large entrance to a city, used both literally and figuratively.
article: πύλη is a gate or entrance, usually a sizable one like the doorway of a city or temple rather than a small house door. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, rendered "gate" 7 times (70%) and "city gates" twice (20%), and it can be used figuratively, as in the narrow and wide gates of Matthew 7 or the "gates of Hades" in Matthew 16:18. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this concrete sense vividly: an Oxyrhynchus document refers to the "north gate of the city," and customs receipts name the gate of a particular village.

definition: A vision or supernatural sight in which something normally unseen comes into view.
article: ὀπτασία refers to a vision—something supernatural that appears to a person's sight, like Zechariah's experience in the temple or Paul's heavenly vision. All four times it occurs in the New Testament, translators render it "vision" with complete agreement. The older lexicon Abbott-Smith notes a broader basic idea of "an appearing" or "coming into view," which shows up in some Septuagint passages, but in the New Testament the meaning consistently narrows to a supernatural vision.
caution: The word is relatively rare (only 4 New Testament uses and 2 in the Septuagint), so its full range rests on limited evidence.

definition: More diligently or earnestly than usual; with greater eagerness, speed, or seriousness.
article: This is the comparative adverb form meaning to do something more diligently, earnestly, or promptly than others or than before. It comes from the adjective σπουδαῖος (earnest, diligent) and carries the sense of heightened zeal or urgency. The lexica agree on the core idea — Strong's and Abbott-Smith both note it can imply 'very promptly,' while the KJV renders it 'very diligently.'
caution: This form does not occur in the Byzantine NT and the digest supplies no measured senses, so the entry rests only on lexicon glosses and the related root.

definition: To set a trap for someone, especially with words, in order to catch them out.
article: Pagideúō means to ensnare or trap someone, used figuratively rather than for literal hunting. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 22:15, where opponents plot to trap Jesus 'in his words' (ἐν λόγῳ). The Septuagint uses it twice to render Hebrew terms for snaring or being caught, and Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, where someone looks for a way 'to trap me' — confirming this was ordinary Koine vocabulary for laying a snare.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, so the measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: A combined word meaning "and there" or "there also," pointing to a place where something else happens.
article: κἀκεῖ is a crasis (a squeezed-together word) formed from καί ("and") and ἐκεῖ ("there"), so it simply means "and there" or "there also." It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and in 6 of those 8 cases it gets folded into the surrounding English phrasing rather than being translated by its own word, which fits its role as a connective pointing to a location. In the Septuagint it shows up only 3 times, standing in for three different Hebrew words, including one (דְּמָמָה) meaning calm or stillness, showing how the translators fit it loosely into varied contexts.
caution: Manuscripts often disagree on whether to write it as one word (κἀκεῖ) or two (καὶ ἐκεῖ), so its exact count varies between editions.

definition: Soft and tender, describing a young plant shoot that is supple and just beginning to grow.
article: Ἀπαλός means soft or tender, and in the New Testament it appears only twice (Matthew 24:32 and Mark 13:28), both times describing the tender new branch of the fig tree as a sign that summer is near. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times in 4 books, almost always translating the Hebrew רַךְ ('soft, tender'), though once it stands in for a word for choice food. In both NT verses it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own standalone English word.
caution: With only two NT occurrences, both in the same parallel saying, the word's full range in biblical usage rests largely on Septuagint evidence.

definition: To breathe, especially in the phrase "breathing out" threats — being filled with hostile intent.
article: This verb literally means "to breathe," formed from "in" plus "breathe." It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 9:1, where Saul is described as "breathing" threats and murder against the disciples — a vivid figure for being consumed by violent intent, here paired with a genitive ("of threat and murder"). In the Septuagint it carries a related sense in passages like Joshua, used of things that still draw breath, rendering the Hebrew words for breath or living soul.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense here rests on a single instance.

definition: To cut something down, off, or out — like felling a tree, severing a limb, or removing an opportunity.
article: ἐκκόπτω is a physical, forceful verb meaning to cut down, cut off, or cut out — built from ἐκ ("out") and κόπτω ("to strike, cut"). In the New Testament's 10 occurrences it usually means felling a tree (4×, "cut down") or severing a limb or branch (2×, "cut off"), and it can also be used figuratively, as when Paul speaks of cutting off an opportunity (2 Cor 11:12). The everyday Koine papyri confirm the literal sense vividly: one A.D. 100 document has a man wanting "to cut down some of the trees," and a later one asks that timber be "cut and delivered" with all speed.

definition: Jonah, a personal name in the New Testament, borne by the Old Testament prophet and by the father of the apostle Peter.
article: Ἰωνᾶς is the Greek form of the Hebrew name יוֹנָה (Jonah), used as a personal name. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Jonah" in 11 of those (85%), most often referring to the prophet whose "sign" Jesus invokes, but also as the name of Peter's father in John 1:42. In the Septuagint it occurs 20 times, almost always translating the Hebrew יוֹנָה (18×), confirming its straightforward role as a transliterated name.
caution: A couple of stray renderings like "asked a son" reflect parsing of surrounding text rather than the name itself, but the meaning of the word is not in doubt.

definition: To set something on fire — to light, kindle, or keep burning, and by extension to burn something up or destroy it with fire.
article: καίω covers the whole life of a fire: lighting a lamp, keeping it burning, and finally burning something to ashes. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "burning" 7 times (50%) and "burned" 4 times (29%), so the active "kindle/keep alight" sense and the destructive "consume with fire" sense are both well attested. Everyday papyri show the same range — one Oxyrhynchus document from 30–29 B.C. talks about supplying "the proper oil for the daily lamps burning in the temples," exactly the lamp-lighting use found in Luke 12:35. In the Septuagint it appears 71 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew בָּעַר (19×).

definition: Lois, the name of a woman—Timothy's grandmother, commended for her faith.
article: Λωΐς is a personal name, that of Lois, the grandmother of Timothy, who is praised for her sincere faith. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 1:5, and its origin is uncertain. The measured rendering shows "reminded" because the word sits within a sentence about Paul being reminded of the faith that lived first in Lois.
caution: This is a personal name appearing only once, so its meaning rests entirely on that single verse rather than any range of usage.

definition: To begin or start doing something, usually paired with another verb to mark the start of an action.
article: This is the middle-voice form of ἄρχω, and in the Byzantine New Testament it almost always means "to begin" — 64 of its 84 occurrences (89%) are rendered "began," and the rest are essentially the same sense bundled into the surrounding phrasing about Jesus. It typically attaches to another verb to mark the start of an action, an idiom Abbott-Smith notes is often an Aramaic pleonasm (as in Mark 1:45, Luke 3:8). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the word's range: surveyors used the participle to mean "beginning from" a boundary point, as in a measurement "beginning from south to north."
caution: Abbott-Smith lists a separate active-voice sense "to rule" (Mark 10:42, Rom 15:12), but the measured NT data for this middle form shows only the "begin" sense.

definition: To set someone free or let them go—whether releasing a prisoner, dismissing a crowd, or divorcing a spouse.
article: At its core ἀπολύω means to loosen and let go, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it across a wide range of situations: it's rendered "release" in 43% of its 68 occurrences and "divorce" in another 22%, with the rest covering dismissing crowds, sending people off, or letting them depart. The shift from "release" to "divorce" simply applies the same idea of letting go to a marriage—Abbott-Smith notes that divorcing a husband (Mark 10:12) reflects Greek and Roman rather than Jewish custom. Everyday papyri confirm this practical range: one document uses it of being "released" from confinement in a temple, and others of sending a person off on an errand.

definition: A piece of parchment, the prepared animal skin used for writing important documents or books.
article: This word names parchment, the durable writing material made from animal skin. It's actually a Greek spelling of the Latin word membrana, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. In the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 4:13, where Paul asks Timothy to bring his parchments—likely scrolls of the Old Testament Scriptures.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To restore a broken relationship by mutual concession after hostility—to reconcile two estranged parties.
article: This verb means to reconcile, specifically restoring friendship where there was enmity, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament—at Matthew 5:24, where Jesus tells the worshiper to be reconciled to a brother before offering a gift. Older lexicons note an underlying flavor of mutual concession after mutual hostility, which is said to set it apart from the related word καταλλάσσω. Strikingly, the same verb form turns up in everyday Koine letters from the papyri, where a mother pleads, "be reconciled to me," showing it was ordinary language for patching up personal quarrels.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, conclusions about its precise range rest on thin evidence.

definition: Describing trees in late autumn, when fruit is expected but the branches are bare and barren.
article: This adjective comes from φθινόπωρον, the fading end of autumn, and describes something that belongs to that season. Applied to trees, it pictures them at harvest time when fruit should be there but isn't — barren when fruit is expected. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 12, where false teachers are called "autumn trees without fruit," and Moulton-Milligan note the same word turns up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: The measured data oddly renders this as "reefs," but every lexicon (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith, Moulton-Milligan) agrees it means "autumnal"; treat the "reefs" label as a tagging error tied to neighboring words in Jude 12.

definition: The aim or effort to please someone, especially conducting oneself in a way that pleases another.
article: This word names the intention to please someone, and in the New Testament it appears just once, in Colossians 1:10, where it gets folded into the wider phrasing rather than translated as a single English word. Greek writers like Aristotle and Polybius usually used it in a bad sense, closer to flattery or obsequiousness, but the everyday papyri and Philo take it positively. A particularly nice parallel to Paul's neutral-to-positive use comes from a papyrus of A.D. 137, where workers irrigate the land 'to the satisfaction (ἀρεσκίαν) of Sarapion.' In the Septuagint it appears once, at Proverbs 31:30, rendering the Hebrew word for grace or favor.
caution: This is a rare word with only one New Testament occurrence, and classical writers used it negatively while papyri and biblical usage take it positively, so its precise force is debated.

definition: A woman who acts as a patron, protector, or benefactor, giving support and aid to others.
article: προστάτις is the feminine form of προστάτης (one who stands before, leads, or protects), and it describes a woman who serves as a patroness or supporter. It appears just once in the New Testament (Romans 16:2), where it is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word, and the KJV calls such a person a "succourer." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan could find no example of the feminine form in the papyri, but the masculine προστάτης is common there, used for a benefactor, a lender, or the chief man of a town.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the feminine form is unattested in the surveyed papyri, so its precise force rests on thin evidence.

definition: To crucify someone together with another person on a cross at the same time.
article: συσταυρόω combines "with" (σύν) and "crucify" (σταυρόω) to mean being crucified alongside someone. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and although the Majority Standard Bible's wording varies—rendering it simply "crucified," "same crucified with," or "crucified with"—the underlying meaning is consistent in every case. Most striking is how Abbott-Smith notes the word takes on a metaphorical sense in Romans 6:6 and Galatians 2:20, describing the believer's spiritual death together with Christ rather than a literal execution.
caution: The varied English renderings reflect translation choices, not distinct meanings, so the three "measured senses" are really one sense applied literally and figuratively.

definition: To give off light or shine, or to come into view and become visible, often with the sense of how something appears.
article: φαίνω covers two related ideas: things shining or giving light, and things coming into view or appearing. The translation data splits almost evenly between "shine" (7×, 28%) and "appeared" (7×, 28%), with further uses meaning to seem or appear a certain way—as in looking outwardly righteous (Matthew 23:28). It relates to the Greek word for light (φῶς), and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew word for light, אוֹר, fitting its "shine" sense well.
caution: The word's range stretches from literal shining to merely seeming or appearing, so the exact shade depends heavily on context.

definition: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the Jewish ruling council who came to Jesus by night.
article: This is the personal name Nicodemus, which appears 5 times in the New Testament, all in John's Gospel (John 3:1, 3:4, 3:9, 7:50, 19:39). Dodson identifies him as a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council. The name is formed from elements meaning "victory" and "people," and Moulton-Milligan notes it was common among both Greeks and Jews, turning up in everyday papyri and inscriptions—including a second-century document where one Nicodemus is called a town councillor.
caution: The second "measured sense" simply reflects an added phrase in one rendering; the word itself is just the proper name.

definition: Eagerness to act quickly, ranging from physical haste to earnest, diligent effort put into something.
article: σπουδή covers a span from literal speed to inner eagerness: it can mean hurrying somewhere or pouring earnest diligence into a task. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "hurried" twice, "earnestness" twice, and "make" twice (the last in phrases like "make every effort"). The everyday papyri confirm the haste sense vividly — one writer says he is sending a letter "in haste" (μετὰ σπουδῆς) so the recipient won't worry, and another asks that freight be loaded "with all despatch."
caution: The senses split fairly evenly between "haste" and "earnestness," so context, not the word alone, decides which is meant.

definition: To dwell or live inside something, often used figuratively of a person, spirit, or quality residing within someone.
article: ἐνοικέω simply means "to dwell in," built from ἐν ("in") and οἰκέω ("to dwell"). In the New Testament it appears 5 times and is rendered "dwell" in 4 of them, but the interesting thing is what does the dwelling: not just God and the Spirit, but also things like the word, faith, and even sin (Rom 7:17). The everyday papyri show the same word with a more physical, sometimes forceful edge — one second-century BC document uses ἐνοικοῦσιν βιαίως for taking forcible possession of a house.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and one of them not rendered by a distinct English word, the measured sense range is thin.

definition: To pass by or go past a place or person, often while traveling alongside it.
article: παραπορεύομαι means to travel past or alongside something — to pass by. In the Byzantine New Testament all 5 occurrences fit this, rendered "passed" 4 times and "walking back" once (Mark 11:20). It's a common everyday Koine word: a papyrus letter from around 258–253 BC scolds someone, "you ought, indeed, not to have passed us by in this way." In the Septuagint it appears 36 times, most often translating the Hebrew עָבַר ("to cross over, pass"), 9 times.
caution: Abbott-Smith lists an additional sense "to go beside, accompany" not reflected in the measured New Testament renderings.

definition: A piece of ground — a field, plot, or property, often a named place.
senseLabels: a piece of land or property
article: χωρίον is a diminutive of χώρα ("region") and refers to a defined piece of ground — a field, plot, or estate. In the Byzantine New Testament's 10 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible splits evenly: half the time it names a specific spot (a place "called" Gethsemane, as in Matthew 26:36 and John 4:5), and half the time it means "land" or property (Acts 4:34; 5:3, 8). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense, using the word for a farmer's field or "the farmstead of Gaianus."

definition: A place on the Jordan River, named in some texts as where John baptized, meaning roughly "place of crossing."
article: Βηθαβαρά is a place name tied to the Jordan River, with the name pointing to a "ferry-house" or "place of crossing," from Hebrew roots meaning house and crossing. It appears in the Septuagint only once, where it renders the Hebrew name Zemaraim, and it does not occur at all in the Byzantine New Testament. The most notable point is textual: at John 1:28 the received text reads Bethabara, but the Westcott-Hort and Revised editions read Bethany instead, so the two readings disagree about the location's name.
caution: Evidence is extremely thin and the manuscripts disagree, with major editions reading "Bethany" rather than "Bethabara" at John 1:28.

definition: To go ahead of others or lead the way, and also to bring or lead someone forward, such as into court.
article: προάγω combines "before" (πρό) with "lead" (ἄγω), and its range splits two ways: most often it means going ahead or preceding someone, but it can also mean leading or bringing a person forward, including into a legal proceeding. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 18 times, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "go ahead" or "ahead" in over 60% of cases and "bring" in two others. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this: one second-century BC letter uses it for telling Timothy to "go before me to Rome," matching the New Testament's most common sense exactly.
caution: The judicial "bring into court" sense rests on only two occurrences, and one of them (Acts 12:6) is textually disputed with the similar word προσάγω.

definition: Someone who hates you or opposes you; a foe or adversary, whether a person, group, or hostile power.
article: ἐχθρός describes an enemy — someone marked by hostility, whether actively hating or being hated. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 32 times, and translators render it "enemies" in essentially every case (31 of 32, 100%). In the Septuagint it appears far more often (345×), mostly standing in for the Hebrew אוֹיֵב, "enemy" (194×); the classical lexica note it can carry both passive ("hated") and active ("hating, hostile") force, and in the Gospels it is sometimes a title for the devil.

definition: The breath or wind, and by extension the inner spirit of a person or a non-physical being—from God's Spirit to human spirits, angels, or demons.
article: Across 384 New Testament occurrences, translators render πνεῦμα as "Spirit" essentially every time (376×, with the BSB independently agreeing 98%), though it covers a wide field: the moving air or wind, the breath of life, the human inner self, and superhuman beings including God's own Spirit. Its core is captured by the Hebrew word it most often translates in the Septuagint, ר֫וּחַ (rûaḥ), found 241 times—a word that itself bridges "wind," "breath," and "spirit." A telling everyday glimpse comes from a 5th-century papyrus where a petitioner pleads that his very "breath of life" (πνεῦμα) is failing, showing how concrete the word could remain even in late Koine.
caution: Moulton-Milligan note that the word's meaning was so deepened by Christian use that everyday papyri shed limited light on its New Testament range.

definition: A part or limb of the body, used both literally for physical body parts and figuratively for members belonging to one another.
article: μέλος refers to a part or limb of the body, and Bible translators render it as "part" in about 43% of its 34 New Testament occurrences and as some form of "member" or "body" in most of the rest. The word stretches naturally from literal anatomy to a figurative sense in which believers are described as members of one another or of Christ's body. Everyday Koine confirms the basic meaning vividly: a papyrus from around A.D. 131 complains of being beaten "on every limb of my body" (μέλος τοῦ σώματος). In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew נֵתַח, a word for a piece or cut portion of an animal.

definition: A person from your own tribe or nation — a fellow countryman who shares your origins.
article: Συμφυλέτης means a fellow member of one's own tribe or country — someone who shares your local roots. It is built from σύν ("with") and a form of φυλή ("tribe"), and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, part of a wave of similar compound words common in later Greek. The most striking fact is its rarity in the Bible: it appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "countrymen."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and, according to Abbott-Smith, is "not found elsewhere," so its precise range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To urge or push someone forward, either by prompting and instructing them or by physically moving them to the front.
article: This verb literally means to move someone forward, and it splits between a figurative and a physical sense in its two New Testament appearances. In Matthew 14:8, Salome is "prompted" by her mother (a sense the Septuagint shares, where the word renders Hebrew terms for giving instruction, as in Exodus 35:34 and Deuteronomy 6:7). In Acts 19:33, by contrast, Alexander is "pushed forward" out of a crowd, the more concrete meaning. Notably, an inscription (Kaibel 947) also uses it with the plain literal sense of being led forward, and Moulton-Milligan argues the Septuagint pattern favors the "instructed" reading in Matthew.
caution: With only two occurrences and the standard rendering disagreeing with the BSB on the Acts verse, the boundary between the prompting and physical senses is genuinely uncertain.

definition: To give someone or something a drink, or to water and irrigate plants.
article: ποτίζω covers two related ideas: giving a drink to people (or animals) and watering or irrigating plants. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times, most often rendered "drink" (4×) or "give drink" (2×), and figuratively for feeding milk to the immature (1 Corinthians 3:2) or being made to drink of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). The Septuagint uses it 61 times, mainly for the Hebrew שָׁקָה ("to give drink, water"), and everyday Koine papyri show the irrigation sense vividly—one third-century text speaks of digging conduits and watering the land.

definition: A commotion or public uproar, when people are stirred up and thrown into confusion.
article: Τάραχος names a stir of agitation — a public uproar or commotion that breaks out among people, as in Acts 19:23 where a "great disturbance" arose. It is a later, masculine form of the more common ταραχή, both built from the verb ταράσσω ("to disturb"). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the word is common in medical writers, and Epicurus used it for inner "disturbance" or "alarm" as well as outward commotion.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin measured data, the range of meaning is hard to pin down precisely.

definition: A pearl, the smooth gem formed inside certain oysters, valued as costly adornment.
article: μαργαρίτης simply means a pearl, and that single sense covers all its uses. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "pearls" in 8 of those (89%), occasionally as "fine pearls." One memorable use is proverbial: in Matthew 7:6 pearls stand for something precious not to be thrown before swine, while in passages like 1 Timothy 2:9 and Revelation 17:4 they appear literally as luxurious adornment.

definition: To have existed or been doing something earlier, before the present moment.
article: προϋπάρχω describes something that was already in place or already happening before the time being discussed. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke's writings, and both times the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it with a sense of prior time — Pilate and Herod had "previously" been at odds (Luke 23:12), and Simon had "before" practiced magic (Acts 8:9). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too: one document from 259 BC speaks of "the already existing dykes" during canal repairs, showing it was ordinary administrative language.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use — so the picture of its full range rests on a small sample.

definition: To hide something away completely or keep it secret, often describing truths concealed by God until revealed.
article: ἀποκρύπτω means to hide something thoroughly or keep it secret, built from κρύπτω ("to hide") with the prefix ἀπό adding the sense of completeness. In the New Testament's 6 occurrences it almost always appears in contexts of divine truth that was concealed—rendered "hidden" in 4 of 6 cases (67%)—as in Matthew 11:25, 1 Corinthians 2:7, and Colossians 1:26. A nice glimpse of its everyday range comes from the papyri: an A.D. 310 census oath swears that no one has been "hidden away," and a much older Ephesus inscription uses it of a bird flying out of sight.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and just 4 in the critical text, the distinctions between the three measured senses rest on thin evidence.

definition: A wrestling match or hand-to-hand struggle, used figuratively for an ongoing fight or conflict.
article: πάλη literally means wrestling or a wrestling bout, and by extension any fight, struggle, or contest. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 6:12, where it pictures the Christian's spiritual combat; the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "against" there, reflecting the verse's phrasing rather than a separate sense. The figurative use is well attested outside the Bible: a 4th–5th century papyrus homily speaks of a "spiritual wrestling" (πνευματικὴ ἡ πάλη), and Marcus Aurelius compares life itself to wrestling rather than dancing.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured data is thin, and the single rendering "against" reflects the surrounding phrase more than the word's core meaning of wrestling.

definition: Darkness, whether literal absence of light or a figurative state of evil, ignorance, or spiritual ruin.
article: σκότος means darkness, and the corpus is overwhelmingly consistent: 29 of 32 Byzantine occurrences (91%) are simply rendered "darkness," with a couple of phrases like "belongs darkness" expressing the idea of people associated with it. The word covers both physical dark and a moral or spiritual sense, as Dodson notes. In the Septuagint it appears 99 times and most often stands in for the Hebrew חֹשֶׁך (60×); a striking detail is that magical papyri pair it with light in creation language—"the one who separated the light from the darkness."

definition: To join or fit together, and in the middle voice, to promise someone in marriage or betroth them.
article: Literally ἁρμόζω means to fit or join things together, but in the New Testament it appears just once (2 Corinthians 11:2), where Paul uses the middle voice to mean he "promised" believers in marriage to Christ. The middle form likely signals Paul's deep personal stake in the match, like someone arranging a betrothal. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan found no exact parallel for this usage in everyday Koine papyri, though a fourth-century document does show a mother arranging a marriage for her son using a related word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and zero times in the critical text, so its sense rests on a single verse with no direct papyri parallel.

definition: A group of people traveling together along the same route, such as a caravan or band of fellow pilgrims.
article: Συνοδία literally combines "together" (σύν) and "way" (ὁδός), describing people sharing a journey. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 2:44, where it is folded into the wider phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word; the KJV simply uses "company." Classical writers like Plutarch could also use it for the journey itself, and everyday Koine papyri show related words for fellow travelers and members of social or cult clubs, hinting at how natural the term was in ordinary life.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence and three in the Septuagint, so the measured range is narrow.

definition: The physical decay or corruption that a dead body undergoes in the grave.
article: διαφθορά means decay or corruption, especially the rotting of a dead body in the grave. All 6 New Testament occurrences cluster in Acts 2 and 13, where Peter and Paul quote a Psalm to argue that the Messiah's body did not undergo this decay. The four 'measured senses' here are really one idea — the Bible renders it as 'decay' every time, with the extra labels just reflecting surrounding phrases. Notably, in the Septuagint it appears 19 times and most often translates the Hebrew word שָׁחַת (shachath), which can mean 'pit' or 'corruption'.
caution: The classical lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) also list a broader sense of 'destruction,' but every New Testament occurrence is the narrower 'decay' of the grave.

definition: Deep mental anguish or distress, the overwhelming fear and inner struggle a person feels under great strain.
article: ἀγωνία describes intense anguish or anxiety of mind — the inner struggle of someone under extreme pressure. It comes from ἀγών (a contest), and the older classical writers used it for an actual wrestling match or athletic contest before it took on the emotional meaning. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 22:44, where the translators folded it into a phrase rather than rendering it as a single English word; the same flavor shows up vividly in everyday papyri, where one writer says "I am at present very anxious" (P Tebt II.423).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests heavily on outside Koine evidence rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: To utterly hate or turn away from something with strong revulsion.
article: ἀποστυγέω means to deeply loathe or detest something, an intensified form of στυγέω (to hate) with the prefix ἀπό. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 12:9, where it describes the believer's response to evil. The classical lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) agree on the sense "abhor" or "detest utterly," and the prefix adds force to the basic idea of hating.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the measured evidence is very thin and the confidence tier is low.

definition: To take on a gloomy or somber look—whether a downcast human face or an overcast, threatening sky.
article: στυγνάζω describes something turning gloomy or somber in appearance. In its two New Testament uses, it does both jobs: in Mark 10:22 a man's face falls in sadness, and in Matthew 16:3 the sky looks dark and stormy. The everyday Koine papyri capture the contrast nicely—one document pairs it with laughter ("laughing, he turned gloomy"), showing it as the opposite of cheerfulness; in the Septuagint it renders Hebrew words for being appalled or laid waste.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (and the Matthew 16:3 reading itself textually disputed), the evidence for the "stormy sky" sense is thin.

definition: The building material or structure built into something, especially the substance worked into a wall.
article: This word describes the material or structure built into something — in its single New Testament appearance (Revelation 21:18), it refers to jasper built into the wall of the heavenly city. It appears in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and one inscription confirms the spelling variant ἐνδώμησις as describing the building of a sacred precinct. Interestingly, the form ἐνδόμησις turns up in Josephus meaning a mole or breakwater, and one scholar even suggested it might mean 'roofing,' though the evidence cited does not support that.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its precise sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To make or establish something by law, or in the passive, to be given laws or have a legal system put in place.
article: This verb has to do with law-making: in its active sense it means to legislate or enact something by law, while in the passive—how the New Testament uses it—it means to be furnished with laws or to be legally established. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (both in Hebrews) and not at all in the critical SBLGNT text; the Septuagint uses it nine times, often translating the Hebrew yarah ("to instruct" or "teach"). A nice everyday glimpse comes from a papyrus letter (P Oxy VIII.1119, A.D. 254), where the verb describes a legal privilege the emperor Hadrian had "clearly enacted" exempting a city's senators from outside public duties.
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only twice in the Byzantine text and not in the critical text, so its measured range here is very thin.

definition: To speak well of someone, to praise or thank God, or to ask for blessing on a person.
article: Built from εὖ ("well") and λόγος ("word"), εὐλογέω literally means "to speak well of," and it covers a range from praising and thanking God to invoking a blessing on someone. In the Byzantine New Testament's 43 occurrences it is rendered "blessed" about 73% of the time and "bless" another 20%, while the Septuagint uses it heavily—337 times—mostly for Hebrew בָּרַך ("to bless"). One nice detail from the inscriptions: the word was not limited to Jewish use, appearing in formulas like "Ptolemaios the Jew blesses God" but also in a pagan inscription praising the god Pan.

definition: To pursue someone closely or track them down, whether to attack them or to catch up with them.
article: This verb means to chase after someone with determination — to hunt them down or follow them up closely. In the Septuagint it appears 83 times, mostly translating the Hebrew רָדַף ('to pursue'), and it can carry either a hostile sense (as in pursuing enemies) or a friendly one (catching up with someone), as Abbott-Smith notes. The word's intensity is its most striking feature: Moulton-Milligan argues the New Testament's single use in Mark 1:36 — where Simon's companions track Jesus down — should be 'pursue after' or 'hunt down' rather than the milder 'follow after' of older translations.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise force in Mark 1:36 is debated — the lexicons favor a strong 'hunt down' over the translated 'went to look for him.'

definition: To exist, be present, or be in a particular state; in the plural participle, the things one owns — possessions.
article: ὑπάρχω most often functions as a quiet way of saying something exists or is in a certain condition, and in 51 of its 62 Byzantine appearances it gets absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own. Its one clearly measured standalone sense is "possessions" — the things one has — rendered that way 10 times (91%), as in Matthew 19:21 and Acts 4:32. The Septuagint stretches it across 23 books to cover Hebrew words like הָיָה ("to be") and מִקְנֶה ("property"), and the older lexicons note an early sense of "to begin," a meaning the everyday papyri show fading over time toward simple existence and ownership.
caution: The verb usually carries no English word of its own (51 of 62 times), so its force depends heavily on context rather than a fixed gloss.

definition: The act or faculty of seeing; by extension, how something appears, or a divinely given vision.
article: ὅρασις covers a range from the basic act of seeing to the way something appears and, further, to a God-given vision. The four New Testament uses split evenly between "appearance" (how something looked, as in Revelation 4:3) and "vision" (an inspired sight, as in Acts 2:17 and Revelation 9:17), and the Septuagint uses it 91 times, mostly for Hebrew words meaning "appearance" (מַרְאֶה) or "vision" (חָזוֹן). A striking piece of evidence: an inscription records Stratia offering a gift to the goddess Demeter "on account of restored sight," showing the plain, everyday sense of physical seeing.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, the measured senses overlap heavily, and how to split a single verse like Revelation 4:3 between "appearance" and "vision" is somewhat arbitrary.

definition: Philetus, a man named in the New Testament who, with Hymenaeus, spread false teaching that wandered from the truth.
article: Φίλητος is a personal name, Philetus, appearing only once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 2:17), where he is identified as someone whose teaching strayed from the truth. The name comes from the verb φιλέω ("to love") and carries the sense "amiable" or "beloved," though as a name it simply identifies the individual. Moulton-Milligan note that this was an ordinary name in everyday Koine, citing a property document from Oxyrhynchus (A.D. 90) that mentions a Tiberius Julius Philetus.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once, so there is no real range of meaning to map.

definition: A mountain, hill, or upland region rising above the surrounding plain.
senseLabels: part of a place name (Jesus context)
article: The basic meaning is a mountain or hill—the high ground rising above the lowlands. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "mountain" 41 times (73%) and as part of a named "Mount" (like the Mount of Olives) 9 times; the cases tagged "Jesus" simply reflect English phrasings where the word disappears into a larger expression rather than a separate sense. In the Septuagint it appears over 600 times, almost always translating the Hebrew har (mountain), and a striking detail is that everyday Koine papyri use ὄρος to mean the desert, since the desert hills were the regular burial ground.

definition: To lease out or rent property to others, typically a landowner letting out a vineyard or field for someone else's use.
article: In the New Testament ἐκδίδωμι appears only 4 times, and every single one comes from the same parable of the wicked tenants, where a landowner "rents out" or "leases out" his vineyard (Matthew 21:33, 41; Mark 12:1; Luke 20:9). The basic idea is giving something forth, but in this commercial middle sense it means letting property out for your own advantage. Interestingly, the everyday papyri stretch this further: the same verb was used for apprenticing a son to a craftsman and even to open marriage contracts, showing it covered the broad notion of formally "handing over" a person or thing by agreement.
caution: The New Testament uses are all from one parable, so its full Koine range is better seen in the papyri than in the biblical text itself.

definition: A child whose parents have died; more broadly, someone left bereft, friendless, or abandoned.
article: ὀρφανός refers to a child who has lost a parent or parents, and by extension anyone left bereft and without support. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just twice, both rendered "orphans," but the word stretches further: in John 14:18 it carries the broader sense of being left desolate or friendless, a usage Abbott-Smith and the classical lexica also recognize. The Septuagint uses it 44 times, overwhelmingly for the Hebrew יָתוֹם (the "fatherless" so often paired with widows), and the papyri show it as an everyday legal term—one Ptolemaic tax list even has a scribbled note insisting a man "is not an orphan, but the son of Daiphantos."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the confidence tier is low, and the lexica spread the meaning from literal orphan to general desolation rather than a single fixed sense.

definition: A lack of belief or trust, especially failure to believe God or his message.
article: ἀπιστία means a want of faith or trust, and the New Testament uses it consistently in this single sense. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "unbelief" in 10 of 12 occurrences (91%), and the BSB independently agrees about 90% of the time, so the word's range is narrow and well-attested. Lexicons like Dodson stretch it slightly toward "unfaithfulness" or "distrust," and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where one illiterate document even spells it with a non-standard form.
caution: Some lexicons allow a sense of "unfaithfulness" or "distrust" beyond plain "unbelief," though the measured renderings overwhelmingly favor the latter.

definition: The state of being God; the full divine nature or essence itself.
article: θεότης refers to deity itself — the very nature and essence of being God, not just godlike qualities. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:9, where it describes the fullness of deity dwelling bodily in Christ; the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it in that context 100% of the time. Abbott-Smith notes a related word, θειότης, and points readers to compare the two, since the distinction between full "deity" and mere "divine quality" can matter.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from usage alone.

definition: Amon, a king of Judah listed in Jesus' genealogy as son of Manasseh and father of Josiah.
article: Ἀμών is simply the Greek spelling of a Hebrew personal name, used in the Byzantine text of Jesus' genealogy where it names King Amon of Judah, son of Manasseh and father of Josiah. It appears just 2 times in the Byzantine New Testament (both in Matthew 1:10) and is rendered "Amon" every time; the critical SBLGNT text has it 0 times. In the Septuagint the related Hebrew name אָמוֹן shows up 15 times across 7 books, mostly translating that same Hebrew form.
caution: The name is absent from the critical text and rests on only 2 Byzantine occurrences, both in a single verse.

definition: To be pleased or take delight in someone or something, or to gladly decide on a course of action.
article: εὐδοκέω covers two closely related ideas: being pleased or taking delight in a person or thing, and gladly choosing or consenting to do something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 21 times, rendered "pleased" in 47% of cases and "well pleased" in 33%, with the latter famously used of God's voice over Jesus at his baptism (Matthew 3:17, Mark 1:11). In the Septuagint it shows up 39 times, most often standing in for Hebrew רָצָה (to be favorable toward); the everyday papyri even use it in legal documents for formally granting or consenting to something.

definition: To count or reckon someone among a particular group, classing them together with others.
article: This verb, built from ἐν ('in') and κρίνω ('to judge'), means to reckon or class someone among a group. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 10:12, where the Majority Standard Bible's rendering reflects the idea of people classing 'themselves' among a certain set. The word is well attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, often in the technical sense of enrolling someone—for example, enrolling youths among the ephebes—and Alexandrian critics used it to mark out or select the best writers.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise force here rests heavily on context and the parallels from inscriptions and papyri.

definition: To make someone or something new again, to renew or restore inwardly.
senseLabels: to renew or make new again
article: This verb means to renew or restore, to make something new again. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul (2 Corinthians 4:16 and Colossians 3:10), describing an inward renewal. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the word has not been traced to any source earlier than Paul, raising the question of whether he coined it himself — though they find no proof he actually did, since it follows the normal pattern of forming new Koine words from old Greek stems.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, and the word's origin and exact range remain uncertain.

definition: To arrange or appoint something beforehand, or to place it in front.
article: προτάσσω combines πρό (before) with τάσσω (to arrange), giving the sense of placing something in front or settling it in advance. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up only once in the Septuagint (2 Maccabees 8:36). The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where the participle means 'the aforesaid' — as in an Oxyrhynchus document (A.D. 188) reading 'Apollonius the aforesaid' — and a later papyrus uses it for what is rightly 'put in the foremost place.'
caution: Evidence is thin: the word never occurs in the Byzantine NT and the one disputed New Testament reading (Acts 17:26) is rejected by modern editors in favor of προστάσσω.

definition: To spend extra money in addition to what one has already paid out.
article: This verb means to spend additional money beyond an initial outlay, built from πρός ("besides") and δαπανάω ("to spend"). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:35, where the Good Samaritan promises to repay whatever extra the innkeeper spends. The same word turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions, such as one from around 165 BC describing a man who "spent additionally from his own funds," confirming it was ordinary financial vocabulary outside the Bible.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Silver metal, and by extension money or silver coins used in payment or trade.
article: This word covers a tight cluster of related ideas: literal silver as a metal, money in general, and specific silver coins. In the Byzantine New Testament it's split fairly evenly—rendered "money" 9 times (50%), "silver" 7 times (39%), and "silver money" twice. The Septuagint uses it heavily, 320 times, almost always for the Hebrew word for silver (כֶּסֶף, 276×), and everyday papyri confirm it routinely meant cash, as in a marriage contract promising 1,000 drachmae of Alexander's coinage.

definition: To taste food or drink, and by extension to eat, or figuratively to experience something firsthand.
article: γεύομαι literally means to taste food or drink, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "taste" in 6 of 15 occurrences (43%) and "eat" in 3 (21%). It stretches naturally into the figurative idea of experiencing something, most famously in the phrase "taste death" (Matthew 16:28; Luke 9:27), which Abbott-Smith links to a Talmudic Hebrew parallel. The word turns up in everyday Koine: papyri from the Decian persecution (A.D. 250) use the standing formula "I tasted of the sacred things," and in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew טָעַם, "to taste."

definition: A person who carries out an official public service, such as a minister, servant, or temple worker acting on behalf of others.
article: λειτουργός describes someone performing official service, whether religious or civic — the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "minister" (3 of 5 times, 60%), with "servant" and one reference to angels as "winds"/ministering spirits filling out the range. In the Septuagint it shows up 10 times, usually translating the Hebrew word שָׁרַת (sharat, "to serve" or "minister"), reinforcing the sense of dedicated service. A nice detail from the papyri: in Ptolemaic-era documents the word could simply mean a workman or laborer — one text lists it alongside builders working on construction — showing how ordinary the term once was before its more official religious flavor.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences, the apparent third "sense" reflects the Hebrews 1:7 angels-as-winds passage rather than a distinct meaning of the word itself, so the measured senses should be read with care.

definition: To throw someone down headlong off a cliff or steep place.
article: This verb means to cast someone down headlong over a precipice. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 4:29, where the crowd tries to throw Jesus off a cliff. The word is built from κατά (down) and κρημνός (a steep cliff), and the Septuagint uses it for similar violent acts, such as in 2 Chronicles 25:12 where captives are thrown down to their deaths.
caution: The measured senses note 'brow,' but this reflects the cliff-edge setting in Luke 4:29 rather than the verb's own meaning, which is to throw down; the New Testament evidence is a single occurrence.

definition: Thyatira, a city in the Lydia district of Roman Asia Minor.
article: Thyatira was a city in the old district of Lydia, within the Roman province of Asia, named all 4 times it appears in the New Testament (Acts 16:14; Revelation 1:11; 2:18, 24). Every translation surveyed renders it simply "Thyatira," with no variation. The most vivid evidence comes from inscriptions: the city was known for its guild of purple dyers, and Lydia, the first convert in Acts 16:14, was herself a seller of purple from Thyatira—a tombstone in Thessalonica even honors a purple dyer from the city.

definition: An adverb meaning without purpose or result — pointlessly, for nothing.
article: μάτην is an adverb describing something done uselessly or without achieving its aim — "in vain." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 2 times, both in the same saying of Jesus (Matthew 15:9 and Mark 7:7) about worshiping God in vain, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way every time. It is far more common in the Septuagint (20 times across 7 books) and shows up in everyday Koine papyri, including one document where a trader "came away after finding six or seven offering in vain to sell" their barley.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both in the same quoted saying, the measured range here is very narrow.

definition: Describing someone or something as strong, powerful, and able to exert force.
article: κραταιός means strong or mighty, describing power and the ability to exert force. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 1 Peter 5:6, where it speaks of God's "mighty" hand, and translators agree on "mighty" 100% of the time. It is far more common in the Septuagint (54 times in 18 books), where it usually renders the Hebrew word for "strong" (חָזָק, 26 times); interestingly, the same word turns up in magical papyri addressing "mighty gods."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on thin evidence, though the Septuagint and lexicons agree on "strong, mighty."

definition: The dry stalks or stubble left after grain is harvested, used as flimsy, easily burned material.
article: καλάμη refers to the leftover stalks of grain — stubble or straw — the cheap, flammable remnant after a harvest. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 3:12, where it joins wood and hay as building materials that fire will destroy. The Septuagint uses it 16 times, most often for the Hebrew קָשׁ ("stubble"), and everyday papyri confirm its plain agricultural meaning, as in a contract stating "the straw shall belong to Diodorus."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: Describing something or someone as Italian, belonging to Italy.
article: Ἰταλικός is an adjective meaning "Italian," describing something that belongs to Italy. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:1, where it identifies the "Italian Cohort" (σπεῖρα Ἰταλική), the military unit to which Cornelius belonged. The word turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions too: one from Delos at the end of the second century BC honors a man on behalf of "the Italians" (Ἰταλικοί) for their fairness and goodwill, showing it was a normal label for people from Italy.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: An indefinite pronoun pointing to an unspecified person or thing—someone, anyone, a certain one, or simply 'a/some.'
article: This is one of the New Testament's most common little words, appearing 533 times in the Byzantine text, and it works as a vague pointer to an unspecified person or thing—'someone,' 'anyone,' 'a certain one,' or just 'a/some.' Its range is wide and slippery: translators rendered it as 'some' 96 times (27%), 'anyone' 64 times (18%), and 'a' 63 times (17%), while in 171 of 533 cases it gets absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own. Notably, Moulton-Milligan flags that it sometimes stands in for the relative pronoun 'who/which' (as in Mark 14:36 and 1 Timothy 1:7), and in the Septuagint it renders several different Hebrew words, including 'man' and 'there is.'
caution: Its sense depends heavily on context, and the many overlapping renderings (plus its occasional use for the relative pronoun) mean translations vary case by case.

definition: To be kind, treating others with active, helpful goodness.
article: χρηστεύομαι means to show kindness — not just a feeling but useful, serving goodness toward others, as the gloss "full of service to others" suggests. In the New Testament it appears only once, in 1 Corinthians 13:4, where it describes what love does. It comes from the adjective χρηστός ("good, kind"), and Moulton-Milligan note that it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary spoken Greek, not a coined religious term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: The skill, insight, or wisdom that guides good thinking and right living, whether human or divine.
article: σοφία means wisdom in a broad sense — from practical skill and intelligence in daily affairs to the highest mental and spiritual excellence. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 51 times, and English translations render it "wisdom" almost without exception (49 of 51, about 98%). It usually translates the Hebrew חָכְמָה in the Septuagint, and one striking detail is that in later everyday papyri it served as a title of honor, as when a writer addresses "your fraternal wisdom" much as we might say "your honor."

definition: To make someone firmly convinced or assured of something; in the passive, to be fully persuaded of what one has learned.
article: πιστόω comes from πιστός ('faithful, trustworthy') and basically means to make something or someone trustworthy or sure. In the New Testament it appears just once, in 2 Timothy 3:14, where the passive form describes being firmly assured of what one has learned. The Septuagint uses it 11 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew root אָמַן ('to be firm, faithful')—the same root behind 'amen'—and everyday Koine papyri show the same idea, as when one writer says he describes reservoirs 'as I was assured' of their nature.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical text), so its New Testament range rests on a single passage.

definition: Being free rather than enslaved, or released from some restraint, obligation, or law.
article: ἐλεύθερος describes someone who is free — most often in the plain civil sense of not being a slave, frequently paired against the word for "slave" (5 of its 23 New Testament uses). It also stretches to freedom from restraint and obligation generally: free from the law, from sin, or exempt from a duty. In the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew חָפְשִׁי (8 times), the word for a freed or free person, and Moulton-Milligan notes it appears in everyday papyri, including the oldest surviving Greek marriage contract where bride and groom are both described as "free."

definition: The act of hunting down and harassing people for their beliefs, especially mistreatment aimed at followers of Christ.
article: διωγμός means persecution—the organized pursuit and mistreatment of people because of what they believe. All 10 New Testament occurrences point to this single sense, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "persecutions" 80% of the time and as "persecution comes" in the other 20%, where it describes trouble arriving on account of one's faith. The word comes from διώκω, "to pursue," and older lexicons preserve that root meaning of "chase" or "pursuit"; in its two Septuagint appearances it translates the Hebrew רָדַף ("pursue") and מָרוּד.

definition: Describing something that came earlier in time, place, or rank — the former or previous one.
article: πρότερος is the comparative form of πρό ("before") and points to whatever came earlier — a former state, a previous time, or an earlier rank. In the New Testament it always refers to time, meaning "former" or "formerly," as in the "former way of life" in Ephesians 4:22; it's strikingly rare, appearing only 11 times in the critical text and never in Luke. The Septuagint uses it 32 times across 11 books, most often to render Hebrew רִאשׁוֹן ("first"). Notably, the papyri show the same pattern of rarity, with everyday documents preferring it for things like "the custom of former years."
caution: Byzantine count is 0 because πρότερος appears only in the critical text (11×), so this entry rests on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: Describing something done according to law, whether a lawful assembly or a person who lives under and obeys the law.
article: ἔννομος combines "in" with "law" (νόμος) and points to whatever is in line with the law. It appears just twice in the New Testament, splitting evenly between two senses: a "lawful" assembly (Acts 19:39) and a person who is "under the law," as when Paul says he is under Christ's law (1 Corinthians 9:21). The everyday Koine papyri back the "legal" sense nicely—one document describes a man "approaching the legal age" (ἐννόμῳ ἡλικίᾳ), the same way Ramsay argued for "lawful assembly" in Acts.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and the senses split one each, the word's exact range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To mock, ridicule, or jeer at someone, treating them with scorn and contempt.
article: This verb means to make fun of or deride someone, and in the Byzantine New Testament it almost always describes the mockery Jesus suffered—appearing 13 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "mocked" or "mock" in 84% of cases. Built from ἐν plus παίζω ("to play"), it carries the sense of playing games at someone's expense. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes a secondary shade of "delude" or "trick" in everyday Koine papyri and in Matthew 2:16, where Herod realizes he has been outwitted by the Magi. In the Septuagint it appears 23 times, most often translating the Hebrew עָלַל (7×).

definition: An image or statue made to represent a god, or by extension the false god itself that people worship.
article: In the New Testament εἴδωλον almost always means an idol — either the physical image set up for worship or the false god behind it — rendered "idols" in 10 of its 11 occurrences (91%). In the Septuagint it appears 74 times, translating several Hebrew words for pagan images, including גִּלּוּלִים (13×) and עֲצַבִּים (10×). Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri preserve the word's older, broader meaning: in one astrological text εἴδωλα refers to the nine constellations, and elsewhere it simply means an image or visible phenomenon, matching the classical sense of a phantom or mental picture.

definition: An adverb meaning 'moderately,' but in the New Testament used with a negative ('not moderately') to mean 'exceedingly' or 'greatly.'
article: On its own μετρίως means 'moderately' or 'to a modest degree,' built from the word for 'measure.' But in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 20:12) it comes with a negative, so 'not moderately' actually means 'greatly' or 'exceedingly' — a turn of phrase the translators count as 'greatly' 100% of the time. The everyday Koine papyri show the same pattern beautifully: a slave writes that she worried 'not moderately' (i.e. terribly) over her master, and a complaint records someone insulted 'not moderately.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests entirely on a single negated phrase rather than a broad range of usage.

definition: To be anxious or worried, mentally unsettled, as if hanging in suspense over uncertain matters.
article: In its one New Testament appearance (Luke 12:29), this verb describes being mentally unsettled or anxious — literally "left hanging" over life's needs. The word's range is striking: it literally means to lift up or suspend in mid-air, and a vivid 5th-century papyrus uses it of a man complaining he was "suspended by ropes" and beaten daily. From that physical image of hanging come two figurative senses — being puffed up or elated (the usual Septuagint sense, translating Hebrew words for "rise high") and being anxiously suspended in suspense, which is how it works in Luke.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical text), so the "anxious" sense rests on a single occurrence supported by classical and papyri parallels.

definition: Jesse, the father of King David and an ancestor of Jesus in the genealogies.
article: Ἰεσσαί is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jesse, and every one of its 5 New Testament occurrences is rendered "Jesse" (100%). He was the father of King David, and he appears mostly in genealogies tracing Jesus' ancestry. In the Septuagint the name shows up 37 times, almost always translating the Hebrew יִשַׁי, which confirms the straightforward transliteration.

definition: A weight or load—literally something heavy, but in the New Testament usually a figurative burden one carries or shares.
article: βάρος means weight, and across its 6 New Testament appearances it consistently points to a burden—rendered "burden" in every measured case (4 times, with 2 more absorbed into phrasing). The range runs from literal heaviness to figurative loads, like Galatians 6:2's call to carry "one another's burdens." The everyday papyri use it of practical hardship: one document complains of a public duty too heavy to bear ("the burden of the service"), and another asks whether a matter "causes you trouble," showing how naturally Koine speakers used it for oppressive obligations. Abbott-Smith notes a rarer late-Greek sense of "dignity, authority," which some translators see in 1 Thessalonians 2:6.
caution: The "dignity/authority" sense in 1 Thessalonians 2:6 is disputed—translations split between "burden" and "weight/authority."

definition: To respond with open thanks and praise, especially giving thanks aloud to God in prayer.
article: This rare word appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 2:38, where the prophetess Anna gives thanks to God upon seeing the infant Jesus. Built from "in return" plus "acknowledge," its range in wider Greek runs from making a mutual agreement to fully confessing, but with a person in the dative it means to declare praise or thanks. The everyday papyri preserve the "agreement" side vividly: one second-century B.C. document uses it for parties who "will come to an understanding" with each other, while the Septuagint applies it to thanking and praising God.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, and its measured English rendering ("forward") reflects translation phrasing rather than the word's core meaning of thanksgiving.

definition: A Jewish liquid measure of roughly eight to nine gallons, used for oil and other liquids.
article: βάτος is a Hebrew loanword (from בַּת) naming a Jewish unit for measuring liquids, equal to about 8¾ gallons. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 16:6, where a steward records a debt measured in this unit. Interestingly, the word was also spelled βάδος in some early sources like Hesychius and the Septuagint, possibly because the softened 'd' sound felt closer to the original Hebrew letter.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering 'manager' reflects the surrounding context rather than the word itself, which the lexicons consistently define as a liquid measure.

definition: A public confession or open acknowledgment of what one believes and holds to.
article: In the New Testament ὁμολογία means a public confession — an open acknowledgment of one's faith — and the Majority Standard Bible renders all three translated occurrences as "confession" (2 Corinthians 9:13; 1 Timothy 6:12-13), with the other three occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday Koine evidence is strikingly different: in the papyri this word is extremely common as a legal term meaning "contract" or "agreement," as in a will headed "deed and agreement" or a contract to nurse an infant slave. In the Septuagint it appears 6 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for a freewill offering (נְדָבָה, 4×), pointing toward something voluntarily declared or pledged.
caution: With only six occurrences and three of those absorbed into phrasing, the biblical evidence is thin, and the New Testament's "confession" sense stands well apart from the dominant "contract/agreement" meaning in the papyri.

definition: The act of teaching, or the body of instruction that is taught.
article: This noun, built from the verb "to teach" (διδάσκαλος), covers both teaching as an activity and the content that gets taught. In the Byzantine NT it appears 21 times, rendered "teaching" in 63% of cases and "doctrine" in 25%, with the two meanings shading into each other; Abbott-Smith notes the objective sense (the body of instruction) is actually the more frequent one. The word was at home in everyday Koine: a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (A.D. 367-70) uses it for a Praefect basing his orders "on instruction" drawn from local practice.

definition: In a manner that fits or matches something, behaving in a way that suits a person, role, or calling.
article: This adverb means acting in a way that matches or befits something — every one of its 6 New Testament uses is rendered "in a manner worthy." It often pairs with a genitive naming the standard you should live up to, as in "worthy of the Lord" (Col 1:10) or "worthy of God" (1 Thess 2:12). Notably, this genitive construction shows up frequently in ancient inscriptions, suggesting it was a familiar formal way to express measuring up to someone's honor or expectations.

definition: To speak, talk, or tell — the everyday act of uttering words to someone.
article: λαλέω is the ordinary verb for speaking, and it shows up everywhere — 294 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 23 books. About 77% of the time it's simply rendered "speak," with "told" and "say" covering most of the rest, so its range is wide but stays firmly in the territory of uttering words. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew דָּבַר ("to speak," 894×). One nice detail: Dodson notes that in classical Greek the word leaned toward "chatter" or idle talk, while the New Testament uses it as a more dignified word for speaking — and the everyday papyri keep that lighter flavor, as in a letter where a man hopes "to escape from the talking."

definition: To produce a good crop or be very fruitful, as land that yields an abundant harvest.
article: εὐφορέω describes land being fertile and yielding well—literally "bearing well," from εὖ (well) and φορέω (to bear). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 12:16, where a rich man's ground produces an abundant crop, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ground" there. The same root shows up in everyday Koine: a third-century BC inscription from Nisyros uses the related noun in a wish that there be a good crop of grain (εὐφορία σίτου).
