caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range here rests on that single verse plus outside evidence.

definition: A hymn or sacred song sung in praise to God.
senseLabels: a hymn of praise to God
article: ὕμνος means a hymn — a song of praise directed to God, appearing only twice in the New Testament (Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16). In the Septuagint it shows up 16 times and most often renders the Hebrew תְּהִלָּה ("praise"), confirming its core sense of praise-singing. The wider Greek world used it more broadly: classical Greek called it a festal song honoring gods or heroes, and an Egyptian inscription from 238 B.C. even mentions temple scribes composing hymns for a choir-master, while a later papyrus speaks of sending up "undying hymns to the Master Christ."
caution: Note that the measured-sense data here mislabels both occurrences as "another," which appears to be a tagging error rather than a real meaning, so rely on the LXX and lexical evidence for the actual sense.

definition: An upper room or chamber built on the flat roof or upper story of a house.
article: ὑπερῷον is simply the upper room or roof-chamber of a house, sitting on the higher level above the main living space. In the New Testament it appears 4 times, all in Acts, where it names the kind of room used for gatherings, prayer, or laying out the dead. The Septuagint uses it 25 times, mostly for Hebrew עֲלִיָּה, and the everyday papyri confirm the plain sense — one Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 179 even mentions a woman owning "two upper-chambers." Classical writers used the word more specifically for the upper rooms where women lived, but in the Bible it just means a roof-top chamber.

definition: The Latin name Silvanus, borne by a Christian companion and co-worker of the apostle Paul.
article: Σιλουανός is a proper name—Silvanus, a helper of Paul—appearing 4 times across 4 New Testament books (1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Peter, and 2 Corinthians). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Silvanus" in 3 of 4 cases, with the 4th occurrence (2 Corinthians 1:19) showing up only as part of a longer phrase. Abbott-Smith notes it is the Latinized form of the name Silas, and Moulton-Milligan points to a fascinating papyrus parallel: a contemporary first-century document (P Oxy II.335, c. A.D. 85) records a Jew named Silvanus buying part of a house in the Jewish quarter.
caution: The manuscripts vary between the spellings Σιλουανός and Σιλβανός, so the exact form is somewhat uncertain.

definition: An adjective meaning belonging to or located in Ephesus, the city; Ephesian.
article: Ἐφεσῖνος is an adjective derived from Ἔφεσος (Ephesus), meaning "Ephesian" or "situated at Ephesus." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament, and Abbott-Smith notes it only as the Received Text reading at Revelation 2:1, where the better-attested texts (WH, RV) instead read ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, "in Ephesus." Moulton-Milligan confirms the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary usage outside the biblical text.
caution: Evidence is very thin: the word has zero New Testament occurrences and survives only as a disputed Received Text variant, so its biblical standing is uncertain.

definition: A figurative or veiled saying, such as a proverb, parable, or illustration that conveys meaning indirectly rather than plainly.
article: In the New Testament παροιμία appears 5 times, and in John's Gospel it describes Jesus speaking in figures or illustrations rather than directly—several occurrences contrast it with speaking "plainly." In the Septuagint it twice translates the Hebrew מָשָׁל, which covers both proverbs and parables, and outside John it can mean a plain old-fashioned proverb or byword (as in 2 Peter 2:22). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan trace the word from παρά and οἶμος, literally "by the way," the sense of a wayside saying that became a maxim or byword.
caution: The word's range is genuinely debated: Abbott-Smith and Strong's lean toward an enigmatic or cryptic saying, while Moulton-Milligan cites Abbott's view that John means a brief, general remark rather than a dark one.

definition: A fire, especially a pile of burning fuel kindled for warmth.
article: πυρά means a fire, typically the kind built up from gathered fuel rather than fire in the abstract. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the same scene at Acts 28:2-3, where the Maltese islanders kindle a fire to warm Paul and his shipwrecked companions; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fire" in both places. It comes from the broader word πῦρ ("fire"), and the Septuagint uses it a handful of times, including in Judith 7:5 and Wisdom 17:6.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences from a single passage, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Illyricum, a Roman province on the eastern Adriatic coast, later called Dalmatia.
article: Ἰλλυρικόν is the place-name Illyricum, a region bordering the Adriatic Sea (later known as Dalmatia, with Pannonia to the north, Macedonia to the south, and Moesia to the east). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 15:19, where it marks the geographic limit Paul describes for his preaching. The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, where Moulton-Milligan note it for the Imperial age.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its 'range' is simply geographic and there is little to say beyond the location itself.

definition: Chorazin, a town in Galilee that Jesus rebuked for refusing to repent despite witnessing his miracles.
article: Χοραζίν is a place name, not a common noun: it refers to Chorazin, a town in Galilee. It appears only twice in the New Testament, in Matthew 11:21 and Luke 10:13, both times in Jesus' rebuke of towns that saw his miracles yet did not repent. The lexicons agree it is a town of uncertain derivation, and every occurrence is rendered simply as the name itself.
caution: This word appears only twice and its derivation is uncertain, so little can be said beyond identifying it as a Galilean town.

definition: A woman's clothing or outward appearance, possibly carrying the wider sense of how one presents and conducts oneself.
article: This rare word appears just once in the New Testament (1 Timothy 2:9), where it's measured as referring to women's apparel. It's equally rare in the Septuagint, showing up once in Isaiah 61:3 to translate the Hebrew מַעֲטֵה (a covering or garment). The most interesting wrinkle comes from the papyri and inscriptions: in an inscription from Priene (c. 120 BC) the word is paired with terms for orderly conduct, suggesting it may carry the broader sense of deportment or demeanor rather than just literal clothing—which is why Abbott-Smith also lists meanings like 'steadiness, quietness in demeanour.'
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall evidence, scholars genuinely disagree over whether it means literal clothing or broader 'deportment,' so its precise force in 1 Timothy 2:9 is uncertain.

definition: A personal name in Jesus' genealogy: Ram, son of Hezron and father of Amminadab.
article: Ἀράμ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Ram, an ancestor of Jesus listed in the genealogies (Matthew 1:3-4, and also Luke 3:33 in some manuscripts). It appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, always referring to this one person, son of Hezron and father of Amminadab. The two "measured senses" here simply reflect how the name sits in genealogical phrasing ("Ram" versus "Ram, father of...") rather than any real difference in meaning. Worth noting: at Luke 3:33 some critical editions read a different name (Ἀρνεί) instead of Ἀράμ.
caution: This is a proper name attested only a few times, and the apparent "second sense" is just phrasing, not a genuine difference in meaning; the Luke reading is also textually disputed.

definition: Describing something that cannot be shaken or moved, whether literally fixed in place or, figuratively, permanently secure.
article: ἀσάλευτος combines the negative prefix with a form of σαλεύω ("to shake"), so it means "unshaken" or "immovable." The New Testament uses it just twice—once of a ship stuck fast in Acts 27:41, and once figuratively of a kingdom "that cannot be shaken" in Hebrews 12:28, where the rendering blends into the surrounding phrase. Everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions used it the same metaphorical way: one fourth-century petition pleads that legal proceedings "remain firm and unshaken," showing the word was at home in documents about lasting, settled arrangements. Curiously, in the Septuagint it translates a Hebrew word for the "frontlets" or phylacteries bound to the forehead (Exodus 13:16; Deuteronomy 6:8; 11:18).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences—one absorbed into surrounding phrasing—the measured data is thin, so confidence in its full range rests largely on outside lexica and papyri.

definition: Describing someone who talks too much, especially spreading idle or foolish chatter and gossip about others.
article: φλύαρος describes a person who babbles or chatters foolishly, particularly someone who spreads gossip. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 5:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gossips." Notably, its only Septuagint appearance is in 4 Maccabees 5:10, where it describes not a person but a philosophy—calling it "babbling" or foolish—which shows the word could apply to ideas as well as people.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range of meaning cannot be confirmed from the biblical evidence alone.

definition: To heal or cure someone of physical sickness, and sometimes to restore them from spiritual harm.
article: ἰάομαι means to heal or cure, used in the New Testament almost entirely of physical sickness — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "healed" or "heal" in about 81% of its 28 occurrences. The range stretches to spiritual or figurative healing too, as Abbott-Smith notes for passages like Matthew 13:15 and John 12:40. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew רָפָא ("heal") 39 of 55 times, and the everyday papyri show the same concrete sense: one inscription records that "a man's finger was healed by a snake," and another that a blind man was cured. Moulton-Milligan distinguishes it from θεραπεύω, which leans toward medical treatment, while ἰάομαι points to the actual healing.
caution: The "done healed" sense (2×, 7%) reflects English phrasing of completed action rather than a distinct meaning, so it overlaps heavily with the main "healed" sense.

definition: A verbal dispute or contradiction—people arguing against one another—and by extension open rebellion or defiant opposition.
article: ἀντιλογία means a dispute, contradiction, or arguing against someone, and at its sharper end can mean rebellion or defiant opposition. In the Septuagint it shows up 20 times and most often (7×) translates the Hebrew רִיב, a word for legal quarrel or contention, with related words for strife adding to the picture. The papyri are especially vivid: Moulton-Milligan cites everyday documents where ἀντιλογία refers to an actual assault, showing the word could escalate from words to physical attack. Note that the measured English renderings here ("greater," "profit") reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself, so lean on the lexical evidence for its true range.
caution: The measured Byzantine renderings don't isolate this word's meaning, so its sense rests mainly on the Septuagint, papyri, and classical lexicons rather than the New Testament translation data.

definition: A person who lives nearby; a neighbor.
article: γείτων simply means a neighbor — someone whose home or land adjoins your own. In the New Testament it appears just 4 times, all in Luke and John, always referring to literal neighbors; the variations the Bible's renderings show ("neighbors," "calls neighbors") just reflect the surrounding sentence, not separate meanings. The everyday flavor of the word shows up vividly in the papyri, where it is extremely common in property descriptions marking who lives to the south, north, and so on of a given plot, and in one letter complaining of suspicion "against my neighbors." In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew shakhen, also meaning neighbor.
caution: The word is rare in the New Testament (only 4 occurrences), so its range there rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: To stay outdoors in the open countryside, especially overnight, as shepherds do while watching their flocks.
article: ἀγραυλέω describes spending the night outdoors in the open country rather than under a roof. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 2:8, where shepherds are out in the fields keeping watch over their flocks; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "residing" there and the BSB agrees fully. The word is built from ἀγρός ("field") plus a root tied to αὐλή ("open courtyard" or "fold"), which fits its sense of camping or bivouacking in the open.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from this evidence.

definition: Libya, the region of North Africa west of Egypt.
article: Libya is a place name for the part of North Africa lying west of Egypt. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:10, where it describes the area near Cyrene from which some of the people at Pentecost had come. Interestingly, the older lexicons note that while early writers (going back to Homer's Odyssey) used the name for this north-African region, later writers sometimes stretched it to mean the whole African continent.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical usage rests on a single verse.

definition: Brightness or brilliant shining, especially the dazzling radiance of a light source like the sun.
article: λαμπρότης means brightness or brilliance, and it appears just once in the New Testament, where Paul describes a heavenly light shining "above the brightness of the sun" (Acts 26:13). Although the Majority Standard Bible's tally labels this single occurrence "noon," the word itself denotes radiance, not a time of day — it refers to the sun's brilliance. Interestingly, in everyday Koine papyri the word took on a social meaning, used as a title of honor (something like "your Excellency"), as in a sixth-century lease document where a property belongs to "your λαμπρότης."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and three in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, and the "noon" label reflects the surrounding phrase about the sun rather than the word's actual meaning of brightness.

definition: A pitcher or jug, originally a Roman liquid measure of a little less than a pint.
article: ξέστης names a small vessel for holding liquids, and it began as the Roman measure called the sextarius (slightly less than a pint), a word that Greek borrowed and reshaped. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Mark 7 (verses 4 and 8), where it refers to pitchers being ritually washed rather than to a precise measurement. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this range: one document lists "twelve xestai of wine" as a measure, while others use the word simply to mean "two cups" or "three bronze cups," showing how it slid from measure to container.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two occurrences, both in one passage—and sources note the meaning shifts between a fixed liquid measure and a generic pitcher or cup.

definition: High-ranking men—nobles, courtiers, or great lords—especially those surrounding a ruler.
article: This word, almost always used in the plural, refers to the great men of a realm—nobles, courtiers, or leading officials around a ruler. It appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament and 18 times in the Septuagint, where it renders Hebrew words for officials and princes; Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. One interesting parallel comes from the Psalms of Solomon, where "the megistanes of the earth" may mean the leading men of Palestine or the victorious party of Caesar.
caution: Confidence is low: only 3 New Testament occurrences, and the digest lists a "never" rendering for Revelation 18:23 that reflects sentence rephrasing rather than a real separate sense.

definition: Describing something done unwillingly or against one's own will, rather than by free choice.
article: This adjective, formed from a negative prefix plus the word for "willing," describes acting against one's own wishes. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) consistently define it as "unwilling" or "unwillingly," though the corpus translation in its single New Testament occurrence (1 Corinthians 9:17) renders it as "voluntary" — note these point in opposite directions and depend on how the verse is read. It was a common everyday Greek word: the papyri include a fourth-century Christian letter saying "unwillingly I cast you into such grief," and inscriptions pair it with its opposite, "willing."
caution: It appears only once in the New Testament, and the corpus rendering "voluntary" runs opposite to the lexicons' "unwilling," so its sense here is genuinely uncertain.

definition: To think ahead about something and take care to provide for it, whether for others or for oneself.
article: προνοέω means to look ahead and make provision—either arranging good things in advance or actively caring for someone's needs. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 3 times: twice the Berean translators render it with the idea of giving careful regard to what is honorable (Romans 12:17; 2 Corinthians 8:21), and once it concerns providing for one's own household (1 Timothy 5:8). The everyday flavor is clear from the papyri, where one writer says he is "by all means looking after the copper," showing the word's plain, practical sense of seeing to a task in advance.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and the word rated low confidence, the surface renderings ("eyes," "anyone") reflect translation phrasing rather than separate meanings, so its true range rests on thin evidence.

definition: A gift given freely, without cost or expectation of repayment.
article: δωρεά means a gift, and specifically one given freely or without charge — the New Testament writers often pair it with God's grace, the Holy Spirit, or righteousness. The Majority Standard Bible renders all 11 occurrences as some form of "gift," and the BSB independently agrees 100% of the time, so the core meaning is solid. One nice detail: in everyday Koine papyri the word describes an emperor's beneficium or largess to his soldiers, showing it could mean a generous benefaction from someone powerful. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew חִנָּם ("freely, without cause"), reinforcing the "free of charge" flavor.

definition: To take care of someone or something, looking after their needs and well-being.
article: ἐπιμελέομαι means to take care of or look after someone, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it consistently this way in all 3 occurrences—the Good Samaritan caring for the wounded man (Luke 10:34–35) and the requirement that a church leader manage his own household (1 Timothy 3:5). The verb takes a genitive object, a construction confirmed by everyday Koine papyri, where letter-writers used phrases like 'take care of yourself, so that you stay healthy.' Its meaning is narrow and well-attested, with all sources agreeing on the same care-giving sense.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint—though the limited data points clearly in one direction.

definition: A short form of the pronoun "me," the object form of "I."
article: μέ is simply a shortened form of the first-person pronoun "me," the object of a verb or preposition. Abbott-Smith notes it stands as an apostrophe for the fuller form με, and rarely (in Homer) does duty for "to me" (μοι). It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all, but shows up over 1,500 times across the Septuagint, where the Greek often lines up with Hebrew particles like אֶל ("to," 337 times) rather than functioning as a standalone pronoun.
caution: The Septuagint counts likely reflect how this short form pairs with surrounding Hebrew words rather than its own independent meaning, so the figures describe context, not a distinct sense of the pronoun itself.

definition: The act of catching fish, or the haul of fish that is caught.
article: ἄγρα covers both sides of fishing: the action of catching and the actual haul brought in. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in Luke 5, where Jesus tells the fishermen to lower their nets "for a catch" (the act) and then they marvel at "the catch" they take in (the result). Abbott-Smith notes the word originally meant a hunt or chase generally, derived from ἄγω ("to lead" or "drive"), though in the New Testament it refers specifically to fish.
caution: With only two occurrences and a low confidence tier, the line between the two senses is thin and rests entirely on these Luke 5 verses.

definition: To send someone or something off on a mission or with a commission, often as an official messenger or representative.
article: ἀποστέλλω means to dispatch a person or thing with a purpose—not just to send, but to send on service or with a commission. The Byzantine NT uses it 132 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sent" in 91% of cases, with a few instances pointing to "one sent" (a messenger) or "sent out." In the Septuagint it appears 533 times and almost always translates the Hebrew שָׁלַח (432 times), "to send," and the everyday papyri confirm it was the common Koine word for sending letters, money, or people, as when one writer promises, "as soon as we receive wages I will send them up to you."

definition: Literally a soldier standing in the front rank; figuratively a ringleader or chief instigator of a movement.
article: πρωτοστάτης literally describes the soldier who stands first in the front line, and the classical writers Thucydides and Xenophon use it that way. By the time of the New Testament it had shifted to a figurative sense of "leader" or "ringleader," which is how Paul's accusers brand him in its single NT appearance (Acts 24:5). Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible's rendering here reads as "dissension" rather than a personal title, and the word's one Septuagint use (Job 15:24) translates a rare Hebrew term, כִּידוֹר.
caution: Evidence is thin: this word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, and the measured rendering "dissension" sits oddly against the lexicons' agreed sense of "leader/ringleader."

definition: To be battered and tossed about by a violent storm at sea.
article: In the New Testament χειμάζω appears just once, in Acts 27:18, where Paul's ship is being violently tossed by a tempest — and every translation surveyed renders it that way ("tossed"). The word's root is connected to χειμών, "winter" or "storm," and older lexicons note a broader range, from exposing to winter cold to being driven by a gale. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: an inscription records people who were "storm-tossed at sea" (χειμασθέντες ἐν πελάγει) making an offering to God in thanks for surviving, almost exactly mirroring the New Testament usage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Able to discern or judge, distinguishing one thing from another.
article: This adjective describes something that has the power to discern, judge, or distinguish — formed from the word for "judge" (κριτής). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 4:12, where it describes God's word as able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. The classical lexica (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) consistently define it as "critical, able to discern or judge," and there it governs a genitive object.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured data shows a rendering of "marrow," which conflicts with the lexicons' "discerner/able to judge" — likely a tagging artifact from the surrounding Hebrews 4:12 phrasing.

definition: To quarrel over words or argue about petty verbal points instead of matters that matter.
article: λογομαχέω combines λόγος (word) and μάχομαι (to fight), so it literally means to fight over words. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 2:14, where Paul warns against such disputes. The lexicons agree on "strive about words" or "contend about words"; interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders the whole phrase as "avoid," capturing the verse's command rather than translating the verb in isolation.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: Ripe fruit, especially the autumn harvest that comes at the end of summer.
article: ὀπώρα originally named the season of late summer and early autumn—roughly late July through early September—and by extension came to mean the ripe fruit of that time. In its single New Testament appearance (Revelation 18:14) it refers to fruit, though the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering here is tied to the phrase 'the fruit your soul longed for.' A nice everyday parallel comes from an Egyptian tax-gatherer's first-century letter, where he complains 'there has not been much fruit in Memphis up to the present,' showing the word was common, ordinary Koine.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: To move something away from its place, or figuratively to be shifted away from a position one holds.
article: μετακινέω means to move or shift something away from where it sits — built from μετά ("change of place") plus κινέω ("to move"). It appears just once in the New Testament, where its sense is carried by the surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word, used figuratively of being shifted away from hope (Colossians 1:23). The literal meaning is well attested elsewhere: in the Septuagint it often describes moving boundary markers (Deuteronomy 19:14), and a Greek inscription on a temple stone near Cephisia warns whoever owns the land never to "move away" any of the sacred images.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use (figurative) — so the precise force in that single verse rests largely on the clearer literal uses outside the New Testament.

definition: To change the outward form or appearance of something, or to disguise oneself as something else.
article: This verb means to change how something looks on the outside while what it really is stays the same. Paul uses it both for genuine transformation (the body remade at Christ's return, Philippians 3:21) and for deceptive disguise — false apostles "masquerading" as servants of righteousness, just as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:13-15). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense of refashioning: legal documents granting permission to "remodel" or "alter" a property use the same word.
caution: The word appears only 5 times and the measured "senses" are mostly tied to specific verses rather than truly distinct meanings, so treat the breakdown as occurrence labels, not sharp categories.

definition: To freely give or bestow something as a favor, and by extension to graciously forgive someone.
article: χαρίζομαι is built on χάρις (grace/favor), and its core idea is doing something freely and graciously for someone. In the Byzantine New Testament's 23 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "forgive" nearly half the time (10×, 48%), with the rest spread across giving, granting, and bestowing — so the word covers both freely handing over a gift and freely pardoning a debt or sin. The everyday papyri capture this warmth nicely: one writer says that if you grant his request, "I shall be eternally obliged to you," showing how giving and showing kindness blur together. Lexicons note the "forgive" sense is a later Greek development (like the Latin condonare).
caution: The senses overlap heavily — even the lexicons admit "show kindness" and "freely bestow" can hardly be separated — so the dividing lines between forgive, give, and grant are softer than the counts suggest.

definition: Describing a Roman citizen punished without first receiving a proper legal trial or investigation of the charges.
article: ἀκατάκριτος literally combines a negative prefix with the idea of being condemned, so older translations like the KJV render it "uncondemned." But in both of its New Testament appearances (Acts 16:37 and 22:25), Paul is protesting the beating of a Roman citizen before any hearing, so the sense "without trial" fits better. Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri, and Ramsay suggests Paul was echoing the Roman legal phrase re incognita, "without investigating our case."
caution: Evidence is thin and sources disagree: Abbott-Smith and the KJV favor "uncondemned," while Moulton-Milligan argues the context demands "without trial."

definition: A four-wheeled carriage or wagon used for riding and transporting goods.
article: This word names a four-wheeled vehicle for carrying people or goods, appearing just once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:13, where it is rendered "carriages." The lexicons note it was originally a Gallic word borrowed into Latin and then Greek, and Quintilian specifically describes it as a four-wheeled vehicle that came from Gaul. Moulton-Milligan confirms the term shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary commercial vocabulary, not a literary rarity.
caution: This is a single occurrence in the New Testament (a hapax) and a loanword, so its precise sense rests on outside evidence rather than NT usage.

definition: To fall off or drop away from something, as scales falling from the eyes.
article: This verb literally means "to fall off" — its single New Testament appearance describes something like scales falling from Saul's eyes in Acts 9:18, where it's absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by one English word. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times across 3 books, translating several different Hebrew words including "gleanings" and even "empty." Interestingly, the Koine papyri use it in a figurative sense of collapsing or losing heart: one letter from around 153 B.C. uses it to mean someone has "given up" and can never show their face again for shame.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use, and that absorbed into phrasing, so the precise force here rests largely on the Septuagint and papyri rather than direct measurement.

definition: To put plants or trees into the ground so they can grow.
article: φυτεύω means to plant something in the earth—whether a single tree, a vineyard, or crops generally. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times, most often (6×, 55%) for vineyards being "planted," with the rest describing the act of "planting" in farming life. It is a thoroughly ordinary word: it shows up 42 times in the Septuagint (chiefly translating Hebrew נָטַע, "to plant"), and Koine farming papyri use it for vineyards too—one third-century BC document literally reports "and all the vine has been planted."

definition: A place where someone lives — a dwelling, home, or residence.
article: οἰκητήριον means a dwelling place or residence, the spot where someone lives. It appears only twice in the New Testament, split evenly between a literal sense (the angels' own 'dwelling' that they abandoned, Jude 6) and a figurative one (our 'heavenly dwelling,' 2 Corinthians 5:2). Everyday papyri confirm the plain meaning: one document from AD 20–50 records a wife taking her destitute husband into her parents' οἰκητήρια, or 'house.'
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences split across two distinct uses, the precise range of this word is hard to pin down from the biblical data alone.

definition: To feel deep compassion or pity for someone, being moved to act on their behalf.
article: This verb means to be moved with compassion or pity, literally describing a stirring in the inner organs (the σπλάγχνα) that the ancients linked to deep emotion. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "compassion" every time — 67% simply as "compassion" and 25% as "moved with compassion." Strikingly, Lightfoot and others suggest the word does not appear in classical Greek and may have been coined by Greek-speaking Jews of the Dispersion, with the few outside examples coming from a sixth-century papyrus petition and even a Modern Greek sailor's prayer.

definition: A serious intestinal illness marked by inflammation of the bowels and severe, often bloody diarrhea.
article: This word names a specific intestinal disease — dysentery, what the KJV calls "bloody flux." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 28:8, where Paul heals the father of Publius on Malta, and modern translations render it "dysentery" 100% of the time. Interestingly, the manuscripts of Acts actually use the neuter form δυσεντέριον, the common spoken Hellenistic form, rather than the Attic feminine δυσεντερία shown in the medical textbooks of Luke's day.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single medical context.

definition: To make a solemn promise or declaration on oath, calling on God or something sacred as witness.
article: This verb means to swear or affirm something under oath, and the meaning is remarkably stable: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "swear" in 20 of its 27 New Testament occurrences (77%), with all the rest being closely related oath-language. In the Septuagint it appears 162 times, almost always translating the Hebrew verb שָׁבַע ("to swear"), 136 times out of its few Hebrew counterparts. Everyday Koine papyri show the same use, including oaths sworn by rulers—one Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 66 reads "I swear by Nero Claudius Caesar."

definition: Describing someone who is devout and reverent toward God, showing genuine piety in attitude and life.
article: εὐσεβής describes a person who is pious, God-fearing, and devout — built from εὖ ("well") and σέβομαι ("to revere"). It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, most often rendered "devout" (50%), as with Cornelius and his soldier in Acts 10. The everyday Koine papyri show a broader, less religious flavor: Moulton-Milligan note it could describe a sensible action or even "dutiful" tax payments, and from the late second century AD it served as the imperial title equivalent to the Latin Pius.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and several different Hebrew counterparts behind it in the Septuagint, the word's precise range is hard to pin down tightly.

definition: To load someone or something down with a heavy burden, used figuratively of people weighed down by demands or worries.
article: φορτίζω means to load up, the way you would pile cargo onto an animal or a vessel, and in the New Testament it is used figuratively of overburdening people. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 11:46 (where Jesus accuses experts in the law of loading people with hard-to-carry burdens) and Matthew 11:28 (the famous "heavy laden"), and in both cases it is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. The everyday Koine flavor comes through clearly in the papyri, where a related verb describes fifty beasts "loaded with dry hay" and boats "loaded with produce."
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use — and the lexica differ on which Hebrew word it renders (Abbott-Smith cites Ezekiel 16:33), so treat the measured sense as low-confidence.

definition: A shrinking or drawing back, used of timidly retreating from faithful commitment.
article: This noun describes pulling back or retreating, the opposite of holding firm. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 10:39, where it contrasts faith that preserves the soul with a fearful drawing back. The classical lexica record an additional sense, "a letting down or lowering" (Plutarch), and Josephus uses it of leaving nothing untried in mischief, showing the word's wider everyday range in Koine documents.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single verse and confidence is low.

definition: The state of being one or united together, especially harmony among people.
article: ἑνότης means oneness or unity, built directly from the number word εἷς ("one"). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Ephesians 4 (verses 3 and 13), where the Berean Standard Bible renders it as "unity" in each case. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the same word in everyday Koine documents and even in an Epicurean philosophical text, where it describes particles maintaining a kind of mutual sympathy and "unity" with one another.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the New Testament, so its measured range is very thin.

definition: To stretch oneself out toward something, and so to long for, aspire to, or reach after it.
article: ὀρέγομαι pictures someone literally stretching out to grasp something, used figuratively to mean reaching after, longing for, or aspiring to a goal. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament (1 Timothy 3:1 and 6:10, Hebrews 11:16), and in each case it is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word. Interestingly, in everyday papyri and inscriptions the related forms could mean simply 'to come to someone's assistance' or 'reach out a helping hand,' showing how the basic idea of stretching out could go beyond mere desire.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament and is always absorbed into phrasing, so its precise force in each passage is hard to pin down.

definition: A brother by birth, or more broadly a fellow member of one's people or religious community.
article: At its core ἀδελφός means a brother born of the same parent or parents, and that literal sense covers nearly all of its 344 New Testament occurrences (98% rendered "brothers"). But the word stretches outward to mean a neighbor, a fellow countryman, or a fellow believer, and the classical lexica spell out all these senses even though the Byzantine measurements just count them as "brothers." One striking detail from the papyri: in a letter from 168 BC a woman addresses her husband as ἀδελφός, reflecting the Ptolemaic habit of calling wives "sisters" even when they were not actually siblings.

definition: A priest — a religious official authorized to offer sacrifices and perform sacred rites for a god.
article: A ἱερεύς is a priest: a person consecrated to serve at an altar, offer sacrifices, and carry out the rites of worship. The word is overwhelmingly stable — the Byzantine New Testament uses it 33 times and it is rendered "priests" in 94% of cases, with the Septuagint using it 779 times, almost always for the Hebrew כֹּהֵן (716×). Though usually Jewish priests in the New Testament, the range is broader: it can name a pagan priest (a priest of Zeus in Acts 14:13) and even Christians figuratively, and the everyday papyri show it used for ordinary temple staff — including a complaint by five elder-priests against a fellow priest for wearing his hair too long.

definition: To pick out and choose someone or something for oneself, especially of God selecting people or things for his purposes.
article: This verb means to select or pick out, and in the New Testament it always appears in the middle voice—meaning you choose for yourself. The Byzantine text uses it 21 times, rendered "chosen" in about 85% of cases (17×) and applied to choosing things twice (10%), as in 1 Corinthians 1:27. In the Septuagint it appears 127 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew בָּחַר ("to choose," 105×), and the everyday papyri show the same middle-voice usage for ordinary acts of selecting and picking out.

definition: The ordinal number "second"—next after the first in order, time, or rank—often used as an adverb meaning "a second time."
article: δεύτερος is the ordinary Greek word for "second," whether in sequence, time, or rank. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 44 times, rendered "second" in 76% of cases and "second time" in another 21%, with the Majority Standard Bible and BSB agreeing fully. The same range shows up in everyday papyri: one second-century BC document pairs it with "first" ("first thank the gods, secondly save many lives"), exactly matching its adverbial use in 1 Corinthians 12:28.

definition: A command form meaning "let him, her, or it be," expressing that something should exist or remain in a certain state.
article: This is the third-person singular imperative of the verb "to be" (εἰμί), so it means "let him/her/it be" or "let it stand." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament corpus measured here, and there are no measured senses to report. The classical lexicon material describes the parent verb's broad range — "to be, to exist" in Homer, Herodotus, and others, including the contrast between truly being and merely appearing to be.
caution: The digest records zero New Testament occurrences and no measured senses, so the description here rests entirely on the form's grammar and the parent verb's classical usage.

definition: To winnow grain by tossing it into the wind, and by extension to scatter or crush something to powder.
article: The literal sense of λικμάω is agricultural: to winnow, throwing threshed grain into the air so the wind blows away the chaff. From this it stretched to mean scatter like chaff or grind to powder, which is how both New Testament uses (Matthew 21:44 and Luke 20:18) describe what happens to anyone who falls on the stone. The everyday Koine papyri keep the original farming sense — one third-century text speaks of winnowing barley on the threshing floor — and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew זָרָה ("to scatter") six times.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and lexicons split between "scatter as dust" and "grind to powder," the exact force in the Gospels is uncertain.

definition: Describing someone whose own actions or choices condemn them, so they stand guilty by their own doing.
article: This word literally combines "self" (αὐτός) with "condemn" (κατακρίνω), meaning a person who is condemned by their own conduct rather than by anyone else. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 3:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "corrupt," though Strong's, the KJV, and the lexicons all point to the more literal "self-condemned." Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and may well be a fresh coinage at Titus 3:11, built on a pattern any writer was free to use.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the MSB rendering "corrupt" differs from the literal "self-condemned" given by Strong's and the lexicons.

definition: The ordinal number meaning ninth, often used in the New Testament for the ninth hour of the day (about 3 p.m.).
article: This is simply the ordinal number "ninth," used 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament. Most often it refers to the ninth hour—around 3 o'clock in the afternoon—the time of prayer and the hour Jesus died on the cross. The Septuagint uses it 26 times, usually rendering the Hebrew word for "ninth" (תְּשִׁיעִי), and everyday papyri and inscriptions show the same word used for dating years and months, confirming it as ordinary Koine vocabulary.
caution: The spelling varies between ἔννατος and ἔνατος, and critical editions (which read ἔνατος) treat the longer form as absent, though this does not affect the meaning.

definition: A stringed musical instrument like a lyre or harp, plucked to produce music.
article: This word names a stringed instrument—a lyre or harp—played by plucking. The three measured senses are really the same object; the differences ("harp," "harp holding," "holding harps") just reflect how the surrounding phrase about people holding harps was translated in Revelation. In the Septuagint it appears 23 times and most often renders the Hebrew כִּנּוֹר (kinnor, 7×), the harp-like instrument of the Psalms, though it also stands in for a few other Hebrew terms.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, three of them in nearly identical Revelation phrases, the apparent "senses" are translation variants of a single meaning.

definition: A putting off or delay in acting, especially postponing something to a later time.
article: Ἀναβολή refers to a delay or putting-off, used just once in the New Testament (Acts 25:17), where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word. The everyday Koine papyri show the word with a wide range of meanings, including the very phrase "to make a delay" found in Acts, though sometimes carrying a quite different sense. In the Septuagint it appears only 3 times across 3 books, translating three different Hebrew words.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 1 NT occurrence, absorbed into phrasing) and the papyri show the same phrase used in different senses, so confidence is low.

definition: Describing something, especially a person's head, that is not covered or veiled.
article: ἀκατακάλυπτος is a compound built from a negative prefix plus a verb meaning 'to cover up,' so it literally means 'not covered' or 'unveiled.' Both of its two New Testament appearances are in 1 Corinthians 11 (verses 5 and 13), where it describes the state of a person's head during prayer. The Septuagint uses it just once, at Leviticus 13:45, to render a Hebrew word for hair left loose or unbound.
caution: With only two New Testament uses and one Septuagint occurrence, the evidence is thin; the second measured sense ('yourselves with head') simply reflects the phrasing of 1 Corinthians 11:13 rather than a distinct meaning.

definition: A person who robs temples or steals sacred objects, hence one guilty of sacrilege against established religion.
article: ἱερόσυλος literally combines "temple" (ἱερόν) with "to plunder" (συλάω), meaning someone who robs sacred places. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 19:37, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "robbed" and the KJV expands it to "robber of churches." Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions also carry a broader sense of disrespect toward established religion, and Ramsay reads the Acts passage as charging the men with sacrilege neither in deed nor in word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and sources differ on whether it means literal temple-robbing or broader sacrilege, so its exact range here is uncertain.

definition: Peleg, a male ancestor in Jesus' genealogy, son of Eber and father of Reu.
article: Φάλεκ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Peleg (פָּלֶג), an ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 3:35, where it is rendered "son" in the chain of names; the name itself is indeclinable in Greek. The Septuagint uses it 6 times in two books, always translating the same Hebrew name Peleg.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its use is fixed and limited to identifying the individual.

definition: The furthest point of something — either the outer edge of a place or the conclusion of a matter.
article: πέρας refers to an extremity: the outermost limit of a space or the end of a process. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 4 times, mostly in the phrase "the ends of the earth" (Matthew 12:42, Luke 11:31), but it can also mean a conclusion that settles a dispute, as when Hebrews 6:16 speaks of an oath ending all argument. Everyday Koine papyri sharpen this second sense: people wrote of asking an official to "put an end" to a legal matter, the same practical idea of bringing something to a close. In the Septuagint it occurs 38 times, most often translating the Hebrew קֵץ, "end."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the measured sense breakdown is thin, and the labels for the single Romans and Hebrews uses reflect rendering fragments rather than clean glosses.

definition: Jeremiah, an Old Testament Hebrew prophet whose name is mentioned in the Gospel of Matthew.
article: This is simply the personal name of the prophet Jeremiah, a Hebrew name that the New Testament always uses to point back to the prophet himself. It appears 3 times, all in Matthew (2:17, 16:14, 27:9), and translators uniformly render it "Jeremiah." In the Septuagint it shows up 107 times, mostly translating the Hebrew name יִרְמְיָה; notably one Matthew quotation (27:9) actually echoes wording from Zechariah 11:13 rather than the book of Jeremiah.
caution: Editions disagree on spelling (Ἱερεμίας vs. Ἰερεμίας), and the citation in Matthew 27:9 is attributed to Jeremiah but matches Zechariah.

definition: To bear and raise children; to become a mother and have a family.
article: τεκνογονέω means to bear children and, by extension, to raise a family — the word combines the roots for "child" and "come to be." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 5:14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the broader idea of managing a household (counted here as "manage"), and the lexicons agree on the core sense of bearing children. An interesting parallel from the papyri is a related compound, τεκνοποιέομαι, found in a 311 BC marriage contract binding a husband not to father children by another woman, showing how everyday Koine documents used similar child-bearing terms.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured precisely; the single rendering "manage" reflects the wider verse rather than the word's own core meaning of bearing children.

definition: To go back, turn back, or return to a place or person.
article: ἀνακάμπτω is built from ἀνά plus κάμπτω ("to bend"), and its measured meaning in the New Testament is consistently "to return" or "turn back" — appearing 4 times, with half the cases rendered simply "return." The word was common in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite papyri using it both literally ("after I had returned") and figuratively, as in Luke 10:6, where peace "returns" to the one who sent it. In the Septuagint it shows up 12 times across 8 books, usually rendering Hebrew words for turning back.
caution: The Acts 18:21 rendering "left" sits oddly alongside the core sense "return," and the BSB does not agree with it, so that occurrence is less certain.

definition: To clothe someone in a garment, or in the middle voice, to dress oneself in or habitually wear clothing.
article: This verb means to put clothing on someone, and in the middle voice (used of oneself) to be dressed in or habitually wear something. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 2 times, both rendered "lived" in the sense of being dressed (as in Luke 16:19, of the rich man clothed in purple). It's a longer form of the more common ἐνδύω, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, with the form even appearing in a second-century B.C. inscription.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and overall thin attestation of this somewhat rare verb, confidence about its full range is low.

definition: Greater or larger — a double-comparative form built on the word for "great," meaning roughly the same as "greater."
article: μειζότερος is a comparative form meaning "greater," built from μείζων, which is itself already the comparative of μέγας ("great"). It stacks one comparative on another — a kind of doubled-up "greater" — but in practice it just means greater. The base word μέγας covers a wide range: physical size (a large stone, a big fish), intensity (great fear, great love), and rank (a greater person or thing). This particular form does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all, showing up only once in the critical (SBLGNT) text.
caution: The evidence is extremely thin: this exact form occurs zero times in the Byzantine text and only once in the critical text, so all meaning is inferred from the parent word μέγας/μείζων.

definition: To calm or quiet a crowd, restraining people from agitation or rash action.
article: This verb means to settle people down — to keep a crowd quiet or hold them back from doing something rash. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 19, where the Ephesian town clerk urges the riotous mob to stay calm and act cautiously. Its literal sense is "to let down" or "lower"; everyday Koine papyri show it used the same way Acts does, for quieting people or restoring peace, as in a document describing Arabs who had been subdued and brought into peace.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a couple of Septuagint instances, the measured data is thin, though the papyri and lexicons agree on the "quiet/restrain" sense.

definition: To turn over or overturn something, knocking it down from its normal position.
article: καταστρέφω means literally to turn something upside down or topple it over. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both describing Jesus overturning the tables of the money changers (Matthew 21:12; Mark 11:15) — which is why the Majority Standard Bible's data shows it bound up with the act of 'selling' in those scenes. The Septuagint uses it 32 times, most often for the Hebrew הָפַך ('to overturn'), and the everyday papyri even apply it metaphorically, as when Vettius Valens speaks of people 'ending their lives' badly.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both in parallel accounts of the same event, the measured range is very narrow and rests on thin evidence.

definition: The way something looks—a face, outward appearance, or what can be seen by the eyes.
article: ὄψις refers to how something appears to the eye—whether a person's face, their outward features, or the general look of a thing. In the New Testament it occurs only 3 times, split between three different uses: judging by appearances (John 7:24), a face wrapped in burial cloth (John 11:44), and a face shining like the sun (Revelation 1:16). A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from a papyrus court case (P Oxy I.37, A.D. 49), where a child was restored to a woman because, from its features (ἐκ τῆς ὄψεως), it appeared to be hers—the same kind of sense-judgment Jesus warns against in John 7:24.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences—each rendered differently—the three 'measured senses' rest on single instances apiece, so the divisions reflect very thin evidence.

definition: Describing something made by bees, specifically a honeycomb.
article: This adjective means "belonging to" or "made by bees," and in the New Testament it appears only in the phrase for a piece of honeycomb. It shows up just once in the Byzantine text, at Luke 24:42, where the risen Jesus is offered fish and honeycomb. Notably, the modern critical text (SBLGNT) drops the word entirely, and the standard English renderings here count it as "broiled" through the surrounding phrase rather than the bee-word itself — a sign that the textual tradition is divided. Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary vocabulary outside the Bible.
caution: This is a single, textually disputed occurrence absent from the critical text, so its New Testament presence rests on weak manuscript support.

definition: To begin something or make a start on it.
article: ἐνάrchomai simply means to begin or make a start, and it shows up only twice in the New Testament (Galatians 3:3 and Philippians 1:6), each time about beginning something that then needs to be carried through. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times across 5 books, where Abbott-Smith notes it chiefly renders a Hebrew word meaning to begin or profane. The most interesting wrinkle is that in classical Greek the word carried a ritual sense (beginning a sacrifice), and Moulton-Milligan suggests this may faintly linger in the two NT uses, though everyday Koine papyri show the plain sense begin had fully taken over.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a possible faint ritual undertone noted by lexicographers, the precise nuance is uncertain.

definition: To raise children, fulfilling the duties of caring for and bringing up the young.
article: This verb combines the words for "child" (τέκνον) and "to nourish or rear" (τρέφω), so it means raising children to maturity. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:10, where it describes a worthy widow. Notably, Aristotle used the same word for bees rearing their young, and the philosopher Epictetus asks why anyone would discourage a wise person from "bringing up children" (τεκνοτροφεῖν), showing it was ordinary Koine vocabulary also found in everyday papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "strangers" appears to be a tagging error that disagrees with every dictionary's "bring up children."

definition: Not in agreement or harmony; describing people whose views clash or sounds that don't blend.
article: ἀσύμφωνος literally means "not sounding together," built from a negative prefix plus the word for harmonious or agreeing. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 28:25), it describes people who could not agree with one another, rendered "disagreed" by the Majority Standard Bible. Interestingly, the term shows up as a technical word in the astrologer Vettius Valens, where planets like Saturn and the Sun are called ἀσύμφωνοι (out of harmony), and Abbott-Smith notes the original sense of "dissonant" or musically discordant.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: The Dioscuri, the twin gods Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus, honored as protectors of sailors and used as a ship's figurehead.
senseLabels: the twin gods Castor and Pollux
article: Διόσκουροι names the divine twins Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus and Leda, who were popular patrons of sailors in the ancient world. The word appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 28:11, where it identifies the figurehead of the Alexandrian ship Paul sailed on. Interestingly, the form here uses the Ionic and common-Koine spelling with -ου-, while the older Attic form was Διόσκοροι; Moulton-Milligan note that this twin imagery was so familiar that personal names like Dioscorus were derived from it in everyday papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the listed measured rendering "wintered" reflects a tagging glitch rather than the word's actual meaning.

definition: Lydda, a town in Palestine on the road to Joppa, within a day's journey of Jerusalem.
article: Lydda is a place name—a town in Palestine, identified with the Hebrew Lod and known today as Ludd. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts 9, and every translation renders it simply as "Lydda." An interesting detail is that the Greek form varies in the manuscripts: it shows up both as the singular Λύδδα and as a plural form (Λύδδων in Acts 9:32, 35), and the genitive flips between Λύδδας and Λύδδης across copies.
caution: This is a proper place name with limited attestation (only 3 occurrences), and its grammatical form varies across manuscripts.

definition: To lay the foundation of something, or figuratively to make it firmly settled and secure.
article: θεμελιόω means to lay a foundation, used both literally for buildings or the earth (Hebrews 1:10) and figuratively for making something firmly established and stable. It appears just 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament but is far more common in the Septuagint (37×), where it usually renders the Hebrew יָסַד, "to found." Interestingly, an inscription preserves it in everyday Koine for founding an association (literally getting a gathering "established"), and the verb still survives in Modern Greek as θεμελιώνω.
caution: In 4 of its 6 New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word, so the measured senses rest on thin direct evidence.

definition: Harsh, unsparing treatment of oneself — severe self-denial or bodily discipline imposed without mercy.
article: This rare word describes unsparing severity, especially the kind of rigorous self-denial people impose on their own bodies. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Colossians 2:23, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "restrictions" (matching the Berean Standard Bible). It comes from a negative prefix joined to the verb "to spare," so it literally points to not sparing — and Moulton-Milligan confirm the related words show up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including phrases meaning "giving oneself unsparingly."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the exact shade is uncertain — lexicons range from "severity" to even "extravagance."

definition: Belonging to one's own house or family; close kin, family members, or those connected as if by household ties.
article: οἰκεῖος comes from οἶκος ("house") and basically means "of one's own house" — whether literal relatives or people bound together like family. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, each used a bit differently: the "household of faith" (Gal 6:10), "members of God's household" (Eph 2:19), and one's own relatives whom a person should provide for (1 Tim 5:8). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this family sense vividly, describing people as the οἰκεῖος of a named relative, and the Septuagint uses it 17 times to translate Hebrew words for kin and close relations.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, each rendered differently, the measured "senses" reflect varied contexts rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: Naphtali, a son of Jacob and the Israelite tribe descended from him that settled in northern Palestine.
article: Νεφθαλείμ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Naphtali, used both for Jacob's son and for the tribe descended from him. It is an indeclinable proper name, appearing only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 4:13 and Revelation 7:6), where it is rendered "Naphtali" 100% of the time. The Septuagint uses it far more often—61 times across 13 books—almost always translating Hebrew נַפְתָּלִי, though once each it stands in for two unrelated Hebrew words.
caution: This is a proper name with only two New Testament occurrences and none in the critical SBLGNT text, so the corpus evidence is thin.

definition: A net, especially the kind fishermen cast or drag through water to catch fish.
article: δίκτυον is the everyday word for a net, used in the New Testament almost exclusively for the fishing nets of Galilean fishermen — rendered "nets" in 10 of its 12 occurrences (83%). Abbott-Smith calls it the general term for a net, distinct from the more specialized ἀμφίβληστρον (a casting-net) and σαγήνη (a dragnet). In the Septuagint it covers several Hebrew words, most often רֶשֶׁת (9×), and it appears widely in ordinary Koine documents; a Christian epitaph from Aegina even uses it figuratively, picturing the dead as having escaped the "grievous nets" of sin, and the word still survives in Modern Greek as δίχτυ.

definition: Herod, the family name of several Jewish rulers in the New Testament era, including Herod the Great and Herod Antipas.
article: Ἡρώδης is a proper name, rendered "Herod" in 36 of its 44 Byzantine occurrences (88%), with the BSB independently agreeing 97% of the time. The lexicons note it covers several distinct rulers—Herod the Great, Herod Antipas, and Herod Agrippa I—so context decides which man is meant. The handful of "When" or "time" renderings (2×, plus a few rare ones) aren't a separate meaning of the name; they come from English phrasing like "when Herod's birthday came," where the translation reshapes the clause. Interestingly, the name also turns up in everyday Koine papyri attached to ordinary people—a ship-master and a weaver—so it wasn't reserved for royalty.

definition: Describing a person who does what is good and acts rightly.
article: ἀγαθοποιός is an adjective meaning someone who does good or acts rightly, formed from the words for "good" (ἀγαθός) and "to do" (ποιέω). In the New Testament it appears only once, in 1 Peter 2:14, where the Berean and Majority renderings both treat it as "those" who do well. Interestingly, the word also had a life outside the Bible: papyri of the 4th century AD use it as an astrological term for stars of benign or favorable influence, and the Septuagint uses it in Sirach 42:14 of a woman who acts pleasantly in order to corrupt.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: A connecting particle that introduces a reason, explanation, or confirmation for what was just said — roughly "for" or "because."
article: γάρ is one of the most common little words in the New Testament, appearing 1,062 times, and it works to link a statement to its reason or explanation. Most of the time (80%) it lands as "for," with "because" capturing the same causal idea more explicitly; the many odd-looking labels like "for is" or "is" simply reflect how the particle gets folded into surrounding English phrasing — in fact it's absorbed with no word of its own 260 times. In the Septuagint it most often stands in for Hebrew כִּי (483 times), the all-purpose word for "for/because," and Moulton-Milligan shows it doing the same explanatory work in everyday papyri, as in a letter where a writer says "for, what's more, his father is employed here."

definition: A city in the Lycus valley of Roman Asia Minor, near Colossae and Hierapolis.
article: Λαοδίκεια is simply the name of a city, Laodicea, located on the Lycus river in Phrygia within the Roman province of Asia, close to Colossae and Hierapolis. It appears 6 times across 2 New Testament books, and translators render it "Laodicea" in every case (the single odd reading counted at 17% is a measurement artifact, not a real second meaning). The name derives from a compound of λαός (people) and δίκη (justice or judgment), though it functions purely as a place name in the text.
caution: The digest lists a second "sense" at 17%, but this reflects a tagging quirk rather than any genuine difference in meaning.

definition: To weave or entwine something together, used figuratively for getting tangled up or caught in affairs you cannot easily escape.
article: ἐμπλέκω literally means to weave or twist things together, and in its two New Testament appearances it always carries the figurative sense of being tangled in something. The Majority Standard Bible splits its two occurrences evenly: in 2 Timothy 2:4 a soldier "refrains" from civilian affairs, and in 2 Peter 2:20 people become "entangled" again in the world's corruption. The papyri show the word's vivid everyday color: one second-century BC document uses it of a man and his wife who "closed with" the writer and beat him, so the picture is one of being physically grappled and held fast.
caution: Only 2 occurrences in the Byzantine NT and none in the critical text, so this entry rests on thin evidence.

definition: Ink, the black writing fluid used for letters and documents.
article: μέλαν is simply the word for ink, the black substance used for writing letters. It appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament and is rendered "ink" in every single one (2 Corinthians 3:3; 2 John 12; 3 John 13). The word is actually the neuter form of μέλας, "black" — so it literally means "the black stuff," which Abbott-Smith notes stands opposite λευκός ("white") elsewhere; in the Septuagint the related adjective translates the Hebrew shachor ("black").
caution: This is a low-confidence tier word due to its rarity, but its meaning as "ink" is consistent across all occurrences and sources.

definition: The office, duty, or active service of being a priest.
article: ἱερατεία refers to the priesthood understood as the actual office and service of a priest. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Luke 1:9 and Hebrews 7:5) and 15 times in the Septuagint, where it usually translates the Hebrew word for priesthood, כְּהֻנָּה. Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions use it for the working service of a priest — as distinct from the more abstract ἱερωσύνη — though they add that this distinction often blurs in practice.
caution: The MSB rendering of "descended" at Hebrews 7:5 reflects phrasing in that one verse rather than the word's core meaning, and with only two NT occurrences the measured data is thin.

definition: To feel intensely about someone or something—whether burning with eager desire and zeal, or burning with envy and jealousy.
article: ζηλόω describes strong, hot feeling that can run in two directions: positively as eager desire or zeal for something good, and negatively as envy or jealousy. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "zealous" in 3 of its 11 New Testament occurrences, with the BSB agreeing 100% and the KJV also listing it; in another 3 cases it disappears into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. In the Septuagint it appears 31 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew קָנָא (24×), the verb behind both "be jealous" and "be zealous," and the everyday papyri show the same range—one second-century text reads "for he is eager for learning."
caution: With only 11 New Testament occurrences and "zealous" covering just 38% of them, the word's full swing between eager desire and outright jealousy depends heavily on context.

definition: A vessel for burning frankincense, that is, a censer used to offer incense.
article: In the New Testament λιβανωτός means a censer—a container for burning incense—appearing only twice, both in Revelation 8 (verses 3 and 5), once as a censer used to offer incense and once as one hurled to the earth. This sense is actually a later Greek development: in classical Greek and the Septuagint the word normally meant frankincense itself, the gum of the libanus tree, and its single Septuagint use translates the Hebrew word for spices or sweet incense. A fun detail from the papyri: a medical prescription from Oxyrhynchus tells you to dilute frankincense in sweet wine and syringe it into the ear.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and lexicographers noting a possible confusion between "frankincense" and "censer," the censer sense rests on thin evidence.

definition: To make someone glad or, more often in the passive, to rejoice, celebrate, and make merry, especially at a feast.
article: εὐφραίνω means to gladden someone, but it usually appears in the passive—to be happy, rejoice, or celebrate. Across its 14 New Testament uses it leans toward festive joy: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "celebrate" 4 times (33%), notably in the parable of the prodigal son's homecoming feast (Luke 15:23–24, 29). The festive flavor is confirmed outside the Bible: a 2nd-century AD papyrus from the Fayum has a writer borrowing wine for a local festival so the group can "make merry," and in the Septuagint the word appears 204 times, most often translating the Hebrew שָׂמַח ("rejoice," 80×).

definition: To buy or purchase something, paying a price for it.
article: ὠνέομαι means to buy or purchase, paying a price for something. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 7:16, where it describes the purchase of a tomb. One interesting note from Abbott-Smith: the form used here (ὠνήσατο) replaced the classical equivalent ἐπρίατο, showing how the Koine vocabulary had shifted by this period.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range is too thin to map confidently; the rendering 'Shechem' reflects the proper name in the verse, not the verb's own meaning of 'buy'.

definition: The genitive form of the pronoun "I," meaning "of me," "my," or "mine."
article: This is simply the unemphatic genitive form of the first-person pronoun ἐγώ ("I"), meaning "of me" or "my." It attaches to nouns, adjectives, verbs, and prepositions where no special emphasis is intended, as in "my words" (Matthew 7:24) or "after me" (Matthew 3:11). It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament count here, but it shows up about 4,101 times across 37 books of the Septuagint, where it translates a wide spread of Hebrew words including "I" (266×), "lord" (183×), "soul/life" (151×), and "name" (93×). When emphasis is needed, the fuller form ἐμοῦ is used instead.
caution: This is a grammatical pronoun form rather than a content word, so its "meaning" is structural; the Hebrew counterparts vary widely depending on the noun it modifies.

definition: An adverb meaning by necessity or as a binding requirement; something that is compulsory or must be done.
article: ἐπάναγκες is an adverb built from ἐπί and ἀνάγκη ("necessity") that means "of necessity" or "it is compulsory." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 15:28, where it introduces the requirements laid on Gentile believers. Everyday Koine papyri use the word in legal contexts—for example a contract stating that anyone breaking the agreement is compelled to pay a fine—which fits its sense of a binding obligation.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the rendering "seemed" reflects the surrounding phrasing rather than the word's own meaning of "necessarily," so its precise force here is hard to pin down from the NT alone.

definition: An arrangement, ordinance, or order put in place by a recognized authority.
article: διαταγή refers to something formally arranged or commanded by an authority — an ordinance or institution. It appears only twice in the New Testament, where it covers both the law "ordained" through angels (Acts 7:53) and the governing "ordinance" of God that one must not resist (Romans 13:2). Grimm once claimed this was a purely biblical and church word, but Deissmann overturned that: the papyri show it in ordinary commercial life, such as an order for the payment of wine (P Oxy I.92) and an arrangement for a grape harvest (P Fay 133).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and the lexicons themselves debate the exact sense in Acts 7:53.

definition: A judgment of guilt and the punishment that follows—an adverse verdict against someone.
article: This noun comes from the verb "to condemn" (κατακρίνω) and names the sentence handed down against a guilty party, including the penalty that comes with it. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Paul's letter to the Romans (5:16, 5:18, 8:1), and the Majority Standard Bible renders every occurrence as "condemnation." The most interesting evidence is from everyday Koine papyri: Deissmann found the word used technically for a burden or servitude attached to a piece of land by a judicial ruling, suggesting it could carry the sense of a real, enforceable penalty rather than just a verdict.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 occurrences, all in one book—and the lexicons differ on whether it means "condemnation" (the verdict) or "penalty/punishment" (its consequence).

definition: Foolish, silly talk; the kind of empty or buffoonish speech that has no good purpose.
article: μωρολογία combines the words for "foolish" (μωρός) and "speak" (λέγω), so it literally means silly or foolish talking. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 5:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "obscenity," though older glosses like the KJV and Strong's lean toward "foolish talking" or "buffoonery." Interestingly, the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and in Plutarch, who pairs it with drinking — noting that it is foolish chatter, not the wine itself, that turns tipsiness into real drunkenness.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lexicons' "foolish talking" differs in tone from the MSB's stronger "obscenity," so the precise force is uncertain.

definition: To be more than enough—to overflow, abound, excel, or have plenty.
article: περισσεύω is about going beyond what is merely sufficient—whether something overflows, is abundant, surpasses others, or remains left over. Its range is wide: of the 39 New Testament occurrences, the Berean Standard Bible renders it "overflow" 7 times (29%), "abound" 5 times, and "excel" 4 times, with 15 cases woven so tightly into the phrasing that no single English word carries it. It can be intransitive (something abounds) or transitive (causing something to abound), and Moulton-Milligan note the plain sense "remain over" in everyday Koine papyri—including a 2nd-century BC inscription about whatever surplus is "left over from the interest."

definition: Describing someone who loves their brothers or fellow believers with warm, family-like affection.
article: φιλάδελφος literally means "loving one's brother" and describes the warm affection family members share, here applied to how Christians should treat one another. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 3:8, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sympathetic" while the underlying sense is loving fellow believers as siblings. A striking detail comes from the papyri: the word turns up on a first-century tomb inscription bidding farewell to a beloved actual brother ("Eision, brother-loving, good man, farewell"), showing it was everyday language for family devotion before it described the church.

definition: Thick darkness or gloom, especially the kind that comes with a storm cloud.
article: γνόφος means deep darkness or gloom, often the heavy blackness associated with a storm. It appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 12:18), where it blends into the phrasing rather than getting its own English word, but it is far more common in the Septuagint, showing up 26 times across 15 books. There it usually translates the Hebrew עֲרָפֶל (11×), the dark cloud of God's presence, and a papyrus citation from Vettius Valens pairs it directly with storm winds — "unsettled winds arise, and gloom."
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin (a single occurrence absorbed into a phrase), so the precise shade of meaning there leans on Septuagint and classical usage.

definition: A small particle that signals a conclusion or inference, much like saying "then," "so," or "therefore."
article: ἄρα is an inferential particle—a little connecting word that draws a conclusion from what came before, best translated "then," "so," or "therefore." It appears 34 times in the Byzantine New Testament, most often (43%) rendered "then," and Abbott-Smith notes it expresses a more subjective or informal inference than the heavier οὖν. Because it does so much of its work in the structure of a sentence, it slips into the phrasing without its own English word in 6 of its 34 occurrences. Worth noting: this word does not appear at all in the SBLGNT critical text, so its 34 Byzantine occurrences reflect a textual difference between manuscript traditions.
caution: Because it has no occurrences in the critical text and frequently dissolves into phrasing rather than a single English word, its exact force in any given verse can be uncertain.
