definition: A month, the roughly thirty-day period originally tied to the cycle of the moon.
article: μήν simply means a month, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: in the Byzantine New Testament it appears 18 times and is rendered "months" in 13 of them (81%), while the rest are just absorbed into phrasing. The Septuagint uses it heavily—262 times—mostly translating the Hebrew word for month (חֹדֶשׁ, 236×). One nice detail: in Galatians 4:10 the plural points to observing the new-moon festivals, and everyday papyri show the same word marking calendar dates and monthly interest payments in ordinary business.

definition: Moral filth or dirtiness — the kind of pollution or vileness that needs to be cleaned away.
article: ῥυπαρία means filthiness, and in its single New Testament appearance (James 1:21) it is used metaphorically for moral defilement, rendered "filth" in 100% of cases. The word comes from ῥυπαρός (dirty) and shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; one document even uses it of the impurity washed away in baptism. Interestingly, Plutarch applies the word to avarice — much like the English "shabbiness" — suggesting it could describe a debased or cheapened moral character.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on a single example.

definition: As an adverb, meaning given freely, without payment or earning—and occasionally without cause or in vain.
article: δωρεάν is the accusative of the noun δωρεά ("gift") used as an adverb, and it appears 9 times in the New Testament. The measured sense is "freely" or "as a free gift" (5 of 9 times, 56%), describing something given or received without payment, as in "freely you received, freely give" (Matthew 10:8) and being "justified freely" (Romans 3:24). The Septuagint uses it 13 times, most often translating the Hebrew חִנָּם (8×), the same word that can mean both "for free" and "without cause"—which explains the secondary sense "in vain" or "without a cause" noted by lexicons in passages like John 15:25 and Galatians 2:21.
caution: The word carries two distinct senses—"freely/as a gift" and "in vain/without cause"—so context determines which is meant.

definition: To discuss something back and forth, often as a debate, dispute, or joint inquiry between people.
article: συζητέω describes people talking something over together — sometimes as friendly discussion, sometimes as sharp dispute or arguing. It appears 10 times in the New Testament across 3 books, often built into phrases rather than rendered by a single English word (5 of 10 times). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this range vividly: one second-century document has a man asking another to come "dispute with you about it," and another speaks of "much discussion and complication" with men who took a donkey. The earlier classical sense of "search or examine together" lies behind it, but in the New Testament the meaning settles on discussing or debating.

definition: A spirit of cheerfulness and gladness, especially the glad readiness with which one gives or shows mercy.
article: ἱλαρότης describes a cheerful, glad disposition, and in its single New Testament appearance (Romans 12:8) it points to the cheerfulness with which acts of mercy should be done. The word is rare—just once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint—but it was at home in everyday Koine, with related forms turning up in papyri and inscriptions alongside words for joy and laughter (one document pairs it with 'all joy and gladness'). Note that the measured rendering 'let' simply reflects how the surrounding sentence was translated; the core idea consistently captured by the lexicons is 'cheerfulness.'
caution: Evidence is thin—only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use—so its precise range cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: Satan, the adversary or accuser—the chief opponent of God and his people.
article: Σατανᾶς is a Greek form of an Aramaic word meaning "the adversary" or "accuser," used in the New Testament as a name for the devil. It appears 36 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "Satan" in 86% of cases; the remaining occurrences come in rebukes like "Get behind me, Satan," where it is the same name addressed to a person. A striking detail: a third-century magical papyrus invokes Jesus to drive out "this unclean demon of Satan," showing the word's reach into everyday Koine usage beyond the Bible.

definition: To cool or grow cold; in its one New Testament use, figuratively, of love losing its warmth.
article: At its root ψύχω means to breathe gently and so to cool something down, distinct from forceful blowing. The Septuagint uses it 6 times across 4 books, translating two Hebrew words, and everyday papyri show the active sense plainly—one third-century BC document uses it of 'drying the foundation' in building work. In its single New Testament appearance (Matthew 24:12) it is passive and metaphorical, describing how love will 'grow cold,' which is how the Majority Standard Bible renders it 100% of the time.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the SBL critical text), so its New Testament range rests on a single figurative occurrence.

definition: To wash off or wash away completely, used figuratively of cleansing oneself from sins.
article: ἀπολούω literally means to wash something off, but in the New Testament it appears only in the middle voice with a figurative sense of cleansing oneself from sin. It occurs just twice in the Byzantine text—once of having sins washed away (Acts 22:16) and once of believers who 'were washed' clean (1 Corinthians 6:11)—and is absent from the critical SBLGNT. Notably, its single Septuagint appearance (Job 9:30) translates the Hebrew for washing with snow-water, preserving the plain physical meaning that the NT then applies metaphorically.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 Byzantine occurrences, none in the critical text, and a single Septuagint instance, so confidence is low.

definition: Lacking water; dry, barren, or arid — used of places, springs, or clouds that hold no water.
article: Ἄνυδρος literally means "waterless," built from the negative prefix and the word for water (ὕδωρ). In the New Testament's 4 occurrences it describes different dry things: arid places where unclean spirits wander (Matthew 12:43, Luke 11:24), springs without water (2 Peter 2:17), and rainless clouds (Jude 12). The Septuagint uses it 22 times, often rendering Hebrew words for parched land or desert (צִיָּה, יְשִׁימוֹן), and everyday papyri use it for "waterless deserts" and land too dry to farm.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences across 3 distinct applications, the apparent "senses" are really one meaning—waterless—applied to places, springs, and clouds.

definition: To comfort, console, or encourage someone, especially a person who is grieving or in distress.
article: This verb means to comfort or console, often someone who is mourning, and can also shade toward encouraging or urging someone on. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, twice in the story of Lazarus where people come to console Martha and Mary in their grief (John 11:19, 11:31), and in Paul's letters about caring for fellow believers (1 Thessalonians 2:11). An everyday papyrus letter captures the sense perfectly: a servant writes that the household is "comforting her by hourly expecting your arrival" while their mistress lies ill.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and a range running from "console" to "encourage," the precise force in any given verse can be hard to pin down.

definition: Describing things that are necessary or suitable, especially the basic supplies and provisions needed for daily living.
article: This adjective describes what is fitting, useful, or necessary, and in its plural form (τὰ ἐπιτήδεια) it means "the necessities of life." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in James 2:16, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as the "physical" things a needy person requires. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: documents speak of making payments "for necessaries" and furnishing provisions and supplies, even for huntsmen, showing the word was common business language for basic goods.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint match, the measured evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: Elisha, the Old Testament prophet who succeeded Elijah in Israel.
article: Ἐλισσαῖος is the Greek form of the Hebrew name אֱלִישָׁע (Elisha), the prophet who followed Elijah. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 4:27, where Jesus recalls how only Naaman the Syrian was cleansed of leprosy in Elisha's day. Note the data oddity: the measured rendering shows up as "Syrian" 100% of the time, which reflects the surrounding phrase about Naaman rather than the name itself, since lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree the word simply means Elisha.
caution: This is a proper name attested only once in the New Testament, and the measured "Syrian" rendering comes from neighboring words rather than the name, so treat the sense data cautiously.

definition: To rise up together against someone, making a concerted attack or hostile move.
article: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 18:12, where a crowd rose up together against Paul and brought him before the proconsul. The lexicons agree on its meaning: to make an assault or insurrection against someone, built from κατά and ἐφίστημι, the latter meaning to stand over or come upon. Notably, the measured rendering label here reads "proconsul," which reflects a quirk in how the surrounding verse was tagged rather than the verb's own sense — the word itself describes the rising-up action, not the official.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be confirmed from usage, and the measured "proconsul" label appears to be a tagging artifact rather than the verb's actual meaning.

definition: A negative connecting word that links items in a list, meaning "neither...nor" or "and not."
article: μήτε is a negative connector used to tie together items being denied, typically in the pattern "neither...nor" (as in Matthew 5:34-36, where one swears neither by heaven nor by earth). The Majority Standard Bible most often renders it simply "or" (10×, 38%) within these chained negations, with "nor" and "neither" also common. Abbott-Smith notes it differs from οὔτε the same way μή differs from οὐ — a softer or more conditional kind of negation. About 10 of its 36 occurrences get absorbed into the surrounding phrasing without a distinct English word of its own.

definition: Deep darkness or gloom, the kind of thick blackness associated with a place of punishment.
article: ζόφος refers to deep, murky darkness or gloom, and in the New Testament it consistently describes the blackness held in store as judgment. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine text (5 in the critical SBLGNT), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as plain "darkness" in half its occurrences (as in 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6) and as "blackest darkness reserved" in the other half (2 Peter 2:17, Jude 13). Interestingly, the word began as a poetic term—in Homer it named the gloom of the underworld—but Moulton-Milligan note it later passed into everyday Koine speech, and it even survives in Modern Greek as ζοφός, "dark."
caution: With only 4 occurrences, all in similar contexts of judgment, the evidence base is thin.

definition: A violent windstorm or whirlwind, the kind of raging tempest that brings darkness and terror.
article: θύελλα refers to a furious windstorm — a hurricane, cyclone, or whirlwind. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:18, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "blackness" rather than a storm word, reflecting how it describes the dark, terrifying scene at Mount Sinai. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it twice translates the Hebrew עֲרָפֶל, a word for thick darkness or gloom, which helps explain why the storm here is bound up with imagery of impenetrable blackness.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the standard storm-related glosses sit oddly beside the "blackness" rendering, so its precise force here is uncertain.

definition: A rotating division or shift of priests assigned to serve in the Temple for a set period.
article: In the New Testament ἐφημερία refers to one of the rotating divisions of Jewish priests who took turns serving in the Temple, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "division" in both of its two occurrences (Luke 1:5, 1:8). The word is built from ἐφήμερος ("daily"), reflecting the idea of a daily or scheduled rotation of duty. In the Septuagint it appears 21 times, most often translating the Hebrew מַחֲלֹקֶת ("division"), and Abbott-Smith notes it can mean both the course of daily services and the class of priests detailed for that service.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, this entry rests on limited evidence.

definition: To gather or be present together with others, sometimes implying coming to someone's aid or support.
article: This compound verb stacks σύν ('with') onto παραγίνομαι ('to arrive'), so its core idea is people showing up together. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament: once of the crowd assembling for the spectacle of the crucifixion (Luke 23:48), and once of supporters standing by someone in need (2 Timothy 4:16, where critical texts read a different word). Moulton-Milligan found it in everyday Koine, including a papyrus from around 257 B.C. where people 'asked him to come along with' them.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences, one of which (2 Timothy 4:16) drops out of the critical text, leaving a single firmly attested use.

definition: An adverb pointing back to a place, source, or cause—'from where,' or, when reasoning, 'therefore' or 'for which reason.'
article: ὅθεν is a flexible little connector that can mean 'from where' (pointing to a place or source) or 'therefore' (pointing to a cause or conclusion). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times across 5 books, and in 11 of those cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word; where it is rendered, the Majority Standard Bible uses 'since' twice. A vivid papyrus example survives in a traveler's letter (P Lond 854) describing the spot 'from where the Nile flows out,' showing the everyday spatial sense alongside the inferential 'wherefore' used in passages like Hebrews 2:17.
caution: Because the word is so often absorbed into phrasing, only a small slice of its occurrences yields a measured English rendering, so the sense breakdown rests on limited data.

definition: The visible gray cloud given off by fire or burning material.
article: Καπνός simply means smoke, the cloud produced by burning. Its meaning is remarkably stable: all 13 New Testament occurrences refer to smoke, and the two measured senses differ only in phrasing ('smoke' 54% versus 'smoke rose' 46%) rather than in actual meaning. In the Septuagint it almost always renders the Hebrew word עָשָׁן (20 of 24 times), and the word still survives in Modern Greek today.

definition: A particular point or stretch of time, often the right or appointed moment for something to happen.
senseLabels: a point or period of time
article: καιρός refers to time in the sense of a specific moment, period, or appointed occasion, rather than time as a flowing quantity. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "time" in 92% of its 86 occurrences and "seasons" in another 6%, with classical lexicons adding the nuance of fitting opportunity or seasonable time. The everyday papyri make this opportunity-sense vivid: one document describes a woman who "seized a favorable opportunity" (καιρὸν εὑροῦσα) to burst into a house and carry off a child. In the Septuagint it appears 309 times, most often translating the Hebrew עֵת ("time," 192×).

definition: To act with wary caution, fearing or being anxious about something; sometimes to treat with religious reverence.
article: This middle-voice verb covers a range from being cautious and wary to feeling afraid, and in religious contexts shading into reverence. The New Testament uses are slim and even disputed: in Acts 23:10 the Majority text renders it "afraid," while the critical text (SBLGNT, WH, RV) reads a different word (φοβηθείς) there entirely. Everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth sense of being wary of someone, as in a letter where a writer says "I am cautious of the magistrate." In the Septuagint it appears 21 times and most often translates the Hebrew חָסָה, "to take refuge."
caution: Very thin evidence: the Byzantine text has only 2 occurrences (one absorbed into phrasing), and the critical text disputes whether the word even stands in Acts 23:10.

definition: To feast or revel together with others at a shared, lavish meal.
article: This verb describes joining others in a sumptuous shared meal or banquet, almost always in the middle or passive form. Its range is narrow: in both of its two New Testament appearances (2 Peter 2:13 and Jude 12), it is rendered "feast," and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100%. A nice everyday confirmation comes from the papyri: a letter from AD 84 (BGU II.596) uses the same word in an invitation, "you are also invited to come down and feast along with us."
caution: This word appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament and zero times in the critical text, so its biblical evidence is thin.

definition: Describing something with a keen cutting edge, or by extension moving quickly and eagerly.
article: ὀξύς basically means "sharp" or "keen," like a blade with a fine cutting edge, and the Byzantine NT uses it this way 6 of 8 times (75%)—often of the sharp sword in Revelation. By extension it can describe swift motion, as in Romans 3:15 ("swift to shed blood"), where the Septuagint background lies behind the imagery. A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri: a 4th-century Egyptian document uses ὀξύς of the "express-post," the fast horse-relay mail service, showing how naturally Greek speakers stretched "sharp" into "speedy."
caution: The word is uncommon (only 8 NT uses) and carries two distinct senses—"sharp" and "swift"—so context, not the word alone, decides which is meant.

definition: Having two cutting edges, used to describe a sword sharpened on both sides.
article: δίστομος literally means "two-mouthed," but in the New Testament it always describes a sword with two cutting edges, appearing 4 times across Hebrews and Revelation. The word's root sense is striking: a sword's edge is pictured as a "mouth" that consumes, which is why Dodson notes the image of a blade as a "drinker of blood." Beyond swords, the classical lexicon Abbott-Smith records a separate sense for rivers and roads that are "double-branching," though that meaning never surfaces in the biblical text; a Koine papyrus magical text even refers to an all-iron double-edged dagger.
caution: The two measured senses ("double edged" and "held double edged") reflect translation phrasing rather than a real difference in meaning—the word simply means two-edged in every New Testament occurrence.

definition: To stay or remain close by, continuing alongside someone or persisting in something over time.
article: παραμένω combines παρά ("beside") with μένω ("remain"), so its core idea is staying near or continuing on. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, rendered by the Majority Standard Bible as "stay" (as in 1 Corinthians 16:6) and, in Hebrews 7:23, as part of the phrase describing priests prevented from continuing in "office." The everyday papyri make the personal sense vivid: one fourth-century letter asks someone to "stay with me until I know the position of my affairs."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the evidence base is thin, so the measured senses are illustrative rather than a full map of its range.

definition: Canaan, the ancient name for the land of Palestine, especially the region west of the Jordan River.
article: Χαναάν is the early name for the land of Palestine, transliterated straight from the Hebrew כְּנַעַן. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both in Acts (7:11 and 13:19), each time rendered "Canaan." It shows up far more often in the Septuagint—98 times across 13 books—where it usually translates that Hebrew word but occasionally stands in for other place-related terms like מַמְרֵא (Mamre) and מוֹשָׁב (dwelling).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences this is thin evidence, though as a place name its meaning is not in doubt.

definition: An overflowing amount of something — more than enough, a surplus or abundance.
article: Περισσεία means an overflow or surplus — having more of something than is needed, whether grace, joy, or wickedness. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, and the Septuagint uses it 12 times (all in Ecclesiastes) to render the Hebrew word for "profit" or "gain" (יִתְרוֹן). A nice detail from everyday papyri and inscriptions: one inscription describes a games official who handed over to the city "the whole surplus" (περισσεία) of the money belonging to the presidents — showing the word's plain commercial sense of leftover funds.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and each rendered differently, the measured "senses" mostly reflect varied English phrasing of one core idea rather than distinct meanings.

definition: Foolishness or absurdity — the quality of being silly or lacking sense.
article: This word names the state of being foolish or absurd. In the New Testament it appears only 5 times, all in 1 Corinthians, and every occurrence is rendered "foolishness." It's rare elsewhere too — the only Septuagint instance is in Sirach 20:31 — so its range is narrow and consistent. It derives from μωρός, the adjective for "foolish."
caution: Evidence outside Paul's letters is thin, with just one Septuagint occurrence, so the word's broader range is hard to map.

definition: The number eleven, often used in the New Testament for the group of eleven apostles after Judas's departure.
article: ἕνδεκα simply means the number eleven, formed from the words for "one" and "ten," and it never changes its form. In the New Testament it appears 6 times, almost always as a shorthand for "the Eleven" — the apostles remaining after Judas left, as in Matthew 28:16 and Acts 1:26. The everyday, non-biblical reach of the word shows up in the papyri: it appears on an ostracon receipt from A.D. 79 recording a poll-tax payment, written simply as the numeral.

definition: To press in on someone from all sides, as a crowd squeezes against a person.
article: συνθλίβω means to crowd or press in on a person from all sides, picturing the squeeze of a packed throng. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Mark chapter 5, describing the crowd pressing against Jesus, and the King James simply renders it "throng." Outside the New Testament it shows up rarely in the Septuagint and related texts, and in Ecclesiastes 12:6 it translates a Hebrew word for being crushed or broken.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and thin wider attestation, confidence in the full range of this word is low.

definition: A load or burden someone carries, including a ship's cargo, and figuratively a task or responsibility laid on a person.
article: φορtίον is a diminutive of φόρtος and refers to something carried — a load, burden, or the freight of a ship. In the New Testament's 6 occurrences it ranges from literal cargo (Acts 27:10) to figurative burdens of responsibility, as when Jesus speaks of his easy burden (Matthew 11:30) or the heavy loads experts pile on others (Luke 11:46). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: one second-century account lists "9 donkeys, 8 loads," and others record payments by boatmen for shipping their freights.
caution: With only 6 occurrences, several of the listed sense labels reflect single passages rather than broad, well-attested distinctions.

definition: A key — the device used to lock or unlock a door, lock, or gate, often used figuratively for the authority to grant or deny access.
article: κλείς simply means a key, the tool that shuts or opens a lock. In the New Testament it appears 6 times, and the so-called 'measured senses' here are really one literal meaning applied in several figurative settings: keys of the kingdom (Matthew 16:19), the key of knowledge (Luke 11:52), and keys of death, the abyss, and Hades in Revelation. Everyday papyri confirm the ordinary usage — one second-century letter (P Oxy I.113) reports sending someone an actual key, and an account from the third century B.C. even mentions paying a locksmith for keys.
caution: The labeled 'senses' beyond 'key' are really figurative phrasings of the same literal word, so treat them as contexts rather than distinct meanings.

definition: An axe — a sharp cutting tool used for chopping or felling wood.
article: ἀξίνη refers to a simple axe, the kind of everyday tool used to chop and fell trees. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in the same vivid image of an axe laid at the root of the trees ready to cut down what bears no good fruit (Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "axe" every time. The word was ordinary in daily Koine life: a papyrus from 218 B.C. even lists an axe priced at two drachmas alongside a harvesting sickle, and the Septuagint uses it for the Hebrew words for axe (קַרְדֹּם and גַּרְזֶן).
caution: The sense is clear and undisputed, but the New Testament evidence is thin, with only two occurrences, both in the same phrase.

definition: The Jewish Festival of Tabernacles, when people built temporary booths or tents to live in during the celebration.
article: This word names the Jewish Festival of Tabernacles, a major autumn feast; its single New Testament appearance (John 7:2) is rendered "Jewish Tabernacles" in every count. Literally it means the "setting up of tents," combining the words for tent and to fasten, which fits the custom of erecting booths during the festival. The Septuagint uses it five times, where it translates the Hebrew words for "to keep a feast" (3×) and "booth" (2×); interestingly, although some have thought Greek-speaking Jews coined the term, it actually already appears in Aristotle and in a Greek inscription reading "at the assembly of the Tabernacles."
caution: Confidence is low: this word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: A male goat, especially one used in animal sacrifices.
article: τράγος refers to a he-goat, and in the New Testament it appears only 4 times, all in Hebrews, where it describes the goats whose blood was used in sacrifice. The Septuagint uses it 30 times across 8 books, mainly translating the Hebrew word עַתּוּד (20×). It was also an ordinary word in everyday life: Koine papyri use it in mundane livestock records, such as a document listing "two kids, one he-goat," and even in reports of hunting goats.
caution: In Hebrews 9:19 it is rendered together with calves, so the count reflects how it appears in a list rather than a separate meaning.

definition: A prickly plant or thorn-bush, always mentioned in the plural in the New Testament.
article: This word names a thorn-bush or prickly plant, and in the New Testament it always appears in the plural. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "thorns" in 7 of its 14 occurrences (58%), and the BSB agrees 86% of the time; the variation in other renderings mostly comes from how the surrounding phrase is translated, as in "seed among thorns." Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri show a related sense: one document from Hadrian's time lists a couch made of acantha-wood, identified as the Egyptian acacia.

definition: To breathe out air onto or into someone or something.
article: This verb means to blow or breathe air at or onto a person or object. It appears just once in the New Testament, in John 20:22, where Jesus breathes on his disciples. The same word turns up in the Greek Old Testament six times, notably in Genesis 2:7 where God breathes life into the first human, and an everyday medical recipe in the papyri even uses it for blowing powdered hellebore into the nostrils to stop sneezing.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: A fig tree, the common Mediterranean tree that produces figs.
article: συκῆ simply means a fig tree, derived from σῦκον ("fig"). The meaning is remarkably stable: in all 16 Byzantine New Testament occurrences it refers to a fig tree, with no real variation in sense. In the Septuagint it appears 31 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew word for fig trees (27 of 31 times), and everyday Koine papyri confirm the word's ordinary use—one letter from 257 BC even urges someone to send along some fig-tree shoots.

definition: A title meaning "the baptizer," used in the New Testament only for John, who baptized people in preparation for Jesus.
article: Βαπτιστής literally means "one who baptizes," formed from the verb βαπτίζω ("to baptize"). In the New Testament it functions almost like a surname, applied solely to John, son of Zechariah—the forerunner of Jesus—appearing 14 times across 3 books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Baptist" in 10 of those occurrences (71%), and the lexicons agree it is used only of John.

definition: Caught in the very act of doing something wrong, with the crime witnessed as it happens.
article: This word describes catching someone red-handed, right as the wrongdoing is taking place. It comes from roots literally meaning "a thief caught in the act," and originally referred specifically to theft before broadening to any crime witnessed in progress. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 8:4, where the woman is said to be caught in the very act of adultery; notably it does not appear in the critical SBLGNT text at all.
caution: This is a one-time word found only in a passage that the critical text omits, and the spelling itself varies between manuscripts, so the evidence is thin.

definition: A piece of fine linen cloth, used either to wrap a dead body for burial or as a garment worn over the body.
article: σινδών is a fine linen cloth, and in the New Testament it appears most often as the wrapping used for a dead body — three of its six occurrences (50%) refer to the linen Jesus was buried in. Its range is fairly tight: besides the burial cloth, it can mean a linen garment or wrap, as in Mark 14:51-52 where a young man flees and leaves his σινδών behind. Notably, the everyday Koine papyri use the word constantly, including a description of one as καθαρά ("clean" or "pure"), the very word Matthew 27:59 uses of the burial linen.
caution: The word may be of Semitic or foreign origin, and scholars disagree on this point; in the Septuagint it consistently renders Hebrew sādîn.

definition: Cunning, calculated trickery — scheming aimed at deceiving or trapping someone.
article: In the New Testament μεθοδεία always carries the negative sense of scheming or craftiness, appearing just twice (Ephesians 4:14 and 6:11), both times rendered "scheming." The word is built from parts meaning "method" or "way of pursuing" something, and that more neutral root shows clearly in everyday papyri: a 5th-century document (P Oxy VIII.1134) uses it simply to mean a "method" of collecting rents. So the New Testament's deceptive sense is a sharpened, negative use of a word that elsewhere just meant a way of going about things.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and sources noting it appears nowhere else in early literature except later papyri, the evidence for its range is thin.

definition: Barnabas, the personal name of a Cypriot Jew and early Christian companion of Paul.
article: Barnabas is a proper name, the byname of Joseph, a Cypriot Jew who became an early Christian leader and traveling companion of Paul. It appears 29 times in the Byzantine New Testament and is rendered "Barnabas" in 79% of cases, with the rest simply pairing his name with others ("Barnabas along"), so there is essentially one meaning here. Acts 4:36 explains the name as "son of encouragement," but Deissmann argued from Syrian inscriptions that it actually derives from a Semitic name meaning "son of Nebo," a derivation accepted by later scholars like Dalman.

definition: To put up with someone's behavior or ways, patiently enduring their conduct over time.
senseLabels: to put up with someone's ways
article: This rare verb means to bear with or tolerate another person's behavior, and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:18, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as 'conduct.' It comes from τρόπος ('manner, way') and φορέω ('to bear'), and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and even in a letter of Cicero, where someone is asked to 'bear with my pride.' The most interesting wrinkle is a textual one: some manuscripts read a near-identical word, τροφοφορέω ('to bear like a nurse'), drawn from the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 1:31, so it's debated whether God endured Israel's ways or cared for them like a nurse.
caution: This is essentially a one-off word with disputed manuscript readings, since editors split between τροποφορέω ('bear their manners') and τροφοφορέω ('care like a nurse').

definition: A type of Roman soldier, probably a spearman or light-armed guard accompanying a military escort.
article: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:23, where it refers to a group of soldiers in a military escort and is rendered "spearmen." Its exact meaning is uncertain: formed from the words for "right hand" and "take," it likely describes a soldier carrying a weapon in his right hand, perhaps a spearman, slinger, or light-armed guard. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note it may have been coined to translate a Roman military title, and an ancient scholion explains the word as meaning "guards" or sentries.
caution: This is a one-time word (hapax) whose precise meaning is genuinely uncertain, and the sources offer several competing guesses.

definition: Reverence for God expressed through devout worship and a godly, pious life.
article: θεοσέβεια describes reverence for God shown in devout, godly living, and the single New Testament use in 1 Timothy 2:10 is rendered "worship." In the Septuagint it appears twice, both times translating the Hebrew word for "fear" (יִרְאָה), tying the idea closely to the fear or reverence of God. A striking detail from the papyri is that the word became a quasi-technical term for worship of the one true God and was even used as a polite Christian title—one fourth- or fifth-century letter addresses a recipient as "your holiness."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, so this entry rests on a very small sample.

definition: To change one's mind and turn away from sin, reconsidering one's whole inner direction toward God.
article: μετανοέω means literally to think differently or afterwards — to have a genuine change of mind that, in the New Testament, almost always involves turning from sin. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "repent" in 25 of 34 occurrences (86%), and apart from a couple of passages in Luke 17, it consistently refers to repentance from sin involving real amendment. In the Septuagint it usually stands in for the Hebrew נָחַם (14 of 19 times), and everyday papyri show the same sense: one second-century inscription speaks of seeing people "having repented over their former wrongs," strikingly close to Paul's language in 2 Corinthians 12:21.

definition: A hollow body cavity, used most often for the womb that carries a child or the stomach that digests food.
article: The literal core of κοιλία is a hollow part of the body, and in the New Testament it lands almost evenly on two meanings: the womb (7 times, 47%) and the stomach or belly (6 times, 40%). The Septuagint uses it heavily, 92 times, most often for the Hebrew בָּ֫טֶן ("belly," 38×) and מְעֵי ("inner parts," 24×). Everyday Koine papyri confirm its plain physical sense — one document describes a name written on the κοιλία of a dead body — and Abbott-Smith notes a rare figurative use for the inner self or heart in John 7:38.
caution: Eight of the 23 occurrences are absorbed into English phrasing without a word of their own, so the womb/stomach split reflects only the cases that were directly translated.

definition: A person who is foreign to Greek language and culture, especially someone whose speech sounds unintelligible.
article: βάρβαρος describes anyone outside Greek language and culture — a foreigner whose speech can't be understood. In its 6 New Testament uses it splits evenly: half the time the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "islanders" (the people of Malta in Acts 28), and half as "foreigner" (notably in 1 Corinthians 14:11, where the point is that unintelligible speech makes someone a foreigner to you). Abbott-Smith notes the word is probably onomatopoeic, imitating the unintelligible sounds of non-Greek speech, and that after the Persian war it picked up an added sense of "rude" or "brutal."
caution: With only 6 occurrences and the renderings split between "islanders" and "foreigner," the English wording is driven heavily by context rather than a fixed meaning.

definition: Cheerful, glad, and willingly glad rather than reluctant—as of someone who gives happily.
article: ἱλαρός describes a cheerful, glad disposition, especially one that acts gladly rather than grudgingly—Paul says God loves a "cheerful" giver in its single New Testament appearance (2 Corinthians 9:7). It appears 3 times in the Septuagint and shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where one writer says "I am cheerful about our safety." An interesting detail: Moulton-Milligan notes that in the magic papyri ἱλαρός was used almost interchangeably with its relative ἵλεως ("propitious, gracious"), reflecting its kinship with that word.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range here rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A common preposition that locates something within a place, time, or state, usually meaning "in," but also covering "on," "among," or "by."
article: ἐν is the workhorse preposition of the New Testament, appearing 2,786 times across all 27 books, and it overwhelmingly means "in" — 1,659 of its translated occurrences (98%). It marks position in space, time, or condition, but stretches to "with," "on," "by," and "among" depending on context. Notably, in 1,098 of those occurrences it carries no English word of its own, getting absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it is even more frequent (11,557 times) and stands in for the Hebrew prefix בְּ, including its pairing with words like "day" (524×) and "Jerusalem" (504×).
caution: Moulton-Milligan calls it the "maid-of-all-work" among prepositions whose extended uses cannot be exhaustively catalogued, so its precise force in any given verse often depends on context.

definition: To bring something powerful or wild under control by taming, subduing, or breaking its strength.
article: δαμάζω means to subdue or bring under control, whether taming wild animals, breaking the strength of chains, or restraining human behavior. In its 4 New Testament occurrences it leans toward 'tame' (half the time), but Mark 5:4 stretches it to describe how no one could 'shatter the strength' of the demon-possessed man. James 3:8 uses it figuratively for the tongue, which no one can tame; meanwhile the word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it was ordinary vocabulary, not a specialized term.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the measured senses largely reflect translation choices in a handful of verses rather than a broad, independently established range.

definition: The condition of being cold, especially chilly weather or low temperatures.
article: ψύχος simply means "cold" — the chill of cold weather or low temperature. All 3 New Testament occurrences are rendered "cold" (100%), as when people warmed themselves by a fire (John 18:18), the islanders kindled a fire because of rain and cold (Acts 28:2), and Paul listed cold among his hardships (2 Corinthians 11:27). The everyday Koine flavor shows up in the papyri, including a first-century acrostic that reads "for it is winter, much cold" (χιμών γάρ ἐστι, ψύχος πολύ).

definition: Fickleness or lightness of purpose—the inconsistency of someone who makes plans carelessly or cannot be relied upon.
article: This noun describes a kind of lightness of character—being fickle, unreliable, or wavering in one's decisions. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 1:17, where Paul asks whether he made his travel plans with such inconstancy. It derives from ἐλαφρός, meaning "light" in weight, so the figurative sense extends a physical lightness to a moral flightiness. Abbott-Smith notes the abstract form is found in the New Testament but not in earlier classical usage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be confirmed from biblical usage alone.

definition: A connecting word that introduces a purpose or result, showing why something is done or what it leads to.
article: ἵνα is one of the most common connecting words in the New Testament, appearing 670 times, and it normally introduces purpose or result—telling you why something happens or what it leads to. Its meaning is so flexible that it absorbs into English phrasing 230 of those 670 times, leaving no single word of its own; the rest spread across renderings like "so that" (104×), "so that may" (93×), and plain "that" (89×). In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew מָה (119×) and מַ֫עַן (99×), and Moulton-Milligan note from everyday papyri that even ordinary letter-writers used it so broadly that the exact shade of meaning is not always easy to pin down.
caution: Its sense is genuinely fluid—so much so that nearly a third of its uses carry no English word at all and even the everyday papyri make its precise shade hard to fix.

definition: Jorim, a man listed as one of Jesus' ancestors in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ἰωρείμ is simply a personal name, Jorim, appearing once in the New Testament as one of the ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:29). It is an indeclinable Hebrew name, and Strong's identifies the bearer as an Israelite. The form may be a variant of Ἰωράμ (Joram).
caution: This name occurs only once in the Byzantine NT and not at all in the critical text, so the evidence is very thin.

definition: To watch or observe someone closely, looking on at how they live and behave.
article: ἐποπτεύω means to watch or observe someone, keeping an eye on how they conduct themselves. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Peter (2:12 and 3:2), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "see" in every case. The word turns up in everyday Koine sources too: Moulton-Milligan cite a memorial inscription and an astrological text where it describes the sun "watching over," hinting at a sense of overseeing that the older lexicons (like Abbott-Smith's note on Homer) also record.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in one book, the measured evidence is thin, so the fuller "oversee/inspect" range comes from outside sources rather than New Testament usage.

definition: In a kind, warmly friendly manner, treating someone with hospitable courtesy.
article: This adverb describes treating someone kindly and warmly, the way a gracious host welcomes guests. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 28:7, and is rare in the Septuagint as well (just 2 Maccabees 3:9 and 4 Maccabees 8:5). Everyday Koine papyri show it as a stock courtesy phrase—one letter from 103 B.C. instructs the writer to "greet you warmly (philophrónōs) on our behalf."
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "Nearby" conflicts with every lexicon, which agree the sense is "kindly" or "in a friendly manner."

definition: Sarah, the wife of Abraham, named as a model of faith and a mother in Israel's story.
article: Σάῤῥα is simply the proper name Sarah, Abraham's wife, transliterated from the Hebrew שָׂרָה. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament and 37 times in the Septuagint, always rendering that one Hebrew name. The two 'measured senses' above are really the same name — the '"Sarah what"' entry in 1 Peter 3:6 just reflects how she is mentioned alongside other words there. Interestingly, the name turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, including documents where men are identified as the son of a mother named Sarah.
caution: The name is straightforward, but note that Hebrews 11:11 has been suggested to be a marginal interpolation, which could affect whether Sarah is the verse's subject.

definition: To execute someone by nailing or fixing them to a cross, the Roman method of death.
article: σταυρόω overwhelmingly means "to crucify," rendered that way in 44 of its 46 New Testament appearances (96%). The word's earliest sense, preserved in the papyri and classical Greek, was actually "to fence with pales" or build a palisade—one sixth-century papyrus still uses it of a room shut off with laths. The crucifixion meaning is the later development, and Paul stretches it figuratively to speak of believers having "crucified" their passions (Galatians 5:24; 6:14).

definition: To foam or froth at the mouth, as during a convulsive seizure.
article: ἀφρίζω means to foam or froth at the mouth, and in both its New Testament appearances it describes someone in the grip of a violent convulsion. The word comes from ἀφρός, the noun for foam, and shows up only twice — both in Mark chapter 9, describing a boy who falls down foaming. The two measured renderings are really one sense viewed up close: the act of foaming and the picture of someone collapsing with a foaming mouth.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in a single passage of Mark, the evidence is thin, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: A lack of understanding or sense — foolishness, sometimes flaring into furious, mindless rage.
article: ἄνοια describes the condition of being without understanding, ranging from plain folly to anger so intense it overrides reason. It appears only twice in the New Testament and 5 times in the Septuagint, where it mostly renders the Hebrew word for 'folly' (אִוֶּלֶת, twice). Notably, in Luke 6:11 the scribes and Pharisees are 'filled with ἄνοια' — and Abbott-Smith, citing Plato, reads this as folly that boils over into violent rage rather than mere foolishness.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the measured-sense data showing odd labeling, the precise shade between 'foolishness' and 'rage' in any given passage is uncertain.

definition: To speak to or converse with someone.
article: προσλαλέω simply means to speak or talk to someone, often with a sense of conversing with them. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 13:43 and Acts 28:20), and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. A vivid classical example comes from Theophrastus, where a talkative man is described "chattering at this rate to the trainers and masters," capturing the conversational flavor of the word.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin and the precise nuance in each passage is uncertain.

definition: In a way that never stops or lets up; doing something continually and without interruption.
article: This adverb means doing something steadily and without interruption — Paul uses it for praying, remembering, and giving thanks. All four New Testament occurrences point to the same idea: an action that keeps going without a break, which the Majority Standard Bible renders with phrases like "without ceasing" and "continually." The word also turns up in the Septuagint (1 and 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees), so it was at home in Greek-speaking Jewish writing of the period.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, the varied English renderings reflect translators smoothing the surrounding sentence rather than different meanings of the word itself.

definition: Adultery — voluntary sexual unfaithfulness by a married person.
article: μοιχεία means adultery, sexual unfaithfulness within marriage, and that single sense is consistent across every source. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often in lists of sins (Matthew 15:19, Mark 7:21), where Greek sometimes uses the plural form. An astrological papyrus (P. Tebtunis II.276) even pairs it with fornication, listing both as effects when Venus meets Mars, showing the word was at home in everyday Koine.
caution: The apparent extra senses ('adultery theft', 'obvious adultery') are just adjacent words in list passages, not separate meanings; the word means only adultery.

definition: A fuller — a worker who cleaned, bleached, and finished cloth to make it white.
article: A γναφεύς was a tradesman who washed, whitened, and finished woolen cloth, essentially a professional launderer of fabric. The word appears only once in the New Testament (Mark 9:3), where it describes clothing made whiter than any fuller on earth could bleach it. It was an ordinary, everyday term: the papyri attest fullers by name in business and even funeral records, and tax documents mention a special 'fullers' tax,' showing how common the trade was in Koine life.
caution: This word appears just once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be tested beyond that single verse.

definition: To cut someone in two, or possibly to punish them with severe flogging.
article: This rare word literally means to cut something in half, built from parts meaning "two" and "cut." In the New Testament it appears only twice (Matthew 24:51 and Luke 12:46), both in the same parable about a master punishing a wicked servant, where modern translations render the idea as the master dealing out a brutal sentence. Lexicons disagree on whether the meaning is literal cutting in two or a metaphor for severe scourging, and one ancient grave inscription from Lycaonia poignantly uses the word of a firstborn son who "cut short" his father's long life by dying young.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT uses and 1 in the Septuagint), and sources genuinely disagree over whether it means literal bisection or severe flogging.

definition: The feeling of shame or disgrace, or something disgraceful that one ought to be ashamed of.
article: αἰσχύνη is the standard Koine word for shame, covering both the inward feeling of disgrace (as in Hebrews 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 4:2) and the outward object or deed that brings shame (as in Philippians 3:19 and Revelation 3:18). Its range stretches from a subjective emotion to a concrete "shameful thing," and in Jude 13 the plural points to actual shameful deeds. The Septuagint uses it 56 times, most often for the Hebrew בֹּשֶׁת (17×), and a marriage contract from 311 BC shows the everyday legal sense: a bride caught doing wrong "to the shame of her husband." The measured senses include odd renderings like "seat" in Luke 14:9, which simply reflects how the translation phrased the disgrace of being moved to a lower place.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and several one-off renderings, individual sense labels rest on thin data, though the core meaning of shame is well established across all sources.

definition: A short cloak worn over the tunic, especially by soldiers and officers.
article: χλαμύς is a short cloak draped over the χιτών (tunic), commonly associated with soldiers and officials. The two New Testament uses both come from one scene—the soldiers mocking Jesus (Matthew 27:28, 31)—where translators render it variously as a "robe" they put on and took off Him. Everyday Koine papyri confirm its ordinary use, including one third/fourth-century order instructing people "to wear cloaks when we entered" for an official function, showing the garment carried connotations of formal or military dress.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only twice in the New Testament (both in one passage) and once in the Septuagint, so its full range rests largely on outside papyri.

definition: The love and pursuit of wisdom, or a particular system of teaching claiming such wisdom.
article: φιλοσοφία means literally the love and pursuit of wisdom, and by extension a particular system of teaching or way of life. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Colossians 2:8, where the wording (with the definite article and the phrase "empty deception") shows that it is not wisdom-seeking in general being condemned but one specific system. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and in 4 Maccabees in the Septuagint, where it can refer concretely to a disciplined mode of life rather than abstract theory.
caution: The single measured rendering shows up as "captive," which reflects the surrounding verb in Colossians 2:8 rather than the meaning of φιλοσοφία itself, so the corpus data here is thin and should be read alongside the lexicon definitions.

definition: Augustus, the title of the Roman emperor, used as the name of Octavian, the first emperor.
article: This is a borrowed Latin word ("august") used as the title-name of the Roman emperor, appearing just once in the New Testament, at Luke 2:1, where it refers to Octavian. The Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "Augustus" 100% of the time, and the older lexicons agree. Interestingly, Greek writers usually translated this title as Σεβαστός rather than keeping the Latin word, and Moulton-Milligan notes the title carried far more weight than just "august," being tied to the emperor's near-divine status.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A natural cave or cavern, often used as a hiding-place or shelter.
article: σπήλαιον is a straightforward word for a cave or cavern, and in the New Testament it splits evenly between two uses: literal caves (as Lazarus's tomb in John 11:38) and the phrase "den of robbers" that Jesus quotes against the temple traders (Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46). In the Septuagint it appears 52 times, mostly translating the Hebrew מְעָרָה, the ordinary word for a cave. An everyday papyrus about renting a house even mentions "one chamber in your cave," showing the word naturally pointed to a cave used as a living or storage space.

definition: Describing something or someone useless, unprofitable, or of no real worth or merit.
article: ἀχρεῖος literally means "not useful" — built from a negative prefix on the word for "useful" — and so points to something or someone unprofitable, worthless, or without merit. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Matthew 25:30, where the Majority Bible renders it "worthless," and in Luke 17:10, where the servants call themselves "unprofitable." The everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth sense: one document (P Magd 29, 217 BC) uses it of a plot of land that was "useless and narrow," showing this was ordinary, practical Koine vocabulary.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one Septuagint use, evidence is thin, and Moulton-Milligan even suggests the Luke 17:10 occurrence may be a mistaken gloss.

definition: A dream — something seen while asleep.
article: ἐνύπνιον means a dream, something seen during sleep, built literally from the words for "in" and "sleep." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 2:17, where it is rendered "dreams," but it shows up 75 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew word for dream (חֲלוֹם, 50×). It was common everyday Koine: a papyrus from around 153 B.C. has a writer saying "I see evil dreams," and another speaks of people "trusting in dreams" after being deceived.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: To take someone else's property secretly and without permission; to steal.
article: κλέπτω means to steal — to take what belongs to another by stealth. The meaning is remarkably consistent: across all 13 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "steal" 9 times (69%), with the remaining cases being minor variations of the same idea. In the Septuagint it appears 29 times and almost always translates the Hebrew גָּנַב ("to steal," 24 of 29 times), and the everyday papyri show the same plain sense — one document from A.D. 34 even reports that a man's pig was stolen from his village.

definition: Made from the fragrant, ornamentally veined wood of the African thyia (citron) tree, prized as a luxury material.
article: This adjective describes something made of thyine wood — the aromatic, decoratively grained timber of an African tree (related to Latin 'citrinus'), valued as a costly material. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:12, where it is rendered "wood" in a list of luxury cargo. The papyri confirm it was a real commodity in everyday Koine: documents even record a tax on thyia-wood, and the timber was used for things like oil-presses.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Rebecca, the wife of the patriarch Isaac and mother of Jacob and Esau.
article: Ῥεβέκκα is the Greek spelling of the personal name Rebecca, the wife of Isaac, and it appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 9:10. It is borrowed straight from the Hebrew name רִבְקָה (Ribkah), which the Septuagint renders 32 times out of its 34 uses of this Greek form. Interestingly, those same 34 Septuagint occurrences also include one each translating two unrelated Hebrew words, likely reflecting incidental textual overlaps rather than other meanings of the name.
caution: This is a proper name with only one New Testament occurrence, so its range cannot be measured from the text.

definition: The language or speech spoken by people of a particular country, region, or group.
article: In the New Testament, διάλεκτος consistently means the language or local speech of a people — all 3 rendered occurrences translate it as "language," and the BSB agrees 100%. The word can range from a general way of speaking to a specific regional dialect, and the classical lexica add the broader sense of "conversation" or "discourse" (from its root διαλέγομαι, "to converse"), though that wider sense isn't measured in the NT. A vivid bit of evidence comes from an everyday Koine papyrus where a dog-headed figure is said to greet the reader "in his own dialect" — showing how the word marked distinctive ways of speaking.
caution: The classical lexica list a broader range (conversation, discourse, manner of speaking) that the measured NT data does not reflect, so the everyday sense here is narrower than the word's full potential.

definition: Trust or confidence placed in someone, especially religious faith in God or Christ.
article: πίστις means trust or confidence, and in the New Testament it consistently points to religious faith — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "faith" in 235 of its 242 occurrences (the rest absorbed into phrasing). In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew אֱמוּנָה, which carries the sense of faithfulness or reliability, showing the word's deep connection to steadfastness. Notably, everyday Koine papyri use πίστις in ordinary settings, such as a legal document where a witness is called "trustworthy" (worthy of πίστις), confirming its plain meaning of confidence in a person.

definition: A Sadducee, a member of the aristocratic Jewish party from which the high priests were usually drawn.
article: Σαδδουκαῖος names a member of the Sadducees, one of the major Jewish parties in the New Testament era; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Sadducees" in 9 of its occurrences (69%), with the rest being minor phrasing variants. Dodson describes them as the aristocratic party from whom the high priests were almost invariably chosen. The name probably derives from Σαδώκ (Zadok), tied to the Hebrew name צָדוֹק, suggesting a link to the priestly Zadokite line.

definition: A particle that adds a generalizing, indefinite force to a word, meaning roughly "of whatever kind" or "any at all."
senseLabels: of whatever kind, any at all
article: δήποτε is a small Greek particle built from δή and ποτέ that broadens whatever word it attaches to, giving the sense "-soever" or "of any kind at all." It is well attested in everyday Koine: papyri like P Lond 904 and P Tebt 381 use phrases such as "for whatever reason" and "in whatever manner." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, in John 5:4, in the phrase "with whatever disease" he was afflicted; the Majority Standard Bible's single rendering there is folded into "stirred."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the Byzantine text, is absent from the critical text (its John 5:4 verse is disputed), and even the manuscript reading there varies between ᾧ δήποτε and οἵῳ δηποτοῦν.

definition: The comparative form of "great," meaning greater, larger, or more important than something else.
article: μείζων is the irregular comparative of μέγας ("great"), so it means "greater" or "larger" — whether in size, degree, rank, or importance. Its range is broad, since μέγας itself covers everything from physical size (a stone, a fish, a city) to intensity (a great fear, a great love) to rank among persons and things. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times and notably renders the Hebrew גָּדֵל ("great/elder") twice, and even gets used for the proper name Cain once and for צָעִיר ("younger/smaller") once, reflecting comparisons between older and younger.
caution: Direct New Testament evidence is thin — it appears 0 times in the Byzantine text and only once in the critical SBLGNT — so most of its measured sense comes from the Septuagint and from its parent word μέγας.

definition: To tell a lie, speak falsely, or try to deceive someone with untrue words.
article: ψεύδομαι means to tell a lie or deceive someone through falsehood, and in the New Testament it always appears in the middle voice. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "lie" in 6 of its 12 occurrences (55%), and it can be used absolutely ("do not lie") or with a person as the one being lied to, as in Acts 5:4 where Peter says Ananias lied to God. The everyday Koine papyri capture its plain force vividly, as in one letter that bluntly accuses, "you lie in all things and your gods likewise." In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew kachash, to deny or deceive.
caution: The 2 cases the data labels "belong" (Acts 5:4, Rev 3:9) reflect English phrasing choices rather than a separate meaning of the verb, which consistently denotes lying.

definition: To be fully awake, or to stay awake throughout, especially in contrast to falling asleep.
article: This verb describes being thoroughly awake, built from the preposition διά ("through") and the verb meaning "to be awake." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 9:32, where Peter and his companions, having been weighed down with sleep, become fully awake and see Jesus' glory at the Transfiguration. Lexicons split on the nuance: it can mean either "to remain awake (the whole time)" or "to become fully awake," and the single occurrence doesn't settle which the author intended.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the lexicons disagree on whether it means staying awake or waking up fully, so its precise sense is uncertain.

definition: A connecting word meaning "since" or "because," giving the reason for something, or sometimes "otherwise" when introducing what would happen.
article: ἐπεί is a common little connecting word that mostly means "since" or "because," pointing to the reason behind a statement — measured this way in about 21% of its 27 New Testament appearances. It also slides into the sense of "otherwise" or "else," introducing what would or would not be the case (about 17%), and three times it disappears into the English phrasing entirely. Built from ἐπί and εἰ, it shows up constantly in everyday Koine papyri; one letter from 168 B.C. uses it just as the New Testament does: "since your mother is much annoyed about it."

definition: To tear or break something apart violently, such as cloth ripping or wineskins bursting open.
article: At its core ῥήγνυμι means to rend or break something asunder by force. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, and in the Gospel examples it describes old wineskins bursting when new wine is poured in (Matthew 9:17, Mark 2:22, Luke 5:37). The lexicons show a wider range than the Gospel uses suggest: it can mean to break forth into speech (Galatians 4:27, quoting the Septuagint) or to throw someone down in a convulsion (Mark 9:18, Luke 9:42), and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew בָּקַע, "to split."
caution: With only 7 occurrences and 4 of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured English senses cover just the "bursting" idea, while the lexicons document additional senses not reflected in the corpus counts.

definition: One who creates or founds something, especially God as the maker of all things.
article: κτίστης names the one who brings something into being — a creator, or in older usage the founder of a city. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Peter 4:19), where it refers to God as the faithful Creator, and once in the Septuagint. Everyday papyri and inscriptions show the word being applied as an honorary title; for instance, it was given five times to the chief magistrate of Oxyrhynchus as "founder of the city," and even to emperors like Domitian and Trajan.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its biblical range rests on very few examples.

definition: The pointing word "this" (or plural "these"), used to single out a person or thing already in view or about to be named.
article: This is the everyday Greek demonstrative pronoun "this/these," used to point at someone or something near at hand or just mentioned. It's enormously common—1,408 times in the Byzantine New Testament—and most often simply renders as "this" (65%) or "these" (16%), though in 416 cases it gets absorbed into English phrasing with no word of its own. In the Septuagint it stands behind several Hebrew demonstratives, chiefly זֶה (932×) and זֹאת (540×), and the papyri show it filling out common stock phrases like "on this account" (διὰ τοῦτο) and "for this reason" (ἐκ τούτου).

definition: An adverb meaning "here" — in this place, or sometimes "to here" or "in this situation."
article: ὧδε is the ordinary Koine word for "here," and that meaning dominates: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "here" in 53 of 60 New Testament occurrences (96%). Beyond plain location it can mean "to here, hither" (Mark 11:3) or, figuratively, "in this circumstance" — as in Revelation 13:10. Everyday papyri confirm the sense vividly: one letter writer says "I have been idle here for two months," and another "as I am staying here a few days."

definition: To write—to form letters, record words, or set something down in a document, especially the authoritative texts of Scripture.
article: γράφω simply means to write—to form letters or commit something to writing—and the New Testament uses it that way almost exclusively, rendered "written" in 185 of 195 occurrences. It very often appears in the perfect form "it is written" (γέγραπται), pointing to Scripture as a standing authority. The everyday papyri show why this carried such weight: legal documents used the same phrase to mean a contract was binding, as in a marriage agreement penalizing anyone who failed to act "as it is written." Older classical writers also used the word for scraping, sketching, or drawing, but that sense does not surface in the measured biblical data.

definition: To stir someone up to jealousy or rivalry, deliberately rousing strong feelings of envy or resentment.
article: παραζηλόω means to provoke someone to jealousy or rivalry — to stir up envy on purpose. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in Paul's letters (Romans 10:19; 11:11, 14; 1 Corinthians 10:22), and the Majority Standard Bible renders every occurrence with some form of "jealous" or "provoke," with the BSB agreeing in all cases. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew קָנָא ("be jealous"), but Moulton-Milligan notes a striking twist: in Psalm 37 the same verb means "fret not yourself" — "do not get worked up" over the world's disorder — showing the word can swing toward agitation more broadly than simple jealousy.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and varied Septuagint Hebrew counterparts, the precise force in any given verse depends heavily on context.

definition: Melchi, the name of two ancestors of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy.
article: Μελχί is a personal name appearing twice in the New Testament, both times in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:24 and 3:28). It is an indeclinable name of Hebrew origin, derived from a word meaning "my king." According to Strong's, it identifies two different Israelites in the ancestral list, and translations consistently render it simply as "Melchi."
caution: This is a proper name appearing only twice, so there is little to define beyond identifying the individuals.

definition: The official coin or money in circulation within a state, recognized as legal currency.
article: In the New Testament νόμισμα appears just once, in Matthew 22:19, where Jesus asks to be shown the coin used for paying the tribute tax, and every translation surveyed renders it as 'coin' or 'money' (100% agreement). The word comes from νομίζω and originally meant anything established by custom; the lexicographer Abbott-Smith still lists 'custom' as its first sense, even though the measured New Testament usage is purely monetary. The papyri preserve that older meaning vividly: an Egyptian petition from A.D. 186 uses the word for native Egyptian law and marriage customs, showing how the same term once covered both 'established usage' and 'official currency.'
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured monetary sense rests on a single occurrence, and the lexica preserve an older 'custom' meaning not seen in the NT.

definition: To stay or reside somewhere, whether for a short visit or a longer settled dwelling.
article: καταμένω means to stay or live in a place, formed from κατά plus the common verb μένω ("to remain"). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 1:13, where the disciples "arrived staying" in their upper room. Older lexicons like Abbott-Smith call it "to remain permanently, abide," but the everyday papyri tell a different story: Moulton-Milligan cite a police officer's edict (A.D. 158) using the word for strangers who were only temporarily staying at a farmstead, suggesting the "permanent" sense is overstated.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and the standard lexicons disagreeing with the papyri over whether the staying is permanent or temporary, the precise force is uncertain.

definition: To breastfeed a baby, said both of a mother nursing and of an infant sucking at the breast.
article: θηλάζω covers both sides of breastfeeding: the mother giving suck and the baby taking it. The grammars (Abbott-Smith) split it cleanly this way, and in the New Testament the mother sense shows up in the warnings about pregnant and nursing women (Matthew 24:19, Mark 13:17, Luke 21:23), while the infant sense appears in Matthew 21:16 and Luke 11:27. The most vivid evidence comes from the papyri: the word is common in actual nursing contracts, including one from 13 B.C. where a woman named Didyme agrees to nurse a child with her own pure, untainted milk.
caution: The display labels here mix in surrounding words like "saying" and "miserable," so the raw rendering counts don't cleanly track the two real senses the lexica describe.

definition: Describing someone or something as unworthy of, or inadequate for, a particular task or standing.
article: ἀνάξιος is built from a negative prefix plus ἄξιος ("worthy"), so it literally means "unworthy" or "not up to" something. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 6:2, where Paul asks whether believers are "competent" to judge trivial cases. The word also turns up twice in the Septuagint and in everyday Koine papyri; interestingly, it survives into Modern Greek with the sense "incapable," which fits the inadequacy nuance well.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: The recovery or restoring of sight to those who cannot see.
article: This word means the recovery of sight, the act of being able to see again. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:18, where Jesus reads from Isaiah, and once in the Septuagint at Isaiah 61:1, where it translates a Hebrew phrase about releasing or opening (פְּקַח־קוֹחַ). Notably, the corpus rendering data records it as "brokenhearted" in that one verse, while every lexicon (Strong's, KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agrees the word means "recovery of sight" — a clear disagreement worth flagging.
caution: Evidence is thin (one NT and one LXX occurrence), and the measured rendering "brokenhearted" conflicts with every lexicon's "recovery of sight," likely reflecting a verse-mapping issue rather than the word's true meaning.

definition: Swept away or carried off by a river or flood.
article: This compound word literally means "river-borne" — carried off by a stream or flood, built from the words for "river" (potamós) and "to carry" (phoréō). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 12:15, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "spewed" (with the sense of the woman being swept away by the water). Older lexicons once suspected John coined the word, but the papyri prove otherwise: it shows up in everyday legal documents as early as 110 BC, including a land agreement describing fields "carried off by the river."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests on a single verse plus outside papyri evidence.

definition: An intense longing or eager desire for someone or something.
article: ἐπιπόθησις names a strong, heartfelt longing or eager desire. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians (7:7 and 7:11), where every translation renders it consistently as "longing." Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes the word also surfaces in Aquila's Greek version of Ezekiel 23:11, showing it was used outside the New Testament too.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in a single chapter of one letter, the evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: To arm or equip oneself, used figuratively in the New Testament for taking up a mental attitude like a weapon.
article: ὁπλίζω means to make ready or equip, especially to arm soldiers with weapons, and in the middle voice to arm oneself. Its single New Testament appearance (1 Peter 4:1) is figurative: believers are to "arm" themselves with a certain mindset, where the verb gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word. Greek writers used the same figurative move elsewhere — Sophocles' Electra speaks of arming oneself with boldness, and a poem in the Greek Anthology has someone arm reason about the chest against Eros, a close parallel to Peter's image.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears just once in the Byzantine NT and not at all in the critical text, so confidence is low.

definition: Having expert, practiced knowledge; skilled and understanding in a particular area.
article: ἐπιστήμων describes someone who not just knows facts but has genuine expertise and practical skill. It appears only once in the New Testament (James 3:13) and 7 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew word for "wise" (חָכָם, 4 times). The everyday papyri reinforce this professional flavor: an Oxyrhynchus document calls a public surveyor "ἐπιστήμων of those places," the way we might say someone is an expert in their field.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence, where it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated as its own word.

definition: The practice of treating people unequally based on outward status or appearance rather than fairness.
article: προσωποληψία describes partiality—judging or favoring people by their outward standing instead of treating everyone evenly. Across its 4 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "favoritism" 75% of the time and "show favoritism" once, a narrow and consistent range that the BSB matches completely. The older King James phrase "respect of persons" captures the same idea, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, showing it was ordinary usage rather than purely religious language.
caution: This word appears in the Byzantine text but not in the SBLGNT critical text, so its presence varies by manuscript tradition.

definition: Something that trips a person up — an obstacle or cause of offense that blocks someone's path or causes them to stumble.
article: προσκοπή describes something that causes a person to stumble — figuratively, an offense or obstacle placed in someone's way. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "obstacle" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully. The word is built from προσκόπτω ("to strike against, stumble"), and the Greek Venetus version uses it in Proverbs 16:18 to translate the Hebrew word for "falling" or "downfall."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured confidently from biblical usage.

definition: The marrow, the soft tissue inside bones, used figuratively for the innermost, deepest part of a person.
article: μυελός means the marrow found within bones, the body's deepest and most hidden tissue. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 4:12, where Scripture is described as piercing to the division of soul and spirit, joints and marrow. Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders this occurrence as "joints" rather than "marrow," while every lexicon (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) and the King James Version all give "marrow" — so the standard meaning and this one translation choice disagree. In the Septuagint it occurs three times, including Job 21:24, where it translates the Hebrew word for marrow.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured translation "joints" conflicts with every lexicon, which gives "marrow."

definition: To give someone, especially a daughter, in marriage to another person.
article: This verb means to give a person in marriage, the active counterpart to getting married. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 20:34, where it is rendered "given in marriage" in every count.
