Notably, the critical text drops the word entirely in favor of the simpler form γαμίσκω, and Moulton-Milligan report that both ἐκγαμίσκω and the related ἐκγαμίζω have effectively vanished from the true New Testament text, with almost no evidence elsewhere.
caution: This is a single, textually disputed occurrence that modern critical editions replace, so its independent existence is uncertain.

definition: Rhodes, an island in the Mediterranean Sea off the southwest coast of Asia Minor.
article: Ῥόδος is the name of the Mediterranean island of Rhodes, which lies in the Aegean Sea southwest of Asia Minor. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 21:1, as a stop on a sea voyage. The lexicons trace the name back as far as Homer's Iliad and connect it, probably, to the word for a rose.
caution: The measured rendering of "ourselves" reflects how the surrounding travel narrative was translated rather than the word itself, which is simply a place name appearing only once.

definition: A harbor or haven — a sheltered place along the coast where ships can safely anchor.
article: λιμήν refers to a harbor or haven, a coastal spot where ships could shelter or dock. All 3 New Testament occurrences cluster in the sea-voyage narrative of Acts 27, and the word is solidly attested in everyday Koine: papyri mention the harbor of Memphis and a harbor tax, showing it was ordinary commercial vocabulary. The measured rendering 'harbor' appears once, while the other two renderings ('difficulty' and 'Phoenix') reflect surrounding context and a proper place name rather than separate meanings of the word itself.
caution: Evidence is thin and confidence is low: only 3 New Testament uses, and two of the measured renderings reflect context or a place name rather than distinct senses.

definition: To lay something open or expose it completely, leaving it bare and unable to be hidden.
article: This verb appears just once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 4:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as everything being "hidden" (here describing what nothing can be) — that is, all things lie exposed and laid open before God. The word literally comes from τράχηλος, "neck," and Strong's traces it to wrestlers seizing an opponent by the throat or to exposing a victim's throat for killing, but in Hebrews the plain meaning is simply "laid bare." Most interestingly, Moulton-Milligan found it in an everyday Koine papyrus (around 241–239 B.C.), though the broken text leaves its exact sense there frustratingly unclear.
caution: This is a one-time New Testament word, and the lexica openly admit uncertainty about how its "laid open" sense developed from its literal neck-and-throat origins.

definition: An intensified word meaning "high above" or "far above," used to place something over everything else in position or rank.
article: ὑπεράνω is a compound adverb (from ὑπέρ, "over," and ἄνω, "above") that means "far above" and can function as a preposition with the genitive. All three of its New Testament uses point upward in either place or rank — Christ seated far above every power (Eph 1:21), ascended above all the heavens (Eph 4:10), and the cherubim above the ark (Heb 9:5). The word was at home in everyday Koine: papyri and inscriptions use it freely, and a third-century memorial even stacks it on itself in the phrase "the one above the gods who are above."
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences, each rendered once, so the apparent three senses are really one meaning shaped by context.

definition: Adam, the first man and ancestor of humankind, used in the New Testament both for that individual and as a representative figure.
article: Ἀδάμ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name אָדָם, and it appears 9 times across 5 books of the Byzantine New Testament. It is rendered "Adam" in 7 of those occurrences (78%), and the name functions both for the original man and as a representative figure — Paul famously contrasts him with Christ, the "last Adam," in 1 Corinthians 15:45. The Hebrew word it translates is interesting because אָדָם means both the personal name "Adam" and the ordinary word for "man" or "humankind," which is why the Septuagint uses the term broadly, appearing 28 times across 3 books.
caution: As a transliterated proper name it is indeclinable and its meaning is stable, so confidence is high despite the moderate computed tier.

definition: The act of putting on or wearing clothing.
article: ἔνδυσις refers to the act of putting on or wearing clothes, derived from the verb ἐνδύω ("to clothe"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 3:3, where it describes the outward wearing of garments, and twice in the Septuagint. An interesting parallel comes from the Letter of Aristeas, which uses the word to describe the amazement caused by the high priest Eleazar's wearing of his richly adorned coat and precious stones.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range in biblical use cannot be measured beyond that single context.

definition: Someone who has personally seen something with their own eyes, a firsthand witness.
article: An αὐτόπτης is a person who saw an event firsthand rather than merely hearing about it secondhand. The word appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 1:2), where Luke notes that his account rests on those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning. A papyrus letter (P Oxy 1154, late first century) shows the everyday flavor of the word: a man reassures his sister, "I am personally acquainted with these places and am not a stranger here," using αὐτόπτης to mean direct, personal familiarity.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: A horse-drawn chariot, the wheeled vehicle used for travel, transport, or war.
article: ἅρμα means a chariot — a wheeled vehicle drawn by horses. Although the digest splits the four New Testament occurrences across three labels, all of them point to the same thing: the chariot the Ethiopian official rode in (Acts 8:28-38) and the war chariots of Revelation 9:9; the extra labels just reflect phrases like "over his chariot" or "stop the chariot." In the Septuagint it appears 162 times, usually translating Hebrew words for riding-vehicles, and Moulton-Milligan find it throughout everyday papyri — including a poem celebrating Hadrian's accession in which Apollo describes Trajan riding skyward in a white-horsed chariot.
caution: The three measured "senses" are really one meaning (chariot) described in different surrounding phrases, not distinct definitions.

definition: The steady, patient endurance that holds firm under hardship or opposition without giving up.
article: ὑπομονή describes staying firm and not giving up when life presses hard — translated 32 times as "perseverance" (19×, 61%), "endurance" (7×, 23%), or with the verb "persevere" (4×, 13%), with the BSB agreeing 100% each time. It comes from ὑπομένω ("to remain under, hold out"), and Abbott-Smith notes it can literally mean "a remaining behind" before taking on its main sense of patient enduring. Notably, in later Jewish writings like 4 Maccabees the word came to describe the special steadfastness shown by martyrs.

definition: To come or to go—to move toward a place, arrive there, or set out from where you are.
article: This is one of the most common motion verbs in the New Testament, appearing 639 times, and it covers both arriving and departing depending on context. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "come" in about 89% of cases and "went" in roughly 10%, with a handful of time-related "when" phrases; Strong's sums it up as "to come or go, in a great variety of applications." In the Septuagint it shows up 869 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew בּוֹא ("come/go in"), 706 times. A papyrus from around A.D. 100 uses it for an everyday report—"Teuphilus the Jew has come saying…"—showing how ordinary this verb was in daily Koine speech.

definition: To yoke or join two things together, used figuratively of uniting a man and woman in marriage.
article: This verb literally means to yoke two things together, and both New Testament occurrences (Matthew 19:6 and Mark 10:9) use it figuratively for God joining a husband and wife in marriage. Outside the Bible it kept its plain, everyday sense: the papyri use it for yoking horses together as well as for marriage unions. In the Septuagint it appears just twice (Ezekiel 1:11, 23), where Abbott-Smith notes it translates a Hebrew word for joining, though the digest's Hebrew counterpart listing differs.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the marriage meaning is well attested but the sources disagree on which Hebrew word it renders in the Septuagint.

definition: A master-builder or chief architect who designs and oversees major construction work.
article: ἀρχιτέκτων combines the ideas of "chief" and "builder" to mean a master-builder or architect, the person who designs and supervises construction. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 3:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "expert," and once in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew word for a craftsman or artisan (חֶרֶשׁ). The papyri make the term vivid: it shows up repeatedly in the third-century B.C. correspondence of Cleon the architect, and one document even names a subordinate, Theodorus, who worked under Cleon before succeeding him.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range in Scripture rests on a single example.

definition: Describing someone who attentively listens and submits to another's authority, ready to do what is commanded.
article: ὑπήκοος describes a person who is obedient or submissive—the underlying sense is of someone attentively listening and then doing what is asked. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "obedient" in the one case where it gets its own English word (Philippians 2:8), with the other two occurrences absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri and inscriptions: one inscription describes Ptolemy III as having made all the local rulers ὑπηκόους ("subject") to him, capturing the note of submission to authority.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences with just one rendered by its own English word—so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: To come to someone's aid, to help or rescue them, especially when they are in trouble or distress.
article: βοηθέω means to come to someone's aid, often picturing a quick response to a cry for help — the word combines the ideas of a shout (βοή) and running (θέω). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times and is rendered "help" or "helped" in every clear case, a consistency the BSB independently confirms 100% of the time. It's a workhorse word: the Septuagint uses it 74 times, mostly for the Hebrew עָזַר ("to help"), and the papyri show it everywhere in petitions where people begged officials to "come to their aid."

definition: Aristarchus, a Christian man from Thessalonica in Macedonia who traveled with and supported the apostle Paul.
article: Aristarchus is simply a personal name, rendered "Aristarchus" in all 5 of its New Testament occurrences (100%), with both the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles agreeing fully. He appears as a Macedonian from Thessalonica who accompanied Paul, showing up in scenes like the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:29) and named among Paul's fellow workers (Colossians 4:10, Philemon 24). The name itself is built from Greek roots meaning "best" and "ruler," so it carries the sense of "best-ruling," though as a proper name it just identifies the individual.

definition: Material wealth or financial resources; money and the prosperity that comes from a profitable trade or business.
article: εὐπορία refers to wealth or financial resources — the money and prosperity a person or trade brings in. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 19:25), where the silversmith Demetrius reminds his fellow craftsmen that their wealth comes from making shrines of Artemis. The everyday papyri back this up vividly: one document from around AD 303 has a man declaring, "I have no other resources (εὐπορία) than this money in question," showing the word's plain commercial use.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the listed measured rendering ("assembled") appears to be a tagging error that conflicts with every lexicon's clear sense of "wealth."

definition: To come to the end of life — that is, to die.
article: Although its root sense is to finish or complete (as in completing one's life), in practice τελευτάω simply means to die. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times, rendered "died" in 5 of them and absorbed into surrounding phrasing in another 5. The Septuagint uses it heavily — 72 times — and it most often stands for the Hebrew word מוּת ("die"), used 61 of those times; everyday Koine papyri likewise use it plainly for someone's death, as in a first-century notice reporting "my brother Peneouris has died."

definition: A person who listens to something, such as the law or a message, but who does not necessarily act on what they hear.
article: ἀκροατής simply means a hearer or listener — someone who takes in what is spoken. In all 4 New Testament occurrences (Romans 2:13 and three times in James 1) it sits in contrast with being a "doer," so the word stresses passive listening over active obedience. Strong's even calls it a hearer "merely." Moulton-Milligan note the related verb in an everyday magic papyrus describing something "dreadful to hear," and in the Septuagint it renders a Hebrew word at Isaiah 3:3, showing the word lived in ordinary Koine well beyond Scripture.
caution: The measured senses split evenly across only 4 occurrences, and the apparent "doer" rendering reflects the surrounding hearer-versus-doer contrast rather than a separate meaning of the word itself.

definition: To take someone or something to yourself—to welcome and accept a person, take someone aside, or take food.
article: In the New Testament this verb always appears in the middle voice, carrying the idea of taking someone or something to yourself. Its range runs from physical actions—pulling someone aside (17%) or taking food (17%)—to the warmer sense of accepting and welcoming people (17%), as in Romans 14:1 and 15:7. Everyday papyri confirm this last meaning vividly: one document from 14 BC describes someone twice taking a person 'into the house to myself,' echoing the language of Philemon 17.
caution: Across all 14 Byzantine occurrences no single rendering dominates, so context decides whether the word means take aside, partake of food, or welcome.

definition: Describing someone who acts to win human approval rather than to serve God sincerely.
article: ἀνθρωπάρεσκος describes a person who works to please other people—especially with an eye on being seen and approved—rather than serving genuinely. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22), both times rendered with the idea of "pleasing" people, and in both places it contrasts surface-level service with wholehearted obedience. Built from the words for "human being" and "to please," it was likely a coined compound; Moulton-Milligan note it first surfaces in the Septuagint and Psalms of Solomon, much as English coined "men-pleasers."
caution: This word is rare—only 2 New Testament uses and 1 in the Septuagint—so its precise shade of meaning rests on thin evidence.

definition: A preposition meaning 'with' (alongside, in the company of) when used one way, or 'after' (following in time) when used another way.
article: μετά is one of the most common prepositions in the New Testament, appearing 471 times, and its meaning splits cleanly along two lines: it means 'with' about 79% of the time (295 occurrences) and 'after' about 17% (62 occurrences). The reason is grammatical—when joined to one case it signals accompaniment ('with'), and when joined to another it signals succession ('after'), which is why classical lexica describe it as taking either the genitive or the accusative. In the Septuagint it appears a striking 1,908 times, most often standing in for Hebrew עִם ('with', 772×), but also frequently for אַחַר ('after', 265×)—the same with/after split shows up in the underlying Hebrew. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, as in a document referring to 'those acting with Demetria.'

definition: Seth, the third son of Adam in the biblical genealogy.
article: Σήθ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name שֵׁת (Seth), the patriarch listed as a son of Adam. It is an indeclinable proper name that appears only once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Luke 3:38, where it is rendered "son." In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times across 3 books, consistently translating the Hebrew name, and Genesis 4:25 records its origin as Adam's third son.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its single rendering simply reflects its place in a genealogy.

definition: An adverb meaning next or following in sequence, used in the New Testament chiefly of the next day or what comes next in time.
article: ἑξῆς is an adverb pointing to whatever comes next in a sequence, and in the New Testament it always concerns time. In its 5 Byzantine occurrences it is rendered "next day" 3 times (75%) and "next" once (25%), with one occurrence absorbed into the surrounding phrasing; it often appears in an elliptical form like τῇ ἑξῆς, where the word "day" is understood but unstated. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this temporal use: an Oxyrhynchus document speaks of "the following 8th year" and another of "the next month Phamenoth," matching the New Testament pattern exactly.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on its temporal meaning.

definition: To be bent over or bowed down, unable to straighten up.
senseLabels: bent over and unable to straighten
article: This verb describes a body permanently bent forward, stooped over and unable to straighten up. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 13:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "disabled" and describes a woman bowed double for eighteen years. The classical sources record a related general sense, "to bend forwards," and Abbott-Smith notes Septuagint uses (Job 9:27; Sirach 12:11; 19:26), with one occurrence translating a Hebrew word for being bowed down.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and few Septuagint uses — so the precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: An adverb meaning "today" — on this present day, as opposed to yesterday or tomorrow.
article: σήμερον is a straightforward adverb meaning "today," rendered that way in 28 of its 41 New Testament appearances (80%), with the remaining uses still pointing to "this day" in fuller phrases like "the present day." Its range is narrow and stable: every source, from Strong's to Abbott-Smith, agrees it marks the current day, often set against αὔριον ("tomorrow"). The everyday Koine flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where one writer laments "a year today I have been away from you," and in the Septuagint it overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew word for "day" (יוֹם, 193 times).

definition: Religion expressed through worship and outward observance—the practice of reverencing God or the gods.
article: θρησκεία refers to religion as it shows up in worship and outward practice, the visible side of reverence toward God or the gods. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 4 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "religion" in every case where it gets its own English word (Acts 26:5; James 1:26-27). Scholars debate its core meaning: Strong's calls it "ceremonial observance," but Moulton-Milligan cite Hort's argument that the underlying idea is simply reverence or worship of the gods, which then often expresses itself in ritual acts—an everyday Koine papyrus from the 2nd century AD uses the plural form for such acts of worship.
caution: Sources disagree on whether the word means ritual observance specifically or reverence/worship more broadly, and the New Testament evidence is limited to 4 occurrences.

definition: A person who gives something, especially someone who hands over a gift.
article: δότης simply means a giver — someone who hands something over. It is a rare word, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament (2 Corinthians 9:7) and once in the Septuagint, where it translates a Hebrew word in Proverbs. Notably, Paul appears to borrow the term directly from the Septuagint of Proverbs, and Moulton-Milligan confirm the form turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a pre-Christian inscription.
caution: The evidence is thin: the word appears just once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its full range is hard to measure.

definition: To mark something off by boundaries, and from there to fix, appoint, or decree something in advance.
article: At its root ὁρίζω means to draw a boundary line — the source of our word "horizon" — and from that literal sense it easily extends to fixing, appointing, or decreeing something definite. It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where translators handle it loosely: in 2 cases the Majority Standard Bible folds it into "through" (as in Romans 1:4 and Hebrews 4:7), elsewhere it becomes "determined," "appointed," or "ordained," and 3 times it disappears into the surrounding phrasing. The everyday concreteness shows up in the papyri, where a second-century document uses it for fixing the actual boundaries of a plot of land.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and 3 absorbed into phrasing, the English renderings vary widely and depend heavily on context.caution placeholder

definition: Describing someone or something that can be relied upon, or a person who trusts and believes.
article: πιστός is the standard New Testament word for being trustworthy, dependable, or faithful, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "faithful" in 44 of its 67 occurrences (98%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. It applies to faithful people, to God himself, and to reliable things like a "trustworthy saying." In the Septuagint it almost always translates the Hebrew root אָמַן (22×), the same root behind "amen." Everyday Koine papyri show the very same usage—one document hands a person over "to the good and faithful grave-diggers" for safekeeping, echoing the language of Matthew 25:21.
caution: Lexicons note a secondary active sense "believing/trusting" (as in Acts 16:1), but the measured data tracks only the dominant "faithful" meaning.

definition: A word meaning "except" or "apart from," or, as a noun, "the things besides" or extra matters.
article: παρεκτός is a rare word that mostly works as a preposition meaning "except" or "apart from" (as in Acts 26:29 and Matthew 5:32). It can also function like a noun, "the things besides," which is how Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 11:28 to mean everything else on top of what he just listed. In everyday Koine, papyri show the related form παρέξ used for accounting—"four golden solidi less 600 myriads"—nicely capturing the sense of subtracting or setting something aside.
caution: It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, each rendered differently, so its range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To fly, moving through the air on wings as a bird does.
article: πέτομαι simply means "to fly," used of birds moving through the air. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, all in Revelation, and in three of those the Majority Standard Bible renders it within phrases describing an eagle (Rev 4:7, 8:13, 12:14); the other two occurrences are absorbed into surrounding wording. In the Septuagint it mostly translates the Hebrew עוּף (13 of 17 times), the ordinary verb for flying, and a charming fourth-century papyrus uses it figuratively in a plea: "for my sake fly and come to me."
caution: Note that some printed editions read the alternate form πετάομαι in these verses, which lexicographers treat as a false form for πέτομαι.

definition: To find fault with someone or something, to blame, criticize, or discredit them.
senseLabels: to find fault with or blame
article: This verb means to blame, criticize, or find fault with someone — often with the aim of discrediting them. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians (6:3 and 8:20), where Paul is concerned that his ministry or his handling of money should give no occasion for criticism. It comes from the noun μῶμος ("blemish, fault"), and in the Septuagint it shows up in Proverbs 9:7 rendering a Hebrew word for blame or disgrace.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences and one in the Septuagint — so the range of meaning is hard to pin down precisely.

definition: Describing something that cannot be approached or drawn near to.
article: ἀπρόσιτος describes something so removed that no one can come near it. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:16, where God is said to dwell in "unapproachable" light — and even there it is folded into a phrase rather than translated as a single English word. The form is built from a negative prefix plus a verb meaning "to go to," literally "not to be gone toward."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from corpus use.

definition: Cooked by fire — roasted, broiled, or baked — describing food prepared over heat.
article: ὀπτός is a simple adjective meaning "cooked by fire," whether roasted, broiled, or baked. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:42, where the risen Jesus is given a piece of broiled fish, and twice in the Septuagint at Exodus 12, both times rendering the Hebrew צָלִי (roasted) for the Passover lamb. The everyday flavor of the word shines through in the papyri, where it shows up in a feast shopping-list as ὀπτοῦ δέλφακος, "roast pork," and very commonly with bricks (ὀπτὸς πλίνθος, "baked brick").
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use and two in the Septuagint — though the meaning is well confirmed by papyri and lexica.

definition: A craftsman who works silver, beating and shaping it into objects.
article: This word names a silversmith, literally a "beater of silver" from the words for silver and to strike. It appears just once in the New Testament, describing Demetrius in Acts 19:24, and twice in the Septuagint. Everyday papyri and inscriptions confirm it was the ordinary Koine job title for such a worker, and one early first-century payment order even names a silversmith called Apollonius.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the evidence is thin, though the meaning is consistent and unambiguous across all sources.

definition: To test or try someone or something, either to prove its quality or to tempt it toward wrongdoing.
article: This verb covers a spectrum from neutral testing to malicious tempting. In the Byzantine New Testament it most often means "test" (13×, 36%) or "tempted" (11×, 31%), with the surrounding context deciding which way it leans—Jesus being put to the test by hostile questioners versus being tempted to sin. In the Septuagint it almost always (27 of 34 times) renders the Hebrew נָסָה, the word used when God "tested" people like Abraham, and Moulton-Milligan notes that even in everyday Koine the idea of probation or trial always clings to it.
caution: The line between "test" and "tempt" depends heavily on context rather than the word itself, so individual passages can be read either way.

definition: A good deed or kind service done to benefit someone.
article: εὐεργεσία refers to a good deed, kindness, or beneficial service rendered to another person. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both rendered "service" by the Majority Standard Bible — in Acts 4:9, where it describes the act of healing done to a lame man, and in 1 Timothy 6:2. The word was common in everyday Koine: the papyri show it used for the benefits or generosity conferred by an emperor, as when one document speaks of "the εὐεργεσία of our lord Hadrian Caesar."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin Septuagint evidence, confidence in the full range is low.

definition: To do what is good and honorable; to keep acting rightly without giving up.
article: καλοποιέω is a compound of καλός ("good, fine") and ποιέω ("to do"), meaning literally to do the fair or honorable thing. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Thessalonians 3:13, where Paul urges believers not to grow weary in doing good — Abbott-Smith compares the similar phrase in Galatians 6:9. Moulton-Milligan note the verb also turns up in everyday Koine documents, such as a later Egyptian papyrus, showing it was ordinary working vocabulary and not just a religious term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range can only be inferred; note also that the measured rendering label "grow" reflects the larger phrase ("grow weary in doing good") rather than the verb's own meaning of doing good.

definition: A modius — a Roman dry-measure container of about a peck (nearly two gallons), used in the New Testament as a bowl-like vessel.
article: A μόδιος was originally a Roman dry measure holding about 16 sextarii (roughly a peck), and the word names both the quantity and the utensil used to measure it. In all 3 of its New Testament occurrences it refers to the container itself — the bowl or basket you might put over a lamp to hide it — and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "basket" twice and "basket sets" once. The everyday character of the term shows up in the papyri, where it appears constantly in grain accounts, such as one listing 49 modii of barley (P Thead 32, A.D. 307).
caution: This is a borrowed Latin term appearing only 3 times in the New Testament; the modern "basket" renderings describe a vessel, while the original word strictly means a dry measure, so the precise object intended is somewhat uncertain.

definition: To die, or in the perfect tense, to be dead.
article: θνήσκω means to die, and in its perfect-tense forms it describes someone being dead. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times across 6 books, with translators rendering it "dead" in 7 cases (54%) and "died" in 3 cases (23%). In the Septuagint it shows up 76 times and mostly stands in for the Hebrew מוּת ("to die"), used 29 times, so its core meaning is consistent across both Testaments. Abbott-Smith notes it can also describe spiritual death, as in 1 Timothy 5:6.

definition: To fasten a belt around oneself or someone else, getting dressed and ready for work, service, or travel.
article: περιζώννυμι means to gird or belt clothing around the body, often picturing someone tucking up their garment to be ready for active work or travel. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times, and translators render it fairly evenly as "dress," "around," "dressed around," and "dressed" — all clustering on the same image of belting up. In the Septuagint it appears 37 times, most often translating the Hebrew חָגַר (22×), and it shows up in everyday Koine documents, even in a magic charm from a London papyrus that speaks of a "heart girded with a serpent."
caution: The measured senses are spread thinly across only 7 occurrences, so the labels reflect translation wording more than sharply distinct meanings.

definition: A soldier who fights or rides on horseback; a cavalryman.
article: ἱππεύς simply means a horse-soldier or cavalryman, and its meaning is remarkably consistent. Both of its New Testament appearances are in Acts 23 (verses 23 and 32), describing the mounted troops sent to escort Paul, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "horsemen" in 100% of cases. It shows up 45 times in the Septuagint, usually for the Hebrew word for horsemen, and the everyday papyri use it for members of cavalry units in the Ptolemaic army — for instance, mercenary horsemen and Macedonian cavalry settlers.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the measured sample is small, though the meaning is firmly confirmed by Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: An exact imprint or precise reproduction, like the image a stamp or seal leaves behind.
article: χαρακτήρ originally named the engraving tool, then the mark it pressed into something — the stamp on a coin or seal — and finally any exact reproduction or distinguishing feature. The word appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 1:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "radiance." A striking parallel comes from an inscription (OGIS 383) where χαρακτήρ describes a statue as the exact "impress" of someone's form, which fits the lexicons' core idea of a precise copy.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the standard lexicons ("exact imprint, stamp") differ from the measured rendering "radiance."

definition: A person bound to you by affection or loyalty; a friend or close associate.
article: φίλος almost always means a friend—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "friends" in 28 of 30 cases (93%), and the BSB independently agrees 96% of the time. Though classical sources note it can mean "beloved, dear" or "loving, friendly" as an adjective, in the New Testament it functions overwhelmingly as a noun for a friend, often paired with a person's name as in "friend of the bridegroom" or set against "servant" in John 15:15. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew רֵעַ ("neighbor, companion," 24×), and everyday Koine papyri show it used naturally for a friend, as in a 255 B.C. letter of recommendation.

definition: To dig down deep, as when laying a foundation by excavating into the ground.
article: βαθύνω comes from βαθύς ("deep") and means to deepen or dig down, picturing the careful work of excavating before building. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 6:48, where a wise builder digs deep to set a foundation on rock; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "flood" there, though the verb itself describes the deepening, not the flood. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it just three times, and Moulton-Milligan note it is rare enough that they could point to only a single comparable instance (Philo) of this transitive verb being used to mean "go deep."
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with very thin attestation, and the lexical sources ("to deepen, dig deep") do not match the measured rendering "flood," so the meaning rests on sparse evidence.

definition: To spend or waste time, lingering somewhere instead of moving on.
article: χρονοτριβέω literally combines the ideas of "time" and "wearing away," so it pictures someone using up time by lingering. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 20:16, where Paul chose not to spend time in Asia, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "past" in every occurrence. Moulton-Milligan note that the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri from 162–161 BC, showing it was ordinary, practical vocabulary rather than a specialized term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical evidence alone.

definition: To make a deep, loud animal sound, like the bellowing of an ox or the roar of a lion or the sea.
article: This verb describes a deep, booming cry — originally the lowing or bellowing of cattle, but also the roar of a lion or even the sea. It appears just once in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sounded" (Revelation 10:3), and the BSB independently agrees. Interestingly, an inscription cited by Moulton-Milligan uses the same word for the heavy roar of the sea surging in deep caverns, showing its range beyond animals.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single passage.

definition: To turn your mind toward something — to pay close attention, watch carefully, or be on guard against danger.
article: At its core προσέχω means to direct your mind toward something, which in the New Testament spreads across three closely related ideas: being on guard (beware), watching over (yourself or others), and paying attention. The senses are evenly distributed — "beware" accounts for 6 of 24 uses (46%), with "watch" and "pay attention" each at 3 (23%) — and the Berean Standard Bible agrees with every measured rendering. One nice detail: in everyday Koine papyri a father from B.C. 152 used it to mean "taking heed lest he should find anything to say against you," the same wary sense behind warnings like Luke 21:34.
caution: In 11 of 24 occurrences the word is absorbed into the phrasing without its own English word, so its exact force often depends on context.

definition: The act of making something openly known or visible, a disclosure that brings what was hidden into plain sight.
article: φανέρωσις refers to making something openly known or visible—a manifestation or disclosure. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 12:7 and 2 Corinthians 4:2), so its range is narrow; the Majority Standard Bible renders one occurrence as "manifestation" and the other in terms of "open" disclosure. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, where Moulton-Milligan note it paired with εἴδησις ("knowledge") in documents as late as A.D. 710, showing it stayed in ordinary use.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and disagreement between the two measured renderings, the precise range of this word is hard to pin down.

definition: The flat roof or top of a house, used in ancient times as a place to stand, sleep, or proclaim things.
article: In the New Testament δῶμα almost always means the flat roof of a house, which served as a usable space where people could stand or call out (housetop, 4 of 7 occurrences, 80%). The one outlier in Luke 12:3 still refers to the rooftop as a place from which something is openly proclaimed. Though the classical lexica note it could mean a whole house or hall in poetry, the Septuagint and New Testament settle firmly on "roof," matching Hebrew גָּג (the roof) 22 of 28 times. A vivid everyday parallel comes from a papyrus (P Oxy III.475, A.D. 182) describing a young slave who leaned out from the δῶμα of a house to watch street performers below.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and 2 absorbed into phrasing, the single "proclamation" sense rests on just one verse.

definition: A Greek unit of distance equal to about 600 Greek feet, or one-eighth of a Roman mile.
article: Στάδιον is a unit of length—roughly an eighth of a Roman mile, or about a furlong. In the Byzantine New Testament it shows up 6 times across 4 books, and translators usually convert it into modern terms: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "miles" 3 times (75%) and keeps the transliterated "stadia" once (25%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Because a stade was the length of the Olympic racecourse, the word also came to mean the racetrack itself (as in 1 Corinthians 9:24), and everyday papyri even use σταδίου as the heading for lists of athletes.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 6 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use—so the measured senses cover distance only and miss the well-attested "racecourse" meaning noted by the lexica.

definition: To nail or fasten something firmly to a surface, used figuratively for fixing a document or record in place.
article: προσηλόω literally means to nail or spike something fast to a surface. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Colossians 2:14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "canceled" (and the BSB agrees), picturing a record of debt nailed up and so done away with. The word is solid everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite inscriptions about gold objects nailed on, bronze tablets fastened up, and a workshop boarded shut, plus its one other Greek Bible appearance in 3 Maccabees 4:9.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its figurative range in Scripture rests on a single verse.

definition: The act of speaking evil about someone behind their back; slander or harmful gossip.
article: καταλαλία refers to speaking against someone — slander, backbiting, or running someone down when they aren't present. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and translators render it consistently as "slander" in both places (2 Corinthians 12:20 and 1 Peter 2:1). Outside the New Testament it is rare even in the Septuagint, showing up just once, in Wisdom 1:11.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and minimal wider attestation, the evidence base for this word is thin.

definition: To have sexual relations with someone other than one's own spouse; to break the marriage bond by being unfaithful.
article: This verb means to commit adultery—to violate marriage through sexual unfaithfulness. All 14 New Testament occurrences point to the same core idea, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "commit adultery" in 71% of cases and the remaining instances being grammatical variations of the same act. The Septuagint uses it 11 times, mostly for Hebrew נָאַף (8×), the verb in the Ten Commandments' prohibition of adultery; interestingly it also stands twice for רָצַח ("to murder"), and Revelation 2:22 stretches it metaphorically to describe idolatry. The everyday papyri confirm it was ordinary Koine, with one astrological text noting men who "commit adultery" against their own wives.

definition: The metal iron, used for tools, weapons, and as a valuable trade commodity.
article: σίδηρος means iron, the common and useful metal. Every reference work here—Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith, and Moulton-Milligan—agrees on this single meaning, and the Septuagint backs it up with 58 uses, most of them translating the Hebrew word בַּרְזֶל ("iron") 35 times. The everyday papyri make the word feel concrete: one document from 256 B.C. mentions "ten talents of iron," and another describes laborers pledging their iron tools as collateral.
caution: The single New Testament occurrence (Rev 18:12) is here rendered "silk," which contradicts every lexicon's gloss of "iron"—this is almost certainly a data error, since all sources and the LXX point firmly to "iron."

definition: Belonging to or produced by the Spirit, or relating to the human spirit as opposed to the physical or worldly.
article: πνευματικός is the adjective built from πνεῦμα ("spirit" or "breath"), and across the Byzantine New Testament it almost always means "spiritual" — 22 of 25 times (88%) — describing things or people connected to the Spirit, in contrast to what is physical, fleshly, or worldly. Twice (8%) the same word stands in for "spiritual gifts" in passages like 1 Corinthians 12:1 and 14:1. Abbott-Smith notes its older sense "of the wind or breath," and the everyday papyri confirm it was common Koine vocabulary, even appearing in a fourth-century letter about a "spiritual threatening."

definition: A wall, especially the wall of a house or building.
article: τοῖχος means a wall, particularly the wall of a house or dwelling, distinct from a city wall (τεῖχος, its close relative). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 23:3, where it is used figuratively in Paul's outburst about a "whitewashed wall." In the Septuagint it shows up 71 times, most often translating the Hebrew קִיר (49×), and the everyday papyri confirm its ordinary sense — one document from 221 B.C. mentions someone wanting to finish building a half-completed wall.
caution: The measured NT sense is labeled "violate," which reflects how the figurative Acts 23:3 phrase was rendered rather than the word's actual meaning of "wall"; with only one NT occurrence, lean on the Septuagint and papyri evidence for its plain sense.

definition: Set against or in opposition to someone or something; as a noun, an adversary or opponent.
article: ὑπεναντίος describes something or someone set in opposition — either contrary to a person (as in Colossians 2:14, where the written record stood against us) or, used as a noun, an outright adversary (as in Hebrews 10:27). It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, but turns up 25 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew word for "foe" or "adversary" (צָר, 7 times). Everyday Koine papyri use it in a legal sense: an early second-century will (P Oxy III.493) forbids anyone to do anything "opposed to" its provisions.
caution: Confidence is low: with only two New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing rather than translated as a single English word, the precise force in each passage is somewhat uncertain.

definition: To love being first, craving the top position and recognition over others.
article: φιλοπρωτεύω describes someone who craves preeminence — literally a love of being first. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 3 John 1:9, describing Diotrephes, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "loves" (to be first), with the BSB agreeing 100%. The word is built from φίλος (loving) and πρῶτος (first); Moulton-Milligan note that while a once-cited papyrus example turned out to be erroneous, the closely parallel verb φιλοπονέω ("I love labor, I am industrious") shows up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from corpus usage alone.

definition: A casting-net thrown out over the water to catch fish.
article: This word names a fishing net, specifically the round casting-net a fisherman flings out so it spreads over the water — the name literally pictures something "thrown around." It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament and five times in the Greek Old Testament, where it renders several different Hebrew words for nets and snares, including חֵרֶם, the term it most often translates. Abbott-Smith notes that beyond fishing the underlying idea is simply "something thrown around," even a garment, though the fishing sense dominates.
caution: Evidence is thin — only a handful of occurrences, and in the New Testament both uses are blended into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word.

definition: To open something—such as a door, mouth, eyes, book, or the heavens—so that it is no longer shut.
article: ἀνοίγω is the everyday verb for opening things: doors, mouths, eyes, books, tombs, and even the sky. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 78 times, with the renderings "opened" (46%) and "open" (45%) accounting for nearly all uses, plus a small idiomatic sense where someone "opens" their mouth and so "began" to speak (3×, as in Matthew 5:2 and Acts 8:35). In the Septuagint it shows up 139 times, most often translating the Hebrew פָּתַח ("to open," 89×), and Moulton-Milligan note that this verb's tangled augmented spellings tripped up ancient scribes in the papyri much as they would a modern schoolboy.
caution: The "began" sense is really an idiom for opening the mouth to speak, not a separate meaning of the verb itself.

definition: A previously fixed deadline or appointed day, especially one set in advance by law or agreement.
article: προθέσμιος refers to a time set beforehand, most often a deadline fixed in advance. In Galatians 4:2, its only New Testament appearance, it describes the date a father has set for his child to come of age. This was a common legal term in everyday life: the papyri use the related noun προθεσμία for things like "the appointed time for the second year" and "the stipulated date" in contracts and claims.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A brood of young birds, or the nest where they are gathered together.
article: νοσσιά refers to a brood of baby birds, and by extension the nest that holds them. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 13:34, where Jesus pictures gathering Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her brood. It is more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 15 times and most often translates the Hebrew קֵן ("nest," 8 times); Moulton-Milligan note it is a later, contracted form of the classical νεοσσιά and turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: The digest's measured sense label "unwilling" plainly mismatches the actual meaning ("brood"), so the single NT rendering data should be treated with caution.

definition: Syracuse, a city on the eastern coast of the island of Sicily.
article: This is simply the name of Syracuse, a town on the eastern coast of Sicily, which appears just once in the New Testament when Paul's ship stops there (Acts 28:12). Every source agrees on the meaning, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Syracuse" in its single occurrence. Interestingly, the Greek form is plural (literally "the Syracuses"), which Moulton-Milligan explains came from the city being both a fortified citadel and a settlement in the valley, though a singular form later appeared in everyday usage.
caution: This is a proper place name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests on its single context and outside historical knowledge rather than varied usage.

definition: To construct a building or structure, and figuratively to build up and strengthen a person or community.
article: οἰκοδομέω means literally to build—houses, towers, barns, city walls—and the Byzantine New Testament uses it this way overwhelmingly, with "build" accounting for 23 of 39 occurrences (88%). It's a thoroughly everyday word: papyri from as early as 218 B.C. use it for digging foundations and constructing dams "at the expense of no small sum." In the Septuagint it appears 371 times, almost always rendering Hebrew בָּנָה ("to build"), 292 times. Beyond the literal, the lexica note a figurative sense of building up character or encouraging—"edify"—which surfaces in renderings like "edified."

definition: Joanna, a woman who followed Jesus; she was the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward.
article: Ἰωάννα is a personal name, the female form of the name behind Ἰωάννης (John), tracing back to an Aramaic original. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in Luke (8:3 and 24:10), and is always rendered "Joanna." The two "senses" simply reflect the same name appearing in different contexts — once among the women supporting Jesus, where Dodson identifies her as the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, and once among the women at the empty tomb.
caution: This is a proper name with only two occurrences, so its range is fixed by context rather than meaning; the two measured senses are the same name, not distinct meanings.

definition: An attention-grabbing call meaning roughly "come now!" or "look here!" used to address one or more people.
article: Strictly speaking ἄγε is the command form of the verb ἄγω ("to lead"), but it had hardened into a fixed exclamation, like saying "come on!" or "now then!" to grab a listener's attention. Abbott-Smith notes it works just like another such interjection, φέρε, and can be addressed to either one person or several. Though it does not appear in the Byzantine NT counted here, the lexicon points to James 4:13 and 5:1, where it opens a pointed address.
caution: The digest records zero Byzantine occurrences and rests almost entirely on a single lexicon entry, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: Crescens, the name of a Christian associate of the apostle Paul.
article: Crescens is a personal name borne by a Christian co-worker of Paul, mentioned just once in the New Testament. In 2 Timothy 4:10 Paul notes that Crescens had gone to Galatia. The name is of Latin origin (related to the idea of "growing"), which fits the Roman naming background of many believers in this period.
caution: This name appears only once in the entire New Testament, so almost nothing can be said about the person beyond that single mention.

definition: A populated settlement, large or small, often walled, where people live together as a community.
article: πόλις refers to any settled human community, from a large city to a modest town — the size distinction is left to the translator, since the Majority Standard Bible renders it "city" 99 times (61%) and "town" 61 times (38%). It is frequently set in contrast to villages and open countryside (κῶμαι, ἀγροί), and can stand for the inhabitants of a place as well as the place itself. In the Septuagint it appears over 1,300 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew word עִיר (996×); it could also designate Jerusalem as "the holy city." One curiosity: the papyri preserve an ancient by-form πτόλις, which even shows up as a personal name in tax records from the reign of Caligula.

definition: A person who treats others with violent, insolent contempt, trampling on their dignity and rights.
article: This word describes someone whose arrogance spills over into outright cruelty — a person who not only despises others but mistreats them. Paul uses it of his own pre-conversion self in 1 Timothy 1:13, and it appears again in Romans 1:30; the Byzantine New Testament has just two occurrences. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times and most often translates the Hebrew word for "proud" or "haughty," linking the violence to underlying arrogance, while Moulton-Milligan notes its everyday sense in the papyri stresses an outrageous disregard for other people's rights.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the translations ranging from "violent" to "insolent" to "injurious," the precise force is hard to pin down.

definition: An impersonal verb meaning it is necessary, one must, or one ought to do something.
article: δεῖ is an impersonal verb ("it is necessary") that links to an infinitive to say something must or ought to happen. It is so woven into the grammar that in 84 of its 103 Byzantine occurrences it carries no English word of its own, and where it does surface the Majority Standard Bible splits evenly between rendering it as "things" (in phrases like what "must" take place) and "ought." An everyday papyrus captures the same flavor: "even if you have to pawn your cloak," showing this was ordinary Koine for plain obligation or necessity, not a special religious term.
caution: Because δεῖ is usually absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single word, the measured sense percentages cover only a minority of its occurrences.

definition: A personal name of a man greeted by Paul in Rome, described as his kinsman and fellow prisoner.
article: Andronicus is a proper name, appearing just once in the New Testament at Romans 16:7, where Paul greets him alongside Junia as a kinsman or fellow-countryman who was outstanding among the apostles. The name was widely used across the Roman Empire, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including one from Priene dating to the first century BC. It derives from the Greek words for 'man' and 'victory,' which is why Strong's offers the literal sense 'man of victory,' though as a name it simply identifies this individual.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage rests on a single verse.

definition: To handle or teach a message correctly, literally to cut something straight, as one would cut a straight road or path.
article: This word combines "straight" (ὀρθός) and "cut" (τέμνω), giving a literal idea of making a straight cut, which the Septuagint uses twice in Proverbs for cutting straight paths, translating the Hebrew yashar ("to make straight"). In the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 2:15, where it describes correctly handling "the word of truth." Its exact metaphor is genuinely uncertain: Moulton-Milligan compares it to a similarly built word for making a new assertion and concludes the stress falls on "straight," so it likely means "teach the word rightly," while Sophocles renders it "expound soundly"; the familiar KJV "rightly divide" reflects the literal cutting image.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only two further Septuagint occurrences, and the lexicons openly admit its precise metaphor is unclear.

definition: A house or dwelling place, or by extension the family and people who live in it.
article: οἶκος covers both the physical building and the people inside it. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 114 times, rendered "house" 62 times (61%), "home" 27 times (26%), and "household" 13 times (13%), with all three readings confirmed independently by the BSB. It is a workhorse word of everyday Koine, documented across ordinary papyri and inscriptions, and in the Septuagint it appears nearly 1,900 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew בָּ֫יִת ("house"). It also stretches to cover a sanctuary or temple — the "house of God" — as well as figurative uses like the body or a city.

definition: A word, saying, or statement that is spoken—and, by extension, the matter or thing being talked about.
article: At its core ῥῆμα is something said—a word, saying, or statement—and in the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "word" 32 of 69 times (59%). But it also stretches to mean the matter or thing being discussed, which is why translators sometimes give it as "what" or even "made," especially in the more Hebraic parts of Luke's writings. This wider "thing, affair" sense comes straight from the Hebrew: in the Septuagint ῥῆμα renders דָּבָר 355 times, a word that itself means both "word" and "thing," and everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain "spoken word" meaning alongside it.

definition: To plead or intercede on someone's behalf, stepping in to make a petition for them.
article: This verb means to step in and make a petition for someone else, combining the idea of "on behalf of" (ὑπέρ) with "intercede" (ἐντυγχάνω). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 8:26, where the translators folded it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that the word does not seem to occur outside early Christian literature, though the simpler verb ἐντυγχάνω is well attested in everyday papyri with a wide range of meaning, including someone literally going to a person to petition them about a matter.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and apparently nowhere else outside early Christian writings, so its range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Being without God—not knowing or having no relationship with the true God.
article: In its single New Testament occurrence (Ephesians 2:12), ἄθεος describes Gentiles as living "without God" in the world—not knowing the true God rather than actively denying his existence. Classical writers used the word with a wider range, including slighting or denying the gods, being ungodly, or even being abandoned by the gods. Strikingly, the everyday papyri and inscriptions preserve the popular cry "Away with the atheists," which was hurled at the early Christians themselves—as in the account of Polycarp's martyrdom—showing how flexible and loaded the term could be.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical sense rests on a single verse and is illuminated mainly by classical and documentary parallels.

definition: To throw or toss something onto something else, used both for physical objects and figuratively for handing over one's worries.
article: This verb means to throw or cast one thing upon another. In its 2 Byzantine New Testament appearances it splits evenly: once literally, when people threw their cloaks over a colt (Luke 19:35), and once figuratively, urging believers to cast their anxiety onto God (1 Peter 5:7). The Septuagint uses it 13 times, most often translating the Hebrew שָׁלַך ("to throw"), and Abbott-Smith notes the figurative "cast your care" wording in Peter echoes that Old Testament background.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 occurrences in the Byzantine text and none in the SBLGNT critical text, so confidence is low.

definition: To take someone captive in war and lead them away as a prisoner.
article: This verb means to capture people and carry them off as prisoners, the way conquerors did with the defeated. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 2 times, both rendered "led" (as in leading captive), but it is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 35 times across 16 books. There it most often translates the Hebrew שָׁבָה (18×), the word for taking captives in battle. Lexicons treat it as equivalent to the closely related αἰχμαλωτίζω.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin—only 2 occurrences (1 in the critical text)—so the meaning rests largely on Septuagint usage.

definition: To rekindle or fan a fire back into full flame, used figuratively for stirring something up again.
article: This vivid compound literally means to relight or fan a fire back to life, built from the words for 'living' and 'fire.' In the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 1:6, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'fan,' urging Timothy to fan into flame the gift within him. Though rare in Scripture (only here and once in the Septuagint, at 1 Maccabees), the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri — including an occult pamphlet that speaks of something 'rekindling all the books.'
caution: Confidence is low because the word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its full range rests on slim evidence.

definition: A literal covering or veil, used figuratively for a cover-up or pretext that hides something underneath.
senseLabels: a covering used as a pretext
article: This noun comes from the verb meaning "to cover over," and at root it names a literal covering or veil. Its single New Testament appearance (1 Peter 2:16) uses it figuratively, warning against using freedom as a cover for wickedness. The Septuagint shows the literal side, using it of a covering for the tabernacle in Exodus 26:14 and 39:34, where it renders the Hebrew word for a covering (מְכַסֶּה).
caution: The word appears only once in the Byzantine NT and is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, so the measured "Live" rendering reflects translation of the surrounding phrase rather than the word's core meaning of "covering/pretext."

definition: Eubulus, a male Christian who was with Paul in Rome and sent greetings in 2 Timothy.
article: Eubulus is a personal name, mentioned just once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 4:21), where he is among the Christians in Rome who send greetings to Timothy. The name is built from the Greek words for "well" (εὖ) and "to wish" or "to will" (βούλομαι), which is why Strong's glosses it as "good-willer," but in practice it simply functions as someone's name. Note that the measured rendering data here labels the occurrence as "Claudia," which appears to be a slip, since Eubulus and Claudia are listed together in that same verse.
caution: Evidence is thin: this is a single-occurrence proper name, and the measured rendering oddly shows "Claudia" rather than "Eubulus," suggesting a data alignment error.

definition: Salamis, the chief city at the eastern end of the island of Cyprus.
article: Σαλαμίς is the name of the principal city of Cyprus, located at the eastern end of the island. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:5, where Paul and Barnabas proclaim God's word there, and every translation surveyed renders it simply "Salamis." Its name probably derives from σάλος, the surge or swell of the sea on the shore, and Moulton-Milligan note that some manuscripts read an alternate dative form, Σαλαμίνῃ, in Acts 13:5.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage rests on a single attestation.

definition: The act of correcting or setting something right again, especially the restoring of a person's life or conduct.
article: This noun describes putting something back into proper order — correction, restoration, or reformation. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:16, where Scripture is said to be useful for "correction." In everyday Koine it had both a literal and a figurative sense: an inscription uses it for the physical repair of the temple of Artemis, while Oxyrhynchus papyri use it for the official "correction" of legal abstracts, matching the moral sense in 2 Timothy.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament; note that the measured rendering "breathed" reflects a data glitch rather than the actual meaning, which the glosses and papyri consistently give as "correction."

definition: The mustard plant, known for its tiny seed that grows into a large shrub.
article: σίναπι simply means mustard, the plant grown from a famously tiny seed, and all five New Testament occurrences refer to it. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "mustard" in 60% of cases, with the remaining instances adding context like being planted (Matthew 13:31) or being the smallest of seeds (Mark 4:31) — these reflect the verse's wording, not separate meanings. Everyday Koine papyri confirm it was an ordinary commodity: one letter from around AD 100 asks that "the mustard that is with you" be handed over to the bearer, and others list it being measured out in choinices and artabas.
caution: Dodson notes it probably refers to the shrub rather than the herb, but the precise plant species is not fully certain.

definition: To say something in advance—either predicting what will happen or giving an earlier warning or statement.
article: προλέγω combines πρό ("before") with λέγω ("say"), and its meaning hinges on what that "before" points to: sometimes it means foretelling the future (foretold, 4× or 31% in the Byzantine NT), and sometimes simply saying or warning someone in advance of an event (told before, 3×; warn, 3×). The senses overlap and translators split fairly evenly between them. A nice glimpse of the everyday sense comes from a marriage contract from the time of Augustus, where προλέγω just means the two parties "settle terms beforehand"—the plain, non-prophetic use Moulton-Milligan highlights.
caution: Abbott-Smith notes the same passages (2 Cor, Gal, 1 Thess) can be read either as "tell beforehand" or "tell plainly," so individual cases are genuinely disputed.

definition: To set something or someone straight again — physically straightening a bent body or rebuilding a fallen structure.
article: ἀνορθόω means to set upright or restore something that had been bent, broken, or fallen. The New Testament uses it both ways: of straightening a person's body (Luke 13:13) and of rebuilding a structure (Acts 15:16), with its three occurrences split evenly between these uses. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the building sense vividly — one second-century inscription says a man "restored" a gateway that had decayed over time at his own expense — and in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew כּוּן, "to establish."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, the measured sense range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Producing fruit; describing something that bears crops or yields produce.
article: καρποφόρος literally means "fruit-bearing," built from καρπός (fruit) and φέρω (to bear or carry). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 14:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it loosely as "goodness" in describing fruitful seasons God provides. The everyday Koine evidence is vivid: a Median parchment from 88 B.C. describes a vineyard with vine-stocks "both those in bearing and those not" (καρποφόροις τε καὶ ἀκάρποις), and the word even served as a title for the goddess Demeter, "the fruit-bearer."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the MSB's "goodness" is a contextual paraphrase rather than the word's core meaning of "fruit-bearing."

definition: To announce something publicly, telling it out openly so others hear and know it.
article: This verb means to declare or proclaim something out loud and in the open, built from the parts meaning "out" and "announce/messenger." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Peter 2:9), where believers are called to proclaim God's praises. The word was at home in ordinary Koine: a fourth-century magical papyrus uses it for "announcing" things that had happened, and inscriptions use it for publicly reporting or proclaiming, while in the Greek Old Testament it shows up 9 times, often for telling out God's deeds.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single passage, so confidence is low.

definition: To engage in sexual immorality, especially giving oneself over completely to it; in the Septuagint often picturing unfaithfulness to God.
article: This is an intensified form of the verb πoρνεύω ("to commit fornication"), built with the prefix ἐκ- to suggest going all the way into sexual immorality. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Jude 1:7, where both the Majority Standard Bible and BSB render it with reference to sexual sin. The most striking evidence comes from the Septuagint, where it occurs 46 times and almost always translates the Hebrew זָנָה (45 times) — frequently used figuratively for Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness to God, not just literal sexual sin.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the single measured "sexual" sense gives a thin basis, though the broader Septuagint figurative usage is well attested.

definition: A possessive word meaning "your" or "yours," pointing to what belongs to a single person being addressed.
article: σός is the possessive form of "you" (singular), meaning "your" or "yours." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 27 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "your" in 63% of cases, with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. It often stands on its own as a noun: οἱ σοί means "your kinsfolk or friends" (Mark 5:19), and τὰ σά means "your goods" (Luke 6:30) — a usage the everyday Koine papyri confirm, where ὁ σός could mean "your household, agent, or friend."

definition: To be away from home, living somewhere other than one's own place or residence.
article: This verb describes being away from home or abroad, the opposite of being settled in one's own residence. Paul uses it just 3 times, all in 2 Corinthians 5, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it twice with the idea of being away from "home" and once folds it into the surrounding phrasing. Everyday papyri confirm the plain sense: one Tebtunis document (A.D. 99) requires people to give notice "if we change our residence, or go abroad," showing the word was ordinary Koine for leaving town.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences, all from a single passage in 2 Corinthians.

definition: To cast someone down into Tartarus, the underworld place of punishment, and hold them imprisoned there.
article: This verb means to thrust someone into Tartarus, the Greek name for the deepest pit of the underworld where the damned were confined. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 2:4, describing how God cast the sinning angels down into that prison; the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "deep" there. Strikingly, outside the Bible the word is so rare that Moulton-Milligan can cite it only from a scholion on the Iliad, though they note a related noun "Tartarus" appears on a third- or fourth-century magic tablet.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire New Testament and is extremely rare elsewhere, so its precise force rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Set apart for God — sacred, pure, and worthy of reverence; as a noun, God's consecrated people.
article: At its core ἅγιος means set apart for God: holy, sacred, belonging to him and so worthy of reverence. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "holy" in 173 of 240 New Testament occurrences (74%) and "saints" in the other 61 (26%), the latter referring to God's consecrated people rather than to morally perfect heroes. In the Septuagint it appears 635 times, chiefly translating Hebrew קֹדֶשׁ ("holiness, sacred thing"), and the everyday papyri and inscriptions show the same word used as a title of the gods — for example "to the holy most high God" — confirming that "sacred, set apart" was its ordinary public meaning.

definition: To assign or render to someone what is properly due to them, such as honor or rights.
senseLabels: to assign or render what's due
article: This verb is built from "apo" plus the root behind "nomos" (law), and its core idea is apportioning to people what rightly belongs to them. In the everyday Koine papyri it shows up in administrative contexts—one Prefect is praised for "rendering to all their due," and the Rosetta Stone uses it for granting justice to everyone. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:7, where husbands are told to render honor to their wives. The classical and documentary evidence consistently points to "assign, render as due," so the Majority Standard Bible's single rendering as "delicate" reflects a particular interpretive choice in that verse rather than the word's measured range.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "delicate" sits oddly against the lexicons and papyri, which all point to "assign or render what is due."

definition: The owner or operator of a merchant ship, the person responsible for the vessel and its cargo.
senseLabels: owner or captain of a ship
article: Naúklēros refers to the man who owned or ran a cargo ship, distinct from the helmsman who actually steered. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "pilot," though the older lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) and the KJV favor "shipowner" or "shipmaster." Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine papyri use the word freely, including two receipts from 221 BC showing the Ptolemaic rulers themselves owned ships and hired them out for transporting grain.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the sources disagree on whether it means "owner" or "captain/pilot," so its precise force here is uncertain.

definition: To become angry or enraged, feeling strong displeasure toward someone or something.
article: This verb means to become angry, and in the New Testament it always appears in the passive sense—someone is provoked to anger rather than provoking others. The eight Byzantine occurrences split evenly between milder "angry" (3×) and stronger "enraged" (3×), so the same word covers a range from personal irritation to full fury, as when a king is enraged in Matthew 22:7. In the Septuagint it shows up 68 times and most often translates the vivid Hebrew חָרָה (29×), an idiom meaning roughly that anger "burned" within a person.
caution: It appears 8 times in the Byzantine text but 0 in the critical SBLGNT, so witnesses disagree on where it actually occurs.

definition: Chaff — the dry husks and straw separated from grain during threshing and winnowing.
article: ἄχυρον refers to chaff, the worthless husks and bits of straw left over after grain is threshed and winnowed. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17), both times in the image of chaff being burned with unquenchable fire, and the Septuagint uses it 22 times, mostly to render Hebrew תֶּבֶן ("straw"). A nice detail from the Koine papyri: documents show straw being mixed into bricks for building, echoing the brick-making of the Exodus story and confirming this was an ordinary, everyday word.
caution: Though confidence is computed as low due to only two New Testament occurrences, the sense is consistent and uncontested across all sources.

definition: A drinking party or carousing—a social gathering centered on drinking alcohol, often to excess.
article: πότος names a drinking-bout or carousal, a social event built around heavy drinking. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 4:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it loosely within a phrase about one's past way of life. In the Septuagint, where it occurs 27 times across 9 books, it most often translates the Hebrew מִשְׁתֶּה (21×) and there carries the broader sense of a feast or banquet, as in Genesis 19:3, rather than strictly a drunken party.
caution: Evidence is thin—just one New Testament occurrence—and the Septuagint's broader "banquet" sense sits alongside the narrower "drinking-bout" meaning the lexicons emphasize.

definition: To cover something over, hide it from view, or conceal it, whether literally or figuratively.
article: καλύπτω means to cover, hide, or conceal — used both literally (a lamp covered by a jar) and figuratively (sins veiled or forgiven). In the New Testament it appears only 8 times, where the Berean Standard Bible renders it "covers" in the clearest cases like Luke 8:16 and 23:30. Its strongest footprint is in the Septuagint, where it occurs 76 times across 19 books and almost always translates the Hebrew כָּסָה ("to cover"), 58 of those times.
caution: With only 8 New Testament occurrences, the figurative range (veiling, concealing, forgiving sins) rests mostly on Septuagint and lexical evidence rather than measured NT senses.

definition: The leg, the part of the body from the hip downward.
article: σκέλος is a plain, everyday word for a leg, the part of the body from the hip down. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in John 19 (verses 31-33), describing how the soldiers broke the legs of those crucified but not those of Jesus. Everyday Koine papyri use the word the same literal way — one document from 157 B.C. even records a man slashing someone's leg with a knife. (The two "senses" measured here are really just one literal meaning split by how the Bible rendered neighboring phrases.)
caution: The word is rare in the New Testament (only 3 occurrences, all in one passage), but its single literal meaning is well supported by the Septuagint, papyri, and lexicons.

definition: To obtain or attain something, to happen or chance, or (in a participle) to be ordinary or commonplace.
article: τυγχάνω literally means to hit a mark, and from there it stretches to obtain something, to happen by chance, or to describe what is merely commonplace. In the Byzantine NT it appears 13 times but is so woven into Greek idiom that 6 of those uses carry no separate English word at all; the measured sense the Berean translators settled on is "extraordinary" (2 times, as in Acts 19:11 and 28:2), where the negated participle "not ordinary" describes God's striking miracles. Tellingly, this word turns up constantly in everyday papyri — petitions asking that someone "receive" justice or relief — which is why its core idea is simply attaining or meeting with whatever comes one's way.
caution: Most of its NT uses are idiomatic phrasing rather than a single clean gloss, so the lexicons spread its range widely (obtain, happen, perhaps, ordinary) and no one English word captures it.

definition: A state of public shame or disgrace, especially the social humiliation that brings reproach upon a person.
article: Ὄνειδος refers to disgrace or reproach — the kind of public shame that damages a person's standing. It appears only once in the New Testament, where Elizabeth says God has taken away her "disgrace" among the people (Luke 1:25), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "disgrace" every time. It is far more common in the Septuagint (39 times), most often translating the Hebrew word חֶרְפָּה, "reproach."
