definition: One's life as it is lived out over time, or the resources and possessions that sustain that life.
article: βίος covers life in the practical, lived-out sense — both the span of a person's life and the material means (money, goods, property) that keep that life going. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times, but in 7 of those the Majority Standard Bible folds it into a phrase rather than rendering it with a single English word; the most common standalone rendering is simply "live." Lexicographers note that βίος differs from ζωή: ζωή is the inner vital principle, while βίος is the life we actually live and the resources by which we sustain it — and the everyday papyri confirm this, using βίος for "the rest of your life" and a person's lifespan.
caution: With only 11 occurrences and 7 of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured English evidence is thin, so the two-sense split rests mainly on the lexica rather than the corpus data.

definition: To step or climb into something, especially to board a boat or vessel.
article: ἐμβαίνω means to step into something, and in the New Testament that something is almost always a boat — the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "got (into)" in over 80% of its 19 occurrences. The word is built from ἐν ("in") plus the root for stepping, so its core idea is literally "to step in." Everyday papyri show the same broad range: one document warns about what happens "if an ox trespass" (literally steps) onto another person's land, while others describe boarding a ship, showing the word covered both casual stepping-in and formal embarking.
caution: In John 5:4 (the stirring of the pool) the word appears only in the Byzantine text and is omitted by some critical editions.

definition: Describing a person who loves and prioritizes themselves above others; selfish.
article: φίλαυτος is built from φίλος (loving) and αὐτός (self), so it literally means "self-loving" and carries the negative sense of being selfish. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:2, where it heads a list of bad traits in the last days; the Septuagint never uses it. The word was current in everyday Koine, showing up in papyri and inscriptions, and Philo memorably pairs it with "godless" to describe the mind that thinks itself equal to God.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured from multiple uses.

definition: Active hostility or enmity—a state of opposition and ill-will between people, or between people and God.
article: ἔχθρα means hostility or enmity—an active state of opposition, whether between human groups or between people and God. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "hostility" in 3 of its 6 New Testament occurrences (60%), with the remaining cases either rephrased ("hostile," or absorbed into wider wording like "abolishing this"). Everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: one second-century BC document (P Hib I.170) hopes "that we may not make enmity instead of friendship," pairing ἔχθρα directly against φιλία (friendship), and a royal ordinance even uses the spelled variant ἔκθρα for a "private quarrel."
caution: With only 6 occurrences, two of the three measured "senses" are really just translation rephrasings of the same core idea—enmity—rather than genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: To fall into something, whether a literal pit or trap, or figuratively into trouble, judgment, or temptation.
article: ἐμπίπτω literally means to fall into something—a pit, a hole, or someone's hands—and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times, all rendered "fall," both literally (a sheep falling into a pit in Matthew 12:11) and figuratively (falling into judgment or temptation in 1 Timothy). In the Septuagint it appears 31 times and lends itself to vivid phrases like "fall into the hands of God" (Hebrews 10:31 echoes this). One nice detail from the papyri: the word was everyday commercial language, where money could "fall into" an account, and it could even carry the stronger sense of falling upon someone in attack.

definition: Describing something magnificent or splendid; used as a noun for great deeds or mighty works.
senseLabels: great deeds of a mighty one
article: This adjective comes from μέγας ("great") and means magnificent or splendid, usually appearing as a noun for "great things" or mighty works. It is rare in the New Testament, occurring just twice in the Byzantine text and only once in the critical text (Acts 2:11), where it describes the "wonderful works of God." An interesting detail from the papyri is that μεγαλεῖον became a ceremonial title of honor—"his highness" or "your magnificence"—used for Caesar and even officials like a Prefect.
caution: With only two occurrences and disagreement among renderings, the precise sense in each passage rests on thin evidence.

definition: A person from the city of Laodicea.
article: This word simply names someone who lives in Laodicea, a city in Asia Minor. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Colossians 4:16, where Paul mentions a letter going to or from the Laodiceans. The same form shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions and decrees from outside the Bible—one inscription from around 200 B.C. records 'a decree from the Laodiceans,' confirming it as a normal civic term for the city's residents.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: A lack of knowledge or understanding, especially a culpable or shameful ignorance.
article: ἀγνωσία is the negative of γνῶσις (knowledge), so it means simply "ignorance" — being without knowledge or understanding. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 15:34 and 1 Peter 2:15), and both times it carries a sense of blameworthy or shameful ignorance rather than innocent unawareness. A papyrus from the first or second century AD uses the word with exactly that flavor of "disgraceful ignorance," matching the tone of both biblical occurrences.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the standard rendering of one of them flagged as "Sober" (where the BSB instead reads "ignorance"), the measured data here is thin and the first sense label is uncertain.

definition: In a wasteful, reckless way that throws money and resources away.
article: This adverb describes how someone spends or lives in a reckless, wasteful manner — its single New Testament appearance is the prodigal son who "squandered" his inheritance in Luke 15:13. The traditional renderings stretch toward "riotous" or "dissolute" living, but Abbott-Smith notes the word does not necessarily imply immorality, only wastefulness. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it once for the Hebrew word for being defiant or unruly (Proverbs 7:11), and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday papyri, where the company it keeps points to a loose, undisciplined way of life.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its exact shade — pure wastefulness versus dissolute living — is genuinely disputed among the sources.

definition: A number—a count or total amount of people or things reckoned up.
article: ἀριθμός simply means a number—the total you get when you count something up, whether people coming to faith or a crowd too vast to tally. The New Testament use is remarkably consistent: of 19 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "number" in 12 (86%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing rather than carrying a separate sense. In the Septuagint it appears 144 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew מִסְפָּר (115×), and Moulton-Milligan note an interesting twist in everyday Koine: the dative ἀριθμῷ could mean "a few" (as in papyri instructions to deliver "a few" rather than a precisely counted lot).

definition: To spread something out flat, such as cloaks on a road or coverings to furnish a room or bed.
article: στρώννυμι means to spread something out — cloaks laid across a road, or coverings and carpets arranged to furnish a room. In the New Testament it appears 7 times across 4 books, used both for spreading garments on the path (Matthew 21:8, Mark 11:8) and for a furnished upper room (Mark 14:15, Luke 22:12). A nice parallel comes from the papyri: a London document from A.D. 212 describes a ship as ἐστρωμένον — "furnished and boarded over" — matching the passive sense found in Mark 14:15.
caution: The measured "senses" here partly reflect how surrounding phrases were translated (e.g. "upper" room, "cut" branches) rather than distinct meanings of the verb itself, which centers on the single idea of spreading or furnishing.

definition: Describes something as being so great, so large, or so vast in size, importance, or degree.
article: τηλικοῦτος points to magnitude — something "so great," "so large," or "so mighty" that it stands out. In the four New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "such" two-thirds of the time (as in 2 Corinthians 1:10 and Hebrews 2:3), while the dramatic earthquake of Revelation 16:18 draws out the "so mighty" force the KJV also recognized. Beyond the Bible, the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including an early first-century alphabetical nursery rhyme where someone complains a theft "was nothing to one like him."
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the precise force in any given verse rests on thin measured evidence.

definition: To come into being, happen, or become — covering birth, events taking place, and one thing turning into another.
article: γίνομαι is one of the most common and flexible verbs in the New Testament, appearing 675 times in the Byzantine text. Its core idea is coming into being, but in practice it splits almost evenly between "become" (42%) and "came" (42%), with smaller shares meaning "happened" (12%) or marking time as "when" (3%). Tellingly, in 522 of 675 cases it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing and never surfaces as a single English word. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew הָיָה, "to be" — used 1304 times — which fits its broad sense of existing, occurring, or coming to pass.

definition: A two-word phrase meaning "if not" or "unless," introducing a condition that must be met for something else to hold true.
article: This is a compound conditional phrase built from ἐάν ("if") plus μή ("not"), so it literally means "if not" and functions like the English "unless." It sets up an exception or a required condition — the thing in the main clause holds only when the stated condition is met. The standard lexicons (Strong's and Abbott-Smith) agree on this straightforward reading.
caution: No occurrences were measured in the Byzantine corpus, so this entry rests on the lexicons and the meaning of its component words rather than corpus data.

definition: To raise and care for a child—nursing, feeding, and educating them as they grow up.
senseLabels: to raise or bring up a child
article: ἀνατρέφω means to rear a child—covering the whole process of nursing, nourishing, and educating someone as they grow up. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all describing how Moses or Paul was raised (Acts 7:20-21, 22:3). The word combines ἀνά with τρέφω ('to feed'), and it shows up in the Septuagint too, in passages like Wisdom 7:4 and 4 Maccabees.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 occurrences—and in 2 of the 3 the verb is absorbed into the phrasing without its own English word, so its precise force is hard to pin down.

definition: Describing land that is sown with grain; as a noun, the grainfields where crops grow.
article: σπόριμος literally means "fit for sowing" or "sown," and in the New Testament it always appears as a noun in the plural (τὰ σπόριμα), meaning grainfields. It shows up just 3 times, all in the same scene where the disciples pick heads of grain as they walk through the fields (Matthew 12:1, Mark 2:23, Luke 6:1). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this farming sense vividly, repeatedly describing plots of "land ready for sowing" in property and land-transfer documents.
caution: The word is rare, appearing only 3 times in one shared Gospel scene, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond "grainfields."

definition: To hold or press something together tightly, and figuratively to grip, confine, compel, or overwhelm a person—often with sickness or strong emotion.
article: At its root συνέχω means to hold or press things together, and that physical idea stretches in many directions: hemming in a crowd, holding a prisoner, closing the ears, or gripping someone with illness or urgency. In the Byzantine New Testament's 12 occurrences, the only sense the Majority Standard Bible measures consistently is being "suffering" from a disease (3×), as in Matthew 4:24 and Luke 4:38. The everyday Koine flavor shows up nicely in the papyri, where the same verb covers keeping a field flooded, closing a piece of business quickly, and even acknowledging receipt of 124 drachmas.
caution: Only one sense was measured cleanly; the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) list a much wider range—constrain, compel, hem in, hold fast—that the rare renderings and absorbed phrasings hint at but don't pin down.

definition: The possessive or "of us" form of "we" — meaning our, of us, or belonging to us.
article: ἡμῶν is simply the genitive plural of the pronoun "I" (ἐγώ), meaning "our" or "of us." It carries no meaning of its own beyond pointing to the speaker's group, and English usually renders it "our," "us," or "we." Though it does not appear in the Byzantine NT count here, it shows up 992 times across 33 books of the Septuagint, where it frequently translates the Hebrew אֲנַ֫חְנוּ ("we," 100×) and attaches to nouns like אֱלֹהִים ("God," 146×) and אָב ("father," 37×) to mean "our God," "our father," and the like.
caution: The digest reports zero Byzantine NT occurrences, which is unusual for so common a pronoun and likely reflects how the data was counted rather than its true frequency.

definition: Tryphosa, the personal name of a Christian woman in Rome whom Paul greets and commends for her hard work.
article: Tryphosa is a personal name, belonging to a Christian woman in Rome whom Paul greets in Romans 16:12, noting that she 'worked' hard in the Lord. The name derives from the Greek word for luxury or daintiness (τρυφή), but in the New Testament it functions purely as a name, not a description. Moulton-Milligan confirms the name was common well beyond Rome, turning up in inscriptions from Magnesia, and Dodson notes she may have been a sister of Tryphaena, who is greeted alongside her.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament, so the evidence for it is very thin.

definition: Someone or something that runs ahead of others, arriving first to prepare the way for those who follow.
article: πρόδρομος literally means "running forward" or "going in advance," built from the idea of running ahead (related to προτρέχω). Used as a noun, it names an advance guard or forerunner—the one who arrives first. It appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 6:20), where the corpus data shows it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it twice translates Hebrew words for early or first-ripe produce (the "firstfruits" of figs in Isaiah 28:4), and Moulton-Milligan note its everyday use even in a building inscription from Delos referring to a forward part of a structure.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only two Septuagint occurrences, so its measured range is very thin and confidence is low.

definition: Something shown as a pattern to follow or to learn from — an example, model, or a copy of an original.
article: ὑπόδειγμα covers two related ideas: an example meant for imitation or warning, and a copy or figure of an original. Across its 6 New Testament occurrences it serves both purposes — Jesus sets an example of service (John 13:15), the prophets are examples of patience (James 5:10), Sodom is a warning example (2 Peter 2:6), while in Hebrews it describes earthly things as copies of heavenly realities (Heb 8:5; 9:23). The everyday papyri confirm the "example" sense vividly: a first-century BC inscription praises someone for "presenting a fine example of a citizen," and the word even appears for a physical "specimen" sent for inspection.
caution: Abbott-Smith notes this is a later word used in place of the older παράδειγμα, and the Septuagint evidence is thin (just a handful of occurrences), so its precise range rests mostly on the small New Testament sample.

definition: To drift away, slip past, or be carried off course, used of gradually losing hold of something important.
article: παραῤῥυέω literally means to flow or glide past, and figuratively to drift away or slip off course. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 2:1, where it warns against drifting away from what has been heard; the single occurrence is absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by one English word. In the Septuagint it shows up twice, once translating a Hebrew word meaning to flow, and an ancient writer, Clement, uses it of women losing their grip on the truth through vain conceit  y drying by".
caution: Evidence is thin: only one (non-critical-text) New Testament occurrence and two Septuagint uses, so confidence is low.

definition: The comparative of "much/many," meaning more in number, quantity, or value, and as a noun the greater part or majority.
article: πλείων is the comparative form of πολύς ("much, many"), so it means "more" — whether more in number, larger in amount, or higher in value. It appears 42 times across 17 books of the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew רָב ("many, great"), though interestingly it also translates the near-opposite מָעַט ("few, little") four times, presumably in comparative phrasing. The everyday papyri show its plain commercial flavor: phrases like πλείονος τιμῆς ("at a higher price") and "for more or less in proportion" turn up in business documents from the third century B.C.
caution: This word does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament corpus, so the sense breakdown rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than measured NT usage.

definition: Describing something that brings no benefit and is actually harmful or to one's loss.
article: This word means "unprofitable" or "detrimental"—not merely neutral, but a loss with no payoff. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 13:17, where disobeying leaders would be "unprofitable" to the readers. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: one document (Tebtunis, c. 117 BC) uses it for "inferior crops," unprofitable by comparison with wheat.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse; the digest's "submit" rendering reflects the surrounding clause, not the word's own meaning.

definition: To owe something to someone, or more often to be morally bound or obligated to do something.
article: At its root ὀφείλω means to owe a debt, and that literal sense shows up in everyday Koine — a Will from 285 BC uses it of children responsible for their parents' debts. In the New Testament the word leans heavily toward the figurative meaning of being under obligation, which is why translators most often render it "ought" (6 of 35 times, 43% of the visible cases). The remaining 21 of 35 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew נָשָׁא, the language of lending and owing.
caution: Because 21 of its 35 occurrences are blended into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, the measured sense breakdown rests on a fairly small visible sample.

definition: The killing of animals or people, especially the violent slaughter of a victim led to be butchered.
article: σφαγή refers to slaughter — the killing of an animal or person, as in leading a sheep to be butchered. All three New Testament occurrences mean "slaughter," with one of them absorbed into phrasing rather than getting its own English word. In the Septuagint it appears 20 times across 8 books, usually standing in for the Hebrew word טָ֫בַח ("slaughter"), and the New Testament uses vivid set phrases like "sheep of slaughter" (Rom 8:36) and "day of slaughter" (Jas 5:5).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, all from Old Testament quotations or set phrases, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Relating to law, or, used as a noun, a person who is an expert in the law.
article: This adjective comes from νόμος ("law") and shifts between two roles. Most often (6 of 9 times, 75%) it works as a noun naming an expert in the law, while in the remaining cases (25%) it stays an adjective meaning "relating to law," as in the "quarrels about the law" of Titus 3:9. The papyri show its everyday range too: one second-century document calls a man a νομικὸς Ῥωμαϊκός, a Roman legal expert who certifies a will matches its original, leaving open whether the term implied Roman or Hebrew law.
caution: Used only 9 times in the New Testament, so the split between "legal expert" and "relating to law" rests on a small sample.

definition: To laugh, expressing joy or satisfaction.
article: γελάω means simply to laugh as an expression of joy or satisfaction. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke (6:21 and 6:25), where it contrasts laughter with weeping. In the Septuagint it shows up 12 times, most often rendering the Hebrew verbs צָחַק and שָׂחַק (both 'to laugh'). A charming bit of evidence comes from the papyri, where an ancient text actually spells out the sound of divine laughter as 'cha, cha, cha,' proving the ancients laughed much as we do.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament uses — and the measured rendering label ('well fed for') reflects surrounding phrasing in Luke rather than the verb's own meaning, which is plainly 'to laugh.'

definition: To let oneself be seen, to appear or show oneself to others over a period of time.
article: ὀπτάνομaι is a middle-voice verb meaning to allow oneself to be seen or to appear, closely related to ὁράω (to see). It is extremely rare in the New Testament, occurring just once, in Acts 1:3, where Jesus showed himself alive to his disciples; the digest's labeling of this as "convincing" reflects the surrounding context rather than the word's own meaning. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that this word was once thought to be a uniquely "Biblical" term, but everyday papyri from as early as 164–158 BC show it was ordinary spoken Koine.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance rests on its single occurrence plus eight Septuagint uses and scattered papyri.

definition: To reject someone or something after examination, judging them unworthy or unfit.
article: This verb means to reject or repudiate after a process of testing or evaluation — not a careless dismissal but a considered verdict that something fails to measure up. In the Byzantine NT it appears 9 times and is consistently rendered "rejected," most famously of the stone the builders rejected (Matthew 21:42, 1 Peter 2:4). The Septuagint uses it 8 times, mostly translating the Hebrew מָאַס ("to despise, reject"), and a Hadrian-era papyrus shows the same everyday sense: a man declines to buy a dagger "that might be rejected" as unsuitable.
caution: The two measured senses differ only in grammar (passive participle versus active verb), not in core meaning, so the word's range is quite narrow and well-attested.

definition: Made of wood; describing objects fashioned from timber.
article: ξύλινος is a simple descriptive adjective meaning "wooden," derived from ξύλον ("wood"). It appears only twice in the New Testament, and both times the Majority Standard Bible renders it "wood" (e.g., the wooden household vessels in 2 Timothy 2:20 and the wooden idols in Revelation 9:20). The everyday, non-theological flavor of the word shows clearly in the papyri, where it describes ordinary items like a small wooden box, a wooden stool, and a wooden ladder for a pigeon-house.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences the corpus evidence is thin, though the meaning is consistent and uncontested across all sources.

definition: The divine nature of God — the sum of qualities and attributes that mark something as belonging to God.
article: This word points to God's divine nature — the bundle of attributes and qualities that reveal who God is, rather than his essence or personhood. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 1:20, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "qualities" (100% of its single occurrence, with the BSB agreeing). Lexicographers distinguish it from the related θεότης ("deity, godhead"): θειότης is more about divine quality, while θεότης concerns divine essence; in everyday Koine the papyri even use it as a flattering term for the "divinity" of emperors, as in a 4th-century document referring to a visit to the imperial court.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range here rests largely on lexicons and outside usage.

definition: To strongly desire or set one's heart on something, whether in a good way (to long for) or a bad way (to covet or lust after).
article: ἐπιθυμέω means to set your heart on something, and the evidence shows it swings both ways: it can be a wholesome longing or a sinful craving. In the Byzantine New Testament it was rendered "long" 3 times (23%) and "covet" 2 times (15%), with the rest scattered across renderings like "lust" and "crave" or absorbed into phrasing. The Septuagint uses it 41 times, most often translating the Hebrew אָוָה (to desire, 18×) and חָמַד (to covet, 7×, the verb behind the tenth commandment); an interesting grammatical wrinkle is that everyday Koine papyri confirm the later construction with the accusative, seen in a third-century inscription warning against desiring another man's wife.
caution: The moral coloring (good longing versus sinful coveting) depends entirely on context, so the same word can mean very different things.

definition: A deep respect and godly fear shown toward God, expressed in worship and reverent caution.
article: In the New Testament, εὐλάβεια names the reverence or godly fear that a person directs toward God; both of its 2 occurrences (Hebrews 5:7 and 12:28) are rendered "reverence." Classical writers, however, used it more broadly to mean caution or discretion, and only in later Greek did the "reverence" sense develop, as Abbott-Smith notes. Everyday Koine documents add a charming twist: the papyri use εὐλάβεια as a title of respect, much like our "Your Reverence."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT occurrences) and the sources diverge, with the classical lexicons giving "caution/discretion" rather than the "reverence" measured in the New Testament.

definition: To receive someone as a guest into one's home and entertain them hospitably.
article: This verb means to receive a person under your roof and host them hospitably—a warm, practical kind of welcome rather than a mere greeting. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, and the renderings cluster tightly around hospitality, whether "welcomed" or specifically "welcomed into home." Everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions back this up: one inscription praises a gymnasiarch because he "entertained all who were in training," and another speaks of hosting an association at one's own expense.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the range is narrow but the meaning is consistent across the NT, Septuagint, and papyri evidence.

definition: Cursed; placed under a divine curse and so condemned to ruin.
article: ἐπικατάρατος means being cursed — the object of a curse that calls down doom or destruction. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, twice meaning "curse" (Galatians 3:10, 3:13) and once "under a curse" (John 7:49), but it is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 42 times and almost always renders the Hebrew אָרַר, "to curse." Though older lexicons claimed the word was limited to biblical and church usage, Deissmann found it in a pagan tomb inscription warning that "cursed" be anyone who damages the monument, showing it was at home in everyday Koine.
caution: Confidence is computed as low because of only three New Testament occurrences, so the sense range rests heavily on Septuagint and inscriptional evidence.

definition: A strong forward movement — either a hostile rush or assault, or the impulse that steers or drives something.
article: ὁρμή names a forceful movement, but the New Testament's two uses pull in two directions: in Acts 14:5 it is a hostile rush — an attempt set in motion to attack — while in James 3:4 it is the impulse or drive by which a pilot steers a ship. The Septuagint uses it seven times across four books, and everyday Koine papyri show the same range, from soldiers repelling an enemy's onset to two pigs "making a rush" onto someone's land. The classical lexica reflect both meanings, listing a violent movement or impulse alongside a hostile assault.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences split evenly between two different senses, the evidence is thin and the word's range here is hard to pin down.

definition: Demas, the personal name of a man who worked alongside the apostle Paul during his imprisonment in Rome.
article: Δημᾶς is simply the proper name "Demas," used 3 times in the New Testament for a companion of Paul, always rendered "Demas" by every consulted source (Colossians 4:14, 2 Timothy 4:10, Philemon 24). Abbott-Smith notes the name may be a shortened form of Δημήτριος (Demetrius). It was an ordinary name in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan track it across papyri and inscriptions, including one document (BGU III.715, A.D. 101–2) where a Demas appears among several Jews.
caution: This is a proper name with only 3 occurrences, so there is no semantic range to debate, though the suggestion that it contracts from Δημήτριος is only a guess.

definition: To set free or release someone from something; in the middle or passive, to be rid of a person or to depart.
senseLabels: to be released or settled with
article: This verb basically means to release or remove, built from ἀπό ("away from") and ἀλλάσσω ("to change"). It only appears 3 times in the New Testament, and in 2 of those it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than mapping to one English word; in Luke 12:58 it carries the legal sense of being "quit of" or settling matters with someone before a magistrate. The everyday Koine papyri make this concrete: one of the oldest surviving Greek marriage contracts uses it for a wife who "desires to be released" from her husband, showing the word's practical, contractual flavor.
caution: Confidence is low: with only 3 New Testament occurrences and two of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured English data is thin and the labeled "officer" rendering reflects context rather than the word's core meaning.

definition: To begin something beforehand or earlier, having already made a start on an action or undertaking.
article: This verb means to have started something earlier, before the present moment. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 8 (verses 6 and 10), where Paul speaks of the Corinthians who had already begun their collection for others. The word is built from πρό ("before") plus ἐνάρχομαι ("to begin"), and Abbott-Smith notes it appears nowhere else, so its meaning rests entirely on these two passages.
caution: With only two occurrences both in the same chapter and no usage elsewhere, the sense rests on very thin evidence; note also that the two measured renderings ("help act started" and "opinion") reflect fuller phrases rather than the verb alone.

definition: Justice as a principle, a legal case or judgment, and the punishment or penalty that carries out a sentence.
article: δίκη covers a span from a formal legal proceeding to the justice or penalty that results from it. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it two ways evenly: once as a requested judgment (Acts 25:15) and once as the goddess-like figure "Justice" who would not let a murderer live (Acts 28:4). The everyday legal flavor is confirmed by the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan cites a document warning that "the case will be drawn up against you in the court at Heracleopolis," and in the Septuagint it most often stands behind Hebrew words for vengeance (נָקָם, 4×) and dispute (רִיב, 4×).
caution: With only 4 occurrences—2 of which are absorbed into phrasing—the measured senses rest on thin data, though the lexicons agree on the legal-to-punishment range.

definition: Property or wealth one owns, especially a piece of land such as a field or vineyard.
article: κτῆμα refers to something a person has acquired and possesses, most often material wealth or a piece of land. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times: twice the Majority Standard Bible renders it "wealth" (as in the rich young man's story, Matthew 19:22, Mark 10:22), and once it points to a specific property in Acts 5:1. The everyday Koine papyri are especially vivid here — the word frequently names a vineyard or a farm allotment, as in one document describing a κτῆμα lying neglected and untilled.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the split between abstract "wealth" and a concrete "piece of land" rests on thin evidence, and the lexicons lean toward the landed-property sense.

definition: A mulberry tree, mentioned by Jesus as something that could be uprooted and cast into the sea by faith.
article: Sykáminos refers to a mulberry tree, and the New Testament uses it exactly once, in Luke 17:6, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "mulberry." The word appears throughout everyday Koine papyri, where it shows up in business documents about buying, selling, and harvesting from these trees, even in a recipe-like reference to "mulberry milk." Interestingly, in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew shiqmim and seems to stand for the sycamore-fig, but Luke carefully keeps sykáminos distinct from the related word for sycamore (συκομορέα).
caution: It appears only once in the New Testament, and the Septuagint apparently uses it for a different tree (the sycamore-fig), so the precise species behind the word is debated.

definition: A woman who sells sex for money; also used figuratively in Revelation for a corrupt, idolatrous city.
article: πόρνη refers to a prostitute, and that single meaning covers all 12 New Testament occurrences (rendered "prostitute" in 10 of them, 83%). In Revelation the word turns figurative, describing Babylon (understood as Rome) as the great "whore." The everyday reality behind the word shows up vividly in the papyri: one document (BGU IV.1024) recounts a man named Diodemus who, infatuated with a public prostitute, killed her and was imprisoned for it. In the Septuagint it appears 40 times, mostly translating the Hebrew root זָנָה (26×) meaning to be a prostitute or act unfaithfully.

definition: The hair of the head, especially long hair worn as a natural covering or adornment.
article: κόμη refers to the hair of the head, often the longer, ornamental kind, which Strong's distinguishes from θρίξ (G2359), the word for a single hair or hair as mere bodily growth. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 11:15, where it is rendered "covering." The Septuagint uses it 7 times, mostly for Hebrew words about hair or locks, and the everyday papyri offer a vivid touch: κόμη could also mean the leafy "foliage" of plants, and one inscription describes a son's hair grown long to be later consecrated to a god.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To double something, or to pay it back twice over.
article: This verb means to double or render something two-fold, and it appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:6, where it occurs in the phrase "double the double" (δίπλωσον τὰ διπλᾶ) — a call to repay twice over. It derives from the adjective διπλοῦς, meaning "double." In its single Byzantine occurrence, it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than carrying its own English word, reflecting how tightly it pairs with the noun "double" in that verse.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: Something to be thrown away or rejected as worthless or unfit.
article: This adjective describes something fit to be cast off or refused. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 4:4, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render it "rejected," agreeing 100%. The lexicons trace it to ἀποβάλλω ("throw away"), and notably Aquila and Symmachus used it in Greek versions of the Old Testament for things ritually unclean (e.g. Hosea 9:3, rendering the Hebrew word for "unclean").
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: Describing something forceful or violent in its power or motion.
article: βίαιος means "violent" or "forceful," built from the noun βία (force). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 2:2, describing the "rushing" wind of Pentecost, and six times in the Septuagint. Everyday papyri use it of people too — one document from A.D. 203 describes a man as βίαιος, "a violent man," who attacked someone by force.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests almost entirely on the Septuagint and outside evidence.

definition: To punish or correct someone, typically as discipline for wrongdoing.
article: κολάζω means to punish, chastise, or discipline, and it appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament. In Acts 4:21 the rulers cannot find a way to punish the apostles, while 2 Peter 2:9 speaks of the unrighteous being held for punishment; both passages center on the single idea of inflicting penalty. The lexica note an older, more literal meaning—"to curtail, dock, or prune"—from a root meaning "docked" or "cut short," and the everyday papyri even use it for someone "feeling the want" of needed tools, showing how its sense of cutting back could shade into deprivation.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and thin Septuagint evidence, the measured sense range here is narrow and the rendering "godly" in 2 Peter 2:9 reflects translation phrasing rather than a distinct meaning of the word itself.

definition: Idumea, the region south of Judea also called Edom, named after the descendants of Esau.
article: Ἰδουμαία is the Greek name for Idumea, the territory east and south of Judea also known as Edom. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Mark 3:8, where it names a region from which crowds came to Jesus. In the Septuagint it shows up 50 times and chiefly renders the Hebrew name אֱדוֹם (Edom), the land linked to Esau's descendants.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests entirely on that single passage.

definition: A likeness or resemblance — something made or appearing similar to another thing, whether concretely or abstractly.
article: ὁμοίωμα points to a likeness or resemblance between two things, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it six times across three books, rendered "likeness" twice and "like" once (the other three times it gets absorbed into phrasing). The Septuagint leans on it heavily, using it 38 times to translate Hebrew words for image, pattern, and form, especially דְּמוּת (16×). Lexicographers note that, unlike εἰκών (which implies an actual archetype), the likeness in ὁμοίωμα can be merely accidental — as Moulton-Milligan puts it, the way one egg resembles another.
caution: With only six New Testament occurrences and half absorbed into phrasing, the precise weight between "concrete image" and "abstract resemblance" rests largely on the broader Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: A particular sail on an ancient ship, probably one set toward the bow of the vessel.
article: ἀρτέμων refers to a sail on a sailing ship, though exactly which sail is uncertain — proposals range from a foresail or jib to a topsail or mainsail. It appears only once in the New Testament, in the account of Paul's shipwreck at Acts 27:40, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding action as the sail being "loosened" or hoisted. Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and points to a Roman case (cited from Juvenal) where a disabled ship limped into harbor under this single sail, set on the bow.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources openly admit which sail is meant remains uncertain (foresail, topsail, or mainsail).

definition: A word meaning all, every, or the whole — covering totality or each individual member of a group.
article: πᾶς is one of the most common words in the Greek Bible, used as an adjective or pronoun to express totality — "all," "every," "whole," "everyone," or "everything." Its sense shifts subtly with grammar: with the article it tends to mean "the whole," while without it leans toward "every kind of," but the core idea of completeness stays constant. In the Septuagint it appears over 5,400 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew כֹּל ("all, whole"), which it matched more than 4,300 times — a remarkably tight correspondence. Notably, in the Byzantine New Testament 181 of its 1,248 occurrences are absorbed into English phrasing without a word of their own.

definition: To make strong, or in the passive, to grow strong or become powerful, whether physically or inwardly.
article: κραταιόω means to make strong, and in the New Testament it almost always shows up in the passive—someone or something growing strong. In its 4 Byzantine occurrences it covers physical growth (the child John and Jesus "became strong") and inner or spiritual fortifying ("be strengthened" in the inner being in Ephesians 3:16). It's a heavily Septuagint word—appearing 57 times across 13 books, mostly translating the Hebrew חָזַק ("to be strong," 18×).
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences (and none in the SBLGNT critical text), the sense range here leans heavily on Septuagint usage.

definition: To use power against people, oppressing or harshly mistreating those who are weaker.
article: καταδυναστεύω means to wield power over others to oppress them, and it always points downward—the strong pressing on the weak. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (once in James 2:6 about the rich oppressing believers, and once absorbed into the phrasing of Acts 10:38), but it is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 28 times and most often translates the Hebrew עָשַׁק (10×) and יָנָה (7×), both words for exploitation and mistreatment. A vivid everyday example survives in the papyri: a prisoner writes that he is "being harshly treated" and perishing from hunger, showing the word's reach into ordinary physical suffering.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences—one of which carries no English word of its own—the measured sense rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: The place a person comes from — their hometown or native region.
article: πατρίς refers to the place someone is from — most naturally one's hometown or native town rather than a whole country. In the New Testament it appears 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "hometown" (sometimes "hometown own") every time, as in the saying that a prophet has no honor in his own πατρίς. Everyday Koine papyri back this up: in one document from 4 B.C. a man fears being deprived of "his own πατρίς," his native place, and Moulton-Milligan note the word means native town rather than native land.
caution: Strong's mentions a figurative "heavenly home" sense, but the measured New Testament data shows only the literal "hometown" meaning.

definition: David, the celebrated king of Israel, named throughout the New Testament.
article: This is the proper name of David, king of Israel, appearing 59 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 9 books. It is an indeclinable name borrowed straight from Hebrew דָּוִד, and in the Septuagint it shows up over 1,000 times, mostly rendering דָּוִיד. The renderings only differ for grammatical emphasis ("David himself," "David's"), and the name anchors important phrases like "Son of David" for the Messiah and "key of David" in Revelation.

definition: A planted area where grapevines are cultivated to produce grapes for wine.
article: ἀμπελών simply means a vineyard, a plot of cultivated grapevines, and that is how it is rendered in 13 of its 23 New Testament occurrences (57%). The other measured sense, "owner's vineyard" (5×, 22%), is the same place viewed in relation to its proprietor, often in parables about laborers or tenants. The word is heavily used in the Septuagint (92×), where it almost always translates the Hebrew kerem, "vineyard," and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Egyptian papyri, including a Ptolemaic document about the taxes due on vineyards.

definition: Stephanas, a Corinthian Christian and one of the first converts in Achaia.
article: Stephanas is a personal name belonging to a Corinthian Christian, appearing three times in the New Testament, all in 1 Corinthians (1:16; 16:15; 16:17). Paul mentions baptizing his household and calls his household the firstfruits of Achaia, devoted to serving fellow believers. The name itself was common in everyday Koine, showing up in papyri and inscriptions, and is probably a shortened form of Στεφανήφορος or a development of Στέφανος.
caution: The second measured sense ('Stephanas devoted Now') is just the name caught up in surrounding phrasing, not a distinct meaning.

definition: Strong anger or wrath, whether human rage or God's settled reaction against sin, sometimes including its punishing effects.
article: ὀργή covers intense anger, ranging from human rage to the divine wrath that God directs against sin. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 36 times, rendered "wrath" in 23 cases (68%) and "anger" in 10 (29%), with the BSB agreeing on every one. In the Septuagint it shows up 235 times, most often translating the Hebrew אַף ("nose/anger," 70×), and the everyday flavor of the word shows in a papyrus where a man "not restraining his anger" murdered a woman with a sword.

definition: An outline or sketch that serves as a pattern or example for others to follow.
article: ὑποτύπωσις literally means a rough sketch or outline, and from there a pattern or example worth imitating. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Timothy 1:16 and 2 Timothy 1:13), and the standard lexicons agree it conveys an outline rather than a fully detailed model. One interesting detail: Moulton-Milligan, drawing on the physician Galen, stresses the 'sketch in outline' nuance — a summary account without the full substance — and the verb shows up in third-century BC papyri for drafting a contract.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and the measured rendering of one as "worst" clearly reflecting surrounding context rather than the word itself, the evidence here is thin.

definition: To stick or join firmly to someone or something, usually meaning to attach oneself closely or keep company with.
article: Literally κολλάω means "to glue" things together, and that physical image carries into its figurative uses—joining oneself to a person, sticking close, or keeping company. In the Septuagint it appears 28 times and most often (14×) translates the Hebrew דָּבַק, the very word for "cleave" used when a man joins his wife. The papyri preserve the concrete sense vividly: one fourth-century document warns against "gluing the stone to your left ear," while another speaks of uniting cattle.
caution: In 8 of its 11 Byzantine occurrences the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English equivalent, so its exact force often depends on context.

definition: The act of striking down or killing enemies in battle; slaughter.
article: In the New Testament κοπή appears just once, in Hebrews 7:1, where it means the defeat and slaughter of kings in battle. The everyday papyri tell a very different story: there κοπή commonly means simple "cutting," as in cutting grass or harvesting a crop. The biblical and military sense of "smiting in battle" actually developed in the Septuagint, where it renders Hebrew words for striking down enemies, while the classical lexicons trace the word back to the plain idea of a stroke or pounding.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A needle, the small pointed tool used for sewing thread through cloth.
article: ῥαφίς simply means a sewing needle, and that single sense covers all 3 of its New Testament appearances, each in Jesus' saying about a camel passing through the eye of a needle (Matthew 19:24, Mark 10:25, Luke 18:25). The word comes from the verb meaning "to sew," and everyday papyri confirm this ordinary use—one account from around A.D. 1 lists "thread and needle" costing one obol. Interestingly, Luke swaps in a different word, βελόνη, a term used for the surgical needle, where Matthew and Mark use ῥαφίς.
caution: This word appears only 3 times in the Byzantine text (just 2 in the critical text), all in the same camel-and-needle saying, so the evidence base is narrow.

definition: The act of forgetting; failure to remember what one has heard or learned.
article: This noun names forgetfulness or oblivion — the state of not remembering something. It appears only once in the New Testament, in James 1:25, in the phrase "a forgetful hearer" (literally "a hearer of forgetfulness"), describing someone who hears the word but fails to act on it. Outside the New Testament it shows up just once in the Greek Old Testament, at Sirach 11:27, so the surviving evidence for it is very thin.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its range cannot be measured with confidence.

definition: Female; belonging to the female sex, used of women or female animals.
article: θῆλυς simply means "female," whether describing a woman or a female animal, and often appears as a noun ("the female") paired with its opposite "male." It shows up only 5 times in the New Testament across 4 books, where the Majority Standard Bible consistently renders it "female," and it occurs 33 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "female" (נְקֵבָה, 20×). A striking everyday example comes from a 1 BC papyrus letter (P Oxy IV.744) in which a husband chillingly instructs his wife that if their unborn child is female, she should expose it.
caution: The four measured senses are really one and the same meaning, "female," just appearing in different phrasings.

definition: A joint or place where parts of the body are joined together.
article: This word means a joint — the point where bones or limbs are joined in the body. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 4:12, where God's word pierces "to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow." The Septuagint book 4 Maccabees 10:5 uses it vividly of torturers wrenching limbs out of their sockets, and everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions even apply it to the fitted joints of temple walls.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on thin evidence.

definition: To recommend or present someone favorably, or to demonstrate and prove something; also, intransitively, to hold together or be composed of parts.
article: Built from σύν ("with") and ἵστημι ("to set, stand"), this verb literally means to set things together, and from there it spreads into two main directions: presenting a person favorably ("commend, recommend") and establishing or proving a point. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 16 times, with the three measured senses—proving, commending, and commending oneself—each accounting for about a quarter of uses, especially clustered in 2 Corinthians. A nice detail from the papyri: Moulton and Milligan show this was an everyday word for introducing or recommending someone, the same way a letter-writer might vouch for a friend.
caution: The lexica also note an intransitive sense "hold together, consist" (as in Colossians 1:17), but that meaning barely registers in the measured Byzantine renderings.

definition: To look attentively at something or someone, paying close watchful attention so as to consider, guard against, or keep in view.
article: σκοπέω means to fix your attention on something—to watch, observe, and consider it carefully. In the New Testament's 6 occurrences the focus shifts with context: half the time (2×) it means watching out for people, once it warns someone to be careful about what's inside them (Luke 11:35), and once it means looking to others' interests (Php 2:4). Everyday Koine papyri use the same word for practical consideration, as in one document where an official, 'after consideration,' gave his ruling.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, though the sources broadly agree on its core meaning.

definition: A child, son, or daughter — anyone born to a parent, and by extension a descendant or someone treated as one's own child.
article: τέκνον means a child of either sex — literally one who has been born or begotten. It is overwhelmingly stable in meaning: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "children" in 91 of 99 occurrences (99%), and the Septuagint most often uses it for the Hebrew בֵּן ("son"). The word stretches naturally from literal offspring to wider posterity, and was also used as a warm form of address from an elder to a younger person or a teacher to a disciple; everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary family sense, including one letter that uses "other children" to mean a second family.

definition: To put someone to death, or figuratively to kill off and be done with something.
article: θανατόω means to put to death, and nearly all of its 11 New Testament appearances carry that plain sense, whether someone is executed, betrayed to be killed, or, in Matthew 26:59 and 27:1, conspired against in order to be killed. The word also reaches into figurative territory: Paul uses it of putting the deeds of the body to death (Romans 8:13) and of being made dead in relation to the law (Romans 7:4). The Septuagint backs this up overwhelmingly, using it 149 times—125 of them rendering the Hebrew verb מוּת, "to die" (in causative forms, "to put to death").

definition: Rome, the capital city of the Roman Empire on the Tiber River.
article: Ῥώμη is simply the proper name for Rome, the capital of the Roman Empire, and that is how it is rendered in all 5 cleanly measured occurrences (with the BSB agreeing 100%). The word appears 8 times across 3 books, always pointing to the literal city—as the destination of Paul's travels and the place where the gospel was preached. Interestingly, the name derives from the root of ῥώννυμι (G4517), which carries the idea of "strength," matching Strong's note glossing it as "strength."
caution: The "strength" sense comes only from the word's derivation, not from any measured New Testament usage, where it always means the city.

definition: To go up, climb, or ascend—whether a person traveling to a higher place or a thing rising, growing, or coming up.
article: ἀναβαίνω is a common, everyday word meaning to go up or ascend, used over and over in the New Testament—80 times—for people climbing a hill, boarding a boat, or traveling up to Jerusalem. It also stretches to things that rise: plants springing up, smoke ascending, even prayers or thoughts "coming up" before God or into the mind. The Septuagint uses it more than 600 times, overwhelmingly to render the Hebrew עָלָה ("go up"), and papyri show its plain Koine flavor—one ancient letter complains, "I have no time to come up to you," while others describe going up to the temple to worship.

definition: A setting right or reforming of something, especially a new order that corrects or replaces an older arrangement.
article: διόρθωσις means a making straight, hence a reform or correction of an existing system. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 9:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the phrase about regulations imposed until "the time of reformation." The classical lexica note it was a favorite term in later writers for the reforming of laws, and the everyday papyri stretch its range further still — it could even mean the settlement of a payment, while one Leiden papyrus uses it of putting one's life in order.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise New Testament force rests on a single passage and on outside parallels.

definition: A flock of sheep, used in the New Testament as an image for a group of believers under a leader's care.
article: ποίμνιον means a flock, properly of sheep, and in all five New Testament occurrences it pictures a community of believers being shepherded. The two 'over flock' and 'flock over' senses are not different meanings but reflect English phrasing in passages like Acts 20:28 and 1 Peter 5:2, where leaders are told to oversee the flock. Although Dodson lists 'a little flock,' Moulton-Milligan note from everyday papyri (such as a widow's complaint about seized flocks) that the diminutive force cannot be pressed in later Greek. In the Septuagint it appears 69 times, most often rendering the Hebrew words for 'herd/flock' (עֵדֶר) and 'sheep' (צֹאן).
caution: With only five New Testament occurrences, the measured 'over flock' and 'flock over' labels reflect English rendering choices rather than truly distinct senses.

definition: A fragrant resin gum from a tree, used as perfume, ointment, and for embalming the dead.
article: Myrrh is a sweet-smelling resinous gum harvested from a tree, valued in the ancient world as a perfume, ointment, and embalming spice. The New Testament uses the word only twice—when the magi present it to the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:11) and when it is used to prepare his body for burial (John 19:39). In the Septuagint it appears 9 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word mor; a medical papyrus from Oxyrhynchus even prescribes pounding myrrh together with alum, showing its everyday practical use.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences the word is thinly attested there, though the Septuagint and papyri confirm the consistent meaning.

definition: To act with deceit or treachery, using one's words to mislead and betray others.
article: This rare verb means to be deceitful or treacherous, especially through speech, and is built from the adjective δόλιος ("deceitful"). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 3:13, which quotes the Septuagint, and shows up only 4 times in the Greek Old Testament. Notably, the Romans verse uses the form ἐδολιοῦσαν, a spelling for the third-person plural imperfect that was common in everyday Koine Greek of the period.
caution: Evidence is very thin — only one New Testament use (a quotation) and four Septuagint occurrences — so the word's full range is hard to pin down, and the measured sense label "throats" reflects the surrounding phrase in Romans 3:13 rather than the verb's own meaning.

definition: Describing the natural, physical life of a person, contrasted with the spiritual.
article: ψυχικός describes what belongs to the ordinary, natural human life — the living, breathing self — as opposed to the spiritual (πνευματικός). The Byzantine New Testament uses it 6 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "natural" in every measured occurrence, with the BSB independently agreeing 100%. An interesting parallel turns up in the ancient Liturgy of Mithras, which speaks of "my human natural powers" (ψυχικῆς δυνάμεως), showing the same contrast between natural life and a higher kind of existence.
caution: Older lexica also list "sensual" or "animal" for passages like Jude 19 and James 3:15, where the sense leans more negative than the measured "natural" suggests.

definition: To bring back word about something, reporting or announcing it, often in detail.
article: ἀναγγέλλω means to bring back word and report it, or more broadly to announce and declare something. In the Byzantine NT it appears 18 times across 7 books, most often rendered "told" (4×) or referring to "what" is disclosed (2×); in 4 of those 18 cases it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. The most striking evidence is its sheer dominance in the Septuagint, where it appears 218 times and mostly translates the Hebrew נָגַד, "to tell or declare," 134 times — and the papyri confirm it was everyday Koine for the older Attic ἀπαγγέλλω.
caution: Lexicons note that in later Greek ἀναγγέλλω overlaps heavily with ἀπαγγέλλω, and manuscripts sometimes swap the two, so the precise sense in a given verse can be uncertain.

definition: A person who does evil or commits crimes; a wrongdoer or criminal.
article: This word combines "bad" (κακός) and "do" (ποιέω), so it literally means "someone who does evil." Across its 5 New Testament occurrences the rendering shifts between the general "evildoer" (twice) and the sharper "criminal" (once, in John 18:30 where it accuses Jesus before Pilate). The most striking outside evidence comes from a first-century B.C. papyrus where a woman promises not to make "harmful" potions, leading Moulton-Milligan to suggest the word in 1 Peter 4:15 may point specifically to a sorcerer or poisoner.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and a possible specialized sense of "sorcerer/poisoner" suggested by the papyri, the precise force in any given verse is somewhat uncertain.

definition: Macedonia, a region in northern Greece that the Romans organized as a province north of Achaia.
article: Μακεδονία is simply the place name Macedonia, rendered "Macedonia" in 20 of its 22 New Testament occurrences (91%), with the BSB agreeing 100%. It appears across 7 books, often paired with Achaia (its southern neighbor) as in Acts 19:21, Romans 15:26, and 1 Thessalonians 1:7-8. Dodson describes it as a Roman province north of Achaia, and it derives from G3110, Μακεδών, meaning a Macedonian.

definition: The process of being made new again — a renewal or transformation of a person's inner life.
senseLabels: renewal that makes a person new
article: This noun describes a renewal or renovation, the making-new of a person's inner life. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 12:2 and Titus 3:5), and the Majority Standard Bible renders one of those occurrences as 'righteous new birth,' while absorbing the other into surrounding phrasing. Abbott-Smith pairs it with παλινγενεσία ('new birth'), treating this word as the renewal that follows from that new birth — a process in which both God and the person take part.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice and confidence is rated low, so its precise force is hard to pin down.

definition: A message or announcement—news communicated from one party to another.
article: ἀγγελία means a message or piece of news passed along, and it's closely tied to ἄγγελος (messenger), from which it derives. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in 1 John (1:5 and 3:11), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "message" 100% of the time, with the BSB and other glossaries in full agreement. In the Septuagint it shows up 12 times, most often translating the Hebrew שְׁמוּעָה ("report" or "tidings"), and a delightful papyrus fragment on bodily twitches uses it for "unexpected news"—if your right ankle quivers, it signals surprising tidings are coming.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the sources fully agree on the meaning.

definition: To violently convulse someone, throwing them into a fit that shakes the whole body.
article: This rare verb describes a violent convulsion that seizes a person's whole body, the kind seen when a demon throws a boy to the ground in distress. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 9:42), with the critical text counting two occurrences. It builds on σπαράσσω, intensified by the prefix σύν to stress how completely the convulsion grips the person, and Abbott-Smith notes it always takes a person as its object (Mark 9:20; Luke 9:42).
caution: With only one Byzantine occurrence and the measured sense recorded oddly as "approaching," the lexical glosses ("convulse," "throw down") are the more reliable guide here.

definition: The flame or blaze of a fire — the bright, burning tongues of light and heat that a fire gives off.
article: φλόξ simply means the flame or blaze of a fire, and across its 7 New Testament occurrences it stays within that single image, whether describing literal flames (Acts 7:30, Heb 1:7), the torment of fire (Luke 16:24), or eyes that look "like blazing" fire (Rev 1:14; 2:18; 19:12). It frequently pairs with the word for fire (φλὸξ πυρός, "flame of fire"), which is why translations render it variously as "flames," "blazing," or just "fire." In the Septuagint it appears 41 times, most often translating the Hebrew words לַהַב and לֶהָבָה for "flame," and it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri — including a sun-hymn praising fire's "tireless light" and an amulet listing "light, fire, flame."
caution: The different English renderings reflect translators' wording choices, not separate meanings — the word consistently denotes one thing: flame.

definition: To have strength or power to do something — to be able, strong, or capable, often used of what one can or cannot accomplish.
article: ἰσχύω is about having the strength or capability to do something, and the New Testament uses it both ways: 5 times the translation shows someone is "able" and 5 times "unable," since the verb itself just measures whether the power is there. Twice it means to "prevail" or carry power, as when the word of God grew and prevailed (Acts 19:20). The Septuagint uses it 69 times, often for Hebrew words for being strong like חָזַק and אָמַץ, and the everyday papyri even apply it to money's worth and to a possession being legally "valid" — an unjust claim that "has no force."

definition: To sprout, grow, or spring up, as plants emerge from the ground.
article: φύω describes how plants sprout and grow, used both of seeds coming up and of something springing into existence. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, twice in Jesus' parable of the sower where seed "comes up" (Luke 8:6, 8) and once in Hebrews 12:15 of a bitter root that "springs up." Everyday Koine papyri confirm this farming sense, mentioning "growing trees," "sprouting mustard," and "all the plants growing in the garden." The older lexicons note a transitive meaning "to bring forth, produce," but every measured New Testament use is about growing or springing up.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this is thin evidence, and the transitive "produce" sense noted by lexicons does not appear in the measured data.

definition: Something missing or insufficient — either a gap that needs filling or a state of want and poverty.
article: ὑστέρημα points to a lack — either a specific gap that needs to be filled (like absent friends or incomplete work) or a general condition of want and poverty. The word's range stretches between these two poles, and notably it stands opposite περίσσευμα ("surplus") in 2 Corinthians 8, capturing the contrast between having too little and having extra. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew מַחְסוֹר (6 of 9 times), the ordinary word for "need" or "lack."
caution: With only 9 New Testament occurrences and the word twice absorbed into phrasing without its own English equivalent, the precise sense often depends on context rather than the word alone.

definition: To fall out, fall off, or fall away from something, including a ship being driven off its course onto land.
article: ἐκπίπτω literally means to fall out of or fall away from something, and the New Testament stretches it across vivid pictures: stars dropping from the sky, chains falling off Peter's wrists, and flowers withering and fading. In Acts 27 it carries a nautical sense, describing Paul's ship being driven off course and running aground, which the BSB renders "run aground" twice. The everyday papyri show the same range, including a wife complaining that her husband "left the country and disappeared" and even coins that "fell out of use." In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew words tied to withering flowers, matching its figurative use in James 1:11.
caution: About a quarter of its uses (3 of 12) get absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, so some figurative shades are harder to pin down.

definition: Eager and ready to do something, willingly disposed toward an action.
article: πρόθυμος describes someone who is eager, ready, and willing — predisposed to act rather than reluctant. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "willing" in both Matthew 26:41 and Mark 14:38 (the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak); the third occurrence, in Romans 1:15, is folded into the phrasing as a neuter noun ("the willingness/eagerness in me"). In the Septuagint it twice translates Hebrew נָדִיב, the idea of a generous or freely-willing heart, and everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense of keen eagerness — one letter has a man offering his services without hesitation.
caution: Only 3 New Testament occurrences and one is absorbed into phrasing, so confidence in the measured range is low.

definition: The number one thousand, often used to count people or groups in large round figures.
article: χιλιάς is simply the number one thousand, used as a counting word for people, soldiers, or units. Its range is narrow and stable: of 23 New Testament occurrences, it's rendered "thousand" in 6 cases and absorbed into surrounding phrasing the other 15 times, so the meaning never really shifts. In the Septuagint it appears 318 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew word אֶלֶף ("thousand"), confirming this single, consistent sense across both Greek and Hebrew evidence.

definition: To be anxious or worried about something, or to give it careful, attentive concern.
article: μεριμνάω means to be anxious or worried, and the New Testament uses it heavily this way—in 8 of its 19 occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "worry," famously in Jesus' teaching not to fret about food and clothing (Matthew 6). But the word also carries a positive side: to care attentively for something, as when Paul speaks of being concerned for the things of the Lord or members of the body caring for one another. A papyrus letter (P. Tebt. II.315) shows the everyday flavor nicely, where a writer hurries to send word "to prevent your being anxious."

definition: The outward appearance or visible form of something, or by extension its kind or sort.
article: εἶδος means what something looks like — its outward appearance or shape — and from there it stretches to mean a kind or sort of thing. It appears 5 times in the New Testament, rendered "form" twice (50%), and once each as "form" (of God) and "sight" (in 2 Corinthians 5:7, where we walk by faith, not by sight). The Septuagint uses it 48 times, mostly for Hebrew words for appearance (מַרְאֶה) and figure or shape (תֹּאַר), and the papyri confirm the "kind" sense: business documents use the formula παντὸς εἴδους meaning "of every kind," which supports the rendering "every form of evil" in 1 Thessalonians 5:22.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences spread across distinct senses, the word's range rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: A fence, wall, or hedge that encloses or separates an area, used literally and sometimes figuratively for a dividing barrier.
article: φραγμός is a physical barrier — a fence, wall, or hedge that encloses land or keeps things apart. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, rendered "wall" in 3 of them (75%) and as a roadside "hedge" once in Luke 14:23. In Ephesians 2:14 Paul uses it figuratively, pairing it with "dividing wall" to picture a barrier between people. It was a thoroughly ordinary word: the papyri show it in everyday leases and contracts, such as a B.C. 5 lease requiring a tenant to return "the fence sound, just as he received it."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the boundary between "wall" and "hedge" reflects translation choices in specific contexts rather than sharply distinct meanings.

definition: To say no to something or someone—denying a fact, disowning a person, or refusing to acknowledge them.
article: This verb covers the whole range of saying "no": denying that something is true, disowning a person, or rejecting and refusing to acknowledge someone. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 31 times and is most often rendered "deny" (73%), but it shades into "reject" when a person is the object, as in Acts 3:14 and 7:35. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where one document (about 6 BC) describes a man who "persisted in his denial"—the same plain refusal we hear in the Gospels.

definition: The act of stealing — taking what belongs to someone else without permission.
article: κλοπή means theft, the act of stealing, and comes from the verb κλέπτω (to steal). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in lists of evils that come from the heart (Matthew 15:19 and Mark 7:22). In the Septuagint it shows up 4 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew word גָּנַב ("to steal"), and everyday papyri use it plainly for theft — one document even refers to "contraband" oil with the related adjective κλόπιμος.
caution: The word's plain meaning is "theft," but one of its two New Testament renderings was measured as "slander," so treat that label as a quirk of how a single verse was translated rather than a separate sense of the word.

definition: The Jewish rite of cutting away the male foreskin, or by extension the resulting state or the people who undergo it.
article: This noun refers to circumcision—the rite itself (rendered "circumcision" 17× of 36) or the condition of being circumcised ("circumcised" 12×). By extension it can stand for the circumcised people, that is, the Jews, as Abbott-Smith notes for phrases like "those of the circumcision." A striking piece of evidence comes from a second-century AD papyrus, where a man describes the trouble he went through to get a boy's circumcision done because the high priest wanted to inspect the child—showing the word in plain everyday use.

definition: To come near or draw close to something, in space or in time, or to bring something near.
article: ἐγγίζω means to come near or draw close — used both of physical nearness (approaching a place or person) and of time (an hour, day, or season drawing near). Its range is broad but unified: in the Byzantine NT it appears 42 times, most often rendered simply "near" (11×) or with past forms like "drew near" and "approached". The lexica note it can also be transitive ("bring near"), as in the Septuagint, where it occurs 130 times, usually translating Hebrew verbs for drawing near such as נָגַשׁ and קָרַב. An everyday papyrus from AD 217 uses it just as the NT does — "as the contest of each year approaches".

definition: Apelles, the personal name of a Christian man greeted by Paul in Rome.
article: Apelles is a man's name, appearing just once in the New Testament when Paul greets him in Romans 16:10 and commends him as approved in Christ. The name was widely used in everyday Greek; Moulton-Milligan note the same accusative form (Ἀπελλῆν) on an inscription from Priene dating to about 1 B.C. Interestingly, the name was sometimes confused with the similar-sounding Apollos, and a related form Ἀπελλᾶς turns up in a Carian inscription about a military officer who served under Vespasian against the Jews.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once in the New Testament, so the evidence is necessarily thin.

definition: A person who inflicts torture or pain, especially a jailer who punishes prisoners.
article: This word names someone who inflicts physical torment, literally a torturer, though it was also used of a jailer who carried out such punishment. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Matthew 18:34, where a king hands his unforgiving servant over to these men until the debt is paid. Worth noting: the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering shows up as 'turned' here, which reflects the surrounding phrase ('turned him over to the tormentors') rather than the word itself, since the term clearly means a torturer or jailer as the lexicons agree.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force—pure torturer versus jailer—rests on thin evidence.

definition: Describing something grand and impressive, befitting greatness or high honor.
article: μεγαλοπρεπής describes what is magnificent or majestic — literally fitting for a great person, built from the words for "great" and "to be fitting." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 1:17, where it is rendered "Majestic," and the major translations agree on that meaning. The Septuagint uses it a handful of times, including Deuteronomy 33:26, and Moulton-Milligan note that the related adverb shows up in inscriptions praising people for living honorably, as in an inscription describing Apollonis, wife of Attalus I.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall data, confidence in the precise range is low.

definition: The grinding or gnashing of teeth, a physical expression of anguish or rage.
article: βρυγμός refers to the grinding or gnashing of the teeth, an action that in the New Testament signals deep anguish—it appears 7 times, almost always in the phrase "weeping and gnashing of teeth." In the Septuagint it shows up just once, where it renders the Hebrew word נַהַם, suggesting a growl or roar of distress. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that an early non-biblical citation from Eupolis (5th century BC) uses the related word in the sense of "biting" rather than "gnashing," hinting at a slightly broader range outside the Bible.
caution: The automated sense data here is garbled (showing "where" and "yourselves"); the actual measured meaning, confirmed by every lexicon, is the gnashing of teeth.

definition: The comparative form of "evil," meaning more wicked, evil, or harmful than something else.
article: This is the comparative form of πονηρός ("evil, wicked"), so it means "more evil" or "more wicked." The base word carries a range from morally wicked to painful or harmful, and the comparative simply intensifies that by comparison. Notably, this exact comparative form does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all, so any discussion of its meaning rests on the parent word πονηρός rather than measured uses of the comparative itself.
