caution: This comparative form has no occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so its sense is inferred entirely from the base word πονηρός.

definition: The quality of being beyond decay or destruction — undying, imperishable existence or, figuratively, genuine soundness.
article: ἀφθαρσία describes a state that cannot rot, perish, or break down — used for the immortal life believers hope for and for the imperishable body raised at the resurrection. The word centers on physical incorruptibility but extends figuratively to moral genuineness, which is how the KJV reaches "sincerity." One striking witness comes from the papyri: a fourth-century Gnostic Gospel fragment (P Oxy VIII.1081) contrasts what is born "from corruption" with what is born "from incorruption" and therefore remains imperishable, while the same word is quoted from Epicurus describing blessedness joined with imperishability.
caution: The word appears only 8 times in the Byzantine NT (7 in the critical text) and is rare in the Septuagint, so its figurative "sincerity" sense rests on thin evidence.

definition: Describing someone or something that is two years old or that lasts for a period of two years.
article: διετής means "two years old" or "lasting two years," formed from the words for "twice" and "year." In the New Testament it appears only once, in Matthew 2:16, describing the children Herod ordered killed "from two years old and under." The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical, ordinary use: one land lease from A.D. 125 guarantees a tenancy "for the period of two years" (εἰς τὸν διετῆ χρόνον).
caution: The measured rendering label "outwitted" reflects how the surrounding verse was tagged, not the actual meaning of this word, which the glosses and papyri consistently give as "two years old"; note also it appears only once in the New Testament.

definition: Chosen together with others, used of someone who shares in being selected alongside fellow believers.
article: συνεκλεκτός means "chosen together with" or "co-elect," combining the ideas of "with" and "to choose." It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:13, where the feminine form ("she who is in Babylon, chosen together with you") most likely refers to a church, with the word "church" understood. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "chosen," and the BSB agrees fully; Moulton-Milligan also notes the related verb συνεκλέγω showing up in an everyday papyrus.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin attestation, the precise reference of this rare word in 1 Peter 5:13 is genuinely uncertain.

definition: The load a ship or animal carries — its freight, cargo, or merchandise.
article: γόμος means the load something carries, most often a ship's cargo or freight. It is a narrow, concrete word: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "cargo" in 2 of its 3 New Testament occurrences (67%), with the remaining instance pointing to merchandise being bought and sold. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this same use vividly — one Oxyrhynchus document asks that a man's freight "be embarked with all despatch," and ostraca even use it as a unit of measure, as in "one load of chaff."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and one measured sense label garbled ("over there left"), the evidence is thin, though sources agree the core meaning is cargo or freight.

definition: To serve as a proconsul, the Roman official governing a province on behalf of the Senate.
article: This verb means to hold the office of proconsul, a Roman provincial governor. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 18:12, where it describes Gallio's term of office in Achaia, and it is built from the noun ἀνθύπατος, "proconsul." Notably, the critical text (SBLGNT) does not include this verb form at all, reading the noun instead, which is why the standard lexicons flag it as a textual variant.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word present only in the Majority/Received text and absent from critical editions, so the evidence is thin and the reading is disputed.

definition: Describing people who meddle in others' affairs, or things connected with prying into hidden knowledge such as magic.
article: This adjective, built from "around" (περί) and "work" (ἔργον), literally suggests working all around things that aren't your concern. It splits into two directions: applied to people it means meddlesome or a busybody (1 Timothy 5:13), and applied to things—as the neuter plural τὰ περίεργα—it means "curious arts" or magic (Acts 19:19). The magical sense is nicely confirmed by a 3rd–4th century papyrus (P Leid V) where περιεργία refers to the curious magical practices of the crowd, showing this was ordinary Koine usage and not a biblical invention.
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, one occurrence for each sense, so the measured range is thin; note that one rendering listed ("drachmas") reflects surrounding text in Acts 19:19 rather than the word itself.

definition: A possessive word meaning "our" or "ours," marking something as belonging to the speaker's group.
article: This is simply the first-person plural possessive adjective: it marks something as belonging to "us." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, rendered "our" in the majority of cases, with the other measured renderings just reflecting added words in the surrounding phrase. The everyday papyri show its ordinary flexibility nicely — one document uses it interchangeably with "my" ("my wife and my virgin daughter"), so it could shade toward a single speaker as well as a group.
caution: The derivation listed here (linking it to θνητός, "mortal") looks like a data error, since this word straightforwardly comes from the pronoun "we."

definition: Cyrene, an ancient city in Libya on the North African coast west of Egypt.
article: Κυρήνη refers to Cyrene, a city in the region of Libya on the Mediterranean coast of North Africa, west of Egypt. The New Testament uses it just once, in Acts 2:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it in terms of "Libya." An interesting detail from the papyri and inscriptions: a Jewish community decree set up at Berenice in Cyrenaica honoring the Roman governor M. Tittius confirms a significant Jewish population in this area.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single occurrence.

definition: To move away from a place, to depart or leave; transitively, to remove or transfer something.
senseLabels: to depart or leave a place
article: In the New Testament, μεταίρω means to move on or depart, and it appears just twice—both times in Matthew, marking Jesus leaving a place after finishing his teaching (Matthew 13:53; 19:1). The Septuagint shows a transitive flavor, meaning to remove or transfer something (translating Hebrew verbs like "remove" and "carry away"). A Cilician rock inscription from near a temple confirms this transitive sense, forbidding anyone to erase, deface, or 'remove' the temple offerings.
caution: With only two New Testament uses—both in the same departure formula—the measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To openly confess, acknowledge, or agree to something, often declaring it publicly.
article: At its core ὁμολογέω means "to say the same thing" as someone else—to agree—and from there it stretches to publicly confessing or acknowledging something. In the Byzantine New Testament's 24 occurrences, translators render it "confess" 14 times (74%) and "acknowledge" twice, with 5 instances absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word. The everyday Koine papyri preserve its original flavor vividly: it appears in legal contracts and the formula "in answer to the formal question I have given my consent," showing that confession began as plain agreement before taking on its public, declarative force.
caution: Dodson notes a Hebraistic sense "praise, celebrate," reflecting its rare Septuagint use to translate יָדָה, but this meaning is not among the measured New Testament senses.

definition: The powdery residue left after something burns, especially used as a sign of mourning or repentance.
article: σποδός means "ashes" — and that meaning is remarkably stable, rendered the same way in all 3 New Testament occurrences and confirmed across every source consulted. In the New Testament it appears mainly in the phrase "in sackcloth and ashes," a gesture of grief or repentance (Matthew 11:21, Luke 10:13), plus a reference to sacrificial ashes in Hebrews 9:13. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew word for ashes (אֵפֶר) 18 of 23 times, and everyday papyri even use a related adjective, σπόδιαι, to describe "ash-colored" or grey goats.
caution: The word is rare in the New Testament (only 3 occurrences), but its meaning is consistent and undisputed across all sources.

definition: A Roman lictor, an officer who carried a rod or staff of office and attended magistrates to enforce their orders.
article: ῥαβδοῦχος literally means "rod-holder" and refers to the Roman lictor, an attendant who served magistrates and carried out their commands. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 16 (verses 35 and 38), where these officers act on the orders of the magistrates at Philippi. Interestingly, the papyri broaden the picture: Moulton-Milligan cites a 164 BC document using the word for a rod-bearing temple-attendant in the Serapeum at Memphis, a religious rather than civil role.
caution: The measured-sense data here looks garbled ("daylight" and "relayed alarmed Silas" reflect surrounding words, not the term itself), so rely on the lexical evidence; with only two occurrences, confidence is low.

definition: A message or answer from God; a divine response or oracle.
article: χρηματισμός refers to a divine response or oracle — God's answer to a question or situation. It appears only once in the New Testament (Romans 11:4) and once in the Septuagint, where it renders a Hebrew term in Proverbs 31:1. Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri use the word more plainly to mean an official report or document, so its biblical sense of a divine answer is a specialized application of a common business term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force in that single verse rests on limited evidence.

definition: To find, discover, or come upon something or someone, whether by deliberate searching or by chance.
article: εὑρίσκω is the everyday verb for finding—coming upon a person, locating an object, or discovering a fact—with or without prior searching, and the Byzantine NT renders it "found" in 156 of 177 occurrences (98%). Its range stretches naturally from physical finding to figurative discovery: finding out by inquiry, learning, or being "found" in a certain state, and the passive can even mean to disappear ("not be found"). In the Septuagint it appears 459 times and overwhelmingly stands for the Hebrew מָצָא (365×), confirming "find" as its core. The everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth use, as in one account-keeper's complaint, "I cannot find the entry in the books."

definition: To tie or wrap something around a person or object, such as cloth bound around the body.
article: περιδέω means to tie or wrap something around—a band of cloth, a wrapping, a binding. It appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:44, where the raised Lazarus has his face bound about with a cloth, and once in the Septuagint at Job 12:18, translating a Hebrew word for a belt or sash. Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri preserve it in a healing inscription from the temple of Asclepius at Epidaurus, where a god wraps a band around an injured eye.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one in the Septuagint, the measured range is very thin, though the lexica and papyri agree on the basic meaning.

definition: In a careful, diligent, thorough way — doing something with attentive effort.
article: ἐπιμελῶς is an adverb meaning "carefully" or "diligently," describing an action done with attentive effort. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 15:8, where the woman searches "carefully" for her lost coin. Everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor of meaning vividly — one document instructs the reader to "carefully grease" a new yoke-band, while others use the comparative form for handling tasks with greater diligence.
caution: The measured-sense data here mislabels the rendering as "silver" — a clear glitch, since the lexica (KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) and the single NT occurrence all agree the word means "carefully/diligently."

definition: The south, whether the southern direction, the southern region, or the south wind.
article: νότος points toward the south — used for the compass direction, a southern territory, or the south wind that blows from that quarter. In the Byzantine New Testament all 7 occurrences are rendered "south," though the broader range is real: the lexica note it can mean the actual south wind (as in Acts 27:13) as well as the southern region. In the Septuagint it appears 75 times and most often translates Hebrew נֶ֫גֶב (33×), the Negev, the dry southern land of Israel, and everyday papyri use it for things like "the South Lane" of a town.
caution: The single measured sense "south" blends what the lexica distinguish as direction, region, and the south wind, so context determines which is meant.

definition: Unstable or unsettled, lacking steadiness and firm direction.
article: This word describes something or someone that is unsettled and lacking stability. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in the critical SBLGNT text), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "unstable" every time, as in James 1:8 of a double-minded person. The Septuagint uses it once in Isaiah, and Moulton-Milligan note its everyday use in Koine — including a striking curse tablet from Cnidus (around 300–100 BC) calling for someone's house to be made "unstable." Dodson even reaches for "almost anarchic," suggesting the word can carry a stronger sense of disorder than "unstable" alone conveys.
caution: Evidence is thin, with only one or two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: A dream experienced while sleeping, especially one through which a divine message is given.
article: Ὄναρ means a dream — the kind you have while asleep. In the New Testament it appears only 6 times, all in Matthew, and always in the phrase κατ᾽ ὄναρ, "in a dream" (as when angels warn Joseph or the Magi). The apparent multiple "senses" in the data are really just one meaning: the measured renderings ("dream," "after a dream," "Magi a dream") are all fragments of that same fixed phrase. One interesting wrinkle: in votive inscriptions the same phrase κατ᾽ ὄναρ tends to mean "in consequence of a dream" rather than "during a dream," and the ancient grammarian Photius even branded the construction as thoroughly "barbarous."
caution: All 6 occurrences sit inside one fixed phrase in a single book, and the supposed separate senses are really phrase fragments rather than distinct meanings.

definition: A man's name, Sosthenes, borne by two different people in the New Testament.
article: Sosthenes is a Greek personal name appearing twice in the New Testament, always rendered "Sosthenes" in every translation surveyed. Abbott-Smith notes it covers two distinct men: a Jewish synagogue ruler at Corinth (Acts 18:17) and a Christian named with Paul (1 Corinthians 1:1). The name was common in everyday life, showing up in papyri and inscriptions across several centuries, from third-century BC Egypt onward, as documented by Moulton-Milligan.
caution: With only two occurrences, the evidence is thin and the name is shared by two separate individuals, so context determines who is meant.

definition: To be set out or placed in front of someone, whether a goal, an offer, or something already present.
article: πρόκειμαι is built from πρό ("before") and κεῖμαι ("to lie"), so it literally means "to lie before" — something laid out in plain view, whether a hope, a race, a joy, or an offering. In the New Testament's 5 occurrences it covers both a thing set before someone (Hebrews 6:18; 12:1-2) and what a person already has on hand (2 Corinthians 8:12). The everyday Koine papyri use the participle constantly to mean "aforesaid" or "the above-mentioned," as in a contract to purchase "the office of prophet in the aforesaid temple" — a practical legal sense.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences spread across 3 senses, the evidence base is thin for any single nuance.

definition: To make room for something — either to hold or contain it physically, or to accept and have space for it in one's mind or heart.
article: χωρέω centers on the idea of "room": physically it means to hold or contain something, and figuratively it means to make room for an idea by accepting it. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times across 5 books, but only twice (50%) does it surface as a clear English word — "accept" in Matthew 19:11–12 — while 6 of 10 occurrences get absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it of measures and capacities (translating Hebrew terms tied to holding and quantity), and Moulton-Milligan notes a striking papyrus where it describes the deceased Emperor Claudius having "withdrawn" or "joined" his ancestors, showing the same range as the New Testament.
caution: With only 10 occurrences and 6 of them absorbed into phrasing, just one measured sense is visible, though the lexica document a much wider range (go, hold, contain, advance).

definition: The end, finish, or final point of something—whether the conclusion of an act, a period of time, or the outcome of a course of events.
article: τέλος most often means "end"—the termination or limit of an action, state, or stretch of time—which accounts for about 70% of its 41 New Testament occurrences. It also stretches to mean the "outcome" or fate of something (about 15%), as in the destiny that follows a way of life. The Septuagint connection is striking: across 127 occurrences it most frequently renders Hebrew נָצַח (37×), often in the phrase "to the end," and everyday papyri use τέλος ἔχει to mean a matter is "finished" or settled, much like a completed decree.
caution: Strong's and the older lexicons also list a "tax" or "levy" sense, but that meaning is not among the measured New Testament renderings here.

definition: The fist or clenched hand; in its single New Testament use it describes a particular way of washing the hands before eating.
article: At its core πυγμή means the fist or clenched hand, a sense confirmed by the classical lexica and by its everyday appearance in Koine papyri. It shows up only once in the New Testament, at Mark 7:3, where it describes how some washed their hands before eating—rendered "ceremonially" in the Majority Standard Bible. In the Septuagint it appears twice (Exodus 21:18 and Isaiah 58:4), both times translating the Hebrew אֶגְרֹף, "fist," matching the literal sense. The exact force of the phrase in Mark is genuinely debated: proposals range from washing "with the fist," "diligently," or "up to the elbow," and some manuscripts even read a different word entirely (πυκνά, "often").
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and its meaning there is openly disputed, with the lexica and manuscripts disagreeing on how to read the Mark 7:3 phrase.

definition: A person who uses force or energetic effort, applied either to those who forcefully press in or to those who violently seize.
article: βιαστής describes someone who acts with force or vigorous energy, and the single ancient lexica behind it stretch the meaning two ways: "strong, forceful" and "violent." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 11:12, and the Majority Standard Bible there renders it with "subject" (the verse's grammatical subject), while the KJV's traditional gloss is "violent." Abbott-Smith notes it is a late form of the earlier word βιατάς, and the "violent" shading is specifically credited to Philo.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources disagree on whether it leans toward forceful eagerness or outright violence.

definition: Abraham, the Hebrew patriarch regarded as the forefather of the Jewish people.
article: This is the personal name of Abraham, the founding patriarch, and it shows up 72 times across 11 books of the Byzantine New Testament. It is a fixed, indeclinable name—the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "Abraham" 88% of the time and "Abraham's" (possessive) in 6 cases like Luke 16:22 and John 8:33. The Septuagint uses it 185 times, almost always for Hebrew אַבְרָהָם, and Moulton-Milligan notes the name turns up in everyday Egyptian papyri, including a Grecized form Ἄβραμος, showing it circulated as a real name in ordinary documents.

definition: Having no children; describing a person who has died or lives without offspring.
article: ἄτεκνος simply means "childless," formed from the negative prefix and the word for "child" (τέκνον). In the New Testament it appears only in Luke 20:28-30, in the discussion of a man who dies without children, where it can describe either the person's state or the manner of dying. The word was common in everyday legal documents: papyri use it in property and inheritance settlements, such as one phrase meaning "childless and intestate" (dying without children or a will).
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (2 in the critical text), all in a single Luke passage, so the apparent two senses really reflect one straightforward meaning.

definition: A person who betrays others, handing them over to enemies or breaking trust.
article: Προδότης means a betrayer or traitor, someone who hands another person over into enemy hands (the word comes from προδίδωμι, "to give forward"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders one of these as "became traitor" (Luke 6:16, of Judas), while absorbing the other two into surrounding phrasing. A striking witness comes from an ancient tomb inscription at Delphi cited by Deissmann, which curses any grave-robber with "the portion of Judas, the betrayer (προδότης) of our Lord Jesus Christ."
caution: With only 3 occurrences and most absorbed into phrasing, the measured evidence is thin, though the classical and papyri sources agree consistently on "traitor."

definition: An animal's burrow, hole, or den—the sheltered hideaway where a wild creature lives.
article: φωλεός refers to the hole, lair, or den that a wild animal lives in. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in Jesus' saying that foxes have dens (Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it consistently in those passages. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes it is a late Greek word well attested in everyday papyri and inscriptions, and its modern Greek descendant φωλιά means "nest."
caution: With only two occurrences—both in the same saying—the evidence is thin, though the lexicons agree closely on its meaning.

definition: To host someone as a guest, or — in the passive — to be taken aback by something that strikes you as strange.
senseLabels: to host or lodge a guest
article: ξενίζω carries two related ideas: welcoming a guest into your home, and being struck by something unfamiliar. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "staying" or "strange" about a third of the time each, with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The hospitality sense is well grounded in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cites a Coan sacrificial calendar from the 4th–3rd century B.C. where temple officials "entertain" the sacred offerings and heralds for the night, and Abbott-Smith notes the "surprise, astonish" sense belongs to later writers like Polybius.

definition: Warm affection and loyalty shared among people who belong to the same family, used in the New Testament for love between fellow Christians.
article: φιλαδελφία means the kind of love that brothers and sisters in a family feel for one another, and in the New Testament it consistently describes the mutual affection of Christians toward each other as members of one family. Across its 6 occurrences the rendering varies only slightly — "brotherly kindness" (2×), "brotherly love," and the like — all pointing to the same core idea. What's striking is the shift in scope: Moulton-Milligan notes that in non-biblical Greek and the Septuagint the word was limited to love between literal blood relatives (one papyrus uses it of kindness to sisters), while the New Testament redirects it to the wider Christian brotherhood.

definition: To do wrong or commit sin, whether against God or against another person.
article: ἁμαρτάνω is the standard New Testament verb for sinning, appearing 42 times. Half of its occurrences (20×) are simply rendered "sinned," while in 9 cases (23%) it means sinning "against" someone specific. The word's literal root sense is "to miss the mark," and everyday Koine papyri preserve this broader meaning: in a private letter from the time of Augustus, a writer protests "I have not wronged you in anything" (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἡμάρτηκά τι εἰς σέ), the same construction Paul uses in Acts. In the Septuagint it appears 200 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew חָטָא.

definition: Describing something that is needed or required, or sometimes a person bound to you by close ties of kinship or friendship.
article: At its core ἀναγκαῖος means "necessary" — something that has to be done or supplied. The Byzantine NT uses it 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders the clearest cases as "necessary" (4×, 57%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing or shaded as "more necessary" and the like. The lexicons add a second, warmer sense not visible in the measured renderings: applied to people, it can mean "near" or "intimate," as in Acts 10:24 where Cornelius gathers his close friends — a usage the everyday papyri confirm when they pair the word with φίλος ("intimate friend").
caution: The measured data only captured the "necessary" sense; the "close/intimate" meaning rests on the lexicons and papyri rather than on counted NT renderings.

definition: A split or tear, whether a literal rip in cloth or a figurative division and disagreement among people.
article: σχίσμα means a split or gap—literally a tear, as in a garment, or figuratively a division between people. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across 4 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "divisions" or "division among" in the measured cases, all referring to disagreement and factions among people (as in John 7:43 and 1 Corinthians 1:10). The literal sense survives elsewhere too: Abbott-Smith notes its use for a rent in cloth in Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21, and the papyri even apply the word to a furrow opened by ploughing.
caution: Two of the eight occurrences were absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, so the measured senses cover only part of the usage.

definition: A spirit believed to give the power to foretell the future, the kind that possessed a fortune-telling slave girl.
article: Πύθων appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 16:16), where it describes the spirit that gave a slave girl her fortune-telling ability. The word originally named the serpent of Greek legend slain by Apollo at Delphi, but by the time of Plutarch it had become a label for ventriloquist soothsayers thought to have a familiar spirit speaking from inside them. Notably, in its one NT use the English translations absorb it into a phrase ("a spirit of divination") rather than giving it its own word, and the Septuagint uses related language for forbidden mediums in Leviticus 19:31 and 1 Samuel 28:7.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests heavily on outside sources like Plutarch and the Septuagint parallels.

definition: A man's name, Eliezer, used in the New Testament for an ancestor of Jesus.
article: Eliezer is a Hebrew personal name carried over into Greek as an indeclinable proper noun. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 3:29, naming an ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy. The name is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 14 times across 6 books, almost always translating the Hebrew name אֱלִיעֶזֶר (13 of those times).
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament use rests on a single passage.

definition: To make something hard or, figuratively, to make a person stubborn and unyielding—or, in the passive, to become stubborn.
article: σκληρύνω comes from σκληρός ("hard") and means literally to harden, but in the New Testament it is used figuratively of making a person stubborn or unyielding. It appears 6 times across 3 books, most often in the warning "do not harden your hearts" (Hebrews 3:8, 15; 4:7), and in Romans 9:18 of God hardening whom he wills; the passive describes people who "become hardened" (Acts 19:9). The Septuagint uses it 34 times, chiefly translating Hebrew קָשָׁה ("to be hard," 17×), and a chemistry recipe in the papyri uses it literally of a substance hardening as it cooks down.
caution: One measured sense labeled "daily" reflects how the surrounding phrase in Acts 19:9 was rendered, not the verb's own meaning, which is "become hardened."

definition: To bring something completely to an end, whether finishing an activity, fulfilling a plan, or accomplishing a task.
article: συντελέω means to carry something all the way through to completion, ranging from finishing speaking to fulfilling a promised event. It appears 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament but is hugely common in the Septuagint (158 times), where it most often renders the Hebrew כָּלָה, "to finish" or "complete." Everyday Koine papyri use it the same practical way—construction records speak of work being "completed" and landing-stages being finished on time—so this was ordinary working vocabulary, not just religious language.
caution: Several New Testament occurrences are blended into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word, so the measured sense breakdown is thin and uneven.

definition: Belonging to this present physical world rather than to the heavenly or future order.
article: κοσμικός describes something that pertains to this world or universe, often with the sense of "earthly" as opposed to heavenly. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "earthly" once (Hebrews 9:1), while the other instance is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing without its own English word. The most interesting wrinkle is that Abbott-Smith records a further ethical sense, "worldly," pointing to desires (Titus 2:12), even though the measured data only captures the "earthly" rendering.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the evidence is thin, and the lexica list a "worldly" ethical sense the corpus measurements do not capture.

definition: A member of an Eastern priestly or learned caste who studied the stars, or more negatively, a practitioner of magic.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament μάγος appears 6 times and splits into two ideas: the respected Eastern scholars who came seeking the infant Jesus (the "Magi" of Matthew 2, 3×), and the negative figure of a "sorcerer" (Acts 13, 2×). The classical lexicons trace it to a Median priestly caste who studied religion and the heavens, which fits the Matthew usage well. Moulton-Milligan find the word in everyday papyri and inscriptions specifically in the "sorcerer" sense, including a third-or-fourth-century reference to an "arch-magus," showing the negative meaning was alive in common speech.
caution: One of the six occurrences was counted under an odd "After during time" label that looks like a data artifact rather than a real sense, so treat the percentages loosely.

definition: The act of seizing others' property by force—plundering, robbery, or the greed that drives it.
article: ἁρπαγή names the violent taking of what belongs to others, ranging from the inner "greed" that grasps to the outward act of robbery or pillage. In the three New Testament uses it covers the greed filling a cup and dish (Matthew 23:25, Luke 11:39) and, in Hebrews 10:34, the plundering of believers' possessions. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this concrete sense: one inscription speaks of "the seizure of livestock that occurred," and a document pairs it with "violence," showing it was a normal word for theft and looting.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 NT occurrences) and confidence is low; the rendering tied to Hebrews 10:34 is uncertain, since the BSB does not independently support the "accepted" label listed here.

definition: To pay a penalty or suffer punishment, especially the price owed for wrongdoing.
article: τίνω is a legal-sounding word meaning to pay the price or penalty for something, most often paired with the word for "penalty" (δίκην) in the phrase "pay the penalty." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Thessalonians 1:9, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "suffer." The everyday papyri confirm this courtroom flavor: one document from A.D. 134 uses the same phrasing for offenders who "may pay the fitting penalty," matching how classical writers used the verb.
caution: Evidence is thin—the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range here rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri parallels.

definition: Happening early in the morning, at or near dawn.
article: ὀρθρινός is an adjective meaning "early" or "belonging to the dawn," formed from ὄρθρος ("dawn, daybreak"). It is a late Koine form of the older ὄρθριος, and the Atticists actually condemned it as substandard, though Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in ordinary everyday papyri and inscriptions. It appears just once in the critical Greek New Testament (Luke 24:22, of the women who came early to the tomb) and three times in the Septuagint, where in Hosea it renders Hebrew words tied to the early morning.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word does not occur in the Byzantine NT text and appears only once in the critical text and three times in the Septuagint.

definition: To bind something under the feet—that is, to put on sandals or shoes, or to be shod.
article: This verb literally means "to bind under," and it is used almost exclusively of footwear—putting sandals or shoes on your feet. It appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, though it gets its own English word in only one of those (in Mark 6:9, rendered "sandals"); the other two are absorbed into phrasing like "shod." The everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense vividly: one document (P Lond 121) speaks of someone "having put on Lycian sandals," exactly the construction Paul uses in Ephesians 6:15.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences with just one rendered as a standalone English word—so confidence is low.

definition: A Hebrew personal name meaning the name of two Israelites, including the father of John the Baptist.
article: Ζαχαρίας is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Zechariah, appearing 11 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "Zechariah" in 10 of them (91%). It refers to two different men: the priest who was father of John the Baptist (most of the occurrences, as in Luke 1), and an earlier Zechariah killed in the temple, mentioned in Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51. In the Septuagint the name shows up 44 times and translates the Hebrew זְכַרְיָה 39 times, confirming its straightforward function as a personal name.
caution: Abbott-Smith notes the New Testament text in Matthew 23:35 calls this Zechariah "son of Barachiah," which he regards as a mistaken identification of the figure described in 2 Chronicles 24.

definition: To set oneself in opposition, resisting or pushing back against someone or something.
article: This verb describes someone placing themselves against another, opposing or resisting them—it appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 2:25, where it refers to people who stand in opposition. The classical and lexical evidence is consistent on the core idea of opposition: Longinus uses it of someone who "steels himself utterly against persuasive words." Notably, Moulton-Milligan confirms the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary language, not a specialized term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's lone measured rendering ("gently") reflects a translation choice for the surrounding phrase rather than the word's own meaning, which the lexica agree is "to oppose."

definition: To need or have need of something or someone.
article: χρῄζω simply means to need or have need of something, whether a thing or a person. It appears only 5 times in the New Testament, and although the renderings cluster into three measured groups, they all express the same core idea of lacking or requiring something. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary usage—one letter from A.D. 264 pleads "come up because I urgently need you," matching the personal use seen in Romans 16:2.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, though its meaning is consistent across all sources.

definition: To bear witness to something, confirming or testifying solemnly that it is true.
article: ἐπιμαρτυρέω means to testify or bear witness to something, built from μαρτυρέω ("to witness") plus the prefix ἐπί. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the phrase translated "briefly" (the construction names Peter's solemn testimony). In the Septuagint it occurs 6 times across 4 books and five of those translate the Hebrew עוּד, and Moulton-Milligan note the stronger related form ἐπιμαρτύρομαι showing up in papyri where someone "calls those present to witness" an assault.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "briefly" reflects translation of the whole phrase rather than the verb's core meaning of bearing witness.

definition: Moral and personal purity, especially blamelessness in conduct and chaste behavior.
article: ἁγνεία refers to purity—a clean, blameless quality of life that includes chastity. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Timothy (4:12 and 5:2), where it is consistently rendered "purity." In the everyday Greek of papyri and inscriptions the word often carried a ceremonial sense, describing the ritual cleanness required at temple sites, as in a Cilician inscription and the decree of Canopus (239 BC).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and limited Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the entry rests on a small sample.

definition: A third-person pronoun meaning he, she, it, or they, also used for emphasis to mean the very same or himself.
article: This is one of the most common words in the Greek New Testament, appearing 5,752 times across all 27 books and functioning as the everyday third-person pronoun — he, she, it, they, and their possessive forms. Because Greek folds pronouns into verb endings and phrasing, the word is so woven into sentences that 2,188 of those occurrences carry no separate English word at all. Beyond a plain pronoun it can mean 'self' or 'the same,' and the papyri show a notable use where αὐτός marks something already mentioned — 'the said Horus' — much like our 'aforesaid.' In the Septuagint it appears over 23,000 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew pronoun הוּא, 'he.'
caution: The many overlapping 'measured senses' here are largely grammatical combinations rather than distinct meanings, so the sense list reflects translation patterns more than genuine differences in meaning.

definition: An emphatic connecting word meaning "for this very reason" or "therefore," drawing a strong conclusion from what was just said.
article: διόπερ is an emphatic form of the ordinary word "therefore" (διό), strengthened to mean "for this very reason." It draws a firm conclusion from a preceding argument, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "therefore" in 2 of its 3 New Testament occurrences. Beyond the Bible, Moulton-Milligan show it was common in everyday Koine, appearing in legal documents and even an imperial edict ("therefore let all in every city know...").
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament (2 in the critical text), so confidence is low.

definition: An adverb meaning "last year" or "a year ago," pointing to the year before the present one.
article: Πέρυσι is a simple adverb meaning "last year" or "a year ago." It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians (8:10 and 9:2), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "last year" 100% of the time. It was common, everyday Koine: papyri use phrases like "which we dug last year," and the construction ἀπὸ πέρυσι ("since last year") shows up in business documents tracking debts and deliveries.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the meaning is unambiguous and confirmed by everyday papyri.

definition: To rescue or deliver someone from danger, harm, or destruction by drawing them to safety.
article: ῥύομαι means to rescue or deliver a person from danger or destruction, often pictured as drawing someone out to safety. The four measured senses ('deliver,' 'delivered,' 'rescue,' 'rescued') are really just present and past forms of one tight idea, and the Majority Standard Bible's renderings line up with the BSB at 75–100%. It shows up heavily in the Septuagint (151× in 17 books), most often translating the Hebrew נָצַל ('snatch away, deliver') 52 times; a sixth-century Christian amulet even quotes the Lord's Prayer with this verb, asking to be delivered 'from evil.'

definition: Corinth, a major Greek city in the northeastern Peloponnese, the capital of the Roman province of Achaia.
article: Κόρινθος is simply the place name Corinth, a prominent city in Greece and the capital of the Roman province Achaia. It appears 6 times across 4 New Testament books, always referring to this one city. The two extra "senses" in the digest ("Corinth together" and "order Corinth") are just artifacts of the surrounding words in a phrase, not separate meanings — the word means Corinth in every instance, as the lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith, Strong's, KJV) all agree.
caution: The three listed senses are not real distinctions; all six occurrences refer to the single city of Corinth.

definition: An edible garden plant or vegetable, the kind of herb grown for food.
article: λάχανον means a garden herb or vegetable — an edible plant raised in a garden, as opposed to a wild or grain plant. The classical lexica are unanimous on this single sense, and the everyday papyri confirm it vividly: documents speak of "vegetables of all kinds," the price of vegetables sold, and even "vegetable ground" for growing them. Note that the measured renderings labeled "largest" and "person" reflect surrounding phrasing in passages like Matthew 13:32 (the mustard seed becoming the largest of garden plants) and Romans 14:2, not separate meanings of the word itself.
caution: The measured sense labels come from how whole verses were translated rather than the word alone, so they don't capture λάχανον's actual meaning, which the lexica agree is simply "vegetable."

definition: A noose, slip-knot, or halter; figuratively a restraint that ties someone down.
article: βρόχος literally means a noose, slip-knot, or halter — a loop of cord. The New Testament uses it only once, in 1 Corinthians 7:35, where it appears figuratively for a restraint placed on someone, which is why translations speak of not throwing a 'restraint' rather than a 'snare.' The everyday Koine sense is vividly preserved in a 2nd-century papyrus, where a public physician reports examining a body found 'hanged by a noose' (βρόχῳ).
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and three times in the Septuagint, and lexica note the figurative 'restraint' sense rather than the 'snare' rendering of older versions.

definition: To lead or take someone away, often to trial, prison, or execution; also of a road that leads somewhere.
senseLabels: led away to trial or death
article: ἀπάγω means to lead or take someone away, and the New Testament uses it most often (7× of 14) for leading a person off—especially to trial, prison, or death—a usage that matches its role as a legal term in Attic Greek. In about a third of cases it simply describes the direction a road or path "leads," as in the narrow and broad ways of Matthew 7:13. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: it appears four times in one second-century document (P Oxy I.33) of someone being led off to death, which led Moulton-Milligan to suspect that in Acts 12:19 the guards were not merely jailed but led away to execution. In the Septuagint it occurs 34 times, frequently rendering the Hebrew נָהַג (8×).

definition: To see or know something in advance, perceiving an event before it happens.
article: προείδω means to see beforehand or foresee, functioning as the aorist of προοράω (no present form is actually used). In the Greek Old Testament it can mean simply to catch sight of someone in advance (Genesis 37:18, where Joseph's brothers see him coming) or to perceive ahead of time (Psalm 139:3). The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, as Moulton-Milligan note from a document around 10 B.C., showing it was ordinary language rather than a specialized term.
caution: This word does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament text used here, so no measured senses are available and the description rests on lexica and Septuagint usage.

definition: Sodom, an ancient city in Palestine destroyed in a famous judgment and remembered as a byword for sin.
article: Σόδομα is simply the Greek name for the city of Sodom, a place-name borrowed from the Hebrew סְדֹם. It appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament and is rendered "Sodom" every single time, so there is no real range of meaning to debate. One striking detail: Moulton-Milligan notes wall-scratchings reading "Sodoma, Gomora" found in Pompeii, which may reflect early Christian presence — and an eerie echo of that town's own destruction.

definition: A lack of knowledge or understanding, sometimes shading into deliberate or willful blindness.
article: Ἄγνοια means a lack of knowledge or understanding, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ignorance" in some form across all 4 New Testament occurrences. The word's range stretches from honest inadvertence to a more loaded sense of willful blindness, which Abbott-Smith and Dodson both note for Ephesians 4:18. Tellingly, Moulton-Milligan found the same "willful blindness" connotation in an everyday papyrus (P Tebt I.24, 117 BC), where an official describes people who finally "left off their ignorance" and departed the district. In the Septuagint it appears 17 times, often translating the Hebrew words for guilt (אָשָׁם, 6×) and unintentional sin (שְׁגָגָה, 2×).
caution: The three measured "senses" really reflect different English phrasings of one underlying meaning rather than distinct definitions, and the BSB does not back the "ignorance due" rendering.

definition: In a spiritual way—either by the Holy Spirit's help or in a non-literal, figurative sense.
article: This adverb, formed from πνευματικός, describes doing or understanding something "spiritually" rather than by ordinary physical perception. The evidence splits its two New Testament occurrences evenly: in 1 Corinthians 2:14 it means perceiving things by the aid of the Holy Spirit, while in Revelation 11:8 it points to a figurative or symbolic sense—the city "spiritually called" Sodom and Egypt. Abbott-Smith neatly captures both poles, distinguishing the Spirit-empowered meaning from the symbolic one.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a measured 50/50 split between two quite different senses, the confidence tier is low.

definition: In a way that pleases or satisfies someone, especially in serving or worshiping acceptably.
article: This adverb describes doing something acceptably or in a way that pleases another, and in its single New Testament appearance (Hebrews 12:28) it speaks of serving God in a pleasing manner. It is built from the adjective εὐάρεστος ("well-pleasing"). The inscription evidence is striking: in pre-Christian texts a woman "completed her water-carrying duty acceptably (εὐαρέστως) to the citizens," and a priest "was praised by all the citizens for serving acceptably" — showing it was ordinary public-service language for satisfactory, commendable conduct.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the corpus rendering "unshakable" conflicts sharply with every lexicon (which gives "acceptably"), likely reflecting a measurement quirk rather than the word's actual meaning.

definition: The best seat at a meal, the place of honor at a banquet table.
article: πρωτοκλισία refers to the most honored spot at a dinner table, where ancient diners reclined to eat. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 3 books, always tied to wanting recognition at meals, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as a "place of honor" in 4 of those 5 cases. Built from πρῶτος ("first") and κλισία (a reclining or seat), it is a vivid social term, and Moulton-Milligan note that it appears confined to the Gospels and writers quoting them, even though related words like πρωτοκλίναρχος show up as a title in everyday documents.

definition: Describing something unbroken or continuous, used in Hebrews in the phrase "for all time" to mean perpetually or without interruption.
article: This word means "unbroken" or "continuous," and in the New Testament it appears only 4 times, all in Hebrews, always in the set phrase "for all time" (εἰς τὸ διηνεκές). Although the Majority Standard Bible renders the four occurrences with different surrounding words like "all time," "time," and even "realities," each instance reflects the same core idea of perpetual continuity. Outside the Bible the word was common everyday Koine: it shows up in papyri and inscriptions, including an Imperial-era inscription honoring someone "for all time" and a prayer for the emperor's permanence.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, all in a single fixed phrase in one book, the measured "senses" reflect translation wording rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: A coming or arrival, especially the advent of a person who is expected.
article: ἔλευσις means a coming or arrival, derived from the verb ἔρχομαι ("to come"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 7:52, where Stephen speaks of the prophets who foretold the coming of the Righteous One. The classical lexica agree it points specifically to an advent or arrival, with later usage tied to the coming of Christ.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from usage, and the lone rendering tag ("fail") in the digest appears to be a data error rather than a genuine sense.

definition: An official registration of people, especially for a government census or tax enrollment.
article: In the New Testament ἀπογραφή refers to an official census or registration, used both times (100%) for the enrollment under Roman authority (Luke 2:2; Acts 5:37). The word had a wider range in Greek—Abbott-Smith notes it could mean a written copy or, as a legal term, a sworn deposition—but the measured biblical sense is consistently "census." Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan observe that a very large number of surviving everyday papyri are themselves census papers, with the oldest firmly dated one from A.D. 34, showing how routine this kind of registration was in the Roman world.
caution: Only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, so the measured "census" sense rests on thin biblical evidence even though it is unanimous.

definition: To bear witness or give evidence about something you have seen or know, and so to confirm, attest, or speak well of it.
article: μαρτυρέω means to act as a witness — to testify to what you know or have seen — and it appears 76 times across 14 New Testament books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "testify" in 79% of cases, with a smaller group meaning "testimony" (10%) and a notable shade where it means to be "commended" or well spoken of (about 6%, clustered in Hebrews 11). The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where it was the standard term written after a signature to confirm wills, sales, and deeds — exactly as we write "witness" today.

definition: A spy or scout—someone sent secretly to observe and gather information about an enemy or place.
article: κατάσκοπος is a watcher sent to size up the situation, built from κατά and σκοπός ("watcher"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:31, where it refers to the spies Rahab welcomed; in the Septuagint it occurs 8 times in 3 books, always rendering the Hebrew רָגַל ("to spy out"). The word was at home in everyday Koine, attested in papyri and inscriptions, and Menander even uses it figuratively for someone who becomes "an observer of the whole situation."
caution: The measured sense is labeled "perish," which contradicts every dictionary gloss ("spy"); this almost certainly reflects a data mismatch in the single Hebrews 11:31 occurrence rather than the word's real meaning.

definition: To split something in two, and figuratively to set people against each other or turn them into enemies.
article: At its root διχάζω means to cut something apart or divide it in two, but its single New Testament use is figurative: setting family members against one another, as in Matthew 10:35. The word appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, and in that one place it gets absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan could find no everyday papyrus examples of the verb itself (Plato uses it), though the related word δίχα, meaning 'apart' or 'without,' shows up commonly in documents like a second-century Oxyrhynchus papyrus meaning 'without an order from the record-office.'
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and no papyrus attestation of the verb itself, the evidence for its range is thin.

definition: An adverb meaning "as for the rest," used to mean "finally," "from now on," or "moreover" as a writer moves on.
article: λοιπόν is the neuter singular of the adjective meaning "remaining" or "the rest," pressed into service as a connecting adverb. In context it can point forward in time ("henceforth, from now on") or simply signal a transition ("besides, moreover, for the rest"), the way a speaker says "and finally..." before a closing thought. The everyday papyri confirm this practical flavor: documents use the related forms for "the rest of the price for the hay" and "the remaining portions," showing it routinely meant whatever was left over.
caution: The word does not appear in the Byzantine NT text and shows up only in the critical text, so its New Testament range rests on a small number of passages.

definition: To eat or chew food; in the New Testament it simply means to eat, often with a vivid, physical sense.
article: τρώγω is a plain word for eating, appearing only 6 times in the New Testament across 2 books, mostly in John's Gospel. Originally it described animals gnawing or crunching, and then people munching raw food like vegetables and fruit, before becoming a general word for eating in everyday Koine speech. Interestingly, where Matthew 24:38 uses τρώγω, the parallel in Luke 17:27 swaps in the more common word ἐσθίω, and the everyday papyri show it used literally—one school exercise even has someone eating something cold and getting burned.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and overlapping renderings, the four measured senses are mostly grammatical variations of one basic meaning, 'to eat.'

definition: To stand firmly against something, resisting or opposing it as one would set up forces to withstand an attack.
article: This compound verb combines ἀντί ('against') with καθίστημι ('to set, establish'), giving the sense of setting yourself up to withstand opposition. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Hebrews 12:4), where it describes resisting to the point of bloodshed. The lexica spread its range wider than the New Testament shows it—Abbott-Smith and Dodson list 'replace,' 'supersede,' and 'oppose' alongside 'resist'—and the everyday papyri use it for confronting an opponent before a magistrate, as in an Oxyrhynchus document where someone 'confronted them before the strategus.'
caution: Evidence is thin: just one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, and the cited Hebrew counterparts in the digest don't fully match across sources, so the exact range is uncertain.

definition: A sharp stirring up of feeling — either a positive push toward good action or a heated, angry falling-out.
article: παροξυσμός captures an intense stirring up that can cut two ways: in Acts 15:39 it names the bitter falling-out between Paul and Barnabas, while Hebrews 10:24 uses it positively for spurring one another on to love and good works. The Byzantine NT has it just twice, and the Majority Standard Bible renders one occurrence "disagreement" and the other "spur" — a 50/50 split that neatly shows the word's double edge. Notably, the papyri use it as a medical term: a Tebtunis document speaks of "the paroxysms" of a fever, the recurring flare-ups of an illness.
caution: With only two NT occurrences split evenly between opposite tones, the range rests on thin evidence and depends heavily on context.

definition: To fill something or someone completely, and figuratively, to complete or fulfill a period of time.
article: At its core πλήθω means to fill—whether a banquet hall packed with guests, a sponge soaked with vinegar, or a person overcome by an emotion or by the Holy Spirit. The same word stretches to mean the completing or fulfilling of a span of time, which is how Luke describes the months of a pregnancy reaching their end. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 25 times and is rendered 'filled' in 84% of cases; the Septuagint uses it 104 times, most often for the Hebrew מָלֵא ('to be full'). A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri, where one document instructs someone to 'fill the vessel with green mustard,' showing the plain, practical sense behind the word.
caution: This is the present/imperfect form of the verb usually listed under πίμπλημι, which supplies its other tenses, so dictionaries treat them together.

definition: The job of managing a household or estate, and by extension any administration or arrangement of affairs entrusted to someone.
article: οἰκονομία starts with the concrete idea of running a household or estate—the office held by an οἰκονόμος (steward)—and stretches to mean administration or a planned arrangement of affairs more generally. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible most consistently renders it "stewardship," though in 2 of those 9 cases the word gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single word. The everyday Koine papyri confirm its practical range: in one document from 114 BC it names the official post of an oeconomus, while in another it simply means "measures" or actions taken, showing how widely the term could flex.
caution: The corpus-measured "stewardship" rests on only a couple of clear occurrences, and the classical lexica add a broader "administration/dispensation" sense not strongly captured by the measured renderings.

definition: To happen or take place, especially of events that occur, often befalling a particular person.
article: συμβαίνω means simply that something happens or comes to pass, and in the Byzantine New Testament every measured rendering points to this single meaning — three of its eight occurrences are translated "happened" (60%), with the rest absorbed into the surrounding phrasing or rendered "came." The Septuagint uses it 20 times, often translating Hebrew קָרָה ("to befall"), and it frequently takes a dative to mark the person to whom something happens, as in Acts 3:10 and 1 Corinthians 10:11. Notably, the classical lexicon traces a more literal root sense — "to stand with the feet together" or "come to terms" — but this physical meaning does not appear in the measured New Testament data, which is purely about events occurring.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and 3 of them carrying no English word of their own, the corpus evidence is moderate, though all sources agree on the core sense of "happen."

definition: A woman who sells purple cloth or fabric for a living.
article: This word describes a woman whose trade was selling purple cloth, a luxury fabric in the ancient world. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:14, describing Lydia, which is why the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it as her name in that single instance. The everyday reality of this profession is confirmed outside the Bible: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription from Cos naming both a male and a female purple-seller, showing it was a recognized trade with its own job title.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Flax, the plant fiber, and by extension the linen cloth or garments made from it.
article: λίνον refers to flax — the plant and its fiber — and by extension to the linen woven from it. The word appears only twice in the New Testament, once meaning a smoldering flax wick (Matthew 12:20, where the MSB renders the phrase "bruised") and once describing linen sashes worn by angels (Revelation 15:6). Everyday Koine papyri show it commonly used for cloths and garments — one Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 21 even prices "a hundred cloths of Sinaru," confirming the practical, commercial sense of linen goods.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the two cited lexica differing on the Revelation 15:6 reading, the evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: Smyrna, a major Ionian port city on the Aegean coast in the Roman province of Asia.
article: Σμύρνα is simply the name of Smyrna, a great port city in Asia Minor, mentioned twice in the New Testament (Revelation 1:11 and 2:8) as one of the seven churches. Every source agrees it refers to this one place, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. One interesting detail: the spelling wavered between Σμύρνα and Ζμύρνα, and the Ζ- form is actually supported by Smyrnaean coins minted down to the emperor Trajan's reign.
caution: This is a proper place name with only 2 occurrences, both pointing to the same city, so the two 'measured senses' reflect rendering quirks rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To spend or pass one's time or life, living in a certain way.
article: In the New Testament διάγω means to spend or pass one's life, usually with a description of how — Titus 3:3 uses it for the way people once lived. It appears only twice in the Byzantine text, and in 1 Timothy 2:2 it pairs with βίον ("life") to describe living a peaceful, quiet existence. The classical and papyri evidence shows a wider range: lexicons note an older sense "to carry over," and a striking inscription from an Asclepieum describes a god in a blind man's dream using his fingers to "draw apart" the closed eyelids — a literal, physical use far removed from the New Testament's "passing time."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of those absorbed into a phrase, the measured evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To peddle something for profit, treating it like cheap merchandise and possibly cheapening or corrupting it in the process.
article: This verb pictures a huckster or street-trader hawking goods for personal gain, and in its single New Testament appearance (2 Corinthians 2:17) it describes those who would 'peddle' the word of God. The Majority Standard Bible renders the lone occurrence as 'peddle' (100%), while older translations like the KJV chose 'corrupt'—reflecting a real ambiguity over whether the word means simply trading for profit or adulterating the goods. Moulton-Milligan favors the 'deal in for gain' sense and cites an everyday Koine papyrus (BGU IV.1024) using the verb, plus a parallel where Apollonius rebukes someone for 'peddling wisdom.'
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and sources genuinely disagree on whether it means merely 'trade for profit' or 'corrupt/adulterate.'

definition: A wide public street or open square in a town or city.
article: πλατεῖα is technically the feminine form of the adjective πλατύς ("broad"), used on its own to mean a broad public way — what we'd call a street or open square. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "streets" in 7 of them (78%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew רָחָב, which likewise means a broad, open place, and Moulton-Milligan confirms the word was common in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.

definition: The dative feminine plural form of the demonstrative "this/these," meaning "to, with, or by these (women or things)."
article: This is simply an inflected form of the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος ("this, these"), specifically the dative feminine plural, used to point at a group of things or people already mentioned. Because it is a case form rather than a separate word, it carries the relational sense "to these," "with these," or "by these," depending on context. The digest records zero occurrences of this exact form in the Byzantine New Testament, so its meaning is drawn entirely from its grammatical relationship to the parent word οὗτος.
caution: This entry rests only on grammatical derivation, since the digest shows no measured occurrences and no corpus translation data for this specific form.

definition: The booth or office where a tax collector sat to collect tolls and duties.
article: τελώνιον is the workplace of a tax collector — the small booth or office where tolls and customs were gathered. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the same scene where Jesus calls Matthew (Levi) as he sits at his post, rendered "booth" twice and "tax booth" once. Everyday Koine documents confirm the meaning: papyri and inscriptions use it for a "revenue office" or "custom-house," and the word survives in Modern Greek as τελωνεῖον.
caution: With only 3 occurrences, all in one parallel Gospel scene, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Describing someone wearing a gold finger-ring, a visible sign of wealth.
article: This adjective describes a person adorned with a gold ring on the finger, marking them out as wealthy. It appears only once in the New Testament, in James 2:2, where it describes a rich visitor entering an assembly. Moulton-Milligan note that the word itself does not seem to occur outside James 2:2, though similar expressions appear in classical authors — Lucian uses χρυσόχειρ ("gold-handed"), and Epictetus describes "a gray-haired old man wearing many gold rings."
caution: The word is a New Testament hapax that the standard translation renders as part of a broader phrase rather than as "clothes," so the single measured sense reflects how the verse is phrased rather than the word's own meaning.

definition: To graft a branch into a tree, inserting a shoot so it grows as part of the host plant.
article: ἐγκεντρίζω means to graft a shoot or branch into a plant so it becomes part of it. The word is fairly narrow: all 6 New Testament occurrences are in Romans 11, where Paul uses the image figuratively of people being grafted into a tree, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "grafted" two-thirds of the time. Moulton-Milligan notes the word belongs to refined Koine Greek and appears in everyday papyri and inscriptions, and outside the New Testament it shows up in the Septuagint only once, at Wisdom 16:11.
caution: Every New Testament use is concentrated in a single passage (Romans 11), so its range beyond Paul's grafting metaphor is thinly attested.

definition: A word meaning directly opposite, facing, or in front of something or someone, and figuratively before God's presence.
article: κατέναντι means "opposite" or "directly in front of," whether describing a village across the way, a place facing the temple treasury, or, figuratively, standing before God. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, and the lexicons agree on the core sense of "over against" or "facing." Built from κατά plus ἔναντι, it shows up routinely in everyday Koine documents — Moulton-Milligan cites a papyrus from 160 BC describing a woman seated on the sand with a child positioned opposite her. In the Septuagint it occurs 59 times, most often translating the Hebrew נֶ֫גֶד ("in front of").
caution: Some New Testament renderings like "into" reflect how a phrase reads in context rather than the word's own meaning, so weigh translations against the consistent "opposite/facing" sense in the lexicons.

definition: To live in self-indulgent luxury, spending freely on pleasure and comfort without restraint.
article: This word describes living for pleasure and luxury, with a sense of wanton extravagance. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just twice (in James 5:5 and, in other texts, 1 Timothy 5:6), and translators often fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. A vivid window into everyday Koine comes from an inscription quoted by Moulton-Milligan: "while you have the chance, bathe, perfume yourself, indulge, give, spend what you can — for whom are you saving it?" In the Septuagint it appears only once, rendering a Hebrew word, and scholars note it often pairs with τρυφάω (to live luxuriously), perhaps carrying somewhat worse overtones.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one Septuagint use, the evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: Alexander, a personal name borne by several different men in the New Testament.
article: Ἀλέξανδρος is a Greek personal name rendered "Alexander" in all 5 of its translated occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament (it appears 6 times total, with one instance absorbed into the surrounding phrasing). The name itself means something like "man-defender," built from elements related to defending and to ἀνήρ ("man"). It refers to several different individuals, including the son of Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21), a kinsman of the high priest (Acts 4:6), a Jew at Ephesus (Acts 19:33), and a coppersmith (1 Timothy 1:20).
caution: Lexicons differ on whether the Alexanders of 1 Timothy 1:20 and 2 Timothy 4:14 are the same man, since the name applies to multiple distinct people.

definition: Made of glass; glassy or transparent like glass.
article: ὑάλινος is an adjective meaning "of glass" or "glassy," describing something clear and transparent like glass. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Revelation, where it describes the sea before God's throne (Rev 4:6; 15:2). The word also shows up in everyday Koine documents: a third-century BC papyrus and an inscription from around 300 BC both mention glass vessels ("four glass bowls"), so this was ordinary household vocabulary, not a specialized term.
caution: The three measured senses here are an artifact of word-counting within phrases; the word itself simply means "of glass" in every occurrence.

definition: To release or let go—whether forgiving a debt or sin, leaving something or someone behind, or permitting an action to happen.
article: ἀφίημι is a workhorse verb covering the whole range of "letting go," and the corpus splits it almost evenly between two big ideas: forgiving sins or debts (48×, 40%) and leaving someone or something behind (45×, 37%), with "let" or "permit" close behind (17×, 14%). The Septuagint shows the same spread, rendering it for Hebrew words meaning "set down/leave" (יָנַח, 17×), "forgive" (סָלַח, 14×), and "abandon" (עָזַב, 4×). One nice detail: classical lexica note it was the standard word for releasing a spouse in divorce and even for releasing one's breath in death—"yielding up the spirit."
caution: The small "man" category (3×) is a tagging artifact, not a real meaning of the word—the BSB agrees with it 0% of the time.

definition: To pluck or pull something off, such as picking heads of grain from their stalks.
article: τίλλω means to pluck or pull something off. In all 3 of its New Testament appearances it describes disciples plucking heads of grain as they walked through fields (Matthew 12:1, Mark 2:23, Luke 6:1), and the Majority Standard Bible renders the context as "grainfields" every time. The everyday Koine papyri stretch the verb further: one document uses it for plucking hairs off hides to prepare them, so the word naturally covers any kind of pulling-off, not just grain.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, all in the same grain-plucking scene, the measured evidence shows just one narrow use even though the word's broader range is clear from other sources.

definition: To be overwhelmed with shock or alarm — deeply distressed, frightened, or awe-struck by something startling.
article: This verb describes a powerful emotional jolt — being utterly amazed, alarmed, or shaken by something unexpected. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, all in Mark, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "troubled" or "alarmed," capturing both inner distress and sudden fright. Notably, the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri: a fourth-century letter uses it (spelled ἐχθαμβῶν) of someone "alarming us," showing it was ordinary vocabulary, not just biblical language.
caution: The measured senses come from only 4 occurrences (none in the SBLGNT critical text), and the lexica list both "be amazed" and "terrify" so the precise shade depends on context.

definition: Full of something, whether literally packed with physical contents or figuratively brimming with thoughts and feelings.
article: μεστός means "full" — completely filled with whatever the surrounding genitive names. In the New Testament it works both literally (a net full of fish in John 21:11) and figuratively (a heart full of hypocrisy or wickedness, as in Matthew 23:28 and Romans 1:29), and the Byzantine text uses it this way in all 7 of its translated occurrences. Everyday Koine papyri show the same dual range, from "one basket full of sweetmeats" to a fourth-century letter describing replies "full of falsehood."
caution: The Septuagint evidence is thin and inconsistent, with sources listing different Hebrew counterparts for its handful of occurrences.

definition: To look directly at someone or something, often with a fixed or attentive gaze, and figuratively to consider closely.
senseLabels: to gaze or look directly at
article: ἐμβλέπω means to fix one's eyes on someone or something—a direct, attentive look rather than a casual glance. Of its 12 New Testament occurrences, it is rendered "looked" 7 times and "Look" 3 times, and it often introduces speech, as when Jesus "looked at" people before speaking. The figurative sense of "consider" shows up clearly in the Greek papyri: a second-century B.C. petition uses it to beg an official to "look into" a person's ruin and losses, the same metaphorical move found in Matthew 6:26 where people are told to consider the birds.

definition: An adverb meaning "in this way" or "thus," pointing to how something is done, either as just described or about to be described.
article: οὕτω (more commonly spelled οὕτως) is a workhorse adverb meaning "in this way" or "thus," used to point either back to what was just said or forward to what comes next. It is extremely common — 212 times across 21 books in the Byzantine text — and so woven into the flow of a sentence that 156 of those occurrences don't get a separate English word at all. In the Septuagint it appears 685 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew כֵּן ("so, thus," 311×), and everyday Koine papyri show the same usage, as in a letter phrase "this being so" (τούτων δὲ οὕτως ἐχόντων).

definition: Something that causes a person to stumble—literally or, more often, a moral obstacle that trips someone up spiritually.
article: πρόσκομμα comes from the verb προσκόπτω ("to strike against") and pictures something you trip over. In the New Testament it appears 6 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it most clearly as "stumbling" or "stumbling block," with the meaning ranging from a literal stumble to a moral obstacle that causes another believer to fall (Romans 14:13, 20; 1 Corinthians 8:9). In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew מוֹקֵשׁ (a snare or trap), which sharpens the sense of a hidden danger that ensnares.
caution: Several of the measured renderings ("pursuit were over," "let") reflect English phrasing rather than the word itself, so lean on the clearer "stumbling" senses.

definition: To make something go up, especially to haul or pull a net up onto the shore.
article: ἀναβιβάζω is the causal form of "to go up," so it means making something rise or hauling it upward — in its single New Testament appearance (Matthew 13:48), it describes fishermen pulling a full net up onto the beach. The word ranges more widely in the Greek Old Testament, where it appears 38 times in 17 books, often rendering the Hebrew עָלָה ("to go up") and רָכַב ("to ride/mount"). An interesting everyday touch comes from the papyri: a document from A.D. 184 uses the word for raising a price up to eighteen hundred drachmas, showing how flexible "make go up" could be.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense there rests on a single example.

definition: Issachar, one of Jacob's sons and the tribe of Israel descended from him.
article: Ἰσαχάρ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Issachar, one of the twelve sons of Jacob and the tribe named after him. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Revelation 7:7, where the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB both render it "Issachar" 100% of the time. The name comes from Hebrew יִשָּׂשכָר (first appearing in Genesis 30:18), and ancient writers like Josephus spelled it Ἰσάχαρις.
caution: This name occurs only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the SBL critical text, and the spelling varies across manuscripts.

definition: To work together with someone, cooperating or laboring alongside them toward a shared goal.
senseLabels: to work alongside as fellow laborer
article: συνεργέω means to work together with someone, to cooperate or labor side by side. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament (5 in the critical text), and the Majority Standard Bible's renderings cluster around the idea of being a 'fellow worker' or partner, though in 2 of the 4 cases the word gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain meaning: one document speaks of a man 'cooperating with' his wife, and Marcus Aurelius famously wrote that 'we are all fellow-workers toward the fulfilment of one object.'
