caution: With only 4 occurrences and grammarians noting a possible transitive sense ('cause to work together') in Romans 8:28, the precise range in some verses is genuinely debated.

definition: A fitting return or repayment made to someone in response to what they have done for you.
article: ἀμοιβή means a return or recompense — giving back something appropriate in exchange for what you have received. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:4, where the phrase "to make ἀμοιβάς to one's parents" means to repay them fittingly; the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding idea as "grandchildren," though the word itself signifies the repayment, not the people. The everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions illustrate it well: a man named Zosimus, granted citizenship, is praised for showing "no fruitless return" (ἀμοιβήν) for the honor, capturing exactly this sense of a worthy reciprocal gesture.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "grandchildren" reflects the verse's wording rather than the word's own meaning of "repayment," so treat the gloss with care.

definition: A rope or band used to fasten and control a ship's rudders.
article: This word refers to a fastening rope on a ship — specifically the band tying down the steering rudders, which sailors would loosen before steering. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:40, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the act of freeing them as 'hoisted.' Abbott-Smith notes the word is found nowhere else in surviving literature, but Moulton-Milligan shows the related adjective living on in everyday Koine papyri, where the neuter plural means 'yokes' or fastenings — one third-century document lists them at sixty drachmae.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is otherwise unattested in literature, so its precise meaning rests largely on context and a few papyri parallels.

definition: To hold someone up for public shame or disgrace by making a humiliating example of them.
article: παραδειγματίζω means to expose someone to public shame, putting them on display as a humiliating example. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (once in the critical text), and in both cases English translations fold it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own word. The Septuagint uses it 5 times, and outside the Bible Plutarch uses it of the poet Archilochus making himself infamous through his verses, while everyday papyri show the related noun simply meaning "example."
caution: Evidence is thin—the word is absorbed into phrasing in both NT occurrences and the digest's listed Hebrew counterparts vary between sources, so confidence is low.

definition: To bow down or prostrate oneself before someone in reverence or homage, especially in worship of God or other beings.
article: προσκυνέω describes the physical act of bowing or prostrating oneself before someone, which is why it shades from literal kneeling "before" a person (4×) into full "worship" — the meaning the Byzantine NT carries in the great majority of its 60 occurrences. The word's root sense points to crouching or making obeisance, and the Septuagint confirms this physical background: it translates the Hebrew שָׁחָה ("bow down") 148 of 190 times. An interesting grammatical detail from the papyri is that Ptolemaic inscriptions construct the verb with the accusative rather than the dative, matching the construction often found in the New Testament.

definition: A person who does evil deeds and breaks the law; a criminal or wrongdoer.
article: κακοῦργος literally combines "evil" and "work," so it names an evildoer, and in practice the New Testament uses it consistently to mean a criminal. All 4 occurrences are translated this way—three describe the men crucified with Jesus (Luke 23), and one is Paul's image of being chained "like a criminal" (2 Timothy 2:9). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary legal sense: people use the word in census disputes, robbery accusations, and complaints about being thrown in prison as a supposed "criminal."

definition: To carry or bring something from one place to another, or to bear up under a load or hardship.
article: φέρω is a common, everyday verb for carrying or bringing things, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 64 times across 12 books. The dominant measured sense is straightforward physical movement—"brought" accounts for 28× (61%) and "carry" appears as well—while a smaller group of uses means "bear" or "endure" (7×, 15%), as in bearing fruit or enduring hardship. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, where one writer asks his brother to "come up and bring my wife with you," exactly the ordinary Koine usage. In the Septuagint it appears 240× and often renders Hebrew words for an offering or tribute (מִנְחָה 13×, תְּרוּמָה 6×), reflecting the idea of bringing something to present.
caution: Some "senses" in the data ("Jesus," "ourselves," "proving") are artifacts of how the verb folds into surrounding phrasing rather than distinct meanings, and 18 of 64 occurrences contribute no English word of their own.

definition: Sharon, a coastal plain in Palestine stretching between Carmel and Joppa.
article: Σάρων is the Greek form of the Hebrew place name Sharon (שָׁרוֹן), the flat maritime plain along the coast between Mount Carmel and Joppa. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 9:35, where every translation surveyed renders it simply as "Sharon"; it also shows up 3 times in the Septuagint. It is a proper name for a specific district, so its meaning is fixed rather than variable.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond this single place name.

definition: So vast or hidden that it cannot be traced out, searched out, or fully understood.
article: ἀνεξιχνίαστος describes something that simply cannot be tracked down or fully explored — built from a negative prefix on a verb meaning "to track out" (related to ἴχνος, a footprint or trace). All 2 New Testament occurrences are rendered "unsearchable" (Romans 11:33 and Ephesians 3:8), and the BSB and KJV agree. The most interesting detail: Moulton-Milligan note Paul seems to have borrowed the word straight from the Greek of Job, where it appears 3 times translating the Hebrew חֵקֶר (a searching or investigation), as in Job 5:9 and 9:10.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences plus a handful in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is rated low.

definition: Relating to or having a physical body; bodily or corporeal as opposed to spiritual or non-physical.
article: σωματικός means "of the body" or "physical," derived from σῶμα ("body"). It appears only twice in the New Testament, splitting evenly between two shades: at Luke 3:22 the Spirit descends in "bodily" (visible, corporeal) form, and at 1 Timothy 4:8 it describes "bodily" training or exercise. Abbott-Smith helpfully distinguishes these as bodily versus incorporeal (Luke) and of or for the body (1 Timothy), and notes the word also appears in the Septuagint at 4 Maccabees 1:32 and 3:1.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and thin overall attestation, confidence is low, so the two measured senses rest on very few examples.

definition: Proof or evidence that demonstrates something to be true, or a rebuke that exposes wrongdoing.
article: ἔλεγχος refers to the kind of proof or evidence that settles a matter, and by extension a reproof that exposes fault. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (once in the critical text), and in both cases it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word, so the English Bible doesn't show it directly. The everyday legal flavor stands out in the papyri: in a document from A.D. 186 it means the "proofs" of a legal accusation that let someone press a more serious lawsuit. In the Septuagint it shows up 23 times, most often translating the Hebrew תּוֹכֵחָה ("rebuke," 13×), which points to the reproof side of its range.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament, where it is twice absorbed into phrasing and never rendered as a standalone English word, so the measured sense rests largely on the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: To come up to or stand beside someone or something, often suddenly arriving or being present at hand.
article: ἐφίστημι combines "upon" with "stand," and across its 21 New Testament uses it pictures someone arriving and standing right beside or over a person or place — sometimes a gentle approach, sometimes a hostile rush. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "stood" 5 times, "came" 3 times, and "came up" twice, while in 6 of 21 cases it simply blends into the phrasing without a word of its own. Outside the Bible it had practical everyday meanings: the papyri show it used for delaying a shipment of wheat, stopping a flow of blood, or fixing a door in place, and in the Septuagint it appears 58 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew word נָצַב, "to take a stand."

definition: A crowd or group that gathers and bands together, often a riotous mob or a secret plot.
article: συστροφή literally means "a twisting together," and in everyday use it describes people drawn into a tight knot — either a riotous gathering or a secret coalition. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times where translators fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word: once for an unruly crowd (Acts 19:40) and once where men "banded together" in a conspiracy (Acts 23:12). The Septuagint uses it 8 times, including for the Hebrew קֶ֫שֶׁר ("conspiracy"), and a papyrus even applies it metaphorically to a terse, compressed style of writing.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing, so the precise force in each context is somewhat uncertain.

definition: Naaman, the Syrian army commander healed of leprosy, mentioned by Jesus in Luke 4:27.
article: Νεεμάν is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Naaman (from H05283), referring to the Syrian commander whom Jesus cites in Luke 4:27 as the only leper cleansed in Elisha's day. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament and is treated as indeclinable. One interesting wrinkle is the spelling: the manuscripts of Luke 4:27 vary between Ναιμάν and Νεεμάν, a difference noted by Moulton-Milligan and the grammarians.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once, and the measured rendering shows "Elisha" rather than "Naaman," so the tagging may reflect the surrounding context rather than the name itself.

definition: Loud grief expressed through weeping and lamentation, especially the wailing of someone mourning a loss.
article: ὀδυρμός is the audible side of grief — the weeping and lamentation of people in deep sorrow. In both of its two New Testament appearances the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mourning" (100%), whether it is Rachel weeping for her children (Matthew 2:18) or Paul speaking of the Corinthians' sorrow (2 Corinthians 7:7). The everyday papyri preserve the related verb vividly: one petitioner writes that he submits his complaint "lamenting this impious act," and a tomb inscription recalls how even children "bewailed my death."
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, so the word's full range is hard to map confidently.

definition: A married woman who commits adultery, or—figuratively—a person or generation unfaithful to God.
article: At its core this word names an adulteress—a married woman who is sexually unfaithful—and it can also work as an adjective, "adulterous." The Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times, and beyond the literal sense it stretches figuratively to describe a faithless generation or people who turn away from God, as in "an adulterous generation" in the Gospels. The Septuagint uses it 7 times, mostly translating the Hebrew נָאַף ("to commit adultery"), and the everyday papyri show it was ordinary Koine vocabulary, not just biblical language.
caution: Sources agree on the literal sense, but the figurative "adulterous generation" usage blends literal and spiritual unfaithfulness in ways translators handle differently.

definition: In a state of readiness; being prepared and willing to do something.
article: This adverb means "readily" or "in readiness," describing someone prepared and willing to act. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, almost always in the fixed phrase ἑτοίμως ἔχω ("to be ready"), as in Acts 21:13 and 2 Corinthians 12:14. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this exact idiom—one document from the second century B.C. has people "being ready to subscribe the royal oath"—showing it was ordinary, practical language rather than special religious vocabulary.
caution: Confidence is low because the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament and the two measured senses are really the same idea applied in different phrasings.

definition: To strike or cut something off, and in the middle voice, to beat one's breast in grief — that is, to mourn or wail.
article: In the New Testament κόπτω splits into two clear uses: in its middle form it means to beat one's breast in grief, which the Majority Standard Bible renders "mourn" 5 of 8 times (63%), and in its plain active form it means to cut, here cutting branches that crowds "spread" on the road (2×, 25%). The Septuagint leans heavily toward the grief sense, using it 82 times and rendering the Hebrew סָפַד ("to mourn, lament") 24 times. The everyday papyri preserve the literal edge of the word beautifully — one document speaks of people who "have cut down wood on their own property," and another of machinery "for cutting."
caution: With only 8 New Testament occurrences, both measured senses rest on a small sample, though the mourning and cutting uses are well supported by the wider Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: Feeling sorrow so deep it surrounds and overwhelms a person.
article: περίλυπος describes sorrow at its most intense — grief so heavy it presses in on every side, which fits its construction from περί ("around") and λύπη ("sorrow"). The measured renderings all cluster around the same idea, from Jesus' soul being "consumed with sorrow" in Gethsemane to the rich ruler who became "very sad," so the word's range is narrow and consistent. In the Septuagint it appears 5 times, notably translating Hebrew terms in Psalm 42 where the soul is cast down within a person.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and several distinct phrasings, the English wordings vary even though the underlying sense is uniform.

definition: A sheepskin worn as a rough garment or cloak, the kind associated with prophets like Elijah.
article: μηλωτή means a sheepskin, a coarse animal-hide cloak. The word appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 11:37, describing persecuted believers who wandered about in sheepskins) and five times in the Septuagint, where it always renders the Hebrew אַדֶּרֶת and always refers to Elijah's mantle. It also turns up in everyday Koine documents — for example a tax list from Palmyra (AD 137) levies duties on imported hides including the μηλωτή.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense there rests on limited evidence; note the lexicons (Dodson) also allow it could mean other animal hides, not strictly sheep.

definition: The region of Asia lying between the Euphrates and Tigris rivers.
article: Mesopotamia is a place name meaning literally "between the rivers" — built from the Greek words for "middle" (μέσος) and "river" (ποταμός), referring to the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 2:9 and 7:2), and every translation surveyed renders it the same way, with no variation in meaning. In the Septuagint it shows up 17 times, often standing in for Hebrew terms like "Paddan Aram" (11×) and "Aram of the two rivers" (3×), which reflect the same river-country idea.
caution: Despite the low confidence tier, the meaning is secure: as a proper place name all sources agree completely.

definition: To sober up after drunkenness, used figuratively for shaking off mental dullness and coming to one's right mind.
article: This verb literally means to sober up after being drunk, and Paul uses it figuratively in its only New Testament appearance (1 Corinthians 15:34) to urge his readers to wake up to clear, sober thinking. The Majority Standard Bible's rendering as "ought" reflects the surrounding sentence rather than the word itself, since its core force is "get sober out of your drunken condition." In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times in 4 books, several times translating the Hebrew יָקַץ (to awake), and Moulton-Milligan note it as a strong, non-classical word marking Paul's polished Greek.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests on slim corpus evidence.

definition: A Mede, a person from Media, the ancient region east of Assyria.
article: Μῆδος names someone from Media, a region east of Assyria, and appears just once in the New Testament, in the list of nations present at Pentecost in Acts 2:9. The Septuagint uses it 15 times across five books, where it generally points to the Medes as a people or kingdom. Curiously, the measured New Testament rendering reads "Parthians" rather than "Medes" at its single occurrence, even though the standard glosses and lexica all give "Mede" or "Median."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and the measured rendering ("Parthians") differing from the lexical glosses ("Mede"), the evidence here is thin and apparently inconsistent.

definition: Describing something that pertains to or is worked by a donkey, especially a large millstone turned by a donkey.
article: ὀνικός is an adjective built from ὄνος ("donkey") and means "belonging to or worked by a donkey." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both times describing a millstone (μύλος ὀνικός) — the large kind turned by a donkey rather than by hand — in Jesus' warning about causing a little one to stumble (Matthew 18:6; Luke 17:2). Scholars once thought the word was unique to the New Testament, but papyri and inscriptions later proved it was ordinary Koine: documents from the first and second centuries AD speak of "donkey animals" (ὀνικὰ κτήνη) and a "donkey-load" (γόμος ὀνικός).
caution: The word occurs only twice in the New Testament and the two measured rendering fragments overlap heavily, so the evidence base is thin even though the sense is clear.

definition: To treat someone or something as worthless, despising or rejecting them as if they counted for nothing.
article: This strong compound means to set someone or something at nothing — to despise utterly or treat with total contempt. It appears 11 times in the Byzantine New Testament, applied to people (as in 1 Corinthians 6:4) and to things, like a rejected message (2 Corinthians 10:10) or the despised stone (Acts 4:11). The everyday papyri preserve it too: a contract from 13 B.C. uses it in the sense of nullifying or setting at nought an obligation, showing the word lived in ordinary Koine, not just literary Greek.
caution: The translation data is messy — only 2 occurrences map to a clean English word, while 4 of 11 dissolve into surrounding phrasing, so the renderings vary widely across contexts.

definition: A person who sins or is morally guilty, or the quality of being sinful.
article: ἁμαρτωλός covers both the person who sins and the quality of being sinful, and the New Testament uses it overwhelmingly as a noun: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sinners" 36 times (80%) and "sinful" 9 times (20%). In the Septuagint it appears 91 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew רָשָׁע ("wicked," 14×) and חַטָּאּים ("sinners," 11×). One striking detail comes from the papyri and inscriptions: an inscription from 240 B.C. and grave epitaphs in Asia Minor use the word in a threat, "let him be a sinner before the gods," showing it was at home in everyday Koine.

definition: To kill someone by cutting off their head.
article: This verb simply means to behead someone, and that single meaning holds across all 4 of its New Testament appearances. It is built from ἀπό ("off") and κεφαλή ("head"), so the literal sense is "to take the head off." The few variations in how it gets translated—"beheaded," "man," "beheaded man kept"—reflect English phrasing of the surrounding story rather than different meanings; it appears in the accounts of John the Baptist's death (Matthew, Mark, Luke). It also turns up once in the Greek Old Testament, at Psalm 151:7.
caution: The three differently worded renderings all point to the same single sense, so the variation is grammatical rather than a real difference in meaning.

definition: Describing someone outside the Jewish people, a non-Jew or pagan, often pointing to their way of life rather than just their ethnicity.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament ἐθνικός appears just twice, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "pagans" both times (100%), as in Matthew 6:7 and 18:17. The word comes from ἔθνος ("nation") and originally meant "national" in classical authors like Polybius, but in the New Testament it works as a noun meaning "the Gentile" — and Abbott-Smith notes it describes character rather than mere position. The papyri preserve a striking twist: in one sixth-century document from Oxyrhynchus, ἐθνικός is used of a tax collector, a sense found nowhere else.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two Byzantine occurrences (four in critical texts) — so confidence is low and the rendering rests on a very small sample.

definition: The direction where the sun rises, the east; also the act of light rising, like dawn.
article: ἀνατολή literally means a "rising" and overwhelmingly refers to the east, the quarter where the sun comes up — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "east" in 8 of 10 New Testament occurrences (89%). It comes from the verb ἀνατέλλω ("to rise"), and Strong's and Dodson note it can also mean the dawn or rising of light, as in Luke 1:78. A nice detail: the plural form for "the east" shows up in everyday documents, including a parchment from Media (22 B.C.) marking property boundaries "from the east" — fittingly close to the home of the Magi in Matthew 2.
caution: The dawn/rising-light sense is real but rare in the New Testament, so most occurrences simply mean the compass direction "east."

definition: To arrive at or reach a place or goal, whether a physical destination or a state one attains to.
article: καταντάω basically means to arrive at or reach a destination, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 13 times across 4 books, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "came" 4 times (67% of the explicit cases) and "reached" twice (33%); in 7 of the 13 it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing without its own English word. The lexicons stretch it further: it can mean to attain to a goal (Abbott-Smith cites Ephesians 4:13 and Philippians 3:11), reflecting both literal travel and figurative arrival. The most striking outside evidence comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show that "καταντᾶν εἰς" was a common legal term for property descending to an heir after someone's death.
caution: Septuagint evidence is thin (cited just once or a few times), and the Hebrew counterpart it translates is reported inconsistently between sources.

definition: To deny, disown, or refuse to acknowledge someone—including refusing to recognize and set aside one's own interests.
article: This compound of ἀπό ("from") and ἀρνέομαι ("deny") means to deny or disown someone, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "deny" in 10 of its 13 New Testament occurrences (83%). It covers two related situations: refusing to acknowledge another person—as in Peter's denials of Christ—and "denying oneself," which in Mark 8:34 means losing sight of one's own interests. The single Septuagint use translates a Hebrew word for worthless idols (Isaiah 31:7), and the Mimes of Herodas show the word in literary Koine, where one scholar even renders it "failed to see" rather than "was denied."

definition: A person habitually given to drunkenness; a drunkard.
article: μέθυσος means a drunkard—someone marked by habitual drinking. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Corinthians (5:11 and 6:10), where Paul lists it among vices to avoid; the Byzantine and critical texts agree on both occurrences. The grammarians note an interesting shift: the word originally described only women, but by the later Koine period it was applied to men, exactly as Paul uses it here, and similar vice-lists (including πλεονέκτης, 'covetous') turn up on ancient game counters and in the papyri.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences), and the second 'covetous drunkards verbal' sense reflects how it sits in a vice-list rather than a distinct meaning.

definition: To beat or drive something back, and so to hinder, check, or stop it.
article: This verb combines ἀνά with κόπτω ("to strike") and basically means to beat something back and thereby stop or hinder it. The classical lexica trace a range from physically driving back (Homer) to repelling an attacker (Thucydides) to simply stopping something short (Lucian). Everyday Koine papyri use it for halting actions or processes \u2014 one fourth-century document speaks of crimes being checked by punishing the criminal, and another petition asks an official to order a woman's lawsuit to be stopped.
caution: This word never appears in the Byzantine New Testament, so the senses given rest entirely on classical lexica and papyri rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: An attempt or trial — putting something to the test, or gaining experience of it firsthand.
article: πεῖρα means a test, attempt, or firsthand experience of something. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Hebrews 11, and both times inside the fixed phrase "πεῖραν λαμβάνειν," literally "to take a trial of" — rendered "tried" in Hebrews 11:29 and "endured" in 11:36. The same idiom turns up in everyday papyri: one second-century BC letter warns people not to "experience the penalties" (πεῖραν λαμβάνειν τῶν ἐπιτίμων), showing this was ordinary Koine for putting something to the test or finding out for yourself.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both locked in one idiom, the measured senses rest on very thin evidence.

definition: To make new again, to renew or restore something to a fresh state.
article: ἀνανεόω means to renew or make new again, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Ephesians 4:23, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "renewed." The Septuagint uses it just twice, and it shows up frequently in everyday Koine inscriptions and papyri (the Syll and OGIS collections), where the most striking parallel comes from a Cnossus inscription describing someone "renewing" the ancestral goodwill toward his city. So the word's measured range is narrow but consistent: it points to a fresh restoration of something that already existed.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense in that context rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: A garland or wreath, especially the kind used to decorate animals and altars for a pagan sacrifice.
article: Στέμμα refers to a wreath or garland, formed from a root meaning to wrap or encircle. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 14:13), it names the garlands the priest of Zeus brought to adorn the sacrificial animals when the crowd at Lystra tried to worship Paul and Barnabas. Everyday papyri broaden the picture: the word shows up in connection with guilds and even names an official "in charge of the stemmata," showing it was common administrative vocabulary in Koine Egypt.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on that single sacrificial scene.

definition: To search, examine, or investigate something carefully to find out the truth about it.
article: This verb means to search something out carefully, whether God examining human hearts or people investigating a matter. The single sense covers all its New Testament uses; the one occurrence rendered "Aren't" (John 7:52) is simply that same searching idea phrased as a probing question ("search and see"). In the Septuagint it appears 13 times, most often translating the Hebrew chaphas, "to search out," and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday papyri—including a fragmentary report apparently written by a professional searcher.
caution: With only 6 Byzantine occurrences (none in the critical SBLGNT text) and two absorbed into phrasing, the measured evidence is thin.

definition: Lycia, a small Roman province on the southern coast of Asia Minor.
article: Lycia is a place name—a small Roman province on the south coast of Asia Minor. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:5, during Paul's sea voyage. As a proper noun it has no real range of meaning; it simply names a geographic region, and the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on this.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the single measured rendering 'open' reflects surrounding context rather than the place name itself.

definition: To be overwhelmed with amazement or shock, struck by something extraordinary you have just seen or heard.
article: This vivid verb describes being knocked off balance by amazement—literally "struck out" with shock. In all 13 New Testament occurrences it carries this one measured sense, "astonished," most often describing crowds reacting to Jesus' teaching (as in Matthew 7:28 and Mark 1:22). It shows up in everyday Koine documents too: a third-century BC healing inscription uses it for a father struck with amazement when his mute son suddenly speaks. Note that none of these occurrences appear in the SBL critical text, only in the Byzantine text tradition.

definition: Gain, profit, or advantage—especially material or financial benefit obtained from something.
article: κέρδος means gain or profit, the benefit you get from something. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, always pointing to advantage—whether the spiritual gain Paul speaks of in Philippians or the "dishonest gain" condemned in Titus 1:11. The everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, usually of money; one papyrus letter even uses it in a context the editor reads as a bribe or bakshish, showing how the word could shade toward shady profit.
caution: With only 3 occurrences—all rendered "gain" by the same translation—the measured evidence is thin, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: Service or care given to someone, including a household of servants or, by extension, medical treatment and healing.
article: θεραπεία covers the broad idea of attending to or caring for someone, ranging from the people who staff a household to the medical treatment that produces a cure. In its four New Testament uses it splits evenly: it can mean a master's body of servants (Luke 12:42) or it can mean healing, as in the leaves for the "healing" of the nations in Revelation 22:2. An everyday papyrus from 114 BC nicely confirms the medical sense, where a writer says he stayed in the temple of Isis ἐπὶ θεραπείαι—for medical treatment of his sickness, not for worship.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences spread evenly across distinct senses, and lexicons emphasizing the "service" sense over "healing," the balance between these meanings rests on thin evidence.

definition: To bring something or someone back to a former, proper, or healthy condition; to restore or give back.
article: ἀποκαθίστημι means to put something back the way it was—whether healing a body, returning a thing, or reestablishing affairs. In the Byzantine New Testament's 8 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "restored" 7 times (88%), most often of physical healing like the withered hand in Matthew 12:13 and Mark 3:5. The everyday Koine papyri sharpen the "give back" side of the word: one early document uses it for making restitution, demanding that a defaulting priest's guarantors pay back what is owed.

definition: To stand beside someone or something, or to bring, present, or set something before another person.
article: At its root παρίστημι means to stand beside, and the New Testament uses it both ways: intransitively for people standing nearby (about a third of its 41 occurrences are rendered "stood") and transitively for bringing or presenting something before someone. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "present" in 7 cases, as when believers present their bodies to God. A nice window into everyday Koine comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan note its use in legal proceedings—a weavers' guild pledging to "produce" (παραστήσιν) accused members in court—showing the same idea of formally setting someone before authorities.
caution: Almost a quarter of its 41 occurrences (11×) are absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, so the rendering counts understate how flexibly it is translated.

definition: Luke, a personal name belonging to a companion of Paul mentioned in his letters.
article: Λουκᾶς is simply the proper name "Luke," appearing 3 times in the New Testament, always referring to Paul's companion. The two measured senses ("Luke" and "Luke Get") reflect translation phrasing in different verses rather than any real difference in meaning—it is one name throughout. Scholars debate its origin: it is generally treated as a shortened pet form of Λουκανός, though some derive it from Λούκιος, and inscriptions from Pisidian Antioch show the two names used interchangeably.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a single name-meaning, the two listed "senses" are just translation artifacts, not distinct meanings.

definition: A house or dwelling place, and by extension the home life or family living inside it.
article: οἰκία refers to a house in the everyday sense of a building where people live, and this dominates its use—rendered "house" 67 times (75%) and "home" another 13 times (15%) in the Byzantine New Testament. It can also shift from the structure to the people in it, the "household" or family, which accounts for 5 occurrences. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary meaning, with documents speaking of building up the doors of houses or throwing an empty box into someone's house; in the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew בַּיִת (104 times).
caution: Lexicons note a rarer metonymic sense of "property" or "goods" (as in Mark 12:40), which the measured renderings here do not separately register.

definition: Describing someone who is physically sick, weak, or unwell, in need of healing.
article: ἄῤῥωστος describes a person who is sick, weak, or feeble in body. It appears 5 times in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible consistently renders it "sick" — the other listed phrasings (like "any their sick" or "why among sick") are just fragments of the surrounding wording, not separate meanings. Built from a negative prefix on the verb meaning "to be strong," it literally points to a lack of strength; in everyday Koine the related verb "to be ill" was common, as in a third-century BC papyrus describing someone lying sick at Memphis.
caution: The four "measured senses" are really one sense (sick) showing through different sentence fragments, so treat them as a single meaning.

definition: A go-between who stands between two parties to mediate, arbitrate, or bring them together.
article: μεσίτης names a person who stands in the middle between two sides, whether to mediate, arbitrate, or reconcile them. The New Testament uses it for a mediator, sometimes specifying the parties involved (as in 1 Timothy 2:5, "mediator between God and men"). The everyday Koine papyri show this word was at home in legal life: people would appoint a μεσίτης to serve as their arbiter and judge in disputes, and Abbott-Smith notes the single Septuagint use (Job 9:33) translates a Hebrew word for "between."
caution: The third measured rendering "however" (1×, in Hebrews 8:6) reflects surrounding sentence flow, not a separate meaning of the word itself.

definition: To regain one's senses, like a person sobering up from intoxication and thinking clearly again.
article: This word literally means to become sober again, used figuratively for snapping back to clear thinking. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 2:26, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "come to their senses," and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully. The image is built from the prefix ἀνά (again) and νήφω (to be sober), and Abbott-Smith compares the closely related ἐκνήφω, which carries a similar sobering-up sense.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: To walk straight, used figuratively for living and behaving in a way that goes directly along the right course.
article: This verb literally means "to be straight-footed" — to walk straight ahead — built from the words for "straight" (ὀρθός) and "foot" (πούς). In the New Testament it appears only once, in Galatians 2:14, where Paul uses it figuratively for behaving in line with the truth of the gospel. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and that one scholar (Westcott) even suspected it had a kind of "sporting ring" to it, perhaps a local word of Antioch or Tarsus.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is barely attested before Paul, so its exact flavor rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A lack of reverence toward God shown in godless attitudes and wicked, irreverent actions.
senseLabels: godlessness, lack of reverence for God
article: ἀσέβεια describes living without proper reverence for God — impiety that produces both godless attitudes and concrete wicked deeds. Across its 6 New Testament appearances the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "godlessness," "ungodliness," and "wickedness," and in Jude 1:15 it widens to "ungodly deeds." One striking detail comes from the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew פֶּשַׁע ("transgression," 26×) and חָמָס ("violence," 12×), and the everyday papyri use it of violating sacred oaths and temple taboos — showing it was a real-life word for impious offense, not just an abstract idea.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences, each rendered just once, the fine distinctions between "godlessness," "ungodliness," and "wickedness" reflect context more than separate fixed meanings.

definition: To restore a broken relationship, changing people from enmity to friendship—especially restoring people to God or a spouse to a partner.
article: This verb originally meant to change or exchange one thing for another, even of swapping money, but in the New Testament it always describes reconciliation—a shift from hostility to peace. All 6 Byzantine occurrences are rendered "reconciled," and both the BSB and KJV agree completely; Paul uses it both for people being reconciled to God (Romans 5:10) and for a wife being reconciled to her husband (1 Corinthians 7:11). One striking witness comes from the everyday Koine papyri: an oracle question from Oxyrhynchus asks "am I to be reconciled with my offspring?"—showing the word at work in ordinary family disputes.
caution: The everyday-Greek senses (changing, exchanging money) are documented in the lexica but never appear in the New Testament, where every measured use means "reconcile."

definition: An interrogative word asking about amount, number, size, or degree—how much, how many, or how great.
article: πόσος is a question word asking about quantity, number, or extent—"how much," "how many," or "how great." Across its 27 New Testament uses the renderings cluster tightly around amount ("how much," 28%) and count ("how many," 16%), but it can also ask about degree or time, as in Mark 9:21 ("how long has this been happening?"). The everyday flavor of the word shows up vividly in the papyri, where merchants write things like "send me word how many bundles you have received" and "inform me how many came out"—the same practical counting question we see in Jesus asking how many loaves the disciples had.

definition: A conjunction meaning "when" or "as soon as," marking the time at which something happens once a condition is met.
article: ἐπάν is a small time-marking conjunction meaning "when" or "as soon as," pointing to the moment an action takes place once its condition is fulfilled. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the three renderings the translation data records ("when too," "when," and "also") all reflect this single core idea of timing in different sentence settings. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one lease from A.D. 208 has "ἐπὰν δὲ μή τις προσθῇ σοι," meaning roughly "as long as no one makes you a higher offer," showing it was common contract language for "when/as soon as."
caution: With only 3 occurrences, the measured "sense" labels mostly reflect surrounding phrasing rather than distinct meanings—all three uses carry the same basic "when/as soon as" force.

definition: A state of confusion or chaos, especially the uproar of a disorderly, agitated crowd.
article: σύγχυσις describes confusion or disorder, and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 19:29) it refers to the uproar of an agitated crowd. Built on the verb συγχέω (to pour together, mix up), it carries the idea of things thrown into chaotic disorder. In the Septuagint it appears four times, including Genesis 11:9, where it stands behind the name Babel; elsewhere it translates the Hebrew word for tumult or panic. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one inscription even speaks of someone as the "instigator of the whole confusion."
caution: The Majority Standard Bible's rendering "Soon" in the measured data does not match the lexical sources, which consistently define the word as "confusion" or "disturbance"; treat the listed sense label with caution given only one New Testament occurrence.

definition: An adverb meaning 'five times,' counting how often something happens.
article: πεντάκις is a numeral adverb built from πέντε ('five') that means 'five times.' It appears just once in the New Testament, where Paul recounts that he received the thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). The Septuagint also uses it only once, in a verse linked to the Hebrew word קָצַף.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: To urge or advise someone toward a particular course of action, often by way of friendly counsel.
article: παραινέω means to advise, exhort, or urge someone toward doing something, typically with a person named and a following infinitive showing what is recommended. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 27, where Paul advises the sailors during the storm; in each case the word is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than given its own English word. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, as in a 2nd-century document urging soldiers to obey their orders, confirming this was ordinary language for giving practical counsel.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both in one chapter, the evidence base is thin, though papyri and lexica agree on its meaning.

definition: A personal name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, identifying one of his distant ancestors.
article: Addi is simply a personal name, listed once in the New Testament (Luke 3:28) as one ancestor in Jesus' genealogy, the son of Cosam and father of Melchi. The name is of probable Hebrew origin, and in the Septuagint a similar form translates Hebrew names like Issachar (twice) and Jathrai (once). There's nothing to define here beyond the man it points to.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament, and the spelling varies between editions (Ἀδδί and Ἀδδεί).

definition: A visible appearance or manifestation, used in the New Testament especially of Christ's coming, whether His first arrival or His future return.
article: ἐπιφάνεια means an "appearing" or "manifestation"—a moment when someone or something becomes visibly present. In the New Testament it shows up 6 times across 4 books, always in the letters to Timothy and Titus, and the Majority Standard Bible consistently renders it "appearing" or "appearance," referring to Christ's arrival (past, as in 2 Timothy 1:10, or future). The most telling background comes from the papyri and inscriptions: this word was commonly used in everyday Greek for any striking intervention by a god or higher power—Moulton-Milligan cites inscriptions describing "the manifestation of the goddess."
caution: The measured sense breakdown contains several garbled labels ("charge view His," "now His appearing") that appear to be data artifacts; the genuine consistent meaning is simply "appearing/appearance."

definition: An adjective meaning Galatian, describing something that belongs to or is located in the region of Galatia.
article: Γαλατικός is simply the adjective form of "Galatia," used to describe the region or territory connected with that province. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Acts (16:6 and 18:23), where it describes the "Galatian region" through which Paul traveled. The lexical sources are unanimous that it means "of Galatia," and although the measured data lists two labels, both occurrences point to this single geographic meaning.
caution: With only two occurrences and a single clear geographic meaning, the evidence is thin, and one of the two measured renderings reflects surrounding phrasing rather than a distinct sense.

definition: To make a profit through business dealings, by trading or investing actively.
article: This verb describes earning a profit through active business or trading, used just once in the New Testament at Luke 19:15, where servants are called to account for what they made with their master's money. It is a strengthened ("perfective") form of the ordinary verb for doing business, and Moulton-Milligan note it appears in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. Interestingly, the classical lexica record an older sense—"to examine thoroughly" (Plato)—that shifted in later writers to the commercial "gain by trading" meaning seen here.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured sense label "each" reflects how the translation phrases the verse rather than the verb's actual meaning, so lean on the lexical evidence.

definition: Sin — wrongdoing or moral failure measured against God's standard, whether a single act or sin as a controlling power.
article: In the New Testament ἁμαρτία overwhelmingly means "sin," rendered that way 166 of 174 times (98%), with only two cases nuanced as "guilty sin" (John 8:46; 15:24). Though its root sense is "missing the mark," the NT always uses it in a moral and ethical sense, and Paul can even personify it as a ruling power that reigns or enslaves. The Septuagint uses it more than 400 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew words for sin, guilt, and iniquity (חַטָּאָה, עָווֹן, חֵטְא), and a striking second-century inscription even pairs it with paying off a "sin" owed to a god that cannot be expiated.

definition: A talent—a large unit of weight, and by extension a very large sum of gold or silver money equal to that weight.
article: A τάλαντον was originally a weight (roughly 108 to 130 pounds), and from that it came to mean a sum of money worth that weight in gold or silver—an enormous amount. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times, almost all in Jesus' parables in Matthew, where servants are entrusted with talents and some earn "more besides." The Greek Old Testament uses it 47 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew kikkar (a measured weight), and everyday papyri show it as a real commercial sum—one letter even mentions selling goods "for a talent."
caution: The "more besides" sense reflects the parable's context (talents gained in addition), not a separate meaning of the word itself.

definition: To contend fiercely or argue strongly against someone, especially in a heated verbal dispute.
article: This verb combines the idea of "through" with "fight," giving a sense of struggling hard against an opponent—either physically or, in the New Testament, in heated argument. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 23:9, where some scribes "contended sharply" on Paul's behalf (the Majority Standard Bible renders the moment as taking his "party"). Abbott-Smith notes the Septuagint uses it for the Hebrew verb "to fight," preserving the more literal combative force seen in passages like Daniel and Sirach.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and limited Septuagint data, the precise force here rests on thin evidence.

definition: Ramah, a town in Palestine north of Jerusalem, mentioned in a prophecy about weeping for lost children.
article: Ῥαμᾶ is the place name Ramah, a town in Palestine that Dodson locates in Ephraim, about two hours north of Jerusalem. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 2:18, quoting the Old Testament image of weeping heard in Ramah. The word transliterates the Hebrew רָמָה, which the Septuagint represents 23 times out of its 30 occurrences across 9 books, alongside a few related Hebrew forms.
caution: The measured rendering reads as "Rachel," which the BSB does not independently support, so treat this lone New Testament occurrence as a place name (Ramah) rather than a personal name.

definition: Unrestrained indulgence in sensual or shameful behavior, especially open, shameless sexual misconduct that flouts public decency.
article: ἀσέλγεια describes a reckless, shameless lack of moral restraint, most often in sexual matters. It appears 10 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "debauchery" or "acts of debauchery" in the clearest cases, with KJV alternatives like "lasciviousness" and "wantonness" pointing to the same idea of brazen excess. Lexicons emphasize the public, shocking quality of the conduct — outrageous behavior that openly affronts decency — and Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a use of the adjective among technical astrological terms.
caution: In 3 of its 10 occurrences the word is absorbed into broader phrasing without a distinct English equivalent, so its precise force in those passages is harder to pin down.

definition: An emphatic particle that strengthens a statement, meaning "surely" or "truly," almost always paired with another word.
article: μήν is a small emphatic particle used to reinforce a statement, conveying something like "surely" or "truly." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (in Hebrews 6:14, quoting the Septuagint), where it's part of a fixed phrase "εἶ μήν" ("surely") rather than a word translated on its own. It shows up 33 times in the Septuagint and is well attested in everyday Koine papyri, often in the combination "οὐ μήν" ("and yet," "nor is this all"), as in a 2nd-century B.C. letter urging someone to act because their mother was in great distress.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one Byzantine NT occurrence, used inside a set phrase, so its independent force is hard to pin down.

definition: Gallio, the Roman proconsul of Achaia before whom Paul was brought in Corinth.
article: Γαλλίων is a proper name borrowed from Latin, referring to Gallio, the Roman proconsul (governor) of the province of Achaia. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts 18 (verses 12, 14, and 17), and is always rendered "Gallio." Strikingly, a Delphic inscription pins down when Gallio entered his proconsulship, giving scholars a fixed date for working out the chronology of Paul's life — and the name also turns up in an everyday papyrus document.
caution: This is simply a personal name with only 3 occurrences, so there is no range of meaning to weigh.

definition: Something done willingly and of one's own free choice, rather than under pressure or compulsion.
article: This adjective describes an action taken freely and spontaneously, not forced. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Philemon 1:14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "consent" — Paul wants Philemon's good deed to be voluntary rather than compelled. The word was common in everyday legal language: the papyri show it in contract formulas like "I have of my own free will covenanted with you," and the Septuagint uses it 13 times, most often for the Hebrew nedabah (a freewill offering).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, though the wider Koine and Septuagint evidence agrees on the basic meaning.

definition: An inner thought, reasoning, or pondering—sometimes the back-and-forth of arguing or doubtful questioning in the mind or out loud.
article: διαλογισμός covers what goes on in the mind: thoughts, inward reasoning, and the questioning or weighing of things. In the Byzantine NT's 14 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "thoughts" 5 times (45%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing or scattered renderings like "doubts" and "thinking," reflecting how the word slides between private thought and outward dispute. In the Septuagint it appears 12 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew מַחֲשָׁבָה ("thought, plan"), and the everyday Koine papyri show a notably judicial flavor—Moulton-Milligan points to legal decisions, which sharpens passages like James 2:4 where corrupt judges "reason" wrongly.
caution: The range is genuinely broad—evidence and lexica split between private "thought" and outward "dispute," so the right shade depends heavily on context.

definition: The precious yellow metal gold, including objects made from it such as ornaments, images, or coins.
article: χρυσός means gold, whether the raw metal, jewelry and ornaments, golden images, or even gold coins used as money. The range is consistent: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gold" in 8 of 10 New Testament occurrences (80%), and the Septuagint uses it chiefly for the Hebrew word זָהָב (zahav, "gold"). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense, with documents specifying things like "gold of full value" and "common gold" when grading the metal's purity for trade.

definition: Something a person undergoes, usually painful suffering or affliction, and sometimes an inner emotion or passion that drives someone.
article: πάθημα refers to something one undergoes — most often hardship or suffering. In the Byzantine NT it is rendered "sufferings" 8 times (50%) and "suffering" 4 times (25%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% on both. The lexicons add a notable extra range the corpus counts barely capture: it can also mean a passive emotion or passion (Abbott-Smith cites Galatians 5:24 and Romans 7:5), and Moulton-Milligan notes the word was originally fairly colorless — a disposition or propensity — before drifting toward the sense of evil experience or suffering.
caution: The measured NT senses center on "suffering," but the lexicons document a distinct "passion/emotion" sense that the raw rendering counts underrepresent.

definition: To weigh someone down or burden them, especially by imposing a financial or other demand upon them.
article: καταβαρέω means to weigh someone down or place a burden on them, used figuratively of imposing a demand on a person. It appears just once in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 12:16) and twice in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew words for "weigh" (שָׁקַל) and "press/oppress" (דָּחַק). The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: an Egyptian document from A.D. 156 uses it of a man "weighed down by my official duties," showing this was ordinary everyday Koine, not a literary or technical term.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint — so the sense rests heavily on the papyri and lexicons.

definition: The quality of being uncertain or unreliable, something that cannot be counted on to last.
article: This noun describes the state of being uncertain or unpredictable. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:17, where it warns against setting hope on the uncertainty of riches. The standard Bible translations agree on rendering it "uncertainty," and Dodson notes a related underlying idea of being unseen or fading from view, which fits the sense of wealth that cannot be relied upon.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range of meaning cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: To announce something publicly like a herald, especially to proclaim or preach the gospel message.
article: κηρύσσω means to announce openly as a public herald would, and in the New Testament it almost always describes proclaiming or preaching God's message. The Majority Standard Bible renders it with some form of "preach" or "proclaim" in all 61 occurrences, so its range is narrow and consistent. Originally the word pictured a herald crying out an announcement; one interesting note is that scholars debate whether Paul's use in 1 Corinthians 9:27 alludes to the herald of the public games, with Field arguing against that connection.

definition: Having great variety; richly diverse in many different forms or aspects.
article: πολυποίκιλος describes something marked by enormous variety—literally "much-variegated," built from "much" (πολύς) and "many-colored" (ποικίλος). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 3:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "manifold" (100%), with the Berean Standard, Dodson, and KJV all agreeing. Abbott-Smith notes a literal sense in Euripides of greatly differing colors, while Moulton-Milligan points out the figurative use in the Orphic hymns, showing the word was at home in everyday Koine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: Someone who teaches what is good, noble, and honorable to others.
article: This compound word joins kalós ("good, noble") with didáskalos ("teacher"), so it literally describes a person who teaches what is good. It appears only once in the entire New Testament, in Titus 2:3, where older women are urged to be "teachers of good things." The classical lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on this "teacher of the good" meaning, though the single measured rendering here landed on the broader word "behavior" within its verse.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be confirmed from usage alone.

definition: A green precious stone, usually identified as an emerald, used in the New Testament as a foundation gem.
article: This word names a green precious stone, traditionally translated "emerald," though scholars note it could refer to other transparent green stones. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Revelation 21:19, where it is listed among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem. Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence as "chalcedony," while the classic glosses (KJV, Strong's, Dodson) all give "emerald" — the standard meaning supported by both the Septuagint and everyday Koine papyri, including a fourth-century magical text mentioning a "smaragdos stone."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and the precise gem disputed (emerald versus other green stones, and one modern rendering as "chalcedony"), confidence is low.

definition: Feeling fear or alarm; gripped by fright in response to something frightening or awe-inspiring.
article: This word describes a person seized by fear or alarm, built from the parts "in" and "fear." Across its 6 New Testament occurrences the measured renderings split evenly between "frightened" and "terrified," though in 4 of those cases the fear is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word. Abbott-Smith notes a wider range in older usage, listing "terrible" alongside "in fear," and a striking magical papyrus from the 2nd–3rd century even describes the moon itself becoming "full of fear" as the earth shakes.
caution: The two measured senses each rest on a single occurrence and most uses are absorbed into phrasing, so the boundary between "frightened" and "terrified" is fuzzy rather than firm.

definition: A strong, uncontrolled emotion or craving — in the New Testament always a sinful passion or lust.
article: πάθος refers to a violent, ungoverned emotion or passionate desire, and in all three of its New Testament appearances it carries a negative meaning — a sinful passion or lust. The word's root sense is actually "that which one suffers," something that happens to you, and you can see that passive flavor in how it differs from ἐπιθυμία, the more active and comprehensive word for desire. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show the same range: one first-century BC document speaks of someone acting "from his own passion," while another inscription uses the plural to invoke "all the evils and sufferings" that befall people as a curse on tomb-robbers.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the sense labels reflect translation choices in specific phrases rather than three distinct meanings.

definition: To drag or pull something or someone forcibly along the ground.
article: σύρω means to drag, pull, or haul something along, whether nets full of fish or a person being forced away. In all 5 New Testament uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "dragged" in 4 of them (with one absorbed into phrasing), and it commonly describes hauling people off to trial or punishment, as when Saul drags believers away in Acts 8:3. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this physical sense vividly: one third-century document uses it for oxen dragging logs along a canal.

definition: The mind — the faculty of understanding, reasoning, and forming purposes and judgments.
article: In the New Testament νοῦς overwhelmingly means the mind — the reasoning, understanding part of a person. It's rendered "mind" in 20 of its 24 Byzantine occurrences (95%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. Beyond this core sense, the lexicons note a related shade meaning a thought or purpose (as in Romans 11:34, "who has known the mind of the Lord?"), and everyday Koine papyri show it stretching to mean the sense or interpretation of a document — one complaint from 164 BC accuses officials of not putting the best construction on "the meaning" (νοῦν) of a farming decree.

definition: To look around at one's surroundings or at the people nearby, sweeping the eyes across a whole scene.
article: περιβλέπω means to cast your eyes all around, taking in the whole scene or surveying the people present. It combines περί (around) with βλέπω (to look), and in the New Testament it appears 7 times, all in Mark and Luke, most often as Jesus looking around at a crowd. Notably, every measured sense is just a variation on the same core act of looking around, and Abbott-Smith points out it usually appears in the middle voice, meaning to look about oneself.
caution: It appears only 7 times in the Byzantine text and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text, so the evidence base is modest.

definition: Arimathea, a town in Palestine, known as the home of Joseph who buried Jesus.
article: Arimathea is a place name, the hometown of Joseph who took Jesus' body for burial. It appears 4 times across all four Gospels, always referring to the same location. The measured renderings differ only because translators attach surrounding phrases like "himself" or "who himself" describing Joseph; the place name itself is consistent. The Septuagint connects it to the Hebrew Ramah (רָמָה), giving the form Arimathaim in 1 Samuel 1:1.

definition: Jason, a personal name borne by an early Christian, including a host of Paul in Thessalonica and a relative who greeted the Romans.
article: Ἰάσων is simply a proper name, "Jason," appearing 5 times across 2 books of the Byzantine New Testament and always rendered "Jason." The two measured senses differ only in phrasing — one occurrence (25%) is grouped with others in Acts 17:6 — so this is really one name, not two meanings. It refers to a Christian who hosted Paul in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5-9), perhaps the same Jason called a relative of Paul in Romans 16:21. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that Jews sometimes used the Greek name Ἰάσων as a substitute for Ἰησοῦς (Jesus), and the name is well attested in everyday papyri and inscriptions.
caution: It is uncertain whether the Jason of Thessalonica and the Jason of Romans 16:21 are the same person; the sources only say "perhaps."

definition: Korah, the Israelite who led a rebellion against Moses, mentioned as a warning example.
article: Κορέ is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name קֹ֫רַח (Korah), an Israelite remembered for rebellion. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:11, where Korah is cited as a cautionary figure. In the Septuagint the name shows up 42 times across 6 books, almost always rendering the same Hebrew name (34×), often in connection with the family or sons of Korah.
caution: The measured NT sense label "rushed" appears to be a data error, since this is a proper name (Korah) and occurs only once.

definition: To run away from danger, threat, or harm, whether literally taking flight or escaping and avoiding something.
article: φεύγω means to run away — from a threat, an enemy, or a duty — and by extension to escape or avoid something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 31 times, rendered "flee" in 52% of cases, "ran" in 23%, and "escape" in 16%, all closely related shades of the same basic idea. The word turns up constantly in the Septuagint (185 times, mostly translating Hebrew נוּס, "to flee"), and everyday papyri use it the same way, as in a first-century letter reporting that "Seleucus came here and has fled."

definition: Describing speech or conduct that gives no fair grounds for criticism or condemnation.
article: ἀκατάγνωστος combines a negative prefix with a word for condemning, so it literally means "not able to be condemned" — something or someone that leaves no opening for fair rebuke. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:8, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "wholesome" (the BSB agrees 100%). The most interesting evidence comes from everyday Koine: an epitaph from Thessalonica (A.D. 165) applies it to the deceased, and another inscription pairs it with ἄμεμπτος ("blameless"), showing it was a real-life term of praise for irreproachable character.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the rendering rests on a single passage supported by scattered papyri and inscriptions.

definition: Work done only while the boss is watching, to make a good impression rather than from genuine commitment.
article: This compound word literally joins "eye" (ophthalmos) and "slavery/service" (douleia), describing the kind of work a servant performs only while the master's eye is on them. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22), and Abbott-Smith notes it is found nowhere else in Greek literature. Strong's captures the flavor well with "sight-labor... that needs watching," pointing to remissness rather than honest effort.
caution: This word is extremely rare, appearing only twice in the New Testament and nowhere else in surviving Greek, so its precise range cannot be tested against wider usage.

definition: To step onto or into something — whether to set foot in a place, climb onto an animal, or board a ship.
article: ἐπιβαίνω literally means "to step on," and its uses fan out from there: setting foot in a region, mounting an animal, or boarding a boat. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times, all in Acts, mostly for arriving somewhere or going aboard a vessel; three of those six are folded so smoothly into English phrasing that no single word translates it. In the Septuagint it shows up 53 times and most often renders the Hebrew רָכַב (26×), "to ride" or "mount" — fitting its sense of climbing onto a horse. A nice everyday touch: a second-century papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses it simply to say "as soon as I arrived at Alexandria."
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences spread evenly across three rather different senses, each meaning rests on a single example.

definition: To cut something by sawing, dividing it through with a saw.
article: πρίζω means to saw something apart, splitting it through with a saw. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 11:37, where it describes the violent death of the faithful who 'were sawn in two.' The everyday Koine papyri show the word at work in ordinary contexts—one document uses it of date-palms being sawn, and another (A.D. 378) is an order to pay two sawyers for boat repairs. In the Septuagint it occurs once, rendering the Hebrew דּוּשׁ.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence for this word's range is thin.

definition: A man named Hamor, the father of Shechem, who owned land near Shechem in Old Testament times.
article: Ἐμμόρ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Hamor (חֲמוֹר), a Canaanite man whose sons sold a field at Shechem to Jacob. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 7:16, within Stephen's speech recalling Israel's history. Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders this single occurrence as 'Shechem' rather than 'Hamor,' likely tied to the place named after Hamor's family.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and the standard rendering as 'Shechem' rather than the personal name 'Hamor' reflects translation choices worth checking against your Bible.

definition: Describing someone who avoids fighting and quarreling—peaceable rather than contentious.
article: άμαχος literally combines a negative prefix with the word for "fight" (μάχη), so it pictures a person who refuses to brawl or quarrel. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the Pastoral letters (1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 3:2), describing the peaceable character expected of believers and leaders. Interestingly, everyday Koine evidence backs this gentle sense: a husband's grave inscription for his wife and an epitaph from Apameia both use the word to praise a peaceful life lived among friends and relatives. Classical writers, however, often used the same word to mean "invincible" or "non-combatant," a meaning never found in the New Testament.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the New Testament, and classical lexica record an older sense ("invincible") that differs from the peaceable meaning measured here.

definition: The act of remembering or mentioning someone, especially recalling a person fondly in prayer.
article: μνεία is about holding someone in mind — remembering or mentioning them, often warmly. All four measured senses are really one idea seen from different angles: the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "remembering" or "remember" in five of its seven New Testament appearances, with the Berean Study Bible agreeing 100% each time. The most striking evidence is from everyday papyri: the phrase μνείαν ποιεῖσθαι ("to make mention of") shows up in private letters, including a wife writing of family who "continually make mention" of her husband and another mentioning someone before the gods in prayer — exactly Paul's usage when he says he remembers people in his prayers.
caution: The four labels reflect translation choices rather than truly distinct meanings; the word essentially carries one sense of remembrance or mention across all uses.

definition: Describing a road, gate, or area that is wide, broad, and spacious.
article: εὐρύχωρος combines the words for "broad" (εὐρύς) and "space" (χώρα) to describe something wide and open. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 7:13, where Jesus speaks of the broad road that leads to destruction. In the Septuagint the word carries a positive feel of freedom and prosperity, and everyday papyri use a related noun for "an open space" on the north side of a property.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single verse; note also that the Majority Standard Bible's "through" reflects the surrounding phrase rather than the word's own meaning of "broad."

definition: To drive someone away or send them off, removing them from a place.
article: This verb means to drive or push someone away from a place, built from ἀπό ("away from") and ἐλαύνω ("to drive"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 18:16, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berea Standard Bible both render it "drove them away." Everyday Koine papyri show its practical range nicely: one document uses it of setting a boat sailing, another of robbers driving off three goats, confirming it covered both pushing people and moving animals or vessels.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, the sources show a thin but consistent picture; note that Abbott-Smith and the digest cite different Hebrew counterparts.

definition: To set or place someone onto an animal, such as a horse, mule, or donkey, so they can ride.
article: This word means to put a person up onto a riding animal — a donkey, horse, or mule. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as setting someone on a beast (Luke 10:34, 19:35) or providing mounts (Acts 23:24); the Berean Standard Bible agrees in all three. In the Septuagint it shows up 10 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew רָכַב ("to ride"), confirming its tie to mounting animals.
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament, so its range is hard to pin down precisely.

definition: To state something firmly and with full confidence, insisting that it is true.
article: This verb means to affirm or insist on something with confidence, presenting it as certain. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Pastoral Epistles—once of false teachers who 'confidently assert' things they don't understand (1 Timothy 1:7) and once of Paul telling Titus to keep stressing sound teaching (Titus 3:8). The everyday papyri are revealing: legal documents use it for formally 'confirming' facts in inheritance disputes, such as one person attesting that certain people had died before the mother (BGU I.19), which shows the word's force of solemn, binding assertion.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the two listed senses are really one idea (confident assertion) rendered two ways in English rather than a genuinely divided range.

definition: To nod in agreement, giving consent or approval to a request.
article: ἐπινeύω literally means to nod, and by extension to nod in approval—that is, to consent or agree to something. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 18:20, where it describes (in the negative) someone declining a request. The everyday Koine papyri make the sense vivid: one document uses it for granting permission to prepare hides, another for refusing a request, and several for a request being approved or assented to.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its New Testament range rests on thin evidence.

definition: The act of building, used figuratively for spiritual growth or strengthening.
article: This word literally means the act of building, and that everyday sense is well attested in Koine papyri and inscriptions—one second-century BC inscription uses it for contributing toward a building project, and others speak of the structures around a tomb. In the New Testament it appears nowhere in the Byzantine text and only as a variant reading in 1 Timothy 1:4 in some manuscripts, where most witnesses instead read οἰκονομία (stewardship). KJV renders this variant as "edifying," extending the building image to spiritual upbuilding.
caution: The word does not occur in the main NT text at all—it survives only as a disputed variant in 1 Timothy 1:4, easily confused with the similar οἰκονομία.

definition: Rough, uneven, or rocky—describing surfaces, ground, or terrain that is jagged rather than smooth.
article: τραχύς describes something physically rough or uneven, whether a bumpy road or a rocky stretch of coastline. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Luke 3:5, where rough ways are to be made smooth (quoting Isaiah), and in Acts 27:29, where sailors fear running onto rocky places. Everyday Koine papyri use it just as concretely—rough sponges, rough cockles, even a medical prescription for "rough eyelids"—confirming it was an ordinary word for a coarse or jagged texture.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 4 in the Septuagint, the measured range is thin, though all sources agree on the basic sense of "rough."

definition: A potter — a craftsman who shapes vessels and other objects out of clay.
article: κεραμεύς simply means a potter, the worker who molds clay into vessels. The meaning is stable and narrow: every New Testament use refers to a potter, and in two of its three occurrences it appears in the phrase "the potter's field" (as in Matthew 27:7) rather than as a standalone English word. In the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew יָצַר, "to form" or "shape," the same word used of a craftsman molding clay; Moulton-Milligan also shows it was a common everyday term in the papyri, appearing in business accounts and personal letters about real working potters.
caution: Only three New Testament occurrences, but the sense is consistent and the Septuagint, papyri, and lexicons all agree.

definition: A person who practices magic or sorcery; a magician.
article: φάρμακος refers to someone who practices magical arts — a sorcerer or magician. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Revelation (21:8 and 22:15), where it is rendered "sorcerers," and the Septuagint uses it 12 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew word for those who practice witchcraft. Interestingly, the related verb φαρμακεύω shows up in everyday Koine papyri with the sense of poisoning: one Oxyrhynchus document (c. A.D. 130) has a man complaining that he "had been poisoned," hinting at the close ancient link between magic potions and poison.
caution: The word occurs only twice in the New Testament, so its range there rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To argue or wrangle with someone, especially in a contentious or quarrelsome way.
article: ἐρίζω means to wrangle, contend, or quarrel with someone. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 12:19), where the wording is absorbed into a larger phrase quoting the Septuagint, and four times in the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew words for rebellion or strife such as מָרָה. The papyri show the same everyday flavor: one second/third-century document has a man arguing, "I am stronger than this one," capturing the ordinary sense of squabbling.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence, and there the verb is folded into a Septuagint quotation rather than standing on its own.
