definition: Demetrius, a personal name borne by two different men in the New Testament.
article: Demetrius is a proper name appearing 3 times across 2 books in the New Testament. It refers to two distinct men: a silversmith of Ephesus who stirred up a riot against Paul (Acts 19:24, 38), and a Christian disciple commended by the apostle John (3 John 12). The name was common in everyday Koine, well attested in inscriptions and papyri documented by Moulton-Milligan.

definition: To waver mentally between two opinions; to doubt or hesitate when faced with uncertainty.
article: διστάζω describes the mental act of wavering—being pulled between two views and unable to commit, hence "to doubt" or "hesitate." It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew (14:31 of Peter sinking, and 28:17 of disciples seeing the risen Jesus), and the Majority Standard Bible renders both simply as forms of "doubt." The everyday Koine papyri preserve the same flavor: one document speaks of applying "the doubtful cases" (τὸ δισταζόμενον) to a fixed rule, showing the word's ordinary sense of unsettled, uncertain matters needing resolution.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both in Matthew, the measured range is very thin, though the sources agree on the meaning.

definition: Work, labor, or the business and profit-making activity by which someone earns a living.
article: ἐργασία covers practical work and the business or trade one does for a living, and by extension the gain or profit that work produces. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times, but in 4 of those the translators folded it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word; one notable use is the idiom 'give diligence' (δὸς ἐργασίαν) in Luke 12:58. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where it can mean physical labor or even the work owed by slaves, as in a second-century document about a master receiving back 'the slaves and their labour.' In the Septuagint it occurs 34 times, most often rendering the Hebrew word for 'work' or 'craft' (מְלָאכָה, 12×).
caution: The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) describe a broader range—business, trade, performance, gains—than the single measured sense captured here, partly because most NT occurrences were absorbed into phrasing.

definition: Legally answerable or accountable to someone, liable to face their judgment in court.
article: ὑπόδικος is a courtroom word describing someone who is answerable to a judge or party and liable to face judgment. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 3:19, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "held" and where the whole world is shown to be accountable to God. The everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions confirm this legal force: contract texts from the third century B.C. use the phrase ὑπόδικος ἔστω ("let him be answerable") for someone who breaks the agreed terms, suggesting the sense is "liable to be brought to trial" rather than already "guilty."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lexica note a subtle distinction—"answerable to" versus "guilty before"—so its precise force is somewhat debated.

definition: Hard, wearying work or the trouble it causes—labor that drains your strength and energy.
article: κόπος points to effort that exhausts you—not just work, but labor that wears down your strength, often paired in the New Testament with words like μόχθος ("hardship"). The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "labor" in 13 of 19 occurrences (72%), while in a couple of cases (Matthew 26:10, Mark 14:6) it appears in the phrase "why are you bothering this woman?"—the idiom κόπους παρέχειν, "to give trouble to someone." That same phrase turns up in everyday Koine papyri, where one letter from 115 BC warns "if he gives you trouble, go up with him," showing this was ordinary, practical language. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew עָמָל ("toil, trouble"), reinforcing the sense of burdensome effort.

definition: Careful attention or kind care given to someone, such as looking after their needs or comfort.
article: This noun describes attentive care or kind concern for someone's wellbeing. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 27:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "consideration" — the friendly attention Paul was allowed to receive. The everyday papyri make the meaning vivid: it covers a nurse caring for a child, officials doing their duties, and estates receiving "proper attention," all centered on the idea of taking care of something properly.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a translation the BSB does not independently match, the precise nuance rests mainly on the papyri and Septuagint evidence.

definition: The main meal of the day, especially a substantial evening dinner or formal banquet to which guests are invited.
article: δεῖπνον is the chief meal of the day—the big evening dinner—and by extension a formal banquet with invited guests. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 16 times, rendered "banquets" 5× and "supper" 4×, with the rest scattered across similar terms like "dinner" and "meal." Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary sense: one private expense account even lists asparagus bought "for the dinner" of a man attending a funeral feast. In the Septuagint it appears only 4 times, all translating the Hebrew phrase for the king's rich food (פַּת־בַּג in Daniel).

definition: To listen intently and attentively to someone, paying close attention to what is being said or heard.
article: This verb means to listen closely or attentively, and it appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:25, where the prisoners listen to Paul and Silas singing in jail. The everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions documented by Moulton-Milligan show it was a normal word in ordinary speech, while it also carried a special medical usage that fits its appearance only in Luke's writing. The standard lexicons agree it carries the sense of attentive, focused listening rather than mere hearing.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the biblical evidence alone.

definition: A person's way of life or conduct — the pattern of behavior by which someone lives.
article: ἀγωγή literally means a leading or guiding, but in the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 3:10, where it refers to Paul's manner of life or conduct. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this figurative sense: documents from as early as 156 B.C. use the word for a person's behavior or way of living, and an inscription praises someone for being 'orderly in character and conduct.' In the Septuagint it shows up just twice, translating Hebrew words for things like a charge or duty and for second rank, suggesting the term could stretch across related ideas of guidance and arrangement.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning there rests on a single verse supported by outside Koine evidence.

definition: A young goat or kid, the offspring of a goat.
article: ἐρίφιον is a diminutive of ἔριφος and simply means a young goat or kid. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, where Jesus separates sheep from goats, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including a letter (c. B.C. 245) asking that a goat be sent for a coming festival. Some manuscripts read the simpler form ἔριφος in places like Luke 15:29, but the diminutive is well attested in ordinary documents listing livestock.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament: it appears only once, with manuscripts sometimes preferring the related form ἔριφος.

definition: To put or place someone on board a ship; to make them embark.
article: ἐμβιβάζω is a causative verb meaning to put or place someone aboard a vessel — literally to make them step in. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 27:6, where it is rendered "board" and describes a centurion putting Paul and the others onto a ship. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including one (Syll 266) that records twelve volunteer sailors being put aboard, matching the nautical sense exactly; in the Septuagint, however, it carries the broader sense of setting someone on a course or path (translating Hebrew verbs for riding or treading).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and few attestations overall, the confidence tier is low, and the Septuagint uses it more broadly than the single nautical NT sense.

definition: To be carried along with someone or something, whether swept into bad company or willingly adapting oneself to others.
article: This compound verb literally means to lead or carry away together with, and in the New Testament it appears in the passive, picturing someone being swept along like in a current. It occurs only 3 times, and in 2 of those the translators absorbed it into broader phrasing rather than giving it a single English word. The sense ranges from being dragged into others' error to the gentler idea of accommodating oneself to people, which is why older versions like the KJV rendered it both "carry away with" and "condescend"; in the Septuagint it shows up once, at Exodus, translating a Hebrew word meaning to take.
caution: Confidence is low: the word appears only 3 times, sources disagree on whether Romans 12:16 means "associate with" or "accommodate oneself to," and the digest reports conflicting Hebrew counterparts.

definition: To move through or across a place, travel from one spot to another, or (of news) to spread around.
senseLabels: go or pass through a place
article: διέρχομαι combines "through" (διά) with "come/go" (ἔρχομαι), and at its core means traversing some distance — whether passing straight through a place, traveling around a region, or simply going from here to there. The Byzantine NT uses it 42 times, and the measured renderings show how flexible it is: 26% are "through," but it also covers "passed through," "went," "traveled," and even "let us go across." An interesting wrinkle is the secondary sense of news "spreading" or "going abroad" (Luke 5:15), and Moulton-Milligan notes from the papyri that the preposition shouldn't be pressed too hard — it just signals that some distance, long or short, gets covered.
caution: The strict "through" force can be overstated; as Moulton-Milligan warns from the papyri, the word often means simply traversing a distance rather than passing strictly through something.

definition: Pamphylia, a coastal region (Roman province) of southern Asia Minor visited by Paul.
article: Pamphylia is simply a place name: a region, later a Roman province, on the south coast of Asia Minor, named five times in the New Testament and all within Acts. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Pamphylia" in every occurrence; the variant phrasings the digest lists ("after in Pamphylia," "after Pamphylia") just reflect surrounding words, not different meanings. One curious detail is Strong's note that the name comes from a compound of πᾶς ("all") and πυρά, suggesting an "all-tribes" or mixed-population sense behind the geographic label.

definition: A loud shout or call that gives an order, like a commander signaling those under him.
article: This word names a forceful spoken signal — a shout, summons, or word of command meant to rouse people to action. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 4:16, where it is rendered "command," and just once in the Septuagint (Proverbs 30:27, translating Hebrew חָצַץ). One notable detail: the spelling here (κέλευσμα) is a later form of the older κέλευμα, and Moulton-Milligan confirms the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use — so the precise force of the term rests on very limited data.

definition: A group of people, especially a people united by shared race and language, and most often Israel as God's chosen people.
senseLabels: a people or group of people
article: λαός means a body of people, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it overwhelmingly this way — rendered "people" in 137 of 142 occurrences (100% of the times it gets its own English word). While it can mean people in general, it most often refers to a distinct people of the same race and language, and in the New Testament it especially designates Israel, often standing in contrast to τὰ ἔθνη (the nations or Gentiles). A striking detail from the papyri: λαοί was the everyday term for the native Egyptian population — the fellaheen — as in a salt-tax document where the word names the local farmers paying their dues.

definition: A bag made from animal skin, used to hold liquids like wine.
article: ἀσκός is a leather bottle or bag, almost always rendered "wineskins" in the New Testament (10 of 12 times, about 83%), where Jesus speaks of not putting new wine into old skins. The other two cases simply use "pour" because the act of filling the skins is in view. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words for skin containers, and everyday Koine papyri show it could mean a hide or skin more generally — one document even lists strong straps cut "from the box of skins."

definition: To torment, torture, or cause severe physical or mental distress to someone.
article: βασανίζω means to torment, torture, or subject someone to severe distress, whether physical pain, mental anguish, or—when used of boats—being battered by waves. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times across 5 books, rendered as "tormented" or "torture" in most cases, though 5 of those 12 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing without a standalone English word. The papyri make its everyday brutality vivid: an Oxyrhynchus document records that slaves "under torture said" something, and curse tablets invoke the word against enemies. Interestingly, the word originally meant to test metal on a touchstone, with torture being the means of forcing out the truth.
caution: The Septuagint evidence is thin (just one occurrence), and the lexica trace a broader original sense of 'testing' that the New Testament's torment-focused usage does not display.

definition: To bring shame or disgrace on someone, or in the passive, to be put to shame—often meaning hopes that go unfulfilled.
senseLabels: to disgrace or put to shame
to never be put to shame
article: καταισχύνω means to disgrace or dishonor someone, and in the passive to be put to shame; it can take an object that is a person or a thing. In the New Testament it appears 13 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "shame" in most cases, twice in the negative sense of being "never" put to shame (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6). One notable feature carried over from the Septuagint—where it shows up 64 times, chiefly translating Hebrew בּוּשׁ (18×)—is its use for hopes that are disappointed or left unfulfilled, as in Romans 5:5.

definition: The act of punishing wrongdoing or paying back an injustice — vengeance carried out, often by God.
article: ἐκδίκησις refers to vengeance or the carrying out of justice against wrongdoing, appearing 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "vengeance" in the clearest cases (3×, like Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it shows up far more often (56×), most commonly translating the Hebrew נְקָמָה, "vengeance." A vivid parallel comes from a curse inscription from Phlius, which speaks of "the inexorable vengeance of Nemesis" hanging over a wrongdoer — close to the idea behind Romans 12:19.
caution: The word can lean toward either "vengeance" or "vindication/defense" depending on context, and only 3 of 9 New Testament occurrences yield a clean English rendering, so its exact force in any given verse depends on the surrounding wording.

definition: A situation of danger, peril, or risk that threatens harm.
article: κίνδυνος means danger or peril — a threat of harm. It appears 9 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "danger" in every clear instance, with Paul famously listing all the perils he faced in 2 Corinthians 11:26. Everyday Koine papyri use the word the same way: one writer congratulates his brother on being saved "out of great dangers" (ἐκ μεγάλων κινδύνων), and another notes a time when "there is no danger," showing the word was ordinary speech, not a technical religious term.
caution: The Abbott-Smith and Septuagint notes cite slightly different Hebrew counterparts (מֵצַר versus the forms listed in the digest), so the exact Hebrew background is reported inconsistently.

definition: Ptolemais, a coastal city in Phoenicia between Tyre and Caesarea, named after a Ptolemy.
article: Πτολεμαΐς is a place name for a maritime city on the Phoenician coast, located midway between Tyre and Caesarea. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:7, where Paul stops there during a voyage. The lexica agree it was named after one of the Ptolemies, the Greek-speaking kings of Egypt.
caution: The measured-sense data is unreliable here, listing the rendering as "finished" (a quirk of how the surrounding verse was counted) when the word is simply a proper place name.

definition: The absence of sound; a hush or stillness that falls over a crowd or place.
article: σιγή means silence or stillness — the quiet that settles when people stop talking or a place falls hushed. It appears only twice in the New Testament, once for the crowd quieting down before Paul speaks (Acts 21:40) and once for the famous half-hour of silence in heaven (Revelation 8:1). The two "measured senses" here aren't really different meanings; the word is the same hush in both cases, and Moulton-Milligan notes it was used in everyday Koine, including for the reverent silence kept during temple services.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and thin overall evidence, the apparent split into two "senses" reflects different settings, not genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: Condemned to death, like a prisoner sentenced to die in public.
article: This rare word describes someone sentenced to die — in its single New Testament appearance (1 Corinthians 4:9), Paul pictures the apostles as men 'condemned to death' put on display before the world. Outside the New Testament it shows up in the Septuagint at Bel 1:31, again of someone doomed to death. The word is built from ἐπί ('upon') and θάνατος ('death'), and the lexicons agree it means 'condemned to death,' even though the Majority Standard Bible renders the verse's imagery as 'displayed.'
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and is barely attested elsewhere, so its precise force rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To do good to someone, helping or benefiting them through kind action.
article: εὐεργετέω means to do good or bestow a benefit on someone. It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 10:38), where Jesus is described as going about doing good, and four times in the Septuagint, once translating the Hebrew word for "to deal kindly with" (Psalm 13:6). Everyday Koine inscriptions show the word used for public benefactors — Moulton-Milligan cites a text honoring those who "do good" to the people, and an Egyptian inscription praising the emperor Nero for the benefits he brought to Egypt.
caution: The measured sense is reported as the word "how," which reflects the surrounding phrasing rather than the verb itself, so rely on the standard meaning "to do good" attested in the lexica and Septuagint.

definition: To rise or come early in the morning, especially to do something at daybreak.
article: ὀρθρίζω means to get up at dawn or come early in the morning, often to seek someone out—in its one New Testament appearance, the people came early to hear Jesus teach in the temple (Luke 21:38). It steps in for the classical word ὀρθρεύω and shows up frequently in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew verb שָׁכַם ("rise early") 45 times. Interestingly, scholars dispute whether the "rise early" meaning truly depends on the Hebrew, with Thumb pointing instead to similar everyday Greek verbs built around times of day, like one meaning "work through the night."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests heavily on Septuagint usage.

definition: A small common bird, the sparrow, often used to picture something of very little market value.
article: Στρουθίον is the everyday word for a sparrow, technically a diminutive of στρουθός (a larger bird). The two "measured senses" here are really the same bird in slightly different phrasings—half its New Testament uses come in the expression "worth more than sparrows," stressing how cheap these birds were. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew צִפּוֹר (bird), and a Greek food-account papyrus prices a large στρουθός at 8 drachmae, which the editors think may actually refer to an ostrich.
caution: The word's range is unusually wide—from a tiny sparrow to possibly an ostrich in the papyri—so the parent term στρουθός could mean a much larger bird than the New Testament sense suggests.

definition: To rage arrogantly or behave with proud, defiant insolence, like a high-spirited horse snorting and prancing.
article: This verb originally pictured a spirited horse neighing and prancing, then came to describe the haughty insolence of proud people. The New Testament uses it just once, in Acts 4:25, quoting Psalm 2:1, where it depicts nations 'raging' against God. The Septuagint connection is striking: there it renders the Hebrew רָגַשׁ, and Moulton-Milligan note its everyday use in the papyri, even of arrogant 'prancing proconsuls.'
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (a quotation from Psalm 2:1), the measured evidence is thin, so the sense rests heavily on the Septuagint and classical usage.

definition: A table for eating or doing business, especially a money-changer's counter; by extension, the food or meal served on it.
article: τράπεζα is the ordinary word for a table, appearing 15 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "table" in 11 of them (79%). Its range stretches beyond furniture: it can mean the food laid out (a meal) and, from the table where money-changers sat, it came to mean a bank or money-changer's counter. The papyri show this everyday flavor vividly, including one mention of a table made of box-wood, and in the Septuagint it appears 69 times, usually translating the Hebrew word shulchan, "table."
caution: Whether a few occurrences mean a literal table or a money-changer's bank is debated, and Abbott-Smith notes scholars disagree on Acts 6:2.

definition: To shine upon or give light to something, used figuratively of illumination.
article: This rare verb means to shine upon or give light, and in its single New Testament appearance (Ephesians 5:14) it is used figuratively, as in the call for Christ to shine on the one who awakes. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, with the Septuagint using it just three times, all in Job. Notably, in Job it renders three different Hebrew words, including one tied to the brightness of the moon (Job 31:26), showing its core sense of light shining forth.
caution: This word is barely attested — one Byzantine occurrence (none in the critical text) and only three in the Septuagint — and lexicons note textual variants and confusion with related forms, so confidence is low.

definition: Describing people who act lawlessly, defying the moral and natural restraints of law, custom, and conscience.
article: ἄθεσμος describes someone who throws off the bounds of law and custom, behaving in an unrestrained, criminal way. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Peter (2:7 and 3:17), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lawless" in every case. The word turns up in everyday Koine too: a sixth-century Egyptian papyrus records a father breaking off his daughter's engagement because he heard the man was giving himself over to "lawless deeds" (ἀθέσμοις πράγμασιν).
caution: This is a rare word with only two New Testament occurrences and thin overall evidence, so the precise shade of meaning is hard to pin down with confidence.

definition: To take someone along with you as a companion or helper.
article: This compound verb means to bring someone with you as a personal companion or helper—the kind of associate you choose on your own authority rather than an officially commissioned envoy. It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, all in Acts and Galatians, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "take" or "take along." Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document speaks of a man "taking along" Heracleides as an assistant, fitting the sense of a private helper rather than a sent representative.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, and the labeled senses ("take," "mission," "accompanied took") reflect translation phrasing rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: To gather together with others, possibly while sharing a meal or staying together; its exact meaning is uncertain.
article: This rare verb appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 1:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "discuss" (the BSB agrees 100%). The basic idea is assembling or coming together with people, but the precise force is genuinely debated: some take it as "eating with," while Professor Cadbury argued it is simply an alternate spelling of a word meaning "to live with" or "spend the night together." Moulton-Milligan note the word is so rare they could cite no clear example even from everyday papyri.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word with disputed meaning, and respected sources offer competing interpretations ranging from "assemble," to "eat with," to "stay with."

definition: To be wealthy or to become rich, whether in money and goods or figuratively in some other way.
article: πλουτέω covers both states of wealth—being rich—and the process of becoming rich, depending on the tense. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times, rendered "rich" in about half its uses (5×) and "grown" rich in two more (Revelation 3:17; 18:3). In the Septuagint it stands mostly for the Hebrew עָשַׁר, "to be rich," and the everyday papyri confirm its ordinary use; one document even prays "that you may grow rich forever."

definition: A standing-out or eminence; used of people of high rank or prominence in a community.
article: This word literally describes something that juts out or projects, and it carries that idea into the social realm to mean eminence or distinction. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Acts 25:23, in the phrase "the men of prominence" (κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν), where it picks out the leading figures of the city. The same phrase shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions and papyri (for example honoring a god "par excellence"), so this was familiar idiom outside the Bible; in the Septuagint, by contrast, it appears at Job 39:28 in its concrete sense of a rocky projection.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To signal to someone by nodding or gesturing, especially to beckon them or call for help.
article: κατανεύω means to make a sign to someone with a nod or gesture, typically to beckon them over. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 5:7, where fishermen signal to their partners in the other boat to come help with the overflowing catch. Greek lexicons note a fuller range — both nodding in assent and signaling by a movement of the head — though the single New Testament use is purely the beckoning sense; Moulton-Milligan find the word in everyday papyri, but admit the readings there are unclear.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the papyri evidence cited is described as unclear, so its broader range rests on lexical tradition rather than measured usage.

definition: To become dirty, used figuratively of remaining morally filthy or stained with sin.
article: This verb literally means to make or become dirty, and in its single New Testament appearance (Revelation 22:11) it carries the moral sense of being filthy or stained with sin. The word is rare: it occurs just once in the Byzantine text and is absent from the critical SBLGNT, which uses a related form instead. Everyday Koine papyri show the literal sense vividly—one inscription rules that women in mourning wear gray clothing that is 'not defiled,' the same root in plain daily use.
caution: Evidence is thin: this form appears only once in the Byzantine text, is absent from the critical text, and lexicons note it was likely read as the closely related ῥυπάω ('to be filthy').

definition: To hit or strike someone, usually with a single blow by hand or weapon, or for a creature to sting.
article: παίω means to hit or strike with a single blow—whether by hand, fist, or sword. The measured senses all cluster tightly around this idea: people striking Jesus (Matthew 26:68, Mark 14:47, John 18:10, Luke 22:64) and, in one case, a scorpion stinging (Revelation 9:5). The classical lexica add that it implies a less violent blow than the related word τύπτω, and an everyday papyrus from 118 B.C. uses it of an attacker who "smote me with a rod on the right shoulder."
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and a couple of overlapping renderings like "hit" and "demanding hit," the sense divisions are narrow variations on a single core meaning.

definition: To shave off the hair with a razor, or to have one's hair shaved.
article: ξυράω means to shave hair off with a razor, whether of one's own head or someone else's. The New Testament range is narrow — all 3 Byzantine occurrences refer simply to shaving (a Nazirite vow in Acts 21:24, and a woman's head in 1 Corinthians 11:5–6). It shows up far more often in the Septuagint, where 29 uses most commonly render the Hebrew גָּלַח ("to shave," 23×), and the related noun ξύρησις even appears meaning "baldness" in Isaiah 22:12.
caution: Confidence is low and the form is disputed: in 1 Corinthians 11:6 editors disagree over whether to read ξυρᾶσθαι (from ξυράω) or the aorist ξύρασθαι (from the rarer ξύρω).

definition: An adverb meaning 'perhaps' or 'maybe', expressing that something might possibly be the case.
article: ἴσως is an adverb that signals possibility, best translated 'perhaps' or 'maybe'. It appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 20:13), where it blends into the phrasing rather than standing as its own English word, and shows up 6 times across 3 books of the Septuagint, often rendering the Hebrew אוּלַי ('perhaps'). The lexica note an older sense of 'equally' (it derives from ἴσος, 'equal'), but the everyday Koine papyri confirm the 'perhaps/probably' meaning, as in a letter saying readers have 'probably heard' the news.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there is very thin, and the classical 'equally' sense is unattested in the NT evidence.

definition: Rhoda, the personal name of a servant girl in the house of John Mark's mother in Jerusalem.
article: Ῥόδη is a personal name, that of a maidservant who appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 12:13), where she answers the door to find Peter standing there. The name probably derives from the word for a rose. Outside the Bible it shows up in everyday life: Moulton-Milligan cite it on a third-century B.C. gravestone in Alexandria and note that it also appears in Greek myths and comedies, so it was a familiar, ordinary name.
caution: The measured-sense data here is misaligned — it records the verb 'knocked' from Acts 12:13 rather than the name itself, so the corpus figures shouldn't be read as defining the word.

definition: To lie or be laid down—a body, an object, or something set in place—often described as resting in a position.
article: κεῖμαι functions as the passive of τίθημι, meaning to be laid or to lie, and it covers everything from an infant or a dead body lying somewhere to objects set in place or even foundations laid. In the Byzantine NT it appears 26 times across 10 books, rendered "lying" 8 times and "lay" 4 times, though notably 12 of those 26 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own. A nice real-world parallel comes from a 3rd-century AD papyrus petition where a woman describes her husband's body "lying" on the bed, mirroring the usage at Matthew 28:6.
caution: The word's force is often grammatical rather than lexical—nearly half its occurrences carry no distinct English equivalent—so its exact weight depends heavily on context.

definition: An adverb of time meaning long ago or in times past, pointing to something that happened in the distant past.
article: πάλαι is a time adverb meaning "long ago" or "in times past," pointing to something that happened well before the present. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "ago" in every case where it gets its own English word (3 times); the other 3 times it dissolves into the surrounding phrasing. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense vividly — one document from 258 B.C. complains that securities "ought to have been here long ago," exactly the meaning we find in the New Testament.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and half of them absorbed into phrasing, the lexica note extra shades the corpus data doesn't measure — an adjective use ("ancient," 2 Peter 1:9) and a durative "all this time" in 2 Corinthians 12:19.

definition: A flat dish or platter used for serving food.
senseLabels: a flat serving dish or platter
article: In the New Testament πίναξ always refers to a flat dish or platter, appearing 5 times across 3 books, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "platter" wherever it gives the word its own English term. The most famous use is the platter on which John the Baptist's head was presented. Interestingly, the word originally meant a board or plank (as in inscriptions about gluing boards together), then came to mean anything flat — a tablet, a disc — and finally a dish; everyday Koine accounts and papyri list "a platter" right alongside loaves of bread.
caution: One of the five occurrences is absorbed into phrasing rather than rendered as a distinct English word, so the measured sense breakdown rests on a small sample.

definition: To think something over carefully, turning it over in your mind or reflecting deeply on a matter.
article: This verb describes the mental act of pondering, reflecting, or weighing something carefully in your mind. It built from a compound meaning roughly "in the spirit/mind," and the Septuagint uses it 7 times, while the Byzantine New Testament has just 3 occurrences (e.g. Joseph pondering whether to take Mary as his wife in Matthew 1:20). The everyday Koine papyri show its practical flavor nicely: one document urges the reader to "consider how great an impulse attention to these matters contributes to business."
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (2 in the critical text), so the measured sense range is narrow and confidence is low.

definition: Describing someone who is religious, carefully observing the outward forms and practices of worship.
article: θρησκός describes a person who is religious, especially attentive to the outward acts and ceremonies of worship. It appears just once in the New Testament, in James 1:26, where it is rendered "religious" 100% of the time, and the lexicons agree on this meaning. Abbott-Smith notes it specifically points to someone careful about the external forms of divine service, distinguishing it from related words for piety like εὐσεβής and θεοσεβής.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance rests on very thin evidence.

definition: More exactly, more accurately, or more carefully than before.
article: This is the comparative form of the adverb ἀκριβῶς, meaning to do or know something with greater exactness, accuracy, or care than already achieved. Though it doesn't appear in the Byzantine New Testament, critical texts show it 4 times, used for things like teaching someone the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26) or examining a case more carefully (Acts 24:22). The base adverb ἀκριβῶς turns up in the Septuagint for careful investigation, as in Deuteronomy 19:18, rendering a Hebrew word for doing something thoroughly or well.
caution: This exact comparative form appears in critical texts (4 times) but not in the Byzantine NT, so evidence for it specifically is limited.

definition: To get away from danger, capture, or punishment; to escape, sometimes escaping a specific person or thing.
article: ἐκφεύγω means to flee out of or away from something dangerous, and the New Testament use is remarkably consistent: in every measured case the Majority Standard Bible renders it "escape" (6×, 100%). The word can stand alone or take an object—escaping a thing (Luke 21:36, Romans 2:3), a person (Hebrews 12:25), or even "his hands" (2 Corinthians 11:33). One everyday papyrus from AD 123 shows the same flavor, describing a woman "thinking by this means to escape the consequences of her misdeeds."
caution: Evidence is moderate with only 7 New Testament occurrences, and one of those is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word.

definition: To fall down before someone, usually in supplication or homage, or to fall against and strike something.
article: This compound of "toward" plus "fall" describes a body dropping in one of two ways. Most often (about 63% of New Testament uses) it means falling down before a person—prostrating in homage or pleading, as the unclean spirits do before Jesus in Mark 3:11 and the healed woman in Mark 5:33. The other measured use is physical impact: in Matthew 7:25 the wind and floods "fell" against the house. Outside the New Testament the word was common everyday Koine for "to befall" or "happen," and a sixth-century Christian amulet even uses it to ask a saint to "fall down" (intercede) on a sick person's behalf.

definition: Describing someone whose conduct is orderly, decent, and well-behaved, befitting respect.
article: κόσμιος describes a person whose life and behavior are orderly, decent, and worthy of respect. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Timothy (2:9 and 3:2), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "respectable" in every case. Outside the Bible it was a common term of honor in inscriptions, often praising someone's orderly conduct (ἀναστροφή), and in the Septuagint it appears just once, in Ecclesiastes, tied to a Hebrew word for setting things in order.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (and one Septuagint use), the evidence for its full range is thin, though all sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: A binding agreement, especially the covenant God establishes with people; in everyday Greek, a person's will or testament.
article: In the New Testament this word almost always means a covenant—rendered "covenant" in 31 of 33 occurrences (100% of the times it gets its own English word). The Septuagint backs this up, using it 306 times and translating Hebrew בְּרִית ("covenant") in 231 of them, nearly always for an arrangement between God and his people. The striking twist is that in everyday papyri and inscriptions the word means "will" or "testament" with near-total unanimity—so much so that Moulton-Milligan calls examples superfluous—and this ordinary legal sense surfaces in disputed passages like Hebrews 9:16–17.
caution: The NT measured sense is firmly "covenant," but lexicographers genuinely disagree over whether a few passages (notably Hebrews 9:16–17 and Galatians 3:15) carry the everyday papyri sense of "will/testament."

definition: To roll something up or coil it, like folding a garment or rolling a scroll.
article: This verb means to roll up or coil something, the way you might fold a worn-out cloak or roll a scroll closed. It appears just twice in the New Testament, and in both places the Majority Standard Bible renders it "up" (100%) — Hebrews 1:12, where the heavens are folded like a garment, and Revelation 6:14, where the sky rolls up like a scroll. The everyday papyri make it vivid: one fourth-century magic text instructs the reader to wrap ("having rolled") the rest of a rag around the neck, showing the plain physical act behind the word.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, so the full range of this word cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: To be left remaining or to survive, especially after others have died or departed.
article: περιλείπω means to be left over or to survive—to still be present when others are gone. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in 1 Thessalonians (4:15 and 4:17), where it describes those believers who are still alive at Christ's coming, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "remain" in both places. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain sense: one third-century BC document speaks of a small portion of land that "will be left" uncultivated, and another says "nothing remains to me."
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament (a low-confidence sample), so its full range rests mainly on outside evidence from the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: Sexual activity outside lawful marriage, including prostitution, adultery, and other forbidden unions; figuratively, unfaithfulness to God through idolatry.
article: πορνεία covers a wide range of forbidden sexual behavior, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 26 times across 12 books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "sexual immorality" in 65% of cases and simply "immorality" in another 19%, and lexicons note it is a broader term than μοιχεία (adultery), originally meaning prostitution before widening to cover unlawful sexual intercourse generally. One striking detail: in the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words for whoredom (14 times each for זְנוּנִים and תַּזְנוּת), and it is sometimes used figuratively for idolatry—Israel's unfaithfulness pictured as sexual betrayal.
caution: Lexicons disagree on whether several Revelation passages use the word literally or figuratively for idolatry, so its exact sense there is disputed.

definition: To bring something to full maturity or completion, especially ripening fruit or carrying offspring to term.
article: This verb means to carry something through to its finished, mature state — built from τέλος ("completion") and φέρω ("to bear"). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 8:14, where in the parable the seed choked by worries and pleasures fails to "bring fruit to maturity." The word has a notably wide range outside the NT: ancient writers used it of plants ripening fruit and of women carrying offspring to full term, and 4 Maccabees 13:20 uses it of childbearing.
caution: It occurs only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by its own English word, so its NT sense rests on thin direct evidence.

definition: A sacrifice — either the act of offering something to God, or the victim or gift that is offered.
article: θυσία covers both sides of sacrifice: the physical offering (the animal or gift) and the act of offering it, with the New Testament leaning heavily toward the concrete sense — 82% of its 29 occurrences are rendered "sacrifices." In the Septuagint it appears a massive 333 times, mostly translating two Hebrew words, מִנְחָה ("grain/gift offering," 142×) and זֶבַח ("slaughtered sacrifice," 137×). Everyday papyri show the word was ordinary Koine vocabulary for religious offerings, as in a third-century BC letter noting that "the women need supplies for the sacrifice."

definition: A possessive word meaning "your" or "yours," referring to a group of people (plural "you").
article: ὑμέτερος is the plural possessive pronoun "your" or "yours," used when something belongs to a group being addressed. It carries a bit of emphasis compared to the simple genitive ὑμῶν, which is why Paul mostly drops it in favor of ὑμῶν; Moulton-Milligan note its comparative rarity in the New Testament. It shows up in everyday Koine too: a papyrus from 253 BC uses it for someone's mules being sent off safely. One striking twist is that in 1 Corinthians 15:31 Abbott-Smith reads ὑμετέρα καύχησις as "my glorying in you" rather than "your glorying," showing the word can occasionally point toward its object rather than its possessor.
caution: With only 10 occurrences and just two measured senses each appearing twice, plus rare and confused renderings in the data, the picture is somewhat thin.

definition: Made of silk, or silk itself as a luxury fabric.
article: σηρικός means silk or silken cloth, a luxury good listed once in the New Testament (Revelation 18:12) among the cargo no longer bought after Babylon's fall. The word comes from οἱ Σῆρες, an Indian or Chinese people from whom the ancients first obtained silk, and the fabric appears to have been named after them. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a related term σιρικοποιός (silk-maker), confirming it was ordinary commercial vocabulary.
caution: It appears only once in the New Testament, so its range there cannot be measured beyond this single luxury-goods context.

definition: To strangle oneself to death by hanging.
article: This verb appears just once in the New Testament, describing how Judas died after betraying Jesus (Matthew 27:5), where every translation renders it "hanged." The base word means to press or strangle, and in the middle voice it means to choke or hang oneself. In the Septuagint it shows up once as well, translating the Hebrew word chanaq ("to strangle"), and the related lexicons note a parallel use in Tobit 3:10.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint.

definition: An interrogative word asking what kind, which, or what sort of thing or person is meant.
article: Ποῖος is a question word that asks about the kind, sort, or identity of something — covering English "what," "which," and "what sort of." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 34 times across 10 books, most often rendered "what" (7×) or "which" (6×), though a notable cluster of uses involves the question of "by what authority" someone acts (as in Matthew 21:23 and parallels). The Septuagint uses it 28 times, chiefly to translate the Hebrew interrogative אַי ("which?" or "where?"), 19 of those times.

definition: To pack up one's belongings and set out on a journey, getting ready to travel.
article: This verb describes packing up baggage and heading off, and in its single Byzantine New Testament use (Acts 21:15) it pictures travelers getting their things ready to leave for Jerusalem. Its range is narrow and practical—a word from everyday life rather than theology. The related noun shows up vividly in a 165 BC papyrus referring to seizing the household furniture of city residents, confirming the word's down-to-earth flavor; in the Septuagint it appears just once, and Abbott-Smith notes that many manuscripts read a similar verb meaning to equip or make ready instead.
caution: Evidence is thin—just one Byzantine occurrence and zero in the critical text, and several manuscripts use a different verb here, so the reading itself is disputed.

definition: The faculty or act of hearing, the physical ears, or the thing heard—a message, report, or rumor.
senseLabels: the act or sense of hearing
article: ἀκοή covers a tidy range built around the idea of hearing: the sense or act of hearing (about a third of its 24 New Testament uses), the physical ears (about a quarter), and what gets heard—news, a report, or rumor. The word slides naturally between the act and its object, so context decides whether someone is hearing, listening with their ears, or passing along news. Notably, it appears in everyday Koine papyri in both senses: one sixth-century document (P Oxy I.129) uses it concretely for the ear, while a third-century letter (BGU IV.1080) uses it for hearing at a distance—"absent in body but rejoicing by hearing as if present."

definition: A small pouch or bag for carrying money.
article: Βαλάντιον is simply a purse — a pouch for carrying coins. All four New Testament occurrences are in Luke (10:4, 12:33, 22:35, 36), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "purse" every time; the lone "out without purse" instance is the same noun in a phrase about traveling unequipped. In the Septuagint it appears just twice, where it translates the Hebrew word kis ("purse" in Proverbs 1:14) and a term in Job 14:17, showing the same everyday money-bag sense across both Testaments.
caution: The word is found only in Luke in the New Testament, and the critical SBLGNT text omits it entirely, so the evidence base is narrow.

definition: Having no end or limit; going on without ever reaching completion.
article: ἀπέραντος describes something with no finishing point — endless or interminable. It is built from a negative prefix plus a root meaning "to complete or finish," so it literally pictures what cannot be brought to an end. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Timothy 1:4), where it was absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word; in the Septuagint it occurs once (Job 36:26), translating a Hebrew word for what is great or beyond searching out.
caution: Evidence is thin — just one New Testament use and one Septuagint use — so the confidence tier is low.

definition: To look down on someone or something as worthless, treating them with scorn or disregard.
article: καταφρονέω means to think little of someone, to disesteem or scorn them, often showing it through active disregard. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "despise" in 3 of those cases, with the Berean Standard Bible independently agreeing every time. The everyday quality of the word shows up beautifully in the papyri: one document complains that someone "despises my age" (καταφρονεῖν μου τῆς ἡλικίας), a phrasing strikingly close to 1 Timothy 4:12, while others speak of despising a widow's vulnerability—real people feeling looked down on. In the Septuagint it occurs 12 times and most often translates the Hebrew בּוּז, "to hold in contempt."
caution: Only one sense was actually measured, and the word appears just 9 times, so the full range rests partly on the lexicons rather than counted data.

definition: To make or treat something as ceremonially unclean, profaning it; or to regard something as unclean.
article: In the New Testament κοινόω almost always means to make something ceremonially unclean or to defile it, appearing 14 times across 4 books. About half its uses cluster around defilement (often what comes out of a person), while in Acts 10:15 and 11:9 it shifts to the sense of counting or treating something as unclean—a meaning God's voice to Peter directly overturns. Interestingly, the classical sense of the word was simply 'to make common,' and Moulton-Milligan shows it living on in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; the ceremonial 'unclean' meaning is largely a development seen in the Septuagint and New Testament.

definition: Moloch, a pagan god worshiped by several Semitic peoples, whose idol the Israelites are condemned for carrying.
article: Μολόχ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name for Moloch, the god identified by Abbott-Smith as the deity of the Ammonites. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 7:43, in a quotation from the Septuagint. The Hebrew background is notable: the name was apparently spelled from the consonants for 'king' (melek) but deliberately vocalized with the vowels of the word for 'shame,' a similar treatment to the name Baal.
caution: This is a single-occurrence proper name in the New Testament, and the digest's rendering data oddly lists 'Remphan' rather than Moloch, so the measured sense label should be treated with care.

definition: To make something or someone clean—washing away physical dirt, healing disease, or removing moral and ceremonial impurity.
article: καθαρίζω covers a wide span of "making clean," from healing lepers and scrubbing the outside of a cup to purifying the heart and conscience—context decides which. Across 30 Byzantine occurrences the renderings cluster tightly around "cleansed" (11×), "make clean" (5×), "clean" (5×), and "purify" (4×). In the Septuagint it appears 102 times and most often stands in for the Hebrew טָהֵר (64×), the standard word for ritual cleanness, and everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions—like a Greek mystery inscription from around 93–91 BC—show the same ceremonial "cleanse from" construction found in 2 Corinthians 7:1 and Hebrews 9:14.

definition: Salmone, a promontory or cape on the eastern coast of the island of Crete.
article: Σαλμώνη is the name of a promontory on the eastern end of Crete, a coastal landmark Paul's ship sailed past on its way west. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase as sailing "off" Salmone. Because it is a proper name for a specific cape, it functions as a navigational reference point rather than a word with a broader meaning.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its usage cannot be compared across passages.

definition: Literally 'newly planted,' used figuratively for someone recently converted to the faith and still spiritually immature.
article: νεόφυτος literally means 'newly planted,' and that agricultural sense is its dominant one outside the New Testament. In the Septuagint it appears 4 times for young plants or seedlings, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up frequently in everyday papyri this way—one document refers to 'the young plantations in the olive-yards.' Its metaphorical sense of a 'new convert' is confined to Christian literature, occurring only once in the New Testament (1 Timothy 3:6), where it warns against appointing a recent convert as an overseer.
caution: The figurative 'convert' sense rests on a single New Testament occurrence, while the literal 'newly planted' meaning dominates the surrounding evidence.

definition: Amplias, the personal name of a Roman Christian greeted by Paul.
article: Amplias is a man's name, appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, where Paul sends greetings to him in Romans 16:8. It is a shortened form of the Latin name Ampliatus (meaning "enlarged"), and the longer form shows up widely in inscriptions across Rome, Pompeii, Spain, and Athens. That broad spread, noted by Moulton-Milligan, means the name cannot be tied specifically to the imperial household, despite older suggestions that it could be.
caution: This name appears only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical (SBLGNT) text, which prefers the longer form Ampliatus.

definition: To firmly prevent or stop someone from doing something.
article: This verb means to actively prevent or hinder someone, built from the common word κωλύω ("to hinder") with the prefix διά adding force. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 3:14, where John the Baptist "tried to prevent" Jesus from being baptized by him. Moulton-Milligan show it was ordinary Koine vocabulary, citing a land-survey papyrus from 114 BC where farmers were blocked from watering their crops, and an inscription forbidding grazing in a sacred precinct.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in the biblical text cannot be measured.

definition: Comparative form meaning more free from grief, sorrow, or trouble; less anxious or distressed.
article: This is the comparative of ἄλυπος, literally "more free from grief or trouble," and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Philippians 2:28. The classic lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith, Strong's, KJV) all point to the idea of being relieved of sorrow or pain, while the measured rendering reads it as "eager" — describing Paul's state of mind as less anxious once a worry is removed. Moulton-Milligan show it was a common everyday word in the papyri, as in a third-century BC letter where a writer says he has "used every forethought to keep you free from trouble."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the measured translation ("eager") diverges from the lexicons' "free from grief," so its exact force here is uncertain.

definition: Sceva, a Jewish chief priest in Ephesus whose seven sons tried to use Jesus' name to cast out a demon.
article: Σκευᾶς is a personal name, appearing only once in the New Testament at Acts 19:14, where it identifies a Jewish chief priest in Ephesus. The name is apparently of Latin origin, and it shows up beyond the Bible too: an inscription (CIG II. 2889) records it as the name of a Milesian gladiator. One scholarly curiosity noted by Moulton-Milligan is that 'seven' (sons) in Acts 19:14 oddly becomes 'both' in verse 16, leading to a speculative suggestion that the figure may stem from a textual gloss.
caution: This is a personal name occurring only once, so its meaning is limited to identifying one individual.

definition: A wall, especially the defensive wall surrounding a city or town.
article: τεῖχος refers to a wall, most often the substantial wall encircling a city or town rather than an interior partition. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "wall" in all measured cases, as when Paul is lowered through an opening in the wall at Damascus (Acts 9:25, 2 Cor 11:33). In the Septuagint it appears 145 times, chiefly translating Hebrew חוֹמָה (110×), and everyday papyri confirm the same sense, with documents speaking of property "inside the wall" of a city.

definition: The act of uncovering or making known something previously hidden, especially God revealing truth, his will, or himself.
article: ἀποκάλυψις means an uncovering or unveiling, and in the New Testament's 18 occurrences it overwhelmingly carries the sense of a divine disclosure — rendered "revelation" 16 times (94%), with the BSB independently agreeing 93% of the time. The word literally describes laying something bare, then is applied metaphorically to God making truth or himself known. An interesting twist appears in the Septuagint: there it renders the Hebrew עֶרְוָה ("nakedness") 16 of 17 times, keeping closer to the plain idea of uncovering than the lofty theological sense the New Testament favors.
caution: Jerome claimed the word was uniquely biblical, but Moulton-Milligan note it appears in Plutarch and everyday Koine papyri, so that assertion does not hold.

definition: Serug, an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy.
article: Σαρούχ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Serug, one of the patriarchs listed in the genealogy of Jesus. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 3:35, and is rendered "son" in context as part of the family chain (and "Saruch" by the King James). The name is indeclinable and comes straight from the Hebrew שְׂרוּג, simply transliterated into Greek.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once, and manuscripts differ on the spelling (Σαρούχ versus Σερούχ).

definition: Three Taverns, a roadside stopping place on the Appian Way, about 33 miles from Rome.
senseLabels: a place name on a road
article: Ταβέρναι is a Latin loanword (from taberna, a hut or roadside building) that survives in the New Testament only as part of a place name, "Three Taverns" (Tres Tabernae), a halting station on the Appian Way south of Rome. It appears just once in the Byzantine text, at Acts 28:15, where believers came out to meet Paul there. Though the word literally means huts or wooden buildings, here it functions purely as a geographic marker, which is why the Majority Standard Bible's rendering attaches to "far" in describing how far out the believers traveled.
caution: This is essentially a one-time place name with very thin evidence, and the measured sense ("far") reflects the surrounding phrasing rather than the word's own meaning.

definition: A domesticated bovine animal—an ox, cow, or bull—commonly used for farm work and herding.
article: βοῦς refers to a domestic bovine—an ox, cow, or bull—the kind of animal kept for plowing, hauling, and grazing. The three "measured senses" here are really one meaning: the differing labels ("ox," "ox out," "out") simply reflect how the surrounding phrase was rendered in English, not separate meanings of the word. In the Septuagint it appears 173 times, mostly translating the Hebrew בָּקָר (cattle/herd) 110 times, and Moulton-Milligan note it was ordinary, everyday vocabulary in the Koine papyri.
caution: The three separate "senses" are an artifact of English phrasing, not genuine distinct meanings—the word consistently denotes a single kind of animal.

definition: A feast or banquet given to receive and entertain guests.
article: δοχή refers to a feast or reception held to entertain guests, growing naturally out of the verb δέχομαι, "to receive." It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke (5:29 and 14:13), so its range there is narrow; the Majority Standard Bible renders one as the banquet itself and the other as the act of hosting one. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times and almost always translates the Hebrew word mishteh (8 of those), the standard term for a drinking-feast or celebration.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the apparent split between "banquet" and "host a banquet" reflects translation phrasing more than two distinct meanings.

definition: A light-giving body or luminary, such as a star or other source of brightness in the sky.
article: φωστήρ refers to something that gives light — a luminary like a star, or the quality of shining brilliance itself. It appears only twice in the New Testament, once describing believers shining like lights in the world (Philippians 2:15) and once describing the radiance of a city (Revelation 21:11). In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew מָאוֹר, the word for the "lights" God set in the sky in Genesis 1, and everyday papyri use it the same way; one ancient text even applies it figuratively to the eyes.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the measured renderings recorded as fragments rather than clean glosses, the precise sense range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To hold something firmly, keep or retain it, take possession of it, or hold someone back from leaving.
article: κατέχω is built from κατά plus ἔχω ("have"), and the κατά intensifies it into a firm, holding-down kind of having. Its range is broad: holding fast to something, keeping or detaining a person, and seizing or taking possession. The measured renderings cluster around "hold," "take," "keep," and "hold firmly," while the classical lexica add some specialized senses the NT data barely shows — including a nautical use of "making for" shore (Acts 27:40) and the puzzling "restraining" force in 2 Thessalonians. The everyday papyri use it for legally possessing land or property, which fits Paul's striking phrase in 2 Corinthians 6:10, "having nothing yet possessing everything."
caution: About a third of its 19 occurrences (6×) are absorbed into English phrasing with no word of their own, and a few rare senses like the nautical and "restraining" uses rest on thin evidence.

definition: The person who steers a ship — its helmsman or pilot, the one in charge of navigating.
article: κυβερνήτης means the steersman or pilot of a ship, the one who actually navigates and guides it. The word appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 27:11 and Revelation 18:17) and four times in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew word for a sailor or ship's pilot. It was a thoroughly ordinary term in everyday Koine: papyri repeatedly mention the κυβερνήτης of a named ship, and one inscription even calls an official the "pilot of the Nile." The classical lexica also note a figurative use — a guide or governor — but that sense is not measured in the biblical text here.
caution: The measured-sense labels here ("advice," "fabulous") are mismatched data artifacts and do not reflect the word's actual meaning, which both occurrences and all lexica agree is helmsman/pilot.

definition: A golden-green gemstone, the chrysoprase, named as one of the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem.
article: χρυσόπρασος names a specific precious stone of golden-greenish color, the chrysoprase. The word is built from the Greek for "gold" (χρυσός) plus a root meaning "leek," capturing its leek-green tint, and the lexicons consistently identify it as a gem akin to beryl. Notably, the Roman writer Pliny describes the same stone in his Natural History, confirming it was a recognized gem in the everyday world, and Moulton-Milligan also find the word in ordinary Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament (Revelation 21:20), and the standard renderings here say "topaz" while the lexicons describe it as a green "chrysoprase" — so the exact stone is uncertain.

definition: An adverb meaning instantly or for the present moment, used in Scripture to stress how brief and fleeting something is.
article: παραυτίκα basically means "right at the instant," and in everyday Koine papyri it carried that plain sense of "immediately" — one Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 186 uses it for someone who did not "immediately" deny a debt. In its single New Testament appearance (2 Corinthians 4:17) it shifts to describe brief duration, modifying a noun to mean "momentary" or "for a moment," a usage also found in the classical historian Thucydides. The Septuagint uses it once, where it stands in for the Hebrew word for "throat," an unusual pairing.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and rarely elsewhere, so its precise force here rests on thin evidence.

definition: To clothe or dress someone, putting garments on them.
article: ἀμφιέννυμι means to clothe or dress someone, and in all 4 of its Byzantine New Testament appearances it is rendered "clothes" — a remarkably consistent 100%. Jesus uses it vividly when he says God "clothes" the grass of the field (Matthew 6:30) and describes those "clothed" in fine garments (Matthew 11:8, Luke 7:25). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that this full form was already a literary survival, nearly obsolete in everyday speech, with the simpler vernacular form ἀμφιάζω appearing in the parallel passage at Luke 12:28.

definition: A military commander, specifically the Roman officer in charge of the imperial guard who took custody of prisoners.
article: This word names a high-ranking Roman military officer, the commander to whom prisoners like Paul were handed over. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 28:16) and is dropped entirely from some critical texts, so its place in Scripture is itself debated. The exact title is uncertain: scholars have proposed both 'chief of the foreign troops' (princeps peregrinorum) and 'camp commander' (princeps castrorum), and the everyday papyri and inscriptions where the word appears show it could cover both naval and land forces.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one disputed New Testament occurrence, omitted in critical texts, and scholars disagree on the precise office it names.

definition: Having no defense or excuse; unable to justify oneself.
article: The word means "without an excuse" or "indefensible" — describing someone who has no grounds to defend their conduct. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Romans (1:20 and 2:1), and the two renderings the Majority Standard Bible uses ("excuse" and "pass") simply reflect different phrasings of the same basic idea of being left with no defense. Abbott-Smith notes it was used as a forensic (courtroom) term by Polybius and others, fitting its sense of having no case to plead.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: Someone who steals secretly through stealth, fraud, or cunning rather than by open force.
article: A κλέπτης is a thief — one who steals quietly and deceptively. Across its 16 New Testament uses it always means a thief, rendered "thief" 11 times (69%) and "thieves" 4 times (25%), and in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew word for thief, גַּנָּב. Abbott-Smith notes a useful contrast: a κλέπτης steals in secret by cunning, while a λῃστής is a robber who plunders openly with violence. An interesting bit of evidence comes from a papyrus dated 242–241 B.C. that describes thieves arriving at night, closely echoing the New Testament image of a thief coming in the night.

definition: A loosening or releasing of something bound, used in the New Testament of being freed from a marriage tie.
article: λύσις means a loosening or releasing, the noun form of the verb λύω (to loose). In its single New Testament appearance (1 Corinthians 7:27) it refers to release from marriage, hence the traditional gloss "divorce," though there it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than getting its own English word. The two Septuagint occurrences point a different direction: in Ecclesiastes 8:1 it renders Hebrew פֵּ֫שֶׁר, "interpretation" (of a matter), and in Wisdom 8:8 it carries a sense of solving or explaining.
caution: Evidence is very thin — only one New Testament use and two Septuagint uses — and the divorce sense differs from the "interpretation/solving" sense seen in the Greek Old Testament.

definition: A tax or tribute, especially a payment imposed on people or property by a ruling authority.
article: φόρος is the tribute or tax owed to a governing power, particularly an assessment levied on persons or property. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 5 times, mostly in passages about paying what is owed to the state, as in Luke 20:22 and Romans 13:6–7. In the Septuagint it appears 30 times, usually rendering the Hebrew מַס (forced labor or tribute, 17×), and everyday papyri show it even meant ordinary rent, such as the rent for a vineyard or for pasturelands paid in drachmae.
caution: Strong's distinguishes φόρος as a personal assessment from τέλος (a toll on goods), but with only 5 New Testament occurrences this fine distinction rests largely on the lexicons rather than measured usage.

definition: To be silent or stop speaking; sometimes to keep something secret or hidden.
article: σιγάω mostly means to be silent or fall quiet — to stop talking, hold one's peace, or wait without speaking. In its transitive or passive use it can also mean to keep something secret, as when Paul speaks of a mystery that was kept hidden. The word was at home in everyday Koine: a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus has an advocate demanding, "what reason had you for being silent regarding this?" In the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew words for being silent or still, including חָרַשׁ.

definition: Describing someone or something marked by deceit—treacherous, dishonest, and out to mislead others.
article: δόλιος describes a person or thing that is deceitful and treacherous, working through trickery rather than honesty. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 11:13, where it's rendered "false" of deceitful workers. It's far more common in the Septuagint (22 times, chiefly in Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach), where it usually translates the Hebrew word for deceit (מִרְמָה, 5 times), and Moulton-Milligan note its abstract form turns up in everyday Koine documents.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To unsettle or disturb people deeply, originally meaning to pack up baggage or dismantle and plunder a town.
article: This word originally meant to pack up baggage, and from there developed military senses like dismantling or plundering a town. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 15:24, where it describes people "unsettling" or troubling the souls of believers with their words. A striking detail comes from an everyday papyrus (c. A.D. 1) where it means to go bankrupt — literally to have one's household "broken up" — showing how the packing-up image stretched into ideas of ruin and upheaval.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, so the precise force here is hard to pin down.

definition: A money-changer who exchanged or broke large coins into smaller currency.
article: This word names a money-changer, someone who handled coins and exchanged large denominations for smaller ones. It appears only once in the New Testament, in John 2:14, where Jesus encounters the money-changers in the temple, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "tables" (100%), as does the BSB. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that the noun itself is practically confined to the New Testament and writings dependent on it, though the related verb shows up in everyday papyri — for example, a document from A.D. 60 using a compound form to mean "exchange money."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Describing something only mildly warm or tepid, used figuratively for half-hearted, neither hot nor cold commitment.
article: χλιαρός literally means warm or tepid, the temperature of something that is neither hot nor cold. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 3:16, where it is used figuratively to describe half-hearted people. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, showing it was ordinary, practical vocabulary for describing temperature before Revelation gave it its famous metaphorical punch.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured-sense data here reflects the surrounding 'vomit out' phrasing rather than the word's own meaning, so lean on the lexicons ('lukewarm, tepid').

definition: A gift dedicated and set up in a temple as an offering to God.
article: ἀνάθημα refers to a gift consecrated to God and displayed in a temple, such as a votive offering. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 21:5, where it describes the gifts adorning the temple. The word is closely related to ἀνάθεμα, and the forms overlapped so much that many manuscripts and editions read ἀνάθεμα here instead; inscriptions show both spellings living side by side in the same sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text and even there the manuscripts vary between ἀνάθημα and ἀνάθεμα, so the evidence is thin.

definition: Wide or broad in extent, used of a road, gate, or anything spread out flat.
article: Πλατύς means "wide" or "broad," describing something spread out flat — a gate, a road, or even a physical build. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 7:13, where it describes the wide gate that leads to destruction. Its feminine form often functions as a noun meaning "a street" (the wide way), and in the Septuagint it appears 53 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for a broad open place (רְחוֹב, 29×). The everyday Koine papyri show it vividly: one document describes a strap as "strong and broad," another a fugitive slave as "broad across the shoulders," and another even mentions flat loaves of bread.
caution: The single Byzantine occurrence makes its New Testament range thin, though the abundant Septuagint and papyri evidence confirms the basic meaning is secure.

definition: Evidence or proof presented to confirm something, often a public declaration that bears witness to a fact or person.
article: μαρτύριον is the evidence or proof that backs up a claim—a testimony given so others can know something is true. In the New Testament it appears 20 times, rendered "testimony" in 14 cases (88%) and "witnesses" in 2 cases (13%), with 4 occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The most striking detail comes from the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew מוֹעֵד 138 times—giving the famous phrase "tent of meeting/testimony"—and everyday papyri even use it for a martyr's shrine in later centuries.

definition: A Greek-speaking Jew, one whose language and customs were Greek rather than Hebrew or Aramaic.
article: Ἑλληνιστής refers to a Jew whose primary language and cultural world were Greek, as opposed to those who spoke Hebrew or Aramaic. It is a rare word, appearing only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts (6:1, 9:29, 11:20), and the Majority Standard Bible consistently renders it "Grecian Jews," matching the older KJV "Grecian." Abbott-Smith notes the word derives from Ἑλληνίζω, "to Hellenize" or adopt Greek customs, which captures the cultural distinction rather than ethnicity.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences, all in Acts) and the digest's sense breakdown mixes in the unrelated word "began," so treat the measured senses with care.

definition: A goal or target that one aims at, like the finish-line mark a runner fixes his eyes upon.
senseLabels: a goal or target aimed at
article: σκοπός is the point you fix your eyes on—a goal, mark, or target. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Philippians 3:14, where the Majority Standard renders it "toward" (the goal), though the original noun means the aim itself. The Septuagint uses it 24 times across 11 books, most often (19×) for the Hebrew צָפָה, a watcher or watchman, which is its other major sense; everyday papyri also show the "aim, object" meaning, as in a bishop's sixth-century will describing his "own good purpose and freely-chosen aim."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a translation ("toward") that flattens the underlying noun, the precise nuance here rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than direct measurement.

definition: To turn something into something else, change its nature, or twist and corrupt it from its proper form.
senseLabels: change or pervert into something else
article: μεταστρέφω literally means to turn one thing into another, and from there it ranges from neutral change to a darker sense of twisting or corrupting something. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, and in the Septuagint 18 times across 12 books, where it most often renders the Hebrew הָפַך ("to turn, overturn"), used 9 of those times. A nice everyday glimpse comes from a fourth-century papyrus, where someone speaks of "turning your word however you wish" — showing the verb's plain, ordinary use in changing the sense of what is said.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only 3 times in the Byzantine NT, was absorbed into surrounding phrasing in 2 of those, and one occurrence (James 4:9) is disputed against the variant μετατρέπω.

definition: To go along with someone, accompany them, or follow them—often as a disciple committing to a teacher.
article: This verb means to accompany or go after someone, and in the Byzantine New Testament its 92 occurrences split almost evenly between past-tense "followed" (48%) and "follow" (47%)—essentially the same idea in different tenses. It frequently carries the deeper sense of following as a disciple, as when men leave their nets to follow Jesus.
