Notably, the papyri show that ἀκολουθέω took over the everyday job of the verb ἕπομαι, which never appears in the New Testament at all; one document from Egypt even uses it in its plainest sense of children walking along behind.

definition: "The Anointed One" — God's promised Messiah, the title given to Jesus throughout the New Testament.
article: Χριστός literally means "anointed," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Christ" in 552 of its occurrences (100% of the time it gets its own word), agreed by KJV and Dodson alike. In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew מָשִׁ֫יחַ ("anointed," 27 times), the very word behind "Messiah" — so "Christ" and "Messiah" point to the same idea from Greek and Hebrew. The classical lexica note an older, plainer use as an adjective meaning "to be used as ointment" or "anointed" (as of a priest in Leviticus), but in the New Testament it functions almost entirely as the title for Jesus. Interestingly, scholars cite the Psalms of Solomon as the earliest example of the word used as a Messianic title.

definition: To throw, cast, or more gently put or place something or someone somewhere.
article: βάλλω covers a wide range, from forceful throwing or casting to the much gentler act of putting, placing, or pouring something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 125 times across 8 books, most often rendered "thrown" (45×, 51%), but also "into" (22×), "put" (12×), and "cast" (10×). The everyday papyri make the gentle end of the range especially clear: one document uses it simply for putting a calf in front of sheep, with no hint of violence, and another for giving good measure—so this is far from always a forceful word.

definition: Ephraim, a town near Jerusalem to which Jesus withdrew with his disciples.
article: Ἐφραίμ is a proper name. In the New Testament it appears just once, in John 11:54, naming a town near Jerusalem where Jesus retreated with his disciples. In the Septuagint the same Greek spelling occurs far more often—223 times—mostly rendering the Hebrew name Ephraim (192×), the well-known tribe and territory of Israel, so the New Testament's lone town reference is a narrow slice of the name's broader biblical use.
caution: The measured sense is labeled "result," which appears to be a tagging artifact rather than a real meaning; the word is simply the place name Ephraim, attested only once in the New Testament.

definition: A visible sign or proof that something is true, a concrete piece of evidence pointing to a conclusion.
article: ἔνδειγμα refers to a tangible piece of evidence — a plain token or proof that demonstrates something is the case. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Thessalonians 1:5, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the idea of something being "clear." Abbott-Smith notes a fine distinction: ἔνδειγμα (with its passive form) points to the *thing proved*, whereas the related ἔνδειξις refers to the *act of proving* itself.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage and confidence is low.

definition: To grab something forcibly—snatching it away, seizing it by force, or carrying a person off, sometimes suddenly heavenward.
article: ἁρπάζω is about taking by sudden, forceful action—whether snatching an object away, seizing a person, or being caught up to heaven. The English renderings cluster into three measured patterns: "caught up" (3×, as in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 and the man taken to paradise in 2 Corinthians 12:4), "force" (2×, as when the crowd tries to seize Jesus to make him king in John 6:15), and "snatch out" (2×, where no one can pluck believers from the Father's hand in John 10:28–29). Everyday papyri use the word for plundering and even forcibly carrying people off into custody during the Jewish war under Trajan, and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew גָּזַל (15×, "rob") and טָרַף (11×, "tear").

definition: To perform sacred priestly duties, carrying out service like a priest who ministers and offers sacrifice.
article: This verb describes acting as a priest — carrying out sacred rites and ministering in holy service. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 15:16, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with priestly language and the BSB agrees completely. Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine papyri use the related noun for sacred functions, including a request to perform temple duties, suggesting the word should carry the full weight of sacrifice rather than mere ministry.
caution: With just one New Testament occurrence, the precise force of the word is hard to pin down from biblical evidence alone.

definition: To mix or blend one thing together with another, such as combining liquids or substances.
article: μίγνυμι means to mix or mingle two things together, and that meaning holds across all 4 of its New Testament appearances—whether wine mixed with gall, hail mingled with fire, or, in Luke 13:1, the blood Pilate had mixed with sacrifices. The range is narrow and stable: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mixed" in 3 of 4 cases, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100%. Everyday Koine papyri show the same plain usage, including grain "mixed" with barley in a document from 240 B.C., confirming this was ordinary, non-technical vocabulary.
caution: With only 4 New Testament and 6 Septuagint occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though all sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: Food of any kind; in some contexts the focus is on eating, especially foods permitted or forbidden under Jewish law.
article: βρῶμα is the ordinary Koine word for food, rendered "food" in 11 of its 17 New Testament occurrences (65%) and twice as "eat" where the emphasis falls on the act of eating. Its range is wide but practical: everyday meals, ceremonially clean or unclean items, and even spiritual nourishment in passages like John 4:34 and 1 Corinthians 3:2. It shows up commonly in everyday Koine papyri, and in the Septuagint it appears 51 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "food" (אֹכֶל, 23×). Interestingly, in Modern Greek the same word has drifted to mean rubbish, stench, or dirt.

definition: The sandy edge of the sea or a lake where land meets the water.
senseLabels: shore of the sea or lake
article: αἰγιαλός is the strip of land along the edge of a body of water — a beach or shore. It appears 6 times in the New Testament, where it is rendered "beach" or "shore," most often for the seacoast (Acts 21:5; 27:39-40) but also for the edge of the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 13:2; John 21:4). One interesting detail: the everyday Koine papyri show the word was not limited to the open sea — documents from Egypt use it for the shore of Lake Moeris and even marshy lakes, matching its New Testament use for lakeside settings.
caution: The three measured "senses" largely reflect rendering variation rather than genuinely distinct meanings, so the word's range is narrow and centers on one idea: the water's edge.

definition: A track or path, originally the rut made by a wheel, used figuratively for a course of conduct.
article: τροχιά means a track or path — literally the rut left by a wheel — and by extension the course someone walks. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 12:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as smooth "paths" so the lame are not turned aside. In the Septuagint it shows up twice, mostly translating the Hebrew מַעְגָּל ("track" or "course"), as in Proverbs, which fits its sense of a route of life or behavior.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament use and two in the Septuagint, so the figurative range rests on limited data.

definition: A thought, reasoning, or mental calculation — the inner workings of the mind as it weighs and judges.
article: λογισμός refers to reasoning or thought — the activity of the mind as it weighs, considers, and reaches conclusions. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 2:15 and 2 Corinthians 10:5), where translators render the inner thoughts that accuse or defend a person. The most interesting detail comes from everyday papyri, where the word kept its concrete sense of "reckoning" or "account-taking" — one document from A.D. 275 uses it for a tax payment, and another asks to delay the "account-taking." In the Septuagint it appears 24 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for "plans" or "thoughts" (מַחֲשָׁבָה, 12 times).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing rather than rendered as a distinct word, the measured evidence is thin.

definition: The breaking of law or commission of a wrong act; lawbreaking or transgression.
article: παρανομία means the breaking of law, an illegal or wrongful act. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 2:16, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase as a "rebuke" of Balaam's wrongdoing. Everyday Koine documents confirm the legal flavor: an Oxyrhynchus papyrus from A.D. 254 pairs it with "audacity" to complain about the "illegality" of a local official.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just three in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, so the full range is hard to pin down.

definition: To grow weary from continued effort, or to be sick or ailing.
article: κάμνω basically means to toil or labor, and from the strain of work it comes to mean growing weary or even falling sick. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, and in both cases it's woven into the phrasing rather than carrying its own English word — once for weariness (Hebrews 12:3) and once for sickness (James 5:15). Everyday Koine papyri use it for ordinary toil and fatigue, including one petition urging someone to "labour in a manner worthy of the past," which shows the plain working-life flavor behind the word.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin Septuagint use, the precise weight between "weary" and "sick" rests on very limited evidence.

definition: Prepared and set to act or be used, whether describing things made ready or people poised to respond.
article: ἕτοιμος means "ready" or "prepared," and the Byzantine New Testament uses it consistently this way—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ready" in 11 of 17 occurrences (79%), with the Berean Standard Bible independently agreeing 100% of the time. It applies both to things (a banquet, an upper room, salvation) and to people poised and waiting. The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: one document from AD 25–26 uses it for getting financial statements "prepared," and others describe fields ready for sowing or wine ripe for drinking.

definition: The visible splendor, honor, or radiant majesty belonging to someone, especially God; also reputation or praise given to a person.
article: δόξα overwhelmingly means "glory" — splendor, radiance, and honor — appearing 135 times (89%) that way in the Byzantine NT, with another 16 times (11%) rendered as the adjective "glorious." The range stretches from human reputation and praise (as in Luke 14:10 and John 12:43) to the unspoken, visible majesty of God. Strikingly, the classical lexica note that in non-biblical Greek the word originally meant "opinion" or "expectation," but in the New Testament it always carries the positive sense of repute, honor, or glory; in the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates Hebrew כָּבוֹד (kavod, "weight/honor," 131 times).

definition: Strength or capacity to act, and by extension a display of that power in a miraculous deed.
article: δύναμις centers on power — the strength or capacity to do something — and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "power" in 81% of its 120 New Testament occurrences. In 18% of cases the same word names the visible result of that power: a "miracle" or mighty deed. The everyday Koine papyri use it in just this ordinary sense, as when a writer begs a friend "with all my power" to help a recommended man; in the Septuagint it appears 387 times, most often translating Hebrew words for an army or military strength (חַיִל and צָבָא, over 110 times each).

definition: The act of doing good to others, especially through kind or generous deeds.
article: εὐποιΐα refers to actively doing good for others — beneficence or kind deeds. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 13:16, where readers are urged not to neglect it. While the New Testament uses it for the action of doing good, Abbott-Smith notes a secondary sense found in Josephus where it means "a benefit" — the good thing received rather than the doing of it. Moulton-Milligan confirm it was ordinary everyday vocabulary, citing a fourth-century papyrus that speaks of someone's "good deeds."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single verse.

definition: Elijah, the Old Testament prophet of Israel.
article: This is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Elijah, the famous Israelite prophet, and it is rendered "Elijah" in essentially every one of its 30 New Testament occurrences. The variations the data picks up—like "Elijah still" in passages such as Matthew 16:14 and Mark 8:28—reflect surrounding words rather than any change in meaning, since people often asked whether Jesus or John was Elijah come again. In the Septuagint the name translates the Hebrew Eliyyah, though one of its four appearances oddly lines up with Horeb, the mountain where Elijah encountered God.

definition: A toilet or latrine — the drain or pit where bodily waste is eliminated from the body.
article: ἀφεδρών refers to a privy or drain — the place where waste leaves the body. It appears only twice in the Bible, in Matthew 15:17 and Mark 7:19, both in Jesus' teaching that food passes through the stomach and out into the latrine. The word is rare but genuinely everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan found it used in the same sense in an inscription from the second century B.C. (OGIS 483), and some manuscripts of Mark substitute the related word ὀχετόν, meaning a drain or intestinal canal.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the New Testament and is rare overall, so its precise sense rests on limited evidence.

definition: A small connecting word meaning "however," "nevertheless," or "yet," used to qualify or push back against what was just said.
article: μέντοι is a little Greek particle that signals contrast or qualification — roughly "however," "yet," or "nevertheless." It appears only 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and the lexicons agree it originally was a strengthened form of μέν, sometimes carrying an emphatic "indeed, really" sense. Everyday papyri show it working exactly this way: one second-century letter uses it in the phrase "do not be disturbed, however" (μηδὲν μέντοι θορυβηθῇς), confirming it as common conversational Koine. Note that in James 2:8 it pairs with εἰ to mean something like "if indeed."
caution: The measured rendering data is noisy here (many fragments like "in" or "Nevertheless in did"), since μέντoι is a connector that rarely gets a clean one-word translation, so lean on the lexicons for its real range.

definition: To watch over carefully, either by examining and guarding against something or by tending and caring for people.
article: ἐπισκοπέω combines "upon" with "to look," giving the sense of attentive supervision. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, with each occurrence carried by the surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word, and its two measured uses split between watching out so that something does not happen (Heb 12:15) and exercising oversight over people (1 Pet 5:2). A nice detail from the papyri: the word was a stock phrase in the closing greetings of everyday letters, where writers would tell a recipient to "look after" the sisters or family members back home.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing), so the precise boundary between "guard against" and "care for" is uncertain.

definition: To say something beforehand—whether predicting a future event or warning people in advance about something.
article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to say," so it means to state something in advance. The lexica show two main uses: simply saying something earlier (as in Galatians 1:9 or Hebrews 4:7) and foretelling, as in prophecy (Matthew 24:25, Acts 1:16, Romans 9:29). Abbott-Smith notes a second classical sense, "to proclaim publicly or declare openly," which some translators prefer in passages like 2 Corinthians 13:2 and Galatians 5:21—showing the lexica don't fully agree on which sense fits those verses.
caution: This form does not occur in the Byzantine NT and functions as an alternate of related verbs, and sources disagree on whether several passages mean "foretell" or "declare plainly."

definition: Babylon, the ancient city on the Euphrates where Jerusalem's people were exiled, and a symbolic name for a great oppressive power.
article: Βαβυλών is the proper name Babylon, rendered "Babylon" in 10 of its 12 New Testament appearances (91%). It points literally to the ancient city on the Euphrates—the place of Israel's exile—but several reference works note it also functions symbolically: Abbott-Smith and Dodson take many Revelation passages, and probably 1 Peter 5:13, as standing for Rome. The name comes from Hebrew בָּבֶל, which the Septuagint renders with this Greek form 120 times, and it even shows up in everyday papyri, including a second-century letter instructing that camels be sent to Babylon.
caution: Sources agree on the literal sense but differ on which passages are symbolic, so the figurative use of "Babylon" for Rome is interpretive rather than measured.

definition: A handheld light source — either an oil-fed lamp or a flaming torch carried for illumination.
article: λαμπάς is a portable light, and the New Testament uses it two ways: most often it means a lamp (5 of 9 times, 56%), as in the parable of the ten virgins and the upper room at Troas, but it can also mean a torch (2 times, 22%), as with the soldiers arresting Jesus in John 18:3. The line between the two senses is genuinely blurry — Abbott-Smith notes these torches were frequently fed with oil like a lamp. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, always rendering the Hebrew lappid ("torch"), and everyday papyri list λαμπάδες among household supplies, even silver ones inventoried as temple property.
caution: The lamp/torch distinction is fuzzy, since the same object could be oil-fed like a lamp yet carried like a torch, so individual passages can be read either way.

definition: Perez, a son of Judah listed among the ancestors of Jesus.
article: Φάρες is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Perez (פֶּרֶץ), a son of Judah who appears in the genealogies of Jesus. It is an indeclinable proper name, so it always points to the same person rather than carrying a range of meanings. In the Septuagint the related Hebrew name shows up 19 times across 5 books, usually rendering פָּ֫רֶץ (13 times), the same name family.
caution: The measured senses are misleading: the digest's "Hezron" and "son" tags come from the surrounding genealogy text, not from this name, which simply means Perez.

definition: Literally "out of place," describing something improper or wrong, or in one case physically strange or unexpected.
article: At its root ἄτοπος means "out of place" (from a negative prefix plus τόπος, "place"), and from there it developed an ethical sense of improper, unrighteous, or perverse. In the New Testament it usually carries this moral meaning, as when Paul asks to be delivered from "wicked" people in 2 Thessalonians 3:2, though in Acts 28:6 it describes Paul suffering no "harm" after a snakebite. The Septuagint uses it 7 times and consistently in the ethical sense, most often translating the Hebrew word אָוֶן (āwen), meaning iniquity or wickedness; the classical lexica note that Plato favored a different shade entirely, using it for what is marvellous or odd.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences in the Byzantine text and just 1 rendered with its own English word — so the range here is mapped more from the Septuagint and lexica than from measured New Testament usage.

definition: To be pulled in many directions at once — overwhelmed and distracted by busy tasks or worries.
article: The literal idea is to drag something all around, but in everyday Koine it shifted to a figurative meaning: to be worried, harried, or pulled away by demands. Its single New Testament appearance is in Luke 10:40, where Martha is overwhelmed with the work of hosting, rendered "preparations" by the Majority Standard Bible. The figurative sense is strongly confirmed by everyday papyri — one letter from 163 B.C. has a writer asking to settle a debt "that I may be no more worried," using this very word.
caution: This appears only once in the New Testament and just four times in the Septuagint, so its measured range is narrow.

definition: A proper name in 2 Peter 2:15 identifying Beor, the father of the prophet Balaam.
article: Βοσόρ is a personal name used once in the New Testament (2 Peter 2:15), where it names the father of Balaam. Abbott-Smith treats it as a variant form of Βεώρ, the standard name for Beor (Hebrew בְּעוֹר), and notes the reading Βοσόρ is the Received Text form. The Septuagint does not use this exact spelling for Beor; the related Greek forms there translate several different Hebrew names, including בֶּ֫צֶר and בְּשׂוֹר, showing that similar-looking names get tangled together.
caution: This is a rare proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, and the sources disagree on whether it is simply a variant spelling of Βεώρ (Beor).

definition: Matthias, the man chosen by lot to replace Judas among the twelve apostles.
article: Matthias is a personal name appearing twice in the New Testament, both times in Acts 1 (verses 23 and 26), where he is selected to take Judas's place among the apostles. It is apparently a shortened form of the name Mattathias, going back to the Hebrew Mattithjah. The name shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it as a normal name of the period; interestingly, the Old Syriac Version may have read 'Tholomaeus' rather than 'Matthias' in these verses.
caution: This name appears only twice in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical SBLGNT, so the textual evidence is thin.

definition: To travel around from place to place, or to take someone along with you as a companion.
senseLabels: go around from place to place
article: περιάγω combines "around" (περί) and "lead" (ἄγω), and its core idea is movement here and there. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times across 4 books, usually describing Jesus going about teaching from town to town (as in Matthew 4:23 and 9:35), but in 1 Corinthians 9:5 it carries the transitive sense of "taking along" a companion. Everyday Koine papyri show the same range: one document from 257 B.C. uses it for leading visitors around to show them gardens, and Diodorus Siculus even uses it of taking concubines along on a journey.
caution: With only 6 occurrences, the split between "go about" and "take along" rests on a single passage (1 Corinthians 9:5) for the transitive sense.

definition: A person who worships, especially one who bows down in reverence to God.
article: This noun names a worshiper—someone who performs the act of worship, derived directly from the verb proskyneō ("to worship"). It appears just once in the New Testament, in John 4:23, where it describes the "worshipers" the Father seeks. The most striking evidence is that this is not a coined Christian term: it shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions, including a pre-Christian decree from Apamea in Syria that mentions the worshipers coming up to a shrine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in biblical Greek cannot be measured from the text alone.

definition: To say goodbye and take your leave of someone, or figuratively to give up and renounce something entirely.
article: This middle-voice verb mostly means to say goodbye or take leave of someone, the sense it carries in five of its six New Testament appearances (Mark 6:46, Luke 9:61, Acts 18:18, 21, 2 Cor 2:13). In Luke 14:33 it shifts to a stronger figurative sense — to renounce or give up everything one owns. The everyday Koine papyri confirm the farewell sense vividly: one letter writer asks a friend to come up and visit "so that I may say goodbye to you."
caution: With only six New Testament occurrences and a single figurative use in Luke 14:33, the renunciation sense rests on thin evidence.

definition: To lure or entice someone into something, like fish drawn to bait, usually toward harmful desire.
article: δελεάζω means to lure someone in, the way bait attracts and traps an animal or fish. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "enticed" twice (in James 1:14 and 2 Peter 2:18) and "desire" once (2 Peter 2:14). Abbott-Smith traces it to δέλεαρ, meaning "a bait," which captures the vivid metaphor of someone being hooked or caught.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the range of this word is thinly attested.

definition: Meat or food that has been offered as a sacrifice to an idol or pagan image.
article: This word names food—especially meat—that has been offered to an idol before reaching the table, a real concern for early believers deciding what they could eat. It appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "food sacrificed to idols" in 60% of cases and "food sacrificed" in another 20%, with the rest being shorter variants of the same idea. The compound joins "idol" (εἴδωλον) with a form of "sacrifice" (θύω), and outside the New Testament it shows up only once in the Septuagint, at 4 Maccabees 5:2.

definition: To bring back into a restored, peaceful relationship parties who were previously estranged or hostile.
article: This verb describes fully restoring a broken relationship, turning estrangement into peace. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Paul's letters (Ephesians 2:16, Colossians 1:20-21), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "reconciling" twice and as part of a "hostile" description once. It builds on the simpler verb καταλλάσσω ("reconcile"), with the added prefix ἀπό understood by lexicographers like Lightfoot and Ellicott to intensify the meaning to reconcile *completely*.
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only 3 times, and the second measured sense ("hostile engaging") reflects the surrounding phrasing of Colossians 1:21 rather than a distinct meaning of the verb itself.

definition: A container, tool, or piece of equipment; by extension, household goods, a ship's gear, or figuratively a person.
article: At its core σκεῦος names a physical object you use or store things in — a vessel, implement, or piece of equipment — and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "vessels" in 7 of 23 occurrences (50% of the measured cases). The word stretches easily: 3 times it means a household's "possessions" or goods, and twice it labels the "sheet" lowered to Peter in Acts. Everyday Koine papyri show the same wide reach, listing σκεύη as furniture, household movables, even measures of wool alongside other implements — exactly the ordinary-objects sense. In the Septuagint it appears a massive 260 times, almost always translating the Hebrew כְּלִי (226×), the general word for utensil or implement.
caution: Roughly 9 of 23 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, and the word is also used figuratively of persons (as the lexica note), so context decides much of its meaning.

definition: To receive something, often getting back what is owed, earned, or promised, or sometimes to carry or bring something.
article: In the New Testament, κομίζω overwhelmingly means to receive—especially to get back what belongs to you, what you've earned, or what was promised, as when a servant returns money "with interest" (Matthew 25:27) or believers receive their reward (1 Peter 5:4). The word's range is broader than the NT shows: classical and lexical sources list earlier meanings like "carry off safely," "recover," and even "carry off as booty," and it can simply mean to bring or carry. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plainer sense—letters use it for an agent who "has brought me" an artaba of grain or the "bearer" who carries a letter.
caution: With only 11 NT occurrences and 2 absorbed into phrasing, the measured data captures just the "receive" sense, while the older "carry/bring" meanings come from lexica and papyri rather than NT usage.

definition: To write or inscribe something onto a surface or into a record.
article: ἐγγράφω means to write or inscribe something on a surface, built from ἐν ("in/on") plus γράφω ("to write"). It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and in 2 Corinthians 3:2 it describes a letter "inscribed" on the heart. The everyday papyri show it functioning almost exactly like plain γράφω, including the technical sense of entering something into an official record, and the classical lexica add specialized uses like registering a son among adult citizens or indicting someone on a court list.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the evidence here is thin and confidence is low.

definition: An animal killed as a sacrifice; a victim offered up in worship.
article: σφάγιον refers to an animal slaughtered as a sacrifice — a victim offered in worship. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 7:42, where Stephen quotes the Old Testament and it is rendered "offerings." In the Septuagint it shows up only 5 times across 3 books, mostly translating the Hebrew word for a slaughter or slain animal (טֶבַח), which fits its core meaning of something killed for sacrifice.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence (itself a quotation) and five in the Septuagint — so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: To bring something to its proper end—to finish, complete, fulfill, or carry it out fully.
article: τελέω is about bringing something all the way to its goal—whether ending a task, completing a process, or fulfilling what was promised or written. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 26 times, and the renderings cluster tightly around "finished," "complete," "fulfilled," and "fulfill," with no single sense dominating. One notable detail: the classical lexica and everyday Koine papyri also attest a financial sense, "to pay" (as in paying a debt or tax), which shows up in the New Testament at places like Matthew 17:24 and Romans 13:6—a side of the word easy to miss.
caution: About a quarter of its occurrences are absorbed into broader phrasing without a distinct English word, so individual sense counts should be treated as approximate.

definition: To hold firm and keep going under hardship, staying steadfast and patient instead of giving up.
article: καρτερέω means to stay strong and patient under pressure, persevering rather than giving way. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:27, where Moses "endured as seeing him who is invisible"; in the Septuagint it shows up only twice. Notably, an everyday Koine papyrus (P Grenf I.1, second century BC) lists καρτερεῖν alongside "holding out" in a lover's complaint, confirming the ordinary sense of bearing up under strain.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and very thin Septuagint and papyri evidence, the measured sense rests on a narrow base.

definition: A solemn oath—a formal sworn statement that binds a person to the truth or to a promise.
article: Ὅρκος means an oath: a formal, binding promise sworn before God or witnesses. Its range is narrow and consistent—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "oath" in 7 of 10 New Testament occurrences (70%), and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100% of the time, with the few other renderings still revolving around swearing or promising. The everyday Koine papyri show the same usage: one third-century BC document reads "I swore to you the ancestral oath beside the river," while others mention "the customary oath" in farm leases and deeds of sale—an oath was simply part of ordinary legal life. In the Septuagint it appears 42 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for an oath (25×).

definition: Fortunatus, the personal name of a Christian from Corinth mentioned once in the New Testament.
article: Φορτουνᾶτος is a personal name of Latin origin (meaning roughly "fortunate") borne by a Christian of Corinth who, along with others, visited Paul (1 Corinthians 16:17), its only New Testament occurrence. It is simply a proper name, not a word with a range of meanings, and the name was very common in the Greco-Roman world. Inscriptions and papyri attest it widely — for example, one inscription names a "Fortunatus, freedman of the Emperor" — and some have suggested this Corinthian Christian may be the same Fortunatus mentioned later by Clement of Rome.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament, so the digest's odd listing of "Achaicus" as the rendering looks like a data mismatch; treat the sense data with care.

definition: Jared, a man in the ancestral line before the flood, son of Mahalalel and father of Enoch.
article: Ἰάρεδ is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew personal name Jared, a figure from the genealogies before the flood. It shows up only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:37), where it names a forefather. The name comes straight from Hebrew יֶרֶד, and the Septuagint uses this form 7 times across 2 books, always rendering that same Hebrew name; Dodson identifies him as the son of Mahalalel and father of Enoch.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, and the spelling varies across manuscripts (Ἰάρετ, Ἰάρεδ, Ἰάρεθ).

definition: To send someone or something along with another person or message.
article: Συναποστέλλω means to send a person (or item) together with someone else, built from σύν ('with') plus ἀποστέλλω ('send'). It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:18, where Paul mentions sending a brother along with Titus, and twice in the Septuagint, where it translates a Hebrew word for sending or dispatching. A nice everyday parallel comes from the papyri: in one third-century letter a father tells his son to 'send me ten litres of delicate flax' right along with his letter, showing the word's ordinary commercial use.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one measured occurrence, so its full range cannot be mapped from biblical evidence alone.

definition: The measurement of how long something is — its length or extent in space.
article: μῆκος means length — the distance something spans in space. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, twice paired with other dimensions like width and height (as in describing the proportions of God's love in Ephesians 3:18 or the measurements of the new Jerusalem in Revelation 21:16). The word is common in everyday Koine: the papyri use it for physical measurements in cubits, but it could also stretch to mean length of time, as one document refers to "the length of time." In the Septuagint it shows up 84 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew word for "length."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, the measured sense range is narrow and rests on thin evidence.

definition: To pass by on the opposite side of the road, deliberately keeping one's distance from someone.
senseLabels: passed by on the other side
article: This compound verb combines 'opposite' with 'pass by,' describing how someone goes along the far side of the road to avoid contact. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:31–32), where the priest and the Levite each 'passed by on the other side'; the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'passed' in 100% of cases. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and was even used by the poet Straton, suggesting it was a natural, freely coined word rather than borrowed from earlier biblical usage.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint (Wisdom 16:10), where the sense is markedly different.

definition: In a brief, concise way; using few words.
article: This adverb means doing something briefly or in a concise manner, and it appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in critical editions), at Acts 24:4 where a speaker asks to be heard "briefly." The Septuagint uses it twice, and everyday Koine papyri attest it too — the closest parallel Moulton-Milligan found is a third-century astronomical treatise describing "another shorter way, starting from the beginning." Both the corpus data and the classical lexica agree it consistently means "briefly" or "concisely."
caution: Evidence is thin: only one Byzantine occurrence, so the measured sense rests on a single passage.

definition: A mark, model, or pattern—from the impression a blow leaves to a person or event that serves as an example or prefigures something else.
article: τύπος covers a striking range, starting from the literal mark a blow leaves (as in the nail-marks in John 20:25) and moving outward to a stamp, an image, a shape, and finally a pattern or model. In the Byzantine New Testament's 16 occurrences, translators most often render it "examples" (6×, 43%) or "pattern" (2×), with the moral sense of something worth imitating being the dominant flavor. Moulton-Milligan notes the same wide spread in everyday papyri, where τύπος can simply mean a "pattern" for making pots; the word also developed the special Biblical sense of a "type"—a person or event foreshadowing a future one, as in Romans 5:14.
caution: Only about 57% of occurrences fall into the two clear measured senses, and the remaining renderings are scattered, so the word's exact force depends heavily on context.

definition: To flash or gleam like lightning, describing something so bright it dazzles the eye.
article: ἐξαστράπτω means to flash or gleam like lightning, used of something blindingly bright. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 9:29, where it describes Jesus' clothing during the Transfiguration; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "changed" there, though the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all point to the more vivid sense of being radiant or gleaming. In the Septuagint it appears 4 times and translates Hebrew words including one for lightning-flash, and Moulton-Milligan notes it may suggest light flashing forth from an inner source, or simply intensify the idea to "dazzling."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the standard translation "changed" differs from the lexicons' "flashing/radiant," so its precise force here is uncertain.

definition: Empty, uninhabited land or a lonely, deserted place set apart from settled life.
article: ἔρημος describes places (and occasionally people) that are empty, abandoned, or far from where people live. In the New Testament it most often (73%) means the wilderness — the open, uninhabited country east and south of Palestine — but it also shades into "desolate" (14%) and "solitary" (11%) depending on context. In the Septuagint it appears a remarkable 350 times, mostly translating the Hebrew מִדְבָּר ("wilderness," 240×), and everyday papyri use it of a village left empty because the Nile failed to flood it, even as a legal term for a case lost when the accused fails to show up.

definition: To leave a place, withdraw, or get out of an area, especially to escape danger.
article: ἐκχωρέω means to depart, withdraw, or clear out of a place. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 21:21, where Jesus warns those in the city to get out as judgment approaches. The everyday papyri make its sense vivid: legal documents repeatedly use it for vacating a house or property, as when officials order someone "to withdraw from the house" (P Amh II.30). In the Septuagint it shows up just three times, translating different Hebrew words in each case.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and few Septuagint examples, the evidence base is thin and confidence is low.

definition: A bed or couch used for sleeping, lying down when sick, or reclining—a piece of household furniture for resting.
article: κλίνη is the ordinary Koine word for a bed or couch—something you sleep on, rest on when ill, or even recline on at a meal. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "bed" wherever it appears, and the BSB independently agrees every time, so the core meaning is solid. In the Septuagint it shows up 35 times, most often translating the Hebrew מִטָּה (24×). A striking detail from the papyri: a second-century invitation from Oxyrhynchus asks a guest to "dine at the couch (κλείνην) of the lord Sarapis," showing the word could refer to a dining couch at a ceremonial feast.
caution: Lexicons stretch the range to include a portable mat, a dining couch, or even a bier, but the measured New Testament uses all point simply to "bed."

definition: In a wise, sensible, and shrewd way; acting with practical good judgment.
article: This adverb means doing something with practical wisdom and shrewdness — acting sensibly rather than foolishly. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:8, where the dishonest manager is praised for acting shrewdly. The everyday papyri back up this sense: a fourth-century letter (P Lond 1927) uses it of someone who "prudently" displayed a noble contest, referring to a manner of life. Note that while the lexicons (Strong's, KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) consistently gloss it "wisely" or "prudently," the measured translation in this app's data renders the verse as "commended," which reflects the surrounding phrase rather than the adverb itself.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lone measured rendering ("commended") reflects the broader sentence rather than the adverb's own meaning, which the lexicons agree is "wisely/prudently."

definition: A life of soft, self-indulgent luxury and easy comfort.
article: τρυφή describes a life of softness and pampered luxury — the kind of dainty, indulgent living the digest sums up as "effeminate luxury." It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: Luke 7:25 pictures people in royal palaces living in luxury, while 2 Peter 2:13 uses it of indulgent reveling (the Majority Standard rendering "blots" reflects a translation choice the BSB does not follow). The Septuagint uses it 20 times, most often for the Hebrew word for Eden's delight (עֵ֫דֶן, 8×), and an everyday papyrus describes hot-spring baths sought "not only for luxury but also for health."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT uses) and the sources disagree on the second occurrence, where the Majority Standard's "blots" diverges from the expected sense of luxury or reveling.

definition: To flood or completely cover something with water, overwhelming it as in a deluge.
article: κατακλύζω means to flood or inundate, washing something completely under water. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 3:6, where it describes the world being flooded in Noah's day, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "flood" in 100% of its occurrences. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: documents from as early as 218 B.C. use the word for farmland and plains that have been inundated, with one writer asking for equivalent land in place of fields that flooding had ruined.
caution: Evidence is thin since the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range rests largely on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: To build, construct, or get something ready by equipping or furnishing it for its purpose.
article: κατασκευάζω covers the practical work of putting something in order—building a house or ark, furnishing a tabernacle, or preparing a road for someone to travel. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times, split fairly evenly between "prepare a way" (3×), "built" (3×), "builder" (2×), and "prepared" (2×), with Hebrews accounting for most of the building language. Everyday Koine papyri use it for craftsmen who furnish or manufacture goods, such as a goldsmith who "made" a pair of bracelets, which fits its core idea of equipping something with what it needs.
caution: Strong's distinguishes it from ἑτοιμάζω as preparation by external equipment rather than inner readiness, a fine shade the measured renderings don't independently confirm.

definition: A Greek term of uncertain meaning, traditionally taken as a label for a particular Sabbath, possibly the second after Passover.
article: This is one of the most famously puzzling words in the New Testament, appearing just once across one book in the Byzantine text (Luke 6:1) and dropped entirely from the modern critical text. Its parts mean "second" and "first," and Strong's guesses it labels a specific Sabbath after Passover, but the dictionaries are blunt: Dodson calls it "a word of uncertain meaning" and Abbott-Smith says there is no satisfactory explanation. The most striking note comes from Moulton-Milligan, who searched the everyday papyri and found no support at all, calling it a famous "vox nihili" — a word that may not really be a word — whose only real interest is how it ever slipped into the text.
caution: This is a single, textually disputed occurrence whose meaning no source can explain with confidence, and the modern critical text omits it entirely.

definition: To stretch yourself forward, reaching out eagerly toward something ahead of you.
article: This word pictures someone leaning and reaching ahead, like a runner stretching toward the finish line. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:13, where Paul describes straining forward to what lies ahead. The verb is built from parts meaning "upon," "out," and "stretch," and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine documents with the plain sense of extending or stretching out.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single verse.

definition: Secret, malicious whispering against someone—talking quietly behind their back to spread harmful rumors.
article: This word names the kind of quiet, behind-the-scenes talk meant to damage someone's reputation—secret slander rather than open accusation. It appears just once in the New Testament, where Paul lists it among the disorders he fears finding in the Corinthian church (2 Corinthians 12:20), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gossip" there. Its single Septuagint appearance (Ecclesiastes 10:11) is striking: it translates the Hebrew לַ֫חַשׁ and refers not to slander but to a murmured snake-charmer's enchantment, showing the word's root sense of low whispering.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use carrying a different shade of meaning, the evidence for its precise range is thin.

definition: To make dark or obscure, used of heavenly bodies losing their light or, figuratively, of a mind clouded and unable to see truth.
article: σκοτίζω means to darken or obscure, whether literally or figuratively. In all 8 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "darkened" (100%), and it always appears in the passive — typically of the sun, moon, or stars losing their light, but also of a darkened mind (Romans 1:21; 11:10). A vivid third-century papyrus charm captures both ranges at once, addressing "the God who lights up and darkens the world," while a related text speaks of someone "darkening his mind away from the truth."
caution: Note that the SBL critical text reads this word zero times where the Byzantine text has 8, so its appearance varies by manuscript tradition.

definition: In the New Testament, the day of preparation before a Sabbath or feast—the day Jews readied themselves, what later became the name for Friday.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament παρασκευή appears 6 times, and the Majority Standard Bible always renders it as some form of "preparation"—5 times plainly and once as "preparation before." Although the word literally means getting ready and shows up in everyday Koine papyri for general preparation (for example, preparing a legal case), in Jewish usage it became the technical name for the day before a Sabbath or festival. Strikingly, this sense stuck: the early Christian Didache and even Modern Greek use παρασκευή as the ordinary word for Friday.
caution: The corpus measures only the "day of preparation" sense, but the classical and Septuagint evidence shows the word also meant general preparation or equipment outside the New Testament.

definition: Coarse joking or crude wit—using clever humor in a way that is improper or offensive.
article: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 5:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as coarse or foolish joking and the Berean Standard Bible agrees. Originally the word meant something positive—versatility, wit, or clever speech—and the classical lexica still attest that 'good' sense; Moulton-Milligan cite an ancient writer praising the witty 'pleasantries' of Attic Greek. By the time of Ephesians, however, the word had shifted toward a negative meaning of crude or vulgar jesting, which is how the early lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) read it here.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources disagree on its range—classical usage treats it positively as wit, while the New Testament reading is negative.

definition: An adverb meaning with one's entire household or family together.
article: πανοικί is an adverb formed from "all" (πᾶς) and "house" (οἶκος), describing something done together with one's whole family or household. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 16:34, where the Philippian jailer rejoices along with everyone in his home. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: this word was a stock phrase in the closing greetings of private letters, where writers regularly wished a friend well "with all the household" (e.g. a second-century letter prays for someone to be in good health πανοικεὶ).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and ancient sources disagree on the spelling and form (Abbott-Smith notes strict Atticists rejected it and preferred the form -κίᾳ).

definition: Located beside the sea or along the coast; situated next to a body of water.
article: This adjective describes something positioned next to the sea or coastline, built from the parts "beside" (παρά) and "sea" (θάλασσα). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Matthew 4:13, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Study Bible both render it with "sea." The word was at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan note a close parallel in an inscription from about 107 B.C. that speaks of someone turning back "to the coastal regions."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Cappadocia, a large Roman province in the central-eastern part of Asia Minor.
article: Καππαδοκία is simply the place-name Cappadocia, a Roman province in central-eastern Asia Minor (modern Turkey). It appears only twice in the New Testament—in the list of regions at Pentecost (Acts 2:9) and among the destinations of 1 Peter (1 Pet. 1:1)—and Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith all agree it is a single geographic region. Interestingly, the word is of foreign origin, and in the Septuagint the related Greek is even used to render the Hebrew place-name כַּפְתּוֹר (Caphtor).
caution: The measured data oddly lists "Pontus" for Acts 2:9, which conflicts with the standard sense of the place-name Cappadocia; treat that rendering with care.

definition: The first light of morning; daybreak or dawn.
article: αὐγή refers to brightness or light, but in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 20:11) it means the break of day — Paul talked until dawn. Older lexicons give the basic sense as "brightness" or "radiance," with "daylight, dawn" noted as a later development reflected in the NT and in everyday Koine usage. In the one Septuagint occurrence (Isaiah 59:9) it translates a Hebrew word for brightness, and the word was even used as a personal name on burial inscriptions from Alexandria.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its meaning there rests on a single passage.

definition: A money-changer who exchanged one kind of currency for another for a fee.
article: A κολλυβιστής was a money-changer, someone who swapped one type of coin for another and charged a premium for the service. The word comes from κόλλυβος, originally a small coin and later the rate or fee of exchange. All three New Testament appearances describe Jesus overturning the tables of these men, and the digest shows the translation is stable across every occurrence. Interestingly, the word turns up in everyday Koine documents too, including a Ptolemaic census paper that lists money-changers, even though strict Atticist writers condemned the term as low-quality Greek.

definition: A bull or ox, the large domesticated bovine used for work, food, or sacrifice.
article: Ταῦρος simply means a bull or ox, a large bovine animal. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 4 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "bulls" in 3 of those (the fourth gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing), often in contexts of sacrifice (Hebrews 9:13; 10:4) or pagan offering (Acts 14:13). The everyday Koine papyri show the same plain agricultural sense, including an instruction "as to the oxen, make them work," confirming this was an ordinary farm animal rather than a specialized term.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences the picture rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: The most honored seat in a synagogue or assembly, marking the highest social rank among those present.
article: πρωτοκαθεδρία literally combines "first" (πρῶτος) and "seat" (καθέδρα), and it consistently means the chief or most honorable seat — the place that signals preeminence. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 4 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders all 4 as "chief seats," with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% of the time. Strong's notes it points to "preeminence in council," and Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was a familiar term for a literal place of rank, not just a religious abstraction.

definition: Antioch, the name of two cities in the New Testament — one in Syria and one near Pisidia in the Roman province of Galatia.
article: Ἀντιόχεια is a place name appearing 18 times across three books, rendered "Antioch" in 94% of cases. It actually refers to two different cities: Antioch in Syria, the capital of that province on the river Orontes (as in Acts 11:19 and Galatians 2:11), and Pisidian Antioch, which lay near Pisidia in the province of Galatia (Acts 13:14; 2 Timothy 3:11). According to Strong's the name derives from a Syrian king named Antiochus.

definition: To join someone in a struggle or contest, working alongside them as a partner to help their effort.
article: This word means to throw yourself into a fight or effort alongside another person, sharing in the contest as a helper or partner. It appears just once in the New Testament (Romans 15:30), where Paul asks readers to join him in his struggle through prayer; in that single case it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as one distinct English word. The everyday papyri and inscriptions give it a vivid backdrop: it shows up describing those who fought alongside in actual battles (against the Galatians and Antiochus, c. 228 B.C.) and "working together" for a city's preservation.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense here rests mainly on outside Koine evidence rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: Silver, the precious metal, whether in raw form or made into coins and objects.
article: ἄργυρος means silver, the shining precious metal, and all 5 of its New Testament occurrences are rendered exactly that way. In classical and New Testament Greek there's usually a distinction between ἄργυρος (the metal) and ἀργύριον (silver used as money), though both have exceptions—Matthew 10:9 uses ἄργυρος where you might expect the coin-word. Moulton-Milligan note that in everyday papyri ἄργυρος is actually rare, while the money-word ἀργύριον is everywhere, with ἄργυρος showing up mostly in a long document on metallurgy.
caution: The supposed split between ἄργυρος (metal) and ἀργύριον (money) is not consistent, since the New Testament itself breaks the rule in places like Matthew 10:9.

definition: A journey or the act of traveling, especially on foot over a road.
article: ὁδοιπορία simply means a journey or the act of traveling, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it that way in both of its 2 occurrences (John 4:6 and 2 Corinthians 11:26), rendered "journey" 100% of the time. It was ordinary travel vocabulary in everyday Koine: the papyri preserve a late-3rd-century letter about sending a ferry-boat "on account of the uncertainty of the road," and the philosopher Epictetus lists traveling alongside walking and sailing as a normal part of life. The Septuagint employs it a handful of times as well, in Wisdom and 1 Maccabees.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences this word's measured range is narrow, though the single "journey" sense is well supported by papyri and the lexicons.

definition: Comparative adjective meaning better, more advantageous, or more excellent than something else.
article: κρείττων is the comparative form meaning "better" — whether in terms of advantage and usefulness or of excellence and nobility. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "better" in 60% of its 16 occurrences and "better than" in another 20%, and the Hebrews letter uses it heavily to argue that the new covenant offers a better hope, a better sacrifice, and better promises. Though it derives from a root meaning "strong" (G2904, κράτος), Moulton-Milligan notes it is always strictly comparative in the NT; an everyday papyrus letter even uses it to mean someone "had better things to do."

definition: An upper room or the upper floor of a building, used as living or gathering space.
article: This word refers to a room on the upper story of a building. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both times for the large upper room where Jesus and his disciples prepared the Passover meal (Mark 14:15; Luke 22:12), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "furnished" within the phrase describing that room. Moulton-Milligan show it was an ordinary Koine word for an upper storey, attested in everyday papyri, and it even survives in Modern Greek as "anógi" meaning upper storey.
caution: The form is uncertain—editions vary between ἀνώγεον and ἀνάγαιον—and the word appears only twice, both in parallel accounts, and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text.

definition: To want, wish, or be willing—to set your mind on something as a matter of personal choice or desire.
article: θέλω is the everyday Koine verb for wanting, wishing, or being willing, appearing 208 times in the Byzantine New Testament. Its range is fairly tight—about 67% of the time it simply means "want," with related shades of "wish," "willing," and "desire" filling out most of the rest; when paired with a negative it can mean "refused" (twice). In the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew verbs of willingness and desire, including אָבָה 33 times and חָפֵץ 23 times, and the papyri show it used naturally for personal wishes, as in a will where someone manages affairs "as I want." Strong's distinguishes it from βούλομαι as an active choice from inner impulse rather than passive acquiescence, though Abbott-Smith notes scholars disagree about how sharply the two words differ.
caution: Lexicons disagree on whether θέλω differs meaningfully from the near-synonym βούλομαι, so don't lean hard on a sharp "active choice" distinction.

definition: An inferential particle meaning 'therefore' or 'accordingly,' drawing a conclusion from what was just said.
article: τοίνυν is a connecting particle that signals a conclusion — roughly 'therefore' or 'accordingly.' It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders all three with this same inferential sense (in Luke 20:25, 1 Corinthians 9:26, and Hebrews 13:13). One nice detail of usage: in classical Greek and in Paul's wording at 1 Corinthians 9:26 it follows the first word of the sentence, while later writers moved it to the front, as in Luke and Hebrews — a pattern Abbott-Smith notes and the everyday papyri confirm.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and just one measured sense, the evidence base is thin even though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: Candace, the dynastic title for the queens of the Ethiopians, used as a royal designation rather than a personal name.
article: Κανδάκη refers to the queen of the Ethiopians, appearing only once in the New Testament (Acts 8:27) where her official, the eunuch, is baptized. The lexicons agree it functions as a dynastic title for Ethiopian queens rather than a single woman's personal name. Strikingly, an inscription from 13 BC found near Ethiopia at ancient Pselkis records an embassy honoring "the lady queen," whom scholars have linked to this very Candace.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests on outside inscriptions and lexical tradition rather than measured biblical range.

definition: To put someone or something on public display, often to expose or shame them openly.
article: δειγματίζω means to hold something up for all to see, whether as an example or to expose it publicly. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in the SBLGNT critical text), and in that single instance it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word. Notably, this rare verb shows up in everyday Koine papyri: Moulton-Milligan cite a land record where crops are catalogued and a fragment of the Ascension of Isaiah where it describes exposing a figure named Samael.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word is rare, appears only once in the Byzantine text, and the lexica describe it simply as a rare word.

definition: A conjunction meaning "since" or "because," introducing a reason, or "when, after that" to mark time.
article: ἐπειδή links clauses together, most often giving the reason for something ("since," "because") but occasionally marking time ("when, after that"). It appears 10 times in the New Testament across 5 books, and another 16 times in the Septuagint, where it usually renders the Hebrew word יַ֫עַן ("because"). The everyday papyri show the same causal force: one ancient document reads "whereas Castor has ceded the remainder of his holding... we write to you," exactly matching the New Testament's reasoning use.
caution: The temporal versus causal sense can be hard to separate, and editions disagree on which applies in Luke 7:1.

definition: The personal name of Nero, a Roman emperor, borrowed into Greek from Latin.
article: Νέρων is simply the Greek form of the Latin name Nero, the Roman emperor, and functions as a proper name rather than an ordinary word. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament text or the critical text at all; according to Abbott-Smith it shows up only in a subscription (a closing note) to 2 Timothy in the Received Text. Because it is a borrowed proper name, it has no range of meaning to map—it points to one specific person.
caution: Evidence is extremely thin: the name occurs zero times in the running New Testament text and only in a manuscript subscription, so confidence about its presence in Scripture itself is low.

definition: A burning or fire, used either literally of flames or figuratively of a fiery ordeal that tests people.
article: πύρωσις refers to burning, whether actual flames or a metaphorical "fiery" trial that tests a person. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament: twice in Revelation 18 of a city's literal burning, and once in 1 Peter 4:12 of a refining trial believers face. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri—including a Berlin magic papyrus that speaks of sending "a burning into the air."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences—all absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word—the evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To drive, throw, or send someone or something out of a place, often forcefully.
article: At its core ἐκβάλλω means to eject something — literally throwing it out or forcibly driving it away. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "drive out" 38 times (54%), with another 34% being "out" in various phrases, and it covers everything from casting out demons to expelling people from a home. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew gārash (37×), "to drive away," and a striking parallel survives in the papyri: a third-century magical text is headed with the very phrase ἐκβάλλουσα δαίμονας, "driving out demons," matching the Gospel usage (Mark alone uses it 11 times for casting out demons).

definition: To stay on in a place, or figuratively to keep on doing something or remain firmly in a state.
article: ἐπιμένω combines ἐπί with μένω ("remain"), and means staying put—either physically lingering in a place or figuratively continuing in a course of action. In the Byzantine text it appears 17 times; translators render it "continue" 4 times and "stay" twice, while 9 of the 17 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. Everyday Koine papyri show the same range: one writer says he has decided "to remain in Alexandria," and another wants to "stay on for the men there," matching its plain New Testament use.
caution: More than half its occurrences carry no distinct English word, so the measured sense counts rest on a small portion of the total uses.

definition: The one who brings something to its complete and finished state, the perfecter or completer.
article: τελειωτής describes someone who finishes or perfects something, carrying it all the way to its intended goal. It comes from the verb τελειόω ("to perfect, complete"), and the New Testament uses it just once, in Hebrews 12:2, where Jesus is called the "perfecter" of faith. The word is so rare that Abbott-Smith notes it appears nowhere else, and in that single Byzantine occurrence it is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than standing as its own English word.
caution: This is effectively a New Testament hapax with only one occurrence and no wider attestation, so its precise range cannot be measured.

definition: Describing someone or something that acts or moves with speed—quick, fast, or ready.
article: ταχύς means quick or swift, and in its single New Testament appearance (James 1:19) it describes being "quick to listen," set in deliberate contrast to βραδύς ("slow"). It shows up far more often in the Septuagint—14 times across 12 books—where it usually renders the Hebrew מָהַר, a verb for hurrying or hastening. The lexicons broaden the sense to "prompt" or "ready," but the one measured New Testament use simply gives "quick."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence rendered "quick," the fuller range ("prompt," "ready") rests on the lexicons and Septuagint rather than measured NT data.

definition: Free from contamination or defilement; morally pure and untainted.
article: ἀμίαντος describes something that is unsoiled, pure, and free from any taint or contamination, formed from a negative prefix attached to the verb meaning "to defile." It appears 4 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "undefiled" 75% of the time and "kept undefiled" once (Hebrews 13:4). Abbott-Smith notes it also appears in the Septuagint (Wisdom and 2 Maccabees), and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a use describing the upper air (αἰθήρ) as pure.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the senses are closely related and the sources agree.

definition: Describing someone who is untrained or uneducated, and so behaves foolishly or without good sense.
article: ἀπαίδευτος is built from a negative prefix on the word for training or instruction (παιδεύω), so it literally points to someone who lacks education or discipline. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only once, at 2 Timothy 2:23, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Study Bible both render it "ignorant." In the Septuagint it appears 9 times, mostly in wisdom literature, where it often translates Hebrew words for foolishness — so the idea easily slides from "untaught" to "stupid" or "foolish."
caution: With just one New Testament occurrence and thin overall data, the precise shade between "untrained" and "foolish" rests largely on Septuagint usage.

definition: To follow something closely—whether walking alongside, tracing a matter carefully, or making it the pattern you live by.
article: At root παρακολουθέω means to follow near, and the New Testament stretches that image in several directions across its four occurrences. It can mean to accompany or result from something (Mark 16:17), to investigate or trace a matter thoroughly (Luke 1:3), or to follow a teaching as your standard of conduct (1 Timothy 4:6; 2 Timothy 3:10). The everyday Koine papyri are revealing: one document from 118 B.C. uses the word for the damage that "follows" or results from a broken dyke, showing how naturally "follow closely" slid into "come about as a consequence."
caution: With only 4 occurrences and two of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the precise nuance often depends on context rather than the word itself.

definition: Moral goodness as a personal quality, especially the kind and generous side of being good.
article: This noun names goodness as a character trait, with the stress falling on its kindly, generous side rather than its strict or righteous side. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament (Romans 15:14, Galatians 5:22, Ephesians 5:9, 2 Thessalonians 1:11), and the small variations in how it gets rendered all circle the same core idea. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the word is found only in biblical and church writers, but its abstract -σύνη ending was a productive way to form such nouns in the Hellenistic period; in the Septuagint it shows up 14 times, all in Hebrew books, translating words for 'good' or 'goodness.'
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and a word built from a common ending, the fine shades of meaning rest on thin evidence.

definition: A vessel or kettle made of copper or bronze, used for cooking, washing, or storing things.
article: χαλκίον is a small bronze or copper container — a pot, kettle, or washing vessel. The word appears just once in the New Testament (Mark 7:4) and once in the Septuagint, where it renders a Hebrew word for a cooking pot. It was thoroughly ordinary household vocabulary: everyday papyri mention things like "two machines and a caldron" and "a small kettle," showing it just meant a practical metal pot.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one in the Septuagint, the biblical evidence is thin, though the papyri confirm its everyday meaning.

definition: An attention-grabbing word meaning "look!" or "see!" — pointing to something right in front of the listener.
article: ἴδε is an interjection that grabs the listener's attention and points to something present: "look!", "see!", or even "here!" Across 35 Byzantine occurrences it lands mostly as "See" (11×, 38%) or "Look" (10×, 34%), with a handful rendered "Here" (4×, 14%) when pointing at a person or scene, as in John 19:5. Originally it was simply the command form of the verb "to see" (from εἴδω/ὁράω), and that older sense survives in everyday papyri — one mid-third-century letter uses it for "look out everywhere for a small donkey for him."

definition: A gentle, mild disposition; the quality of being meek and even-tempered toward others.
article: πρᾳότης is the older spelling of a word for gentleness or meekness — a calm, mild temper in dealing with people. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament under this spelling; the New Testament instead uses the later form πραΰτης, found in passages like Galatians 5:23 and Ephesians 4:2. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew words for humility (for example in Psalm 45:4), and Moulton-Milligan note that the related vocabulary turns up in everyday Koine papyri, showing it was ordinary, not just biblical, language.
caution: This exact spelling has zero New Testament occurrences; the measured biblical evidence belongs to the variant form πραΰτης, so confidence here is low.

definition: To welcome someone in, taking them into your care or favor.
article: εἰσδέχομαι means to receive or admit someone, welcoming them into your favor — a sense well attested in everyday Koine, where it could even be used technically for receiving and storing wheat in a treasury. In the New Testament it appears just once, in 2 Corinthians 6:17, quoting the Septuagint, where God promises to "receive" his people. In the Septuagint it shows up 15 times across 7 books, most often translating the Hebrew קָבַץ (8 times), meaning to gather or collect.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (a Septuagint quotation), the measured evidence for its New Testament range is very thin.

definition: To work or labor at a task, trade, or activity, putting effort into producing or accomplishing something.
article: This common verb means to work, labor, or toil — whether at a job, a trade, or any task that produces a result. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 39 times across 17 books, and translators render it as "work" in 63% of cases, though it absorbs into surrounding phrasing about 15 times without an English word of its own. In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 94 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew verb עָבַד ("to serve, work"), and everyday papyri use it just as plainly — one apprenticeship contract promises to produce a brother "to work at the weaver's trade."
caution: The senses labeled "what" and "while" reflect how translators phrase whole clauses rather than distinct meanings of the verb itself.

definition: To break something apart or crush it into pieces, especially something brittle or rigid.
article: This verb means to break or shatter something, and all 4 of its Byzantine New Testament occurrences are rendered "break" — a perfectly stable picture across translations. Famously it appears in Matthew 12:20, where the bruised reed is not broken, and in John 19:31-33, where the soldiers break the legs of the crucified men. The everyday Koine papyri show the same physical sense vividly: documents speak of broken house doors, ruined pack-saddles, and head wounds from being struck, confirming this was ordinary language for things smashed or cracked apart.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the range is narrow, but the consistent single sense across all sources gives solid confidence.

definition: To sit together with others, as in someone's company or as part of a group.
article: Built from σύν ("with") and κάθημαι ("to sit"), this verb simply means to sit alongside others, whether warming yourself by a fire among bystanders or taking a seat as part of a group. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "sat warmed by" once (Mark 14:54), with the other occurrence absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The papyri show the same plain Koine use: in a case before the Emperor Claudius, senators "sit along with" the Emperor as advisors, and a record even notes clerks sitting up through the night by lamplight.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint instance, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To dance, moving the body rhythmically, often to music at celebrations or festivals.
article: ὀρχέομαι means simply "to dance," and the evidence is remarkably consistent: all 4 New Testament occurrences are rendered "dance," and every lexicon agrees. The Septuagint uses it 7 times, mostly to translate Hebrew words for dancing such as רָקַד. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where its related noun ὀρχήστρια ("dancing-girl") appears in a real contract hiring two dancers for an upcoming festival — a vivid parallel to the dancing scene in Matthew 14:6.

definition: The honor, respect, or worth given to someone or something, or the price paid to obtain it.
article: τιμή carries two closely related ideas: the esteem or honor shown to a person, and the price or value placed on something. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "honor" 26 times out of 41 (90%), with rare cases meaning "price" or "city honor." In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for an assessed valuation (עֵרֶךְ, 19 times), highlighting its monetary side, while everyday papyri use it for the high rank and honor given to officials—one inscription has a magistrate gratefully acknowledging "the honor which you do me."

definition: Linus, the personal name of a Christian in Rome who sends greetings in Paul's letter.
article: Linus is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:21, where he is listed among believers in Rome sending greetings. The Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence as a personal name (though the digest's label oddly reads "Pudens," another name from the same verse). Interestingly, the older classical lexicon Abbott-Smith records a completely different background: Linos was a mythical minstrel, son of Apollo, whose name also became a type of mournful work-song sung during the grape harvest in Homer's Iliad.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's sense label ("Pudens") does not match the lemma, so the rendering data should be treated with caution.

definition: To stretch something out so it lasts longer, especially to prolong a speech or extend a period of time.
article: παρατείνω means to stretch or extend something out, most often in the sense of prolonging it in time. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 20:7), Paul "prolonged" his message, which the Majority Standard Bible renders with the idea of speaking at length. Everyday Koine papyri use the same verb in vivid practical ways: one document speaks of postponing a payment, while others use it of land stretching out over a distance.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured biblical range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A diminutive, often contemptuous term for a weak, foolish, or easily-swayed woman.
article: γυναικάριον is the diminutive of γυνή (woman), and its little ending carries a belittling or contemptuous tone — something like "silly little woman" or "poor weak woman." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:6, describing women easily manipulated and led astray. One intriguing suggestion from Sir W. M.
