Ramsay, citing the word's use in Epictetus, is that these were society ladies tossed about by their own whims and idle curiosity, comparable to Cicero's fashionable young dandies.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise tone is hard to pin down with confidence.

definition: An authoritative order, charge, or instruction given by someone with the power to command.
article: παραγγελία is an authoritative directive — an order, charge, or instruction handed down by someone with standing to give it. The five New Testament uses cluster tightly around this idea, rendered as "orders," "instructions," or "instruction," whether it's the Sanhedrin's command not to teach (Acts 5:28) or the apostle's charge to believers (1 Thessalonians 4:2). The everyday papyri sharpen the picture: one document (P Oxy 1411, A.D. 260) warns that those who disobey "this injunction" will face penalties, and the word could even mean a formal summons to appear in court — and classical writers like Xenophon and Polybius used it specifically for a military order.
caution: With only five occurrences, the boundaries between the measured senses are subtle and rest on thin evidence.

definition: An adverb meaning more quickly or sooner, comparing the speed or timing of an action.
article: τάχιον is the comparative form of the adverb ταχύς ("quick"), so it means "more quickly" or "sooner." It can describe physical speed (doing something fast) or timing (something happening soon), and the four New Testament uses split evenly across both shades. Abbott-Smith notes it stands in for the older Attic forms θᾶσσον/θᾶττον, and the related base form ταχύ renders the Hebrew מָהַר ("to hasten") in the Septuagint.
caution: With only four occurrences—each rendered differently—the line between "quickly" and "soon" depends heavily on context.

definition: The ordinal number meaning third in a sequence, or as an adverb, the third time something happens.
article: τρίτος is the ordinary ordinal number "third," used 58 times in the Byzantine New Testament. About 86% of the time it simply means "third" (as in "the third day"), while around 12% functions adverbially to mean "the third time" something occurs, as when Jesus comes to the disciples a third time in Mark 14:41. It can also act as a noun—"a third part"—especially in Revelation, where a third of the earth or sea is struck. In the Septuagint it appears 147 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for "third," and it shows up in everyday papyri, including a document about three men who stole sheaves while gleaning.

definition: An inscription, label, or title written on something, such as the words and image stamped on a coin.
article: This word names something written or stamped onto an object — an inscription, label, or title. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, usually for the inscription on a coin (as when Jesus asks whose inscription a coin bears), but also for the written notice posted above Jesus on the cross. Outside the Bible it was common everyday Koine: a papyrus from A.D. 145 uses it of a written insertion on a document, while a third-century-B.C. letter uses it of a mark or title of honor.
caution: The measured senses are really one core meaning — 'inscription' — split by surrounding phrasing rather than distinct definitions.

definition: Cana, a town in Galilee mentioned in the Gospel of John as the site of Jesus' first miracle.
article: Κανᾶ is a place name, the village of Cana in Galilee, appearing 4 times in the New Testament, all in the Gospel of John. The word is indeclinable and comes from Hebrew, where the related form translates עֶבְרֹן (Hebron) in the one Septuagint occurrence. Although the lexicons list it simply as a place, the Majority Standard Bible's renderings vary because translators sometimes fold the name into surrounding phrasing like "took place at" or "first at Cana," so all the measured senses really point to the same single location.
caution: The differing measured senses reflect translation phrasing, not different meanings; the word always refers to the one place, Cana.

definition: Silas, a leading member of the early church who became one of Paul's traveling companions.
article: Σίλας is the personal name of Silas, a Christian leader sent from Jerusalem and later a key partner in Paul's missionary work; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Silas" in 11 of its 12 occurrences (92%), with the BSB independently agreeing 100%. The name is a shortened, pet-form of Σιλουανός (Silvanus), the Latinized version of the same Semitic name, so the two refer to one person. It traces back to an Aramaic original and turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions, including a sepulchral inscription where a man named Silas also goes by the Greek name Kleonikos.

definition: The number two hundred, used to count people, objects, or measures of distance.
article: This is simply the cardinal number "two hundred," formed from the words for "twice" (δίς) and "hundred" (ἑκατόν). It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "hundred" (as part of "two hundred") in 3 cases and folds it into the surrounding phrasing in the other 4. It is far more common in the Septuagint, occurring 78 times across 16 books, where it counts everything from raisins to male goats.
caution: In half of its New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into English phrasing rather than rendered as a standalone word, though its meaning is not in doubt.

definition: An adjective meaning "relating to sheep," used in the New Testament for the gate or pool in Jerusalem connected with sheep.
article: Προβατικός is an adjective built from the word for "sheep" (πρόβατον) and simply means "pertaining to sheep." In its single New Testament appearance (John 5:2) it stands alone, with a word like "gate" understood, naming the "sheep-gate" near the pool where the Septuagint also uses it (Nehemiah 3:1, 32; 12:39). A striking piece of evidence comes from a Christian amulet found in the papyri (P Oxy VIII. 1151), which invokes "O God of the sheep-pool" (προβατικῆς κολυμβήθρας) to deliver a servant named Joannia from evil—showing how the term lived on in everyday devotion.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the measured rendering "Bethesda" reflects the place name in context rather than the word's actual "sheep-related" meaning.

definition: To take from someone what is rightfully theirs by fraud or unfair dealing; to cheat or deprive someone.
article: This verb means to defraud or rob someone of what belongs to them, often by withholding what is owed. It appears 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, where the Majority Standard Bible mostly renders it with "cheat" or related ideas, while one occurrence is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. Notably, the everyday Koine papyri use it for the misappropriation of trust funds or deposits — refusing to return what was entrusted to you — which fits its biblical sense of withholding what is owed, such as the unpaid wages condemned in James 5:4.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and several spread thinly across distinct grammatical uses (middle and passive), the picture of its full range rests on limited evidence.

definition: Describing something so deep it cannot be searched out, examined, or fully understood by human investigation.
article: This word describes things that resist all human attempts to probe or trace them out, fittingly translated "unsearchable." It appears just once in the New Testament, at Romans 11:33, where Paul marvels that God's judgments are beyond searching out. Although it shows up only once in Scripture, Moulton-Milligan note that it was a normal word in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and it even surfaces in a fragment of the philosopher Heraclitus.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on one verse, though the lexicons agree firmly on its meaning.

definition: A person who learns or follows alongside others, especially a fellow student or fellow disciple.
article: συμμαθητής combines σύν ("with") and μανθάνω ("to learn"), so it literally means someone who learns together with others — a fellow disciple. It appears only once in the New Testament, at John 11:16, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fellow" disciples and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100%. Though it is a New Testament hapax legomenon, Moulton-Milligan notes it was an ordinary word in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and it is also attested in earlier writers like Plato and Diogenes Laertius.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: A strong, eager longing or desire for something or someone.
article: This noun describes an intense yearning or eager desire, built from the verb ἐπιποθέω (to long for). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 15:23, where Paul speaks of his longstanding longing to visit the believers in Rome. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on the sense of 'longing' or 'eager desire,' and treat it as equivalent to ἐπιπόθησις.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single passage; note also that the corpus rendering 'opportunities' reflects translation phrasing rather than the lexically attested sense of 'longing.'

definition: To rule as a tetrarch, a regional ruler governing one part of a divided territory.
article: This verb means to serve as a tetrarch — a ruler over one portion of a divided region. It appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all within a single verse (Luke 3:1), where it describes several rulers governing different territories. The measured renderings labeled "fifteenth" and "Abilene" reflect surrounding words in that crowded verse rather than separate meanings of this verb, which consistently denotes ruling as a tetrarch.
caution: The evidence is thin and clusters in one verse, and two of the three measured 'senses' are artifacts of nearby words rather than genuine meanings of the verb.

definition: Describes something hidden, kept secret, or stored away out of sight.
article: ἀπόκρυφος means hidden, secret, or kept out of view, and all three New Testament occurrences are rendered "hidden" (Mark 4:22, Luke 8:17, Colossians 2:3). It comes from the verb ἀποκρύπτω ("to hide away"), and the Septuagint uses it 11 times across 4 books. Interestingly, the everyday Koine astrologer Vettius Valens favored this word for things like the body's hidden inner organs and "hidden matters" of the future, showing its ordinary range covered anything concealed.
caution: Evidence is thin — only three New Testament uses — and the Septuagint Hebrew counterparts listed here vary, so the word's full range is not firmly fixed.

definition: A grammatical form of "to put" meaning something must be put or placed somewhere.
article: βλητέος is a special verb form (a verbal adjective built from βάλλω, "to throw" or "put") that expresses obligation — "must be put" or "ought to be placed." It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in the saying about putting new wine into fresh wineskins (Mark 2:22 and Luke 5:38), and only once in the critical text. The lexicons agree closely: Abbott-Smith and Dodson both define it as "that which one must put," matching Strong's "fit to be cast." Translators render it loosely within the wider sentence ("instead," "instead is poured"), but the underlying meaning is simply the idea of something that has to be put in place.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two occurrences, both in the same wineskin saying — so this entry rests on a very small sample.

definition: To express deep grief by wailing or loudly lamenting, either on one's own or while mourning over someone.
article: θρηνέω means to mourn out loud, expressing sorrow through wailing and lament. It works both ways: without an object it just means to wail (as in John 16:20), and with an object it means to bewail a particular person, as when the crowds wailed over Jesus in Luke 23:27. It shows up only 4 times in the New Testament but 22 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew word קוּן (7 times), and the related noun forms even appear in everyday Egyptian papyri tied to funeral customs.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences—and two of those absorbed into broader phrasing—the New Testament picture is thin, though the Septuagint and papyri broaden the evidence.

definition: The plural "you" when it is the object of a verb or preposition — that is, "you all" being acted upon.
article: This is simply the accusative (object) form of the plural pronoun "you," used when a group is on the receiving end of an action or follows a preposition. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament count here, but it shows up 556 times across 36 books of the Septuagint, where it often renders Hebrew expressions in declarations and commands. Notably, it frequently translates the Hebrew נְאֻם ("declaration/oracle," 23×) and כֹּה ("thus," 21×), reflecting prophetic speech addressed to a people.
caution: The digest provides no measured New Testament senses for this form, so the sense breakdown rests on grammatical function and Septuagint patterns rather than tabulated meanings.

definition: To choke or stifle something by growing over it or pressing upon it.
article: This compound combines ἐπί ("upon") with πνίγω ("to choke, strangle"), giving the picture of choking or stifling something from above, used figuratively of plants being overgrown and smothered. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all, so no measured senses are available, and the meaning rests entirely on the parts of the word and the lexicon glosses ("choke," "stifle," "overgrow"). Abbott-Smith and Strong's agree on the basic idea of throttling or smothering, with the figurative sense of one growth crowding out another.
caution: This word has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so its meaning is reconstructed from its parts and lexicon glosses rather than from measured biblical usage.

definition: In a godly, devoted way—living with reverence and respect toward God.
article: This adverb describes living in a godly, reverent manner, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both of its two New Testament occurrences (2 Timothy 3:12 and Titus 2:12) as "godly," with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing fully. It is built from the adjective εὐσεβής ("devout, godly"). Outside the Bible it was ordinary Koine vocabulary: papyri and inscriptions use it for being "scrupulously" followed or for being reverently "disposed toward Dionysus and the other gods," showing the word's everyday sense of dutiful reverence whether toward people, gods, or God.
caution: The word appears only twice in the New Testament (and once in the Septuagint, 4 Maccabees 7:21), so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: A turtle-dove, the small wild dove used as an offering in Jewish worship.
article: τρυγών is the turtle-dove, a small wild pigeon whose name comes from the verb meaning "to murmur" or "coo," describing its soft sound. In the Septuagint it appears 16 times in 6 books, almost always rendering the Hebrew תֹּר ("turtledove"), and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri as well. Its single New Testament appearance is in Luke 2:24, where it forms part of "a pair of turtledoves," the offering brought at Jesus' presentation in the temple — which is why the Majority Standard Bible's wording there reflects the phrase "pair."

definition: Daniel, the Hebrew prophet whose name Jesus cites when warning about the abomination of desolation.
article: Δανιήλ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Daniel, an indeclinable proper noun referring to the Israelite prophet. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14), both times where Jesus refers to a prophecy spoken by Daniel. The name shows up far more often in the Septuagint—85 times across 5 books—rendering the Hebrew דָּנִיֵּאל, which Abbott-Smith notes means "God is my Judge."
caution: This is a proper name with only 2 New Testament occurrences, so its range is limited to identifying the prophet.

definition: A conjunction meaning "since indeed" or "seeing that," introducing a reason or cause.
article: ἐπείπερ is a causal conjunction built from ἐπεί ("since") plus the emphasizing particle περ, giving the sense "since indeed" or "seeing that." It is exceptionally rare, appearing in only 1 place in the Byzantine New Testament (Romans 3:30) and not at all in the critical (SBLGNT) text. The everyday Koine papyri show its ordinary use well: a 165 B.C. document reads "since (ἐπείπερ) it is necessary to keep reminding you continuously about the same things."
caution: The reading is disputed — Abbott-Smith notes that while the Received Text has ἐπείπερ at Romans 3:30, Westcott and Hort read εἴπερ instead, and the critical text omits it entirely.

definition: The Roman name Porcius, part of the official name of the governor Porcius Festus.
article: Πόρκιος is a Latin personal name borrowed into Greek, appearing just once in the New Testament as part of the name of the Roman governor Porcius Festus (Acts 24:27). It is not really a vocabulary word but a proper name, which is why the lexicons simply list it as "Porcius." Strong's notes the name apparently derives from a Latin word meaning "swinish," but it functions purely as the man's middle (gentile) name.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament as a proper name, so there is no real range of meaning to measure; the rendering "succeeded" reflects the surrounding sentence, not the name itself.

definition: To shut or close something in on all sides; figuratively, to confine people under a condition like sin or law.
article: συγκλείω literally means to shut or enclose something on every side, as when a net closes around a catch of fish in Luke 5:6. Paul stretches it figuratively in Romans and Galatians to picture people being confined or shut up under sin and the law. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, but 30 times in the Septuagint, where it usually renders the Hebrew סָגַר ("to shut," 13×); the everyday papyri use it concretely for being locked up, as in one document where a man says he was shut into a barracks, or another threatening prison until a debt is paid.
caution: Each of the four New Testament uses is rendered differently, so the senses rest on single occurrences rather than a broad measured pattern.

definition: To beg, especially to ask repeatedly or persistently for money or alms.
article: προσαιτέω means to beg, picturing someone who asks again and again—the kind of persistent appeal a roadside beggar makes. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all describing blind men begging (Mark 10:46, Luke 18:35, John 9:8). Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri show a more literal flavor of the word's parts (πρός + αἰτέω): one document (3rd century B.C.) uses it to mean asking for additional measures of something "in addition" to what was already owed, a sense Abbott-Smith also lists.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 NT uses, just 1 in the critical text and 1 in the Septuagint), and lexicons split between "beg/importune" and the literal "ask in addition."

definition: A tiny piece of dry plant matter—a speck of straw, chaff, or a splinter—used as an image of a minor fault.
article: κάρφος refers literally to a small dry stalk, twig, or bit of chaff—something almost too small to notice. In the New Testament all six occurrences sit in one vivid teaching (Matthew 7:3-5 and Luke 6:41-42), where the speck in someone else's eye is contrasted with the plank in your own. Interestingly, a Greek sepulchral epitaph uses it in the phrase "not even a κάρφος was harmed," meaning the pious man was not hurt one bit, showing how the word stood for the smallest imaginable thing.
caution: The measured senses beyond "speck" (such as "brother's fail notice") are artifacts of how phrases were split, not distinct meanings; the word consistently means a tiny piece of straw or splinter.

definition: A person from Corinth; an inhabitant of the Greek city of Corinth.
article: Κορίνθιος simply means a Corinthian — someone who lives in or comes from the city of Corinth. It's a place-name adjective derived from Κόρινθος (Corinth) and appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 18:8 and 2 Corinthians 6:11. Although the digest splits these into two measured "senses," both occurrences mean the same thing: a resident of Corinth, with the difference coming only from surrounding wording, not from any real shift in meaning.
caution: The two listed measured senses reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings, and with only two occurrences the evidence is thin.

definition: The ordinal number meaning eighth, marking something as eighth in a sequence or count.
article: ὄγδοος is simply the ordinal number "eighth," used to mark a position in a sequence — an eighth day, an eighth person, an eighth stone in a row. It appears 5 times in the New Testament and 39 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always translates the Hebrew word for "eighth" (27 of those times). One nice detail from the papyri: the word never contracts in its NT occurrences, and everyday documents like the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) use it the same way, dating events to "the eighth year."

definition: To fix or fasten something firmly in place, especially to set up or pitch a tent.
article: πήγνυμι means to make something fast or fix it firmly, and is used especially of setting up a tent. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Hebrews 8:2, where it describes the true tabernacle that the Lord—not a human—pitched. The Septuagint uses it 28 times, most often for the Hebrew נָטָה (to stretch out or pitch), and everyday papyri show a related sense of "plant," as in one document where people planted wild heather and figs.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the range of meaning here rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: Galatia, a region and Roman province in central Asia Minor, originally settled by Gauls.
article: Galatia is a place name appearing 4 times in the New Testament (Galatians 1:2, 1 Corinthians 16:1, 2 Timothy 4:10, 1 Peter 1:1). The lexicons note two layers of meaning: a smaller ethnic region in Asia Minor settled by Gauls in the third century B.C., and the larger Roman province that came to include it, with scholars still divided over which sense the New Testament intends. One interesting wrinkle: in 2 Timothy 4:10 some manuscripts read "Gaul" (Γαλλίαν) instead of Galatia.
caution: The corpus shows only one true sense; the second "measured sense" ("Now are of" at 25%) reflects how the surrounding phrase was rendered, not a separate meaning of the word.

definition: Describing a period or age of forty years.
article: This adjective combines the words for "forty" and "year" to describe something measured in a span of forty years, whether a person's age or a stretch of time. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: in Acts 7:23 it marks Moses being about forty years old, and in Acts 13:18 it describes the forty-year wilderness period. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on the basic meaning, while Abbott-Smith also notes a spelling variant, τεσσερακονταετής.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and none in the critical SBLGNT text, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To overpower someone or something, gaining the upper hand, or to press a demand so forcefully that it wins out.
article: κατισχύω means to be strong enough to overpower or prevail against someone, built from κατά plus ἰσχύω ("to be strong"). Its two New Testament uses (Byzantine) split evenly: in Matthew 16:18 the gates of Hades do not "prevail against" the church, while in Luke 23:23 the crowd's voices were "insistent" — pressing their demand until it won out. The word is far more common in the Septuagint, appearing 92 times and most often translating the Hebrew חָזַק ("to be strong," 49 times); a papyrus charm even uses it for a spell that "shall not prevail against me."
caution: With only 2 (or 3 in critical texts) New Testament occurrences, each sense rests on a single verse, so the measured range is thin.

definition: Made of leather or animal skin.
article: δερμάτινος describes something made of animal hide or leather. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both times describing the leather belt worn by John the Baptist (Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6). The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: papyri mention a pair of leather garments, and an old inscription from Andania permits sacred women to wear only felt or consecrated leather sandals.
caution: The digest lists the New Testament rendering as "camel's," but every reference work and the underlying word itself point to "made of leather/skin," so the measured label appears to mislabel the surrounding phrase.

definition: A sacrifice in which the whole animal is burned up completely as an offering to God.
article: ὁλοκαύτωμα refers to a burnt offering—a sacrifice that was entirely consumed by fire rather than partly eaten. The word combines the ideas of "whole" (ὅλος) and "burn" (καίω), and it gives us the English word "holocaust." Though it appears only 3 times in the New Testament, it shows up 191 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always translates the Hebrew עֹלָה (166 times), the standard term for a burnt offering in the sacrificial law.
caution: The three New Testament uses all carry the same single meaning; the apparent variety in the measured renderings reflects surrounding phrasing rather than different senses.

definition: Easily understood or clearly marked, so that something stands out distinctly or makes plain sense.
article: εὔσημος combines εὖ ("well") with the idea of a sign, so it describes something marked clearly enough to be readily grasped. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 14:9), where Paul speaks of producing speech that is intelligible. The everyday papyri show a vivid concrete use: it described people's distinguishing marks, like a scar on the middle of the forehead or a noticeable right eye, while the lexica also note a "conspicuous" sense in the Septuagint.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the listed sources describe slightly different shades ("conspicuous" versus "clear to understand"), so its full range is hard to pin down.

definition: To leave someone or something behind, or to abandon, forsake, or keep something in reserve.
article: καταλείπω means to leave something or someone behind, whether by simply departing, by deliberately forsaking, or by holding something back in reserve. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 25 times and is rendered "left" in 15 of them (68%). It was a common word in everyday life: the papyri show it constantly used for property left or bequeathed in wills, and the Septuagint uses it 224 times, mostly for the Hebrew שָׁאַר ("to remain," 79×) and עָזַב ("to abandon," 44×).

definition: By one's own free choice, willingly and without being forced or compelled.
article: This adverb describes doing something deliberately and by free choice rather than under compulsion. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Hebrews 10:26 and 1 Peter 5:2) and twice in the Septuagint, and in both Testaments it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word. The everyday legal force of the word shows clearly in the papyri: in one document an accused man "persistently refuses to pay voluntarily," and contracts pair it with phrases meaning "of one's own free will."
caution: Confidence is low: with only two New Testament occurrences and neither rendered by a distinct English word, the measured evidence is thin.

definition: To beg for money or food, especially as a poor person asking strangers for help.
article: This word combines "upon/besides" with "to ask," and means to beg — to ask others for money or food the way a poor person does. The lexicons note an older sense of "ask besides," but the practical meaning in everyday Greek and the New Testament is mendicant begging. A nice illustration comes from the papyri: a recluse living at the Serapeum temple around 163 BC described himself as surviving "from what I beg in the temple," using this exact verb — the same kind of public, shame-laden begging Luke 16:3 has in view ("I am ashamed to beg").
caution: Evidence is thin: only 1 Byzantine occurrence (rendered merely as "too" by the MSB) and 1 Septuagint use, so the picture rests mostly on lexicons and papyri rather than measured New Testament senses.

definition: To exercise authority or dominating power over people, lording it over them.
article: This verb means to wield authority over others, with the prefix κατά suggesting a heavy, domineering use of power. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in parallel passages (Matthew 20:25 and Mark 10:42) where Jesus describes how Gentile rulers lord it over their subjects. Abbott-Smith notes it always takes a genitive of the person being ruled and pairs it as a near-synonym with κατακυριεύω ("lord it over"), and Moulton-Milligan confirms the related word group turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions.
caution: With only two occurrences—both in the same parallel saying—the precise force of the word is hard to pin down from usage alone.

definition: The sound of music, whether played together by voices or instruments — or possibly a particular musical instrument.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Luke 15:25), συμφωνία describes the music heard as the prodigal son's brother approaches the house, and every measured rendering translates it simply as "music." The word's range is debated: classical sources like Polybius and the Greek of Daniel use it for an actual musical instrument, and Abbott-Smith lists this second sense. One striking detail is that the scholar Philipps Barry argued συμφωνία in both Daniel 3:5 and Luke 15:25 names an instrument — perhaps a bagpipe — though Moulton-Milligan also cites everyday papyri using it for the general sense of "music."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and sources genuinely disagree over whether it means "music" in general or a specific instrument.

definition: A four-footed animal, especially a beast or quadruped of the land.
article: τετράπους simply means "four-footed," used in the New Testament as a noun (in the neuter plural) for four-footed animals or beasts. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine NT, all referring to land animals, and is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 23 times across 7 books and chiefly renders the Hebrew word בְּהֵמָה ("beast"). Everyday papyri confirm this plain meaning: a document from 256 BC speaks of "four-footed animals at the city of Oxyrhynchus."
caution: One of the three measured renderings ("exchanged" in Romans 1:23) reflects neighboring words in the verse rather than the meaning of τετράπους itself, so treat that sense label as an artifact.

definition: Something that has been made or crafted; a created work or product.
article: ποίημα refers to anything that has been made — a product, fabrication, or finished work — and it comes straight from the verb ποιέω, "to make." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both times pointing to what God has made: the created world in Romans 1:20 and believers themselves as God's handiwork in Ephesians 2:10. The Septuagint uses it far more often (29 times), most frequently translating the Hebrew מַעֲשֶׂה ("work, deed"), and an inscription from 218–217 BC even uses the plural for an artisan's own "pieces of work," showing it was everyday vocabulary for crafted things.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured sense range here is very thin and rests largely on the broader Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: To feel and show joy or gladness; also used as a set greeting like "hello" or "farewell."
article: χαίρω is the common Greek verb for being glad or rejoicing, which is how it's rendered in 40 of its 74 New Testament appearances (83% of the times it gets its own English word). It also serves as a standard social formula — "Greetings" — used when meeting or parting, accounting for 5 occurrences in places like Matthew 26:49 and the letter opening in Acts 15:23. In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew verbs שָׂמַח and גִּיל, both meaning to be glad or exult. The greeting sense is vividly confirmed by everyday papyri letters, where writers like one from 223 BC say they "rejoiced" (ἐχάρην) on receiving a friend's letter and learning he was well.
caution: In 26 of 74 cases the word is folded into surrounding phrasing and gets no English word of its own, so raw counts understate how often it appears.

definition: The act of receiving or taking something, especially in a financial or business transaction.
article: This noun, built from the verb λαμβάνω ("to take, receive"), means the act of receiving. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:15, where Paul pairs it with its opposite—"giving and receiving" (δόσις καὶ λῆμψις)—to describe his financial partnership with the Philippians. Everyday Koine papyri confirm its commercial flavor: one document speaks of "the receipt of wheat," another of taking securities to settle a bond, showing the word was at home in business and legal language.
caution: Evidence is thin—only one New Testament use and two in the Septuagint—so the measured sense rests on a very small sample.

definition: A footstool — a low support for the feet, often used figuratively for something placed under someone's authority.
article: ὑποπόδιον is simply a footstool, the low rest you put your feet on. In the New Testament it appears 9 times, mostly inside the phrase "make your enemies a footstool for your feet" (about 44% of uses), echoing Psalm 110:1, so the word usually carries the figurative sense of something brought under another's power; only occasionally does it name a literal footstool, as in James 2:3. The everyday flavor of the word is confirmed by Koine papyri: Deissmann cites second-century A.D. marriage contracts listing "a chair with a footstool," showing it was ordinary household vocabulary, and in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew word hadom.
caution: The two labels reflect translation phrasing, not two genuinely different meanings — both point to the same single sense of "footstool," literal or figurative.

definition: A flexible connecting word meaning "as" or "like," used to compare, describe manner, or introduce how something is said or seen.
article: ὡς is one of the most common little words in the Greek New Testament, appearing 499 times in the Byzantine text, and it works mainly as a connector meaning "as" or "like." When translators give it an English word at all, it almost always comes out as "like" (117× of the rendered cases), but in 382 of its 499 appearances it simply melts into the surrounding phrasing without a word of its own. Its range is genuinely wide—older lexicons and the KJV list senses like "how," "when," "while," "about," and "so that"—and in the Septuagint it shows up 1500 times, most often standing in for forms of the Hebrew verb הָיָה ("to be"), 82 times. Everyday papyri confirm the plain comparative use, as in "it will be as we desire."
caution: The measured data captures only the dominant "like/as" sense, while the classical lexica and KJV record many more shades ("how," "when," "so that"); most occurrences are absorbed into phrasing, so a single English label understates its real range.

definition: Describing something or someone unmarked and undistinguished — plain, ordinary, with nothing notable to set it apart.
article: At root ἄσημος means "without a mark," combining a negative prefix with the word for a mark or sign. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 21:39, where Paul calls Tarsus no "ordinary" city (using the negative construction "not insignificant"). The most vivid evidence comes from the papyri: Moulton-Milligan note that this word turns up constantly in official documents to describe a person who has no identifying scars on eyebrow, arm, or shin — literally someone "unmarked" and so undistinguished from the crowd.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint — so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: Showing earnest, intense effort or devotion; literally stretched out and strained toward a goal.
article: ἐκτενής comes from the verb meaning "to stretch out," so its core idea is something stretched taut or strained—then, figuratively, effort that is earnest and intense. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just twice: of the church praying earnestly for Peter (Acts 12:5) and of believers keeping love constant "above" one another (1 Peter 4:8). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense well, as in a 164 B.C. document urging someone to "take the most earnest precautions," and inscriptions praising people who showed themselves "earnest and eager" in guarding their city.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text)—so confidence in the full range is low.

definition: Useful, beneficial, or worthwhile — describing something that brings real profit or advantage.
article: ὠφέλιμος describes something that does real good — useful, serviceable, and worth the effort. It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, all in the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus), where it tells us what is profitable, whether godliness, Scripture, or good works. The word was common in everyday Koine: papyri use the stock phrase "in all good and useful works" in contracts, and one letter thanks someone for "having been useful to us" during a trip abroad.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, all in the Pastorals and absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word, the New Testament range is narrow.

definition: To travel from place to place doing business, buying and selling, or to exploit others for profit.
article: This verb means to engage in trade, especially by traveling around for business, and by extension to make a profit off something or someone. In the New Testament it appears only twice: in James 4:13 it describes merchants planning to go to a city and "do business," while in 2 Peter 2:3 the lexicons note it can mean making a gain of people. In the Septuagint it shows up 11 times, usually translating the Hebrew root סָחַר ("to trade"), and an inscription from the oracle of Zeus at Dodona records a traveler literally asking the god whether his trading venture will succeed.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured evidence is thin, so the full range comes mainly from the lexicons and Septuagint.

definition: The ordinal number meaning fourth, the one coming after the third in a sequence.
article: τέταρτος is the ordinary Greek word for "fourth," the ordinal formed from τέσσαρες ("four"). In the New Testament it appears 10 times, rendered "fourth" in 8 of those (89%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. It is thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: the papyri use it for dates ("the thirty-fourth year"), fractions ("a quarter of sesame"), and shares like "the fourth part of the estate." In the Septuagint it occurs 91 times, most often translating the Hebrew רְבִיעִי ("fourth").

definition: Very gladly or most willingly — doing something with the greatest pleasure.
article: This is the superlative form of the adverb ἡδέως ("gladly, with pleasure"), so it means "very gladly" or "most willingly." Both of its two New Testament appearances are in Paul's words to the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 12:9 and 12:15), and translators render it "gladly" 100% of the time. It was ordinary, everyday Koine: the papyri show people writing "I will most gladly do it" in personal letters, and even using a related form in a medical prescription mixing incense with "very sweet" wine.
caution: Only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same letter, place this word in a low-confidence tier.

definition: To lie in wait for someone, setting a trap or ambush to catch or entrap them.
article: ἐνεδρεύω means to lie in wait for someone, ambushing or scheming to catch them off guard. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke's writings (Luke 11:54 and Acts 23:21), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "wait"; in one of those two occurrences the idea is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than carried by a single English word. The Septuagint uses it 22 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew אָרַב ("to lie in ambush"), and the everyday papyri make the sense vivid — one petitioner begs the gods not to ignore "the trap laid for me by this unfeeling man."
caution: Confidence is low: only two New Testament occurrences, with one of them not rendered by a distinct English word.

definition: A connector word linking statements, used to mean "that" when reporting speech or thought, or "because" when giving a reason.
article: ὅτι is one of the most common little connectors in the New Testament, appearing 1281 times, and it does two main jobs: it introduces what someone sees, knows, or says ("that"), and it gives a reason ("because" or "for"). Most of the measured renderings beyond these two are really ὅτι getting absorbed into surrounding English phrasing rather than carrying its own word — in fact it has no separate English word 319 times out of 1281. In the Greek Old Testament it appears a staggering 3346 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew word כִּי (2461×), which does the same double duty. One notable wrinkle: ὅτι can also stand untranslated right before a direct quotation, working almost like an opening quotation mark.
caution: The many "senses" with low percentages are mostly artifacts of English phrasing absorbing the word, not distinct meanings — its real range is the simple "that"/"because" pair.

definition: To feel thirst, needing something to drink, or figuratively to long deeply for something.
article: διψάω covers the plain physical experience of being thirsty and, by extension, an intense longing for something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 16 times, rendered "thirsty" in 63% of cases and "thirst" in 25%, with the Majority Standard Bible and BSB in full agreement on every occurrence. It can take an object, as in Matthew 5:6 where people "thirst" for righteousness, showing how naturally the word stretches from literal to figurative. In the Septuagint it appears 32 times, most often translating the Hebrew צָמֵא (to be thirsty), and a touching Roman epitaph in the papyri asks someone to "share cool water with a thirsting soul."

definition: To remove the roof from a building, taking off its covering.
article: This verb means to take the roof off a structure, built from the prefix ἀπό ("off") and στέγη ("roof"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Mark 2:4, where the friends of a paralyzed man uncover the roof to lower him to Jesus; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "uncovered" in all (one) occurrences, and the Berean Standard Bible agrees. Abbott-Smith notes it also turns up in Symmachus's version of the Old Testament at Jeremiah 29:11, showing the word was known outside this single Gospel scene.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and very thin attestation elsewhere, the precise range of this verb cannot be confirmed.

definition: The tail of an animal or creature.
article: οὐρά simply means "tail." All five New Testament occurrences appear in Revelation, describing the tails of symbolic creatures (Rev 9:10, 9:19, 12:4), and the Majority Standard Bible renders every instance with "tail" in some form. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times, usually translating the Hebrew word זָנָב ("tail"), and Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in a magical papyrus describing a serpent biting its own tail.

definition: A ceremonial washing or dipping, including ritual cleansings and Christian baptism.
article: βαπτισμός refers to the act of ceremonial washing or dipping, derived from the verb βαπτίζω. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible gives it an English word of its own just once — in Hebrews 6:2, rendered "instruction about baptisms" — while absorbing it into the surrounding phrasing the other three times. Abbott-Smith notes the unusual plural and form in Hebrews 6:2 may have been chosen deliberately to include Christian baptism alongside other Jewish lustral rites, and Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin: with only 4 occurrences and a single distinct rendering, the word's range overlaps closely with the related βάπτισμα and is hard to pin down precisely.

definition: An adverb pointing to the present moment—now, at this time—as opposed to the past or the future.
article: νῦν is the common Koine word for "now," the present moment, and it shows up 144 times in the Byzantine New Testament. Translators render it "now" in 91% of cases, with another 9% pointing to "the present" (as in "this age" or "the present time"), often when paired with the article in phrases like "until now." In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly stands in for the Hebrew word עַתָּה ("now"), and the everyday papyri confirm its ordinary use—one Egyptian letter from 2 B.C. uses the classical phrase τὰ νῦν ("and now") just as a writer reports sending a man off to collect rents.

definition: To run or move quickly on foot, and figuratively to put effort into reaching a goal, like a runner in a race.
article: τρέχω basically means to run or hurry on foot, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ran" in 13 of 20 occurrences (72%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. From this literal core the New Testament builds a vivid metaphor drawn from foot races: striving and exerting effort to reach a goal, as in Paul's image of running so as to win. In the Septuagint it appears 61 times, almost always translating the Hebrew רוּץ ("to run," 51×), and everyday Koine papyri show both the plain sense "ran" and the derived sense "strive" in a single document.

definition: Gabbatha, the local Aramaic name for the paved area in Jerusalem where Pilate's judgment seat stood.
article: Gabbatha is not really a word to translate but a place name: it appears just once in the New Testament, at John 19:13, as the local Aramaic term for the spot where Pilate sat to judge Jesus. John pairs it with the Greek word for "stone pavement" (λιθόστρωτον), and the Majority Standard Bible's one rendering reflects that paved or stone setting. The underlying Aramaic word is uncertain, but the lexicons describe it as a paved square where the Roman governor kept his judgment seat.
caution: This is a single occurrence transliterating an uncertain Aramaic word, so its precise meaning is genuinely unknown.

definition: A state of quietness or stillness — being calm, silent, or settling down into peaceful order.
article: ἡσυχία describes a condition of quiet — sometimes literal silence, sometimes a settled, calm way of going about life. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only 4 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "quiet" or "quietness" in most cases, while in 2 Thessalonians 3:12 the sense leans toward calmly settling down to work (rendered there with "earn"). Everyday Koine papyri show the same flexibility: one document from 141 BC uses it for being "completely at rest" in mind, and another speaks of "keeping quiet" so as not to trouble one's master.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and a sense that slides between literal silence and calm conduct, the exact shade in any given verse depends on context.

definition: To sigh or groan deeply, drawing up a heavy breath from within in distress or frustration.
article: This verb describes a deep sigh or groan that comes up from within, expressing weariness or grief. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 8:12, where Jesus sighs deeply over a demand for a sign. The Septuagint and related texts also use it for human sorrow, including Lamentations 1:4, where it renders a Hebrew word for mourning. It is built from the prefix ἀνά ("up") and στενάζω ("to sigh, groan"), giving the sense of heaving a sigh up from deep inside.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and rarely elsewhere, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: An adverb meaning at the very end of life; in the phrase "to be at the point of death," critically ill.
article: ἐσχάτως is an adverb formed from ἔσχατος ("last") and appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 5:23, where Jairus says his daughter "is at the point of death." It occurs only in the fixed phrase ἐσχάτως ἔχειν, literally "to have it at the extreme," matching the Latin idiom in extremis ("in one's last moments"). Interestingly, ancient Atticist grammarians actually criticized this expression as substandard Greek, even though it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions documented by Moulton-Milligan.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single example.

definition: To receive someone or something offered, often warmly welcoming a person or accepting a message.
article: At its core δέχομαι means to take what is offered—whether a person you welcome or a thing you accept. In the Byzantine New Testament's 58 occurrences, it splits mainly between "welcome" (20×, 43%) and "received" (17×, 36%), with many cases woven into phrases about receiving people in Jesus' name. The everyday flavor shows clearly in the papyri, where business receipts use it for acknowledging payment: "I have received from you the sum in full without any arrears."
caution: The various "whoever"-type sense labels mostly reflect English phrasing of the same welcoming/receiving idea rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: To take something in hand, that is, to set out or attempt to do it.
article: ἐπιχειρέω literally means "to put one's hand to" something, and in practice it means to undertake or attempt an action. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Luke's writings, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "tried" or "talked, debated, tried" (Acts 9:29; 19:13), and once it is absorbed into the phrasing. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan cites a 164 B.C. document using it for someone trying "to compel them to accept" the work.
caution: With only 3 NT occurrences and a low confidence tier, the sense range is thinly attested.

definition: To watch over something so it stays safe, or to keep and obey a command or rule.
article: φυλάσσω covers two closely linked ideas: physically guarding or protecting something, and keeping or observing a law, custom, or precept. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 30 times, rendered "kept" 9 times (39%) and "guard" 7 times (30%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing. The Septuagint uses it heavily—423 times—overwhelmingly for the Hebrew שָׁמַר (308×), the everyday word for guarding and keeping, and the everyday papyri show the same flavor, as in a request to "guard and protect Aria from ague" or village elders "guarding the dykes and embankments."

definition: A rooster, the male chicken whose crowing marks the early morning.
article: This word simply means a rooster, the male fowl. Its 12 New Testament uses all cluster around one famous scene—the rooster crowing as Peter denied Jesus—which is why the measured renderings all involve crowing rather than the bird alone. Everyday papyri confirm the plain meaning: roosters appear in farm leases and yearly rent offerings, such as a document from AD 26 promising "one rooster."

definition: Describing someone who is eager, diligent, and earnest, applying themselves wholeheartedly to a task.
article: σπουδαῖος describes a person or quality marked by zeal, diligence, and earnestness. In the Byzantine NT it appears 4 times across 2 books, all clustered in 2 Corinthians 8, where Paul commends a co-worker's eagerness; the Majority Standard Bible captures it with words like "earnestness," though half its occurrences get absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single word. The everyday papyri make the sense vivid: one letter praises a worker's "zeal and attentiveness to the work" (σπουδαῖον), showing this was common, practical vocabulary for a hard-working, attentive person.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 4 NT occurrences, all in one chapter, with a single Septuagint use, so the measured English renderings reflect a narrow sample.

definition: A mirror, in ancient times a polished metal surface used for seeing one's reflection.
article: ἔσοπτρον means a mirror, and in all 2 of its New Testament appearances it is rendered exactly that way. Since ancient mirrors were made of polished metal rather than glass, the reflection they gave was often dim or imperfect — which is the very point Paul draws on in 1 Corinthians 13:12. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including a temple property list mentioning a silver mirror made for a child.
caution: With only 2 occurrences the entry rests on thin corpus evidence, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: To give someone a share of something, passing along part of what you have to another person.
article: This verb combines "with" and "give" to mean handing over a share of what you have, whether material goods or something less tangible. It appears only 5 times in the New Testament, and translators render those occurrences in slightly different ways—"impart," "share," and the like—though all carry the same basic idea of giving someone a portion. One striking detail comes from everyday papyri letters, where the word often means simply "inform" or "pass along news," as in a note telling someone "tell Nicanor that..."
caution: With only 5 occurrences and translators splitting them across three different renderings, the precise shade of meaning in any given verse can be hard to pin down.

definition: To fix one's attention on something or someone, to pay close heed, or to hold something out toward others.
article: At its root ἐπέχω means "to hold upon," and from that come several practical senses. Most often in the New Testament (3 of 5 times) it means to fix attention or pay heed — like the lame man who fixed his eyes on Peter and John (Acts 3:5). It can also mean to take notice of behavior (Luke 14:7) or to hold something out and offer it, as when believers "hold forth" the word of life (Phil. 2:16). Everyday papyri confirm the "pay heed" sense vividly: one letter urges the reader to "give heed to the measurer Zoilus; don't look askance at him."
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences spread thin across three different senses, each meaning rests on just one or two examples.

definition: To set on fire or burn, and by extension to be refined or purified by fire, as metal is.
senseLabels: to burn or be on fire
article: πυρόω comes from πῦρ ("fire") and always appears in the passive in the New Testament. Its range runs from literal burning to the refining of metal by fire, and the Majority text's six uses split between "refined" (2×, of gold) and "burn" (1×, of being inflamed), with three more occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 17 times, most often translating Hebrew צָרַף (6×), the verb for smelting or refining metal. One striking detail: a Jewish-Greek tomb inscription from Tell el Yehudieh uses the word of "father and mother burning [grief over] their nine-year-old," though scholars debate whether it means cremating the body or burning with sorrow.
caution: With only six Byzantine occurrences and none in the SBL critical text, plus lexicons that also note metaphorical "inflamed with grief or lust" senses not isolated in the measured data, the picture is somewhat thin.

definition: Festus, the Roman governor of Judea who succeeded Felix and heard the apostle Paul's case.
article: Φῆστος is simply the personal name Festus, borne by Porcius Festus, the Roman procurator of Judea who replaced Felix and presided over Paul's hearing. It appears 13 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all in Acts, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Festus" in every measured case (the few odd renderings like "Festus myself" just reflect surrounding phrasing). The name is of Latin origin, and Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine documents, such as a London papyrus from A.D. 104 naming a cavalry commander.

definition: A flowing or discharge from the body, used in the New Testament specifically for a flow of blood.
article: Built on the verb "to flow," ῥύσις names a flowing or discharge, and in all three New Testament uses it refers to a flow of blood — the woman healed by Jesus in Mark 5:25 and Luke 8:43-44. The word was common in everyday Greek for other kinds of flow: the papyri use it especially for the yield or flow of wine at harvest. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, most often (15×) translating the Hebrew word zob, a bodily discharge.
caution: The New Testament evidence is thin — just three occurrences, all describing the same woman's bleeding — so its full range comes from the Septuagint and papyri rather than biblical usage.

definition: A member of the Areopagus, the council or court that met on Mars' Hill in Athens.
article: This word names a judge or member of the Athenian council known as the Areopagus, which met on Mars' Hill. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 17:34, describing Dionysius, who came to faith after Paul's speech in Athens. The word is built from Ἄρειος Πάγος (Mars' Hill), and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Greek inscriptions, including some from the third century B.C.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: All at once and without warning; suddenly and unexpectedly.
article: ἐξάπινα is an adverb meaning "suddenly" or "unexpectedly," describing something that happens all at once. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing just once (Mark 9:8), where it is woven into the phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word; it shows up more often in the Septuagint, 11 times across 7 books, translating Hebrew words for suddenness like פִּתְאוֹם and פֶּ֫תַע. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from a second-century papyrus where someone writes that "the accident happened suddenly (ἐξάπινα)" and a reburial is now needed.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence, and the reference sources treat it simply as a variant of the more common ἐξαίφνης.

definition: To feed someone, originally with small morsels, and more generally to nourish or give out food.
article: ψωμίζω comes from the word for a morsel and originally meant feeding someone bite by bite, as you would a child or a sick person. By the time of the New Testament it had broadened to mean simply to feed or nourish, and the Majority Standard Bible renders its two NT uses as feeding an enemy (Romans 12:20) and giving away possessions to feed the poor (1 Corinthians 13:3). Interestingly, everyday Koine documents preserve a related noun ψώμισμα in a food contract from 13 B.C., listing a ration of oil and bread.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise range here rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri parallels rather than New Testament evidence.

definition: A conditional particle introducing a possible or uncertain situation, usually translated "if" and often paired with verbs of willing.
article: ἐάν is the standard Greek word for setting up a condition — "if such-and-such happens." It appears 348 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and translators render it "if" or close variants in the great majority of cases, with "unless" used 16 times for negative conditions. In the Septuagint it shows up 1,163 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew אּם ("if," 509 times), and everyday papyri confirm it was common speech, as in a letter saying "if you must meet Anicetus, meet him."
caution: The many measured "senses" largely reflect how ἐάν combines with neighboring words (especially verbs of willing) rather than separate meanings, and in Hellenistic Greek its distinction from εἰ had already blurred.

definition: A gentle, mild disposition toward others, marked by humility rather than harshness or self-assertion.
article: πραΰτης describes a quality of gentleness or mildness in how a person treats others, often paired with humility. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "gentleness" in 75% of its translatable occurrences, with the remaining four absorbed into broader phrasing; older lexicons like the KJV prefer "meekness." A striking piece of evidence comes from the papyri: an inscription from about A.D. 350 reads "the tomb of the meek Aquilinus," literally "the meekness of Aquilinus," showing the word praised even on a gravestone.
caution: The earlier spelling πραότης appears in the papyri and some manuscripts, so editions vary slightly in form, though the meaning is stable.

definition: To feel or touch something with the hands, or figuratively to grope about searching for something.
article: ψηλαφάω is mainly a hands-on word: it means to feel, touch, or handle something physically, as when the risen Jesus invites the disciples to touch him in Luke 24:39. It also stretches to a figurative sense of groping about or searching after something, used of seeking God in Acts 17:27. In everyday Koine papyri the word developed a further nuance of examining a matter closely, and the Septuagint uses it 16 times, most often rendering the Hebrew מָשַׁשׁ (6×), the verb for feeling or groping with the hands.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences spread across three different renderings, the precise force in any single passage can be debated.

definition: A raised platform or altar, especially one used for religious offerings.
article: βωμός means a raised place — originally just a platform — but it was long ago specialized to mean an altar for worship. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, where Paul in Athens points to an altar inscribed "to an unknown god" (Acts 17:23). The Septuagint uses it 33 times, where it frequently renders Hebrew terms for altars and pagan high places (בָּמָה), and Moulton-Milligan note it was common in everyday papyri — one document even describes people setting altars against their doorways to avoid having officials billeted in their homes.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the word's full range here rests mostly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than NT usage.

definition: A negative connecting word that joins items in a list of things that are not so, meaning "neither," "nor," or "and not."
article: οὔτε is a linking particle used to string together negatives, most often in the paired pattern "neither...nor." It's a flexible connector translated as "nor" (17×), "or" (13×), "neither nor" (11×), or simply "neither" (7×), and in 35 of its 94 appearances it gets absorbed into the phrasing without a separate English word of its own. It was common, ordinary speech: a first-century papyrus loan document uses it just as the New Testament does, in the line "neither I nor any one else having the right to expel you."

definition: An adverb meaning "from childhood" or "since early boyhood," describing something true of a person ever since they were young.
article: παιδιόθεν is an adverb formed from παιδίον ("child") with the ending -θεν that signals source, so it literally means "from childhood." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:21, where it is paired with the preposition ἐκ; the classical equivalent was the phrase ἐκ παιδός. The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Moulton-Milligan compares the parallel formation ἐξ οἰκόθεν ("from home") in a first-century document.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its meaning rests on very thin biblical evidence, though the papyri and classical sources agree.

definition: Tall or high up, describing something raised far above—like a mountain, wall, or heaven—and sometimes used figuratively for status or pride.
article: ὑψηλός basically means "high" or "lofty," used 11 times in the New Testament and rendered "high" in 75% of cases, often of mountains (Matthew 4:8) or, in the phrase "led up a high mountain" (Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2), accounting for the other 25%. It stretches naturally from physical height to figurative heights—heaven itself (Hebrews 1:3) or human pride and esteem (Luke 16:15). In the Septuagint it appears 186 times, most often translating the Hebrew בָּמָה (56×), a word for a "high place" of worship, and the everyday papyri keep the literal sense alive, describing "two tall female asses" and ground lying too high above the water for irrigation.

definition: Describing a person who comes from or lives in Derbe, a city in Asia Minor.
article: Δερβαῖος simply means "of Derbe," identifying someone as a native or resident of that city. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:4, where it describes a companion of Paul named Gaius. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) all agree it is an adjective of origin tied to the place-name Derbe (G1191).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be tested against other uses.

definition: Rhegium, a port city in southwestern Italy across the strait from Sicily (modern Reggio).
article: Ῥήγιον is a place name borrowed from Latin, referring to the Italian port of Rhegium (modern Reggio) on the toe of Italy, just across the strait from Sicily. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:13, as a stop on Paul's sea journey toward Rome, where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word. Moulton-Milligan note that the city's name was traditionally linked to the verb ῥήγνυμι ("to break"), perhaps reflecting the broken or sundered coastline at the strait.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its profile rests on geography rather than measured sense range.

definition: To suffer together with someone, sharing in their pain or hardship.
article: συμπάσχω combines "with" (σύν) and "suffer" (πάσχω) to mean experiencing pain or hardship alongside another person. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and both times the BSB renders the underlying idea as suffering together, though in 1 Corinthians 12:26 the surrounding contrast with shared honor shapes how it reads. The classical lexica add a softer secondary sense, "to sympathize with," and a papyrus letter from Oxyrhynchus uses a related form when one person can no longer "suffer along with" another, showing the word at home in everyday Koine emotional life.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 New Testament occurrences and 1 in the Septuagint), and the two measured renderings differ sharply because of context.

definition: To lie down, especially to lie sick in bed or to recline at the table for a meal.
article: This verb literally means "to lie down," and in the New Testament it splits between two practical situations: being bedridden with illness and reclining at a meal in the customary fashion of the day. It is built from κατά ("down") plus κεῖμαι ("to lie"). The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where one document describes a woman "laid up with sickness" after being beaten, her life endangered — the same medical sense found in passages like Mark 1:30. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times, and notably 7 of those are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word.
caution: With 7 of 11 occurrences absorbed into phrasing and only 2 Septuagint uses, the precise sense in any given verse often depends on context rather than the word itself.

definition: To dig into the ground, as with a spade, for planting, building foundations, or breaking up soil.
article: Σκάπτω simply means to dig — turning over earth with a tool, whether to plant a tree, lay a foundation, or break up ground. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Luke, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "dig" in every measured case. The papyri show it was an ordinary working-life word: one document from 94 AD orders someone to "dig a deep trench round the oil-press," and others describe laborers digging in the sand or digging foundations to build.
caution: The Septuagint evidence is thin (one occurrence, in Isaiah 5:6), and the digest notes the Hebrew counterpart slightly differently across its sources.

definition: A gift or present, especially an offering presented to God at the altar.
article: δῶρον means a gift or present, and the New Testament most often uses it for something offered to God—an altar offering or sacrifice. Of its 19 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders 11 (65%) as "gift(s)" and 2 more as gifts of a sacrificial kind, with the remainder absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it 163 times, most frequently for the Hebrew קָרְבָן ("offering," 77×), and the papyri and inscriptions confirm this same sense, recording gifts presented to gods and temples.

definition: A secret scheme or plot to harm someone, often involving lying in wait.
article: ἐπιβουλή means a hostile plan aimed at someone—a plot or conspiracy, sometimes involving an ambush. All four New Testament occurrences are in Acts and refer to plots against Paul, and the various English renderings ("learned their plot," "formed a plot against," "through plots," "plot against") all point to this single sense. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the meaning vividly: one Oxyrhynchus document uses the phrase "a pretext for plotting against me," showing the word was common legal-complaint language for conspiracy.
caution: Evidence is limited—only four New Testament uses (all in Acts) and two in the Septuagint—but all sources agree on the single sense.

definition: To keep someone alive or rescue them from death; in classical and medical usage, to bring forth or endue with life.
article: In the New Testament and Septuagint, ζωογονέω means to preserve someone alive or rescue them from death, the sense reflected in passages like Luke 17:33 and Acts 7:19. The Septuagint uses it 12 times across 6 books, most often translating the Hebrew חָיָה ("to live," 8×), as in Exodus 1:17 where it describes the midwives keeping the Hebrew babies alive. Interestingly, the word literally means "to produce alive" or "endue with life," and Moulton-Milligan notes a third-century magical papyrus that addresses the sun-god as the one who "gives life and holds the world together."
caution: The Byzantine NT shows only 2 occurrences with very little measured rendering data, so the word's range here rests largely on Septuagint and lexical evidence.

definition: To correspond to or line up with something, the way one thing matches another point by point.
article: συστοιχέω is a military term that originally meant to stand in the same rank or file, like soldiers lined up in formation, and is used this way by the historian Polybius. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Galatians 4:25, where it is used figuratively to say one thing corresponds exactly to another. The everyday papyri back up both flavors: the related adjective shows up in a 28 B.C. document meaning "in agreement" (BGU IV.1205) and in Epicurus for "kindred phenomena."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single verse plus outside Greek sources.

definition: A finger, the slender part of the hand, also used figuratively for God's power at work.
article: δάκτυλος means a finger, the part of the hand, and that physical sense covers nearly all of its uses—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "finger" in 5 of 8 New Testament occurrences. It also appears figuratively in the phrase "the finger of God" (Luke 11:20), an image of divine power that echoes Exodus 8:19. The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: papyri use it in physical descriptions of people, such as a scar "on the little finger of the left hand," and it even shows up in a magical charm invoking "the finger of God."

definition: A Roman — either a person from Rome or someone holding Roman citizenship.
article: Ῥωμαῖος describes a Roman, and the New Testament uses it two ways: about 45% of the time it means a Roman citizen — a legal status with real protections, as when Paul invokes it during his arrest (Acts 22:25-27) — and about 36% of the time it simply means the Romans as a people or nation (John 11:48). The word comes straight from Ῥώμη, the name of Rome itself. Lexicons like Dodson note this same dual use, listing it both as an adjective "Roman" and as a noun "a Roman citizen," which matches the measured pattern well.
caution: The single Septuagint occurrence, listed as translating an unrelated Hebrew word, looks like a data quirk and should not be leaned on.

definition: To draw something together — either by wrapping a body for burial or by shortening a span of time.
article: This verb literally means to draw things together, and it splits into two distinct uses in the New Testament, each appearing just once. In Acts 5:6 it describes wrapping or shrouding a corpse for burial, while in 1 Corinthians 7:29 it describes time being shortened or compressed. The everyday Koine papyri show a vivid third use the NT doesn't have: the curtailing or cutting back of expenses, as in records that order spending to be reduced.
caution: Each of the two senses rests on only a single New Testament occurrence, so the measured range is thin.

definition: To throw a group of people into confusion or uproar, or to leave someone's mind bewildered.
article: συγχέω literally means to pour things together, and from there it came to mean stirring people up into confusion or commotion. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, all in Acts, where translators render it differently each time—from a crowd in turmoil to a mind left bewildered—so no single English word captures it. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from the papyri: one writer (P Oxy XVI.1873) says "I feel my reasoning faculties confused," showing the same sense of mental bewilderment. In the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew words, most often בָּלַל ("to mingle") and רָגַז ("to be agitated").
caution: With only 5 occurrences, each translated by a different English word, the word's force depends heavily on context rather than a fixed meaning.

definition: To crush or shatter something to pieces, as when a falling stone breaks whatever it lands on.
article: Συνθλάω means to crush together or break something into pieces, often pictured as the effect of a heavy blow or fall. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical SBLGNT text), both times describing how a stone breaks anyone who falls on it (Matthew 21:44; Luke 20:18). Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and the Septuagint uses it eight times across three books, often of divine punishment as in the Psalms.
caution: Confidence is low: the word is rare, absorbed into surrounding phrasing in both NT verses, and absent from the critical text.

definition: An adverb meaning "from here" or "from this place," sometimes doubled to mean "on each side."
article: ἐντεῦθεν is an adverb of place meaning "from here" or "from this place," appearing 11 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "here" in 38% of cases, while in 3 of 11 occurrences it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing without a separate English word. When doubled ("ἐντεῦθεν καὶ ἐντεῦθεν"), it means "on this side and on that" or "on each side," and the everyday Koine papyri also use it to mean "from this time"—a money document from A.D. 255 has someone saying they "thereupon received" a sum of drachmas.
caution: The lexicons list additional senses (temporal "thereupon" and causal "therefore") that the measured New Testament data does not clearly distinguish, so the word's range may be broader than the single measured sense suggests.

definition: A strong connecting word marking contrast, used to correct or override what was just said — "but" or "rather, instead."
article: ἀλλά is the New Testament's strong adversative particle, appearing 639 times and overwhelmingly rendered "but" (471×, or 96% of cases where it gets its own English word). It does more than simply join clauses: it typically corrects or overrides a preceding negative, as in "not by bread alone, but by every word." One striking feature from the papyri is that ἀλλά could shade into the meaning "except," especially in the phrase ἀλλ᾽ ἤ — a Greek letter from 241 BC uses it to say "there is no one left here except ourselves." In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew words אם, כִּי, and רַק.

definition: A formal charge or accusation brought against someone, especially in a legal setting.
article: ἔγκλημα is a legal term meaning a formal accusation or charge laid against a person. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts dealing with Paul's trial (Acts 23:29 and 25:16), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it loosely within phrases like "involved" and "opportunity" rather than with a fixed word. The everyday Koine papyri confirm its courtroom flavor vividly: a royal decree of 118 BC (P Tebt I.5) declares an amnesty for "errors, crimes, and accusations (ἐνκλημάτων)," and other documents speak of filing a complaint or making counter-accusations.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and translations that paraphrase rather than render it directly, the measured senses here reflect the surrounding phrasing more than the word itself.

definition: Heli, the name of a man listed as Joseph's father in the genealogy of Jesus.
article: Ἡλί is a personal name, transliterated into Greek from Hebrew, and the lexicons agree it refers to Heli, the father of Joseph in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 3:23) and is indeclinable. Interestingly, in the Septuagint a related form renders the Hebrew name עֵלִי (Eli) 33 of 36 times, and Moulton-Milligan note that a similar Greek spelling reflects the Aramaic cry from the cross in Matthew 27:46.
caution: This is a name with only one New Testament occurrence, and the standard rendering 'ministry' in the measured data appears to be a tagging artifact rather than a real translation of the word.

definition: Without measure or limit; describing something not confined to set boundaries.
article: ἄμετρος literally means "without measure," built from the negative prefix and the word for "measure" (μέτρον).
