It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 10 (verses 13 and 15), where Paul uses the phrase "beyond measure" in talking about the proper limits of his sphere of work; the Majority Standard Bible renders both with "influence." A related form, ἀμέτρητος ("immeasurable"), turns up in a moving second-century BC grave inscription from Rhodes describing a husband and wife who traveled "the immeasurable road" to Hades together.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in the same passage, the evidence base is thin, and the lexicons gloss it as "immeasurable/excessive" while the measured rendering reads "influence," so confidence is low.

definition: Eve, the first woman in the biblical account and wife of Adam.
article: Εὖα is simply the proper name Eve, the first woman, mentioned twice in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Timothy 2:13). The name comes from the Hebrew חַוָּה (Chavvah), introduced in Genesis 3:20. Both occurrences are rendered "Eve" unanimously, with no variation in meaning. One curious detail: in the Septuagint one of its two appearances corresponds not to חַוָּה but to הֶבֶל, suggesting a textual or transmission quirk in that passage.
caution: This is a rare proper name with only two NT uses, and the Septuagint evidence shows an odd Hebrew correspondence worth noting.

definition: Without a recorded father, used of someone whose paternity or genealogy is not documented.
article: ἀπάτωρ combines the negative prefix 'a-' with 'father' (πατήρ), describing someone with no recorded father. In the New Testament it appears only once, at Hebrews 7:3, where it portrays Melchizedek as having no recorded genealogy. The most striking evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where the word appears in routine birth and registration formulas — for example listing a child as 'ἀπάτωρ, mother Thaseti' — to mark someone whose father was unknown or unregistered, sometimes implying illegitimacy.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical sense rests on a single verse alongside the documentary papyri evidence.

definition: To keep or guard something carefully, whether holding it safely or keeping oneself away from it.
article: διατηρέω is a strengthened form of τηρέω ("keep") with διά added, meaning to keep or guard thoroughly. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Luke 2:51 Mary "kept" these things, while in Acts 15:29 it means keeping oneself away from certain things. Strong's notes both directions — observing strictly (positive) and avoiding wholly (negative) — and the Septuagint's 15 uses, mostly translating Hebrew shamar ("keep," 4×), confirm the core idea of careful keeping. Everyday papyri show the same range, including an instruction to "keep it carefully" and a man's claim to have kept himself from troubling anyone.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a measured low confidence tier, the evidence for its full range is thin and rests heavily on the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: To stir up or agitate something, whether literally roiling water or, more often, unsettling a person's mind or a crowd with fear, worry, or confusion.
article: ταράσσω means to stir up or agitate, and the New Testament uses it for everything from a frightened individual to a whole city thrown into turmoil. Of its 17 occurrences, the most common renderings cluster around being "troubled," "troubling," "disturbed," and "terrified" — all shades of inner or social agitation rather than the literal sense. The classical lexicons note its original physical meaning of stirring water (as in roiling a pool), while the everyday Koine papyri use it just as the Gospels do: one document pleads "do not be disturbed on this account." In the Septuagint it appears 91 times, translating Hebrew words for trembling, raging, and dismay.

definition: To feel ashamed of someone or something, or be too embarrassed to acknowledge a connection to them.
article: This verb means to feel shame about a person or thing, often to the point of being unwilling to be openly associated with them. It appears 11 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ashamed" in some form in nearly every case (70% as plain "ashamed," another 20% as "anyone ashamed"). The grammar shows its range: it can stand alone, take a direct object (a person or thing), or be followed by "of" plus what one is ashamed about, as in Romans 1:16. In the Septuagint it shows up only 3 times, translating different Hebrew words for fear, shame, and disgrace.

definition: A man's personal name, Theophilus, the individual to whom Luke addressed his Gospel and Acts.
article: Theophilus is a personal name meaning "friend of God," given to the person to whom Luke dedicated both his Gospel and the book of Acts. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Luke 1:3 and Acts 1:1), and the Berean Study Bible renders it as the name in both cases. The name was common in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan documents it in papyri and inscriptions as early as the third century B.C., including a doctor named Theophilus and even its use as a Jewish name.
caution: With only two occurrences and no description in the text beyond the name itself, almost nothing certain is known about who Theophilus actually was.

definition: A person who speaks for God, declaring or interpreting His will and sometimes foretelling what is to come.
article: A προφήτης is someone who speaks forth God's message — an interpreter or forth-teller of the divine will, and sometimes a foreteller of the future. The word is overwhelmingly stable: of 148 Byzantine occurrences, 137 (94%) are simply rendered "prophets," with the remaining cases just reflecting different sentence phrasing rather than different meanings. In the Septuagint it appears 281 times and almost always translates the Hebrew נָבִיא (233×), the standard word for a prophet. Outside the Bible the term was used in everyday Koine too: an inscription from Upper Egypt describes a προφήτης as the interpreter of an oracle of Apollo, showing the word's wider sense of a spokesman for a deity.

definition: To plunge or be thrown into the sea, and so to sink down or drown beneath the water.
article: καταποντίζω describes going under water, whether sinking down like Peter on the waves or being drowned outright; the two ideas are really one picture viewed from either side. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament (both in Matthew) and 11 times in the Septuagint, where it renders several Hebrew words including בָּלַע, "to swallow up." The most vivid evidence comes from an everyday papyrus letter that uses this very verb for the sinking of an elephant transport ship — confirming it was ordinary Koine for boats and bodies going under.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (and none in the SBLGNT critical text), the evidence base is thin, so the split between "sink" and "drown" reflects translation choice rather than two truly distinct meanings.

definition: To join someone in pretending or playing a false part, going along with their hypocrisy or pretense.
article: This verb means to act out a false part alongside others—to join in someone's hypocrisy or pretense rather than acting alone. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Galatians 2:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "joined," describing other Jews who went along with Peter's pretense. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Moulton-Milligan note a telling parallel in Polybius, where Fabius "pretended to agree" with eager soldiers—a sense that fits Galatians well: going along outwardly with what one does not truly intend.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on a single verse plus a handful of outside parallels.

definition: To throw something alongside another, hence to compare things, or—of travelers and ships—to arrive at or touch in at a place.
article: παραβάλλω literally means to throw one thing beside another, and from that root it branches into two main uses: comparing things side by side, and (of seamen) putting in or touching at a place. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, and in both cases it was absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated as a single English word. The everyday papyri back up the travel sense nicely—one letter from the 3rd century BC scolds a man who 'passed us by' instead of landing to visit for even a quarter of an hour, matching the rendering 'we touched at Samos' in Acts 20:15.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text), both absorbed into phrasing—so the senses rest mainly on Septuagint, papyri, and classical attestation.

definition: To open something completely or thoroughly, whether eyes, ears, and minds physically, or the meaning of scripture by explaining it.
article: This is an intensified form of the ordinary verb "to open" (ἀνοίγω), carrying the sense of opening up fully or completely. In the Byzantine New Testament's 8 uses, it is rendered "opened" 86% of the time (6×), covering both literal openings like ears (Mark 7:34) and eyes (Luke 24:31) and figurative ones like opening a heart (Acts 16:14) or explaining scripture. The Septuagint uses it 34 times, often to translate the Hebrew word for a firstborn that "opens the womb" (פֶּטֶר), which is why Strong's notes the literal birth sense alongside the figurative "to expound."
caution: With only 8 New Testament occurrences, the rarer sense of "explaining" or "expounding" scripture rests on just a couple of passages.

definition: To turn aside and slip away quietly, withdrawing from a place or crowd.
article: ἐκνεύω literally means to bend or turn the head aside, and by extension to quietly withdraw or get clear of a situation. It appears just once in the New Testament (John 5:13), where it describes Jesus slipping away from a crowd and is best rendered intransitively as "had turned aside" or "had retired." The Septuagint uses it 7 times across 3 books, translating several different Hebrew words including פָּנָה ("turn") twice, and Moulton-Milligan note its everyday use in the papyri, where a related form describes men evading an appearance.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise NT sense rests on a single passage plus outside evidence.

definition: Uncleanness or impurity, considered as a state or condition rather than a particular act.
article: This noun means "uncleanness" or "filthiness," the abstract state of being impure, and it is derived from the adjective ἀκάθαρτος ("unclean"). It does not actually appear in the Byzantine New Testament; Abbott-Smith notes it only as a variant reading (the Received text) in Revelation 17:4, where the standard text instead reads the plural adjective τὰ ἀκάθαρτα. In other words, the word survives chiefly as a textual footnote rather than as an established New Testament term.
caution: The evidence is extremely thin — the word has zero New Testament occurrences and is attested only as a disputed variant reading in Revelation 17:4, so any sense assignment is uncertain.

definition: To be furiously angry or locked in a bitter quarrel with someone.
article: θυμομαχέω describes being intensely angry or caught up in a hot quarrel with someone. It is built from two parts meaning 'anger' (θυμός) and 'to fight' (μάχομαι), so it literally pictures fighting in a rage. The word appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 12:20, where Herod is described as deeply angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the corpus translation data here registered the place name 'Tyre' rather than the verb's own meaning, so lean on the lexicon glosses of furious anger or quarreling.

definition: The foot, the body part on which people and animals stand and walk.
article: πούς is the ordinary word for a foot, whether of a person or an animal. In the New Testament it is rendered "feet" 86 of 93 times (99%), and the meaning is remarkably stable. The word often appears in vivid phrases like "at his feet" or "under his feet," and by extension it can stand for a whole person in motion (as in Luke 1:79 or Romans 3:15). One nice everyday touch: the papyri use "from the foot" to describe watering fields by foot-operated irrigation, echoing Deuteronomy 11:10.

definition: The practice of magic or sorcery — using occult arts to manipulate supernatural powers.
article: μαγεία refers to magic or sorcery, the practice of occult arts. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 8:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sorcery" (100% of the time), a choice the BSB and KJV share. The everyday Koine papyri confirm the word, and one magical text (third century AD) even speaks of "sacred magic," reflecting the ancient idea that magic was originally something divine; Abbott-Smith likewise notes an older sense, "the lore of the Magians."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: To make someone strong or fill them with power, strengthening them for a task.
article: This verb is built from "in" (ἐν) and "empower" (δυναμόω), and means to fill a person with strength or power. It usually takes a person as its object and appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often describing being strengthened in the Lord (as in Ephesians 6:10 and 2 Timothy 2:1). In its single Septuagint appearance the underlying Hebrew is a word for "clothing oneself" with strength, and the verb also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, showing it was ordinary working vocabulary, not just a religious term.
caution: The corpus tagged only 2 of 8 occurrences cleanly as "strong," with the rest scattered across odd renderings, so the measured data is thin even though the lexicons agree on the core meaning.

definition: Theudas, the personal name of a Jewish rebel leader mentioned once in the New Testament.
article: Theudas is simply a man's name — that of a Jewish insurgent referenced once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 5:36. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as a person ("somebody") 100% of the time, which fits its function as a proper name. Its origin is uncertain, though it may be a shortened form of Theodorus; Moulton-Milligan note a tomb inscription from Hierapolis where one man named two of his sons Theodorus and Theudas, rather like calling brothers Theodore and Teddy.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once, and its derivation is genuinely uncertain, so little can be said about it beyond identification.

definition: Carpus, a man at Troas with whom Paul left his cloak and other belongings.
article: Κάρπος is a personal name, that of a Christian at Troas mentioned only once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 4:13), where Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left with him. Although the Majority Bible text 'renders' this single occurrence as 'cloak' in the measured data, this is the name of the man, not an object; every lexicon (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) identifies it simply as Carpus, a person. Moulton-Milligan notes the name turns up in everyday Koine, appearing on a Magnesian coin dated A.D. 230 bearing the name M. Aurelius Carpus.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured 'cloak' rendering reflects a data quirk rather than the word's actual meaning, which all lexicons agree is the personal name Carpus.

definition: Uriah, the Hittite soldier whose wife Bathsheba later became the mother of Solomon.
article: Οὐρίας is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Uriah, appearing just once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Matthew 1:6, where Solomon is born to David and the wife of Uriah. In the Septuagint the name shows up 36 times across 7 books, usually rendering the Hebrew אוּרִיָּה (29×). Strong's and Dodson identify this Uriah specifically as the Hittite husband of Bathsheba, which fits the lone New Testament reference.
caution: This is a proper name with only a single New Testament occurrence, so its range cannot be measured beyond that one verse.

definition: A worm or maggot, especially the kind that feeds on dead bodies.
article: σκώληξ refers to a worm or maggot, particularly the type that preys on corpses. In the New Testament it appears 3 times, all in Mark 9 (verses 44, 46, 48) within the same vivid image of future punishment where "their worm does not die." The Septuagint uses it 12 times across 7 books, mostly translating the Hebrew words תּוֹלָע (tola, 4×) and רִמָּה (rimmah, 4×), both ordinary words for worm; the Mark 9:48 wording draws directly on Isaiah 66:24.
caution: The measured "never" rendering reflects the surrounding phrase "never dies" rather than the noun itself, and with only 3 NT occurrences in one passage the evidence base is thin.

definition: Josiah, a king of Judah, listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Matthew's genealogy.
article: Ἰωσίας is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Josiah (יֹאשִׁיָּה), the king of Judah. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10-11), and every translation renders it "Josiah." The name is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 35 times across four books, almost always rendering the Hebrew יֹאשִׁיָּה (32 of those times).
caution: This is a proper name with only two New Testament occurrences, so its sense is fixed but the evidence base is thin.

definition: A wooden stick used as a walking staff, a tool for striking, or a royal scepter symbolizing authority.
article: ῥάβδος is basically a stick, but its use determines its meaning: a traveler's staff (the most common New Testament sense, 67% of occurrences), or a ruler's scepter standing for authority (22%). The word's range is broad, and the Septuagint uses it heavily—114 times—most often for the Hebrew מַטֶּה. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain, physical sense vividly: one document from 114 BC describes a man giving "many blows with the rod he was carrying."

definition: A living creature or animal—any being that is alive, often the symbolic beings worshiping in Revelation.
article: ζῶον means a living creature, and in 74% of its 23 New Testament appearances the Berean Standard Bible renders it "living creatures"—nearly all of these in Revelation, where the term describes the symbolic beings around God's throne. In another 21% it is simply "creatures," as when 2 Peter 2:12 speaks of "unreasoning creatures." Lexicographers note that ζῶον is broader and more neutral than θηρίον (a brute beast), stressing the shared vital element of all living things—a distinction echoed in the papyri, where "sacred animals" (ἱερὰ ζῷα) like Apis are mentioned in everyday documents. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words, including the "wheel" (אוֹפָן) and "likeness" (דְּמוּת) of Ezekiel's visions.

definition: A compelling necessity or pressure to act, ranging from logical obligation to outright hardship and distress.
article: At its core ἀνάγκη describes a force that constrains you — something that must be done, whether by logic, duty, or pressure of circumstance. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 18 times, with translators most often landing on "necessary" (4×) or "need" (2×), though in 7 of 18 cases the idea is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. The classical lexicons stress a second, harder edge — "force, violence, distress" — and this is borne out beautifully in the everyday papyri: a 1st-century BC letter uses "I have been obliged to urge," while an inscription speaks of being caught "in hardships and sufferings," matching Paul's distress language in passages like 2 Corinthians 6:4. In the Septuagint it often renders Hebrew words for trouble or distress (צָרָה, 3×).
caution: The measured renderings cluster on "necessity/need," but the lexicons insist on a strong secondary sense of "distress, violence," so the word's range is wider than the headline glosses suggest.

definition: To shut someone up or confine them, especially by locking them away in prison.
article: κατακλείω means to shut someone in or lock them away, and in the New Testament it appears only twice, both times describing people being put in prison — as when Herod locked John up (Luke 3:20). It's built from κατά and κλείω ("to shut"), and the Septuagint uses it similarly, including at Jeremiah 32:3 to render a Hebrew word for confining. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary sense: one writer complains "I have been shut up in the finance-office until to-day," showing the word covered bureaucratic detention as well as actual imprisonment.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, though all sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: A willing, eager readiness of mind to do something.
article: Προθυμία describes an inner readiness or enthusiasm—a willing eagerness to act. It appears only 5 times in the New Testament, all rendered with the idea of eager willingness, whether straightforwardly as "eagerness" or woven into phrases like "more than eager." The everyday papyri pair it with σπουδή ("zeal"), as in a 164 BC document urging officials to apply "the greatest zeal and eagerness," confirming this was a common, practical word for enthusiastic readiness.
caution: The differing Majority Standard Bible phrasings reflect translation context rather than distinct meanings, so the single core sense is consistent across sources.

definition: Describing something that is welcome and pleasing, especially in God's sight.
article: ἀπόδεκτος describes something that is gladly received or pleasing, and in the New Testament it appears only twice (1 Timothy 2:3 and 5:4), both times rendered "pleasing sight" and both referring to what is acceptable before God. The word comes from ἀποδέχομαι, "to welcome or receive," so the underlying idea is of something one is glad to accept. Interestingly, it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a first-century B.C. inscription where it carries the same sense of something that "ought to be acceptable."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured range for this word is very narrow, though the lexicons agree on its meaning.

definition: To lift someone or something up, or to take a person or thing along with you.
article: This verb combines "up" (ἀνά) with "take" (λαμβάνω), and across its 13 New Testament uses it splits between two closely related ideas. About 55% of the time it means being lifted up — most famously Jesus being "taken up" into heaven — while another 36% means simply taking someone or something along, as when Paul's companions "took" him aboard ship. In the Greek Old Testament it appears 70 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew נָשָׂא ("to lift, carry"), and everyday papyri show people using it for taking up arms or even "receiving" a document.

definition: To set something in motion—to move, shake, or stir it up, whether physically or by provoking action.
article: κινέω means to set something in motion, covering a range from literal shaking and moving to figuratively stirring people up. In the Byzantine New Testament its eight uses split evenly: shaking the head in mockery (Matthew 27:39, Mark 15:29), moving or being moved (Acts 17:28, Revelation 6:14), and stirring up trouble (Acts 21:30, 24:5). The Septuagint uses it 42 times, often for Hebrew נוּעַ (to shake or wander), and the everyday papyri show the concrete sense vividly—one third-century document uses it of "movables," the portable goods someone left behind.
caution: With only eight New Testament occurrences spread evenly across three distinct senses, the boundaries between physical and figurative use depend heavily on context.

definition: To follow closely after someone or something, often used figuratively for accompanying, attending to, or pursuing.
article: This compound verb joins "upon" (epí) with "follow" (akolouthéō), giving the sense of following close behind or accompanying. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times across 3 books and is always used figuratively—of signs that "accompanied" the apostles' preaching (Mark 16:20), of sins, and of following in someone's footsteps. The everyday papyri are especially revealing: the word could mean "see to" or "be personally present at" a task, as when one writer asks for someone to be sent who will "see to" the pouring out of new wine.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences—three of which dissolve into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word—the measured evidence for any single sense is thin.

definition: A small portable oil lamp, usually set on a stand to light a room, or the light such a lamp gives.
article: λύχνος is the ordinary word for a small oil lamp—the kind you light and set on a stand to fill a room with light. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 14 times, rendered "lamp" in 11 cases (79%) and "lamp light" in 2 (14%), and it shows up routinely in everyday papyri, including temple records about "the proper oil for the daily lamps burning" and even "a lamp with a double light." In the Septuagint it appears 41 times, most often translating the Hebrew נֵר (lamp) 32 times, and the New Testament also stretches it figuratively—to the eye, to John the Baptist, and to prophecy.

definition: Magog, a name from Old Testament prophecy used in Revelation for nations gathered against God's people.
article: Μαγώγ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Magog (מָגוֹג), borrowed straight from the Old Testament where it appears in passages like Genesis 10:2 and Ezekiel 38:2. The word does not decline in Greek and shows up just once in the New Testament, in Revelation 20:8, where it is paired with Gog as enemies gathered for battle. Older lexicons note that Magog can name either a people or a country, possibly the Scythians, and is reused in apocalyptic literature.
caution: This is a rare proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its precise reference is uncertain and the renderings differ on whether it names a people or a place.

definition: To watch over someone or something thoroughly, keeping them safe and protected.
article: Built from διά ("thoroughly") and φυλάσσω ("guard"), this verb means to protect carefully or defend. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:10, where it quotes Psalm 91:11 about angels guarding a person—and the Septuagint uses it 15 times across 10 books, most often translating the Hebrew שָׁמַר ("to keep"). The most striking detail is how everyday this word was: Koine papyri use it for the gods watching over a friend's safety, as in one letter thanking "all the gods because they keep you unharmed."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (a quotation of the Septuagint), the measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: The act of going out to meet someone, often a formal welcome to greet an arriving person.
article: ἀπάντησις refers to the act of meeting someone, and in all 4 of its New Testament appearances translators render it as "meet" (100%). It often carries a semi-technical sense of going out to welcome an arriving official or dignitary, a usage confirmed by everyday Koine papyri. One papyrus from 118 B.C. uses the word for going out to greet a newly arriving magistrate, which suggests this formal-reception sense is genuine Greek rather than a borrowed Hebrew idiom. In the Septuagint it appears 35 times, most often rendering the Hebrew phrase for "to meet" (קְרָאת and קָרָא, 10 times each).

definition: A mother city or chief city — the principal town of a region or district.
article: μητρόπολις combines the words for "mother" (μήτηρ) and "city" (πόλις) to mean a region's chief or capital city. It never appears in the body of the Byzantine New Testament — the only New Testament occurrence is in a late editorial subscription to 1 Timothy — but it shows up 7 times in the Septuagint and was common in everyday Koine. The papyri make it vivid: one document is a birth notice addressed to the registry clerks of the metropolis, and a prodigal son's letter expresses surprise that his reader would "come up to the metropolis."
caution: Evidence is thin for biblical study since the word does not occur in the actual New Testament text, only in a late subscription.

definition: To make someone or something useless, worthless, or good for nothing.
article: ἀχρειόω means to render useless or spoil, built from the adjective ἀχρεῖος ("useless"). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 3:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "turned" (in the sense of having become worthless), quoting the Septuagint. An everyday Cilician inscription from the first century AD uses it for the forbidden act of defacing temple inscriptions and offerings — making them useless — showing the word lived in ordinary Koine speech.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence (and none in the critical text), the measured range here rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To make something white or to whiten it.
article: λευκαίνω means simply to make something white. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Mark 9:3 and Revelation 7:14), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "white" each time, with one of those occurrences absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times in 4 books, twice translating the Hebrew לָבַן ("to be white"), as in Isaiah 1:18 about sins becoming white as snow.
caution: With only 2 New Testament uses and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, and Moulton-Milligan found no papyri examples of this exact verb (only the related λευκόω).

definition: Agabus, the name of a Christian prophet mentioned in the book of Acts.
article: Ἄγαβος is a personal name, that of a Christian prophet who appears twice in Acts (11:28 and 21:10). The lexica agree it is a proper name of Hebrew origin, with no separate vocabulary meaning. One of the two measured renderings, "After been several," is a translation-alignment artifact from Acts 21:10 rather than a real sense of the name itself.
caution: This is a rare proper name occurring only twice, and one of the two measured "senses" reflects a translation glitch, not a genuine meaning.

definition: To tear or rip clothing off all the way around, usually stripping a person's garments.
article: This verb means to rip clothes completely off or away, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 16:22, where the garments of Paul and Silas are torn off before a beating. It also shows up in the Septuagint at 2 Maccabees 4:38 and in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was a normal word for the act of rending clothing. One interesting point of disagreement: most translators read Acts 16:22 as the magistrates stripping the prisoners, but the scholar Ramsay argued instead that the praetors tore their own clothes in a show of outrage.
caution: Evidence is thin\u2014only one New Testament occurrence\u2014and scholars disagree over whose clothes were torn in Acts 16:22.

definition: The highest, used either of God as "the Most High" or of physical height, as in "the highest heavens."
article: ὕψιστος is a superlative meaning "highest," and in the New Testament it splits cleanly between two uses: as a title for God, "the Most High" (8× out of 13, about 62%), and of place, "highest" (4×, about 31%), as in the heavens in phrases like "Hosanna in the highest." The Septuagint uses it heavily, 57 times, most often to render the Hebrew עֶלְיוֹן (Elyon), a name for God. The most striking evidence is from inscriptions and papyri: the title "to God the Most High" (θεῷ Ὑψίστῳ) shows up in everyday Jewish dedications, marking it as a recognized name for the God of Israel in the wider Greek-speaking world.

definition: To settle and come to rest upon someone or something, whether literally or by relying and depending on it.
article: This verb describes settling down to rest on something, and figuratively, relying or leaning on it. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice: in Luke 10:6, where peace "rests" on a worthy person, and in Romans 2:17, where someone "rests" or relies on the law. The Septuagint uses it nine times, most often for the Hebrew שָׁעַן ("to lean on," 6×), which fits the sense of relying; the everyday papyri and the Didache also use it for being "refreshed" by something.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into the phrasing, the measured evidence is thin, so the figurative "rely on" sense rests mainly on the Septuagint and lexicons.

definition: Half-dead; so badly injured or exhausted that one is barely alive.
article: ἡμιθανής literally means "half-dead," combining the words for "half" and "to die," and describes someone beaten or exhausted nearly to the point of death. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:30, where robbers leave the traveler half dead, and once in the Septuagint at 4 Maccabees 4:11. A striking everyday parallel turns up in a papyrus from A.D. 350, where a woman complains that her brother and his wife beat her with many blows and "left her half dead" — almost the same scene as in Jesus' parable.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: An adverb meaning in every place, all over, used to describe an action or condition occurring everywhere.
article: πανταχοῦ simply means "everywhere" or "in all places," and the measured senses really just reflect different sentence contexts—sometimes paired with "people" or with words of opposition—rather than separate meanings. It appears 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "everywhere" in 4 of those (57%), with the others being variations on the same idea. The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite papyri like a B.C. 248 letter saying "we have looked for wood everywhere," and legal documents declaring an agreement valid "everywhere."
caution: In Acts 21:28 the form is actually πανταχῇ (a spelling variant), which some editors prefer, so that occurrence is grouped here under the same word.

definition: Describing a person who lacks reverence for God and lives wickedly, without piety.
article: ἀσεβής describes someone who fails to reverence God—impious, irreverent, and so wicked in conduct. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "ungodly" in 5 of its 9 New Testament occurrences (56%), and the Berean Study Bible agrees 100% of the time, so the range is narrow and stable. The word is enormously common in the Septuagint, appearing 195 times and most often translating the Hebrew רָשָׁע ("wicked," 123×). It was also ordinary everyday Greek: a 116 BC papyrus speaks of damage done "by ungodly men," and the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) uses it of those who had stirred up sedition.

definition: A large piece of linen cloth, like a sheet, big enough to hold objects within it.
article: ὀθόνη refers to a piece of fine linen cloth, and in later usage a sheet or even a sail. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Peter's vision of a great sheet lowered from heaven (Acts 10:11 and 11:5), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with reference to its four "corners." Notably, the word never occurs in the Septuagint, and some have suggested its appearance in Acts echoes medical vocabulary, though it is well attested in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same vision, and the classical sense of "fine linen" or "sail" is broader than the single measured use.

definition: Describing someone who comes from Pontus, a region in northern Asia Minor.
article: Pontikós is an adjective meaning 'belonging to Pontus,' a region along the southern coast of the Black Sea. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:2, describing Aquila as a Jew 'from Pontus.' Curiously, the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering reads 'recently' here, which clashes with the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) that unanimously define the word as 'from Pontus' — the rendering 'recently' more likely reflects the neighboring word in the verse rather than this adjective itself.
caution: The single measured rendering ('recently') contradicts every cited lexicon, which all agree the word means 'from Pontus,' so the digest's sense data appears misaligned with the actual word.

definition: A young man or youth, sometimes one serving as an attendant.
article: νεανίσκος means a young man or youth, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it that way in 9 of its 10 occurrences (90%). The range is narrow: Strong's pins it at "under forty," and beyond age it can also describe a young man acting as an attendant or servant (as in Acts 5:10 and Genesis 14:24). The everyday papyri show the same flavor — one second-century document advises not to lease a house to νεανίσκοι so the owner won't be caused vexation and annoyance, while another describes a chosen band of youths.

definition: The proven character or genuineness that results from being tested, or the process of testing itself.
article: δοκιμή carries two related ideas: the actual process of testing or proving, and the tried-and-true character that results once someone passes the test. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times across 3 books, mostly in Paul's letters, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "character" (twice), "proof," and similar test-related phrases. A striking detail is its age: Moulton-Milligan notes this is a new formation of the Hellenistic era, with Paul possibly the earliest surviving author to use it, though he certainly did not invent it.
caution: The word's two senses—the process of testing versus the proven result—overlap in practice, and the lexicons assign individual verses to different categories.

definition: Ruth, the Moabite woman who became the wife of Boaz and an ancestor of King David and Jesus.
article: Ῥούθ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Ruth (רוּת), an indeclinable proper name appearing once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Matthew 1:5. The name comes from the Septuagint, where it shows up 19 times, mostly translating Ruth's own name (12×) but occasionally standing in for other Hebrew words like "mother-in-law" (4×) within her story. The digest's measured sense label of "father" is an artifact of the genealogy formula and does not reflect the name's actual meaning — this is simply a personal name.
caution: The single NT occurrence and the mislabeled "father" sense make the measured data unreliable; this is just a proper name.

definition: The womb, the organ of the body in which a child develops before birth.
article: μήτρα refers to the womb, and it is closely related to the word for "mother" (μήτηρ). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in phrases about the firstborn that "opens the womb" (Luke 2:23) or about Sarah's barren womb (Rom 4:19); in the Septuagint it occurs 28 times, usually translating the Hebrew word rechem ("womb"). Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri show the same word in a magical spell that names a person by "the womb that bore" her, reflecting how the term anchored someone to their mother.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the corpus evidence is thin, though the meaning "womb" is consistent across all the sources.

definition: A sound, balanced mind expressed through self-control and good judgment in how one acts and lives.
article: σωφροσύνη describes a healthy, well-ordered mind that shows itself in self-control and sober judgment. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 3 times, and where it gets its own English word the Majority Standard Bible always renders it "self control" (2 of 3, with the third absorbed into the phrasing). Classical and lexical sources stretch the range a bit wider: Abbott-Smith notes it can mean "soundness of mind, sanity" (opposite to madness) as well as "self-control," and the everyday papyri even use it of frugal restraint, as in an imperial edict where Julian claims he restored order by σωφροσύνη — economy and limiting expenditure.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use — and the measured "self-control" sense is narrower than the broader "sanity, soundness of mind" range the lexica record.

definition: The act of living somewhere temporarily as a foreigner, away from one's true home.
article: παροικία describes a temporary residence in a place that isn't your real home — living as a stranger or sojourner. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just twice, both rendered around the idea of a temporary "stay" (Acts 13:17, where Israel lived as foreigners in Egypt, and 1 Peter 1:17, of the believer's life on earth). The most interesting evidence comes from outside the New Testament: Moulton-Milligan notes that Psalms of Solomon 17:19 may be the earliest case of the word applied to a community temporarily sojourning in a strange land, showing this usage was Jewish before Christians adopted it.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a confidence tier rated low, the precise range of this word rests on limited evidence.

definition: A person who deals in drugs or potions, and by extension a sorcerer or magician who works with such mixtures.
article: φαρμακεύς literally points to someone who handles drugs or potions, but the lexical tradition extends it to mean a sorcerer or magician who works through such means. Abbott-Smith lists it only at Revelation 21:8, but notes this is the 'Received' reading (Rec.), meaning the more widely accepted text uses a different form there. Strong's captures the full range, from 'druggist' or 'poisoner' to 'magician,' all rooted in φάρμακον, a drug or spell-giving potion.
caution: This word does not appear in the Byzantine NT and is absent from the critical text, so its only New Testament attestation rests on a disputed textual reading.

definition: The basic building blocks or first principles of something, like the ABCs you learn before advancing further.
article: στοιχεῖον starts from the idea of things arranged in a row or series, and from there came to mean the most basic units of something — the elementary sounds or letters of the alphabet, and by extension the rudiments or first principles of any subject. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times across 4 books, rendered "basic principles" twice (as in Galatians 4:3 and Hebrews 5:12), while in 4 of those 7 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word. Tellingly, the papyri use it for the letter of the alphabet and even as a numbering label ("element 5, column 17"), showing how concrete and everyday its sense of "item in a series" was.
caution: The classical lexica note senses the New Testament data doesn't settle — material elements of the universe, heavenly bodies, even tutelary spirits — and scholars dispute which is meant in Galatians and Colossians.

definition: An adverb meaning right away, with no delay — at once, immediately, or very soon.
article: εὐθέως is an adverb signaling that something happens without delay — "immediately," "at once," or "soon." It appears 88 times in the Byzantine New Testament, clustered heavily in the narrative Gospels, where it keeps the action moving. The renderings labeled "Jesus" or "away" in the data aren't separate meanings — they're just neighboring words that got tallied alongside the adverb in fast-paced storytelling phrases. Notably, Abbott-Smith points out that Mark prefers the shorter sibling form εὐθύς, while the other Gospels favor this fuller Hellenistic spelling, which also turns up routinely in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: The senses "immediately," "at once," and "soon" overlap heavily and differ mainly in nuance, not core meaning.

definition: Cilicia, a Roman province in the south-eastern corner of Asia Minor, bordering the province of Syria.
article: Cilicia is simply a place name: a Roman province in the south-eastern corner of Asia Minor, hemmed in by the Taurus mountains and the coast and closely tied to Syria. It appears 8 times in the New Testament, always rendered "Cilicia," notably as the home region mentioned by Paul (Galatians 1:21). One charming detail from the papyri: the region's goats gave their name to a coarse hair-cloth called *cilicium*, used even in boat equipment.

definition: To reject, set aside, or treat as invalid something or someone—refusing to accept its authority or breaking faith with it.
article: ἀθετέω means to push something aside as no longer valid—whether rejecting a person, ignoring a command, or making an agreement void. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 16 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "rejects" 5 times (42%) and "set aside" twice (17%), while 4 occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The word built it from the negative particle plus a form of τίθημι ("to place"), so its core idea is "to do away with what has been laid down." Notably, in the Septuagint it translates seventeen different Hebrew words, most often בָּגַד (20×), which carries the sense of betraying or breaking faith—giving the Greek a flavor of treachery, not just polite disagreement.

definition: A personal name, Joses, borne by more than one man in the New Testament.
article: Ἰωσῆς is a proper name, "Joses," likely a variant form of Joseph. The New Testament uses it for at least two different men: a brother of Jesus (Matthew 13:55, Mark 6:3) and a son of a Mary present at the crucifixion (Mark 15:40). The other "senses" the data records—"among them were" and "among them of"—are not meanings of the name itself but just nearby translated phrases that happened to fall in the same verses. Interestingly, the name turns up in everyday Koine sources too, including a Cyrenaic inscription naming "Joses son of Crispus."
caution: This is a personal name, so its "senses" simply reflect which individual is meant; two of the three measured renderings are surrounding words rather than the name.

definition: Handed over or surrendered to someone, especially given up into another's power.
article: ἔκδοτος is an adjective meaning "given over" or "surrendered into someone's hands," built from the verb meaning "to give out." It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 2:23) and a single time in the Septuagint, where the construction is debated enough that older lexicons point readers to specialized notes. The word also turns up in everyday Koine documents: an early inscription uses it of hostages handed over to a city, and an Oxyrhynchus papyrus uses it of a bride "given out" in marriage with her dowry.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use and one Septuagint occurrence, and the meaning was absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word.

definition: A prayer or act of praying to God, and by extension a place set aside for prayer.
article: προσευχή is overwhelmingly the word for prayer addressed to God, rendered "prayer" in 32 of 37 Byzantine occurrences (97%), with the Majority Standard Bible and BSB agreeing. It carries a secondary sense the translation data doesn't capture: a designated "place of prayer," used especially by Jews (as in Acts 16:13), well attested in both papyri and inscriptions. In the Septuagint it appears 68 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew תְּפִלָּה (prayer) 37 times. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show it wasn't a purely Jewish or Christian term—one third-century letter has a father pairing his "prayers and supplications" for his newly married son.

definition: Saul, the Jewish name of the Apostle Paul before he is more often called Paul.
article: Σαῦλος is the Grecized form of the Hebrew name Saul (Σαούλ), used in the New Testament specifically for the Apostle Paul. It appears 17 times in the Byzantine text, almost always rendered simply "Saul" (15× or 88%, with the BSB agreeing 93%). A notable detail is the phrase "Saul, who is also called Paul" in Acts 13:9, which marks the shift to his better-known name; interestingly, Moulton-Milligan found no examples of Σαῦλος in the papyri name-book, though a related indeclinable form Σαῦλ shows up in a document from A.D. 514.

definition: A finger-ring, the band of metal worn on the finger.
article: δακτύλιος means a finger-ring, a band worn on the finger, and it appears just once in the New Testament — when the father in the parable tells his servants to put a ring on the returning son's hand (Luke 15:22). It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 36 times across 6 books, usually translating the Hebrew word for a ring or signet (20×). Everyday papyri confirm the ordinary sense: a will from the second century AD lists a gold ring left to the writer's daughter among a woman's ornaments.
caution: Although the word appears only once in the New Testament, its meaning is well established by abundant Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: The quality of being right and doing right in conformity to God's will, in character, thought, and action.
article: In the New Testament δικαιοσύνη overwhelmingly means "righteousness" — the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 82 of 93 occurrences (98%), and the BSB independently agrees at the same rate. The word stays remarkably consistent across the corpus, covering both moral uprightness and right standing in relation to God. One striking detail from the Septuagint: it usually translates the Hebrew words for "righteousness" and "justice" (צְדָקָה 111× and צֶדֶק 35×), but five times it stands in for חֶסֶד, the word for covenant loyalty or kindness — and it even shows up in everyday papyri and inscriptions, once as a title for Cleopatra.

definition: To set something on fire or set it ablaze, often used figuratively of being inflamed or consumed.
article: φλογίζω means to set on fire or cause to blaze, built from the noun φλόξ ("flame"). It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in James 3:6, where the tongue is described as setting the course of life on fire and itself being set ablaze. In the Septuagint it shows up three times, translating Hebrew words tied to fire and burning, and it occurs in everyday Koine documents; Moulton-Milligan note that the closely related word φλέγω turns up on a magic tablet asking to "inflame the heart," showing the word's figurative pull toward burning passion.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only twice in the New Testament (both in one verse), so confidence is low and the precise force in James 3:6 is debated.

definition: A person from Thessalonica, the Macedonian city; a Thessalonian.
article: Θεσσαλονικεύς simply names someone who comes from Thessalonica, a city in Macedonia. It appears 4 times in the New Testament, and translations split evenly: half the time it's rendered with the city name "Thessalonica" (as in Acts 20:4 and 27:2, describing where a traveling companion was from) and half the time as the people "Thessalonians" (the church addressed in 1 and 2 Thessalonians). The word is built straightforwardly from the city name Θεσσαλονίκη, so the two renderings are just different ways of pointing to the same thing — origin versus people.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the evidence is thin, though all sources agree on its meaning.

definition: A turning back toward God—a change of heart and life that the New Testament calls conversion.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 15:3), ἐπιστροφή means "conversion"—the turning of people, here Gentiles, toward God. It comes from the verb ἐπιστρέφω, "to turn around," and the Septuagint uses it literally for things like a riverbank's bend (Ezekiel 47:7) as well as more figuratively. Strikingly, everyday Koine papyri show the word meaning "attention" or "regard"—a prisoner's petition begs an official to "pay attention" to him—a sense quite different from the religious turning seen in the New Testament.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and limited Septuagint use, the word's biblical range is thinly attested.

definition: The cancelling or setting aside of something previously in force, such as a rule or command.
article: ἀθέτησις means the cancelling, annulling, or setting aside of something that was previously valid. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews (7:18 and 9:26), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once with "set" (aside) and once in the phrase translated "repeatedly." The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: Moulton-Milligan note the technical legal formula εἰς ἀθέτησιν καὶ ἀκύρωσιν, "to be annulled and cancelled," showing it was an everyday term for voiding a decree or document.
caution: With only two New Testament uses, both in Hebrews, and just one Septuagint occurrence, the evidence base is thin.

definition: An emphatic particle combining "and" with "at least" or "even," used to stress or intensify a statement.
article: καίγε is a compound particle formed from καί ("and") and γέ (an emphasizing particle), serving to add emphasis with the force of "and indeed," "at least," or "even." The lexicons give a range covering "even," "even though," and "also" (Abbott-Smith), with Strong's adding "and at least." Notably, this exact spelled-out form does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the critical text as well, so its meaning here rests entirely on its component parts and lexical tradition.
caution: This form has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so its sense is inferred from its components and lexicons rather than measured usage.

definition: To bring a formal charge against someone, accusing them of wrongdoing, especially in a legal setting.
article: ἐγκαλέω means to accuse someone or bring a charge against them, typically in a courtroom context. All 7 New Testament occurrences cluster in legal scenes, mostly in Acts where Paul faces accusations, plus Romans 8:33 ("who will bring a charge?"). Originally the word literally meant "to call in" a debt, but everyday Koine papyri show it had already specialized toward the negative sense of summoning someone to face charges—one document from 311 BC has a man stating "whatever charge he makes against Demetria."
caution: The various sense labels measured here are really one accusing/charging meaning shaped by surrounding phrasing, not genuinely distinct senses.

definition: Something detestable or disgusting, especially an object of idolatry that provokes loathing.
article: βδέλυγμα refers to something utterly repulsive or detestable, often connected with idolatry. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 6 times, rendered "abomination" in 4 of them, including the famous "abomination of desolation" in Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14. Its range is shaped overwhelmingly by the Septuagint, where it appears 104 times and mainly translates the Hebrew תּוֹעֵבָה (62×), "a detestable thing," along with terms for ritually unclean or idolatrous objects.
caution: Moulton-Milligan note this is largely a biblical and church word, with only thin everyday Koine attestation outside religious texts.

definition: To carry someone off as plunder—figuratively, to capture or rob people through deceptive teaching.
article: συλαγωγέω combines the ideas of seizing booty (σύλη) and leading away (ἄγω), so its literal sense is to carry someone off as captured plunder. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Colossians 2:8, where it is used figuratively for being captured by deceptive philosophy; the English translations absorb it into a phrase like "make spoil of" rather than rendering it with a single word. Interestingly, scholars disagree on the focus: Field argued the sense is to "rob" people of their spiritual treasures, while others (citing Heliodorus) defend the picture of the people themselves being carried off.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the evidence is thin, with sources disagreeing over whether it means robbing people or carrying them off.

definition: To burn or scorch something with intense heat, whether plants withered by the sun or people seared by fire.
article: καυματίζω means to burn or scorch up, and across its 4 New Testament appearances it points consistently to damage from intense heat. Half the time it describes seedlings scorched by the sun (Matthew 13:6, Mark 4:6), while the other two uses in Revelation describe fire scorching people. The Abbott-Smith lexicon notes the grammar nicely: in Revelation 16:8 it takes a person as object with "by fire" (ἐν πυρί), and in 16:9 the people are scorched "with great heat" (καῦμα μέγα), the very noun this verb is built from.
caution: With only 4 occurrences the evidence is thin, though all sources agree closely on the meaning.

definition: A small grammatical particle that signals something is hypothetical or conditional, marking what would, might, or could happen rather than what definitely does.
article: ἄν is not really a word you can translate on its own; it's a marker that makes a statement contingent—signaling "would," "might," or "whoever/whatever" depending on the surrounding grammar. Its range in the Byzantine NT is wide, with 174 occurrences spread across many renderings, and notably 62 of those (more than a third) get absorbed into the English phrasing with no word of their own. The most telling evidence is how varied its job is: in the Septuagint it stands in for several different Hebrew words, including אֲשֶׁר (31×) and עַד (28×), reflecting that it shapes meaning rather than carrying its own.
caution: Because ἄν has no fixed English equivalent, its many measured "senses" are really translation by-products of grammar, not distinct meanings, and the BSB itself disagrees on several renderings (as low as 25% agreement for "if").

definition: Good in nature or quality—whether morally upright, beneficial, or pleasing—the broadest, most general word for "good."
article: ἀγαθός is the all-purpose word for "good," covering both the physical sense (good soil, a good tree) and the moral sense (a good heart, good works). The Byzantine New Testament uses it 101 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "good" in 73% of cases, with most of the rest being noun phrases like "good things" or "what is good." In the Septuagint it appears over 400 times, almost always translating Hebrew טוֹב (tov), and an interesting wrinkle is its use in everyday papyri and inscriptions: Nero is hailed as ἀγαθὸς θεός ("good god"), and the phrase ἀγαθὸς δαίμων ("good spirit") was common.

definition: To bring someone completely under your control, reducing them to slavery or total subjection.
article: This verb means to enslave someone utterly or bring them into complete bondage. In the New Testament it appears only twice (Galatians 2:4 and 2 Corinthians 11:20), where it describes people being subjected to control, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "enslave" every time it surfaces as a distinct word. A striking witness comes from the papyri: a 4th–5th century AD magical invocation summons a deity to "subdue" and "enslave" the whole human race, showing the word's force of total domination in everyday Koine.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences—one of which is absorbed into surrounding phrasing—the evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: A violent rushing motion or forceful onset—the sudden, powerful surge of something being thrown or attacking.
article: This word describes a violent rush or forceful onset, derived from ὁρμή (impulse, drive). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 18:21, where an angel hurls a stone into the sea, and the Berean Bibles render it with the idea of a violent "cast." Interestingly, in its 6 Septuagint appearances it usually translates the Hebrew עֶבְרָה (overflowing wrath or fury), and Moulton-Milligan note that scholar R.H. Charles argued the Revelation sense should likewise be "indignation" rather than "rush."
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with disputed meaning—sources split between a physical "rush/onset" and an emotional "indignation," so confidence is low.

definition: To show favoritism, treating some people better than others based on who they are rather than fairness.
article: This verb means to play favorites — to give some people special treatment or undue partiality. It appears only once in the New Testament, in James 2:9, where favoritism is named as sin. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that this word and its two related nouns never appear in the Greek Old Testament and may be among the earliest distinctly Christian words; it grew out of the Hebrew idiom 'to lift the face' on someone, meaning to be favorable to them.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and does not appear in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: To commit adultery — to have sexual relations with someone other than one's own spouse, said of either a husband or a wife.
article: This verb means to commit adultery, and in the New Testament it applies to both men and women — Mark 10:11 uses it of the husband and 10:12 of the wife. The Byzantine text has it 6 times across just 2 books (Matthew and Mark), all in Jesus' teaching on divorce, though the SBL critical text reads it nowhere. The various Majority Standard Bible renderings — "commits adultery," "whoever adultery," simply "adultery" — all reflect the same single meaning; the differences are just phrasing within the verse. Notably, Moulton-Milligan cites Wackernagel's view that this form belonged to a coarser, more everyday layer of Hellenistic Greek than the related noun μοιχαλίς.
caution: The word appears only in the Byzantine text and not in the SBL critical text, and the four listed "senses" are really one meaning split by translation phrasing.

definition: A nation or people group; in the New Testament especially the non-Jewish peoples, the Gentiles.
article: ἔθνος is the standard word for a nation or people group, but in the New Testament it most often points to the non-Jewish world: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Gentiles" 87 times (54%) and "nations" 67 times (42%). The same word can describe Israel itself as a people, so context decides whether it means "the nations at large" or specifically "the Gentiles outside the Jewish community." Strikingly, this word appears 741 times in the Septuagint, where it usually translates Hebrew גּוֹי (450×), and in everyday papyri it could even mean a Roman province, as in an imperial rescript of A.D. 198–201.

definition: Describing words that are made up or fabricated in order to deceive someone.
article: πλαστός literally means "molded" or "shaped" (it comes from πλάσσω, to form), but figuratively it describes something made up or counterfeit. In its single New Testament appearance (2 Peter 2:3), it describes the "deceptive" or fabricated words false teachers use to exploit people, and both the Majority Standard Bible and Berean Standard Bible render it that way 100% of the time. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: a papyrus from AD 186 uses πλαστός for a forged contract, while another from AD 137 keeps the literal sense, describing a vineyard enclosed by a "mud wall."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured biblical range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To point something out so others can see it, or to give a warning by making a coming danger known.
article: ὑποδείκνυμι means to bring something into view — to show, point out, or make known — and by extension to warn someone by showing them what lies ahead. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times, split between plain 'show' (as in Luke 12:5 and Acts 20:35) and 'warn' (Matthew 3:7, Luke 3:7, where John warns of coming wrath). The everyday Koine papyri confirm both halves of this range: one document begs an official to 'look into the matters indicated,' while another asks someone to 'inform' a visitor about his business.
caution: The several 'measured senses' here are really just different surrounding phrases for the same two core uses — showing and warning — so the count overstates the variety.

definition: Salmon, a man in the Old Testament genealogies, son of Nahshon and father of Boaz, listed among Jesus' ancestors.
article: Σαλμών is simply the personal name Salmon, an Israelite who appears in the genealogies of Jesus. It occurs 3 times across the Byzantine New Testament and is always rendered "Salmon." The Greek form is indeclinable and comes directly from the Hebrew name שַׂלְמוֹן, which the Septuagint also represents twice; some manuscripts at Luke 3:32 read the variant form Σαλά instead.
caution: This is a proper name with only a few occurrences and a known textual variant (Σαλά) at Luke 3:32, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: Made of thorns; describing something woven or formed from thorny branches.
article: This adjective means "made of thorns" and appears just twice in the New Testament, both times describing the crown of thorns placed on Jesus' head (Mark 15:17 and John 19:5). It is built from the noun ἄκανθα, "thorn." The Septuagint uses it once, at Isaiah 34:13, where it renders a Hebrew word for thorny growth, and Abbott-Smith notes a second classical sense — "of acantha-wood" — found in Herodotus and the papyri, though that sense does not appear in the biblical text.
caution: Evidence is thin (only two New Testament uses) and the classical "acantha-wood" sense is not attested in Scripture, so the biblical range is narrow.

definition: To press someone with sharp questions, trying to make them speak out and commit themselves on the spot.
article: This rare verb describes the act of barraging someone with questions to provoke them into saying something incriminating. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 11:53, where the scribes and Pharisees begin to interrogate Jesus aggressively. There's a notable shift in meaning over time: in classical Greek the word meant to dictate or recite from memory (a teacher having pupils repeat lessons), while in later Greek it took on the sense of hostile cross-examination, which is how Luke uses it.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and its exact force in Luke 11:53 is debated, since the hostile-questioning sense has thin parallels.

definition: The state of being complete, fully developed, or mature.
article: τελειότης is an abstract noun meaning completeness or maturity, the finished state of something. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the two translation choices reflect its context rather than two different meanings: in Colossians 3:14 love is the bond of "completeness" (rendered as relating to virtues), and in Hebrews 6:1 it marks the maturity that lies beyond "elementary" teaching. In the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew word for blameless integrity (tāmîm), and Moulton-Milligan note it even turns up in a magical papyrus referring to a "compelling emanation of perfection."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the renderings driven by context, the precise sense in each passage is hard to pin down.

definition: Cinnamon, the fragrant spice from tree bark, used as a costly trade good and perfume.
article: Κινάμωμον is simply cinnamon, the aromatic spice and trade commodity. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Revelation 18:13, where it is folded into the listing of luxury cargo) and four times in the Septuagint, three of which render the Hebrew קִנָּמוֹן. The word is borrowed from a foreign source — Herodotus calls it Phoenician — and Moulton-Milligan shows it turning up in everyday Koine, as in a third-century B.C. inscription mentioning "two minas of cinnamon."
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament (a single occurrence) and the spelling varies between κινάμωμον and κιννάμωμον across manuscripts.

definition: A preposition meaning without, apart from, or in the absence of someone or something.
article: ἄτερ is a preposition meaning "without" or "apart from," taking a genitive object. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke (22:6 and 22:35), and just once in the Septuagint (2 Maccabees 12:15). Originally a poetic word, it turns up in everyday Koine documents too—a Priene inscription uses ἄτερ ὀψωνίον, "without salary," and a papyrus letter describes a cobbler refusing to hand things over ἄτερ Ἰούστου, "without Justus."
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences—so the measured sense breakdown reflects the specific contexts rather than the word's full range.

definition: A spoken defense, especially the kind of reply or argument someone makes to answer a charge or justify their position.
article: ἀπολογία means a defense — a reply made to answer an accusation or to justify oneself, often in a legal setting like a courtroom. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "defense" in 38% of its 8 New Testament occurrences, and the lexicons agree, defining it as "a speech in defence," sometimes with the person addressed or used after the preposition πρός. The everyday papyri confirm this courtroom flavor: one fourth-century document uses it for evidence brought "to the tribunal," while a related form even shows a weakened sense meaning a simple written "record" or accounting of sheep.
caution: The word appears only 8 times in the New Testament and just once in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on a fairly small body of evidence.

definition: A Greek silver coin worth two drachmas, used to pay the annual Jewish Temple tax (about a half-shekel).
article: The δίδραχμον was a silver coin worth two drachmas, named simply by combining the words for "two" and "drachma." In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Matthew 17:24, where it refers to the annual Temple tax that worshippers paid; the BSB renders one instance as the coin itself ("drachma") and the other as the act of paying it ("pay two drachmas"). In the Septuagint it shows up 26 times, mostly translating the Hebrew shekel, and Moulton-Milligan note that everyday papyri record a tax of the same amount paid to the Egyptian temple of the god Suchus.
caution: Only two New Testament occurrences exist, both in a single verse, so confidence about its full range in biblical usage is low.

definition: Active power at work—energy that produces visible effects, attributed in the New Testament to God or to Satan.
article: ἐνέργεια describes power that is actually operating and producing results, not merely potential strength. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "working" in 4 of 8 occurrences (57%) and "power" in 2 (29%), with BSB agreeing 100% in both cases. Abbott-Smith notes it specifically means "operative power" as distinct from δύναμις (potential power), and Dodson observes that in the New Testament it is confined to superhuman activity—God's at work in Ephesians and Philippians, Satan's in 2 Thessalonians. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan finds the same divine-power sense in a third-century inscription speaking of "the working of the god Zeus."
caution: With only 8 occurrences, the split between "working" and "power" reflects subtle translation choices rather than two sharply separate meanings.

definition: For a long time, since long ago; describing something established or set in motion in the distant past.
article: This is an adverb meaning "for a long time" or "from of old," pointing back to something settled in the distant past. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Peter (2:3 and 3:5), and is one of those compound adverbs common in later Greek. Everyday papyri confirm the sense nicely: an Oxyrhynchus letter uses it to scold someone who "had been long ago instructed" to send baskets of hay. Note that the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "deliberately" in one place and absorbs it into the phrasing in the other, which leans more on context than the word's basic "long ago" meaning shown in the older lexicons.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and the MSB rendering "deliberately" departing from the lexicons' plain "from of old," confidence is low and the range is thinly attested.

definition: Describing something old, ancient, or worn out by use, as opposed to what is new or fresh.
article: παλαιός means "old" — covering both age and the wear that comes from long use. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 19 times, rendered "old" in 15 cases (79%) and as part of the phrase "old self" in 3 cases (16%), as in Romans 6:6 and Ephesians 4:22. Abbott-Smith notes it stands opposite to νέος and καινός ("new"), and the everyday papyri sharpen the "worn" nuance: one document contrasts old, previously-gathered dates with fresh new ones, and another mentions "the old cushion" in the dining-room. In the Septuagint it commonly translates the Hebrew word for something aged or worn (יָשָׁן, 8 times).

definition: To use clever scheming or trickery against someone in order to outwit or take advantage of them.
article: This verb describes using cunning or cleverness against someone, scheming to outsmart or get the better of them. It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 7:19), where it is quoted directly from the Septuagint of Exodus 1:10, and there it translates a Hebrew word meaning 'to be wise' or 'act shrewdly' — here turned to a hostile, manipulative purpose. Moulton-Milligan note that the word also shows up in ordinary everyday Koine papyri, so it was familiar outside the Bible.
caution: Evidence is thin: it occurs only once in the New Testament (a quotation from the Septuagint) and only a handful of times in the Greek scriptures overall.

definition: To warm or keep warm, used figuratively to mean caring for someone tenderly, nurturing, or comforting them.
article: θάλπω literally means to warm or heat, but in the New Testament it always carries the figurative sense of caring for someone tenderly. It appears only twice — once where a husband "cherishes" his own body (Ephesians 5:29) and once describing a nurse being "gentle" with her children (1 Thessalonians 2:7). The most striking parallel comes from the papyri: a marriage contract where a husband promises to love, cherish (θάλπειν), and care for his wife, showing this was everyday language for tender devotion.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and an overall low confidence rating, the precise shading between "cherish" and "gentle" rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Knowledge—the understanding or awareness someone has, especially of spiritual or divine truth.
article: γνῶσις means knowledge or understanding, and in the New Testament it usually carries a spiritual sense—the knowing of God, salvation, or divine truth. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "knowledge" in 24 of 29 occurrences (89%), and that one sense covers nearly all its biblical uses. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew דַּעַת ("knowledge"). Everyday Koine papyri show a broader, more practical range: in one document it means the body of expertise the ancient Egyptians handed down, and in legal papyri it can even mean the "decision" of a lawsuit.

definition: Complete and sound in every part, whole and undamaged—used of someone fully intact in body and character.
article: ὁλόκληρος describes something that is whole and intact, lacking nothing in any of its parts. It appears just 2 times in the New Testament, in both cases blended into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word; in James 1:4 it pairs with τέλειοι ("complete and perfect"). The everyday papyri are revealing: the word is common for material soundness, as in a reference to a "complete house" (P Lond 935) and to bringing back a survey of dykes and canals to completion, showing its plain sense of physical wholeness before it took on an ethical meaning in the New Testament.
caution: Confidence is low: with only 2 New Testament occurrences—both absorbed into phrasing—and a small Septuagint sample, its precise force here rests largely on outside evidence.

definition: Lacking reason — either an unreasonable, illogical action or a creature that acts on instinct rather than thought.
article: The word literally combines "without" (a-) and "reason/word" (logos), so it means something done or existing without rational thought. In the New Testament it covers a small range: once it describes an unreasonable action (Acts 25:27), and twice it labels creatures as "irrational animals" acting purely on instinct (2 Peter 2:12; Jude 1:10). The everyday Koine papyri show the adverb form vividly — one writer says a garment "was taken without cause," capturing the sense of something happening with no good reason.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences split evenly across two related senses, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on the overall meaning.

definition: A complete overturning that destroys something, whether a literal demolition of cities or the ruin and upsetting of people who hear empty words.
article: καταστροφή describes a violent overturning that leaves destruction behind. In the two New Testament uses it covers both the literal sense — the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah — and a figurative one, the ruin worked among people through quarreling over words. It is the source of our English word "catastrophe," and a papyrus inscription even uses it for a sudden death, memorializing a woman whose death "cut short the marriage."
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word, and one of those (2 Peter 2:6) is omitted in some critical texts.

definition: To lead or bring someone or something out from one place to another, such as out of a city, prison, or country.
article: ἐξάγω literally means to lead or bring out, and across its 13 New Testament uses the rendering stays remarkably stable—"led out," "led," or "leads them out" cover three quarters of the cases. It's a workaday word: the Septuagint uses it 206 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew verb יָצָא ("to go out"), often for God bringing Israel out of Egypt. One vivid detail from the papyri is that this verb was used for leading someone out of prison—an Egyptian document from 114 B.C. even uses it of a prisoner who had escaped.

definition: A ship or boat of any size, used for travel or transport on water.
article: Ναῦς is the classic Greek word for a ship, found freely in literary Koine writers and everyday papyri alike — one Zeno letter and a business document both use it for an ordinary vessel. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 27:41, where the ship runs aground; everywhere else the NT prefers the word πλοῖον. The Septuagint uses it 14 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for ship (אֳנִי) and the related אֳנִיָּה.
caution: The single NT occurrence makes its New Testament range thin, and the digest's measured rendering 'struck' reflects the verb of the verse rather than the noun itself, which simply means 'ship.'

definition: To shine or be clear like crystal, sparkling with transparent brilliance.
article: This rare verb describes something gleaming with the transparent clarity of crystal. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:11, where it pictures the radiance of the holy city. The lexicons agree it means "to shine like crystal" or "be crystal-clear," and it comes from the noun κρύσταλλος (crystal).
