caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its precise range cannot be confirmed from usage; note the measured "most" reflects translation phrasing rather than the word's meaning.

definition: To make thick or fat, used figuratively of a heart that grows dull, callous, and unable to respond.
article: Literally παχύνω means to thicken or fatten, but in the New Testament it appears only twice (Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27), both times figuratively of a heart that has "grown gross" or become unfeeling—and in both cases it's absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. The Septuagint uses it 5 times across 4 books, mostly translating the Hebrew שָׁמַן ("to be fat"), keeping that same image of physical thickness standing for spiritual dullness. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show the word in its plain medical sense: it turns up in a (badly damaged) medical prescription, confirming "thicken" as the literal background.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 Byzantine occurrences (none in the critical text) and both folded into phrasing, so the figurative sense rests on a small sample.

definition: A maker or builder who designs and constructs something, used in the New Testament for God as the builder of the heavenly city.
article: δημιουργός literally combines "people" (δῆμος) and "work" (ἔργον), originally meaning one who works for the public, and it broadened to mean a craftsman, builder, or maker. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:10, where it describes God as the builder of the city Abraham looked forward to. Abbott-Smith notes a subtle distinction in that verse: a related word (τεχνίτης) points to the plan, while δημιουργός points to carrying it out. The papyri show the word in everyday use and even in early Christian prayers, where God is called both "almighty" and δημιουργός.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "looking" reflects the surrounding verse rather than the word's actual meaning of "builder."

definition: A male, used of humans or animals to mark the male sex.
article: ἄῤῥην simply means "male," applied to people and animals alike to distinguish the male sex from the female. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 6 books, rendered "male" in 5 of those cases and absorbed into phrasing in 3 others; the Septuagint uses it 52 times, most often (41×) for the Hebrew זָכָר ("male"). A nice glimpse of its everyday use comes from a papyrus from 1 B.C. giving instructions about a birth: "if it is male, let it live; if it is female, expose it" — showing the word's plain, practical sense in ordinary Koine.
caution: The word has two spellings (ἄῤῥην and ἄρσην) that vary across manuscripts, and it does not appear in the SBLGNT critical text.

definition: To think too highly of yourself; to be arrogant or overly proud.
senseLabels: to think too highly of oneself
article: This verb describes having an inflated opinion of yourself — being conceited or proud beyond what is warranted. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 12:3, where Paul plays on words by warning against thinking of yourself more highly than you ought to think. Outside the NT it shows up in 4 Maccabees and everyday Koine papyri, and classical writers also used it in a second sense — to look down on or think slightly of something — though that meaning does not appear in the New Testament.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests entirely on a single verse.

definition: The braiding or elaborate plaiting of hair as a form of adornment.
article: ἐμπλοκή refers to the braiding or plaiting of hair, used as a form of personal adornment. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:3, where it is rendered "adornment," and is built from the verb ἐμπλέκω (to weave in or entwine). Interestingly, the papyri show this word with a quite different everyday meaning of "struggle" or "scuffle" — one document describes a woman losing a golden ear-ring "in the struggle" — while an inscription regarding the mysteries of Demeter parallels the New Testament's concern with braided hair.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical sense rests on a single verse, and the papyri attest a separate meaning ("struggle") not found there.

definition: Peter, the personal name of the apostle Simon, a Greek word that literally means "rock" or "stone."
article: Πέτρος is almost always simply the name of the apostle Peter, used that way in 153 of its occurrences (99%) across the Byzantine New Testament, with a couple more cases where it identifies who is speaking. The name itself means "rock" or "stone," larger than the ordinary λίθος, and the lexica connect it to the noun πέτρα. A nice detail: the name Peter shows up in everyday Koine papyri, including early Christian letters addressing "my lord brother Peter," showing it was a real personal name in circulation, not just a New Testament label.

definition: A small Greek particle that flags a word or clause as the first of a pair, usually setting it against something that follows.
article: μέν is one of Greek's little signpost words: it marks the clause it sits in as the first half of a pairing, typically answered later by δέ ("this one... but that one"). It is so dependent on context that it is genuinely untranslatable — in the Byzantine New Testament it absorbs into the surrounding phrasing 136 of its 194 times, with no English word of its own. When it does surface, translators render it all sorts of ways ("is," "indeed," "one," "they," "with," "there"), and notably the BSB agrees 0% of the time on the "indeed" renderings, showing how loosely it maps to English. Moulton-Milligan even cites an everyday papyrus letter (BGU II.423) where μέν stands alone in a greeting, "first of all I pray that you are well."
caution: The measured "senses" here are mostly translation artifacts of how μέν gets folded into English clauses, not distinct meanings, and the lexica agree it is essentially untranslatable, so treat the sense labels loosely.

definition: A healing or cure—the result of being made well, often used in the plural for acts of healing.
article: ἴαμα refers to a healing or cure—the actual effect of being made well rather than the process. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in 1 Corinthians 12, where Paul speaks of "gifts of healing" using the plural form. The word has a rich life outside the Bible: the inscription heading from Epidaurus literally lists the "cures" (Ἰάματα) worked by Apollo and Asclepius at their healing shrine, showing how naturally Greeks used this word for documented recoveries. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew מַרְפֵּא, meaning a remedy or healing.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences, all from one chapter—and Abbott-Smith notes classical Greek more often used it for "a means of healing" rather than the healing itself.

definition: The basic connector that links words, phrases, and sentences together, most often meaning "and."
article: This is the workhorse connecting word of the New Testament, appearing 9,203 times across all 27 books and overwhelmingly meaning "and" (5,848 times where it gets its own English word). It connects single words, numbers, whole clauses, and strings of sentences one after another. About a third of the time (3,353 occurrences) it disappears into the phrasing with no English word of its own, because translators often smooth it out. Interestingly, scholars note its piling-up style of "and... and... and" is a hallmark of plain, popular Koine — the same pattern shows up in everyday papyri like a recorded dream from the Serapeum dated to 160 BC.

definition: The outward look or appearance of someone or something.
article: Ἰδέα refers to how something looks—its visible appearance or aspect. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 28:3, where the angel's "appearance" was like lightning, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way 100% of the time. In everyday Koine papyri it could even mean "quality," as in a document describing linen cushions "of the same quality," and in modern Greek the word has shifted to mean "thought" or "idea."
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine NT (and not at all in the critical text), so its New Testament range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A bird, and specifically a hen or domestic fowl that gathers her chicks under her wings.
article: ὄρνις is a general word for a bird, but by New Testament times it had narrowed to mean a hen or domestic fowl, much as English "fowl" once did. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in Jesus' lament over Jerusalem where he compares himself to a hen gathering her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34). The papyri confirm this everyday sense vividly: the word shows up in food and provision accounts, such as a Tebtunis text simply listing "2 birds."
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences and four in the Septuagint — and the measured rendering data here is unclear, so lean on the lexica and papyri for the hen/fowl sense.

definition: An established custom, habit, or practice — sometimes verging on a prescribed law or rite.
article: ἔθος refers to a settled way of doing things — a custom or habit — and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "customs" in 5 of 11 occurrences (50%) and in phrases like "according to custom" 4 times (40%). In several passages, especially in Luke and Acts (such as Acts 6:14, 15:1, and 21:21), Abbott-Smith notes the word shades into the narrower sense of "law." The everyday flavor of the word shows in the papyri, where phrases like κατὰ τὸ ἔθος ("according to custom") appear in ordinary financial and legal documents from the first century onward.

definition: The ground or floor — the solid surface beneath one's feet.
article: ἔδαφος means the ground, soil, or bottom surface — the solid base under your feet. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 22:7, where Paul falls to the ground, and it is rendered "ground" in every count. The everyday papyri give it a vivid concrete flavor: leases and petitions use ἔδαφος for plots of land, vineyards, and (in the plural) "lands" to be irrigated, showing it was ordinary language for cultivated soil and property.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Service performed on behalf of others, whether a religious ministry, priestly duty, or charitable giving for the public good.
article: λειτουργία covers service rendered for others, ranging from priestly and ritual ministrations (Luke 1:23) to acts of Christian generosity (2 Corinthians 9:12). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "service" in all 4 of its translated occurrences, with 2 of the 6 total absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In classical Greek the word originally meant discharging a public office at one's own expense, but in the Septuagint it shifted toward religious service, most often translating Hebrew עֲבֹדָה (35 of 43 times); papyri show it used of Egyptian priestly duties as well.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences, the word's full range—from secular public duty to priestly ritual to charitable gift—rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than the NT itself.

definition: The genitive form of "the rest/remaining," used adverbially to mean "from now on" or "henceforth."
article: This is the genitive singular form (τοῦ λοιποῦ) of the broader word λοιπός, which means "the rest" or "remaining." In this specific case form it works as a time expression — "from now on," "henceforth" — understood with the implied word χρόνου ("time"). Abbott-Smith notes it carries this future-time sense in Galatians 6:17 and Ephesians 6:10, where Paul uses it to mean "for the rest of the time" going forward.
caution: This form appears 0 times in the Byzantine NT and only twice in the critical text, so the evidence for this exact spelling is thin.

definition: Not clearly visible or recognizable; either hidden from notice or sounding unclear and indistinct.
article: ἄδηλος combines the negative prefix with δῆλος ("clear, evident"), so it describes something that fails to be obvious. In its two New Testament occurrences it splits evenly between two shades of meaning: hidden from sight, as with unmarked graves people walk over without knowing (Luke 11:44), and indistinct in sound, like a trumpet giving an unclear call (1 Corinthians 14:8). The everyday Koine papyri use it the same practical way, speaking of an "uncertain" inheritance or the "uncertainty" of a journey.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base for this word is thin.

definition: The rich, oily fatness of a plant — specifically the nourishing sap that flows through an olive tree's roots.
article: Πιότης describes the fatness or oily richness of a plant, the nourishing life it draws up through its roots. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 11:17, where Paul pictures a wild branch sharing in the richness of an olive tree's root. In the Septuagint it shows up 12 times across 7 books, most often translating the Hebrew דָּ֫שֶׁן ("fatness," 5×), and a striking parallel from the Testament of Levi speaks of an olive branch "of fatness" (πιότητος).
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests largely on Septuagint and other Koine usage rather than New Testament evidence.

definition: Achim, a man listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Zadok and father of Eliud.
article: Ἀχείμ is simply the personal name Achim, a man appearing in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. According to the digest, he was the son of Zadok and the father of Eliud, and the name occurs only in Matthew 1:14. The lexica (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree it is a proper name, probably of Hebrew origin (compare H03137). One quirk in the measured data: of its 2 Byzantine occurrences, one was rendered as "Zadok" rather than "Achim," which likely reflects how the surrounding genealogical text was tabulated rather than a true second meaning.
caution: Evidence is thin (only Matthew 1:14) and confidence is low; the "Zadok" rendering appears to be a tabulation artifact, since the name itself only ever means Achim.

definition: To sail slowly, making little progress, especially when struggling against the wind.
article: This is a compound word from "slow" (βραδύς) and "sail" (πλέω), and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:7. The measured rendering picks up the place name "Cnidus" from that verse, but the word itself describes the slow sailing of Paul's ship as it labored along. Moulton-Milligan notes that one scholar suggested it may be a technical sailing term for working to windward by tacking, though in Artemidorus (2nd century AD) it simply means making a slow voyage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance — ordinary slow sailing versus a technical tacking maneuver — cannot be settled from the evidence.

definition: A journey made by ship across the sea; a voyage.
article: πλόος refers simply to a voyage or trip by sea. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Acts (21:7; 27:9, 10), and is consistently rendered "voyage." The word was common in everyday Koine: papyri and inscriptions record sailings to Egypt and even a merchant who reportedly made seventy-two voyages, showing it was the ordinary term for a sea journey rather than anything specialized.

definition: A female disciple or follower, the feminine form of the word for a male disciple.
article: μαθήτρια is the feminine counterpart of μαθητής ("disciple"), meaning a woman who follows or learns from a teacher. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 9:36, where it describes Tabitha (Dorcas). Beyond Scripture, Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and in the later Gospel of Peter the term is applied to Mary Magdalene.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range within the biblical text cannot be confidently measured.

definition: To finish putting things in order, setting right what still remains to be arranged or corrected.
article: This verb means to bring something to fuller order — to set right what is left unfinished or still needs arranging. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:5, where Titus is told to complete what was left undone, and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering captures this idea of finishing the job. Beyond the Bible, Moulton-Milligan note the same verb in an inscription about a council voting to 'set in order, remove, or add' matters for the common good, showing it was ordinary administrative language for tidying up arrangements.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on that single verse plus a handful of inscriptions.

definition: To set something on fire or burn it up, such as a city or building.
article: This verb means to set something ablaze and destroy it by fire. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Matthew 22:7, where a king burns a city, and it's missing from the SBLGNT critical text. The word is well-attested in everyday Koine: the Septuagint uses it 25 times (mostly for Hebrew שָׂרַף, "to burn"), and the papyri show real-life examples like burning stores of wheat or torching a house on purpose. One related lexical note: Abbott-Smith records a passive sense "to become inflamed" of the body in Acts 28:6, though that text more likely reflects the variant form πίμπρημι.
caution: With only one Byzantine occurrence and a disputed form overlapping with πίμπρημι, the evidence for this exact lemma is thin.

definition: Describing a person who is unlearned, untaught, or lacking in knowledge.
article: ἀμαθής describes someone without learning or instruction — literally "untaught," built from a negative prefix plus the verb "to learn." It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 3:16, where it pairs with "unstable" to describe people who twist Scripture. The lexica gloss it as "unlearned" or "ignorant," yet Moulton-Milligan notes it is oddly rare in biblical Greek, with related words like ἰδιώτης taking its place; they cite a third-century BC Epidaurus inscription using the related noun ἀμαθία for a votive silver pig.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the Septuagint, so its biblical range rests on a single verse; note also that the digest's single rendering 'hard' does not match the standard gloss 'unlearned.'

definition: To restrain or hold oneself back from something, taking care to avoid it.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament στέλλω appears only twice, both times in the middle voice meaning to restrain oneself, withdraw, or steer clear of something—as in avoiding any criticism (2 Corinthians 8:20) and keeping away from disorderly believers (2 Thessalonians 3:6). The word's root sense is to set, place, or arrange, and the everyday papyri show it commonly meaning to send (for instance, P Oxy 1843 mentions linen garments "sent me"). Notably, the seafaring world used it of furling or shortening sails (Homer), and from that image of drawing things in came the New Testament sense of pulling oneself back.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 New Testament occurrences (and none in the critical SBLGNT text), so the range here rests on a very small sample.

definition: Suddenly, without warning; describing something that happens unexpectedly and all at once.
article: This adverb means "suddenly" — something happening without warning. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, all in Acts, and every translation renders it the same way: the rushing wind at Pentecost (Acts 2:2), the earthquake that frees Paul and Silas (Acts 16:26), and the moment islanders watch Paul shake off a snake (Acts 28:6). In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times and most often translates the Hebrew word פִּתְאוֹם, which itself means "suddenly," confirming the consistent sense across both Greek and Hebrew evidence.
caution: The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, so the evidence base is thin, though all sources agree firmly on its meaning.

definition: A two-word combination ("not anyone") used to ask whether anyone or anything is the case, often expecting a negative answer.
article: μήτις is really the negative particle μή joined to the indefinite pronoun τὶς, written as one word in some older printed texts but treated as two words (μή τις) by modern editors. It functions in questions, where it signals "whether anyone" or expects the answer "no," sometimes carried only by the questioning tone of the sentence rather than a separate translated word. A nice everyday example survives in a papyrus from 13 B.C. (BGU IV.1141), where a writer says he asks the doorkeeper daily "whether anyone has slept outside" — showing the same construction in ordinary indirect questions.
caution: The evidence digest records zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament and notes that grammarians treat it as the two separate words μή τις, so its status as a distinct "word" is disputed.

definition: To shine or give off light, whether physically gleaming or figuratively radiating brightness.
article: λάμπω means to shine or beam with light, and the New Testament uses it both for literal brilliance—Jesus' face shining at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:2) or the angel's light filling Peter's cell (Acts 12:7)—and figuratively for letting one's good works shine before others (Matthew 5:16). The Majority Standard Bible's renderings cluster evenly around "light," "shine," and "shone," all describing the same basic action of radiating brightness. A vivid parallel comes from an inscription over a church built on a former pagan temple site, which proclaims that "saving light shone (ἔλαμψεν) where darkness had covered"—strikingly close to Paul's language in 2 Corinthians 4:6.

definition: The heart as the inner center of a person—where thoughts, feelings, will, and moral and spiritual life all reside.
article: In the Greek New Testament καρδία almost always points to the inner person rather than the physical organ—the seat of thought, emotion, and will, the core of who someone is morally and spiritually. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "hearts" in 153 of 159 cases (100% of the times it gets an English word at all), with the remaining 6 simply folded into phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears a remarkable 767 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew words lev and levav, the same Hebrew terms for the inner self. A vivid trace of its everyday use shows up in the papyri, where the word pairs with "soul" (psychē) in love charms and curse tablets, echoing Jesus' command to love God "with all your heart and soul."

definition: Without sound or voice—mute, silent, or producing speech that carries no meaning.
article: Ἄφωνος literally means "voiceless," built from the negative prefix and φωνή ("voice, sound"). In its 4 New Testament uses the sense splits between literal muteness—a lamb silent before its shearers (Acts 8:32, echoing Isaiah 53:7), and Balaam's donkey speaking against natural mutness (2 Peter 2:16)—and the figurative idea of sound without meaning, as in Paul's note that no language is truly "voiceless" or unintelligible (1 Corinthians 14:10). Strikingly, the word was applied to dumb idols (1 Corinthians 12:2), and Moulton-Milligan cite a Galatian inscription where a once-"voiceless" marble pillar is made to "speak" through its carved words; it survives even in Modern Greek.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and the Majority Standard often absorbing the word into surrounding phrasing, the measured sense labels are rough and don't fully capture the plain "mute" meaning that the lexicons emphasize.

definition: A feeding trough or stall where animals eat, especially the manger where the infant Jesus was laid.
article: φάτνη refers to a feeding trough for animals, and by extension the stall or stable area where they were kept. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, all in Luke: rendered "manger" 3 times (the famous birth narrative in Luke 2) and "stall" once in Luke 13:15. The everyday character of the word is confirmed by Koine papyri, including a third-century BC document (P Lille I.17) that literally mentions putting grain "in one manger."
caution: Moulton-Milligan notes a scholar (Cadbury, 1926) argued φάτνη may instead be an open-air feeding place rather than a stall, so the precise setting is somewhat debated.

definition: Sweat, the perspiration produced by the body, especially under strain or distress.
article: ἱδρώς simply means sweat or perspiration. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 22:44, describing Jesus in the garden, and the Septuagint uses it for the Hebrew word זֵעַת ("sweat") in Genesis 3:19. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, where Moulton-Milligan even spot it possibly meaning "sweaters" (sweat-cloths or garments) in commercial documents.
caution: Evidence is thin (a single NT occurrence, omitted in some critical editions), and the digest's measured rendering "earnestly" reflects translation of the surrounding phrase rather than the word itself, which means "sweat."

definition: A question-particle that signals the speaker expects a negative answer, like asking "surely this isn't...?" or "can it be...?"
article: μήτι is a Greek interrogative particle that usually has no direct English word of its own — it shapes the whole question to expect the answer "no." Built from μή ("not") plus the neuter of τις ("any"), it shows up 20 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and in 6 of those it simply gets absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by a single word. In hesitant questions like "Could this be the Christ?" (John 4:29) it softens to a tentative "could"; in the phrase εἰ μήτι it can mean "unless" (Luke 9:13). Its sole Septuagint appearance translates the Hebrew yaqqîr.
caution: The translation choices vary widely because μήtι carries tone rather than fixed meaning, so any single English rendering is approximate; even the standard reference works point readers to a special discussion of how to translate it.

definition: To agree with something, admitting or consenting that it is right or true.
article: σύμφημι is built from σύν ("with") and φημί ("to say"), so it literally means "to say along with" — to voice agreement or admit that something is so. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Romans 7:16, where Paul admits that the law is good. The classical lexica add a slightly broader range, listing "consent" and "confess" alongside "agree."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: The quality of being like or resembling something else; a similarity or correspondence between things.
article: ὁμοιότης means likeness or resemblance — the state of one thing being similar to another. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, both inside the fixed phrase καθ᾽ ὁμοιότητα, which the lexica explain as meaning "in like manner" or "after the likeness of" (Hebrews 4:15; 7:15). Everyday Koine papyri use exactly this phrase in a weakened sense of "in the same way as," as when a legal petition asks for treatment "after the likeness of others" — showing it was ordinary administrative language, not just a biblical term.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the New Testament and always within one set phrase, so its independent meaning is hard to isolate.

definition: Something given back in return for what someone has done — a repayment that can be either a reward or a punishment.
article: ἀνταπόδομα names the thing paid back for someone's actions, the concrete repayment rather than the act of repaying. It works both ways: in Luke 14:12 it is a favorable return (a gift given back), while in Romans 11:9 it is unfavorable (a punishment), so context decides whether it is reward or retribution. In its 14 Septuagint appearances it most often renders the Hebrew גְּמוּל (8 times), which itself covers this same two-sided idea of recompense; Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and in the Didache.
caution: Both New Testament occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than mapped to a single English word, so the measured sense-range rests mainly on Septuagint and lexicon evidence.

definition: A donkey, the common pack and riding animal of the ancient world.
article: ὄνος simply means a donkey, the everyday work animal used for riding and carrying loads. The single sense is solid: the Byzantine New Testament uses it 5 times, all rendered "donkey," and the word shows up constantly in the Septuagint (117 times, mostly for Hebrew חֲמוֹר). The everyday Koine papyri make its ordinary, practical flavor vivid—one third-century BC letter requests "send me the donkey," and another mentions readying forty pack-donkeys.
caution: The three listed "senses" are really one meaning—the variants "donkey her beside" and "O donkey" just reflect surrounding phrasing, not different meanings.

definition: To cut something short or shorten it, especially to reduce a period of time.
article: This verb means to cut off or shorten, originally in the literal sense of amputating or docking something. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times, all in Jesus' words about the days of tribulation being "cut short" (Matthew 24:22 and Mark 13:20). The Septuagint uses it just once, where it translates a Hebrew phrase, and everyday papyri show related forms like κολόβιον, "a shirt with shortened sleeves," confirming the core idea of trimming something down.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 4 New Testament uses, all in the same saying, plus a single Septuagint occurrence.

definition: A precious gemstone used in the foundations of the New Jerusalem, traditionally identified as chalcedony.
article: This word names one of the precious stones decorating the foundations of the New Jerusalem, and it appears just once in the entire New Testament (Revelation 21:19). Strong's links it to the word for copper, and Abbott-Smith notes it may refer to a green copper-silicate stone found in mines near the city of Chalcedon. Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'sapphire' here, while the older glosses (KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all favor 'chalcedony' — a small stone of various colors.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word with low confidence, and the modern translation ('sapphire') disagrees with the traditional lexicons ('chalcedony'), so its exact stone is uncertain.

definition: To learn something, whether by being taught, by inquiry, or through experience and practice.
article: μανθάνω is the ordinary Greek verb for learning, and the New Testament keeps it firmly in that everyday range: 54% of its 25 occurrences are rendered "learn" and another 38% "learned," with the BSB agreeing 100% in both cases. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew לָמַד ("to learn"), appearing 37 times across 11 books. A nice everyday glimpse comes from the papyri, where a writer congratulates someone for "learning Egyptian letters" — the same plain sense of picking up knowledge or a skill. Lexicons note it can also mean learning by use and practice (becoming accustomed to something) and, in the aorist, simply ascertaining a fact.

definition: A small fish, the diminutive form of the ordinary word for fish.
article: ἰχθύδιον is the diminutive of ἰχθύς ("fish"), so it literally means a little or small fish. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in feeding-miracle scenes (Matthew 15:34 and Mark 8:7), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as "small fish" and once simply as "fish." Moulton-Milligan show it was a perfectly ordinary word in everyday Koine, appearing in second- and third-century papyri such as a Florence document from A.D. 254 that lists "fish."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree that the core meaning is a small fish.

definition: A person who kills another human being; a murderer or manslayer.
article: ἀνδροφόνος is built from the words for "man" (ἀνήρ) and "killing" (φόνος), so it literally means a man-slayer or murderer. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:9, where it lists the kinds of people the law targets. The word turns up in everyday Koine sources too: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription (OGIS 218) declaring certain people to be murderers, and a metrical epitaph from Corcyra referring to "murderous bandits."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured-sense data appears garbled (labeling it "mother"), so rely on the lexical glosses of murderer/man-slayer.

definition: To worship or show religious reverence and awe toward something or someone.
article: σεβάζομαι means to worship or revere with religious awe, a stronger relative of the more common σέβομαι. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:25, describing those who worshiped created things rather than the Creator. The word is rare overall, though Moulton-Milligan note it does turn up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; Abbott-Smith adds that in Homer it carried the older sense "to fear" before later writers used it for worship.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on very thin evidence, and the measured rendering "rather" reflects translators reworking the surrounding clause rather than the verb's own meaning of "worship."

definition: The act of declaring or pronouncing someone righteous; acquittal.
article: δικαίωσις refers to the act of pronouncing someone righteous, an acquittal or justification. It is rare, appearing only twice in the New Testament (Romans 4:25 and 5:18), where the Berean Standard Bible renders one occurrence as "for righteousness" and absorbs the other into surrounding phrasing. It derives from the verb δικαιόω ("to justify"), and in its single Septuagint appearance it stands in for a Hebrew word tied to legal judgment or statute, fitting its courtroom flavor of declaring a verdict.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and sparse Septuagint evidence, confidence in its precise range is low, and the lexica disagree on which Hebrew term it translates.

definition: Lycaonia, a region in central Asia Minor that included the cities of Lystra and Derbe.
article: Lycaonia is a place name for a district in Asia Minor, part of the Roman province of Galatia. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 14:6, where Paul and Barnabas flee into its cities, Lystra and Derbe. The lexicons agree closely, and one note suggests the name may be remotely connected to the word for "wolf" (λύκος), though this is only a possibility.
caution: This is a proper place name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from broader usage.

definition: Describing something sharp or bitter, whether literally to the taste like undrinkable water or figuratively as harsh, resentful feelings.
article: πικρός means "bitter" or "sharp"—literally to the senses (the opposite of sweet) or figuratively of a harsh, resentful attitude. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in James 3: once of bitter water from a spring (3:11) and once of harboring bitter envy (3:14). In the Septuagint it shows up 20 times and most often renders the Hebrew מָר (mar, "bitter," 14×); the everyday papyri use it both for bitter nuts in a medical recipe and for something that "appears to be harsh."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured sense range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A name used in the Gospels for Satan, the ruler of demons or evil spirits.
article: Beelzebul is a proper name that appears 7 times in the New Testament, always as a title for Satan, identified as the chief or ruler of evil spirits. Every one of its occurrences carries this single meaning; the variations the Bible translations show ("only by Beelzebul," "possessed by Beelzebul") simply reflect surrounding sentence structure, not different senses of the word. The most interesting detail is the name's background: Abbott-Smith traces it to Hebrew roots meaning "lord" combined with either a word for "dung" or "habitation," while the familiar spelling "Beelzebub" entered English through the Latin Vulgate from 2 Kings 1:2, where the name means "lord of flies."
caution: Scholars disagree on the name's exact origin and meaning, with proposed roots including "dung," "habitation," and the "lord of flies" form behind the traditional spelling Beelzebub.

definition: Describing a wife who loves her husband.
article: φίλανδρος describes a wife's affection for her husband, built from the words for "friend/loving" (φίλος) and "man/husband" (ἀνήρ). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:4, where older women are to encourage younger women to love their husbands. Abbott-Smith notes the word turns up frequently in ancient tomb inscriptions praising a devoted wife, which fits the warm, everyday tone of its single biblical use; in classical Greek (Aeschylus) it could mean simply "loving men."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense rests on outside evidence like epitaphs rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: To remind someone of something, or in the passive, to remember or call something to mind.
article: This verb covers both sides of memory: actively reminding another person (as Paul reminds Timothy and the Corinthians) and passively calling something back to one's own mind (as when Peter remembered Jesus' words). The three measured senses split evenly, each appearing twice across its 6 New Testament occurrences. In the Septuagint it shows up 20 times, almost always translating the Hebrew verb זָכַר ("to remember"), and the papyri preserve a touching everyday line where a writer says "pain grips me when I recall" how things are.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences spread evenly across three closely related senses, the boundaries between "remind" and "remember" depend mainly on grammatical voice.

definition: Willing or acting of one's own free will, by choice rather than compulsion.
article: ἑκών describes doing something voluntarily, of one's own free will, as opposed to being forced. It appears just twice in the New Testament, and in both places it actually works through negation or contrast: in Romans 8:20 creation was subjected to futility "not willingly," and in 1 Corinthians 9:17 Paul weighs preaching willingly against being compelled. The word is solid everyday Koine — Moulton-Milligan cites a deed of gift from 127 B.C. where signatories "willingly" drew up the contract, and an inscription where priests complain of being obliged to do things "not willingly."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both leaning on negation or contrast, the measured range is very thin.

definition: Rescue or deliverance from danger, harm, or enemies — and especially God's saving of people from sin.
article: σωτηρία means rescue, safety, or deliverance, and in the New Testament it overwhelmingly carries the spiritual sense — translated "salvation" 37 of 46 times (93%). A handful of places use it of physical rescue or well-being, and the everyday Koine papyri confirm that broader range: people wrote letters simply asking about a friend's σωτηρία, meaning their health and safety. In the Septuagint it appears 107 times, most often rendering the Hebrew words for deliverance and victory, יְשׁוּעָה and תְּשׁוּעָה.

definition: Treating sacred things as common; showing no reverence for what is holy.
article: βέβηλος describes a person or thing that is irreverent—treating the holy as if it were ordinary. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, and where the Majority Standard Bible gives it a distinct English word it always renders it "irreverent" (3×, with the BSB agreeing 100%); the other 2 occurrences are folded into the surrounding phrasing. The word literally relates to a threshold that may be "trodden" or walked across, hence accessible and unhallowed, and in the Septuagint it usually translates Hebrew חֹל (5×), the "common" as opposed to the sacred. Notably, Moulton-Milligan stress it was a technical religious term rather than everyday street speech, yet it does turn up in inscriptions like the Gadatas rescript translated from Darius I.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences—2 of them absorbed into phrasing—and a confidence tier rated only moderate, the measured range rests on thin data.

definition: Describing something or someone impure — ceremonially, morally, or as an evil spirit that is not clean.
article: ἀκάθαρτος means "unclean" or "impure," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 25 of 31 occurrences (86%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% of the time. The word covers a wide range: things impure physically, ceremonially (as in Acts 10), or morally, but in the Gospels it almost always pairs with "spirit" (πνεῦμα) to describe an unclean demon. In the Septuagint it appears 155 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew word טָמֵא, which carries the same idea of ritual impurity; the everyday Koine papyri show the same range, including a magical text that uses it of an unclean demon.

definition: Describing something that brings shame or disgrace, regarded as improper or unfitting for honorable people.
article: αἰσχρός describes things that are shameful or dishonorable — actions or speech that decent people should be ashamed of. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, split evenly between "shameful" (twice) and "dishonorable" (twice), and it is used only by Paul. The everyday papyri show its force vividly: in one second/third-century document a judge tells a scoundrel he killed a woman "shamefully" (αἰσχρῶς), and an astrological text uses it for an "unfavorable" position.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, all from Paul, the evidence base is thin, and Moulton-Milligan notes the word is not common even in the papyri.

definition: To name or call something by a particular name, or in the middle voice, to choose someone for oneself.
article: This verb appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so the evidence is thin. In John 5:2 it means to call something by a name (rendered "covered" in one translation), while in Acts 15:40 it means to choose for oneself, as when Paul chose Silas. The Septuagint backs up the "choose" sense strongly, using it 7 times mostly for the Hebrew בָּחַר ("choose"); everyday papyri also show both meanings, including a contract about hunters being chosen and an instruction about "pronouncing the name in addition."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (none in the critical text) and two quite different measured senses, confidence is low and the precise meaning in each verse is debatable.

definition: Samaria, the capital city and surrounding region of central Palestine, lying between Galilee and Judea.
article: Σαμάρεια refers to Samaria, which can mean both the ancient capital city and the broader region named after it, bounded by Galilee to the north and Judea to the south. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times and is rendered "Samaria" in 8 of them (73%), with lexicographers noting the word covers both the city (as in Acts 8:5) and the region (as in John 4:4-5 and Acts 1:8). The Septuagint uses it 112 times, almost always translating the Hebrew Shomeron (98×), and Moulton-Milligan even document a village called Samaria in the Egyptian Fayum papyri, evidence of early Jewish settlement there.
caution: It is sometimes uncertain whether a given verse means the city or the region (e.g. Acts 8:9, 14).

definition: To lead or guide someone along a way, and figuratively to instruct or guide toward truth.
article: ὁδηγέω means to show someone the way, whether literally leading a person or figuratively guiding them into understanding. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, rendered "lead" in 3 of them (60%), with the rest carrying the sense of guiding into truth or instructing. It shows up 40 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew נָחָה ("to lead"), and Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in Hermetic literature where the mind "guides" the soul toward the light of knowledge—close to the figurative use in John 16:13.
caution: The figurative "guide into truth" and "instruct" senses each rest on a single occurrence, so the boundaries between them are thin.

definition: Hail — frozen pellets of rain, often described falling as a storm.
article: χάλαζα simply means hail, the frozen rain that falls from the sky. All four New Testament occurrences are in Revelation, where it appears in scenes of judgment, sometimes as part of a hailstorm. In the Septuagint it shows up far more often (31 times) and almost always translates the Hebrew word בָּרָד, the ordinary word for hail.
caution: The two measured senses ('hail' and 'hailstorm') reflect a single basic meaning, with the second just describing how the hail falls.

definition: The number seven thousand.
article: This is simply the cardinal number seven thousand, built from the words for "seven times" and "thousand." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:4, where God says he has kept seven thousand who never bowed to Baal. The Septuagint uses it twelve times across seven books, usually translating the ordinary Hebrew word for "seven" (five times) in counted totals.
caution: The measured-sense tag of "divine" is a data artifact from the Romans 11:4 context; every lexicon agrees the word plainly means "seven thousand," and it occurs only once in the New Testament.

definition: Melchizedek, the king and priest of Salem named in Genesis and presented in Hebrews as a model for Christ's priesthood.
article: Μελχισεδέκ is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Malki-tsedek, the priest-king of Salem, and it never changes form (it's indeclinable). All 9 New Testament occurrences sit in Hebrews, where the rendering splits between naming the man himself (3×) and the recurring phrase "the order of Melchizedek" describing a priesthood (5×). One nice detail from the papyri evidence: the name is never spelled in Greek with a ζ in either Testament, and Hebrews famously describes him as "without father, without mother" (Heb 7:8).
caution: This is a proper name confined to Hebrews, so its meaning is tied entirely to that book's argument rather than a flexible word range.

definition: More diligent, eager, or earnest than someone or something else.
article: σπουδαιότερος is the comparative form of σπουδαῖος, meaning "more diligent," "more eager," or "more earnest." It describes a heightened degree of zeal or promptness relative to another, and the available glosses also include the older sense "more forward." There are no measured senses to report, since the word does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament corpus used here.
caution: This word occurs zero times in the Byzantine New Testament, so the entry rests entirely on lexical glosses rather than measured usage.

definition: The superlative of "much/many": the greatest amount, the most, or very many of something.
article: πλεῖστος is the irregular superlative of πολύς ("much, many"), so it points to the largest quantity, the greatest degree, or—in the plural—very many. It carries two flavors: a true superlative ("the most") and an intensive or elative sense ("very great, very many"). The papyri are especially telling here: Moulton-Milligan note the word is "generally elative," as in phrases like "with very many others," though genuine superlative uses also appear. It does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up only 4 times in the Septuagint, where it renders three different Hebrew words.
caution: Evidence is thin—zero New Testament occurrences and only 4 in the Septuagint—and the papyri show the elative ("very great") and true superlative ("the most") senses overlapping.

definition: To be mentally sound and clear-thinking, and so to behave with calm self-control and good judgment.
article: σωφρονέω covers a span from literally being in one's right mind to living a measured, self-controlled life. In Mark 5:15 and Luke 8:35 it describes the formerly demon-possessed man now sane, and Abbott-Smith notes it stands opposite to "being out of one's mind" (2 Corinthians 5:13); elsewhere it shades into discretion and restraint (Romans 12:3, Titus 2:6, 1 Peter 4:7). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one fourth-century text pairs it with "keeping quiet" to mean being sensible and discreet, and Xenophon even applies it to prudent household management.
caution: With only 6 occurrences split across two related ideas (soundness of mind versus self-restraint), the line between senses is blurry and somewhat context-dependent.

definition: In an earnest, intense, wholehearted way; doing something with sustained fervor and sincerity.
article: ἐκτενῶς is an adverb describing action done intensely and earnestly — putting your whole self into it. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in the critical SBLGNT), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "genuine" in 1 Peter 1:22, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing entirely. The classical lexica lean toward "fervently" or "earnestly," and the everyday Koine papyri reinforce this: an inscription pairs it with "zealously" to describe someone who "continued serving fervently."

definition: A gift or offering dedicated to God, and by extension the temple treasury where such gifts were kept.
article: This is a Hebrew loanword (קׇרְבָּן) that the Greek text keeps essentially untranslated, meaning an offering consecrated to God. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament: in Mark 7:11 it names something a person has declared 'Corban,' or dedicated to God, and in Matthew 27:6 the related sense points to the temple treasury where consecrated money was held. The most telling detail is that the word is left in its Hebrew form rather than translated, so readers meet the original religious term directly.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences, low confidence tier), and the lexica treat the offering sense as primary while the 'treasury' sense leans on the related form κορβανᾶς.

definition: A person from Nazareth, used especially as a title for Jesus and, by extension, his followers.
article: Ναζωραῖος identifies someone as coming from Nazareth, and in the New Testament it functions almost like a title for Jesus. The Byzantine text uses it 15 times across 5 books, and translations render it as "of Nazareth" in 86% of cases, occasionally folding it into a longer phrase. Strong's notes that by extension the word came to designate a Christian — a sense reflected in Acts 24:5 where the early believers are called "the sect of the Nazarenes," though the basic geographic meaning dominates.

definition: Someone's arrival or being present, especially used for the future coming of Christ.
article: παρουσία basically means a "coming" or "arrival," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 14 of its 24 New Testament appearances (93%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In classical Greek the word more often meant simply "presence" (the opposite of absence), but in the New Testament it frequently becomes a near-technical term for the future advent of Christ. One striking detail: everyday Koine papyri use παρουσία for the official visit of a king or dignitary—for example, a man writing "we await your presence"—which fits how the word came to describe Christ's arrival.
caution: The classical lexicons stress "presence" as the primary sense, while the New Testament usage measured here leans heavily toward "coming/arrival," so the emphasis depends on context.

definition: To be like or closely resemble something else.
article: παρομοιάζω means to resemble or be similar to something, used with a dative object. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 23:27, where Jesus says the Pharisees are like whitewashed tombs. Although the Majority Standard Bible's rendering registers as "men's" in the measured data (an artifact of the verse's phrasing), the lexicons agree the verb itself means "to be like" or "to be somewhat similar to." Moulton-Milligan notes it is found in Biblical Greek only in this verse, though the word is otherwise documented in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This is a near-hapax occurring just once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on minimal scriptural evidence.

definition: Describing ground that is rocky or stony — shallow soil with rock lying just beneath the surface.
article: Πετρώδης literally means "rock-like," built from πέτρα (rock) and εἶδος (form or appearance). In all 4 New Testament occurrences it refers to shallow, stony soil with underlying rock, appearing only in the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:5, 20; Mark 4:5, 16). The two measured "senses" are really the same meaning, since the 25% case is just "some rocky ground" with an added quantifier; Abbott-Smith and Strong's agree on the basic idea of rocky, stony terrain.
caution: This word appears only 4 times, all in one parable and absent from the critical SBLGNT text, so its range cannot be tested across varied contexts.

definition: To bring or lead someone or something into a place or situation.
senseLabels: to bring in or lead in
article: εἰσάγω is a straightforward compound of εἰς ("into") and ἄγω ("lead"), meaning to bring or lead someone or something in. The Byzantine NT uses it 10 times, rendered "brought" in 60% of cases (as when Mary and Joseph brought Jesus into the temple, Luke 2:27) and as "into" in another 20%. It is heavily used in the Septuagint (141 times), most often translating the Hebrew bo ("come, go"), and the papyri show a notable legal sense of being "brought into court," as in a second-century BC document about a defendant entering a trial.

definition: A queen — a female ruler or the wife of a reigning king.
article: βασίλισσα simply means "queen," used for a female sovereign or a king's wife, and all four New Testament occurrences are rendered exactly that way. The word is a Koine form (Attic preferred βασιλίς or βασιλεία), and Moulton-Milligan note it was the standard term in everyday papyri for the wife of the ruling sovereign, as in a 225 BC document naming "king Ptolemy and queen Berenice." In the Septuagint it appears 39 times, most often translating the Hebrew מַלְכָּה (25×).

definition: To undergo or endure something, especially a punishment or penalty that one is made to bear.
article: ὑπέχω literally means to hold oneself under something, and figuratively to undergo or endure it. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Jude 1:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "indulged" (and BSB agrees), though the classical lexica and KJV point more toward "suffer" or "undergo" a penalty. The papyri make the legal flavor vivid: it shows up repeatedly in the common phrase τὸ δίκαιον ὑπέχειν, "to give satisfaction" or face justice, in everyday legal documents.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the modern "indulged" rendering sits uneasily beside the classical and papyri sense of "undergo a penalty," so the range is genuinely uncertain.

definition: To brand with a hot iron, used figuratively of a conscience burned numb and unable to feel guilt.
article: καυτηριάζω literally means to brand or cauterize with a hot iron, and by extension to deaden feeling—exactly how it works in its single New Testament appearance, 1 Timothy 4:2, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "influenced" (100%), describing a conscience seared past sensation. It appears only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the SBL critical text. Moulton-Milligan note the related branding-word turning up in everyday Koine papyri, including a possible restoration in a second/third-century document referring to branding gypsum.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its figurative range rests on very thin evidence, and the lexicons even differ over spelling (καυτηρ- vs. καυστηρ-).

definition: First in time, order, place, or importance — the foremost or earliest in a sequence or ranking.
article: πρῶτος means "first" in the broadest sense: earliest in time, foremost in place, or highest in rank. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "first" in 78 of 99 Byzantine occurrences (96%), with 18 more absorbed into phrasing rather than getting their own English word. One notable wrinkle: in the Septuagint and everyday Koine papyri, πρῶτος often does the work of πρότερos ("former"), reversing the usual Greek pattern — a papyrus from AD 54 uses it for an earlier annual return of lambs.

definition: Stubborn hardness of heart — an obstinate inner refusal to perceive, trust, or obey.
article: σκληροκαρδία combines the words for "hard" and "heart" to describe a stubborn, unyielding inner disposition. It appears just 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all rendered by the Majority Standard Bible as some form of "hardness of heart," and the BSB independently agrees in two of those three places. Notably, in its 2 Septuagint occurrences (Deuteronomy 10:16 and Jeremiah 4:4) it translates the Hebrew for "foreskin" (עָרְלָה), picturing an uncircumcised, unresponsive heart — which is why the older lexicons stretch the sense to "perverseness" or "obstinacy."
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament uses and 2 in the Septuagint — so the full range rests on a small sample.

definition: An adverb meaning again or once more, sometimes pointing back to a previous position or place.
article: πάλιν is a very common adverb, appearing 140 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the overwhelming majority of the time it simply means "again" or "once more" (about 78% of cases combined). Originally, as the papyri and Moulton-Milligan note, it meant "back" — a return to a previous position — and that older spatial sense still surfaces in roughly 13% of New Testament uses (e.g. Mark 2:1, John 8:2). One nice detail: in everyday Koine papyri it shows up in routine letters, as when a writer says he will "write to you again" once a payment comes through, showing how ordinary the word was.

definition: To wait for or look forward to someone or something, or to receive a person or thing favorably.
article: This verb carries two closely related ideas: waiting expectantly for something to come, and warmly receiving someone or something that arrives. In the Byzantine New Testament's 14 occurrences, the waiting sense dominates the measured data (4× rendered "waiting"), as with those who were "waiting for the consolation of Israel," while the welcoming sense appears in passages like Romans 16:2 and Philippians 2:29. The everyday papyri show both flavors vividly — one inscription speaks of welcoming freed slaves into the citizen body, while an Oxyrhynchus letter uses it for telling Lucia to "wait until the year."
caution: About 3 of the 14 occurrences were absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, so the measured sense breakdown only covers part of the data.

definition: To feel and show strong displeasure or anger at something seen as wrong or improper.
article: This verb describes a flash of indignation — being upset, displeased, or angered when something strikes you as unfair or wrong. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times across 3 books, almost always rendered "indignant" (5 of 7 times), with the remaining cases tied to scenes of people complaining about wasted resources. The everyday Koine papyri confirm the same flavor: people writing in anger over wrongs done to them, as in a London papyrus from 161 B.C. where someone is "indignant" at things carried on in a temple.
caution: The "waste" labels reflect single occurrences where the indignation is about wasted ointment, not a separate meaning of the word itself.

definition: To store up or set aside something valuable, like money or goods, saving it for the future.
senseLabels: to store up or lay up
article: θησaurízō means to amass and reserve something—literally goods or money, or figuratively. It comes from θησαυρός (treasure), and across its 8 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "up" (as in "store up" or "lay up") in 4 of them, with BSB agreeing 100% of the time. The word can take a striking metaphorical turn: in Romans 2:5 it describes "storing up wrath" for oneself, showing the same idea of accumulation applied to judgment. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words, most often צָפַן (3 times), meaning to hide or treasure away, and Moulton-Milligan note it was common in everyday Koine documents, including an inscription recording a sum that was "stored up."

definition: A word meaning behind or after, used of place, time, or following someone, especially as a disciple.
article: ὀπίσω is a flexible little word covering both space and time: it can mean physically "behind," temporally "after," or describe "following" someone as a disciple, as in Jesus' call to fishermen. The Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "after" (33%) or "behind" (27%), with about 17% expressing the idea of following. A notable detail: in everyday Koine papyri it served as shorthand for "continued on the back" or "turn over" — the ancient equivalent of P.T.O. on a document — and in the Septuagint it appears 351 times, mostly translating the Hebrew preposition אַחַר ("after").

definition: Belonging to human beings, especially as contrasted with God or the divine.
article: ἀνθρώπινος is the adjective form of ἄνθρωπος ("human being") and means "human" — pertaining to people rather than to God. The Byzantine NT uses it 7 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "human" in 5 of them (83%); the remaining instance, in 1 Corinthians 10:13, describes a temptation that is "common to man" or such as people can bear. A neat detail from the papyri: in Ptolemaic-era wills the phrase ἀνθρώπινόν τι πάσχειν (literally "to suffer something human") was a stock euphemism for dying.
caution: With only 7 occurrences, the second "what humans can bear" sense rests on a single verse, so the split reflects very thin data.

definition: A sound, disciplined state of mind that produces self-control and clear, level-headed judgment.
article: σωφρονισμός describes the quality of a sound, well-ordered mind that expresses itself in self-control and self-discipline. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 1:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fear" (paired with power and love) and the older KJV captures the same idea as "sound mind." Interestingly, its word-ending suggests the active sense "power to make someone sound-minded," and the classical lexica note a secondary meaning of "admonishing"; but Moulton-Milligan, drawing on everyday Koine papyri, judges that the context here points to self-control.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the classical lexica allow a range (admonishing versus self-control) that the single occurrence cannot settle.

definition: To shake or make something move back and forth, whether literally (the earth, a tree) or figuratively (people stirred up by strong emotion).
article: σείω describes shaking or agitating something so it moves to and fro, used both of physical events like an earthquake splitting rocks (Matthew 27:51) or a fig tree dropping fruit (Revelation 6:13), and figuratively of a whole city or guards being stirred up with emotion (Matthew 21:10; 28:4). It appears only 5 times in the New Testament but 34 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew רָעַשׁ ("to quake," 17×). One striking detail: the papyri show a specialized everyday sense — in a third-century document σείω means "to extort," as people affirm that "nothing has been extorted from us by him."
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences (each counted as a separate measured sense) the picture rests heavily on the broader Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament frequency.

definition: An adverb asking "how often?" or "how many times?"—used in questions about the number of times something happens.
senseLabels: how often or how many times
article: ποσάκις is an interrogative adverb meaning "how often?" or "how many times?" It appears just 3 times in the New Testament—Matthew 18:21, Matthew 23:37, and Luke 13:34—and the Berean Standard Bible renders it with "how" in every case. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew word פָּ֫עַם ("time, occurrence") twice, and a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (2nd century A.D.) uses it vividly in an everyday complaint: "see how many times I have sent to you!"
caution: Confidence is rated low because the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: Describing actions or people that violate sacred custom or law — forbidden, unlawful, or detestable.
article: ἀθέμιτος describes something that breaks accepted custom or law, ranging from "unlawful" to "detestable." It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 10:28 and 1 Peter 4:3), and in the Septuagint it shows up in Maccabees, where it can describe lawless people as well as forbidden acts. A papyrus from 116 B.C. uses it of dead bodies being "forbidden" to certain goddesses, which lexicographers cite to support the stronger sense "abominable" in 1 Peter 4:3.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the precise force — "unlawful" versus "abominable" — rests on thin evidence.

definition: The way or manner in which something is done, and by extension a person's way of living or character.
senseLabels: just as, in the manner that
article: τρόπος is a flexible little word meaning the "way" or "manner" something happens, often appearing in fixed phrases like "in the same way" (καθ᾽ ὃν τρόπον). In the New Testament it shows up 13 times, rendered "way" in half its uses and "just (as)" in another quarter, while 5 of its 13 occurrences melt into English phrasing without a word of their own. Beyond manner, it can describe a person's manner of life or character, as in Hebrews 13:5. A nice everyday touch: the same phrase καθ᾽ ὃν τρόπον turns up in a second-century papyrus letter from a prodigal son writing home about being punished.

definition: The first or best portion of a harvest offered to God, used figuratively for the first people or things dedicated to him.
article: In the New Testament ἀπαρχή refers to firstfruits — the earliest or best part of a crop given to God — and by extension the first members of a group, like early converts or Christ as the first to rise. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "firstfruits" in half its eight occurrences and "first" in another quarter, with the rest being slight variations. Most striking is its rich Septuagint background, where it appears 68 times and usually translates the Hebrew terms תְּרוּמָה ("contribution/offering," 47×) and רֵאשִׁית ("beginning/first," 13×); the everyday papyri even use it for fees and inheritance taxes.
caution: Strong's and Dodson note an older sacrificial sense ("the beginning of a sacrifice" or "gift"), but the measured New Testament renderings only show "firstfruits" and "first."

definition: The act of falling down or collapsing, used both for something physically crashing and for a person's downfall or ruin.
article: πτῶσις means a fall or collapse, and it shows up only twice in the New Testament, split evenly between a literal and a figurative use. In Matthew 7:27 it describes the great collapse of the house built on sand, while in Luke 2:34 it refers metaphorically to the falling—the ruin—of many in Israel. The Septuagint uses it 21 times across 9 books, most often translating the Hebrew מַפֶּ֫לֶת ('downfall,' 7×), which fits its sense of a crash that can be physical or figurative.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured range is thin, though the literal and figurative senses match the broader Septuagint and classical evidence.

definition: The condition of being unable to sleep or staying awake, often through hardship.
article: ἀγρυπνία describes sleeplessness — being kept awake, whether by toil, anxiety, or hardship. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's lists of his sufferings (2 Corinthians 6:5 and 11:27), and earlier in the Septuagint at Sirach 9 and 2 Maccabees 2:26. A third-century BC inscription uses it of a man "gripped by sleepless nights because of the pain in his head," which fits the everyday Koine sense of sleeplessness caused by suffering.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences, both in similar hardship lists, so the measured "senses" are really one meaning seen through different translation contexts.

definition: More earnestly or intensely; with greater fervor than before.
article: This is the comparative form of ἐκτενής, used adverbially to mean doing something "more earnestly" or "more intensely." In the New Testament it appears just once in the Byzantine text, at Luke 22:44, where Jesus prays the more fervently. Interestingly, the lexicons (Strong's, KJV, Abbott-Smith) consistently point to "more earnestly" or "intensely" as the meaning, while the measured rendering at Luke 22:44 captures the surrounding "anguish" of the scene rather than the adverb itself.
caution: With only one occurrence and a measured rendering ("anguish") that reflects the context rather than the word's own sense, the lexicons' "more earnestly" should be weighed carefully.

definition: A person who habitually complains about their lot in life, grumbling and discontented with their circumstances.
article: This adjective describes someone who finds fault with their fate or lot, the grumbler who is never satisfied. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:16, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render the surrounding phrase the same way. The word is built from μέμφομαι (to blame) plus μοῖρα (fate, lot), and Moulton-Milligan notes a related form ἀμεμψιμοίρητος ('blameless') in a papyrus from 164 B.C.; the term also turns up meaning 'censorious' in the astrologer Vettius Valens.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on slim evidence supplemented by a few outside attestations.

definition: The form of the word "you" used when addressing a group as the indirect object — meaning "to you" or "for you."
article: This is simply the plural pronoun "you" in its dative form, used when something is given, said, or done "to" or "for" a group of people. It appears 609 times across 32 books of the Septuagint, frequently in passages where God commands or gives something to the people — its top Hebrew counterparts include צָוָה "command" (35×) and נָתַן "give" (30×). It is a grammatical workhorse rather than a word with distinct meanings, which is why no separate senses are measured.
caution: The digest reports zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, which is surprising for such a common pronoun and likely reflects how the data was tabulated rather than the word's actual rarity.

definition: To treat someone spitefully — to mistreat, insult, or abuse them, especially out of malice.
article: ἐπηρεάζω means to deal spitefully with someone — to mistreat, revile, or treat wrongfully. It appears only three times in the Byzantine New Testament, where Jesus urges prayer for those who do this to us (Matthew 5:44, Luke 6:28) and Peter speaks of those who abuse believers (1 Peter 3:16). The word was common in everyday Koine: a papyrus from the first or second century shows worried parents taking precautions lest a wayward youth 'deal despitefully' with them.
caution: Evidence is thin — only three New Testament occurrences (two in the critical text), and the second measured sense reflects an awkward rendering of one verse rather than a clearly distinct meaning.

definition: The main or chief point of a matter, or a sum total of money.
article: In its two New Testament uses κεφάλαιον carries two related ideas: the chief point or summary of something, and a sum total of money. The Byzantine occurrences are split — one is rendered as part of a phrase about a large "sum" of money (Acts 22:28), while Abbott-Smith notes Hebrews 8:1 uses it for "the chief point." Everyday Koine papyri strongly back the money sense: documents like BGU IV.1200 and P Oxy II.268 use it for sums or capital amounts that people agreed to pay.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences, one absorbed into phrasing, so the measured data captures only the money sense even though the lexica also document the "chief point" meaning.

definition: To let someone see something, whether by physically pointing it out or by making a truth clear and known.
article: δεικνύω means to show—to put something in front of someone so they can see it, whether literally or figuratively. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 31 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "show" in 27 of those (90%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The word stretches naturally from the concrete (showing the kingdoms of the world, a healed body to the priest) to the abstract (making something known, even proving a point, as in James 2:18); the everyday papyri capture both flavors, from "showing signs" to a man unable to "point to" any wrong done against him.

definition: To make someone or something low, used mostly figuratively for humbling or lowering a person in rank, status, or heart.
article: Ταπεινόω means to bring low. In the New Testament it is used almost entirely in the figurative sense of humbling, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "humbles" in 7 of 14 occurrences (58%); it covers both humbling others and humbling oneself, as in "whoever humbles himself" (Matthew 18:4, 23:12). The literal sense survives in the Septuagint and in Luke 3:5, where mountains are made low, and across its 149 Septuagint uses it most often translates the Hebrew עָנָה (41×), tied to ideas of affliction and submission. One striking witness: a Jewish prayer in the papyri says every soul "is humbled" before God with supplication, which scholars connect to a day of fasting.

definition: A contest or struggle—originally an athletic competition, used figuratively for the strenuous effort and conflict of living out one's faith.
article: ἀγών originally named a gathering for games and then the athletic contest itself, but in the New Testament it is used figuratively for the demanding struggle of the Christian life. The word's measured renderings in the Majority Standard Bible scatter across phrasings like "race" (2 Timothy 4:7, Hebrews 12:1) and contextual words like "since" or "face," reflecting how often the noun gets absorbed into the surrounding sentence—2 of its 6 occurrences carry no English word of their own. The papyri show this same range vividly: a fourth-century document (P Flor I.36) speaks of "the contest for one's life," the very ethical, life-and-death sense the New Testament draws on.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and most of them folded into English phrasing rather than a single word, the measured sense labels are approximate; note also that Col 2:1 may mean inward anxiety or outward conflict, a point on which sources differ.

definition: Living for a long time; lasting many years.
article: μακροχρόνιος combines the words for "long" and "time" to describe someone who lives a long life. It appears just once in the New Testament (Ephesians 6:3) and twice in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew root meaning "to be long" — typically in the promise that honoring one's parents leads to long life. Moulton-Milligan note that this word and its related verb show up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary vocabulary rather than a specialized term.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use (where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing) plus two Septuagint occurrences.

definition: A tree, a woody plant with a trunk and branches.
article: δένδρον simply means "tree," and the evidence is remarkably consistent: it is rendered "tree" in 25 of 26 New Testament occurrences (96%). The Gospels often pair it with descriptive adjectives — a "good" tree, a "fine" tree, or a "rotten" tree — to contrast healthy and worthless plants. In the Septuagint it stands behind several Hebrew words for trees and wood, including עֵץ ("tree/wood"), אַלּוֹן ("oak"), and רַעֲנָן ("luxuriant"), and an everyday papyrus from around 250 B.C. even uses it in a rule that an olive or fig tree be planted nine feet from a neighbor's boundary.

definition: Wild, wasteful living marked by reckless self-indulgence and a lack of moral restraint.
article: ἀσωτία describes a wasteful, undisciplined way of life—the kind of profligacy that squanders both resources and good sense. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "indiscretion" in two of its three New Testament occurrences (67%) and "reckless indiscretion" once (33%), and the dictionaries push the meaning further toward prodigality and wastefulness. A striking witness comes from the everyday papyri: a 165 B.C. letter (P Par 63) describes a family home that had been "utterly ruined through ἀσωτία," showing how the word evoked financial wreckage caused by loose living.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the precise force ranges from general indiscretion to outright profligacy.

definition: To react with strong, deep emotion—either being powerfully stirred inside or sternly warning someone with displeasure.
article: This vivid verb literally pictures snorting like an angry horse, and in the New Testament it conveys intense feeling that breaks through the surface. Across its 5 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "deeply moved" twice (as when Jesus is stirred at Lazarus's tomb in John 11:33, 38) and "sternly" once (Matthew 9:30), with the other 2 absorbed into the phrasing. Its single Septuagint appearance translates the Hebrew כָּאָה, and Moulton-Milligan note the broader Greek evidence leans toward "being angry" or expressing violent displeasure, perhaps inwardly.
caution: The word is genuinely difficult: it occurs only 5 times, and lexicons stretch from inner emotion to anger to stern command, so the exact force in each verse is debated.

definition: Moisture or dampness, especially water in the ground that a plant needs to grow.
article: ἱκμάς means moisture or dampness. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 8:6, where seed withers because it has no moisture, and every translation surveyed renders it the same way. It shows up twice in the Septuagint and turns up in everyday Koine papyri; though once thought to be a medical term, Cadbury showed it was used widely by writers like Josephus, Plutarch, and Lucian, so it carries no special technical flavor.
