caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint — but the meaning is consistent across all sources.

definition: A raised platform reached by steps, especially the official seat where a Roman magistrate or ruler sat to render judgment.
article: In the New Testament βῆμα almost always means a judgment seat—the elevated tribunal where a Roman official sat to hear cases and pronounce verdicts, rendered "judgment seat" in 8 of its 12 occurrences (80%). The original sense was simpler: a step or pace, which is how it appears in the Septuagint, where Acts 7:5 quotes Deuteronomy 2:5 about not even a "foot's breadth" of land. That literal meaning survives in everyday papyri too—one inscription from A.D. 207 uses it of a scar on the sole of someone's right foot, and other monuments carved actual footprints into stone to mark a safe journey's end.

definition: Firmly settled or steadfast, especially of someone whose mind or commitment cannot be shaken.
article: Built from the Greek word for a seat (ἕδρα), ἑδραῖος literally pictures something fixed in place, and by extension describes moral or mental firmness — being settled and unmovable. In the New Testament it appears 3 times across 2 books, and where it is translated, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "established" both times (with the BSB agreeing 100%), as in 1 Corinthians 7:37 and Colossians 1:23. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri: a sixth-century document describes a household servant in a "fixed position" (φαμιλιάριος ἑδραῖος), using the same idea of being settled in place.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences, one of which is absorbed into surrounding phrasing — so this entry rests on a small sample.

definition: To bring something in secretly or slip it in alongside, especially false ideas introduced under the surface.
article: This compound literally means "to bring in from the side," and in 2 Peter 2:1, its only New Testament appearance, it carries the sense of introducing false teachings secretly. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "secretly" in all 1 occurrence, and Abbott-Smith notes this stealthy meaning belongs to late writers. Interestingly, the everyday papyri tell a different story: Moulton-Milligan cite documents where the prefix conveys no idea of secrecy at all, just plain introduction—as in a 116 B.C. papyrus and in Aristeas, where it simply means people brought into a kingdom.
caution: With only 1 New Testament occurrence and papyri evidence showing no inherent sense of secrecy, the "secretly" nuance may come from the context of 2 Peter rather than the word itself.

definition: To roll a heavy object, such as a large stone, away from a position.
article: This verb means to roll something heavy away — in the New Testament always the great stone sealing Jesus' tomb. It appears 4 times across Matthew, Mark, and Luke, and every source agrees on the core meaning "to roll away." In the Septuagint it shows up 3 times in Genesis, where it consistently translates the Hebrew גָּלַל, describing rolling the stone off the mouth of a well.
caution: The three measured "senses" reflect surrounding translation wording rather than genuinely different meanings, so the word's actual range is narrow and consistent.

definition: A physical blow or wound, and by extension a calamity or plague sent as affliction.
article: πληγή starts from the literal idea of a blow or stroke—something that strikes the body and leaves a wound—and stretches to mean a wider calamity or plague. In the Byzantine New Testament its most common rendering by far is "plagues" (12 of 22 times, 71%), driven heavily by Revelation, with "wounds" appearing only twice. The everyday Koine papyri keep the concrete sense vivid: people report being dragged off "with insults and blows" (P Fay 12) or beaten on every limb of the body (P Tebt II.331), and in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew makkah, a "blow" or "stroke."

definition: A young boy or lad, originally a diminutive form but sometimes used more loosely for older youths.
article: παιδάριον is a small-form version of παῖς (child) and basically means a young boy or lad. In the New Testament it appears just once, in John 6:9, describing the boy with the loaves and fish, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "boy" every time. What's interesting is that the diminutive sense often faded in everyday Koine: papyri and inscriptions use it for everything from an unborn child to, in Tobit 6:2-3, a young man strong enough to haul a fish ashore. In the Septuagint it appears 206 times, most often translating the Hebrew na'ar (158×), a word for a young man or servant.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and evidence that its diminutive force was often lost, the precise age it implies in any given passage is uncertain.

definition: Unable to speak; describing a person or spirit that prevents speech.
article: ἄλαλος literally means "without speech" — it joins the negative prefix to the root for talking. In Mark's Gospel it appears 3 times, describing people who cannot speak and a spirit blamed for causing that muteness (Mark 9:17). The lexicons agree it means "dumb" or "speechless," and in the Septuagint it renders Hebrew words for being mute (Psalms 38:13).
caution: The MSB's renderings as "deaf" and "someone that makes" don't cleanly match the lexicons' "mute/speechless," and the word is rare, so treat the precise sense with care.

definition: To shine upon, appear, or become visible, whether of natural light or of someone making themselves known.
senseLabels: to shine and guide a path
article: At its core ἐπιφαίνω means to shine upon and so become visible or known, built from ἐπί ("upon") and φαίνω ("shine"). In the New Testament it appears just 4 times, half rendered "appeared," while individual cases describe light shining to guide a path (Luke 1:79) and God's saving grace appearing (Titus 2:11). The most striking evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions: the same word was used for the "epiphany" of the goddess Artemis appearing to worshippers, the very language Moulton-Milligan links to its use in Titus.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the three rendered "senses" overlap heavily and largely reflect context rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To go or come into a place, or to enter something (including food going into the body), sometimes used figuratively.
article: εἰσπορεύομαι means to go or come into something, built from εἰς ("into") and πορεύομαι ("go"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 17 times, rendered "enter" in about half the cases and "went" in others; it can describe people entering a place, food entering the body (Mark 7:15-19), or figuratively things like cares "entering" the heart (Mark 4:19). In the Septuagint it shows up 144 times, mostly translating Hebrew בּוֹא ("to come/go in"), and an everyday papyrus from 1 B.C. uses it of people simply going into their homes. One notable idiom pairs it with ἐκπορεύομαι ("go out") to mean associating with someone (Acts 9:28).

definition: The breast or chest of a person, especially a woman's breast used for nursing a child.
article: μαστός refers to the breast or chest, most often a woman's breast as the place where infants nurse. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, and the Septuagint uses it 31 times, mainly to translate the Hebrew word shad ("breast"), though it occasionally renders other Hebrew words too. One vivid piece of evidence comes from a second-century AD inscription where a man describes a healing at a temple of Asclepius, saying the god "touched my right hand and my breast."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and the measured senses essentially identical, the evidence here is thin, and the word's spelling varied (μασθός, μαζός) across early manuscripts.

definition: The process or means of testing something to prove whether it is genuine, especially in reference to faith.
article: This rare word appears only twice in the New Testament (James 1:3 and 1 Peter 1:7), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as the 'testing' that develops endurance and once as proven 'character.' The senses cluster closely: both point to putting something through a trial to show it is real. A striking detail comes from the papyri, where Deissmann found this word used commercially of 'tested' or assayed gold of certified purity (e.g. BGU IV.1065), which fits 1 Peter's image of faith tested like gold; in the Septuagint it appears twice, in Proverbs, of a crucible that refines metal.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences — and scholars debate whether the word is a noun meaning 'a test' or an adjective meaning 'genuine,' so its exact force is uncertain.

definition: The most exact or strict — describing something carried out with the greatest precision or rigor.
article: This is the superlative form of ἀκριβής ("exact, precise, careful"), so it means "most exact" or "strictest." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament — in Acts 26:5, where Paul describes the strictest party of the Jewish religion — and in that one spot it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. The base adjective shows up in the Septuagint in books like Daniel, Esther, and Sirach, where it can render a Hebrew word meaning "reliable" or "sure."
caution: This exact superlative form occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, so the evidence is thin.

definition: To treat or season something with salt, as in preserving food or preparing sacrifices.
article: ἁλίζω means to salt or season with salt, derived from the noun ἅλς ("salt"). It appears just 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 2 books, and the Septuagint uses it twice to translate the Hebrew מָלַח. The lexicons add color the bare gloss misses: Dodson notes it can mean to keep something fresh and sound, used of sacrifices or those offering them, and so acceptable to God.
caution: This word is very rare, appearing only 3 times in the New Testament with 2 of those instances absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as a standalone English word.

definition: To take away or remove someone, especially in the New Testament used of a person being taken from others.
article: At its root ἀπαίρω means to lift off or take away. In all 3 of its New Testament appearances (Matthew 9:15, Mark 2:20, Luke 5:35) it shows up in the same passive phrase about the time when the bridegroom "will be taken away" from his companions. The Septuagint, however, uses it much more broadly—92 times, mostly translating the Hebrew נָסַע (to set out or journey), and the everyday papyri attest a related sense of "departing."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences—all in the same idiom—the measured sense is narrow, while the wider Septuagint and papyri evidence points to a much broader range of meaning.

definition: A craftsman who builds and shapes materials—especially wood—commonly understood as a carpenter.
article: τέκτων refers to a skilled craftsman, most often a worker in wood, though the word could also cover working in stone or metal. In the New Testament it appears only twice (Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3), both times describing the trade of Jesus and his family. The everyday papyri confirm the carpenter sense vividly: one document from AD 94 tells carpenters to "put up the doors," and an AD 316 report comes from the guild of carpenters at Oxyrhynchus. In the Septuagint it appears 25 times, mostly translating the Hebrew חָרָשׁ.
caution: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on the broader Greek and papyri evidence rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: A royal headband or crown worn as the badge of a king's authority.
article: Διάδημα refers to a crown or headband that marks someone as a king, signaling royal authority rather than victory. All three of its New Testament appearances are in Revelation (12:3, 13:1, 19:12), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it consistently as "royal" or "royal crowns." The word literally comes from "to bind around," and Abbott-Smith notes it originally described the band wrapped around a Persian king's tiara; in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew kether ("crown") among other terms. It is worth distinguishing from στέφανος, which marks victory or celebration rather than kingship.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences, all in Revelation, so confidence in its full range is limited.

definition: A word marking the space, position, or time that lies between two people, places, or moments.
article: μεταξύ marks what falls between two things — whether physical space, persons in relationship, or intervening time. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 5 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "between" in 5 of those (71%), with the remaining occurrences either absorbed into the phrasing or used of time, as in John 4:31 ("meanwhile"). Everyday Koine papyri show the very same prepositional use: legal documents speak of an agreement "between him and Isidora" or of mediating "between" two named parties, exactly matching the New Testament's sense of relationship between persons.
caution: Some standard lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) note a temporal sense meaning "after" or "afterwards" in Acts 13:42, which goes beyond the simple "between" the corpus measures most often.

definition: To serve or attend to someone, meeting their needs as a subordinate or helper.
article: ὑπηρετέω means to serve or minister to someone, always with a person as the object in the three New Testament occurrences. Though the three measured renderings look different—"served," "own," and "needs"—they all turn on the same idea of providing service or supplying what is needed, with the English wording shaped by context. Originally the word meant to serve as a rower on a ship, but the lexica note that in classical Greek it was always used metaphorically for serving or ministering. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense, as in one letter promising "I will serve you again."
caution: With only 3 occurrences and each rendered differently, the confidence tier is low, so the apparent range partly reflects translation context rather than distinct meanings.

definition: Feeling very hungry; experiencing a strong, intense hunger.
article: This word describes being intensely hungry, formed from the preposition πρός joined to the root for hunger (πεινάω). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:10, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "hungry"; Strong's, KJV, and Dodson emphasize the intensity with "very hungry." The most interesting note is from Moulton-Milligan, who report that this is one of the dwindling number of New Testament words once thought not found elsewhere, though they document it in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range is hard to confirm.

definition: To share together in something with others, whether participating jointly in good deeds or becoming a partner in wrongdoing.
article: This verb combines "with" (σύν) and "share" (κοινωνέω), so it means joining others in a common activity—either positively, by partnering with someone, or negatively, by taking part in something. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the renderings split evenly: once as "fellowship" (Eph 5:11), once as "done share" (Php 4:14, where Paul thanks the Philippians for sharing in his troubles), and once absorbed into the phrasing. Abbott-Smith notes a grammatical detail worth knowing: the word takes the dative for things shared in but the genitive for persons shared with, matching the classical pattern.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and the translations split evenly between two senses, the evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: To pay a tenth of something as a tithe, or to collect a tithe from someone.
article: This verb covers both sides of tithing: paying a tenth of your goods, or collecting that tenth from others. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "pay tithes" in the measured cases (Matthew 23:23, Luke 11:42, Luke 18:12). Abbott-Smith notes the verb can take a thing as its object (to tithe goods) or a person as its object (to exact tithes from people, as in Hebrews 7:5), and in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew עָשַׂר; one rare classical sense is even "to decimate."
caution: The collecting sense (exacting tithes from people) is identified by Abbott-Smith but does not show up among the measured Byzantine renderings here, which all reflect paying.

definition: To separate or distinguish one thing from another; to judge or decide; or, in the middle voice, to waver and be divided in one's own mind.
article: διακρίνω is built from κρίνω ("judge") and διά, giving the core idea of separating things in order to distinguish, evaluate, or decide between them. In the New Testament it stretches across a wide range: in some places it means to discern or make a distinction, in others to judge or settle a matter, and in still others—reflexively—to be split in one's own thinking, hence to doubt or waver. The everyday papyri confirm the practical legal flavor: one document (A.D. 139) uses it for examining tax-collectors, and a third-century B.C. inscription uses it for judges deciding disputed contracts. Notably, the "doubt, hesitate" sense is described as a later Hellenistic development found in the NT but not in the Septuagint, where it instead renders Hebrew words like שָׁפַט ("to judge," 10×).
caution: The measured renderings only capture a fraction of the word's range—4 of 19 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing with no English word, and the lexica list several senses (distinguish, contend, decide) that the counted data barely reflects.

definition: A preposition meaning "before," "in the presence of," or "in the sight of" someone, often God as witness or judge.
article: ἐνώπιον is a preposition built from "in" plus a word for "eye" or "face," so it literally puts you face-to-face with someone. The Byzantine NT uses it 96 times, and over half of those (53%) are simply rendered "before," while the rest cluster around closely related ideas of presence and sight — these are really shades of one core meaning rather than separate senses. It's a favorite of Luke, Acts, and Revelation but never appears in Matthew or Mark, and a common phrase is "in the sight of God," picturing God as the one watching or judging. The Septuagint uses it 454 times, most often to translate the Hebrew words for "face" (192×) and "eye" (114×), which fits its eye-and-face origins perfectly.

definition: Mysia, a region in the northwest of the Roman province of Asia, in Asia Minor.
senseLabels: Mysia, a region of Asia Minor
article: Mysia is a place name referring to a district in the northwest corner of Asia Minor, within the Roman province of Asia. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 16:7-8, where Paul's missionary route passes through it, and every translation surveyed renders it simply "Mysia." The lexicons agree it is a geographic region, though its origin as a word is uncertain.
caution: This is a rare proper name with only 2 occurrences and an origin the sources call uncertain.

definition: A combined form meaning "and that one" or "that one also," pointing back to a person or thing previously mentioned.
article: κἀκεῖνος is a crasis (squeezed-together form) of καί ("and") plus ἐκεῖνος ("that one"), so it means "and that one," "that one also," or simply "they/he/she/it." Because it does double duty as a connector and a pointer, translators handle it loosely: across its 21 Byzantine occurrences the standard rendering "they" covers only about a quarter of cases, and in 5 of 21 it is absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own. In the Septuagint it appears just 3 times, in a single book, where it stands in for ordinary Hebrew expressions.

definition: A personal name, the form of "Joses" used in Luke's genealogy for a son of Eliezer in Jesus's ancestry.
article: Ἰωσή is a personal name rather than an ordinary word, and the digest shows it does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all. According to Abbott-Smith, this exact spelling reflects an older printed reading (the "Received Text") at Luke 3:29, where the KJV rendered it "Jose"; it is a variant form of the name Joses (Ἰωσῆς). Dodson notes the name attaches to several different men in the Gospels — a son of Eliezer, a son of Mary and brother of Jesus, and the man also called Barnabas — though here it specifically marks the genealogical entry.
caution: The evidence is thin: this form has zero Byzantine occurrences and survives mainly as a textual variant, so sources treat it as a spelling of Joses rather than a distinct word.

definition: A thing that causes terror — a frightening sight or alarming portent that fills people with dread.
article: φόβητρον is something that strikes fear into people — a terrifying sight or an alarming sign. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 21:11, where it sits alongside other dread-inspiring signs, and translators consistently render it as a "fearful sight." Interestingly, the early physician Hippocrates used the word for the frightening objects that present themselves to the imagination of the sick, and in its single Septuagint use (Isaiah 19:17) it translates a Hebrew word for terror.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its precise range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: Timothy, a Christian companion and helper of the apostle Paul.
article: Τιμόθεος is the personal name Timothy, used in the New Testament for a Christian from Lystra who traveled with and assisted Paul. It appears 23 times across 11 books in the Byzantine text and is rendered "Timothy" in every single occurrence. The name combines the Greek words for "honor" (τιμή) and "God" (θεός), and Moulton-Milligan note that it was a common proper name in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, also showing up in spelling variants like Τιμόθειος and Τιμώθεος.

definition: To come into view or be brought to light, whether something becoming visible or, in sailing, sighting a place.
article: This verb means to make something appear or, in its passive form, to come into view out of the unseen. Its range is genuinely broad: the lexica list a nautical sense (in Acts 21:3, sighting Cyprus), a passive sense of becoming manifest (Luke 19:11, the kingdom of God), and an active sense of bringing to light. A striking parallel comes from a fourth-century Christian papyrus letter (P Oxy VI.939) which uses the very same wording as Luke 19:11, saying "the knowledge of God appeared to us all."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one of those absorbed into phrasing, the single measured sense rests on thin evidence, so the lexicons' fuller range is hard to confirm from the corpus alone.

definition: Knowing something in advance, especially God's prior knowledge or determination of events and people.
article: πρόγνωσις means knowing or determining something ahead of time, and in the New Testament it always refers to God's foreknowledge. It appears just twice (Acts 2:23 and 1 Peter 1:2), both rendered "foreknowledge" in every measured occurrence. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri—including a magical text seeking "foreknowledge" via the constellation Aries—showing it was ordinary vocabulary, not a specialized religious term; in 1 Peter the commentator Hort took it to mean foreknowledge of a person in relation to their role.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences this word's full range is hard to map, so confidence in its biblical sense rests on a thin sample.

definition: Used to describe being by oneself, in private, away from others.
article: This adverb describes doing something on one's own, apart from other people. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and in both places it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word. Notably, most editors treat it as two separate words, κατὰ μόνας ('by oneself'), and it does not appear at all in the critical (SBLGNT) text; in the Septuagint the related word μόνος chiefly renders the Hebrew לְבַד ('alone').
caution: Evidence is thin — only two Byzantine occurrences, none in the critical text, and scholars dispute whether it is even one word.

definition: Niger, a Latin surname meaning "black," used to identify one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch.
article: Niger is a proper name of Latin origin, appearing just once in the New Testament (Acts 13:1), where it identifies Simeon among the prophets and teachers at Antioch. The Latin word literally means "black," and the name turns up in everyday Koine documents — Moulton-Milligan cite a tax receipt from A.D. 174–175 naming a collector called Niger, plus a tombstone inscription. One scholar has suggested it may have started as a nickname given to Simeon at Antioch, though that remains speculation.
caution: This is a name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its sense is fixed by that single context rather than a measurable range.

definition: To place a financial or emotional burden on someone, weighing them down with expense, demands, or harsh treatment.
article: This verb literally means "to put a weight upon" and, in the New Testament, usually describes being a financial drain on others — Paul uses it twice (67%) to insist he worked so as not to burden the churches (1 Thessalonians 2:9, 2 Thessalonians 3:8). The remaining use (2 Corinthians 2:5) shifts toward not overstating or piling on grief. Everyday papyri confirm this ordinary sense beautifully: a soldier writes home to his mother, "do not burden yourself to send me anything."
caution: With only 3 occurrences and two distinct shades of meaning, the evidence base is thin and the range should be treated cautiously.

definition: To not believe something, refuse to trust, or fail to remain faithful.
article: ἀπιστέω covers two related ideas: refusing to believe a report and failing to stay faithful. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, and about half the renderings (3×) are simply "believe" (in the negative), as when the disciples did not believe the report of the risen Jesus (Mark 16:11, Luke 24:11). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one Oxyrhynchus letter from the 2nd century AD promises to add "a fact which will excite your wonder and disbelief" until the documents are read. In a few places, notably Romans 3:3 and 2 Timothy 2:13, it shades toward unfaithfulness rather than mere disbelief, and Abbott-Smith notes some scholars even tie it to "disobey."
caution: With only 7 occurrences and a real overlap between "disbelieve" and "be unfaithful," the sense in Romans 3:3 and 2 Timothy 2:13 is debated among the lexicons.

definition: A legal document that formally ends something, especially a written certificate of divorce releasing one spouse from the marriage.
article: In the New Testament ἀποστάσιον always means a written certificate, and all 3 occurrences refer specifically to a bill of divorce. The Greek Old Testament uses it 4 times to translate the Hebrew word for "cutting off" or divorce (כְּרִיתוּת). The everyday papyri reveal a broader legal flavor: the word shows up in contracts for renouncing or relinquishing property rights, so its core idea is a formal document of release or separation, of which divorce is the biblical example.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single measured sense, the broader "relinquishment" range comes from papyri rather than the biblical text itself.

definition: To cut, gash, or batter the body, striking it so as to wound or mangle the flesh.
article: This verb means to cut, gash, or beat the body, often violently enough to wound or mangle it. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Mark 5:5, where a demon-possessed man kept gashing himself with stones; the Septuagint uses it 19 times, frequently for the Hebrew כָּתַת (to crush or break in pieces). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this physical, brutal sense: one document describes a man beaten with blows all over his legs and limbs, matching the derived meaning of 'bruise' or 'batter' seen in Mark.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise force in Mark 5:5 rests on slim evidence and supporting parallels.

definition: A person living in a place that is not their home, staying only as a temporary resident or foreigner.
article: παρεπίδημος describes someone who lives in a place only for a time—a stranger settled in a district without belonging to it. The Byzantine NT uses it just 3 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders all 3 as "exiles" (Hebrews 11:13, 1 Peter 1:1, 2:11), where it pairs with words for "strangers" and "resident aliens." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan show the same everyday sense in Greek papyri, including a will from 238 B.C. that calls a man named Apollonius a παρεπίδημος, confirming this was ordinary legal language for a temporary resident.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 NT occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint—so the confidence tier is low, though the sources agree on the meaning.

definition: Physical or inherent power and might — the capacity to act with full force.
article: ἰσχύς means strength, might, or power — the inherent capacity to exert force. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, and where it gets an English word it is rendered "strength" every time (8×), as in Jesus' call to love God "with all your strength" (Mark 12:30, Luke 10:27). It was a thoroughly everyday word: the Septuagint uses it 265 times, most often for the Hebrew כֹּחַ (97×), and the papyri apply it to the legal "validity and force" of a receipt, showing the same idea of effective power extended to documents.

definition: Referring to the left side or left hand, as opposed to the right.
article: ἀριστερός simply means "left" — the left hand or the left side, in contrast to the right. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament but 58 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always renders the Hebrew word for "left" (שְׂמֹאול, 44 times). The phrase ἐξ ἀριστερῶν ("on the left"), used in Luke 23:33 of the criminal crucified beside Jesus, shows up in everyday legal papyri, where the word was common in physical descriptions of witnesses and litigants.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences spread across three different uses, the measured sense breakdown rests on very thin evidence.

definition: An interval or gap, whether of time or of physical space between two points.
article: διάστημα names a gap or interval — it can mark a stretch of time or a distance between physical objects. In the New Testament it appears only once, at Acts 5:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "later," referring to a span of about three hours that passed. The everyday papyri show both uses vividly: an astronomical document measures the interval of day and night, while a land survey speaks of a ditch and a considerable space between plots, and a Septuagint preface (Sirach) likewise uses it of a time interval.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests almost entirely on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: Belonging to or living in Smyrna, an Ionian city on the Aegean coast.
article: Σμυρναῖος simply means "of Smyrna" — a resident or native of that Ionian city on the Aegean. It is derived from Σμύρνα, the city name, which appears in Revelation 1:11 and 2:8. Note that some manuscripts spell the city name with an initial zeta (Ζμύρνα) rather than sigma, a variation the lexicons flag in the textual tradition.
caution: This word has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so its meaning rests entirely on the related city name Σμύρνα rather than direct measured usage.

definition: The period of darkness between sunset and sunrise; nighttime.
article: νύξ simply means "night," the dark hours of the day, and it is remarkably consistent: across all 65 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "night" 63 times (the other 2 are absorbed into broader phrasing). In the Septuagint it appears 232 times and almost always translates the Hebrew word for night, לַיְלָה (189×). Greek often used special grammatical forms with this word to mark time—"by night" or "at night"—and everyday papyri show the same usage, as in a complaint about an Arabian ewe lost from the pen "at night."

definition: To grieve or mourn, expressing deep sorrow either inwardly as a feeling or outwardly as lamentation.
article: πενθέω means to mourn or grieve, covering both the inner feeling of sorrow and its outward expression. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mourn" in 7 of those cases, with the other 2 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. A striking piece of evidence comes from the papyri: a man's letter to his wife (P Oxy III.528) pairs πενθέω with "weep," writing that since she left he has been "weeping by night and mourning by day" — the same pairing of mourning and weeping found in Mark 16:10. In the Septuagint it appears 48 times, most often translating the Hebrew אָבַל ("to mourn").

definition: Describing someone who loves and actively promotes what is good and virtuous.
article: φιλάγαθος combines the words for "loving" (φίλος) and "good" (ἀγαθός), so it literally means a lover of goodness — someone who is drawn to and promotes virtue. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:8 listing qualities of an overseer, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "upright" (and the Berean Standard Bible agrees). One vivid piece of evidence comes from an Oxyrhynchus papyrus, where someone praises the emperor Marcus Aurelius as φιλάγαθος, "a lover of virtue," alongside being a lover of wisdom and no lover of money.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament (and once in the Septuagint, Wisdom 7:22), so its full range cannot be measured from limited evidence.

definition: A formal question, request, or pledge, especially the appeal or solemn commitment a person makes toward God.
article: This noun comes from the verb ἐπερωτάω ("to ask, inquire") and appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 3:21, where it describes something offered to God in connection with baptism. The classical lexica (Herodotus, Thucydides) settle on the basic sense "a question or inquiry," but Abbott-Smith treats the 1 Peter use as the distinct sense "a demand." The most telling evidence comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show the word used as a legal technical term equivalent to Latin stipulatio — a formal pledge sealed by question and answer — which may illuminate the difficult Peter passage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and its precise meaning there is genuinely disputed, with the classical "inquiry" sense, the lexical "demand" sense, and the legal papyri "pledge" sense all in play.

definition: A palm branch, especially the leaf or frond of a palm tree.
article: βαΐον means a palm branch or frond, appearing only once in the New Testament, in John 12:13, where crowds wave them to welcome Jesus into Jerusalem. The word is rare in the Bible, found elsewhere only in 1 Maccabees 13:51, and is apparently of Egyptian origin. Interestingly, it turns up in everyday Egyptian papyri, including one document from the 5th or 6th century A.D. where a palm branch is used as a measuring rod.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone, though the lexica agree on its meaning.

definition: To strain a liquid through a filter or sieve, removing tiny particles like an insect.
article: This word means to filter a liquid carefully, straining out even the smallest bits. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 23:24, where Jesus pictures people who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel. In the Septuagint it shows up just once (Amos 6:6) rendering a Hebrew word, and Abbott-Smith notes the sense shifted over time from 'strain thoroughly' (in the older writer Archytas) to 'strain out.' Note that the King James 'strain at a gnat' is widely regarded as a printing error for 'strain out.'
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so confidence is low.

definition: The roof of a house, often used to refer to the house or home itself.
article: Στέγη simply means the roof of a building, and that is how it is rendered in all three of its New Testament appearances. In two passages (Matthew 8:8, Luke 7:6) it is part of the phrase "to come under my roof," where the roof stands for the whole home—the centurion saying he is unworthy to host Jesus. Everyday Koine papyri use the word the same way, including a tax-dodging case where owners had "taken down the upper story" (στέγας) of a building to avoid having officials lodged there.
caution: With only three New Testament occurrences and two in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, though every source agrees on the basic meaning.

definition: Unable to walk normally because of an injured or disabled leg or foot; lame or limping.
article: χωλός describes someone who cannot walk properly because of a disabled leg or foot — lame or limping. The meaning is remarkably stable: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lame" in 14 of its 15 New Testament occurrences (93%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing at the same rate. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew word for a lame person (11 of 12 times), and the everyday papyri confirm the literal sense — one Egyptian sale document from 99 B.C. describes a person as "straight-nosed, near-sighted, lame."

definition: To receive someone or something gladly—to welcome a person warmly or accept news with approval.
article: This compound of ἀπό and δέχομαι means to receive with genuine gladness, whether welcoming a person or accepting something offered. In the Byzantine New Testament's 6 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "welcomed" 75% of the time, with the rest absorbed into phrasing or describing a glad reception. A nice glimpse of its everyday warmth comes from a fourth-century papyrus letter where a dependent begs his master to "receive me kindly"—the same word at work in ordinary life.
caution: Evidence is fairly thin with only 6 occurrences, but the measured senses and the lexicons agree well.

definition: A dwelling place, homestead, or farm property where someone lives.
article: This word names a place where people live — a house, farmstead, or estate. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 1:20, quoting Psalm 69:25, and there it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word. In the Septuagint it shows up 45 times, most often rendering the Hebrew חָצֵר ('settlement' or 'enclosure'), and everyday papyri use it concretely for a working homestead — one property return even describes 'a common homestead that is in a state of ruin.'
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing there, so its sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: A preposition meaning directly in front of or in the presence of someone or something.
article: κατενώπιον is a preposition meaning "in front of" or "in the presence of," taking a genitive object. The measured renderings cluster around this single idea: it appears with "presence" (in phrases like standing in God's presence) and in phrases translated "before" someone, as in 2 Corinthians where Paul writes that he speaks before God. The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a sixth-century Christian amulet that reads "I bow my head before you," and Moulton-Milligan stresses it should not be treated as a Hebrew-style construction.
caution: It occurs only 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament (3 in the critical text), so some of the listed "senses" are really just translation fragments rather than distinct meanings.

definition: The ear, the physical organ of hearing, often used as a figure for the ability to listen, perceive, and understand.
article: οὖς simply means "ear," the organ you hear with, and across its 37 New Testament appearances the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ears" in 53% of cases and "ears" within the famous call "he who has ears, let him hear" in another 42%. That second pattern shows how readily the word stretches from the physical organ to the faculty of perceiving and understanding. In the Septuagint it appears 163 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew אֹ֫זֶן ("ear") 115 times; the everyday papyri capture both the literal sense and a vivid idiom, with one Oxyrhynchus document (A.D. 186) using "I turned a deaf ear to him" much like Acts 7:57.

definition: To walk or move about on foot, and figuratively to live one's life or conduct oneself in a particular way.
article: At its core περιπατέω means to walk or go about on foot, and that literal sense dominates: the Byzantine NT uses it 96 times, with 'walk' or 'walked' accounting for 76 of those (about 88%). But it also stretches into a figurative meaning of how someone lives or conducts their life, rendered as 'live' or 'way (of life)' a handful of times each. This ethical sense follows the Hebrew הָלַךְ, which it most often translates in the Septuagint, and the everyday papyri show the same range — one second-century letter even has a writer complaining he is 'going about in a disgraceful state.'

definition: The act of hunting or catching, and by extension the trap or snare used to capture prey.
article: θήρα basically means hunting or the chase, and by extension can mean the prey caught or the net used to catch it. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Romans 11:9, where it is rendered "trap" alongside the idea of retribution. The Septuagint uses it 24 times across 9 books, most often translating the Hebrew word for "game" or "hunt" (9×) and "prey" (6×), and everyday papyri show it used quite literally—for elephant hunting, fishing taxes on Lake Moeris, and provisions "for the hunt."
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, and lexicons differ on whether Romans 11:9 means "net/trap" or another shade of "hunting/prey," so the precise sense there is debated.

definition: To eat a meal together with someone, sharing food in their company.
article: συνεσθίω is simply σύν ("with") joined to ἐσθίω ("eat"), and it means to share a meal in someone's company. All five New Testament uses carry this single idea, taking the person you eat with in the dative (Luke 15:2, Acts 10:41, 11:3, 1 Corinthians 5:11) or with μετά (Galatians 2:12); the measured senses ("man eats," "ate," "visited ate") are just different English phrasings of the same act. The word was ordinary everyday Koine — Moulton-Milligan cites an inscription pairing it with "drinking together" and "coming under the same roof," capturing the social weight of sharing a table.

definition: To serve as a soldier or wage war, often used figuratively of spiritual or inner conflict.
article: This verb describes military service—either fighting battles or simply serving in the army—and the New Testament also stretches it to picture spiritual struggle, as in waging war against the desires of the soul (2CO 10:3, 1PE 2:11). It appears 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "war" twice and "soldier" once, while the other 4 occurrences are folded into surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word. The everyday papyri confirm its ordinary sense: documents speak plainly of "the Greeks serving in the army" and lists distinguishing soldiers from civilian inhabitants of a district.
caution: Most NT uses are absorbed into phrasing rather than translated by one word, so the precise sense often depends on context.

definition: To utter a sound or speak aloud, whether a person making clear speech or an animal giving voice.
article: φθέγγομαι means to produce a clear, audible sound — usually speaking, but it can apply to animals as well as people. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 3 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "speak" every time it gets its own word (as in Acts 4:18 and 2 Peter 2:16). A vivid touch comes from the papyri: one third-century epigram describes a painted portrait so lifelike that you'd say the man Eupepios "already speaks" (φθέγγεται), showing how everyday Koine used the word for giving voice.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 New Testament occurrences) and the word's confidence tier is low, so its full range is hard to pin down.

definition: The past-tense form of the verb "to be," meaning "was" or "were," used to describe how someone or something existed in the past.
article: ἦν is simply the imperfect (past) tense of the verb εἰμί, "to be" — it means "was" or "were." Like the English verb "to be," it covers a wide range: existing, happening, being present in a place, or just linking a subject to a description. One striking use is in Revelation, where "the one who is and who was" (ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν) treats this past-tense form almost as a name, using ἦν where you would normally expect a participle.
caution: The digest reports zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament being counted under this lemma, so the usage examples here come from the lexicon rather than measured corpus senses.

definition: The great value, costliness, or preciousness of something, especially wealth and luxury goods.
article: τιμιότης refers to preciousness or costliness — the high worth of valuable things. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Revelation 18:19, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "enriched" in describing how a city's wealth came from costly cargo. One striking detail: the papyri show this word commonly used as a title of respect ("your honour"), as in a 4th–5th century letter where a writer politely says he does not wish to weary "your honour."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: In a similar way; in much the same manner as something or someone else.
article: This adverb means "in like manner" or "similarly" — pointing to two things being nearly the same. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 2:14, where the BSB renders it in connection with "humanity," describing how Jesus shared in flesh and blood in much the same way people do. The lexicons agree on the basic sense, and Moulton-Milligan notes it was ordinary Koine vocabulary found in everyday papyri and inscriptions, with one parallel suggesting it can carry the nuance of "almost equally" or "also."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise shade of meaning rests largely on outside evidence rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: Eaten or destroyed by worms or maggots.
article: This compound word, built from σκώληξ ('worm') and a form of βιβρώσκω ('to eat'), describes something consumed by worms or maggots. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 12:23, where it describes Herod's death. Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri show the word applied to crops: one third-century BC document even uses the negative form for grain that was 'not worm-eaten,' and Theophrastus likewise used it of diseased grain, so its original range was broader than human disease.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single passage.

definition: Susanna, a woman who traveled with Jesus and helped support his ministry from her own means.
article: Susanna is a personal name belonging to one of the women who accompanied Jesus and supported his work, mentioned just once in the New Testament (Luke 8:3). The name comes from Hebrew and originally means "lily," and it shows up beyond the Bible too — Moulton-Milligan note it appearing in a list of accounts in an everyday Koine papyrus. The measured rendering here is labeled "household," but this reflects the surrounding context of Luke 8:3 rather than the name itself, which is simply the woman's name.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, and the single measured sense ("household") reflects the verse's context rather than the meaning of the name itself.

definition: Describing a person who has no law, either lacking it or breaking it, and so acting wickedly.
article: ἄνομος combines the negative prefix "a-" with "law" (nomos), so at root it means "lawless." In the New Testament it splits two ways: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lawless" 40% of the time (as in Acts 2:23 and 2 Thessalonians 2:8) and as someone "without law" another 40% — strikingly, all those "without law" uses cluster in a single verse, 1 Corinthians 9:21, where Paul speaks of those who do not have the Mosaic law. In the Septuagint it appears 75 times, mostly translating Hebrew words for the "wicked" (רָשָׁע, 14×). Everyday papyri use it for an "illegal" claim, showing the plain legal sense was common in ordinary Koine.
caution: The two main senses — merely "without law" versus actively "wicked" — depend heavily on context, and the "without law" sense rests almost entirely on one verse.

definition: A mixture or blend of substances combined together.
article: μίγμα refers to a blend of substances mixed together, derived from the verb μίγνυμι ("to mix"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at John 19:39, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the phrase describing a mixture of myrrh and aloes brought to prepare Jesus' body. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, including a magical text from the third century AD that instructs the reader to mix clay with a "mixture" of sulfur, showing its ordinary practical use.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and some manuscripts read a different word (ἕλιγμα, "a roll") instead, so its presence here is disputed.

definition: To walk in step or stay in line with a standard, meaning to live or conduct yourself according to an agreed rule.
article: στοιχέω literally pictures things arranged in rows—waves, plants, or soldiers marching in file—and from there came to mean ordering your life by a fixed standard or rule. In the Byzantine NT it appears 5 times, rendered "walk" in 3 (60%) and "live" in 2 (40%), with the BSB independently agreeing both ways. A striking parallel comes from an inscription where a man named Aristagoras is praised for "walking in the steps" of his ancestors, matching the sense behind Romans 4:12.
caution: Evidence is moderate: only 5 NT occurrences and a single Septuagint use, so the "walk" versus "live" split reflects translation choices for one underlying metaphor rather than two sharply distinct meanings.

definition: Amminadab, a male personal name belonging to an Israelite listed among the ancestors of Jesus.
article: Ἀμιναδάβ is an indeclinable Hebrew name, transliterated into Greek, and it appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Amminadab" every time. He is identified as the son of Ram and father of Nahshon, placing him in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:4, Luke 3:33). In the Septuagint the same Greek form appears 27 times and translates several different Hebrew names — most often עַמִּינָדָב (13×), but also אֲבִינָדָב (10×) and even the woman's name הֲדַסָּה (Hadassah) once, showing how transliteration can blur distinct underlying names.
caution: This is a proper name with few New Testament occurrences, and Abbott-Smith notes that Westcott-Hort omit it at Luke 3:33.

definition: Cornelius, the name of a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea in the book of Acts.
article: Κορνήλιος is simply the personal name Cornelius, a name of Latin origin borne by a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea. It appears 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all within the story of Acts chapter 10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Cornelius" in 7 of those occurrences (the rest are phrases like "Cornelius among"). The lexicons agree completely: it is a Roman name, and Abbott-Smith flags its Latin background.

definition: A small smooth pebble, especially the kind once used for casting a vote or recording a verdict.
article: ψῆφος is literally a little stone worn smooth by handling, the kind people kept in their pockets and used as counters. Because such pebbles were dropped into urns to cast votes, the word also came to mean a "vote" or "verdict." The everyday sense shows up vividly in the papyri, where one stone contract (P Petr II, 258-253 BC) speaks of clearing away the ψήφους, the pebbles lying over rock to be quarried. In the Septuagint it renders three different Hebrew words, and in Revelation 2:17 it names the white stone given to the one who overcomes.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences, and the measured renderings reflect the wider phrase rather than the word itself, so lean on the lexicons for the pebble-and-vote range.

definition: Sinai, the mountain in Arabia where God gave the law to Moses.
article: Σινᾶ is simply the Greek spelling of the place-name Sinai, the mountain where, according to the biblical account, God met Moses and gave the law. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all referring to this one mountain, though one passage (Acts 7:38) ties it to the gathering of Israel there, which is why the Bible renders it once as "assembly Mount Sinai." The name is borrowed straight from the Hebrew סִינַי, which it translates 33 of its 37 times in the Septuagint.

definition: To be greatly upset, troubled, or worn out in spirit over something.
article: In its 2 New Testament appearances, διαπονέω describes being deeply annoyed or troubled, rendered "greatly disturbed" in passages like Acts 4:2 where the religious leaders react to the apostles' preaching. The word literally means "to work through with labor," and that everyday sense survives in the papyri—one Oxyrhynchus letter from 2 B.C. uses it to mean "I am quite upset." The Abbott-Smith lexicon notes it can also mean "to be worn out, sore troubled," fitting the emotional strain captured in the biblical uses.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 Byzantine occurrences (none in the critical SBLGNT text) and a single Septuagint use, so confidence is low.

definition: A person who works the land, especially one who tends a vineyard or farms a plot, often as a tenant rather than the owner.
article: γεωργός is a worker of the soil — a farmer, vine-dresser, or husbandman. Of its 19 New Testament uses, the great majority cluster in the parable of the vineyard tenants (rendered "tenants" 7×, with related phrasings), while just 2× it means a plain "farmer" (2 Timothy 2:6; James 5:7). Papyri show it was a ubiquitous everyday word; one document from 223 BC even concerns tenants who went insolvent because their farming burden was too heavy.
caution: The many parable renderings ('tenants,' 'tenants another,' 'harvest tenants collect') reflect a single underlying sense shaped by context, so the count of distinct meanings is narrower than it first appears.

definition: To win an overwhelming victory; to be far more than just a conqueror.
article: This vivid word combines "over/beyond" (ὑπέρ) with "to conquer" (νικάω), so it means not merely winning but gaining a decisive, overwhelming victory. It appears only once in the entire New Testament, in Romans 8:37, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "conquerors" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100%. Though rare in scripture, Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and the Septuagint uses it a couple of times (Daniel and the Psalms in later translations).
caution: This is a New Testament hapax (appearing only once), so its precise force rests on a single passage plus thin outside evidence.

definition: To examine a matter carefully in order to determine or decide it, especially in a legal context.
article: This compound of διά ("through") and γινώσκω ("know") means to know something thoroughly—to investigate closely and reach a decision. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts: once of inquiring more exactly into Paul's situation (Acts 23:15) and once of Felix deciding Paul's case (Acts 24:22). The legal flavor is well supported outside the Bible: everyday Koine papyri use it for officials deciding matters, including a phrase meaning "the king shall take cognisance" of someone's affairs.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, each carrying a different shade of meaning, the evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: A person who kidnaps people to enslave or sell them, a slave-dealer or trafficker in human beings.
article: ἀνδραποδιστής refers to someone who captures and trades human beings as slaves — a kidnapper or slave-dealer. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:10, where it sits in a list of lawless behaviors. The related noun for "slave" turns up regularly in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a document mentioning payment of a "slave-duty" and property catalogues listing slaves, showing this was ordinary commercial vocabulary of the time.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on a single occurrence and the broader documentary evidence.

definition: A branch or shoot of a vine, the leafy growth that grows out from the main stem.
article: κλῆμα means a branch or shoot, especially of a grapevine. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times, all clustered in John 15, where Jesus speaks of branches connected to the vine; the apparent variety in the digest's rendering ("branch," "branch itself," "branch away") simply reflects surrounding words, not different meanings — the core sense is always "vine branch." The Septuagint uses it 11 times, mostly for Hebrew words for vine shoots, and a third-century papyrus from a vineyard tells workers to "gather the branches," showing it was everyday farming vocabulary.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament, where the word occurs only in one passage (John 15).

definition: Describing customs, beliefs, or ways of life handed down from one's ancestors and inherited from past generations.
article: πατροπαράδοτος combines the words for "father" and "hand down," describing something inherited from previous generations — a traditional, ancestral way of life. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 1:18, and outside the Bible Moulton-Milligan note it in everyday Koine, including a Pergamene inscription where a man describes the god Sabazios as "handed down" (πατροπαράδοτον) by his Cappadocian mother. Notably, the measured rendering tags this single occurrence as "redeemed," which reflects the surrounding verse rather than this word itself — the lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) consistently define it as "inherited from one's fathers."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured "redeemed" rendering reflects the broader verse rather than the word's actual meaning, which the lexicons agree is "inherited from one's ancestors."

definition: To lay waste a place or strip a person, leaving them ruined, deserted, and empty.
article: ἐρημόω means to turn something into a wasteland — to leave a place desolate or to strip a person of everything. It is closely related to ἔρημος, "desert," and the family shows clearly in the Septuagint, where it appears 54 times and most often translates the Hebrew חָרַב, "to be laid waste" (20×). The same word turns up in everyday Koine documents; one papyrus from around A.D. 245 reports that "the lands happened to be laid waste," showing the very physical, practical sense of ruin.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament — only 5 Byzantine occurrences (none in the SBL critical text), and 3 of those are absorbed into phrasing without their own English word.

definition: A place near Jerusalem named in Aramaic "field of blood," linked to the death of Judas.
article: Akeldama is a proper name—a specific plot of ground near Jerusalem—transliterated from Aramaic words meaning "field of blood." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 1:19, and the critical SBLGNT text does not include it. The lexicons agree on the Aramaic sense "field of blood" and traditionally place it south of the valley of Hinnom, with the name drawn from Hebrew roots for "field" and "blood."
caution: This is a place-name attested only once, so its meaning rests on the Aramaic etymology and tradition rather than broad usage.

definition: A relative pronoun meaning "whoever," "anyone who," or simply "who," pointing to people or things in a general or descriptive way.
article: ὅστις is a flexible relative pronoun that ranges from the general "whoever, anyone who" to a plain "who" identifying a particular person or thing. In the New Testament it appears 142 times but almost only in the nominative form, and translators render it most often as "who" (38×, 41%); strikingly, in 50 of those 142 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding English with no word of its own. Classically ὅστις was distinguished from the simpler ὅς, but Moulton-Milligan note that this distinction "has worn very thin in the papyri" — an everyday dinner invitation from second-century Egypt uses ἥτις just to mean "which is the 15th."
caution: The renderings vary widely and the classical ὅστις/ὅς distinction is inconsistently maintained in the NT, so the exact shade of meaning often depends on context rather than the word itself.

definition: To think something through with oneself—reasoning, weighing options, or calculating—before reaching a conclusion.
article: This verb combines "together" (σύν) with "reckon" (λογίζομαι), giving the sense of working things out in one's mind—deliberating, reasoning, or computing. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 20:5, where the chief priests "deliberated" among themselves; the Septuagint uses it five times across three books. A nice glimpse of its everyday range comes from the papyri, where it carries the accountant's sense of "compute"—one document has people "having reckoned up" both a loan and its valuation.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical sense rests on a single passage, with the broader "compute" meaning drawn mainly from external evidence.

definition: An opening in a wall to let in light or air; a window.
article: θυρίς means a window, an opening in a wall, and is a diminutive form of θύρα ('door'). Both of its New Testament occurrences (Acts 20:9, where a young man falls from one, and 2 Corinthians 11:33, where Paul escapes through one) are rendered 'window,' and the Majority Standard Bible and BSB agree 100%. In the Septuagint it appears 32 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word חַלּוֹן ('window'), and everyday Koine papyri describe houses fitted 'with doors and windows and locks,' confirming the plain household meaning.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences this is a thinly attested word, though all sources agree on its meaning.

definition: The act of sleeping or resting, especially natural sleep as opposed to death.
senseLabels: the act of sleeping or resting
article: κοίμησις refers to sleeping or taking rest, and in its single New Testament appearance (John 11:13) it points specifically to ordinary sleep. There the word matters precisely because of a misunderstanding: when Jesus spoke of Lazarus "sleeping" as a figure for death, the disciples assumed he meant this natural κοίμησις, the rest a sick person takes to recover. Interestingly, the everyday papyri and inscriptions tell a fuller story: the word was also used for the "rest" of death, as in a Jewish epitaph reading "in peace be your κοίμησις," the very nuance the disciples missed.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament (a hapax) and just twice in the Septuagint, so its range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: To faint or lose heart from overwhelming fear or anxiety, as the breath seems to fail.
article: ἀποψύχω literally means "to breathe out," and it describes people fainting or losing heart when overcome by dread. In its single New Testament appearance (Luke 21:26), the Majority Standard Bible and the Berea Standard Bible both render it as fainting from anxiety, and Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith all agree on this "faint" sense. Notably, Abbott-Smith records two distinct shades elsewhere: in 4 Maccabees 15:18 it means "to breathe out life, expire," while in Homer's Odyssey it carries the milder "faint" sense that fits the Luke passage.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single occurrence.

definition: An impersonal phrase meaning "it is enough" or "it is sufficient," marking that something is settled or complete.
article: This is a specific form of the verb ἀπέχω (apéchō, "to have in full," "to be distant," or in the middle voice "to abstain") used impersonally to mean "it is enough." The base verb has a broad range: it can describe receiving payment in full (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16; Luke 6:24; Philippians 4:18), being physically far off (Luke 7:6), being estranged in heart (Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6), or abstaining from something. The notable point is that this impersonal sense "it is enough" appears in Mark 14:41, where the underlying idea of "having in full" shades into "that's sufficient."
caution: This exact form has zero Byzantine NT occurrences in the digest and no confidence tier was computed, so all evidence here comes from the broader verb ἀπέχω rather than from measured uses of this specific form.

definition: To pour a liquid down over someone or something.
article: καταχέω means to pour a liquid down upon a person or object, and in the New Testament it appears just twice—both times describing a woman pouring costly ointment over Jesus' head (Matthew 26:7; Mark 14:3). The verb is typically construed with the genitive of what is poured over, and it shows up in everyday Koine: a 218 B.C. papyrus (P Magd 24) uses it in a rather earthy complaint about someone whose urine poured down on the writer from an upper room. In the Septuagint it occurs three times, translating Hebrew words including יָצַק and נָטָה.
caution: With only 2 New Testament uses, both in the same anointing scene, the measured evidence is thin even though the meaning is clear.

definition: To make, create, or produce something, or to do, perform, or carry out an action.
article: ποιέω is one of the most common and flexible verbs in the New Testament, appearing 574 times and covering everything from making and creating to doing, performing, and carrying out. About 38% of the time it's rendered "made," while the rest splits among "what," "done," "doing," and "things," reflecting how broadly it stretches across both production and action. In the Septuagint it appears a staggering 2,817 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew עָשָׂה ("to do/make") over 2,200 times; everyday papyri also show the polite phrase "you will do well" used much like our "please" when making a request.
caution: The verb is so broad that in 381 of 574 occurrences it carries no English word of its own, getting absorbed into surrounding phrasing.

definition: The act of placing or laying something on someone, especially the laying of hands on a person in a formal or official setting.
article: In the New Testament, ἐπίθεσις always refers to the laying on of hands, appearing 4 times and rendered "laying" in 100% of cases, as when hands were laid on people to confer a gift or office (Acts 8:18, 1 Timothy 4:14, 2 Timothy 1:6). The word comes from ἐπιτίθημι, "to put upon." Interestingly, the evidence outside the New Testament tells a different story: in the Septuagint it can mean a "conspiracy" (translating Hebrew קֶ֫שֶׁר), and the everyday papyri use it exclusively in a hostile sense — an "attack" or "machination," as in a complaint describing a violent assault. So the same word that means a gentle laying on of hands in the New Testament more often meant an aggressive onslaught in common Greek.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the gentle "laying on" sense is narrow, and the broader Greek evidence (papyri and Septuagint) points instead to "attack" or "conspiracy."

definition: Eager to gain money through shameful or dishonest means; greedy for dishonorable profit.
article: This adjective describes someone driven by a shameful love of money, willing to pursue gain in dishonorable ways. It is built from two Greek parts meaning "shameful" (G150) and "gain," so the disgrace is baked right into the word. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all in the pastoral letters listing qualifications for church leaders (1 Timothy 3:3, 3:8; Titus 1:7), where overseers and deacons must not be this way. The various English renderings — "greedy for money," "given to greedy," and the older KJV "given to filthy lucre" — all point to the same idea of shameful greed.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences) and the lexica disagree on which verses contain the word, so treat the range as approximate.

definition: To roll something heavy, like a stone, up against or toward an object so it sits in place.
article: This verb describes the physical act of rolling a large stone up to or against something, and in the New Testament it is used only of sealing a tomb with a stone. It appears just twice, both times rendered "rolled" (100%), in Matthew 27:60 and Mark 15:46. Abbott-Smith notes the grammar shifts slightly between the two: Matthew pairs it with a direct object and indirect object, while Mark uses it with a stone rolled "upon" (ἐπί) the entrance.
caution: With only 2 occurrences the word is barely attested, so its full range cannot be measured from the New Testament alone.

definition: To formally confirm or ratify something in advance, settling it beforehand as a binding agreement.
article: This compound joins "before" (πρό) with "to ratify" (κυρόω), so it means to validate or settle an agreement in advance. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 3:17, where Paul speaks of a covenant established beforehand. Notably, while the lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) and Strong's all define it as "establish or ratify before," the Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence as "revoke" — likely shaped by the surrounding context of a law that cannot annul the prior covenant.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lexicons ("ratify beforehand") sit oddly against the MSB rendering "revoke," so its precise force rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To wear someone down through harsh treatment, oppressing or overpowering them until they are worn out.
article: καταπονέω describes grinding someone down through mistreatment or hardship, leaving them oppressed and worn out. It is rare in the Byzantine New Testament, appearing only twice (Acts 7:24, describing the Israelite being mistreated, and 2 Peter 2:7, of Lot distressed by lawless living), and in both cases it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. The everyday papyri make the sense vivid: petitioners complain of being "worn down" by tax-collectors (BGU IV.1188), and one document speaks of a desire to thoroughly "worst" one's adversaries in a lawsuit (P Oxy VIII.1101).
caution: Confidence is low: only two New Testament occurrences, both blended into phrasing, so the precise force rests largely on outside papyri evidence.

definition: Colossae, a city on the Lycus River in Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia.
article: Colossae was a city in the Lycus valley of Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, located near Laodicea and Hierapolis. The name appears just once in the New Testament, in Colossians 1:2, where the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB both render it "Colossae." The spelling varied even in antiquity: some manuscripts and editions read the form with a double sigma (-ασσαί), as Abbott-Smith notes.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage cannot be measured across multiple contexts.

definition: To solemnly put someone under oath, urgently charging or appealing to them by a higher power to do something.
article: ὁρκίζω means to bind someone with an oath — to charge or appeal to them solemnly, often invoking God or another power. In its 3 New Testament appearances it splits evenly between an urgent plea ("beg before") and a binding command ("charge before"), and once it dissolves into the surrounding phrasing. The most striking evidence comes from the papyri: an imprecatory tablet from Hadrumetum reads "I adjure thee, demonic spirit... by the God of Abraham," matching exactly how the demon-possessed man uses the word against Jesus in Mark 5:7. In the Septuagint it appears 27 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew verb for swearing an oath (שָׁבַע, 22 times).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences split across two senses, the precise English range rests on thin measured evidence.

definition: A feeling of gladness, joy, or cheerful delight.
article: Euphrosýnē names a state of joyful gladness or cheerful celebration. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 2:28 and Acts 14:17), but it is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 112 times across 24 books. There it most often renders the Hebrew śimḥâ ("joy," 68×), and also stands in for several other Hebrew words for rejoicing and exultation, showing it covers a wide and well-attested range of glad emotion.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences—one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than given its own English word—the measured NT evidence is thin, so its fuller range rests mainly on Septuagint usage.

definition: A remnant — the small portion of people or things left over after most are gone.
article: κατάλειμμα means a remnant or leftover portion, what remains when most has been removed or destroyed. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Romans 9:27, where it speaks of a remnant being saved; many critical editions actually read the near-synonym ὑπόλειμμα here instead. The Septuagint uses it 16 times, most often to render the Hebrew word שְׁאֵרִית ('remnant'), and Moulton-Milligan even found the related word in an everyday wine account on papyrus.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the Byzantine NT and zero times in the critical text, where the synonym ὑπόλειμμα is read instead.

definition: To harm or influence someone through what was popularly believed to be the power of the evil eye, or to slander.
article: βασκαίνω appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Galatians 3:1, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render Paul's metaphor of bewitching the Galatians. The classical lexica note a broader range: Demosthenes used it to mean "slander," while in the Septuagint (Deuteronomy 28:54, 56; Sirach 14:6, 8) it carries the idea of harming through a grudging or envious eye. The most vivid evidence comes from everyday papyri, where letter-writers routinely closed with prayers that the recipient stay healthy "unharmed by the evil eye" (ἀβασκάντως), showing how alive this popular belief was in ordinary Koine.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall attestation, the precise force in Galatians is uncertain, and the lexica split between "slander" and "bewitch by the evil eye."

definition: Extremely frightened or terrified, overwhelmed by fear.
article: ἔκφοβος describes someone in a state of intense fear — terrified or frightened out of their wits. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and in both places it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word, so its force comes through expressions like 'sore afraid' or 'exceedingly fear.' In its single Septuagint appearance it renders the Hebrew יָגֹר ('to dread'), in Deuteronomy 9:19, reinforcing the sense of overwhelming terror. The word is built from ἐκ ('out of') and φόβος ('fear').
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences and one in the Septuagint — so the picture of its range is limited.

definition: A small boat or skiff, especially a ship's lifeboat carried aboard a larger vessel for landing or escape.
article: σκάφη is a small open boat — literally something "scooped out" or hollowed, from the verb σκάπτω (to dig). In all three New Testament uses, which fall in the single shipwreck scene of Acts 27, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lifeboat" (100%), describing the small craft carried aboard Paul's ship. The everyday papyri back this up nicely: documents speak of "a boat with three sculls" and even "the pilot of a public vessel," showing it was a common word for a small working boat.
caution: This word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all within one narrative, so the measured sense reflects a single context rather than a broad range.

definition: Nicopolis, a city where Paul planned to spend the winter, mentioned once in the New Testament.
article: Nicopolis is a place name, built from the words for "victory" (G3534) and "city" (G4172), so it literally means "victory city." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Titus 3:12, where Paul tells Titus to meet him there for the winter. The sources differ on which Nicopolis is meant: Strong's and Dodson place it in Macedonia, while Abbott-Smith favors the city of that name in Epirus.
caution: This word occurs only once and the lexicons disagree on which Nicopolis is intended, so its exact location is uncertain.

definition: A ghostly apparition or spectral appearance—something seen that seems to be a spirit rather than a real person.
article: φάντασμα refers to an apparition or ghostly appearance, something that looks like a spirit. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 14:26 and Mark 6:49), both times when the disciples mistake Jesus walking on the water for a ghost; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ghost" once, while the other occurrence is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The word turns up in everyday Koine too: Moulton-Milligan cite a third-century protective charm invoking a bodyguard "against demons, against apparitions, against every sickness," showing the word's place in popular fears of the supernatural.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin Septuagint attestation, this entry rests on limited evidence.

definition: To say, speak, or tell something — the basic verb for putting words to thoughts, whether spoken aloud or in writing.
article: This is one of the most common verbs in the entire New Testament, appearing 2,313 times across 25 books, and it covers the whole range of speaking: stating, telling, asking, replying, and answering. Over half the time (53%) it simply means "said," and in about a third of cases it shades into telling, asking, or replying depending on context.
