In the Septuagint it translates the ordinary Hebrew verb for speaking, אָמַר, more than a thousand times, but it also renders נְאֻם, the solemn formula "declares the LORD" — so the same word stretches from casual conversation to prophetic announcement. Many of its labeled "senses" here are really just where Jesus happens to be the speaker, which is why entries like "Jesus said" show up so often.
caution: Several of the listed senses ("Jesus," "Jesus said," "said tell") reflect surrounding phrasing and subject rather than distinct meanings of the verb itself, and 666 of 2,313 occurrences were absorbed into English phrasing with no word of their own.

definition: To let things grow up together side by side until a later time of separation.
article: συναυξάνω means to cause or let things increase and grow together, and in its single New Testament appearance (Matthew 13:30) it describes letting wheat and weeds grow side by side until the harvest. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the SBL critical text, with a couple of Septuagint occurrences (2 Maccabees 4:4; 4 Maccabees 13:27). The word was at home in everyday Koine: an inscription from the third century B.C. (OGIS 233.19) uses it of people eager to 'increase together' the population of the Antiochenes.
caution: This is essentially a one-occurrence word in the New Testament with very thin attestation, so its range cannot be measured with confidence.

definition: A long or unbounded stretch of time — an age, an era, or, in fixed phrases, eternity itself.
article: αἰών names a span of time, and the New Testament uses it two ways that flow into each other: the concrete sense of an "age" or era of history (rendered "age" 29 times, 26%), and the looser sense of unbounded duration that fills set phrases like "forever" (49×), "ever" (23×), and, when negated, "never" (10×). The same Greek expression flips between "forever" and "never" depending on whether a negative is attached, so the word's force depends heavily on its surrounding phrasing — in fact 14 of its 126 occurrences carry no English word of their own. In the Septuagint it stands overwhelmingly for the Hebrew עוֹלָם (190×), and an everyday papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος ("from life") to describe a man being led off to death, showing how ordinary the time-sense could be.
caution: The split between concrete "age" and abstract "forever/never" is real, and the latter readings depend on Greek prepositional and negative constructions rather than the bare noun, so renderings can shift with phrasing.

definition: To honor or show respect to someone, or to set a value or price on something.
article: τιμάω overwhelmingly means to honor or revere someone, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "honor" in 15 of 19 cases (83%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% of the time. The lexicons add a second shade the NT itself rarely shows: to fix a value or price on something, as in Matthew 27:9. The Septuagint backs both ideas, translating it most often for Hebrew כָּבַד ("to be heavy, honor," 10×) and also עָרַךְ ("to arrange, value," 6×); everyday papyri confirm both, using it in civic decrees honoring officials and in accounts where something is "priced."

definition: To have sinned at an earlier time, before the present moment being addressed.
article: This compound joins "before" (πρό) with "to sin" (ἁμαρτάνω), so it means to have sinned at some earlier point. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's letters (2 Corinthians 12:21 and 13:2), and the translation "earlier" is used in every case. The word also shows up in everyday Koine documents: one inscription speaks of people who have "repented of their earlier sins," using exactly this term alongside a word for changing one's mind.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the evidence base is thin, so the word's full range cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: The comparative form meaning "nearer" or "closer," used of time drawing closer.
article: This is the comparative of ἐγγύς ("near"), the neuter form used as an adverb to mean "nearer" or "closer." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Romans 13:11), where it speaks of something being nearer in time. In that single use it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than standing as its own English word, and Abbott-Smith notes it as the comparative of the adjective used adverbially.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense range for this exact form rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Describing people as unusually attentive to religious matters or the divine, more so than others.
article: This is a comparative form meaning something like "more religious" or "more reverent toward the divine" than others. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:22, where Paul addresses the Athenians. The word famously sits on a knife's edge: the KJV renders it "too superstitious" with a negative tint, while Dodson and others lean toward the more positive "religious" or "God-fearing," and Moulton-Milligan notes the everyday Koine usage offers little to settle which shade Paul intended.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine NT, the measured-sense label ("meeting") looks like a data artifact rather than a real gloss, and the sources openly disagree over whether it praises or criticizes.

definition: To bend or bow, especially to bend the knee in an act of submission or worship.
article: κάμπτω means to bend or bow, and in the New Testament's four uses it always describes bending the knee before God in worship or submission. The range is narrow in Scripture, but the wider Koine world used it more literally—everyday papyri mention things like "a bent little finger" and even ships "turning" toward the north or east. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew word kāraʿ (8 of 11 times), which also means to kneel or bow down.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, all in the single sense of bowing the knee, the measured biblical range is quite thin.

definition: To sound out or resound, used of news or a message ringing forth so widely it becomes generally reported.
article: ἐξηχέομαι describes a sound carrying outward, like a trumpet blast or thunder rolling out, and figuratively a report spreading far and wide. In its single New Testament appearance (1 Thessalonians 1:8) it is rendered "ring," picturing the message of faith echoing out from the believers. In the Septuagint it shows up in passages tied to noise or multitude (Abbott-Smith notes Joel 3:14, Sirach 40:13, and 3 Maccabees 3:2), and one digest links it to the Hebrew חָרוּץ, while Abbott-Smith connects the Joel verse to הָמוֹן, a word for a roaring crowd.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and rarely elsewhere, and the sources differ on which Hebrew word it renders, so its precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: To set on fire or kindle something, and figuratively to be inflamed with strong passion or desire.
article: ἐκκαίω literally means to burn up or kindle, but its single appearance in the New Testament (Romans 1:27) uses the passive sense of being inflamed—here with desire. The Septuagint employs it far more often, 39 times across 18 books, most frequently translating the Hebrew בָּעַר ("to burn," 6×). The everyday papyri and a Menander fragment confirm this fiery, metaphorical edge: feelings "fanned into flame," as one slave is told she sets her mistress "on fire with fury."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text, so its single measured sense rests on limited New Testament data.

definition: Lysias, the Roman commander (Claudius Lysias) who oversaw Paul's protection and transfer in Jerusalem.
article: Lysias is a personal name, belonging to Claudius Lysias, the Roman tribune who commanded troops in Jerusalem and intervened to protect Paul. It appears twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 23:26 and 24:22), once with his title rendered "Lysias, Excellency" and once simply as "Lysias." The name itself was ordinary in everyday Koine, since Moulton-Milligan notes it turning up in common papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This is a proper name with only two occurrences, so its range is limited entirely to this one Roman official.

definition: A going down or descent, such as the downward slope of a road or hillside.
article: κατάβασις refers to a descent — the act or place of going down, like the slope of a hill. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 19:37, where it marks the "descent" of the Mount of Olives, and the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "descent" there. The word comes from καταβαίνω ("to go down"), and in everyday Koine it could be quite concrete: one papyrus from A.D. 237 uses it for transporting dancing girls "down and back" (κατάβασις and ἀνάβασις) for a village festival.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single passage, though the Septuagint and papyri agree on the basic meaning.

definition: The neuter form used as a noun meaning either the cause or reason for something, or the grounds for an accusation—a fault or crime.
article: This word is the neuter form of αἴτιος and works as a noun with two related senses: 'the cause' or reason behind something, and 'the fault' or crime someone is charged with. It never appears in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up only once in the critical text (SBLGNT), so our New Testament evidence is thin. Abbott-Smith notes the related forms in Luke 23:4, 14, 22, where the sense is the legal 'fault' or charge against the accused—the most concrete picture of how the word lands in practice.
caution: Evidence is very thin: the word does not occur in the Byzantine text and appears only once in the critical text, so its precise range rests largely on the related form αἴτιος.

definition: Archippus, the personal name of a Christian associated with the church at Colossae.
article: Ἄρχιππος is a personal name appearing twice in the New Testament, both times referring to a believer connected with Colossae (Colossians 4:17 and Philemon 2). The Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "Archippus" in 100% of cases, and the lexicons agree completely. The name is built from ἀρχή ("ruler") and ἵππος ("horse"), giving it the literal sense "horse-ruler" or "master of horses," a typical Greek name formation that carried no theological meaning in its New Testament use.

definition: A personal name belonging to an early Christian greeted in Colossians, possibly a man (Nymphas) or a woman (Nympha).
article: Νυμφᾶς is a proper name appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Colossians 4:15, where it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated as a separate English word. The name's form is genuinely disputed: it may be the masculine Nymphas or the feminine Nympha, since the Greek spelling can be read either way. Moulton suggests the feminine reading 'Nympha' arose by analogy, where the genitive Νύμφης produced a short nominative Νύμφα, comparing it to a similar form in a Christian inscription.
caution: This name occurs only once, appears in none of the SBLGNT critical text, and the sources genuinely disagree over whether it names a man or a woman.

definition: A dish or plate, especially the small one used to serve choice foods at a meal.
article: παροψίς is a serving dish, and in the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Jesus' rebuke of the Pharisees in Matthew 23:25-26. Originally the word meant a fancy side-dish of dainties, but in comic poets and later prose it came to mean the plate or platter on which the food was served — the sense used here. Interestingly, this later usage was condemned by the Atticists as bad Greek, yet papyri and inscriptions confirm it was ordinary everyday Koine, with documents listing carved παροψίδες among household items.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a sense disputed by ancient Atticist purists, the precise nuance (the food versus the dish) is debated.

definition: In a way driven by greed for shameful or dishonest gain.
article: This adverb describes doing something out of eagerness for dishonest profit. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:2, where shepherds of God's flock are told not to serve this way. It comes from the adjective αἰσχροκερδής, meaning greedy for shameful gain, and the lexicons agree it points to an attitude of grasping after base profit.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: The act of equipping or preparing people so they are fully ready and fit for a task.
article: καταρτισμός refers to bringing something or someone into a state of readiness — equipping, furnishing, or preparing for use. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 4:12, where the Berean Standard Bible renders it "equip" (100% of its single occurrence). The everyday Koine papyri show its concrete, practical flavor: one document from 112 BC speaks of "the things for the furnishing of the guest-chamber," and another mentions the preparation of woof and warp for a cloak.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests on a single verse plus outside evidence.

definition: A turning away from sin and change of heart and mind toward God.
article: Repentance is the dominant and nearly exclusive meaning of this word, used 24 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "repentance" in 83% of cases (with the BSB independently agreeing 89%). Beyond simply feeling sorry, the underlying idea is a change of mind in the inner person, which is why John's baptism is called a "baptism of repentance" and why it can be paired with turning from sin. A nice glimpse of its life outside the Bible comes from the papyri: a sixth-century Egyptian church calendar even lists a "day of repentance," and a monastery at Alexandria bore the same name.
caution: The Septuagint evidence is thin, appearing only once, so most of this word's biblical weight rests on its New Testament usage.

definition: Belonging to Adramyttium, a seaport in the region of Mysia in Asia Minor.
article: This adjective simply describes something as coming from or belonging to Adramyttium, a seaport in Mysia in Asia Minor. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:2, where it describes the ship Paul boarded on his journey toward Rome. The lexicons note a spelling variation, with some manuscripts reading Ἁδραμυντηνός rather than Ἀδραμυττηνός.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be tested across multiple contexts.

definition: A red gemstone (the sardius or carnelian) mentioned as part of a vision's description.
article: σάρδινος refers to a reddish precious stone, the sardine or sardius, and is essentially a variant form of σάρδιον. It appears in the textus receptus reading of Revelation 4:3, where God's appearance is compared to gemstones, though it is not part of the Byzantine count here (0 occurrences). Abbott-Smith treats it as simply equal to σάρδιον, the more standard term for the same stone.
caution: The evidence is extremely thin: this form is a textual variant tied to Revelation 4:3 with no Byzantine occurrences, and lexicons equate it with σάρδιον rather than treating it as a distinct word.

definition: To make one thing resemble another, or to compare two things in order to show how they are alike.
article: ὁμοιόω covers two closely related ideas: drawing a comparison between things ('to what shall I compare this generation?') and making or becoming similar to something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times, rendered 'compare' in 5 cases and 'like' in 4, with the passive often meaning 'to be made like.' In the Septuagint it shows up 30 times, most often translating the Hebrew דָּמָה, which itself carries the sense of resembling or likening.

definition: A pointing out or display that proves or makes something clearly evident.
article: ἔνδειξις refers to the act of showing something so clearly that it serves as proof or evidence. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times across 3 books; the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "demonstrate" twice (67%, as in Romans 3:25-26 where God demonstrates his righteousness) and "view" once (33%, in 2 Corinthians 8:24, a visible token shown to others). Built from ἐνδείκνυμι ("to point out"), it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a Lesbian-dialect inscription documented by Moulton-Milligan, confirming it was ordinary public language.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the word's range is narrow, and one instance is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word.

definition: To be advantageous or profitable; in the New Testament, to be better or good for someone, often used impersonally as "it is beneficial."
article: At its root συμφέρω means to "bring together," but in the New Testament it almost always works impersonally to say that something is advantageous — rendered "better" 4 times (31%), "good" 4 times (31%), and "beneficial" twice (15%), with another 4 of 17 occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The literal sense survives in places like Acts 19:19, where it describes physically gathering or bringing things together. Everyday Koine papyri show the same range, even using the word for a marriage union when a couple "come together," alongside the very common impersonal "it is expedient."

definition: The act of breaking something, used in the New Testament specifically of breaking bread at a shared meal.
article: κλάσις refers to the act of breaking, and in both of its New Testament appearances it describes the breaking of bread (Luke 24:35; Acts 2:42). It comes from the verb κλάω, "to break," so the word names the action itself rather than a piece or fragment. Every translation in the evidence agrees on this single meaning, and both occurrences pair it with bread, giving it a strong association with shared meals among early believers.
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times with "bread," so its broader range cannot be measured from this evidence.

definition: Haran, a town in northwestern Mesopotamia where Abraham lived before moving to Canaan.
article: Χαῤῥάν is simply the Greek spelling of the place name Haran, a town in northwestern Mesopotamia. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Stephen's speech in Acts 7, recalling Abraham's journey before he settled in Canaan. The Septuagint uses it 14 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew חָרָן, and Josephus spells it variously as Κάρρα or Χαρρά, showing the name was transliterated several different ways in Greek.
caution: This is an indeclinable proper name with only two New Testament occurrences, so the two "measured senses" simply reflect translation phrasing rather than genuinely different meanings.

definition: A soldier — a member of an army serving under military authority.
article: στρατιώτης simply means a soldier, and the New Testament uses it that way consistently — 24 of its 26 occurrences (92%) are rendered plainly as "soldiers," with the remaining two differing only because of an attached object. The word was common, everyday vocabulary; Moulton-Milligan cites it in soldiers' letters and complaints from the papyri, including one Oxyrhynchus document about extortion "by the soldier" that echoes the language of Luke 3:14. Abbott-Smith notes one figurative use, where Paul calls Timothy a "soldier of Christ Jesus" (2 Timothy 2:3).

definition: A man named Cosam, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.
article: Cosam is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:28), where he is named as the son of Elmadam and father of Addi. Every source treats it strictly as a proper name, and the translation evidence agrees completely. Strong's notes it is of Hebrew origin, comparing it to a Hebrew word (H7081).
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so there is little beyond the genealogy itself to draw on.

definition: To grab someone or something forcibly and either carry them off or hold them fast.
article: συναρπάζω is a strengthened form of ἁρπάζω ("snatch"), and means to seize with force — sometimes grabbing and dragging away, sometimes grabbing and keeping a tight grip. In the Byzantine New Testament its four uses split evenly: twice the person is "seized" (Luke 8:29; Acts 6:12), and twice a person or ship is swept "into" or away by force (Acts 19:29; Acts 27:15). Everyday papyri confirm both shades — one document complains that the writers "have been robbed on every side" by a man using this same verb.

definition: Describing something bright and shining, or by extension fine, splendid, and impressive in appearance.
article: λαμπρός describes things that gleam — a bright star or river — and by extension clothing or objects that look fine, splendid, and impressive. In the New Testament's 9 occurrences it splits between these two ideas: it's rendered "fine" 3 times (often of garments) and "bright" twice, with the rest absorbed into phrasing or rare wordings. A vivid touch from the papyri: a Christian-era inscription uses the word for "the shining land" of the afterlife, where a young woman "departed to the bright place," and in modern Greek the related form means Easter.
caution: With only 9 occurrences and renderings ranging from "fine" to "bright" to "gorgeous," the exact shade depends heavily on context.

definition: To know, understand, or come to recognize something or someone through experience or perception.
article: γινώσκω is one of the most common verbs in the New Testament, appearing 222 times, and it covers the whole range of "knowing" — from grasping a fact to recognizing a person to coming to understand a truth over time. The dominant rendering is plainly "know" (142×, 80%), with "understand," "realized," and "be aware" filling out the picture; in 44 of those cases it is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. In the Septuagint it appears 603 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew יָדַע ("to know"), the same word used for everything from intimate personal knowledge to factual awareness. Everyday papyri show its ordinary force well: one letter opens "know that the runaway will try not to let us stay," exactly the plain "be informed that" sense.

definition: To write something beforehand or earlier, whether in the past, above in a text, or publicly posted.
article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to write" (γράφω), and in the New Testament it mostly means simply something written previously — as in Romans 15:4, where the Scriptures were "written" in earlier times, or Ephesians 3:3, "already written briefly." In Jude 1:4 the Majority Standard Bible renders it more loosely ("among"), describing people designated beforehand for judgment. The everyday papyri are illuminating here: a phrase like τὸ προγεγραμμένον ἐκφόριον ("the above-written rent") shows the prefix often just meant "written above" in a document, with the time-sense weakened.
caution: Classical lexica list additional senses not measured here — "to placard publicly" and "to portray openly" (proposed for Galatians 3:1) — so the word's full range exceeds the New Testament samples.

definition: To love someone or something—to feel and show esteem, goodwill, and delight toward a person or thing.
article: ἀγαπάω is the standard Greek verb for love, and it is remarkably consistent: of its 142 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "love" 130 times (98%), with the BSB agreeing 100%. It covers a wide range—love between people, love for things, God's love for people, and Christ's love—and in the Septuagint it appears 215 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew אָהַב ("to love," 130×). One striking detail: the Rosetta Stone and a Munich papyrus use the same form for kings "beloved by" a god, mirroring Paul's phrase "brothers beloved by God" in 1 Thessalonians 1:4.

definition: The practice of sorcery or witchcraft, often involving magic potions or spells.
article: In the New Testament, φαρμακεία always appears with the meaning "sorcery" or "witchcraft" — all 3 Byzantine occurrences (Galatians 5:20, Revelation 9:21, 18:23) are rendered that way. The word's literal root, however, has to do with drugs and medicine: in the Septuagint it covers the magic arts of Egypt's sorcerers (Exodus 7–8) and Babylon's spells (Isaiah 47), and classical writers used it for everything from medical drugging to poisoning. A vivid example comes from the papyri: an Egyptian document from B.C. 258 has a man explaining he can't leave the house because a dose of medicine has made him sick, while a later record (A.D. 131) uses the same word to accuse a mother of poisoning.
caution: This entry rests on only 3 New Testament occurrences (2 in the critical text), so the consistent "sorcery" sense is real but thinly attested in the corpus itself.

definition: In a way that gives no cause for blame or complaint; conducting oneself so that no one can find fault.
article: This adverb describes acting in a way nobody can criticize—living "blamelessly." It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Thessalonians (2:10 and 5:23), and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "blameless" (with BSB and KJV agreeing). It is rare in the Septuagint too, showing up only once, in Esther 3:13.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: The city of Jerusalem, the capital of ancient Palestine, named in its Greek form.
senseLabels: Jerusalem, the city or its people
article: Ἱεροσόλυμα is one of two Greek forms of the city name Jerusalem, this one being a Greek-style neuter plural built from the Hebrew name (יְרוּשָׁלִַם). It is rendered "Jerusalem" in 56 of its occurrences (95%), and it can refer to the city itself or, by extension, to its inhabitants (as in Matthew 2:3). Interestingly, the form turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including one second-to-third century AD text that speaks of the great divine name "in Jerusalem."
caution: Scholars have long debated whether the two New Testament forms (Ἱεροσόλυμα and Ἱερουσαλήμ) carry a deliberate distinction, especially in Luke and Paul, and the sources note this remains unsettled.

definition: The ceremonial act of purifying oneself to become ritually clean, especially through a prescribed religious rite.
article: ἁγνισμός is the act of ritual purification—going through the prescribed ceremony to become ceremonially clean. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 21:26) and 6 times in the Septuagint, where it translates several different Hebrew words, including terms tied to the Nazirite vow and to sin offerings. Notably, the word also shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions: one third-century BC inscription speaks of an official charged with overseeing 'the purifications,' showing the term was at home in ordinary Greek religious life, not just the Bible.
caution: The measured NT data labels the single occurrence as "notice," which conflicts with every lexicon's "purification"; with only one NT instance, the measured rendering should be treated with caution.

definition: A Greek title meaning "revered" or "august," used in the New Testament for the Roman Emperor or things connected to him.
article: This word originally meant "reverend" or "august" — worthy of being honored — but in late Greek it became the official equivalent of the Latin title "Augustus" given to the Roman Emperor. In the New Testament it appears 3 times, all in Acts: twice as a title for the Emperor himself (Acts 25:21, 25), and once as an adjective describing an Augustan military unit, the "σπείρα σεβαστή" (Acts 27:1), which the Berean Study Bible renders with "decided" in context. Everyday papyri confirm the imperial use: an Oxyrhynchus letter from A.D. 16 dates itself to "the 3rd year of Tiberius Caesar Augustus."
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence is thin, and the "decided" rendering reflects a phrase in context rather than a separate independent meaning of the word.

definition: A person who worships idols or images instead of the true God.
article: This word always means an idol-worshipper, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: in all 7 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "idolaters," with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100%. It comes from combining εἴδωλον (idol/image) with a root tied to service or worship, literally something like "image-servant." Interestingly, scholars regard this word and its relative "idolatry" as Christian coinages, though it does show up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a 5th-century account of martyrs that mentions fire killing the souls of idolaters.

definition: Describing someone who loves and is devoted to their own children.
article: This adjective combines "loving" (philos) with "child" (teknon) to describe a parent who is devoted to their children. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Titus 2:4, where it is paired with "loving their husbands" as a quality urged on younger women. The word turns up frequently in everyday Koine memorial inscriptions, where the dead are fondly remembered as "loving their children" alongside "loving their spouse" — a touching glimpse of how ordinary families described one another.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: The twelve tribes of Israel considered together as a single body or nation.
article: This is a collective noun meaning "the twelve-tribe people" — the nation of Israel viewed as one whole made up of its twelve tribes. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:7, and the standard Bible rendering captures it simply as "twelve." A telling detail: Moulton-Milligan note we should not expect to find this word outside Jewish circles, though its form parallels the common everyday term δωδεκάμηνον, "twelvemonth."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from usage; the single rendering "twelve" reflects part of a larger phrase rather than the full collective sense given by the lexicons.

definition: Describing someone who insists on having their own way, stubbornly arrogant and self-pleasing.
article: αὐθάδης describes a person who pleases only themselves — stubborn, arrogant, and determined to have their own way. Both New Testament uses (Titus 1:7 and 2 Peter 2:10) render it "self-willed," with full agreement across translations, and the Septuagint uses it for the Hebrew words עָז ("fierce" or "strong") and יָהִיר ("proud"). A papyrus from A.D. 184 shows the word in ordinary life, where a writer complains of a man's "audacity" reaching a pitch he can no longer endure.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and limited overall evidence, this entry rests on a thin sample.

definition: A heap of burning charcoal or a charcoal fire used for warmth or cooking.
article: This word names a pile of burning coals — a charcoal fire used for keeping warm or cooking. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in John's Gospel: the fire Peter warms himself by (John 18:18) and the one Jesus prepares with fish on the shore (John 21:9). Built from ἄνθραξ (charcoal), it also turns up in the Septuagint at Sirach 11:32 and 4 Maccabees 9:20.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the two listed senses really describe the same thing — a bed of burning coals — viewed as the material or the fire itself.

definition: To fall into or come upon something that surrounds you, like robbers, a sandbar, or troubles you stumble into unexpectedly.
article: περιπίπτω describes falling into circumstances that close in around you — built from περί ('around') and πίπτω ('fall'). In its three New Testament appearances it covers a traveler falling among robbers (Luke 10:30), a ship striking a sandbar (Acts 27:41), and believers encountering trials (James 1:2), so the word can be literal or figurative. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one document speaks of meeting with anger, another of being 'involved in much' worry and hardship — which fits the New Testament range closely.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the apparent two-sense split is really one flexible idea of 'falling into' circumstances.

definition: To choke or strangle something completely, or figuratively to press in and crowd around a person.
article: συμπνίγω is an intensified form of πνίγω (to choke), built with σύν, and it appears 5 times in the New Testament. In the parable of the sower it describes weeds choking the seed so it bears no fruit (Matthew 13:22, Mark 4:7, 19, Luke 8:14), rendered "choke" or "choked" in most occurrences. Interestingly, Luke 8:42 stretches the word in a more literal direction—of crowds physically pressing around Jesus—which is why it's also translated "pressed around" or "throng."
caution: With only 5 occurrences, the "pressed around" sense rests on a single verse (Luke 8:42).

definition: A trembling or quaking, usually caused by fear, sometimes expressing deep respect or awe.
article: τρόμος is the trembling or quaking that fear produces, and the New Testament uses it 5 times for everything from the women fleeing the empty tomb (Mark 16:8) to Paul arriving "in fear and trembling" (1 Corinthians 2:3). The range stretches from literal shaking to a posture of deep respect, as in Ephesians 6:5. Notably, it pairs so often with the word for "fear" that this combination ("fear and trembling") echoes Greek Old Testament phrasing found in Genesis 9:2 and Exodus 15:16, and the word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri.

definition: The lower back or hip region around the waist, also used as the body's seat of reproductive power.
article: ὀσφῦς literally names the loin, hip, or waist area, the part of the body you wrap a belt around — which is why it appears in phrases about girding up one's waist. The Hebrews, and the New Testament writers following them, also treated this region as the seat of generative power, so it can refer to a person's offspring or descendants. In the Septuagint it shows up 58 times and most often translates the Hebrew word for loins (מָתְנָ֫יִם, 40×). A nice everyday-Koine detail: it appears in a 4th-century AD fortune-telling text saying that if the right part of the loin twitches, a poor man will prosper.
caution: The word's plain anatomical sense is secure, but in several New Testament passages it is absorbed into phrases (like girding the waist or fruit of the loins), so the exact English rendering varies.

definition: The shoulder, the part of the body on which loads and burdens are carried.
article: ὦμος simply means the shoulder, especially viewed as the body part used to bear loads. It appears only twice in the New Testament—of religious leaders piling heavy burdens on people's shoulders (Matthew 23:4) and of the shepherd joyfully laying the found sheep across his shoulders (Luke 15:5)—and the two measured 'senses' are really one anatomical meaning in different contexts. The Septuagint uses it far more often (43 times), translating the Hebrew words for shoulder, and everyday papyri even show it referring to a cut of meat for sacrifice and, intriguingly, to a wooden beam.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences the measured data is thin, so the two listed senses simply reflect different contexts of the same basic meaning.

definition: A wonder or portent—a startling, awe-inspiring sign that points beyond itself, in the New Testament always appearing in the plural.
article: τέρας refers to a marvel or portent—something so striking it draws attention as a sign. In the New Testament it appears 16 times and is always plural, almost always paired with "signs" (σημεῖα), rendered "wonders" in 69% of cases and "wonders among" in another 19%. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew מוֹפֵת (25 of 39 times), the word for a divine wonder or portent, and Moulton-Milligan note its everyday use in Koine, where one astrology text uses it for an ominous prodigy.

definition: To be enough or sufficient for a need, or in the passive, to be satisfied and content with what one has.
article: ἀρκέω centers on the idea of sufficiency: something being enough to meet a need, or (in the passive) a person being content with what they have. It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often used impersonally ("it is enough"), as when Philip says "it is enough for us" in John 14:8. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one document about a disputed inheritance records a father leaving half an acre to a son, saying "it is enough for him." The older lexicons note a primary sense "to ward off" or "keep off," but the measured New Testament data shows only the meanings of sufficing and being content.
caution: The classical sense "to ward off/keep off" listed in the lexicons does not show up in the measured New Testament usage, and 3 of the 8 occurrences are absorbed into phrasing rather than rendered by a distinct English word.

definition: To physically set something out or expose it, or figuratively to lay out an explanation in an orderly way.
article: In the New Testament ἐκτίθημι splits evenly between two senses across its 4 occurrences: the literal act of setting out or exposing (as with the infant Moses in Acts 7:21) and the figurative act of laying out an explanation point by point (Acts 11:4; 18:23, 26). The everyday papyri show both poles vividly — one document uses it for exposing an abandoned infant, while others use it for posting up a public notice in large letters, which fits naturally with the "set forth, explain" sense. In the Septuagint it appears 11 times across 3 books, most often rendering the Hebrew word דָּת ("decree" or "law") six times.
caution: With only 4 occurrences split evenly between two senses, the measured picture rests on thin data, though the lexica agree on the overall range.

definition: In a good, proper, or correct manner; expressing that something is done well or said rightly.
article: This adverb, formed from καλός ("good"), covers the whole range of doing or saying something the right way — well, properly, correctly, rightly. The Byzantine NT uses it 36 times, with "well" the most common rendering (12×, 40%), though it also slides into "good," "correctly," "correct," and "right" depending on context. A nice detail from the papyri: the polite formula καλῶς ποιήσεις ("you will do well to...") was essentially the everyday Koine way of saying "please," a pattern reflected in passages like 3 John 6, Acts 10:33, and Philippians 4:14. In the Septuagint it stands behind forms of the Hebrew יָטַב ("to be good/go well," 7×) and טוֹב ("good," 2×).

definition: To till or cultivate the ground, growing crops by farming.
senseLabels: to till or cultivate the ground
article: γεωργέω means to farm or cultivate land, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 6:7, where it describes ground that is tilled and receives blessing. The word's range is narrow and concrete—it's about working the soil. Moulton-Milligan notes that since agriculture was Egypt's main industry, this word and its relatives are very common in everyday papyri, including a letter where a father scolds his son for leaving their land unfilled because no farmer was willing to work it.
caution: Evidence is thin—only one New Testament occurrence and one in the Septuagint—and the digest's labeling of the rendering as "falling" appears to be a data error rather than a genuine sense.

definition: To train or discipline oneself through repeated practice, like an athlete conditioning the body, but used figuratively for sharpening the mind, character, or habits.
article: γυμνάzō literally meant exercising the body, but in the New Testament it's always used figuratively for training and discipline. Across its 4 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "trained" 3 times (the fourth is absorbed into surrounding phrasing), covering senses, conscience, and the discipline that produces righteousness. The word ties back to γυμνός ("naked"), reflecting the ancient practice of athletes exercising unclothed, and Moulton-Milligan note that everyday papyri even use it for having a vigorous "bout" or confrontation with someone.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, all clustered in one rendering, the measured range is narrow even though the figurative meaning is well attested elsewhere.

definition: To suffer labor-like pains together with others, used figuratively of shared groaning under suffering.
article: This rare verb combines "with" (σύν) and "to be in labor" (ὠδίνω), picturing the agony of childbirth experienced jointly. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 8:22, where creation is described as "groaning together" — rendered "groaning" in 100% of measured occurrences, with the BSB agreeing fully. The classical lexica show its literal sense of being in travail together (Aristotle) alongside a figurative, metaphorical use (Euripides), and Paul's usage clearly draws on that vivid birth-pang imagery.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise force of this word rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: To show reverence or dutiful devotion, whether worshiping God or respecting and supporting one's family.
article: εὐσεβέω is a verb of reverence — acting out devotion, either toward God in worship or toward parents and family in dutiful respect and support. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 17:23, where Paul speaks of what the Athenians worship, and 1 Timothy 5:4, of children showing piety to their household), and the lexicons split it neatly between these religious and family-duty uses. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the worship sense vividly: recently discovered libelli record people declaring they have "always sacrificed and shown piety to the gods."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the measured-sense data oddly tagging it as "altar," the corpus evidence here is thin and should be read alongside the lexicons.

definition: To glue or stick one thing tightly to another; figuratively, to join oneself closely and faithfully to someone.
article: Literally προσκολλάω means to glue something onto something else, and figuratively it describes one person clinging or bonding tightly to another. In the Byzantine New Testament all 3 occurrences are about a man being joined to his wife (Matthew 19:5, Mark 10:7, Ephesians 5:31), echoing the Greek Old Testament, where it appears 15 times and usually translates the Hebrew דָּבַק, "to cleave." A striking everyday parallel comes from a 6th-century Egyptian will, where a man arranges affairs for "the wife who had been joined to me," using this very word.
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only 3 times in the Byzantine text and is absent from the critical SBLGNT, so its New Testament range rests on thin evidence.

definition: Describing something new in form or quality—fresh, unused, or novel—rather than merely recent in time.
article: καινός points to something new in kind or quality: fresh, unused, or novel, often standing opposite to what is old (παλαιός). The Byzantine New Testament uses it 44 times, and translations render it "new" in 40 of those (95%), so the meaning is remarkably stable. Lexicons traditionally distinguish it from νέος (new in age), but the papyri tell an interesting story: in everyday Koine the two words were used almost interchangeably, with one town called both "Ptolemais the new (καινή)" and "Ptolemais the new (νέα)" in different documents.
caution: The classic distinction between καινός (new in quality) and νέος (new in age) is sharper in the lexicons than in actual papyrus usage, where the two words often overlap.

definition: An adverb meaning badly or ill, used most often of being physically sick or, in a moral sense, of doing or speaking wrongly.
article: κακῶς is the adverb form of κακός ("bad"), and in the New Testament its dominant use is physical: in 7 of its 16 occurrences (54%) it appears in the phrase "to have it badly"—that is, to be sick (e.g. Matthew 8:16, Mark 1:32). It also carries a moral edge in some passages, meaning to speak or act wrongly (as in John 18:23 and Acts 23:5). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the medical sense: an Oxyrhynchus letter reports that a man "was ill" (κακῶς ἔχειν), and another notes oxen being "in a bad way."
caution: The single measured sense covers only about half of occurrences; the moral sense ("wrongly") and a literary idiom in Matthew 21:41 are well attested by the lexica but not separately measured here.

definition: A chief tax-collector who supervised others gathering taxes for the Roman authorities.
article: This word describes a senior tax official, someone above the ordinary tax-collectors who oversaw or directed their work. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:2, where it describes Zacchaeus, and the lexicons agree it means a chief tax-collector or head of a custom-house. The word is built from ἀρχή (chief, head) plus τελώνης (tax-collector), and in that single verse it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from usage.

definition: A physical injury to the body, such as a cut or wound that needs treatment.
article: τραῦμα means a wound or bodily injury. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 10:34, where the Good Samaritan bandages the injured man's wounds; everywhere else the NT uses πληγή instead. The everyday papyri confirm this plain medical sense: one document from 178 AD describes a man with "three wounds on his head," and the Septuagint uses the word ten times, translating several Hebrew terms for wounds and injuries.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full New Testament range cannot be measured from a single example.

definition: Not able to be seen; hidden or concealed from view.
article: ἀφανής means hidden, unseen, or not visible—built from a negative prefix attached to the verb meaning "to appear." It occurs only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 4:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "uncovered," describing how no creature is hidden from God's sight. The everyday papyri are striking here: the phrase ἀφανὴς ἐγένετο ("became hidden" or "disappeared") shows up repeatedly in second-century documents, and one inscription even contrasts things "visible" (ἐμφανέα) with things "hidden" (ἀφανέων).
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Prisca, a Christian woman married to Aquila, mentioned by name in Paul's letters.
article: Prisca is a personal name, a Christian woman who, with her husband Aquila, was active in the early church. The name is Latin in origin, the formal form of the more familiar diminutive "Priscilla" used elsewhere in the New Testament. One striking footnote in the evidence: the scholar Harnack suggested Priscilla may have authored the Epistle to the Hebrews, a speculation noted in the lexical sources.
caution: Both measured "senses" are simply the same proper name in different greetings, so there is really only one meaning here.

definition: A contracted reflexive pronoun meaning himself, herself, or itself, equivalent to the fuller form heautou.
article: This is simply a shortened spelling of the standard reflexive pronoun heautou, carrying the same meanings — himself, herself, itself, or their own. Editors disagree about how often this contracted form should even be recognized in the text: it does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all, though Abbott-Smith points to spots like Matthew 6:34 and Luke 12:17 where it may stand. The most interesting evidence is the regional split in the papyri: in Attica between 300 and 30 BC the fuller heautou outnumbered this form roughly 100 to 7, yet in third-century BC Egyptian papyri Mayser found the reverse, with this contracted form about three times as common.
caution: This form's very existence is debated — it appears zero times in the Byzantine text, and scholars disagree on whether it should be read as distinct from heautou at all.

definition: A wild animal, especially a dangerous or predatory one; in Revelation, a symbolic monstrous figure.
article: θηρίον refers to a wild animal, often one that is dangerous or predatory, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "beast" in 36 of its 46 New Testament appearances (90%). In Revelation it takes on a symbolic role, naming the monstrous figure that acts and even causes others to act. The Septuagint uses it 106 times, most often translating the Hebrew words for "living thing" (28×) and "bird/flying creature" (24×), and the documentary papyri even record it in everyday tax records charged on animals.

definition: The time when daylight first appears at the start of the day; dawn or early morning.
article: ὄρθρος refers to daybreak, the first light of morning, and in the New Testament it always appears in phrases marking the early hour at which something happened. It shows up only 3 times in the Byzantine text (2 in the critical text), each describing the early morning — at the empty tomb (Luke 24:1), Jesus teaching (John 8:2), and the apostles arrested at daybreak (Acts 5:21). Notably, the exact phrase ὑπὸ τὸν ὄρθρον ("about dawn") in Acts 5:21 turns up in an everyday papyrus from around A.D. 171, showing this was ordinary, real-world Koine vocabulary. In the Greek Old Testament it appears 28 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for dawn (shachar).
caution: This word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament, and the digest's third sense is listed as "people" — likely a tagging artifact from the Acts 5:21 phrase rather than a genuine meaning.

definition: Describing something that is much like or closely similar to another thing.
article: Παρόμοιος means "much like" or "closely similar," built from παρά ("alongside") and ὅμοιος ("like"). The ancient grammarian Pollux explained it neatly as "nearly similar"—something that comes within a little of being identical. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament (only once in the critical text), both in Mark 7 where Jesus speaks of human traditions, and Moulton-Milligan note it was common in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: The measured sense labels here reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself, so rely on the lexical meaning "much like, similar"; evidence is thin with only two occurrences.

definition: Justus, a personal name (actually a surname) borne by three different Christian men in the New Testament.
article: Ἰοῦστος is a proper name of Latin origin (meaning "just") used as a surname for three separate Christians in the New Testament. It appears 3 times, always rendered "Justus," and the men are distinct: Joseph Barsabbas (Acts 1:23), Titius Justus of Corinth (Acts 18:7), and Jesus called Justus in Rome (Col 4:11). What stands out is that this single Latin nickname is shared across three unrelated people, showing how common such Roman surnames were among early believers.
caution: This is a personal name with only 3 occurrences, so it carries no general meaning beyond identifying the three individuals who bore it.

definition: Light, whether sunlight, lamplight, or fire, often used figuratively for spiritual truth and God's presence.
article: φῶς covers light in its widest sense — daylight, the glow of a lamp or torch, the heat of a fire, or heavenly radiance — and the Byzantine New Testament renders it simply as "light" 63 of 70 times (95%). It contrasts directly with darkness and frequently carries figurative weight, standing for spiritual truth or for God himself. The everyday Koine usage backs this up nicely: a second-century papyrus uses the plural φῶτα for the glass "lights" of windows, while another from A.D. 359 uses it for the torches an intruder carried — exactly the torch sense found in Acts 16:29. In the Septuagint it almost always translates Hebrew אוֹר ("light," 86 times).

definition: To reckon or count something to someone's account, or to weigh a matter mentally and reach a conclusion.
article: λογίζομαι is a bookkeeping word at heart, meaning to credit or charge something to an account, and by extension to consider, calculate, or conclude a matter in the mind. Its range stretches from the literal—reckoning sums of money or grain—to the figurative crediting of righteousness, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "credited" in 9 of 41 occurrences and "consider" in 3, while 21 occurrences get absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word. The everyday accounting sense is vividly documented in the papyri, where one ledger reads "the due amounts in money and corn are reckoned here." In the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew חָשַׁב ("to think, reckon") in 53 of its 79 appearances, anchoring the link between mental calculation and crediting an account.
caution: Nearly half of its New Testament occurrences (21 of 41) carry no English word of their own, so its precise force often depends on context rather than a fixed gloss.

definition: Rahab, the Canaanite woman of Jericho who hid the Hebrew spies and was later praised for her faith.
article: Ῥαάβ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Rahab, a woman of Jericho who sheltered the Israelite spies. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25), both times recalling that same episode, and both occurrences center on her welcoming the spies. One curiosity is that the Greek spelling varies: Matthew uses Ραχάβ, and Josephus writes it as Ραχάβη; the form Ῥαάβ also turns up 12 times in the Septuagint, though there it often renders unrelated Hebrew words for "broad" or "open square," not the personal name.
caution: This is a proper name with only two New Testament occurrences, so the entry rests on thin evidence and the variant Greek spellings.

definition: A formal conjunction meaning "since" or "forasmuch as," used to introduce a reason or cause.
article: This is a stately, formal conjunction meaning "since" or "forasmuch as," used to introduce the grounds or reason for something. It appears just once in the New Testament, at the opening of Luke's Gospel (Luke 1:1), where its dignified tone fits a formal preface; the Majority Standard Bible's rendering there reflects "have" only as part of the surrounding phrase. Outside the Bible it was ordinary everyday Koine: the papyri show it with its usual meaning "since," as when a 3rd-century letter writer explains a request because "I have kept the mule for my own use."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: To speak against someone harmfully, especially to slander or spread damaging talk behind their back.
article: καταλαλέω means to speak evil of someone, ranging from outright slander to simply speaking against a person. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times across just 2 books, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "slander" in 60% of cases. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this hostile sense: one second-century inscription worries about ill-natured people who like to "speak against us" (καταλαλεῖν).
caution: The measured senses all cluster in James 4:11 and 1 Peter, so the word's full range rests on a small number of occurrences.

definition: The company you keep — close association or fellowship with others, especially the influence it has on character.
article: ὁμιλία refers to associating with people — keeping company or being in close fellowship, with conversation as a related sense. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Paul's quotation of the playwright Menander at 1 Corinthians 15:33: "bad company corrupts good character." The single most telling detail comes from everyday papyri, where the word can describe a person's "intercourse" or dealings with someone in a negative sense, matching the warning tone of Paul's quoted line. In the Septuagint it appears just twice, once translating a Hebrew word for marital duty.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word appears only once in the New Testament and could mean either "conversation" or "companionship," so its precise range here is uncertain.

definition: Complete physical wholeness or perfect health, the restored soundness of the whole body.
article: ὁλοκληρία means full, undamaged wholeness, especially the healthy soundness of the entire body. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 3:16, describing the complete healing given to the lame man. The everyday Koine papyri illuminate it nicely: one letter (P Oxy I.123) uses the word simply to mean a person's good health and well-being, the way we might ask how someone is doing.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on a single verse; the measured-sense label shown here reflects a data artifact rather than its actual meaning of physical soundness.

definition: An interrogative phrase asking the reason behind something — "why?" or "for what purpose?"
article: This word is a question phrase meaning "why?" or "for what reason?" — literally formed from ἵνα ("in order that") and τίς ("what"), so it asks what end or purpose lies behind an action. It does not appear in the Byzantine NT this digest counts, but the critical text (SBLGNT) has it 6 times, and Abbott-Smith lists six occurrences including Jesus' words in Matthew 9:4 and the cry from the cross in Matthew 27:46. It probes motive and purpose, not just cause.
caution: The Byzantine text records no occurrences while the critical text has six, so attestation depends on which Greek edition you use.

definition: From or on all sides; surrounding something completely from every direction.
article: πάντοθεν is an adverb meaning "from all sides" or "on every side," built from πᾶς ("all"). It appears only a handful of times in the New Testament — twice in the Byzantine text, three times in critical editions — typically describing something completely surrounded, as when Jesus warns that enemies will hem Jerusalem in on every side (Luke 19:43). The papyri show it was everyday Koine: a property sale from 88 BC uses it for whatever "adjoins on all sides," and Moulton-Milligan note it replaced the older Attic form πανταχόθεν.
caution: The measured sense labels here ("hem" and "jar") reflect surrounding English phrasing rather than the word's actual meaning, and with so few occurrences the data is thin.

definition: A sandal — a simple shoe consisting of a sole strapped to the foot.
article: σανδάλιον is the everyday word for a sandal, a sole held to the foot by straps, and it appears just twice in the New Testament (Mark 6:9 and Acts 12:8). The Septuagint uses it sparingly, in places where the Hebrew refers to footwear, while the more common Greek term for shoes is ὑπόδημα. Interestingly, it shows up in ordinary Koine papyri and inscriptions: one inscription lists σανδάλια among the ornaments adorning a god's statue, and a papyrus mentions "walking-shoes," showing this was plain, practical vocabulary.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 NT occurrences, one of which is absorbed into phrasing — and the word's exact sense in some papyri is uncertain.

definition: To appear or become visible, especially as a striking or terrifying sight or spectacle.
article: φαντάζω is built on φαίνω ("to shine, appear") and means to make visible or become visible. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 12:21, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the participle as "terrifying" (the sight that was so frightening). The everyday papyri show its breadth: one address to the moon-goddess uses the passive participle for something "appearing," while a fifth-century letter uses it for vividly picturing a riot "in imagination," and Abbott-Smith notes that classical Greek uses it only in the passive, meaning simply to appear.
caution: This word occurs just once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical text), so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: Describing something empty, useless, or pointless—lacking real value or any power to accomplish what it claims.
article: μάταιος describes things that are empty, useless, or ineffective—whether worthless idols, futile reasoning, or pointless religious practice. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 6 times, where the Berean translators split fairly evenly between "worthless" and "futile," but the word is far more common in the Septuagint (69×), where it most often renders Hebrew שָׁוְא ("emptiness, falsehood," 20×) and הֶבֶל ("vapor, vanity," 13×). A nice everyday glimpse comes from an Egyptian papyrus of A.D. 288 that speaks of τὰ μάταια ἀναλώματα, "useless expense"—the same plain sense of money wasted on nothing.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences, the boundaries between "worthless," "futile," and "empty things" reflect contextual translation choices rather than sharply distinct meanings.

definition: To press a point with greater force, insisting all the more strongly.
article: This verb combines "upon" (ἐπί) with "to be strong" (ἰσχύω), giving the picture of someone strengthening or intensifying their effort — in practice, pressing a point more urgently. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 23:5, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "insisting" (matched 100% by the Berean Standard Bible). The everyday flavor is confirmed by Koine papyri, and a striking parallel from Vettius Valens uses it of an argument that "will be stronger" for advice or instruction; in the Septuagint (Sirach 29:1, 1 Maccabees 6:6) it can simply mean to make or grow stronger.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and an overall low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin.

definition: A road, path, or route — and by extension a journey along it or a way of living and acting.
article: At its core ὁδός means a way, road, or path, and by extension the journey taken on it; the Byzantine NT uses it 101 times, with "way" (54×) and "road" (19×) covering most cases. Several measured senses are really the same idea showing up in travel phrases like "along the road" or "along the path," and in 13 places the word is absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own. The Septuagint uses it heavily — 766 times — chiefly for Hebrew דֶּרֶךְ (558×), and everyday papyri confirm its plain sense, as in P Oxy 1068 with καθ᾽ ὁδόν, "on the road," exactly matching the Gospel usage.

definition: To escort travelers on their way, helping them set out by providing company, supplies, or assistance for the journey.
article: προπέμπω literally means "to send forward," but in all nine of its New Testament appearances it means to help travelers on their way — escorting them, equipping them, or seeing them off. In 5 of the 9 cases the idea gets absorbed into phrasing rather than a single English word, since English often packs "send on their way" into a verb phrase. The everyday papyri back this up: one document uses it of a "packet of letters previously sent," while a sixth-century letter of recommendation asks that some people be sent on "with all honor."
caution: Abbott-Smith lists a "send before" sense from the Septuagint, but the measured New Testament usage all falls under the travel-escort meaning.

definition: A mark, stamp, or impression made by engraving or branding, including a sculpted figure or image.
article: χάραγμα refers to something scratched, etched, or stamped onto a surface — a mark or impression. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mark" in 5 of those (63%), most famously for the mark of the beast in Revelation. Beyond this, Acts 17:29 uses it of a graven image or sculptured figure, and Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine papyri use it for the official seal stamped on bills of sale, giving the emperor's year and name — which Deissmann suggested may illuminate the Revelation imagery.
caution: The precise sense behind Revelation's "mark" has been much discussed, and the word also carries a separate "graven image" sense in Acts 17:29.

definition: To show or point out openly, especially to publicly declare or appoint someone to a role or office.
article: This verb combines the ideas of pointing out and lifting up to public view, ranging from openly declaring something to formally appointing a person to a task. In Acts 1:24 the disciples ask God to "show" which candidate He has chosen, while in Luke 10:1 the Lord "appoints" seventy others to go ahead of Him. The word turns up often in inscriptions in a sacrificial or proclamation sense — one striking example uses it to mean officially declaring war.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and just 3 in the Septuagint, the sense range rests on thin biblical evidence.

definition: The fine, loose grains found on beaches and in deserts — sand, often used to picture a number too vast to count.
article: ἄμμος means sand — the loose grains heaped on a shore or filling a riverbed. Across the New Testament it appears 5 times, and where it is rendered meaningfully it always means "sand" (the digest's odd entries like "act sand" and "out" are fragments of phrases, not separate senses). In the Septuagint it shows up 27 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew חוֹל, also meaning sand; everyday Koine papyri use it in a very practical way, as when workers are hired to clear the sand choking up an irrigation canal.
caution: The measured data splits one plain sense into three through phrase-fragment artifacts, so treat "act sand" and "out" as noise rather than real meanings.

definition: The neuter form of "this," pointing to a single thing, idea, or statement just mentioned or about to be said.
article: τοῦτο is simply the neuter singular form of the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος ("this"), used as either subject or object. It points to a specific thing — sometimes a literal object, but very often an idea, statement, or situation, either one just mentioned ("this is what I said") or one about to follow ("this: that..."). The classical lexicon notes it can even carry a tone of contempt, as in "this fellow," and it appears in many fixed phrases like εἰς τοῦτο ("for this purpose") and μετὰ τοῦτο ("after this"). In the Septuagint the parent word chiefly renders the Hebrew demonstratives זֶה and זֹאת.
caution: The digest reports zero Byzantine NT occurrences and only one Septuagint instance for this exact form, so the measured evidence here is thin and most detail comes from the lexicon rather than counts.

definition: A person's deliberate purpose or intention — what someone has decided or wants to bring about.
article: βούλημα means a settled purpose, will, or intention — what someone has resolved to do. It's closely related to θέλημα (will), and Abbott-Smith lists the two as synonyms. Interestingly, the everyday papyri use the word for the contents of a will or testament: documents speak of carrying out or making known a person's βούλημα regarding property and freeing slaves, showing how naturally it expressed someone's expressed wishes in ordinary Koine.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word appears only 2 times in the Byzantine NT (3 in the critical text), and in one of those it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by a distinct English word.

definition: Manasseh, a Hebrew personal name borne by several figures, including Joseph's son and a king of Judah.
article: Manasseh is a Hebrew proper name that the New Testament uses for distinct people: in Matthew 1:10 it names a king of Judah in Jesus' genealogy, while in Revelation 7:6 it refers to the Israelite tribe descended from Joseph's firstborn son. It appears only 3 times across 2 books in the Byzantine text, and one of those occurrences is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as its own word. The name is far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 158 times and almost always translates the Hebrew מְנַשֶּׁה (139×), though it occasionally stands in for other names like Reuben (3×) or Ephraim (2×).
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament, with only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier.

definition: The act of being brought to or having approach to someone, especially the right to come into God's presence.
article: In the New Testament this noun describes being brought near or having the right of approach, and the Majority Standard Bible renders all three occurrences with "access" or "gained access." It comes from the verb προσάγω (to bring to) and appears just three times across two books. The everyday papyri show a surprisingly wide concrete range: it could mean a landing stage, the carting of gravel, or even additions to revenue—and one scholar suggested Romans 5:2 pictures approach in a nautical sense, like reaching a haven.
caution: Evidence is thin (only three occurrences) and Abbott-Smith notes some argue for a transitive sense "introduction" rather than "access."

definition: A person who speaks against others, spreading damaging talk; a slanderer or backbiter.
article: κατάλαλος describes someone who talks against other people — a slanderer or defamer. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:30, where it sits in a list of behaviors and is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than given its own English word. The word is built from κατά ("against") and the root of λαλέω ("to speak"), so its literal sense is "speaking against," and Abbott-Smith contrasts it with ψιθυριστής, a "whisperer."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be confirmed from biblical usage alone.

definition: A lying in wait or ambush, especially a secret plot or treacherous scheme to attack someone.
article: ἐνέδρα refers to lying in wait — setting an ambush or hatching a treacherous plot against someone. In Acts 25:3 the religious leaders ask a favor while secretly planning to ambush Paul on the road, and the Septuagint uses the word for literal military ambushes (Joshua 8) translating the Hebrew אָרַב, "to lie in wait." Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri show the word stretched to mean ordinary fraud or deception — one Oxyrhynchus document uses it for cheating during the loading of cargo.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one Byzantine occurrence, and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering as "grant" appears to reflect the surrounding request rather than the word itself, which the lexica consistently define as ambush or plot.

definition: To give someone, especially a daughter, in marriage to another person.
article: γαμίσκω means to give a person—typically a daughter—into marriage, as opposed to the one who actually marries. It is rare, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament, where the translators folded it into surrounding phrasing rather than rendering it as a separate English word. Its close variant γαμίζω shows up in passages about marrying and being given in marriage, and the grammarian Apollonius distinguished γαμῶ ("I take in marriage") from γαμίζω ("I give someone in marriage"), though Moulton-Milligan note no outside examples have yet been found to confirm exactly how that rule applies.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one Byzantine occurrence, no clear non-biblical examples, and the exact sense depends on a debated grammatical rule.

definition: To cancel something so it no longer has any force or authority, like voiding a legal agreement.
article: ἀκυρόω means to revoke or invalidate something, stripping it of authority — the prefix comes from κῦρος, "authority," with a negating sense. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "nullify" each time (Matthew 15:6, Mark 7:13, Galatians 3:17). Moulton-Milligan show that the related adjective ἄκυρος was standard legal language in everyday Koine papyri, where it voided contracts or even a person's action deemed illegal — so the word carries a courtroom flavor of declaring something legally void.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences and a handful of Septuagint uses — so the measured range is narrow.

definition: To travel along with someone, or to gather together in a crowd.
senseLabels: to come together as a crowd
article: This compound of "with" (σύν) and "to go" (πορεύομαι) means traveling alongside someone, and by extension a crowd assembling around a person. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 4 times, where it mostly describes people accompanying Jesus, with Luke 24:15 capturing two travelers walking together. The Septuagint uses it 18 times, chiefly for the Hebrew verb "to walk" (הָלַךְ), and Moulton-Milligan shows it was ordinary travel vocabulary in the papyri, as in a 3rd-century BC document mentioning someone "journeying with him."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the split between "journey with" and "come together" rests on thin evidence.

definition: A man's name, Aristobulus, mentioned in a greeting in Paul's letter to the Romans.
article: Aristobulus is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:10, where Paul greets the household associated with him. The name itself is built from Greek words meaning "best" and "counsel," but in practice it simply functions as a proper name. Moulton-Milligan note it was a widely spread name, attested in everyday Koine inscriptions across places like Leros, Delos, and Priene from the second and third centuries BC.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once, and the measured rendering oddly lists "Apelles" rather than "Aristobulus," so the occurrence data should be treated with care.

definition: A person from Elam, a region in southern Persia north of the Persian Gulf.
article: This word names a member of the Elamite people, who lived in what is now southern Persia near the Persian Gulf. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 2:9, in the list of nations present at Pentecost. The name comes from the Hebrew אֵילָם (Elam), and the Septuagint uses related forms like Ἐλυμαίος and Ἀιλαμείτης in passages such as Isaiah 11:11 and 21:2.
caution: This term appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured data labels it "Medes," which differs from the standard gloss "Elamite" reflected in the lexicons.

definition: A comparative particle meaning "than," used to mark what one thing is preferred over or compared with.
article: This is a strengthened form of the comparative particle ἤ ("than") combined with the emphatic περ, so it means something like "than" with added force — "rather than" or "more than." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 12:43, where people "loved the praise of men more than (ἤπερ) the praise of God." The classical lexica (Abbott-Smith) treat it under ἤ, which works both as a disjunctive "or" and as a comparative "than"; ἤπερ specifically belongs to the comparative use.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone and rests mostly on its components and lexical tradition.

definition: Describing something as breathed out by God, that is, originating from God's own inspiration.
article: This word combines "God" (θεός) with the idea of "breathing" (πνέω), so it literally means "God-breathed" — produced by God's own breath or inspiration. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:16, describing Scripture. Note the gap between the lexicons and the corpus measurement: every dictionary glosses it as "inspired by God," but the translation data here oddly registers "useful," which likely reflects a tagging quirk from the surrounding phrase ("God-breathed and useful") rather than the word's actual meaning. The papyri and inscriptions confirm the "divine inspiration" sense, including a second-century BC decree at Magnesia speaking of a "divine inspiration" moving the people to rebuild a temple.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "useful" conflicts with every lexicon's "inspired by God," so treat the corpus label with caution.

definition: Money, wealth, or possessions—useful goods that a person owns, usually mentioned in the plural.
article: χρῆμα refers to money, wealth, or possessions—essentially the useful things a person owns. In the New Testament's 7 occurrences it clusters around two ideas: the rich (those who 'have possessions,' 2 times) and money itself (Acts 8:18, 8:20, and a specific sum in Acts 4:37). The Septuagint uses it to render several Hebrew words for property and riches, including נְכָסִים three times, and the everyday papyri confirm its plain commercial meaning—one freedman wrote that his patron's loyalty 'means the same as money' to him.
caution: Two of the seven occurrences are absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, and the 'perish' sense reflects the surrounding clause rather than the word itself, so the sense breakdown is looser than it looks.

definition: On or from the outside; the external part of something, as opposed to the inside.
article: ἔξωθεν is an adverb built from ἔξω ("out"), and the New Testament uses it consistently to mean "outside" or "the outer part" — it is rendered "outside" in 9 of its 13 occurrences (100% of the times it gets its own English word), as in Jesus' image of cleaning the outside of a cup while the inside stays dirty (Matthew 23:25). Strictly it answers the question "from where?" (from outside), but in practice it often just means "on the outside," and it can function as a preposition with the genitive ("outside of"). The everyday flavor shows up in a papyrus from A.D. 94 instructing someone to "dig a deep trench round the oil-press outside." In the Septuagint it appears 41 times, most often translating the Hebrew word חוּץ ("outside"), 27 times.

definition: A gathering of people, especially a Jewish religious assembly, or the building where such an assembly meets.
article: In the New Testament this word almost always means a synagogue — either the Jewish religious assembly itself or the building where it gathers — rendered that way in 54 of 57 occurrences (96%). The root sense is simply a 'bringing together,' and the Septuagint uses it 204 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word עֵדָה ('congregation,' 128×). That literal sense survives in everyday papyri, where it can describe a boat's awning 'converging' over three cubits or a 'gathering in' of grain, and the lexicons note it could also mean a Christian assembly (as in James 2:2).

definition: To come rushing together toward one spot, as a crowd quickly gathering at a particular place or occasion.
article: This verb describes people swarming or rushing together toward a single place, built from prefixes meaning "upon" and "together" attached to a verb for running. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 9:25, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "come running" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully.
