Notably, Moulton-Milligan could find no actual papyrus citation of this exact word, though the closely related ἐπιτρέχω shows up as the title of a village inspector or overseer in everyday documents.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax legomenon with only one occurrence and no direct papyri attestation, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: The quality of being deathless or undying — a state of life that cannot be ended.
article: ἀθανασία means immortality, literally a "deathless" state, built from the negative prefix and the word for death (θάνατος). It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, all in Paul's letters, where the Berean Standard Bible consistently renders it "immortality." Outside the New Testament it shows up in the wisdom literature (Wisdom of Solomon) and in everyday Koine, where Moulton-Milligan note an inscription describing the emperor Caligula's "greatness of immortality" and the common tomb formula "no one is immortal."
caution: The digest lists three "measured senses," but two of them ("saying pass," "unapproachable") appear to be artifacts of surrounding text rather than genuine meanings; all real evidence points to a single sense, "immortality."

definition: Fiery — having the bright, flame-like color or appearance of fire.
article: πύρινος describes something that looks like fire, whether in its flaming color or glowing brightness. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 9:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as a fiery "color" of breastplates. The Septuagint uses it twice (Ezekiel 28:14, 16) for Hebrew words connected with fire, and an inscription on the statue of Memnon at Thebes (A.D. 95) speaks of being struck by "fiery" rays — showing the word was at home in everyday Koine.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just two in the Septuagint, the measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To call something or someone to mind, to remember; sometimes to act on that memory by showing care, rewarding, or forgiving.
article: At its core μνάομαι means to remember or keep someone or something in mind. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament, but it is common in the Septuagint, occurring 118 times across 25 books, where it most often renders the Hebrew זָכַר, "to remember" (72 times). Notably, Abbott-Smith points out that when used with a negative for sins, the sense shifts to "forgive" (as in Hebrews 8:12), and in some contexts the verb stretches toward actively caring for someone rather than merely recalling them.
caution: Because this form is absent from the Byzantine New Testament, its New Testament usage is described under the related lemma μιμνήσκω, so treat the cited verses with that in mind.

definition: A person's outward bearing, demeanor, or settled manner of conduct that reflects their inner character.
article: κατάστημα refers to a person's bearing or demeanor — the consistent way they carry and conduct themselves. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the description of older women whose manner should be reverent. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including one (OGIS 669) using it of keeping a city in its proper, fitting condition, and the Letter of Aristeas applies it to the bearing of virtue and piety.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and the digest's own translation tag reading 'Older' rather than the demeanor sense the lexica describe, the evidence here is thin.

definition: An abnormally high body temperature accompanying illness; a fever.
article: πυρετός means a fever, the bodily heat that comes with sickness, and the New Testament uses it consistently this way across all 6 occurrences. Though the Majority Standard Bible's renderings break out as "fever," "left fever," and "fever began," these all reflect the same single sense, just wrapped into different English phrasings of healing accounts (Luke 4:38–39, John 4:52, Acts 28:8). The word derives from πῦρ (fire), and the everyday papyri confirm its medical use: one document from A.D. 316 describes a man lying in bed "seized with a slight fever," matching Luke and Acts' phrasing of being gripped by fever. In its single Septuagint appearance (Deuteronomy 28:22) it translates a Hebrew word for fever or inflammation.
caution: The multiple sense labels reflect English phrasing differences only; all evidence points to one stable meaning, "fever."

definition: Describing someone who has no love for what is good.
article: This word combines a negative prefix with φιλάγαθος ("loving good"), so it literally means "without love of what is good." It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "unloving," though older lexicons aim closer to "despiser of those that are good" or "hostile to virtue." Interestingly, although it shows up nowhere else in surviving Greek literature, Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine documents use closely related compounds — an Oxyrhynchus papyrus praises an emperor's father as φιλάγαθος ("good-loving"), the very positive form this word negates.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence with no other appearances in Greek literature, and the modern rendering "unloving" is looser than the lexicons' "not loving what is good," so the precise force is uncertain.

definition: To be at leisure or free, and so to devote oneself to something; of a house, to stand empty and unoccupied.
article: σχολάζω comes from the noun for leisure (σχολή) and basically means having free time. In everyday Koine papyri it constantly means "to have leisure," as in a letter complaining "I have no leisure to remain longer." In the New Testament it appears just twice: once figuratively of a house standing "vacant" (Matthew 12:44), and once absorbed into a phrase about devoting oneself to something (1 Corinthians 7:5). In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew words for being idle or slack, fitting the same leisure-and-emptiness range.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is very thin (only 2 occurrences, one not even rendered by a distinct English word), so the measured picture rests heavily on outside sources.

definition: A festive public gathering, especially a joyful assembly held to celebrate or honor someone or something.
article: πανήγυρις describes a grand festive assembly — originally a national gathering held in honor of a god, but used more broadly for any joyful public celebration. It appears just once in the New Testament (Hebrews 12:23), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "joyful," capturing the celebratory mood. In the Septuagint it shows up 4 times across 3 books, usually translating the Hebrew word חָג ("festival," 3×), and the papyri show it was a common everyday word for festivals and public meetings — at Fayum it even appears alongside markets, marking a clear festal occasion.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise nuance in Hebrews 12:23 rests on thin direct evidence.

definition: Coarse, dark cloth woven from goat hair, worn as a garment to express grief, mourning, or repentance.
article: σάκκος is a coarse cloth—usually woven from goat hair—and the garments made from it, worn as a sign of grief or repentance. In the Byzantine New Testament all 4 occurrences point to this mourning-garment sense (the listing of "empower they sackcloth" at Revelation 11:3 just reflects the surrounding clause, not a separate meaning). The word is borrowed from Hebrew שָׂק, which it renders 37 times in the Septuagint, and everyday papyri show its plainer, original use—shopping lists and receipts mention a hair sack or "a sack full of cnecus," reminding us the material started as ordinary sacking before becoming a symbol of sorrow.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the measured data captures just the mourning-garment use, though the broader evidence shows σάκκος also meant a plain sack for carrying goods.

definition: A personal name: the father of the blind beggar Bartimaeus.
article: Τιμαῖος is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Mark 10:46, where it identifies the father of the blind beggar Bartimaeus. Lexicographers treat the name as Aramaic in origin, though the form is also a common Greek name written with a different accent (Τίμαιος). One papyrus from around 250 BC even uses the Greek form in a legal context, listing 'the case against Timaeus, 20 drachmae.'
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and sources disagree on whether it is genuinely Aramaic or simply the common Greek name Τίμαιος.

definition: Samos, an island in the Aegean Sea off the western coast of Asia Minor, near Ephesus and Miletus.
article: Σάμος is a proper name for an island in the Aegean Sea, lying off the coast of Asia Minor near Ephesus and Miletus. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:15, as a stop on Paul's sea journey. Note that the measured rendering data here is misleading: it lists the sense as "day" at 100%, which clearly reflects a tagging error rather than the word's actual meaning, since every lexicon agrees Σάμος is simply the place name Samos.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured sense data conflicts with the lexicons, so rely on the standard identification as the island Samos.

definition: Genuine purity of motive or character, with no hidden mixture of deceit or pretense.
article: This word describes moral sincerity — being genuine and unmixed, without hidden agendas. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sincerity" in two of those (67%); the third (2 Corinthians 1:12) is folded into a phrase about how Paul conducted himself, which is why it shows up there as "relation." An interesting detail: this word isn't found in classical Greek, but it does turn up in everyday Koine papyri, where one document (P Oxy 1252) uses it to mean a person's "probity" or uprightness.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint instance — so the precise range of meaning is hard to pin down.

definition: To burn with intense heat, used of physical elements being consumed by fire.
article: καυσόω means to burn with great or fervent heat. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in 2 Peter (3:10 and 3:12), where it describes the elements being destroyed by fire; the Berean Standard Bible agrees with this rendering in both spots. Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes that outside the New Testament the word was used in the passive sense of burning with a fever (as in the physician Galen), so the New Testament's application to cosmic heat is a distinct usage.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice, both in a single book, and is absent from the critical text, so confidence is low.

definition: The state of being unclean or impure, whether physically dirty or, more often, morally corrupt.
article: ἀκαθαρσία refers to impurity—a lack of cleanness that can be literal filth or moral corruption. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times and is rendered "impurity" in 8 of them (80%), most often pointing to moral uncleanness, though Matthew 23:27 uses it physically of the rot inside whitewashed tombs. The everyday papyri show the down-to-earth side of the word: house-rental agreements required tenants to leave the property "clean and free from all uncleanness" (P Oxy 1128, A.D. 173). In the Septuagint it appears 49 times, usually translating the Hebrew טֻמְאָה ("uncleanness," 32×).

definition: The act of sowing seed, and by extension the seed itself—including human offspring or descent.
article: σπορά comes from the verb σπείρω, "to sow," and basically refers to a sowing or the seed that gets sown. In its single New Testament appearance (1 Peter 1:23) it carries the collective sense of "seed," and could extend to human parentage or offspring. The everyday papyri use it plainly for agricultural sowing—one document speaks of "three arouras for the sowing of vegetables"—while a magical-religious papyrus stretches it to the cosmic "seed through which all things were sown."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its New Testament range rests on very thin direct evidence.

definition: A reply or response given when someone asks a question.
senseLabels: a verbal response in a confrontation
article: ἀπόκρισις simply means an answer or reply, the response someone gives when questioned. Built from the verb ἀποκρίνομαι ("to answer"), it appears only 4 times in the New Testament, and in each case the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "answer" — whether the boy Jesus astonishing teachers with his replies (Luke 2:47) or messengers needing an answer to bring back (John 1:22). The Septuagint uses it 10 times, most often for the Hebrew מַעֲנֶה, and the everyday Koine papyri show it as a standard word for official replies and responses delivered to magistrates.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the apparent "senses" are really one core meaning shaped by context, not distinct definitions.

definition: To be inactive or idle, especially used of something that delays or holds back from acting.
article: ἀργέω means to be idle or inactive, and by extension to delay or hold back. In its single New Testament appearance (2 Peter 2:3) the Majority Standard Bible renders it figuratively, describing how judgment does not 'linger' or stay idle. The everyday papyri make the literal sense vivid: a group of quarrymen complain that they 'are idle' because they lack the labor to clear away sand, showing the ordinary working-life flavor of the word.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and just twice in the Septuagint, so its measured range in Scripture is very thin.

definition: A boat, originally meaning a small boat but in practice used for any ordinary vessel.
article: πλοιάριον is technically a diminutive of πλοῖον ("ship"), so it literally means "little boat," but in actual use it is hardly distinguishable from the regular word for a boat. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "boat" in every case where it gets its own English word (3 of 6 occurrences in the Byzantine NT). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this overlap: one document interchanges πλοιάριον with the ordinary πλοῖον, showing the "small" sense had largely faded in common speech.

definition: To exercise self-control or restrain one's own desires, especially regarding appetite or sexual urges.
article: This verb means to hold yourself back—to practice self-restraint over bodily desires like food or sex. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Corinthians, where Paul applies it to sexual continence (7:9) and to the disciplined training of an athlete who controls everything (9:25). In the Septuagint it twice renders the Hebrew אָפַק, used of someone forcibly holding back emotion, and an everyday inscription honors a woman named Orestina who "lived in continence," though scholars note no extreme asceticism is implied.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament and two Septuagint occurrences—so the precise range is hard to fix.

definition: Puteoli, an Italian port city on the Bay of Naples where Paul landed on his way to Rome.
article: Ποτίολοι is the Greek name for Puteoli, the modern Pozzuoli, a coastal city on the Bay of Naples. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 28:13, where Paul reaches it during his journey toward Rome, and every source renders it the same way. The name is of Latin origin and Strong's connects it to 'little wells,' likely referring to local mineral springs; Dodson notes it was the great harbor for shipping traffic with Alexandria.
caution: This is a place name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests entirely on identifying the city rather than on a range of usage.

definition: A dove or pigeon, the familiar bird used in the Bible for sacrifice and as a symbol of gentleness.
article: This word simply means a dove or pigeon, a single steady sense found across all 10 New Testament occurrences, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "doves" wherever an English word is needed. It appears in famous scenes like Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:16, Luke 3:22) and the cleansing of the temple (Mark 11:15). The Septuagint uses it 35 times, mostly for the Hebrew word for dove (28×), and Moulton-Milligan note it was common in everyday papyri\u2014one document from around AD 82 mentions ordering "a hundred doves," and another offers a half-jar of preserved pigeons.

definition: A going out or departure from a place, used figuratively of a person's death.
article: ἔξοδος literally means a "going out" or "departure," built from the parts meaning "out of" and "road." In the New Testament's three uses it splits between a literal departure—the exodus of Israel out of Egypt in Hebrews 11:22—and a figurative one, where it gently names a person's death (Luke 9:31, 2 Peter 1:15). Everyday Koine papyri show how flexible the word was: it could mean "expenditure" (paired with income), and contracts even use it for "divorce," a "judicial decision," or a "voyage." In the Septuagint it appears 56 times, most often rendering the Hebrew מוֹצָא (8×), a word for an exit or place of going out.
caution: With only three NT occurrences—each rendered differently—the sense divisions rest on thin evidence, though the lexicons agree on the basic "departure/death" range.

definition: A temple-keeper or guardian; also used as an honorary title claiming a city is the official caretaker of a god's temple.
article: Νεωκόρος literally means "temple-sweeper," pointing to someone who tends and guards a sacred building, and by extension it became an honorary title a city could claim for itself as caretaker of a god's temple. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 19:35, where the city clerk calls Ephesus the guardian of Artemis. The most striking outside evidence is a papyrus from 217 BC mentioning a man who held this title (in its Doric form) for a Jewish synagogue, and Moulton-Milligan notes the word still survives in Greece as the title of a church or synagogue sacristan.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering of "Finally" reflects a neighboring word rather than this term's actual meaning, so rely on the lexical evidence instead.

definition: To practice or exert effort toward something, as in striving or making it your earnest aim.
article: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 24:16, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the idea of striving or making something one's aim (counted under "hope"). Its broader range in classical Greek runs from "to adorn" in poetry to "to practice or exercise" (as in Herodotus and Xenophon) and "to endeavor." The everyday Koine papyri preserve a telling example—someone "practicing piety" (eusebeian askēsanta)—which fits the New Testament sense of devoting earnest effort to a goal.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise New Testament force rests on a single verse plus thin outside evidence.

definition: To share something with others, whether by giving a portion or by taking part together in it.
article: κοινωνέω means to have a share in something together with others, covering both giving and partaking. In the Byzantine New Testament all 7 translated occurrences are rendered "share" (one further occurrence is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing), so its measured range is tight, though the older lexica spread it across "communicate," "distribute," and "have fellowship with." One interesting detail: Moulton-Milligan notes that everyday Koine inscriptions use κοινωνέω and μετέχω as practically synonymous, undercutting any fine distinction between the two words.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and KJV/Dodson listing a broader "have fellowship with" sense, the single measured "share" gloss may understate its full range.

definition: Subject to death; describing a person or body that will eventually die.
article: θνητός describes anything that is liable to die—most often the human body or human nature, in contrast to what is undying. It appears just 6 times in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mortal" in the clearest cases (Romans 8:11; 1 Corinthians 15:53–54). An inscription quoted by Moulton-Milligan captures the contrast neatly, calling the sun an "imperishable" thing within a "mortal nature" (thnētēs physeōs), and in the Septuagint it stands behind Hebrew words for death and the living human being.
caution: Two of the six measured renderings ("consigned sake also" and "swallowed") reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself, so the real range is narrower than the raw list suggests.

definition: Describing the early rain that falls at the start of the growing season, before the later rains.
article: πρώϊμος describes something early in the year, used especially of the early rains that begin the agricultural season as opposed to the late rains (ὄψιμος). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at James 5:7, where a farmer waits patiently for the early and late rains. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times across 6 books, most often translating the Hebrew word for the early rain (מַלְקוֹשׁ, 5×), and an Egyptian decree from 238 BC uses it of the 'early sowing,' which has led some to apply the James passage to the early crop rather than the early rain.
caution: Evidence is thin (only one NT occurrence), the spelling and derivation are disputed between πρώϊμος and πρόϊμος, and scholars disagree on whether James means early rain or early crop.

definition: A Chaldean—a person from the region of the lower Euphrates, or the land where the Chaldeans lived.
article: Χαλδαῖος refers to a Chaldean, a native of the lower Euphrates region. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 7:4, in the phrase "land of the Chaldeans," describing where Abraham lived before leaving. The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 83 times across 10 books and most often renders the Hebrew כַּשְׂדִּי (Kasdi).
caution: It appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "settled" reflects the surrounding sentence rather than the word itself, which simply names the Chaldeans.

definition: A person, typically a man, who is sexually unfaithful by having relations with someone else's spouse.
article: μοιχός is the standard Koine word for an adulterer—a man guilty of sexual unfaithfulness with a married woman. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, always rendered "adulterer(s)," and 4 times in the Septuagint, where it consistently translates the Hebrew נָאַף ("to commit adultery"). One vivid bit of everyday evidence: a 3rd–4th century papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses the word for a sexual "paramour," with a jealous correspondent demanding, "Write and tell me, who is my paramour?"

definition: To make someone a eunuch by castration, or figuratively to choose a celibate, unmarried life for oneself.
article: This verb means to make a eunuch of someone, literally by castration, and it appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew 19:12. The two measured renderings reflect the same verse's contrast: some are made eunuchs by other people, while others figuratively 'make themselves eunuchs' by choosing to live unmarried for the sake of God's kingdom. Abbott-Smith notes this metaphorical use of doing it to oneself, where the bodily image stands for voluntary celibacy.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in a single verse, the evidence base is very thin and the measured 'senses' simply split one passage's two clauses.

definition: To pick up or carry something, whether lifting it with the hands, hauling a load, or figuratively bearing and enduring it.
article: βαστάζω covers a range from physically lifting an object to shouldering a load, and by extension enduring something hard. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 27 times, rendered "carry" in 45% of cases and "bear" in 23%, with the literal sense of picking up stones to throw at Jesus in John 10:31. The everyday papyri back this up nicely: one document uses it for sluice-gates being "lifted" as much as inspectors wished, while a tax formula stretches it to mean a region cannot "bear" so heavy a payment.
caution: Some late writers and lexica add a sense of "carry off" or even "steal" (as in John 12:6), but this nuance is not reflected in the measured renderings.

definition: The sky or heavens above the earth, including the realm of God and the place opposite to the earth.
article: οὐρανός covers the whole vertical world above us — the visible sky where birds fly and stars shine, and the spiritual dwelling place of God. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "heaven" in all 253 cases where it gets its own English word (and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 97% of the time), so its meaning is remarkably consistent. In the Septuagint it almost always stands in for the Hebrew שָׁמַיִם ("heavens"), 342 times, and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, as in a prayer for dominion over "the regions under heaven."

definition: A preposition meaning "under" something, or "by" someone—naming who or what does the action, especially after passive verbs.
article: At its core ὑπό means "under," but in the New Testament its most common job is to name the agent—the "by" after a passive verb, as when people were baptized "by" John. Of 229 occurrences, 60% are rendered "by" and another 24% "under," so these two ideas cover most of its range. Everyday papyri show exactly this agent use—one document reads "I, Antigonus, am unjustly treated by Patron"—and in the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew תָּ֫חַת, meaning "under" or "beneath."
caution: Many of the listed senses ("was by," "was," "be by") reflect English phrasing of passive verb constructions rather than distinct meanings of the preposition itself, and 72 of 229 occurrences contribute no separate English word.

definition: A strong feeling of anger or indignation, especially the kind that rouses a person to act against wrongdoing.
article: This noun, built from the verb ἀγανακτέω, names the feeling of indignation or righteous anger. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 7:11, where it describes the response stirred up in the Corinthians. An everyday papyrus (P Grenf II.82, c. A.D. 400) illustrates the word in a legal threat, where offenders are warned they could face "judicial indignation" — that is, legal proceedings and penalties — showing the term could carry a formal, enforcing sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range is hard to pin down from biblical usage alone.

definition: An adjective describing nard (an aromatic ointment) as genuine or pure, used only in the phrase 'pure nard.'
article: In the New Testament this word appears just twice (Mark 14:3 and John 12:3), both times describing the expensive nard ointment poured on Jesus, and translators consistently take it to mean 'pure' or 'genuine.' Since it derives from πίστις (faith, trust), the underlying idea is 'trustworthy' or 'unadulterated,' which fits an unmixed, authentic perfume. The classical lexica record broader senses the New Testament never uses, including 'persuasive' (Plato) and 'faithful, trusty' of persons (Plutarch), so its everyday biblical sense is narrower than its full range.
caution: This is a rare word with only 2 New Testament occurrences, and scholars have debated whether it comes from 'true/genuine' or from a word for liquid, leaving its precise meaning somewhat uncertain.

definition: A member of a Jewish religious group known for strict observance of the law and its traditions.
article: Φαρισαῖος names a member of a well-known Jewish sect, almost always appearing in the plural and rendered "Pharisees" in 85% of its 101 Byzantine occurrences. The various measured "senses" beyond the first are really just contextual phrasings tied to encounters with Jesus rather than separate meanings — the word itself consistently refers to the same group. The most interesting detail is its origin: it comes from an Aramaic/Hebrew root (compare H06567) carrying the idea of a "separatist," which is why Strong's glosses it as "a separatist, an exclusively religious" person.
caution: The listed senses after the first reflect surrounding wording (e.g. "Pharisees Jesus") rather than distinct meanings of the word itself.

definition: Midday or noon, and by extension the direction south, where the sun stands at noon.
article: μεσημβρία literally means "midday," built from the words for "middle" and "day," and from there it came to mean "south" — the direction the sun faces at noon. It appears just twice in the New Testament, once for each sense: Acts 22:6 ("noon") and Acts 8:26 ("south"). It is far more common in the Septuagint, showing up 24 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for noon or midday; everyday Koine papyri also use it for clock-time, as in an astronomical text dating the equinox to about an hour after noon.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences split evenly between two meanings, the sense in any given passage depends heavily on context.

definition: To wash or bathe the whole body, whether for cleaning or for ceremonial purposes.
article: λούω means to wash or bathe the entire body, as opposed to rinsing just a part (νίπτω) or laundering garments (πλύνω). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times, rendered "washed" 5 times and "bathed" once. The Septuagint uses it 44 times, mostly for the Hebrew רָחַץ, often of ceremonial washing, and the everyday papyri illustrate its common middle use "to bathe oneself," frequently at the public bath (βαλανεῖον).
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences, the small sample limits how finely the "washed" and "bathed" senses can be separated.

definition: In a way that is devoted to God and morally pure; piously and uprightly.
article: This adverb describes living in a manner devoted to God and morally clean. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:10, where Paul stacks it with two related words ("devoutly, righteously, and blamelessly"). The everyday papyri show the same pairing was common: a writer in 162 BC describes himself as "piously disposed toward the divine," using the very combination of pious-and-just that Paul echoes.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the Majority Standard Bible renders it broadly as "righteous," so its precise shade is hard to pin down from such thin evidence.

definition: To rule over, master, or have power over someone or something.
senseLabels: to be lord or rule over
article: κυριεύω means to rule over or be master of someone or something, built directly from κύριος ("lord"). The Byzantine NT uses it 7 times, where translators render it variously as "Lord," "dominion," "master," and "lord over," reflecting one core idea of holding power. Paul applies it strikingly to abstract powers — death, sin, and the law all "rule" over people in Romans. In the Septuagint it appears 32 times, most often translating the Hebrew מָשַׁל ("to rule," 16×), and the everyday papyri show it used plainly of owning property and exercising control over possessions.
caution: The varied measured renderings reflect translation phrasing more than distinct meanings, so treat the single sense of "ruling over" as central.

definition: All together as one crowd, with the whole multitude acting at the same time.
article: This adverb describes a whole crowd doing something simultaneously, in a single united outburst. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 23:18, where the entire crowd cries out together against Jesus, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "unison" while older versions say "all at once." Built from the words for "all" (πᾶς) and "multitude" (πλῆθος), it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and a related form appears in Aristeas describing a "vast accumulation" of sacrificial blood.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on limited evidence.

definition: A bone, the hard part of the skeleton in humans or animals.
article: ὀστέον simply means a bone, and that single meaning holds across all its uses. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament and a hefty 111 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always renders the Hebrew word עֶצֶם ("bone", 88×). The everyday concreteness of the word shows up nicely in the papyri: one document describes donkeys "laden with bones," and a tomb inscription near Jerusalem marks "the bones of Nicanor of Alexandria."
caution: The second "sense" measured at 20% ("Myself does bones" from Luke 24:39) is a tally artifact, not a real distinct meaning — the word still just means "bones."

definition: To call or summon people to gather together in one place.
article: συγκαλέω means to summon people so they assemble together, built from σύν ("together") plus καλέω ("to call"). In its 8 New Testament uses it consistently carries this sense, whether a governor convening officials (Luke 23:13) or, in the middle voice, a person calling friends and neighbors to themselves to rejoice (Luke 15:6, 9). The everyday Koine papyri confirm the same range — including a marriage contract where a husband promises his wife not to bring (συγκαλέσαι) any unsuitable person into the house.
caution: The Septuagint shows it translating several different Hebrew words, so its background sense is somewhat broader than the New Testament's tight "summon together" usage.

definition: To make meaning clear by explaining it fully or by translating it from one language into another.
article: This verb covers two related actions: explaining something so people understand it, and translating words from one language to another. It is an intensified form of the simpler verb ἑρμηνεύω, and the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "interpret" (3 of 6 times), with one place where Jesus "explained" the written Scriptures (Luke 24:27). A nice detail from everyday Greek: a papyrus from 116 B.C. uses this very word for Egyptian documents "translated into Greek," matching the translation sense seen when Tabitha's name is rendered into Greek in Acts 9:36.
caution: With only 6 occurrences, the translating sense rests on a single instance, so the "explain" and "translate" meanings are not sharply separable here.

definition: Describing an animal that has been deliberately fattened for eating, especially fattened cattle prepared for a feast.
article: σιτιστός means "fattened," describing livestock raised and fattened for slaughter, and as a noun (in the plural) it refers to the fatlings themselves. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 22:4, where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. The word is rare overall but turns up in everyday Koine documents, and Symmachus uses it in his Greek versions of Psalm 22:13 and Jeremiah 46:21.
caution: This word appears just once in the New Testament and is rare elsewhere, so its range rests on thin evidence.

definition: Verbal abuse — harsh, insulting speech aimed at attacking or shaming another person.
article: λοιδορία refers to abusive, insulting speech directed against someone, the kind of railing or reviling meant to wound. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "insult" in one place (as in 1 Peter 3:9), folding it into surrounding phrasing the other two times. The Septuagint mostly uses it for the Hebrew מְרִיבָה ("strife" or "quarreling"), and everyday papyri show it paired with ὕβρις ("insolence") to describe "abusive action," confirming it was common, real-world language for hostile speech.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and two of them absorbed into broader phrasing, the precise range here rests on thin direct evidence.

definition: Pentecost, the Jewish festival held on the fiftieth day after Passover.
article: This word literally means "fiftieth" and, when used on its own, refers to the Jewish Feast of Pentecost—the second of the three great festivals, falling fifty days after Passover. All three New Testament occurrences point to this single festival; the two measured "senses" are really the same feast viewed slightly differently, once as the named celebration and once as the specific day it began (Acts 2:1). Interestingly, in everyday Koine papyri and ostraca the same word had nothing to do with religion at all—it named a 2% tax, as in an inscription listing "the fiftieth (tax) and the recording of oaths."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences) and the two listed senses both denote the same festival rather than genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: Shameful or obscene behavior, especially indecent or crude talk that is improper for godly people.
article: αἰσχρότης refers to shamefulness or obscenity, the kind of indecency that disgraces a person. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 5:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "crude" (and the Berean Standard Bible agrees), in a list of things that should have no place among believers. The word derives from αἰσχρός ("shameful, base"), and older lexicons like Abbott-Smith simply gloss it as "baseness," while the King James tradition reads it as "filthiness."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured and rests on a single context.

definition: An emphatic particle meaning roughly "surely" or "let me tell you," used to stress a point — but in the New Testament it appears only fused onto other particles.
article: τοί is a small emphatic particle that adds weight to an assertion, with the flavor of "surely" or "verily." According to the lexicons it can express an inference ("then, consequently") or introduce a general statement, and it goes back at least to Homer. The most telling fact in the evidence is that it never stands alone in the New Testament — zero standalone occurrences — and instead survives only as a building block inside compound particles like καίτοι, μέντοι, ἤτοι, and τοιγάρτοι.
caution: There are no measured New Testament uses of τοί on its own, so its sense here rests entirely on the lexicons and its appearance within other particles.

definition: A lot — an object cast or drawn to decide something by chance — or, by extension, the portion or inheritance assigned to someone.
article: At its core κλῆρος is the physical lot — a marker cast or drawn to settle a decision, as when soldiers divided Jesus' clothing (Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24, Acts 1:26). From there it stretches to mean the portion or inheritance secured by such a drawing, which is why the King James Version also renders it "heritage," "inheritance," and "part." The Septuagint shows this same double range vividly: it uses κλῆρος 147 times, mostly for the Hebrew gôrāl ("lot," 74×) but also for naḥălâ ("inheritance," 49×). Everyday papyri keep the original sense alive too — one second-century letter urges a brother not to neglect "the ballot for the strategus."
caution: The Majority Standard Bible measured only the "lots" sense (3×), with four occurrences absorbed into phrasing, so the broader "portion/inheritance" range rests mainly on the Septuagint and lexica rather than measured NT renderings.

definition: The north, as a direction or region; originally the personified north wind.
article: βοῤῥᾶς refers to the north — either the direction or the people and lands lying that way. It appears only twice in the New Testament, once for people coming from the north to feast (Luke 13:29) and once for the north side of the heavenly city (Revelation 21:13), and the Septuagint uses it 153 times, almost always for the Hebrew צָפוֹן ("north," 129×). The contracted form found in both NT verses is also the standard spelling in everyday Ptolemaic papyri, where people gave directions like "from south to north," and classical lexica note its older meaning as Boreas, the personified north wind.
caution: With only two NT occurrences this entry rests largely on Septuagint and papyri evidence, and the "north wind" sense classical lexica record does not appear in the measured New Testament data.

definition: A genealogy — a tracing of family descent through successive generations.
article: This noun refers to a genealogy, the listing or tracing of someone's descent through generations. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Timothy 1:4 and Titus 3:9), where it is always rendered "genealogies," and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions as well. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that Polybius pairs the plural with "myths," referring to legendary stories about the births of a city's founders — which has led some scholars to read the word in these passages as such tales rather than as later Gnostic lineage schemes.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a single measured sense, the precise nuance Paul intended is debated among the sources.

definition: The act of praising God, especially praise offered to him as a kind of sacrifice or thank-offering.
article: αἴνεσις is the act of giving praise, often tied to the idea of a thank-offering brought to God. It appears just once in the New Testament (Hebrews 13:15) but turns up 56 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew words for thanksgiving (תּוֹדָה, 14×) and praise (תְּהִלָּה, 7×). A telling clue is the phrase 'sacrifice of praise' (θυσία αἰνέσεως), which in Leviticus 7:12 translates a Hebrew term for a thank-offering, linking praise with worship one physically brings to God.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the single rendering measured here ('continually') reflects the surrounding phrase rather than the word's core meaning of 'praise,' so treat the NT data cautiously.

definition: Lacking sense or understanding; foolish, thoughtless, failing to grasp what should be obvious.
article: ἀνόητος describes someone who fails to understand or think clearly — foolish or thoughtless rather than merely uninformed. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "foolish" in 5 of its 6 New Testament uses, with the remaining instance in Romans 1:14 part of a paired phrase. Notably, the classical lexicon (Abbott-Smith) records an older sense "not thought on, not understood" in Homer and Plato, but the measured biblical data shows only the active sense of being foolish, and Moulton-Milligan notes the word survives in modern Greek meaning "unreasonable."
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and a classical sense ("not understood") that never surfaces in the measured biblical data, the range is narrower in practice than the lexica suggest.

definition: To give off a smell, especially a bad one, as a decaying body emits an odor.
senseLabels: to smell or give off odor
article: This verb means to emit a smell, almost always a foul one — to stink. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 11:39, where Martha warns that Lazarus, dead four days, would already smell. (Note the digest's measured rendering reads as "four," which reflects the surrounding verse rather than the verb itself; the lexica uniformly define ὄζω as "to stink" or "emit a smell.") The Septuagint uses it once at Exodus 8:14, where the heaped-up dead frogs make the land reek, and the papyri attest the same sense vividly — one document speaks of a body "emitting a pungent odour."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the NT, and the digest's measured "four" rendering disagrees with the lexica, which consistently define it as "to stink."

definition: The sharp pain of childbirth, often used as an image for sudden, intense suffering or distress.
article: ὠδίν is the pang of childbirth, and the New Testament uses it both literally and as a vivid picture of sudden anguish—Jesus calls wars and famines the "beginning of birth pains" (Matthew 24:8, Mark 13:8). In the Septuagint it appears 29 times across 13 books, mostly rendering Hebrew words for labor or writhing pain, including the striking phrase "birth pains of death" (cf. Psalm 18:4) that lies behind Acts 2:24, where Christ is freed from death's pangs. The word turns up movingly in everyday Koine too: ancient tomb inscriptions describe women who died in bitter labor, escaping their own "birth pains."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the sense labels "releasing" and "pains" reflect translation choices in single verses rather than distinct meanings, and the Acts 2:24 phrase is debated.

definition: To empty something out, or figuratively to drain it of its meaning, power, or effect.
senseLabels: empty out a reason for boasting
article: κενόω basically means "to empty," but in the New Testament's 5 uses it almost always works figuratively—draining something of its content or effect, whether faith (Romans 4:14), the cross (1 Corinthians 1:17), or a ground for boasting (1 Corinthians 9:15; 2 Corinthians 9:3). It famously describes Christ "emptying himself" in Philippians 2:7. In the Septuagint it appears only twice, both translating the Hebrew word for languishing or being drained, and a second-century papyrus uses it vividly of a god "emptying" a greedy usurer of his swinish wealth.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the measured "senses" are really shades of one figurative "empty," so the four labels reflect different translation contexts rather than sharply distinct meanings.

definition: To communicate by gestures—nodding, beckoning, or making signs—when speaking is impossible.
article: This word describes signaling to someone with motions of the head or hands instead of words. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 1:22, where Zechariah, struck mute, keeps making signs to the crowd—which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders the moment as his being "unable" to speak. The Septuagint and lexicon evidence point more directly to the gesturing itself: Abbott-Smith notes it translates Hebrew terms for winking or beckoning in Psalm 35:19 and Sirach 27:22.
caution: With only one New Testament use, and the standard rendering capturing the muteness rather than the gesturing the lexica emphasize, the precise nuance is hard to pin down.

definition: Worthy of respect because of serious, honorable character or conduct; dignified and venerable.
article: σεμνός describes someone or something that commands respect through serious, honorable bearing — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "dignified" or "honorable" across all 4 New Testament occurrences. It applies both to people (church leaders and older men in 1 Timothy and Titus) and to things worth thinking about (Philippians 4:8). Outside the Bible the word turns up constantly in everyday papyri and tombstone inscriptions, where it praised respectable family lines and honored the dead, and it was even used of gods like Isis — showing how naturally it carried the sense of "venerable."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and a slim 3-time Septuagint footprint, the evidence base is modest, and the "things"/"dignified things" labels simply reflect how the adjective is translated when it modifies impersonal nouns.

definition: An adverb meaning truly or really, used to affirm that something is genuinely the case.
article: ἀληθῶς is an adverb meaning "truly" or "really," affirming that something is genuinely so — as when the centurion says Jesus was "truly" the Son of God (Matthew 27:54, Mark 15:39). It is overwhelmingly stable: of 21 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "truly" 11 times (61%), with the rest mostly absorbed into surrounding phrasing or minor variants. In the Septuagint's 13 uses it translates several Hebrew words for genuineness, including אֻמְנָם ("truly, indeed") three times, showing the same core idea of real, certain truth.

definition: An Aramaic title of respect meaning "my master" or "my teacher," used to address Jesus.
senseLabels: a title of address: my master
article: ῥαββονί is a respectful Aramaic title meaning roughly "my master" or "my teacher," closely related to ῥαββί. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament — once when blind Bartimaeus addresses Jesus (Mark 10:51) and once when Mary recognizes the risen Jesus (John 20:16), where the text explains it means "Teacher." Abbott-Smith traces it to the Aramaic רַבּוֺנִי ("my master"), and notes the word does not appear in the critical SBLGNT text at all.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 occurrences with 0 in the critical text, and the standard renderings vary between leaving it untranslated and explaining it, so confidence is low.

definition: To travel over land, by foot or otherwise, rather than going by sea.
article: This verb describes making a journey across land instead of sailing, and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 20:13, where Paul goes by land while his companions take the ship. Although Strong's and the older lexicons render it 'go on foot,' the evidence shows it can mean land travel more broadly: as Blass noted, it refers to a journey over land, not necessarily on foot. A nice parallel comes from Plutarch's life of Cato, who regretted having sailed to a place where he could have traveled by land instead.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and its exact force—'on foot' versus simply 'by land'—is genuinely disputed among the sources.

definition: Belonging to the beginning or earliest times; original, ancient, or long-standing.
article: ἀρχαῖος describes something that goes back to the beginning or origin, not merely something that is old. In the New Testament it shows up 11 times, often pointing to "the ancients" or people of former times (about 44% of uses), and twice in Luke describing an old prophet thought to have risen. What's striking is the distinction lexicons draw from παλαιός: while παλαιός just means "old," ἀρχαῖος carries the idea of original or primeval, and everyday Koine papyri preserve this same shade—an inscription describes an "ancient initiate" set against the newcomer, much like Acts 21:16 calls Mnason an "original disciple" belonging to the earliest days of the gospel.

definition: Describing worship or nourishment that engages the mind and spirit rather than physical ritual or literal substance.
article: This rare word, appearing only twice in the New Testament (Romans 12:1 and 1 Peter 2:2), comes from λόγος (word, reason) and basically means "rational" or "reasonable." The Majority Standard Bible renders both occurrences as "spiritual," though the older KJV captured the literal idea with "reasonable" and "of the word." One striking parallel comes from the Hermetic writings, where λογικὴ θυσία describes a pure offering from the soul, contrasted with ceremonial sacrifice — closely echoing Paul's call in Romans 12:1.
caution: With only two occurrences and a documented gap between the modern "spiritual" rendering and the lexicons' "reasonable, rational," the precise force of this word is genuinely uncertain.

definition: A dead body or corpse, especially one fallen in death; literally a limb or member of the body.
article: In the New Testament κῶλον appears just once, in Hebrews 3:17, where it refers to the bodies of those who died in the wilderness. The classical sense is a 'limb' or 'member' of the body, but in actual biblical use the word always means a corpse or carcass. The Septuagint confirms this: all 8 of its occurrences translate the Hebrew פֶּגֶר (peger), meaning a dead body, so the figurative 'carcass' sense has fully taken over from the literal 'limb' sense.
caution: The word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests heavily on the eight Septuagint uses, and the lexicons' 'limb' sense is not the meaning actually attested in Scripture.

definition: To begin to grow light, as dawn breaks or a new day starts to draw near.
article: This verb describes the early light of dawn or the moment a new day begins to draw on. It appears only twice in the New Testament, rendered once with "day" (Matthew 28:1) and once with "beginning" (Luke 23:54), both pointing to the same idea of light breaking. Notably, the everyday papyri show the same usage: a horoscope from A.D. 81 and a later festal letter both use the participle to mark the dawning of a particular day.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and thin evidence, the exact shade of meaning (literal dawn versus the approach of a day) is not always certain.

definition: To suppose, suspect, or guess at something privately based on what one observes.
article: ὑπονοέω means to form a private guess or suspicion about something—to surmise based on what you notice rather than what you know for certain. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts, and the renderings split evenly between "suppose" (Acts 13:25) and a negated "not suppose" (Acts 25:18), with one occurrence absorbed into the phrasing. The everyday flavor shows up nicely in the papyri: one document from A.D. 34 has a writer saying "I suspect that this has been done by the inhabitants of the so-called Winepress," exactly the same nuance of cautious conjecture.
caution: With only 3 occurrences (all in Acts) and one absorbed into phrasing, the measured range is thin, though the sources broadly agree on the meaning.

definition: A winnowing tool—a wooden shovel or fork used to toss threshed grain into the air so the wind separates grain from chaff.
article: πτύον is a farmer's winnowing tool, a wooden shovel or fork used to throw grain into the air so the breeze carries off the lighter chaff. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17), and in both places it is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. A nice glimpse of its ordinary use comes from the papyri: an illiterate landowner named Gemellus (around A.D. 100) wrote asking a supplier to send him two forks, two shovels, and one winnowing-fan—using this very word.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences, both from the same source material, so the picture rests mainly on everyday papyri and lexicon entries.

definition: The outward form or appearance of something, which may match its substance or merely imitate it.
article: μόρφωσις refers to the shape, outline, or appearance that something presents. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and in both cases English translations fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a single word of its own. The two uses pull in slightly different directions: in Romans 2:20 it points to a genuine embodiment of knowledge, while in 2 Timothy 3:5 it describes a mere outward "form" of godliness set against its missing power (δύναμις). Notably, Moulton-Milligan reports a suggestion that in Romans the word functions as a Stoic term meaning "education," comparing a Modern Greek word for a well-educated person.
caution: With only two New Testament uses, both absorbed into phrasing, and the two contexts pointing in different directions, the precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: A period of three months.
article: τρίμηνον is a compound of "three" (τρεῖς) and "month" (μήν), used as a noun for a three-month span. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:23, where Moses is hidden for three months, and shows up 5 times in the Septuagint. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the word's ordinary use: one document from 256 BC speaks of sowing "three-month wheat," showing the term applied beyond just stretches of time.
caution: The measured rendering "unafraid" is a data error tied to the Hebrews 11:23 verse and does not reflect this word, which clearly means "three months"; the New Testament evidence is also limited to a single occurrence.

definition: A member of the Israelite tribe of Levi, especially one who assisted the priests in the temple.
article: A Λευΐτης is a man descended from Levi, the tribe set apart to help the priests with temple duties. The meaning is narrow and stable: all 3 New Testament occurrences are rendered "Levite," and Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith all agree. In the Septuagint the word shows up far more often (282 times), almost always translating the Hebrew word for Levi (לֵוִי, 270 times), which shows how central this tribe was to Israel's worship.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin direct evidence, though its single clear meaning is not in doubt.

definition: A price paid to set someone free, such as the money used to release a slave or captive.
article: Lýtron is a ransom — the payment that buys someone's freedom. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both saying Jesus came to give his life "as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28, Mark 10:45), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ransom" in 100% of cases. The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri: Deissmann showed that ordinary people would have recognized lýtron from the purchase money used to set slaves free, as in an Oxyrhynchus document where a slave named Euphrosyne is freed "for a ransom." In the Greek Old Testament it appears 20 times, often translating Hebrew words for ransom-payment (kopher), redemption, and the price of release.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured evidence is thin, though it agrees fully on "ransom."

definition: The smallest copper coin in everyday use, worth very little money.
article: λεπτόν refers to the tiniest piece of money in circulation, the coin famously given by the poor widow in Mark and Luke. The word started life as an adjective meaning "peeled, thin, small, light" (from λέπω, to peel), and only in later Greek did the neuter form come to mean a small coin. All three New Testament uses are about money, and the papyri and inscriptions confirm this everyday financial sense — one inscription (OGIS 484) even distinguishes the small provincial copper coinage (λεπτὸν χαλκόν) from the imperial silver denarius.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and the three measured renderings really pointing to the same coin sense, the apparent variety reflects translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings.

definition: To keep company or closely associate with someone, mixing socially into their circle.
article: This word literally means to "mix up together," and in the New Testament it always appears in the figurative middle voice meaning to associate or keep company with someone. All 3 Byzantine occurrences carry this social sense (1 Corinthians 5:9, 5:11, and 2 Thessalonians 3:14), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "associate" or "associate with people" every time. It turns up in everyday Koine documents too: a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses the related adjective for parcels of land "included" or mixed in together with other property, showing the plain mixing-together idea behind the social metaphor.
caution: Evidence is thin, with only 3 New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence, so confidence is low.

definition: A person who greedily wants more than their share, often by taking advantage of others.
article: πλεονέκτης describes someone driven to have more — a covetous, grasping person — built literally from the words for "more" and "have." In its 4 New Testament uses the Majority Standard Bible renders it "greedy," and the BSB independently agrees every time. Everyday Koine documents confirm the same flavor: a papyrus from 221 B.C. labels someone simply as "being greedy," and a later ethical fragment lists the greedy person alongside the liar and the swindler.
caution: With only 4 occurrences the evidence is limited, though the corpus and lexicons agree closely on the meaning.

definition: Someone called to your side to help, especially an advocate who pleads your case or speaks in your favor.
article: παράκλητος literally describes someone "called alongside" to help, and in legal settings means an advocate or pleader who speaks on another's behalf. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Advocate" in all 5 New Testament occurrences (one as "Advocate" expressing benefit), and the term appears only in John's writings, applied to the Holy Spirit (John 14:16, 26; 16:7) and to Christ (1 John 2:1). Notably, the King James Version translated it "comforter," and Strong's and Dodson add the sense of consoler or helper—so older sources stretch the word toward comfort while the measured renderings favor the courtroom idea of an advocate; the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: Sources disagree on range: measured renderings consistently give "Advocate," but older lexica (KJV, Strong's, Dodson) also list "comforter/consoler," and the word occurs only 5 times.

definition: To suffer hardship and misery, or to feel wretched and grieve over one's own distress.
article: This verb describes enduring severe hardship and feeling wretched — in James 4:9, its single New Testament appearance, it's a call to grieve and lament. In the Septuagint it occurs 16 times across 7 books, almost always (14×) rendering the Hebrew shadad, meaning to be devastated or laid waste. The classical lexica note an interesting extra range: occasionally the word is used transitively to mean wearing down or distressing someone else (as in Psalm 17:9 and Isaiah 33:1).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, so the broader range comes mainly from Septuagint and classical evidence.

definition: To an overwhelming degree; beyond all measure or limit.
article: This adverb intensifies the idea of abundance, describing something done or felt to an overwhelming, beyond-all-limits degree. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 7:37, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "utterly" and the King James renders it "beyond measure." It is built from two pieces — ὑπέρ ("over, beyond") and περισσῶς ("abundantly") — so the word literally stacks one intensifier on top of another to mean something like "super-abundantly."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on a single passage.

definition: Not subject to regret or a change of mind; something that will not be taken back.
article: This adjective describes something that brings no regret or cannot be reversed — a decision that stands. It is built from a negative prefix plus a word for changing one's mind (μεταμέλομαι), so it literally means "not repented of." It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Romans 11:29, where God's gifts and call are irrevocable, and in 2 Corinthians 7:10, where godly sorrow produces a salvation that leaves no regret. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) agree closely on "not repented of, unregretted."
caution: With only 2 occurrences, the per-verse renderings ("call," "worldly") reflect surrounding wording rather than this word's own narrow meaning, so weigh the lexicon glosses more heavily.

definition: A firm foundation or steadiness underlying something, used either as inner confidence or as the assurance that gives substance to what we hope for.
article: ὑπόστασις literally means something "standing under" — a base or support — and from that root it stretches in two directions in the New Testament's 5 occurrences. In Paul's letters it twice (50%) describes inner confidence (2 Corinthians 9:4; 11:17), while in Hebrews it carries the weight of "assurance," most famously the firm ground beneath what we hope for (Hebrews 11:1). The everyday Koine papyri are striking here: the word commonly meant one's property, estate, or actual possessions, as when an Oxyrhynchus document speaks of owning "more land than I actually possess" — a concrete sense that may color the idea of faith as the real substance of things hoped for.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and a range running from "confidence" to "substance" to a possible "title-deed" nuance (per Moulton-Milligan), the precise force in Hebrews remains genuinely debated.

definition: To announce good news, especially to preach the Christian gospel of salvation.
article: This verb means to announce good news, and in the New Testament it overwhelmingly carries the specific sense of preaching the Christian gospel of salvation. Its range is fairly tight: across 55 occurrences the renderings cluster around "preach the gospel" (13×, the single most common) and "good news" (9×), with all the other renderings being variations on proclaiming or hearing that message. A nice piece of background comes from the papyri: a document from around the reign of Trajan or Hadrian uses the rare active form for a slave arriving to announce a military victory, showing the word's everyday Koine use for spreading good tidings. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew בָּשַׂר ("to bring news," 18 of 22 times).

definition: Egypt, the land of the Nile to which Israel went down and from which God delivered them.
article: Αἴγυπτος is simply the name of Egypt, the country along the Nile, and that is how it reads in 23 of its 24 Byzantine New Testament occurrences (96%). In the Septuagint it appears a striking 598 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew name מִצְרָ֫יִם, and it often comes in the phrase 'land of Egypt' (γῆ Αἰγύπτου). The most interesting twist comes in Revelation 11:8, where Abbott-Smith notes the name is used figuratively of Jerusalem as a city hostile to God.

definition: Utterly astounded or overcome with amazement.
article: ἔκθαμβος describes someone completely overwhelmed by astonishment, built from the prefix ἐκ ('out') and θάμβος ('amazement'). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 3:11, where the crowd is utterly astounded after the lame man is healed. It is a rare word: outside the Bible it was previously known only from the historian Polybius, and Moulton-Milligan add a striking third-century imprecatory tablet from a necropolis at Hadrumetum, where demons are roused 'astounded and terrified.' In the Septuagint it can carry a darker shade of 'dreadful' or 'terrible' (Daniel 7:7).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and one digest measurement renders it 'clung,' which reflects the surrounding verse rather than the word itself, so treat the data cautiously.

definition: The number twelve, used for counting and as a standing label for Jesus' twelve apostles.
article: δώδεκα is the plain cardinal number "twelve," rendered that way in 51 of its 74 Byzantine occurrences (86%). Besides ordinary counting, it serves as shorthand for Jesus' inner circle of apostles, called simply "the Twelve" about 8% of the time, as in Mark 6:7 and Luke 8:1. In the Septuagint it appears 87 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for "ten" (עָשָׂר) within larger number phrases, and Moulton-Milligan note it survives unchanged into Modern Greek.

definition: To gather a crowd in order to stir up a public disturbance or riot.
senseLabels: gather a crowd, cause a riot
article: This verb combines ὄχλος (crowd) and ποιέω (make), so it literally means to "make a crowd" — but the sense is hostile: rounding up a mob to start trouble. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 17:5, and lexicographers like Abbott-Smith note it occurs nowhere else in the Bible. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan record that the word does show up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Hobart compares the similar phrase ὄχλον ποιέει in the ancient physician Hippocrates.
caution: This word is a New Testament hapax with thin attestation, and the digest's measured rendering as "marketplace" conflicts with every lexicon's meaning of gathering a crowd, suggesting a tagging issue rather than a real sense.

definition: A personal name, Abiud, listed in Matthew's genealogy as the son of Zerubbabel and father of Eliakim.
article: Abiud is simply a proper name, appearing twice in the New Testament (both in Matthew 1:13) and rendered "Abiud" by every translation tracked. It comes from Hebrew and shows up 13 times in the Septuagint, where it usually stands for the name Abihu (12×) and once for Abihud. Beyond its place in Jesus' genealogy as Zerubbabel's son, there is nothing here to define beyond the name itself.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the same verse, so confidence is rated low.

definition: Agreement or harmony between parties, the state of being in accord with one another.
article: συμφώνησις means concord or agreement—the harmony that exists when two parties are aligned. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:15, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "between" ("what harmony is there between Christ and Belial?"). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Moulton-Milligan note its close relative συμφώνημα showing up in a second-century document about settling accounts.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: To grow calm or die down, especially of a raging wind that settles and stops.
article: κοπάζω describes something settling down into stillness, used in the New Testament every time of the wind dropping after a storm. All three Byzantine occurrences refer to the wind, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "died" twice and "died down" once, with the BSB agreeing fully each time. Tied to the root κόπος ("toil, weariness"), the word's original sense is to grow weary and then relax; the Septuagint uses it 22 times across 13 books, often for Hebrew חָדַל ("to cease") and שָׁכַך ("to subside").
caution: Evidence is thin — only three New Testament occurrences, all describing wind, so the measured "died"/"died down" split reflects translation style more than distinct senses.

definition: To pitch a tent over someone, used figuratively for a power that settles upon and dwells with a person.
article: This rare verb literally means to spread a tent or tabernacle over something, built from ἐπί ('upon') and σκηνόω ('to pitch a tent'). It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:9, where Paul speaks of Christ's power coming to 'rest upon' him. Interestingly, the corpus-measured rendering tags it as 'sufficient' here, which actually reflects the surrounding statement ('my grace is sufficient'), while the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, KJV, Dodson) consistently give the image of a power that tents over and covers a person. Moulton-Milligan confirm it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the single measured rendering ('sufficient') reflects the verse's context rather than the verb's own meaning of 'tenting over,' so lean on the lexical image.

definition: To fan or stir something up with air, especially to drive waves or leaves into motion by a breeze.
article: ῥιπίζω comes from the word for a fan or bellows, and its root sense is to fan a fire or make a breeze. In its one New Testament appearance (James 1:6), it describes a person whose doubt makes them like a wave of the sea "blown and raised with the wind," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it in terms of "doubts" 100% of the time. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from the papyri and Aristeas 70, where ornamental metal leaves are crafted so lifelike that they stir when a breath of wind fans them — showing the word's gentle "stirred by shifting breezes" feel rather than violent storm imagery.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text), so its sense rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: To worship or revere a god, showing devotion through reverent religious practice.
article: σέβομαι means to worship, revere, or show devout reverence, almost always toward a deity. In the New Testament it appears only in the middle voice, and several times it describes "God-fearers" — the σεβόμενοι, devout Gentiles drawn to Jewish worship (Acts 13:43, 17:4, 17:17). In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew יָרֵא, "to fear," tying worship closely to reverent awe; everyday papyri use it the same way, as in an inscription urging "worship the divine."
caution: Of its 10 New Testament occurrences, only 2 surface as a standalone word in translation; the other 8 are folded into phrasing, so the measured sense rests on limited explicit data.

definition: The Jewish religion with its beliefs and practices, especially the strict observance of Jewish customs.
article: Ἰουδαϊσμός refers to Judaism—the Jewish faith and its observance of Jewish rites and customs. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Galatians 1:13-14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Judaism" every time. Notably, the word also shows up in the Septuagint's books of Maccabees (2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees), where it likewise describes commitment to the Jewish way of life.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both in a single passage, the evidence base for its full range is thin.

definition: To spend money or resources, sometimes wisely on a cost and sometimes wastefully by squandering them.
article: δαπανάω covers spending in the broad sense of laying out money or resources, and depending on context this can mean a reasonable expenditure or a reckless squandering. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, ranging from a woman spending all she had on doctors (Mark 5:26) to the prodigal son wasting everything (Luke 15:14) to people spending on selfish pleasures (James 4:3). The word was common in everyday Koine: papyri use it for ordinary accounting, including a phrase rendered "I will make an allowance for the expense."
caution: The measured-sense labels here track surrounding phrasing (e.g. "rumors," "motives") rather than the verb itself, so they should be read against the underlying meaning of spending.

definition: Describing the fresh green color of plants, or by extension a sickly pale yellow-green hue.
article: χλωρós basically means "green," the color of fresh growing plants. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 4 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "green" in every case it gives it a word of its own (3×), as in green grass (Mark 6:39) and the green grass burned up (Revelation 8:7). The everyday papyri confirm this farming sense vividly — one letter complains that the writer's working animals "are eating green fodder," and asks for green hay to be brought. Lexicons note a stretched sense of "pale": in Revelation 6:8 the same word describes the sickly color of the rider's horse, where "pale" fits better than "green."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 4 occurrences), and the "pale" rendering for the horse in Revelation 6:8 reflects lexical judgment rather than the dominant "green" sense.

definition: Shealtiel, a personal name of an Israelite man listed in the genealogies of Jesus.
article: Σαλαθιήλ is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Shealtiel, an indeclinable proper name that appears 3 times in the New Testament, always rendered "Shealtiel." It shows up in the genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12, Luke 3:27), identified as the son of Jechoniah. In the Septuagint it occurs 12 times across 4 books, mostly translating שְׁאַלְתִּיאֵל but interestingly sometimes standing alongside or in place of זְרֻבָּבֶל (Zerubbabel) in a few instances.
caution: This is a proper name with only 3 New Testament occurrences, so the evidence is thin and limited to genealogical lists.

definition: To pull or draw something away, ranging from physically drawing a sword to leading people away or departing from a place.
article: ἀποσπάω literally means to pull or drag something off or away, and the New Testament uses cover a real range: a companion of Jesus 'drew' his sword (Matthew 26:51), false teachers try to 'draw away' disciples after themselves (Acts 20:30), and a ship party departs or is 'parted' from others (Acts 21:1). The strength of the action varies from forceful tearing away to a gentle withdrawal. The everyday papyri are illuminating here: one third-century document uses this verb simply for withdrawing a gang of mine workers from a site, with no hint of violence at all.
caution: Whether the passive sense (Luke 22:41, Acts 21:1) means a forceful 'tearing away' or a mild 'withdrawing' is genuinely disputed, with Field and Thayer disagreeing.

definition: A person's stage of growth, measured either by their age in years or by their physical height.
article: ἡλικία refers to where someone stands in the process of growing up or growing older, and the evidence pulls in two directions: it can mean a person's age or stage of life, or it can mean physical stature (height). In the Byzantine New Testament's 8 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible splits evenly across "worrying," "stature," and "age" (2 each). The most telling evidence comes from the everyday Koine papyri: Moulton-Milligan can produce a long list of examples meaning "age" but can hardly find any where "stature" is even possible, which tips the disputed passages (like Matthew 6:27) toward "age."
caution: The two main senses genuinely compete: in passages like Matthew 6:27 and Luke 12:25 the translations and lexica disagree over whether it means "age" or "stature."

definition: The state of being a war captive, or collectively the group of people taken captive.
article: This noun refers to captivity—the condition of being seized and carried off, usually as a prisoner of war—and can also stand for the captives themselves as a group. It is rare in the New Testament (just 2 Byzantine occurrences, 3 in the critical text), but very common in the Septuagint, where it appears 91 times across 20 books. There it most often renders the Hebrew shevi, "captivity" (31×), along with golah, "exiles" (13×), reflecting Israel's experience of being deported. Abbott-Smith notes that in Ephesians 4:8 it is used as an abstract word standing for the concrete "captives."
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin—both Byzantine occurrences were absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word—so the confidence tier is low.

definition: A grammatical form of the feminine word "this," pointing to a particular thing already mentioned or near at hand.
article: This is not really a separate word but an inflected form of οὗτος ("this"), specifically certain case-endings of its feminine singular. Strong's describes it as meaning "(towards or of) this," and the KJV renders it in many ways depending on context, such as "this," "that," "the same," or "it." Because it functions as a pointing word, its exact English translation always depends on the noun it modifies and its role in the sentence.
caution: This entry shows no measured occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so its usage range here rests only on Strong's and Abbott-Smith rather than corpus evidence.

definition: To rub perfumed ointment onto someone or something, especially the body.
article: μυρίζω means to apply scented ointment, and it appears just once in the New Testament, in Mark 14:8, where a woman anoints Jesus' body. It is closely tied to the noun μύρον (perfumed oil), from which it derives, and the standard translations all settle on "anoint."
