Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that in everyday Koine the word shows up in a third-century magical papyrus instructing someone to apply ointment to the face, and that in Modern Greek μυρίζω has shifted to mean simply "to smell."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: The Mediterranean island where Paul was shipwrecked, traditionally identified as modern Malta.
article: Μελίτη is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 28:1, naming the island where Paul's ship ran aground. Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith all identify it with modern Malta. The most interesting wrinkle is textual: some manuscripts (followed by Westcott and Hort) read Μελιτήνη instead, but Moulton-Milligan judges this likely an accidental doubling of the following letters ('dittography'), and they cite inscriptions referring to the 'Melitenses' that support the Μελίτη form.
caution: This word occurs only once and the manuscripts disagree on its exact spelling (Μελίτη versus Μελιτήνη).

definition: A humble attitude of mind that does not exalt itself above others.
article: ταπεινοφροσύνη describes lowliness of mind or humility, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "humility" in 6 of its 7 New Testament occurrences (86%), with the single remaining case in Colossians 3:12 phrased as "yourselves with humility." It is built from ταπεινός (lowly) and the base of φρήν (mind), so the underlying idea is literally a humble mindset. Notably, Abbott-Smith observes the word is rare outside the New Testament and, where it does appear in Josephus and Epictetus, it carries a bad sense — and the New Testament itself uses it negatively of a false humility in Colossians 2:18, 23.

definition: A little scroll or small book, the diminutive of the ordinary word for a book or scroll.
article: βιβλιαρίδιον means a small scroll or little book—it's a double diminutive, built down from βίβλος (book) through βιβλάριον. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both in Revelation 10, where John is told to take and eat the small scroll, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as 'small scroll.' Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes this exact form is not found anywhere else, and the manuscripts vary considerably here (some read βιβλίον or βιβλιδάριον instead).
caution: This is a rare form found only in Revelation, the manuscripts disagree on its exact spelling, and it is absent from the critical SBLGNT text.

definition: A clear, transparent material like glass or crystal, prized for its see-through quality.
article: Hýalos refers to glass or a clear, transparent stone, and in the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Revelation 21 (verses 18 and 21), where it is rendered "glass" 100% of the time. The classical lexica show a wider range: in the earliest writers (Herodotus) it meant a clear transparent stone, and only later (from Plato onward) did it come to mean manufactured glass. Everyday papyri confirm the practical sense vividly — one document lists "4 glass flasks in sound condition," showing the word was ordinary trade vocabulary. The Septuagint uses it once, at Job 28:17, translating the Hebrew word for glass.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences and one in the Septuagint — and the classical lexica note the meaning shifted over time between transparent stone and manufactured glass.

definition: To deliver a public speech or formal address to a gathered crowd or assembly.
article: δημηγορέω means to stand up and make a formal speech before an assembled crowd, built from the words for "people" (δῆμος) and "to speak in public" (ἀγορεύω). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 12:21, where Herod addresses the people. In the Septuagint it shows up only once, oddly translating the Hebrew word zarzir, and it also turns up in 4 Maccabees 5:15, so its overall footprint in the biblical corpus is tiny.
caution: Evidence is very thin: a single New Testament occurrence and only one Septuagint use, and the MSB's measured rendering "appointed" reflects the wider verse rather than the verb's own meaning of public speaking.

definition: Made of hair, describing cloth or material woven from animal hair such as goat's hair.
article: τρίχινος is an adjective meaning "made of hair," built from θρίξ ("hair"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Revelation 6:12, where it describes sackcloth and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "goat" (as in goat-hair sackcloth). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: documents speak of "hairy crests" and a "sack of hair-cloth," showing it routinely described coarse hair-woven goods, and the Septuagint uses it twice (Zechariah 13:4 and Exodus 26:7).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the "goat" rendering is really a contextual translation of hair-cloth, not a separate meaning of the word.

definition: A fresh, new quality or condition of life that replaces an old way of being.
article: καινότης names the quality of being new or fresh, and in the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Romans, describing the "newness" of life or of the Spirit (Romans 6:4; 7:6). It derives from καινός ("new"), and in one of its two NT uses the Majority Standard Bible folds it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a single English word. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it only twice as well, where it renders very different Hebrew words — one tied to separation (בָּדַל) and one to healing or remedy (תְּרוּפָה, in Ezekiel 47:12) — while classical writers like Thucydides used it for "novelty."
caution: Evidence is thin: only two NT occurrences and two Septuagint uses, so the word's full range is hard to pin down with confidence.

definition: To cut down standing grain or grass with a blade; to mow or reap a harvest.
article: This verb means to mow down or reap crops, the work of harvesting grain by cutting it with a blade. It appears just once in the New Testament, in James 5:4, where it describes laborers who mowed the fields. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times and stands in for Hebrew קָצַר (to reap) three times; interestingly, an uneducated papyrus letter from 256 BC pairs it with another word for harvesting ("to mow and to reap"), showing that although the word was mostly poetic in earlier Greek, it had a place in everyday speech.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a word that was chiefly poetic in earlier Greek, the confidence here is low.

definition: A person who attacks others with insulting, abusive speech; a reviler or verbal abuser.
article: λοίδορος describes someone who habitually hurls insults and abusive words at others — what older translations call a "railer" or "reviler." It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's lists of bad behavior in 1 Corinthians (5:11 and 6:10), and turns up a handful of times in the Septuagint, including Proverbs where it renders the Hebrew word for strife or contention. A nice everyday parallel comes from a Roman inscription praising a man named Menophilus who "hurt no one and sent out no abusive words" (λοίδορα ῥήματα), showing the word was at home in ordinary Koine.
caution: The measured sense data here is noisy — the rendering fragments "claims a verbal" and "nor" reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word's actual meaning, so lean on the lexical evidence.

definition: To be nourished or trained up in something, like being raised on and shaped by certain teachings.
article: ἐντρέφω literally means to nurture or feed something, but in its single New Testament appearance (1 Timothy 4:6) it works figuratively in the passive: being raised on and shaped by the words of faith. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "nourished" in that one instance. Moulton-Milligan finds the word in everyday Koine papyri, and notably the philosopher Epictetus uses the same construction—being "nourished" on certain reflections—showing this was a natural way to describe forming a person through steady mental diet.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its measured range here rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Phlegon, a Roman Christian man greeted by Paul.
article: Phlegon is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament when Paul sends greetings to him in Romans 16:14. The name comes from a word meaning "blazing" (a participle of the base behind the word for "flame"), though here it functions purely as a person's name. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the name was once given to a dog in Xenophon and later came to be applied to slaves, suggesting Phlegon may have been of humble or servile background.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so almost nothing is known about the man himself.

definition: A hostile gathering or crowd that rises up against someone, sometimes the pressure of such opposition.
article: ἐπισύστασις pictures people banding together against someone—a riotous throng or hostile combination. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, where editors prefer the similar word ἐπίστασις instead. The Majority Standard Bible renders it once as 'accusers' (Acts 24:12) and once as 'trials' (2 Corinthians 11:28), and an inscription from the first century B.C. uses it of 'risings up' by hostile barbarians, reinforcing the idea of organized opposition.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two disputed New Testament occurrences, the critical text omits the word entirely, and the two measured renderings ('accusers' and 'trials') pull in noticeably different directions.

definition: An unripe fig that grows late and usually drops off before ripening.
article: Ὄλυνθος refers to an unripe fig—specifically the kind that forms out of season, lingers through winter, and falls off in spring before it can ripen. The word is rare: it appears just once in the New Testament (Revelation 6:13), where stars fall like late figs shaken from a tree, and once in the Greek Old Testament. That single Septuagint use translates the Hebrew פַּג in Song of Solomon 2:13, the early green fruit of the fig tree, confirming the picture of fruit that is not yet ripe.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, and its derivation is uncertain.

definition: A sight or spectacle—something gathered to look at or watch.
article: θεωρία refers to a sight or spectacle, the kind of scene people come together to watch. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 23:48, where the crowd had gathered for the spectacle of the crucifixion. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one document from 112 BC describes a Roman senator sailing to Egypt 'to see the sights,' and others mention the spectacles at a village festival; it could even mean a judicial investigation.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin Septuagint evidence, confidence in its full range is low, though papyri usage agrees on the basic 'spectacle' sense.

definition: To be slow or to delay, holding back from doing something at the expected time.
article: βραδýnō means to be slow or to linger, holding back rather than acting promptly. In the New Testament it appears just twice and always in the intransitive sense of delaying or tarrying. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one third-century document reads "since they are delaying" of people putting off a duty—and classical sources also record a transitive sense, "to retard," not found in the New Testament. In the Septuagint it renders Hebrew words for holding back or being late, as in Genesis 43:10.
caution: The measured-sense data here is garbled (it labels this verb "foundation" from 1 Timothy 3:15), so rely on the lexica, which agree it means to be slow or delay.

definition: Describing something or someone as belonging to a particular person or group — their own, personal, or private.
article: This common adjective marks something as belonging to a specific person or group — "his own," "their own," "private." Of its 113 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "own" 72 times (88%) and "privately" 10 times (12%), with 31 more instances absorbed so smoothly into the phrasing that no single English word represents them. Everyday Koine papyri show how worn-down it became: people swore documents were "written in my own hand" (γράψω τῇ ἰδίᾳ μου χειρί), and the word often amounted to little more than a possessive pronoun, as Moulton-Milligan notes.

definition: The form of the word "you" used to show possession or relationship, meaning "your" or "of you," referring to more than one person.
article: This is the possessive form of the plural "you" (ὑμεῖς), translated as "your" or "of you" when several people are addressed. It is one of the most common grammatical words in Greek, appearing 1,569 times across 34 books of the Septuagint, though the Byzantine New Testament digest records no occurrences here. In the Septuagint it lines up with a range of Hebrew words, most often forms tied to God (אֱלֹהִים, 86×) and to personal pronouns like "I" and "you," reflecting how often phrases of belonging and address occur in Scripture.
caution: This is a grammatical pronoun rather than a content word, so its "meaning" depends entirely on the phrase it sits in; the reported zero Byzantine occurrences likely reflects how the data was indexed rather than true absence.

definition: To talk something over among people, so that news or discussion spreads from one person to another.
article: διαλαλέω combines "through" with "to speak," carrying the idea of talk passing from mouth to mouth through a group. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Luke 1:65 of news being talked about everywhere (rendered as part of the phrase "filled"), and in Luke 6:11 of people discussing what to do. Moulton-Milligan note that a related noun appears in an eighth-century papyrus will of an Egyptian bishop, referring to the "Egyptian tongue" in which the document was interpreted to him, and the verb survives in Modern Greek meaning "announce."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin measured data (one of which is absorbed into surrounding phrasing), confidence in the precise range is low.

definition: Describing something that happens every day or day by day.
article: καθημερινός means "daily" — something that recurs or is done every day. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 6:1, describing the daily distribution to widows, and shows up in the Septuagint only at Judith 12:15. Everyday Koine papyri use it freely, including third-century medical and magical texts that speak of a "daily" fever as opposed to one that strikes every other day.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the corpus tool oddly tags its rendering as "increasing," though every traditional source agrees the word simply means "daily."

definition: To praise or express admiration, used in the New Testament almost always of praising God.
article: αἰνέω means to praise, and in the New Testament it nearly always has God as its object. It is fairly narrow in range: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "praising" 4 times and "praise" 2 times across its 9 occurrences. The word is hugely common in the Septuagint (100×), where it usually translates the Hebrew הָלַל (53×), the root behind "hallelujah"; Moulton-Milligan note it appears in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, though Greek writers had largely shifted to the related ἐπαινέω.

definition: An adverb meaning on the ground or to the ground, describing where something falls or rests.
article: This adverb simply locates something in relation to the ground, covering both motion toward it ("to the ground") and position on it ("on the ground"). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in John: Jesus spitting on the ground (John 9:6) and the soldiers falling to the ground (John 18:6). Everyday Koine papyri show the same flexible range — one document uses it for doors "thrown to the ground" and also for doors that "lie on the ground" — confirming this was ordinary, practical vocabulary.
caution: With only two New Testament uses, the entry rests on a thin biblical base, though papyri evidence supports its meaning.

definition: To accuse someone or bring a charge against them, often with a hint of slander or hostility.
article: In the New Testament διαβάλλω appears only once, in Luke 16:1, where the BSB and Majority Standard Bible both render it "accused." The word literally means "to throw across," and from there it stretches to slandering, defaming, or accusing — though the everyday papyri show it could mean simply "complain of" without any necessary implication of malice or falsehood. One papyrus letter even cautions that the charge in Luke 16:1 need not assume slander, since the verb was used for ordinary complaints.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a range running from neutral complaint to malicious slander, the precise force in Luke 16:1 is uncertain.

definition: To put to death or make as good as dead, used both literally and figuratively for deadening something within a person.
article: This verb means to make dead or put to death, and the New Testament uses it both literally and figuratively across its 3 occurrences. It can describe a body so worn by age that it is as good as dead, or it can be a command to kill off carnal impulses, as in Colossians 3:5. A striking parallel comes from an ancient inscription where a tomb pleads, "O man, pass not by my body, now a corpse," using this same word for a literal dead body.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 occurrences, two of which were absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word.

definition: To be cut to the heart, meaning to feel a violent surge of fury that wells up inside a person.
senseLabels: cut to the heart with rage
article: Literally this verb means "to saw through" or "saw apart," but in the New Testament it appears only in the passive and only figuratively, describing people consumed by anger. It shows up just twice in the Byzantine text, both in Acts (5:33 and 7:54), each time picturing listeners enraged to the point of violence. The everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, however, keep the plain woodworking sense: one inscription speaks of Theodemos "having sawed through" a piece of timber.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences (and none in the critical SBLGNT text), so the figurative "cut to the heart" sense rests on a very small sample.

definition: To be present or at hand right now; in some contexts, to be about to come or to loom threateningly.
article: This compound of ἐν ("in") and ἵστημι ("to stand") means something "stands upon" you — most often that it is present and happening now, though it can also point to what is about to come or threaten. In its 7 New Testament appearances the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "present" in various forms, sometimes paired with "future" to contrast the now with the not-yet. The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where ἐνεστώς routinely marks "the current month" or "the present year" — leading Moulton-Milligan to argue that 2 Thessalonians 2:2 means the day of the Lord is "now present" rather than merely "at hand."
caution: The word straddles "present" and "about to come," and the lexicons disagree on which sense fits certain verses, so context matters.

definition: To move forward or advance, used literally for going on ahead and figuratively for being far advanced in age.
article: At its core προβαίνω means to walk forward or advance, and the New Testament shows both its plain and figurative sides. In Matthew 4:21 and Mark 1:19 it describes James and John literally "going farther on" while mending their nets, while in Luke it appears three times in the idiom of being "well advanced" in years (Luke 1:7, 1:18, 2:36). The Septuagint uses it 11 times, most often (6×) for the Hebrew word זָקֵן, "old" or "aged," and the everyday papyri confirm both meanings — one document from 120 B.C. speaks of someone "already advanced in years" much as Luke does.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences split between literal motion and the age idiom, the sense breakdown rests on thin data.

definition: A loud cry or shout — whether from grief, alarm, joy, or angry shouting against someone.
article: κραυγή is a loud vocal outcry, and the situation gives it its color: it can be a midnight alarm (Matthew 25:6), Jesus crying out in anguish (Hebrews 5:7), or the angry "clamor" against others that believers are told to put away (Ephesians 4:31). In the Septuagint it appears 53 times, often rendering Hebrew words for a desperate cry for help or a battle/festival shout. One papyrus is especially vivid: a description of Ptolemy III's triumphal welcome pairs κραυγή with applause as a shout of joy, the same happy note heard in Luke 1:42.
caution: Two of the six New Testament occurrences were counted under fragments of surrounding phrases ("Get," "every") rather than a clear standalone gloss, so the rendering counts understate how consistently it means "cry."

definition: A bear, the large wild animal known for its ferocity.
article: ἄρκτος means a bear, a large and dangerous wild animal. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Revelation 13:2), where the beast's feet are described, and across the Septuagint it shows up 13 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word דֹּב ("bear", 10×). An interesting wrinkle from the papyri and inscriptions is the contracted spelling ἄρκος (and even the further-shortened ἄρξ in a sixth-century inscription), the by-form that eventually gave Modern Greek its word for she-bear, ἀρκούδα.
caution: The measured data oddly labels the single New Testament occurrence as "leopard," but every dictionary source and the Hebrew counterpart point to "bear," so the rendering tag appears to be an error.

definition: An adverb meaning afterward or later in time, and sometimes last of all in a sequence.
article: This little adverb is mostly about time: it marks something that happens later or afterward, and it appears 12 times in the Byzantine New Testament. In a few places it shifts to mean "last of all," as when a woman dies after all her husbands (Matthew 22:27). The everyday flavor comes through clearly in the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan cites phrases like "a very long while afterwards," showing it was common, ordinary Koine for sequencing events.

definition: To put out or extinguish a fire, or figuratively to suppress and stifle something so it stops burning or working.
article: This verb means to extinguish or quench — most often literally, of fire or things on fire, but also figuratively. In the Byzantine New Testament its 8 occurrences split between "quenched" (4×) and "extinguish" (3×), with the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles agreeing fully on each. The Septuagint uses it 36 times, chiefly for the Hebrew word kābāh ("to go out, be quenched," 22×), and the everyday papyri show the same fire sense alongside a striking figurative extension to "wash out" or "erase" something.

definition: A deep ravine or gully, especially one cut by a winter torrent, lying between higher ground.
article: φάραγξ names a steep-sided valley or chasm carved into the landscape, the kind of gully a seasonal torrent would dig. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 3:5, quoting Isaiah's image of every ravine being filled in; the Septuagint uses it far more often (78 times), most frequently rendering the Hebrew words נַ֫חַל (a wadi or stream-valley, 20×) and גָּיְא (a valley, 22×). A nice everyday touch: the related verb φαραγγόω turns up in a late-second-century-BC papyrus survey-list describing land ploughed up into furrows.
caution: The New Testament evidence is thin — a single occurrence, and that one a direct Septuagint quotation — so its range here rests almost entirely on the Greek Old Testament.

definition: To sink or go down, used specifically of the sun setting at the end of the day.
article: δύνω describes something sinking down, and in the New Testament it always refers to the sun going down at sunset. It appears just twice (in Mark 1:32 and Luke 4:40), both times marking the moment after sundown when people brought the sick to Jesus. The word was at home in everyday Koine: papyri use it for the literal setting of stars, as in an astronomical calendar that times festivals by whether a star is 'setting or rising.' In the Septuagint it shows up 21 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for 'sun' (14×).

definition: Eliakim, a personal name borne by men listed among the ancestors of Jesus.
article: Ἐλιακείμ is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name אֶלְיָקִים (Eliakim), always rendered "Eliakim" in English. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 3 times across 2 books, naming ancestors in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:13 and Luke 3:30). It shows up far more often in the Septuagint, 12 times across 4 books, each time translating the same Hebrew name, so its meaning as a proper name is well anchored.
caution: Despite the genealogy appearances, this name is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, so the count rests on the Byzantine tradition.

definition: The natural state of sleep, and figuratively a spiritual drowsiness or unawareness.
article: ὕπνος is the ordinary Koine word for sleep, appearing 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament and 43 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew שֵׁנָה (sleep, 16×) and חֲלוֹם (dream, 11×). Most occurrences simply mean physical sleep, as in Luke 9:32 or John 11:13, while a couple of the measured "senses" listed above ("up embraced Mary," "When") are really just fragments of surrounding phrasing rather than meanings of the word itself. The lexica (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) note a figurative sense of spiritual drowsiness in Romans 13:11; one striking everyday parallel is a papyrus letter from 258 BC in which a man reports the god Sarapis appearing to him repeatedly "in his sleep" (ἐν τοῖς ὕπνοις).
caution: The measured-sense breakdown is misleading, since two of the three "senses" are stray words from adjacent phrasing, not actual meanings of ὕπνος; the word really just means sleep, sometimes figuratively.

definition: To renounce or disown something for oneself, turning away from it deliberately.
article: This is a reflexive past-tense verb meaning to renounce or disown something, literally to "speak it away" from yourself. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (2 Corinthians 4:2), where the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding phrase as "deceit," though the verb itself carries the sense of renouncing. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this middle usage well: one document (Ostr 1156) uses the exact form to mean refusing or giving up a claim, and another (P Giss I.82) pairs it with disowning all expenses incurred. The older lexicons spread its range across "tell out," "forbid," and "renounce," with the Septuagint examples (only 4 times across 3 books) showing it translating several different Hebrew words.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and disagreement among the lexicons over its range, confidence is low.

definition: To kiss someone, often as a warm or demonstrative greeting of affection.
article: καταφιλέω means to kiss someone, and all six New Testament occurrences are simply rendered as some form of "kissed." In the Septuagint it shows up 14 times across 7 books, mostly translating the Hebrew נָשַׁק (12×), the ordinary word for kissing. Lexicons like Abbott-Smith and Dodson suggest a fervent or affectionate kiss, but Moulton-Milligan cites everyday papyri and Epictetus to argue the prefix often stresses the act of kissing itself rather than any extra intensity — making the "kiss fervently" reading doubtful.
caution: Sources disagree on whether the word implies a fervent or affectionate kiss or just an ordinary one, so the intensity is uncertain.

definition: A honeycomb, the wax structure bees build to store honey.
article: κηρίον means a honeycomb — the waxy comb that holds honey, fittingly named since it derives from the word for wax (κηρός). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 24:42, where the risen Jesus is offered a piece alongside broiled fish, and the Septuagint uses it about 10 times, often for Hebrew נֹפֶת (honey from the comb). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the word was ordinary commercial vocabulary, including a document mentioning a contractor dealing in honey and wax.
caution: The word is dropped from Luke 24:42 in the critical text (SBLGNT and others), so its single New Testament occurrence rests on the Byzantine/Majority tradition.

definition: Describing something regarded as unpresentable, indecent, or not fit to be shown openly.
article: ἀσχήμων literally means "shapeless" or "without proper form," and from there came to describe what is unseemly or indecent — something not fit for public display. It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 12:23), where Paul speaks of the body's less presentable parts, and twice in the Septuagint, where the Greek versions used it for Hebrew words tied to disgrace and shameful behavior (Genesis 34:7, Deuteronomy 24:1). The everyday papyri make its force vivid: a petitioner from A.D. 38 complains of being subjected to "much shameful mishandling," showing the word commonly carried a sense of degrading, improper treatment.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by its own English word) and just two in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin.

definition: A negative connector meaning "and not," "nor," or "not even," used to continue or strengthen a negation or prohibition.
article: μηδέ is a negative particle that carries forward a "no" already in play—translating roughly as "nor," "and not," or, more emphatically, "not even." The measured renderings cluster around joining negatives together ("do nor," "or," "do or") and around plain prohibition ("do not," "not"), and it often pairs with itself as "neither...nor" (as in Matthew 10:10 and 1 Corinthians 10:8-9). Notably, 18 of its 58 New Testament occurrences are simply absorbed into the surrounding English phrasing with no word of their own, which is why its sense is more about glue than meaning. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew prohibition word אַל (31×), fitting its role in commands not to do something.
caution: Most of the measured "sense" labels reflect English phrasing patterns rather than distinct meanings, so the divisions are looser than they appear.

definition: Dearly loved; cherished, used of someone held in deep affection by God or by fellow believers.
article: ἀγαπητός means "beloved" or "dearly loved," and the evidence is remarkably uniform: across 62 Byzantine occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "beloved" 58 times (98%), with the BSB independently agreeing 97% of the time. It applies both to those loved by God—famously the voice declaring Jesus "my beloved" in Matthew 3:17, Mark 1:11, and Luke 3:22—and to Christians' affection for one another, where it often serves as a warm form of address. The most striking detail is that this wasn't church jargon: it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, including a third-century letter addressing "Apollo the elder, beloved brother in the Lord," and even in a horoscope from around AD 20–50.

definition: To cover something over or hide it; used figuratively of sins being covered, meaning forgiven.
article: ἐπικαλύπτω literally means to cover or cover up something, and built from ἐπί (over) and καλύπτω (to cover). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Romans 4:7, where Paul quotes the Septuagint about the person whose sins are covered—a figurative way of saying forgiven. It is more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 17 times across 10 books and translates several Hebrew verbs, most often חָפָה (to cover) three times.
caution: The word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured New Testament sense rests on a single quoted verse.

definition: A passing over or temporary overlooking of sin or debt, leaving punishment suspended rather than fully cancelled.
article: πάρεσις means letting something go by — a passing over or toleration, used in the New Testament of God passing over sins previously committed. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 3:25, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the idea of "atoning." The most telling evidence comes from the papyri and ancient writers: Dionysius of Halicarnassus contrasts a full release with a temporary deferral, and a papyrus from Diocletian's time uses the word for a temporary remission of debt — suggesting a suspension rather than a complete cancellation. Lexicographers note it stands close to ἄφεσις but is not identical.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the digest's senses disagree, with the lexica favoring "passing over/suspension" while the measured rendering reads "atoning," so its precise force is genuinely uncertain.

definition: Rahab, a Canaanite woman from Jericho who appears in Jesus' genealogy.
article: Ῥαχάβ is a proper name, the Greek form of the Canaanite woman Rahab, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Matthew 1:5, where every translation renders it "Rahab." According to the supporting lexicons she lived before Israel's monarchy and is first mentioned at Joshua 2:1, where she helped the Hebrew spies at Jericho; Matthew lists her as the mother of Boaz. Abbott-Smith notes the underlying name means "spacious" or "broad," and the word is indeclinable in Greek.
caution: With only one occurrence the entry rests on a single verse, so the confidence tier is low.

definition: To bear up under or endure something difficult, holding firm rather than giving way.
article: In the New Testament στέγω means to bear up under hardship and keep enduring, and that is how the Majority Standard Bible renders all four occurrences—"bear" twice and "bears things" once, with one instance absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The word's root idea is to cover or roof over, and from that came two branches: covering to conceal, or covering to ward off and endure; Abbott-Smith notes the "keep secret" sense is possible at 1 Corinthians 13:7 ("love covers all things"), though the MSB and BSB read it as enduring. A nice everyday parallel appears in an Oxyrhynchus papyrus where a writer says his father did him much harm "and I endured (ἔστεξα) until you came."
caution: With only four occurrences and the "conceal" versus "endure" senses overlapping, the rendering of 1 Corinthians 13:7 is genuinely debated.

definition: A wrinkle or fold in the skin, especially the kind that comes with age.
article: This word literally means a wrinkle or fold, the sort that appears on an aging face. It shows up only once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 5:27, where the Berean translations render it "stain" in describing the church as having no blemish. Outside the Bible it appears in everyday Koine papyri and in classical authors like Aristophanes, and Moulton-Milligan cites Plutarch using it of the wrinkle of age as a witness of experience.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: Indecency or shameful nakedness — something disgraceful, often used as a polite term for exposed private parts.
article: This word covers what is unseemly or disgraceful, and especially serves as a polite way of speaking about nakedness or indecent acts. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "shame" both times (once absorbed into the surrounding phrasing). The strongest signal of its range comes from the Septuagint, where it shows up 41 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew word ʿerwah (38×), the standard term for nakedness or shameful exposure; everyday Koine papyri also attest the word, where it can mean scandals.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single measured sense, the full range of meaning rests mainly on Septuagint and external evidence rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: Enough or sufficient — describing an amount that meets a need or is adequate for the day.
article: ἀρκετός means "enough" or "sufficient," and all 3 of its New Testament appearances are rendered that way, as in Jesus' words that "sufficient for the day is its own trouble" (Matthew 6:34). It's a fairly rare word, derived from the verb ἀρκέω ("to be enough"), and the lexica agree closely on its meaning. The everyday Koine papyri confirm it in ordinary life — one second/third-century document urges someone to "be sufficient" (adequate) for the remaining tasks, showing the word covered both quantities and people's adequacy.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, this is a thinly attested word, though the available evidence is consistent.

definition: A plan, purpose, or decision reached through deliberation, whether by people or by God.
article: βουλή refers to a settled plan or purpose arrived at by thinking something through — it can be a human decision or, often in the New Testament, God's purpose. The renderings spread evenly across its 12 occurrences, covering deliberation ("waiting," "decided") and the resulting plan ("purpose"), frequently in phrases like "God's purpose." In the Septuagint it appears 128 times and most often translates the Hebrew עֵצָה ("counsel," 64×); notably, Moulton-Milligan observe that both the LXX and NT always use it for "counsel" and never in its technical Greek sense of a governing "council."
caution: The four measured senses each cover only 2 occurrences, and 2 of 12 were absorbed into phrasing, so the boundaries between "plan," "purpose," and "decision" are fluid rather than sharply distinct.

definition: Jotham, a king of Judah, son of Uzziah and father of Ahaz, named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.
article: Ἰωάθαμ is a proper name, the Greek form of the Hebrew יוֹתָם (Jotham), a king of Judah. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 2 times, both in Matthew 1:9, where the genealogy lists Jotham along with his father Uzziah and son Ahaz. The Septuagint uses the name 23 times across 7 books, always rendering the same Hebrew name. One of the two measured renderings reads as "Ahaz" rather than "Jotham," which simply reflects how the verse's neighboring names were counted, not a second meaning.
caution: This is a rare indeclinable proper name appearing only in Matthew 1:9, and the "Ahaz" rendering is an artifact of how the genealogy was counted rather than a genuine separate sense.

definition: Kingly rule or sovereignty, and by extension the realm or people over which a king reigns.
article: βασιλεία covers both the abstract idea of royal power or sovereignty and the concrete sense of an actual kingdom — the territory or people a king rules. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 162 times across 17 books, and translators render it "kingdom" in 156 of those cases (100% of the times it gets its own English word), with the other 6 absorbed into phrasing. In the Septuagint it shows up 281 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew words מַמְלָכָה and מַלְכוּת, both of which carry the same blend of "reign" and "realm." The lexicons note an even narrower usage where the word can mean the royal majesty or the king himself, much like calling someone "His Majesty."

definition: A person's way of living—their conduct and behavior in daily life and dealings with others.
article: In the New Testament ἀναστροφή always refers to how someone lives—their conduct, behavior, and manner of life—appearing 13 times across 7 books, rendered as "way of life" or "conduct" about 27% each. Although it comes from a verb meaning to turn back or wheel about, classical writers like Sophocles and Thucydides used it literally for a "turning," and only later writers shifted it to mean behavior. The KJV's old gloss "conversation" reflects this same idea of one's whole conduct, not just speech, and Moulton-Milligan note its somewhat formal flavor, as in a 215 AD edict of Caracalla contrasting civic versus rustic conduct.

definition: A connecting word meaning "just as" or "even as," introducing a comparison between two things.
article: καθάπερ is a comparison word that links two ideas, meaning "just as" or "even as" — for example, just as the body has many parts (Romans 12:4). It appears 13 times in the New Testament, but in 7 of those it gets folded into the surrounding English phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word. One fascinating detail comes from the papyri: it was very common in a legal formula, καθάπερ ἐκ δίκης, meaning "as if a formal court decree had been obtained," found in marriage contracts as early as 311 BC.

definition: Tarsus, a city in Cilicia in Asia Minor, known as the home of the apostle Paul.
article: Ταρσός is the name of a city in Cilicia, a region of Asia Minor. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, always referring to this same place, and every source agrees on this rendering. In all three occurrences (Acts 9:30, 11:25, 22:3) it is tied to Paul, who is identified as a man of Tarsus.
caution: This is a proper place name appearing only 3 times, so its range is fixed and there is no question of varied meaning.

definition: Describing something of very high value or great cost.
article: βαρύτιμος describes something that is very costly or of great value, and in the New Testament it appears just once, in Matthew 26:7, where it refers to the expensive perfume a woman poured on Jesus. The word is built from βαρύς (heavy) and τιμή (price or value), literally suggesting something "heavy in price." Notably, some manuscripts read πολυτίμου instead at this spot, a near-synonym meaning "of great price."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and some textual witnesses replace it with πολυτίμου, so the evidence is thin.

definition: To burst open noisily, splitting apart—as a body does when it falls.
article: λάσχω appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical SBLGNT text), describing in Acts 1:18 how Judas, after falling headlong, burst open. The Majority Standard Bible renders this single occurrence as "fell," though the older sense behind the word is much more graphic: to crack, crash, or burst with a loud noise. Classical lexicons note that in poetry the word could even mean to scream or shout, and one interesting detail from the papyri is that a related form λάσκομαι in Pontus came to mean "seek aimlessly," showing how the word's force softened over time.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and may actually derive from the alternate form λακέω, so its precise form and sense are uncertain.

definition: To split, tear, or rip something apart; figuratively, to divide a group into opposing factions.
article: σχίζω means to tear, split, or rend something physically — like the temple veil torn in two (Matthew 27:51) or the unshrunk cloth that tears a garment (Luke 5:36); the Majority Standard Bible renders it "torn" in 6 of its occurrences. The word can also be used figuratively in the passive voice for a crowd being divided into rival factions, as in Acts 14:4 and 23:7. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew בָּקַע (to split open, 4 times), and everyday Koine papyri use it for cleaving stones and even for "split" tunics, showing it was ordinary, practical vocabulary.

definition: To settle accounts or make a reckoning, especially in figuring out who owes what.
article: This verb literally means "to take up together," but in the New Testament it always pairs with "word/account" (λόγον) to mean settling accounts or making a financial reckoning. It appears just 3 times, all in Matthew's parables about masters reckoning with servants over money owed. A nice piece of evidence: this accounting sense was once thought absent from Greek literature, but everyday business papyri now confirm it—a London papyrus from AD 78–79 uses the exact phrase "settling the account with Epimachos."
caution: With only 3 occurrences—all the same accounting idiom in Matthew—the evidence is thin, and the financial sense rests largely on parallel papyri usage.

definition: To leap or spring upon someone, typically as an attack or assault.
article: ἐφάλλομαι literally means to spring or leap upon someone, formed from ἐπί ('upon') and ἅλλομαι ('to leap'). In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 19:16) the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'overpowered,' capturing the violent result of the leaping assault. In the Septuagint it appears 3 times, always translating the Hebrew צָלַח, and an inscription from the healing shrine at Epidaurus uses it of a god 'leaping upon' a powerless hand to restore it.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: Sufficient or considerable—enough in amount, large in number, or competent and fit for a task.
article: ἱκανός describes something that measures up: either ample in quantity (many, a large number, enough) or, when applied to people, competent and qualified for a task. Its range is broad, and in fact 26 of its 41 New Testament occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew דָּי, meaning "enough" or "sufficiency," and the everyday papyri use it the same way—one tax document speaks of "a large quantity" of wheat coming in.
caution: The word's meaning shifts heavily with context (number, quantity, time, or personal fitness), so its sense depends on the specific verse rather than a single fixed gloss.

definition: To live somewhere as a foreigner or temporary resident rather than as a permanent inhabitant.
article: παροικέω means to dwell in a place as a stranger or temporary resident, not as a settled native. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and Hebrews 11:9 captures its sense well: Abraham living in a foreign country. The Septuagint uses it 60 times, most often for the Hebrew גּוּר (38×), 'to sojourn,' and Moulton-Milligan note that in later Greek it specifically signaled transitory living as opposed to κατοικέω, which meant settling down permanently — a contrast that classical writers used the word differently, where it could simply mean 'to dwell beside.'
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the measured English evidence is thin, though the abundant Septuagint usage supports the 'sojourn as a stranger' sense.

definition: The act of receiving or taking someone to oneself; acceptance into a relationship or group.
article: Πρόσληψις refers to the act of accepting or receiving someone, taken from the verb προσλαμβάνω ("to take to oneself"). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 11:15, where it stands in deliberate contrast to "rejection." Notably, while the New Testament use centers on "acceptance" or "receiving," the classical lexica (Abbott-Smith citing Plato) also record an older sense of "assumption," showing the word's range narrowed by the time of the New Testament.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: To escape from a sinking or dangerous situation by swimming away from it.
article: This verb describes swimming away to safety, formed from ἐκ ("out of") and κολυμβάω ("to swim"). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 27:42, where soldiers worry that prisoners might swim away and escape during Paul's shipwreck. The standard lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) consistently define it as "to swim out," and Abbott-Smith notes the word goes back as far as the classical playwright Euripides.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "freedom" is a loose paraphrase rather than the literal "swim out" given by the lexicons.

definition: A fathom, a unit of depth equal to the span of a person's outstretched arms, about five or six feet.
article: This word names a fathom — the distance measured by your outstretched arms, used here for sounding the depth of water beneath a ship. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in the same verse (Acts 27:28), where sailors measure the sea depth as they near land. An ancient measurement papyrus (P Oxy IV.669) helpfully defines it as 4 cubits, calling it "the distance of the outstretched hands," which matches the word's link to the verb meaning to reach out.
caution: Both occurrences are in a single verse, and the two "measured senses" simply reflect different wordings for the same nautical depth measurement.

definition: A chain or fetter used to bind or restrain a person or thing.
article: ἅλυσις means a chain or fetter, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: of its 11 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, the Majority Standard Bible renders 10 as "chains" (100% of the rendered cases), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing fully. The word covers everyday physical chains—those that couldn't hold the demoniac in Mark 5:3, the chains binding Peter in Acts 12:6, and the chain Paul wore as a prisoner in Ephesians 6:20. The papyri confirm this was ordinary Koine vocabulary, and even preserve two diminutive forms (a "little chain"), showing the word was at home in daily Greek life, not just biblical texts.

definition: To lack or fall short of something, whether through being deficient, being in need, or being inferior to others.
article: ὑστερέω covers a connected range built on the idea of coming up short: lacking what you need, being in want, or failing to measure up. In the Byzantine New Testament's 16 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lack" 3 times, "need" twice, and "fall short" twice, with another 4 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri: one third-century document complains that it is "no use if a person comes too late," preserving the literal sense of arriving behind or being late that underlies the metaphorical meanings.

definition: A sense of proper appearance or dignity; the seemly presentability that something is given to make it look fitting.
article: εὐσχημοσύνη describes outward seemliness or a fitting, presentable appearance. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 12:23, where Paul says the body's less honorable members are treated with greater "presentability" — rendered "parts" in the measured translation. The everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions are illuminating here: the word shows up describing good order and decorum in a gymnasium and the dignified bearing of a person, confirming a general sense of orderly, becoming appearance.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint use (4 Maccabees 6:2) — so the full range rests largely on outside sources.

definition: Wine, the fermented drink made from grapes, common in everyday meals, celebrations, and religious life.
article: οἶνος simply means "wine," and the evidence is remarkably consistent: in 32 of 33 Byzantine New Testament occurrences it is rendered "wine," with the remaining instance absorbed into surrounding phrasing. It appears 194 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew יָ֫יִן ("wine," 121×) and תִּירוֹשׁ ("new wine," 35×), and it was such an ordinary word in everyday Koine that the papyri even use a diminutive, οἰνάριον, as in one document referring to "a quantity of quite thin wine." Abbott-Smith notes a metaphorical use in Revelation (the "wine" of God's wrath) and a figure where the word stands in for the vine itself in Revelation 6:6.

definition: The act of expecting or anticipating something, whether feared or simply awaited.
article: προσδοκία means expectation or anticipation — the state of waiting for something to come. It appears only twice in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as "coming" (Luke 21:26) and once as "sure" (Acts 12:11), with the BSB independently agreeing 100% in both spots. Everyday Koine papyri use the word the same way: one document from B.C. 117 speaks of people being "in expectation," and a wartime report describes it as the people's last remaining "hope" — showing the word covers both dread and longing. Strong's leans toward the fearful sense ("apprehension of evil"), but the broader evidence simply means anticipation of any kind.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a thin overall record, the precise range of this word is hard to pin down, and Strong's narrower "apprehension of evil" reading is not supported by the measured usage.

definition: Describing someone or something just born, very recently brought into life.
article: This adjective combines "just now" (ἄρτι) and "born" (γεννητός), so it literally means newly born. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 2:2, where it pictures believers as "newborn" infants who should crave pure spiritual milk. Lexicographers note that the writer Lucian also used the word, which gives ancient warrant for Peter's usage, and Moulton-Milligan point to a late imperial epitaph showing the term in everyday Koine.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical evidence.

definition: To be healthy and physically well, and figuratively, to be sound or uncorrupted in teaching, faith, or character.
article: ὑγιαίνω basically means to be in good health, healthy, well—the literal sense behind our word "hygiene." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "sound" in 8 of 12 occurrences (73%), covering both physical health (as in Luke 15:27) and a figurative sense common in the Pastoral Epistles, where Paul speaks of "sound" doctrine, words, faith, and love (1 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 1:13). One striking detail: in the Septuagint it usually stands for the Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (peace/wellbeing, 10 of 12 times), and Moulton-Milligan note it was the standard everyday word for "be well" in private letters, used as a greeting like "I hope you are in good health" or even "good-bye."

definition: A woman who nurses and cares for a young child; a wet-nurse or nursing mother.
senseLabels: a woman who nurses a child
article: τροφός refers to a nurse — a woman who feeds and tends a small child, drawn from the verb τρέφω, "to nourish." It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 2:7, where Paul compares his gentle care to a nursing mother. The everyday papyri make the picture vivid: one third-century document has a relative insisting a newborn be given a nurse rather than letting his own daughter breastfeed.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and four scattered Septuagint uses, the measured evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To place a crown or wreath on someone as a mark of honor or victory.
article: στεφανόω means to crown someone, either literally with a victor's wreath or figuratively with honor and glory. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 3 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "crowned" in 2 of those, with the third folded into surrounding phrasing. The everyday papyri make the imagery vivid: in a letter from 257 B.C. a writer hopes his nominee will be "crowned" — that is, win — in the games, and the verb was also used technically for the ceremonial crowning of magistrates.
caution: This word is rare in the New Testament (only 3 occurrences), so its full range rests largely on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: Abijah, a Hebrew personal name borne by several biblical figures, used as a proper name.
article: Ἀβιά is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Abijah, and it appears 3 times in the New Testament, always rendered "Abijah" (100%). It refers to more than one person: a son of Rehoboam who became king, and a priest who founded one of the priestly divisions (the line Zechariah belonged to in Luke 1:5). In the Septuagint the name turns up 24 times, mostly translating Hebrew אֲבִיָּה (21 times), though a few odd cases map it to entirely different Hebrew names like Tamar.
caution: This is a proper name with few NT occurrences, so its range simply reflects the different individuals who happened to bear the name.

definition: A person who originates or leads something—either the founder/author who begins it or the chief leader who heads it.
article: ἀρχηγός combines the ideas of beginning (ἀρχή) and leading (ἄγω), so it points to someone who is both the source and the head of something. In the New Testament it appears 4 times, rendered by the Majority Standard Bible as "author" half the time (Hebrews 2:10; 12:2) and as "Author" or "Prince" in Acts 3:15 and 5:31. Moulton-Milligan notes that everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions use it closely like the Latin auctor ("author"), as in a proconsul's edict calling someone the ἀρχηγός—the instigator—of a whole disturbance.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and overlapping renderings, translators genuinely disagree whether it means "founder/author" or "prince/leader" in each verse, as both Moulton-Milligan and Abbott-Smith point out.

definition: Having only one eye, or able to enter life with just one eye.
article: μονόφθαλμος simply means "one-eyed." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in nearly identical sayings of Jesus about it being better to enter life one-eyed than to be thrown into hell with both eyes (Matthew 18:9 and Mark 9:47). It's a Koine compound from μόνος ("only") and ὀφθαλμός ("eye"); ancient grammarians (per Ammonius) carefully distinguished it from ἑτερόφθαλμος, the word for someone who lost one eye by accident, whereas μονόφθαλμος describes one naturally having just one eye, like the Cyclops.
caution: The two measured "senses" listed here ("sin better with" and "better") just reflect the surrounding translation phrasing in two verses, not distinct meanings; the word itself means only "one-eyed."

definition: Failing the test and therefore rejected as unfit, useless, or worthless, whether describing metals, land, or people.
article: ἀδόκιμος is the negative of δόκιμος ("approved"), so it describes something that has been tested and failed — rejected, unfit, worthless. It applies to objects like unproductive land (Hebrews 6:8) and, more often, to people who have been examined and found wanting (Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, 2 Timothy, Titus). The word's roots show clearly in the Septuagint, where it twice describes metal: at Isaiah 1:22 it renders the Hebrew word for the dross or impurity skimmed off silver, capturing the sense of material that won't pass inspection.
caution: The word is uncommon (8 New Testament uses, only 2 in the Septuagint), and in 3 of its 8 occurrences it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single word, so renderings vary.

definition: To come back to life or regain life, used both literally and figuratively of moral or spiritual revival.
article: This verb describes coming back to life or regaining life, and the New Testament uses it in two distinct ways. In Luke 15:32 it pictures a son who 'is alive again,' a figurative moral revival, while in Romans 7:9 sin 'springs to life,' showing how broadly the word stretches from a person to an abstract force. A striking parallel turns up in everyday Koine: an inscription from Crete records a woman named Archonica fulfilling a vow to Artemis as one 'being alive once more,' confirming the word's ordinary use outside the Bible.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences (2 in the critical text), and one of these is absorbed into phrasing with no English word of its own.

definition: An interrogative word asking who, what, which, or why, used in both direct and indirect questions.
article: τίς is the basic Greek question word, covering "who," "what," "which," and "why" depending on context — it appears 570 times across 20 books of the Byzantine New Testament. The single most common rendering is "what" (170×, 35%), followed by "who" (79×, 16%) and "why" in various forms; because question words shape whole phrases, it gets absorbed into the surrounding English wording 87 times with no separate word of its own. In the Septuagint it appears 1,267 times, mostly translating the Hebrew מָה ("what," 596×) and מִי ("who," 382×), confirming its dual who/what range. It should not be confused with its unaccented cousin τὶς, which means "someone" or "something" and shows up in everyday Koine papyri.

definition: To turn something around, used figuratively of driving a person's mind toward madness.
article: περιτρέπω literally means "to turn around" or "turn about," but in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 26:24) it is used figuratively: Festus tells Paul that his great learning is "turning him to madness." The Majority Standard Bible renders this occurrence as "stage," and the BSB agrees independently. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and in the Greek historian Josephus, who uses it for turning people toward joy, showing the verb could swing in either emotional direction.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range is very thin.

definition: The preparation of a dead body for burial, such as washing, anointing, and wrapping it.
article: This word refers to getting a body ready for burial, including the customary anointing and laying out, rather than the act of burial itself. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Mark 14:8 and John 12:7), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "burial" in one of its two occurrences. Moulton-Milligan note that it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and they argue that in John 12:7 it is better translated "laying out" or "preparation for burial" rather than simply "burying."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences), and sources differ on whether to render it "burying" or the more precise "preparation for burial."

definition: The date palm tree, or by extension the branches cut from it.
article: φοῖνιξ is the date palm tree, and by extension the leafy branches taken from it. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just twice, once for palm branches waved at Jesus' entry (John 12:13) and once for the palm branches held by the great multitude (Rev 7:9). It shows up far more in the Septuagint (38 times, usually rendering Hebrew words for palm), and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday papyri, where it often means the palm's fruit—dates—as in a tax document noting that 'as regards the dates, we did not find any old ones.'
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a computed low-confidence tier, the evidence base here is thin.

definition: Describing something that resembles or corresponds to another thing in form, nature, condition, or character.
article: ὅμοιος means "like" or "resembling" — pointing to something that matches another in appearance, nature, condition, or rank. It's a remarkably stable word: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "like" in 41 of its 44 Byzantine appearances (100% of the times it gets a word of its own), and the BSB agrees independently 98% of the time. Everyday Koine papyri show a sharper shade — marrying "from one's own rank" (ἐκ τῶν ὁμοίων) — and the phrase ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν ὁμοίων meant "as in similar cases," showing how naturally it covered equality of station as well as mere resemblance.

definition: Nard, a costly fragrant oil made from an aromatic plant, used as a perfume or ointment.
article: Nard refers to a luxury perfume or ointment derived from an aromatic plant, and in both New Testament occurrences (Mark 14:3 and John 12:3) it describes the costly oil poured on Jesus. The word came into Greek from a Semitic source (Hebrew נֵרְדְּ, ultimately from Sanskrit), and the Septuagint uses it three times in the Song of Songs. Everyday Koine papyri confirm it was a real trade commodity: one early first-century document from Oxyrhynchus even prices nard by the obol.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single rendering, the measured evidence is thin, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: Near in space or time—close by in place, or soon to happen.
article: ἐγγύς is a flexible little adverb meaning "near," whether of physical distance or of time about to arrive. In the Byzantine NT it's rendered "near" 78% of the time across 30 occurrences; the other instances simply specify what is near—a Jewish feast drawing close (John 2:13; 6:4) or events that are "near, right at the door" (Matthew 24:33). In the Septuagint it appears 49 times, mostly translating the Hebrew קָרוֹב ("near," 31×), and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday papyri, as in BGU III.698 "near the threshing-floor."

definition: To burn something completely to ashes, destroying it by fire.
article: τεφρόω means to burn something down to ashes — to incinerate and so destroy it. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:6, describing the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the closely related noun τέφρα means "ashes." Strikingly, ancient writers used this same word for volcanic devastation: commentators cite Dio Cassius describing Mount Vesuvius's eruption with people "being parched and overwhelmed with ashes."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range in biblical usage cannot be measured from internal evidence.

definition: To force someone into compulsory public service, especially to make them go somewhere or carry a load.
article: ἀγγαρεύω means to press a person into compulsory service, originally a Persian term for impressing someone to act as a courier. The three Byzantine occurrences all turn on this idea of forced labor: being made to go a mile (Matthew 5:41) or being compelled to carry a load, as when Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry Jesus' cross (Matthew 27:32; Mark 15:21). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too — one Ptolemaic document from 252 BC uses it of a post boat being requisitioned, and an Egyptian prefect's order forbids anyone from impressing the local population.
caution: Only 3 occurrences, all in the same Gospel episode-type, so the measured range is narrow and rests on thin data.

definition: Describes wine that is undiluted, full-strength, poured out without being mixed with water.
article: ἄκρατος describes something unmixed or undiluted, built from a negative prefix plus a root tied to mixing or blending. In its single New Testament appearance (Revelation 14:10) it describes wine poured out at full strength, which the Majority Standard Bible renders simply as "poured." Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri stretch the word beyond drinks: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 186 uses it for the "untempered" severity of the law, showing the image of something not watered down.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured biblical range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To turn around in one's thinking — to change one's mind or opinion about something.
article: μεταβάλλω literally means "to throw over" or "turn about," and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 28:6) it carries the figurative sense of changing one's mind — the Maltese onlookers reverse their opinion about Paul. In the Septuagint it shows up 24 times across 7 books, most often translating the Hebrew הָפַךְ ("turn over," 5×) and לָבָן (8×). One striking parallel comes from the papyri: a letter of Darius I to the governor Gadatas uses the verb the same metaphorical way, threatening punishment on one who would not change his attitude toward the king's gods.
caution: This verb occurs only once in the New Testament, and the listed "islanders" rendering reflects the surrounding context of Acts 28:6 rather than the verb's own meaning, so its measured range here is very thin.

definition: A stately seat of state symbolizing royal or divine authority, and by extension the power or rule that seat represents.
article: θρόνος is overwhelmingly a single, stable idea: in 58 of 62 New Testament occurrences (98%) it is simply rendered "throne," the ceremonial seat of a king, of God, or of Christ. It can also stand by association for the power or sovereignty that the seat represents, as the lexica note (for example in Luke 1:32). In the Septuagint it appears 134 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word כִּסֵּא ("seat/throne," 100×), and the papyri confirm its everyday use for an official chair of state, as in a rescript of Commagene referring to ancestral royal thrones.

definition: A region or geographical district, a tract of land in a particular area.
article: In the New Testament κλίμα always means a region or district—a stretch of land in a particular part of the country—and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "regions" in all three of its occurrences (Romans 15:23, 2 Corinthians 11:10, Galatians 1:21). The everyday papyri confirm this geographical sense, as in an inscription (c. A.D. 245) referring to "the region of the Appiani" and a magical text speaking of "the four regions of the world." Interestingly, the word comes from κλίνω ("to lean, slope") and originally meant a slope or incline—Aristotle used it for the earth's slope from equator to pole—but that literal sense never appears in the New Testament.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only 3 times in the New Testament and just once in the Septuagint, so its full range rests largely on outside sources.

definition: A person who must work hard to earn their daily living and has little to spare; a poor laborer.
article: πένης describes someone who works for their daily bread — a laborer or poor person who scrapes by, as opposed to outright beggary. It appears only once in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 9:9, where it's absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own) but turns up 70 times in the Septuagint, most often rendering the Hebrew אֶבְיוֹן ('needy,' 18×) and עָנִי ('afflicted, poor,' 8×). Everyday papyri capture the flavor vividly: one document describes a 'poor man wearing cheap clothes,' and another advises that 'being poor, do not associate with the rich.' Lexicons note it implies less severe poverty than πτωχός, which properly means a beggar.
caution: The word appears just once in the New Testament and is absorbed into phrasing there, so its precise New Testament nuance rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: To anoint someone with oil, especially to set them apart by God for a sacred role or mission.
article: χρίω means to anoint, but in the New Testament it is always God who does the anointing, marking someone out for a special role or task. It is rare in the Byzantine NT—just 5 times across 4 books—and four of those are rendered "anointed," referring to Christ (as in Luke 4:18 and Acts 4:27); the fifth, in 2 Corinthians 1:21, extends the picture to believers. The Septuagint uses it far more (71×), mostly for Hebrew מָשַׁח, the word for consecrating priests, prophets, and kings, and everyday papyri even apply the term to greasing camels and providing oil.
caution: The two measured senses really reflect one meaning; the second "establishes both anointed" label simply captures the phrasing of a single verse (2 Cor 1:21) rather than a distinct sense.

definition: A genitive form linked to the article or pronoun, sometimes standing in for "of this person" or "his."
article: τοῦ is properly the genitive case of the Greek article ὁ ("the"), and Strong's notes it is sometimes used for τούτου, "of this person." In that role it can carry the sense rendered "his" in older translations like the KJV. The digest records no Byzantine New Testament occurrences under this specific entry, so its meaning here rests on its grammatical function rather than measured usage.
caution: With zero Byzantine occurrences logged for this entry and a "none" confidence tier, this is essentially a grammatical form, and the evidence here is too thin to support firm sense claims.

definition: A non-Jew who has come over to and adopted the Jewish faith.
article: In the New Testament προσήλυτος always means a Gentile who has converted to Judaism, appearing 4 times across 2 books and rendered "convert" or "convert to Judaism" every time. The word literally means "one who has arrived," and the Septuagint uses it 84 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew גֵּר (76×), the word for a resident foreigner or stranger. That broader sense of "stranger" is preserved in older lexicons like Abbott-Smith, though the measured New Testament usage has narrowed entirely to the religious-convert meaning; a Cyrenaic inscription even records a woman named Sarra labeled προσήλυτος.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the evidence is thin, and lexicons note a broader "stranger" sense not reflected in the measured New Testament usage.

definition: To strike or smite someone or something, with a hand, a weapon, or a deadly or punishing blow.
article: πατάσσω means to strike or hit, ranging from a single sword blow to a fatal or punishing strike. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times and is rendered "strike" in 8 of them (80%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. The Septuagint uses it heavily—about 400 times—mostly for the Hebrew נָכָה ("to strike," 331×), and everyday Koine papyri show it for everything from a slave hitting a free man to God striking enemies. Abbott-Smith notes it can also describe disease striking someone, as in Acts 12:23.

definition: A gift freely given, especially a grace or spiritual endowment bestowed by God rather than earned.
article: χάρισμα means a freely given gift, and in the New Testament it most often points to gifts of grace and spiritual endowments. The Byzantine NT uses it 17 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "gift" in 14 of those (88%), with the remaining handful framed as a particular gift someone is given. Everyday papyri confirm the word was used for ordinary gifts too — one fourth-century letter says "you know the gifts I have given you" — so the term is not purely religious in origin, though the NT writers, especially Paul, give it a strongly spiritual sense.

definition: Moral excellence or goodness of character; in some contexts the praise or honor that excellence earns.
article: This word points to excellence or moral goodness — the quality that makes a person or thing stand out. In the New Testament it appears only 5 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it mostly as "virtue," though the phrasing shifts with each context, and it describes both God (2 Peter 1:3) and people (Philippians 4:8; 2 Peter 1:5). Interestingly, in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew תְּהִלָּה (5 times), meaning "praise" — so the word carries not just the excellence itself but the renown that excellence produces, as seen in 1 Peter 2:9.
caution: The word's range is genuinely broad — sources note it had "nearly all the forces of our adjective good," and its blend of intrinsic excellence and outward praise makes any single rendering imprecise.

definition: A person who instructs others, especially a teacher of religious truth or a recognized authority addressed as such.
article: διδάσκαλος is the standard Greek word for a teacher, and the New Testament uses it that way almost without exception—53 of 58 times (91%) it is simply rendered "Teacher." Its range is narrow but its objects are varied: it labels Jewish teachers, John the Baptist, Jesus (often as a title of address), apostles, and Christian teachers, as well as false teachers. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where it appears three times in an apprenticeship contract from A.D. 183, with one inscription even specifying a "teacher of military tactics."

definition: An adverb meaning entirely or altogether, and—when paired with a negative—"not at all."
article: ὅλως is an adverb formed from ὅλος ("whole") and basically means "entirely" or "altogether." Its range stretches from emphatic affirmation ("actually," "assuredly") to strong denial when joined with a negative verb, as in Matthew 5:34's "do not swear at all." Everyday Koine papyri confirm both ends: one writer says he is "quite upset" (ὅλως) over lost money, while a wife writes that her son "did not lodge with me at all" (οὐ... ὅλως). It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, spread across just two books.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and each rendered differently, its precise force in any given verse depends heavily on context, especially whether a negative is present.

definition: To talk someone into doing something, often by pushing or coaxing them toward a wrong or harmful course.
article: ἀναπείθω means to persuade or incite someone, frequently with a negative edge of pushing people toward something improper. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 18:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "persuading" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully. A vivid papyrus example (P Magd 14, 221 BC) shows the darker shade: a father complains that a courtesan "induced" his son to sign a bill for 1000 drachmas in her favor, illustrating the sense of crooked persuasion that some sources see lurking behind the word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and just twice in the Septuagint, so its precise force is hard to pin down with confidence.

definition: A command or rule, especially a religious instruction or precept laid down for people to follow.
article: ἔνταλμα means a command or precept, particularly a religious rule that someone is taught to keep. It is rare, appearing only 3 times in the New Testament—and in all three cases the translators absorbed it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a single English word. Strikingly, all three New Testament uses (Matthew 15:9, Mark 7:7, Colossians 2:22) echo the same Old Testament passage, Isaiah 29:13, where it renders the Hebrew word for 'commandment.'
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences (all quoting the same source) and 4 in the Septuagint, with sources disagreeing about which Hebrew words it translates.

definition: In a way marked by intense grief or harshness; weeping bitterly with deep sorrow.
article: This adverb means "bitterly," describing weeping that is intense and full of grief. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both times in the same scene where Peter "wept bitterly" after denying Jesus (Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62), and the rendering is unanimous across translations. The everyday Koine papyri show its harsher edge too: one third-century BC letter complains that the king "dealt bitterly" with someone, and a comparative form means to handle someone "more harshly" — so the word can describe rough treatment as well as sorrow.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (both in the same episode), the measured range is very narrow, though the Septuagint and papyri evidence confirm the meaning.

definition: Describing someone or something that has been taught, instructed, or communicated through teaching.
article: Derived from the verb διδάσκω (to teach), διδακτός means "taught" or "instructed," appearing only 3 times in the New Testament.
