It can describe people who are taught—as in those "taught by God" (John 6:45, echoing the Septuagint's Isaiah 54:13)—or describe words communicated by teaching (1 Corinthians 2:13). Interestingly, the same Greek phrase "taught by God" appears in the Psalms of Solomon to describe Israel's king as one "instructed by God," matching the Hebrew word לִמֻּד behind the Isaiah passage.
caution: This is a rare word with only 3 New Testament occurrences, so its full range of meaning is hard to map confidently.

definition: A sparkling white stone, namely marble, used as a luxury building and decorative material.
article: μάρμαρος refers to marble, a glistening crystalline stone prized as a costly material — the name itself derives from a verb meaning "to glisten." In the New Testament it appears only once, in Revelation 18:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it among the luxury goods of fallen Babylon (the digest's "citron" label appears to be a tagging error; the actual gloss across all sources is "marble"). Everyday Koine papyri confirm its ordinary use: one third- or fourth-century text mentions writing in gold letters "on polished marble," and inscriptions even attest a related word for a marble-mason.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured sense label ("citron") conflicts with every dictionary source, which uniformly gives "marble."

definition: God's righteous judgment—a just verdict that reflects the fair character of the judge handing it down.
article: δικαιοκρισία is a compound built from δίκαιος (just) and κρίσις (judgment), and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 2:5. Every lexicon agrees it means "righteous judgment," and Moulton-Milligan note an interesting nuance: the word emphasizes the just character of the judge rather than the judgment itself. That fits its use in everyday Koine papyri—one Oxyrhynchus petitioner from A.D. 303 appeals confidently to a magistrate to obtain his δικαιοκρισία, his righteous verdict.
caution: The measured rendering "unrepentant" reflects nearby wording in Romans 2:5, not the word itself, which all sources define as "righteous judgment"; with only one occurrence, confidence is low.

definition: A person secretly planted to lie in wait and entrap someone by pretending to be sincere.
article: This word describes someone secretly set up to watch and trap another person, often by posing as honest. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 20:20, where opponents send such planted men to catch Jesus in his words, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "spies." The Septuagint uses it twice in Job, where it relates to the Hebrew idea of lying in wait, fitting the sense of an ambush or covert agent.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and twice in the Septuagint, so its precise range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Describing a person who lacks faith or trust, especially someone who is not a Christian believer; also, of things, hard to believe.
article: ἄπιστος describes someone without faith or trust, and in the New Testament it most often means an unbeliever as opposed to a Christian — rendered "unbelievers" 9 times (41%) and "unbelieving" 7 times (32%). It can also describe things rather than people, meaning "incredible" or hard to believe, as Abbott-Smith notes for Acts 26:8. An interesting detail comes from the papyri: a third-century BC inscription plays on the word, using it first to mean "incredible" (about recorded healings) and then "incredulous" of a doubting person, even turning it into a nickname, "Doubter."
caution: In the 1 Corinthians passages the word's exact reference (unbelieving spouse versus unbeliever in the assembly) depends heavily on context, so renderings vary.

definition: To separate or divide things, or—when used of oneself—to depart, withdraw, or part from someone.
article: χωρίζω means to put space between things, hence to separate or divide; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "separate" in 6 of 13 occurrences (50%), as in Jesus' saying that what God has joined together no one should separate (Matthew 19:6, Mark 10:9). When used reflexively or passively it shifts to mean depart or withdraw, rendered "leave" 3 times (25%), and it can describe divorce. The everyday flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where one document (P Fay 110, A.D. 94) uses it to mean "take away the manure to the manure-heap."

definition: The Sabbath, the seventh day of weekly rest in Jewish life, and by extension the seven-day week itself.
article: σάββατον overwhelmingly means the Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest, rendered that way in 51 of its 68 New Testament appearances (80%). It can also stretch to mean a whole week, as in counting days "the first of the Sabbath" (4×, 6%), which is why English versions sometimes say "week." The word came into Greek from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabbat), which it translates 102 of 109 times in the Septuagint, and Moulton-Milligan note the plural form τὰ σάββατα was originally mistaken for a plural even when it meant a single Sabbath day.
caution: The two "Sabbath Jesus" renderings reflect awkward phrasing in the surrounding text rather than a distinct meaning of the word itself.

definition: The side of the body, especially the human flank or torso area.
article: πλευρά refers to the side of the body, the flank or torso region. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all in John and Acts, and is rendered "side" in every case—most memorably when a soldier pierces Jesus' side in John 19:34. The Septuagint uses it 25 times, most often translating the Hebrew צֵלָע ("rib" or "side"), and everyday papyri stretch it further to mean the lung or chest, as in one Oxyrhynchus letter where a man complains of "a cough from my side."

definition: Legally liable, answerable, or bound—facing a charge, penalty, or punishment, or held fast by something.
article: ἔνοχος is a legal term meaning someone is answerable or liable—facing a charge, deserving a punishment, or held fast by something. Across its 10 New Testament uses, translators land on "subject" only 3 times, with the rest scattered across phrases like "deserves to die," "guilty of," or "verdict deserving," showing how flexibly it bends to context. The classical lexica fill out its range: it can mean liable to a court (with the dative of the tribunal, as in Matthew 5:22), liable to a punishment like death ("liable to death," Mark 14:64), or guilty against the thing injured (1 Corinthians 11:27). Everyday papyri confirm the legal flavor—one B.C. document uses it for being "liable to the impiety of the oath."

definition: To be king and exercise royal rule over people or things, whether literally as a monarch or figuratively as a controlling power.
article: βασιλεύω means to reign or rule as a king, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "reign" or "reigned" in most of its 21 New Testament occurrences. Its range stretches from literal monarchs to figurative powers — Paul speaks of death, sin, and even believers "reigning," while Revelation uses it of God and Christ. The Septuagint uses it heavily (353 times), almost always for the Hebrew מָלַךְ (to be king), and the papyri show it in the grand Persian-style title "king of kings reigning" (P Sa\u012bd Khan, 1st century BC).

definition: To travel toward or come to someone, making one's way to a destination.
article: This verb combines "to" (ἐπί) with "to journey" (πορεύομαι) and basically means to travel toward or come to a person or place. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 8:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as people "gathering" to Jesus, though the underlying idea is of crowds journeying to him. The everyday papyri show some striking uses: one document describes an official who "comes to see" villagers and demands twelve geese for his entertainment, and in legal texts the word can mean "proceed against" someone.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just two in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, and the sources disagree on the Hebrew words it translates.

definition: A mass or bulk that weighs you down; figuratively, an encumbrance or hindrance that holds you back.
article: At root ὄγκος means physical bulk or mass, but in the New Testament it appears just once (Hebrews 12:1), where it is used figuratively for an encumbrance or weight that a runner must lay aside. Lexicons like Abbott-Smith and Dodson trace it from the literal idea of bulk to this metaphorical sense of a burden or hindrance. A nice glimpse of the everyday word comes from Menander, who quipped that an expensive corpse 'comes to the same bulk' as a cheap one — a handful of ashes — and the word also turns up in ordinary Koine papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured biblical range rests on a single verse.

definition: To challenge or provoke others, especially by stirring up rivalry or daring them to react.
article: This verb literally means "to call forth," and in the middle voice it carries the sense of challenging, provoking, or daring someone. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Galatians 5:26, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the whole phrase as "conceited" — the idea being a self-important attitude that provokes others into rivalry. The word was common in everyday Koine, showing up in classical writers from Homer onward and in papyri and inscriptions, including a letter to the Smyrnaeans addressed to the emperors Septimius Severus and Caracalla.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a translation rendered as "conceited" rather than the lexicons' "provoke" or "challenge," the measured sense reflects the larger phrase rather than the verb's own range.

definition: A greeting or word of welcome, whether spoken in person or written at the close of a letter.
senseLabels: a written greeting in one's own hand
article: Ἀσπασμός means a greeting or salutation, and all three measured senses really describe the same act in different settings—spoken or written. In the Gospels it covers the public greetings that proud religious leaders craved in the marketplaces (Mark 12:38, Luke 11:43, 20:46), while in Paul's letters it marks the personal sign-off written in his own hand (1 Corinthians 16:21, Colossians 4:18). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note the noun is curiously rare in everyday papyri, appearing apparently only once in the large Oxyrhynchus collections (P Oxy III.471) plus one sixth-century instance.
caution: The three measured senses are really one meaning (a greeting) split by context rather than distinct definitions.

definition: On the contrary; the adverb that flips to the opposite of what was just said.
article: τοὐναντίον is an adverb meaning "on the contrary" or "instead," used to pivot to the opposite of what came before. It is really a contraction (crasis) of the article τό and ἐναντίον, the neuter accusative used adverbially. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 2:7, Galatians 2:7, 1 Peter 3:9), and in 2 of those 3 cases it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences, with just one rendered as a distinct word, so confidence is low.

definition: The general bent of someone's thinking — the mindset, attitude, or aspirations that shape how a person is inclined.
article: φρόνημα refers to the content and direction of one's thinking — not a single thought, but the overall mental inclination, purpose, and outlook a person carries. In all 4 New Testament occurrences (clustered in Romans 8), the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mind," and the BSB and KJV agree, often expanding it into phrases like "carnally minded" or "spiritually minded." Moulton-Milligan show the word at home in everyday Koine: one source speaks of someone taking on "the mind of Odysseus" — the cunning bent of thought that defines a person — which captures the word's sense of a whole disposition rather than a passing idea.
caution: This is a rare word, appearing only 4 times in the New Testament (all in Romans 8) and just twice in the Septuagint, so its measured range is narrow.

definition: The act of going out to meet someone, an encounter or meeting.
article: Συνάντησις refers to going out to meet someone — an encounter or meeting. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 8:34), where it's rendered "meet," though the critical text reads the near-synonym ὑπάντησις instead. The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 64 times across 15 books, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew קְרָאת (54×), typically in the sense of going to meet a person; Moulton-Milligan also notes a parallel in later Koine, where a nurse "went out as usual to meet her."
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin — only one occurrence, and the critical text replaces it with ὑπάντησις, so the reading itself is disputed.

definition: Fame, glory, or credit that comes from a good reputation being spoken about by others.
article: κλέος refers to the renown or credit a person earns when others speak well of them, fittingly tied to its root in καλέω, "to call." It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Peter 2:20), where it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word, and twice in the Septuagint (Job 28:22; 30:8). The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: one inscription speaks of "hearing the fame of the city," and another tells someone it is "glory" to die for one's beloved homeland. Older lexicons note an additional sense of "rumor" or "report," though the New Testament use carries the positive meaning of good repute.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, and lexicons split between "rumor/report" and "fame/glory."

definition: The condition or act of disregarding God's law — living or behaving in a lawless, wicked way.
article: ἀνομία describes a state of being without or against the law, ranging from "lawlessness" to "wickedness" — and the Byzantine NT splits evenly between the two, each rendered 5 of 15 times in the Majority Standard Bible. It is heavily a Septuagint word, appearing 199 times and most often translating the Hebrew עָווֹן (iniquity, 46×), but also תּוֹעֵבָה (abomination, 28×) and פֶּשַׁע (transgression, 10×). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one second-century BC document complains of being assaulted with "unbearable lawlessness."

definition: A Philippian — a person from the Roman colony city of Philippi in Macedonia.
article: Φιλιππήσιος means an inhabitant of Philippi, and it appears just once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:15. The most interesting detail is the form itself: it is a Latin-style spelling (Philippensis) rather than the pure Greek Φιλιππεύς or Φιλιππηνός, and one scholar (Ramsay) saw this as a sign of Paul's preference for Roman administrative terms when addressing this Roman colony. Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the single measured sense was tagged 'early' — almost certainly a data artifact rather than a real meaning, so rely on the lexicons here.

definition: To knock or rap, especially at a door, in order to be let in.
article: This verb means to knock or rap, almost always at a door to gain entry, and that's exactly how it works in all 9 New Testament occurrences. The range is narrow: the Majority Standard Bible splits its renderings evenly between "knock at a door" (4×) and "knocks" (4×), but both point to the same simple action. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, including a 160 B.C. document describing someone "knocking at the door," and in the Septuagint it consistently translates the Hebrew verb dāphaq, also meaning to knock.
caution: Attic Greek writers preferred κόπτω for knocking at a door, so this word's door-knocking sense reflects later Koine usage rather than classical preference.

definition: The worship or service of idols — treating images or false gods as objects of devotion.
article: εἰδωλολατρεία means idolatry, the worship or service of an idol, built straightforwardly from the words for "image" (εἴδωλον) and "service/worship" (λατρεία). It appears 4 times in the Byzantine NT, and although the Majority Standard Bible's renderings get grouped under labels like "lust idolatry" or "idolatry factions," these reflect the surrounding vice-lists (in Colossians 3:5, Galatians 5:20, 1 Peter 4:3) rather than separate meanings of the word itself. The lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on the single sense: worship of an idol, sometimes used figuratively as Strong's notes.
caution: The word occurs only 4 times and drops to zero in the critical (SBLGNT) text, so its attestation is thin and partly disputed.

definition: A stone or rock, whether a building block, a millstone, a gem, or one sealing a tomb.
article: λíthos is the ordinary Greek word for a stone, and across its 60 New Testament occurrences it means exactly that 94% of the time. Its range is wide but concrete: building stones, millstones, the stone rolled over Jesus' tomb, and even precious gems. In the Septuagint it appears 259 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew אֶבֶן ("stone"), and Moulton-Milligan finds it everywhere in everyday papyri — including a contract for squared building-stones "transportable by camel." Several New Testament passages also use it figuratively of Christ as the chief cornerstone or stumbling stone, though that is a metaphorical application of the same plain meaning.

definition: Describing something that cannot stop or be restrained — restless and unceasing in its activity.
article: ἀκατάπαυστος is built from a negative prefix plus a form of the verb "to cause to cease," so it literally means "that cannot cease" or "unable to be restrained." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 2:14, where it describes eyes that never stop seeking sin. Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and even suggests, given the common vulgar shift of "au" to "a," that the spelling ἀκατάπαστος may be what was intended in that verse.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured sense is labeled "adultery," which reflects the sin described in 2 Peter 2:14 rather than the word's own meaning of "unceasing" given by the lexica.

definition: A fellow soldier; in Paul's letters, used figuratively for a companion in Christian work and struggle.
article: συστρατιώτης literally means a fellow soldier, someone serving alongside you in a military campaign, but Paul uses it both times figuratively for a partner in Christian labor (Philippians 2:25 and Philemon 2). The word shows up in everyday Koine outside the Bible too—Moulton-Milligan cite a soldier's letter to his mother (BGU III.814) where he mentions borrowing money from a συστρατιώτης, confirming its ordinary military sense. One of the two measured renderings reads oddly as "thought back soldier," which appears to be a data glitch rather than a real meaning; the genuine sense in both verses is "fellow soldier."
caution: The word appears only twice in the NT, and one of the two measured renderings looks garbled, so treat the sense data with caution.

definition: Narcissus, the name of a person whose household members in Rome are greeted in Paul's letter.
article: Narcissus is a proper name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Romans 16:11), where Paul greets believers from his household. The name comes from the narcissus flower, itself linked to a word meaning stupefaction because of the plant's narcotic properties. Interestingly, the inscriptions and papyri (from Magnesia, Hierapolis, and Thasos) show the name was common well beyond Rome, so the old assumption that this is the famous imperial freedman named Narcissus is far from certain.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and the evidence shows the popular identification with a specific historical figure is uncertain.

definition: Miletus, an ancient seaport city on the coast of Caria in Asia Minor.
senseLabels: Miletus, a city in Asia Minor
article: Miletus is a proper name for a maritime city in the region of Caria, on the coast of the Roman province of Asia. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, always rendered "Miletus," twice in Acts 20 (verses 15 and 17) and once in 2 Timothy 4:20. Interestingly, the name also shows up once in the Septuagint, where it stands in for the Hebrew word חֶלְבּוֹן (Helbon), suggesting it was occasionally used to translate other place-related terms.
caution: This is a proper place name with only 3 New Testament occurrences and uncertain origin, so the lone Septuagint match to a different Hebrew word should be treated carefully.

definition: A connecting word that draws a conclusion from what came before, meaning "therefore" or "for this reason."
article: διό is a conjunction that links a statement to its consequence, telling readers that what follows results from what came before. It's a compound formed from διά ("through") and ὅς ("which"), literally "through which thing," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "therefore" half the time (23 of 51 occurrences), with "so" and "is why" filling out most of the rest. The everyday papyri show the same plain usage—one A.D. 108 document reads "execute the deed therefore, as is fitting"—confirming this was ordinary connective language, not specialized vocabulary.

definition: A body of priests, or the office of priesthood; a priestly community considered collectively.
article: This rare word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Peter (2:5 and 2:9), where it describes believers collectively as a "holy priesthood" and a "royal priesthood." It can mean either the group of priests as a body or the act and office of being a priest, and scholars genuinely disagree on which sense fits 1 Peter best. Notably, the word has never been found outside Biblical and church Greek, though Moulton-Milligan compares a parallel formation, τεχνίτευμα, used in a third-century-BC inscription for a body of skilled workers.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two occurrences, no attestation outside Biblical and ecclesiastical Greek, and sources disagree on whether it means a body of priests or the office of priesthood.

definition: As quickly as possible; the superlative form meaning with the greatest speed.
article: τάχιστα is the superlative adverb from ταχύς ("swift"), meaning "most quickly" or "as soon as possible." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 17:15, where it occurs in the phrase ὡς τάχιστα, "as quickly as possible"; in that verse the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding action as Paul's escorts being told to bring Silas and Timothy to him with all speed. It belongs to the same family as the more common ταχύ ("quickly"), which the Septuagint mostly uses for the Hebrew מָהַר ("to hasten").

definition: To travel by water in a ship; to sail or make a sea voyage.
article: πλέω simply means to travel by sea in a ship. All six New Testament uses point to the same basic action of sailing, and the three measured "senses" are really just different English phrasings of one idea rather than distinct meanings — half the occurrences get absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own. The everyday papyri are vivid here: one writer apologizes that he "could not sail without you," and another that he was "unable through sickness to make the voyage," showing this was ordinary travel vocabulary in common Koine.
caution: With only six occurrences, the three listed senses are phrasing variants of a single meaning rather than genuinely separate senses.

definition: To rest or be refreshed together with someone, whether physically lying down or being renewed in spirit.
article: This compound verb combines the ideas of "together with" and "resting," so it means to lie down to rest alongside another, and by extension to be mutually refreshed in spirit. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament and once in the Septuagint, where it renders a Hebrew word and pictures animals lying down peacefully together in Isaiah 11:6. A nice parallel comes from the early historian Hegesippus, who used a related form to say he and the Corinthians "were mutually refreshed in the true doctrine," capturing the same sense of shared renewal.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, and that New Testament instance is textually disputed in some manuscripts.

definition: The act of making or taking a solemn oath, or the oath itself.
article: This noun refers to swearing a solemn oath—both the act of making one and the oath that results. It is a rare word, appearing only 4 times in the New Testament, all clustered in Hebrews 7, where it contrasts a priesthood established without an oath against one confirmed by God's oath. The Septuagint uses it twice, rendering Hebrew words for a sworn curse or oath, and Moulton-Milligan notes the related neuter form turns up in everyday inscriptions referring to sacrifices made for oath-taking ceremonies.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only 4 times in the New Testament, all within a single passage in Hebrews.

definition: To benefit someone or something, to do good, or to gain advantage from a thing.
article: ὠφελέω means to help, benefit, or do good — and by extension to gain profit or value from something. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 15 times, where the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "profit" (4×, 31%), with "value" and a few other shadings filling out its range. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew יָעַל ("to profit" or "be of use," 11×), and everyday papyri confirm the same plain sense, as in a third-century letter saying "I know that this letter of mine also will be of much help to him."
caution: Two of its fifteen occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, so a third of the data is less directly observable.

definition: A large, oblong shield, originally door-shaped, that covers most of the body in battle.
article: θυρεός names a big, rectangular shield—the kind that protects nearly the whole body—and its name comes from θύρα, "door," because of its door-like shape. The New Testament uses it only once, in Ephesians 6:16, where it is the "shield of faith," and translators are unanimous in rendering it "shield." In the Septuagint it appears 23 times, usually translating the Hebrew words for shield (מָגֵן 10×, צִנָּה 9×), while everyday Koine papyri list it alongside other military gear like the round shield (ἀσπίς) and the quiver. Abbott-Smith notes that in Homer the word meant a door-stone, with the large-shield meaning emerging in later Greek writers like Polybius and Plutarch.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests largely on Septuagint and classical evidence rather than direct New Testament range.

definition: A private inner room of a house, used for storage, retreat, or seclusion away from public view.
article: This word refers to an inner chamber of a house — a place for storage, privacy, or quiet retreat. The New Testament uses it just 4 times, always for a private inner room (as in Matthew 6:6, where Jesus tells people to pray behind a closed door), but the Septuagint shows its broader range across 39 occurrences, mostly rendering the Hebrew chedher ("chamber," 30×) and sometimes a storehouse or granary. The everyday papyri confirm this practical sense: one document speaks of "the bank of the store-houses," using the same contracted spelling found in the New Testament.
caution: The New Testament range is narrow (only 4 occurrences, all "inner room"), while wider Greek usage also covers treasuries and storehouses.

definition: A pig or hog, the domestic farm animal raised for meat.
article: χοῖρος simply means a pig, and the meaning is steady across all its uses: the Byzantine New Testament has it 14 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "pigs" 71% of the time and the other renderings being garbled fragments rather than real alternate meanings. It was an everyday word in ordinary life, well documented in Koine papyri—one early text records the price of a pig at 8 drachmas, and another mentions handing over "the pig and the two nice sucking pigs" to a cook. The classical lexicons and the measured corpus usage fully agree: this is just the common farm animal.

definition: To yield to someone's authority by giving way, submitting, or letting them lead.
article: This verb means to give way or submit to someone in charge, built from the idea of yielding or stepping back. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Hebrews 13:17, where readers are urged to yield to their leaders. The Septuagint uses it just once as well, in 4 Maccabees 6:35, and Abbott-Smith notes its more literal sense of retiring or withdrawing alongside the metaphorical sense of submitting.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and very thin overall attestation, the precise nuance rests on a single verse.

definition: A person who knows something well, an expert who is familiar with a particular subject or matter.
article: γνώστης means "one who knows" — an expert or someone well-acquainted with a subject. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:3, where Paul calls Agrippa knowledgeable about Jewish customs and controversies. In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 4 times, mostly translating a Hebrew word for a spirit-medium or one who claims hidden knowledge, and the papyri preserve a striking parallel where an official says he "became aware" (γνώστης) of the good news of an emperor's proclamation; the word could even mean a legal surety or witness.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: Describing a hand, foot, or limb that is crippled, maimed, or deformed so it cannot function normally.
article: κυλλός describes a part of the body—especially a hand or foot—that is crippled, deformed, or maimed. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, twice in warnings that it is better to enter life crippled than to keep a limb that leads you into sin (Matthew 18:8, Mark 9:43), and twice in accounts of crippled people brought to Jesus and healed (Matthew 15:30–31). The word lived in ordinary Koine: a sixth-century papyrus speaks of a "crooked wheel" used for irrigation, and the ancient writer Herodas used it for "limping" verse, showing how the basic idea of being bent or crooked stretched beyond bodies.
caution: The evidence is thin (only 4 occurrences), and Abbott-Smith notes the Matthew 15:30–31 readings are textually uncertain.

definition: To twist or distort the meaning of words, bending them out of their true sense.
article: στρεβλόω literally means to twist or wrench something, and by extension to torture someone on the rack — but in the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Peter 3:16, where it describes people who "distort" the Scriptures. The Septuagint uses it just once too, at 2 Samuel 22:27, translating the Hebrew פָּתַל ("to twist"). The everyday papyri preserve the older physical sense vividly: Herodas has a character say "take me, Thales, and torture me," showing the literal meaning behind the figurative "twist words" usage Peter intended.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its figurative "distort" sense rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To give rest or refreshment to someone, or in the middle/passive voice, to rest, relax, and recover from labor.
article: This verb covers giving rest to others and taking rest yourself, ranging from physical refreshment to recovery from work. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times across 8 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "rest" in nearly half its appearances, as in Jesus' invitation in Matthew 11:28. A striking detail from the papyri: ἀναπαύω was a technical farming term for "resting" land by sowing only light crops on it, so the fields could recover — a vivid everyday picture behind the idea of rest. In the Septuagint it appears 63 times and most often translates the Hebrew נוּחַ ("to rest"), 24 times.

definition: Describing something positioned on the outside or farthest out, the outer region beyond an inner space.
article: This adjective is the comparative form of ἔξω ("outside") and means "outer" or "outermost," the opposite of "inner." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, every one in Matthew and always describing "outer darkness" (Matt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30); the Majority Standard Bible renders it "outer" each time, with one occurrence phrased as part of a larger expression. The Septuagint uses it far more often, 22 times across 4 books, where it most commonly translates the Hebrew word חִיצוֹן ("outer"), 17 of those times.
caution: The evidence base is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences, all in a single fixed phrase, and the digest's confidence tier is low.

definition: To touch or handle something, often with the sense of coming into contact with what is forbidden or dangerous.
article: θιγγάνω means to touch or handle something, appearing only 3 times in the New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "touch" twice (67%) and "handle" once (33%), and these meanings sit close together. Abbott-Smith notes a possible third sense, "to injure," for Hebrews 11:28, but the measured renderings don't reflect that nuance. A nice everyday parallel comes from a papyrus (P Oxy IX.1185, c. A.D. 200) warning "do not touch the sauce," showing the word was common in ordinary Koine speech.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the boundary between "touch," "handle," and the lexicon-listed "injure" sense remains uncertain.

definition: The personal name Philemon, borne by a Christian man addressed in Paul's letter to him.
article: Philemon is a proper name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Philemon 1:1) as the recipient of Paul's short letter; every translation surveyed renders it simply "Philemon." Dodson identifies him as a Christian man of Colossae. The name derives from the verb meaning "to love" (G5368) and turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions—Moulton-Milligan even notes its connection to Phrygia through the legend of Philemon and Baucis.
caution: This is a personal name attested only once in the New Testament, so its meaning beyond identifying the man himself is minimal.

definition: Lamech, a personal name in biblical genealogy, borne by the patriarch who was father of Noah.
article: Λάμεχ is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Lamech (לֶמֶךְ), an indeclinable proper noun. In the New Testament it appears just once, in the genealogy of Luke 3:36, where it names Noah's father; the Septuagint uses it 11 times across 2 books, always rendering the same Hebrew name. As a name it carries no separate meaning of its own — every occurrence is just the man himself in a family line.
caution: This is a proper name attested only once in the New Testament, so its range is essentially fixed by genealogy rather than meaning.

definition: To make someone blind, used in the New Testament always in a figurative sense of darkening the mind or understanding.
article: τυφλόω means to make blind, and in all 3 of its New Testament occurrences it is used figuratively—of minds or hearts that cannot perceive (John 12:40, 2 Corinthians 4:2, 1 John 2:11). Everyday Koine papyri, however, use it literally, as in a sixth-century document describing a man who lost his sight, and another from imperial times warning that no one "blinded by wealth" should think lightly. In the Septuagint it appears just once, where it renders a Hebrew word in Isaiah; Abbott-Smith links it to Hebrew terms for blindness.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence, so the measured senses reflect very few examples.

definition: A surplus or overflow — more than enough, the abundance left over after a need is met.
article: περίσσευμα is the noun for an excess or surplus — what spills over once enough is present. Across its 5 New Testament occurrences the renderings vary widely because translators follow the context: the overflow of the heart (Matthew 12:34; Luke 6:45), the leftover broken pieces gathered after feeding the crowd (Mark 8:8), and Paul's idea of one person's surplus supplying another's lack to create equality (2 Corinthians 8:13-14). Abbott-Smith notes it stands as the opposite of ὑστέρημα ('lack'), which is exactly the contrast Paul draws in 2 Corinthians; its one Septuagint appearance (Ecclesiastes 2:15) renders the Hebrew word for 'advantage' or 'what is more.'
caution: Evidence is thin — only 5 New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence — and each instance is translated differently, so the labels reflect context-driven renderings rather than five distinct senses.

definition: Punishment inflicted on someone for wrongdoing, the penalty or suffering imposed as a consequence.
article: κόλασις means punishment or penalty, and both of its New Testament appearances (Matthew 25:46 and 1 John 4:18) are rendered exactly that way. The classical lexicons add nuances like correction, chastisement, or torment, and Aristotle even drew a distinction between κόλασις as disciplinary (aimed at the sufferer) and τιμωρία as retributive (aimed at satisfying the one who punishes) — though Abbott-Smith notes this distinction wasn't always kept in later Greek. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan finds the word in everyday papyri and inscriptions for ordinary punishment, and suggests that in 1 John 4:18 the idea of deprivation or loss may be in view.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a confidence tier of low, the finer shades of meaning (correction versus mere penalty) rest on classical sources rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: An adverb meaning together—people or things being in the same place or at the same time.
article: ὁμοῦ is an adverb meaning "together," describing people or things gathered in the same place or acting at the same time. In all 3 Byzantine New Testament occurrences it is rendered "together" (100%), as in John 4:36, 20:4, and 21:2; the SBLGNT counts a fourth use. The everyday papyri add a vivid wrinkle: ὁμοῦ was commonly used in account-keeping to mark a total, as in one receipt reading "total 46 denarii and a quarter."
caution: Evidence is thin overall—only 3 Byzantine occurrences and a single Septuagint use—so the confidence tier is low.

definition: To provide food and nourishment, or to raise and bring up a living thing to maturity.
article: At its core τρέφω means to nourish or feed, and by extension to rear and bring up a child or animal to maturity. The New Testament uses center on feeding—God feeds the birds (Matthew 6:26, Luke 12:24)—while Abbott-Smith also notes a sense of fattening animals and even a mother giving suck. Everyday papyri show the same practical breadth: one third-century BC document arranges for grown sons to maintain their aging parents, and an apprenticeship contract from AD 66 stipulates that a boy be fed and clothed throughout his service.
caution: One of the four measured renderings is the placeholder "where" (Rev 12:14), reflecting how the word was absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than a distinct meaning; with only seven occurrences the sense breakdown rests on thin data.

definition: Parmenas, the personal name of one of the seven men chosen to assist the early church in Jerusalem.
article: Parmenas is a man's name appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 6:5, where he is listed among the seven men selected to help serve the Jerusalem church. The name is a shortened, affectionate form of Parmenides, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday life as a wall-scratching in the Serapeum at Memphis. As a proper name it carries no broader meaning beyond identifying this individual.
caution: This is a personal name appearing only once in the New Testament, so there is no range of meaning to assess.

definition: To take hold of a task alongside someone, sharing the load and helping them carry it.
article: This word literally pictures grabbing hold of a burden at the side, next to someone else, to share the work — so it means to help by taking part rather than just standing by. In both of its 2 New Testament appearances it is rendered "help," once of Martha wanting Mary to pitch in (Luke 10:40) and once of the Spirit helping us (Romans 8:26). Notably, Deissmann traced this word right across the Hellenistic world: an inscription from Delphi (around 260 BC) uses it of helping "in things profitable to the city," showing it was ordinary, everyday Koine rather than a special biblical term.
caution: The New Testament evidence is thin — only 2 occurrences — so the full "share the load alongside" nuance leans on Septuagint and papyri usage rather than the New Testament itself.

definition: To urge someone forward, encouraging or persuading them to take action.
article: This verb means to urge or push someone forward—to encourage and persuade them toward a course of action. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:27, where the brothers encourage Apollos. The Septuagint shows the same sense in a handful of places like Wisdom 14:18 and 2 Maccabees 11:7, and classical lexicons agree it carries the meaning of exhorting or persuading.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense rests almost entirely on outside evidence from the Septuagint and classical usage.

definition: Lasting forever, without end (and sometimes without beginning); everlasting or eternal.
article: ἀΐδιος describes something that endures permanently—everlasting or eternal—and in the New Testament it appears just twice, both times rendered "eternal" (Romans 1:20 and Jude 6). The word was common in everyday Koine inscriptions: one Delphi inscription speaks of a gift staying "eternal for all time," and Ptolemaic decrees ordered "eternal honors" and an "eternal memorial" for royalty. Strong's notes it can point both forward and backward in time (or forward only), but Abbott-Smith observes that any sharp distinction from its near-synonym αἰώνιος was no longer kept in late Greek.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a sense that overlaps heavily with αἰώνιος, the precise nuance is hard to pin down.

definition: Boaz, a personal name in Jesus' genealogy; the husband of Ruth, father of Obed, and great-grandfather of King David.
article: Βοόζ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Boaz, an Israelite who married Ruth and fathered Obed. It is an indeclinable proper name, so it never really shifts meaning — the three different renderings in the measured data ('Boaz,' 'Obed,' and 'son') simply reflect how the surrounding genealogy lines were segmented in Matthew 1:5 and Luke 3:32, not separate senses of the word. The Septuagint uses the name 28 times, almost always for the same Hebrew בֹּעַז, the figure from the book of Ruth.
caution: The three 'senses' here are artifacts of genealogy formatting, not genuine meanings, and the word appears only 3 times in the Byzantine text and not at all in the SBLGNT critical edition.

definition: A father — one's male parent, an ancestor, or by extension a respected elder or originator.
article: πατήρ is the ordinary Greek word for "father," and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 417 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "Father" in 388 cases (96%) and as the possessive "Father's" in 17 more (4%). The range stretches from a literal male parent to forefathers and ancestors, and figuratively to an originator or archetype. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew אָב (1,041 of 1,166 times); the everyday papyri show its looser use as a title of respect, as in one Oxyrhynchus letter where the writer calls two men besides his actual father "father" out of honor.

definition: The temple complex in Jerusalem, including its outer courts and entire sacred precincts, not just the central sanctuary building.
article: This neuter noun refers to the whole sacred temple area, including the surrounding courts where worshippers gathered. The Majority Text renders it "temple" 37 times (54%) and "temple courts" 26 times (38%), with translators choosing between the two based on context. Lexicons stress that ἱερόν covers the entire precincts, unlike ναός (G3485), which means the inner sanctuary proper—and an everyday papyrus from 99 BC shows the word used for a local Egyptian temple, confirming it applied to any deity's shrine, not only Jerusalem's.

definition: In the manner of non-Jews, living the way Gentiles do rather than following Jewish customs.
article: This adverb describes acting "in Gentile fashion" — living the way non-Jews do rather than keeping Jewish customs. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Galatians 2:14, where Paul confronts Peter for living like a Gentile yet pressuring Gentiles to adopt Jewish ways. It is the adverb formed from the adjective ethnikos ("Gentile"), and the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on this single straightforward meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: Not subject to control or authority; describing either rebellious people or, of things, what is not yet placed under someone's rule.
article: ἀνυπότακτος literally means "not made subject," built from a negative prefix plus the verb "to put under, subject." The New Testament uses it both ways: of people it means rebellious or unruly (as in Titus 1:6), and of things it means not yet placed under someone's authority (as in Hebrews 2:8, where nothing is left "not subject"). The word also lived in everyday Koine — Moulton-Milligan note it in a magical papyrus alongside words like "fierce-tempered," and an ancient lexicographer paired it with terms for the proud and defiant.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and half of those absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the evidence base is slim though sources agree on the meaning.

definition: A relative word meaning 'as much/many as' or 'all who/whatever,' linking a thing to the full extent or whole group it covers.
article: ὅσος is a correlative relative pronoun that points to quantity, extent, or the full membership of a group — 'as much as,' 'all who,' 'whatever,' 'everything that.' Its meaning shifts heavily with context, which is why 42 of its 115 New Testament occurrences are simply absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own. In the Septuagint it appears 519 times and most often stands in for the Hebrew relative אֲשֶׁר (248×), and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, as in 'how much trouble I had' or 'all else that is fitting.'
caution: The word's force is highly context-dependent, with measured senses spread thinly across eight renderings and over a third of cases carrying no distinct English equivalent.

definition: To gain benefit, advantage, or satisfaction from someone or something.
article: This verb means to derive profit, benefit, or satisfaction from someone, and in its only New Testament appearance (Philemon 1:20) it shows up in a special wishing form that the Majority Standard Bible renders "benefit" 100% of the time. It is a rare word built on an old primary verb, and the middle voice carries the sense of personally gaining advantage. Moulton-Milligan note that Philemon's optative form ("may I have satisfaction") is the only such form from this kind of verb in the entire NT, and they point to similar wording on ancient inscriptions from the third century B.C. onward.
caution: With just a single New Testament occurrence in an unusual grammatical form, the evidence here is thin even though sources agree on the sense.

definition: To be startled or terrified, thrown into fear by something threatening.
article: πτύρω means to be frightened or startled, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Philippians 1:28, where both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it "frightened" every time it occurs. Though rare in Scripture, it was an ordinary word in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan note its use in papyri and inscriptions, and the historian Eusebius later wrote "I am not frightened" using this same verb. Abbott-Smith notes it usually appears as a deponent (πτύρομαι, "to be startled, frightened"), while the active form πτύρω turns up mainly in later writers.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: Arphaxad, a son of Shem who appears in the genealogy from Adam to Jesus.
article: Ἀρφαξάδ is simply the Greek spelling of a personal name, transliterated from the Hebrew אַרְפַּכְשַׁד. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 3:36, where it sits in the line of descent leading to Jesus; every source renders it the same way. The Septuagint uses the name 7 times across 2 books, always for the same Hebrew name, identifying Arphaxad as one of Shem's sons.
caution: This is a proper name occurring just once in the New Testament, so there is no measurable range of meaning beyond the person it identifies.

definition: A state of madness or irrational folly that overrides sound judgment.
article: παραφρονία describes a loss of rational sense — madness, or the reckless folly that comes with it. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 2:16, where Balaam's senseless conduct is rebuked; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "transgression" there, while the older lexicons and KJV favor "madness." An interesting wrinkle: Moulton-Milligan can find no other example of this exact spelling, noting that some manuscripts read the more standard form παραφροσύνη instead.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and in an unusual spelling, and the modern "transgression" rendering differs sharply from the lexicons' "madness," so its precise force is uncertain.

definition: To formally call someone by a name or title; to designate or address them officially.
article: This verb means to address or call someone by a particular name or title, essentially to designate them officially. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 5:10, where it is rendered "designated." The Septuagint uses it for greeting or saluting (sometimes translating Hebrew darash), and everyday Koine papyri show both senses — one inscription even uses it of someone "called Onouris in Egyptian but Ares in Greek," matching the "designate" meaning seen in Hebrews.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: To see something clearly or perceive it distinctly, often grasping what would otherwise be hidden.
article: καθοράω combines κατά ("down") with ὁράω ("see"), and means to look down on or, figuratively, to grasp something distinctly. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:20, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "divine," though the underlying idea is that God's invisible qualities are clearly perceived. A striking witness comes from the ancient epitaph of Abercius (late second century A.D.), which describes Christ as having "great eyes that see all things" (πάντα καθορόωντας), showing the word's sense of comprehensive, penetrating sight.
caution: This is the word's only New Testament occurrence (a hapax), and with just 5 Septuagint uses the evidence base is thin.

definition: A large flexible woven basket used for carrying food and provisions.
article: σπυρίς is a sturdy, flexible woven basket big enough to carry provisions — in Acts 9:25 it was even large enough to lower Paul through a wall. It appears 5 times in the New Testament, and the measured data shows 4 of those clearly meaning "basket"; the fifth "however" reading is a translation artifact from surrounding words, not a real sense of σπυρίς. The everyday papyri back this up nicely: one document from A.D. 29 mentions "a basket in which were fifty loaves," and others list baskets of seeds and pitch.
caution: The fourth measured "sense" ("however") is a counting artifact from the verse context, not an actual meaning of the word.

definition: To abandon or desert someone, especially leaving a person stranded in trouble; sometimes simply to leave behind.
article: ἐγκαταλείπω most often means to abandon or desert a person, particularly someone already in distress—the cry "why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34) is the best-known example. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "forsaken" in 43% of cases, with the rest tending toward synonyms like "leave" or being absorbed into surrounding phrasing. It can also carry the milder sense of leaving something behind, but the desertion sense dominates. Everyday Koine papyri sharpen the picture vividly: one letter describes a brother who "deserted me, leaving me in a state of destitution," capturing the verb's flavor of leaving someone in the lurch.
caution: The dominant sense is well established, but the New Testament occurrences are few (9) and two of them carry no distinct English rendering, so fine distinctions rest mostly on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: To make a sound by calling out, shouting, summoning someone, or—of a rooster—crowing.
article: φωνέω covers a range of sound-making: shouting aloud, calling someone over, addressing a person by name, and even a rooster's crowing. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 42 times, most often (58%) translated simply "called," with about 16 occurrences absorbed into broader phrasing rather than getting their own English word. One vivid detail: the same word used for the cock's crow in Matthew 26:34 shows up in everyday papyri for a city council or senators crying out together, as in a document where "the council cried out" over a matter of business.

definition: To look away from everything else and fix your gaze on one thing, or simply to see how a situation turns out.
senseLabels: to see how things turn out
article: This verb combines "away from" (ἀπό) with "to see" (ὁράω), giving the sense of turning your eyes from all distractions toward a single focus. In its only two New Testament uses it splits evenly: in Hebrews 12:2 it means to fix one's gaze (on Jesus), while in Philippians 2:23 it simply means to see how things turn out. A nice parallel comes from the philosopher Epictetus, who used the same phrase for "looking away to God" in everything great and small.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences carrying two different senses, the evidence is thin and the word's range is hard to pin down.

definition: A herald who publicly announces a message on behalf of someone, used in the New Testament for one appointed to proclaim the gospel.
article: This noun comes from the verb κηρύσσω ("to proclaim") and basically means a herald—someone who makes a public announcement on another's authority. The New Testament uses it just 3 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders all of them as "preacher" (twice) or "appointed as preacher" (once), always pointing to one charged with proclaiming the gospel. The everyday flavor of the word is striking in the papyri, where a κῆρυξ is a paid public official: one Oxyrhynchus record shows eight drachmae handed to a herald at the games, and the Septuagint even uses it of the herald announcing Joseph before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:43).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and just 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, so the entry is rated low confidence.

definition: Describing someone or something belonging to a particular place; a local person or resident.
article: ἐντόπιος is built from ἐν ("in") and τόπος ("place"), so it simply means "of that place" — a local or resident. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:12, where it blends into the phrasing rather than getting its own English word. The everyday Koine papyri make the sense vivid: people used it of "local purple" dye, gold weighed by the "local standard," and "native stone," while one document contrasts a list of locals (ἐντοπίων) with Alexandrians.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in biblical usage rests largely on outside papyri evidence.

definition: The act of doing or carrying something out; a performance or making.
article: ποίησις means "a doing" or "a making" — the noun built from ποιέω, "to do/make." It appears just once in the New Testament, at James 1:25, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the phrase "intently" as part of describing someone who acts on what they hear; the classical lexica (Herodotus, Thucydides) and the Septuagint's seven uses lean toward the basic ideas of "making" and "doing." A nice everyday witness comes from an inscription (211/210 BC) about "the making of the image," and in Modern Greek the word has narrowed to mean "poetry."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a measured rendering ("intently") that reflects a translation phrasing rather than the word's own "doing/making" core, the evidence here is thin.

definition: Fond of arguing or quarreling; eager to push a dispute rather than seek peace.
article: φιλόνεικος describes someone who loves a fight—a person disposed to quarrel and keep an argument going. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 11:16, where Paul brushes aside anyone who wants to be contentious about a practice. The word also shows up once in the Septuagint at Ezekiel 3:7, rendering a Hebrew phrase about a hard or stubborn forehead, which fits its sense of obstinate combativeness; note that the Majority Standard Bible's rendering 'inclined' there reflects the wider phrase rather than a separate meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To spend something completely or use it all up, often used of pouring oneself out entirely for others.
article: ἐκδαπανάω is a strengthened form of the verb δαπανάω ("to spend"), with the prefix ἐκ adding the sense of spending fully or exhausting. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 12:15, where it is rendered "spend" and carries a reflexive force — to spend oneself wholly for others. Abbott-Smith notes it occurs there in the passive, paired with ὑπέρ ("on behalf of"), giving the picture of being completely poured out for someone.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine NT and is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, so its range rests on a single passage.

definition: A small piece of food, such as a bit of bread broken off and dipped to eat.
article: ψωμίον is a diminutive meaning a little bit or morsel of food, and all four New Testament occurrences cluster in one scene: John 13:26-30, where Jesus dips the morsel and hands it to Judas. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "morsel" each time (the variant labels just reflect the surrounding words about Judas); the KJV famously called it a "sop." The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too — one document from 112 B.C. even lists the customary titbits fed to sacred crocodiles.
caution: The three separate "sense" labels really reflect one meaning ("morsel"); the differences are just neighboring words about Judas, not distinct senses.

definition: A precious stone of deep blue color, named after the hyacinth flower, listed among the foundation gems of the New Jerusalem.
article: In the New Testament ὑάκινθος appears only once, in Revelation 21:20, where it names one of the gemstones in the wall of the New Jerusalem; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "chrysoprase" there, though the KJV and others say "jacinth." In classical Greek the word named a flower, probably the dark blue iris, and only later writers used it for a blue gem, perhaps the sapphire. Interestingly, in the Septuagint the word appears 32 times and most often (18×) translates the Hebrew תְּכֵלֶת, the blue or violet dye used in tabernacle fabrics, so the underlying idea is consistently a deep blue color.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence and the exact stone is uncertain — sources variously suggest jacinth, sapphire, or chrysoprase.

definition: To bring something out or produce it, drawing it forth from a source.
article: προφέρω literally means to bring forth or produce something, pulling it out from a store or source. In its only New Testament use (Luke 6:45), it appears twice in the same verse, describing how a person brings good or evil out of the heart. The everyday Koine papyri show the verb's flexibility: in legal documents it could mean to "set forth" or "bring forward" a claim, as when one writer declares that his father had purchased a house.
caution: The two listed senses are really one meaning split across a single verse, so the evidence base is very thin.

definition: To give or share advice with others, often by deliberating together to reach a decision or plan a course of action.
article: At its core συμβουλεύω means to advise or take counsel jointly — the prefix σύν ('with') gives it a strongly cooperative, deliberative flavor. In the New Testament it appears only 5 times (4 in the critical text), and in the Gospels and Acts it leans toward the darker sense of plotting together, as when the chief priests 'conspired covertly' to seize Jesus (Matthew 26:4). The Septuagint shows the neutral, original range much more clearly, where it renders the Hebrew יָעַץ ('to advise') 15 times, and everyday papyri use it plainly for one person counseling another — for example, advising someone to enlist in military service.
caution: The few New Testament occurrences skew toward 'plotting,' but the broader Septuagint, papyri, and classical evidence show the word's basic meaning is simply 'to advise.'

definition: A need, lack, or necessity—something required or wanted in a given situation.
article: χρεία means a need or necessity—something you require, lack, or want. It's a remarkably stable word: across all 48 Byzantine occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "need" 86% of the time, and where it isn't translated directly it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing (6× of 48), as in the common idiom "to have need of." The everyday papyri preserve the same down-to-earth flavor—one second-century letter asks someone to send fish "as we want to make use of him," using χρεία for a practical, ordinary requirement.

definition: A narrow cloth garment, such as a workman's apron, worn by laborers and artisans.
article: This word appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 19:12, where it describes cloths taken from Paul's body to heal the sick; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "handkerchiefs," while the older KJV tradition and the standard lexicons favor "apron." Borrowed from the Latin semicinctium (a "half-girding"), it refers to a narrow covering worn by artisans, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. Interestingly, one scholar (Nestle) argued the reference must be to underclothing in actual contact with Paul's skin rather than an apron worn over regular clothes.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word, and sources disagree: the lexicons say "apron," the MSB renders "handkerchiefs," and one scholar proposes "underwear," so its exact sense is uncertain.

definition: To watch someone or something closely—often with hostile intent to catch them—or to observe rules and days scrupulously.
senseLabels: watch closely or for a chance
article: παρατηρέω means to keep a close eye on something, and the New Testament's 6 occurrences lean heavily toward watching with bad intent—half the time (3×) it describes opponents watching Jesus to trap him, as in Mark 3:2 and Luke 14:1. A second strand is scrupulous religious observance, used once in Galatians 4:10 of "observing special" days and seasons. The everyday Koine flavor shows up in the papyri, where one letter from 156 B.C. asks someone to "keep a watchful eye on the criminals"—the same suspicious surveillance the Gospels describe.
caution: With only 6 occurrences spread across distinct uses, the boundary between hostile watching and neutral observation rests on context rather than the word itself.

definition: A personal name borne by two ancestors of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ματταθίας is a Hebrew-derived personal name that appears twice in the New Testament, both in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:25-26), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Mattathias" every time. It comes from the Hebrew name מַתִּתְיָה (Mattithjah), which shows up 7 times in the Septuagint. The name is closely related to the form Μαθθίας (Matthias), as Abbott-Smith notes.
caution: This is a proper name with only 2 New Testament occurrences, so its evidence base is thin.

definition: A connecting word meaning either "because" (giving a reason) or "according as, just as" (matching one thing to another).
article: Καθότι is a connector that works two ways: it can introduce a reason ("because") or signal correspondence ("according as, just as"). The Byzantine New Testament uses it 5 times, and the Majority Standard Bible mostly renders it "because," though in passages like Acts 2:45 and 4:35 it carries the "as" sense of distributing things to each person as they had need. It is a word peculiar to Luke in the New Testament, and the everyday papyri confirm its ordinary administrative flavor, with phrases like "just as has been written above" appearing in contracts and official letters.
caution: The two senses ("because" versus "just as") are both well attested, so the right meaning depends on context in each verse.

definition: To be present in overwhelming, more-than-enough amounts; to overflow far beyond measure.
article: ὑπερπλεονάζω means to abound exceedingly, combining the prefix ὑπέρ ("over, beyond") with πλεονάζω ("to abound"), so it pictures something pouring out far past what is needed. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 1:14, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render it "overflowed." The word turns up in everyday Koine too: Moulton-Milligan cite Psalms of Solomon 5:19, where it carries a darker edge — "if a person superabounds, he sins" — showing the same idea of going beyond proper limits.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament (a hapax), so its measured range rests on a single verse plus a handful of outside attestations.

definition: To add up or calculate amounts together, as when totaling a sum.
article: This verb means to reckon or compute things together, built from "with" (σύν) and "to count" (ψηφίζω). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 19:19, where people in Ephesus added up the value of their burned magic books. The everyday nature of the word is confirmed by a London papyrus from A.D. 114/115 that uses it for tallying up three thousand drachmas for a rebuilding project.
caution: The lone measured sense is labeled "magic," which reflects the verse's subject matter rather than the word itself, which the lexicons consistently define as "reckon up"; with only one occurrence, confidence is low.

definition: Showing the warm, tender affection that naturally binds family members to one another.
article: φιλόστοργος describes the deep, warm affection that relatives naturally feel for one another, built on στοργή, the word for family love. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 12:10, where Paul urges Christians to show this kind of tender devotion to each other; here English versions fold it into a phrase like "kindly affectioned" rather than giving it its own word. The related noun φιλοστοργία turns up often in everyday papyri, especially in wills, where people leave bequests "out of affection" (κατὰ φιλοστοργίαν), showing how naturally this term belonged to ordinary family life.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint (4 Maccabees 15:13), so its New Testament range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To cry out loudly or exclaim, raising one's voice in a strong, emphatic utterance.
article: ἀναφωνέω means to raise the voice and cry out, built from ἀνά (up) and φωνέω (to make a sound). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 1:42, where Elizabeth "exclaimed" with a loud voice — the only New Testament occurrence, rendered the same way by both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for cymbals (4 of 5 times), pointing to a loud, sounding-out quality, while the everyday papyri show a weakened sense, as in a Fayum document of 124 B.C. where it refers to a crown tax being formally "decreed."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources note differing senses (the lexica also cite Hebrew counterparts that disagree with the digest's listed ones), so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: Cyprus, a large island in the eastern Mediterranean Sea.
article: Κύπρος is simply the name of Cyprus, the Mediterranean island, and it appears 5 times in the New Testament, all in the book of Acts. Every source agrees on the meaning, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Cyprus" in all cases — the one instance counted as "sailed Cyprus" (Acts 27:4) is just the place name caught up in a sailing phrase, not a separate meaning. As a proper noun its sense is fixed and not open to range or debate.

definition: To reach or extend as far as a particular point or place.
article: ἐφικνέομαι means to come to or reach as far as something. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in 2 Corinthians 10 (verses 13 and 14), where Paul speaks of his authority and ministry extending or reaching all the way to the Corinthians. Outside the New Testament it shows up in the Septuagint at Sirach 43:27 and 30, though some manuscripts there read the related verb ἀφικνέομαι instead.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both from the same passage, the evidence for this word's range is thin.

definition: The state of being clean or pure, whether ceremonially or in moral and ethical conduct.
article: καθαρότης means cleanness or purity, derived from the adjective καθαρός ("clean"). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:13, where it refers to the ceremonial cleansing of the flesh under the old covenant. The everyday papyri show a fascinating moral and figurative range: one fifth-century petition appeals to the "purity" of a judge's righteous judgment, and another official letter uses it as a flattering term meaning something like "impartiality."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there is extremely narrow and rests on a single verse.

definition: Lacking self-control, unable to restrain one's impulses or desires.
article: This adjective is built from a negative prefix plus the word for "power" or "strength," so it literally means "without mastery" — either physically powerless or, in a moral sense, unable to govern one's own appetites. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, KJV's "incontinent") consistently point to "lacking self-control," and it appears just once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 3:3) and once in the Septuagint (Proverbs 27:20). Interestingly, third-century BC inscriptions from a temple of Asclepius use it in the purely physical sense of "impotent," describing a man whose fingers were powerless.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering "slanderous" disagrees with the lexicons' consistent sense of "lacking self-control," so the precise nuance in 2 Timothy 3:3 is uncertain.

definition: Gabriel, an angel of God who delivers divine messages to people.
article: Γαβριήλ is the name of the angel Gabriel, appearing twice in the New Testament, both in Luke chapter 1 (verses 19 and 26). The name comes from Hebrew גַּבְרִיאֵל, which the lexicon Abbott-Smith explains as "hero of God," and the Septuagint uses the same Greek form twice to render this Hebrew name. The two measured "senses" are really just the same name in different sentence contexts — once as a description ("Gabriel") and once introducing his speech ("Gabriel called"). Strong's and Dodson identify him specifically as an archangel and messenger of God.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only twice, so the two "senses" reflect translation phrasing rather than any real difference in meaning.

definition: To share in glory together with someone, especially being raised to honor alongside them.
article: This compound joins σύν ('with') and δοξάζω ('to glorify'), meaning to be brought into glory in company with another. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 8:17, where it speaks of believers being glorified together with Christ; in that single case it is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by its own English word. Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes an older sense found in Aristotle — 'to join in approving' — which the New Testament does not use, where it carries only the meaning of shared glorification.
caution: Evidence is very thin: the word occurs just once in the Byzantine text (and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text), so confidence is low.

definition: The public showing or presenting of someone, the point at which they appear openly before others.
article: This noun describes the moment of being shown forth or publicly presented — in its single New Testament use it marks when John the Baptist appeared openly to Israel. The word is rare: it occurs just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 1:80) and once in the Septuagint (Sirach 43:6). Older lexicons stretch the sense toward a formal proclamation of an appointment to office or admission to a society, though the New Testament evidence only supports a general 'showing forth' or public appearance.
caution: This word is essentially a hapax in the New Testament with only one further Septuagint occurrence, so its precise range is uncertain and lexicons differ on whether it implies a formal appointment.

definition: A leather pouch or bag used to carry food and provisions on a journey.
article: πήρα is a leather pouch or wallet that travelers carried for food and supplies, appearing 6 times in the New Testament, all in instructions Jesus gives about traveling light. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "bag" half the time, with the rest emphasizing journeying without provisions. One intriguing wrinkle: the scholar Deissmann argued it could instead mean a collecting-bag carried by pagan beggar-priests for alms, citing an inscription where a slave of the Syrian goddess says each begging trip "brought in seventy bags."
caution: The evidence is thin and the sources disagree on whether πήρα is a provisions bag or a beggar's collecting-bag.

definition: The act or result of judging — a decision, verdict, or sentence, often referring to God's judgment.
article: κρίσις centers on the act of judging and its outcome, and the Byzantine NT renders it "judgment" in 35 of 48 occurrences (95%), with eleven more cases absorbed into phrasing. Beyond a general decision or verdict, it frequently points to divine judgment, including the final judgment, and can carry a forensic, courtroom sense. The Septuagint mostly uses it to translate Hebrew מִשְׁפָּט (115×), the broad word for justice and legal verdict, and everyday Koine papyri confirm the courtroom usage — one petition even asks that no action be taken "before the trial of the case."

definition: To lay violent hands on someone and kill them, used in the New Testament of putting a person to death.
article: In the New Testament διαχειρίζομαι means to kill someone by laying violent hands on them, and it appears just twice, both in Acts (5:30 and 26:21). The word's original everyday sense was much milder, though: papyri and inscriptions use it for handling money, administering funds, or managing public affairs—literally 'to have in hand.' The sense 'to kill' is a later development found in writers like Polybius and Josephus, and that violent meaning is the only one the New Testament uses.
caution: Only 2 occurrences in the New Testament, both meaning 'kill,' so the corpus shows none of the word's broader 'manage/handle' range seen in the papyri.

definition: To cover something by casting a shadow over it, to overshadow.
article: Κατασκιάζω means to overshadow or cover something, built from κατά ("down") plus a word related to σκιά ("shadow"). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:5, where the cherubim of glory "overshadow" the mercy seat of the ark. The same word shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions — one funerary text (Kaibel 495) uses it to say the common earth "covered over" a dead man, a vivid example of its plain sense of shading or burying.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the range of this word in biblical usage cannot be measured precisely.

definition: A burning piece of coal or charcoal, glowing with fire.
article: ἄνθραξ means a coal or piece of charcoal, especially a live, glowing one. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 12:20, where it speaks of heaping "burning coals" on an enemy's head. The word was ordinary enough to show up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a Delos temple account listing wood and coal among its expenses, and in the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew word for hot coals (11 of 27 times), though it also stands in twice for a gemstone.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: A person from Cyrene, a city in North Africa, or someone belonging to that place.
article: Κυρηναῖος is simply an ethnic label meaning "of Cyrene" — a native or inhabitant of the North African city of Cyrene. It appears 6 times across 4 New Testament books, always pointing to specific people such as Simon, who carried Jesus' cross (Matthew 27:32, Mark 15:21, Luke 23:26). The everyday nature of the term shows up in the papyri, where a man's will from 237 BC describes someone as Κυρηναῖος τῆς ἐπιγονῆς, "a Cyrenean by descent." The varied English renderings in the digest reflect translators fitting the word into phrases rather than any real shift in meaning.
caution: The differing measured renderings simply reflect surrounding phrasing, not distinct senses; all sources agree the word means "of Cyrene."

definition: A questioning or debate—the back-and-forth of arguing over an issue or disputed point.
article: ζήτησις comes from the verb "to seek" (ζητέω) and basically means the act of inquiring, which in the New Testament shades into questioning, debating, and arguing. Its seven occurrences cluster around disputes—translators render it "dispute," "speculation," or "engaging" in debate, often something the writer views as unproductive (as in 1 Timothy and Titus). One nice detail: everyday Koine papyri use the word in a more technical legal sense, with an Oxyrhynchus petition from A.D. 186 speaking of "private suits" (ἰδιωτικῶν ζητήσεων) and official "inquiries."
