caution: The translations vary widely ("speculation" appears in 33% of cases but BSB never independently agrees), reflecting how flexibly the same word is rendered.

definition: The act of confirming or guaranteeing something so it stands firm and assured.
article: βεβαίωσις means a confirmation or guarantee that makes something secure and dependable. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both rendered "confirmation" — the confirmation of the gospel in Philippians 1:7 and an oath given as final confirmation in Hebrews 6:16. The most telling evidence comes from everyday papyri, where the word was a standard legal term: sellers promised to back a sale "with every guarantee" (πάσῃ βεβαιώσει), even guaranteeing that goods owed nothing to the tax authorities.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: A position word meaning in front of, ahead of, or in the presence of someone or something.
article: ἔμπροσθεν is a spatial word marking position: standing in front of, going ahead of, or being in someone's presence. In the New Testament it appears 48 times and is rendered "before" most often (18×, 39%), but it spreads across a range of phrasings—"ahead," "in front of," and the courtroom-flavored "in the presence of." The Septuagint uses it 133 times, most often to translate the Hebrew word for "face" (פָּנִים, 43×), which fits its sense of being before someone's face; everyday papyri use it the same spatial way, as in a lease describing people who "live opposite the admiralty."
caution: Abbott-Smith notes the word can mark time as well as place in classical Greek and the papyri, but the New Testament uses are spatial.

definition: Describing something that cannot be set aside, broken, or transferred to another, and so remains permanent.
article: ἀπαράβατος describes something that cannot be violated or passed on to someone else, and so stays permanently in force. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 7:24, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "permanent" in every count (and the BSB agrees fully); older lexicons offer "inviolable" and "unchangeable." The most telling evidence comes from everyday papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show it as a fixed legal phrase—judgments declared "valid and inviolate"—from 67 B.C. clear through a sixth-century A.D. sale document, proving the sense "inviolable" was rooted in real legal language.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: To send someone to another party, especially up to a higher authority or back to the sender.
article: ἀναπέμπω combines "up/back" with "send," and it covers two related actions: sending a person up to a higher official (like Pilate sending Jesus to Herod) and sending them back. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times across 2 books, mostly in Luke's trial scenes, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sent" in two-thirds of cases. The most striking evidence comes from everyday papyri and inscriptions, where the word regularly means "to remit, to send up to a higher authority" — a precise legal sense matching its New Testament use in courtroom settings.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and the senses clustered in one author, the "send back" meaning rests more on the lexica and one disputed passage than on clear measured data.

definition: To destroy something or someone utterly, wiping them out completely.
senseLabels: to utterly destroy or wipe out
article: This strong verb means to destroy completely — to root out, exterminate, or annihilate. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 3:23, where it quotes Deuteronomy and warns that anyone who refuses the prophet will be "utterly destroyed" from among the people. The word is far more at home in the Septuagint, where it shows up 207 times across 27 books, most often translating the Hebrew כָּרַת ("to cut off," 65×); its sheer force is also seen in everyday Koine, as in a text where someone fears an angel will be sent to wipe out a whole army.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence (and none in the critical text), the New Testament range rests entirely on that one quoted verse.

definition: To make something or someone less—lower in rank or status, or reduced in amount or influence.
article: ἐλαττόω means to make something smaller, lower, or less—whether in rank, importance, or quantity. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times: twice rendered "lower" (as in Hebrews 2:7, 9, about being made lower than the angels) and once "decrease" (John 3:30, where John the Baptist says he must become less). The everyday papyri show the same practical range: one document warns an official against "diminishing" a report compared to an earlier one, and a lease specifies that a man should "incur no loss."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, this is thin evidence, though the measured senses and the lexica agree well.

definition: Without anything blocking or stopping you; freely and unhindered.
article: This adverb describes doing something without anyone or anything getting in the way. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:31, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render it "freely" (100% of its single occurrence). The most telling detail comes from the papyri: it was standard legal vocabulary, showing up constantly in everyday contracts and leases (for example, an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 164 uses it to mean holding a property "without hindrance" for the agreed time).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: Gaza, one of the five main Philistine cities, located in southern Palestine near the seacoast.
article: Γάζα is a place name—the city of Gaza in southern Palestine, on the coast, known in the Old Testament as one of the five chief Philistine cities. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 8:26), describing the road that leads down toward Gaza through desert country. The name comes from Hebrew עַזָּה (Azzah), which the Septuagint renders 21 of its 25 times, and Moulton-Milligan notes a linguistic detail: the Greek γ stands in for a Semitic consonant in this borrowed name.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, so its New Testament evidence is thin.

definition: Made of clay or pottery; earthen, like the work of a potter.
article: This adjective describes something made of clay or fired pottery, the kind of thing a potter produces. It appears only once in the New Testament (Revelation 2:27), where it describes earthen vessels being broken to pieces — which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase with "shatter." Abbott-Smith notes that in classical Greek the word usually meant "of a potter," but in the Septuagint and New Testament it shifted to simply mean "earthen"; its single Septuagint appearance, in Daniel 2:41, translates the Hebrew word for potter's clay.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: The act of polluting or defiling, especially moral corruption or contamination.
article: μιασμός refers to the act of polluting or contaminating, typically in a moral sense. It appears only once in the New Testament (2 Peter 2:10), where translators struggle to render it cleanly—the Majority Standard Bible's wording here doesn't isolate a clear single gloss, while traditional sources give "uncleanness" or "defilement." Abbott-Smith notes that in 2 Peter it functions like its close relative μίασμα, and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and in the Septuagint at Wisdom 14:26 and 1 Maccabees 4:43.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering does not yield a clear gloss, so its precise force in context is somewhat uncertain.

definition: Describing something dirty or shabby, used both of soiled clothing and, figuratively, of moral filthiness.
article: ῥυπαρός describes things that are dirty, soiled, or shabby. In its two New Testament appearances it splits evenly: in James 2:2 it refers literally to a poor person's filthy clothing, while Revelation 22:11 uses it figuratively for moral defilement ("let the filthy continue to be filthy"). The everyday papyri are striking here — the word turns up describing "soiled cloaks," unwinnowed (dirty) grain, and even debased coinage, showing how ordinary and concrete this term was in daily Koine.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a couple of Septuagint uses, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To cry out or shout loudly, often with strong emotion, to call out a message or to call on someone for help.
article: βοάω means to shout, cry out, or call aloud, usually with intense feeling. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times, and the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "calling" (3×, as in Matthew 3:3 and Mark 1:3, echoing the voice crying in the wilderness), with related shades like "cried out" elsewhere. It shows up 123 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating Hebrew words for crying out (זָעַק 34×, צָעַק 23×), and the papyri capture its emotional force well — one excited petition reads "so I was shouting and crying out."
caution: With only one consistently measured sense and just 11 occurrences, the full range (such as calling on someone for help) rests more on the lexica and Septuagint than on the New Testament data.

definition: To take a tenth from someone as a tithe, or in the passive, to have a tenth taken from you.
article: δεκατόω covers both sides of the tithing transaction: actively taking a tenth from someone (Hebrews 7:6) and, in the passive, paying a tenth (Hebrews 7:9). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews, and just once in the Septuagint, where it translates a Hebrew word for tithing in Nehemiah. Moulton-Milligan note this verb is hard to parallel outside the Septuagint, suggesting it was a freshly coined term—natural in Jewish writing because tithing was a procedure with no real equivalent in everyday Greek life.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, and the word appears to be a specialized coinage rather than common Greek.

definition: Bithynia, a Roman province in northwest Asia Minor, lying along the southwest coast of the Black Sea.
senseLabels: Bithynia, a region of Asia Minor
article: Bithynia was a Roman province in the northwest of Asia Minor, bordering the southwest of the Black Sea. The word appears just twice in the New Testament and is always simply the place name: Paul and his companions are kept from entering it in Acts 16:7, and Peter addresses believers there in 1 Peter 1:1. Both the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB render it "Bithynia" 100% of the time, and all the listed lexicons agree.
caution: This is a rare proper name (only 2 occurrences) of uncertain derivation, so the evidence is thin even though its meaning is not disputed.

definition: To move something from one place or direction to another — to lead, steer, or turn it about.
article: This verb's basic everyday meaning is to transfer or transport something from one spot to another, as the papyri show clearly — one document from AD 23 uses it for moving 320 sheep between districts. In the New Testament, though, it appears only twice, both in James 3:3-4, where it describes steering a horse with a bit and turning a ship with a small rudder; the lexicographers note this 'turn about, direct' nuance is otherwise unattested elsewhere. In the Septuagint it shows up 5 times across 3 books, translating several different Hebrew words, mostly in the sense of leading people away or carrying them off.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and Abbott-Smith noting the 'turn about' sense as 'otherwise unknown,' confidence in the precise James meaning is low.

definition: Cleopas, the personal name of one of the two disciples who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus.
article: Cleopas is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Luke 24:18) for one of the two travelers Jesus joined on the road to Emmaus. Every source agrees on the rendering "Cleopas," and the name turns up in everyday Koine documents, including three times in Wilcken's collection of second-century Egyptian ostraka. Scholars note it may be a contracted form, and there is discussion of whether Cleopas (Κλεόπας) could be linked to the similar name Clopas (Κλωπᾶς).
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and its possible identification with the name Clopas remains an open question.

definition: Friendly and kind in attitude, showing warm, courteous goodwill toward others.
article: φιλόφρων describes a friendly, kind-hearted disposition toward others. It is built from φίλος ("loving, friend") and φρήν ("mind"), so it literally points to a mind inclined toward friendliness. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 1 Peter 3:8, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "courteous"; note that it is part of the Received Text reading and is absent from the critical text (SBLGNT).
caution: This is a single, textually disputed occurrence dropped by the critical text, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: Gideon, an Israelite military leader and one of the judges, praised among the heroes of faith.
article: Γεδεών is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Gideon (גִּדְעוֹן), the Israelite judge whose story is told in Judges chapters 6-8. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:32, where Gideon is listed among the great examples of faith. The name is indeclinable in both the Septuagint and the New Testament, and in the Septuagint it stands for the Hebrew Gideon 78 times.
caution: The single 'allow' rendering reported in the measured data is a digest artifact; this is a proper name, not a verb.

definition: A woman from Phoenicia in the region of Syria, identifying her ethnic and geographic background.
article: This word names a woman who was a native of Phoenicia within Syria, as opposed to Phoenician territory elsewhere like Carthage in North Africa. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Mark 7:26, and the critical text uses a different form, with Westcott-Hort printing 'Σύρα Φοινίκισσα' in their margin. Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Abbott-Smith points to a parallel phrase in the historian Diodorus.
caution: This is a single rare occurrence, it carries no English word of its own in translation, and the manuscripts and lexica disagree over its exact spelling.

definition: To measure something back to someone in return, giving an equivalent amount in response.
senseLabels: measured or given back in return
article: This word combines "in return" (ἀντί) with "to measure" (μετρέω), so it literally means to mete back out the same measure someone gave. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 6:38, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "poured" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees 100%. It was a rare word even in its day, but Moulton-Milligan note that it does show up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, with a parallel sense of paying back a fitting return for how one has lived.
caution: This is a rare word with only one New Testament occurrence, and some manuscripts read the plainer μετρέω instead.

definition: A person who owns property, especially land — an owner or proprietor.
article: κτήτωρ means an owner or possessor, particularly of land or property, formed from the verb κτάομαι ("to acquire"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 4:34, where it describes those who owned land or houses. The everyday Koine papyri make this sense vivid: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 186 uses the very word for property-owners commanded to register their holdings at the record-office, and a Tebtunis lease calls landlords "the owners" (κτήτορες) responsible for State dues.
caution: The measured data labels its single occurrence "needy," which actually reflects the surrounding context of Acts 4:34 rather than the word itself — every lexicon and the papyri agree the word means "owner."

definition: To turn someone completely inside out morally — to corrupt or pervert a person away from what is right.
article: This compound of ἐκ ("out") and στρέφω ("to turn") literally means to turn something out or inside out, and figuratively to change a person entirely for the worse — to corrupt or pervert. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Titus 3:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sinful" (and the BSB agrees), describing a divisive person as warped or self-condemned. The classical sources fill out the picture: Homer used it for turning something out, Aristophanes for the metaphorical sense of perverting, and the Septuagint uses it four times to translate several different Hebrew words.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical SBLGNT text), so its New Testament range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Verbal instruction or warning meant to correct someone, gently calling their attention to better conduct.
article: Νουθεσία refers to admonition — the act of warning, counseling, or correcting someone by drawing their attention to a fault or a better way. Built from νοῦς (mind) and a form of τίθημι (to put), it literally suggests "putting something in the mind." It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and in every case translators folded it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word; outside the Bible it is a comparatively rare and mostly late word, turning up in everyday Koine papyri but unfortunately in broken, unreadable contexts.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, all absorbed into phrasing, and papyri evidence surviving only in damaged contexts, the precise force of the word rests on thin evidence.

definition: To busy oneself with matters that are not your own concern; to meddle in other people's affairs.
article: This word literally combines "around" with "to work," picturing someone bustling about in business that isn't theirs. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Thessalonians 3:11, where Paul describes people who aren't working but are instead being busybodies. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this everyday sense beautifully: in a letter from Emperor Claudius to the Alexandrines (A.D. 41), the Jews are told "not to busy themselves about anything beyond what they have held." The lexicons add an older sense—"to waste one's labor about a thing"—but the New Testament use points to meddling.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on a single passage.

definition: To put someone on public display in order to expose them to scorn or humiliation, as if making them a spectacle.
article: θεατρίζω means to make a public spectacle of someone, holding them up to contempt and ridicule. It comes from θέατρον, "theater," so the picture is of a person put on stage before a watching, mocking crowd. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 10:33, where it describes believers being publicly humiliated; in that single use the verb gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as one English word. Abbott-Smith notes the form is otherwise mainly ecclesiastical, with the related compound ἐκθεατρίζω attested in the historian Polybius.

definition: A secret truth that people cannot know on their own, but which God has now made known through the gospel.
article: In the New Testament μυστήριον overwhelmingly means a divine secret—something once hidden but now revealed in Christ and the gospel—and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "mystery" in 20 of its 27 occurrences (80%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing every time. Importantly, the word does not mean something puzzling or hard to grasp in the modern sense; it points to truths kept hidden until God chose to disclose them. The background is striking: in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions the word was a technical term in pagan religion for secret rites known only to those formally initiated, who were forbidden to reveal them. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times, and Abbott-Smith notes it translates the Aramaic word for "secret" in Daniel.

definition: To weep or wail aloud, expressing grief or sorrow openly, often loudly enough for others to hear.
article: κλαίω means to weep, and across all 40 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "weep" 35 times (97%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing. Unlike quiet crying, Strong's notes this word implies sobbing or wailing aloud, and Abbott-Smith calls it any loud expression of pain or sorrow, especially mourning for the dead. The everyday reality of the term shows up vividly in a second-century papyrus letter where a husband writes to his departed wife that he has been "weeping by night and lamenting by day." In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew בָּכָה ("to weep") 102 of 124 times.

definition: The dirt rinsed off something — used as a cutting insult for the lowest, most despised rubbish of society.
article: περικάθαρμα literally means the filth scraped or rinsed off a dirty vessel, and was used as a term of deep contempt for the most wretched, outcast people. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 4:13, where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. The one Septuagint use, in Proverbs 21:18, translates a Hebrew word for ransom or expiation, and Abbott-Smith notes a related sense of a sacrificial victim — possibly because the lowest people were once offered as expiatory victims.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use and one Septuagint occurrence — so the range from "refuse" to "expiatory victim" rests on very few examples.

definition: At an inconvenient or unsuitable time; when the moment is not right.
article: This adverb means doing something at the wrong or unfitting time — the opposite of εὐκαίρως, "in season." It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 4:2, where preaching is urged "in season and out of season," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it under the "season" pairing in 100% of its single occurrence. Everyday Koine papyri use the same word: a famous letter from a prodigal son (BGU III.846, second century A.D.) complains that someone "unseasonably related all to you."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, this reading rests on very thin corpus evidence.

definition: An orderly arrangement or fixed sequence, and by extension an appointed office, rank, or position in a recognized succession.
article: τάξις describes things set in proper arrangement — from the orderly turn of a priest's duty (Luke 1:8) to the appointed "order" of a succession, as in the repeated phrase "after the order of Melchizedek" in Hebrews. Most of its 10 New Testament occurrences are absorbed into English phrasing (6 of 10) rather than getting their own word, since it usually works inside expressions like "in the order of." The papyri make the rank-and-office sense vivid: a Tebtunis document from about A.D. 123 uses τάξις for a priestly office that "ought to be sold," and another for the post of water-guard.
caution: With only one clearly measured sense and most occurrences absorbed into phrasing, the precise shade in any given verse depends heavily on context.

definition: The cold rainy season of the year, or by extension a violent storm with heavy rain.
article: χειμών mainly means "winter," the cold rainy time of year, which is how the Majority Standard Bible renders it in 4 of 6 occurrences (80%). In 1 case (20%) it shifts to "storm" or "tempest," as in the shipwreck account of Acts 27:20, and the classical lexica note that the storm sense actually underlies the word—a winter storm of pouring rain. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the seasonal meaning vividly, including one that simply says "it is winter, there is great cold."
caution: With only 6 occurrences, the two senses rest on thin evidence, and the lexica treat "storm" as the original idea while the NT mostly uses "winter."

definition: To create a noisy disturbance—whether loud wailing, an uproar, or throwing a crowd into confusion.
article: θορυβέω covers two related kinds of disturbance: making a loud commotion (often the ostentatious wailing of mourners) and stirring a crowd or city into confusion. It appears just 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the same 4 times in the Septuagint, where it renders several different Hebrew words tied to panic and dread. A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri: a second-century letter reassures the reader, 'do not be disturbed, for when you come you will know what it means.'
caution: The MSB rendering count here is split confusingly—some occurrences were absorbed into surrounding phrasing or attached to nearby words like 'Paul' and 'went'—so the measured senses are best read alongside the clearer lexicon definitions.

definition: To arrange, assign, or appoint someone or something to a specific place, position, or task.
senseLabels: appointed or assigned to a position
article: τάσσω is about putting things in their proper place — arranging, assigning, or officially appointing someone to a role or task. In the Byzantine New Testament it shows up 9 times, and where it gets its own English word the Majority Standard Bible renders it "appointed" in 4 of those (67%), as in Acts 13:48 and Romans 13:1. The everyday papyri make the flavor vivid: it described officials "appointed to the administration" or even the governor put in charge of a prison, and Abbott-Smith notes its original military sense of drawing troops up in order.
caution: Three of its nine occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own, and the active-versus-middle sense in passages like Acts 13:48 is debated.

definition: A feeling of deep distress or anguish that grips a person, as if they were being squeezed in a tight, confined place.
article: συνοχή literally means a pressing or holding together, and from there a narrow, confining place — which became a vivid image for emotional distress and anxiety. In the New Testament it appears only twice (Luke 21:25 and 2 Corinthians 2:4), always pointing to anguish or being hemmed in. A striking witness comes from the papyri: a 4th-century magical text from London pleads "deliver me from all συνοχή," showing the word was everyday Koine for the straits people prayed to escape.
caution: Evidence here is thin: the word occurs only twice in the New Testament, and in our measured data both renderings were absorbed into phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word.

definition: To agree with or give one's assent to a decision or course of action.
article: This verb literally means to "deposit together," coming from the image of casting your vote alongside someone else's. In the middle voice—the form used in the New Testament—it means to agree with or assent to a decision. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 23:51, describing Joseph of Arimathea, who had not "consented" to the council's plan against Jesus. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this usage: legal records use it when someone "agreed" to a statement during proceedings.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: A group of people united by shared ancestry or homeland, especially one of the tribes of Israel.
senseLabels: a tribe or clan of people
article: φυλή refers to a body of people bound together by kinship, most often one of the twelve tribes of Israel, but also extended to the wider tribes, peoples, and nations of the earth. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "tribe" in 30 of its 31 New Testament occurrences (97%), and the meaning is consistent across sources. It shows up heavily in the Septuagint (394 times), where it translates the Hebrew words maṭṭeh (171×) and shēveṭ (137×), both terms for tribe or staff. Notably, the everyday Koine papyri use it for priestly "tribes" in Egypt, as in a document where a man identifies himself as a priest of "the fifth tribe" of the local gods.

definition: A distinction or difference that sets one thing apart from another.
article: διαστολή points to a separation or distinction between things — the quality of one thing being marked off from another. In the New Testament it appears 3 times across 2 books, always woven into the phrasing rather than translated as a single word; in Romans 3:22 and 10:12 it expresses that there is "no distinction" (between Jew and Greek), and in 1 Corinthians 14:7 it concerns distinguishing musical notes. Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri use the same word quite differently — for an injunction, notification, or memorandum, as in a Tebtunis document referring to "the memoranda given by them" — a sense not found in the biblical texts.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences, all absorbed into phrasing, and the papyri attest a quite different administrative meaning than the biblical "distinction."

definition: To give orders, arrange, or formally set something in place, often as an authoritative instruction.
article: διατάσσω means to arrange thoroughly or to give authoritative directions, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 15 times across 6 books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "directed" in a third of cases (as in Acts 7:44, 1 Corinthians 16:1, and Titus 1:5), while in 6 of 15 occurrences it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. A striking detail comes from the papyri: the verb had a technical legal use in connection with wills, where it meant a sum "bequeathed" — one document records twenty silver drachmae left by a deceased father.
caution: Only one clear measured sense emerged, and 6 of 15 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing, so its full range is hard to pin down from the rendering data alone.

definition: A person who mocks or ridicules others, especially someone who scornfully dismisses what is sacred.
article: Ἐμπαίκτης is a noun built from the verb ἐμπαίζω ("to mock"), naming someone who derides or ridicules. It appears only twice in the New Testament (2 Peter 3:3 and Jude 1:18), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "scoffers" in both places, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing fully. Its single Septuagint appearance is in Isaiah 3:4, where it translates the Hebrew תַּעֲלוּלִים, suggesting a sense connected to capricious or abusive behavior. Strong's adds the implied notion of "a false teacher," but the measured renderings stay with the plain idea of a mocker.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament uses and one Septuagint occurrence — and Strong's expanded sense of "false teacher" goes beyond what the measured renderings support.

definition: The act of eating, or by extension the food that is eaten; figuratively, the rust or corrosion that eats away at things.
article: βρῶσις covers both the act of eating and the food itself, and the New Testament uses it about evenly: "food" (3×), "store" in the sense of corroding rust (2×), and "eating" (2×). The Septuagint uses it 37 times across 16 books, most often translating Hebrew מַאֲכָל ("food," 8×). One nice detail comes from the everyday papyri, where the word turns up describing fodder "for the pasturing of sheep" — ordinary feeding language, not just religious vocabulary.
caution: In Matthew 6:19–20 the word means "rust" or corrosion rather than food, so context decides whether it refers to eating, what is eaten, or what eats away.

definition: In the Jewish way; living or behaving according to Jewish customs and practices.
article: Ἰουδαϊκῶς is an adverb meaning "in a Jewish manner" — describing behavior that follows Jewish customs. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 2:14, where Paul confronts Peter about forcing Gentiles to live like Jews. The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was part of ordinary usage; Moulton-Milligan even notes an unusual rough breathing (οὐχ Ἰουδαϊκῶς) in the Galatians text that drew scholarly comment.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: The number six.
article: ἕξ is simply the number six, an indeclinable word used the same way for masculine, feminine, and neuter. It appears 13 times in the New Testament and very heavily in the Septuagint (121×), where it almost always renders the Hebrew word for six, שֵׁשׁ (109 times). It shows up in everyday Koine documents too, such as a papyrus from A.D. 18 mentioning "six arouras" of land. The "half" rendering you may see in places like Luke 4:25 and James 5:17 comes from the phrase "three years and six months," where the six is folded into the English wording rather than meaning anything other than the number itself.

definition: The act of pulling down, tearing down, or demolishing something, whether a structure or, figuratively, opposing strongholds.
article: καθαίρεσις means the act of pulling something down or demolishing it, and in the New Testament Paul uses it figuratively as the opposite of "building up" (οἰκοδομή), as in 2 Corinthians 10:8 and 13:10. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all in 2 Corinthians, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "tearing" or "tearing down." Everyday Koine papyri confirm its concrete meaning: one third-century BC document concerns a shrine of Isis that was in danger of collapse, using this very word for its demolition or repair.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (all in one book) and a single Septuagint use — so the measured range rests on a small sample.

definition: To pierce or stab deeply, used figuratively of being struck to the heart by strong emotion.
senseLabels: pierced or cut to the heart
article: κατανύσσω literally means to pierce or strike violently, but in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 2:37) it describes people being emotionally "cut" to the heart by what they heard. The Septuagint uses it 11 times across 5 books, where it can render Hebrew words for being stunned, silent, or grieved. A striking parallel comes from an early Christian text quoted by Moulton-Milligan, where a whole crowd was so "cut" by the Holy Spirit's words that the church floor was wet with their tears — and the modern Greek form still means "to be seized with contrition."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and varied Hebrew counterparts in the Septuagint, the measured evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: The bearing of children; childbirth, and by extension a mother's role of raising a family.
article: τεκνογονία means childbearing — the act of bringing children into the world. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 2:15, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "childbearing." Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; one scholar (Ramsay) argued the abstract noun points beyond physical birth toward motherhood or maternal instinct, though Moulton-Milligan doubts the writer meant anything different from the plain physical sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and scholars disagree over whether it means literal childbirth or the broader role of motherhood.

definition: A person put in charge of someone else's affairs—either a household manager or a legal guardian appointed over minors.
article: ἐπίτροπος is someone entrusted with another's responsibilities, ranging from a household steward or estate manager (Matthew 20:8, Luke 8:3) to a legal guardian set over children (Galatians 4:2). All 3 of its New Testament occurrences are folded into surrounding phrasing rather than mapped to a single English word. The everyday papyri make the legal sense vivid: one document records 'Aurelius Hermodorus, guardian of the minors,' taking an oath on their behalf, and wills routinely name ἐπίτροποι to oversee heirs until they came of age.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences across 3 books, all absorbed into phrasing, so the sense divisions rest mainly on context and outside sources.

definition: The highest point of the sky directly overhead, where the sun stands at noon — the zenith or mid-heaven.
article: This word names the very top of the sky, the point straight overhead where the sun sits at midday — what we'd call the zenith. The Majority Standard Bible renders all three occurrences with motion language: "flying" twice and "flying overhead" once, picturing creatures soaring at that high point. A nice detail from the papyri: the word turns up in an ancient horoscope (P Oxy II.235), where it described a star's position in mid-sky — showing this was everyday astronomical vocabulary, not just a biblical term.
caution: This word appears only 3 times, all in Revelation, so its sense rests on a thin and narrow body of evidence.

definition: A council of elders; in the New Testament, the assembly of leading Jewish elders forming the Sanhedrin.
article: γερουσία refers to a body or council of elders, a term used for governing assemblies in Greek cities under Roman rule. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 5:21), it describes the Jewish Sanhedrin, the high council of elders. In the Septuagint it shows up 27 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "elder" (זָקֵן, 24 times). One striking detail: scholars note that this word, rather than the more common βουλή, came to be applied to the Sanhedrin, mirroring the prominent role such councils played in cities like Ephesus.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering as "apostles" reflects translation context rather than the word's own meaning of an elders' council.

definition: Nicolaus, a personal name belonging to one of the seven men chosen to serve the early church in Jerusalem.
article: Νικόλαος is a Greek personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 6:5, where Nicolaus is named among the seven chosen to assist the apostles. The name is built from elements meaning "victory" and "people," and Moulton-Milligan confirms it was a common everyday name found across Koine papyri and inscriptions. Interestingly, this same name-meaning fueled later attempts to link Nicolaus with the "Nicolaitans" of Revelation 2:6, though some scholars like Harnack reject reading any hidden meaning into the name.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and the standard rendering as "Nicanor" in the measured data conflicts with the lexica, which all give "Nicolaus."

definition: The Roman province of Asia, occupying roughly the western third of Asia Minor.
article: Ἀσία refers to the Roman province of Asia—not the continent—covering roughly the western third of Asia Minor, with cities like Ephesus at its heart. It appears 18 times across 6 New Testament books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "province Asia" in 12 of those (67%) and simply "Asia" in 4 more (22%), showing how translators clarify the geography for modern readers. Strong's notes that the name usually points only to the western shore, and Abbott-Smith consistently treats every occurrence as this same Roman province.

definition: Something entrusted to another person for safekeeping; a deposit or trust placed in someone's care.
article: παρακαταθήκη refers to something handed over to another for safekeeping — a deposit or entrusted possession. The word doesn't appear in the Byzantine New Testament, but it shows up twice in the Septuagint (in one book) and was the more usual form in Greek writers, often replacing the variant παραθήκη in some New Testament textual traditions. Everyday papyri richly illustrate its commercial flavor: one third-century document (P Oxy I.71) speaks of "a secure deposit, subject to no claim or charge," showing it was the ordinary word for a legally protected entrusted sum.
caution: This word does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament and appears only twice in the Septuagint, so its biblical sense rests on thin attestation and the related form παραθήκη.

definition: Skilled in music, or as a noun, a musician or singer.
article: This adjective means "skilled in the arts, especially music," and when used as a noun it names a musician, minstrel, or singer. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Revelation 18:22, where it refers to musicians whose sound will no longer be heard in fallen Babylon. In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times across 3 books, rendering Hebrew words for stringed and piped instruments, and the everyday papyri preserve a sharp exchange before Emperor Claudius where a man is taunted as the "son of a female musician."
caution: The measured rendering "again" is a tagging artifact from the surrounding verse and does not reflect the word's actual meaning, which is "musician"; with only one New Testament occurrence, confidence rests mainly on the Septuagint and lexica.

definition: A man's name, Sopater, a Christian from Beroea in Macedonia who traveled with Paul.
article: Σώπατρος is a personal name, Sopater, occurring just once in the New Testament (Acts 20:4), where it names a Christian who originally belonged to Beroea in Macedonia and accompanied Paul. Moulton-Milligan note that it is a pet-form (shortened version) of the longer name Σωσίπατρος and that the name shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. The name derives from the roots behind σώζω ("save") and πατήρ ("father"), which Strong's renders "of a safe father."
caution: The lone measured sense is labeled "province," which conflicts with every lexicon listing this as the proper name Sopater — treat the measured label as a tagging error.

definition: An attendant or subordinate official who carries out the orders of someone in authority, such as a court officer, guard, or assistant.
article: This word describes a subordinate who serves under someone's authority, ranging from a magistrate's officer or guard (rendered "officers" 11 of 20 times, 61%) to a general servant or attendant ("servants," 4 times, 22%). It covers a wide span: synagogue attendants, royal attendants, and even ministers of the gospel like the "servants of the word" in Luke 1:2. Its literal root meaning is striking — it originally meant an "under-oarsman" or rower on a ship — and the everyday papyri confirm the practical, official flavor, describing assistants to tax collectors and administrators.

definition: To test or examine something to find out its true quality, and by extension to approve what proves genuine.
article: δοκιμάζω means to put something to the test to see whether it is genuine, and then—once it passes—to approve it. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 23 times, and the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "test" (3×), "try" (2×), or "approves" (2×), with the rest absorbed into phrasing or scattered renderings. Its original force was concrete: it was used of testing metals like gold, and everyday Koine documents show officials using it to "sift" or vet matters—an inscription has officials inspecting sacrificial animals, and a papyrus speaks of an official examining a case with the utmost fairness. In the Septuagint it usually stands in for Hebrew בָּחַן, "to test or examine" (9 times).

definition: Chuza, the personal name of the household manager of Herod Antipas, mentioned once in the New Testament.
article: Χουζᾶς is a proper name, not an ordinary word: it belongs to Chuza, identified in Luke 8:3 as the household manager (steward) of Herod Antipas, whose wife Joanna supported Jesus. It appears just once in the New Testament. The most interesting clue about him comes from outside the Bible — the name has turned up in a Nabataean inscription, which led some scholars to suggest Chuza was a Nabataean rather than a Jew.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament and its origin is uncertain, so the evidence is thin.

definition: Anxious worry or care that weighs on the mind, especially over life's concerns and wealth.
article: μέριμνα names the anxious care that distracts and burdens a person, and all six New Testament uses lean toward this negative sense of worry rather than neutral concern. Its range is fairly tight: it covers worry about life, wealth, and daily survival, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "worries" every time. The everyday papyri capture this vividly: a wife writes to her husband that, lying awake night and day, she has "one care" (μίαν μέριμναν) for his safety, showing the word's pull toward genuine fear for a loved one.
caution: With only six occurrences and two of those absorbed into phrasing, the measured sense distinctions are thin and reflect context more than fixed meanings.

definition: In the middle voice, to consult with someone or to add further instruction or status to a person.
article: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Galatians, and its middle-voice meaning centers on bringing something to someone—either consulting them for guidance or contributing extra instruction or standing to them. The two occurrences pull in slightly different directions: in Galatians 1:16 it means consulting others (the rendering 'rush' here is loose), while in Galatians 2:6 it concerns the leaders adding nothing to Paul (rendered 'favoritism'). One vivid clue comes from everyday Koine: ancient writers like Diodorus Siculus used it for consulting soothsayers about an omen, and it shows up in a tax report from a papyrus (c. 148 BC).
caution: Evidence is thin—only two NT occurrences with quite different renderings, so the precise sense in each verse is genuinely debated.

definition: The benefit, profit, or advantage that something brings.
article: ὠφέλεια refers to the benefit, profit, or advantage gained from something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both rendered as "advantage" (Romans 3:1 and Jude 16), and the lexicons add the related ideas of usefulness, gain, and help. The everyday flavor of the word shows up nicely in the papyri: one document from AD 278 speaks of "the benefit resulting from these works" of repairing dykes, showing how ordinary and practical the term was.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and limited measured data, confidence in its precise range is low.

definition: In a forceful, vigorous way — doing something intensely, energetically, or with great determination.
article: This adverb describes doing something with intense energy or force; both New Testament uses involve people speaking or accusing with great vigor. It appears only twice — once of chief priests accusing Jesus "vehemently" (Luke 23:10), and once of Apollos powerfully refuting opponents in debate (Acts 18:28). It surfaces in everyday Koine papyri too, where the comparative form means writing to someone "more forcefully" or "more urgently," and in the one Septuagint use it oddly renders the Hebrew word for a ram's-horn trumpet (Joshua 6:8).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the translations differing on the second instance, the precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: Causing wonder or amazement; marvelous and remarkable, often describing what God has done.
article: θαυμαστός describes something that makes people marvel — wonderful, amazing, remarkable. It appears 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "marvelous" (3 times, 43%), as in the quoted line "this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes" (Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:11). The Septuagint uses it 27 times, frequently translating Hebrew פָּלָא and related words for wonder, and a Christian amulet from the papyri calls God's name "the wonderful and exceeding glorious and fearful" (P Oxy VIII.1151).
caution: Several of the measured "senses" (such as "God's" or "marvelous final") reflect how the word sits within longer phrases rather than truly distinct meanings, so the core sense is simply "marvelous, wonderful."

definition: The act of burying someone, or the place where a body is buried.
article: ταφή refers to burial — the act of putting a body in the ground — and by extension the burial place itself. The lexica and the everyday papyri agree on this range: a will from 236 BC sets aside money "for my own burial," and the word could even stretch to mean a mummy or its wrappings in Egyptian documents. In the Septuagint it shows up 11 times in 9 books, mostly translating the Hebrew words for "grave" or "burial" (קְבוּרָה and קָ֫בֶר). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 27:7, where the chief priests buy a field "to bury" foreigners.
caution: The measured NT rendering "together" is clearly a data artifact from a single verse and does not reflect the word's actual meaning, which all the lexical sources give as "burial."

definition: Describing something that happens early, at or near daybreak in the morning.
article: This adjective describes something belonging to the early morning, derived from the noun ὄρθρος (dawn). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 24:22, where the women came to the tomb 'early' — though note it is absent from the critical (SBLGNT) text there, replaced by a related form (ὀρθρινός). An interesting detail comes from everyday papyri: one document uses τὸ ὄρθριον for a person's 'morning greeting' or first act of the day, showing how naturally the word fit ordinary Koine speech about morning activity.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one Byzantine occurrence (dropped in the critical text), so confidence is low, and the MSB rendering 'Furthermore' reflects sentence flow rather than the word's actual time-of-day meaning.

definition: The attractive, dignified beauty or graceful appearance of something, especially its impressive outward splendor.
article: εὐπρέπεια describes a fine outward appearance — beauty, comeliness, or stately splendor. It appears only once in the New Testament (James 1:11), where it is woven into the phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word, and 10 times across the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew words for a dwelling-place, beauty, and song. Moulton-Milligan note an added flavor of majesty and stateliness, citing an inscription where emperors wish their realm to continue in the same εὐπρεπείᾳ, suggesting more than mere prettiness — a dignified grandeur.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade there leans heavily on Septuagint and inscriptional parallels.

definition: Tertius, a man who wrote down Paul's letter to the Romans as Paul dictated it.
article: Tertius is a personal name of Latin origin (it means "third"), borne by the scribe who physically wrote out Paul's letter to the Romans. The word appears just once in the New Testament, at Romans 16:22, where Tertius adds his own greeting to the readers. Moulton-Milligan note that the name also turns up in a first-century inscription in the Cemetery of Priscilla in Rome, confirming it was a real, everyday name in that period.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range rests on that single verse plus outside inscriptional evidence.

definition: The number forty.
article: This is simply the cardinal number forty, an indeclinable word built from τέσσαρες ("four"). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "forty" in 16 of its 22 Byzantine New Testament appearances (94%), with the remaining occurrences absorbed into larger phrasing; the Septuagint uses it 133 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for forty (120× out of 133). One small point of interest is spelling: the New Testament consistently writes it τεσσεράκοντα, a form that was actually uncommon in everyday papyri of the first to third centuries A.D.

definition: By compulsion or under constraint, as opposed to acting willingly or by free choice.
article: This adverb describes doing something because you are forced to, not because you choose to. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:2, where it is explicitly contrasted with ἑκουσίως ('willingly') — shepherds are told to serve God's flock not by constraint but freely. Moulton-Milligan note that the word and its relatives turn up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary language rather than a specialized term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical evidence alone.

definition: To make a grating sound, especially to grind or gnash the teeth.
article: τρίζω basically means to make a creaking, squeaking, or chirping sound — originally used of noises made by animals — and by extension to grind the teeth together. It appears only once in the New Testament (Mark 9:18), where it is used of a boy gnashing his teeth, and in that verse it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. The lexicographers note its wider range of sounds, and Moulton-Milligan confirm it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests almost entirely on a single verse, so confidence is low.

definition: To cause someone pain or grief, or in the passive, to feel sorrow, sadness, or distress.
article: λυπέω covers the whole territory of emotional pain — grieving, feeling sorrow, being distressed — and it appears 25 times in the Byzantine New Testament. Often it shows up in the passive, describing someone who is grieved or made sad, as when Matthew 26:37 pairs it with another word for being troubled. The everyday flavor comes through clearly in the papyri: a first-century letter of condolence uses it for weeping over a death, and another writer says he "read the letter and was grieved." In the Septuagint it does double duty, sometimes rendering Hebrew words for anger or wrath (קָצַף, חָרָה) as well as words for pain.

definition: Completely clear or obvious, leaving no room for doubt.
article: κατάδηλος means something is plainly clear or evident — the prefix κατά intensifies the base word δῆλος ("clear"), giving the sense "quite manifest." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 7:15, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "clear" (the BSB agrees fully). Moulton-Milligan note that it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including a 4th-century document where someone is told to "make the measure quite clear" to those involved.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: To speak openly and boldly, with confidence and without fear, especially when proclaiming a message.
article: This verb describes speaking out frankly and fearlessly, often paired with the bold proclamation of a message. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it simply "boldly" (2×), with related phrasing like "speak boldly" or "freely" in other places; 2 of the 9 cases get folded into the surrounding wording without a word of their own. Moulton-Milligan note that in the New Testament the word is confined to the free and bold preaching of the Gospel, the privilege of a servant of Christ, and the same idea of open speech shows up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: Roughly 29% of occurrences map to a single clear sense and others are absorbed into phrasing, so the evidence for a sharply defined range is moderate rather than strong.

definition: Free from fault or defect—either a sacrificial animal without physical blemish or a person who is morally blameless.
article: ἄμωμος literally means "without blemish," built from a negative prefix plus μῶμος ("blemish, fault"). It moves between two closely linked uses: the technical sacrificial sense of an animal without physical defect (as of Christ in Hebrews 9:14 and 1 Peter 1:19) and the ethical sense of a person who is morally blameless (Ephesians 1:4, Revelation 14:5). The Septuagint uses it heavily—79 times in 8 books—mostly to render Hebrew תָּמִים ("complete, sound"), 58 of those times, which is why the sacrificial overtone carries into the New Testament; the word also turns up as a personal name and in everyday Koine inscriptions and epitaphs.
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences spread thinly across five renderings, the sense divisions are fine-grained and most rest on a single example each.

definition: To give someone a full hearing, especially when a judge listens to a legal case or plea.
article: This verb means to hear someone out completely, and in practice it carries a courtroom flavor: a judge or official giving a prisoner or petitioner a full hearing. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 23:35, where the governor says he will hear Paul's case. The judicial sense is strongly confirmed by everyday Koine papyri, where officials are repeatedly petitioned to "hear" a person's matter, and the Septuagint uses it twice, including in Deuteronomy 1:16 where it translates the Hebrew word for hearing disputes.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament (only one occurrence), so the judicial sense rests mainly on the papyri and Septuagint rather than NT range.

definition: A pig or sow, the domestic farm animal kept for meat.
article: ὗς simply means a pig — specifically a female sow in its one New Testament appearance (2 Peter 2:22), where a washed sow returns to wallow in the mud. The word was thoroughly ordinary in everyday Greek; the papyri show it in farm contexts, including a brood sow about to give birth and notes about a pig being unwell. In the Septuagint it appears 6 times and usually renders the Hebrew word for swine (חֲזִיר), the same unclean animal of Jewish dietary law. The digest lists its measured sense as 'proverbs,' but that reflects the proverbial saying in which the word is embedded, not the meaning of ὗς itself, which is the animal.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's labeling of its sense as 'proverbs' comes from the surrounding proverbial saying rather than the word's actual meaning, which is consistently 'pig.'

definition: To mark or take note of someone, often for the purpose of keeping one's distance from them.
article: σημειόω means to mark or note someone, and in its single New Testament appearance (2 Thessalonians 3:14) it carries the added sense of marking a person out so as to avoid them. The word shows up only once in the Byzantine NT and once in the Septuagint, where it renders a Hebrew word. It was common in everyday Koine documents — papyri and inscriptions use it for officials 'noting' matters in correspondence — and Polybius even uses it of marking an ominous sign, which fits the disapproving tone in Paul's command.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the measured evidence is thin, so the disapproving nuance rests mostly on context and outside sources.

definition: To struggle or work hard alongside others toward a shared goal, as teammates contending together.
article: συναθλέω pictures people striving together like athletes on the same team, combining "with" (σύν) and "to compete" (ἀθλέω). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Philippians, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the idea of being at someone's "side" in a shared effort (Php 1:27; 4:3). Abbott-Smith treats it as equivalent to συναγωνίζομαι, noting it takes a dative of advantage in 1:27 and a dative of the people one labors with in 4:3.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in one book, the evidence base is thin and the confidence tier is low.

definition: Careful exactness or strictness, especially in following rules or doing something with precise attention to detail.
article: ἀκρίβεια refers to exactness, precision, and scrupulous attention to detail. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 22:3, where Paul says he was trained according to the "strictness" of the law. The word was at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite a papyrus from the second century B.C. using the phrase "with all exactness" (μετὰ πάσης ἀκριβείας), showing it was common, practical language for careful, thorough work.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single context.

definition: Last or final—coming at the very end, whether in time, sequence, or rank, or located at the farthest point.
article: ἔσχατος means "last" in nearly every sense: the final one in a series, the latest in time, the lowest in rank, or the most distant in place. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 52 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "last" in 88% of cases (38×), with BSB independently agreeing 97% of the time. Everyday papyri confirm the same range—one Oxyrhynchus document speaks of "the last year" of a lease, exactly matching the temporal sense seen throughout the New Testament. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew אַחֲרוֹן (34×) and אַחֲרִית (28×), both pointing to what comes afterward or at the end.

definition: Martha, the personal name of a woman in the Gospels, sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany.
article: Μάρθα is simply a personal name, appearing 13 times across Luke and John for Martha of Bethany, the sister of Mary and Lazarus. The name is Aramaic in origin (related to a word meaning "mistress" or "lady"), and Strong's identifies her as a Christian woman. Interestingly, the papyri show it was a common everyday name: Moulton-Milligan cite a nursing contract from 14 B.C. and a debt-payment record from 10 B.C. that both name women called Martha, confirming it was in ordinary circulation in Greek-speaking communities.

definition: Deep suffering or wretched misery brought on by calamity, hardship, or distress.
article: ταλαιπωρία describes the wretched condition of someone overwhelmed by suffering or calamity. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both times rendered "misery" (Romans 3:16, quoting the Old Testament, and James 5:1). The Greek Old Testament uses it 27 times, most often to translate the Hebrew word for violent ruin or devastation (שֹׁד, 12×), and an everyday papyrus letter from 113 B.C. uses it of a person who "still continues in the same miserable condition."
caution: Only two New Testament occurrences, so the measured sense rests on thin evidence; classical sources also record an earlier meaning of "hard work" not seen in the biblical data.

definition: To receive something, especially what is due to you, get something back, or take a person aside privately.
article: At its core, ἀπολαμβάνω means to receive—but with shades the simple verb lacks. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times, and translators render it "receive" in just over half the cases (5×, 56%), often with the sense of getting what one deserves or what is owed. The lexica add two narrower senses not separated out in the measured data: receiving something back (as in the prodigal's father getting his son back) and taking someone aside privately—a usage vividly matched in everyday papyri describing recluses "shut up" in the Serapeum temple.
caution: The measured data shows only one dominant sense ("receive"), but the lexica list two further senses—"receive back" and "take aside"—that the corpus counts didn't separate out, so the word's full range is broader than the single measured label suggests.

definition: To prove someone guilty by exposing wrongdoing, often with the implication of conviction or punishment.
article: ἐξελέγχω is an intensified form of ἐλέγχω (to convict or reprove), built with the prefix ἐκ to mean fully proving someone guilty and exposing their wrongdoing. It is essentially absent from the New Testament's main text and appears just once in the Septuagint evidence here; the older Textus Receptus read it in Jude 1:15, where critical editions prefer the simpler ἐλέγχω. The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine documents: papyri and inscriptions use it in legal contexts, such as a 117 B.C. official letter and a Delphi inscription about "those who had committed sacrilege," and a first-century text condemning anyone "proven to have lied."
caution: Evidence is very thin — the word is absent from the Byzantine NT, appears only once in the cited Septuagint data, and its New Testament reading in Jude 1:15 is disputed between manuscript traditions.

definition: To mix or blend things together into a unified whole; figuratively, to combine or join people into agreement.
article: This verb means to mix or blend separate things into one, like compounding ingredients. In its 2 New Testament occurrences it works both ways: God "combines" the body's parts into a unified whole (1 Corinthians 12:24), and in Hebrews 4:2 the sense shifts toward people being "united with" or sharing in something, though translators differ here. The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor in a touching inscription describing a spirit "blended with" a most loving soul, and a bride "united in" auspicious marriage.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and genuine disagreement among manuscripts and translators over the Hebrews 4:2 sense, the precise range is uncertain.

definition: To call someone blessed or fortunate, or to consider them happy.
article: μακαρίζω means to pronounce or regard someone as blessed, happy, or fortunate. In its two New Testament appearances—Luke 1:48 and James 5:11—both are rendered "blessed," and it always takes a person as its object. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri: Moulton-Milligan cites a text where a man born under certain planetary influences "will be called blessed by many," showing the verb's common, non-religious use of calling someone lucky.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the measured evidence for its range is thin.

definition: To stumble or trip, used figuratively to mean failing morally, making a mistake, or falling into sin.
article: πταίω literally means to stumble or trip, and the New Testament uses it figuratively for moral failure or sin. It appears only 5 times in the Byzantine text, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "stumble" 60% of the time; the other two cases involve negated phrases like "never" stumbling. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri too — a sixth-century legal letter uses it to ask whether some workers "made an error or did not," matching this same sense of failing or going wrong.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and the same James 3:2 verse counted under two different sense labels, the measured breakdown reflects translation phrasing more than truly distinct meanings.

definition: To instruct or teach someone, passing on knowledge or giving direction.
article: διδάσκω means to teach or instruct, and that single sense dominates: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "teach" in 88 of 97 occurrences (94%), with another 4× as "began teach" — really just "teach" with a starting verb attached. It covers teaching a person, teaching a thing, or simply teaching in the absolute sense, and the lexica agree completely on this broad range. In the Septuagint it usually stands for the Hebrew לָמַד (learn/teach, 31×); one charming papyrus shows a mother congratulating her son that, having finished his own education, he can now teach children and earn a living into his old age.

definition: An object used for burning incense, understood either as a portable censer or as the altar of incense in the sanctuary.
article: θυμιαστήριον refers to incense equipment, but exactly which piece is genuinely disputed. The word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 9:4, where the Majority text describes Aaron's incense object; older glosses like the KJV render it "censer," while Abbott-Smith notes it can mean the altar of incense, citing Philo and Josephus for that sense. In the Septuagint it occurs just twice (translating Hebrew מִקְטֶ֫רֶת), and the everyday Koine papyri Moulton-Milligan cite point clearly to "censer"—a portable container for burning coals.
caution: Evidence is thin (one NT occurrence, two LXX) and the sources openly disagree on whether it means a portable censer or the fixed altar of incense.

definition: To appoint or choose someone for a role, originally by a show of hands in a vote.
article: χειροτονέω literally means to stretch out the hand, and originally described voting by raised hands in the Athenian assembly, but in everyday Koine it came to mean simply to select or appoint. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 14:23 and 2 Corinthians 8:19), where it covers both appointing without a formal vote and choosing by vote. The papyri show the word still alive in ordinary administrative life — one document from A.D. 192 has a man who "nominated himself" for the urgent office of cosmetes.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a broad range spanning formal voting to plain appointment, the precise sense in any given verse is hard to pin down.

definition: Literally soft to the touch, as with fine clothing; of people it means delicate or effeminate, and in one context refers to a man in a same-sex role.
article: At its core μαλακός means "soft," especially soft to the touch. In its 4 New Testament occurrences it describes fine, soft clothing (Matthew 11:8; Luke 7:25) and, in 1 Corinthians 6:9, is applied to persons in a sense lexicons take as effeminate or sexually so. A striking parallel comes from the papyri: a musician named Zenobius is labeled "ὁ μαλακός" (P. Hib. I.54, c. B.C. 245), which Moulton-Milligan reads in the same sense as the 1 Corinthians usage rather than merely describing his dancing.
caution: The exact force in 1 Corinthians 6:9 is debated, with lexicons noting it probably carries an obscene sense, so the precise meaning of that single occurrence remains uncertain.

definition: In a splendid, lavish way — describing someone living luxuriously, especially feasting in fine, sumptuous style.
article: This adverb describes living splendidly or lavishly, and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 16:19) it pictures the rich man dressing and feasting in luxurious style — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fine" there. The lexica add shades like "sumptuously," "magnificently," and "splendidly," and Abbott-Smith notes it was a common word for rich fare. The papyri and inscriptions back this up, including one describing a councilman who carried out his public offices "splendidly and conspicuously" (λαμπρῶς καὶ ἐπιφανῶς), showing the word's broader sense of doing something with brilliant display.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured biblical range rests on a single verse.

definition: An adverb meaning "ever" at any time, which with a negative becomes "never at all."
article: πώποτε is a small adverb meaning "ever" or "at any time," and when paired with a negative it sharpens into "never at all." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times, all but one in John, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ever" in half the cases and "never" in the rest — the difference comes entirely from whether a negative particle is present. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this: one second-century BC letter says "you would never have seen my face," and another declares that defiled women "shall never at all be pure," matching the New Testament usage closely.
caution: The third "measured sense" listed ("answered Whoever never") is just a fragment of a verse rendering, not a genuine separate meaning, so this word really has only two functions.

definition: To supply or provide something generously, often abundantly, whether God giving or people contributing.
article: This compound verb means to supply or provide, frequently with a sense of generosity or abundance — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "lavish" in two of five occurrences and "supplies" in another. It appears 5 times across 4 New Testament books, with two more occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. A papyrus complaint from around A.D. 30 captures the generous flavor nicely: a man says he "provided for my wife in a manner that exceeded my resources," showing the everyday Koine sense of giving beyond what is required.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and two of them blended into phrasing, the measured English renderings rest on a thin sample.

definition: Maath, a man in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed as one of his distant ancestors.
article: Maath is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament (Luke 3:26), where it falls in the list of Jesus' ancestors between Semei and Josech. It is an indeclinable name of Hebrew origin, and the Septuagint uses a related form twice to render the Hebrew name Machath (מַחַת). Because it is simply a name in a genealogy, it carries no broader meaning or range of usage.
caution: This is a proper name attested only once in the New Testament, so there is little evidence beyond its place in Luke's genealogy.

definition: A theft — either the act of stealing or the thing that has been stolen.
article: κλέμμα refers to theft, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Revelation 9:21, in a list of sins people refused to repent of. The word can mean either the act of stealing or the stolen object itself, and the Septuagint uses it four times to render Hebrew words for both 'stolen thing' and 'theft.' A nice glimpse of its everyday range comes from an inscription where a thief — free man or slave — had to repay 'double the stolen item' (τὸ κλέμμα), showing the 'thing stolen' sense in real legal use.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence — and lexicons split the meaning between the act of theft and the stolen object.

definition: Belonging to or inherited from one's fathers or ancestors.
article: πατρῷος describes something handed down from one's ancestors — a law, custom, or god received from past generations. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Acts, where it always blends into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word (for example, the "law of our fathers"). The everyday papyri show the same usage strikingly: a document from Oxyrhynchus (A.D. 108) speaks of "the ancestral gods" (τοὺς πατρῴους θεούς), exactly matching the phrasing of Acts 24:14.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament uses (all in one book) and 1 in the Septuagint — so confidence is low.

definition: A plow, the farming tool pulled to break up soil for planting.
article: This word names a plow, the basic farm implement for turning soil. It appears just once in the New Testament (Luke 9:62), where it is folded into the phrase rather than translated as a standalone English word, and four times in the Septuagint. The everyday papyri are striking here: business letters and inventories list plows being shipped between people and paired with oxen or yokes, showing this was plain agricultural vocabulary in ordinary Koine life.
caution: Evidence is thin (a single NT use), and the Septuagint Hebrew counterparts listed are pruning and threshing tools rather than a plow, so the cited equivalents look inconsistent.

definition: To be torn away from someone like an orphan separated from a parent, feeling the pain of forced absence.
article: This rare verb pictures the grief of being suddenly cut off from people you love, built from the word for 'orphan.' It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 2:17, where Paul describes being torn away from the believers. The lexicons note the literal sense is being bereaved as of a parent, though one scholar (Field) suggests here it simply means 'having been separated.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force is hard to pin down and the sources differ on whether it means full bereavement or simple separation.

definition: Worthless leftovers fit only for throwing out — garbage, refuse, or dung.
article: σκύβαλον means waste material that gets discarded — refuse, dregs, or specifically dung. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 3:8, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "things" (and BSB agrees), though the underlying force is much stronger and cruder. Moulton-Milligan note it was probably a vulgar street coinage and that everyday Koine papyri (such as P Fay 119, around A.D. 100) illustrate the "dung" sense well; the older lexica (Strong's, KJV, Abbott-Smith) all lean toward "dung" or "refuse."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on a single verse plus outside papyri evidence, and the standard translation softens its blunt original meaning.

definition: A bundle, especially of plants or stalks tied together for handling or storage.
article: δέσμη means a bundle — something bound together, typically stalks or plants. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 13:30, where weeds are tied into bundles to be burned, and once in the Septuagint, where it renders a Hebrew word at Exodus 12:22 (the sources cited differ on which Hebrew word — מַשְׁקוֹף or אֲגֻדָּה). The everyday papyri make the meaning vivid and concrete: documents order specific quantities of "bundles" of hay and fodder, showing this was common commercial Koine vocabulary for tied loads.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the digest's measured rendering of "grow" does not match the lexicons' agreed meaning of "bundle," so treat the measured sense with care.

definition: A situation that tests a person, whether an enticement to sin or a hardship sent to prove one's faith.
article: πειρασμός covers a spectrum from outright temptation to sin to a neutral or even positive testing of character. In the Byzantine NT the Majority Standard Bible renders it "temptation" 9 times (47%), "trials" 6 times (32%), and "testing" twice (11%), so the same word swings between enticement and proving. One striking detail: Moulton-Milligan note the word is essentially confined to Biblical Greek, with a rare medical use in Dioscorides for "trials" of drugs to test their effect — and a scholar even proposed that "the temptation" in Galatians 4:14 might mean the devil himself.
caution: Whether a given occurrence means "temptation to sin" or a faith-proving "trial" depends on context, since the Greek word itself does not distinguish the two.

definition: To gain or win something or someone, whether by making a profit or by drawing a person over.
article: κερδαίνω means to gain—either turning a profit on goods or talents, or winning a person over, such as an unbelieving spouse or a brother who has sinned. Its range stretches from the commercial (gaining money or the whole world) to the personal (winning people to faith), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "win" 6 times (55%) and "gained" twice (18%).
