An everyday Oxyrhynchus papyrus even shows someone asking an oracle whether they will "profit by the transaction," confirming how ordinary this commercial sense was; meanwhile Acts 27:21 stretches the word to mean avoiding or being spared a loss.
caution: In about 5 of 16 occurrences the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing without its own English word, so the rendering counts only partly reflect its full use.

definition: To uncover or disclose something hidden, especially to make known a truth or person that was previously concealed.
article: At its root ἀποκαλύπτω means "to take off the cover" — to uncover or disclose. The Byzantine NT uses it 26 times, and over half (54%) are simply rendered "revealed," most often of God making known truths, persons, or his purposes. It's worth noting how concrete the word stays in everyday Koine: papyri from the second and third centuries use it of farmland that becomes "uncovered" along the shore and can then be leased and sown. In the Septuagint it appears 74 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew גָּלָה (60×), which likewise means to uncover or expose.

definition: Joel, the Hebrew prophet whose words are quoted in the New Testament.
article: This is simply the personal name Joel, an indeclinable Greek form borrowed from the Hebrew יוֹאֵל. It appears just once in the New Testament, where Peter quotes the prophet Joel in Acts 2:16. In the Septuagint it shows up 23 times across 6 books, and interestingly, while it usually renders the name יוֹאֵל (19 times), in a few places it stands in for other Hebrew words entirely, including בָּרִיחַ, יְעִיאֵל, and שְׁמָעָה.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, this entry rests on very thin direct evidence, though its meaning as a proper name is not in doubt.

definition: To fill something or someone completely, or by extension to satisfy a need, hunger, or desire.
article: At its core ἐμπίπλημι means to fill up completely, and from there it stretches to mean satisfying hunger or desire — like filling the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53). The New Testament uses are few (5 times in the Byzantine text, none in the SBL critical text), and the renderings range widely: "filled," "wasted" (John 6:12), and "enjoyed" (Romans 15:24, taking one's fill of someone's company). The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 129 times, usually translating Hebrew מָלֵא ("to fill," 40 times) and שָׂבַע ("to be satisfied," 40 times); everyday papyri use it plainly, as in an instruction to fill a jar with salted fish.
caution: The English renderings vary quite a bit across only a handful of occurrences, so the figurative senses ("wasted," "enjoyed") rest on single examples each.

definition: The way a person lives — their manner of life or conduct over time.
article: βίωσις refers to someone's manner of life — how a person actually lives and conducts themselves. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:4, where Paul speaks of the life he had led from his youth. The most telling outside evidence is a Jewish inscription from about A.D. 60–80 honoring people for their virtuous βίωσις, and the word also shows up in the Prologue to Sirach summarizing the practical goal of living by the law.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering ('Surely') looks like a data mismatch — the lexica consistently define it as 'manner of life.'

definition: Water falling from the sky as rain, especially a shower that waters crops and land.
article: ὑετός simply means rain — water falling from the sky — and that is what it means in all six New Testament occurrences. The various Majority Standard Bible renderings ("rain," "rain crop," "fall rains") are just contextual variations on this one idea, such as the "fall rains" of James 5:7 or the rain that produces a crop in Hebrews 6:7. In the Septuagint it appears 71 times, usually translating the Hebrew words for rain, and Moulton-Milligan notes a striking parallel: an Athenian prayer asking Zeus to "rain upon the cornland," which echoes the agricultural rain-and-crop imagery of Hebrews 6:7.
caution: With only six occurrences, the listed "senses" are really one core meaning split by translation context rather than distinct meanings.

definition: A birthday celebration or feast held in someone's honor.
article: γενέσια refers to a birthday feast or celebration, appearing only twice in the New Testament, both describing Herod's birthday (Matthew 14:6 and Mark 6:21). Interestingly, in classical Attic Greek the word originally meant a commemoration of the dead, while a living person's birthday feast was γενέθλια; but this distinction faded in later Greek, and in the everyday papyri γενέσια always means a birthday feast. One papyrus even orders fish be sent for someone's birthday celebration, showing how ordinary the word was in daily Koine life.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the New Testament, both referring to the same kind of event, so its full range rests largely on outside sources.

definition: The status of belonging to a state, or the commonwealth one belongs to—one's citizenship.
article: πολίτευμα refers to citizenship—the status and rights of belonging to a political community, or by extension the commonwealth itself. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 3:20, where the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB both render it "citizenship" (the older KJV used "conversation," reflecting an outdated sense of conduct or way of life). Everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions back this up: a decree of King Philip (219 BC) uses related terms about granting πολιτεία—citizen status—to resident Greeks, showing the word's grounding in real civic life. Note that lexicons such as Abbott-Smith list a wider range, including "a form of government" and "community/commonwealth."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and lexicons disagree on whether it means "citizenship" or "commonwealth/community," so the single measured rendering rests on thin evidence.

definition: Beyond, farther out; pointing to places or regions lying past a given boundary.
article: ὑπερέκεινα is an adverb meaning "beyond" or "farther out," and in the New Testament it functions as a preposition taking the genitive — "the regions beyond you" (2 Corinthians 10:16). It is rare: it appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "regions" and the Berean Standard Bible independently agrees 100%. Built from ὑπέρ ("over, beyond") plus the neuter plural of ἐκεῖνος ("those"), it literally points to "those parts beyond," and Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs just once in the New Testament and is otherwise limited to papyri and ecclesiastical writers, so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: Lucius, the personal name of one or two early Christians mentioned in the New Testament.
article: Λούκιος is a Latin personal name, Lucius, that appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament and is rendered "Lucius" in every instance. One bearer is among the church leaders at Antioch (Acts 13:1), said by some to be from Cyrene, and another is a companion of Paul sending greetings (Romans 16:21). Interestingly, the papyri and inscriptions usually show the related spelling Λεύκιος, which scholars connect to the genuine Greek word λευκός ("white"), suggesting the Latin name was sometimes reshaped to resemble a native Greek one.
caution: Evidence is thin (only two occurrences) and it remains debated whether the two Lucius references point to the same person, or even to Luke the evangelist.

definition: To have, hold, or possess something—whether in your hand, on your body, in your circumstances, or as an ability or condition.
article: This is one of the most common verbs in the Greek New Testament, appearing 708 times, and it covers an enormous range from physically holding something in your hand to wearing clothing, being pregnant, or simply being in some condition. Strikingly, in 692 of those 708 cases the word disappears into English phrasing—'have' blends into expressions like 'be able,' 'be with child,' or 'keep'—so it almost never gets its own standalone English word. The classical lexica back up this breadth, listing dozens of constructions; in the Septuagint it even renders the Hebrew word for 'beside' or 'next to' (אֵ֫צֶל) 23 times, reflecting how flexibly it could express relation and nearness.
caution: Because the verb is so often absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word, its meaning depends heavily on context and construction rather than the verb alone.

definition: The office, rule, or period of authority held by a governing official such as a ruler or governor.
article: ἡγεμονία refers to rule, sovereignty, or the official term of a governing authority. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 3:1, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it in connection with a ruler's reign (the BSB independently agrees). The papyri make its everyday sense vivid: documents from Roman Egypt use it for the office or 'praefecture' of a prefect, as in a phrase praising the 'delightful praefecture of Larcius Memor.' In the Septuagint it shows up only 3 times, where it translates Hebrew words for a tribal 'standard' or banner (דֶּגֶל) and for a clan chief (חֹרִי).
caution: With just one New Testament occurrence and only 3 in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, so this single sense should be held loosely.

definition: Lysanias, the man named in Luke 3:1 as ruler (tetrarch) of the region of Abilene.
article: Lysanias is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:1, where he is identified as the tetrarch of Abilene during the time of John the Baptist. Although the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering shows "Trachonitis," the lexical sources (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all treat the word straightforwardly as the personal name of a governor of Abilene. A notable piece of evidence comes from an inscription found at Abila, the capital of Abilene, which mentions a "Lysanias the tetrarch," though scholars cannot determine for certain which Lysanias is meant.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and the inscriptional evidence cannot confirm which historical Lysanias is intended.

definition: A sandal or shoe — a sole tied or bound under the foot.
article: ὑπόδημα literally means something bound under the foot, which in practice was a sandal or shoe. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, half rendered simply as "sandals"; the other occurrences cluster in phrases about being unworthy to untie or carry someone's sandals. The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: papyri mention paying for shoes and even asking a friend to send some, and one inscription forbids bringing shoes into a sacred enclosure. In the Septuagint it appears 24 times, usually translating the Hebrew נָ֫עַל (na'al).
caution: The second and third measured "senses" are really fragments of the same sandal-untying expression, not distinct meanings.

definition: The physical need for water; the dry, uncomfortable craving caused by lack of drink.
article: δίψος simply means thirst, the bodily craving for water. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:27, where Paul lists it among his hardships alongside hunger and sleeplessness, but it is more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 13 times and usually translates the Hebrew word for thirst (צָמָא, 9 times). Interestingly, δίψος is a later form of the older word δίψα, and the Septuagint uses the two interchangeably, sometimes within the same passage—Wisdom 11 even swaps between them.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured.

definition: A splitting into opposing sides; division or discord that breaks apart unity.
article: διαμερισμός describes a division that splits people into opposing camps, the opposite of peace (εἰρήνη). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 12:51, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as a division Jesus brings rather than peace—a rendering the Berean Standard Bible and KJV both share. The Septuagint uses it just 3 times across 2 books, translating one Hebrew word for an allotted portion or division (מַחֲלֹקֶת in Ezekiel 48:29) and another that elsewhere means siege or distress.
caution: Evidence is thin—a single New Testament occurrence and only three Septuagint uses—so the full range of meaning cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: Describing something as genuine, real, and corresponding to what it truly claims to be.
article: ἀληθινός means "true" not just in the sense of "correct" but in the sense of real, genuine, and authentic — the thing that lives up to its name. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "true" in 24 of its 27 Byzantine occurrences (96%), and the meaning is remarkably stable. In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew אֱמֶת ("truth/faithfulness"), though it also covers words for "complete" (שָׁלֵם), "blameless" (תָּם), and "innocent" (נָקִי), showing it can shade toward wholeness and integrity as well as factual truth.

definition: Refers to a different or additional person or thing, often the second of a pair or one set apart from others.
article: ἕτερος points to something or someone other than what's already mentioned — sometimes a different kind of thing, sometimes simply the second of two. Across its 98 New Testament occurrences it is rendered "other" 38 times (42%) and "another" 30 times (33%), with smaller groups translated "one," "else," or "someone." Originally this word strictly marked duality (the second of a pair) as opposed to ἄλλος, and the papyri confirm this careful usage — one document uses it to request "a second ass" — though by New Testament times it was already drifting toward the broader sense of "another." In the Septuagint it appears 187 times, mostly translating the Hebrew אַחֵר, "other."
caution: The line between ἕτερος ("the second of a pair") and ἄλλος ("another in general") was already blurring in Koine, so the precise force can be uncertain in individual verses.

definition: The number three thousand.
article: Τρισχίλιοι simply means "three thousand," a compound built from τρίς ("three times") and χίλιοι ("a thousand"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 2:41, where about three thousand people were added to the church, and shows up 21 times across 11 books of the Septuagint, where it usually renders the Hebrew word for "thousand." The word is well attested far beyond the Bible, going back as early as Homer's Iliad.
caution: The single Byzantine occurrence was tagged as "embraced" in the measured data, which conflicts with the actual meaning "three thousand" given by every lexicon, so treat that label as a data artifact.

definition: A personal name borne by a Corinthian Christian whose visit, with two others, cheered the apostle Paul.
article: Ἀχαϊκός is a proper name, mentioned just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 16:17, where Achaicus is one of three Corinthian believers whose arrival encouraged Paul. The name derives from Ἀχαΐα, the Greek region of Achaia, so it effectively means "the Achaian" or "man from Achaia." Both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible simply transliterate it as the personal name in every instance, and the lexica (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree it refers to this individual Christian.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its usage rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To practice divination or fortune-telling, claiming to foretell the future through pagan or supernatural means.
article: This verb means to tell fortunes or practice divination, and in the Bible it always carries a negative ring. It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 16:16), where the Majority Standard Bible and Berean Standard Bible both render it as "divination." In the Septuagint it shows up 12 times across 6 books, usually translating the Hebrew קָסַם (9×) and always describing lying prophets or forbidden practices; interestingly, the everyday papyri preserve a more neutral sense, as in a Thessalian inscription about people consulting an oracle of Apollo.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament, with only a single occurrence to measure.

definition: A split-second moment, as quick as the blink of an eye.
article: ῥιπή names an extremely brief moment, the time it takes to blink—every one of its single New Testament uses (1 Corinthians 15:52) is rendered "instant," matching the famous KJV phrase "twinkling of an eye." The word comes from ῥίπτω ("to throw"), and in classical Greek it covered any rapid movement: a thrown javelin, a rush of wind or flame, the flapping of wings, the flicker of lights. Notably, some manuscripts (D*EFG and others) read the similar-looking ῥοπή instead, a word meaning the tipping or turn of a balance-scale, which everyday Koine papyri use for "a moment" or to tip the scales in someone's favor.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and several manuscripts substitute the similar word ῥοπή, so the textual reading is disputed.

definition: A flute or pipe, a wind instrument played by blowing.
article: αὐλός is a wind instrument — a flute or pipe — that produces sound when air is blown through it, fitting its likely derivation from a root meaning "to blow." In the New Testament it appears just once, in 1 Corinthians 14:7, where Paul lists it alongside other instruments. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew חָלִיל (chalil), itself a pipe or flute. The word was also common in everyday Koine, turning up in papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Note the measured NT rendering shows up as "lifeless," reflecting how the surrounding verse is translated rather than the instrument itself; with only one NT occurrence the evidence is thin.

definition: Antipas, a Christian man and martyr at Pergamum named once in Revelation.
article: Ἀντίπας is a personal name, appearing only once in the New Testament (Revelation 2:13), where it identifies a faithful witness who was killed at Pergamum. The name is a contracted form of the longer name Antipatros, built from the elements meaning "against" and "father," and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. Interestingly, an inscription at Pergamum uses the full form Antipatros, which suggests that later resident was probably not named after the martyr.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage rests on a single passage.

definition: Hard, wearisome labor that wears a person out, often paired with physical hardship and exhaustion.
article: μόχθος means strenuous, tiring labor—the kind of work that leaves you worn out. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Paul's letters, where it sits alongside related words for effort and hardship. In the Septuagint it shows up 39 times and most often translates the Hebrew עָמָל (24×), a word for toil and trouble; the everyday papyri use it the same way, including a dream-omen text where a quivering leg signals "threats and labor" for slaves. The two measured senses reflect translation choices in specific verses rather than truly distinct meanings—both center on toil.
caution: Confidence is low: with only 3 New Testament occurrences, the split between "toil" and "food toil" reflects context-specific wording rather than two genuinely separate senses.

definition: To stay awake or spend the entire night doing something, such as praying.
article: This verb means to pass the whole night doing something, built from "through" (διά) and "night" (νύξ). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:12, where Jesus spends the whole night in prayer, and once in the Greek Old Testament (Job 2:9). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, including a copy of a history of the Trojan War, showing it was ordinary vocabulary rather than specifically religious language.
caution: With only one New Testament use and one Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: To conduct oneself or live in a certain way; also literally to overturn or turn back and return.
article: At its root ἀναστρέφω means to turn something over or turn back, but in the New Testament it most often shifts to a moral sense: how a person lives and behaves. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "lived" twice (40%), while six of its eleven occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing without a single English word. In the Septuagint it appears 92 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew שׁוּב ("return," 39×), and Moulton-Milligan note that the "behave, conduct oneself" sense shows up in everyday papyri and inscriptions, so no Semitic borrowing is needed to explain it.
caution: The word's range is wide — from "overturn" to "return" to "live" — and most New Testament occurrences are absorbed into phrasing rather than mapped to one clear English sense.

definition: The left side or left hand, often used to describe positions opposite the right.
article: εὐώνυμος almost always means "left" in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 6 of its 10 occurrences and one occurrence simply gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The literal parts mean "good-named" or "of good omen," and this was actually a polite substitute for the ordinary word for "left" (ἀριστερός), apparently to soften the unlucky associations the left side carried for ancient Greeks. The most striking evidence comes from a fifth-century inscription from Ephesus about reading omens from birds: a bird raising its εὐώνυμος (left) wing carried meaning in augury, which fits the word's original sense of "good omen." In the Septuagint it appears 17 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "left" (שְׂמֹאול, 14 times).

definition: Free from blame or fault; deserving no criticism.
article: ἀμώμητος describes someone or something that is free from blame or fault, with the negative prefix turning the idea of finding fault into its opposite. In its 2 New Testament uses it is rendered "blameless" 100% of the time (Philippians 2:15 and 2 Peter 3:14). Interestingly, the word turns up in everyday Koine epitaphs found in the papyri, where it praises a small child and a young man who died prematurely as "blameless," showing it functioned as ordinary heartfelt language, not just a moral or theological term.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament occurrences (with one being a single critical-text reading), so the measured range is narrow.

definition: Lacking wisdom; foolish or unwise in how one lives.
article: ἄσοφος means "unwise" or "foolish," formed by adding the negative prefix "a-" to σοφός ("wise"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 5:15, where it contrasts how believers should and should not walk. Outside the Bible it shows up in everyday Koine: a third-century papyrus (P Ryl II.62) uses it for someone "unskilled in wisdom," pointing to a sense of lacking practical skill as well as good judgment.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: A solemn promise made to God (a vow), or a prayer offered to him.
article: εὐχή covers two closely related ideas: a vow or solemn promise made to God, and a prayer addressed to him. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 3 times, split evenly between vow-related uses (Acts 18:18; 21:23) and prayer (James 5:15). The Septuagint heavily favors the 'vow' sense, using εὐχή to translate the Hebrew neder (vow) 48 times; everyday Koine papyri, by contrast, often use it simply for 'prayer,' as when a mother writes that her son's wellbeing is her whole εὐχή.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a label like "advise There taken" reflecting a phrase rather than a clean gloss, the measured split between 'vow' and 'prayer' rests on very thin evidence.

definition: One who rescues or delivers, used in the New Testament as a title for God and for Christ.
article: σωτήρ means a savior or deliverer, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Savior" in 21 of its 23 New Testament occurrences (91%). It applies both to God (as in Luke 1:47) and to Christ (as in John 4:42, where he is called "Savior of the world"). The most striking background comes from the papyri and inscriptions: the title σωτήρ was routinely given to the Ptolemaic kings and Roman emperors, so calling Jesus "Savior" carried a pointed contrast with these rulers.

definition: A preposition meaning "on account of" or "for the sake of," pointing to the reason or cause for something.
article: This little connecting word links an action to its reason or motive, most naturally translated "for the sake of" or "on account of." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 26 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it variously — "for" (5×), "for sake" (4×), and so on — while 6 times it simply dissolves into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. It is far more common in the Septuagint (119 times in 22 books), where it most often stands in for the Hebrew עֲבוּר ("because of," 13×) and מַ֫עַן ("for the sake of," 10×); everyday papyri use it the same way, as in an Oxyrhynchus letter saying "I do this not on account of us but on account of the camel-drivers."
caution: Several measured "senses" (like "whoever wills it" and "will give account") reflect the surrounding clause rather than the word itself, so the labels overstate its actual range, which is consistently just "on account of."

definition: To travel away from home, especially to a distant or foreign country, leaving for an extended absence.
article: ἀποδημέω describes leaving home to travel abroad, often to a far country and for a long while. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times across 3 books and always carries this travel sense, rendered either simply as "went" (3×) or as "went on a journey" (2×). The everyday papyri show the word was common business and personal language: one third-century BC letter has someone writing "I am on the point of departure," and a marriage contract pairs it neatly with its opposite, "staying at home and going abroad" (ἐνδημῶν καὶ ἀποδημῶν).

definition: A weed that closely resembles wheat as it grows but is worthless, also known as darnel or tares.
article: Ζιζάνιον refers to a weed—commonly called darnel or tares—that looks much like wheat while growing, making it hard to tell apart until harvest. The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, all clustered in Jesus' parable of the wheat and the weeds, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "weeds" in every measured case. Interestingly, this is a borrowed Semitic word (appearing as זוּנִין in the Talmud), and Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, confirming it was an ordinary agricultural term.
caution: The word's range is narrow and tied almost entirely to one parable, and its ultimate origin is uncertain.

definition: To cross over or pass from one place to another, often across a body of water or boundary.
senseLabels: to cross over or pass through
article: διαβαίνω means to step across or cross over, often a river, sea, or boundary, built from διά ("through") plus the base meaning "step." In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 118 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew verb עָבַר ("to pass over"), 102 of those times. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, and everyday papyri use it the same way—one document urges someone to "go over to Dionysias and find out," the same construction with εἰς that we see in Acts 16:9.

definition: A flood or surge of water, whether from a river or the sea, that rises and overwhelms.
article: πλήμμυρα refers to a flood — a rising surge of water from a river or sea — and appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 6:48, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "deep" in describing a flood striking a house. It shows up just once in the Septuagint, where it translates a Hebrew word in Job, and the lexicons consistently gloss it as "flood." Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri use the related verb to describe the flooding of the Nile, and one inscription praises a Roman official for making Egypt "overflow with all good things."
caution: This word is a single occurrence in the New Testament with thin overall evidence, so its measured range rests on one verse.

definition: A small portable case or money-box used for carrying coins or valuables.
article: In the New Testament γλωσσόκομον means a money-box — both times it appears (John 12:6 and 13:29) it refers to the bag Judas kept and managed for Jesus' group, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "bag" in 100% of cases. The Septuagint uses it more broadly for a chest or box, translating the Hebrew word for the ark (אָרוֹן). The most striking detail is its forgotten origin: the word literally named a case for holding the reeds or mouthpieces ("tongues") of flute-like instruments, but by Koine times that sense had vanished and only the idea of a small, portable container remained, as everyday papyri confirm.
caution: Confidence is rated low because the word appears only twice in the New Testament, though its meaning there is consistent and well supported by Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: To wrap clothing around someone, so as to dress or clothe a person, or to be wearing a garment.
article: At its root περιβάλλω means to throw something around, and in the New Testament it almost always describes wrapping a garment about a person — being dressed, clothed, or wearing something. All 24 Byzantine occurrences cluster around clothing, rendered "dressed" (47%), "clothed" (29%), or "wearing" (24%), and the Majority Standard and Berean translations agree completely. The wider sense survives elsewhere: Strong's notes it can mean to surround with a palisade, and a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses it for building enclosing walls around a vineyard, while another describes a man stripped of "the garment in which I was clothed."
caution: The siege-wall sense appears in lexica and papyri but not in the measured New Testament senses, where the meaning is consistently about clothing.

definition: To weigh down, burden, or oppress someone or something, whether physically heavy or figuratively troubled.
article: βαρύνω means to weigh down or burden, used both literally for physical heaviness and figuratively for being oppressed or troubled. It appears 38 times in the Septuagint but never in the Byzantine New Testament; in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew כָּבַד (25 times), the verb behind the idea of being heavy or weighty. The everyday papyri capture its emotional sense vividly — one writer says he is 'excessively vexed,' and another complains 'I am very much annoyed by him.'
caution: Sources note this classical verb was steadily replaced by βαρέω, so it does not appear in the New Testament except in a compound and a disputed reading at Luke 21:34.

definition: To block, hinder, or get in the way of someone's progress or actions.
article: ἐγκόπτω means to impede or hold someone back, getting in their way. The picture behind it is literally cutting into something, like breaking up a road to make it impassable, which then became a figure for hindering someone's progress. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and translations consistently land on "hinder" or "obstruct" — in Galatians 5:7 someone obstructs believers from obeying, and in 1 Thessalonians 2:18 Paul says Satan tried to block his coming.
caution: Translations agree the core sense is "hinder," but with only 5 occurrences and 2 absorbed into phrasing, the evidence is thin.

definition: To deeply disturb or agitate someone, throwing them into alarm or confusion.
article: This verb describes being thoroughly shaken or agitated, with a sense of alarm — the Latin equivalent is perturbare, 'to throw into confusion.' It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 1:29, where Mary is deeply disturbed by the angel's greeting. Abbott-Smith notes it also turns up in the Septuagint at 3 Kings (1 Kings) 20:43, so its use is extremely sparse across the biblical corpus.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and very thin attestation overall, the precise force of this word cannot be confirmed from biblical usage alone.

definition: An outer tunic or coat worn over other clothing.
article: ἐπενδύτης refers to an outer garment, a tunic or coat worn over one's other clothes. It appears just once in the New Testament, at John 21:7, where Peter puts it on before jumping into the water, and the word is so embedded in the phrasing there that it gets no distinct English word of its own. In its single Septuagint appearance it renders the Hebrew פַּסִּים, though the lexicon Abbott-Smith notes manuscript instances where it instead translates מְעִיל (a robe or mantle).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint use, the precise type of garment intended remains uncertain.

definition: The quality of remaining calm and forbearing over a long time, especially when wronged or facing trouble.
article: μακροθυμία describes a steady, long-lasting patience—the willingness to hold back anger and endure difficulties without giving up. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 14 times and is rendered "patience" in 11 of them (79%), with the lexicons adding "longsuffering" and "forbearance" as close partners; it is used both of human endurance and of God's forbearance toward people. A vivid glimpse of its force comes from a papyrus fragment of the Apocalypse of Baruch, where wrath is said to be "restrained by long-suffering as it were by a rein"—patience pictured as a bridle holding anger in check.

definition: To brace a ship by passing cables around the hull to hold it together in rough seas.
senseLabels: to undergird or brace a ship
article: This is a nautical term meaning to wrap a ship with cables or ropes to strengthen its hull against storm damage, a procedure sailors called 'frapping.' It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as 'crew' undergirding the ship in a storm. The wider Koine evidence is broader than this single sense: the related noun ὑποζώνη simply means a girdle or belt, showing up in everyday papyri lists of household items, and the Septuagint uses the verb at 2 Maccabees 3:19 of women girding themselves beneath the breasts.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its specialized nautical meaning rests on a single passage.

definition: A physical chain or shackle binding a prisoner, or figuratively any bond or restraint that holds something fast.
article: δεσμόν refers to the physical chains or shackles that hold a prisoner, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "chains" in 13 of its 20 New Testament appearances (76%), with BSB independently agreeing 77% of the time. The word stretches beyond literal fetters into figurative bonds — the Septuagint uses it 36 times across 19 books, translating several Hebrew words including עֲבֹת (8×) and מוֹסֵר (7×). The most striking example is "the bond of the tongue" in Mark 7:35: Moulton-Milligan notes this had a technical sense rooted in the old belief that a person could be bound by demonic forces, so loosening it meant more than restoring speech.

definition: An action, deed, or thing done; in the plural often someone's practices or conduct, and sometimes a role or function.
article: πρᾶξις means simply something done — an act or deed — and across its 6 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it three ways: as "deeds" (Rom 8:13), as deeds tied to magic (Acts 19:18), and as a "function" or role (Rom 12:4). Notice that the same noun stretches from a single action to ongoing practices to the job a body part performs, and in 3 of its 6 uses it gets absorbed into phrasing without its own English word. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one fourth-century dream manual says that if both of a woman's legs quiver it denotes πράξεις, "great achievements," and travel — the very word that titles the book of Acts ("Acts of the Apostles").
caution: With only 6 occurrences spread thinly across senses, the line between "deeds," "wicked practices," and "function" rests on context rather than the word itself.

definition: Tamar, an Old Testament woman who bore Perez and Zerah by Judah and appears in Jesus' genealogy.
article: Θάμαρ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Tamar, borne by the woman who became mother of Perez and Zerah through Judah. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:3, where she is one of the few women named in Jesus' genealogy. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times across 3 books, almost always rendering Hebrew תָּמָר (7×), with one instance instead standing for שֵׁלָה.
caution: The measured sense is labeled "father," which reflects how the surrounding genealogy was tagged rather than the name itself; Θάμαρ is simply the personal name Tamar.

definition: To dig or break through a wall to burglarize a house.
article: This vivid verb literally means "to dig through," picturing a burglar tunneling through the mud-brick wall of a house to rob it. In all four New Testament uses it describes thieves breaking in to steal, whether by daylight against stored treasure (Matthew 6:19–20) or under cover of night (Matthew 24:43, Luke 12:39). The everyday reality behind the word shows up in the papyri: a document from 260 B.C. uses the exact same phrasing, reporting that someone "broke into a house," and in the Septuagint it consistently renders the Hebrew חָתַר, "to dig through."

definition: Describing a person who stirs up division or factions within a community.
article: αἱρετικός describes someone who causes division or forms factions, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Titus 3:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "divisive" and the BSB agrees 100%. Although the KJV famously translated it "heretic," the single measured occurrence points to a divisive or factious person rather than someone holding wrong doctrine. Interestingly, the classical lexicon (Abbott-Smith) preserves an older sense, "capable of choosing," found in Plato, alongside the later meaning of "causing division."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a noticeable gap between the classical sense ("capable of choosing") and the later factional sense, confidence is low.

definition: To hand over or deliver something, such as presenting a letter or document to its intended recipient.
article: ἀναδίδωμι means to hand over or deliver, built from ἀνά and δίδωμι ("to give"). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 23:33, where soldiers deliver a letter to the governor — though the digest's measured rendering oddly shows "horsemen," which reflects the surrounding verse rather than the verb itself. The papyri show this was an everyday word: Moulton-Milligan note it was the regular term for presenting an official list of well-to-do citizens, while Abbott-Smith adds an older sense of plants "giving forth" or sending up shoots.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured "horsemen" rendering does not match the verb's actual meaning, so the corpus evidence here is thin and likely mislabeled.

definition: The pay, wages, or provision-money given for work or service, originally a soldier's rations and stipend.
article: ὀψώνιον means the pay or wages owed for service, and it carries a military flavor from its origins—the rations and stipend given to soldiers. Across its 4 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it around the idea of serving or wages, as when John the Baptist tells soldiers to be content with their wages (Luke 3:14) and when Paul declares that the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). A nice historical detail: Moulton-Milligan note this word was "banned by the Atticists" as too colloquial, yet it became very common in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Polybius even records soldiers receiving two obols a day as their ὀψώνιον.
caution: With only 4 occurrences the sense breakdown rests on thin data, though the lexicons agree closely on its meaning.

definition: To hear something but refuse to heed it, ignoring or disobeying what was said.
article: παρακούω literally means to hear alongside or imperfectly, but in everyday Koine it came to mean hearing without heeding — that is, ignoring or disobeying. The Majority Bible renders both Byzantine occurrences in terms of refusal (in Matthew 18:17, refusing to listen to the church), and the everyday papyri back this up nicely: one ancient letter pleads that the recipient "no longer ignore us, so that we don't turn friendship into enmity." In the Septuagint it appears 5 times across two books, often paired with negatives to mean disregard or take no heed, while the classical lexica also note an older sense of simply overhearing or mishearing.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 Byzantine occurrences — and the lexica list an older "overhear/mishear" sense not found in the measured New Testament data.

definition: To point something out or make it known, often by giving a sign or hint about how something will happen.
article: σημαίνω means to indicate, signify, or make something known—sometimes by giving a sign or hint. In the New Testament's 6 occurrences across 3 books, the Berean translators rendered it as "indicate" in two cases (each 50% of the explicitly translated uses), while the other 4 were folded into the surrounding phrasing. It's an ordinary, well-attested Koine word: everyday papyri from the second century B.C. onward use it for sending word or signaling news through letters, as when one writer says he had "decided to indicate it by letter."
caution: With only 6 occurrences and 4 of them absorbed into phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word, the measured English sense data is thin.

definition: Paphos, a city at the western end of the island of Cyprus.
senseLabels: the city of Paphos in Cyprus
article: Paphos is a place name, a city at the western end of Cyprus. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 13, marking points in Paul's first missionary journey: arriving at Paphos (Acts 13:6) and sailing on from there (Acts 13:13). The lexicons agree completely that it simply names this Cyprian city, and Strong's notes only its location.
caution: This word occurs just twice and is a proper place name, so its sole meaning is fixed but the evidence base is small.

definition: The liquid that flows from the eyes when a person weeps, whether from sorrow, joy, or distress.
article: δάκρυ simply means "tears" — the drops that come from crying — and every one of its 11 New Testament appearances is rendered that way. The range is narrow and stable: in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew דִּמְעָה ("tears," 13 times), and it shows up in everyday Koine letters too, including one papyrus where a wronged writer says the outrage done to him "would have been tears for you to read" had he set it down. Grammatically the word is a little quirky — the dative plural δάκρυσιν (used in Luke 7:38, 44) belongs to the alternate form δάκρυον, which papyrus scholars note must be kept distinct.

definition: A covered walkway lined with columns, like a roofed porch or colonnade attached to a building.
article: A στοά is a roofed walkway supported by columns — a colonnade or covered porch, often running along the edge of a larger structure. In the New Testament all 4 uses describe such a feature in the Jerusalem temple, and half of them name the famous "Solomon's Colonnade" specifically; older translations like the KJV simply render it "porch." The everyday papyri confirm how ordinary this word was: it shows up describing public colonnades and porticoes in marketplaces and buildings, including an edict of Caracalla "published at Babylon under the public colonnade."

definition: A tanner, a worker who turns animal hides into leather.
article: βυρσεύς simply means a tanner, someone who processes animal hides into leather. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts and all referring to one person—Simon the tanner, in whose house Peter stayed. Abbott-Smith notes it is a later form of the older word βυρσοδέψης, and the everyday Koine papyri confirm the trade: one document even mentions "the hunch-backed tanner."
caution: All three New Testament occurrences refer to the same person, so the word's range is narrow but its single meaning is well attested.

definition: A unit of ten thousand, or, by extension, a vast and countless multitude.
article: μυριάς literally names a specific number—ten thousand—but it stretches naturally to mean an immense, uncountable crowd. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "myriads" 6 times (67%) for huge numbers and "thousand(s)" twice (22%), as in Acts 19:19 and 21:20. Everyday Koine papyri keep the precise sense alive: one tax document prices 20,000 papyrus stalks as "two myriads," while a later Christian amulet uses it for the looser "countless" idea. In the Septuagint it appears 24 times, usually translating the Hebrew רְבָבָה.

definition: A person from the city of Antioch.
article: Ἀντιοχεύς simply means a native or inhabitant of Antioch, the city whose name it is built from. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:5, describing Nicolas, one of the seven chosen to serve. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) agree completely that it means "an Antiochian"; the word is a straightforward demonym with no contested range.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: A blow or slap delivered to the face with the open hand.
article: ῥάπισμα is a slap or blow struck to the face with the open hand, derived from the verb ῥαπίζω. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in scenes of Jesus being struck during his trial, and once in the Septuagint where it renders the Hebrew word for spitting (רֹק). One notable wrinkle: the phrase in Mark 14:65 is genuinely difficult, with translators divided over whether the blows were struck with rods or with open hands—Swete renders it "they caught Him with blows."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 NT uses) and the rendering in Mark 14:65 is disputed, so the precise force of "slap" versus a more general "blow" is uncertain.

definition: Mary, a personal name borne by several women in the New Testament, most notably the mother of Jesus.
article: Μαρία is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Miriam, and it is rendered "Mary" in 52 of its 54 Byzantine occurrences (98%). The same name is carried by at least six different women in the New Testament, including the mother of Jesus, Mary Magdalene, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, and a Christian woman Paul greets in Rome. In the Septuagint it usually translates מִרְיָם (14 times) but once stands in for a different Hebrew name, יוֹכֶ֫בֶד (Jochebed), and an Egyptian ostracon from A.D. 116 records a real "Mary, daughter of Abietas," showing the name in everyday Jewish use.

definition: To beat someone with a rod, especially as the Roman form of physical punishment.
article: This verb comes from ῥάβδος, a rod or staff, and means to beat someone with a rod. In both of its New Testament appearances (Acts 16:22 and 2 Corinthians 11:25) it describes the Roman punishment of beating with rods, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way 100% of the time. Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri use the same word for threshing grain — one document from A.D. 40 has workers "threshing out" loads of anise — and the Septuagint applies it the same agricultural way, translating the Hebrew word for beating out grain in passages like Judges 6:11 and Ruth 2:17.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a confidence tier rated low, the evidence base is thin, even though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: To patiently put up with someone or something difficult, bearing with them and enduring rather than reacting.
article: ἀνέχομαι means to hold up under someone or something — to bear with, tolerate, or endure patiently. In the New Testament it always appears in the middle voice and usually takes a genitive of the person or thing being endured, as in Jesus' words "how long shall I put up with you?" (Matthew 17:17, Mark 9:19, Luke 9:41). Interestingly, in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew אָפַק, used four times, which carries the sense of restraining or holding oneself back, and a vivid papyrus example (P Oxy VI.903) shows a man saying "I refused to send her away," capturing the everyday flavor of forbearance.
caution: In nearly half its NT occurrences (7 of 15) the word is absorbed into English phrasing without a distinct rendering, so its force is felt more in context than in any single word.

definition: Gold—the precious metal itself, or things made from it like coins, ornaments, or plating.
article: χρυσίον means gold, whether as the raw metal, gold coins, or golden jewelry, and the Majority Standard Bible renders all 11 New Testament occurrences simply as "gold." Technically it is the diminutive of χρυσός (G5557), and lexicons note it can specify gold ornaments (1 Peter 3:3) or coin and money (Acts 3:6). The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri: one third-century letter tells a traveler, "when you come bring your gold ornaments, but do not wear them on the boat." In the Septuagint it appears 235 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew word זָהָב (gold) 178 times.

definition: A person who teaches false or untrue doctrine, posing as a legitimate teacher.
article: This compound word joins "false" (ψευδής) with "teacher" (διδάσκαλος), naming someone who spreads untrue teaching while claiming the role of a genuine instructor. It is rare, appearing only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 2:1. In that single occurrence the term is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word, and the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree it means simply "false teacher."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from broader usage.

definition: Describing a tomb or space that has been cut and carved directly out of solid rock.
article: λαξευτός means "hewn in stone" — carved out of solid rock by a stonecutter. It appears just once in the New Testament (Luke 23:53), describing the rock-cut tomb where Jesus' body was laid, and once in the Septuagint (Deuteronomy 4:49). The papyri are especially vivid here: a stonecutters' contract from Oxyrhynchus uses the related verb λαξεύω ("we will cut the stones"), and the everyday Koine term λάξος, a stone-mason, turns up in documents like a child's alphabet acrostic listing trades. Abbott-Smith notes other Koine writers preferred λατομητός for the same idea.
caution: With only one New Testament and one Septuagint occurrence, the evidence is thin and the precise Hebrew counterpart varies across sources (אֲשֵׁדוֹת versus פִּסְגָּה).

definition: To choose or pick out someone or something for oneself.
article: This verb means to choose or select, functioning much like the related middle verb αἱρέομαι. It appears just once in the New Testament (Matthew 12:18), where it quotes the Septuagint, and is far more common in the Greek Old Testament, where it shows up 21 times across 12 books. Most tellingly, the Septuagint uses it mainly to translate the Hebrew בָּחַר, 'to choose' (8 times), confirming the core meaning, and an inscription from the second century A.D. uses it of God choosing.
caution: Its single New Testament use is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word, so its sense rests largely on Septuagint and inscriptional evidence.

definition: A spiritual or mental dullness, like a hard callus forming over the heart so that people cannot perceive or respond.
article: πώρωσις literally means a covering with a callus, and the New Testament uses it figuratively for a hardening of heart or mind. It appears only 3 times, rendered "hardness" twice (67%) and once tied to the "hardening" of Israel until the full number of Gentiles comes in (Rom 11:25). Moulton-Milligan notes a scholarly discussion arguing that in the NT the contextual meaning is closer to obtuseness or intellectual blindness, a sense most ancient translators and commentators also assigned.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, and sources differing between "hardness/callousness" and "obtuseness/blindness," the precise shade of meaning is uncertain.

definition: A colony — specifically a Roman settlement, often founded for veteran soldiers and granted special civic status.
article: This word names a Roman colony, a city settlement that carried official Roman status and was frequently established for retired soldiers. It is borrowed straight from the Latin colonia and appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 16:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Roman" 100% of the time. The everyday papyri make it vivid: Moulton-Milligan cites third-century documents describing a settlement of veteran soldiers near a village in the Egyptian Fayum, even showing how the land for such colonies was obtained.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense rests on a single verse, though the meaning is well supported by Latin origin and papyri evidence.

definition: A leather strap or thong, used either to fasten a sandal or to bind and lash someone for flogging.
article: Ἱμάς is a plain everyday word for a leather strap. In the New Testament's 4 occurrences it shows up two ways: as the strap of a sandal (in the Gospels, where John says he isn't worthy to untie Jesus' sandal strap) and as the strap used to bind a prisoner for flogging (Acts 22:25). Everyday papyri confirm how ordinary the word was — one receipt covers oil for greasing straps, and a basket is described as tied with "a good strap" — while a 4th-century edict even uses ἱμάντες to mean the whips used to punish people.
caution: The three measured "senses" all refer to the same physical object (a strap), differing only in wording and context rather than meaning.

definition: To tear down or demolish a structure, especially by digging out its foundations.
article: κατασκάπτω means to demolish something by undermining it — literally digging beneath a structure until it collapses. The Septuagint uses it 31 times, most often for the Hebrew נָתַץ (12×, "pull down") and הָרַס (7×, "tear down"), confirming the sense of razing buildings or walls. It shows up in the New Testament only twice (in Romans 11:3, quoting the Old Testament), and the related noun appears in an inscription from Teos (303 BC) describing the demolition of a city's acropolis.
caution: Only 2 New Testament occurrences, with the word absorbed into the phrasing in one of them, so the corpus evidence is thin.

definition: To pray—to speak to God in worship, request, or supplication.
article: This verb means to pray to God, and across all 87 Byzantine occurrences it is rendered with a form of "pray" in nearly every case—60% simply as "pray." Notably, the word is always used of prayer directed to God (or, in classical Greek, to the gods), never of ordinary speech between people; in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew פָּלַל (62 times). A vivid example outside the Bible comes from a 257 BC Egyptian papyrus, where a man named Zoilos, struck with serious illness for neglecting the god Sarapis, finally prays to the god for relief.

definition: To move people from one place to settle elsewhere, often by force, as in resettling, deporting, or exiling them.
article: μετοικίζω means to transfer people to a new dwelling place, whether by peaceful resettlement or forced exile. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 7 (verses 4 and 43), and the Septuagint uses it 9 times across 6 books, chiefly for the Hebrew word for being carried into exile. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: one inscription describes a ruler who "resettled" the people of Pergamon back into their old city, and Aristeas speaks of those "removed into Egypt from Judea."
caution: The Byzantine sense labels here ("God" and "into") are artifacts of how surrounding words were counted in just two verses, not real meanings of this rare word.

definition: To happen to be present or to meet someone by chance, especially encountering whoever is around at the moment.
article: This verb describes happening to be in a place or meeting people by chance — Paul in Acts 17:17 reasoned daily with whoever happened to be present in the marketplace. It appears only once in the New Testament, but everyday Koine papyri show the same ordinary usage, as in a letter where a writer thanks the gods that he "came upon" a man named Plution in the Oxyrhynchite district. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the idea of pure chance is not necessarily present, despite Strong's gloss "to chance near."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range rests mainly on outside papyri evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: An adverb meaning in the morning or early in the day, around dawn.
article: πρωΐ is an adverb formed from πρό that simply means "in the morning" or "early in the day, around dawn." Its range is narrow and consistent: in the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "morning" 4 times and "early morning" 4 times, two ways of saying the same thing. It shows up everywhere in the Septuagint (186 times), where it almost always translates the Hebrew word בֹּקֶר ("morning," 160 times), and it was equally at home in everyday speech, appearing in Greek papyri and surviving into Modern Greek.

definition: To bring or lead someone or something toward a person or place, or simply to approach.
article: προσάγω combines πρός ("toward") with ἄγω ("lead"), and it means just that: to conduct someone or something near. In the Byzantine NT it appears only 4 times, twice rendered plainly as "bring" (as in Luke 9:41 and Acts 16:20) and once in the rich phrase about Christ bringing us "to God" (1 Peter 3:18). The Septuagint uses it far more heavily—148 times—mostly to translate the Hebrew קָרַב ("draw near," 89×), and everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth sense of hauling stones or bricks to a building site, even extending to "collect" or "add."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences—and one absorbed into phrasing with no English word of its own—the NT range is thin, though the abundant Septuagint and papyri evidence agrees on the core meaning.

definition: A piece of cloth, a scrap or rag torn from a larger fabric.
article: ῥάκος is simply a piece of cloth — a scrap, rag, or remnant torn off something larger, which fits its derivation from a verb meaning 'to tear.' Both New Testament uses appear in the saying about patching an old garment with a piece of unshrunk cloth (Matthew 9:16; Mark 2:21); the translation 'unshrunk' actually renders the accompanying word, not ῥάκος itself, which just means the cloth. Everyday papyri confirm this plain sense, listing things like 'two rags,' a 'linen rag,' and even a 'fine piece of cloth,' and the word could also describe mummy wrappings.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT occurrences), and the measured sense 'unshrunk' reflects neighboring wording rather than ῥάκος itself, which the lexica define simply as a cloth or rag.

definition: Andrew, the apostle and brother of Simon Peter, one of Jesus' twelve disciples.
article: Ἀνδρέας is a personal name, always referring to the apostle Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter from Bethsaida. It appears 13 times across five New Testament books and is rendered "Andrew" in every case. The name comes from the Greek word for "man" (ἀνήρ), and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up as an ordinary name in everyday Koine inscriptions, including a memorial from the 2nd century B.C.

definition: Strips of cloth used to bind a body, especially the wrappings placed around a corpse for burial.
article: In the New Testament κειρία appears just once, in John 11:44, describing the bands of cloth wrapping the body of Lazarus; the Byzantine text uses it in a phrase where it has no standalone English word and translators render it as "graveclothes." The word's range is broader than burial cloth alone: it was an everyday Koine term, and in its single Septuagint use (Proverbs 7:16) it translates a Hebrew word for bed coverings or cords, while classical sources also attest the sense of a bed-cord. The most interesting detail is from a medical papyrus, where a related form κηρία appears, and an old definition explains it as the kind of swaddling band used for infants and also to bind the dead.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its precise sense rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: The cardinal number seventy.
article: This is simply the Greek word for the number seventy, and it stays the same in every grammatical setting. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times across 2 books, always meaning seventy — for example the seventy others Jesus sends out in Luke 10:1. It is hugely common in the Septuagint (106 times), where it almost always renders the Hebrew word for seventy (89 of those times), and old papyri use it for everyday counting, including a document granting a kind of pension to people who had lived over seventy years.
caution: The measured "board" rendering at Acts 27:37 and the split between "seventy" and "seventy even" reflect translation phrasing, not separate meanings; the word always means the number seventy, which Moulton-Milligan notes can sometimes be an approximate figure.

definition: Cunning, fraudulent wrongdoing — trickery or deceitful schemes that twist what is right.
article: This word appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 13:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "perverting" (and the Berean Standard agrees 100%). At root it carries the idea of "easiness" or doing things carelessly, which slid into the negative sense of recklessness and outright fraud. The everyday Koine papyri are especially telling here: a document from Oxyrhynchus (A.D. 186) lists ῥᾳδιουργία alongside forgery and false pretenses as a formal legal charge, confirming the sense of deceitful, fraudulent dealing.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a range that classical sources spread across "ease," "laziness," and "wickedness," the precise force here rests on thin evidence.

definition: To be completely at a loss, overwhelmed to the point of despair with no way out.
article: ἐξαπορέομαι describes being so cornered by trouble that you give up hope of any escape. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's letters to the Corinthians, and in each case it is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word — in 2 Corinthians 1:8 Paul says he despaired even of living. The prefix ἐξ ('out, utterly') intensifies the simpler ἀπορέω ('to be at a loss'), and one Egyptian papyrus from 285 BC uses a milder form simply to mean 'be in want of something,' showing the word's everyday range was broader than the biblical despair.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing, the evidence for its precise force is thin.

definition: Half — one of two equal parts of something, or the midpoint of an amount.
article: ἥμισυ simply means "half," whether used as an adjective agreeing with a noun ("half of my possessions," Luke 19:8) or as a standalone noun ("the half"). It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament and is remarkably common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 125 times—most often translating the Hebrew word חֵצִי ("half"), 97 times. In Mark 6:23 it forms the phrase "up to half of my kingdom," which the translators rendered with "up half" to capture that limiting sense.

definition: To beat, strike, or thrash someone physically, usually as punishment or violent assault.
article: δέρω means to beat, thrash, or strike someone—usually a violent physical blow given as punishment or in an attack. All 15 New Testament uses point to this physical sense, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "beat" or "strike" in every case. Interestingly, Strong's notes the word properly meant "to flay" (skin an animal), a sense found in its few Septuagint appearances translating Hebrew פָּשַׁט; the everyday Koine papyri (Moulton-Milligan) confirm that by New Testament times it had shifted to the colloquial "beat, thrash" meaning, much like the English slang "hide."

definition: To secretly persuade or bribe someone to make false statements; to induce by underhanded means.
article: Literally this verb means "to throw or put under," but it took on a figurative life meaning to suggest, whisper, or prompt someone—and in its sharpest sense, to bribe people into giving false testimony ("to suborn"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 6:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prompted" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully. The most telling evidence comes from Field's note, citing the historian Appian, where false accusers were similarly "thrown forward" against a priest of Zeus—a vivid parallel for the corrupt, planted-witness sense.
caution: This appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force here rests on a single passage and outside parallels.

definition: Welcome and well-received; describing something that is gladly accepted or pleasing to the one receiving it.
article: This word describes something that is gladly welcomed or favorably received, built from εὖ ("well") and a form of προσδέχομαι ("to receive"). It is consistent and narrow in range: in all 5 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "acceptable" 4 times, with one absorbed into phrasing, and the BSB agrees 100%. Moulton-Milligan note that the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, showing it was ordinary language rather than a specialized religious term.
caution: Evidence is moderate, resting on just 5 occurrences, though the renderings are fully consistent.

definition: Victory; the winning or successful overcoming of an opponent or obstacle.
article: νίκη means victory — the act or result of overcoming. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 John 5:4, where it is rendered "victory" in every measured occurrence and confirmed independently by other translations. The papyri preserve a vivid everyday example: in a letter the Emperor Claudius thanks a club for a golden crown sent to celebrate his victorious campaign in Britain in A.D. 43, using this very word.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just two in the Septuagint, the evidence base for this word is thin.

definition: To form, shape, or mold something into its full and proper form.
article: Μορφόω means to give something its shape or form, like a craftsman molding material into a finished object. It appears only once in the Greek Bible, at Galatians 4:19, where Paul speaks of Christ being formed in believers; the Majority Standard Bible renders this with the image of childbirth, and the BSB agrees. The most striking detail is that commentators see the verb extending Paul's earlier picture of his readers as babies in the womb, now reimagined as pregnant mothers awaiting the full development of the Christ growing within them.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Greek Bible, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Describing someone who fights or struggles against God.
article: θεομάχος combines the words for "God" and "to fight," and labels a person as an opponent of God. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:39, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "fighting." The Septuagint uses related forms in Job 26:5 and Proverbs, and Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine writing, including the astrologer Vettius Valens, who pairs "ignorant" people with "God-fighters."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Jephthah, one of the judges of Israel mentioned among the heroes of faith.
article: Ἰεφθάε is the Greek form of the Hebrew name יִפְתָּח (Jephthah), one of Israel's judges. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Hebrews 11:32, where Jephthah is listed among the people of faith. The name is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 59 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew Jephthah (58×).
caution: The Majority Standard Bible's rendering is logged here as "Samson," which conflicts with every lexicon listing this name as Jephthah, so treat that single measured sense with caution.

definition: Standing out so as to be noticed, whether favorably as distinguished or unfavorably as notorious.
article: ἐπίσημος literally means "bearing a mark," and the everyday papyri show this concrete sense vividly: shops and districts marked with numbers, and especially money described as ἐπίσημος, meaning "stamped" or "coined." From that root it stretches metaphorically to mean someone who stands out, which can be positive ("notable, illustrious") or negative ("notorious"). In the New Testament both occurrences are absorbed into phrasing rather than given a single English word, and Abbott-Smith neatly captures the two-sided range with examples in both directions.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into surrounding phrasing, and a range that swings between praise and disgrace, the precise force in any given verse depends heavily on context.

definition: A wide, impassable gap or chasm separating two places so that no one can cross from one side to the other.
article: χάσμα refers to a yawning gap or chasm — a wide space that cannot be crossed. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:26, where it describes the unbridgeable gulf fixed between the rich man and Lazarus. The word is rare in the Greek Bible overall; in the Septuagint it shows up just once, translating the Hebrew פַּחַת (a pit or trench) in 2 Samuel 18:17.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its range in biblical Greek rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To wail or cry out loudly in grief or distress, often as a public expression of sorrow.
article: This verb means to howl or wail loudly, the kind of unrestrained crying that goes with grief or distress. It appears just once in the New Testament, in James 5:1, where the rich are told to weep and wail over coming miseries, but it shows up 21 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew יָלַל ('to wail,' 16 times). Interestingly, in older Greek (Homer) the word described women crying out to the gods in prayer or thanksgiving, and it surfaces in everyday papyri—including a magical spell where an old woman 'wails' and flees.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise New Testament range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A fellow slave or servant who shares the same master, whether human or divine.
article: σύνδουλος combines σύν ('with') and δοῦλος ('slave/servant'), so it literally means a slave who serves alongside another under the same master. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, split evenly between the renderings 'fellow' and 'fellow servant,' and it covers a wide range: ordinary servants in Jesus' parables, Christians serving the same Lord, and even angels who call themselves fellow servants. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain workplace sense — one document pairs it with 'fellow-freedman,' showing it was common labor vocabulary, not just religious language.

definition: Doing something eagerly and willingly, with a ready and cheerful attitude rather than reluctantly.
article: This adverb describes the spirit in which an action is done — eagerly, readily, with a ready mind. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:2, where elders are told to shepherd God's flock willingly. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document asks for someone's "zealous co-operation" in a task, confirming the sense of cheerful, prompt readiness.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than broad biblical usage.

definition: The direction of the setting sun — the west, or by extension the place where the sun goes down.
article: δυσμή literally points to the sunset, and from there comes to mean the western region; it appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "west" in every case. The three "senses" the data records are really one meaning shaped by context — the basic direction in passages like Luke 12:54 and Revelation 21:13, the gathering of people "from east and west" in Matthew 8:11, and the lightning that flashes across the sky in Matthew 24:27. In the Septuagint it shows up 52 times, often translating Hebrew words for "west" (מַעֲרָב) or even "desert/plain" (עֲרָבָה). Everyday papyri confirm the usage: documents pair "from the east" (ἀνατολῶν) with "from the west" (δυσμῶν) exactly as the Gospels do.
caution: The split into three labeled senses reflects translation phrasing in context, not distinct meanings — the word consistently signifies "west."

definition: A question-word asking how great, how large, or how small something is, with the exact size shown by context.
article: ἡλίκος is a sizing word that asks "how great?" or "how large?" — and, depending on context, can even mean "how small." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 2 times, both rendered "how" (in Colossians 2:1 and James 3:5), though critical editions count a third instance at Galatians 6:11. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document from 113 BC asks readers to "consider how great an impulse" attention gives to business, and a medical prescription uses it to mean "the size of an Egyptian bean."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT occurrences) and the word's range stretches from "how large" to "how small," so the precise force depends entirely on context.

definition: An adverb meaning down or below, pointing to a lower place or direction.
article: κάτω is a simple directional adverb meaning "down" or "below," used either with verbs of motion (going downward) or to mark something located beneath. In the New Testament it appears 11 times, but in 6 of those it gets absorbed into English phrasing rather than translated as its own word; where it stands out, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "below." In the Septuagint it shows up 24 times, most often translating the Hebrew מַ֫טָּה ("below, downward," 9×), and everyday papyri use it the same plain way—one document describes items "at the bottom" of a little basket.

definition: Describing something fresh or recent in time, or someone young or younger in age.
article: Νέος covers two closely related ideas: things that are new or fresh (like new wine, rendered "new" in 41% of New Testament occurrences) and people who are young or younger (about 36% combined). The comparative form νεώτερος often contrasts the young with the elders, as in 1 Timothy 5:1 and 1 Peter 5:5. In everyday Koine papyri the word frequently described the "new year," and in the Septuagint it commonly translated Hebrew words for young (נַעַר, צָעִיר) or small (קָטָן), spanning the full range from age to freshness.
caution: Greek has a near-synonym, καινός, also meaning "new," and the papyri sometimes pair the two words, so the precise distinction between them can be subtle.

definition: In many parts or installments — describing something delivered piece by piece rather than all at once.
article: This adverb describes how something happens in many separate portions or stages, built from the words for "many" (πολύς) and "part" (μέρος). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 1:1, where it pairs with πολυτρόπως ("in many manners") to describe how God spoke through the prophets — πολυμερῶς specifically points to the many portions or installments, while its partner points to the many methods. The word was at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan note its adjective form describing the god Fire as "manifold" in a papyrus, and both forms turn up commonly in the astrologer Vettius Valens.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence (a hapax), so its precise nuance rests mainly on the Hebrews 1:1 context and outside Greek sources rather than broad biblical usage.

definition: A boast, or the thing that gives someone reason to boast or take pride.
senseLabels: a boast or grounds for boasting
article: καύχημα is the proud claim a person makes, or—more often—the thing that gives them a reason to make it. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times, and translators render it "boast" in about 64% of cases, with the rest scattered across phrases involving glorying or rejoicing. In the Greek Old Testament it most often translates Hebrew words for "praise" (תְּהִלָּה) and "glory" or "splendor" (תִּפְאָרָה), which shows the word can carry a positive sense of something genuinely worth celebrating, not just empty bragging.
caution: Scholars distinguish two shades—the act of boasting versus the ground for it—and disagree on which applies in places like Galatians 6:4, so the exact nuance can be context-dependent.

definition: The finest, most refined wheat flour, the high-grade flour used in baking and offerings.
article: σεμίδαλις means fine, top-quality wheaten flour. It appears just once in the New Testament (Revelation 18:13), but it is common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 60 times across 10 books, chiefly translating the Hebrew word סֹ֫לֶת ('fine flour') 54 times. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the same down-to-earth meaning, listing rations of this flour and even σεμιδαλίτης ἄρτος, 'fine wheaten bread' — and Pliny notes it was made from the most prized wheat.
caution: The measured rendering 'cinnamon' is almost certainly a data-alignment error from the long cargo list in Revelation 18:13; all the lexica and Septuagint evidence agree the word means fine wheaten flour.

definition: Describing a calm, untroubled, peaceful manner of living, free from disturbance.
article: This adjective means calm or tranquil, describing a peaceful, undisturbed way of life. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 2:2, where Paul prays that believers may lead a tranquil and quiet life. The papyri offer a striking parallel: a document from around A.D. 245 uses nearly the same phrase Paul does, speaking of those "living a calm and untroubled life," showing this was ordinary everyday Koine rather than a literary word.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured.

definition: Thunder, the loud rumbling sound that accompanies a storm or a powerful display of divine presence.
