article: βροντή simply means thunder, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: in all 12 New Testament occurrences it is rendered "thunder" (or related forms like "thundered"), and the Septuagint uses it the same way, mostly translating the Hebrew word raʿam. The word is concentrated in Revelation, where thunder marks dramatic scenes of God's presence and judgment. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note they could find no example of this exact noun in the everyday papyri, though related forms turn up in magical papyri describing a being who "flashes lightning and thunders."

definition: To go up or ascend, especially traveling up to a city or higher place.
article: This verb combines ἀνά ("up") with ἔρχομαι ("come, go") and simply means to go up or ascend. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament: once of Jesus going up a mountain (John 6:3) and twice in Galatians of Paul going up to Jerusalem (Gal 1:17-18). The everyday papyri show a vivid specialized use—"going up to the capital city"—as in a letter urging someone to "come up instantly" because an official was asking for him.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences and 4 in the Septuagint, so the picture of its full range is limited.

definition: In a bodily or physical way; in concrete, tangible reality.
article: This adverb means "bodily" or "corporeally" — describing something present in physical, concrete reality rather than in mere appearance or abstraction. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:9, where the fullness of Deity is said to dwell in Christ "bodily." Moulton-Milligan note that the word turns up in everyday Koine documents too: one inscription uses it to contrast being punished "either in money or in bodily form" (κατὰ πᾶν ἢ ἀργυρικῶς ἢ σωματικῶς).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force in Colossians 2:9 has long been debated and is best understood from the broader Koine evidence.

definition: To draw water up out of a well or container, originally to bail water out of a ship's hold.
article: This verb means to draw water, typically lifting it out of a deep well with a bucket or jar. The Majority Standard Bible renders all four New Testament occurrences this way, and they all appear in John—filling the water jars at Cana (John 2:8–9) and the Samaritan woman at the well (John 4:7, 15). Its original sense was nautical: to bail out bilge-water from a ship's hold, and the everyday papyri preserve this watery range vividly—one sixth-century receipt covers a rope for the machine used to raise water for a church font.

definition: A young man, typically someone in the prime of life (anywhere up to about forty years old).
article: Νεανίας simply means a young man — a male in his youth or prime, which ancient usage could stretch as old as about forty. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, all in Acts, and translators render it consistently as "young man" (the apparent variety in the measured senses is just phrasing differences around the same idea). It's a common everyday word: a second-century papyrus from Oxyrhynchus uses it of a seventeen-year-old boy expected to attend school and the exercises "proper for the young," and in the Septuagint it stands behind Hebrew terms like נַעַר and בָּחוּר.
caution: The three "measured senses" all point to the same meaning and reflect translation phrasing rather than genuinely distinct senses.

definition: The comparative of "up," used as an adverb to mean either a higher (more honored) position or an earlier point in a text.
article: This is the comparative form of ἄνω ("up"), and it appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament. In Luke 14:10 it describes moving up to a more honored seat at a dinner table (rendered "honored" in the Majority Standard Bible), while its other use points backward to an earlier part of a text, meaning "above" or "before." An interesting wrinkle: the everyday Koine papyri use this word for time as well, as in an inscription meaning "in the third year previous" — the same idea of "earlier" that shows up in its textual sense.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into the surrounding phrasing, the measured evidence here is thin.

definition: The harvest — the act of reaping, the time when crops are ripe, or the gathered crop itself, often used figuratively.
article: θερισμός refers to harvest in its full range: the act of reaping, the season when crops are ready, and the crop that gets gathered. In the New Testament it appears 13 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "harvest" most often (38%) and the rest in fuller phrases like "harvest plentiful" or "ripe harvest." The everyday Koine background is clear from the papyri, where farm leases speak of renting land "for one seed-time and harvest" — the same plain agricultural sense the Gospel writers draw on. In the Septuagint it almost always translates the Hebrew word קָצִיר ("harvest"), used 30 of its 32 times.

definition: The head of a person or animal, or figuratively a person who leads, governs, or holds the foremost place.
article: κεφαλή is the ordinary word for the head, the body part, and that literal meaning covers 69 of its 76 New Testament occurrences (99%). But it stretches naturally into figurative uses—a husband or Christ described as the "head," and the "head of the corner" (cornerstone) that joins two walls. The Septuagint uses it over 354 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew rosh ("head"), and everyday papyri show the same plain sense, as in a second-century document describing a man with "three wounds on his head."

definition: To feel strong sensual or self-indulgent desires that pull a person away from a prior commitment.
article: καταστρηνιάω appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 5:11, where it describes younger widows whose physical desires draw them away from their pledge to Christ. The lexica (Strong's, KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on the sense "to wax wanton against" or "grow voluptuous against," and it takes a genitive object. Notably, the measured rendering in the digest reads "enroll," which clashes sharply with every classical lexicon's sense of wanton desire — the lexica should be trusted here over that single tag.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the measured rendering ("enroll") conflicts with the lexicons ("wax wanton against"), so the sense should be drawn from the lexical evidence.

definition: To go all the way through something, reaching deep inside and penetrating it completely.
article: This rare verb describes something passing completely through and reaching the inside of an object. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 4:12, where the word of God is described as penetrating deep within a person; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "active" there. In its single Septuagint appearance it translates a Hebrew word for a crossbar that runs through (Exodus 26:28), showing the same idea of passing all the way through.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To shake physically, especially out of fear or awe.
article: τρέμω means to tremble or shake, most often because someone is afraid. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "trembling" just once (Mark 5:33), with the other two occurrences folded into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. In everyday Koine the word carried the same sense of alarm: a 2nd-century papyrus letter reassures a son not to suppose his mother is in any "tremble" or worry over a matter. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew verbs of wavering, dread, and quaking.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences, two of which lack their own English rendering, so the measured picture rests on a single clear example.

definition: A follower of Christ; a name first given to Jesus' disciples by outsiders at Antioch.
article: Χριστιανός means a Christian — a follower of Christ — and it appears only 3 times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26, Acts 26:28, and 1 Peter 4:16). The three measured renderings all point to the same single sense; the variations simply reflect how the word sits in different sentences. The most interesting detail is its origin: Moulton-Milligan and Abbott-Smith agree it was a word of Latin formation, apparently coined by outsiders at Antioch as a nickname for Christ's partisans, and Codex Sinaiticus actually spells it Χρηστιανοί, leading some scholars to debate the original form.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only 3 times — and sources note genuine uncertainty about its original spelling (Χριστ- vs. Χρηστ-).

definition: A little dog or house dog, the small pet kept around a household rather than a wild or stray animal.
senseLabels: a little dog or pet dog
article: κυνάριον is a diminutive of the ordinary word for dog (κύων), pointing to a small household or pet dog rather than a wild scavenger. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in the same exchange between Jesus and the Syrophoenician woman about dogs eating crumbs under the table (Matthew 15:26-27; Mark 7:27-28). The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri and in the philosopher Epictetus, who lists 'a dog, a horse, an estate' as common possessions.
caution: The three 'measured senses' all reflect the same single household-dog meaning broken up by translation phrasing, so treat it as one sense.

definition: A very young child or infant, often used figuratively for someone who is immature, simple, or still unlearned.
article: Νήπιος literally describes a very young child—rendered "children" in 6 of 14 New Testament occurrences (43%) and "infants" in 4 more (29%). Beyond the literal sense, it carries a figurative meaning of being immature or unskilled, which lexicons like Strong's and Dodson note (a simple-minded person, an immature Christian), often standing opposite to "mature" (τέλειος). The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, where one woman describes leaving behind a daughter "quite young" (κομιδῆ νηπίαν), and in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for a small child (עוֹלָל, 14 times).
caution: The literal "child/infant" sense dominates the measured data, but the figurative "immature" or "unskilled" sense rests mainly on the lexicons rather than the rendering counts.

definition: To tie or wrap something around yourself like a garment, used figuratively for clothing yourself with an attitude toward others.
article: This rare verb pictures fastening a garment onto yourself, drawn from κόμβος, a 'knot.' The related noun referred specifically to an apron or frock that slaves tied on over their other clothing, which gives the word its overtone of humble service. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:5, where believers are told to clothe themselves with humility toward one another; the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'yourselves' there, agreeing 100% with the BSB.
caution: This is essentially a one-occurrence word with very thin evidence — Moulton-Milligan found no examples in the papyri, and even classical interpretations of the Peter passage are described as doubtful.

definition: Strips or pieces of fine linen cloth, especially the wrappings used to bind a body for burial.
article: ὀθόνιον refers to fine linen, used in the New Testament for the strips of cloth that wrapped Jesus' body, appearing 5 times across John and Luke. The renderings cluster tightly around "linen cloths" or simply "linen" — every occurrence describes the same burial setting. Egyptian papyri studied by Wilcken show the word meant fine linen stuff both as finished product and raw material, and its manufacture was actually a government monopoly. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words, including סָדִין (a linen garment) in Judges 14:13.

definition: A Hebrew-derived shout, originally meaning "save now!" but used in the Gospels as a cry of praise to God.
article: Ὡσαννά is a transliterated Hebrew/Aramaic exclamation that the Majority Standard Bible simply carries over as "Hosanna" in every one of its 6 occurrences, found in Matthew, Mark, and John. The variations in the data ("were Hosanna," "is that Hosanna") are just surrounding sentence words, not different meanings — the word itself is always the same cry. The most interesting detail is its history: Moulton-Milligan notes it began as a genuine plea for help in Psalm 118:25 ("save now!"), but by the time the Evangelists used it, it had become a shout of praise.
caution: It appears only 6 times and is a foreign loanword, so its force comes from its Old Testament background rather than ordinary Greek usage.

definition: In a way that shows gladness or delight; willingly and with pleasure.
article: This adverb describes doing something with gladness or delight, built from a root meaning "to be glad." Its two New Testament uses both fall in Acts and are rendered "gladly" (Acts 2:41) and "joyfully" (Acts 21:17), so the range is narrow and consistent. It also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, where one first-century example pairs it with another word for "willingly" (ἀσμένως καὶ ἑκουσίως), reinforcing the sense of acting freely and happily.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text), so the precise shade of meaning rests mostly on outside sources.

definition: To promise or pledge to do something, and sometimes to profess or openly claim something about oneself.
article: The word almost always means to promise or pledge, and that is how the Majority Standard Bible renders it in 8 of its 15 New Testament uses (57%), with the BSB independently agreeing 88% of the time. Beyond promising, the lexicons note a secondary sense of "profess" — to openly claim something about oneself, as in professing godliness or knowledge. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary commercial meaning, including a document where someone "promised that you would be present today," showing the word at home in routine pledges and agreements.
caution: The measured data captures only the dominant "promise" sense; the "profess" meaning rests on the lexicons rather than the corpus counts here.

definition: To locate something or someone by asking questions and following up the answers until you find it.
article: This compound verb joins "through" (diá) with "to ask" (erōtáō), giving the sense of asking persistently until you track something down. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 10:17, where the men sent by Cornelius "found" Simon's house by making inquiries. The Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "found," capturing the idea that the discovery came through repeated questioning rather than chance.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical evidence alone.

definition: A building or place for storing harvested crops, such as a barn or granary.
article: ἀποθήκη is a storehouse, most often a barn or granary where harvested grain is kept. Across all 6 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "barn" 100% of the time, with the BSB independently agreeing, as in Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri — though Moulton-Milligan notes it is surprisingly uncommon there, appearing just once in the indexes to Oxyrhynchus Papyri I–X.

definition: To sing, especially songs of praise to God, originally meaning to pluck or play a stringed instrument.
article: In the New Testament this word always means singing, usually praise to God — it appears just 5 times across 4 books, rendered "sing," "sing hymns," or "sing praises." Its older meaning was far more physical: to pull, twitch, or twang a string, and so to play a stringed instrument with the fingers, a sense found in classical writers and even an inscription that pairs it with playing the lyre. The shift toward "sing" happened in the Septuagint, where it appears 45 times and most often translates the Hebrew zamar ("make music, sing praise") and nagan ("play an instrument").
caution: The word's range shifted over time from "play a stringed instrument" to "sing," so the older instrumental sense lingers behind its New Testament use even though every measured occurrence means singing.

definition: To make someone a slave or bring them into bondage, used both literally and figuratively for being controlled by something.
article: δουλόω means to enslave or bring into bondage, built directly on the noun δοῦλος ("slave"). It appears 7 times in the Byzantine New Testament, ranging from literal slavery (Acts 7:6) to vivid figurative uses—being enslaved to righteousness (Rom 6:18), to God (Rom 6:22), or even to wine (Titus 2:3 per Abbott-Smith). A striking witness comes from the papyri: an honorific decree from Pergamon (46 BC) praises a proconsul for restoring the city's democracy "unenslaved" (ἀδούλωτον), showing the word's everyday political weight.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and 2 absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, the measured sense divisions rest on thin data.

definition: To move quickly or act urgently — to hurry, or to be eager to do something without delay.
article: σπεύδω basically means to hurry — to do something fast and without delay. In the Byzantine New Testament all 6 uses point this way, and the Majority Standard Bible and BSB agree completely on rendering it "hurry," as when Zacchaeus came down quickly or Paul rushed to reach Jerusalem. In the Septuagint it appears 51 times, most often translating the Hebrew מָהַר ("to hasten," 25×), and the everyday papyri show people writing things like "I am anxious to make haste" — so it was common, ordinary Koine. Classical lexicons note a fuller transitive range, including "urge on" or even "desire eagerly," but those shades don't show up in the measured New Testament data.
caution: The senses beyond plain "hurry" (such as "urge on" or "desire eagerly") come from classical sources and a disputed reading of 2 Peter 3:12, not from the measured New Testament usage.

definition: A visible cloud of vapor, mist, or steam that rises and quickly disappears.
article: ἀτμίς means a rising cloud of vapor, steam, or mist — something visible but short-lived. It appears just twice in the New Testament: in Acts 2:19 it describes "vapor of smoke" (quoting the Septuagint), and in James 4:14 a human life is compared to a mist that appears briefly and then vanishes. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the ordinary sense: one magical papyrus uses it for the smoke rising off burning incense, and an inscription describes a censer "steaming."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and limited Septuagint data, the evidence for this word is thin.

definition: To help together with others, joining in service or assistance toward a shared purpose.
article: Συνυπουργέω means to pitch in alongside others to assist or serve, combining the idea of working under a task with doing it together. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 1:11, where Abbott-Smith notes it takes a dative and where the word's force is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. The lexicons agree on its sense, and its build from σύν ('with') plus a compound of ὑπό and the root of ἔργον ('work') makes the meaning of cooperative service transparent.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word with only this one New Testament use, so its full range cannot be confirmed from the evidence.

definition: To ask someone a question, inquire of, or question a person directly.
article: This verb means to put a question to someone or to inquire of a person, and across all 59 Byzantine occurrences nearly every rendering circles around the same idea of asking or questioning. The measured senses differ mostly in English wording — "asked," "questioned," "ask," "inquired" — rather than in real meaning, and many examples involve people questioning Jesus or Jesus questioning others. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew שָׁאַל ("to ask," 38×) but also דָּרַשׁ ("to seek or consult," 9×), and a papyrus from 241 B.C. uses it of a man sent to ask whether a seal was still in the temple. The lexica note a later Greek sense of "beg" or "demand of," which Abbott-Smith ties to Matthew 16:1.
caution: The many measured senses are mostly translation-style variations of one core meaning, so the apparent range is narrower than the list suggests.

definition: To arrive at, reach, or come to a place; figuratively, of news that travels and reaches people.
article: ἀφικνέομαι basically means to arrive at or reach a destination, and the lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on this core sense. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 16:19, where it is used figuratively of a report that has "reached" or spread to everyone, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "about" in that context. The papyri evidence is striking: Moulton-Milligan note it was almost a technical word for pilgrimages, used in inscriptions where worshippers record that they "arrived" at a sacred place, sometimes noting their immediate cure.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured New Testament range is extremely thin and the single rendering reflects a figurative use.

definition: Agreement or shared consent between parties; a coming together in accord.
article: συγκατάθεσις means agreement or accord — the mutual consent of parties who share the same mind. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:16, where Paul asks what agreement a temple of God can have with idols. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense vividly: one document (BGU I.194, A.D. 177) speaks of villagers undertaking public duties 'by agreement' (ἐκ συνκαταθέσεως), and another refers to acting 'without my consent.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests largely on outside evidence from papyri and classical authors.

definition: To give way or yield, backing down before someone's pressure or demands.
article: εἴκω means to yield or give way, the act of backing down before pressure. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Galatians 2:5, where Paul refuses to "give place" to those pressuring him. The Septuagint uses it only a handful of times (2 Kings 12:7, Wisdom 18:25, 4 Maccabees 1:6), and Abbott-Smith notes its relation to the compound form ὑπείκω.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: It means continually or on every occasion, marking something that happens without stopping or that recurs each time.
article: ἀεί is a small adverb meaning "always" or "ever," and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "always" in every one of its 6 translated occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament (BSB agrees 100%). The standard lexicons split it into two shades: continuous, unbroken time ("unceasingly," as in Acts 7:51 and 2 Corinthians 4:11) and repeated occasions ("on every occasion," as in 1 Peter 3:15). A nice etymological detail from Moulton-Milligan: ἀεί is built from the same root as αἰών ("age"), so the idea of "continued duration" sits right inside the word.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and 2 of them absorbed into phrasing, the corpus is thin, and the "on every occasion" sense comes from the lexicons rather than the measured renderings.

definition: A personal name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed as one of the ancestors in the line of David.
senseLabels: a man's name in a genealogy
article: Μαϊνάν is a proper name appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in the genealogy of Jesus at Luke 3:31, where it sits in the line descending from David. It is probably of Hebrew origin, though the digest gives no further detail about its meaning. The most notable point is textual: the critical text does not contain this form at all, and the lexica record the alternate spelling Μεννά (Menna), so different manuscript traditions disagree on the name.
caution: This name occurs only once, is absent from the critical text, and the sources differ over its spelling (Μαϊνάν versus Μεννά).

definition: A convincing demonstration or proof that establishes something as certain.
article: ἀπόδειξις refers to a demonstration that proves a point and carries conviction. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 2:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "persuasive" (the BSB agrees 100%). Everyday Koine papyri repeatedly use the word in a concrete legal sense — producing "proofs" against someone in a dispute — and Greek philosophers used it for rigorous, certain demonstration.
caution: With just one New Testament occurrence, the precise force here is hard to pin down, and the lexicons range from "showing off" to "certain proof."

definition: Rhesa, a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as one of his ancestors.
article: Rhesa is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:27, where he is listed as an ancestor of Jesus. The name is indeclinable in Greek and is probably of Hebrew origin, apparently corresponding to the Hebrew name behind H07509 (Rephaiah). Because it occurs only here, there is little to say about its range beyond its role in the genealogy.
caution: This name appears only once in the New Testament, and its proposed Hebrew counterpart (Rephaiah) is only tentative.

definition: Rain, especially a heavy downpour of water falling from the sky.
article: βροχή means rain, and in the New Testament it appears just twice, both in the same parable about the houses built on rock and sand (Matthew 7:25, 27). The Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render every occurrence as "rain," matching Strong's, KJV, and Dodson, who specifies "a heavy rain." The most interesting wrinkle is from the papyri: in everyday Egyptian documents the word often means a "wetting" or irrigation of land, as in a Ptolemaic-era papyrus about watering soldiers' allotment fields — so the original sense leans more toward soaking than toward storms.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences, both in one passage — and the papyri use the word for irrigation rather than falling rain, so its full range is uncertain.

definition: A negative connecting word meaning "and not," "nor," or "neither," and as an adverb "not even."
article: οὐδέ is a negative particle built from οὐ ("not") and δέ, used 134 times in the Byzantine New Testament. It works two ways: as a conjunction linking negatives ("and not," "nor," "neither"), and as an adverb meaning "not even," as in "not even Solomon was arrayed like one of these" (Matthew 6:29). The everyday papyri show this adverbial force vividly — one third-century letter complains, "not even once have you deigned to write me" — and in the Septuagint it most often renders the plain Hebrew negative לֹא (137 times).
caution: The many measured renderings reflect English phrasing of negative clauses rather than truly distinct meanings, so the long sense list is more granular than the word's actual range.

definition: A pointing demonstrative meaning "this" or "these," especially introducing the exact words that follow, as in "these are the words."
article: ὅδε is an old demonstrative pronoun (built from the article ὁ plus δέ) that points to something present or about to be named, basically "this here." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 11 times, and in 7 of those (78%) it sets up a quotation as "these are the words," while twice (22%) it works more like a relative "who." The neat detail from the papyri is that the phrase τάδε λέγει ("thus says") mirrors the standard formula τάδε διέθετο used to introduce a person's wishes in ancient wills, so the New Testament's "thus says" echoes everyday legal language.
caution: New Testament occurrences are few (only 11), so the measured senses rest on a thin sample even though usage is consistent.

definition: Describing someone arrogant and haughty, who shows themselves above others with contempt and disdain.
article: ὑπερήφανος describes a person who lifts themselves above everyone else—arrogant, haughty, disdainful. Built from ὑπέρ ("above") and φαίνω ("to show"), it literally pictures someone making themselves conspicuous over others. In the New Testament it appears 5 times and is always negative, usually rendered "proud"; in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 it stands as the direct opposite of ταπεινός ("humble"). One nice detail: an Oxyrhynchus papyrus from the 2nd century AD uses it as a nickname, greeting "Leontas the proud," showing it was everyday vocabulary.
caution: Classical Greek could use this word in a good sense ("splendid, pre-eminent"), but in biblical Greek it is always negative.

definition: A person held in custody or bound as a captive; a prisoner.
article: δέσμιος refers to a person who is bound or held captive—simply, a prisoner. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 16 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prisoner" in every occurrence where it carries its own English word (14×, with the other 2 absorbed into surrounding phrasing). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary legal sense: one second-century document (P Oxy III.580) speaks of guarding prisoners in custody, and the Septuagint uses the word to translate the Hebrew אָסִיר, "captive."

definition: The act of rising from the dead, especially God's raising of people back to life after death.
article: In the New Testament ἀνάστασις almost always means resurrection from the dead, rendered that way in 34 of 42 occurrences (87%), whether of Christ, of people in Old Testament accounts, or of the general resurrection. The handful of other renderings are just grammatical variations of the same idea ("the resurrection whose..."). The most striking evidence comes from everyday Koine: papyri and inscriptions use this word for the "erection" or "setting up" of a monument or statue, a plain physical "standing up again" that lies behind the theological sense.

definition: A flat wooden board or plank, such as those used in a ship's structure.
article: σανίς refers to a flat wooden board or plank. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:44, where shipwreck survivors reach shore on planks, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "planks" in every occurrence. Beyond plain boards, everyday Koine sources stretch the word in interesting directions: papyri and inscriptions use it for a wooden writing-tablet, and in Herodas it even names a wooden bench to sit on.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To travel or be on a journey, moving along a road from one place to another.
article: ὁδεύω means simply to travel or be on the road, and it comes from ὁδός, the ordinary word for a road or way. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 10:33, where the Samaritan is journeying and comes upon the wounded man. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain sense — one Oxyrhynchus document uses it of someone in the middle of a trip, while the Septuagint employs it both literally and figuratively.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from the text itself.

definition: A physical disease, sickness, or illness that afflicts the body.
article: Νόσος means a bodily disease or sickness, and the New Testament uses it consistently this way—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "diseases" in 6 of its 12 occurrences, with related renderings like "sicknesses" filling out the rest. The word's range is narrow and well-attested, appearing often in healing accounts like Matthew 4:23 and Luke 4:40. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the same meaning vividly: one fourth-century letter describes a woman "oppressed by sickness" (νόσῳ), and a Christian amulet praises the one "who healed every disease." In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words for illness, including מַחֲלֶה and חֹלִי.

definition: Describes a person who neither trips others into sin nor stumbles themselves—morally clear, blameless, and giving no offense.
article: This adjective combines the negative prefix with the idea of 'striking against' or stumbling, and it works in two directions: actively, not tripping others into sin (1 Corinthians 10:32), and passively, staying blameless and not stumbling yourself (Acts 24:16; Philippians 1:10). It's rare in the Bible—only three New Testament occurrences and a couple in the Greek Old Testament—but everyday papyri give it a warmer, more concrete flavor. In one slave's letter to her master, the writer thanks the gods for keeping him ἀπρόσκοπον, meaning simply 'safe and free from harm.'
caution: Evidence is thin (only three New Testament uses), and the standard translation absorbs the word into surrounding phrasing two out of three times, so the precise English rendering is uncertain.

definition: A pointed stake or the palisade and siege-rampart built from such stakes to encircle a city under attack.
article: χάραξ refers to a sharpened stake and, by extension, the wall of stakes or earthwork that an army threw up around a besieged city. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 19:43, where Jesus foretells that enemies will build such a barricade around Jerusalem; the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding action as "surround." Everyday Koine papyri preserve its plainer agricultural sense too, where χάραξ means a stake or vine-prop—one document even mentions thirty thousand reed stakes—showing the word lived in both farming and military settings.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on limited biblical evidence supplemented by external usage.

definition: To wrong someone or to harm them, whether by unjust treatment, injury, or causing damage to a person or thing.
senseLabels: to do wrong or act unjustly
article: ἀδικέω covers a range from outright moral wrongdoing to physical harm or injury, and can be used both for treating a person unjustly and for damaging things. In the Byzantine New Testament it's most often rendered "harm" (8×, 38%) or "wrong" (5×, 24%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing or rendered as a wronged person. The word was everyday legal vocabulary in the Greek world: Moulton-Milligan notes it is common in petition papyri where people complain of being wronged, such as a second-century B.C. document of someone "exceedingly wronged by Harmiysis," and even the sense of harming inanimate things (as in Revelation) has a parallel in Thucydides.

definition: To get something or someone ready in advance, making the necessary preparations.
article: ἑτοιμάζω means to make ready or prepare, and the corpus bears this out: of its 40 New Testament occurrences, 30 (79%) are rendered "prepared" and another 3 simply "make," with the rest minor variations. It covers everything from practical hospitality—preparing a meal or a room—to God's ordaining of coming events, blessings, or judgment. The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: papyri from the third century BC use it for equipping a relief force, cultivating land, and preparing grain to deliver to the State, and in the Septuagint it appears 136 times, most often translating the Hebrew kun ("to establish, make firm") 82 times.

definition: To move suddenly and violently toward something — to rush, charge, or dash forward.
article: ὁρμάω describes a sudden, forceful surge of motion — people, animals, or crowds dashing toward a place or target. In all 5 New Testament occurrences it works the same way: a herd of pigs plunging down a slope, or an angry mob charging at someone. The everyday papyri show the same flavor, where people "took to flight" (εἰς φυγὴν ὥρμησαν), though one later document weakens it to simply going after something you wanted. The three "senses" measured here are really one core meaning of rushing, just colored by what's added — "whole," "together," or alone.
caution: With only 5 occurrences, the distinctions between the measured senses reflect translation phrasing rather than truly separate meanings.

definition: The cardinal number five hundred.
article: This is simply the Greek number "five hundred," formed from πέντε (five) and ἑκατόν (hundred). It appears only twice in the New Testament — describing a debtor who owed five hundred denarii (Luke 7:41) and the more than five hundred believers who saw the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:6). In the Septuagint it shows up 52 times, most often rendering the Hebrew word for five (חָמֵשׁ), and everyday papyri use it for ordinary counting, such as a record of "five hundred bundles of hay."
caution: The digest's second measured sense is labeled "five" rather than "five hundred," likely an artifact of how the rendering was counted, since all the lexical sources agree the word means "five hundred."

definition: The front or forward part of a ship, the prow.
article: Πρῶρα is a nautical term for the forward part of a ship—the prow or bow—standing opposite the πρύμνα (stern). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the shipwreck account of Acts 27 (verses 30 and 41), and the two measured senses ("bow" and "ship bow") are really the same meaning. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too, including a third-century BC document that also preserves a related adjective, showing it was ordinary sailors' vocabulary.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in a single chapter, the evidence base is thin, though its meaning is not in doubt.

definition: Patmos, a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea, southwest of Ephesus, where John received the Revelation.
article: Πάτμος is the name of a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, lying southwest of Ephesus. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Revelation 1:9, where John says he was on Patmos when he received his visions; every translation simply transliterates it as "Patmos." Its derivation is uncertain, and the lexicons add only its geographic location.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its usage range cannot be measured beyond that single occurrence.

definition: Describing a garment made in one piece, without any seam where pieces were sewn together.
article: This word describes cloth that has no seam—a garment woven as a single piece rather than stitched together from parts. It comes from a negative prefix plus the root for sewing (ῥάπτω, "to sew"), so literally "unsewn." It appears only once in the New Testament, at John 19:23, describing Jesus' tunic, which the Majority Standard Bible renders "woven" (matching the BSB), while older lexicons and the KJV favor "without seam" or "seamless."
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its sense rests on a single passage.

definition: A teacher, instructor, or guide—someone who leads others by going before them in learning.
article: καθηγητής means a teacher or instructor, literally one who "goes before" to guide others, from the verb meaning to lead the way. In the New Testament it appears only a handful of times, all in Matthew 23, where Jesus warns against claiming such titles. The everyday papyri show the word in its plain sense: one letter asks someone to "send to my daughter's teacher that he may bestir himself about her," exactly the way we'd talk about a private tutor today.
caution: The three "measured senses" here are an artifact of how the verse was split—the word really carries a single meaning of teacher/guide, and the evidence overall is thin.

definition: A thought, plan, or intention formed in the mind — in its one New Testament use, a wicked scheme of the heart.
senseLabels: a thought or intention of the mind
article: At its root ἐπίνοια means a thought, design, or purpose conceived in the mind, built from ἐπί and νοῦς. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 8:22, where it refers to the wicked intent of someone's heart, and the Byzantine text renders it as "wickedness" in that context. The everyday Koine papyri confirm the broader, neutral range: documents speak of acting on one's own ἐπίνοια (one's own initiative or design), and one even mentions an "unjust" intention — showing the word itself is neutral and takes its moral color from the surrounding text.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax legomenon with only one occurrence, so its full range there can only be inferred from outside evidence like the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: Describing someone who breaks agreements and stays untrue to promises or covenants they have made.
article: ἀσύνθετος literally means "not put together" or "not agreed" — someone who fails to keep faith with the agreements they have made. It appears just once in the New Testament (Romans 1:31), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "heartless, merciless," though the older lexicons (KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) consistently define it as "covenant-breaker" or "faithless." The Septuagint uses it 4 times, all in Jeremiah, to translate Hebrew words for treachery and faithless backsliding, and the related verb εὐσυνθετέω ("to keep faith") shows up in Ptolemaic papyri about honoring obligations.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the modern translation "heartless" differs sharply from the lexicons' "covenant-breaker," so its precise force here is uncertain.

definition: Describing someone falling forward, headlong, or face-first to the ground.
article: πρηνής describes a body pitching forward, headlong or face-first, and appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:18 describing the death of Judas. It is a rare word—found in only a few Septuagint passages and in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions—and the standard glosses (KJV "headlong," Dodson "falling headlong, prone") all point to falling forward. One striking complication: Moulton-Milligan notes that Chase argued πρηνής could instead be a medical term meaning "swollen up," which would change how Acts 1:18 is read.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and scholars genuinely disagree on whether it means "falling headlong" or "swollen up."

definition: Not able to be tempted, or having no experience of something, especially of evil.
article: This rare word combines a negative prefix with a root tied to testing or tempting, so it describes someone who cannot be tempted or who is untried. It appears only once in the New Testament, at James 1:13, where it states that God is ἀπείραστος of evil. Moulton-Milligan note that the everyday Koine papyri use similar negative adjectives with a genitive construction, like an allotment described as 'subject to no dispute,' which supports reading James as 'untempted by evils.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and lexicons list a range of senses (untried, inexperienced, untemptable) whose exact force here is debated.

definition: Without distraction; in a way that is free from competing concerns or anxieties.
article: This adverb describes doing something free from distraction or competing worries—in 1 Corinthians 7:35, its only New Testament appearance, Paul speaks of serving the Lord with undivided attention. Though it occurs just once in the New Testament, the adjective form was common in everyday Koine, showing up in papyri where people sought to be secured "without trouble" from liabilities or debts (e.g., a tax document from 157 B.C.). The note in the Majority Standard Bible labeling this "promote" likely reflects how the surrounding phrase was rendered rather than the word itself, which all sources agree means "without distraction."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "promote" seems to capture the phrase rather than the word's actual meaning of "without distraction."

definition: Jesus, a personal name; the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, borne by Jesus of Nazareth and several other men.
article: Ἰησοῦς is a proper name, the Greek form of Hebrew Joshua (Jehoshua). It appears 972 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Jesus" in all 959 of the cases that get their own English word; the other 13 are absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it 258 times, mostly translating יְהוֹשׁוּעַ (214×) and יֵשׁוּעַ (28×), and everyday papyri show it was a common Jewish name both before and after the start of the Christian era — one census return even records a man's mother as "Iēsous." Strong's and Dodson note it also names other Israelites besides Jesus of Nazareth.

definition: Philippi, a major city in the Roman province of Macedonia.
article: Φίλιπποι is the name of Philippi, a leading city in the Roman province of Macedonia, mentioned 4 times in the New Testament. Notably the name is grammatically plural in Greek, and Acts 16:12 describes the city as a Roman colony. Moulton-Milligan note this colonial status meant Philippi functioned as a miniature likeness of Rome itself, which helps explain the strong Roman flavor of the city in Acts.
caution: This is a proper place name with only 4 occurrences, so its meaning is fixed rather than carrying a range of senses.

definition: An adjective meaning Hebrew, describing the Hebrew language or script.
article: Ἑβραϊκός is a simple adjective meaning "Hebrew," used of the Hebrew language. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 23:38, where it describes one of the languages of the inscription placed above Jesus on the cross. Notably, this word is absent from the critical text (SBLGNT) and is part of the Received Text reading, which is why Abbott-Smith marks it as a Received-text occurrence; the lexicons agree it derives from the name Eber (Ἐβέρ).
caution: Evidence is very thin — a single occurrence that does not appear in the critical text, so confidence is low.

definition: To suffer shipwreck, whether literally at sea or figuratively as a ruin or disaster in one's life.
article: ναυαγέω means to suffer shipwreck, built from the words for "ship" and "to break." It appears just twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "shipwrecked" (100%). One use is literal — Paul recounting his sea disasters in 2 Corinthians 11:25 — while in 1 Timothy 1:19 it is metaphorical, describing those who have "shipwrecked" their faith. Moulton-Milligan notes this same figurative image was common in popular Greek philosophy, describing people who "drag out their existence as derelicts on life's ocean."
caution: With only two occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though the literal and figurative senses are well attested in wider Koine usage.

definition: Lacking good sense or sound judgment; being foolish, senseless, or recklessly thoughtless.
article: ἄφρων describes someone without reason or sound judgment—built literally from a negative prefix plus the word for "mind" (φρήν). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 11 times and is consistently rendered "fool" or "foolish," with no real disagreement among the standard sources. The Septuagint uses it heavily (113 times) to translate several Hebrew words for foolishness, most often כְּסִיל (46×); strikingly, a second-century papyrus letter uses it to call a man defrauding his mother "quite mad," showing it carried real bite in everyday speech.

definition: To search for, look for, or seek after something or someone, often with eager intent.
article: ἐπιζητέω is ζητέω ("to seek") with the prefix ἐπί added, and the evidence suggests this prefix mostly gives a "directive" force — seeking toward a particular object — rather than intensifying it. In the Byzantine NT it appears 15 times, rendered "seeking" in 6 cases (55%) and "after" in 3 (27%), with about 4 occurrences blending into the phrasing rather than getting their own English word. The everyday Koine papyri are a nice touch: one second-century letter uses it simply to mean "in answer to your inquiry," showing the plain "ask about" sense alongside the stronger "long for" range. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew דָּרַשׁ ("to seek/inquire"), 5 times.
caution: The lexicons split on whether the ἐπί prefix is merely directive or genuinely intensive ("crave, demand"), so the exact force in any verse is uncertain.

definition: Someone who meddles in other people's affairs—interfering in business that isn't their own.
article: This rare word combines "belonging to another" with "overseer," so it literally means someone who oversees affairs that aren't theirs—a meddler or busybody. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 4:15, where it's listed alongside murderers and thieves; the Majority Standard Bible renders it broadly as "wrongdoer" there. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine papyri form similar compound titles (like inspectors and overseers of public works), which helps explain how this odd word was built.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise meaning is uncertain, and translations range from the specific "meddler" to the general "wrongdoer."

definition: The Greek letter iota, the smallest letter, used figuratively to mean the tiniest possible part of something.
article: Iota is simply the name of the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, used as an image for the smallest imaginable detail. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Matthew 5:18, where Jesus says not even an iota will pass from the Law until everything is accomplished. Dodson notes it parallels the Hebrew yod, the smallest letter of that alphabet, making it a natural stand-in for the tiniest part of the written text; the word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and even a third-century BC inscription about wind directions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its figurative range rests on that single verse plus outside parallels.

definition: To stay patient and long-suffering, holding back anger and waiting calmly when wronged or when things take time.
article: μακροθυμέω means literally being "long-tempered" — slow to anger, willing to wait and endure rather than react. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "patient" in just over half its occurrences (5×), with the rest using related words like "patience" or "longsuffering." One intriguing detail: classical sources also record an active sense "to persevere" (like καρτερέω), and Moulton-Milligan note a debated case in Luke 18:7, where the word may ask whether God delays in helping his people — a nuance beyond simple patience.
caution: The classical lexica list an active "persevere" sense alongside the dominant "be patient," and at least one verse (Luke 18:7) has a disputed shade of meaning.

definition: An exclamation of surprise, wonder, or mockery, like English "Aha!" or "Ha!"
article: οὐά is a shout of surprise or ironic mockery, best rendered "Aha!" or "Ha!" It appears just once in the New Testament, in Mark 15:29, where passersby jeer at Jesus on the cross, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "saying, Aha" in all (1×) of its uses. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and that Epictetus uses it the same mocking way ("say to me, Aha, and wonderfully!"); importantly, it expresses derision or amazement, not the pity carried by the similar-looking word οὐαί.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise tone rests on that single passage and a handful of outside examples.

definition: The act of throwing cargo overboard from a ship to lighten it during a storm.
article: ἐκβολή literally means "a throwing out," and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 27:18) it refers to the sailors jettisoning cargo to keep their storm-tossed ship afloat. The Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase "violently" in that one passage, though the word itself names the act of throwing overboard rather than the storm's force. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: Moulton-Milligan cite a mummy-ticket using the very phrase ἐκβολὴν ποιεῖσθαι for jettisoning, showing this was standard shipping vocabulary. In the Septuagint it appears just twice, where it can carry the broader sense of driving out or expelling.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there rests on a single verse and confidence is low.

definition: To bury someone, placing their body in a grave and carrying out the customary funeral rites.
article: θάπτω simply means to bury the dead, and its meaning is remarkably stable: in the Byzantine New Testament all 11 uses involve burial, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "buried" or "man buried." It's heavily used in the Septuagint (133 times), where it almost always translates the Hebrew קָבַר, "to bury" (124 times). The everyday papyri show the same down-to-earth sense, including one Egyptian document where a body had to be buried a second time in a fresh mummy-wrapping.

definition: A thought, plan, or mental purpose; by extension the mind or faculty that produces such thoughts.
article: νόημα centers on the activity of thinking—a thought, design, or purpose—and by extension can stand for the mind itself. Across its 6 New Testament occurrences (all in Paul) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "minds" 3 times, once as a hostile "scheme," and once within the phrasing about God's peace guarding hearts and minds in Philippians 4:7. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan argues from everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions that "thoughts" fits best every time, doubting the "mind" sense that many commentators prefer—so the measured renderings and this lexicon partly disagree.
caution: The word is rare (only 6 NT uses, all in Paul) and sources disagree on whether it ever means "mind" rather than simply "thoughts."

definition: Foolish or stupid; lacking sense or sound judgment, and as a noun, a person who acts that way.
article: μωρός describes someone or something dull-witted, senseless, or lacking sound judgment, and it works both as an adjective ("foolish") and as a noun ("a fool"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times, rendered "foolish" in 54% of cases and "fool" in 23%, with the Majority Standard Bible and BSB in full agreement. One vivid detail from the papyri: in an early first-century nursery acrostic about a lost garment, it reads "a lion he was who took it, a fool who lost it," and elsewhere the word even shows up as a personal nickname, much like the Latin name Brutus.

definition: To make someone angry, or to stir them up to anger or exasperation.
article: παροργίζω means to provoke someone to anger or exasperate them, built from παρά plus ὀργίζω ("to anger"). It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Romans 10:19 and Ephesians 6:4), but it is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 47 times and most often renders the Hebrew כָּעַס (31×), meaning to vex or provoke. A striking inscription over a former pagan temple turned Church of St. George in Syria captures the sense vividly: "where God was provoked to anger, God now shows Himself gracious."
caution: The measured rendering "instead" reflects the surrounding clause rather than the verb itself, so lean on the lexical evidence ("provoke to anger") for the actual meaning.

definition: To engage in sexual immorality, or figuratively to be unfaithful to God by practicing idolatry.
article: This verb covers sexual immorality and, by extension, the unfaithfulness of idolatry — picturing a people who abandon God like an unfaithful partner. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across just 2 books, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "immoral" in 3 cases and "commit sexual immorality" in 2. The metaphorical sense is rooted in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew זָנָה 12 times and is used by the prophets for spiritual unfaithfulness; everyday Koine papyri also attest the plain literal sense.
caution: The metaphorical "idolatry" sense in Revelation is debated, with Abbott-Smith noting that Swete reads those passages differently.

definition: Authority or commission given to someone, the power to act or decide on another's behalf.
article: ἐπιτροπή refers to delegated authority — the official power or commission to act, decide, or carry something out on behalf of someone else. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "pursuit" while the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) favor "power to decide, authority" and the KJV reads "commission." The everyday papyri are especially telling here: in one document a person says they handed over the ἐπιτροπή "to the gods," and the word commonly means the office of a legal guardian, as in receipts demanding proof of guardianship.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use — and the measured rendering "pursuit" diverges from the lexicons, which point to "authority" or "commission."

definition: A person who copies or follows someone else's example or way of life.
article: μιμητής names someone who deliberately models their conduct on another person, and in the New Testament it always carries a positive sense — copying a good example worth following. The Majority Standard Bible renders all 7 occurrences with "imitate" or "imitator," and the KJV's older "follower" points to the same idea. One striking detail: in every New Testament use the word is paired with the verb "to become" (γίνεσθαι), framing imitation as deliberate moral effort rather than passive copying; Moulton-Milligan also confirms it was ordinary, everyday Koine, found in papyri and inscriptions.
caution: The labeled senses are really one meaning split by phrasing, so don't read them as distinct definitions.

definition: To bite with the teeth, used figuratively for attacking or harming someone in a quarrel.
article: δάκνω literally means to bite, the way an animal sinks its teeth in, but its single New Testament appearance (Galatians 5:15) uses it figuratively for people tearing into one another in conflict. The Septuagint uses it 13 times in 8 books, almost always for the Hebrew נָשַׁך (12×) and once for שָׂרָף, often of literal snakebites. Moulton-Milligan notes a striking detail: the word has survived essentially unchanged in Greek for 3000 years, continuing in Modern Greek as δαγκάνω.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the figurative "attack/harm" sense rests on that single verse plus lexicon inference rather than broad measured data.

definition: To cover something with a shadow or cloud, enveloping it so completely that it is wrapped in haze or brilliance.
article: ἐπισκιάζω literally means to cast a shadow over something, but in the New Testament it usually describes being wrapped or enveloped by a cloud—often a bright, shining one rather than a dark one. All five Byzantine occurrences are rendered with words like "envelop" or "overshadow," and the Majority Standard and Berea Standard Bibles agree completely on every one. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew for "cloud" and even "to cover/shelter," and the word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary vocabulary, not a special religious term.
caution: Strong's and Abbott-Smith note a figurative sense of investing with divine influence (as in Luke 1:35), but the measured renderings treat this simply as enveloping, so the metaphorical reading is interpretive rather than confirmed by the data.

definition: A Hebrew personal name, Eleazar, borne by an ancestor of Jesus in Matthew's genealogy.
article: Eleazar is a Hebrew proper name (from אֶלְעָזָר) that appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both within Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, where Eleazar is the son of Eliud and father of Matthan. The name was common in everyday Koine life, showing up in papyri and inscriptions such as a first-century tombstone addressing 'Eleazar, untimely dead, good, friend to all.' In the Septuagint it occurs 75 times across 11 books, almost always for אֶלְעָזָר but occasionally for other Hebrew names like מָכִיר and יָרִיב.
caution: The two listed senses are an artifact of measurement—one occurrence was tallied as the adjacent name 'Matthan'—so this is simply one indeclinable personal name.

definition: To trace someone's ancestry or reckon their descent through a family line.
article: This verb means to trace or reckon someone's ancestry through a recorded family line, built from the words for "generation" and "to count." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 7:6, where it is used in the passive to describe Melchizedek, who did not trace his descent from a known lineage. Notably, in its single Septuagint appearance at 1 Chronicles 5:1, it again carries this sense of recording genealogical descent, matching a Hebrew word for being counted in a family register.
caution: Evidence is thin: just one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, so the measured range rests on very few examples.

definition: A whip or lash made of cords, like the Roman flagellum used for public punishment.
article: φραγέλλιον is a whip or scourge, appearing just once in the New Testament when Jesus makes one of cords to drive merchants from the temple (John 2:15). It is a Latin loanword (from flagellum) that passed into Koine Greek, and Moulton-Milligan find it in an everyday papyrus inventory from around A.D. 103–117 referring to a whip of Indian reed. The Majority Standard Bible, the Berean Study Bible, Strong's, and Dodson all agree on the meaning "whip" or "scourge."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To not know, not understand, or be unaware of a person, thing, or fact—sometimes implying a willful ignorance.
article: ἀγνοέω covers the whole range of not knowing—from simple unawareness to a deeper failure to understand. In the New Testament's 22 occurrences it clusters into being unaware (15%), simply 'not' knowing (15%), being ignorant (15%), and failing to understand (10%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing. The everyday papyri provide a striking parallel to Paul's recurring phrase 'I do not want you to be unaware,' where a letter (P Tebt II.314) reads 'I believe you are not unaware,' and another papyrus even hints at the willful ignorance Dodson and Strong's note.
caution: The measured senses spread fairly evenly with no dominant meaning, and renderings like 'unaware' versus 'ignorant' versus 'fail to understand' depend on context rather than a sharp distinction in the word itself.

definition: Mahalalel, a man listed among the ancient ancestors in the genealogy leading to Jesus.
article: Μαλελεήλ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Mahalalel (מַהֲלַלְאֵל), one of the early descendants of Adam before the Flood. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:37, where it is part of the genealogy tracing Jesus' line, and the translation simply renders it as a name within the list of ancestors. The Septuagint uses it 7 times across 3 books, always translating that same Hebrew name.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so it carries no meaning beyond identifying the individual.

definition: A going away or leaving, used in the New Testament for someone's departure.
article: This word appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 20:29, where it means Paul's departure. Interestingly, the classical and papyri evidence pulls the other way: in everyday Koine documents the word usually means "arrival" — Moulton-Milligan cites a papyrus where roads are leveled in preparation for King Ptolemy's ἄφιξις (his coming), and Abbott-Smith notes the "departure" sense is rare. So the New Testament's one use sits at the uncommon end of the word's range.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence, and the lexicons note that its "departure" sense is rare compared to the usual classical meaning "arrival."

definition: A promise—especially God's pledge to give something good—or, more rarely, a formal announcement.
article: In the New Testament ἐπαγγελία almost always means a promise: it's rendered "promise" in 49 of its 52 occurrences (96%), and the Berean Study Bible agrees 100%. It's used especially of God's promises, as in Luke 24:49, Acts 1:4, and Romans 4:13. Interestingly, the word's older sense was "announcement"—papyri and inscriptions from the third century BC use it for public notices—but by NT times it had settled into the meaning "promise," which Moulton-Milligan notes it apparently always carries in the New Testament.
caution: Abbott-Smith records an older legal sense "a summons," but that meaning does not appear in the measured New Testament data.

definition: Sour wine, the cheap everyday drink of laborers and Roman soldiers.
article: Ὄξος is sour wine—a cheap, vinegary drink (Latin posca) commonly carried by laborers and Roman soldiers, which is why it appears in the crucifixion scenes of all four Gospels. Though it shows up in the digest's measured data under several phrasings ("sour wine," "sour wine up," "wine"), these are just surrounding words from translation, not separate meanings; the word itself consistently means sour wine. The everyday papyri confirm this: a London receipt from A.D. 357 records four thousand measures of ὄξος supplied to soldiers, and other documents carefully distinguish it from regular wine (οἶνος). In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew chomets, meaning vinegar.

definition: Someone who does or carries out something, especially one who actively obeys a law or message rather than just hearing it.
article: ποιητής comes from the verb ποιέω ("to do, make") and means a person who acts on something. In the New Testament it appears 6 times, regularly in phrases like "doer of the law" or "doer of the word" (James and Romans), where it stresses carrying something out rather than merely listening. Interestingly, in everyday Greek the same word commonly meant "poet" or "maker" — papyri and inscriptions call Homer "the divine poet" using this exact term, and Acts 17:28 uses it that way too.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and the measured rendering folding it into surrounding phrasing almost every time, the English wording varies by context.

definition: Abiathar, a Jewish high priest who served during King David's reign.
article: Ἀβιαθάρ is the Greek form of a Hebrew personal name, indeclinable in Greek, naming Abiathar, a priest in King David's time. It appears just once in the New Testament (Mark 2:26) and 29 times in the Septuagint, where it always renders the Hebrew name אֶבְיָתָר. One measured note: the single Majority Standard rendering shows up as "priesthood" because the verse refers to events in Abiathar's time, but lexicons agree the word itself is simply the man's name.
caution: This is a personal name occurring only once in the New Testament, so the lone "priesthood" rendering reflects context rather than the word's own meaning.

definition: To struggle or fight against an opposing force.
article: This verb means to struggle or contend against something, picturing an active fight with an opponent. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 12:4, where it describes struggling against sin. It often takes the preprosition πρός ("against"), and an inscription from Priene (shortly after 278 B.C.) uses the same construction for fighting "against the barbarians."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: To bring someone to their senses, training or coaching them toward sound, self-controlled behavior.
article: This verb means to make someone σώφρων—level-headed and self-controlled—whether by correcting them, recalling them to their senses, or training them in good habits. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Titus 2:4, where older women are to train the younger ones; the digest's lone measured rendering tags it oddly as "husbands," reflecting the surrounding context rather than the verb itself. A striking parallel comes from the papyri: in an Oxyrhynchus document an emperor declares he is accustomed to "bring to their senses" those who are mad or beside themselves, which fits the corrective edge of the word.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence and the one measured rendering ("husbands") clearly reflects context rather than the verb's meaning, so lean on the lexical evidence here.

definition: The act of calling something to mind again; a deliberate remembering or recollection.
article: ἀνάμνησις means a calling-to-mind, a deliberate act of remembrance. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, rendered "remembrance" in 3 of them (75%), most famously in Jesus' words over the bread and cup in Luke 22:19 and 1 Corinthians 11:24-25. The one outlier, Hebrews 10:3, speaks of a yearly reminder of sins through sacrifices. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words, including אַזְכָּרָה in Leviticus 24:7, tied to the memorial offering, and it also turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions and papyri.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the second "annual" sense really reflects context in Hebrews 10:3 rather than a separate meaning of the word itself, which consistently denotes remembrance.

definition: To move or go from one place to another, or to leave and depart from where you are.
article: μεταβαίνω is a movement word meaning to pass from one place to another, and by extension simply to leave or withdraw from where you are. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "leave" 3 times and "Move" 2 times across its 12 New Testament occurrences, matching its everyday use in Koine papyri, where one Tebtunis document (A.D. 99) uses it for changing one's residence: "if we change our abode or go abroad." Abbott-Smith notes a striking metaphorical stretch in John, where it describes moving from death into life (John 5:24) and even departing this world to go to the Father (John 13:1).

definition: Purple cloth or a purple garment, prized as a sign of wealth and high rank.
article: In the New Testament πορφύρα refers to expensive purple fabric or a purple robe, worn to signal power and wealth—as with the rich man in Luke 16:19 and the robe mocking Jesus in Mark 15. The Septuagint uses it 33 times, most often for the Hebrew אַרְגָּמָן (17×), the prized purple dye of tabernacle and royal fabrics. The lexicons note an older, more basic meaning: the word originally named the shellfish that produced the dye, then the dye itself, and only later the finished garment—and everyday papyri accounts confirm it was a common trade commodity, with one listing 'purple, 20 drachmae.'
caution: Confidence is rated low: the word appears only 3–4 times in the New Testament, and the classical sense of 'purple shellfish/dye' is not what the NT occurrences actually mean.

definition: Describing a person who is skilled at teaching others.
article: διδακτικός describes someone who has the ability and aptitude to teach. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Timothy 3:2 and 2 Timothy 2:24), and in both places the Majority Standard Bible renders it "able to teach," with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing completely. Interestingly, this is the later Koine form of the word; Abbott-Smith notes that the classical form was διδασκαλικός, and Moulton-Milligan observes that even Vettius Valens still used the older spelling.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice and confidence is rated low, though all sources agree on its meaning.

definition: To feel inner joy or delight in something, taking deep personal satisfaction in it.
article: This word describes an inner, heartfelt joy or satisfaction in something—in its single New Testament appearance (Romans 7:22), Paul says he delights in God's law in his inner self. The verb is middle voice and is built from σύν ("with") and the root behind ἡδονή ("pleasure"). Everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions use it to mean "congratulate," as when one writer tells a friend "I congratulate you on your dear protector" (P Oxy XIV.1663), showing the word could be directed warmly toward others as well.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single passage.

definition: The act of throwing something away or casting it off, or the experience of losing something.
article: ἀποβολή is a noun built from the verb ἀποβάλλω (to throw off) and covers two related ideas: actively rejecting or casting something away, and passively suffering a loss. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and in both cases English translations fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a single word. Abbott-Smith neatly separates the two uses: in Romans 11:15 it is the "casting away" set opposite to acceptance (πρόσλημψις), while in Acts 27:22 it is the "loss" of life that Paul says will not happen.
caution: With only two occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word, the evidence for its range is thin.

definition: Someone who brings a charge against another person, especially a prosecutor or complainant in a legal setting.
article: κατήγορος is a legal term for the person who brings charges against someone—an accuser, prosecutor, or plaintiff. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times and is rendered "accuser(s)" in 5 of them, with the one exception in Revelation 12:10 referring to Satan as the accuser of believers. The word is well attested in everyday Koine: papyri use it for legal accusers and plaintiffs, including a "public prosecutor" (δημοσίου κατηγόρου), and the Septuagint employs it in Proverbs 18:17 for the one who argues a case at law.
caution: The lexica (Abbott-Smith) cite different verse references than the measured occurrences, partly because critical texts (SBLGNT counts only 4) omit some readings found in the Byzantine text.

definition: Characteristic of youth—the kind of desires or tendencies typical of young people.
article: This adjective describes things that are characteristic of youth, especially youthful qualities or impulses. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:22, where it modifies "desires" (epithymiai) that are to be fled. Interestingly, the same word shows up in an everyday papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (A.D. 213-217) describing a bronze folding mirror "in the new style," showing that the term could also mean simply newfangled or modern.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint use (3 Maccabees), the evidence is thin, though sources agree on the basic sense.

definition: The number three.
article: τρεῖς is simply the cardinal number "three," and it works exactly as you'd expect across the New Testament. It's overwhelmingly stable: of 66 Byzantine occurrences, 62 (97%) are rendered "three," with the rest absorbed into phrases. In the Septuagint it appears 324 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for three (שָׁלוֹשׁ, 282×), and it even shows up in a place name—"Three Taverns" (Τρεῖς Ταβέρναι), a stopping point on the Appian Way mentioned in Acts 28:15.

definition: Iconium, a city in the Roman province of Galatia in Asia Minor (modern Konya).
article: Ἰκόνιον is simply a place name: Iconium, a city in central Asia Minor, in the Roman province of Galatia. It appears 6 times in the New Testament, all in Acts and 2 Timothy, marking Paul's travels and the persecution he faced there. The two "measured senses" both refer to the same city; the only difference is phrasing in one verse (Acts 16:2). Interestingly, inscriptions show the city's name likely came from an older non-literary Phrygian form, later hellenized and reshaped to suggest a link with the Greek word for "image" (εἰκών).

definition: Excessive drinking of wine; habitual drunkenness or boozing.
article: οἰνοφλυγία refers to heavy, excessive drinking of wine — drunkenness or wine-bibbing. The word literally combines "wine" with a root meaning "to bubble up" or "overflow," picturing drink running over the top. It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Peter 4:3), but Moulton-Milligan finds it in everyday Koine papyri and in writers like Musonius and Philo, who list it alongside gluttony and lust as a vice; the related verb also shows up in Deuteronomy 21:20.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with thin biblical evidence, and the lone measured rendering "detestable" reflects translation phrasing rather than the word's core meaning of drunkenness, which the lexicons agree on.

definition: To shine out or beam forth light; possibly also to see clearly or discern.
article: This rare verb appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 4:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as light dawning or shining forth. The word's range is genuinely disputed: in the Septuagint it appears 7 times in Leviticus, all translating the Hebrew term for a bright or white skin spot, so it means "appear white or bright" there. Moulton-Milligan notes that Nägeli reads the Pauline passage differently, taking it in the old poetic sense "see clearly" (as in Sophocles), which would make Paul speak of unbelievers being unable to see the light of the gospel.
caution: The evidence is thin and the sources genuinely disagree: the single NT use could mean "shine forth" or "see clearly," and the LXX usage points to a third, unrelated sense.

definition: Paul, a Latin personal name borne in the New Testament chiefly by the apostle and once by a Roman official.
article: Παῦλος is a Latin name (Paulus) that appears 163 times across 15 books of the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "Paul" in essentially every instance. It overwhelmingly refers to the apostle Paul, but Abbott-Smith notes it also names the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus in Acts 13:7. The most interesting detail is the double name in Acts 13:9, "Saul who was also called Paul": Moulton-Milligan reports that Deissmann showed the apostle already held both names by this point, and Ramsay even suggested his full Roman name may have been C. Julius Paullus.

definition: To make strong or healthy; in its perfect imperative form, used as a polite closing word meaning "farewell" or "goodbye."
article: The base meaning of ῥώννυμι is "to strengthen" or "make firm," but in the New Testament it appears only twice (Acts 15:29 and Acts 23:30), both times in its perfect passive form as a closing word meaning "Farewell" — literally something like "be strong" or "keep well." Moulton-Milligan shows this was the standard sign-off in everyday Koine letters, both private and official, with the forms ἔρρωσο and ἔρρωσθε working exactly like the Latin uale/ualete. A nice detail from the papyri: writers often warmed it up with terms of endearment, as in one second-century letter reading "farewell to me, most honored one."
caution: This word does not appear in the critical SBL Greek text and occurs only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: To lower or let something down, such as lowering a person or net by ropes from a height.
article: χαλάω means to lower or let something down, often by ropes or other means.
