All seven New Testament uses center on this physical action—lowering a paralyzed man through a roof, letting down fishing nets, or lowering Paul in a basket through a window. The papyri show the same everyday sense, with one document describing workers slackening ropes around a piece of equipment; in Modern Greek the word later shifted to mean "break to pieces" or "ruin."
caution: The few related senses (slacken, loosen) come from lexicons rather than measured New Testament data, where every occurrence means lowering something down.

definition: To boast or take pride in something, whether arrogantly or as confident, joyful exultation in a worthy object.
article: καυχάομαι is the verb for boasting, used 38 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "boast" in 82% of cases. But it carries a notable double edge: it can also mean joyful exultation, which is why translators sometimes render it "rejoice" (as in Romans 5:2-3). Both Strong's and Abbott-Smith confirm this good-or-bad range, and the Septuagint often used it for triumphant rejoicing, frequently translating Hebrew words for being rich or glorying.

definition: To run around or all through an area, moving quickly from place to place.
article: This verb combines "around" (περί) with "run" (τρέχω) to describe rushing about through a region. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Mark 6:55, where people run all through the area carrying the sick to Jesus. The word also shows up twice in the Septuagint, both times rendering the Hebrew שׁוּט (to roam or rove), and a papyrus from A.D. 254 uses it of someone "going round the threshing floors" — everyday Koine for moving about a property.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: To feed and raise someone to maturity, covering both physical nourishment and the longer-term work of bringing up children.
article: ἐκτρέφω combines ἐκ with τρέφω (to feed) and means to nourish someone or rear them all the way to maturity. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, split evenly across feeding (Eph 5:29), bringing up children (Eph 6:4), and being sustained (Rev 12:6), and the Septuagint uses it 19 times, most often for Hebrew גָּדַל, "to grow up." An everyday early first-century papyrus contract preserves the word vividly: a nurse agrees "I will nurse the infant slave Thermoutharion for two years."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and one rendered "wrath" in the digest (which conflicts with the verb's actual meaning and likely reflects context, not the word itself), the evidence here is thin and should be read carefully.

definition: The cherubim — angelic winged figures associated with God's presence, especially over the ark's cover.
article: Χερουβίμ is a Hebrew word brought straight into Greek, naming the angelic figures linked with God's presence. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 9:5, describing the figures overshadowing the ark's mercy seat, and it is consistently rendered "cherubim." The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 82 times and almost always translates the Hebrew כְּרוּב; Moulton-Milligan even finds it in everyday papyri, including the phrase "the one seated upon the cherubim."
caution: This is a transliterated Hebrew loanword appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament, so its sense rests mainly on Septuagint and Old Testament usage.

definition: A dragon or huge mythical serpent, used in Revelation as a symbol of Satan.
article: Across all 13 New Testament occurrences, every one in Revelation, δράκων is rendered "dragon" 100% of the time, and the lexicons agree it names a mythical serpent-monster — in Revelation explicitly identified with Satan. In the Septuagint it appears 28 times, most often translating the Hebrew word תַּנִּין (12×), a term for a sea-monster or great serpent. The word turns up frequently in everyday magical papyri, including a vivid description of an ouroboros, "the dragon devouring its own tail."

definition: To serve or wait on someone, often by attending to practical needs like food, support, or care.
article: διακονέω covers the practical act of serving or waiting on people, especially attending to needs like food at a table. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "serve" in 20 of 37 occurrences (69%), with "ministered" and "minister" filling out the rest, and the Berean Standard Bible agrees with every choice. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary sense: an apprenticeship contract from A.D. 66 uses it of a boy hired "to serve and do everything commanded him." Lexicons note a narrower technical sense, "to serve as a deacon," though that meaning doesn't surface in the measured renderings here.

definition: To be at peace, keep peace, or live peaceably with others.
article: εἰρηνεύω means to be at peace or to keep peace, especially in how you live with other people. All four New Testament uses point the same way, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "peace" three times and "live" once (as in "live in peace"). A striking example comes from an inscription of the time of Augustus that says "land and sea are at peace" — a vivid snapshot of the Pax Romana using this very word.
caution: Abbott-Smith notes a separate transitive sense "to bring to peace, reconcile" in 1 Maccabees 6:60, but that meaning does not appear in the four New Testament occurrences.

definition: A system of religious belief or worship, referring neutrally to someone's religion or, in a negative slant, to superstition.
article: δεισιδαιμονία describes religious belief or worship, and it can be heard either neutrally ("religion") or critically ("superstition"), depending on the speaker. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 25:19, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "contentions," though the older lexicons treat it as a person's religion. A nice piece of supporting evidence comes from an inscription (OGIS 455, 39 BC) where the word names the legal religious status of a temple of Aphrodite, showing its plain, non-judgmental use in everyday Koine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "contentions" sits oddly against the lexicons, which read it as "religion" or "superstition" — so its precise force in Acts 25:19 is uncertain.

definition: To find someone guilty and pass sentence against them, as a judge issuing a formal condemnation.
article: καταδικάζω is a legal term meaning to give a verdict against someone and declare them guilty. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, rendered "condemned" in 3 of them, with the contrast between being acquitted and condemned in view at Matthew 12:37. It carries the same courtroom meaning in everyday Koine: a third-century B.C. legal code uses it of a master being formally convicted in a lawsuit, and Moulton-Milligan note the word kept this exact form and sense all the way into Modern Greek.

definition: To strip something off completely from oneself, like removing clothing, or to disarm and despoil an opponent.
article: This verb means to strip something off entirely, built from pieces meaning "off," "out of," and "to undress." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Colossians: once of God disarming or despoiling rulers and authorities (2:15), and once of believers stripping off the old self like discarded clothing (3:9). The translation labels here ("having," "since") just reflect how the surrounding sentence is phrased, not separate meanings of the word itself.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in one book, the evidence is thin, and lexicons note the despoiling sense in Colossians 2:15 is debated.

definition: Connected with the marketplace—either an idle rabble-rouser who hangs around it, or the court sessions that are held there.
article: This word literally means "belonging to the marketplace," and it pulls in two directions across its 2 New Testament uses. In Acts 17:5 it describes loafers or agitators recruited from the marketplace (rendered "troublemakers"), while in Acts 19:38 it refers to the court days held in that public square (the "fellow" rendering reflects this legal setting). An inscription from the 2nd century BC uses the same word simply for merchants and dealers, and a scholar cited by Moulton-Milligan points to a Plutarch parallel that paints the marketplace crowd as low-born agitators able to stir up a mob.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 occurrences with two distinct senses—and the lexica note that even the manuscripts and grammarians disagree over the word's accent and exact meaning.

definition: A place where two seas or currents meet, such as a reef or sandbar with water on both sides.
senseLabels: a place where two seas meet
article: This word literally combines "twice" and "sea," describing a spot caught between two bodies of water — a tongue of land, reef, or sandbar with sea on both sides. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:41, where Paul's ship runs aground on such a place; the Majority Standard Bible renders the scene with "stuck." Abbott-Smith notes the term could also mean "divided into two seas," as ancient writers applied it to the Black Sea, but in Acts it points to the reef or shoal that grounded the ship.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and lexicons differ on whether it means a sea split in two or a place where two seas meet.

definition: The ability to perceive and discern, especially moral or spiritual insight that helps you judge what truly matters.
article: αἴσθησις refers to perception that goes beyond raw sensing into discernment — the kind of insight that lets you tell good from bad. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 1:9, where translators render it "depth insight." In the Septuagint it shows up 23 times, mostly standing in for the Hebrew word דַּעַת ("knowledge"), and the everyday papyri use it for ordinary "perception" alongside words for body, spirit, and mind, showing it could mean plain sense-perception too.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning there rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Referring to an earlier time or prior state — "before," "formerly," or "the former."
article: πρότερον is the neuter form of πρότερος used as an adverb, pointing to something that came earlier in time. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 11 times, and translators split it fairly evenly between "first" (30%), "formerly" (30%), and "former" (20%), which all share the same core idea of priority in time. In the Septuagint it appears 32 times and most often renders the Hebrew רִאשׁוֹן ("first," 13 times), confirming the consistent "earlier/first" sense across both Testaments.

definition: A scaly, spreading skin disease that made a person ritually unclean and socially isolated until cured.
article: λέπρα names a serious skin disease, rendered "leprosy" in all 4 of its New Testament appearances and across the lexicons. The word is built from the same root as λεπίς, reflecting the scaly appearance behind Strong's note of "scaliness." In the Septuagint it shows up 39 times, almost always translating the Hebrew צָרַעַת, the condition that required priestly inspection and rendered a person ceremonially unclean.

definition: To boast or triumph against someone or something, treating it with proud contempt.
article: This compound joins κατά ("against") with καυχάομαι ("to boast"), giving the sense of boasting over or exulting against something. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, split evenly between Romans 11:18 and James, where it can describe both prideful contempt and, positively, mercy that "triumphs over" judgment. Notably, Abbott-Smith records a second Septuagint sense, "to glory in" (with ἐν), where it translates the Hebrew for walking or rejoicing, showing the word could carry a more neutral celebratory tone outside the NT.
caution: With only 4 NT occurrences, the breakdown into four measured senses reflects very thin per-sense evidence, and the renderings overlap heavily around the single idea of boasting against.

definition: A violent, sudden windstorm or squall that whips up dangerous, churning conditions.
article: Λαῖλαψ names a sudden, fierce windstorm — a squall or whirlwind that strikes without warning. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, in all three cases tied to dramatic weather: the storm that nearly swamps the disciples' boat (Mark 4:37; Luke 8:23) and a figurative storm in 2 Peter 2:17. In the Septuagint it renders several different Hebrew words, including סַעַר (a tempest), and Abbott-Smith notes it is close in meaning to θύελλα, another word for a violent gust.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and an uncertain derivation, this is a thinly attested word; translators split between specific renderings like 'windstorm' and the more general 'storm'.

definition: To cut hair short or shear an animal's wool, often used of having one's own hair cut.
senseLabels: to shear or cut hair short
article: κείρω means to cut hair very short or to shear an animal's fleece. In the New Testament it appears 4 times, often in the middle voice for cutting one's own hair, as when Paul had his head shorn (Acts 18:18); it also describes a sheep silent before its shearer (Acts 8:32). In the Septuagint it occurs 21 times and most often translates the Hebrew גָּזַז ("to shear," 14×), while everyday Koine papyri use it literally for shearing sheep and figuratively for "fleecing" or ravaging people.
caution: Of its 4 New Testament occurrences, only one is rendered by a distinct English word, so its measured range rests on thin data.

definition: Matthat, the personal name of two ancestors of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy.
article: Matthat is a Hebrew personal name (from מַתָּת) belonging to two different men in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke's Gospel. It appears just twice, in Luke 3:24 and Luke 3:29, and is consistently rendered simply as the name "Matthat." Strong's notes it is probably a shortened form of Mattathias (G3161), meaning it carries the same Hebrew naming tradition.
caution: This name appears only twice and the spelling varies across manuscript traditions (Μαθθάτ vs. Ματθάτ).

definition: To take something on oneself—either by accepting responsibility for it or by welcoming someone as a guest.
article: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, and its two uses pull in slightly different directions. In Hebrews 11:17 it describes Abraham, who had "received" or taken up the promises—the sense of accepting and holding something as one's own; in Acts 28:7 it means to welcome guests. The everyday papyri are especially telling here: ἀναδέχομαι was a common legal term meaning to assume liability or stand as security, as in an Oxyrhynchus document where a man writes, "I will take the responsibility upon myself."
caution: With only 2 occurrences and one of them absorbed into the surrounding phrasing, the evidence is thin and the word's range is hard to pin down.

definition: Someone who takes over another person's office or position; a successor.
article: διάδοχος means a successor — someone who steps into another person's official role. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 24:27, where Porcius Festus succeeds Felix as governor (the MSB happens to render the surrounding phrase as the name "Porcius"). The most interesting detail comes from the papyri: Deissmann showed that διάδοχος could be a formal court or military title, originally applied to Alexander's reinforcements before it came to mark a particular rank or privilege among his successors.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured from usage alone.

definition: To circumcise, meaning to cut away the foreskin as a ritual or covenant act.
article: This verb literally means "to cut around," but in the New Testament it consistently refers to circumcision, the rite of cutting away the foreskin; it's rendered "circumcised" in 13 of 18 occurrences (72%). The Septuagint uses it 32 times, almost always for the Hebrew word mul, "to circumcise," and the lexicons agree it became the standard term for this ceremonial act. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan note that an everyday Koine papyrus from 163 BC uses the same word for an Egyptian circumcision custom, suggesting the Greek translators picked it because it was already a recognized technical term. Paul also stretches it metaphorically in Colossians 2:11 to speak of a spiritual circumcision.

definition: Lacking understanding or discernment; failing to grasp or perceive, sometimes with a hint of moral as well as mental dullness.
article: ἀσύνετος describes someone who fails to understand or discern, built from a negative prefix plus the word for "understanding." In the New Testament it shows up 5 times, where translators render it around understanding in two-thirds of cases and as being "still dull" once, with the remaining two absorbed into broader phrasing. The Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew word nāḇāl (the senseless "fool"), and Moulton-Milligan's everyday papyri include a line meaning "he was not stupid" alongside an inscription where the word points less to lack of brains than to moral failing.
caution: Lexicons note a possible moral dimension ("wicked," "moral defect") beyond plain mental dullness, so the exact shade can be uncertain in a given verse.

definition: Loud mourning for the dead, expressed by beating the breast and head in grief.
article: κοπετός means a public, physical display of grief — wailing and beating the chest and head over someone who has died. Although the Majority Standard Bible's rendering registers as "buried" here (the word appears alongside the burial of Stephen in Acts 8:2, its only New Testament occurrence), the classical and Septuagint evidence is clear that the word itself denotes the lamentation, not the burial. In the Greek Old Testament it appears 14 times and almost always translates the Hebrew מִסְפֵּד ("mourning, wailing"), and a Greek inscription even pairs it with words for dirges and laments, where a mother is urged to cease her "laments and breast-beating."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "buried" reflects the surrounding verse rather than the word's actual meaning of loud mourning.

definition: A written notice or placard posted publicly to state something, such as the charge against a condemned person.
article: τίτλος is a Latin loanword (from titulus) meaning a written placard or inscription posted for public reading. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in John 19:19-20, referring to the notice Pilate fixed to Jesus' cross. The most interesting evidence comes from Christian inscriptions from Iconium, where the word was used to mean an epitaph on a tombstone, showing its everyday life in ordinary Koine.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in the same passage, and the two measured senses really describing one object, the apparent range is very thin.

definition: A rare word describing the bread asked for in the Lord's Prayer, most likely meaning needful for today or for the coming day.
article: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:11 and Luke 11:3), and is almost always rendered "daily." Its meaning is genuinely uncertain because the word may break down several ways: as "for the coming day," as "for subsistence" or "needful," or as "pertaining to the day." The most striking piece of evidence is that Moulton-Milligan, who normally find words in everyday papyri, report that the documents "have as yet shed no clear light" on it, suggesting it may have been a fresh coinage to translate an Aramaic original.
caution: This is effectively a hapax phrase whose derivation is disputed; the major lexicons list several competing meanings, so any single rendering is provisional.

definition: A placeholder for a person whose name is known but left unstated — "so-and-so" or "a certain person."
article: δεῖνα is the Greek equivalent of saying "so-and-so" or "Mr. X" — a stand-in for a name the speaker knows but doesn't say. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 26:18, where Jesus tells the disciples to go to "such a man" in the city; interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders that occurrence as "house" rather than naming a person. Everyday papyri make the word's flavor vivid: the magic papyri leave a literal blank into which any name could be inserted, exactly like a fill-in-the-blank form.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range rests almost entirely on outside evidence, and the single measured rendering ("house") doesn't match the lexicons' "a certain person."

definition: Balaam, the Old Testament soothsayer hired to curse Israel, named in the New Testament as an example of false teaching.
article: Βαλαάμ is simply the proper name Balaam, the Mesopotamian diviner from the book of Numbers, and the Majority Standard Bible renders all 3 New Testament occurrences this way. The New Testament writers point back to him as a warning, citing him in 2 Peter 2:15, Jude 11, and Revelation 2:14. The name is far more common in the Septuagint, appearing 62 times and translating the Hebrew בִּלְעָם in 59 of those cases.
caution: This is a proper name, so it has no real semantic range, and the low confidence tier reflects only its few New Testament occurrences.

definition: In a way marked by eagerness and urgency — doing something earnestly, diligently, or without delay.
article: This adverb describes acting with eager effort and a sense of urgency, whether that comes across as earnest diligence or as moving quickly. The two shades overlap so closely that lexicons split on the comparative form in Philippians 2:28: Abbott-Smith and others read it as "more earnestly," while Thayer and Zorell take it as "more speedily." Moulton-Milligan show the word was common in everyday Koine, citing a papyrus where a writer asks someone to pass along information "earnestly" — that is, promptly and in earnest.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 Byzantine occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing) and sources genuinely disagree on whether the sense leans toward 'earnestly' or 'speedily.'

definition: To spread out or stretch forth, as one extends the arms wide or unfurls a sail.
article: This verb means to spread or stretch something out fully — the prefix ἐκ pushes the action as far as it will go, like unfurling a sail. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 10:21, where God spreads out his hands all day toward a disobedient people. In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times across 4 books, every time translating the Hebrew פָּרַשׂ ("to spread out"), and Romans 10:21 itself quotes Isaiah 65:2.
caution: The measured sense label "obstinate" reflects how the surrounding verse is rendered, not this verb itself, which means "stretch out"; with only one New Testament occurrence, confidence is low.

definition: A city magistrate or local civic official who governed a town, especially in Thessalonica.
article: Both New Testament occurrences (Acts 17:6 and 17:8) refer to the same kind of local civic rulers, and the Majority Standard Bible renders them "officials" 100% of the time. The word combines πόλις ("city") and ἄρχω ("to rule"), so it literally means a city-ruler or town magistrate. The most striking evidence is from inscriptions: Moulton-Milligan notes that this title is confirmed in stone for Thessalonica and elsewhere, with about seventeen inscriptions documenting that the city had 5 politarchs under Augustus and 6 under Antoninus and Marcus — a precise match to Luke's usage.
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the biblical text alone, and the confidence tier is low.

definition: In a way that is just, fair, or morally right.
article: This adverb describes acting in a manner that is just or righteous, formed from the adjective δίκαιος ("righteous"). It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament; the Majority Standard Bible renders 2 occurrences as "justly" and folds the other 3 into surrounding phrasing rather than giving them a separate word. In the Septuagint it appears 5 times, usually translating the Hebrew צֶ֫דֶק ("righteousness") three times, though once it stands in for the unrelated עָקַב.
caution: Lexicons split the range between "righteously" and "justly," and the measured data covers only 2 of the 5 occurrences as an explicit English word, so the sense boundary is somewhat soft.

definition: To thoroughly deceive someone, leading them astray by trickery or false reasoning.
article: This is an intensified form of ἀπατάω, meaning to deceive someone completely or thoroughly. The five Byzantine New Testament uses all carry this single core sense, whether of people deceiving others with smooth talk (Romans 16:18), sin deceiving and killing (Romans 7:11), or self-deception (1 Corinthians 3:18). The everyday papyri show the word's down-to-earth flavor: one document warns against debtors who would "fraudulently mortgage" property, and another asks whether someone "was deceived or took bribes."
caution: The translation variations in the digest reflect surrounding phrasing rather than distinct meanings; the word consistently means "deceive," and it appears only 5–6 times in the New Testament and just once in the Septuagint.

definition: A furnace or oven — an enclosed structure for intense heat, used for baking, smelting, or burning.
article: κάμινος is a furnace or kiln, an enclosed structure built to hold intense heat. In the New Testament it appears 4 times, split evenly: twice as a "fiery furnace" (Matthew 13:42, 50) and twice simply as a "furnace" (Revelation 1:15, 9:2). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense — one document mentions "the oven built to receive the rye intended for the food of the calves," and others reference brick-carriers working at a furnace. In the Septuagint it occurs 33 times, often translating Hebrew words for fire (אֵשׁ) and smelting-furnace (כּוּר).

definition: A person who sets others free or buys them back, used in Scripture of God as redeemer and deliverer.
article: λυτρωτής means a redeemer or deliverer — one who rescues people, often by paying a price to set them free. It is rare: it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 7:35, where it describes Moses) and 4 times in the Septuagint, where it twice renders Hebrew words for redemption and is used of God himself as redeemer. Moulton-Milligan note that the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was real working vocabulary, not just a religious term.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and a handful in the Septuagint — so the confidence tier is low.

definition: A large dragnet pulled through the water to sweep up fish, distinct from smaller throwing nets.
article: σαγήνη refers to a large fishing dragnet, or seine, that sweeps up everything in its path. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Matthew 13:47, where it is rendered "net" in every counted instance. Moulton-Milligan note that it was a sizable, expensive piece of equipment, often worked by two boats that drew it together to the shore, setting it apart from the smaller circular ἀμφίβληστρον. In the Septuagint it occurs 6 times across 4 books, translating several different Hebrew words.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on thin evidence.

definition: A helmet, the protective covering worn over the head, used both literally and as a figure of speech.
article: περικεφαλαία simply means a helmet—literally something that encircles the head, as the word's parts suggest. Both of its New Testament appearances use it figuratively, picturing the helmet as part of a believer's spiritual armor (Ephesians 6:17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8). The everyday reality behind the metaphor shows up in the papyri, where one third-century BC account lists 60 drachmas for a helmet and sheath, and an inscription names a helmet as first prize in a javelin-throwing contest. In the Greek Old Testament it occurs 9 times, usually rendering the Hebrew word for helmet (kova').

definition: To officially register or enroll someone onto an approved list.
article: In its single New Testament appearance, καταλέγω means to enroll or register someone onto an official list — in 1 Timothy 5:9 it describes putting a widow on the church's roster of those to be supported. The classical lexicons show a wider range: it could mean to lay down, to narrate, or to choose out, and was especially used of enrolling soldiers. The everyday papyri confirm this technical sense vividly, with one document from A.D. 274 using it of someone enrolled into a sacred assembly, and an inscription describing a girl enrolled as a basket-bearer.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical meaning rests on a single occurrence supported by outside evidence.

definition: A kiss, given as a greeting or as a sign of affection and brotherhood among believers.
article: φίλημα simply means a kiss, and that single meaning covers all 7 of its New Testament appearances (the lone "here with a" reading just reflects how a phrase got split in counting, not a separate sense). It comes from the verb φιλέω ("to love") and shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions as well. In the letters it often appears in the phrase "a holy kiss" (φίλημα ἅγιον), used as a token of Christian fellowship; in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew word for kiss in Proverbs 27:6 and Song of Songs 1:2.

definition: A crowd, throng, or gathered company of people.
article: ὅμιλος means a crowd or throng — a body of people gathered together. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament, but the Textus Receptus reads it at Revelation 18:17, and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. One striking piece of evidence is a literary papyrus fragment (PSI II.130.7) that uses the phrase "a great crowd around," possibly drawn from Hesiod, with parallels reaching back to Homer's Iliad.
caution: The word does not appear in the Byzantine or main critical New Testament text and is attested there only in the Textus Receptus reading of Revelation 18:17, so its New Testament footing is very thin.

definition: Barak, an Israelite military leader named among the heroes of faith.
article: Βαράκ is the indeclinable Greek form of the Hebrew name Barak, a leader in the book of Judges who appears once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:32 among the heroes of faith. In the Septuagint the same form occurs 28 times, almost always translating the Hebrew בָּרָק (27×), with one instance standing in for בְּדָן. Curiously, the measured rendering data shows the single NT occurrence labeled as "Gideon," which conflicts with the standard lexica (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) identifying him as Barak the judge.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering ("Gideon") disagrees with the standard lexica, which identify him as Barak.

definition: To shape yourself to match an external pattern or mold, conforming outwardly to the same form as something else.
article: This verb means to fashion yourself after a pattern, conforming to the same shape or mold as something around you. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament and is missing from the SBLGNT critical text, but the meaning is consistent: in 1 Peter 1:14 it warns against conforming to former desires, and in Romans 12:2 against being conformed to this world. Moulton-Milligan note an intriguing nuance from Field: in Romans 12:2 the word may mean being outwardly conformed, deliberately contrasted with the inward transformation of the following verb.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two occurrences, none in the critical text, and the Romans 12:2 rendering 'renewing' clashes with the expected 'conform,' so treat the senses with care.

definition: Describing something more bearable or easier to endure than another situation, used in the New Testament to compare degrees of coming judgment.
article: ἀνεκτότερος is the comparative form meaning "more bearable" or "more tolerable" — it describes a situation that is easier to endure when set against a worse one. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times across 3 books, always in Jesus' warnings that judgment will be more bearable for some places than others (as in Matthew 10:15 and Luke 10:12). It also turns up in everyday Koine: a fourth-century Christian letter from Oxyrhynchus uses it to describe being "in a more tolerable state," showing it was ordinary language and not a specialized religious term.
caution: This is always a comparative form, so even where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "bearable," the underlying sense is "more bearable."

definition: The physical tongue as the organ of speech, and by extension a language or tongue that people speak.
article: At its core γλῶσσα means the tongue—the body part used for speaking—and it carries this meaning in 48 of its 50 New Testament occurrences (100% of the rendered cases). By natural extension it also means a language or way of speaking, which is how it works in phrases pairing it with tribe, people, and nation. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew לָשׁוֹן ("tongue") 56 times, and everyday papyri show a delightfully ordinary side: a cook's monthly meat bill from Oxyrhynchus lists tongue as a favorite food, and sacrificial inscriptions treat the victim's tongue as a special portion.

definition: Describing a person who is wild, fierce, and untamed in temperament, like a savage beast.
article: ἀνήμερος describes someone wild and untamed, behaving like a savage animal rather than a civilized human. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:3, where it lists traits of people in the last days. The word literally combines a negative prefix with a root meaning 'tame,' and a striking parallel comes from the philosopher Epictetus, who described people forgetting their divine origin as 'like lions—wild, beastly, and untamed (ἀνήμεροι).'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering 'without' looks like a fragment of a phrase rather than the true meaning, which the lexicons consistently give as 'savage' or 'untamed.'

definition: Seed that is sown, and by extension a person's offspring, descendants, or children.
article: σπέρμα literally means seed—the kind a farmer sows in a field—but it ranges easily into the human realm to mean offspring, descendants, or children, which together make up over half of its 44 New Testament uses. The agricultural sense (8×) and the family senses overlap so much that translators sometimes keep the word "seed" even when people are meant, as in Galatians 3:16 where Paul builds an argument on whether "seed" is singular or plural. The Septuagint uses it heavily—218 times, mostly for the Hebrew zera' ('seed')—and everyday papyri show it in the plain sense of seed carried out to the fields and loaned for planting.
caution: The boundaries between 'descendants,' 'offspring,' and 'children' are fluid and translator-dependent, so the sense counts reflect rendering choices rather than sharp distinctions in meaning.

definition: The chest or bosom, the fold of a garment used as a pocket, or by extension a curved hollow like a bay or gulf.
article: At its core κόλπος means the bosom or chest, and it stretches naturally to the fold of a loose garment that hangs over a belt and serves as a pocket (as in Luke 6:38, where something is poured "into" it). It can also describe a bosom-shaped hollow in the landscape, namely a bay or gulf, as in Acts 27:39. The word frequently pictures close, affectionate association — reclining at someone's side or being held in "Abraham's bosom" — and strikingly, the same comforting image turns up in burial inscriptions that ask God to rest the dead "in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and the measured senses split across single-instance phrase fragments, the labeled breakdown is thin and best read alongside the broader lexical range.

definition: Animals kept and raised on a farm, such as cattle or other livestock.
article: θρέμμα refers to farm animals—livestock kept and raised by their owner. It appears just once in the New Testament, in John 4:12, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "livestock." Built from the verb τρέφω ("to nourish, raise"), it literally means something reared or nurtured; the everyday papyri confirm this farming sense, as in an Oxyrhynchus document where a man registers twelve lambs born from his sheep.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on that single verse plus papyri evidence.

definition: The mind as the faculty of thinking, understanding, and disposition—the seat of one's thoughts and intentions.
article: διάνοια refers to the mind as the inner faculty of thought and understanding. In the Byzantine New Testament's 12 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "minds" 7 times (70%) and "thoughts" twice (20%), often appearing in the command to love God with all your mind (Matthew 22:37, Mark 12:30, Luke 10:27). In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for "heart" (לֵבָב, 6×), showing how the Greek mind and the Hebrew heart overlap as the center of inner life; an everyday papyrus from 258 BC even uses it in the phrase "keep this in mind."

definition: The singular form of "you" used as the direct object of a verb, meaning "you" or "thee."
article: This is simply the object form of the singular pronoun "you" (the accusative case of σύ), used when a single person is on the receiving end of an action. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament text as listed here, but it occurs about 1,495 times across 37 books of the Septuagint. Interestingly, the Hebrew words it stands in for vary widely, including בָּרַך ("bless," 62×), אָנֹכִי ("I," 42×), and אַתְּ ("you," 39×), reflecting how a pronoun like this gets folded into many kinds of Hebrew phrasing.
caution: The Hebrew counterparts listed (such as "bless" and "I") suggest the digest reflects broad phrase-level alignments rather than this single word's narrow grammatical role, so treat those mappings cautiously.

definition: Describes an animal that has been specially fed and fattened, ready for slaughter.
article: σιτευτός means "fattened" — an animal deliberately fed up, derived from the word for grain (σῖτος). In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Luke 15, every one describing the fattened calf in the parable of the prodigal son. The most telling evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where third-century BC documents list "fattened geese" (χῆνας σιτευτούς), confirming this was a common term for prized, well-fed livestock.
caution: The three Byzantine occurrences all come from a single passage (Luke 15), so the word's range in the NT is very narrow despite the consistent meaning.

definition: The scattering of a people away from their homeland, or the scattered people themselves living among foreigners.
article: διασπορά describes the scattering of a people far from home, and by extension the dispersed community itself living in foreign lands. It comes from a verb meaning to scatter (like seed broadcast by a sower) and was used especially of Jews exiled and spread across the ancient world; the New Testament writers also apply it metaphorically to Christians (James 1:1, 1 Peter 1:1). In the Septuagint it stands behind several Hebrew words tied to exile and scattering, such as נָדַח and זַעֲוָה, and could even name the exiles themselves rather than the act of scattering.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 New Testament occurrences), and the John 7:35 rendering "intend" reflects translation of the surrounding phrase rather than a distinct meaning of this word itself.

definition: A mill-house, the building where grain was ground into flour.
article: μύλων refers to the mill-house, the place where grain was ground. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 24:41), where it is rendered "mill," and the Septuagint uses it only once as well, at Jeremiah 52:11. Notably, the critical text reads μύλος (the millstone itself) rather than μύλων here, and Abbott-Smith flags that several editions prefer that alternative reading.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word whose reading is disputed—major critical editions favor μύλος (millstone) over μύλων (mill-house) in Matthew 24:41.

definition: A hole dug in the ground for water—a well or cistern—or, figuratively, a deep pit or shaft.
article: φρέαρ is a dug hole in the ground, most concretely a water well or cistern, though it also names a deep pit or shaft. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times: rendered "pit" 3 times (43%), "well" twice (29%), and in Revelation 9 for the shaft of the abyss. Everyday papyri confirm the down-to-earth sense—one will from 126 BC bequeaths a vineyard "and the wells of baked brick in it," and a lease even mentions a well's reel fitted with a new rope. In the Septuagint it appears 57 times, mostly translating the Hebrew בְּאֵר ("well," 34 times).
caution: The MSB sense list splits one Revelation 9:2 phrase into separate "star pit" and "out" labels, which reflect rendering quirks rather than distinct meanings of the word itself.

definition: A severe shortage of food affecting a region or a person, ranging from widespread famine to personal hunger.
article: λιμός is the standard Koine word for a lack of food, covering everything from a region-wide famine to one person's gnawing hunger. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "famine" in two-thirds of its 12 New Testament occurrences, but a few times it means simply personal hunger, as when the prodigal son begins to be in need (Luke 15:14, 17) or Paul lists "hunger and thirst" among his hardships (2 Cor 11:27). In the Septuagint it appears about 100 times, almost always translating Hebrew רָעָב (79×), and the everyday papyri show people pleading not to be left to die of λιμός in prison.
caution: The word's gender wavers between masculine and feminine in both the New Testament and the papyri, but its meaning is well established.

definition: A group of sheep or goats kept together, or figuratively a group of people under a shepherd's care.
article: ποίμνη means a flock, normally of sheep, and in all 5 Byzantine New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "flock" (4 times explicitly, once absorbed into the surrounding phrasing). It comes from the verb ποιμαίνω, "to shepherd," and can be used figuratively for people, as when Jesus speaks of his followers as one flock (John 10:16). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and a third-century wax tablet even shows it spelled φήμνης, a window into how it was actually pronounced.

definition: A watercraft used for fishing, travel, or transport, ranging from a small fishing boat to a larger seagoing ship.
article: πλοῖον covers any kind of vessel that floats and carries people or cargo. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 66 times, rendered "boat" in 65% of cases and "ship" in 30%, the smaller-versus-larger choice depending mostly on context, like the fishing boats of the Gospels versus the seagoing ships of Acts and Revelation. Interestingly, this everyday Koine word came to absorb the role of the older word ναῦς ("ship"), which had nearly vanished from common speech, and the papyri even mention a papyrus boat seen in a dream sailing to Memphis. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew אֳנִיָּה ("ship") 23 of 31 times.

definition: The plural "of these," pointing to people or things just mentioned or close at hand.
article: τούτων is simply a grammatical form of the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος ("this"), specifically the genitive plural masculine or neuter, meaning "of these" persons or things. The base word works much like English "this" versus "that," pointing to what is near, recently mentioned, or about to be named. In the Septuagint οὗτος most often stands in for the Hebrew words zeh and zoʾth ("this"), and it can even carry a tone of contempt, as when people dismissively ask about Jesus, "Is not this the carpenter's son?"
caution: This is just an inflected case form rather than a distinct word, so it has no measured senses of its own and zero separate Byzantine occurrences were tabulated.

definition: The inner organs of the body, used figuratively for deep feelings of affection, compassion, and tenderness toward others.
senseLabels: the heart as seat of feeling
article: Literally σπλάγχνον means the inward parts of the body—the heart, liver, and lungs—but in the New Testament it almost always points to deep emotion, rendered "affection" in 3 of its 11 occurrences (33%) and "hearts" in 2 (22%). The figurative range centers on warmth, kindness, and pity, the sense the Septuagint and New Testament settle on. Strikingly, a papyrus from 5 BC uses the phrase ὑπὲρ σπλάγχνου, "for pity's sake," showing this tender meaning was already common in everyday Koine.
caution: In 2 of 11 cases the word is absorbed into English phrasing without a direct equivalent, and the literal "inner organs" sense survives only outside this set, so the measured senses capture only part of its range.

definition: To stir up or disturb someone's mind, leaving them agitated and troubled about many things.
article: τυρβάζω means to disturb or agitate, especially mentally, and appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 10:41), where Jesus tells Martha she is troubled about many things. The word is related to θόρυβος (uproar, commotion) and connects to the idea of making something turbid or stirred up, like muddied water. Notably, the critical text (SBLGNT) reads not τυρβάζω but the related word θορυβάζω here, and Abbott-Smith flags that major editors prefer that alternate reading.
caution: This word rests on a single, textually disputed occurrence, since the major critical editions read θορυβάζω instead, making the evidence thin.

definition: Describing something that is peaceful, marked by peace, or tends toward peace rather than conflict.
article: This adjective, built from the noun εἰρήνη ("peace"), describes things or qualities that are peaceful or disposed toward peace. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both times rendered "peace" — describing the "fruit of peace" born of discipline (Hebrews 12:11) and heavenly wisdom that is "peaceable" (James 3:17). It was an ordinary working word in Koine: an Egyptian papyrus from A.D. 392 uses it for night-watchmen "entrusted with the care of the peace," showing its everyday administrative flavor.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin evidence, though the Septuagint's 36 uses and the lexica agree well on its meaning.

definition: An adverb meaning "in Hebrew," used to mark a word or name given in the Hebrew (or Aramaic) language.
article: Ἑβραϊστί is an adverb meaning "in Hebrew," used to introduce a name or term in that language. It appears 6 times in the Byzantine NT, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "Hebrew" in 4 of 6 cases (67%), with the other instances expanding it to "Hebrew called" or "called in Hebrew" depending on phrasing. A nice detail comes from the papyri: a magical text (P Leid W, 2nd–3rd century AD) pairs it with words written ἱερογλυφιστί ("in hieroglyphics"), showing it as an ordinary label for a language. Note that lexicons like Dodson and Abbott-Smith point out that in several Gospel passages the underlying language is actually Aramaic, even though the word literally means "in Hebrew."
caution: Sources note that in several Gospel verses this word likely refers to Aramaic rather than literal Hebrew, so the language it names is not always certain.

definition: To earn or produce something extra through work or trading, gaining more in addition to what one already had.
article: This verb combines "toward/in addition" (πρός) with "to work" (ἐργάζομαι), describing the act of earning more on top of what you started with. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:16, where a servant reports that his pound "produced more" — the sense rendered there 100% of the time. Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine documents, and the classical lexica note a fuller range, including "to do service besides" alongside this trading sense found in Xenophon.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured meaning rests on a single verse, though papyri and classical evidence support it.

definition: Having a fiery red color, like flame; bright or ruddy red.
article: πυρρός describes something fiery red, the word being built straight from πῦρ, 'fire.' In the Septuagint it appears 8 times across 5 books, almost always rendering the Hebrew word אָדֹם ('red'), and it shows up in Revelation for the red horse (6:4) and the great red dragon (12:3). The everyday papyri are revealing: the same word is used in a milder 'ruddy' sense to describe the complexion of a witness to a will, and even shows up in a recipe for making a hippopotamus figure out of red wax.
caution: Note that the similar-looking proper name Πύρρος ('Pyrrhus') in Acts 20:4 is a different word, not the color term.

definition: A standard or instrument for measuring quantity, length, or amount, whether a measuring vessel, a measuring rod, or the measured amount itself.
article: At its core μέτρον is anything used for measuring — a vessel, a rod, or the resulting amount. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "measure" in 5 of 14 places (45%) and "use" twice (as in the proverb about the measure you use being measured back to you), while 3 of 14 occurrences are absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own. It appears 71 times in the Septuagint, most often for the Hebrew מִדָּה, and the everyday papyri show it concretely: a loan repaid "by just measure" calculated against the royal bronze standard.

definition: Not working or active—whether a person standing around with nothing to do, or a thing that produces no effect.
article: ἀργός literally combines a negative particle with the word for "work," so its core idea is "not working." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times and is rendered "doing nothing" or "idle" in equal measure, describing both unemployed workers standing in the marketplace (Matthew 20:3, 6) and people who are lazy or useless. Beyond people, lexicons note it can describe things that are ineffective or worthless, such as an idle word or a barren faith. The papyri make this vivid: a census return from A.D. 160–161 describes a man as belonging to the "leisured class" using exactly this word.
caution: Three of the eight occurrences are absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word, so the measured sense split is based on a small sample.

definition: A woman from Magdala, a town in Galilee; used as the identifying surname of Mary Magdalene.
article: This word simply means "of Magdala," identifying a woman by her hometown, a fishing village in Galilee. In all 12 New Testament occurrences it attaches to Mary, marking her as Mary Magdalene to distinguish her from other women named Mary. The two measured renderings aren't really separate meanings—the "Magdalene mother" cases (2×, in Mark 15:47 and 16:1) just reflect the wider phrasing where she is named alongside her role, while the basic sense stays the same. The form is a feminine derivative of the place name Magdala (G3093).

definition: The training and correction that shapes a person, especially the discipline a parent or God gives to guide growth.
article: παιδεία covers the whole process of forming a person—training, education, and the corrective discipline that goes with it. In the Byzantine New Testament its six uses lean toward "discipline" (4 of 6, 67%), with "instruction" once and disciplined suffering once, while classical lexica note it could also simply mean rearing or schooling a child. The Septuagint uses it 57 times, most often (32×) for the Hebrew מוּסָר, the word for moral correction, and the papyri confirm its everyday sense of education "befitting freeborn children."
caution: With only six New Testament occurrences, the balance between "correction" and broader "training" depends heavily on context, and the lexica stress the wider educational range more than the measured NT usage.

definition: To be diseased — used figuratively of an unhealthy mental obsession, like being sick with a craving for arguments.
article: Literally νοσέω means "to be sick," but in the one New Testament occurrence (1 Timothy 6:4) it is used figuratively of a diseased mind — someone who is morbidly obsessed, here with disputes and word-battles, which the Majority Standard Bible renders "abusive." The everyday papyri confirm the plain literal sense: one Oxyrhynchus letter has a woman writing "I write this to you in sickness, being very ill." The Septuagint also uses it metaphorically (Wisdom 17:8), matching the figurative "sick in the mind" idea found in the New Testament.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its figurative range there rests on a single passage.

definition: Describing something so great it cannot be fully put into words.
article: This adjective describes a thing too wonderful or vast to be fully expressed in speech. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:15, where Paul calls God's gift 'indescribable' — the measured data renders that whole phrase 'Thanks be for' since the word sits inside an exclamation of thanks. Although it was once thought Paul may have coined the term, Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up as a variant reading in the Letter of Aristeas, describing 'wonder beyond description,' and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the corpus.

definition: The good news of God's kingdom and salvation through Christ — the gospel message itself.
article: In the New Testament εὐαγγέλιον means the good news — almost always the message of salvation through Christ — and it is rendered "gospel" in 73 of its 77 Byzantine occurrences (97%). The word often carries a defining genitive: it can name the giver (God), the subject (Christ, the kingdom), or the human messenger who delivers it. One striking piece of evidence is the Priene calendar inscription from about 9 B.C., which uses the plural to call the birthday of the Emperor Augustus the beginning of "tidings of joy" for the world — showing the word's wider Koine use for any momentous good announcement, while in classical Greek it could even mean a reward for bringing good news.

definition: The act of teaching, or the body of instruction and doctrine that is taught.
article: διδαχή covers both the activity of teaching and the actual content—the doctrine—that gets passed on. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 30 times across 12 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "teaching" in 22 of those (81%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time, so the range is remarkably tight. One striking detail: a papyrus letter from Hadrian's time (A.D. 119) uses the same word for military training, while another early gospel fragment echoes the very phrase from Mark 1:27 by asking what "new teaching" Jesus proclaims.

definition: To give, hand over, or grant something to someone, covering a very wide range of actions depending on context.
article: δίδωμι is the ordinary Greek verb for giving, and it appears 416 times in the Byzantine New Testament — overwhelmingly rendered "give" or "given" (310 times, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 99% of the time). Its range is enormously flexible: depending on context it can mean bestow, grant, deliver, commit, put, or yield, which is why the KJV translators reached for dozens of different English words. In the Septuagint it shows up a staggering 1,722 times, mostly translating Hebrew נָתַן ("to give") in 1,390 of those cases. Everyday papyri confirm how common the word was — one Oxyrhynchus letter simply says "give the silver to Zoilos my friend," the same plain sense found throughout the Bible.

definition: An emphatic adverb meaning "in no way" or "by no means," denying something completely.
senseLabels: by no means, not at all
article: This word is a strong, emphatic way of saying "not at all" or "by no means" — it negates something completely rather than partially. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 2:6, which quotes the Old Testament. Everyday Koine papyri show the same emphatic force, as in a document from 113 B.C. accusing someone of making "no improvement whatever" in their behavior; in the Septuagint it surfaces only in 2-4 Maccabees.
caution: The single Bible occurrence shows up here oddly as rendered "means rulers" because Matthew 2:6 reads "by no means least among the rulers," so judge its meaning from the lexical evidence rather than that one quotation.

definition: Genuine and without pretense, describing love or faith that is real rather than play-acted.
article: ἀνυπόκριτος literally means "unfeigned" or "without hypocrisy" — it's built from a negative prefix on the same root as the word for a stage actor, so it describes feelings or qualities that aren't put on for show. It appears 6 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sincere" in 4 of them (80%), used of love (Rom 12:9, 2 Cor 6:6) and faith (2 Tim 1:5). Beyond the Bible it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it was ordinary, real-world vocabulary rather than purely a religious term.
caution: The two listed senses are really the same meaning; the second is just an artifact of phrasing in 1 Tim 1:5, so treat "sincere/unfeigned" as the single sense.

definition: Jehoshaphat, a king of Judah listed among the ancestors of Jesus in Matthew's genealogy.
article: Ἰωσαφάτ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jehoshaphat, a king of Judah who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. The name is indeclinable and shows up only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in Matthew 1:8, where he is named as the father of Joram. In the Septuagint it appears 90 times, mostly translating Hebrew יְהוֹשָׁפָט (79×), though it also stands in for a few other names like עָמְרִי (Omri, 7×).
caution: The measured senses show one occurrence rendered "Joram" alongside "Jehoshaphat," which reflects the genealogical phrasing of Matthew 1:8 rather than two separate meanings of the name.

definition: An Aramaic cry meaning "my God," spoken by Jesus on the cross and kept untranslated in the text.
article: This is the Aramaic word for "my God," which the Gospels carry over directly into Greek rather than translating it. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in Jesus' cry from the cross (Mark 15:34 and the parallel passage), and the translators leave it as the proper-name-like "Eloi." Strikingly, a Christian protective amulet from the 5th or 6th century AD (P Oxy VIII.1152) uses the same form alongside other divine names, showing the word lived on in everyday devotional and magical use.
caution: Evidence is thin and the spelling varies across manuscripts (ἐλωΐ, ἑλωΐ), so treat this as a low-confidence transliterated form rather than a settled Greek word.

definition: To feel envy or jealous resentment toward someone, often in a way that stirs up rivalry.
senseLabels: to envy or provoke through jealousy
article: φθονέω means to envy someone, harboring jealous resentment that can spill over into rivalry. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Galatians 5:26, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "provoking" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees—both capturing the idea of stirring up jealousy between people. The everyday Koine papyri sharpen the picture: in one third-century document a man complains that someone "envied" him, and in another a malicious spirit is said to have begrudged a household its marriage, showing the word's reach into resentment and ill-will in daily life.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and sparse Septuagint use (Tobit), the word's range here rests largely on outside papyri and classical evidence.

definition: Neri, a man listed as an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.
article: Neri is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:27, within the genealogy tracing Jesus' lineage. The Greek form is indeclinable, borrowed directly from a Hebrew name (related to Nerijah), which is why every translation simply renders it as the proper name 'Neri.' The single measured occurrence is rendered as 'son' in context, reflecting his place in the chain of fathers and sons in Luke's family tree.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage rests on a single passage.

definition: To divide something into parts, or to distribute, assign, or share it out among people.
article: μερίζω basically means to split something up—either literally cutting it into portions or distributing and assigning shares to people. In the Byzantine New Testament its measured uses lean toward conflict imagery, with 7 of 10 clear cases describing a kingdom or house "divided against itself" or "divided against" something, while the rest cover ordinary division or apportioning. The everyday Koine papyri show the practical financial side vividly: one document describes a mother who "bestowed" four arourae of land each upon her children, and another mentions land "assigned" instead of a subvention. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew חָלַק, the standard word for dividing or apportioning.

definition: In a genuine, sincere way—acting from honest and true motives.
article: γνησίως is an adverb meaning to do something sincerely and genuinely, from the heart. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 2:20, and the classical lexicons agree on the range: truly, honorably, sincerely. Note that the measured rendering tag here reads "nobody"—that reflects the surrounding phrase in Philippians 2:20 rather than the word itself, while Strong's, KJV ("naturally"), and Abbott-Smith all point to the core sense of genuine sincerity, with Abbott-Smith citing a papyri parallel for honorable conduct.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a measured-sense label ("nobody") that captures the surrounding phrase rather than the word's meaning, lean on the lexicon glosses for the actual sense.

definition: To do evil or harm—either by injuring someone or by acting wickedly in general.
article: This verb covers doing wrong in two related ways: harming or injuring someone directly, and behaving wickedly in a broader moral sense. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, with the moral sense clear in 1 Peter 3:17 and 3 John 1:11. The everyday papyri back this up nicely—one document from around 245 BC warns a troublemaker to "stop your malpractices in the village" or he will regret it, while in the Septuagint it shows up 25 times, most often translating the Hebrew רָעַע (to do evil).
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and the measured sense labels here being fragmentary, the precise shade—injure versus do wrong morally—must be read from context.

definition: The color black, the opposite of white; in its neuter form it also means ink.
article: μέλας means "black," the color opposite to white (λευκός), as in Jesus' words about being unable to make one hair white or black (Matthew 5:36) and the black horse and darkened sun of Revelation 6. The Septuagint uses it the same way, five times rendering the Hebrew word שָׁחֹר ("black"). The most interesting wrinkle comes from the neuter form τὸ μέλαν, which means "ink" — Paul and John use it that way in the New Testament, and everyday Koine papyri even preserve a recipe for making writing ink.
caution: The Byzantine New Testament has only three occurrences (all "black"), so the common "ink" sense rests on the Septuagint, papyri, and a few verses outside this count.

definition: Without honor; treated as unworthy of respect, slighted, or held in low esteem.
article: ἄτιμος combines the negative prefix with τιμή ("honor"), so it means lacking honor or being treated as unworthy of respect. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times across 3 books, including Jesus' saying that a prophet is not without honor except in his own hometown and household (Matthew 13:57, Mark 6:4); it also appears in a comparative form for "less honorable" body parts (1 Corinthians 12:23). The most interesting evidence comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show it had an old technical legal sense in Attic law of being stripped of civic rights, with property confiscated by the state.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and 2 of them absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word, the sense breakdown rests on thin evidence.

definition: To serve as the governor or ruler of a province or region.
article: This verb means to hold the office of governor over a territory, and both of its New Testament appearances use it exactly that way: Luke 2:2 (Quirinius governing Syria) and Luke 3:1 (Pilate governing Judea). Everyday Koine documents back this up — papyri repeatedly use it for the rule of a Roman prefect or praefect, such as a tax record dated A.D. 7 referencing "the prefecture" of Petronius. The classical lexicon Abbott-Smith notes a broader range the New Testament doesn't show, including "to lead the way" and "to command in war," reserving the provincial-governor sense specifically for these two Luke passages.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in Luke and both meaning "to govern a province," the wider senses listed in classical lexica aren't attested in the New Testament itself.

definition: To remove or take away completely, especially to drive out or expel someone from a group.
article: ἐξαίρω means to lift something off and carry it away, hence to remove or expel completely. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in 1 Corinthians 5 about expelling a wicked person from the church, and the verse in 5:13 echoes Septuagint wording. The Septuagint uses it heavily—189 times—often for Hebrew verbs of pulling up stakes (נָסַע), dispossessing (יָרַשׁ), or cutting off (כָּרַת); a vivid papyrus from A.D. 33 uses it of a dam in danger of being "entirely carried away."
caution: New Testament evidence is very thin (only two occurrences in one chapter), so its full range rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: The setting free of someone, like a ransom paid to release a captive, used especially for God's deliverance of people from sin.
article: ἀπολύτρωσις is the act of buying someone's freedom — a release secured by paying a ransom. In the Byzantine New Testament's 10 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "redemption" 8 times (89%), and the New Testament applies it mainly to deliverance through Christ from sin and its consequences. One vivid contrast comes from Abbott-Smith: in Hebrews 11:35 the word describes a literal release from torture, while elsewhere it carries the figurative sense of spiritual rescue. Its roots lie in ἀπό ("from") combined with λύτρον ("ransom"), which keeps the original idea of payment in view.
caution: Scholars debate how strongly each occurrence still carries the literal sense of a paid ransom versus a more general "deliverance," and the Septuagint offers only a single supporting example.

definition: To question someone formally as part of a legal investigation, sometimes using torture to get the truth.
article: ἀνετάζω means to examine or interrogate someone in a judicial setting, the kind of formal questioning a court or official would conduct. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 22, where a Roman commander orders Paul questioned under flogging—so the legal, even coercive, edge of the word fits the scene exactly. The papyri confirm this everyday administrative flavor: in one Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 127, a prefect uses the word for clerks tasked with examining official documents.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 1 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, so the precise range of meaning is hard to pin down.

definition: A horn of an animal, or a horn-shaped projection on the corners of an altar, often used as a symbol of strength.
article: κέρας means an animal's horn, and by extension the horn-shaped projections at the corners of an altar. In the Majority Standard Bible it is rendered "horns" in 10 of 11 occurrences (91%), spanning literal beasts, the altar's corners (Revelation 9:13), and the figurative "horn of salvation" in Luke 1:69, where it signals strength. The everyday Koine papyri show just how concrete the word was: it appears for the horn of a roast suckling pig, gilded ram's horns, and even the yard-arm of a ship's sail. In the Septuagint it occurs 85 times, mostly translating the Hebrew קֶרֶן.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning "father," used to address God directly and intimately in prayer.
article: Ἀββᾶ is the Aramaic word for "father," carried straight over into Greek without translation. In all three New Testament occurrences (Mark 14:36, Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6) it appears in the same phrase, "Abba, Father," where the Greek word for father immediately follows and explains the Aramaic. Abbott-Smith notes it is the emphatic form of the Aramaic word for father, and it shows up only once in the Septuagint, where it stands in for the Hebrew name Abijah.
caution: This word appears only 3 times and is essentially a single fixed phrase, so the two "senses" reflect translation wording rather than genuinely different meanings.

definition: To slaughter an animal, whether to make a sacrifice to a deity or simply to kill it for food or other purposes.
senseLabels: offer a sacrifice to a god
article: θύω covers a spread of meanings tied to slaughtering animals, from plain killing for a feast to ritual sacrifice offered to a god. In the Byzantine New Testament's 14 occurrences it splits fairly evenly, with about 29% rendered "kill" and the rest involving sacrifice, fattened animals, or passover lambs. In the Septuagint it appears 120 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew זָבַח (89×), "to sacrifice or slaughter," anchoring the word firmly in sacrificial language; a Koine papyrus royal edict from around 265 BC even uses it for citizens being told to "sacrifice" once recognized by their phratry.

definition: A preposition meaning "without" — apart from something or someone, including without their knowledge or consent.
article: This little preposition (always with the genitive) means "without" — describing the absence of something or someone. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, and in Matthew 10:29 it carries a slightly richer shade: a sparrow does not fall "without" your Father, meaning apart from his will. The everyday papyri confirm an interesting nuance: scholars like Wilcken showed that in certain contexts ἄνευ means not just "in the absence of" but "without the knowledge or consent of" someone — exactly the force at work in 1 Peter 3:1, where wives might win husbands "without a word."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, this is thin evidence, and Abbott-Smith notes it is rarer than the near-synonym χωρίς.

definition: Describing something that has lost its salt and become flat or tasteless.
article: This adjective means salt-free or having no taste, formed from a negative prefix joined to the word for salt. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:50, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "saltiness" and the Berean Standard Bible agrees completely. Beyond the New Testament, the translator Aquila used it in a handful of passages in Ezekiel, showing it could describe other things lacking what they should contain.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage.

definition: Showing no mercy or pity; harsh and unrelenting toward someone.
article: This word describes a complete absence of mercy — a judgment or treatment that is utterly unrelenting. It appears just once in the New Testament, at James 2:13, where it warns that judgment will be merciless toward those who have shown no mercy. The form is unusual: Moulton-Milligan note it is a remade spelling found in everyday Koine, including a papyrus from A.D. 390 that uses a related word to describe someone being beaten 'mercilessly.'
caution: This is a single-occurrence word whose exact form and accentuation were debated even by ancient grammarians, so confidence is low.

definition: Cowardly or fearful, lacking the courage to trust or act when facing danger.
article: δειλός describes someone gripped by fear or cowardice, unable to muster courage. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice spoken by Jesus to his frightened disciples (Matthew 8:26 and Mark 4:40) where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as being "afraid." The Septuagint uses it 11 times across 8 books, translating several different Hebrew words including רַךְ (rak), and Strong's notes the word can carry the further implication of being faithless—the opposite of trusting courage.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise force of the word (mere timidity versus faithless cowardice) cannot be pinned down from the measured data alone.

definition: To wash something off oneself, especially to wash one's own hands as a symbolic act.
article: This verb means to wash dirt or impurity off, and in its single New Testament appearance (Matthew 27:24) it is used reflexively of Pilate washing his own hands to disown responsibility. The reflexive 'wash off' sense also shows up in everyday Koine: a third-century BC inscription describes a fraudulent patient at a healing shrine told to wash his face, only to find his deceit branded there. Note that the measured rendering 'accomplishing' looks like a tagging artifact rather than the word's actual meaning, which lexicons agree is 'to wash off.'
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the lone measured rendering ('accomplishing') conflicts with every lexicon's plain meaning of 'wash off,' so treat the corpus label with caution.

definition: The number ninety-nine, used for the sheep left behind while one is sought.
article: This is simply the cardinal number ninety-nine, an indeclinable Greek numeral. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament across just 2 books, every instance tied to Jesus' parable of the sheep where the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find the one that wandered (Matthew 18:12–13, Luke 15:4, 7). Strong's and the King James tradition render it "ninety and nine," and the measured renderings ("ninety" 3× and "moreover ninety" 1×) all reflect this same count within the parable's phrasing.
caution: The two listed senses are not really distinct meanings but the same number split by phrasing, and the spelling varies (ἐννεν-/ἐνεν-) across editions; the word is absent from the critical SBLGNT text.

definition: The seed a farmer sows, or by extension the act of sowing.
article: σπόρος refers to seed that is sown in the ground, and it can also mean the sowing itself or seedtime. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times across 3 books, almost always meaning the literal seed scattered by a farmer, though Paul stretches it metaphorically toward almsgiving in 2 Corinthians 9:10. The everyday papyri are especially telling: documents speak of leasing land 'for the sowing of year 25,' showing how ordinary the word was in farming contexts and reminding us it could name the season as readily as the grain.
caution: The measured sense labels here are fragmentary phrases from longer verses, so they describe contexts more than distinct meanings; the real range is essentially 'seed' and 'sowing.'

definition: A cluster or bunch of grapes growing on the vine.
article: βότρυς refers to a cluster or bunch of grapes, the kind that hangs from a vine. It appears just once in the New Testament (Revelation 14:18) and 13 times in the Septuagint, where it consistently renders the Hebrew word eshkol, meaning a grape cluster. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain agricultural sense — one document from 22 B.C. lists "eighty clusters of grapes," and the lexicons agree throughout.
caution: The word appears only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests almost entirely on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: A chief or ruling angel, the highest rank among angels.
article: ἀρχάγγελος combines the ideas of "ruler" (ἄρχω) and "angel" (ἄγγελος) to mean a chief or superior angel. It appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Jude 9, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "archangel," with the BSB agreeing fully. Interestingly, the word spread well beyond the Bible into everyday Koine: the magical papyri use it for named figures such as "my lord the archangel Michael," and a gnostic inscription from Miletus invokes an archangel as the city's guardian.
caution: With only two occurrences—one of which is absorbed into surrounding phrasing—the evidence base is thin, so the entry carries low confidence.

definition: Hezekiah, a king of Judah listed among the ancestors of Jesus.
article: Ἐζεκίας is the Greek form of the personal name Hezekiah, a king of Judah who appears in Jesus' genealogy. It shows up just twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew 1 (verses 9 and 10), each time rendered "Hezekiah." The name is far more common in the Septuagint, appearing 123 times across 9 books, where it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew חִזְקִיָּה (116 times); Abbott-Smith notes the Hebrew name means "strength of Jehovah."

definition: To use strength to seize, take hold of, or firmly keep something or someone.
article: κρατέω is about applying strength to grasp or retain something—physically taking hold of a hand, arresting a person, or firmly keeping a teaching or possession. Its range runs from literal seizing (it's rendered "arrest" or "took" in nearly a third of its 47 New Testament uses) to the figurative sense of holding fast to something. The classical lexicons add a stronger primary sense the New Testament rarely shows: "to be master, rule, prevail," which is the dominant meaning in everyday Koine papyri, where it describes Caesar conquering Cleopatra's kingdom. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew חָזַק (33×), meaning to be strong or take firm hold.
caution: The classical and papyri "rule, prevail" sense is largely absent from the measured New Testament data, where "seize/hold" dominates instead.

definition: A household or estate manager—often a trusted slave or freedman—who runs another person's property and finances on their behalf.
article: An οἰκονόμος is the person put in charge of running someone else's household, estate, or money—what we'd call a manager, steward, or treasurer. The word appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where it ranges from the literal estate manager to a figurative "steward" of Christian ministry; in Romans 16:23 it even names the city treasurer.
