It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 10:4 and Hebrews 9:10), and the Septuagint uses it just once, in Psalm 102:9, where it corresponds to the Hebrew word for a drink (שִׁקּוּי). Abbott-Smith notes that πόμα is a later form of the older Attic Greek πῶμα, and Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions.
caution: The first listed "sense" ("same they that") reflects surrounding words in one verse rather than the meaning of πόμα itself, so treat "drink" as the word's only genuine sense; evidence is thin (only two NT occurrences).

definition: In a way that shows good sense and sound judgment; thoughtfully and prudently.
article: This adverb describes acting or speaking with sound judgment — sensibly, prudently, and reasonably. It is built from the words for "mind" (νοῦς) and "to have" (ἔχω), literally meaning to do something "with mind engaged." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 12:34, where Jesus sees that a scribe has answered "wisely." Moulton-Milligan note that the word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions and was used from Aristotle onward, so it was common, ordinary Greek even though the New Testament uses it just once.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on a single verse.

definition: The act of stripping or taking off, as one removes a garment.
article: ἀπέκδυσις means the stripping or putting off of something, like removing a piece of clothing. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Colossians 2:11, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it with the idea of "off" 100% of the time. The most striking fact is that Moulton-Milligan note this word seems to have been coined by Paul himself — there's no clear earlier attestation, and even its related verb is barely saved from being unique by a single manuscript of Josephus.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and may have been newly minted by Paul, so its precise range is hard to establish.

definition: To hand out land or property as an inheritance, distributing it among recipients as if by lot.
article: This rare verb describes the act of parceling out an inheritance—especially land—so that each party receives an allotted share. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 13:19, where it refers to God giving Israel the land), and there it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word; it is absent from the critical text. The most striking detail is that wherever the word turns up in the Septuagint, the manuscripts show a competing variant, κατακληρονομέω, and Moulton-Milligan note an overlooked passage in Theophylact using it of a general distributing honors and trophies to a city.
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs just once in the Byzantine NT, is dropped from the critical text, and is consistently swapped with κατακληρονομέω in the Septuagint manuscripts.

definition: Generous giving to help the poor, or the act of showing mercy through charitable gifts.
article: ἐλεημοσύνη centers on charitable giving—handing over money or goods to relieve the needy—and the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "give," "charity," "alms," or "gifts to the poor" depending on context. It comes from the word for mercy (ἔλεος), and its range stretches from the inner quality of compassion to the concrete gift placed in a beggar's hand. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew צְדָקָה ("righteousness"), showing how Hebrew thought linked right living with caring for the poor; our English word "alms" is actually a worn-down descendant of this very Greek term.
caution: The standard lexica disagree on the leading Hebrew counterpart—Abbott-Smith names חֶסֶד and צְדָקָה while the corpus data shows צְדָקָה leading—and the measured senses overlap heavily, so the precise shade often depends on context.

definition: To live together with someone, sharing the same life and existence whether now or beyond death.
article: συζάω combines "with" (σύν) and "live" (ζάω) to mean sharing life in common with another person. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "live" in two of those, while the third is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. Abbott-Smith notes it stands opposite "to die together with" in 2 Corinthians 7:3 and elsewhere describes life in union with Christ; a charming touch from the papyri is a second-century BC epigram on the playwright Menander, praising one who "lived along with" him.
caution: This is a rare word with only 3 occurrences, so its full range rests on thin evidence.

definition: Hagar, the slave woman of Sarah and concubine of Abraham, used in Paul's allegory of the two covenants.
article: Ἄγαρ is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Hagar, the slave woman who bore Abraham a son; it appears just twice in the New Testament, both in Galatians 4 where Paul uses her as a figure of the covenant of slavery. The two measured 'senses' are really the same name showing up in two verses, not distinct meanings. The name comes straight from Hebrew הָגָר and is used 13 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating that same Hebrew name (12 of 13 times).
caution: This is a proper name appearing only twice in the New Testament, so the two listed 'senses' reflect different verses rather than genuinely different meanings.

definition: To wake someone or raise them up — from sleep, from sitting or lying down, or from death.
article: This common verb (138 times in 17 books) covers a whole range of "rising": waking from sleep, getting up from a chair or sickbed, and being raised from the dead. The death-related sense dominates the New Testament — "raised" and "risen" together account for over 60% of its uses — but the plain everyday meaning of "get up" appears 27 times. A vivid papyrus example survives in a saying attributed to Jesus from Oxyrhynchus: "Lift up the stone and there you will find me," showing the literal physical sense alive in ordinary Koine; in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew word for waking or rousing.

definition: A standing or position, but most often a violent public uprising or a heated dispute.
article: στάσις literally means "a standing" or fixed position, but in the Byzantine New Testament's 9 uses it usually points to something far more disruptive — a popular uprising (as with Barabbas, jailed for a riot) or a sharp quarrel among people. The word's range is wide: from the neutral "standing" in Hebrews 9:8 to violent sedition to mere argument. Everyday Koine papyri show the same spread, including a striking plural use for "buildings" or "erections" and the literal "a standing for grazing," reminding us the calm root sense was alive alongside the turbulent ones.
caution: With only 9 New Testament occurrences and 6 of them absorbed into phrasing rather than translated as a single word, the boundary between "uprising" and "dispute" can be hard to fix in a given verse.

definition: A sound or tone, especially one made by a voice or musical instrument.
article: φθόγγος refers to a sound or audible tone, whether produced by a voice or an instrument. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 10:18 and 1 Corinthians 14:7), and the word comes from φθέγγομαι, "to utter." Everyday Koine papyri use it in a notably musical sense, including a magical text that speaks of "the harmony of the seven tones" (φθόγγων), which fits Paul's reference to distinguishable notes on an instrument.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured English-rendering data is too thin to define the word's range on its own.

definition: To set someone free, releasing them from bondage, sin, or some controlling power.
article: ἐλευθερόω means to liberate or set free, and in the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, rendered "set free" in 6 of them (86%) and "sets free" once. The two measured senses really describe the same action, differing only in grammar, and the word covers both physical and figurative freedom—from sin (John 8:32, 36), from a master, or from a controlling power (Rom 6:18). Strikingly, the verb shows up in countless everyday papyri documenting the legal manumission of slaves, such as one Oxyrhynchus text where slaves are freed "in consequence of their goodwill and affection," rooting this religious term in ordinary life.
caution: Evidence is thin outside the New Testament, with only a single Septuagint occurrence.

definition: To hold first place; to rank above all others in importance or influence.
article: πρωτεύω means to be first or preeminent—to occupy the top rank or chief position. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Colossians 1:18), where it describes holding preeminence over all things. Everyday Koine papyri use it for civic leaders: one document calls a man "preeminent" among the people of Hermopolis, and another addresses a "most renowned patrician holding first place," showing the word commonly marked official or social rank. In the Septuagint it appears just once, translating the Hebrew word for "riches" (Esther 5:11).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and rarely in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: To give someone, especially a daughter, in marriage to another person.
article: This verb means to give a person in marriage, with Strong's specifying the giving of a daughter. It appears 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament but drops out of the critical text entirely, where the simpler form γαμίζω stands instead. Most occurrences cluster in Jesus' sayings about marrying and being given in marriage (Matthew 24:38, Luke 17:27, Matthew 22:30), with one in Paul's discussion of marriage (1 Corinthians 7:38).
caution: Editors disagree about this word: Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan note it has dropped from the true text in favor of γαμίζω, and outside the New Testament evidence for it is very thin.

definition: A tetrarch — a minor ruler who governed a small territory, originally one fourth of a region, under a larger empire.
article: τετράρχης names a low-ranking ruler, literally the governor of a fourth part of a territory, though in practice it could apply to any petty local prince. All 4 of its Byzantine New Testament appearances point to the same person — Herod Antipas — so the four "measured senses" here simply reflect different phrasings around a single role, not different meanings. The classical lexica back this up: Strabo uses it in the strict "fourth-part" sense, while Plutarch already broadens it to any minor ruler, and Moulton-Milligan shows the title (and related forms like τετραρχία) was common in everyday Greek inscriptions long before the New Testament.
caution: This word appears in the Byzantine text but is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, which prefers the spelling τετραάρχης, so the form itself is disputed.

definition: Sharing the same form or shape as something else; conformed to, made to match.
article: σύμμορφος describes one thing being shaped like or conformed to another, built from σύν ('together with') and μορφή ('form'). It appears only twice in the New Testament, and in one of those cases the translation absorbs it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. Abbott-Smith notes it can take either a dative (Philippians 3:21) or a genitive (Romans 8:29), and that in the classical writer Lucian it simply means 'similar.'
caution: With only 2 occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To take someone into your arms and hold them in an embrace.
article: This verb means to fold or take someone into your arms — a physical embrace. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Mark, where Jesus takes children into his arms (Mark 9:36 and 10:16). The Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew חִבֻּק, and Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions, including one referring to embracing children.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences, both in Mark, so the word's full range is hard to gauge.

definition: To be fully strong or completely able to do something, especially a demanding task.
article: ἐξισχύω means to have enough strength to accomplish a difficult task — to be entirely competent for it. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Ephesians 3:18, where it describes being able to grasp something fully, and just once in the Septuagint (Sirach 7:6). The everyday papyri are especially telling: one document describes people who tried to force open a machine and "were not able" (οὐκ ἐξείσχυσαν), while another uses it for a man whose influence "managed to procure" the rejection of a petition.
caution: This word appears just once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: To throw people into great confusion or agitation, deeply disturbing them.
article: ἐκταράσσω means to throw someone into serious upset or turmoil — an intensified form of the common verb ταράσσω, built with the prefix ἐκ-. It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 16:20), where translators fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word, plus twice in the Septuagint. The everyday flavor of the word shows up nicely in the papyri: a document from A.D. 213 uses it of someone disturbing or harassing farmers, and Moulton-Milligan reads it as 'gravely trouble' rather than a fully completed 'thoroughly confound.'
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with very thin overall attestation, so confidence in its precise force is low.

definition: Empty, fruitless talk—words that sound impressive but say nothing of real value.
article: κενοφωνία describes talk that is hollow and pointless, the kind of babbling discussion that produces no real benefit. It combines the ideas of "empty" (κενός) and "sound/voice" (φωνή), and both of its two New Testament occurrences (1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 2:16) are rendered as some form of "chatter." Abbott-Smith notes a related word, κενολογέω, stands behind the Hebrew term for muttering in Isaiah 8:19, and Moulton-Milligan find a close parallel in the philosopher Epictetus, showing the word was at home in everyday Koine.
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its measured range is necessarily narrow.

definition: Bearing a name or label that does not match reality—falsely named or wrongly called.
article: ψευδώνυμος combines the words for "false" and "name," describing something that goes by a label it does not deserve. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:20, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible both render it as warning against knowledge "falsely called" by that name. Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions, including a grave epitaph (Kaibel 42) that calls a name "false" because death snatched the person away too soon.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on a single occurrence plus outside sources.

definition: The fruit of trees, vines, or fields—and, figuratively, the deeds, results, or produce that something yields.
article: καρπός is the everyday Koine word for fruit and the produce of the land, and it dominates the New Testament: of its 65 Byzantine occurrences, 57% are rendered "fruit" and another 20% as "bear fruit," with "crop" and related verbs covering most of the rest. Beyond literal fruit of trees, vines, and fields, the word stretches metaphorically to deeds, actions, and results—as in the "fruit of the Spirit" or the "fruit of the womb." The everyday papyri confirm this earthy range, using καρπός for the produce of an oliveyard and a vineyard, while in the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew פֶּרִי (72 of 107 times).

definition: Syria, a region and Roman province in the ancient Near East, north and east of Israel.
senseLabels: the region or province of Syria
article: Συρία names the region of Syria, which the New Testament treats as a Roman imperial province; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Syria" in 6 of its 8 occurrences (75%), and the Berean Study Bible agrees 100%. In the Septuagint it appears 115 times across 14 books, almost always standing in for the Hebrew name Aram (87×). One striking detail from everyday Koine papyri: the same word could describe "Syrian cloth," with one document from 245 BC pricing Syrian clothes at 6 drachmae.
caution: The few odd renderings like "Syria where" are just fragments of phrases, not separate meanings, so the single sense is secure.

definition: A song or chant, especially one sung in praise of God or Christ.
article: ᾠδή is the general term for any words set to singing, and in the New Testament it appears 7 times—rendered "song" in 5 cases and "sing" in 2. While the word can describe a song that is sad or joyful, in both the Septuagint and the New Testament it always refers to praise of God or Christ, as in Ephesians 5:19's "spiritual songs." Tellingly, the Septuagint uses ᾠδή to translate the Hebrew שִׁיר ("song") 41 times, and everyday inscriptions show it used for a hymn sung during a sacrifice—confirming its broad public, ceremonial range.

definition: To strike or trip against something — literally stubbing a foot or beating against a surface, or figuratively stumbling and taking offense.
article: προσκόπτω covers a range from physical impact to figurative stumbling. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times: about half (4×) render it "stumble" and the rest (3×) describe striking "against" something — as when wind beats against a house (Matthew 7:27) or a foot dashes against a stone (Matthew 4:6). The Septuagint uses it 10 times, mostly for the Hebrew verbs כָּשַׁל and נָגַף, both meaning to stumble or be struck down, and the figurative sense of taking offense (as in 1 Peter 2:8) shows up in everyday Koine writers too.
caution: The two senses overlap and shade into figurative "taking offense," so context decides whether a given verse means literal striking or metaphorical stumbling.

definition: A group of animals kept or moving together, especially pigs as described in the Gospels.
article: ἀγέλη refers to a herd of animals—in every New Testament use it describes the herd of pigs into which Jesus sent demons. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "herd" in 6 of its uses (75%), with occasional variations like "large herd." In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew עֵ֫דֶר, and the word turns up in ordinary life too: Moulton-Milligan note it appears twice in a farm account from 8 B.C., confirming it was the everyday term for livestock.

definition: Salty; relating to salt, as of brackish or salt water.
article: ἁλυκός means "salty" or "briny," derived from ἅλς (salt). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in James 3:12, where it describes salt water that cannot yield fresh, contrasted with a spring. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for salt (מֶלַח, 5×), and the papyri preserve everyday uses like "salted cheeses" and possibly "salted beer," showing it was common Koine vocabulary.
caution: The Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering here ("grow grapevine produce") clearly reflects surrounding context rather than the word itself, which all the lexica agree simply means "salt/salty."

definition: Siloam, the name of a pool fed by a spring in the southeastern corner of Jerusalem.
article: Σιλωάμ is a place-name: the pool of Siloam in Jerusalem, which appears 3 times across the New Testament (Luke 13:4; John 9:7, 11). It comes from the Hebrew שִׁלֹחַ (Shiloach) and shows up once in the Septuagint translating that same Hebrew word. One intriguing note: a scholar suggested the final 'm' in 'Siloam' might mark a Hebrew dual form, hinting at two pools, though this idea has been questioned.
caution: This is a rare proper name with only 3 New Testament occurrences, and the suggestion that its ending points to a dual 'two pools' is disputed.

definition: The number ten, the cardinal figure counting ten items, people, or units.
article: δέκα is simply the number "ten," and it behaves that way throughout the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ten" in 23 of 27 occurrences (96%). It's a common, everyday word that shows up in the Septuagint 286 times, usually translating the Hebrew words for ten. One interesting wrinkle: "ten" can be used loosely to mean simply a short period of time, as in Revelation 2:10's "ten days"—a usage Moulton-Milligan illustrates from a papyrus where a prisoner complains he has been starving "for the last ten months."

definition: A freedman — a former slave (or descendant of one) who had been legally set free, especially under Roman law.
article: Λιβερτῖνος is a Latin loanword (libertinus) for a freedman, a person freed from slavery. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:9, which mentions a synagogue 'of the Libertines' in Jerusalem — apparently a community of such freed people. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it as ordinary Roman legal vocabulary, though some scholars have proposed the original text read Λιβυστίνων, referring instead to Jews from Libya.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and scholars dispute whether the original reading was actually Λιβυστίνων (Libyans) rather than Λιβερτίνων.

definition: A worker who tends and prunes grapevines in a vineyard.
article: This word names someone who cultivates grapevines—pruning, tending, and caring for the vineyard. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 13:7, where it's rendered "keeper," though older translations like the KJV prefer "vine-dresser." In the Septuagint it shows up 4 times, always translating the Hebrew word for vine-growers, and Moulton-Milligan notes it was an ordinary working-life term, appearing in an inscription from 46/45 B.C. about employing a vineyard worker.
caution: This is a one-time word in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on limited evidence.

definition: The number twelve, written as "ten-two" instead of the more common form.
article: This word simply means "twelve." It is an alternate way of writing the number, built from "ten" plus "two," and appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 19:7 and 24:11), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "twelve" 100% of the time. The Moulton-Milligan papyri evidence is the interesting part: in the Ptolemaic-era documents this "ten-two" form was actually the regular spelling for twelve, even though the smoother form δώδεκα dominates elsewhere and in the critical text of these verses.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences and 0 in the critical text, which prefers δώδεκα), so this entry rests on a low confidence tier.

definition: To explain something fully or tell it clearly, making the whole matter plain to someone.
article: This verb means to make something completely clear—to explain it fully or report all the details. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears once, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "recounted" (Matthew 18:31), describing servants telling their master everything that happened. It was a common word in everyday Greek: Moulton-Milligan cites several early papyri letters using it for "explain to us" or "tell me clearly," and in the Septuagint it once renders the Hebrew בָּאַר, "to make plain."
caution: Evidence is thin, with only one Byzantine occurrence, so the precise range rests heavily on the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: To travel together with someone, accompanying them on a journey.
article: This verb means to travel in company with another person, formed from σύν ('with') and ὁδεύω ('to journey'). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 9:7, describing the men traveling with Saul on the road to Damascus, and shows up a few times in the Septuagint (Zechariah 8:21, Tobit, Wisdom). It was ordinary travel vocabulary in everyday Koine, attested in papyri and inscriptions, with the related form συνοδοιπορέω turning up in a second-century papyrus.
caution: The word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: The hair growing on a person's head or on an animal's body, including a single strand of it.
article: θρίξ refers to hair, whether on a human head or covering an animal. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times, rendered "hair" 11 times (79%) and "a single hair" twice, as when Jesus says no one can make one hair white or black (Matthew 5:36). It was an ordinary everyday word: papyri use it in personal descriptions on wills and deeds ("a scar on the forehead under the hair") and even in a tax receipt for cut hair, and in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word שֵׂעָר (24 times).

definition: To be present together with someone, as part of a group gathered in one place.
article: This verb describes being on hand alongside other people—literally "present together with" someone, taking a dative for the persons involved. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just once, in Acts 25:24, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as the assembled "community" present with the speaker. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain meaning: contracts and reports note people who "were present along with" others as witnesses, exactly the sense of bodies gathered in one spot.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and limited Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, and the rendering "community" reflects the gathered group rather than the word's core idea of simply being present together.

definition: To dip something into a liquid, especially dipping food or one's hand into a dish at a meal.
article: ἐμβάπτω simply means to dip one thing into another, formed from ἐν ("in") plus βάπτω ("dip"). In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all describing the same Last Supper moment when someone dips a hand or piece of food into the dish (Matthew 26:23, Mark 14:20, John 13:26). The translation data splits the renderings three ways, but this reflects how the phrase is worded in each verse rather than any real difference in meaning — Abbott-Smith confirms a single sense, "to dip in."
caution: With only 3 occurrences, all from the same scene, the evidence is thin and the three "measured senses" really reflect phrasing differences, not distinct meanings.

definition: To stop someone or something from happening, whether by physically preventing, restraining, or forbidding it.
article: κωλύω means to keep something from happening — to hinder, restrain, or forbid it, whether by action or by spoken command. The Majority Standard Bible splits its renderings fairly evenly between "hinder" (3×) and "forbid" (3×), with the remaining occurrences blended into surrounding phrasing in 11 of its 23 appearances. Everyday Koine papyri show the same down-to-earth range: one second-century document asks "why then did not you stop him?", while a third-century B.C. letter speaks of someone being prevented from building a wall. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew כָּלָא (6×), meaning to shut up or hold back.

definition: The number five thousand, used in the New Testament chiefly to count the men whom Jesus fed.
article: This is simply the cardinal number "five thousand," formed from the parts meaning "five times" and "thousand." It appears 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and every occurrence refers to the same crowd-feeding event, which is why the rendering sometimes expands to phrases like "five thousand fed." In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times as a plain counting word, where it once stands in for the Hebrew term for Persian gold coins (darics), confirming its straightforward numerical use.
caution: The measured sense "thousand" (3 times) reflects how translators split the phrase "five thousand" across words; the word itself always means five thousand.

definition: An oven or furnace, typically an earthen container, used for baking bread or producing heat.
article: κλίβανος refers to a baking oven or furnace, and in both of its New Testament appearances (Matthew 6:30 and Luke 12:28) it describes where dried grass is thrown to fuel the fire. The classical lexica note an interesting shift: originally the word meant a specific earthen vessel for baking bread, but in the Septuagint and New Testament it broadened to mean a furnace or oven generally. Everyday papyri confirm this practical sense, including one Ptolemaic document describing a furnace fed with logs of wood. The form κλίβανος is actually the Ionic spelling, used consistently in the Septuagint in place of the Attic κρίβανος.
caution: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, and the digest's two listed senses both point to the same meaning, so its measured range is very thin.

definition: Phrygia, an inland region of Asia Minor that the Roman Empire split between the provinces of Asia and Galatia.
article: Phrygia is a place name, used the same way every one of its 3 New Testament appearances, all in Acts (2:10; 16:6; 18:23). It refers to an ethnic district in Asia Minor whose northwestern part fell within the Roman province of Asia and whose southeastern part lay in Galatia. One detail worth noting: the word began life as an adjective ("Phrygian"), and in Acts 16:6 it still functions adjectivally, describing the territory rather than naming it outright.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences) and the word's grammatical status shifts between noun and adjective, so its exact reference in Acts 16:6 and 18:23 has long been debated.

definition: The act of opening, especially opening the mouth to speak.
article: ἄνοιξις is a noun built from the verb ἀνοίγω ("to open") and names the act of opening. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 6:19, where Paul speaks of the opening of his mouth to proclaim the gospel — so the phrase functions like "whenever I open my mouth." An interesting twist: in everyday Koine the word turns up in documents like a fourth-century magical papyrus, and in Modern Greek it came to mean "springtime."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: To issue a decree or rule by statute; in the middle voice, to submit oneself to regulations or ordinances.
article: δογματίζω comes from δόγμα (decree) and basically means to lay down a rule by official decree. In its single New Testament appearance, Colossians 2:20, it shows up in the middle voice asking why believers submit themselves to regulations, which the Majority Standard Bible renders with "belonged." The Septuagint uses it three times across two books for the issuing of decrees, and Moulton-Milligan shows the same official sense in inscriptions, where it describes formal decisions of the Roman Senate.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its precise force in Colossians rests on a single passage.

definition: To speak in one's own defense, especially answering charges in a legal or formal setting.
article: This is a courtroom word: it means to plead your case or answer accusations, whether literally before a judge or more generally defending yourself in argument. Across its 10 New Testament uses it clusters tightly around legal defense — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "make defense," "defend," or "defense" in nearly every case, and Abbott-Smith notes it can take an object naming what you say in your defense. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this judicial flavor: a 163 BC petition to King Ptolemy uses it for someone appointed "to make my defence."

definition: A pointing word meaning "of this kind" or "such as this," describing the character or type of a person or thing.
article: τοιοῦτος is a correlative pointer that means "such" or "of this sort," describing what kind of person or thing is in view rather than naming it. Its range is fairly tight, but English translators handle it many ways depending on context, and notably it disappears entirely into the phrasing 13 of 61 times, since English often expresses "such" without a separate word. It frequently stands alone as a noun-like "such a one," as in the Septuagint and the everyday papyri, where a contract describes "a female donkey, just as it is."

definition: To scatter people abroad, dispersing them from one place into many regions, like seed thrown over a field.
article: διασπείρω literally means to sow seed throughout, but in practice it describes people being scattered and dispersed into other places. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in Acts (8:1, 8:4, 11:19), where believers are scattered by persecution. The word is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 58 times and most often renders the Hebrew פּוּץ (33×), "to scatter." It also turns up in everyday Koine documents — Moulton-Milligan cite a tax list mentioning people "scattered" across registers.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, confidence is low, though the meaning is consistent and well supported by abundant Septuagint usage.

definition: The knee, especially in expressions for kneeling or bowing in worship, supplication, or mockery.
article: γόνυ simply means the knee, but in the New Testament it almost always appears in expressions about kneeling or bending the knee—whether before Jesus in supplication, in prayer, or even in mockery. Of its 12 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it literally as "knees" 7 times (58%) and as "knelt" 3 times (25%), the latter capturing phrases like "placing the knees." In the Septuagint it appears 28 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for knee (24 of those times). A nice everyday detail: the word shows up in census documents from the papyri, where a person could be identified by "a scar on the right knee."

definition: A small herb (dill) whose seeds and leaves were used as seasoning and grown in gardens.
article: Ánēthon names a common garden herb, rendered "dill" in every one of its single New Testament occurrences (Matthew 23:23, in Jesus' rebuke of Pharisees who tithed even tiny herbs). The KJV translates it "anise," but the measured evidence and modern translations agree on "dill." The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri among medical prescriptions—one early first-century recipe from Oxyrhynchus mixes it (spelled ἀννήσου) into a sleeping potion with henbane and opium, and an inscription pairs it with oil for headache.
caution: Evidence is thin—just one New Testament occurrence—and older sources gloss it as "anise" while the measured data points to "dill."

definition: The bent or curved arm, especially as used to hold or carry something or someone.
article: ἀγκάλη refers to the arm seen as a curve or bend, particularly the way you cradle your arms to receive a burden or hold a child. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 2:28, where Simeon takes the infant Jesus into his arms. Everyday Koine papyri stretch the word further: it could mean an armful or bundle, as in a document about transporting bundles of goods, showing how naturally the "curved arm" idea extended to whatever the arms carry.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and three in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin.

definition: To throw or fling something away, or to throw oneself off—as overboard from a ship into the water.
article: At its core ἀποῤῥίπτω means to hurl or cast something away; used reflexively it means to throw oneself off, as in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 27:43), where prisoners cast themselves overboard to swim ashore. The word ranges widely in the Septuagint, where it appears 41 times across 16 books, most often translating the Hebrew שָׁלַך, "to throw" (18×). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this concrete sense vividly: in one petition a man complains of being shoved "into a hidden corner," and in another someone's belongings are "thrown into the road."
caution: It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its New Testament sense rests on a single verse.

definition: Phoenix, a harbor town on the southern coast of Crete.
article: Phoenix is the name of a harbor on the south coast of Crete, mentioned only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 27:12). In that passage it appears as the destination the sailors hoped to reach to spend the winter. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Phoenix" in its single occurrence, and the BSB agrees fully; the older KJV used the spelling "Phenice."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so the evidence is very thin.

definition: To take something away or remove it, including cutting something off such as an ear.
article: ἀφαιρέω means to take away or remove something, whether literally pulling it off or figuratively removing things like reproach or sins. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times, mostly for things being "taken away" (6×, 67%), but twice for the dramatic "cutting" off of a servant's ear at Jesus' arrest (Mark 14:47, Luke 22:50). It was a very common everyday word: the papyri show it used in a mathematical sense of "deduct" (subtract from a total) and in complaints about garments being violently seized.

definition: Describing something that does not wither or fade, made of or like the unfading amaranth flower.
article: This adjective appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 5:4, describing the crown of glory that faithful shepherds will receive. Abbott-Smith notes it originally meant "of amaranth," a flower that holds its color, and from there came to mean simply "unfading" or "enduring." Worth noting: the measured rendering data labels its single occurrence as "Chief," which clashes with every lexicon here (KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith all agree on "that does not fade away"); the lexical sense of fadelessness is the well-supported one.
caution: A single New Testament occurrence and a confusing measured-sense label that conflicts with all the lexica make this entry low-confidence.

definition: A person from the Roman province of Asia; an Asian.
article: Ἀσιανός describes someone from the Roman province of Asia, used in the New Testament as a noun for inhabitants of that region. It appears only once, in Acts 20:4, where it identifies traveling companions of Paul. Interestingly, the measured rendering pairs it with the name "Secundus" in that verse, reflecting how the word functions there to mark a man's regional origin rather than carrying a meaning of its own.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be confirmed from biblical evidence alone.

definition: Deserving pity; in a wretched or miserable condition that calls for compassion.
article: This adjective describes someone in a pitiable, miserable state who deserves to be pitied. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in the critical text), where Paul says that if hope in Christ is only for this life, believers are the most to be pitied (1 Corinthians 15:19). One nice detail: the word turns up in everyday Egyptian papyri, where a writer calls himself "Anoup, your wretched servant" — showing it served as a humble, self-deprecating term in ordinary speech.
caution: Evidence is thin (only one Byzantine occurrence), and the Septuagint's use to render Hebrew חָמַד, "to desire," sits oddly with the New Testament sense of "pitiable."

definition: Punishment given to an offender as the penalty they deserve, with no implied aim of correction or discipline.
article: In the New Testament τιμωρία appears just once, in Hebrews 10:29, where it means the punishment an offender deserves. The papyri sharpen this picture: in a first-century document (P Lond 1171) a prefect threatens wrongdoers with the 'highest' τιμωρία, and Moulton-Milligan note that the word carries the idea of giving an offender his just deserts, unlike κόλασις, which normally includes the thought of correction or discipline. Interestingly, the older lexicon Abbott-Smith also lists an earlier sense of 'help, assistance,' which does not show up in the biblical evidence at all.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lexicons disagree about its range—Abbott-Smith records an older sense of 'help' not reflected in the measured biblical data.

definition: Describing something that cannot be dissolved, broken up, or brought to an end.
article: ἀκατάλυτος describes something that cannot be taken apart or ended — built from the negative prefix and a form of καταλύω (to dissolve or tear down). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 7:16, where it describes a life that cannot be destroyed; the lexicons render it "indissoluble" or "endless." Outside the New Testament, the word is rare, with one Septuagint appearance in 4 Maccabees 10:11, showing it was a recognized but uncommon term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and only once in the Septuagint, so its range cannot be measured from many examples.

definition: Showing no mercy or compassion toward others; hard-hearted and unwilling to pity.
article: This adjective combines the negative prefix "a-" with the word for "merciful," so it literally means "without mercy." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Paul's list of human failings in Romans 1:31, and six times in the Septuagint, where it consistently translates the Hebrew word for "cruel" (אַכְזָרִי, 4 times). The lexicons (Strong's, KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) all agree on "merciless" or "unpitying," though the Majority Standard Bible renders the single NT occurrence as "senseless."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and the MSB rendering ("senseless") differing from the lexicons' consistent "merciless," the evidence is thin and the sources disagree on the best translation.

definition: Belonging to the Stoics, a school of Greek philosophers in Athens who debated with Paul.
article: This adjective names an adherent of Stoicism, one of the philosophical schools Paul encountered in Athens. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 17:18) and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text. The word derives from στοά ("porch"), referring to the colonnade in Athens where these philosophers taught, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions; the spelling varies between Στωϊκός and Στοϊκός in the manuscripts.
caution: This word occurs only once and the measured "said" rendering reflects surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself, so treat the data cautiously.

definition: A braided or twisted arrangement of hair, woven up into an elaborate hairstyle.
article: πλέγμα comes from the verb πλέκω ("to weave or twist") and literally means something woven or interwoven — basketwork, nets, and, when applied to hair, an elaborate braid. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 2:9, where it describes the kind of fancy hairstyling Paul contrasts with modest dress. Outside the New Testament the only noted occurrence is in the later translators Aquila and Theodotion at Isaiah 28:5, showing how rare the word is in the Greek Bible.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering "modesty" is a loose contextual gloss that differs from the lexicons' literal sense of "braided hair," so the evidence is thin.

definition: To set or lay something down, deposit it, or—in the middle voice with "favor"—to do someone a favor, often hoping for one in return.
article: At its root κατατίθημι means to put something down or deposit it, a usage common in everyday Koine papyri—where people deposit seed into the ground or pay money into a bank. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, and the one rendered sense is the middle-voice idiom "to do a favor" (literally "lay up favor for oneself"), as when a governor wishes to please others in Acts 24:27. The classical phrase χάριν κατατίθεσθαι, paying out a favor with a view to receiving one in return, is the most striking feature here, attested both in Acts and in older Greek authors.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences with just 1 yielding a measured English rendering, so confidence is low.

definition: To bring things together—physically uniting them, mentally piecing facts into a conclusion, or instructing someone by drawing knowledge together.
article: This verb covers a surprisingly wide range, all built on the idea of bringing things together. It can mean physically uniting or knitting parts into one (Ephesians 4:16; Colossians 2:2,19), mentally putting facts together to prove a point (Acts 9:22) or reach a conclusion (Acts 16:10), or teaching someone—which is its constant meaning in the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew verbs for instructing or making someone know (יָרָה, יָדַע). Moulton-Milligan notes the same shift toward "instruct" in 1 Corinthians 2:16, comparing the everyday papyri verb ἐκβιβάζω used for a lawsuit being decided.
caution: With only 6 occurrences spread across six distinct senses and lexicons disagreeing on whether Colossians 2:2 means "knit together" or "instruct," individual renderings rest on thin evidence.

definition: A tenth part of something, given as a tithe or offering.
article: δεκάτη means a tenth part—a tithe—and every one of its 4 New Testament appearances comes from a single passage in Hebrews 7 discussing Melchizedek. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for tithe (מַעֲשֵׂר). Interestingly, the everyday papyri reveal a striking inversion of the biblical idea: one document records a δεκάτη as a 10 percent tax levied on profits priests made, rather than an offering given to them.
caution: The two measured senses both mean "a tenth" and reflect the same Hebrews 7 passage, so the second is essentially a contextual label rather than a distinct meaning.

definition: A Galatian — a person living in the Roman region of Galatia.
article: Γαλάτης simply means a Galatian, someone from the region or province of Galatia, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Galatians 3:1. The word was originally interchangeable with the classical term for a Celt (Κέλτης), reflecting the Celtic peoples who settled the area. One wrinkle worth noting: the related place-name Galatia could point either to the inland Asian province or to European Gaul, as its proximity to Dalmatia in 2 Timothy 4:10 suggests — a question scholars still debate.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "bewitched" reflects the surrounding verse rather than the word itself, which plainly means "Galatian."

definition: A fox, the wild animal, sometimes used figuratively to describe a sly or cunning person.
article: At its core ἀλώπηξ simply means the animal we call a fox, and that is how it's used twice in the New Testament when Jesus says foxes have holes. The third occurrence applies it figuratively to Herod in Luke 13:32, where Jesus calls him 'that fox' — the sense both Strong's and Dodson note as a crafty or cunning person. In the Septuagint it appears 10 times across 7 books, most often translating the Hebrew word שׁוּעָל (shu'al, 'fox'), though it also stands in for a few other Hebrew words.
caution: The figurative 'cunning person' sense rests on a single New Testament occurrence (Luke 13:32), so its range there is narrow.

definition: Describing something held in equal honor or value, placing one person or thing on the same level as another.
article: ἰσότιμος combines ἴσος ("equal") and τιμή ("honor, value"), so it describes something that ranks on the same level as something else. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 1:1, where it describes a faith equally privileged with that of the apostles; the King James Version renders it "like precious," but Field argued the emphatic idea is equality rather than preciousness. A striking parallel comes from an inscription (OGIS 234) where "Apollo Isotimos" marks that this god was held in no less honor than Zeus.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and translators disagree over whether it stresses equal value ("like precious") or equal standing ("equally privileged").

definition: To clothe someone, or to provide them with clothing.
article: ἱματίζω means to clothe a person or to provide them with clothing; it comes from ἱμάτιον, the word for a garment. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Mark 5:15 and Luke 8:35), in both cases describing the formerly demon-possessed man found sitting clothed and in his right mind. Though Grimm thought the word was found neither in the Septuagint nor in classical authors, Moulton-Milligan shows it was ordinary in everyday Koine papyri, where parents and guardians promise to clothe a child—proof that the Gospel writers did not coin it.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences—and one absorbed into surrounding phrasing—the evidence is thin, so this entry rests largely on papyri usage.

definition: Rich, sumptuous, or luxurious — literally "fatty," used of fine and dainty things.
article: λιπαρός comes from a word for fat or grease and literally means "oily" or "fatty," but it is regularly used in a figurative sense for rich, dainty, or luxurious living. It appears just once in the New Testament (Revelation 18:14), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within a phrase about the lost luxuries of fallen Babylon. In the Septuagint it shows up 3 times, each translating the Hebrew word shamen ("fat"), as in Isaiah 30:23 describing rich, plentiful produce.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the way the cited translation renders it as "fruit" reflects the broader phrase rather than the word's own literal sense of "fatty" or "sumptuous."

definition: Crete, the large Mediterranean island south of the Aegean Sea.
article: Κρήτη is simply the place name Crete, a large island in the Mediterranean, appearing 5 times in the New Testament across 2 books. Four of those uses (80%) name the island directly, while one (20%) describes sailing past it, as in the voyage narrative of Acts 27. It shows up once in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew כְּרֹת, and its ultimate derivation is uncertain.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: Bethsaida, a town near the Sea of Galilee linked with several Gospel events and with some of Jesus' disciples.
article: Bethsaida is a place name appearing 7 times across 4 books of the Byzantine New Testament, always rendered "Bethsaida" (the other measured "senses" are just neighboring words pulled in from each verse). The name reportedly comes from a Syriac or Aramaic phrase meaning "house of fish," fitting for a lakeside town near the Sea of Galilee. Interestingly, lexicons note there may have been two towns by this name—one northeast of the lake (Luke 9:10) and possibly a second on the western shore referenced elsewhere—though scholars do not fully agree on this point.
caution: It is a proper noun with a single real sense; the only genuine uncertainty is whether one or two towns named Bethsaida are in view, on which the sources differ.

definition: The living self of a person—their life, breath of life, or inner soul that feels, wills, and desires.
article: ψυχή covers the whole range of what makes a creature alive and self-aware. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "soul" 40 times (49%) and "life" or "lives" in another 39 times, so it swings between the inner self and physical life depending on context—and in 23 of its 105 occurrences it's folded into a phrase with no English word of its own. In the Septuagint it appears 748 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew נֶפֶשׁ (523×), and Strong's notes it points to the sentient "animal" life, distinct from πνεῦμα (spirit) and ζωή (mere vitality). Strikingly, it can also serve simply as a way of saying "person" or "self," and the phrase ἐκ ψυχῆς means "heartily" or "from the heart."
caution: The line between "soul" and "life" is genuinely blurry, and translators differ case by case rather than following a fixed rule.

definition: Samuel, the Hebrew prophet and judge of Israel.
article: Σαμουήλ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name שְׁמוּאֵל (Shemuel), the prophet and judge Samuel. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament (Acts 3:24; 13:20; Hebrews 11:32) but turns up 143 times in the Septuagint. Interestingly, the name also shows up in everyday documents: a sixth-century Oxyrhynchus papyrus names a man called Samuel in an order to pay a monk 12 measures of corn, showing it stayed in use as a personal name long after the prophet.
caution: This is simply a proper name; the three NT occurrences all point to the same person, so the listed "senses" just reflect surrounding phrases rather than distinct meanings.

definition: Pacatiana, the western part of the Roman province of Phrygia as it was organized in the fourth century AD.
article: Pakatianḗ is a place name referring to western Phrygia, a region in Asia Minor that was administratively organized as "Pacatiana" in the fourth century AD. The word does not appear in the body of the Byzantine New Testament; it shows up only in the subscription (the closing note) attached to 1 Timothy in the Received Text, identifying where the letter was supposedly written or sent. The form is the feminine of an adjective whose origin Abbott-Smith calls uncertain.
caution: This term appears only in a late textual subscription, not in the actual New Testament text, so the evidence is extremely thin and the word's derivation is unknown.

definition: A very young child, from an unborn baby in the womb to a newborn or infant in arms.
article: βρέφος covers the earliest stage of human life, stretching from an unborn child still in the womb to a newborn or nursing infant. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "baby" in every occurrence it translates (6 of 8), with the other 2 absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The everyday papyri make this vivid: one third-century letter discusses arranging a wet-nurse for a βρέφος, and Abbott-Smith notes the phrase "from infancy" (apo brephous) in 2 Timothy 3:15.
caution: With only 8 occurrences the evidence is limited, and the word spans both unborn and newborn children, so context determines which is meant.

definition: To assign or choose someone by lot, and so to make them part of an allotted portion or inheritance.
article: This verb comes from κλῆρος ("lot") and basically means to assign or choose by lot, often with the sense of being made part of an inheritance. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Ephesians 1:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "chosen" and the passive form points to believers being given a share or made a heritage. The everyday papyri are illuminating here: people write of being "assigned" to farming work (P Iand 27) or "allotted" to herding cattle (BGU II.625), showing the plain administrative force of the word. In the Septuagint it appears just 3 times across 2 books and reflects ideas like casting or seizing by lot.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and thin Septuagint evidence, the precise nuance at Ephesians 1:11 is genuinely disputed, and translations split between "chosen" and "obtained an inheritance."

definition: Describing something clear or evident to the mind — plainly obvious or easily understood.
senseLabels: clear or evident to the mind
article: δῆλος means "clear" or "evident" — not visible to the eye so much as obvious to the understanding. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often in the phrase "it is clear that" (as in 1 Corinthians 15:27 and Galatians 3:11). Abbott-Smith draws a nice contrast: φανερός means manifest to outward sight, while δῆλος means evident to inner perception; everyday Koine papyri confirm this, repeatedly using δῆλον for what is plainly so, like a petition stating that something "is forbidden by the law — that is clear." In the Septuagint it interestingly stands in for the Hebrew Urim (3×), the priestly objects used to make God's will known.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and the measured renderings ("one," "put," "certainly") reflecting surrounding phrases rather than the word itself, the corpus data is thin and best read alongside the lexical sense "clear, evident."

definition: To tie someone up with chains or bonds, restraining them physically.
article: δεσμέω means to bind or shackle someone, restraining them with chains. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 8:29, where it describes a demon-possessed man being kept bound. Abbott-Smith notes this form is actually a textual variant for the more common δεσμεύω, which in the Septuagint translates the Hebrew word for 'bind' (אָסַר) and is used both for putting people in chains and for tying loads together.
caution: This word occurs just once in the Byzantine text and may be a textual variant for δεσμεύω, so the evidence is thin.

definition: To marry a relative by family obligation, especially a dead brother's widow to continue his line.
article: This rare verb describes forming a marriage tie within a family, and in the New Testament it specifically means taking a dead brother's widow as wife to raise up children in his name. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 22:24, where the Sadducees describe the levirate marriage custom. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times across 4 books, always translating the Hebrew root חָתַן ("to become a son-in-law" or "intermarry"), where it more often means simply to enter into a marriage alliance—a slightly broader sense than the specific levirate meaning in Matthew.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise levirate sense here is shaped by Genesis 38:8 rather than broad attestation.

definition: To be short-sighted, squinting or closing the eyes to see, the way a near-sighted person peers at distant things.
article: This rare verb describes the squinting of a near-sighted person — screwing up the eyes to make out what is far off. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 1:9, where it sits alongside the word for "blind." Moulton-Milligan note it is documented in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, yet outside 2 Peter the only other known instance in Greek literature is a passage in Pseudo-Dionysius; they argue the word actually limits rather than intensifies the preceding "blind," meaning the person can still see only what is close at hand.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament and is almost unattested elsewhere in Greek literature, so its precise force is genuinely uncertain and debated.

definition: To suddenly cry out or shout aloud, often in fear, distress, or strong emotion.
article: This verb means to shout or cry out suddenly and forcefully — it combines κράζω ("cry out") with the prefix ἀνά. All five New Testament uses describe a loud outcry, frequently from people in distress or possessed by unclean spirits, and the standard renderings cluster around the simple phrase "cried out." A vivid papyrus example (BGU IV.1201, second century AD) shows villagers crying out for help when the temple of Serapis caught fire, confirming the word's everyday sense of urgent, vigorous shouting.
caution: The five measured renderings are really one sense ("cried out"); the variations come only from surrounding words, not different meanings.

definition: Describing a person or statement as false, lying, or untrue rather than truthful.
article: ψευδής means "false" or "untrue," applied both to people who lie and to things that aren't true. In its 3 New Testament appearances it twice describes liars (Revelation 2:2; 21:8) and once refers to the false witnesses brought against Stephen (Acts 6:13). The word was common in everyday Koine: papyri use it for false reports, lying accusations, and fabricated charges, and the Septuagint uses it 88 times, most often to render the Hebrew word for falsehood, שֶׁקֶר.
caution: Only 3 New Testament occurrences, so the measured senses rest on thin evidence.

definition: To capture someone and lead them away as a prisoner, often used figuratively for being conquered or held under control.
article: αἰχμαλωτίζω means to take someone captive, especially in war, and lead them away as a prisoner. The New Testament uses it both literally (Luke 21:24, of people led off after Jerusalem falls) and figuratively (Romans 7:23 and 2 Corinthians 10:5, of being held captive by sin or of taking thoughts captive). In the Septuagint it appears 10 times and chiefly renders the Hebrew שָׁבָה, the standard word for capturing prisoners; the verb also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and the ancient grammarian Phrynichus dismissed it as substandard — which actually confirms it was good common speech.
caution: With only 3 or 4 New Testament occurrences, the split between literal and figurative use rests on thin evidence.

definition: Refusing to change one's mind or turn from sin; unrepentant and stubbornly set in one's ways.
article: This adjective combines a negative prefix with a word for repentance, describing a heart that refuses to turn around. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 2:5, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "hard" and the Berean Study Bible agrees fully. Interestingly, everyday legal papyri from the third and fourth centuries A.D. use it in a fixed phrase meaning a decision made of one's own free will and not to be retracted, showing the word could carry the active sense of "unchangeable" as well as "unrepentant."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range here rests on a single verse plus outside evidence.

definition: The enjoyment or pleasure one gets from possessing or experiencing something.
article: ἀπόλαυσις means enjoyment or pleasure — the satisfaction that comes from having or doing something. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Timothy 6:17 and Hebrews 11:26), and in everyday Koine it was common: inscriptions and papyri pair it with words like 'sweetest' or 'shared,' as in a Commagene inscription describing reverence as giving people 'the sweetest enjoyment.' Note that the measured rendering data for 1 Timothy 6:17 looks garbled (it lists 'conceited'), which doesn't match the word's actual meaning of enjoyment.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 NT occurrences), and the digest's measured rendering 'conceited' appears to be a data error inconsistent with the word's well-attested sense of enjoyment.

definition: A physician—someone whose work is healing the sick.
article: ἰατρός is simply the everyday word for a doctor, the person who heals the sick, and all 7 New Testament occurrences point to that single meaning. The measured senses only differ in form and setting: it appears as the general figure of the doctor (as in Jesus' saying that the healthy don't need one), as physicians people actually consulted (Luke himself is called 'the beloved physician' in Colossians 4:14), and once inside the proverb 'Physician, heal yourself' in Luke 4:23. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the word was common, even listing it in an alphabet acrostic and documenting official 'public physicians' in Egypt who could be ordered to inspect a dead body.

definition: To stay firmly committed to something—a faith, an agreement, or a written rule—remaining true to it over time.
article: ἐμμένω is built from "in" plus "remain," and it means to stay put—but in the New Testament it's almost always figurative, describing someone staying loyal to a faith, a covenant, or a body of rules. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine text (4 in the critical text), rendered "continue," "rely/continue," and "abide," so its range centers on persevering and being true to something. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: ἐμμένω was a standard legal formula meaning to abide by a contract or comply with a judgment, and that legal flavor echoes in Galatians 3:10's phrase about abiding by what is written.
caution: With only 3–4 New Testament occurrences, each rendered differently, the sense divisions rest on very thin evidence.

definition: A person from Cyprus, the Mediterranean island; a Cypriot.
article: Κύπριος simply means someone who comes from the island of Cyprus — a Cypriot. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts, always describing a person's home origin (such as Barnabas in Acts 4:36 and Mnason in Acts 21:16). The word is built straight from Κύπρος, the name of the island itself, so it carries no meaning beyond identifying nationality.
caution: The measured senses look like three different translations, but this reflects how the word sits inside longer phrases rather than any real variation in meaning — it consistently just means "Cypriot"; with only 3 occurrences the evidence is thin.

definition: A person who strongly craves or desires something, often in a bad sense of lusting after what one should not have.
article: ἐπιθυμητής describes someone who eagerly longs for something. Built from the verb ἐπιθυμέω ("to desire"), it appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 10:6, where Paul warns against being "cravers" of evil things. The everyday papyri show both sides of the word: one man insists he is no "coveter of others' goods," while an inscription speaks admiringly of people becoming "desirers of glory"—so the craving can be shameful or noble depending on its object.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense there rests on a single passage.

definition: An adverb meaning in a different way, or otherwise than expected.
article: This adverb means "differently" or "otherwise," built from the word for "other" (ἕτερος). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 3:15, and the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) agree on the sense "differently, otherwise." Notably, Moulton-Milligan document it in everyday Koine inscriptions, including one from A.D. 147 reading "even if this turned out otherwise," showing it was ordinary, idiomatic Greek.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering label "embrace" does not match the lexicons' "differently/otherwise," so treat the corpus tag with caution.

definition: A custom or established practice, or the force of habit that shapes what people regularly do.
article: συνήθεια refers to a settled custom or practice—the way things are usually done. In its three New Testament uses it points to a Passover custom (John 18:39), accepted church practice (1 Corinthians 11:16), and the lingering force of habit shaping how someone acts (1 Corinthians 8:7). Notably, the everyday Koine papyri and the classical lexica also attest a warmer sense the New Testament does not use: 'intimacy' or 'friendship,' as in a fourth-century letter speaking of 'the knowledge of our intimacy with one another.'
caution: The word appears only 2 or 3 times in the New Testament and is always absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word, so confidence is low and the 'intimacy' sense comes only from outside the NT.

definition: To make something clear or known to someone, whether by reporting information or by pointing to its meaning.
article: δηλόω means to make something plain to the mind—to inform, declare, or point out a meaning. In the Byzantine NT it appears 7 times, most often rendered "informed" (about two-thirds of cases, as in 1 Corinthians 1:11 and Colossians 1:8), and once as "signify" in Hebrews 12:27. Tellingly, the everyday papyri show this same plain sense: people closed letters with phrases like "when you have received it, let me know" (δήλωσόν μοι), making it a routine word for passing along information. Abbott-Smith notes a useful distinction from ἐμφανίζω: that word means to make visible to the sight, while δηλόω makes something evident to the mind.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and 4 of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured English renderings rest on thin data.

definition: Someone who debates or argues over difficult questions, especially a clever academic arguer.
article: This word names a person who debates or disputes, the kind of skilled academic arguer reflected in older glosses like 'disputer' and 'sophist.' It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 1:20, where it is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word. It is built from the verb συζητέω, 'to discuss or dispute together.'
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence and thin attestation, the precise shade of meaning is hard to pin down.

definition: Levi, a personal name borne by several men in the Bible, including a son of Jacob and an apostle.
article: Λευΐ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name לֵוִי (Levi), used as a proper name for several different men. In the New Testament it can point to the patriarch Levi, the third son of Jacob and founder of the tribe (as in Hebrews 7:5 and Revelation 7:7), to ancestors of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, or to the tax collector also called Matthew. It appears 5 times in the Byzantine text but far more often in the Septuagint, where it shows up 73 times, mostly translating לֵוִי itself but occasionally standing in for other names like Merari or Mahli.
caution: Although the spelling is consistent, the name refers to at least four different individuals, so context determines who is meant.

definition: A teaching or custom handed down from one generation to the next, whether human or divinely received.
article: παράδοσις comes from the verb παραδίδωμι, "to hand over," and its root idea is the act of passing something on. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times across 6 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "tradition" in 12 of those (92%), with the BSB agreeing 100%. The everyday Koine papyri preserve the more literal sense beautifully: documents speak of the official "transmission" or "delivery" of freight and of seed (P Oxy X. 1262), reminding us the word first meant a concrete handing over before it came to mean inherited teaching.

definition: Lasting only for a short time; temporary, fleeting, and not enduring.
article: Πρόσκαιρος describes something that lasts only for a season rather than permanently, built from πρός ("for") and καιρός ("time"). It appears 4 times in the New Testament, where translators render it with phrases about endurance — "remains" only briefly in Matthew 13:21 and Mark 4:17 (the seedling that withers), and "what" is temporary in 2 Corinthians 4:18. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show a second shade of meaning: an edict of Caracalla (A.D. 215) uses it to mean "in season" or "opportune," matching Abbott-Smith's first listed sense, even though the New Testament always uses the "temporary, transient" sense.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and the lexica noting an "in season" sense not measured in the New Testament, the full range carries some uncertainty.

definition: To act before someone else does, getting ahead of them by speaking or moving first.
article: προφθάνω means to get ahead of someone, anticipating their action by doing or saying something first. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 17:25, where Jesus speaks before Peter can, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "preempted." In the Septuagint it occurs 17 times, mostly translating Hebrew קָדַם ("to come before, meet"), and a papyrus from 161 B.C. uses it of a man who got to the temple door first and shut it before others could reach him.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise New Testament shade of meaning rests on a single verse.

definition: To respond or reply to something said, often beginning a speech in answer to a person or situation.
article: This is the standard New Testament verb for answering or replying, and the meaning is remarkably stable: across 248 Byzantine occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "replied" (49%), "answered" (39%), or "answer" (9%), with the BSB independently agreeing nearly every time. In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew עָנָה ("answer") 161 times, and from that Hebrew background it picked up a distinctive use: "to begin to speak" when a response is expected, even where no one has literally asked a question. One small surprise comes from the papyri, where a 2nd-century AD document uses a passive form to mean fulfilling a duty rather than answering — a reminder that the word's older sense of "separate" or "choose" lingered in everyday Greek.
caution: Classical lexica list older senses like "separate" and "choose," but these do not appear in the New Testament, where the meaning is overwhelmingly "answer."

definition: To produce fruit or crops, whether literally from plants or figuratively from a person's life and conduct.
article: This verb means to be fruitful, used both for plants yielding a crop and, figuratively, for the results a person's life produces. Across its 8 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible splits its renderings evenly—"produce crop," "bear fruit," and "fruit" each appear twice—and the BSB independently agrees with all of them. Abbott-Smith notes the literal sense in Mark 4:28 (bearing grass or vegetation) versus the metaphorical sense of conduct in passages like Matthew 13:23 and Colossians 1:10.
caution: The Septuagint evidence is thin (just one occurrence), and the listed Hebrew counterpart in the digest appears garbled, so the LXX background should be treated with care.

definition: A fish, especially one prepared to be eaten alongside bread, as in a meal.
article: ὀψάριον means fish—specifically the kind eaten as a tasty accompaniment to bread. All 5 New Testament occurrences are in John's Gospel (6:9, 6:11, 21:9-10, 13), and the Berean Standard Bible renders it "fish" every time, agreeing fully with the measured senses. Originally a diminutive meaning a relish or dainty added to a main dish, it came to mean fish in particular; everyday Koine papyri show this clearly, with one letter asking someone to "send me the loaves and the relish" and another mentioning a jar of pickled fish.
caution: The three listed senses are really one meaning, "fish," split only by surrounding words in the translation; the broader "relish" sense comes from papyri and lexica, not the New Testament occurrences.

definition: To be driven or tossed about by the wind, used of something moved by gusts of air.
article: ἀνεμίζω describes being blown or tossed about by the wind, built from the noun ἄνεμος ("wind") with the productive -ίζω verb ending. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at James 1:6, and even there it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than standing as its own English word. Interestingly, the lexicographer Mayor suggested the writer of James — who liked -ίζω verbs — may have coined this term himself, since other parallels in the dictionaries come from much later.
caution: This word occurs only once and may be a fresh coinage, so its exact range cannot be pinned down from usage.

definition: The ordinal number meaning twelfth, marking something as number twelve in a sequence.
article: δωδέκατος simply means "twelfth," the ordinal form derived from δώδεκα ("twelve"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Revelation 21:20, where it marks the twelfth foundation stone of the heavenly city; the Majority Standard Bible renders the verse with "jacinth," the name of the stone tied to that twelfth position. Everyday papyri confirm the same plain usage—for example, a document from A.D. 127 refers to "the coming twelfth year of Hadrian Caesar," exactly how we still count years and items today.
caution: The single NT occurrence is rendered as "jacinth" because of the stone it numbers, but the word itself only means "twelfth"; with just one attestation, treat the measured sense cautiously.

definition: To tell a story or report in full detail, recounting what happened from start to finish.
article: διηγέομαι means to tell something out in full — to narrate, describe, or give a detailed account of events. It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, often paired with what was seen or done ("what they saw," "all that he did"), and 51 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew סָפַר, "to recount" (26 times). Everyday papyri show the same plain use: a prodigal son's letter complains that someone "unseasonably related everything to you," showing this was a common word for ordinary storytelling.
caution: In 5 of its 8 New Testament uses the word is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word, so glosses vary.

definition: A short comparison or illustrative story drawn from everyday life to teach a deeper truth, often told by Jesus.
article: παραβολή literally means setting one thing beside another, and across its 50 New Testament uses it almost always points to the vivid comparisons and illustrative stories—parables—found in the synoptic Gospels, rendered "parable" or a variation 81% of the time. In the Septuagint it usually stands in for the Hebrew מָשָׁל (25 times), a word that covers proverbs and sayings as well as comparisons, which is why the classical lexica also list senses like "proverb," "figure," and "analogy" (for example in Hebrews 9:9 and 11:19). The most telling detail is that Hebrew background: the same term that gives us "parable" also produced the broader "adage" or "figure" range the NT only occasionally uses.

definition: To feel grief alongside others, sharing in their sorrow out of sympathy.
article: This verb combines "with" (σύν) and "to grieve" (λυπέω), so its basic idea is feeling sorrow together with or on account of someone. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Mark 3:5, where it is rendered "sorrow," and the passive form there carries the sense of being moved to grief by sympathy. In its two Septuagint appearances it stands for Hebrew words tied to distress and devastation (Psalm 69:20 and Isaiah 51:19), and Abbott-Smith notes an active sense in Aristotle—"to make someone grieve along with you."
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, and it does not appear in the SBLGNT critical text.

definition: A split into opposing groups; division or dissension that breaks apart a community.
article: Διχοστασία describes a falling-out that divides people into opposing camps — built from parts meaning "two" and "standing," so literally a "standing apart." It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "divisions" in two of three cases (the third reading reflects a textual difference rather than a separate meaning).
