The word was ordinary Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite a second-century BC inscription describing affairs left "in the greatest turmoil and division," and it also turns up in the Greek Old Testament at 1 Maccabees 3:29.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (and just 2 in the critical text), so the confidence tier is low.

definition: A stone-paved area, especially a surface laid out in mosaic or tessellated stonework.
article: Literally meaning "strewn with stones," this word describes a paved surface, particularly the kind made of fitted decorative stonework. In the New Testament it appears just once, as a noun naming the "Pavement" where Pilate's judgment seat stood (John 19:13). The same word shows up in everyday Koine: a papyrus from A.D. 268 mentions a "paved street of Hermes," and the Letter of Aristeas uses it for a temple floor entirely paved with stone, while in the Septuagint it three times renders the Hebrew word for a stone floor (rītspāh).
caution: This is the word's only New Testament occurrence, so its measured range rests on a single verse, though the wider Koine and Septuagint evidence agrees.

definition: To form and pronounce a decision about someone or something—whether in a courtroom, in everyday opinion, or by deciding on a course of action.
article: At its core κρίνω means to separate things out and reach a decision, which is why it covers everything from a courtroom verdict to a private opinion to simply deciding to do something. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "judge" 53 times (67%), with smaller groups meaning "judgment," judging a person, and "condemn" (3×); notably, it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing 36 of 115 times with no English word of its own. The everyday Koine papyri show the practical edge of the word vividly: people wrote "we have decided" (ἐκρίναμεν) and "I have decided once and for all" (κέκρικα) about ordinary plans. In the Septuagint it appears 202 times, most often translating Hebrew שָׁפַט ("to judge," 105×).
caution: The word's range is genuinely broad—the lexica list senses like "decide," "esteem," and "think" that the measured renderings fold into phrasing, so context matters more than any single gloss.

definition: A precious gemstone of sea-green color, listed among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem's wall.
article: βήρυλλος names a precious stone, the beryl, traditionally described as sea-green in color. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:20, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "chrysolite" (with the Berean Study Bible agreeing). Interestingly, the Septuagint uses the word in Tobit 13:17, while a related form appears in Exodus 28:20 standing for the Hebrew stone shoham among the high priest's breastpiece jewels.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and its exact stone is uncertain, since translations vary between "beryl" and "chrysolite."

definition: Unable to see, whether physically sightless or, figuratively, lacking spiritual or moral perception.
article: τυφλός means "blind," and the three measured senses are really one idea expressed differently: "blind" as a description (55%), "blind man" as a noun (25%), or "man blind" in phrasing (12%). The word covers both physical blindness and a figurative blindness of understanding, as Abbott-Smith notes in passages like Matthew 15:14 and Revelation 3:17. It was thoroughly ordinary Koine: census rolls and tax papyri simply list men as "so-and-so, blind," and one Oxyrhynchus papyrus even uses it for a "blind alley" (a dead-end street).

definition: A person who unlawfully and intentionally kills another; a murderer.
article: φονεύς means a murderer—someone guilty of intentional, criminal killing. All 7 New Testament occurrences point to the same idea; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "murderer(s)" every time, with the small variations in the data ("murderer released," "One murderers") simply reflecting surrounding wording rather than separate meanings. Strong's notes it specifically implies criminal or at least intentional homicide, and everyday Koine papyri confirm the legal weight of the word—one fourth or fifth-century document orders that someone "be struck down by the sword as a murderer."

definition: To shake something off vigorously, like dust from one's feet or clothing.
article: This verb means to shake something off forcefully—in the New Testament always dust from one's feet or a garment, often as a symbolic gesture of rejection or protest. It appears just 4 times in the Byzantine text, but the Septuagint uses it 20 times across 10 books, most often rendering the Hebrew נָעַר (to shake). The everyday papyri are especially vivid: one document instructs someone to shake out the wool and clothes as part of spring cleaning, and another to shake out a mat 'so you can be carefree.'

definition: Samothrace, an island in the Aegean Sea south of Thrace, mentioned as a stop on Paul's voyage.
article: Σαμοθρᾴκη is the proper name of an island in the Aegean, lying south of the province of Thrace. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:11, where Paul's ship puts in there on the way from Troas toward Neapolis. The name is built from "Samos" and "Thrace," and Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This is a place name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single passage.

definition: A state in which the mind is overwhelmed—either a divine trance or a rush of amazement and astonishment.
article: ἔκστασις literally means a "standing outside" oneself, and in the New Testament it covers two related experiences: a God-given trance in which a person receives visions (as with Peter in Acts 10:10 and 11:5), and the sweeping amazement that grips people who witness something astonishing. Of its 7 occurrences, translators render it "trance" twice and use amazement-related wording elsewhere, with three cases absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Tellingly, the Septuagint uses it 27 times to translate Hebrew words for dread and terror (חֲרָדָה, פַּחַד), and everyday papyri even employ it as a legal term for the surrender of property—showing how broadly this "displacement" idea could stretch.
caution: The measured senses split the word between "trance" and "amazement," and several occurrences are blended into translation phrasing, so the exact boundary between these senses in any given verse can be debated.

definition: Shaking with fear, trembling because one is terrified.
article: ἔντρομος describes someone physically shaking because they are afraid. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament (Acts 7:32, Acts 16:29, Heb 12:21), and across all three the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB consistently render it as some form of "trembling" or "trembling with fear." In the Septuagint it shows up twice and renders Hebrew words for shaking and quaking; interestingly, an ancient magical papyrus uses a closely related form (ἔκτρομος) to describe making the very foundations of the earth tremble.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, and the manuscripts vary at Heb 12:21 between ἔντρομος and ἔκτρομος.

definition: To let something or someone down to a lower place, as by lowering on ropes or through an opening.
article: καθίημι means to send or let something down to a lower position. All four New Testament occurrences appear in Luke and Acts, describing acts like lowering a paralyzed man through a roof (Luke 5:19) or letting Paul down the city wall in a basket (Acts 9:25). It is well attested in everyday Koine papyri, and in the Septuagint it appears 24 times, though there it often renders the Hebrew word for 'throne' (כִּסֵּא, 7×), reflecting a different sense of placing or setting down.
caution: The single measured 'sense' here reflects how translators absorb this verb into varied phrasing rather than distinct meanings, so the consistent underlying idea is simply 'to lower.'

definition: An olive grove or orchard; in the New Testament the name of the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem.
article: ἐλαιών literally means an olive-grove or olive-orchard, and that is exactly how it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where people speak of an olive-yard they own or of young plantations in their groves. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once (Acts 1:12), where it names the Mount of Olives, the hill described as a Sabbath day's journey from Jerusalem. The Septuagint uses it 9 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "olive" (זַיִת, 7×). The word also stands very close to the related ἐλαία ("olive"), and scholars have long debated whether the form in Acts 1:12 should be read as ἐλαιών or as a form of that other word.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a long-standing textual dispute over its exact form in Acts 1:12, the evidence here is thin.

definition: To flourish or come to life again, like a plant that puts out fresh growth after a dormant season.
article: ἀναθάλλω pictures something blooming or thriving anew, built on θάλλω (to flourish) with the prefix ἀνά giving the sense of "again." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Philippians 4:10, where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Study Bible both render it "revived" (100%). It shows up in everyday Koine papyri and three times in the Septuagint, where Moulton-Milligan notes that it translates several different Hebrew words and even raises the curious question of where the Septuagint translators picked it up.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on limited evidence.

definition: To say, speak, or tell something; also to ask or to name what was foretold.
article: This verb covers the broad act of speaking—saying, telling, declaring—and supplies the future and certain other tenses for the more common verb ἔπω/λέγω. In the Byzantine NT it appears 95 times, most often rendered "say" (30×, 38%) or "spoken" (17×, 22%), and it frequently introduces what was foretold by the prophets ("what was spoken"). In the Septuagint it is enormously common (412×), almost always translating the Hebrew verb אָמַר, "to say," along with the prophetic formula כֹּה ("thus") and even אָמֵן.
caution: The critical SBLGNT text reads it 0 times where the Byzantine text has 95, so the count reflects the Majority/Byzantine tradition rather than all editions.

definition: Hard or difficult to accomplish; describing something that is not easy to do.
article: In the New Testament this word appears only once, in Mark 10:24, where Jesus says how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God. Though the New Testament uses it of a difficult situation, the older Greek lexicons note that it properly described a person who was "hard to please" or fussy about food (the word literally combines "bad" with "food"). The everyday Koine confirms this everyday range: a private letter from Oxyrhynchus reassures a father that "there is nothing unpleasant at your house."
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single verse.

definition: A viper or poisonous snake, also used figuratively to condemn malicious, deadly people.
article: This word names a viper—a poisonous snake—and appears 5 times in the New Testament. Four of those uses are figurative: Jesus and John the Baptist call hostile crowds and leaders a "brood of vipers," condemning them as dangerous and deadly. The single literal use is the snake that fastens onto Paul's hand in Acts 28:3; interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes Ramsay's argument that this may have been a non-venomous constrictor that merely clamped down, which fits the verb meaning "fastened upon" rather than "bit."

definition: To scratch or tickle; in its only New Testament use, the passive describes ears that itch for pleasing words.
article: Literally κνήθω means to scratch or tickle, and in the passive it means to itch. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 2 Timothy 4:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it in terms of people who will not 'tolerate' sound teaching but instead want their ears scratched by agreeable speech. Moulton-Milligan note this rare Hellenistic verb shows up in everyday papyri, and a striking parallel from Clement of Alexandria speaks of 'scratching and tickling the ears of those who wish to be tickled,' aimed at the empty jargon of the Sophists.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its sense rests on a single passage and outside parallels.

definition: The act of guarding something — either holding a person in custody or keeping rules and commands faithfully.
article: τήρησις covers two related ideas of guarding: the literal holding of a person in custody (a prison or ward) and the figurative keeping of rules or commands. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice meaning imprisonment (Acts 4:3; 5:18) and once meaning keeping God's commandments (1 Corinthians 7:19). Everyday Koine papyri use it for practical 'protection,' such as guarding crops or being entrusted with the keeping of a whole household, which fits the word's basic sense of watching over something.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences split across two distinct senses, the evidence here is thin and confidence is low.

definition: The cardinal number fifty.
article: πεντήκοντα is simply the number fifty, an indeclinable word built from πέντε (five). It appears 7 times in the New Testament and a hefty 144 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always renders the Hebrew word for fifty (122 of those times). The varied phrases in the measured data—"Take fifty," "fifty old," and so on—are just the surrounding sentence wording; the word itself never means anything but fifty, as in Mark 6:40, where people sit in groups of fifty.
caution: Several of the listed "senses" (like "aboard ashore large" and "took") are artifacts of how the verse was sliced, not real meanings of the word, which consistently means fifty.

definition: Persis, the personal name of a Christian woman in Rome greeted by Paul.
article: Persis is a proper name—it belongs to a Christian woman in Rome whom Paul commends in Romans 16:12, the only place it appears in the New Testament. The measured rendering "worked" simply reflects the surrounding verse, where Paul praises her hard labor in the Lord, rather than any meaning of the name itself. Moulton-Milligan notes the name shows up in everyday inscriptions and papyri from Rome, Greece, and Egypt, so it offers no clue about where the church Paul addressed was located.
caution: Evidence is thin—only one New Testament occurrence—and the word is a personal name, so it carries no general dictionary meaning.

definition: From now on; henceforth, marking the present moment as the start of something continuing forward.
article: ἀπάρτι is an adverb meaning "from now on" or "henceforth," built from ἀπό ("from") plus ἄρτι ("now"). It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament text used here, though editors like Westcott-Hort write it as two words (ἀπ᾽ ἄρτι) in passages such as John 13:19, 14:7, and Revelation 14:13. The most interesting wrinkle is in the classical evidence: the look-alike form ἀπαρτί meant "exactly" in Ionic Greek and, ironically, "quite the contrary" in Attic—a completely separate word with a different history, which is why Moulton-Milligan insists the two should not be confused.
caution: This word shows zero occurrences in the Byzantine text used here and is absent from the Septuagint, so its New Testament range rests on editions that print it as two words and on everyday Koine papyri rather than measured biblical data.

definition: The name of a violent storm-wind that struck the ship carrying Paul, blowing from the northeast.
article: This is the name of the tempestuous wind that battered Paul's ship in Acts 27:14, the only place it appears in the New Testament. The form Εὐροκλύδων combines the Greek word for the east wind with κλύδων (a surging wave), though many editors prefer the alternate spelling Εὐρακύλων, likely a sailor's blend of Greek εὖρος and the Latin aquilo (northeast wind) — what we might today call a Levanter or northeaster. The most interesting wrinkle is this textual disagreement: it shows up as a vivid bit of working sailors' vocabulary, and the lexicographers think one spelling is a corruption of the other.
caution: This word occurs only once and is absent from the critical text, with sources disagreeing over both its spelling (Εὐροκλύδων vs. Εὐρακύλων) and the exact direction of the wind.

definition: Called or invited—in the New Testament always describing those summoned by God, whether to an office or to salvation.
article: κλητός means "called" or "invited," and in the New Testament it always carries a divine sense—people summoned by God either to a specific role (like Paul being a "called" apostle in Rom 1:1 and 1Co 1:1) or to salvation. The Byzantine New Testament renders it "called" in 9 of its 11 occurrences (90%), and the modern BSB independently agrees about 89% of the time, so its meaning is remarkably stable. The Septuagint connection is illuminating: in 13 of its 18 appearances it translates the Hebrew מִקְרָא, often a "holy convocation," and it even describes the invited guests of Adonijah in 1 Kings 1:41, showing the older, ordinary sense of someone invited to a banquet before it narrowed to God's call.

definition: An impressive public display of pomp and ceremony, suggesting grand show or splendor.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 25:23), φαντασία describes the grand show with which Agrippa and Bernice entered the auditorium, and the MSB renders the setting as 'auditorium' while the word itself points to the accompanying pomp and display. The term has a wide range elsewhere: philosophers like Plato and Aristotle used it for 'imagination' or a mental impression, while later writers such as Polybius used it for 'show' or 'display.' Everyday papyri confirm the 'pomp, dignity' sense, with one document even applying it to idols, and Epictetus shows the philosophical use for sense-impressions reason must handle.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its sense there rests on a single occurrence supported by outside Koine evidence.

definition: To add extra provisions to a legal document like a will, after it has already been settled.
article: This verb describes adding fresh terms or a codicil to a document that has already been finalized, such as a will or testament. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 3:15, where Paul argues that no one adds to a ratified covenant. The most telling evidence comes from everyday papyri and inscriptions from Asia Minor, where related words carry the specialized legal sense of "determine by testamentary disposition" — showing Paul borrowed real-world legal language familiar to his readers.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range is hard to measure from the biblical text alone.

definition: To trouble, annoy, or burden someone, especially by piling extra difficulties onto them concerning a matter.
article: This verb means to harass or bother someone, typically with a person in the dative case as in its single New Testament appearance at Acts 15:19. Although the Majority Standard Bible renders that one occurrence with the word "cause," the lexicons agree the underlying idea is troubling or annoying people. Moulton-Milligan shows it was ordinary Koine vocabulary: everyday papyri use it for pestering officials or petitioning a king through repeated appeals, though the more common construction there takes the accusative rather than the dative.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single passage.

definition: An adverb meaning "then" or "at that time," pointing to when something happens—whether in the past, the future, or as the next step in a sequence.
article: τότε simply marks time—"then" or "at that time"—and can point backward to past events, forward to future ones, or signal what happens next in a sequence of actions. It appears 158 times in the Byzantine New Testament, far more often in Matthew than anywhere else, though in 137 of those cases it blends so smoothly into the English sentence that no single word translates it. In the Septuagint it shows up 193 times, usually rendering the Hebrew אָז ("then"), and an everyday papyrus letter uses it just the way the New Testament does: "if my son had not then been ailing, I should have sent him to you."

definition: The end of someone's life — that is, death.
article: τελευτή means death, the end of a person's life. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Matthew 2:15, where it is rendered "death," and the Septuagint uses it 10 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for death (מָוֶת, 8 of those times). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense: legal documents use the phrase "after his death" (μετὰ τὴν τελευτήν) when arranging wills and freeing people from obligations once someone has died.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its meaning there rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: To testify or declare something in advance, bearing witness beforehand to what is going to happen.
article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to bear witness" (μαρτύρομαι), giving the sense of testifying or predicting something ahead of time. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 1:11, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the phrase "trying" but the underlying idea is the Spirit witnessing in advance to the sufferings of Christ. Notably, the word is otherwise almost unknown in ancient sources—Hort claimed it appeared nowhere else except in a writer around AD 1300—yet a Greek papyrus from AD 710 has now turned up using it for someone "calling beforehand to witness" the fear of God.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with extremely thin attestation, so its precise force rests on a single occurrence and very limited outside evidence.

definition: To pierce or stab someone through, driving a sharp point deep into the body.
article: ἐκκεντέω means to pierce or transfix someone with something sharp. In both of its New Testament appearances (John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "pierced," with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing fully. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times, most often translating the Hebrew דָּקַר ("to pierce"), which fits the bodily-stabbing sense closely; Abbott-Smith also notes an older meaning in Aristotle, "to prick out" or "put out," though that sense never appears in the biblical texts.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (both quoting or echoing the same Old Testament image), this word's biblical range is narrow and rests on thin evidence.

definition: A person who collected taxes or tolls for the Roman authorities, often despised in Jewish society.
article: A τελώνης was someone who gathered public revenue—taxes and tolls—on behalf of the governing authorities. The word appears 22 times in the Byzantine New Testament, almost always rendered "tax collectors," and the Gospels frequently pair them with "sinners" or "prostitutes," reflecting their low social standing. The everyday papyri make this reputation vivid: one document from 156 B.C. warns against tax-gatherers who wrong people, and a line from Herodas says "every door now shudders" at them—the same idea behind the Gospels' grouping of them with outcasts.

definition: To see with the eyes, look at something, or—figuratively—perceive, notice, and pay careful attention.
article: βλέπω is the common Koine verb for seeing and looking, used 132 times across 16 books of the Byzantine New Testament. About 73% of the time it simply means "see," with "look" accounting for another 9%; the remaining renderings mostly reflect how the word folds into surrounding phrasing rather than distinct meanings. Beyond physical sight, the lexica show it can stretch to mental perception and to "take heed" or "beware," warning someone to watch out. One curiosity: the papyri preserve a rare perfect form βέβλοφα in a woman's letter from Ptolemaic Egypt, showing the verb was thoroughly at home in everyday speech.
caution: Several measured "senses" (like "one," "what," "see what") are artifacts of phrasing rather than separate meanings, so treat them as the same core idea of seeing or looking.

definition: Belonging to or coming from Sidon, an ancient coastal city; a person or thing identified as Sidonian.
article: Σιδώνιος simply means "of Sidon" or "Sidonian," pointing to people or places connected with the city of Sidon. It can describe the region (as in Luke 4:26) or the people themselves (as in Acts 12:20). In the Septuagint it appears 19 times and mostly renders the Hebrew word for "Sidonian" (14 of those times), though it occasionally stands in for unrelated Hebrew words, including ones meaning something like "lazy."
caution: The Byzantine text has only one occurrence, and the lone measured rendering came through as "king's" — almost certainly a quirk of phrasing in context rather than the word's actual meaning, so treat the measured sense with care.

definition: Sergius, the Roman family name of the proconsul of Cyprus who summoned Paul and Barnabas.
article: Σέργιος is a Latin family name carried by Sergius Paulus, the proconsul of Cyprus, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 13:7). Lexicons agree it is simply a proper name — a Roman official's surname — not a common noun, even though the measured rendering label here reads "attendant." The most striking outside evidence is an inscription from Soloi on Cyprus dated "in the proconsulship of Paulus," which scholars commonly link to this very man and which shows the Sergian family's close ties to Cyprus.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once, and the digest's measured sense label "attendant" conflicts with all the lexical sources, which treat it purely as the name Sergius.

definition: To wait for someone whose arrival is expected, often with a sense of patience and confidence.
senseLabels: await one whose coming is expected
article: ἀναμένω means to wait for someone or something that is expected to come, and the lexicon Abbott-Smith notes it can carry an added flavor of patience and confidence. It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Thessalonians 1:10, about awaiting God's Son from heaven) and four times in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew קָוָה ('to wait, hope for') three times. The everyday papyri give a vivid practical edge: in Alexandrian documents the word describes debtors who are to pay up 'without waiting' for the time allowed them.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise nuance in the biblical text rests on limited evidence.

definition: Something valuable handed over to someone for safekeeping; a trust or deposit committed to one's care.
article: παραθήκη refers to a deposit—something valuable placed in another person's keeping to guard and return safely. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the Pastoral letters (1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 1:12, 14), where the renderings cluster around "entrusted" and "treasure entrusted." The everyday backdrop is striking: Koine papyri use the word for ordinary financial deposits, with one document recording someone receiving 1500 drachmae "as a deposit," and in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew piqqadon, the legal term for property left in another's charge.
caution: The translations spread evenly across three differing renderings (one of which, "even though as," reflects sentence phrasing rather than the word itself), and with only 3 occurrences the confidence is low.

definition: Mitylene, the chief city of the island of Lesbos in the northern Aegean Sea.
article: Mitylene is a proper name—the main city of Lesbos in the northern Aegean—appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 20:14, where Paul's ship stopped there. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, where one interesting detail is the shifting spelling: the older Attic form was Μυτιλ-, and the form Μιτυλ- only became regular around 100 BC through dissimilation, which matches the spelling used in Acts. As a place name, its meaning is fixed and there is no range to interpret.
caution: This is a place name occurring only once in the New Testament, so there is no measured semantic range.

definition: The red fluid in the body of humans or animals, often used to speak of bloodshed, violent death, or human kinship and nature.
article: αἷμα means "blood" — that is overwhelmingly how it works, rendered "blood" in 93 of 98 New Testament occurrences (100% of the times it gets its own English word), with the other 5 absorbed into phrasing. Beyond the literal liquid, the classical lexica trace a useful range: bloodshed and violent death, family kinship or origin (as in John 1:13), and the Hebrew pairing "flesh and blood" for frail human nature as opposed to God. A striking piece of evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions: a Jewish tombstone prayer for vengeance from the 2nd century BC echoes the biblical phrase "to shed innocent blood," the very wording found in the Septuagint at Deuteronomy 19:10.

definition: Happening on its own, without outside help or human effort—spontaneously or by itself.
article: αὐτόματος describes something that acts or happens by itself, without anyone making it happen. In the New Testament it appears just twice: the earth producing crops "of itself" (Mark 4:28) and a prison gate that opened "by itself" (Acts 12:10). The classical lexica note it can also describe people acting of their own will, but every measured New Testament use applies it to things rather than persons—the Septuagint similarly uses it three times for the Hebrew word for crops that grow up untended (sāphîaḥ).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the fuller "acting of one's own will" sense noted by lexica is not measured in the New Testament.

definition: Jezebel, a personal name used in Revelation as a symbol for a woman promoting false teaching in the church.
article: Ἰεζαβήλ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jezebel, the Tyrian queen of the Old Testament, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Revelation 2:20), where it labels a false prophetess in Thyatira. In the Septuagint it shows up 22 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew אִיזֶבֶל (14×), the name of Ahab's wife, queen of Israel. The single New Testament use is symbolic rather than literal—a stand-in for someone leading believers astray. One curious thread in the evidence: some scholars proposed identifying this 'Jezebel' with a local pagan prophetess at Thyatira, but that suggestion has not been widely accepted.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the Byzantine NT (and not in the SBLGNT critical text), so its New Testament evidence is very thin and its symbolic application is debated.

definition: A personal name belonging to a Christian man in Rome whom Paul greets.
article: Olympas is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, in Paul's list of greetings in Romans 16:15. It is probably a shortened form of a longer name like Olympiodorus. Moulton-Milligan note that this abbreviated name was not unique to Rome but turns up commonly across the Empire, in inscriptions from Athens, Ostia, and Olympia.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so nothing is known about the man beyond Paul's brief greeting.

definition: To speak badly of someone—to curse, revile, or abuse them with hurtful words.
article: κακολογέω means to speak ill of someone—to revile, abuse, or curse them, built from the words for "bad" (κακός) and "word" (λόγος). It appears only 4 times in the New Testament and always takes an object: a person (as in Matthew 15:4 and Mark 7:10, quoting the command not to curse father or mother) or a thing (Acts 19:9). The everyday Koine papyri show the same usage in striking terms—one document from around 103 BC complains of being "abused in the most unmeasured terms"—and Moulton-Milligan notes that in the New Testament the verb tends toward the weaker sense of simply "speak evil of" rather than formal cursing.
caution: The second measured sense shows up as "around" only because of how that verse was phrased in translation, so it does not reflect a separate meaning of the word.

definition: To measure water depth by dropping a weighted line, called taking a sounding.
article: βολίζω is a nautical term for dropping a weighted line to measure how deep the water is — what sailors call taking a sounding. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the same verse (Acts 27:28), where the crew of Paul's ship checks the depth as they near land. The word comes from βολίς, a word for the sounding-lead, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary working vocabulary rather than literary.
caution: Both occurrences fall in a single verse, so the measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A city in Macedonia that Paul passed through on his way to Thessalonica.
article: Amphipolis was a leading city in Macedonia, named because the river Strymon flowed around it. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:1, as a place Paul traveled through on his journey to Thessalonica. The name itself combines elements meaning "around" and "city," reflecting the river that encircled it.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage rests on a single passage.

definition: A person from Galilee, the northern region of ancient Israel.
article: Γαλιλαῖος simply means a Galilean — someone who lived in or came from the region of Galilee. It appears 11 times in the Byzantine New Testament across five books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Galilean" in 73% of cases, with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. The word is built directly from Γαλιλαία (Galilee), and all the standard lexicons agree on its single, straightforward meaning.

definition: A Jew — a person belonging to the people of Judah, by descent, religion, or homeland.
article: Ἰουδαῖος refers to a Jew — someone belonging to the people of Judah by ancestry, faith, or region — and is rendered "Jews" in 170 of its occurrences (99%). It can describe the people broadly, but in John's Gospel it often points specifically to the ruling class who opposed Jesus, and it can also function as an adjective ("a Jewish man," "a Jewish woman"). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note abundant papyri and inscriptional evidence for Jews living in Egypt, where special districts were set aside for them in towns like Alexandria and Oxyrhynchus.

definition: Compassion or mercy—an active kindness shown toward someone, whether by God or by people.
article: ἔλεος means mercy, pity, or compassion, especially the kind that is actively shown rather than merely felt. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 28 times and is rendered "mercy" in 21 of them (78%), with a couple of cases stressing mercy actually extended to someone ("mercy shown"). Its range is quite stable, and the Septuagint anchors it firmly: across 246 occurrences it most often translates the Hebrew חֶסֶד (91 times), God's covenant loyalty and steadfast love—which is why the word so often describes God's mercy in benedictions and praise.

definition: Something eaten along with bread, especially fish, served as a relish or side dish to the main staple.
article: In Koine Greek προσφάγιον means whatever you eat together with bread—a relish or side dish—and in practice especially fish. It appears just once in the New Testament, at John 21:5, where the risen Jesus asks the disciples whether they have caught any fish, and translators render it "fish" 100% of the time. Everyday papyri confirm the broader sense: a private account from Oxyrhynchus (around A.D. 1) lists small sums spent on προσφάγιον, which the editors translate simply as "relish."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on a single passage plus outside evidence.

definition: A part or portion of something larger, whether a physical piece, a share, a region, or a side of an issue.
article: μέρος is a flexible everyday word for a "part" set against a whole — a share, a piece, a portion, or a region of a country. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 43 times, with "part" being the clearest sense (11×, 58%), while it often shows up in set phrases like "in part" (1 Corinthians 12:27) and, in 24 of 43 cases, gets absorbed into the surrounding wording with no English word of its own. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew קָצֶה ("edge" or "end," 30×), and the everyday papyri confirm its ordinary use, including a deed dividing property into "one part out of nine."

definition: Eliud, a man named in Matthew's genealogy as an ancestor of Jesus, son of Achim and father of Eleazar.
article: Eliud is a personal name appearing only in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, occurring 2 times in both the Byzantine and critical texts (Matthew 1:14-15). Every translation renders it the same way—"Eliud"—since it is simply a proper name. The name comes from Hebrew roots (H0410 and H01935), and Strong's suggests it means something like "God of majesty," though this is an etymological note rather than a translated meaning.
caution: This is a proper name attested only twice, so there is little to say beyond identifying the person.

definition: The time of day around sunset; evening.
article: ἑσπέρα refers to evening, the part of the day around sunset, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it this way in all 3 occurrences (100%), such as Luke 24:29 and Acts 28:23. In the Septuagint it appears 119 times, most often translating the Hebrew word עֶרֶב (102×), which also means evening. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, but interestingly some examples shift the sense to geography, where it means "the west" — the direction of the setting sun — as in a document describing arriving at the "western border."
caution: This entry rests on only 3 New Testament occurrences (a low-confidence tier), though the Septuagint and papyri evidence strongly back the "evening" sense.

definition: Lot, Abraham's nephew, the man rescued from Sodom before its destruction.
article: Λώτ is simply the name of Lot, Abraham's nephew, who lived in Sodom and was rescued before the city was destroyed. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all referring to the same person; the four "senses" the digest lists are just grammatical variations (possessive "Lot's," or "Lot rained down") rather than different meanings. The name is indeclinable in Greek, borrowed straight from the Hebrew לוֹט, and the Septuagint uses it 35 times, mostly translating that same Hebrew name (32 of 35).

definition: A personal name belonging to a Christian in Rome greeted by Paul.
article: Patrobas is a proper name, appearing just once in the New Testament when Paul sends greetings to him in Romans 16:14. It is an abbreviated form of the name Patrobius, and Moulton-Milligan notes it appears in everyday Koine inscriptions; interestingly, a well-known freedman of the emperor Nero bore this name. Scholars differ on the accentuation and on whether the ending was a dismissive form sometimes attached to slaves' names.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so almost everything known about the person comes from outside the text.

definition: The Jewish Passover — the festival, the meal, or the lamb sacrificed in remembrance of Israel's deliverance from Egypt.
article: πάσχα refers to the Passover, appearing 29 times across the Byzantine New Testament, and is rendered "Passover" in 72% of cases (with "Passover was" in another 7%). Though the word can point to the festival as a whole, the paschal supper, or the lamb itself, the digest measured these uses as essentially one sense. Notably, it is an indeclinable transliteration of the Hebrew פֶּסַח, which it translates 28 of 29 times in the Septuagint, and it turns up in everyday Koine papyri as well.

definition: To kneel down or fall on one's knees before someone, often as an act of respect or earnest pleading.
article: γονυπετέω describes the physical act of dropping to one's knees before another person. It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, split evenly between Matthew and Mark, and the renderings cluster tightly around "kneel" and "knelt before." The word is built from γόνυ ("knee") and a form of πίπτω ("fall"), so it literally pictures falling onto the knees; Abbott-Smith notes it can mean simply kneeling before someone (with ἔμπροσθεν, as in Matthew 27:29) or kneeling down before a person directly (with an accusative object).
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the nuance of supplication or entreaty suggested by Dodson rests on context rather than the bare word, so render it cautiously.

definition: Nathan, a Hebrew personal name; in the New Testament a son of David listed among Jesus' ancestors.
article: Ναθάν is the proper name Nathan, a Hebrew personal name carried into Greek as an indeclinable form. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 3:31, where it names a son of David in Jesus' genealogy, and every translation counted renders it as that ancestor. In the Septuagint it shows up 46 times, almost always (41×) translating the Hebrew name נָתָן, though it occasionally stands in for other names like בְּנָיָה (2×).
caution: This is a proper name with only a single New Testament occurrence, so its range rests almost entirely on Septuagint usage.

definition: A star or other bright point of light in the night sky.
article: ἀστήρ means a star, the literal point of light in the sky, and it is used this way nearly all 24 times in the New Testament (88% rendered simply "star"). The handful of remaining cases still refer to stars, just in phrases like "the stars of the sky." In the Septuagint it almost always translates the Hebrew word for star (17 of 19 times). One striking detail: a late fourth-century B.C. temple-account from Delphi uses ἀστήρ for a "wooden star," a carved pattern, showing the word could name a star-shaped object, not only a heavenly one.

definition: To fasten a belt or sash around oneself or another, often as preparation for work or travel.
article: Ζώννυμι means to gird—to tie a belt around the waist, sometimes for someone else and sometimes (in the middle voice) for oneself, often as a prelude to active work or movement. It's rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice in the Byzantine text and three times in critical editions, but the Septuagint uses it 18 times across 10 books, mostly to render the Hebrew חָגַר ("to gird," 9 times). The image is concrete and physical: in John 21:18 Jesus contrasts a young man who dressed and went where he wished with an old man who would stretch out his hands and be girded by another.
caution: New Testament evidence is very thin—only two or three occurrences—so the measured sense data is limited, though the Septuagint usage and lexicons agree on the basic meaning.

definition: A skill, craft, or trade — the practical know-how by which someone earns a living or makes things.
article: τέχνη means a craft, skill, or trade — the practical expertise behind a profession. The Byzantine New Testament uses it just 3 times across 2 books, and where it gets its own English word the Majority Standard Bible renders it "trade" both times (100%), as in Acts 18:3 where Paul shares Aquila's tentmaking trade. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this workaday sense vividly: one apprenticeship contract speaks of learning "the trade of weaving," and another names a man "a river fisherman by trade."
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (one absorbed into phrasing), and some manuscripts omit the word at Revelation 18:22, so confidence is low.

definition: To travel along with someone, going as their companion on a journey.
article: συνέπομαι means to go along with someone as a traveling companion, formed from σύν ('with') and a root meaning 'to follow.' It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 20:4, where it describes the men who accompanied Paul. The everyday Koine papyri show a slightly different use: in one third-century document (P Oxy XII.1415) an official uses the word to mean 'add' a further statement to a case, suggesting the broader idea of one thing going together with another.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering ('Derbe') reflects an adjacent place name rather than the verb's actual meaning, so corpus evidence here is thin.

definition: A region northeast of the Sea of Galilee, partly inhabited by the nomadic tribe called Ituraeans.
article: Ἰτουραΐα is a place name for a district about 60 miles east of the Sea of Galilee, also linked with Trachonitis and partly home to the nomadic Ituraean people. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 3:1, where it names part of the territory Philip governed. The word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a reference to Ituraeans in Mount Lebanon around A.D. 6, and classical writers like Strabo used it of the Ituraean highlands.
caution: The digest's measured sense oddly labels this occurrence "Tiberius," which conflicts with every other source identifying it as the region Ituraea, so treat the measured data with caution.

definition: Describing beings or things that belong below the ground, in the realm of the dead.
article: καταχθόνιος literally means "under the earth" and describes those who dwell in the underworld realm of departed spirits. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Philippians 2:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "earth" (under the earth), set alongside the heavenly and earthly. Inscriptions and papyri show the word used in everyday formulae invoking "the gods below the earth" (theois katachthoniois), as in a second-century inscription where an Armenian king dedicates a sarcophagus to such gods.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single verse.

definition: The choicest part of war spoils, originally the top of a heap, dedicated as an offering or gift.
article: ἀκροθίνιον literally means "the top of a heap" (from ἄκρος, "top," and θίς, "heap") and came to mean the very best portion of plunder taken in war. The New Testament uses it just once, in Hebrews 7:4, describing what Abraham gave to Melchizedek. The lexica note an older sense of first-fruits offered to a god, and an inscription from Delphi (c. 395 B.C.) records τὰ ἀκρόθινα dedicated to Apollo, while Moulton-Milligan show the word living on in everyday Koine documents.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin direct evidence, this word's full range rests heavily on classical sources rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: To stop feeling pain or moral sensitivity, becoming emotionally numb, callous, or reckless toward right and wrong.
article: This rare word literally means to cease feeling pain, and by extension to grow numb and callous, no longer caring about right or wrong. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 4:19, where both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it as having 'lost' all sensitivity. The classical and later Greek sources trace an interesting development: Thucydides uses it for ceasing to feel pain, while Polybius and the everyday Koine papyri shift it toward despairing or becoming hardened and reckless.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force here rests heavily on outside Greek sources, and the secondary lexica differ between 'despair' and 'become callous.'

definition: Describing something that cannot be done, or a person who lacks the strength or ability to act.
article: ἀδύνατος combines the negative prefix with the word for "able," so it means literally "not able." In the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "impossible" 7 of 10 times (88%), as in the famous saying that with God all things are possible (Matthew 19:26, Mark 10:27, Luke 18:27). The lexicons note a second, more personal use—of people who are powerless or incapable—and the papyri vividly confirm it, where ἀδύνατοι names men not strong enough to work and a woman unable to act through bodily weakness.
caution: The personal "powerless" sense rests on lexicons and papyri rather than the measured NT renderings, which only recorded "impossible."

definition: The air around us — the lower atmosphere we breathe and move through.
article: ἀήρ simply means the air — the lower atmosphere surrounding the earth, the stuff we breathe. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "air" in all 7 New Testament occurrences, and the BSB agrees every time, so the core meaning is rock-solid. What's interesting is how the word slots into vivid expressions: Paul "boxing the air" to no purpose (1 Corinthians 9:26), speaking "into the air" without being understood (1 Corinthians 14:9), and in Ephesians 2:2 the air appears as the realm of a spiritual power. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the word stayed in common use, and classical writers contrasted this lower air with the purer αἰθήρ of the upper regions.
caution: The three labels the digest lists ("air," "conformed air," "air done") reflect minor rendering artifacts; in practice every occurrence means simply "air."

definition: To look at or watch something, often attentively, taking in what is happening with one's eyes.
article: θεωρέω is overwhelmingly a word for seeing or watching: in 45 of its 57 Byzantine occurrences (90%) the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it "see." Its range stretches from casual looking to attentive observation, and the older lexica add nuances like behold, consider, and perceive. One nice detail from everyday Koine: a third-century BC papyrus uses it of someone "watching" another's daily attendance, showing the word could describe ordinary keeping-an-eye-on rather than solemn beholding.

definition: A piece of body armor worn over the chest to protect it in battle, a breastplate.
article: θώραξ refers to the breastplate, the protective armor covering a soldier's chest, and the New Testament uses it consistently this way—4 of 5 occurrences are rendered "breastplate," with Paul applying it figuratively in phrases like "breastplate of righteousness" (Eph 6:14) and "breastplate of faith" (1 Thess 5:8). In the Septuagint it appears 11 times, most often translating the Hebrew שִׁרְיוֹן, the word for armor or coat of mail. Everyday papyri confirm the down-to-earth military sense: one second-century letter even praises a breastplate made of fine brass for being finely woven and light enough not to tire the wearer.

definition: A strong craving or longing for something, whether a neutral or good desire or a sinful, forbidden urge.
article: ἐπιθυμία covers the whole range of strong wanting, from an innocent longing to a sinful craving. In the Byzantine New Testament's 38 occurrences, it is rendered "desires" 27 times (77%) and "passions" 7 times (20%), and the context usually decides whether the desire is good (as in Luke 22:15) or forbidden. Tellingly, everyday Koine papyri use the word in a purely neutral commercial sense — one letter speaks of buying cheaply "in accordance with your desire" — showing the word itself carries no built-in negative charge.

definition: Moral straightness or uprightness; doing what is right and fair.
article: εὐθύτης means moral straightness — uprightness or fairness in conduct and rule. It comes from εὐθύς ("straight"), carrying the idea of a path with no crooks in it, applied here to character. It appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 1:8) but turns up 19 times in the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew words for straightness and fairness such as יֹשֶׁר and מֵישָׁרִים, which helps anchor its sense of righteous, even-handed rule.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise rendering here is uncertain, and the measured "sense" reflects a translation artifact rather than a clear gloss.

definition: To crucify again, or to lift up and crucify on a cross.
article: This verb combines the prefix ἀνά with the word for "crucify," and in Hebrews 6:6 — its single New Testament appearance — it describes crucifying Christ again. The classical lexica show a wider range: Herodotus used it to mean "impale," Polybius and others to mean "raise up on a cross," and the sense "crucify again" appears specifically in this Hebrews passage. The interesting wrinkle is that the prefix ἀνά can mean either "up" (raise on a cross) or "again" (recrucify), which is exactly the ambiguity the sources flag.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the lexica disagree over whether it means "raise up on a cross" or "crucify again."

definition: To live in self-indulgent luxury, indulging excessively in wealth and pleasure.
article: This verb describes living it up in extravagant, wanton luxury, and both of its two New Testament appearances are in Revelation 18 (verses 7 and 9), where the MSB renders it "lived" and "lived luxury." It first turns up in Greek middle comedy, and originally meant something more neutral like feeling strong and hearty, but in Revelation it carries the harsher sense of growing wanton through wealth. A nice everyday glimpse comes from the papyri: one document warns "let Lukias not live it up, but let her work" — the same word used to scold someone for idle indulgence.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in a single chapter, and a confidence tier rated low, the evidence base for this word is thin.

definition: A person who receives property, status, or promised blessings as an inheritance.
article: κληρονόμος is the standard word for an heir—someone who receives an inheritance. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times across 8 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "heir" in 10 of those (71%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. Everyday Koine documents confirm this plain legal sense: an Oxyrhynchus papyrus from around AD 117–137 uses it for a father naming his daughter Ammonous as heir in his will. Abbott-Smith notes a secondary sense, "a possessor" (drawn from Septuagint usage), in a few Hebrews passages.
caution: In Hebrews 6:17 and 11:7 lexicons suggest the broader sense "possessor" rather than strictly "heir," so the precise shade can vary by context.

definition: The daytime between dawn and dark, or a full 24-hour day, and by extension a defined period or appointed time.
article: This common word covers both the daylight hours as opposed to night and the whole 24-hour day, with context deciding which. The Majority Standard Bible renders all 325 translated occurrences as "day" (with the BSB agreeing 98% of the time), while another 64 of its 389 New Testament appearances are absorbed into broader phrasing rather than given their own English word. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew יוֹם (1,794 times), and the everyday papyri show the same flexible range — phrases like "during the day," "every day," and "at daybreak" all appear in ordinary Koine letters and contracts.

definition: Naggai, a man listed as one of Jesus's ancestors in Luke's genealogy.
article: Naggai is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Jesus at Luke 3:25. It is an indeclinable form probably of Hebrew origin (compare H05052), and translators consistently treat it simply as the name of an ancestor. The Majority Standard Bible renders it in the genealogical 'son of' chain in its single occurrence, with the BSB agreeing fully.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its background and exact Hebrew connection remain uncertain.

definition: To greet, welcome, or pay respects to someone, including sending greetings to others in a letter.
article: This is the standard Greek word for greeting or welcoming people, used 60 times across the New Testament. Just over half the time (53%) it means greeting someone directly, but nearly a third of its uses (28%) are about sending greetings to people, especially at the close of letters. The papyri confirm this: Moulton-Milligan show it was the regular technical term for conveying greetings at the end of a letter, with everyday examples like 'Greet Diodorus' and 'Greet Capito warmly and my brothers.'

definition: A person or thing placed under a divine curse and devoted to destruction; in older usage, something set apart for God.
article: In the New Testament ἀνάθεμα names something handed over to God's judgment — a person or thing under a curse — and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "curse" in 60% of its 6 occurrences. It originally meant a votive offering set apart for God, and in the Septuagint it appears 23 times, almost always translating the Hebrew חֵרֶם, a thing devoted (often to destruction). Strikingly, Deissmann found this same cursing sense on a pagan curse-tablet from Megara of the first or second century A.D., showing the word carried this force even outside Jewish circles.
caution: The senses overlap heavily and the word is rare (6 NT occurrences), so the distinctions between "curse," "declared accursed," and "under a curse" reflect translation phrasing more than sharply separate meanings.

definition: To be fearful or cowardly; to lose one's nerve and shrink back in fright.
article: δειλιάω means to be timid or fearful, to let fear take hold so that you shrink back. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 14:27, where it is rendered "afraid" in every measured rendering. In the Septuagint it shows up 13 times across 5 books, usually translating the Hebrew חָתַת ("be shattered, dismayed"); and a vivid papyrus letter has a condemned man telling the Emperor he "will not be afraid" (δειλιάσω) to speak the truth.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single passage.

definition: To deceive one's own mind, fooling yourself with false ideas about who you are.
article: φρεναπατάω means to mislead the mind—literally to deceive yourself by holding an inflated or false self-image. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Galatians 6:3, where someone who thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself. Though rare in Scripture, Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was part of ordinary speech; Lightfoot suggested the nuance of being deceived by fancies.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A strong word of refusal meaning "by no means" or "not at all," used to firmly reject something.
article: μηδαμῶς is an emphatic negative adverb meaning "by no means" or "not at all." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both times on Peter's lips refusing the heavenly command to eat unclean food (Acts 10:14 and 11:8), where the Majority Standard Bible renders the surrounding refusal of anything "impure." In the Septuagint it shows up 14 times, most often translating the Hebrew חָלִילָה (9×), a horrified "far be it!" — and everyday Koine papyri confirm it was common, ordinary speech for flat denial.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (both the same scene) this is thin evidence, though the broader Septuagint and papyri usage supports the meaning confidently.

definition: A reed plant or its hollow stalk, used for various purposes such as a staff, a measuring rod, or a writing pen.
article: At its core κάλαμος is simply a reed—the marsh plant or its hollow stem. In the New Testament its 12 uses split evenly: a third refer to the plant itself, a third to a reed pressed into service as a staff (notably mocking Jesus), and about a fifth to a measuring rod in Revelation. The word's flexibility shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where farmers promised to deliver fields cleared of reeds and people even burned κάλαμος to heat the public baths; one further sense, a reed-pen for writing, appears at 3 John 13.
caution: Three of the 12 occurrences were absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word, so the percentages cover only the rest.

definition: A time of refreshment or relief, like catching your breath again after strain.
article: ἀνάψυξις means a refreshing or revival — literally a recovery of breath, used figuratively for relief that comes after hardship. It is extremely rare, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 3:19) and once in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew word for 'relief' (רְוָחָה) in Exodus 8:15, describing the relief Pharaoh felt when the plague of frogs lifted. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, KJV) agree it means 'a refreshing,' though the measured rendering in Acts ('back be wiped') reflects how the surrounding phrase was parsed rather than the word's core sense.
caution: With only one New Testament and one Septuagint occurrence, the evidence is very thin and the measured rendering does not cleanly isolate this word's meaning.

definition: To make a loud cry — wailing in grief, shouting in triumph, or, of a cymbal, clanging noisily.
article: This is an onomatopoeic word built from the battle-cry "alala," and originally meant to raise a war-cry or shout with triumph and joy. The New Testament uses it just twice, in quite different ways: in Mark 5:38 it describes people wailing in grief over a death, and in 1 Corinthians 13:1 it describes a cymbal clanging. The Septuagint shows the word's wider range, using it 17 times across 6 books, most often to translate the Hebrew rûaʿ (to raise a shout).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (one absorbed into phrasing) spanning meanings as different as wailing and clanging, the word's English range here is thin and context-dependent.

definition: Someone who seizes other people's property through greed, fraud, or force — a swindler, extortioner, or predatory grabber.
article: ἅρπαξ describes a person who grabs what isn't theirs, whether through cheating or sheer rapacity. In 4 of its 5 New Testament uses (80%) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "swindlers," listing such people alongside other wrongdoers, while the one outlier (Matthew 7:15) uses the predatory image of false prophets who are inwardly ravenous beneath their sheep's clothing. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that Deissmann found the word current as a Latin loan-word in comedy, and argues that in Paul it is better translated "swindler" than "robber" — pointing to a financial, fraud-related flavor rather than violent theft.
caution: The single Septuagint occurrence (Genesis 49:27) and the lone Matthew use show the word also carried a more violent, predatory sense, so its range spans both fraud and rapacity.

definition: Useful, serviceable, or beneficial — something that brings real profit or advantage.
article: χρήσιμος means "useful" or "serviceable" — describing something that brings real benefit. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:14, where the MSB renders the surrounding phrase as warning that quarreling about words is not useful but instead ruins those who listen. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain sense: one third-century BC letter describes a person as "useful to us," and others speak of looking after "useful" matters, showing the word was common business and personal vocabulary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: Behaving in a way that fits a sacred or holy character; reverent and dignified, as befits a person devoted to God.
article: ἱεροπρεπής describes conduct that suits a sacred character—the kind of dignified, reverent bearing appropriate to someone set apart for holy things. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:3, where the Berean Standard Bible and Majority Standard Bible both render it "reverent." The word turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions: Moulton-Milligan cite examples where ἱεροπρεπῶς describes religious functions and sacrifices carried out fittingly, which fits the sense "like those employed in sacred service."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament (and is not found in Attic writers), so its precise shade of meaning rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To put something into proper working order—mending what is broken or fully preparing and equipping it for its intended use.
article: καταρτίζω is about bringing something into its proper condition, whether that means mending what is broken (like fishermen repairing nets) or fully preparing and equipping something for its purpose. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times, but only 2 of those are rendered with a clear English word—both as "prepared"; in 9 of the 13 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no single English equivalent. A nice everyday example survives in a first-century papyrus letter (P Oxy VIII.1153), where garments are described as κατηρτισμένα—"made ready" or finished for use—matching the lexicons' sense of preparing a thing for its full purpose.
caution: Only 2 of 13 occurrences map to a distinct English word, so the measured-sense picture is thin; the lexicons document a wider range (mend, restore, perfect) that the corpus rendering data does not fully capture.

definition: Resentful ill-will toward another person, especially displeasure at their success or advantages.
article: φθόνος is the resentful jealousy or spite you feel toward someone else's good fortune or standing. It is consistent across the New Testament, rendered "envy" in 7 of 9 occurrences and "out of envy" in the other 2, where it explains the motive behind an action (as in Matthew 27:18 and Mark 15:10, where leaders hand Jesus over "because of envy"). Everyday papyri show the word stretching a little wider toward general malice or spite — one document speaks of someone bringing "baseless accusations of malice," and another lists it alongside "vexation and annoyance."
caution: The two measured senses are really the same idea in different grammatical settings, and the LXX evidence is thin (only a handful of occurrences).

definition: To kill someone, often by execution or violence; in the middle voice, to take up or adopt.
article: In the New Testament ἀναιρέω overwhelmingly means to kill or put someone to death, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "kill" 8 times (42%) and "put to death" 4 times (21%). It carries one notably different sense too: in the middle voice it means to take up or adopt, as when Pharaoh's daughter takes up the infant Moses (Acts 7:21). The Septuagint uses it 56 times, most often translating the Hebrew הָרַג ("to slay"), confirming its violent edge; meanwhile everyday papyri show a purely commercial use, where the word means borrowing or receiving money.
caution: The killing senses overlap heavily and four of 23 occurrences carry no distinct English word, so the boundaries between "kill," "put to death," and "death" are partly a matter of translation phrasing.

definition: The collapse or ruin of something that breaks apart, like a house falling into pieces.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Luke 6:49), ῥῆγμα names the dramatic collapse of a house built without a foundation, rendered "destruction" or "ruin." The word literally points to something torn or broken — the Septuagint uses it five times, often translating the Hebrew for a torn piece of cloth (קְרָעִים, 3×). Everyday papyri show the same root meaning concretely: a "breach" in the Nile embankments, and Greek physicians even used it for a bodily rupture, showing how this idea of a break or tear stretched across many settings.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests on a single verse.

definition: An adverb meaning "afterward" or "later," pointing to a time that follows an earlier event.
article: μετέπειτα is a time adverb meaning "afterward" or "thereafter," built from μετά ("after") and ἔπειτα ("then"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 12:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "afterward." The word turns up in everyday Koine documents as well: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription (OGIS 177) using the phrase εἰς τὸν μετέπειτα χρόνον, "for the time thereafter," showing it was ordinary, practical language for marking later time.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, so the entry rests on a very small sample.

definition: To draw back or hold back, especially to withdraw timidly out of fear or to keep something from being shared.
article: ὑποστέλλω carries the picture of pulling back—whether physically withdrawing yourself, timidly shrinking away, or holding something back from others. In its 4 New Testament uses it covers both Paul's claim that he held nothing back from his teaching (Acts 20:20, 27), Peter's cowardly withdrawal in Galatians 2:12, and the warning against the one who shrinks back in Hebrews 10:38. A striking parallel comes from a papyrus property return of A.D. 66, where the sender swears by the Emperor Nero not to have kept anything back or prevaricated, matching Paul's exact sense of full disclosure.
caution: With only 4 occurrences clustered into closely related shades of meaning, the boundaries between the measured senses are subtle rather than sharply distinct.

definition: To raise oneself upright from a bent or stooped position, sometimes used figuratively for lifting one's head in hope.
article: ἀνακύπτω means to unbend and raise yourself from a bent-over posture, the literal opposite of stooping. In the Byzantine New Testament's 4 occurrences it stays close to this physical sense—half the time rendered "straightened up" (John 8:7, 8:10) and once "stand up" of a woman bent double (Luke 13:11)—but in Luke 21:28 it shifts to lifting the head in hopeful anticipation. The everyday papyri capture both edges of this range vividly: one letter complains that a man can never "show his face again" for shame, while another predicts a person will "emerge again" from his troubles.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the figurative "be elated" sense rests on thin evidence.

definition: The state of forgetting or failing to remember something.
article: λήθη means forgetfulness or oblivion — the condition of having let something slip from memory. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:9, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as part of a phrase about someone who "lacks" memory of being cleansed from sin; the Greek idiom there is literally "to take forgetfulness." The Septuagint uses it just four times across four books, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine documents and even survives into Modern Greek.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin Septuagint usage, the precise nuance rests largely on a single idiomatic phrase in 2 Peter 1:9.

definition: A bucket or vessel used to draw water up from a well.
article: ἄντλημα refers to the tool you'd lower into a well to bring water up — a bucket or drawing-vessel. It appears only once in the New Testament, in John 4:11, where the Samaritan woman points out that Jesus has no ἄντλημα and the well is deep. The classical lexica note it can also mean, more literally, "what is drawn" (the drawn water itself), though the New Testament use points to the container.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range is hard to pin down from biblical evidence alone.

definition: The open town square where people gathered to shop, trade, and meet — a city's public marketplace and social center.
senseLabels: in or out of the marketplace
article: ἀγορά is the open public square at the heart of a town, where people bought, sold, and gathered. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "marketplace" in 6 of 11 occurrences (60%) and "marketplaces" as part of a phrase in 2 more, with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% on these. The papyri show how everyday this word was: it could even mean the "provisions" or "supplies" bought there, and bankers' tables were set up in the agorá for business.

definition: To verbally attack someone, hurling insults and abuse at them, often directly to their face.
article: λοιδορέω means to abuse someone with words — to revile, insult, or hurl reproaches. All four New Testament occurrences point to the same idea, whether someone "heaped insults" (John 9:28), challenged "how dare you insult" (Acts 23:4), or endured being reviled without retaliating (1 Peter 2:23). In the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew רִיב ("to dispute, quarrel"), and everyday papyri show real people filing complaints about being verbally abused, as in a third-century BC document where a writer protests "you insulted me."
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences all carrying one sense, the range here is narrow but consistently attested.

definition: Describing something complete or total; in the New Testament it always appears in a phrase meaning "completely" or "finally."
article: This adjective means "complete, entire, perfect," but in the New Testament it only ever shows up in the fixed phrase "εἰς τὸ παντελές," which the Majority Standard Bible renders "completely" in Hebrews 7:25 (the "hunched" rendering in Luke 13:11 actually translates the surrounding clause, not this word itself). It appears just twice across two books. The most interesting clue comes from the papyri: a property sale dated A.D. 212 uses the same phrase to mean "from now on forever," suggesting the Hebrews passage may carry a time sense — to save "finally" or permanently — which fits the "always lives" idea right after it.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and both inside one fixed phrase, whether it means "completely" or "forever" in Hebrews 7:25 is genuinely disputed.

definition: On the other side of, or across, a body of water or river that lies between.
article: πέραν means "on the other side" or "across," almost always with the idea of water—a sea, lake, or river—lying in between. In the New Testament it usually appears with a noun in the genitive, such as "across the Jordan" or "the other side of the sea," and the phrase τὸ πέραν simply means "the region beyond." The Septuagint uses it 98 times, mostly to render the Hebrew עֵבֶר ("side, region across"), and everyday papyri confirm the same sense—one document speaks of a place "opposite the city of Oxyrhynchus."
caution: In 6 of 22 occurrences the word is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own, so some renderings like "disciples" reflect translation context rather than the word's own meaning.

definition: A threshing floor — the flat area where grain is beaten out — and by extension the harvested grain lying on it.
article: ἅλων refers to a threshing floor, the hard flat surface where grain was beaten loose from the stalk; by association it can also stand for the grain piled there. In the Septuagint it appears 43 times and almost always renders the Hebrew word for threshing floor (32 of those times). Curiously, the Byzantine New Testament uses it just twice (Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it 100% of the time inside the phrase about clearing the threshing floor; Abbott-Smith notes that in these verses the word likely means the grain on the floor rather than the floor itself. The papyri show the everyday farming flavor, with one document urging workers not to be in a hurry with the threshing floor.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the lexica suggesting the word there may mean the grain rather than the floor itself, the precise sense in those verses is somewhat uncertain.

definition: A prison or jail — a place where people are locked up in confinement.
article: δεσμωτήριον means a prison or jail, a place where people are held in bondage. It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, and the meaning is stable: every occurrence is rendered as 'prison' or 'jail.' The word is built from a root meaning 'to bind,' and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where documents speak of people being thrown into the local δεσμωτήριον — in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew word for the prison where Joseph was held.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the meaning is consistent across all sources.

definition: Alpha, the first letter of the Greek alphabet, used to mean the very beginning.
article: Alpha is simply the first letter of the Greek alphabet, and in the New Testament it always appears paired with Omega, the last letter, in the phrase "the Alpha and the Omega" — a way of saying "the first and the last" or "the beginning and the end." It occurs only 3 times in the Byzantine text, all in Revelation (1:8; 21:6; 22:13), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Omega" in those pairings, agreeing fully with the BSB. The word does not appear at all in the critical SBLGNT text, which reflects a textual difference in these passages.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences, all in Revelation, and none in the critical text), and the Abbott-Smith note about an unrelated interjection "ἔα" does not apply to this letter.

definition: A region east of the Jordan made up of ten cities of Greek type.
article: Δεκάπολις is a place name, built from the words for "ten" (δέκα) and "city" (πόλις), describing a district of ten Greek-style cities lying mostly east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, always as the proper name Decapolis, and the various renderings ("come Decapolis," "toward Decapolis") simply reflect the surrounding sentence, not different meanings. An inscription from A.D. 134 (Cagnat III.1057) attests the same name for a man from Abila "of the Decapolis," confirming the term was in real-world geographic use, and similar formations like Τρικωμία ("three-village") show the standard way such names were coined.
caution: As Dodson notes, ancient sources disagree on the exact names and number of the ten cities, so the region's precise boundaries are uncertain.

definition: Sharing the same inner life and feelings with others; united in soul and purpose.
article: σύμψυχος literally combines "with" (σύν) and "soul" (ψυχή), describing people who are joined together in spirit, sharing the same feelings and aims. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:2, where the lexicons render it "like-minded" or "of one accord." Because it occurs just this single time and is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word, all we can say about its range comes from that one verse.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense and range cannot be confirmed from multiple uses.

definition: To make a calf as an idol — that is, to fashion an image of a young bull for worship.
