article: This rare compound verb combines "calf" (μόσχος) and "to make" (ποιέω), meaning to fashion the image of a young bull. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:41, where it replaces the longer phrase "made a calf" (ἐποίησε μόσχον) from Exodus 32:4. The most interesting detail is that this word occurs nowhere else in the Septuagint or in secular writers — it appears to be a newly coined term modeled on similar compounds like Plato's εἰδωλοποιέω ("to make an idol"), though Moulton-Milligan note it does turn up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and nowhere else in the Septuagint or classical authors, so its range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To kill someone, putting them to death; sometimes used figuratively for destroying or abolishing something.
article: This is the standard Koine verb for killing or putting someone to death, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 76 times across 10 books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it almost entirely as "kill" (55%) or "killed" (43%), with very high independent agreement from the BSB. In the Septuagint it appears 184 times and most often translates the Hebrew הָרַג ("to slay," 118×); the lexica also note a figurative use, as when Paul says the letter "kills" (2 Corinthians 3:6) or speaks of putting hostility to death (Ephesians 2:16). It was an ordinary, everyday word, well attested in the papyri — one fourth-century document graphically describes someone "half killed with blows."

definition: The base or supporting structure on which a building rests, used both literally and figuratively for what something is built upon.
senseLabels: a foundation that bears or supports
article: θεμέλιος is the foundation of a building—the substructure or foundation stone laid down first—and the New Testament uses it both literally (a house's base in Luke 6:48) and figuratively (the basis for ministry or teaching in Romans 15:20). Across 16 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "foundation" 13 times (81%) and "foundation" in a bearing or supporting sense twice. The word turns up in ordinary Koine: papyri record people paid "to those who dug the foundation," and one inscription speaks of the earth's foundations being shaken, echoing Acts 16:26.

definition: An adverb meaning "twice," marking that something happens two times.
article: δίς is an adverb built from δύο ("two") and simply means "twice" or "a second time." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times across 5 books, and translators handle it three ways—"twice" (3×), "again" (2×), and once in the phrase "twice broke down"—but all three really express the same idea of something occurring two times. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew word פַּעַם ("time, occurrence"), and everyday Koine papyri use it in ordinary phrases like δὶς μηνός ("twice a month").

definition: A wooden box or chest, used in the New Testament for Noah's ark and the ark of the covenant.
article: At its root κιβωτός simply means a wooden box or chest, and everyday Koine papyri show it used very plainly — for example, depositing official documents "into the chest" (P Tebt II.279, 231 BC) or storing wineskins in one. In the New Testament, though, all 6 occurrences refer to a sacred "ark": either the vessel Noah built (as in Matthew 24:38 and Luke 17:27) or the ark of the covenant (Hebrews 9:4). The Septuagint reflects both ideas at scale, using the word 217 times to translate the Hebrew אָרוֹן (the covenant ark, 179×) and תֵּבָה (Noah's vessel, 27×).

definition: To serve as a slave or servant, whether by force or willingly, devoted and subject to a master, person, or thing.
article: δουλεύω means to serve as a slave or bound servant—being subject and devoted to a master, whether a person, God, sin, or even money. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "serve" in 15 of 25 cases (79%) and "slaves" twice (11%), with another 6 cases absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 139 times, almost always (110×) translating the Hebrew עָבַד (to serve, work for), and Moulton-Milligan note that a religious use of the word is unattested in pagan literature, surfacing only in a later occult papyrus—suggesting its devotional sense is distinctive.

definition: Kish, the Israelite who was the father of King Saul.
article: Κίς is simply the Greek spelling of a Hebrew personal name, Kish, used for the father of King Saul. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 13:21) and is rendered "Kish" every time, while the Septuagint uses it 20 times to translate the Hebrew name קִישׁ. The word is indeclinable in Greek, meaning its form never changes, which is typical for names borrowed from Hebrew.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests entirely on its Hebrew source rather than any range of usage.

definition: The refusal to obey or submit; stubborn, willful disobedience toward God or his commands.
article: ἀπείθεια names a settled refusal to obey — stubbornness or rebellion rather than mere doubt. It appears 7 times in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders every occurrence as some form of "disobedience" (the other measured senses are just longer phrases built around that same core word). Moulton-Milligan stress that the everyday papyri and inscriptions consistently point to disobedience and rebellion, and they explicitly reject the older idea that the word means "unbelief" — even though Strong's, the KJV, and Dodson still list "unbelief" or "willful unbelief" among the glosses.
caution: The classical and traditional sources include "unbelief" among the meanings, but the corpus and papyri evidence point firmly to "disobedience" alone.

definition: Describes a person who is either hated by God or who hates God—a hostile relationship with God, occurring just once in the New Testament.
article: This rare word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:30, within Paul's list of human vices. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "slanderers," but this sits oddly against the classical and traditional readings, which break two ways: passively "hateful to God" (the more common ancient usage, per Abbott-Smith and KJV) or actively "hating God." The most interesting feature is the ambiguity baked into the word itself—built from "God" plus the root meaning "to hate," it can point in either direction depending on who is doing the hating.
caution: This is a near-hapax with thin evidence and the sources genuinely disagree: the measured "slanderers" rendering differs from both the passive "hateful to God" and active "hating God" readings found in the lexica.

definition: To slap someone, especially across the face, with the open palm of the hand.
article: In the New Testament ῥαπίζω means to slap or strike, particularly hitting someone's face with an open hand, appearing both times in Matthew (5:39 and 26:67). Originally the word meant to strike with a rod, but later writers shifted it to mean a slap of the palm — the lexica note this development, and the ancient lexicographer Suidas defines it as striking the cheek with a bare hand. The Septuagint uses it only twice, and the word also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and an evidence tier rated low, the range rests on thin attestation.

definition: Fully fitted, complete, and ready for what is required.
article: This adjective describes someone or something that is complete, fully equipped, and ready for a task. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "complete" (all sources agree). The everyday Koine evidence backs this up nicely: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription where it equals τέλειος ("perfect") and a papyrus where the related adverb means doing something properly "according to command," while classical lexica add the shades "fitted" and "ready."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise force has to be drawn largely from outside evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: To fill something completely, or to load up a vessel or container until it is full.
article: γεμίζω means to fill something entirely or load it up, and across all 9 New Testament uses the Majority Standard Bible renders it "filled" in every case it gets its own English word. Its range is narrow and consistent—whether it's filling water jars (John 2:7) or a sponge (Mark 15:36)—though the Septuagint uses it just once, translating the Hebrew word for "load" in Genesis 45:17. The most telling evidence comes from everyday papyri: the word repeatedly describes loading a ship with grain, matching the older classical sense Abbott-Smith notes for vessels (Mark 4:37).
caution: Thin Septuagint evidence (only one occurrence), and lexica distinguish an older nautical "load a ship" sense from the general "fill" sense the New Testament data measures.

definition: A trusted servant or attendant, one who serves a master closely and faithfully rather than as a mere slave.
article: θεράπων describes a servant who serves with personal devotion and trust, carrying a warmer, more confidential sense than ordinary words for slave. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Hebrews 3:5, quoting the Old Testament description of Moses as God's faithful servant; the Majority Standard Bible there renders the phrase as "testifying." The Septuagint uses it 53 times, most often for the Hebrew word for servant (14×), and Thackeray noted that later Greek books gradually replace it with the more distant terms for slave and household servant, reflecting a growing emphasis on the gap between God and humanity.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is extremely thin\u2014a single occurrence in an Old Testament quotation\u2014so the measured sense rests almost entirely on Septuagint and classical usage.

definition: A large, broad sword or saber, used literally as a weapon or figuratively for piercing grief.
article: ῥομφαία refers to a large, broad sword—originally a Thracian weapon, according to the lexica. In the New Testament it appears 7 times, almost all in Revelation, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sword" in 71% of cases; the one striking exception is Luke 2:35, where Simeon tells Mary a sword will "pierce" her soul, a figurative image of grief. In the Septuagint it occurs a remarkable 222 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew chereb ("sword") 181 times, where it is used interchangeably with the more common word μάχαιρα.

definition: Difficult to explain or interpret clearly.
article: δυσερμήνευτος combines the prefix δυσ- ("hard, difficult") with a derivative of ἑρμηνεύω ("to interpret"), so it literally means something that is hard to put into words or explain. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 5:11, where the author says he has much to say that is "hard" to explain to listeners slow to understand. The lexicons agree closely: Strong's gives "difficult of explanation," Dodson "difficult to interpret," and the KJV renders it "hard to be uttered."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage.

definition: A formal charge or accusation brought against someone, especially the kind raised in a legal setting.
article: αἰτίαμα refers to an accusation or formal charge laid against a person, and it appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 25:7, where opponents bring charges against Paul. It comes from the same family as αἰτία ("cause, charge"), and lexicons like Dodson and Abbott-Smith agree on the meaning "charge, accusation." Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan note that this exact word had no outside parallel until it turned up in a papyrus from A.D. 95–96, where a donkey-driver "shifted the blame" off himself, though they caution the document is rather illiterate.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and rests on thin evidence, so its range cannot be measured with confidence.

definition: To throw or cast someone or something into a place, often used of being thrown into a punishment.
article: ἐμβάλλω simply means to throw or cast something into a place, built from ἐν ("in") and βάλλω ("throw"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 12:5, in the phrase "to cast into hell (Gehenna)," though in that single verse it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word. The Septuagint uses it far more freely (67 times), and everyday papyri show both literal and figurative uses\u2014one fourth-century letter says "unwittingly I cast you into such distress."
caution: With just one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense here rests almost entirely on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than the NT itself.

definition: To punish someone, inflicting a penalty in response to their wrongdoing.
article: In the New Testament τιμωρέω means to punish or inflict a penalty, and both of its two occurrences (Acts 22:5 and 26:11) describe Paul punishing believers before his conversion. The classical lexica note a wider range: the word originally relates to protecting one's honor, and Abbott-Smith records an older sense "to help" alongside the more common "to avenge oneself on, punish." The everyday Koine papyri back up the punishment sense vividly — an Oxyrhynchus document (A.D. 127) warns that violators "will receive condign punishment."
caution: Only 2 New Testament occurrences and limited Septuagint use mean confidence is low, and the lexica preserve an older sense ("to help") not seen in the biblical text.

definition: Well-suited or ready for a particular use, task, or position.
article: εὔθετος describes something or someone that is well-placed and ready for its intended purpose. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 3 times across 2 books, rendered "fit" in the Majority Standard Bible (and agreed by BSB), applying both to people (Luke 9:62) and to things like saltless salt (Luke 14:35) or productive ground (Hebrews 6:7). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document from 113 B.C. urges that "suitable persons" be appointed to public offices, showing how naturally the word meant "qualified for the job."
caution: This word is rare, occurring only 3 times in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To look forward to something good with confident expectation, or to place one's trust and confidence in someone.
article: ἐλπίζω covers both the inner act of hoping or expecting and the relational act of placing one's hope and trust in someone, with the Byzantine New Testament rendering it "hope" in 77% of its 31 occurrences and "put hope" in another 13%. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew בָּטַח (13×), "to trust," which explains why the word leans toward confident reliance rather than mere wishing. A nice everyday glimpse comes from the papyri: a soldier writes to his father, "I hope to be quickly promoted, if the gods will" — showing the same forward-looking confidence found in the biblical texts.

definition: A fitting time or favorable moment to do something — a good opportunity.
article: εὐκαιρία means a well-timed, convenient chance to act — the right moment for something. Both New Testament occurrences (Matthew 26:16 and Luke 22:6) describe Judas looking for a good opportunity to betray Jesus, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both with "opportunity." The everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary sense: one document (BGU II.665) simply says someone "has no opportunity," and another (BGU I.46) speaks of "if I get the opportunity" to do something.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both in the same betrayal narrative, the measured range is narrow, though the papyri and lexicons agree on the meaning.

definition: To live among or settle down in a place, residing in the midst of other people.
article: This compound verb combines "in/among" with the common verb "to dwell," producing the sense of living or settling among a group of people. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Peter 2:8, describing Lot living among the people of Sodom, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "saw" within the surrounding clause about what he witnessed daily. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) agree on the basic meaning "to dwell among."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured, and the single rendering reflects translation of the wider clause rather than the verb in isolation.

definition: Truth or reality—what is genuinely so—including a person's truthfulness, sincerity, and integrity of character.
article: ἀλήθεια overwhelmingly means "truth": the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 93 of its measured occurrences (98%), with only 2 instances tied to the act of speaking truth. The word's range is fairly broad—lexicographers note it covers both objective reality (the true essence of a matter) and subjective truthfulness or sincerity of character, not merely truth in words. One nice detail: in the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew אֱמֶת (50×), and the phrase ἐπ᾽ ἀληθείας ("in truth") shows up in everyday Koine oath formulas in the papyri, confirming it was idiomatic Greek and not awkward translation-speak.

definition: An interrogative word introducing a question between two options, meaning "whether" this or that is the case.
article: Πότερον is the neuter form used as an adverb to introduce a question that weighs one possibility against another — "whether this or that." It appears only once in the New Testament, at John 7:17, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "desires whether," and it is well attested in everyday Koine: a Tebtunis papyrus from A.D. 23 uses it exactly this way, "I shall thus know whether I shall leave you in employment... or..." Classical lexica note a related adjectival sense meaning "which of two," seen in an inscription of the Emperor Claudius asking which group was at fault.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: A large, generous amount of money or gift collected for others.
article: ἁδρότης refers to a large, lavish amount — in the New Testament specifically the bountiful collection of money gathered for the believers in Jerusalem. It appears only once, in 2 Corinthians 8:20, where Paul is careful about how this generous gift is administered so no one can criticize him. The classical lexicons trace the word back to ἁδρός, meaning "thick" or "well-grown," so its root sense is plumpness or vigor, which then extends figuratively to abundance and generosity; Moulton-Milligan notes the related adjective shows up in everyday papyri describing a "stout" dish.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise range in biblical usage rests on a single verse.

definition: A participle meaning the day or night that comes next or follows after.
article: This is the feminine participle of a verb meaning "to come upon" or "approach," and in the New Testament it always refers to time—the day or night that comes next. It appears 5 times, all in Acts, and the translations cluster tightly around "next" and "following," usually paired with an implied or stated word for "day" (or "night" in Acts 23:11). In the Septuagint the underlying verb shows up in Exodus 8:22 rendering a Hebrew word for "stand," though there the meaning leans toward the verb's literal sense rather than the time idiom.
caution: All five occurrences are translated slightly differently and it appears only in Acts, so its measured range is narrow and the varied renderings reflect context more than distinct senses.

definition: Help, aid, or assistance, especially the kind of support that comes to someone facing opposition or danger.
article: ἐπικουρία means aid or assistance—the help that backs someone up, sometimes specifically support against enemies or foes. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:22, where Paul speaks of the help he has received; fittingly, it shows up nowhere else but in Luke's writing within the NT. The everyday papyri and inscriptions broaden the picture: a related word was used for auxiliary or mercenary troops, and one inscription describes a priestess offering ἐπικουρία on behalf of her city.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its full range rests largely on outside sources.

definition: A woman who shares the same parents, or a fellow female member of the Christian community.
senseLabels: a sister, naturally or in the faith
article: ἀδελφή is the feminine counterpart of ἀδελφός and overwhelmingly means "sister" in the family sense, rendered that way in 20 of its 25 New Testament appearances (83%). It also stretches to mean a fellow Christian woman, as when Paul commends Phoebe in Romans 16:1. An interesting wrinkle comes from the papyri: in an Oxyrhynchus letter from 1 B.C., a man named Hilarion greets "his sister" Alis, who was apparently his wife as well — reflecting an Egyptian custom and a religious echo of Isis seeking her brother-husband Osiris.

definition: Lacking strength — whether physically frail, ill, or morally and spiritually unable to stand firm.
article: At its core ἀσθενής simply means "without strength," and the New Testament stretches that idea across a wide range. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "weak" 13 times (68%) and "sick" 6 times (32%), so the word covers both general feebleness and bodily illness, plus a moral or spiritual weakness seen in passages like Matthew 26:41 and 1 Corinthians 8. The everyday papyri make the range vivid: it describes a defenseless widow, someone being taken advantage of, and even villages that are "weaker" financially — showing the word reached into social and economic vulnerability, not just physical health.

definition: To be poorly clothed, wearing little or only an undergarment.
article: γυμνητεύω describes the condition of being scantily clothed or going without proper clothing, used by Paul to list the hardships he endured. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text), where translators folded it into a larger phrase rather than giving it its own English word. Worth noting: the lexica disagree on form (γυμνιτεύω vs. γυμνητεύω), and in wider Koine writers the verb could also mean to go light-armed, a military sense not present in the New Testament use.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one Byzantine occurrence, absorbed into phrasing, with the spelling and exact range disputed among the sources.

definition: A person who gives advice or counsel to someone, especially regarding a decision or course of action.
article: Σύμβουλος means a counselor or adviser — someone whose advice you seek. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:34, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "counselor." The word was at home in everyday life: in the Septuagint it shows up 18 times across 8 books, usually translating forms of the Hebrew verb יָעַץ ("to advise"), and a 3rd-century BC papyrus uses it when a writer asks someone to act as his "adviser" on a building contract.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

definition: To announce or proclaim something in advance, like a herald giving public notice before an event.
article: This verb combines "before" (πρό) with "to herald" (κηρύσσω), so it means to proclaim something ahead of time. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:24, where John the Baptist proclaimed Jesus' coming in advance. The everyday papyri are especially telling here: the word shows up in business and legal contexts meaning to issue a public notice or advertise — for example, one document instructs someone to "issue a public notice and advertize."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured from usage alone.

definition: To have come or arrived, and so to be present, whether of a person reaching a place or of a time or event drawing near.
article: ἥκω is a steady, everyday verb meaning to have come or arrived, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it that way in all 27 occurrences—the Majority Standard Bible renders it "come" 86% of the time, with 5 cases simply absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. It stretches naturally from people arriving somewhere to time or events that have "come" upon someone. In the Septuagint it appears 219 times, most often for the Hebrew בּוֹא ("come"), and the papyri preserve a lovely religious formula—"I have come to the lady Isis"—that parallels its use for coming to worship in passages like John 6:37.

definition: Julius, the Roman centurion who guarded Paul on the voyage toward Rome.
article: Ἰούλιος is simply the Latin name Julius, used for a specific person. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Acts 27 (verses 1 and 3), naming the Roman centurion who took charge of Paul and other prisoners on the sea journey to Rome. The name is of Latin origin, and every source agrees it refers to this one centurion, who is shown treating Paul kindly.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only twice, so its meaning is fixed and limited rather than a word with a range of senses.

definition: A tent or temporary dwelling, used figuratively for the human body as the soul's lodging.
article: σκῆνος literally means a tent or temporary shelter, and in its two New Testament occurrences (both in 2 Corinthians 5) Paul uses it figuratively for the human body as the temporary home of the soul. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "tent" in one of those two places, absorbing it into the surrounding phrasing in the other. A striking parallel comes from the everyday papyri and inscriptions: Moulton-Milligan cite a tomb epigram placed over a recumbent skeleton that calls the body a σκῆνος, showing how naturally Greek speakers pictured the body as a shell one moves out of.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint instance (Wisdom 9:15) — so the figurative range rests on limited data.

definition: Describing someone or something that is hated by others — detestable, odious, deserving of contempt.
article: This adjective describes a person or thing that is hated and detestable. It appears only once in the New Testament (Titus 3:3), where it characterizes the way people lived before being changed. The measured rendering 'too' reflects an alignment quirk rather than the word's meaning; the lexicons consistently give 'hateful, hated, detestable,' and Moulton-Milligan cites Philo pairing it with 'hated by God' (στυγητὸν καὶ θεομίσητον), reinforcing the sense of something deeply odious.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so the measured-sense data is thin and the rendering 'too' does not reflect its actual meaning.

definition: The "of this" form of the demonstrative pronoun meaning "this one" or "this thing," pointing to a nearby person or object.
article: This is simply the genitive ("of/from/concerning") form of the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος, meaning "this" — pointing to a person or thing close at hand, much as English "this" contrasts with "that." In practice it shows up in phrases like "because of this," "after this," or "of this man," and the lexicon notes it can even carry a tone of contempt, as when crowds dismiss Jesus with "isn't this the carpenter's son?" The Septuagint mainly uses οὗτος to render the Hebrew demonstratives זֶה and זֹאת ("this").
caution: The digest records zero Byzantine occurrences of this exact form and assigns no measured senses, so the description rests on lexical sources rather than corpus data.

definition: A tent or dwelling place, used in the New Testament both literally and as an image of the body as the soul's temporary home.
article: σκήνωμα means a tent or dwelling, and in the New Testament it stretches naturally to figurative use. Peter twice calls the human body a σκήνωμα — a temporary tent for the soul (2 Peter 1:13-14) — while Acts 7:46 uses it of David seeking a dwelling place for God. The Septuagint employs it 71 times across 19 books, most often translating the Hebrew word for 'tent' (אֹהֶל, 28×), and Moulton-Milligan notes a parallel form in an edict of Germanicus (A.D. 19) referring to seizing lodgings.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and one rendered loosely as 'provide,' the measured sense data here is thin.

definition: Describing something or someone in the middle of a place, group, or time — often translated as 'among,' 'midst,' or 'between.'
article: μέσος points to the middle — of a space, a crowd, or even a time of day or night. In the New Testament it most often means being 'among' a group (19 of 60 occurrences, 49%), though it also marks the literal middle of something and appears in fixed phrases like 'stand in the midst.' It's a workhorse word: the Septuagint uses it 755 times, mostly to render the Hebrew בֵּין ('between,' 343×) and תָּוֶךְ ('midst,' 269×), and everyday papyri use it in physical descriptions, such as a man with 'a scar on the middle of the forehead.'
caution: In about a third of its New Testament uses (21 of 60) μέσος is absorbed into English phrasing and has no word of its own, so its exact force depends heavily on the surrounding construction.

definition: To formally arrange or establish something binding, such as making a covenant, assigning an inheritance, or drawing up a will.
article: This middle-voice verb means to formally set something in place — most often to make a covenant, but also to assign or bequeath. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, rendered "made" 5 times (often paired with "covenant") and tied to bestowing once in Luke 22:29. In the Septuagint it shows up 81 times and overwhelmingly translates Hebrew כָּרַת ("to cut," 63×), reflecting the Hebrew idiom of "cutting" a covenant; everyday papyri also use it as the standard legal formula for drawing up a will.
caution: Sources differ on whether Hebrews 9:16-17 means "covenant" or "will/testament" — a genuine translation dispute also flagged in the lexicons.

definition: To work to the point of exhaustion, putting in hard, tiring physical or mental effort; sometimes simply to grow weary.
article: κοπιάω covers strenuous, tiring effort — the kind of work that wears you out — and sometimes the resulting weariness itself. The Majority Standard Bible renders it most often as some form of "labor" or "work" (about 21% as "labor"), and the lexicons note two related shades: growing weary (as in Matthew 11:28 and John 4:6) and toiling with effort. In the Septuagint it appears 37 times and most often translates the Hebrew יָגַע, "to grow weary," and Moulton-Milligan finds the everyday "work hard" sense in the papyri, with Lightfoot suggesting it may carry an undertone of the grueling training an athlete endures.
caution: The measured senses cluster tightly around "work/labor," but the lexicons add a distinct "grow weary" sense that the corpus renderings barely surface, so the full range is slightly broader than the numbers alone show.

definition: Being equal or matching in amount, size, quality, or kind; when used of testimony, agreeing rather than conflicting.
article: ἴσος describes things that match—equal in amount, size, quality, or number. In the New Testament it appears just 8 times, split evenly between two uses: "equal" (as in equal pay or making oneself equal with God in MAT 20:12 and JOH 5:18) and a special application to testimony, where the witnesses' statements did not match or "agree" (MAR 14:56, 14:59). Everyday papyri confirm both shades, including a document describing payment of equal quality and another referring to the same length of time.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and the renderings split evenly between "equal" and the testimony-specific "inconsistent," the sense depends heavily on context.

definition: To be removed from something or to depart life — that is, to die.
article: This is a past participle of a compound verb meaning "to be away from" or "to depart," and in practice it came to mean simply "to die." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Peter 2:24), where it is woven into the phrasing about being dead to sins rather than translated as its own English word. The everyday papyri make its meaning vivid: documents speak of "corpses" and of someone's "departed father," showing it was a common, plain word for the deceased.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence (absent from the SBLGNT critical text) and a single Septuagint use, so confidence is low.

definition: An interrogative phrase meaning "why?" or "for what reason?", asking the cause behind something.
article: διατί is simply the preposition διά ("through, because of") joined to the question word τί ("what"), producing the question "why?" or "for what reason?" It appears in the Gospels in everyday challenges and complaints, as in "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors?" (Matthew 9:11). When followed by the article τό plus an infinitive, it shifts toward "because" or explaining a cause, as in Mark 5:4 and James 4:2.
caution: The digest records zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament used here, though Abbott-Smith cites several Gospel passages, so the textual data and the lexicon do not line up cleanly.

definition: Diotrephes, the personal name of a man who opposed the apostle John in his third letter.
article: Διοτρεφής is a Greek personal name appearing only once in the New Testament, in 3 John 9, where it identifies a man who resisted the apostle John. The name itself is built from "Zeus" and the verb "to nourish," meaning something like "nourished by Zeus," though by John's time it functioned simply as a name. It shows up in everyday Koine sources too: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription from the third century BC (OGIS 219) listing a man named Diotrephes, confirming it was a real, ordinary name and not unique to the Bible.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its 'meaning' is just its identity, not a translatable word.

definition: To move up to a higher or more honorable place, as a guest invited to a better seat at a meal.
senseLabels: to move up to a better seat
article: This compound verb literally combines "toward" and "go up," and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 14:10) it describes a banquet guest being told to come up to a more honorable seat. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "better" there, though the underlying picture is physically moving up or forward to where the host sits. Abbott-Smith records two senses—"to go up besides" and "to go up higher"—and Moulton-Milligan notes that the prefix may carry the sense of approaching the host, comparing the related verb προσβαίνω used in papyri for people "approaching the age of 14."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force here rests on thin biblical evidence and competing scholarly preferences ("go up higher" versus "come up higher").

definition: To a degree that closely resembles or comes near to something — in practice, 'nearly' or 'almost.'
article: This word appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 2:27, where it is used adverbially with a dative to mean 'nearly' — describing how Epaphroditus came close to death. The standard lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) give it a slightly broader basic sense of 'coming near' or 'nearly resembling,' and the everyday papyri bear this out: a document from 164 B.C. uses the related form to mean 'other similar persons,' and another from 116 B.C. speaks of bringing forward 'matter similar to' something else. So the core idea is closeness or resemblance, which in Philippians narrows to 'almost.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single passage.

definition: Describing a city or place that is full of idols or completely given over to idol worship.
article: This adjective describes a place packed with idols — its meaning combines κατά (here used intensively) with εἴδωλον ("idol"), so it literally pictures somewhere crammed with images. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:16, where it describes Athens, and in that single occurrence it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word. Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine documents and is built on the same pattern as other κατά-intensified adjectives, glossing it as describing a city "crammed with idols."
caution: This is a New Testament one-off, so its precise force rests on a single verse plus the word-formation pattern.

definition: A leaf of a tree or plant.
article: Φύλλον simply means a leaf, used in the New Testament 6 times across 3 books, always referring to the leaves of trees like the fig. The two measured senses ('leaves' at 60% and 'except leaves' at 40%) are not really different meanings—the difference just reflects how translators handle the phrasing of finding nothing on the fig tree but leaves (Matthew 21:19, Mark 11:13). In the Septuagint it appears 16 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew word עָלֶה ('leaf'), though once it stands in for a quite different word meaning 'plans' or 'counsels.'

definition: To muzzle an animal, or figuratively to silence someone or something.
article: φιμόω literally means to muzzle, as you would an ox, and from there it stretches to mean putting someone or something to silence. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 8 times; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "silence" in 29% of cases, and where it isn't translated that way the idea of being quieted still drives the phrasing (as when Jesus stills the storm in Mark 4:39 or muzzles the wind). In the Septuagint it appears just once, translating the Hebrew חָסַם (chasam, "to muzzle") in Deuteronomy 25:4, the very verse Paul quotes literally in 1 Corinthians 9:9 and 1 Timothy 5:18. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the word may have been treated as slang or nonliterary, vanishing from literature between Aristophanes and the Septuagint.
caution: The literal "muzzle" sense survives mainly in Old Testament quotations, so most New Testament uses are figurative "silence," and the small number of occurrences limits confidence.

definition: Salome, a woman who followed Jesus and was among those who came to anoint His body.
article: Σαλώμη is the personal name Salome, a woman mentioned only twice in the New Testament, both in Mark (15:40 and 16:1). The name probably comes from a Hebrew root tied to the word for peace (shalom). Dodson identifies her as the wife of Zebedee and mother of the apostles James and John, though the bare text simply lists her among the women who watched the crucifixion and later came to anoint Jesus' body.
caution: The two measured senses are an artifact of phrasing — both occurrences refer to the same person named Salome — and her family identity beyond the text is supplied by later lexicons, not stated in the verses themselves.

definition: To put forth or sprout, as a tree pushing out its leaves.
article: ἐκφύω describes a plant pushing out new growth, especially a tree putting forth its leaves. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 24:32 and Mark 13:28), both in Jesus' lesson about the fig tree whose tender branch and emerging leaves signal that summer is near. The word lived on in everyday Koine—Moulton-Milligan note it survives in Modern Greek as ξεφυτρώνω, "to shoot up, flourish."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same fig-tree saying, the measured evidence for its range is thin.

definition: To become quiet—to stop talking, give up an argument, rest from work, or live peacefully.
article: This verb means to grow still or quiet, covering a range from falling silent in conversation to resting from labor to simply living a peaceful life. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, and the rendered cases all involve people ceasing to argue—dropping their objections (Acts 11:18) or being talked out of a course of action (Acts 21:14). It was a favorite word of Luke and shows up commonly in everyday papyri; one second-century petition uses it of someone who could no longer keep quiet and so appealed to an official. In the Septuagint it occurs 43 times, most often translating the Hebrew shaqat, "to be still or at rest."
caution: Most New Testament uses get absorbed into surrounding phrasing (3 of 5), so the measured senses rest on just two occurrences.

definition: A moral stain or defilement — the corrupting pollution that taints a person or community.
article: μίασμα refers to defilement or pollution, especially the moral kind — the contaminating residue left behind by corruption. It is rare, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament (in its plural form in 2 Peter 2:20) and three times in the Septuagint, where it renders several different Hebrew words including פִּגּוּל (a term for unclean or rejected sacrificial meat). The lexica note it belongs chiefly to tragedy and later writers, and Strong's stresses that it denotes the effect of defiling rather than the act itself.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and a handful in the Septuagint, so its precise range is hard to fix with confidence.

definition: To keep yourself away from something, refraining or staying at a distance from it.
article: This is the middle (reflexive) form of ἀπέχω, meaning to hold yourself back or stay clear of something. The Byzantine New Testament does not use it at all, and it appears only 3 times in the Septuagint across 3 books, where it translates three different Hebrew words including רָחַק (to be far). The lexicons line up on the basic idea: refrain, keep away, or stay at a distance, with KJV simply rendering it 'abstain.'
caution: Evidence is very thin — no New Testament occurrences and only three scattered Septuagint uses, each translating a different Hebrew word.

definition: A star or group of stars in the night sky, often the heavenly lights collectively.
article: Ἄστρον refers to the stars in the sky, and in the New Testament it usually appears in the plural for the heavenly lights as a group, as in Luke 21:25, Acts 27:20, and Hebrews 11:12. In Acts 7:43 it points instead to a star as a symbol or image (an object of worship), the only singular use among the four occurrences. In the Septuagint it shows up 25 times across 14 books, most often translating the Hebrew word for star (כּוֹכָב, 18 times); everyday Koine papyri use it too, including a calendar describing astronomers tracking the risings and settings of the stars.
caution: The second listed sense reflects a single occurrence (Acts 7:43), and one rendering label appears garbled in the data, so treat that sense breakdown loosely.

definition: To wear one's hair long, letting it grow out rather than keeping it short.
article: This verb describes the practice of letting one's hair grow long, and in the Greek New Testament it appears only in 1 Corinthians 11:14-15, where the two occurrences are rendered as "hair" and "long hair." It comes from the noun κόμη, meaning hair. A vivid example from everyday Koine comes from a papyrus dated A.D. 159-160, where a priest faces a formal charge for letting his hair grow too long and wearing woolen clothing.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same passage, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Not made by human hands; describing something formed by God rather than crafted by people.
article: This word always carries a single core idea: something that human hands did not make. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice describing a temple or dwelling 'not made with hands' (Mark 14:58, 2 Corinthians 5:1) and once, metaphorically, of a spiritual circumcision (Colossians 2:11). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that Grimm found this negative form in neither classical authors nor the Septuagint, suggesting it may have been coined for the occasion in the earliest source, even as the simpler word it negates was well established.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a word that may have been freshly coined, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: The time or fact of being born; one's birth.
article: γενετή refers simply to birth, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in John 9:1, describing a man blind "from birth" (ἐκ γενετῆς). The phrase ἐκ γενετῆς was a common expression in everyday Koine, and Moulton-Milligan notes that documentary and literary sources use it especially of conditions present from birth, such as blindness. The Septuagint uses the word twice, where it stands behind a Hebrew term in Leviticus 25:47.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint — so the word's full range cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: The act of reading, especially the public reading of Scripture aloud in a synagogue or church gathering.
article: ἀνάγνωσις means reading, and in all 3 New Testament occurrences it refers to reading Scripture aloud in a gathering (Acts 13:15; 2 Corinthians 3:14; 1 Timothy 4:13). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "reading" in 2 of 3 cases, with the third being part of the phrase about reading in the synagogue. Interestingly, the older classical lexica note an earlier sense of "recognition" (Herodotus), and a papyrus from 118 BC preserves an unusual administrative use meaning the "revision" of a land survey, but none of these appear in the biblical text.
caution: This word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament and the two "senses" measured are really one meaning split by phrasing, so the entry rests on thin evidence.

definition: To come back or return to a place after having gone away.
article: ἐπανέρχομαι means to return or come back to where one started. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke (10:35 and 19:15), and in both cases the idea is folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than carried by a single English word. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from the papyri: an A.D. 104 census order from Egypt uses this very verb to command people living away from home to "return" to their own households.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 4 in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: To violently mistreat, ruin, or do harm to someone or something.
article: This verb means to outrage, maltreat, or do violent harm — in its one New Testament appearance (Acts 8:3) it describes Saul ravaging the church, which the Majority Standard Bible renders "destroy." The word has a wider range than that single occurrence shows: in the Septuagint (14 times across 8 books) it can also mean to corrupt or defile, and the lexica add senses like insulting or maltreating. Everyday Koine papyri use it concretely too, as in a phrase warning that fire should not "harm my flesh."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense here rests on a single example, though the Septuagint and papyri confirm the broader meaning.

definition: A mist or dimness that clouds the eyes and dims sight.
article: This word names a mist or haze, used especially of a dimness that clouds the eyes and blocks normal vision. It appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 13:11), where the magician Elymas is struck and a mist or darkness falls over his eyes; the lexica describe it as dimness of sight, possibly even a cataract. Aquila and Symmachus used it in their Greek versions of the Old Testament (Ezekiel 12:7; Job 3:5), confirming its sense of obscuring gloom.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and its derivation is uncertain, so its precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: A dog, the animal—often used as an insult for a despised or contemptible person.
article: Κύων means a dog, an animal looked down on in the ancient Near East. In all 5 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "dogs," sometimes for the literal animal (as in Luke 16:21) and sometimes as a sharp term of reproach for people (Matthew 7:6, Philippians 3:2). In the Septuagint it appears 35 times, usually translating Hebrew kelev (22×), and a soldier's letter in the papyri shows the same insulting use when he complains his mother abandoned him "like a dog."

definition: A heavy rain or downpour, especially a sudden rainstorm.
article: ὄμβρος refers to a storm of rain or a heavy downpour, and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 12:54, where it is consistently rendered "shower." It shows up just twice in the Septuagint, once translating a Hebrew word for rain in Deuteronomy 32:2. Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri use the word in a technical sense for land that has become waterlogged, showing how it could describe the practical effects of heavy rain on farmland.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured.

definition: A summons or invitation; in the New Testament, always God's call inviting people to salvation.
article: κλῆσις means a calling or invitation, and in the New Testament it consistently refers to God's call to salvation — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "calling" in 5 of its 11 occurrences, with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. The word also appears in everyday Koine: the papyri use it in a narrower legal sense, where a heading like "εἰς μαρτυρίαν κλῆσις" means "a call to witness" before a legal procedure. Both Dodson and Abbott-Smith note that, whatever its broader range elsewhere, in the NT it is always the divine call.
caution: With only 11 NT occurrences and a single Septuagint instance, the evidence is solid but limited, and a few renderings vary depending on phrasing.

definition: To manage and rule one's own household as its head.
article: This verb means to be in charge of a household and run its affairs, formed from the noun οἰκοδεσπότης (master of the house). It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 5:14, where Paul urges younger widows to marry, bear children, and manage their homes. Interestingly, this is a later Greek word that turns up in everyday papyri, including astrological horoscopes where it describes a planet 'ruling' a chart, as in P Oxy II.235.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering 'advise' differs oddly from the lexicons' consistent 'rule/manage a household.'

definition: To owe something in addition to what is already owed, or to be still in debt.
article: This verb combines "toward/in addition" with "to owe," meaning to owe something extra or still be in debt. In its single New Testament appearance (Philemon 1:19), the Majority Standard Bible renders it "repay," with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing fully. The word turns up commonly in everyday Koine papyri about money: one account from around 270 BC has a writer saying "I owed an additional sum with expenses," though papyri scholars note it's not always easy to tell apart from the plain verb "owe."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: To see something reflected as in a mirror, or to reflect it like a mirror does.
senseLabels: seeing or reflecting as in a mirror
article: This word comes from the Greek for "mirror" and means to look at a reflection or to reflect something like a mirror. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 3:18, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "unveiled," though that translation reflects interpretive choices rather than the word's core meaning. A nice piece of evidence comes from a third-century BC inscription, where the word describes someone washing his face and then looking at his own reflection in the water.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and translators disagree on whether it means "reflect" or "behold as in a mirror," so its precise force here is genuinely uncertain.

definition: To send for someone or summon them to come to you from another place.
senseLabels: to summon or send for someone
article: This verb means to call someone from one place to another — essentially, to send for them — and in the New Testament it always appears in the middle voice, meaning 'summon to myself.' It occurs 4 times, all in Acts, though the measured English renderings ('guest' in Acts 10:32, 'Paul' in Acts 20:17) reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the verb itself, which is absorbed into the sentence in half its uses. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from the papyri: in one document an emperor 'sent for' a man (μετεκαλέσατο), showing the word's plain summoning sense in ordinary Koine.
caution: The corpus data shows English labels like 'guest' and 'Paul' because the verb's action gets folded into the phrasing, so those labels don't reflect the word's actual meaning, which is consistently 'to summon.'

definition: A feeling of shame or embarrassment, the sense of being put to disgrace.
article: In the New Testament ἐντροπή means shame or embarrassment, used both times by Paul (1 Corinthians 6:5 and 15:34) to provoke a sense of disgrace meant to wake people up. The Septuagint uses it the same way, often translating the Hebrew word kelimmah, meaning disgrace or humiliation, in passages like the Psalms. Interestingly, the classical lexica and everyday papyri also record a quite different sense — 'respect' or 'reverence' — as in an inscription honoring a man who rightly earned respect and glory, but that meaning never appears in the New Testament.
caution: The word occurs only twice in the New Testament, and its classical/papyri sense of 'respect' diverges sharply from the biblical sense of 'shame.'

definition: An adverb meaning three times or on three occasions.
article: τρίς is a simple adverb meaning "three times" or "thrice," formed from the number τρεῖς ("three"). It is remarkably consistent: of its 12 New Testament occurrences, 10 are rendered "three times" (83%), with the rest being slight variations on the same idea. The Greek phrase ἐπὶ τρίς ("three times over") in Acts 10:16 and 11:10 has a close parallel in everyday papyri, where one fourth-century document uses ἐπὶ τρὶς to describe someone "thrice stepping backwards."

definition: To bring or cast something down from a higher place to a lower one.
article: καταβιβάζω means to cause something to go down or be cast down, often to a much lower place. In the New Testament it appears just twice—in Matthew 11:23 and Luke 10:25—both in the dramatic image of a city being brought down to Hades. The Septuagint uses it 10 times across 6 books, mostly rendering Hebrew words for going or being made low, and Moulton-Milligan even found it in an everyday horoscope papyrus describing a star 'descending' near a constellation.
caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text)—and the two listed senses are really one meaning split by wording.

definition: An emphatic particle of affirmation meaning "surely" or "certainly," used to strengthen a solemn statement or oath.
article: This is a particle that adds emphasis and certainty to a statement, best rendered "surely" or "truly." In the New Testament it appears only once, in Hebrews 6:14, where it strengthens a divine oath ("I will surely bless you"), and there it is always paired with the particle μέν. The Septuagint shows it 34 times across 7 books, though the listed Hebrew counterparts vary widely, suggesting it answered to no single Hebrew word.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and zero in the critical SBLGNT text, the evidence for its range here is extremely thin.

definition: Describing a person who is gentle, mild, and humble in manner rather than harsh or self-assertive.
article: πραΰς describes a gentle, mild disposition, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it just 4 times—rendered "gentle" in 3 cases and "meek" once (Matthew 5:5). The two senses overlap heavily, differing more in English flavor than in Greek meaning. In the Septuagint it appears 15 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew words עָנָו and עָנִי, terms for the humble or afflicted. A nice everyday witness comes from a grave inscription at Pergamon, where a man named Aelius Isidotus is praised as "meek in private life," showing the word at home in ordinary Koine.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the split between "gentle" and "meek" reflects translators' English choices more than a real difference in the Greek.

definition: To make someone or something firm and secure, especially to strengthen or steady a person inwardly so they stand fast.
article: στηρίζω basically means to fix something firmly in place, then by extension to strengthen or steady a person so they hold steady. The New Testament uses it almost entirely in this strengthening sense — the Berean Study Bible renders it "strengthen" in all 9 of its translatable occurrences, with another 4 of its 13 uses absorbed into broader phrasing. A vivid older sense survives in Luke 9:51, where Jesus "set his face" toward Jerusalem, echoing a Hebrew idiom; the everyday Koine papyri likewise show it used quite literally, as in propping something against a beam.

definition: To drink together with someone, sharing a beverage in their company.
article: συμπίνω means to drink alongside another person, combining the words for "with" (σύν) and "drink" (πίνω). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 10:41, where it describes those who ate and drank with the risen Jesus. Interestingly, the closely related noun συμπόσιον (a drinking party or the guests at one) shows up several times in the Septuagint, often rendering Hebrew expressions for a wine-feast, and the word is well documented in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on very thin evidence; note also that the digest's "beforehand" label appears to be a tagging error rather than a real meaning.

definition: A trusted household slave who escorted and supervised boys, guiding their conduct rather than teaching lessons.
article: A παιδαγωγός was a household slave charged with escorting boys and overseeing their behavior and morals — not a teacher in the strict sense, as Abbott-Smith notes by distinguishing him from the διδάσκαλος. The word appears 3 times in the New Testament across 2 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "guardian" (the two GAL 3:25 and 1CO 4:15 phrases counted separately are really the same single sense). An everyday papyrus letter (P Oxy VI.930) captures the role perfectly: a mother urges her son and his παιδαγωγός to find a suitable teacher, then sends greetings to "your highly esteemed attendant Eros" — showing the close, affectionate place such an attendant often held.
caution: Confidence is low: only 3 occurrences, and the three "measured senses" are really one meaning split by translation phrasing.

definition: To move someone or something from one place or position to another — to remove, transfer, depose, or figuratively turn away.
senseLabels: remove or put out of a place
article: μεθίστημι combines μετά ("change") with ἵστημι ("to stand"), so at root it means to make something stand somewhere else — to shift, remove, or transfer. In the New Testament's 5 occurrences it ranges from a steward being put out of his job (Luke 16:4), to God removing King Saul (Acts 13:22), to believers transferred into Christ's kingdom (Col 1:13), and it can even stretch to "pervert" or turn people away (Acts 19:26). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sweep: it appears in a house-rental contract for moving tenants, and strikingly in the phrase "to depart from life," meaning to die.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and two of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured sense data is thin, though the classical and papyri evidence agree on its core meaning.

definition: A compressed form of 'and if,' used to mean 'and if,' 'even if,' or simply 'at least,' depending on context.
article: κἄν is a contraction of καί ('and') and ἐάν ('if'), and it carries a range of meanings: it can mean 'and if,' 'even if' (in a concessive sense), or act as an intensive meaning 'even' or 'at least.' In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 13 times, but the Majority Standard Bible renders it plainly as 'if' only twice, and in 4 of those 13 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing without its own English word. The everyday Koine papyri show this last 'at least' sense vividly: one fourth-century letter scolds a brother to act 'now at least' (κἂν νῦν), capturing the urgent, pleading tone the word could carry.
caution: Its meaning shifts noticeably with context, ranging from 'and if' to 'even if' to a bare intensive, so the right rendering depends heavily on the surrounding sentence.

definition: One who carries out justice by punishing wrongdoing; an avenger who brings the penalty a wrong deserves.
article: In the New Testament ἔκδικος describes someone who enforces justice by punishing wrongdoing — in Romans 13:4 the governing authority acting as God's agent of punishment, and in 1 Thessalonians 4:6 the Lord who avenges wrong done to others. It appears only twice, so its measured range is narrow, but the broader Koine evidence is rich: Moulton-Milligan show that in everyday papyri ἔκδικος was the standard term for a legal representative or advocate (advocatus), as when a husband 'defends' his wife in a lawsuit. Abbott-Smith also records an older, opposite-sounding sense, 'without law, unjust,' though that meaning does not appear in the New Testament occurrences.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a computed low confidence tier, the everyday papyri sense of 'legal advocate' differs markedly from the NT meaning of 'avenger,' so use the lexical range with care.

definition: The smallest, least, or very little — whether in size, amount, or importance.
article: ἐλάχιστος is the superlative of the word for "short," meaning smallest or least, and it stretches across size, quantity, and dignity. The Majority Standard Bible's measured uses split evenly between "very little" (17%, as in Luke 16:10) and plain "small" (17%, as in Luke 19:17 and James 3:4), with many remaining occurrences rendered "least." Lexicons note an interesting wrinkle: while it can be a true superlative ("least," as in 1 Corinthians 15:9), in later Greek it often weakened to simply mean "very small" — and the papyri back this up, with the phrase ἐπὶ τὸ ἐλάχιστον ("at least") found in an official document from 117 B.C. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew word for "young" or "little" (צָעִיר).
caution: Sources note the word swings between a strict superlative ("least") and a weakened intensive ("very small"), so context decides which is meant.

definition: A fallen or lifeless body — a corpse or dead body left where it lies.
article: In the New Testament πτῶμα consistently means a dead body or corpse — that's how all of its uses turn out, whether it's John the Baptist's body (Mark 6:29) or the bodies lying in the street (Revelation 11:8-9). The measured renderings showing "permit" and "John's about body" reflect how the word gets folded into surrounding phrasing rather than separate meanings; the core sense is simply a corpse. Interestingly, the broader Greek word literally points to something that has fallen: classical and later writers used it for a building's ruin, and a papyrus from A.D. 325 even speaks of the "collapse" of a man's house. Everyday Koine inscriptions confirm the corpse sense, including one where a man guards against another body being placed in his family tomb.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and a couple of those absorbed into phrasing, the labeled "senses" reflect translation mechanics rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: A person who catches fish for a living; a fisherman.
article: This word simply means a fisherman, someone who catches fish for a living, and the New Testament uses it consistently that way in all five occurrences. Most of those uses cluster around Jesus calling fishermen to follow him, which is why translations sometimes render it as Jesus' "fishers" of people. Although Strong's links the root to the salt sea and suggests "sailor," the actual usage is plainly about fishing; the papyri even preserve a related epithet meaning a fisherman who worked the Nile river.
caution: Strong's broader gloss "sailor" is not borne out by the measured biblical usage, which always means fisherman.

definition: A drinking cup, and by extension its contents or, figuratively, the lot or experience God allots someone.
article: At its core ποτήριον simply means a cup for drinking, and that is how it's rendered 32 of 33 times (97%) in the Byzantine New Testament. The word was thoroughly ordinary in everyday Koine: papyri list things like "2 drinking-cups of tin" and even "a little cup for little Theonas." Beyond the literal vessel, it can stand for the cup's contents and, figuratively, for the portion or fate someone receives — whether prosperity, suffering, or divine punishment — a usage rooted in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew kos (15×).

definition: What is left over after most is gone—a remnant or small remaining portion.
article: λεῖμμα means a remnant or leftover portion, what remains when the rest has been removed or used up. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 11:5, where it describes a remaining group of people. The same word shows up in everyday Koine business documents—one papyrus from around 115 B.C. uses it for the leftover amount of wheat—which shows it was ordinary commercial vocabulary, not a specially religious term.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in that corpus cannot be measured from biblical use alone.

definition: A faculty or organ of perception by which a person discerns and judges what is good or bad.
article: This word names the inner capacity for perceiving and discerning, much like we speak of trained "senses." It appears only once in the New Testament (Hebrews 5:14), where mature believers have their senses trained to distinguish good from evil, and the Majority Standard Bible, BSB, and KJV all render it "senses." Though it sounds technical—classical writers like Aristotle and Epicurus used it—Moulton-Milligan note it had passed into everyday Koine speech, and the Septuagint uses it for the body's inward faculties of feeling.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from multiple contexts.

definition: The act of mocking or making fun of someone, especially scornful ridicule directed at a victim.
article: ἐμπαιγμός means mocking or derision — the scorn heaped on a person to humiliate them. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:36, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as part of the suffering of faithful people; the word also turns up twice in the Septuagint, translating Hebrew words for shame and contempt. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan could find no example of this exact word in everyday papyri, though they did locate the related form συμπαιγμός meaning "collusion" in a document from around 117 B.C.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament and is otherwise rare, with no clear attestation in everyday papyri, so its full range is hard to pin down.

definition: Moral soundness and integrity, especially the freedom from corruption that marks a person's character and teaching.
article: ἀδιαφθορία describes incorruptibility — being free from the kind of moral decay that ruins character. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Titus 2:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "integrity" (and the Berean Standard Bible agrees fully). Moulton-Milligan notes the related adjective ἀδιάφθορος turns up in everyday Koine inscriptions, including a 4th-century BC honor praising the Athenian statesman Lycurgus as "incorruptible" on behalf of his homeland; they also point out that only some late manuscripts give the noun form here, while critical texts omit it.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine text and is absent from the critical text, with even the manuscript reading at Titus 2:7 disputed, so the evidence is thin.

definition: With great difficulty or effort; barely, hardly, scarcely.
article: μόγις is an adverb meaning something happens only with toil and difficulty—'barely' or 'hardly.' It appears just once in the New Testament (Luke 9:39, in the WH/critical reading), where a spirit 'hardly' or with great difficulty leaves a boy. Everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor: one document from 221 B.C. describes sailors 'hauling the vessel with difficulty' into harbor, capturing exactly the sense of effort and struggle behind the word.
caution: Evidence is thin—a single New Testament occurrence, and the manuscripts vary between μόγις and the related form μόλις, so the reading itself is disputed.

definition: Without having the law, or in a way that is outside the law's reach.
article: This adverb describes acting or being judged without reference to the law. In its two New Testament appearances—both in Romans 2:12—it is rendered "apart" (from the law), meaning people who never had the Mosaic law. Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes a different shade in its only Septuagint occurrence (2 Maccabees 8:17), where it means "lawlessly," so the sense shifts between sources from "outside the law" to "in violation of law."
caution: Evidence is thin—just two New Testament occurrences (both in one verse) and a single Septuagint use—and the lexicons divide its meaning between "without law" and "lawlessly."

definition: Describing something that cannot be admitted or allowed to not happen — in other words, unavoidable or impossible to prevent.
article: Ἀνένδεκτος is a negative compound meaning something that simply cannot be admitted or allowed — that is, impossible or inadmissible. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 17:1, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "inevitable" (Jesus saying that stumbling blocks are bound to come). Interestingly, the modern measured rendering ("inevitable") flips the angle of the older glosses: the KJV and lexicons like Abbott-Smith and Dodson read it as "impossible/inadmissible," but the sense is the same — it is impossible for these things not to come.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured, and the modern "inevitable" rendering differs in emphasis from the lexicons' "impossible."

definition: To deceive or mislead someone through false reasoning or misleading arguments.
article: In its two New Testament appearances (Colossians 2:4 and James 1:22), this word means to deceive or mislead, especially by persuasive but false reasoning. Its literal root sense is "to miscalculate" or "cheat in reckoning," and the Greek papyri show exactly this: tax documents speak of expenses being "fraudulently reckoned," and other records use it plainly to mean "cheat" or "swindle." In the Septuagint it appears 12 times across 7 books, most often standing in for the Hebrew רָמָה ("to deceive"). The classical lexicons agree, listing both "to miscalculate" and the derived sense "to mislead."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured evidence is thin, though the papyri and Septuagint usage strongly support the deceive/mislead range.

definition: A treasure, or the place where valuables are stored, such as a chest, treasury, or storehouse.
article: θησαυρός covers both a treasure itself and the place it is kept—a chest, treasury, or storehouse. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 18 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "treasure" in 14 of those (78%), with a couple of cases (Matthew 12:35) describing a person bringing things out of a "store." The everyday Koine papyri make the "storehouse" sense vivid: there θησαυρός very commonly means a granary holding agricultural produce like corn and wine, or even a public/temple treasury. In the Septuagint it appears 77 times, mostly translating the Hebrew אוֹצָר ("storehouse, treasury").

definition: Describing something happening at night or in the dark, used in the New Testament for the very early hours before dawn.
article: This adjective literally means "nightly" or "by night," formed from the words for "in" (ἐν) and "night" (νύξ). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Mark 1:35, where it describes Jesus rising while it was still dark, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "still" there 100% of the time. Originally a poetic word, it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a verse inscription from the fifth century AD that speaks of "when night-dawn takes you."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so its range rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: Gall — a bitter substance, literally bile, used both for a bitter drink and figuratively for poisonous bitterness.
senseLabels: a bitter drink mixed with wine
article: χολή literally means gall or bile, a notoriously bitter fluid. In its two New Testament appearances it is split evenly: once it is the bitter substance mixed into the wine offered to Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:34), and once it is used figuratively for spiritual corruption, the "gall of bitterness" (Acts 8:23). In the Septuagint it shows up 10 times, most often rendering the Hebrew words for wormwood (לַעֲנָה, 5×) and a bitter poison plant (רוֹשׁ, 2×), and Moulton-Milligan note its prominence in ancient medical and magical recipes.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the sense in Matthew 27:34 is uncertain — Abbott-Smith suggests it may actually mean myrrh there, comparing the parallel in Mark 15:23.

definition: Describing something long in extent or duration, or far away in distance.
article: μακρός covers both space and time — it can mean physically "far away" (a distant country in Luke 15:13 and 19:12) or "long" in duration, as in the "long" prayers criticized in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. It comes from μῆκος ("length") and shows up in everyday Koine papyri, where one writer complains that affairs were neglected "owing to our long absence from home." In the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew word for "far/distant" (רָחוֹק, 3 times).
caution: The measured data labels three uses as "defraud," which conflicts with every dictionary here (all give only "long/far"); that label likely reflects a tagging quirk rather than a real sense of this word.

definition: An emphatic phrase meaning "not to mention" or "how much more," used to point from a smaller case to a greater one.
article: μήτιγε is a strengthened form of μήτι that introduces a comparison, meaning roughly "not to speak of" or "how much more" depending on context. In its single New Testament appearance (1 Corinthians 6:3), Paul argues that if believers will judge angels, then "how much more" can they handle ordinary matters of daily life (βιωτικά). Moulton-Milligan compares it to the parallel μὴ ὅτι γε found in a papyrus letter from 168 B.C., where a wife writes "not to mention how long a time has passed," showing this was a real turn of phrase in everyday Koine.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and does not occur in the Byzantine text used here, so its exact force ("much less" versus "much more") depends entirely on context.

definition: To flow or stream, as water moves from a source.
article: ῥέω means to flow or run the way water does. In the New Testament it appears only once, in John 7:38, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "streams." In the Septuagint it shows up 38 times across 14 books, most often translating the Hebrew זוּב (23 times); the everyday papyri use it plainly too, as in a traveler's note that "the Nile flows out" from its source.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there rests on a single verse.

definition: To explain or settle something that is unclear, such as interpreting a teaching or resolving a dispute.
article: In its two New Testament appearances, ἐπιλύω means to clear up something that needs explanation—in Mark 4:34 Jesus privately explained his teaching to the disciples, and in Acts 19:39 it refers to settling a matter in a lawful assembly. Built from ἐπί and λύω ("to loose"), it carries the idea of "unloosing" or untangling what is obscure. Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri use this verb in money matters, such as discharging a loan, while a later astrological writer (Vettius Valens) uses it much like the New Testament for explaining things written obscurely.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the range of meaning rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Violent harm or loss, whether physical disaster or the insults and abuse one person inflicts on another.
article: ὕβρις is a strong word covering both the damage that befalls someone and the deliberate outrage one person heaps on another. In the New Testament's 3 occurrences it splits between these: twice (67%) it names a 'disaster' — strikingly, a metaphorical loss at sea in Paul's voyage (Acts 27:10, 21) — and once (33%) the 'insults' Paul endures (2 Cor 12:10). The everyday papyri sharpen the harsher sense: a marriage contract bars a husband from bringing in another woman to the abuse of his wife, and a complaint describes being dragged away 'with insults and blows.' In the Septuagint it appears 49 times, most often translating Hebrew words for pride or arrogance (גָּאוֹן 23×).
caution: Confidence is low: only 3 New Testament occurrences, and the senses range widely from 'disaster' to 'insult' depending on context.

definition: To swear a false oath, or to break an oath you have sworn.
article: This verb refers to violating a sworn promise — either by swearing falsely or by failing to keep an oath you made. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 5:33, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "break" (an oath), and the Berean Standard Bible agrees. Notably, it shows up frequently in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions in a standard legal oath formula: "if my oath is kept, may it be well with me, but if false, the reverse."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured evidence is thin, and lexicons stress the "swear falsely" sense slightly differently than the rendering "break."

definition: To pledge or promise someone in marriage; in the passive, of a woman, to be betrothed or engaged.
article: This verb means to promise someone in marriage, and in the New Testament it appears only in the passive, describing a woman who is betrothed. All 3 Byzantine occurrences point to the same idea, and the Septuagint uses it 8 times to render the Hebrew word אָרַשׂ ('to betroth'). A real-life touch comes from the papyri: a fourth-century document (P Flor I.36) records a father betrothing his niece to his son from early childhood, showing the word's plain everyday use for arranging marriage.
