caution: Confidence is low because the word appears only 3 times in the Byzantine text and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text, and all three uses are the same passive sense.

definition: To raise someone up together with another, used of believers being spiritually raised together with Christ.
article: συνεγείρω combines "with" (σύν) and "raise/awaken" (ἐγείρω), so its core idea is being raised up alongside someone else. In all 3 New Testament occurrences it describes the Christian's mystical resurrection with Christ (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 2:12; 3:1), and in every case the word is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it in an entirely physical sense — Abbott-Smith notes Exodus 23:5, where it refers to helping raise up a fallen animal, far from the spiritual meaning seen in the New Testament.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a handful of differing Septuagint uses, this is a rare word whose attested range is thin and confidence is low.

definition: To grind grain into flour, usually by working a hand-operated mill.
article: ἀλήθω means to grind grain into flour, the everyday task of working a hand mill. In the New Testament it appears only twice (Matthew 24:41 and Luke 17:35), both picturing two women grinding together, one taken and one left. Abbott-Smith notes it is the common (Koine) form of the older Attic ἀλέω, and in the Septuagint it shows up five times, mostly rendering the Hebrew verb טָחַן ("to grind").
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences, and in one of them the verb is absorbed into the English phrasing rather than translated by its own word.

definition: A rented dwelling or lodging that someone pays to occupy.
article: In the New Testament μίσθωμα appears just once, in Acts 28:30, where Paul stays two years in his own rented quarters. The word literally has to do with payment, and in the Septuagint and everyday papyri it usually means the price, rent, or hire paid for something. Abbott-Smith notes that the meaning "a hired dwelling" in Acts is actually not found elsewhere, making Paul's lodging a distinctive use; in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew אֶתְנָן (8 times), the wages or hire of a prostitute.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sense "rented dwelling" there is, by Abbott-Smith's account, not attested elsewhere.

definition: A connecting word meaning "and yet" or "although," used to introduce a qualifying point that slightly contrasts with what was just said.
article: καίτοιγε is a strengthened form of καίτοι that links two clauses with a sense of "and yet" or "although indeed," softening or qualifying a previous statement. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (just once in the critical SBLGNT text), and the two measured renderings — "although it was" in John 4:2 and "His" in Acts 14:17 — really reflect how the word's concessive force gets folded into the surrounding translation rather than two distinct meanings. Notably, Moulton-Milligan documents it in everyday Koine, including a second-century BC inscription about restrictions in the temple of Zeus, showing it was ordinary connective language, not a specialized term.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences and the two "senses" are translation artifacts of one concessive connector, not genuinely different meanings.

definition: In a way that follows the rules or law; properly and according to what is required.
article: This adverb means doing something the right way — in keeping with the law or the established rules. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's letters to Timothy: once about using the law "lawfully" (1 Timothy 1:8) and once about an athlete who must compete "according to the rules" to win the prize (2 Timothy 2:5). The athletic sense is striking — the philosopher Epictetus uses the very same word for competing lawfully in the games, and the everyday papyri show it covering anything from "legitimate priests" to "illegally" (without the legal forms).
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint instance, the evidence base is thin, so the precise shade of meaning leans on outside sources like the papyri and Epictetus.

definition: A title for Simon the apostle, marking him as a member of the Jewish party called the Zealots.
article: Ζηλωτής is used as a surname or label for Simon, one of Jesus' apostles, distinguishing him from Simon Peter. Abbott-Smith notes the word appears in the Jewish historian Josephus and the New Testament as the name of a Jewish party, the Zealots, who were partisans for Jewish political independence. In this form it shows up specifically in Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13.
caution: This form has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament used here, and the supplied evidence does not include measured translation data, so the sense rests on the lexicon notes alone.

definition: Continually, always, at all times — without interruption through the whole period in view.
article: This is the adverbial phrase "dia pantos," literally "through all," used to mean constantly or always. It is built from the preposition "dia" (through) plus the genitive of "pas" (all), and the lexicons gloss it as "alway(-s)" and "continually." Notably, Abbott-Smith records it written as one word (διαπαντός) in places like Mark 5:5 and Luke 24:53, where it describes something happening without ceasing.
caution: This phrase has no occurrences recorded in the Byzantine NT digest and no confidence tier, so the evidence here rests on lexical definitions rather than measured corpus usage.

definition: The act of giving false testimony or bearing untrue witness against someone, especially in a legal or accusatory setting.
article: This word names the giving of false testimony — lying about another person, often in a courtroom or accusation context. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Matthew 15:19 and 26:59), and the two renderings the Majority Standard Bible uses ("false testimony" and "false") really reflect the same single meaning. A related form, ψευδομαρτύριον, shows up six times in a mid-third-century BC papyrus dealing with court procedure, confirming the term's at-home use in everyday legal Koine.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the sources fully agree on the meaning.

definition: The state or process of resembling something — being made like or similar to it.
article: ὁμοίωσις means a likeness or the act of becoming like something, built on the verb ὁμοιόω ("to make like"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at James 3:9, where it speaks of humans being made in the likeness of God; classical sources like Plato also use it for "a making like" or "becoming like." In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times across 4 books, most often rendering the Hebrew דְּמוּת ("likeness," 4 times). One commentator (Hort, cited by Moulton-Milligan) distinguishes ὁμοίωσις from εἰκών, suggesting ὁμοίωσις points to a resemblance in developing character rather than fundamental nature.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the evidence base is thin, so its precise nuance in James 3:9 should be treated with caution.

definition: Being without sin or fault; not having committed wrongdoing.
article: ἀναμάρτητος describes someone who is free from sin or fault. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in John 8:7, where Jesus invites whoever is "without sin" to throw the first stone. Classical lexica record a wider range: it could mean "unerring" or "not missing" (Xenophon) as well as the moral sense "faultless" (Plato), and everyday Koine papyri use it for "sinless," as in a quote from Musonius noting that virtue alone keeps one from sinning in life.
caution: This word occurs just once in the Byzantine NT and is absent from the critical text, and the digest's measured rendering label ("continued") reflects the surrounding verse rather than the word itself, so lean on the lexical evidence.

definition: A tender, affectionate way of addressing those one cares for, literally meaning "little children" but used as a term of endearment.
article: τεκνίον is a diminutive of τέκνον ("child") and works as a warm term of endearment, almost like saying "dear little ones." Across its 9 Byzantine New Testament appearances it is rendered "little children" 4 times (44%) and simply "children" twice (22%), always used to address people the speaker loves rather than to describe actual infants. The everyday warmth of the word shows up beautifully in a third-century Egyptian papyrus, where a writer sends greetings to someone's τεκνία ("children, whom the evil eye will not harm").
caution: With only 9 occurrences and several rare phrasings counted, the evidence base is modest, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: To forcibly drag someone away, especially hauling a person before a judge or court.
senseLabels: to drag someone before a judge
article: κατασύρω means to drag or pull someone forcibly away, and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 12:58) it describes being hauled before a magistrate or judge. The word is rare, occurring just once in the Byzantine New Testament and three times in the Septuagint, where it can also carry the sense of pulling down. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew שָׁטַף (twice), a verb associated with sweeping or flooding away, which fits the picture of being swept along under force.
caution: The New Testament evidence rests on a single occurrence, and the Strong's gloss ('magistrate') reflects the judicial setting rather than the verb's own core meaning of dragging, so treat the labeled sense loosely.

definition: A person who kills another human being; a murderer.
article: This word straightforwardly means a murderer or killer of human beings, built from the words for "man" and "to kill." It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 2 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "murderer" twice and "reside a murderer" once (the second simply reflecting the surrounding phrasing rather than a different meaning). Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and that it was originally a poetic term—Euripides is the only classical author cited—which Hellenistic prose later adopted.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 occurrences and the two listed senses really reflect one core meaning, so the second label is a phrasing artifact rather than a distinct sense.

definition: A piece of cloth used to wipe the face, wrap an object, or cover the face of the dead.
article: A σουδάριον is a small cloth—the word comes straight from Latin (sudarium, a sweat-cloth)—used to wipe the face, wrap up an item, or bind the face of a corpse. It appears 4 times in the New Testament, where a servant wraps his money in one (Luke 19:20) and Jesus' face is covered with one (John 11:44; 20:7). Everyday Koine papyri confirm how ordinary the object was: one even lists a σουδάριον among the items in a bride's dowry, and another uses it in a charm for procuring dreams.
caution: The corpus tool split the occurrences into separate "senses," but these are really phrase fragments, not distinct meanings—the word consistently denotes a single kind of cloth.

definition: A formal legal decision or ruling, made after examining a case in court.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 25:21), διάγνωσις means a judicial decision—the verdict reached after a case has been examined, here referring to the emperor's ruling on Paul. The word's range covers both general distinguishing or discernment and, more technically, a formal legal determination, and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri as a courtroom term. A striking detail: an Egyptian papyrus from about 250 BC uses it for an official 'decision about his case,' which proves the legal sense was already current centuries before the New Testament.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise shading rests heavily on outside papyri and lexical evidence.

definition: The sick, heavy aftereffects of heavy drinking — the nausea or hangover that follows a drunken binge.
article: κραιπάλη refers to the physical misery that follows excessive drinking — what the older translations call "surfeiting" and medical writers described as drunken nausea. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 21:34, where Jesus warns against letting hearts be weighed down by it. Interestingly, the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and was used in medical contexts, and Westcott and Hort read the variant spelling κρεπάλη at that single verse.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise force of the word rests largely on outside lexical and medical evidence rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: A man's father-in-law, the father of one's wife or spouse.
article: πενθερός refers to a father-in-law, the father of one's spouse. It appears only once in the New Testament (John 18:13, where Annas is called the father-in-law of Caiaphas), and the Septuagint uses it 5 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word חָם (4×). The word was common in everyday life: it shows up in ordinary Koine papyri and inscriptions, such as an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 186 naming a man's father-in-law.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single instance, though the Septuagint and papyri confirm the meaning.

definition: To know or recognize something by focusing your attention on it, often coming to fully understand or identify a person or thing.
article: This verb builds on the ordinary word for knowing (γινώσκω) by adding a sense of directing your attention toward a particular person or thing. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 42 times, rendered "know" in 38% of cases, "recognize" in 34%, and "understand" in 14%, with the rest absorbed into phrasing. A neat confirmation comes from the papyri: an everyday letter (P Fay 112, A.D. 99) uses it to mean "find out" whether an olive grove had been dug, matching the idea of knowledge reached by paying attention rather than simply deeper knowledge.

definition: A pattern or model to be copied, like a writing-sample children trace to learn letters.
senseLabels: a pattern or example to follow
article: ὑπογραμμός literally means a "writing-copy" — the master sample of letters a student traces over to learn how to write — and from there it comes to mean a model or example to imitate. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 2:21, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "leaving" (the idea that Christ left us a pattern to follow), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100%. The word is rare overall, also appearing in 2 Maccabees 2:28 in the Septuagint; Moulton-Milligan could cite no papyrus examples of the word itself, though its close relatives ὑπογραφή and ὑπογράφω are very common in everyday documents.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is rare elsewhere, so its precise range rests on thin evidence.

definition: Complete or fully developed—whether something flawless and whole, or a person grown to full maturity.
article: τέλειος comes from τέλος ("end" or "goal") and describes something that has reached its proper end—either complete and perfect, or fully grown and mature. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "perfect" 10 of 19 times (56%) and "mature" 7 times (39%), and these two ideas blend together rather than competing. Everyday Koine papyri show the "mature" sense vividly: legal documents use it for a woman "of age" or for an heir who has come of age, and the Septuagint mostly uses it for Hebrew words meaning whole or blameless (שָׁלֵם, תָּמִים).

definition: A sacred place or thing set apart for God, especially the holy place or sanctuary of the temple.
article: ἅγιον is the neuter form of the adjective ἅγιος ("holy, sacred"), and in practice it names a holy place — a sanctuary or the inner "holy of holies." The broader word group describes whatever belongs to God or deserves reverence: God himself in his purity and majesty, sacred places like the temple, and persons set apart for his service such as angels, prophets, and apostles. The Greek root carries the idea of religious awe, and in the Septuagint the family chiefly translates the Hebrew קֹדֶשׁ (qodesh, "holiness, sacredness").
caution: This neuter form has no occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament and is not separately attested in the critical text, so the entry rests on the parent adjective ἅγιος rather than measured uses of ἅγιον itself.

definition: A beaten track or well-worn path made by repeated use, especially one that people travel.
article: τρίβος means a beaten track—a path worn down by feet or traffic, literally something "rubbed" smooth by repeated use. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in the same prophetic quotation about preparing the Lord's paths (Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4), where translations render it simply as "paths." The Septuagint uses it far more often (53 times) for several Hebrew words for roads and trails, and everyday papyri confirm its plain sense, as in one document marking out land "to the west of the path."
caution: All 3 New Testament uses come from a single repeated quotation, so the measured range is narrow, though the Septuagint and papyri evidence agree on the basic meaning.

definition: A connecting particle that links words or clauses, often working in pairs to mean "both...and" or simply adding "and."
article: τέ is a small linking particle, similar to Latin -que, that ties words and sentences together a bit more tightly than the ordinary "and" (καί). It often pairs up — "both...and" or "as well...as" — and frequently has no standalone English equivalent at all; in fact 149 of its 208 Byzantine occurrences get absorbed into the phrasing without their own English word. A striking feature is its concentration in one book: Abbott-Smith notes that more than two-thirds of all New Testament occurrences are in Acts, where it knits narrative together. Moulton-Milligan confirms it was standard everyday Koine, showing up in contracts and sales documents on conditions like "discharge all the debts."
caution: Because this particle so often blends into surrounding phrasing, the measured "senses" mostly reflect translation context rather than distinct meanings of the word itself.

definition: To violate or break a command, rule, or tradition; figuratively, to turn aside and abandon something rightfully held.
article: At its core παραβαίνω means to step over a line — to break a command, rule, or tradition you were meant to keep. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only 4 times, three of them clearly about violating commands or traditions (as in Matthew 15:2–3), with one occurrence in Acts 1:25 describing Judas turning aside and abandoning his rightful position. The Septuagint employs it 37 times, often rendering the Hebrew סוּר ("to turn aside") and פָּרַר ("to break"), and Greek classical authors like Homer used it literally for standing beside before it took on its dominant metaphorical sense; everyday papyri also use it for transgressing oaths and contracts.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and the Acts 1:25 "turn aside" sense differing from the more common "transgress," the precise range in a given verse can be debated.

definition: The emphatic genitive form of "I," meaning "of me," "mine," or "my."
article: This is the emphatic genitive of the Greek first-person pronoun "I," used where the speaker is stressed — "of me" or "mine" — as opposed to the lighter unstressed form μου. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament as a separately counted form here, but the broader pronoun is everywhere in Scripture, with the Septuagint showing 389 occurrences across 33 books. Interestingly, the related nominative ἐγώ often translates Hebrew expressions like הִנֵּנִי ("here I am") and אֲנִי ("I am"), as in John 1:23 and Acts 7:32.
caution: The digest reports zero Byzantine New Testament occurrences of this specific form, so its New Testament range is inferred from the pronoun system as a whole rather than measured directly.

definition: To accuse or charge someone beforehand, having already laid a formal complaint against them.
article: This verb means to make a prior accusation — to have already charged someone before the present moment. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 3:9, where Paul says he has already brought the charge that all people are under sin. Moulton-Milligan note that the word has not been found anywhere else, though the related noun προαιτία shows up in a later source, so its everyday range is essentially undocumented.
caution: This is effectively a hapax with no parallel attestation, so its precise force rests almost entirely on its single use in Romans 3:9.

definition: To leave someone or something behind, especially so that they remain or survive after others are gone.
article: ὑπολείπω means to leave behind or leave remaining, and in the passive it describes those who are left alive — the survivors. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 11:3, where Elijah laments that he alone is left, and it is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up about 80 times across 22 books. Tellingly, it almost always renders the Hebrew verbs שָׁאַר and יָתַר, both meaning to remain or be left over, and everyday papyri use it commercially — one writer keeps half a sum back for necessities, another wants nothing left owing.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (absorbed into the phrasing rather than a standalone English word), the New Testament evidence is thin, though the Septuagint and papyri usage is consistent.

definition: To wrap a newborn baby snugly in strips of cloth, following the customary practice of the time.
article: This verb means to swathe an infant in bands of cloth, the standard way of bundling newborns in the ancient world. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Luke 2 (verses 7 and 12), describing the baby Jesus. The Septuagint uses it just twice as well, in Job 38:9 and Ezekiel 16:4, and everyday papyri confirm it was ordinary Koine vocabulary — one inscription even speaks tenderly of a child being kept warm "from swaddling clothes."
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences and two in the Septuagint, so the confidence tier is low.

definition: To insult or verbally abuse someone back in response to their insults.
article: This verb combines "against/in return" with "to revile," meaning to throw insults back at someone who has insulted you. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, where in that single instance it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. A nice detail: Moulton-Milligan found it in an everyday papyrus from the late third century B.C., where one person describes another "reviling me in return" after first being abused — the same back-and-forth sense the New Testament uses.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A name for Satan, appearing in the New Testament as the wicked opposite set against Christ.
article: Βελίαλ is a Hebrew loanword used as a name for Satan, set in stark contrast to Christ. It comes from the Hebrew בְּלִיַּעַל, which means "worthlessness," and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:15. An interesting wrinkle is the alternate form Βελιάρ, which Abbott-Smith notes may reflect a "harsh Syriac pronunciation" of the same name.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical (SBLGNT) text, and the measured rendering label "harmony" reflects the surrounding verse rather than the word itself, so the evidence is thin.

definition: Cnidus, a coastal city and peninsula on the southwest tip of Asia Minor near the island of Cos.
article: Cnidus was a city and peninsula on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor (in the region of Caria), mentioned just once in the New Testament. It appears in Acts 27:7 as a point Paul's ship struggled to reach during his voyage to Rome. The name is probably of foreign origin and refers solely to this place.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "slowly" reflects the surrounding sailing narrative rather than the meaning of the place-name itself.

definition: A follower of Epicurus, belonging to the Greek philosophical school he founded.
article: Ἐπικούρειος names a member of the Epicurean school, the followers of the philosopher Epicurus. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 17:18, where Epicurean philosophers encounter Paul in Athens. Inscriptions in everyday Koine confirm the word's real-world use: Moulton-Milligan cite one honoring a man called an 'Epicurean philosopher' who greatly benefited his city.
caution: The measured rendering 'debate' reflects a quirk of how the occurrence was tagged, not the word's actual meaning, which all lexicons agree is 'Epicurean'; with only one occurrence, evidence is thin.

definition: To leave something behind for others, such as an example to follow.
article: ὑπολιμπάνω means to leave behind, and it appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 2:21, where it speaks of Christ leaving behind an example to follow. It is a prolonged Ionic form of the more common ὑπολείπω, and the everyday papyri show its plainer business sense: one document from 257 B.C. urges people not to 'leave behind' unpaid arrears, while another refers to a small sum 'we were leaving behind.' So the underlying idea is simply leaving something for others, which in Peter's single usage becomes leaving an example.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its translation as 'example' reflects that single context rather than a broad measured range.

definition: To speak against something, contradicting or denying what someone else has said.
article: ἀντέπω combines the prefix ἀντί ("against") with the verb "to say," so it literally means to speak in opposition or gainsay. It is used only in the second aorist (ἀντεῖπον), with no present form in actual use, and the New Testament shows it twice, in Luke 21:15 and Acts 4:14, both times describing opponents unable to contradict or answer. The Septuagint employs it 11 times across 5 books, where Abbott-Smith notes it renders Hebrew verbs for turning back, speaking, and answering.
caution: The sources offer differing notes on which Hebrew words it translates, and the digest lists some surprising counterparts (such as proper names), so the Septuagint correspondence data should be treated with care.

definition: To be out of one's mind, talk or act like a madman, or be mentally deranged.
article: παραφρονέω means to be beside oneself or to think and speak like someone who has lost his senses. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 11:23, where Paul says he is talking 'like a madman,' and once in the Septuagint at Zechariah 7:11 rendering the Hebrew word for being stubborn or rebellious. The papyri give a vivid parallel: a document from around A.D. 200 describes a condemned man scornfully asking what choice he has 'except to give way to a mad king,' using this same verb.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its full range is hard to pin down.

definition: To bind up or bandage something, especially a wound, by wrapping it.
article: καταδέω means to bind or wrap something up, and in the New Testament it describes the Good Samaritan bandaging the wounded traveler's injuries (Luke 10:34), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the surrounding act of "pouring." It appears 8 times in the Septuagint, often translating the Hebrew חָבַשׁ (to bind up), and Sirach 27:21 likewise uses it of binding wounds. The most striking evidence comes from the papyri: the word turns up in magical curse formulae, where someone "binds" an enemy's hands, feet, tongue, and soul on leaden tablets buried in graves.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: The means by which sin is dealt with and a holy God is satisfied; an atoning sacrifice.
article: In the New Testament ἱλασμός appears just twice, both in 1 John, where the Berean Standard Bible renders it as Christ being the "atoning sacrifice" for sins. The Septuagint uses it five times for several different Hebrew words, including kippurim (the Day of Atonement language in Leviticus and Numbers) and, in Psalms and Daniel, simply "forgiveness." Notably, the classical lexica record a broader range than the New Testament shows: Abbott-Smith lists an abstract sense "an appeasing" from Plutarch, the concrete "means of propitiation," and the Septuagint sense of "forgiveness" — so the word can point either to the act, the means, or the resulting pardon.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and just five in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, and the lexica show a wider range (appeasing, means of propitiation, forgiveness) than the measured New Testament uses capture.

definition: The cardinal number sixty, used either for an exact count or, in the parable of the sower, for a sixtyfold yield.
article: Ἑξήκοντα is simply the number sixty, built as ten times six (ἕξ). In the New Testament it appears 9 times across 5 books, often blended into a larger phrase, but where it stands out it renders the "sixtyfold" harvest in the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:8; Mark 4:8). One nice everyday glimpse comes from the papyri: a marriage contract from A.D. 170 sets sixty days as the period within which a dowry must be repaid if the couple separates.

definition: Describing something that belongs to or is part of a mill, as in a millstone.
article: μυλικός is an adjective meaning "belonging to a mill," used in the New Testament of a millstone (the heavy stone used for grinding grain). It appears just once in the Byzantine text and the broader manuscript tradition, in the saying about hanging a millstone around someone's neck (Mark 9:42; Abbott-Smith cites the parallel at Luke 17:2). Moulton-Milligan note related millstone forms in everyday papyri and inscriptions—one inscription even describes a marble statue set on a "millstone" pillar, referring to the type of stone millstones were made from.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "anyone" reflects how the whole verse was translated rather than the word's actual meaning of "belonging to a mill."

definition: Describing someone who shares your own spirit, mind, and outlook so closely that they feel like a true partner.
senseLabels: of the same mind or spirit
article: ἰσόψυχος combines ἴσος ("equal") and ψυχή ("soul"), literally meaning "of equal spirit" — someone whose heart and outlook match your own. It is very rare, appearing only once in the New Testament (Philippians 2:20), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "genuinely" and Paul uses it of Timothy as a like-minded co-worker. The one Septuagint use is in Psalm 55:13, where it translates a Hebrew word for someone counted as your equal or close companion, and Moulton-Milligan note it surfaces in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions too.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and one in the Septuagint — so the precise shade of meaning is hard to pin down.

definition: To be, to exist, or to be present — the basic verb linking or asserting that something is.
article: Εἶναι is simply the present infinitive form of the verb εἰμί, "to be." Like the English verb "to be," it covers a wide range: asserting that persons or things exist (as in John 1:1 or Acts 17:28), saying that an event happens or takes place, or stating that someone is present in a place. Abbott-Smith notes one striking usage where the form ὁ ὤν καὶ ὁ ἦν ("the one who is and who was") substitutes for a past participle in Revelation.
caution: This form does not occur in the Byzantine NT as counted here, so the description rests on the lexical entry for the parent verb εἰμί rather than on measured occurrences of εἶναι itself.

definition: A fine, expensive linen cloth made from high-quality flax, used for costly garments.
article: βύσσος refers to fine linen — a costly fabric made from a high-quality species of flax. It appears just once in the New Testament (Luke 16:19), describing the rich man's luxurious clothing, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it "linen." The word is a Hellenized borrowing from a Semitic source, and in the Septuagint it shows up 40 times, most often translating the Hebrew שֵׁשׁ (22×); everyday Koine papyri likewise use it for measured lengths of byssus cloth, confirming its commercial sense as a fine textile.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the meaning rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than the Greek New Testament itself.

definition: To separate or move apart, whether in space, in time (with an interval passing), or by withdrawing from someone.
senseLabels: an interval of space or time passing
article: διΐστημι combines "through/apart" with "to stand," giving the sense of setting apart or putting distance between things. In its three New Testament uses it covers space and time alike: in Acts 27:28 the sailors moved "a little further" before sounding the depth again, while in Luke 24:51 Jesus "was parted" from the disciples; a related form elsewhere marks an interval of time passing (an hour). Notably, everyday Koine papyri use the word for a quite different shade — a dispute or disagreement between parties, as in marriage contracts and loan documents where people had "differed" over something.
caution: With only three New Testament occurrences spread thinly, and the papyri showing a "dispute" sense not found in the biblical text, the word's full range is hard to pin down.

definition: To write or carve something onto a surface, or figuratively to imprint it on the mind or heart.
article: ἐπιγράφω means to write or inscribe something onto a surface—like the charge inscribed above Jesus on the cross (Mark 15:26) or the names written on the gates of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "inscribed" in every clear case, and it also works figuratively, as when God's laws are written on people's hearts and minds (Hebrews 8:10). In everyday Koine papyri the same verb took on a bureaucratic flavor—used of taxes or supplies "imposed," and even of someone appointed or assigned to an office.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences (one of which is absorbed into surrounding phrasing), the measured evidence is thin, though the sources agree on the core meaning.

definition: To draw something over oneself; in its one New Testament use, to surgically reverse or hide the mark of circumcision.
article: Literally this verb means "to draw over" or pull something across, a sense seen in everyday Koine papyri where it describes grabbing a cloak or even bringing people in to help. In the New Testament it appears just once, in 1 Corinthians 7:18, where it is absorbed into the phrasing and refers specifically to a man trying to undo or conceal his circumcision to look uncircumcised. The Septuagint uses it three times in its plainer literal sense of drawing or pulling, translating different Hebrew words each time.
caution: With only one New Testament use—and that one absorbed into a phrase rather than translated as a standalone word—the specialized "reverse circumcision" meaning rests on context and outside sources rather than broad measured evidence.

definition: To put together in an orderly account, compiling and arranging material into a written narrative.
article: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 1:1, where Luke notes that many had "undertaken" to draw up an orderly account of the events among them. The core idea is arranging things in proper sequence, and the Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence as "undertaken" 100% of the time, with the BSB agreeing. Intriguingly, the one parallel from non-biblical literature is Plutarch describing an elephant "rehearsing" its learned tricks by moonlight, which led some scholars to suggest the sense "bring together or repeat from memory" for Luke's usage.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and is extremely rare elsewhere, so its precise nuance—orderly compilation versus recollection from memory—remains genuinely uncertain.

definition: Going without food; having eaten nothing, whether by circumstance or choice.
article: ἄσιτος combines the negative prefix ἀ- with σῖτος (food/grain) to describe someone who has eaten nothing. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:33, where Paul notes the storm-tossed sailors have gone without food. The everyday Koine papyri back this up nicely: one letter describes a writer who was sick and went without food (ἀσειτήσαντος) for two days, so that he could not even dine with the local officials — pointing to actual absence of food rather than deliberate fasting.

definition: To throw or strike someone down, or to lay down something like a foundation.
article: This compound of κατά ("down") and βάλλω ("throw") means to cast or strike something down, and it appears only twice in the New Testament. In 2 Corinthians 4:9 it describes being struck down but not destroyed, while in Hebrews 6:1 the middle voice means to lay down a foundation. The Septuagint uses it 31 times, often for the Hebrew word הָרַס ("to tear down"), and the papyri show a common everyday sense not seen in the NT: "to pay," as in paying taxes through a banker.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences carrying two different senses, the measured evidence is thin and the rendering of Hebrews 6:1 as "teachings" reflects context rather than the verb's core meaning.

definition: To suffer loss, forfeit, or be deprived of something, often as a penalty or damage incurred.
article: In the New Testament ζημιόω always appears in the passive, describing someone who suffers loss or forfeits something—whether one's soul (Matthew 16:26, Mark 8:36) or, in Paul, all worldly things counted as loss (Philippians 3:8). The everyday Koine papyri sharpen the picture: there it carries the sterner sense of being fined or penalized, with one document recording a man fined fifteen bronze talents and another threatening death as the penalty. In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew עָנַשׁ (5 of 6 times), which likewise means to fine or impose a penalty, so the underlying idea is loss imposed as a consequence.
caution: The four measured sense labels reflect how the word is woven into translated phrases rather than four distinct meanings, and the New Testament's 'suffer loss' sense is gentler than the 'fine/penalize' force seen in the papyri.

definition: A public lodging-house where travelers could find shelter for the night.
article: πανδοχεῖον refers to a public lodging-place — what we might call an inn, khan, or caravanserai — where travelers could stop and be taken in. Its parts literally suggest a place that "receives all," and the word was everyday colloquial Koine, showing up in comic writers and ordinary papyri and inscriptions. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:34, where the Good Samaritan brings the wounded man to an inn; related papyri even use a form for the innkeeper's trade.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on outside evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: A linking word meaning "just as" or "according as," introducing a comparison or showing how one thing matches another.
article: καθώς is a connector that joins two things by comparison, meaning "just as," "according as," or "even as." It appears 182 times in the New Testament, but in 122 of those the translators folded it into the surrounding phrasing without giving it its own English word — when it does surface, it shows up as "just" (as in "just as") in all 60 measured cases. A common fixed pattern is καθὼς γέγραπται, "just as it is written," used to introduce scripture quotations (e.g. Matthew 26:24, Mark 9:13).

definition: A close companion or partner — literally someone yoked together with you in shared work.
article: σύζυγος literally means "yoke-fellow," describing someone harnessed together with you in a common task, and by extension a loyal colleague or partner. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Philippians 4:3, where Paul addresses a faithful coworker. Interestingly, the word is also attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions — including a Magnesian graffito (probably first century AD) reading "yoke-fellows Baibios Kallipos" — and several scholars think Paul may actually be using it as a proper name, Synzygus.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources genuinely disagree on whether Paul means "yoke-fellow" as a description or as someone's actual name.

definition: Nazareth, the town in Galilee where Jesus lived before beginning his public ministry.
article: Ναζαρέθ is simply the name of Nazareth, a town in Galilee, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Nazareth" in 10 of its 12 New Testament occurrences (83%). The spelling of this place name is notably unstable in the manuscripts—the same town appears as Ναζαρά, Ναζαρέθ, and Ναζαρέτ across different verses and editions, and its underlying Semitic form is uncertain. Moulton-Milligan note that the form of the name has drawn scholarly attention, including studies of its Syriac spellings.
caution: The exact original spelling and Semitic derivation of the name are uncertain, with manuscripts varying between Ναζαρά, Ναζαρέθ, and Ναζαρέτ.

definition: An adverb meaning barely, with difficulty, or scarcely — something that happens only through great effort or hardship.
article: μόλις is an adverb meaning that something is done only with difficulty or barely accomplished. Though the Byzantine NT uses it 6 times across 3 books, in 4 of those it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word, so its sense surfaces clearly only in places like Romans 5:7 (one would scarcely die even for a righteous man) and 1 Peter 4:18 (if the righteous are saved with difficulty). The everyday Koine papyri confirm this meaning vividly — one writer says he was "with difficulty able" to settle a debt only by selling all his property, and another that people "scarcely live" on their meager holdings.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 6 NT uses with most absorbed into phrasing, and Abbott-Smith notes some editors read μόγις instead at Luke 9:39.

definition: Property, possessions, or status received as an heir, especially the lasting share God grants to his people.
article: κληρονομία refers to an inheritance—property or possessions handed down to an heir, and by extension the secure portion God promises to those who belong to him. In the New Testament it appears 14 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "inheritance" in 11 of them (79%), with the rest being close variations of the same idea. It was an ordinary legal word in daily life: a property registration from A.D. 110–111 describes two arurae of land "forming part of the inheritance" of a deceased mother. In the Septuagint it shows up 185 times, mainly translating the Hebrew נַחֲלָה (130×), the term for Israel's allotted land.

definition: A walled garden or park, used in the New Testament for the heavenly home of the blessed dead.
article: The word originally meant a garden or enclosed park, and in everyday Koine papyri it very commonly refers to an orchard of fruit-trees, usually walled. The Greek Old Testament uses it 27 times, mostly to render the Hebrew word for "garden" (20×), including the garden of Eden in Genesis. In the New Testament, however, all three occurrences point to Paradise as the dwelling place of the blessed dead, as in Jesus' promise on the cross (Luke 23:43). Interestingly, the word is a foreign borrowing of Iranian origin, related to the modern Persian word for garden.
caution: Confidence is low: there are only 3 New Testament occurrences, and the everyday "garden/park" meaning seen in the Septuagint and papyri does not appear in the New Testament's spiritual usage.

definition: Held in honor or high value—describing people who are esteemed or things regarded as precious.
article: ἔντιμος describes someone or something held in honor or treated as valuable, built from ἐν (in) and τιμή (honor/value). It applies both to people—an esteemed servant in Luke 7:2 or honored guests in Philippians 2:29—and to things, like the "precious" cornerstone in 1 Peter 2:4-6. Everyday papyri use it the same way: a retired soldier's certificate of "honourable release" (ἐντείμῳ ἀπολύσσει) after 26 years of service, showing this was ordinary language for being held in esteem.
caution: The five New Testament uses split evenly across slightly different shades (valued, honored, precious), so the exact emphasis depends on context.

definition: An assassin who carried a hidden dagger, especially a member of the Jewish rebel group known as the Sicarii.
article: σικάριος is a Latin loanword (from sica, a small dagger or stiletto) describing an assassin who concealed a blade under his clothing, and it specifically named the Sicarii, a band of Jewish rebels. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:38, where the Roman commander asks Paul whether he is the Egyptian who led four thousand of these men into the wilderness. The most telling outside evidence is a papyrus (P Oxy X.1294) using the related form σικάριον for an ordinary knife — "of these take one for yourself" — alongside Josephus, who uses σικάριος repeatedly for the rebel assassins.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there cannot be measured from the biblical text alone.

definition: A group of people living at the same time, or those descended from a common ancestor — a generation or family line.
article: γενεά refers most often to a generation — all the people living during a particular period — and is rendered "generation" in 35 of 42 Byzantine occurrences (97%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. It also carries a broader collective sense of race, family, or lineage, rooted in its tie to γένος; the papyri show it in wills meaning simply "issue" or "offspring," with no individual reference. In the Septuagint it appears 187 times and renders Hebrew דּוֹר ("generation") in 95 of those cases, confirming its core meaning across both Testaments.

definition: A hidden trap or scheme to attack someone by surprise, or more broadly a treacherous plot.
article: ἔνεδρον means an ambush — lying in wait to attack — and by extension a treacherous, murderous scheme. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 23:16, the plot against Paul) and is absent from the critical text, but it shows up 32 times in the Septuagint, where it usually translates the Hebrew verb אָרַב, "to lie in wait." An everyday papyrus from AD 338 stretches the word toward the more general sense of "fraud," warning against any ἔνεδρον in connection with the public bath.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament: it occurs only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical text, where the related form ἐνέδρα appears instead.

definition: To hate or strongly detest someone or something; sometimes, to love or value something far less by comparison.
article: μισέω means to hate or detest, and that single sense covers it: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "hate" in 34 of 40 occurrences (87%), with the rest just being slight variations of the same idea. In the Septuagint it appears 149 times and almost always stands in for the Hebrew שָׂנֵא, "to hate." Interestingly, that Hebrew word can carry a softer sense of preferring one thing over another (as in loving one wife and "hating" the other), and lexicographers suggest μισέω may carry this comparative "love less" meaning in passages like Luke 14:26 and Romans 9:13. The everyday papyri confirm the plain sense, as in a phrase about "evil-smelling persons hated by refined women."
caution: Whether certain passages mean literal hatred or merely "loving less by comparison" is a matter the lexicons flag as probable rather than certain.

definition: To spend the night somewhere, lodging or staying overnight, often out in the open or in a courtyard.
article: αὐλίζομαι means to lodge or pass the night somewhere, and the New Testament's 2 occurrences both describe overnight staying — Jesus spending the night at Bethany (Matthew 21:17) and spending each evening on the Mount of Olives (Luke 21:37). The word comes from αὐλή (courtyard), so it originally pictured lodging in a courtyard or out in the open. It appears 43 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating Hebrew לוּן (33×), and Moulton-Milligan note a vivid image in Psalm 30:5, where weeping "lodges" overnight like a passing stranger before joy comes in the morning.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the range here rests mostly on Septuagint and everyday Koine usage.

definition: Laughter, especially the kind expressing joy or amusement.
article: γέλως simply means laughter, and the New Testament uses it only once, in James 4:9, where every translation renders it the same way. It appears more widely in the Septuagint, where it shows up 15 times and most often stands in for the Hebrew word שְׂחוֹק (laughter or mockery). The everyday Koine papyri preserve a vivid example: an invitation to celebrate Hadrian's accession summoned people to sacrifice "with laughter and drink," letting their spirits loose.
caution: The word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single verse.

definition: A young girl or maiden, often a child, used as an everyday and somewhat informal term.
article: κοράσιον is a colloquial Koine word for a girl or young maiden, rendered "girl" in 7 of its 8 New Testament occurrences (88%), with the BSB agreeing 100%. It's a diminutive of κόρη, and Abbott-Smith notes it survived into modern Greek as an ordinary spoken word. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, most often translating the Hebrew נַעֲרָה (8×), while everyday papyri use it strikingly for a female slave being sold or hired out — a deed of sale even prices one such κοράσιον at 350 denarii.

definition: The face or countenance of a person, and by extension someone's presence, outward appearance, or surface.
article: At its core πρόσωπον means a person's face, which is how it's rendered in 36 of its 78 New Testament occurrences (73%). From there it stretches naturally: people fall "facedown" (6×), it can mean the outward "appearance" of things versus what's inside (3×), and in phrases like "in someone's presence" it points to being before a person (3×). In the Septuagint it appears over a thousand times and almost always translates the Hebrew פָּנִים ("face"), and a touching papyrus letter from 152 BC uses it just as personally—a writer says shame would otherwise have kept you from ever seeing "my face" again.

definition: Belonging to or located in heaven, as opposed to earthly or underground things.
article: ἐπουράνιος describes whatever belongs to or is located in heaven, standing in contrast to what is earthly (ἐπίγειος) or below the earth (καταχθόνιος). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "heavenly" in 11 of its 20 New Testament occurrences (55%), with "heavenly realms" (20%) and "heaven" (15%) covering the rest. A striking piece of evidence comes from a third-century Paris magical papyrus, which pairs the word with "earthly" and "underground" much as Paul does in Philippians 2:10 and Ephesians 2:2 — showing the word lived in everyday Koine and was not a uniquely Christian coinage.

definition: Describing something that cannot decay, perish, or fade away, and so endures forever.
article: ἄφθαρτος literally means "not subject to decay," built from a negative prefix plus a root tied to the verb "to destroy" or "corrupt." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "imperishable" 4 of 7 times (57%), "immortal" twice (29%) when describing God or raised people, and "unfading" once. The word reached beyond the Bible into everyday Koine: an inscription from around A.D. 37 contrasts "the imperishable" with "mortal nature," and a later one (A.D. 312) speaks of an "eternal and imperishable" imperial rule.
caution: With only 7 occurrences, the three shades of meaning—imperishable, immortal, and unfading—are closely related rather than sharply distinct senses.

definition: Something that is known or recognized, or—when used of people—an acquaintance.
article: γνωστός describes whatever is known or recognized, and the New Testament uses it 15 times. About 46% of the time the Majority Standard Bible simply renders it "known," but it also appears in expressions like making something known to people (15%) or something that became known (15%), especially in Acts. A notable secondary use applies it to people as "acquaintances" (Luke 2:44; 23:49), and Moulton-Milligan cites a 4th–5th century papyrus using τὸ γνωστόν for "the knowledge of our intimacy," supporting the sense "known" rather than "knowable."
caution: Scholars disagree over whether the personal use means simply "acquaintance" or the stronger "familiar friend."

definition: God's forbearance or restraint, holding back deserved punishment for a period of time.
article: ἀνοχή refers to forbearance — a deliberate holding back, especially the delay or restraint of deserved punishment. The word appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 2:4 and 3:26), where it describes God's patient toleration of sinners. Everyday Koine papyri use it in a more mundane sense: one third-century document speaks of having "a delay of some days," pointing to the underlying idea of a pause or postponement. Lexicons distinguish it from related words like μακροθυμία (long-suffering toward people) and ὑπομονή (endurance of circumstances).
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the digest's second "measured sense" (rendered merely as "one") reflects a translation artifact rather than a distinct meaning.

definition: An adverb meaning "from that place" or "from there," pointing back to a location just mentioned.
article: At its core ἐκεῖθεν simply means "from there," marking movement away from a place already named. The measured senses cluster around this: it most often (39%) describes someone going from a spot, and several renderings like "Jesus," "place," and "area" reflect translators naming the location or subject of the departure rather than a different meaning. It appears 28 times in the Byzantine NT and a hefty 135 times in the Septuagint, where it almost always renders the Hebrew שָׁם ("there"), 104 of those times. One striking detail from the papyri: a 4th-century Christian letter uses it with a causal force meaning "wherefore," showing the word could stretch beyond simple place.
caution: The labeled senses "Jesus," "place," and "area" reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings, and the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing 10 of 28 times, so its true range is narrower than the list suggests.

definition: The cock-crowing, used as a name for the third Roman night-watch, roughly between midnight and 3 a.m.
article: ἀλεκτοροφωνία literally means "cock-crowing" and was used as a label for a stretch of the night — the third night-watch, which the lexica place between midnight and 3 a.m. It is a compound built from ἀλέκτωρ (rooster) and φωνή (sound or voice), so it names the time of night by the sound that marks it. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just once, in Mark 13:35, where it sits in a list of night-watches and gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word.

definition: To cover something completely all around, whether covering a person's face to blindfold them or overlaying a surface entirely.
article: This verb means to cover something fully on all sides, built from "around" (περί) plus "to cover" (καλύπτω). In the New Testament its three uses split between covering a person's face during Jesus' mockery (Mark 14:65, Luke 22:64), rendered "blindfolded," and overlaying a surface with material, as in Hebrews 9:4 where the ark was covered with gold. The Septuagint shows the same range, where it translates several different Hebrew words including ones for covering and overlaying.
caution: Evidence is thin: only three New Testament occurrences and a handful in the Septuagint, so the full range is hard to pin down.

definition: Annas, the name of a Jewish high priest in Jerusalem during the New Testament period.
article: Ἄννας is simply the personal name Annas, borne by a high priest in Jerusalem who appears 4 times across 3 New Testament books. The name comes from Hebrew (related to חָנַן), and Josephus spells it Ananos. All sources agree it always refers to this one man; the different "senses" measured here are just translation phrasing around the same name, such as "during the priesthood of Annas" in Luke 3:2.
caution: The three "senses" reflect contextual wording in translation, not distinct meanings\u2014the word is always the proper name Annas.

definition: To treat someone or something as worth nothing, despising or rejecting them with contempt.
senseLabels: to despise or treat as nothing
article: This verb means to regard a person or thing as utterly worthless — to set them at nought, despise, or reject. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Mark 9:12), but it is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 45 times and renders the Hebrew words מָאַס ("reject," 13×) and בָּזָה ("hold in contempt," 12×). The Hebrew counterparts confirm the core idea: not just ignoring something but actively scorning it as nothing.
caution: The single New Testament occurrence and the odd "things" rendering make the measured data thin, so the fuller sense rests mainly on the Septuagint and lexicons.

definition: A personal name: Mark, an early Christian associate of Paul, Barnabas, and Peter.
article: Μάρκος is simply the name of a man, rendered "Mark" in 7 of its 8 New Testament occurrences (88%). The same person is identified in the sources as also bearing the Hebrew name John, the son of Mary and a companion of Barnabas, Paul, and Peter. The name is Latin in origin (the Roman praenomen Marcus), and Moulton-Milligan note it was very widely spread, showing up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions across the Mediterranean.

definition: Empty, foolish talk or pointless argument that has no real substance or value.
article: This word names useless, empty speech — the kind of babbling or pointless argument that goes nowhere. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 1:6, where people have turned aside to it after wandering from sincere faith. The papyri and a few Koine writers (like Vettius Valens) use it similarly, often pairing it with 'much talking,' confirming it describes wordy speech that lacks genuine meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests largely on a handful of outside Koine examples.

definition: The quality of being devoted to God and living a holy, upright life before him.
article: ὁσιότης describes a God-directed holiness or piety—living rightly toward God. In the New Testament it appears only twice, in Luke 1:75 and Ephesians 4:24, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "holiness" both times, and in each case it stands alongside "righteousness" (δικαιοσύνη). Outside the Bible it was an everyday word: a papyrus from 162 BC speaks of the "piety" (ὁσιότης) a person shows toward the divine, showing the word carried this devotional sense in ordinary Koine speech.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and 4 in the Septuagint translating several different Hebrew words, the evidence base is thin.

definition: To arrive at or reach something, or to come upon someone; in older usage, to get there first or beat someone to it.
article: In the New Testament, φθάνω usually means simply to come, arrive, or reach something, appearing 7 times across 6 books. The four measured senses really cluster into two ideas: coming upon someone (as in "the kingdom of God has come upon you," Matthew 12:28) and attaining or reaching a goal (Romans 9:31; Philippians 3:16). The interesting twist is that the classical sources point to an older, sharper meaning—to anticipate or get there before someone else—which the lexica say faded in later Greek; the everyday papyri likewise show it meaning "previously" or "already," as in a document noting that an inquiry "had already been held."
caution: With only 7 occurrences and a documented shift from the older "anticipate, get there first" sense to the later "arrive" sense, the precise force in a given verse can be debated.

definition: To make wide or enlarge something, whether physically or, figuratively, to open up the heart in warmth and affection.
article: πλατύνω means to widen, broaden, or enlarge something, and Paul uses it both ways in 2 Corinthians: literally of a heart "opened wide" (2CO 6:11) and as an appeal for the readers to do the same (2CO 6:13). It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 2 books, but 20 times in the Septuagint, where it usually renders the Hebrew רָחַב, "to be wide." The everyday Koine papyri also use it for "broadening" or "enlarging," matching the figurative sense Paul draws on.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin—only 3 occurrences—so the confidence tier is low, though the Septuagint and papyri support the same basic range.

definition: Rue, a small garden herb with fleshy leaves used to flavor or garnish food.
article: πήγανον is the name of rue, a common garden plant whose thick leaves were used for flavoring or garnishing food. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:42, where Jesus mentions tithing it alongside other herbs. Interestingly, Matthew's parallel verse (23:23) reads ἄνηθον (anise) instead, and some scholars cited by Moulton-Milligan suggest Luke worked from a Semitic source and misread the underlying word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its sense rests on that single instance plus its well-attested everyday use in Koine papyri.

definition: A feeling of gladness or delight; also sometimes the person or thing that causes such delight.
article: Χαρά means joy or gladness, and the evidence is remarkably consistent: of its 59 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "joy" 50 times (94%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 98% of the time. It can name both the inner feeling and, occasionally, its source (Dodson notes "a source of joy"), and the New Testament sets it in contrast both to grief (λύπη) and to gloom (κατήφεια). The same warm sense shows up in everyday life: a fourth-century papyrus letter uses nearly the words of Matthew 13:20, hoping "that we may welcome you with joy."

definition: The wild olive tree, or a branch from it, which produces poor fruit compared to the cultivated olive.
article: This word combines "wild" (ἄγριος) and "olive" (ἐλαία) to mean the wild olive tree or oleaster. It appears just twice in the New Testament, both in Romans 11 (verses 17 and 24), where Paul uses the image of a wild olive branch being grafted into a cultivated tree; the standard Bible renders it once as "wild" and once as "wild branches." Beyond Scripture, Moulton-Milligan note the adjective in an everyday inscription describing "dry wild-olive wood," showing it was ordinary Koine vocabulary.
caution: With only 2 occurrences (both in Romans 11) confidence is low, and Moulton-Milligan note that Sir W. M. Ramsay specifically debated the precise sense in Romans 11:17.

definition: A woman in relation to her child; also used figuratively for a city or other source regarded as a mother.
article: μήτηρ is the ordinary Greek word for "mother," and across 85 New Testament occurrences it means exactly that 72 times (95%), with the remaining instances simply absorbed into longer phrases. Beyond the literal sense, it stretches to figurative uses: someone who takes a mother's place, a city called "our mother" (Galatians 4:26), and symbolically "the mother of prostitutes" in Revelation 17:5. The everyday Koine papyri show this same loose, affectionate use, where a writer greets multiple unrelated women each as "my mother."

definition: On the opposite side, especially the far shore of a body of water.
article: This adverb means "on the opposite side," and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 8:26) it points to the shore across the lake from Galilee, where Jesus arrived after sailing. It takes a genitive to say what something lies opposite. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document refers to guards protecting estates on the "further bank" of a river, matching the New Testament sense exactly.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the manuscripts vary in its spelling (ἀντιπέραν, ἀντιπέρα, ἀντιπέρας), so evidence is thin.

definition: A connecting word that links what follows to what came before, marking it as a result, sequence, or conclusion.
article: οὖν is one of the most common connecting particles in the New Testament, appearing 523 times in the Byzantine text, and its exact force shifts with context. The measured renderings cluster around three ideas: drawing a conclusion ("so," 31%; "therefore," 23%) and marking simple sequence or resumption of a story ("then," 29%). Notably, in 159 of 523 cases the word is absorbed into English phrasing with no word of its own, since it often just smooths the flow of a narrative. The everyday papyri confirm this range: one letter uses it for plain "therefore" ("I beg you, therefore, my lord father, write me a letter").
caution: The boundaries between "so," "then," and "therefore" are fuzzy, and many translation differences reflect English style rather than distinct meanings.

definition: Isaac, the son of Abraham and father of Jacob, a key patriarch in Israel's family line.
article: Ἰσαάκ is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yitzchak (Isaac), the patriarch son of Abraham; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Isaac" in 16 of its 20 New Testament occurrences. As a personal name it doesn't shift in meaning, and in the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew יִצְחָק (107 times). One striking piece of evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions, where a sepulchral inscription pleads that God grant the dead rest "in the bosoms of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob," showing how the patriarch's name lived on in everyday Koine devotion.

definition: To take in and care for strangers or guests, that is, to practice hospitality.
article: ξενοδοχέω means to welcome and host strangers — to put hospitality into practice by lodging and caring for guests. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:10, where it describes the good works of a worthy widow, rendered "entertaining" by both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible. The word lived on in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan note that the related noun appears in Theophrastus for someone's "entertainments," and the modern Greek descendant ξενοδοχεῖον simply means "hotel."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from the corpus; ancient Atticist grammarians also criticized this spelling.

definition: The comparative form of the adjective "good," used adverbially to mean "better" or "very well."
article: This is the comparative of καλός ("good"), so it carries the sense of "better" or "very well." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 25:10) and not at all in the critical SBLGNT text. The single measured rendering here is unusual — the Majority Standard Bible's wording reflects the surrounding phrase rather than the word in isolation — so older lexicons like Abbott-Smith treat it under the broader family of καλῶς ("finely, rightly, well"), where it commonly introduces statements or expresses approval.
caution: Evidence is very thin — only one Byzantine occurrence and none in the critical text — so the measured "yourself" rendering reflects context rather than the word's own meaning, and confidence is low.

definition: The state of being a virgin, especially the unmarried years of a young woman's life before her first marriage.
senseLabels: the state of being a virgin
article: Παρθενία refers to virginity or maidenhood, the time of life before a woman marries. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 2:36, describing the prophetess Anna, who had lived with her husband only seven years "from her virginity" — that is, from her youth. The word turns up in everyday Koine documents too: a fourth-century papyrus describes a woman joined to her husband "from virginity," showing this was ordinary language for a first marriage, and in the Septuagint it once renders a Hebrew word for one's youth (Jeremiah 3:4).
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall attestation, this entry rests on limited evidence."

definition: An adverb meaning secretly or in private, describing something done out of public view.
article: Κρυφῆ is an adverb built from the verb "to hide," and it simply means "secretly" or "in private." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 5:12, and shows up 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, where it most often renders a Hebrew word for concealment (סָתֶר). One nice detail: the word turns up in an everyday third-century BC ostrakon letter that says to send something "secretly, and let no one notice" — proof it was ordinary Koine vocabulary, not just biblical language.
caution: It occurs only once in the New Testament, so the lexical sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than measured New Testament usage.

definition: Straight or direct, not crooked; also used in a moral sense of being upright, and as an adverb meaning immediately.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament, εὐθύς is rendered "straight" in all 7 of its measured occurrences, most famously in the cry to "make straight" the Lord's path (Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4). But the word's range is wider than that single measured sense suggests: lexicons note both a moral meaning ("straightforward, upright," as of the heart in Acts 8:21) and a very common adverbial use meaning "immediately" or "straightway" — the form Mark especially favors. The Septuagint uses it some 60 times, chiefly for the Hebrew word for "straight" or "upright," and a fourth-century Christian papyrus letter even prays that God would make "a straight way" for the writer, echoing the same imagery.
caution: The measured data only captured the literal "straight" sense, but the lexicons clearly document a moral sense and a frequent adverbial "immediately," so the corpus undercounts the word's real range.

definition: A Roman army officer in command of about one hundred soldiers, a centurion.
article: This word names a centurion, the Roman officer who led roughly a hundred men, and it appears 21 times in the Byzantine New Testament. Its meaning is remarkably stable: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "centurion" in 17 of those occurrences (81%), and the BSB agrees 94% of the time. The name itself is transparent, built from the parts meaning "hundred" and "to rule," so it literally describes a commander of one hundred. In the Septuagint it shows up only twice, where it stands behind Hebrew phrases for military leaders.

definition: In a kind and humane way; treating someone with friendly, considerate care.
article: This adverb describes acting toward people in a friendly, humane manner, built from the words for "friend" and "human being." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:3, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "care" (the King James Version says "courteously"); it also shows up twice in the Septuagint (2 Maccabees 9:27 and 3 Maccabees 3:20). Moulton-Milligan note its softened sense of "kindly" in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, such as an OGIS inscription from 239 B.C. describing someone who "treats the craftsmen kindly in everything."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A domestic animal, especially a four-footed beast used for riding or carrying loads.
article: κτῆνος refers to a domesticated animal, often a beast of burden like a horse or mule used for riding or carrying loads, and is distinguished from fish and birds (1 Corinthians 15:39). In the New Testament it appears only 4 times; in Acts 23:24 it specifically means a mount to set Paul on, which is why the Berean rendering folds it into the verb 'take.' Its much heavier use in the Septuagint (239×) chiefly translates the Hebrew word for beast or cattle (בְּהֵמָה, 146×), and everyday papyri repeatedly show it as flocks, herds, and working animals — one tax-era letter complains 'we have not so much as food for our cattle.'
caution: Only 4 New Testament occurrences, so the measured sense breakdown rests on very few examples.

definition: Comforting, encouraging speech that lifts up or consoles someone in distress.
article: παραμυθία means encouraging or consoling words spoken to lift someone's spirits. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 14:3), where it's woven into the phrasing rather than translated as a single English word, and twice in the Septuagint. A vivid detail from the papyri: one writer addresses his correspondent as 'the consolation of his friends,' and the related modern Greek word παραμύθι means a fable or tale—an echo of the comforting stories a nurse might tell a child. Abbott-Smith notes it pairs closely with παράκλησις (encouragement).
caution: Evidence is thin—just one New Testament use and two in the Septuagint—so the precise shade between 'encouragement' and 'comfort' is hard to pin down.

definition: A close relationship of sharing—either personal fellowship and partnership, or a concrete contribution given out of that shared bond.
article: κοινωνία covers a spectrum of "sharing in common," running from the close personal bond of fellowship (its most frequent sense, rendered "fellowship" in 10 of 19 occurrences, 63%) to partnership and even a concrete monetary contribution given because of that bond (as in Romans 15:26). The everyday Koine papyri show just how intimate the word could be: marriage contracts use it for two people "coming together for a partnership of life," making it the term for the closest of human relationships. In the Septuagint it appears only once, where it stands behind a Hebrew word in Leviticus about a deposit or pledge held in common.

definition: In a proper, decent, and orderly way that looks respectable to others.
article: This adverb describes acting in a fitting, dignified, and presentable manner. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, where it shifts slightly between behaving respectably (Romans 13:13; 1 Thessalonians 4:12, rendered "behave") and doing something properly or orderly (1 Corinthians 14:40). Everyday Koine documents confirm the same flavor: a 1st-century BC inscription pairs it with "orderly" (euschēmonōs kai eutaktōs) to describe officials keeping a procession running smoothly and respectably.
caution: With only 3 occurrences, the evidence base is thin, so the precise boundary between "respectable conduct" and "orderly procedure" rests on very few examples.

definition: To stay temporarily in a place as a visitor or foreign resident, rather than living there permanently.
article: ἐπιδημέω describes the experience of being away from home and lodging somewhere for a while—what we might call sojourning or staying as a visitor. It built on δῆμος (people, district), and classical writers used it both for being at home and for staying in a place; the New Testament uses focus on the latter sense of temporary residence. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: Moulton-Milligan point to a strategus's day-book (A.D. 233) where the word marks his arrival and temporary stay in a place, paired with its opposite ἀποδημέω for his departure.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only 2 times in the New Testament, and one of those is absorbed into phrasing without its own English word.

definition: A staining or pollution that morally contaminates a person, making them unclean.
article: μολυσμός refers to defilement or pollution—a stain that makes something unclean, used figuratively for moral or spiritual contamination. It appears only once in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 7:1), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the idea of what "defiles." In the Septuagint it translates a Hebrew word for godlessness or impiety, and everyday Koine papyri use it similarly: one document (Aristeas) speaks of people being "utterly tainted with the pollution of their impiety."
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A washing or bath — the water used for cleansing or the act of washing itself.
article: λουτρόν refers to a washing or bath — either the water used for cleansing or the act of washing itself (it does not mean the basin or vessel). It appears just twice in the New Testament, both times in vivid images: the "washing of water" (Ephesians 5:26) and the "washing of regeneration" (Titus 3:5), with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "washing" in both. The everyday Koine background is striking: an inscription from Andania (91 BC) lists "anointing and washing" (loutrón) as a heading, and the word turns up regularly in papyri and inscriptions for bathing.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the evidence base is thin.

definition: A petition or request brought before someone, used in the New Testament for prayer and intercession offered to God.
article: In the New Testament ἔντευξις refers to a petition or appeal, appearing only twice—both in 1 Timothy—where the BSB renders it once as "intercessions" (1TI 2:1) and once as "prayer" (1TI 4:5). The most striking evidence comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan shows it was a standard, almost technical term for any petition addressed to a king or ruler, as when the Serapeum Twins petitioned Ptolemy. Dodson notes this royal background literally—"approaching the king"—which fits how the word carried the sense of formally bringing a request before a higher authority. Classical lexica like Abbott-Smith also record older senses such as a chance meeting or a conversation, though these do not appear in the New Testament.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the word's New Testament range is thinly attested and leans heavily on papyri evidence.

definition: Baal, the chief god worshiped by the Phoenicians and other Semitic peoples, used in the Bible as a symbol of idolatry.
article: Βάαλ is the name of the chief deity of the Phoenicians and related Semitic nations, derived from the Hebrew word for "lord" (בַּעַל).
