It appears just once in the New Testament (Romans 11:4) but 79 times across the Septuagint, where it usually translates the Hebrew בַּעַל. A fascinating detail: in Romans 11:4 the name takes a feminine article ("the Baal"), which lexicographers connect to a Septuagint habit of substituting the word for "shame" (αἰσχύνη) when reading the name aloud, avoiding the idol's name directly.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the unusual feminine article reflects a scribal-reading convention that the sources explain but do not treat as fully settled.

definition: A door, gate, or entrance — the opening into a building or room, sometimes used figuratively for an opportunity.
article: θύρα is the everyday word for a door or entrance, rendered "door" in 77% of its 39 New Testament occurrences and "gate" in another 16%. Its range stretches from literal doorways — the door of a house, a tomb, a prison — to figurative uses like "a door of opportunity" (as in Acts and 1 Corinthians) and even Jesus calling himself the door of the sheep. The Septuagint uses it over 200 times, mostly for the Hebrew words for an entrance (102×) and a physical door or leaf (69×), and the papyri show it as plain household vocabulary, as when a man describes sleeping "at the door of the house" he lives in.

definition: Ephesus, a major coastal city in Asia Minor that served as a center of early Christian activity.
article: Ephesus was an important coastal city in Asia Minor (the capital of the Roman province of Asia), and the word names that place in all 16 of its New Testament occurrences. Both the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB render it "Ephesus" consistently, with a lone variant phrasing "Ephesus man" being the only exception. The name is probably of foreign (non-Greek) origin, and grammarians have noted a peculiarity in how its genitive form is constructed.

definition: To sit, be seated, or take a seated position.
article: καθέζομαι simply means to sit or be seated, and all six of its New Testament appearances express this single, plain idea. The translations vary only in surrounding phrasing—'sat,' 'sitting,' 'finally sitting'—but the core meaning never shifts. One notable detail comes from Moulton-Milligan, who argue that in the New Testament this verb is always durative, describing the ongoing state of 'sitting' rather than the action of 'sitting down,' a usage backed by everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: The word appears only six times in the Byzantine New Testament, so the evidence for its range is limited, though the sources broadly agree on its meaning.

definition: A group of people who share particular beliefs or opinions—a sect, party, or faction.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament αἵρεσις appears 9 times, and where it gets its own English word it consistently means "sect"—a group bound by shared beliefs, as when Paul speaks of the Pharisees or "the sect of the Nazarenes" (Acts 24:14; 26:5; 28:22). The word comes from the verb meaning "to choose," and lexicons trace it from "choice" to "a chosen opinion" to "a party holding such opinions." Interestingly, the papyri and inscriptions show the same split: one early collection lists fourteen examples meaning "opinion, conviction" but only three meaning "sect, faction," suggesting the "group" sense was the later development that the NT favors.
caution: Lexicons list additional senses like "choice," "opinion," and "heresy" that the measured NT data does not capture, and 2 of the 9 occurrences are absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word.

definition: The number four, used as a cardinal number to count people, objects, or groups.
article: τέσσαρες is simply the number "four," and it works exactly as you'd expect — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "four" in 36 of 41 occurrences (97%), with the rest just absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 213 times and almost always translates the Hebrew word for four, אַרְבַּע (177×). One quirk worth noting: grammarians point out that τέσσαρες is the only early Greek cardinal number that ever developed its own separate accusative form, a detail well attested in everyday papyri and ostraca.

definition: A locust, the insect that swarms over crops and was also eaten as food.
article: ἀκρίς simply means a locust, and the evidence is remarkably consistent across every source. In the New Testament it appears 4 times, rendered "locusts" in all of them — once as part of the phrase "locusts descended" in Revelation 9:3, where the insects swarm. The Septuagint uses it 32 times, most often to translate the Hebrew אַרְבֶּה (19×), the standard word for the devastating swarming locust of plagues, and Matthew and Mark famously list it among John the Baptist's diet.

definition: To see clearly and distinctly, even from a distance.
article: This adverb describes seeing something plainly, with the built-in nuance of clarity even at a distance—the parts of the word combine the ideas of "afar" and "radiance." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 8:25, where a blind man healed by Jesus sees everyone clearly. A nice glimpse of everyday usage comes from a magical papyrus (P Oxy VI.886, 3rd century AD), where the word promises that "you will obtain an illuminating answer."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and some manuscripts read the variant δηλαυγῶς instead, so the evidence is thin.

definition: A person from Gergesa (or Gerasa), a town on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee.
article: Γεργεσηνός is a place-name adjective identifying someone from Gergesa, a town on the eastern shore of the lake, and the lexicons connect it to a Gerasa or Gergesa, possibly modern Kersa, rather than the better-known Gerasa of the Decapolis. The name traces back to Hebrew (the Girgashite people), and the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. Interestingly, the manuscripts vary between Γεργεσηνῶν, Γερασηνῶν, and Γαδαρηνῶν across the parallel Gospel accounts, so the exact spelling and town are genuinely contested.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical text, with manuscripts disagreeing over the place-name, so the evidence is thin and the rendering 'violent' likely reflects context rather than the word's actual meaning.

definition: To be controlled or afflicted by a demon, so that the demon exercises power over the person.
article: δαιμονίζομαι describes a person who is under the power of a demon, and it always appears in the passive or middle—something is being done to the person. The range is narrow and consistent: the Majority Standard Bible renders its 13 occurrences as either "demon possessed" (6×) or simply "possessed" (5×), and the BSB independently agrees with both 100% of the time. Notably, Moulton-Milligan found that this sense of being possessed by demons seems to appear only in later Greek, and a related form shows up in third-century magical papyri, including a charm "for those possessed by demons."

definition: To set yourself against someone or something, standing firm to oppose, withstand, or resist them.
article: ἀνθίστημι literally means to "stand against" someone, and in the New Testament it splits cleanly between two closely related ideas: opposing a person or position (5×, 38%) and resisting or withstanding pressure (4×, 31%). The two are really one stance viewed from different angles, and translators agree closely with Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith on the range. The word was at home in everyday Koine — the papyri show ordinary people writing things like "I cannot stand against" (οὐ γὰρ δύναμαι ἀνθιστάνειν), confirming it was common speech, not just biblical vocabulary.

definition: A plant or shrub that has been planted, or the act of planting itself.
article: φυτεία comes from the verb φυτεύω ("to plant") and basically means "a planting" — either the act of planting or, by extension, the thing that has been planted. In its single New Testament appearance (Matthew 15:13), it refers to a plant that will be pulled up by the roots, and both the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles render it that way. Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri use the word for literal agricultural planting, including the planting of vineyards and gardens, which fits its three Septuagint uses where it translates Hebrew words for what is sown or planted.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its sense there rests on a single occurrence supported by broader Koine and Septuagint usage.

definition: To drive or force people together, used figuratively of pushing two parties toward reconciliation.
article: This verb literally means to drive or force things together, and in its single New Testament occurrence (Acts 7:26) it describes Moses trying to push two quarreling men toward peace. The word is rare and disputed: it appears only once in the Byzantine text and zero times in the modern critical text (SBLGNT), where editors instead read συνήλλασσεν ('he was reconciling'). Moulton-Milligan documents the related reconciliation vocabulary in everyday papyri, where συναλλάσσω names 'the contracting parties' in legal agreements, and the Septuagint uses συνελαύνω in 2 Maccabees.
caution: This is essentially a single-occurrence reading that the critical text replaces with a different verb, so its presence here is genuinely disputed.

definition: A sheep, the woolly grazing animal, often used figuratively for the followers of a shepherd or leader.
article: πρόβατον overwhelmingly means "sheep": the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way 36 times (95%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing. The Greek itself is broader than the English suggests — in older writers like Homer and Herodotus it covered livestock generally, especially small cattle including goats, and it appears constantly in everyday papyri (one document from 246 B.C. counts 38 sheep, eight rams, and 13 lambs). In Scripture it most often pictures people under a leader's care, especially the flock of the Good Shepherd, and the Septuagint uses it 285 times, chiefly for the Hebrew collective word for a flock, צֹאן (193×).

definition: To carry out or fulfill something completely, bringing a promise or obligation to full completion.
article: This verb means to fill something up entirely or to fulfill a promise to the full, and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:32-33, where it describes God fully carrying out his promise. Built from the parts meaning "out" and "to fill," it carries the sense of completing something all the way. A nice example from everyday Koine comes from the papyri: a letter requesting the release of workers so they could "make up" the food supplies for the sacred crocodiles, and another using it for paying off an amount in full.
caution: Evidence is thin: this word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range rests mainly on outside papyri and lexicons.

definition: To suffer the pains of childbirth, used both literally and as a vivid image for intense agonized effort or longing.
article: ὠδίνω means to go through the pains of giving birth, and the New Testament uses it both literally and figuratively. In the three Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders each differently — straightforward birth pains (Galatians 4:19), a labor cry that breaks forth aloud (Galatians 4:27), and the agony of childbirth (Revelation 12:2). In the Septuagint it appears 16 times across 6 books, most often standing in for the Hebrew חוּל (11×), and one charming detail from the papyri is a Pompeian bedroom inscription where the word is taken to mean simply 'is anxious.'
caution: Only three New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, so the figurative range rests on thin evidence.

definition: A conjunction meaning "because" or "for," introducing the reason or grounds for what was just said.
article: διότι is a causal conjunction built from διά ("through, on account of") and ὅτι ("that"), and it usually introduces the reason behind a statement — most often rendered "because" or "for." It appears 24 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the measured renderings cluster tightly around "because" and "for," with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% of the time for the plain "because," "for," and "for because" senses. In the Septuagint it shows up 310 times, overwhelmingly translating Hebrew כִּי ("because/that," 87×). Abbott-Smith notes it is usually stronger than the simple ὅτι, though papyri and later Greek sometimes weaken it to merely mean "that."
caution: Lexica note that in some passages (e.g. Luke 1:13) διότι can shade toward the weaker sense "for/that" like ὅτι, so its exact force is occasionally disputed.

definition: To become poor or destitute, like a beggar reduced to having nothing.
article: This verb describes sinking into poverty—becoming as destitute as a beggar. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 8:9, where it is rendered "became" (poor), set in contrast to being rich. The classical lexicons note an earlier, more concrete sense—"to beg" or "to be a beggar"—which Abbott-Smith marks as the chief classical meaning, while the New Testament use leans toward the broader idea of becoming destitute; in the Septuagint it occurs 6 times across 3 books, translating Hebrew words including דָּלַל.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one New Testament occurrence, and the classical "to beg" sense differs from the destitution sense seen in 2 Corinthians.

definition: A linking word that introduces a result or consequence, meaning "so," "so that," or "therefore."
article: ὥστε is a connecting particle that points to a result or consequence, ranging from "so" and "so that" (the most common renderings, together about 56% of its 83 New Testament uses) to "therefore" and "so then." Its meaning sits on a spectrum: sometimes it simply marks a result ("so that"), and other times it draws a conclusion from what came before ("therefore"). The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where one writer uses it in a complaint about waiting for discharge: "so that up till today no one of us has been let go." It appears 127 times in the Greek Old Testament as well.
caution: In 13 of 83 cases the word is absorbed into the English phrasing with no word of its own, so its exact force often depends on context.

definition: To give an order or instruction, telling someone what to do.
article: ἐντέλλομαι means to command, charge, or give instructions, and the New Testament uses it consistently this way—rendered "command" or "commanded" in nearly 70% of its 17 occurrences. It's a workaday word, not a specialized one: Moulton-Milligan finds it all over everyday Koine papyri, where people use it for giving orders, sending greetings, or assigning tasks. In the Septuagint it appears a remarkable 382 times, almost always translating the Hebrew verb צָוָה ("to command"), making it the standard Greek word for divine and human commands alike.

definition: To overflow or gush out, like a spring pouring forth water; literally to be full to bursting.
article: βρύω describes something so full it bursts out — used of the earth producing plants, buds opening, or springs gushing with water. It appears only once in the New Testament (James 3:11), where it pictures a spring pouring out water, and in that single verse it was folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word. Beyond the Bible it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and the poet Bacchylides uses it five times, as in the image of temples "rife" with sacrifices and streets full of feasting.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on very thin biblical evidence.

definition: A sore, ulcer, or festering wound on the body.
article: ἕλκος refers to an open sore or ulcer—a festering, often painful wound on the skin. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 3 times, describing the sores covering the beggar Lazarus (Luke 16:21) and the painful sores afflicting people in Revelation 16:2, 11. In the Septuagint it appears 14 times, most often translating the Hebrew שְׁחִין (12×), the same word used for the boils of the Egyptian plagues and Job's afflictions; Greek medical papyri from the third century BC likewise use it for a body ulcer.
caution: The New Testament evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences), though the consistent Septuagint and papyri usage makes the basic meaning clear.

definition: A Hebrew word of affirmation meaning "truly" or "so be it," used to begin solemn statements or to confirm prayers and praise.
article: Borrowed straight from Hebrew אָמֵן, this indeclinable word carries the sense of something firm and trustworthy. It works two main ways: introducing Jesus' weighty sayings (rendered "truly," about 33% of its 152 occurrences) and closing prayers or doxologies ("amen," about 27%), with many cases blending into the phrase "truly I tell you." A striking detail from the papyri: early Christian scribes wrote it as the numeral 99, the sum of the Greek letters' values, so a prayer could simply end "γένοιτο, 99"—"so be it, Amen."
caution: The boundaries between its "truly," "amen," and "truly I tell you" senses overlap heavily, so the counts reflect translation choices more than sharp distinctions in meaning.

definition: To think, suppose, or expect something to be the case, often based on one's own assumption or opinion.
article: This verb means to hold an opinion or assumption about how things are — to suppose, think, or expect. It only appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical SBLGNT text), so it's rare, but it was common in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite letters and documents where people use it for what they 'think' or assumed to be true, such as money they 'thought had been lost in the purse.' In the Septuagint it shows up 14 times and renders several different Hebrew words, including one tied to dreaming (as in Joseph's dream in Genesis).
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences, one of which carries no English word of its own, so the measured sense data is limited.

definition: To shut someone's mouth so they cannot speak, putting an end to their talk.
article: ἐπιστομίζω literally pictures putting something over the mouth — like a muzzle or bridle — and is used figuratively to mean shutting people up or silencing them. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:11, where false teachers' mouths must be stopped, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "silenced entire" every time. Moulton-Milligan note it is a rare verb but show it living in everyday Koine, citing Philostratus, who used it of silencing a person.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests on a single verse plus a few outside attestations.

definition: A human being of either sex, a person, often used generically for humankind or to describe humanity as distinct from God or animals.
article: ἄνθρωπος is the everyday Greek word for a human being, used 556 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "man" in 427 of them—though it covers people of either sex, not just males. Its range stretches from the generic (humankind, John 16:21) to contrasts with God (Matthew 19:6) or animals (Matthew 4:19), and it can highlight human frailty (1 Corinthians 3:4). In the Septuagint it does the work of several Hebrew words—chiefly אָדָם (432×) and אִישׁ (382×)—and Moulton-Milligan notes it has held its meaning steady from Homer all the way to Modern Greek.

definition: Describing something so extraordinary that it goes against what people expected to see.
article: Παράδοξος describes events or things that defy normal expectations — remarkable, incredible, even astonishing. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 5:26, where the crowd reacts to a healing, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "remarkable" in every count. Interestingly, the papyri show it became an athletic title: a παράδοξος was a champion who won in multiple events, and it even appears in P Lond 1178 (A.D. 194) describing victorious boxers and wrestlers.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To stir someone up emotionally—usually to anger or irritation, but sometimes to spur them toward action.
article: At its root παροξύνω means to "sharpen," but in practice it almost always describes stirring up strong feeling, especially anger or irritation. The word covers a real range: in the Septuagint (47 times across 13 books) it most often renders Hebrew נָאַץ (to spurn, 10×) and קָצַף (to be angry, 6×), and the New Testament uses both the negative sense (Paul's spirit being provoked, 1 Corinthians 13's love that is not "easily provoked") and a positive one. Everyday papyri show both directions too: a woman complains her husband was turned against her, while an inscription uses it for citizens being roused to civic action.
caution: Evidence is thin and the two Byzantine occurrences were absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word, so no measured senses could be isolated.

definition: Made of clay or earthenware, often suggesting something fragile or of little value.
article: ὀστράκινος describes anything made of fired clay or earthenware, and by implication something frail. It appears only twice in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 4:7 and 2 Timothy 2:20), in both cases paired with the word for "vessel." The everyday papyri confirm this plain sense: one contract lists a "cask of earthenware," and the word commonly attaches to ordinary household pots, jars, and dishes. In the Septuagint it occurs 15 times, most often rendering the Hebrew חֶ֫רֶשׂ ("potsherd" or "earthenware").
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, confidence is low, though the literal "clay/earthen" sense is consistent across the Septuagint, papyri, and lexica.

definition: To twist or bundle things together, or for people to gather themselves into a group.
article: This compound of "with" (σύν) and "turn/twist" (στρέφω) basically means to twist things together into a bundle, and by extension to gather. In the Byzantine NT it appears just once (Acts 28:3), where Paul gathers a bundle of sticks and a snake comes out driven by the heat. It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 20 times across 9 books, usually translating the Hebrew קָשַׁר ("to bind/conspire," 11 times). A nice everyday glimpse comes from an Egyptian medical papyrus that uses it for twisting oily wool around a probe to treat an earache.
caution: With only one Byzantine occurrence, the sense range here rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than NT usage.

definition: To tear something down or destroy it, whether a building, a law, or an undertaking; sometimes to stop traveling and lodge for the night.
article: At its core καταλύω means to "loosen down" — to take apart, demolish, or overthrow, used both literally of buildings ("not one stone left on another") and figuratively of abrogating a law or annulling a work. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 17 times, mostly for tearing down or destroying; in 6 of those it blends into the phrasing and gets no English word of its own. The most interesting wrinkle is a second, gentler sense seen in Luke and the everyday papyri: travelers "unyoking" their animals and stopping to lodge for the night, which connects it to the related word κατάλυμα (lodging).
caution: The measured senses cover only the "destroy/tear down" range, while the lexica and Luke's usage also document a "lodge for the night" sense not captured in the counted renderings.

definition: A field used for crops or grazing, or by extension the rural countryside and farmland outside towns.
article: ἀγρός most often means a field — a piece of farmed or grazing land — which is how it reads in 25 of 35 New Testament occurrences (78%). It can also widen to mean the countryside or rural districts, the area outside towns, in another 5 cases (16%). In the Septuagint it appears 236 times and overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew word שָׂדֶה, 'field' (202×), so the agricultural sense is deeply rooted; interestingly, although Moulton-Milligan note this was once a common word, they found it surprisingly rare in everyday papyri.

definition: The pods of the carob tree, used as cheap animal fodder, that a starving man longed to eat.
article: κεράτιον is a diminutive of κέρας ("horn"), so it literally means "a little horn" — a fitting name for the curved pods of the carob tree. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 15:16, where the prodigal son wishes he could fill his belly with the carob pods fed to the pigs, and translators agree on "pods" 100% of the time. The papyri show the word's everyday life beyond food: from the fifth century AD onward it was used in Egypt, like the Latin siliqua, as a unit of weight or money — the source of our word "carat."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: The act of disappearing, vanishing away, or being wiped out completely.
article: ἀφανισμός means the process of disappearing or being obliterated — something fading from view and ceasing to exist. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 8:13, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as the old covenant "aging" and on the verge of vanishing away. The word is far more common in the Septuagint (50×), where it most often translates the Hebrew שְׁמָמָה, a word for desolation or ruin, giving it a sharper sense of devastation than the gentler English "vanishing" suggests.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and its Septuagint sense of "desolation" is stronger than the mild "aging" rendering at Hebrews 8:13, so confidence is low.

definition: To have courage and confidence, especially as a command telling someone not to be afraid.
article: θαρσέω means to be of good courage or take heart, and in the New Testament it shows up only as a command—"Take courage!"—appearing 8 times across 5 books. The two measured senses are really the same encouragement; both render as "Take courage," the second just carrying an added "up" from phrasing like "Cheer up." In the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew word for fear (יָרֵא, 7 of 13 times), where it appears with a negative, fitting its role as the antidote to being afraid; the papyri preserve a lovely parallel where someone tells the "eye of my soul, take courage."
caution: The two listed senses are essentially one meaning split by surrounding phrasing, so the apparent range is narrower than the labels suggest.

definition: To see something with your eyes or perceive it with your mind, and by extension to watch out or take care.
article: ὁράω is the basic verb for seeing, used 657 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "saw" in 88% of cases. Beyond physical sight it stretches to mental perception ("discern") and to warnings like "take heed" or "beware"—in fact Moulton-Milligan note the word is cognate with our English "be ware." In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates Hebrew רָאָה ("to see," 928 times), and it shows up regularly in everyday Koine papyri, with phrases like "as you see" in first-century documents.
caution: Note that in everyday Koine the present tense was rare, its place often taken by βλέπω and θεωρέω, so ὁράω commonly appears in its aorist and other forms.

definition: A visiting—whether God coming in mercy or judgment, or an opportunity for relief—and also the office or charge of an overseer.
article: ἐπισκοπή centers on the idea of a visit or a looking-in, and the New Testament uses it in two directions: God's coming to His people (whether to help or to judge) and the office held by an overseer. In the Septuagint it appears 30 times across 10 books, most often rendering the Hebrew root פָּקַד and its noun פְּקֻדָּה, both tied to the idea of God 'visiting' or calling to account. A telling everyday parallel comes from the papyri, where a related noun describes government inspections of tax returns, and a later inscription praises a bishop for administering his ἐπισκοπή for twenty-five full years.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences—two of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing—the precise shade in any given verse leans heavily on context and the Septuagint background.

definition: A garden plot or bed of herbs, used figuratively for people seated in neat, orderly groups.
article: Literally πρασιά means a garden bed, the kind where leeks or other herbs are planted in tidy rows. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Mark 6:40, where it describes the crowd settling into orderly 'groups' to be fed. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as 'groups' in every counted occurrence, and a papyrus from the first century (BGU II.530) uses the same word for an irrigated vegetable plot, showing it was everyday farming vocabulary; the repeated 'πρασιαὶ πρασιαί' in Mark stresses the neat arrangement of the people rather than any color or variety.
caution: The figurative sense rests on just two occurrences in a single verse, so confidence is low.

definition: Describing something that cannot be put into words or expressed in ordinary speech.
article: This adjective combines a negative prefix with a word for speaking, so it literally means "unutterable" or "unable to be expressed in words." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 8:26, where it describes the groanings or sighs through which the Spirit intercedes. Notice the gap between the lexicons and the measured data: the classical and reference glosses (Strong's, KJV, Abbott-Smith) all point to "unutterable" or "inexpressible," while the Majority Standard renders the verse with "intercedes" — a translator's choice that folds the word into the surrounding phrase rather than translating it directly.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the dictionary sense ("inexpressible") differs from how translations smooth it into the verse, so its precise force rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A paying back — the recompense or reward given in return for what someone has done.
article: ἀνταπόδοσις names the act of paying someone back, whether as reward or repayment. It appears only once in the New Testament (Colossians 3:24), where the translation folds it into a larger phrase rather than giving it its own English word, but the Septuagint uses it 16 times across 6 books, often for Hebrew words meaning recompense (גְּמוּל), repayment (שִׁלּוּם), or vengeance (נָקָם). Moulton-Milligan note its everyday use in inscriptions and papyri, including a loan document on a house, showing the word lived in ordinary financial language as well as scripture.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (absorbed into surrounding phrasing) and a low confidence tier, the precise English sense rests mostly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than measured NT usage.

definition: A group sharing a common origin — a family, descendants, a people or nation, or a kind or class of things.
article: γένος covers anything bound together by a common origin, from a family or set of descendants, to a whole people or nation, to a category or "kind" of thing. In the Byzantine New Testament it shows up 21 times, but in 16 of those it gets folded into the phrasing rather than translated by its own English word, so the two clearly measured senses — "kind" and "offspring" — each appear only twice. The everyday papyri make the "class of things" sense vivid: phrases like "in kind or in money" and "a loan in kind" use γένος exactly the way we say "in kind" today.
caution: The standard lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, KJV) list a wider range — family, race, nation — than the two senses the corpus measurements isolate, partly because most occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing.

definition: Made by weaving; describing cloth produced in one continuous piece on a loom.
article: This adjective means "woven," describing something made on a loom, and in the New Testament it appears just once, in John 19:23, where Jesus' tunic is described as woven in a single seamless piece. The word was ordinary in everyday Koine: a second-century papyrus uses it of "woven stuffs," and related forms name woven materials and weavers themselves. In the Septuagint it shows up 9 times, rendering several different Hebrew terms tied to fabric and weaving, such as the word for a curtain or tent-hangings.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there rests on a single verse.

definition: Describing a tale or belief as foolish and unfounded, like the superstitious stories associated with old women.
article: γραώδης means 'old-womanish' or 'anile' — used to dismiss something as a silly, superstitious story of the kind old women were said to tell. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 4:7, where Timothy is told to reject such tales and instead train himself in godliness. The word is built from the Greek for 'old woman' plus a root meaning 'form' or 'kind,' literally 'of the old-woman type.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: The number four hundred.
article: This is simply the cardinal number "four hundred," formed from the words for "four" (G5064) and "hundred" (G1540). Though the Majority Standard Bible's renderings appear in the digest as several different phrases, every one is just "four hundred" embedded in a larger statement, and the BSB agrees fully in each case. It shows up 57 times in the Septuagint, almost always translating the ordinary Hebrew counting word for four, and Moulton-Milligan finds it counting money in an everyday papyrus deed of A.D. 314 ("two thousand four hundred silver drachmas").

definition: To sing praise to God, whether singing a hymn or singing in worship before others.
article: ὑμνέω means to praise God in song. In the New Testament's 4 occurrences it splits between singing a hymn (3×, as when Jesus and the disciples sing after the Last Supper) and singing praises among the assembly (1×, in Hebrews 2:12). The Septuagint uses it heavily (52× in 9 books), and Moulton-Milligan note an everyday Koine inscription from 238 B.C. using the transitive sense "to be praised in song," matching its use in Acts 16:25.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the two measured senses really reflect one core meaning differing mainly in setting rather than a genuine split in range.

definition: To carry a body away together for burial, or more generally to gather or collect things together.
senseLabels: carry away a body for burial
article: This rare word literally means to bring or carry things together, and everyday Koine papyri use it for gathering in crops, like harvesting produce from the fields. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 8:2), it takes the specialized sense of taking up a corpse for burial, describing devout men who carried Stephen's body away. The Septuagint uses it just once (Job 5:26), and classical writers like Sophocles also attest the burial sense, so this narrower meaning has solid roots even though the broader "gather together" sense is more common in everyday documents.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its biblical sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Too many to count; countless or innumerable.
article: ἀναρίθμητος describes a quantity so vast it cannot be counted — built from a negative prefix plus a word related to counting (G705, ἀριθμέω). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:12, where it describes Abraham's descendants being as countless as the stars and the sand. The Septuagint uses it 6 times across 4 books, including Job 31:25, where it renders several different Hebrew words for abundance or magnitude.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: To shed tears, to weep silently rather than cry out loud.
article: δακρύω means to shed tears, and in the New Testament it appears just once—famously in John 11:35, where Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb. Abbott-Smith notes it differs from related words: κλαίω is audible crying, θρηνέω is formal lamentation, and ἀλαλάζω is loud wailing, so δακρύω points more to quiet tears. A nice touch from the papyri: the related form survives in modern Greek with the participle δακρυσμένος, meaning "red with weeping," and an undated tombstone pleads, "Let all the earth weep for you, Magna."
caution: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on limited biblical evidence and comparison with related words.

definition: To sprout or send up new growth, or to cause a plant to grow and bring forth fruit.
article: βλαστάnω is a farming word for plant life breaking into growth. Most often it is intransitive — the wheat sprouts (Matthew 13:26) — but Greek of the later period also let it work transitively, meaning to make something grow, as in James 5:18 where the earth "yielded" its crop. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, where related forms describe pruning off young shoots and even speak of children as the "shoots" of a household; in the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew words for sprouting and growing, including צָמַח.
caution: Only 4 New Testament occurrences, two of them absorbed into broader phrasing, so the measured English renderings rest on thin evidence.

definition: An adverb meaning all around or surrounding something, often used to describe what encircles a place or object.
article: κύκλῳ is technically the dative form of κύκλος ("a ring or circle"), but in practice it functions as an adverb meaning "around" or "round about." The Byzantine New Testament uses it 8 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "around" in every case, sometimes with the sense of surrounding or encircling. It is extremely common in the Septuagint (211 times), where it almost always translates the Hebrew word סָבִיב ("around"), and everyday papyri confirm the same usage—one document even speaks of digging "a deep trench round" an oil-press.

definition: Thomas, one of Jesus' twelve apostles, also called Didymus, meaning "the twin."
article: Θωμᾶς is the name of Thomas, one of Jesus' twelve disciples, appearing 11 times across the New Testament and always rendered simply "Thomas." The name comes from a Semitic word for "twin," which is why he is also called Didymus (the Greek word for twin) in John's Gospel. Interestingly, this "twin" name shows up beyond the Bible too—Moulton-Milligan notes it was used as a personal name in Phoenician inscriptions.

definition: To live together as husband and wife, sharing a home in marriage.
senseLabels: live together as husband and wife
article: συνοικέω literally means to dwell together as a family, and in everyday Koine it became the standard term for a married couple sharing a household. The New Testament uses it just once, in 1 Peter 3:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "treat" (as in how a husband treats his wife) even though the word's core meaning is simply living together in marriage. Marriage contracts from the papyri make this vivid: one document records a woman pledging to "live with you as your lawful wedded wife," and another asks whether a couple "wished to live together."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and the standard rendering ("treat") differing from the word's measured "dwell together" sense, confidence is low.

definition: A place to stay or dwell — a room, lodging, or home where someone resides.
article: μονή comes from the verb μένω ("to remain, stay") and means a place where one stays — a room, lodging, or abode. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in John 14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as "rooms" (John 14:2) and once as "home" (John 14:23). The everyday Koine papyri are especially interesting: there μονή was used as a legal term in sureties guaranteeing a person's appearance, showing the word's practical, ordinary range before its later Christian use for a "monastery."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low-confidence rating, the precise nuance rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Reuben, the eldest son of Jacob and founder of one of Israel's twelve tribes.
article: Ῥουβήν is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Reuben (רְאוּבֵן), the firstborn son of the patriarch Jacob and the tribe descended from him. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 7:5, in the list of the sealed tribes of Israel, but it is common in the Septuagint, occurring 89 times across 9 books. The word is indeclinable in Greek, simply carrying over the Hebrew name.
caution: The displayed translation data labels the single occurrence as "Gad," which conflicts with every dictionary identifying this name as Reuben; treat that label as a data artifact.

definition: To grow up together with something, especially plants sprouting and growing alongside each other at the same time.
article: συμφύω describes plants growing up together at the same time, built from σύν ('with') and φύω ('to grow'). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 8:7, where in the parable of the sower the thorns grow up alongside the seed and choke it. Outside the New Testament it shows up in the Septuagint at Wisdom 13:13 and in classical writers like Plato, where it carries the related sense of causing things to grow together.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: In a way that lacks certainty or clear direction, without a definite aim or target.
article: This adverb describes acting without certainty or a fixed direction—running or moving without a clear goal in view. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 9:26, where Paul says he does not run "uncertainly" but with purpose. Note that the measured data labels the single occurrence as "fight," reflecting the surrounding athletic imagery (running and boxing) rather than the word's own meaning, while the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) consistently define it as "uncertainly" or "without certain aim."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured, and the corpus tag of "fight" reflects context rather than the lexical sense given by Dodson and Abbott-Smith.

definition: Refers to something taken in its entirety—a whole thing, all of it, or every part, whether of an object, group, place, or stretch of time.
article: ὅλος points to completeness: the whole, the entire amount, the full extent. Across 113 New Testament occurrences it splits mainly between "whole" (43%) and "all" (38%), with a further 12% used of something spread "throughout" a place or region. Everyday Koine papyri show the same range—"the whole outlay," "seven whole days," "during the whole winter"—and the Septuagint uses it over 200 times, chiefly for the Hebrew word for "all" (kōl).

definition: A comparison word meaning "just as" or "like," introducing how one thing matches or resembles another.
article: ὥσπερ is a strengthened form of ὡς ("as") that draws a comparison, most often translated "just as" (15× of 42, 60%) and sometimes "like" (6×, 24%). It frequently opens a comparison that pairs with "so" (οὕτως) in the matching clause, as in "just as... so also." In about 17 of its 42 New Testament appearances it gets absorbed into the English phrasing without a word of its own, and the everyday Koine papyri confirm this same comparing sense — one physician pleads to be exempted from duties "like myself" (P Fay 106).

definition: An adverb meaning to do something without fear, freely and unafraid.
article: ἀφόβως simply means "without fear" and is built from the negative prefix a- attached to the word for fear (φόβος). All four New Testament uses carry this same meaning — whether serving God without fear, working or speaking the message fearlessly, or (in Jude 12) people feasting without fear. The lexicons agree completely, and the Septuagint uses it once at Proverbs 1:33 for living securely; a third-century papyrus even pairs it with "boldly," capturing the sense of confident freedom from fear.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is limited, though the sources agree on its meaning.

definition: An Aramaic-influenced Hebrew cry meaning "my God," spoken by Jesus on the cross.
article: ἠλί is not really a Greek word but a transliteration of the Hebrew for "my God," carried over into the New Testament text. It appears just twice in the Byzantine text (three times in the critical SBLGNT), all in Matthew 27:46, where Jesus cries out from the cross. Abbott-Smith ties it directly to the Hebrew אֵל ("God") with a possessive ending, and points readers to the parallel form ἐλωΐ used elsewhere.
caution: This is a transliterated Hebrew exclamation with very few occurrences and a low confidence tier, so its handling is more about quotation than ordinary Greek vocabulary.

definition: To make war, fight in battle, or engage in armed conflict—and figuratively, to quarrel.
article: πολεμέω means to make war or fight, whether in literal battle or figurative conflict. In the New Testament it appears only 7 times, six of them in Revelation describing warfare, while James 4:2 stretches it to private quarreling among people. It's a heavily used Septuagint word (165 times), almost always rendering Hebrew לָחַם ("to fight," 114 times); notably, the everyday Koine papyri show it construed with μετά ("war with")—as in a 5th-century document and a 6th-century inscription—so this construction in Revelation reflects ordinary Greek usage, not a Hebraism.
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences, the measured senses are thin, and most simply reflect the single core idea of waging war rendered with slightly different English wording.

definition: The day before today; yesterday.
article: Χθές is a simple time adverb meaning "yesterday." Although the digest lists three measured renderings—"yesterday" in John 4:52, "killed yesterday" in Acts 7:28, and "same yesterday" in Hebrews 13:8—these all reflect the one core meaning, just colored by the surrounding words. In the Septuagint it appears 32 times across 11 books, usually translating the Hebrew תְּמוֹל; it could also be paired with "third day" (LXX Ruth 2:11) to mean "in times past." Everyday Koine papyri confirm the same plain usage, as in an Oxyrhynchus document referring to "the evening time of yesterday."
caution: This word appears only 3 times in the Byzantine NT (and none in the SBL critical text), and the alternate form ἐχθές was actually more common in Koine.

definition: To go ahead of someone, leading the way or going before them as a guide or herald.
article: This verb means to travel out in front of someone, whether as a guide, a herald, or simply moving on ahead. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke's writings (Luke 1:76 and Acts 7:40), but it is very common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 32 times and most often renders the Hebrew הָלַך ("to walk, go"), five times. The word also turns up in everyday documents, including a temple account from Oxyrhynchus where temple-attendants are described as "going before."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise shade of meaning leans heavily on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: Deep grief or mourning, the sorrow felt over loss or distress.
article: πένθος is the noun for deep grief or mourning—the heavy sorrow of loss. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, rendered as "grief" 3× and "mourn" 2×, and the Septuagint uses it 33 times, mostly to translate the Hebrew word אֵבֶל ("mourning"). A vivid everyday example comes from the papyri: a man writes of his πένθος over the death of his daughter's husband, showing the word's plain use for personal grief.

definition: A person from Gadara, a Hellenized town southeast of the Sea of Galilee, used to describe the region's inhabitants.
article: Γαδαρηνός simply means someone who lived in or near Gadara, an important Hellenized town belonging to the Decapolis, southeast of the Sea of Galilee. It appears 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, always describing the region where Jesus encountered the demon-possessed man. Interestingly, the manuscript tradition is unsettled here: Abbott-Smith notes that the major critical editions read 'Gerasenes' (Γερασηνῶν) instead at Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26, 37, and 'Gergesenes' at Matthew 8:28, which is why the critical text counts only 1 occurrence.
caution: Confidence is low: this is a place-name with few occurrences, and the manuscripts disagree sharply, with critical editions preferring 'Gerasenes' or 'Gergesenes' instead.

definition: Malchus, the name of the high priest's servant whose ear Peter cut off when Jesus was arrested.
article: Μάλχος is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, at John 18:10, where it identifies the high priest's servant whom Peter struck with a sword. Abbott-Smith notes it is a Hellenistic form of the Hebrew word מֶלֶךְ ("king"), and Moulton-Milligan points to a comparable Semitic name in a second-century military letter, showing the name was at home in everyday Koine-era usage. Because it is a proper name, it carries no range of meaning beyond identifying this one person.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the evidence is limited to a single passage.

definition: A person who makes tents, working with the fabric or materials used to build them.
article: σκηνοποιός describes someone whose trade is making tents, formed from the words for "tent" and "make." It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:3, where it describes Paul's occupation, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "tentmakers" every time. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it was a normal term for an ordinary trade. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that scholars like Ramsay and Nestle discussed alternative renderings such as "landscape-painter" or "shoemaker," but concluded there is no good reason to abandon the standard "tentmaker."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and some scholars have debated whether it might mean something other than tentmaker, though the standard rendering is well supported.

definition: A false statement or claim that contradicts the truth; a lie.
article: ψεῦδος means a lie or falsehood, and the New Testament consistently sets it in direct contrast to the truth (ἡ ἀλήθεια), as in Romans 1:25 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "lie" in 5 of its 10 occurrences, with the rest absorbed into phrasing or given related terms like "falsehood." In the Septuagint it appears 25 times, most often translating the Hebrew word shéqer (6×) for falsehood, and everyday Koine papyri show the same plain sense — one B.C. 110 document insists "there is no lie in the oath."

definition: Hot or boiling, used figuratively in Revelation for someone spiritually fervent rather than indifferent.
article: ζεστός means literally boiling hot, derived from the verb ζέω (to boil). All 3 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament appear in a single passage, Revelation 3:15–16, where it is used figuratively to describe spiritual fervor as opposed to being lukewarm. Abbott-Smith notes the word also turns up in the Greek translations by Aquila and Symmachus at Leviticus, and in the geographer Strabo, confirming its ordinary sense of physical heat outside the Bible.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only in one Revelation passage, so the metaphorical "fervent" sense rests on a single context rather than broad measured usage.

definition: Describing a person who is devout, reverent, and carefully attentive toward God.
article: εὐλαβής literally means "taking hold well" — carefully or cautiously — and from that root it came to describe someone who is reverent and devout toward God. In the New Testament it appears only a handful of times (3 in the Byzantine text, 4 in the critical text), and the Majority Standard Bible's renderings show the religious sense at work, as in Acts 8:2. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it stands behind Hebrew words like nazar (to separate/consecrate), and in later Koine its superlative form εὐλαβέστατος became a standard honorific title for clergy in papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin — only a few NT occurrences and two in the Septuagint — and lexica split between an older "cautious, circumspect" sense and the "devout" sense the NT measurements favor.

definition: A stated reason offered to justify or disguise an action, usually a false front masking the real motive.
article: πρόφασις is the outward reason given for doing something, and it usually points to a pretense rather than the genuine motive behind an act. Across its 7 Byzantine New Testament uses the word rarely surfaces as a single English word—it was rendered "preached" only once and was absorbed into surrounding phrasing the other 6 times—so its sense lives in context, as in Philippians 1:18 where Paul contrasts preaching from "pretext" versus "truth." Moulton-Milligan confirms this from everyday Koine papyri, citing a Tebtunis document where officials refuse to accept force or "any pretext whatsoever," matching the classic "ostensible-but-false reason" idea found in the older lexicons.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and the word usually absorbed into phrasing rather than translated directly, the single measured rendering "preached" reflects context, not the word's core meaning of pretext.

definition: Zerubbabel, an Israelite leader listed in Jesus' genealogy as the son of Shealtiel and father of Abiud and Rhesa.
article: Ζοροβάβελ is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Zerubbabel, and the New Testament uses it just one way — as a personal name in Jesus' family line, appearing 3 times across Matthew and Luke, always rendered "Zerubbabel." The name comes straight from Hebrew זְרֻבָּבֶל and shows up 22 times in the Septuagint, where it names this same Israelite leader (as in 1 Chronicles 3:19). As a borrowed name it is indeclinable in Greek, though the historian Josephus used a Greek-inflected form, Ζοροβάβηλος.

definition: In a sparing or stingy way — giving or using little, holding back rather than being generous.
article: This adverb means doing something sparingly or stingily, holding back rather than giving freely. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in the same verse (2 Corinthians 9:6), where Paul contrasts sowing sparingly with sowing generously. The word is rare overall — Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and in Plutarch, who uses it of using sparingly what one already has.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only in a single New Testament verse and is rare elsewhere, so its full range cannot be confidently mapped.

definition: To destroy something completely or wear it out, and figuratively to corrupt or morally ruin a person or thing.
article: διαφθείρω describes a thorough, completed process of damage — destroying, wearing out, or in a moral sense corrupting. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times across 4 books, mostly for outright destruction (60%), but it also carries the figurative sense of moral corruption, as Abbott-Smith notes for those "corrupted in mind" (1 Timothy 6:5) and for corrupting the earth (Revelation 11:18). It is a heavily used Septuagint word (66 times), where it most often renders the Hebrew shachat, "to ruin"; everyday papyri use it bluntly for the death of livestock, like sheep and camels that "perished" after a census count.
caution: Roughly 2 of the 7 New Testament occurrences are absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, so the measured sense breakdown rests on a small set of clear cases.

definition: To slip in secretly or sneak into a group without being noticed.
article: This verb describes slipping in quietly and unnoticed, as someone who works their way into a group by stealth. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Jude 1:4) and isn't in the critical text at all, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "crept," matching the King James phrase "creep in unawares." Moulton-Milligan note that the word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and a related form (παρείσακτος) need not always carry a sinister meaning, though here it does.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: A Greek or Gentile woman, that is, a non-Jewish woman of Greek background.
article: Ἑλληνίς is the feminine form of Ἕλλην ("Greek"), describing a woman who is Greek or, more broadly, a non-Jewish Gentile woman. It appears only twice in the New Testament, in Mark 7:26 and Acts 17:12, and both times the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "Greek" (100%), with the BSB independently agreeing. The word is also attested in everyday Koine: a papyrus from 161 B.C. records a legal complaint opening "Thus says the Greek woman Ammonia."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the sources fully agree on the meaning.

definition: To set your mind on something, having a certain attitude, opinion, or outlook that shapes how you think and act.
senseLabels: to hold a view or opinion
to focus the mind on things
to be set in one's mind
article: φρονέω is about the direction your mind takes — not just thinking a thought, but having an attitude, outlook, or settled opinion that points you a certain way. It appears 29 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and translators handle it flexibly: about 14% as "view" and 14% as "think," with many other phrasings like "set your mind on" or "be of one mind," and in 7 of 29 cases it simply melts into the surrounding wording with no English word of its own. Everyday papyri show the same practical flavor — one document has a woman who "changed her mind" (φρονήσασα), left the oil mill, and walked out, capturing the sense of one's thinking taking a new direction.
caution: Because the meaning shades from "think" to "be disposed toward" depending on context, no single rendering dominates, so the right English wording varies passage by passage.

definition: A stand or holder that raises a lamp so its light can shine across a room.
article: λυχνία refers to the stand or holder on which an oil lamp was placed so its light could spread widely. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "lampstand" 7 times (58%) and "stand" 3 times (25%), but both point to the same object — the difference is just phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 31 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew מְנֹרָה (28×), the term for the tabernacle's lampstand, and Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday papyri and inscriptions as early as 284 BC, even describing an iron lampstand.

definition: To an extreme or intensified degree — exceedingly, all the more, or even louder.
article: This adverb pushes the intensity of an action up a notch, covering ideas like 'exceedingly,' 'all the more,' and 'even more.' Its range is fairly wide: across 16 Byzantine occurrences it gets rendered as 'even' 5 times (42%), 'more' 3 times (25%), and 'all louder' twice (17%), while 4 times it disappears into the phrasing with no English word of its own. The everyday papyri preserve a sharper everyday feel — one early letter uses it to mean 'unnecessarily, superfluously' ('you wrote to me needlessly about the wages'), while another uses it for plain 'exceedingly.'
caution: Translations vary widely and the word often dissolves into surrounding phrasing, so its force depends heavily on context rather than a fixed meaning.

definition: A loud cry or shout, especially a call for help or an outcry against injustice.
article: βοή means a loud cry or shout — typically a call for aid or an outcry. It appears only once in the New Testament, in James 5:4, where the cries of cheated harvesters reach God's ears. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times across 6 books, most often translating the Hebrew צְעָקָה ("cry" or "outcry"), which fits the sense of crying out against wrongdoing.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the single measured rendering reflects one context rather than a tested range.

definition: A craftsman who works metal, especially a smith who shapes copper or bronze.
senseLabels: a worker in copper or bronze
article: χαλκεύς names a metalworker—literally someone who works χαλκός (copper or bronze), often rendered "coppersmith." It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 4:14, where Alexander the coppersmith "did harm." The word was ordinary, everyday vocabulary: papyri preserve it in a tax list naming "Ophelion the smith" and in a letter complaining that "the smith is a long way from us." In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times across 5 books, translating several different Hebrew words for craftsmen and metalworkers.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise metal intended (copper versus bronze) can't be pinned down from the evidence.

definition: A Hebrew name-title meaning "God with us," applied to the promised child of Isaiah's prophecy and to Christ.
article: Ἐμμανουήλ is a transliterated Hebrew name, עִמָּנוּאֵל, meaning "God with us." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Matthew 1:23, which quotes Isaiah 7:14 directly from the Septuagint, where the word also occurs only once. Notably, in its single New Testament use the name is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone English word, since Matthew himself supplies the explanation "God with us."
caution: Evidence is very thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, both as a name drawn from Isaiah 7:14.

definition: A word marking that one event happened earlier than another — "before" something else occurred.
article: πρίν is a time-marker meaning "before," connecting one event to another that follows it; in the Byzantine New Testament it appears 14 times and is rendered "before" in 9 of them (64%). It works both as an adverb and as a conjunction, often paired with ἤ ("before that"), as in Jesus' prediction that Peter would deny him "before the rooster crows." In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew word טֶ֫רֶם ("not yet, before"), 20 of 28 times, and everyday papyri use it freely — one Oxyrhynchus letter has a writer say "as I asked you before."

definition: To stir people up into turmoil — unsettling, upsetting, or driving them out of their settled state.
article: This verb means to throw people or a situation into upheaval, whether by causing public disorder or by upsetting someone's settled life. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times across 2 books, always woven into the phrasing rather than translated as a single English word, covering both political tumult and the disruption caused by false teaching. The most striking evidence comes from the papyri: a private letter from A.D. 41 uses it to mean "drive us out" of home, and a boy's letter writes "he quite upsets me" — showing it was living, everyday Koine, even though Grimm noted it appears nowhere in classical authors.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 NT uses and a single Septuagint occurrence (Daniel 7:23, rendering Hebrew דּוּשׁ) — so confidence is low.

definition: A Latin Roman name appearing only in "Appii Forum," a town on the Appian Way south of Rome.
article: Ἄππιος is a Latin Roman name that appears in the New Testament only as part of the place name "Appii Forum" (Market of Appius), a town in Italy that Paul's traveling party reaches in Acts 28:15. It shows up just once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the SBLGNT critical edition, and in that single use it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. According to the lexicons, this market town stood on the Appian Way about 43 Roman miles from Rome.
caution: This is a rare proper name appearing only once, absorbed into a place name, so the evidence is very thin and confidence is low.

definition: To permit someone to do something, or to leave a thing or situation alone without interfering.
article: ἐάω is the everyday verb for permitting an action or leaving something undisturbed. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times, rendered "let" in 5 cases (63%) and "allow" in 2 (25%), with the remaining 4 absorbed into the surrounding English phrasing. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one document permits people "to use the pastures," another allows a man "to carry off 28 artabae" while "leaving the rest under the seals" — showing both the "permit" and "leave alone" sides of the word. Abbott-Smith notes a related nautical sense "to leave" in Acts 27:40, where the sailors leave the anchors.

definition: To make a serious, eager effort to do something, working at it diligently and without delay.
article: σπουδάζω describes putting real energy and earnestness into a task — making every effort, being diligent, and acting promptly. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "make every effort" in 86% of its 11 New Testament uses, and the BSB agrees 100% of the time. The word's root sense includes speed: in the Septuagint it usually translates the Hebrew בָּהַל (6 of 8 times), which carries the idea of haste or urgency, and everyday Koine papyri show people using it to urge one another to "see to it" that something gets done quickly.

definition: To guide or set something on a straight, right course, usually God directing people's hearts, steps, or paths.
article: κατευθύνω literally means to make fully straight, and figuratively to direct or guide someone or something onto the right course. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, and the Majority Standard Bible counts just one clear English rendering ("direct") in 2 Thessalonians 3:5, with the other two occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The word is common in the Septuagint (50 times across 14 books), where it translates several Hebrew verbs including יָשַׁר and כּוּן, and Moulton-Milligan note a fitting parallel in Aristeas where God "directs" people's actions and plans.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the measured English evidence is thin, though the Septuagint and lexicons agree on its meaning.

definition: The forehead, the front part of the face above the eyes.
article: μέτωπον simply means the forehead, the area of the face above the eyes. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "foreheads" in 7 of its 8 New Testament occurrences (88%), all in Revelation, where it is the place where people are marked or sealed. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times and always translates the Hebrew word מֵצַח (mētsach), also "forehead." Notably, the everyday papyri use the word in physical descriptions of people and in references to branding the foreheads of slaves and soldiers, which sheds light on Revelation's imagery of marking.

definition: The superlative of "great," meaning greatest or very great, often used to intensify rather than to compare.
article: μέγιστος is the superlative form of μέγας ("great"), and in the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Peter 1:4, where it functions as an intensifier ("very great") rather than a true comparison. Moulton-Milligan note that this superlative was already fairly rare in Hellenistic Greek, surviving mainly as a grand epithet for gods. The papyri bear this out: a 120 B.C. document calls Hera "the greatest goddess," and an inscription praises a king as "first and greatest" of the kings of Thrace.
caution: Evidence is very thin: the word appears only once in the New Testament and no measured senses are recorded, so its precise range rests largely on classical and papyri parallels.

definition: To dig into the ground, such as excavating a hole, pit, or foundation.
article: ὀρύσσω means simply to dig or excavate in the earth. In all 3 New Testament occurrences it is rendered "dug" (100%), used for digging a winepress (Matthew 21:33), a pit beneath one (Mark 12:1), and a hole in the ground to hide money (Matthew 25:18). The word was common in everyday Koine: the papyri show people paid "to those who dug the foundation" and even instructions to dig around acanthus trees, while in the Septuagint (28×) it most often translates the Hebrew חָפַר, "to dig."
caution: Only 3 New Testament occurrences, so the measured sense rests on thin evidence, though the broader Koine and Septuagint usage agrees.

definition: The act of finishing or completing something, such as a building project carried through to the end.
article: ἀπαρτισμός refers to the completion or finishing of something undertaken. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 14:28, where Jesus speaks of someone building a tower and counting whether he has enough to finish it. The everyday Koine papyri back this up nicely: one document uses it for the 'completion of an audit,' and another for finishing construction work, showing the word was at home in ordinary business and building contexts.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force rests largely on the few papyri examples.

definition: To serve as an official representative or ambassador who speaks on behalf of another.
article: In the New Testament πρεσβεύω means to act as an ambassador, used both times (2 Corinthians 5:20 and Ephesians 6:20) of representing God or Christ. Classical lexica note an older sense — "to be the elder" or "to take precedence" — reflecting its link to the word for an older man, but the measured New Testament usage renders it "ambassadors" 100% of the time. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan show this was the standard term in the Greek East for the Emperor's official legate, as in a letter of Claudius naming the men who "were serving as ambassadors."
caution: With only 2 occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though both uses agree and the documentary parallels are clear.

definition: To please someone well, or to be pleasing to them—often with the sense of doing good that wins approval.
article: In the New Testament this verb appears only 3 times, all in Hebrews, where it consistently means being well-pleasing—especially to God (Hebrews 11:5-6) or, in the passive, God being well pleased with our actions (Hebrews 13:16). The Septuagint uses it 13 times, notably for the Hebrew verb meaning 'to walk,' as in the descriptions of Enoch and Noah who 'walked with God' (Genesis 5:22, 24)—so the idea of pleasing God is tied to faithfully walking with him. Dodson suggests it can carry the added sense of rendering good service, and the word also shows up in everyday Koine, including a marriage contract from Egypt.

definition: A cowardly fearfulness or timidity — a shrinking, faint-hearted fear, never used in a positive sense.
article: δειλία refers to cowardice or timidity — a fearfulness that holds someone back, and the lexicons note it is never used in a good sense, unlike the more neutral φόβος ("fear"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 1:7, and four times in the Septuagint, where it translates several Hebrew words for dread or sluggishness. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan found the word in everyday Koine papyri, including one document (A.D. 215) referring to a "charge of cowardice" (δειλίας αἰτία), showing it was ordinary, real-world vocabulary.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse plus a handful of Septuagint and papyri examples.

definition: A symbolic place-name in Revelation, the site where kings are gathered for the final battle.
article: Armageddon appears just once in the entire New Testament, at Revelation 16:16, where it names the place kings are gathered for battle. Strong's and Abbott-Smith identify it as a symbolic name from Hebrew, combining 'har' (mountain) with Megiddo, the place that appears in the Septuagint as Magedon (2 Chronicles 35:22) and Magedo (Judges 1:27). The exact spelling is itself debated: the received text reads Ἀρμαγεδδών, while Westcott-Hort split it into Ἅρ Μαγεδών.
caution: This is a single-occurrence name with disputed spelling and an uncertain underlying Hebrew form, so its precise meaning cannot be settled from the evidence.

definition: The ordinal number meaning fifth, marking the item that comes after the fourth in a sequence.
article: πέμπτος is simply the ordinal "fifth," derived from πέντε (five). It appears 4 times in the New Testament, all in Revelation, where it marks the fifth seal, the fifth angel, the fifth bowl, and the fifth foundation stone, and renders the Hebrew חֲמִישִׁי 36 times in the Septuagint. The everyday Koine papyri show it in mundane settings—one document records a woman seeking permission to transfer "the fifth part" (πέμπτον μέρος) of a house property, while another assigns a prophet a fifth of temple revenues.
caution: The one rendering "fifth that upheld" (Rev 6:9, 25%) just reflects the surrounding translation rather than a separate meaning of the word itself, which always means "fifth."

definition: A fragrant aromatic substance, the powder of a scented wood, used to prepare bodies for burial.
article: Aloe was a fragrant aromatic, the powdered scented wood used in burial preparations. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 19:39, where it is mixed with myrrh to wrap Jesus' body — which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the phrase "mixture." The word is of foreign origin, and in the Septuagint it shows up in Song of Solomon 4:14, corresponding to the Hebrew word for aloes (אֲהָלִים).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single burial context.

definition: To do what is good, whether as a general way of living rightly or as a kind act done to benefit someone.
article: This verb literally combines "good" with "do," and it means simply to do good. The evidence shows two main shades that overlap: doing good as a general duty or way of life (especially in 1 Peter), and doing good for someone else's benefit (as in the Gospel debates over healing on the Sabbath, Mark 3:4 and Luke 6:9). Abbott-Smith notes it can even take a person as its object, as in Luke 6:33 and 35, meaning to do good to specific people. In the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew yatab, "to do well or make good."

definition: To stretch out or extend something, most often a hand, reaching it toward a person or object.
article: ἐκτείνω means to stretch out or extend, and in the New Testament it almost always describes someone stretching out a hand—to heal, to point, or to act. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "stretch out" or "reach out" in the great majority of its 16 occurrences, and the underlying idea stays consistent across them. In the Septuagint it appears 124 times, most often translating the Hebrew נָטָה (43×), "to stretch out." A vivid touch from the papyri: a sepulchral inscription uses it for a corpse that "stretched out its legs" in death, showing the word's plain physical sense in everyday Koine.

definition: An act of rebuke or reproof that exposes someone's wrong and calls it out.
article: ἔλεγξις refers to a rebuke that exposes wrongdoing — the noun form of the verb ἐλέγχω, "to expose or correct." It is extremely rare, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament (2 Peter 2:16) and twice in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew word שִׂיחַ ("complaint" or "plea," in Job 21:4 and 23:2). The translation data flags it as "otherwise" in 2 Peter 2:16, which simply reflects how the surrounding phrase is rendered rather than the word's core meaning; the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) consistently give "rebuke, reproof, refutation."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, evidence is thin, and the measured rendering "otherwise" reflects phrasing rather than the word's lexical sense of "rebuke."

definition: The number one — a single person or thing, often standing in contrast to many or used as an ordinary indefinite "a" or "someone."
article: εἷς is simply the cardinal number "one," and the data is overwhelmingly consistent: of its 346 Byzantine New Testament occurrences, it's rendered "one" in 252 cases (99%), with the Berean Standard Bible independently agreeing 98% of the time. Notably, 92 of those 346 occurrences get absorbed into English phrasing without a word of their own — Greek uses εἷς where English just says "a" or "someone." In the Septuagint it appears 877 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for "one" (אֶחָד, 740×), and the everyday papyri show it counting wristbands ("one scarlet and one purple") and even doing duty as an ordinal, as in dating documents to "the first day."

definition: The Greek phrase meaning "you are" — the second person singular present of the verb "to be."
article: This is simply the form of the Greek verb "to be" (εἰμί) that means "you are," addressed to one person. Like the English verb "to be," the parent verb covers existence, presence, identity, and what happens or takes place. Abbott-Smith lays out this wide range — from "to exist" (as in John 1:1) to "to be present" or "to come," and even impersonal uses like "there is."
caution: The digest reports zero occurrences of this exact form in the Byzantine New Testament, so all evidence here comes from the parent verb εἰμί rather than measured uses of εἶ itself.

definition: To look upward, or to gain or recover the ability to see.
article: ἀναβλέπω combines "up" (ἀνά) with "see" (βλέπω), and the two meanings track those parts: physically lifting the eyes upward, and—by extension—having sight given or restored. In the Byzantine NT it leans toward the healing sense, with "received sight" the most common rendering at 9 of 26 occurrences (35%), while plain "up"/"looked up" covers the literal looking-up. A striking parallel comes from the papyri: a second-century inscription describes a blind man who "looked up" (ἀνέβλεψεν) and recovered his sight in a temple, using the word exactly as John 9 does. In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew נָשָׂא, "to lift up."

definition: Light in weight and therefore easy to carry or bear.
article: ἐλαφρός describes something light in weight and so easy to carry, whether a literal load or a figurative burden. The New Testament uses it just twice: Jesus calls his yoke "easy" (Matthew 11:30), and Paul speaks of "light affliction" (2 Corinthians 4:17). One charming detail comes from the papyri and inscriptions, where the word appears literally — a breastplate bought because it was "very light" so as not to tire its wearer, and a tombstone wish, "may the earth be light upon you."

definition: A young sheep, especially one used for sacrifice; used in the New Testament as an image for Christ.
