Across its 8 New Testament uses the measured renderings split evenly between active care or leadership ("giving," as in Romans 12:8) and managing one's own household (1 Timothy 3:4-5). Moulton-Milligan notes that the word's everyday spread in the papyri, plus its placement in 1 Thessalonians 5:12 alongside "laboring" and "admonishing," makes it practically certain this was not a fixed title of office but a flexible verb of leading and caring.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and lexicons stretching from "give attention to" to "rule," the precise force in any given verse can be hard to pin down.

definition: Berea, a city in the Roman province of Macedonia, visited by Paul on his missionary travels.
article: Béroia is the proper name of a city in Macedonia, appearing only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 17 (verses 10 and 13), where Paul and Silas traveled there. It is consistently rendered "Berea" in English translations, and the two occurrences differ only in the surrounding wording, not in meaning. The name may derive from a word meaning "the region beyond the coast-line," though this etymology is uncertain.
caution: With only two occurrences and a single, undisputed meaning as a place name, the evidence is thin but unambiguous.

definition: Sharper or more cutting than something else, used to compare how keenly something slices.
article: This is the comparative form of τομός ("sharp"), meaning "sharper" or "more cutting." In the New Testament it appears only once, in Hebrews 4:12, where it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word, and Strong's notes it suggests a decisive single stroke rather than repeated hacking. The everyday Koine flavor shows up in the papyri: a third-century B.C. fragment (PSI VI.624) uses τομώτερον in connection with the cultivation of vines.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin papyri evidence, the precise force of the word is hard to pin down.

definition: Describing someone or something that misleads others; as a noun, a deceiver or impostor who leads people astray.
article: πλάνος appears 5 times in the New Testament and works as both an adjective meaning "misleading" and a noun meaning "a deceiver or impostor." The translations cluster tightly around the idea of deception—"deceiver," "seducing"—and the lexicons agree, though Abbott-Smith preserves an older, more literal sense of "wandering," which fits Strong's image of a roving tramp. Notably, the word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and in the astrologer Vettius Valens, who pairs it with "magicians" and "diviners" (μάγους πλάνους θύτας), suggesting it carried a flavor of charlatans and fraudulent religious figures.
caution: Evidence is thin with only 5 NT occurrences (2 absorbed into phrasing) and 2 in the Septuagint, so the precise range stays uncertain.

definition: The number a thousand, used as a plural adjective to count people, years, or other things.
article: χίλιοι is simply the cardinal number "a thousand," used as an adjective agreeing with whatever it counts. Its meaning is stable and narrow: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "thousand" in 5 of 11 New Testament occurrences (63%), with the remaining cases absorbed into longer numeric phrasing rather than carrying a separate English word. In the Septuagint it appears 99 times and almost always translates the Hebrew אֶלֶף ("thousand," 86×), and everyday Koine papyri show the same plain commercial usage—one document records buying "the thousand bundles for fifteen drachmae."

definition: To search out something thoroughly and carefully, examining it in close, minute detail.
article: ἐξερευνάω means to search something out carefully and minutely — not a quick glance but a thorough investigation. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (1 Peter 1:10), where the prophets "searched" intently into salvation, but it's far more common in the Septuagint, showing up 20 times and rendering Hebrew words like חָפַשׂ (to seek out) and חָקַר (to examine). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way, and one striking parallel in the Psalms of Solomon has God "searching out" a people's offspring so none escape, capturing that sense of exhaustive scrutiny.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and that verse absent from the critical text, the sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than New Testament usage.

definition: More eagerly or urgently; doing something with greater diligence or haste than otherwise.
article: This is the comparative form of an adverb meaning to act with eagerness, zeal, and diligence. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Philippians 2:28), and even there it carries no English word of its own — translators fold it into the surrounding phrasing. The lexicons agree it adds intensity ("more earnestly," "with special urgency"), though Strong's leans toward the idea of speed ("more speedily, sooner") while Abbott-Smith and Dodson stress eagerness and zeal.
caution: This word occurs only once and the sources disagree on whether it stresses speed or eagerness, so confidence is low.

definition: Low or lowly, whether in social position or in attitude — modest and unassuming rather than proud or self-exalting.
article: Across its 8 New Testament uses, the Byzantine text consistently means "humble," rendered that way in 6 of 8 occurrences (75%), and the BSB agrees 100%. The word literally describes something low-lying and stretches from social lowliness — "those of low degree" set against the powerful in Luke 1:52 — to a humble disposition of heart, as in Jesus's self-description in Matthew 11:29. Interestingly, classical Greek often used it in a negative, demeaning sense, and the papyri preserve that edge: P.Oxy I.79 warns against doing anything "mean or ignoble" (tapeinón), whereas the New Testament gives the word an honorable meaning. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew words for the lowly, afflicted, and oppressed (שָׁפָל, עָנִי, עָנָו).
caution: The same word that means "humble" honorably in the New Testament could carry a slighting, negative sense in classical Greek and the papyri, so its tone depends heavily on context.

definition: To stay or continue steadily over time, whether a person standing firm or a thing lasting unchanged.
article: διαμένω means to keep on staying — to remain, continue, or endure rather than change or disappear. Of its 5 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "remain" twice (as in Galatians 2:5 and Hebrews 1:11) and once describes those who "stood" by Jesus through his trials (Luke 22:28), with two further uses absorbed into surrounding phrasing. A papyrus from 113 B.C. captures the everyday flavor vividly, complaining that someone "still continues in the same miserable course" — the same sense of stubbornly staying put.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and two of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured English renderings rest on thin data.

definition: Insincere praise used to win someone over, usually for the flatterer's own advantage or gain.
article: κολακεία means flattery — excessive or false praise aimed at influencing another person, typically for selfish ends. The word appears just once in the New Testament (1 Thessalonians 2:5), where Paul denies ever using such tactics. Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and that it carries the idea of the manipulative methods by which one person tries to gain influence over another, much like the self-serving rhetoricians of the day.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: To fill something completely, often used of being filled with wine to the point of drunkenness.
article: μεστόω means to fill up or fill completely, built from the adjective μεστός ("full"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 2:13, where onlookers accuse the disciples of being "filled with new wine" — which is why the Majority Standard Bible's rendering effectively captures the charge of being drunk (counted here as "mocked" in the data, the scene of mockery). The word also surfaces in everyday Koine papyri and in the Didache, where speech is described as "fulfilled by deed" (μεμεστωμένος πράξει), and Moulton-Milligan notes its use by medical writers.
caution: This verb occurs only once in the New Testament and just twice in the Septuagint, so its range in the biblical text rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To wrap or wind something around a person or object, such as wrapping a body in cloth.
article: This verb means to wrap, roll, or wind something around something else. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 15:46, where Joseph wraps Jesus' body in linen cloth, and once in the Septuagint translating the Hebrew lut. The everyday papyri show a striking range of nuance: people "worming themselves" into official positions, the heat of a violent struggle, or simply the neutral act of a fabric being wound up.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: A look or glance — the act of seeing, and by extension what the eyes perceive.
senseLabels: a look or what is seen
article: βλέμμα comes from the verb βλέπω ("to see") and refers to a look or glance — the seeing eye and what it takes in. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:8, where it is paired with hearing ("sight and hearing"). Interestingly, an Oxyrhynchus papyrus of the second century AD uses the word in a vivid phrase about "the shameless look" of lovers, and Abbott-Smith notes that the precise nuance in 2 Peter is not found in literary Greek but may be recognized in everyday vernacular usage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its exact shade of meaning is uncertain and the lexicons lean on papyri and inference to pin it down.

definition: A community or assembly of people called together, used in the New Testament mainly for a congregation of Christians.
article: In the New Testament ἐκκλησία overwhelmingly means "church" — a community of Christian believers — rendered that way in 109 of 115 occurrences (99%), occasionally as "assembly." The word's range is broader than this single sense suggests: originally it meant any public meeting of citizens summoned by a herald, and the Septuagint used it 80 times for the assembly of Israel, mostly translating the Hebrew קָהָל (65×). Tellingly, in the Gospels it appears only twice (Matthew 16:18 and 18:17), where it points to Christ's new community as distinct from the old.

definition: To travel through or journey across a region, passing from place to place.
article: This verb describes physically traveling through or across an area, built from διά ("through") and ὁδεύω ("to journey"). It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, and lexicons distinguish two shades: traveling *through* a place (Acts 17:1) and traveling *along* through it (Luke 8:1). Everyday papyri confirm this plain sense vividly — a cavalry officer petitions an official about the danger he faced "passing through" certain districts on his way to Thebes.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and the measured rendering reduced to phrasing, the corpus data here is thin and leans on the Septuagint and papyri for its range.

definition: To place something beside or before someone—especially food at a meal—or to hand something over into another's care and keeping.
article: παρατίθημι is built from παρά (beside) and τίθημι (to place), so its core idea is putting something right in front of someone—most often food served at a table. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 19 times, and the Majority Standard Bible most commonly renders it "set before" (43%); it can also mean to "put forth" a parable, as in Matthew 13. The lexicons add an important middle-voice sense not dominant in the measured data: to deposit or entrust something to another's care, as Jesus does in committing his spirit to the Father. A nice everyday glimpse comes from an Oxyrhynchus papyrus (c. A.D. 45) where someone has "set beside" his mother an ink pot.
caution: Almost a third of occurrences (5 of 19) were absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, and the well-attested "entrust" sense from the lexicons appears only as a rare rendering in the measured data.

definition: A miscarriage or premature, lifeless birth — used figuratively for someone born abnormally or at the wrong time.
article: ἔκτρωμα literally means a miscarriage or a baby born dead before its time, from a verb meaning "to miscarry." It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 15:8), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "untimely," and the Septuagint uses it 3 times, including for the Hebrew word נֶפֶל (a stillbirth). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense vividly: one document from A.D. 362 complains that violent men caused a pregnant woman named Taesis to miscarry her child.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise figurative force there rests on thin evidence.

definition: Agrippa, the personal name of Herod Agrippa II, a Jewish king before whom Paul made his defense.
article: This is a proper name appearing 12 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all within Paul's hearing before the king, and rendered "Agrippa" in every case. According to Abbott-Smith, all occurrences refer specifically to Herod Agrippa II (Acts 25:13–26:32). The name itself, by its apparent derivation, combines the Greek words for "wild" and "horse," suggesting a meaning like "wild-horse tamer."

definition: To form a circle around someone or something—surrounding, encircling, or gathering around it.
article: κυκλόω means to encircle or surround, and all its New Testament uses cluster around that single image—whether a crowd standing around Jesus (John 10:24), gathering around the fallen Paul (Acts 14:20), armies surrounding a city (Luke 21:20), or marching around Jericho's walls (Hebrews 11:30) and a camp (Revelation 20:9). It appears just 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament but is common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 72 times, most often translating the Hebrew סָבַב (43×), which also means 'to go around.' Interestingly, the related form κυκλεύω turns up in everyday papyri describing the turning of a water-wheel, capturing the basic idea of moving in a circle.

definition: Literally uncircumcised; used figuratively for people who are stubborn and resistant to God.
article: The word literally means "uncircumcised," and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 7:51) it is used figuratively—Stephen calls his hearers stubborn and resistant in heart and ears, which the Majority Standard Bible renders "stiff." In the Septuagint it occurs 34 times across 12 books, almost always translating the Hebrew עָרֵל ("uncircumcised," 30×), and it sometimes pairs metaphorically with "heart," as in Jeremiah 9:26. Interestingly, scholars suggest this blunt word may have been coined by Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria to express their contempt for the uncircumcised, since Egyptians normally used a milder term.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured New Testament sense rests on a single figurative occurrence.

definition: Describing cloth that is new and unshrunk, not yet washed or treated for finishing.
article: ἄγναφος describes fabric that is fresh off the loom — new, uncarded, and not yet shrunk. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21), both times in Jesus' saying about not sewing a piece of new cloth onto an old garment, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it "patch" both times. Everyday papyri confirm the sense vividly: one second-century document lists a stolen "new white shirt" (κιτῶν ἄγναφος), showing this was ordinary language for unwashed new garments.
caution: The word occurs only twice in the New Testament, so its measured range is thin and rests heavily on outside evidence from papyri and lexica.

definition: To send for someone, summoning or inviting them to come from elsewhere.
article: μεταπέμπω means to send for someone, summoning them to come to you — built from μετά ("after") and πέμπω ("send"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times, always in Acts, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sent" 4 of those times, with the other 4 folded into surrounding phrasing. It was common in everyday Koine: a papyrus from AD 23 uses it of being summoned before the Prefect, and another from AD 192 has officials being "sent for" so something could be said in their presence.
caution: It does not appear in the SBLGNT critical text, and its only handful of Septuagint uses translate different Hebrew words, so the measured sense rests on a narrow base.

definition: By common consent or admittedly — pointing to something everyone agrees is true beyond dispute.
article: This adverb, built from the verb meaning "to confess" or "agree," signals that what follows is acknowledged by everyone as true. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 3:16, where the King James Version renders it "without controversy." Everyday Koine papyri from the 2nd century B.C. use the word in legal contexts to mean "admittedly" — for example, where a person's own testimony makes a charge plainly undeniable. Abbott-Smith also notes an older sense, "as agreed" or "conformably with," though the New Testament use carries the "by common consent" meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word, so its precise force rests largely on the papyri and lexical evidence.

definition: An adjective meaning female or belonging to a woman, used to describe something as womanly or characteristic of women.
senseLabels: belonging to or characteristic of women
article: γυναικεῖος is the adjective form of γυνή (woman), meaning "female" or "belonging to a woman." It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "manner" (in a phrase about the wife as the weaker partner). A striking parallel comes from the papyri: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 55 uses the same word when a woman pleads she cannot attend court "owing to womanly weakness," while another papyrus describes a "woman's woolen chiton," showing the word's everyday range from physical clothing to perceived frailty.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To wash inanimate things, especially clothing, by plunging and cleansing them in water.
article: πλύνω means to wash things—not people—and is used especially for laundering clothes or cleaning objects like fishing nets. In the Septuagint it appears 52 times and most often (44×) translates the Hebrew כָּבַס, the standard word for washing garments. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense: a third-century BC Zenon letter uses it for washing flax before weaving, and an early first-century AD medical recipe calls for "purified" (washed) schist. In the New Testament it shows up just once in the Byzantine text (Revelation 7:14, of robes "washed" white), though critical editions count three occurrences.
caution: The word is rare in the New Testament (only 1 Byzantine occurrence), so its New Testament range rests largely on Septuagint and papyri evidence.

definition: Describing a woman who is unable to bear children; childless.
article: This word describes a woman who cannot have children, and every New Testament use refers to exactly that—it appears 4 times in the Byzantine text, always of barren women (Luke 1:7, 1:36, 23:29, Galatians 4:27). In the Septuagint it shows up 14 times across 8 books, almost always translating the Hebrew word ʿaqar (12 of 14 times), the standard term for childlessness. The form is striking for its staying power: Moulton-Milligan notes that steíra survives unchanged in Modern Greek, and the word appears in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions as well.
caution: The three labels listed by the renderings all reflect the single sense "barren"; differences are just sentence context, not distinct meanings.

definition: A respectful title of honor used when addressing a person of high official rank, like "Your Excellency."
article: This word is the superlative form built on κράτος ("strength, power"), and in the New Testament it always works as a polite title of honor rather than a description of physical might. It appears 4 times, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "most excellent" in 3 of those (the fourth is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing); both Luke's dedication and Paul's speeches before Roman officials use it this way. Strikingly, the everyday Koine papyri show the exact same usage — it was the standard honorific for prefects, procurators, and other exalted officials, much like our "Your Excellency."
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the evidence is thin, though the papyri strongly confirm the honorific use.

definition: At the same time or together with, marking that actions or people happen or belong closely alongside one another.
article: ἅμα points to things happening at the same moment or in close association — "together" or "at once." It works as an adverb, as a preposition with the dative ("together with"), and even in time phrases like "early in the morning" (Matthew 20:1). In the Byzantine NT it appears 10 times, rendered "together" in 3 of them, while 6 of the 10 simply fold into the English phrasing without a word of their own; in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew יָ֫חַד ("together," 38×), as in Romans 3:12's "one and all."

definition: Sulfur, the yellow flammable mineral, often pictured falling in fiery judgment.
article: θεῖον is the Greek word for sulfur, what older Bibles call "brimstone." It has a remarkably narrow range: in all 7 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sulfur" (the three measured "senses" are really just one meaning split by surrounding words). In the Septuagint it consistently translates the Hebrew גָּפְרִית, the same mineral, and it tends to appear in scenes of fiery destruction such as the judgment on Sodom in Luke 17:29 and the lake of fire in Revelation.

definition: To give evidence or testimony against someone, bringing accusations or charges in a legal or formal setting.
article: καταμαρτυρέω means to bear witness against a person, typically in a courtroom or formal accusation. All four New Testament uses occur in the trial scenes of Jesus, where opponents or false witnesses testify against him. The classical lexica agree with the measured data, and the verb shows up in everyday Koine documents too: a papyrus from 117 B.C. uses it of a man whose own words made him 'evidently testifying against himself.'
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences, the distinction between the measured 'bringing charges' and 'testifying charges' senses is slim and the BSB does not always match.

definition: A reconstructed Greek verb meaning to know, see, or understand, never actually written out in the New Testament.
article: This is a theoretical base form that scholars assume lies behind certain irregular forms of the more common verb εἴδω (to see or know), where it appears as a perfect tense carrying a present meaning. It does not occur even once in the Byzantine New Testament, so all its meaning is borrowed from that wider word group: to know, see, or understand. The most notable point is that this lemma is itself an assumption — listed in lexicons mainly to explain odd verb forms rather than as a word readers will encounter.
caution: This lemma has zero New Testament occurrences and is only a reconstructed base form assumed by some grammarians, so its independent existence is uncertain.

definition: Wood as a material, or something made from it—especially a tree, a wooden club, or the cross on which Jesus died.
article: At root ξύλον means wood, and from there it stretches to cover almost anything wooden: a tree, a club, the wooden stocks that held prisoners' feet, and the cross used in crucifixion. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "tree" 11 times (79%) and "clubs" 3 times (21%), with 6 more occurrences blended into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 285 times, almost always translating the Hebrew עֵץ ("tree" or "wood"), and everyday Koine papyri use it for living trees too—one Ptolemaic decree from 118 BC penalizes people for cutting down trees (ξύλα) on their own land.

definition: Describing something that never fades, withers, or loses its freshness, like a flower that stays in bloom forever.
article: ἀμάραντος literally means "unfading," built from a negative prefix plus a word for withering, and it pictures something that never loses its bloom. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 1:4, where it describes the believer's heavenly inheritance and is rendered "reserved." The image comes straight from the flower world: it gives us the name of the amaranth, an unfading flower, and a sepulchral poem from about 145 BC uses the same word to wish that the dead might "remain unfading on earth."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, and the rendering "reserved" reflects the verse's context rather than the word's core sense of "unfading."

definition: To make someone drunk, or in the passive, to become drunk on wine or other alcohol.
article: This verb means to intoxicate or, in its passive form, to get drunk, and all four Byzantine New Testament occurrences point to that single idea of drunkenness (as in Ephesians 5:18). The measured renderings split it across four phrases, but that simply reflects surrounding words like "menservants" or "those" being captured alongside the verb itself. Moulton-Milligan notes from everyday Koine papyri that it's nearly impossible to draw a clear line between this word and its shorter relative μεθύω, since in 1 Thessalonians 5:7 the two are virtually synonymous.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences and the rendering data scattered across neighboring words, the picture rests on a small evidence base.

definition: An enclitic particle meaning "somehow" or "in any way," used only attached to other words to add a sense of possibility or uncertainty.
article: This is a small enclitic particle that never stands alone in the New Testament — it only appears fused into compounds like εἴπως ("if somehow") and μήπως ("lest somehow"). On its own it carries the idea of "in some way" or "by any means," softening a statement with a sense of possibility. In the Septuagint it shows up only twice, both times rendering the Hebrew אוּלַי ("perhaps"), and the papyri confirm its everyday Koine use — one Oxyrhynchus letter uses εἴπως of someone "anxious that you should come to us by every possible means."
caution: Evidence is thin: the bare particle never occurs independently in the New Testament and appears only twice in the Septuagint, so its sense is reconstructed mainly from compounds and documentary usage.

definition: Describing something risky or precarious, likely to cause a fall or lead to harm.
article: This adjective describes a situation that is unsafe or likely to lead to a fall — in the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 27:9, where sailing had become 'dangerous' as the season turned. It comes from a word meaning to trip or cause to fall, so the literal idea of being 'prone to fall' (noted by Plato and Abbott-Smith) shades into the figurative sense of being 'insecure' or precarious. A nice everyday parallel comes from a papyrus letter (P Oxy 76, A.D. 179), where the related adverb describes a person who 'has fallen ill and is in a precarious condition.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is used only by Luke, so its New Testament range is very thin.

definition: To do or take something ahead of time, or to catch someone in the act, surprising or overtaking them.
senseLabels: caught or overtaken in the act
article: This verb combines "before" with "take," and across its 3 New Testament appearances it stretches from doing something in advance to being caught by surprise. In 1 Corinthians 11:21 someone goes "ahead" with their own meal, while in Galatians 6:1 the passive form means a person is "caught" or overtaken in some sin. Everyday Koine papyri use it plainly for money "received in advance" — for example travel expenses paid beforehand — showing how ordinary the word was in commercial life.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and the senses ranging from "take in advance" to "surprise/overtake," the exact force in each verse is debated; Abbott-Smith notes the temporal "before" meaning had largely faded.

definition: The root of a plant, or figuratively the source, origin, or ancestral stock from which something grows.
article: ῥίζα is the underground root of a plant, and in all 17 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "root" (94%), with the BSB independently agreeing 100%. The word stretches naturally from the literal root to figurative source or ancestry: Paul calls the love of money "a root of all evils" (1 Tim 6:10) and speaks of the "root" from which descendants spring (Rom 15:12; Rev 5:5). One nice everyday touch comes from the papyri, where a third-century AD document recommends eating roots of bugloss to keep your breath from smelling after garlic, and an inscription uses ῥίζα for a royal ancestral line.

definition: To put on an additional garment over what one already wears, used figuratively of being clothed with a heavenly body.
article: ἐπενδύομαι is the middle voice of a compound built from ἐπί ('upon') and ἐνδύω ('to clothe'), so it literally means to put something on over yourself, like an extra layer of clothing. It is rare, appearing only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 5 (verses 2–4), where Paul speaks of longing to be 'clothed' with a heavenly dwelling. The Majority Standard Bible renders one occurrence with the 'tent we clothed' image, and the KJV similarly gives 'be clothed upon'; in one of its two appearances it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in a single passage, the evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: The personal name of a Jewish sorcerer at Paphos who opposed Paul, also called Bar-Jesus.
article: Elymas is a proper name, used once in the New Testament (Acts 13:8) for the magician who tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith. It appears to be of foreign (Aramaic or Arabic) origin, and the lexicons simply identify it as the name of the sorcerer at Paphos, the same man called Bar-Jesus. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes scholarly debate over the name: it cannot be a translation of Bar-Jesus, and some have proposed alternate readings such as 'Hetoimas' or even 'the pestilent fellow,' though none of these has won agreement.
caution: This is a single-occurrence proper name of uncertain foreign origin, and scholars disagree about its exact form and meaning.

definition: The act of breaking a law or command—stepping over a known boundary set by God.
article: παράβασις means a transgression—deliberately crossing a line that a law or command has drawn. The Majority Standard Bible renders all 5 visible occurrences as "transgression" (the other 2 of its 7 New Testament uses are absorbed into surrounding phrasing), and it is closely tied to its verb παραβαίνω, "to step across." Interestingly, the classical lexicon Abbott-Smith notes an older sense of simply "a going aside, a deviation," while everyday Koine papyri use the word for the breach or violation of a contract or agreement, complete with stated penalties.
caution: The word appears only once in the Septuagint and just 7 times in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on relatively thin evidence.

definition: To go in or enter a place, often used of stepping into the temple or into someone's presence.
article: εἴσειμι simply means to go into or enter, and all four New Testament occurrences carry this basic idea — entering the temple, going in to see James, or priests entering the tabernacle. The varied English renderings ("enter," "see," "entered," "when") all reflect the same act of going in, just smoothed for context. In the Septuagint it stands for the Hebrew בּוֹא ("to come/go"), and an interesting detail from everyday papyri is that the word was very commonly used in dating notices, as in "the coming month" or "the incoming year."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the apparent variety of senses simply reflects translation choices for one underlying meaning rather than truly distinct senses.

definition: To tie, bind, or fasten something or someone, whether with ropes and chains or, figuratively, by obligation or constraint.
article: δέω means to bind or fasten—literally tying up an animal, wrapping a dead body, or chaining a prisoner. It's overwhelmingly concrete: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "bound" in 80% of its 44 Byzantine appearances, with the BSB independently agreeing 95% of the time. The Septuagint uses it 97 times, mostly translating the Hebrew אָסַר ("to bind," 38×), and one striking thread runs through the papyri: everyday Greek curse tablets use this verb for the "binding" power of a curse, which lines up with Luke 13:16, where a disease is said to bind a sufferer.

definition: Describing something that goes beyond the usual measure—more than enough, greater, or abundant.
article: περισσός points to something that exceeds the normal amount or standard—whether "more" in quantity or "greater" in rank. In the Byzantine NT it appears 26 times, rendered "more" in about a quarter of cases and "greater" in a fifth, while six occurrences simply melt into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own. Its everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, where a private letter uses it for whatever "surplus" is left over after measuring out grain, and grammarians note that in popular Koine its comparative and superlative forms often just stood in for the ordinary words "more" and "most."
caution: The reference works partly disagree on whether the word means simply "more than others" or carries the stronger sense of "pre-eminent, superior" in passages like Matthew 5:47.

definition: To take something or someone down from a higher position, or to pull down and destroy by force.
article: καθαιρέω covers two related actions: physically taking something down — it was the technical term for removing a body after crucifixion (Mark 15:36, 46; Luke 23:53) — and pulling down or destroying by force, the opposite of building up (Luke 12:18, tearing down barns). The Septuagint uses it 69 times, most often for the Hebrew נָתַץ ("break/tear down," 19×) and הָרַס ("demolish," 10×), confirming this demolition sense. Everyday Koine papyri show the same range: one contract pays a man to "take down" dilapidated royal buildings.

definition: A voice, sound, or noise — most often the audible voice of a person speaking or crying out.
article: φωνή is the everyday Greek word for a voice, sound, or noise, and in the New Testament it overwhelmingly means a human or divine voice — rendered "voice" in 99 of 139 occurrences (92%). Its range stretches from a person crying out to the sound of inanimate things like wind or trumpets, and it can even shade into "speech" or "language." In the Septuagint it appears over 530 times, almost always translating the Hebrew קוֹל ("sound, voice"), a match repeated 384 times. The everyday papyri confirm this breadth, using φωνή for speaking "by word of mouth" and for a formal "declaration."

definition: Hierapolis, a city in the Lycus valley of Phrygia in the Roman province of Asia, near Laodicea and Colossae.
senseLabels: Hierapolis, a city in Asia Minor
article: Hierapolis is a place name — a city in the Lycus valley of Phrygia, located near Laodicea and Colossae. The name combines the Greek words for "holy" and "city," and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Colossians 4:13. Inscriptions from the site (cited by Moulton-Milligan) point to a sizable Jewish community there, including tomb inscriptions that threatened fines payable to "the people of the Jews" against anyone disturbing the grave.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage range cannot be measured from the biblical text alone.

definition: The form of the word "you" used when something is given, said, or done to or for a single person.
article: σοί is simply the dative form of the singular pronoun "you" (σύ), used when a single person is the one receiving, being addressed, or being affected by an action — "to you," "for you," "your." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament text as counted here, but it is extremely common in the Septuagint, showing up 1188 times across 34 books. Notably, it often stands in for Hebrew words like אָנֹכִי ("I/myself," 65×), צָוָה ("to command," 45×), and נָתַן ("to give," 40×), reflecting how naturally "to you" attaches to commands and gifts.
caution: The Abbott-Smith entry supplied actually discusses αὐτός rather than σοί, so the lexical excerpt here does not match the word.

definition: To sail under the lee of an island—on the sheltered side where it blocks the wind.
senseLabels: to sail under the lee of
article: This nautical term describes sailing along the protected side of an island, using its bulk as a windbreak. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the storm-tossed voyage of Acts 27 (verses 4 and 7), and Abbott-Smith notes it always takes a direct object. Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and cite a parallel from the writer Philostratus, so it was ordinary seafaring vocabulary rather than a coinage.
caution: Evidence is thin: just two occurrences, both in the same Acts narrative, and the digest's second measured sense ('After we us') reflects a rendering glitch rather than a genuine separate meaning.

definition: A person who tells lies or speaks falsehood, someone whose words cannot be trusted.
article: ψεύστης is a straightforward word for a liar, derived from the verb ψεύδομαι ("to lie"). It appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and every occurrence is rendered "liar" (8× directly), with full agreement across the major glossaries. Notably, Moulton-Milligan observes that ψεύστης has a fixed place in early Christian lists of vices, paralleling similar Jewish and pagan catalogs of wrongdoing.

definition: Wet, dirty mud or filthy mire, the kind of muck an animal wallows in.
article: Βόρβορος means mud or filth — the slimy, foul muck of a wallowing place. It appears just once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:22, where a washed pig returns to the mire, and twice in the Septuagint. The note that the Hebrew counterpart at Jeremiah 38:6 is טִיט ("mud") fits this picture, and ancient texts like the Apocalypse of Peter even describe a great lake "filled with flaming filth," stressing the word's sense of disgusting, stinking sludge.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint — though the sources agree on the meaning.

definition: A symbolic name, paired with Magog, for nations far from Israel that gather for battle in prophetic visions.
article: Γώγ is a Hebrew proper name (transliterating גּוֹג) that appears just once in the New Testament, at Revelation 20:8, where it is rendered as part of the pairing "Gog and Magog." In the Septuagint it occurs 14 times across 3 books, usually translating the Hebrew גּוֹג (9×), though it occasionally stands in for unrelated Hebrew words. The name is best known from Ezekiel, where Gog is described as a king from the remote north, and Revelation carries it forward to picture nations far removed from Israel.
caution: This is a rare proper name with only one New Testament occurrence, so its full sense rests on the prophetic background rather than New Testament usage.

definition: To rush or leap suddenly into a place.
article: This verb describes the action of bursting or leaping suddenly into a place, built from "into" plus a root meaning "to leap." It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice (and just once in the critical text), where it pictures Paul and Barnabas rushing into a crowd (Acts 14:14) and the jailer rushing in to Paul and Silas (Acts 16:29). Everyday papyri sharpen the picture vividly: one document complains that someone "burst into my client's house and carried off the foundling," another that a man "rushed in with staves."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, this entry rests on thin evidence, though the papyri and lexicons agree on its meaning.

definition: The act of building or strengthening something, or the structure that results — used both literally for buildings and figuratively for building people up.
article: οἰκοδομή spans both the action of building and the thing built, and the New Testament uses it both literally and figuratively. In 18 occurrences it most often means strengthening or "building up" people spiritually (6×, 33%), while five times it names an actual "building" and twice the plural "buildings" (as in Mark 13:1-2). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain literal sense — one document from 126 BC uses it for building a dovecote, another for building a fountain.

definition: To jab or pierce something with a sharp point, such as stabbing with a spear.
article: This verb means to prick or pierce with a sharp object, and it shows up only once in the Byzantine New Testament, when a soldier pierces Jesus' side with a spear (John 19:34). The everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions use it freely, so it was an ordinary word for a sharp jab. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that some scholars, like Field, prefer the milder sense "pricked" over "pierced" in John 19:34, especially since a different, stronger word for piercing (exekentēsan) appears just a few verses later in 19:37.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and scholars split between "pricked" and "pierced," the exact force of the word here is genuinely uncertain.

definition: Small coins or coined money, especially the loose change used in everyday transactions.
article: κέρμα refers to coins, particularly the small change people carried for daily purchases. It appears only once in the New Testament, in John 2:15, where Jesus scatters the money changers' coins, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "coins" in that single occurrence. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense vividly: one document mentions "4 drachmae in copper" tucked into a belt, and another tells someone to sell bracelets if the cash on hand runs short. The word literally derives from κείρω ("to cut"), so it originally meant a slice or bit, which is how it came to mean a small cut piece of metal — a coin.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, though the papyri evidence strongly supports it.

definition: The neuter form of "greater," used adverbially to mean "to a greater degree" or "more."
article: μεῖζον is the neuter form of μείζων, the comparative of μέγας ("great"), and works adverbially to mean "more" or "in a greater degree." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up only once in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew אֲדָר. The fuller form μείζων was common in everyday Koine: papyri and ostraca use it to mean "senior" or even "the official in authority" — a person you might petition about a problem.
caution: Evidence for this exact neuter form is very thin: zero New Testament occurrences and only a single Septuagint instance, so its measured range is hard to pin down.

definition: To shatter, crush, or break something into pieces, used both physically and figuratively for being broken down or overwhelmed.
article: συντρίβω means to break something by crushing it, whether smashing a physical object or crushing a person or part of the body. The Septuagint uses it heavily — 181 times — and it most often stands in for the Hebrew שָׁבַר, "to break" (96 times). Everyday papyri show the same range vividly: workmen complaining they were "crushed" by their labor, and looters who "knocked down the street door," giving us a real-world feel for both the figurative and literal force.
caution: Four of the eight Byzantine occurrences were absorbed into broader phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word, so the English renderings vary considerably.

definition: The border region or frontier where two territories meet.
article: μεθόριος refers to the boundary or frontier between two areas — the land lying along a shared border. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Mark 7:24), where translators fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than rendering it with its own English word, and the critical text omits it entirely. In the Septuagint it shows up once (Joshua 19:27), translating a Hebrew place name (Beth-emek), and Moulton-Milligan note it as ordinary, everyday vocabulary in Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: Evidence is thin (one NT occurrence, and the critical text reads ὅριον instead), so confidence in its New Testament use is low.

definition: To whip or flog someone, beating them with a lash as a punishment.
article: μαστίζω means to whip or scourge someone with a lash. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 22:25, and once in the Septuagint, where it renders a Hebrew verb for striking or beating. Interestingly, the Greek inscription Kaibel 303 uses the word figuratively—people 'flogging' someone with words—though the New Testament use is literal physical scourging.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax (one occurrence) with thin overall evidence, so its range cannot be measured confidently.

definition: To go down or travel down together with someone else.
article: This compound verb literally means to descend in company with others, combining "with" (σύν) and "go down" (καταβαίνω). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 25:5, where Festus invites leading men to go down with him, and twice in the Septuagint. Interestingly, later Greek writers used it metaphorically to mean "condescend," a sense Abbott-Smith notes for Wisdom 10:13, though that broader meaning is not measured in the New Testament data here.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence — and the rendering label "wrong" in the digest appears to be a data artifact rather than a real sense.

definition: A spring or fountain — a natural source where water flows out, sometimes used figuratively for any source or supply.
article: πηγή names a spring or fountain, the place where water naturally gushes up, and by extension the source of something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times, rendered "springs" in half its occurrences and simply "water" in two more, while it can also describe a well fed by a spring (John 4:6) or even a flow of blood (Mark 5:29). The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: papyri use it for things like "the spring in a ship's hold" and "the so-called source of the Nile," and in the Septuagint's 84 uses it most often translates the Hebrew word for spring, מַעְיָן.

definition: A high official who rules a Roman province; more broadly, any leader or commander.
article: In the New Testament ἡγεμών almost always means a Roman provincial governor — rendered "governor" in 71% of its 22 occurrences and as the possessive "governor's" another 14%, often referring to the procurator of Judea like Pilate. The wider Greek range is much broader: it can mean any leader, guide, or commander, and the papyri show it stretching from a tiny district official all the way up to the Emperor himself in a single verse (Luke 3:1). In the Septuagint it appears 74 times, most often translating the Hebrew word אַלּוּף for tribal chiefs or leaders.

definition: An adverb meaning almost or nearly, marking that something falls just short of being complete or total.
article: σχεδόν is a small adverb meaning "almost" or "nearly," signaling that something is close to but not quite the full amount. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, where the Berean Standard Bible renders it "nearly" in two cases and "following nearly whole" in the third (Acts 13:44). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one document speaks of "almost all" doors being supplied with water—and Abbott-Smith notes an older spatial sense ("near" in place) that does not show up in the New Testament's measured usage.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence is thin, and the older "near in place" sense noted by lexica is not attested in the New Testament data.

definition: To loosen or untie something fastened, and so to release, free, or break apart what was held together.
article: At its core λύω means to loosen what is bound—a knot, a rope, an animal tied up, or a prisoner held captive. The word stretches naturally from this literal untying (41% of the 42 New Testament uses) to releasing people (31%) and to breaking apart or dissolving a whole, such as breaking a commandment or a ship breaking up. A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri, where λύω is used for a will being 'opened' or a contract being 'dissolved,' showing how the same loosening idea covered legal documents in ordinary Koine.

definition: A raised structure where sacrifices or offerings are presented to God.
article: θυσιαστήριον means an altar — a place where sacrifices are offered. Across all 23 Byzantine New Testament occurrences it is rendered "altar" 100% of the time (22 explicit, 1 absorbed into phrasing), and the meaning is rock-solid. The most striking evidence is its Greek Bible history: the word first appears in the Septuagint, where it shows up 391 times in 25 books, almost always translating the Hebrew מִזְבֵּחַ ("altar," 359×), so it became the standard biblical term for a sacrificial altar.

definition: An adverb of place meaning "here" or "to this place," pointing to the spot where the speaker is.
article: ἐνθάδε is a simple adverb of location meaning "here" or, with motion, "hither" (to this place). In the Byzantine NT it appears 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders the clear cases as "here" in 5 of them, with the BSB agreeing 100%. The papyri show it was ordinary everyday Koine: one third-century letter speaks of worshiping "before the gods of this place" (παρὰ τοῖς ἐνθάδε θεοῖς), and another writer insists he is "not a stranger here."
caution: The handful of odd renderings like "call back" or "out harm here" reflect noisy measurement rather than real senses, so weigh those lightly.

definition: The ordinal number meaning tenth, the one coming after the ninth in a sequence or count.
article: Δέκατος is simply the ordinal "tenth," built from δέκα (ten), and it works exactly like the English word—marking position in a sequence, an hour, a day, or an item in a list. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament but is common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 75 times rendering several Hebrew words, most often עִשָּׂרוֹן (33×) and עֲשִׂירִי (27×). Everyday Koine papyri use it freely too, often for dates, as in a tax receipt referring to "the tenth year of Nero the lord."
caution: One of the two measured senses ("tenth collapsed quake") simply reflects the phrasing of a single Revelation 11:13 occurrence, not a separate meaning—the word straightforwardly means "tenth."

definition: The personal name of an Old Testament Israelite, an ancestor of Jesus listed in the gospel genealogies.
article: Ναασσών is simply the Greek spelling of a proper name, rendered "Nahshon" in all 3 of its New Testament occurrences. It is an indeclinable name borrowed straight from the Hebrew נַחְשׁוֹן, which the Septuagint uses 10 times across 4 books. According to Dodson, this is Nahshon, son of Amminadab and father of Salmon, one of the ancestors of Jesus named in the genealogies of Matthew and Luke.

definition: Bethany, a New Testament place name referring to a village near Jerusalem and also a location beyond the Jordan River.
article: Bethany is a place name appearing 12 times across the New Testament, almost always rendered simply "Bethany" (75% of the time, with the rare alternatives just artifacts of how surrounding words were grouped). The digest identifies two distinct locations: a village about fifteen furlongs from Jerusalem—the home of Lazarus, Martha, and Mary, and today called El Azerîyeh—and a separate place on the east bank of the Jordan. The name comes from Aramaic/Hebrew roots, with early interpreters debating whether it means "house of affliction" (per Jerome) or "house of dates."
caution: The exact meaning of the name is uncertain, with ancient sources disagreeing between "house of affliction" and "house of dates."

definition: To carry or lead someone or something up, or to bring an offering up to an altar.
article: ἀναφέρω literally means to carry something up, used in the Gospels when Jesus leads disciples up a mountain (Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2) or is taken up into heaven (Luke 24:51). It also developed a sacrificial sense, bringing offerings up to an altar, which dominates the Septuagint, where it appears 149 times and often renders the Hebrew word for a burnt offering (עֹלָה, 63×). One intriguing detail: Deissmann argued from everyday papyri that 1 Peter 2:24 may echo a legal usage about transferring one person's debts onto another.
caution: The measured New Testament renderings cluster on the plain "carry up" sense, while the lexicons stress a fuller sacrificial and debt-bearing range drawn from less frequent passages.

definition: Willing to yield to others, ready to listen and comply rather than stubbornly insisting on one's own way.
article: εὐπειθής describes someone who is open to persuasion and ready to obey or yield, built from εὖ ('well') and πείθω ('persuade'). It appears only once in the New Testament, at James 3:17, where it characterizes the wisdom from above; the Byzantine and critical texts agree on this single occurrence. A vivid parallel comes from an everyday Koine contract (P Oxy II.268, A.D. 58), where two women agree to be 'compliant' (εὐπιθεῖς) in accepting a money settlement, showing the word's practical sense of willingly yielding in an agreement.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: To feel and show pity or compassion toward someone in need or suffering.
article: This verb means to take pity on someone, to feel and act with compassion. Both of its two New Testament appearances are in a single verse, Romans 9:15, where it is rendered "compassion" 100% of the time—and that verse quotes the Septuagint, which uses the word 28 times across 10 books, most often translating the Hebrew רָחַם ("to have mercy"). One interesting detail: the related adverb "pitiably" turns up in an everyday Koine school exercise from the second century AD, copying a letter about an emperor's approaching death that was "neither untimely nor unreasonable nor lamentable."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences (both in the same quoted verse) and zero in the critical text, the measured evidence here is thin.

definition: To bring something fully to completion, finishing it off or carrying it through to its final result.
article: ἀποτελέω means to bring a thing to its full completion—to finish, accomplish, or fully form something. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in the critical SBLGNT), and in that single case the verb is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word, so the corpus gives us no measured sense to label. The evidence outside the NT is more telling: Moulton-Milligan cite an astrological papyrus where planetary positions "produce" (ἀποτελεῖ) great kingdoms, and Hort argued that in James 1:15 the sense is sin "fully formed" rather than merely "full-grown."
caution: With only one Byzantine occurrence—and that one absorbed into phrasing with no measured sense—the corpus evidence here is very thin, so this entry leans heavily on the lexica and papyri.

definition: A nail or metal spike, such as those used to fasten things or to crucify a person.
article: This word simply means a nail or metal spike. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in John 20:25, where Thomas insists on seeing the nail marks in the risen Jesus' hands. In the Septuagint it shows up 8 times, usually translating the Hebrew word for nails, and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one letter from AD 261 records someone sending along 'four nails' for a repair job, showing how ordinary the term was.
caution: The two New Testament occurrences are both in the same verse, so its biblical range is narrow, though the Septuagint and papyri confirm the plain meaning.

definition: To carry something along or aside, and so to take it away or cause it to pass by.
article: παραφέρω literally means to bear something along or to one side, and from there it shades into carrying off or taking away. In the New Testament's 4 occurrences it appears in two related ways: in Mark 14:36 and Luke 22:42 Jesus asks the Father to 'take away' the cup, while in Hebrews 13:9 and Jude 1:12 the passive form describes being carried along or swept aside. Tellingly, Moulton-Milligan and Field render the passive uses as 'am turned aside' and point to Plutarch, where the same word means to let a remark pass without notice.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and the renderings split between 'take away' and 'carried/turned aside,' the precise force in passages like Hebrews 13:9 is somewhat uncertain.

definition: To be in danger or peril, or to put oneself at risk.
article: This verb describes being exposed to danger or deliberately risking oneself, and it appears just 4 times in the New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "danger" twice (as in the storm that endangered the boat in Luke 8:23) and as "endanger ourselves" once (1 Corinthians 15:30). A vivid parallel comes from the papyri: a soldier named Apion, after a stormy sea voyage, wrote to his father thanking the lord Serapis for saving him when he was "in danger at sea" — the very same word.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the range is thin; Abbott-Smith also lists an older sense "to be daring, to venture," which the measured New Testament data does not show.

definition: Describing a person who is thankful or grateful, especially toward those who have done them good.
article: εὐχάριστος describes someone who is thankful or grateful, built from εὖ ("well") and a word for showing favor. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Colossians 3:15, where the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering is actually "rule" — reflecting the surrounding phrase rather than the word itself, since the standard glosses are "thankful, grateful." The most interesting evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions, where this word was a common epithet of beneficent gods and Ptolemaic kings and was widely used to express a people's gratitude toward their benefactors.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "rule" reflects the larger phrase rather than the word's own meaning of "thankful," so treat the sense label with care.

definition: A steep bank, cliff, or precipice — a sharp drop-off where land falls away.
article: κρημνός refers to a steep bank or precipice, a place where the ground drops off sharply. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in the same story of the herd of pigs rushing down a steep bank into the sea (Matthew 8:32, Mark 5:13, Luke 8:33). The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too: one document uses it for the steep edges of an irrigation trench, and a grave inscription describes a man who threw himself off the cliffs (κρημνῶν).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, all from one parallel account, the measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Describing a letter that introduces or recommends a person, vouching for their character to others.
article: This adjective always describes letters of introduction or recommendation—the ancient equivalent of a reference letter that vouched for someone being received by strangers. In the New Testament it appears only in 2 Corinthians 3:1, where the Majority text uses it twice (the critical text has it once), which is why the rendering splits between "people" and "recommendation" in that single verse. The papyri make this word concrete: Moulton-Milligan cite an Oxyrhynchus document mentioning "letters of recommendation" (συστατικῶν γραμμάτων), exactly matching Paul's phrase. Lexicons also note a broader root sense of "putting together, constructive," though that meaning does not appear in the biblical use.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs in just one New Testament verse, so its measured "senses" reflect translation choices within that single passage rather than a genuinely broad range.

definition: To urge people on or stir them up, especially provoking them toward hostile action against someone.
article: Παροτρύνω means to spur someone on or stir them up, and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 13:50) it carries a hostile edge — inciting people against Paul and Barnabas. The word is rare in biblical Greek, found only here, but Moulton-Milligan note it was fairly common in ordinary late Greek; Josephus, for example, uses it of people stirring up a king with accusations. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "incited," matching the lexicons' sense of urging on toward action.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Onesiphorus, the personal name of a Christian friend who helped the apostle Paul.
article: Onesiphorus is a personal name belonging to a Christian who supported Paul, mentioned twice in the New Testament (2 Timothy 1:16 and 4:19). The name itself means something like "profit-bringer" or "bringing advantage," built from words for benefit and bearing, and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was a real name in ordinary use. One intriguing note: tradition holds that an Onesiphorus was martyred at Parium in Mysia in the early second century, though scholars like Ramsay argue this figure is unlikely to be the same person as Paul's friend.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only twice, so its meaning rests on the name's parts rather than measured usage, and its identification with later traditions is disputed.

definition: A seat or chair, including the formal seat from which a teacher gives instruction.
article: καθέδρα simply means a seat or chair. In all 3 New Testament occurrences the Berean Standard Bible renders it "seats" (100%), whether the seats of dove-sellers overturned in the temple (Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15) or "Moses' seat" from which teachers taught (Matthew 23:2). The everyday Koine range shows up in the papyri, where one wooden item is simply listed alongside a basket and a perfume-box, and an astrological text playfully uses the word to mean the posterior.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, this entry rests on thin evidence, though the sense is consistent and uncontested.

definition: To look at something carefully and attentively, observing or considering it well.
article: This verb means to observe something thoughtfully and with attention, whether examining objects in front of you or reflecting on a course of life. It appears only twice in the New Testament: once where Paul carefully observes the objects of Athenian worship (Acts 17:23), and once urging readers to consider the outcome of their leaders' way of life (Heb 13:7). Built from ἀνά plus θεωρέω ("to look at"), the prefix adds the sense of looking "again" or attentively. Abbott-Smith notes it also turns up in the classical historian Diodorus.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the first sense recorded as "UNKNOWN," the measured rendering data is too thin to map its full range confidently.

definition: To make something widely known by telling it to others; to spread a report abroad.
article: This rare compound verb means to publish or spread news widely, telling others what you have learned. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 2:17, where the shepherds make known what they had been told about the child. Notably, the modern critical text reads the simpler verb ἐγνώρισεν here instead, so this fuller compound form rests on a single disputed reading.
caution: Evidence is very thin: only one Byzantine occurrence, zero in the critical text, where editors prefer the simpler verb γνωρίζω instead.

definition: To roll up, coil, or wrap something together.
article: εἱλίσσω means to roll or coil something up, the way you might wrap a scroll or fold a garment together. It is simply a longer spelling of the more common form ἑλίσσω, and the lexicons point you there for the fuller picture. It never appears in the Byzantine New Testament, but Moulton-Milligan note that the word shows up in ordinary everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was familiar in regular speech.
caution: There are no measured New Testament senses for this spelling, and the lexicons treat it only as a variant of ἑλίσσω, so its specific range here rests on thin direct evidence.

definition: Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from a son of Jacob.
article: Γάδ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Gad, naming one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It appears just once in the New Testament, in the list of sealed tribes in Revelation 7:5, but shows up about 80 times across the Septuagint, where it almost always renders the Hebrew גָּד. Notice the measured sense label here shows 'Reuben' because the single NT verse listing Gad sits alongside Reuben, so treat the rendering data with that quirk in mind.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a tagging quirk that pairs it with 'Reuben,' the measured rendering data is thin and should be read cautiously.

definition: Describing flat, level, low-lying ground, such as a plain.
article: πεδινός is an adjective describing flat, level, low-lying terrain — the kind of open plain you can walk across easily. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 6:17, where Jesus stands on a level place; the Septuagint uses it 21 times, most often (15×) for the Hebrew שְׁפֵלָה, the lowland region. The word is well attested in everyday Koine papyri, and the Letter of Aristeas neatly pairs it with its opposite, contrasting low-lying (πεδινῶν) land with mountainous (ὀρεινῶν) land.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence, the entry leans heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence, though the sources agree closely on its meaning.

definition: Describing a person unable to speak or unable to hear, depending on context.
article: κωφός literally means "blunted" or "dull," and in the New Testament it describes a sense that doesn't work — either speech or hearing. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "mute" 4× and "deaf" 2×, and the same physical impairment can mean either depending on context, which is why translators sometimes have to decide which sense fits. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for "deaf" (7 of 11 times) but also stands in for "mute," matching this double range; it even appears in everyday papyri as a descriptive nickname for a man.
caution: Because the word covers both "mute" and "deaf," the intended sense in any given verse must be judged from context rather than the word alone.

definition: To have a share in something jointly with others, partaking together in what is distributed.
article: This verb means to share jointly in something—to have a portion alongside others. In the active voice it carries the idea of distributing something in shares, but the New Testament's single use (1 Corinthians 9:13) is in the middle voice, meaning "to have a share in," describing temple servants who partake of what is offered. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and a related noun, συμμεριστής ("one who shares"), appears in a second/third-century document about distributing things according to a will.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single example.

definition: A payment back in kind — a reward, return, or penalty that matches what someone has done.
article: ἀντιμισθία is built from ἀντί ("in return") and μισθός ("wages"), so it means a recompense that corresponds to what was done — a return in kind. It works either way: in Romans 1:27 it points to a deserved penalty (rendered "indecent" in the measured data, where BSB's own wording differs), while in 2 Corinthians 6:13 it carries the positive sense of a fair, matching response ("fair"). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that this Pauline word has not yet turned up outside Christian literature, though they add there is nothing about the word itself that would have excluded it from ordinary everyday Koine.
caution: This word occurs only twice, both in Paul, and the renderings split evenly with the BSB disagreeing on one, so its precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: To store something up or set it aside as treasure for future use.
article: This verb means to put something away in reserve, like building up a store of treasure for later. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:19, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "treasuring" (and the Berean Standard Bible agrees), and once in the Septuagint at Sirach 3:4. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan finds the same word twice in the astrological writer Vettius Valens, confirming it was used in everyday Koine Greek beyond the Bible.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and very limited other attestation, the sense rests on thin evidence.

definition: A personal name, Epaphroditus, borne by a Christian who served Paul.
article: Epaphroditus is a proper name, appearing twice in the New Testament (Philippians 2:25 and 4:18), both times referring to the Christian who carried gifts to Paul and served him. As a name it originally meant something like "charming" or "devoted to Aphrodite/Venus," and the adjective behind it shows up in everyday papyri — one document from A.D. 192 praises a "delightful (epaphroditos) prefecture." Interestingly, the name was common enough that it even appears as a surname of the Roman general Sulla in an inscription from 81 B.C.
caution: Evidence is thin (only two occurrences) and this is simply a person's name, so there is no broader meaning to translate.

definition: The quality of being fast or quick, almost always used in phrases meaning that something happens speedily or soon.
article: τάχος is a noun meaning swiftness or speed, but in the New Testament it almost always appears in the phrase "ἐν τάχει" ("in speed"), which is best translated as "quickly" or "soon." The various measured renderings — quickly, promptly, soon, soon to take place — are really just context-driven shades of the same idea of something happening fast. In the Septuagint it shows up 19 times, mostly translating Hebrew words built from the root מָהַר ("to hasten"), and the everyday papyri use it the same way, as when a writer urges that a letter be sent "as quickly as possible" (ὅ τι τάχος).
caution: With only 7 occurrences, all in adverbial phrases, the separate "sense" labels reflect translation context rather than genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: A person related to you by blood or family, and by extension a member of your own people or nation.
article: Συγγενής describes someone connected to you by birth — a blood relative or kinsman — and it can stretch to mean a fellow countryman from your own tribe or people. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 12 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "relatives" in 60% of cases, with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where one document even uses it of two pigs from the same litter, and an inscription pairs it with "brothers" to mark blood kinship.

definition: A fit of fear or panic — the trembling agitation that overwhelms a person who is frightened.
article: πτόησις describes the fluttering, panicked state that fear stirs up in a person, sometimes translated as terror, dismay, or alarm. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Peter 3:6), where the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase as not letting fear 'refuse' or unsettle you. In the Septuagint it shows up in Proverbs 3:25, standing in for a Hebrew word for sudden dread or ruin, which fits its sense of overwhelming fright.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word in the New Testament with very thin evidence, and the lexicons (terror, dismay) sit awkwardly against the measured 'refuse' rendering, so its precise force in 1 Peter 3:6 is uncertain.

definition: Italy, the region of Europe centered on Rome.
article: Ἰταλία is simply the place-name Italy, the Roman region of Europe. It appears 4 times in the New Testament, across Acts and Hebrews, and the meaning is consistent: every translation surveyed renders it "Italy." The one variation the data shows is in Acts 27:1, where the word sits inside the phrase "sail to Italy" — a translation choice driven by context, not a different meaning of the word itself.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the apparent second sense ("sail Italy") simply reflects surrounding wording rather than a genuinely distinct meaning.

definition: Hard, rough, or harsh — whether physically tough to the touch or, when describing people and words, stern, severe, or difficult to accept.
article: σκληρός literally means "hard" — physically tough or rough, the opposite of soft. The Byzantine New Testament uses it only 5 times, where it describes both a stern person (the harsh master of Matthew 25:24) and difficult things (the hard saying, the violent wind). The everyday papyri keep that literal sense vivid, using it for hard stone and marble in building inscriptions, while the Septuagint applies it 49 times, most often rendering the Hebrew word for "hard" or "stubborn."

definition: To stand around something, and in the middle voice to turn oneself away from something in order to avoid or shun it.
article: This compound of "around" plus "to stand" literally pictures standing around something, but its meaning splits depending on grammar. In the active tenses it means people physically standing around (the crowd in John 11:42, the accusers in Acts 25:7), while in the middle voice — used by later writers — it means to turn yourself away to avoid or shun something, as in Paul's warnings to steer clear of empty chatter (2 Timothy 2:16; Titus 3:9). The everyday Koine papyri show a further twist: the word could describe being "reduced to" dire circumstances, as when one woman complains of being brought to extreme poverty.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences spread thinly across three distinct uses, each sense rests on just one or two examples.

definition: To leave someone alone or forsaken, especially describing a widow left without family or support.
article: μονόω means to leave someone isolated or forsaken, built from μόνος ("alone"). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:5, where its passive participle describes a widow who has been left entirely on her own, with no family to lean on. Moulton-Milligan notes this was a common classical verb, citing Musonius's striking comparison of human nature to a bee, which "cannot live alone, for it perishes when isolated."
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine NT and zero times in the critical text, so its biblical range rests on a single verse.

definition: A loud noise or roar, and by extension a report or rumor that spreads about someone.
article: ἦχος covers both a literal loud sound — like the roaring of the sea or the blast of a trumpet — and the figurative spread of news, a report or rumor about a person. In the New Testament it appears only a handful of times (3 in the Byzantine text, 4 in the critical text), once meaning a spreading report (Luke 4:37) and once tied to the sound heard at Sinai (Hebrews 12:19). It's well attested beyond the Bible: Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday Koine papyri, including a magical text describing how a sound rises up from water.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 Byzantine occurrences) and the word's gender and accent vary across manuscripts, so some renderings get absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated directly.

definition: To learn an inner secret or be let in on something through experience, originally to be initiated into mysteries.
article: This verb appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 4:12, where Paul says he has "learned the secret" of being content in any situation. The word's older technical sense was to initiate someone into the mysteries, as seen in inscriptions cited by Moulton-Milligan and in 3 Maccabees 2:30 in the Septuagint, and that background of being let in on hidden knowledge may underlie Paul's usage. It is built on the same root as the word for "mystery" (μυστήριον), and Abbott-Smith notes it comes from a base meaning "to shut the mouth."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and translations vary between the plain sense "how" and the fuller "I have learned the secret."

definition: To get something ready or make preparations, whether for a meal, a battle, or any anticipated event.
article: παρασκευάζω means to prepare or get ready, and across all 4 New Testament occurrences it is rendered "prepared." The range is fairly flexible: it can be used on its own to mean preparing a meal (as in Peter's vision in Acts 10:10), making ready for battle (the trumpet call in 1 Corinthians 14:8), or readying a gift, as in Paul's eager Corinthians (2 Corinthians 9:2). Everyday papyri show it in a stronger causative sense, where someone "causes" or "arranges" others to act — for instance, instructing leather workers to supply a hide.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the full range rests largely on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than biblical usage.

definition: Bethlehem, a town in Judea about six miles south of Jerusalem.
article: Βηθλεέμ is simply the place-name Bethlehem, an indeclinable word borrowed straight from Hebrew. It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament and is rendered "Bethlehem" in every clear instance. The underlying Hebrew name בֵּית לֶחֶם means "house of bread," and in the Septuagint it shows up 22 times across 6 books, almost always translating that same Hebrew phrase.

definition: In a hidden or concealed way, without others knowing; secretly or privately.
article: λάθρα is an adverb meaning to do something secretly or in private, away from public notice. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "secretly" in two-thirds of cases (as in Matthew 2:7 and Acts 16:37); the one place it is translated "publicly" (Matthew 1:19) actually describes the opposite of acting quietly, so the word itself still carries the idea of secrecy.
