Fittingly, it derives from λανθάνω, "to escape notice," and the papyri preserve a vivid everyday example from 165 B.C. describing someone who "secretly carried off" some flax.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and varied translation choices, the apparent "publicly" rendering reflects sentence context rather than a genuine second meaning of the word.

definition: Actively at work and producing real results; powerfully operative rather than passive or idle.
article: ἐνεργής describes something that is actively at work and getting results — Paul speaks of an "effective" door for ministry (1 Corinthians 16:9) and an "effective" sharing of faith (Philemon 6), and Hebrews 4:12 calls God's word living and active. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, and the "even" rendering in Hebrews simply reflects English phrasing rather than a distinct meaning. The everyday papyri show how concrete this word was: in its related form it described a working mill, wrought iron, and tilled, productive land — the same idea of being operational and effective.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and one rendering being a translation artifact, this word has thin evidence, though the sources agree on its core meaning.

definition: Relating to or belonging to God; having a godlike, divine nature or quality.
article: θεῖος means "divine" — belonging to or characteristic of God. In all 3 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "divine," describing God's power and nature (2 Peter 1:3-4) and, in neuter form, "the Deity" itself (Acts 17:29). One striking parallel comes from the papyri and inscriptions: Moulton-Milligan note that the phrase "sharers of the divine nature" (θείας φύσεως) in 2 Peter 1:4 echoes an inscription honoring Aion that speaks of an eternal "divine nature," showing the word was at home in everyday religious language.
caution: The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on thin evidence.

definition: Describes someone or something that stands by itself—only, alone, or solitary with nothing else added.
article: μόνος points to singleness: it can mark something as the "only" one of its kind (23×, 56%) or describe a person or thing standing "alone" (14×, 34%). The two measured senses overlap closely, and the Byzantine NT and Majority Standard Bible agree on them about 95% and 93% of the time. In the Septuagint it shows up 112 times, most often rendering the Hebrew בַּד (68×), which carries the same idea of being apart or by oneself; one papyrus even uses it in a touching daughter's letter saying "I am alone" (μόνη ἰμὶ ἐγω).

definition: A relative pronoun meaning who, which, what, or that, linking a clause back to a person or thing already named.
article: ὅς is the standard Koine relative pronoun, usually translated "who," "which," "what," or "that" depending on what it points back to. It is extraordinarily common, appearing 1,408 times in the New Testament, and its exact English form shifts so much with context that 730 of those occurrences get absorbed into the phrasing with no single English word of their own. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly stands in for the Hebrew relative particle אֲשֶׁר, used 2,918 times that way. Notably, the lexica also document an older demonstrative use ("the one... the other"), confirmed in everyday papyri, as in a complaint of assault from A.D. 38.
caution: Because this is a grammatical connector, the measured "senses" are really translation forms driven by surrounding words, not distinct meanings.

definition: A preposition meaning in place of, in exchange for, or in return for something, sometimes expressing the reason why something happens.
senseLabels: in exchange or in place of
article: This preposition (used with the genitive case) most often points to substitution or exchange — one thing standing in for or given in return for another, which is why translators render it "for" in 8 of its 22 New Testament uses. In the fixed phrase "ἀνθ᾽ ὧν" it shifts to meaning "because," as in Luke 1:20 and 19:44. The classical lexica note an older, purely physical sense of "over against, opposite" that has largely faded by New Testament times, and the Septuagint most often uses it to render the Hebrew תָּ֫חַת ("under, in place of") 172 times.
caution: In about a quarter of its New Testament uses (5 of 22) the word is absorbed into English phrasing without its own translated word, so its force depends heavily on context.

definition: Describes something heavy or weighty, used figuratively for commands, accusations, or people that are oppressive, severe, or hard to bear.
article: βαρύς literally means "heavy," but in the New Testament it is mostly used figuratively for things that weigh a person down — commands, accusations, even a fierce wolf. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "burdensome" in the two clear cases (Matthew 23:4; 1 John 5:3), while the lexicons stretch its range further to "weighty," "severe," and "violent" or "cruel." In the Septuagint it appears 29 times, most often translating the Hebrew כָּבֵד ("heavy"), and the everyday papyri show colorful uses like "seriously ill" and even "pregnant."
caution: With only 6 occurrences and 4 of them absorbed into phrasing, just two cases were directly measured, so the broader senses listed by lexicons rest on thinner evidence.

definition: To share in someone's feelings or troubles, showing compassion and understanding for what they are going through.
article: συμπαθέω means to feel with another person — to enter into their experience with genuine compassion, whether the object is a difficulty (Heb 4:15) or a group of people (Heb 10:34). The word appears only twice in the New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "sympathize," with the Berean Study Bible agreeing completely. Moulton-Milligan note that no early everyday examples survive, but a later text from the Acts of Paul and Thekla uses it of Christ as the one who "suffered along with" a wandering world.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and no early papyri examples, the evidence base for this word is thin.

definition: Prochorus, one of the seven men chosen to help with daily distribution in the early Jerusalem church.
article: Πρόχορος is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament at Acts 6:5, where Prochorus is listed among the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem. The name derives from πρό ("before") and χορός ("dance"), giving Strong's the literal note "before the dance," though as a proper name it simply identifies one individual. There's little to say beyond the bare fact of his selection, since Scripture mentions him only here.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so virtually nothing is known about the man himself beyond his being named in Acts 6:5.

definition: To run toward someone or something, hurrying to meet, reach, or join them.
article: προστρέχω simply means to run up to or hasten toward someone, combining πρός ("toward") with τρέχω ("run"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, twice rendered "ran" (as crowds rushing to Jesus in Mark 9:15 and the man running to him in Mark 10:17) and once "ran up to a person" (Philip approaching the chariot in Acts 8:30). A nice glimpse of everyday Koine comes from an Egyptian papyrus where the verb is used metaphorically of someone "approaching" the legal age, showing it could mean drawing near in a figurative as well as physical sense.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences this word is thinly attested, though the sources fully agree on its meaning.

definition: A place where goods are bought and sold; a market or trading center.
article: ἐμπόριον means a marketplace or trading center — literally a place where merchants do business, built from the word for "merchant" (ἔμπορος). It appears only once in the New Testament, in John 2:16, where Jesus tells the merchants not to make his Father's house "a house of trade." The everyday Koine papyri confirm this commercial sense richly: tax records mention duties paid "in the market" and goods imported "through the foreign mart," showing it was a standard business term.
caution: The digest's measured-sense label reads "dare," which is almost certainly a data error; all the actual evidence (lexica, papyri, LXX) points uniformly to a market or trading place.

definition: A loud lament or mournful song expressing deep grief, especially weeping over the dead.
article: θρῆνος means a lament or dirge — the wailing cry of grief, often a formal mourning song for the dead. In the Septuagint it appears 23 times across 7 books, most often rendering the Hebrew קִינָה (a funeral lament). The one New Testament occurrence is textually disputed: it shows up in the Byzantine text at Matthew 2:18 (the weeping over Israel's children) but is absent from the critical SBLGNT.
caution: The single NT occurrence appears only in the Byzantine/Received text and is missing from the critical text, so the measured English data is thin and the word's NT presence is itself debated.

definition: A connecting word that pivots to a contrasting or qualifying point, or marks an exception—roughly "nevertheless," "only," or "except."
article: πλήν is a small but versatile linking word that turns a sentence toward a contrasting or limiting point, most often rendered "nevertheless." The Majority Standard Bible translates it that way 5 times, but in 23 of its 31 New Testament occurrences it simply gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing without a word of its own. It can also work as a preposition meaning "except" or "save" (as in Mark 12:32), and in the Septuagint it appears 212 times, frequently rendering the Hebrew רַק ("only," 63×). Moulton-Milligan notes it was the regular everyday word for this kind of pivot in common Koine speech, as the papyri show (e.g. "but we will begin the work").

definition: To stay awake, especially to remain alert and watchful rather than caught off guard.
article: At its core this verb means to stay awake, and from there it stretches into the metaphorical sense of being vigilant or spiritually alert. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 23 times, most often rendered "keep watch" (9×, 47%) or simply "watch" (21%), with "awake" and "wake" filling out the range. It's actually a newer Koine present tense built from the perfect of ἐγείρω ("to raise"), and grammarians of the era condemned it as bad form — yet it shows up freely in the New Testament and in everyday papyri, and even survives in Modern Greek as an adverb meaning "quickly."
caution: Note that this form (γρηγορεύω) is absent from the critical text, which uses γρηγορέω instead, so the headword reflects the Byzantine spelling.

definition: To be afraid or alarmed; also to hold someone in awe, reverence, or deep respect.
article: This very common verb means to be gripped by fear, but it also stretches to cover the kind of awe or reverence you give to God or a ruler. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 93 times, rendered "afraid" in 56% of cases and "fear" in 39%, with the two senses shading into each other. It shows up a remarkable 353 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew יָרֵא (222×), the standard word for fearing or revering God; everyday papyri use it the same way, as when a writer says "I myself am afraid."
caution: In the New Testament the verb is always passive in form ("be afraid," not "frighten someone"), and the line between simple fear and respectful awe depends on context rather than the word itself.

definition: To bless someone, especially God conferring blessing on people or nations.
article: This verb means to bless or grant a benefit, built from the preposition "in/through" plus the common word for "bless." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both quoting the Septuagint promise that all nations would be blessed in Abraham's offspring (Acts 3:25 and Galatians 3:8), so the rendering shifts slightly to "blessed" or "blessed through" depending on context. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew word for "bless" (barak), though it also stands in for several other Hebrew words including one meaning "curse" (arar), a striking mismatch.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both Septuagint quotations, and varied Hebrew counterparts behind it, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Surrounding or lying round about, used of places situated nearby on every side.
article: πέριξ is an adverb meaning "round about" or "surrounding," formed from περί ("around"). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:16, where it describes the towns surrounding Jerusalem. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, such as a papyrus from A.D. 95 reading "all the people round about," so its sense of "in the vicinity" was familiar in ordinary usage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To pierce or run completely through, used figuratively of stabbing oneself with pain or grief.
article: περιπείρω literally means to put something on a spit or run it all the way through, and by extension to pierce or stab. The New Testament uses it once, in 1 Timothy 6:10, where the love of money leads people to "pierce themselves" with many griefs. Moulton-Milligan note this figurative sense in everyday Koine and cite a striking parallel from Philo, who speaks of someone "pierced with incurable evils."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured sense is tagged "money" (from the surrounding verse) rather than the verb's actual meaning, so lean on the lexicon glosses of piercing.

definition: To live in the surrounding area, that is, to be a neighbor to someone.
article: This verb combines the ideas of "around" and "to dwell," so it literally means living in the region surrounding a place or person — being a neighbor. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:65, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "neighbors" (the people living around Zechariah and Elizabeth). Abbott-Smith notes it takes a direct object, describing those who dwell round about a particular spot.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the biblical evidence alone.

definition: A connecting joint or ligament that fastens parts together, allowing a body to be held together and to grow.
senseLabels: a joint holding a body together
article: In the New Testament ἁφή appears only twice, both times describing the connecting joints or ligaments that bind a body together—rendered "grows" in Ephesians 4:16 and "whole" in Colossians 2:19. The word comes from ἅπτομαι, "to fasten," and lexicons consistently treat it as a joint or fastening. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses ἁφή 69 times in a completely different sense, almost always translating the Hebrew נֶ֫גַע (68×), a word for a plague or affliction; the everyday papyri stretch even further, using it for the "kindling" of lamps and even for arena sand.
caution: With only 2 NT occurrences and a measured range that diverges sharply from the dominant Septuagint and papyri senses, confidence here is low.

definition: Relating to prophets or prophecy; describing writings or messages that come from a prophet.
article: προφητικός is the adjective form built from προφήτης ("prophet"), meaning "prophetic" or "belonging to the prophets." It is rare, appearing only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, once describing the "prophetic writings" (Romans 16:26) and once the "prophetic word" (2 Peter 1:19). The two occurrences split evenly between referring to the prophets' writings and to prophecy in general, and the standard lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) agree the word simply means "of prophecy" or "uttered by a prophet."
caution: With only two occurrences in the corpus (one in the critical text), the evidence base is thin, so its full range is hard to map confidently.

definition: Clothing or garments worn on the body, including fine robes, ordinary dress, or distinctive attire.
article: ἐsthḗs is a general word for clothing or garments, covering everything from a king's splendid robe to ordinary dress. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across 3 books, often pointing to notable or fine attire—a royal robe in Acts 12:21 or the well-dressed visitor in James 2:2. The everyday papyri confirm its breadth: documents mention "white garments," torn clothing in a dispute, and even "military dress," showing the word covered plain wear as much as luxury.
caution: The label "man" reflects how translators render James 2:2 ("a man in fine clothes"), not a separate meaning—the word itself always denotes clothing.

definition: Moses, the Hebrew lawgiver who led Israel out of Egypt and through whom God gave the Law.
article: This is the proper name Moses, used 80 times in the Byzantine New Testament and rendered "Moses" in 76 of them (95%). It can also stand by metonymy for Moses' writings — the books of Moses or the Pentateuch — as in phrases like "the law of Moses" and passages such as Luke 16:29 and Acts 15:21. In the Septuagint it appears a striking 796 times, almost always translating the Hebrew name מֹשֶׁה (733×), though it occasionally renders other names like Joshua and Aaron.

definition: The act of killing or putting someone to death.
article: ἀναίρεσις refers to the killing or murder of a person, a noun built from the verb ἀναιρέω ("to kill, do away with"). In the New Testament it appears only twice, both times referring to Stephen's death — and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "approval," reflecting the phrasing where Saul approved of the killing rather than the killing itself. Scholar Field notes that "killing" or "slaying" captures the word better than the older KJV rendering "death," and Moulton-Milligan find it in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: Confidence is low: the measured "approval" rendering reflects the surrounding sentence rather than the word itself, which the lexicons consistently define as killing or slaying.

definition: A change or variation, especially the kind of shifting motion seen in the movement of stars and other heavenly bodies.
article: παραλλαγή means a change or variation, and in its single New Testament appearance (James 1:17) it carries the more specialized sense of the shifting movement of a heavenly body, contrasting God's constancy with the changing lights of the sky. The word is rare and its range runs from plain 'variation' to this astronomical nuance. Moulton-Milligan notes that the periodic-motion meaning is illustrated by a passage in Dio Cassius describing how the Emperor Severus carefully observed the sun's variation in the north of Scotland.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its precise shade of meaning rests on thin evidence and external parallels.

definition: Levi, a personal name, here the tax collector (son of Alphaeus) whom Jesus called to follow him.
article: Λευΐς is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Levi, appearing 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament. In every case it refers to the tax collector, son of Alphaeus, whom Jesus calls to follow him (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27, 29). Abbott-Smith notes that the related indeclinable form Levi is used elsewhere for several different men—the son of Jacob, two ancestors in Luke's genealogy, and this tax collector—but this particular spelling is tied to the publican called by Jesus.
caution: This is a proper name with thin attestation, and the spelling is rare; the measured "senses" largely reflect surrounding phrases rather than distinct meanings, and some manuscripts read James instead of Levi in Mark 2:14.

definition: The special rights and privileges belonging to the firstborn son, including inheritance and family leadership.
article: πρωτοτόκια refers to the birthright — the legal and family privileges that belonged to the firstborn son. It appears just once in the New Testament (Hebrews 12:16, of Esau selling his birthright) and seven times in the Septuagint, where it always translates the Hebrew בְּכֹרָה, the word for the firstborn's portion, including the famous account of Esau and Jacob in Genesis. The classical lexicons note it matches the older Greek term ἡ πρεσβεία, 'the rights of seniority.'
caution: The Majority Standard Bible's single rendering here is recorded as "godless," which conflicts with the consistent "birthright" meaning in every other source, so treat that label as a data quirk rather than the word's sense.

definition: The fermenting agent mixed into dough to make it rise, often used as an image for an influence that quietly spreads through a whole group.
article: ζύμη is the substance you stir into dough to make bread rise, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "leaven" in 9 of 13 occurrences (90%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it translates two Hebrew words, שְׂאֹר (6×) and חָמֵץ (4×), and Abbott-Smith notes that outside the Parable of the Leaven (Matthew 13:33, Luke 13:21) it always pictures a moral influence, usually an evil one, as in "the leaven of the Pharisees." A nice glimpse of everyday life comes from the papyri: a land-lease from A.D. 140 records a tenant promising to pay his landlord 2/3 of an artaba of "prepared leaven" each year.

definition: Lordship or ruling power, used both for abstract dominion and for a class of angelic or heavenly authorities.
article: κυριότης means lordship or dominion, the quality of having ruling power, and it can shift to name actual rulers or authorities collectively. It appears just 4 times across 4 books, split evenly: sometimes it points to abstract rule (Ephesians 1:21), sometimes to a category of beings called "dominions" (Colossians 1:16), and twice it describes an authority that people slander or reject (2 Peter 2:10; Jude 8). The lexicons note that in these letters it often refers to a heavenly or angelic hierarchy, which is why it slides between the abstract idea of lordship and a concrete group of rulers.
caution: With only 4 occurrences spread across distinct contexts, the line between abstract "dominion" and concrete angelic "dominions" is genuinely hard to pin down.

definition: The act of moving or being set in motion, such as the stirring of water.
article: κίνησις refers to movement or stirring, the noun form of the verb κινέω ("to move"). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 5:3, describing the stirring of the pool's water, and shows up just twice in the Septuagint, once rendering the Hebrew word נִיד. Everyday Koine papyri stretch the sense further: one inscription uses κίνησις for a Jewish uprising or sedition in Syria, and a magical text uses it for the movement of one's joints.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and rarely elsewhere, so its full range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To spend money in addition to what one has already spent, especially on top of earlier expenses.
article: προσαναλίσκω means to spend even more money on top of what has already gone out — the prefix πρός adds the sense of "further" to the base verb ἀναλίσκω, "to spend." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 8:43, describing the woman who had spent all her living on doctors. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions too, as in an inscription where someone "spent no small amount of money" finishing a public task, showing it was ordinary financial language.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and some manuscripts and editors (noted by Abbott-Smith) omit it at Luke 8:43, so the evidence is thin.

definition: To shut something firmly and completely, especially to close and lock a door.
article: ἀποκλείω means to close something fully and securely—built from ἀπό plus κλείω, "to shut." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 13:25, where the master of the house has shut the door. The Septuagint uses it 28 times, mostly to render the Hebrew סָגַר ("to shut," 20×), and an everyday papyrus from Oxyrhynchus even has someone reporting, "I shut the door of my house," showing the word's plain, practical use in ordinary Koine.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse, though the Septuagint and papyri confirm the same meaning.

definition: Ruin or destruction that wrecks a person's life, sometimes meaning death or final punishment.
article: ὄλεθρος is a strong word for ruin — the loss of everything that makes life worthwhile, and sometimes death itself. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 4 times, rendered "destruction" in 3 of them (75%) and once in 1 Corinthians 5:5 as "destruction of the flesh" (a kind of physical discipline). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes a somewhat weaker use in everyday papyri, where a fourth-century document speaks of the "great danger" or ruin facing a town council over withheld supplies, showing the word could describe disaster short of total annihilation.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the precise force of the word in passages like 1 Corinthians 5:5 remains debated.

definition: Greece, the geographical region of the Greek-speaking world, used in the New Testament for the area also called Achaia.
article: Ἑλλάς is the native name for Greece, appearing just once in the New Testament (Acts 20:2). Its geographical boundaries varied in usage, and in the New Testament it corresponds to the region also called Achaia (compare Acts 18:12). In the Septuagint it appears twice, where Abbott-Smith notes it translates the Hebrew name Javan (יָוָן), and a Delphic inscription honoring Hadrian as the savior who 'nurtured his own Hellas' shows the word's everyday use in the Greek world.
caution: The measured-sense data here is clearly garbled, listing 'encouragement' for Acts 20:2, which contradicts every lexicon that identifies this word simply as Greece.

definition: Terah, the father of Abraham, named in genealogy.
article: Θάρα is the Greek form of the Hebrew name תֶּרַח (Terah), the father of Abraham. It appears only once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Luke 3:34, and shows up 11 times in the Septuagint across 3 books, always rendering the same Hebrew name. As a proper name it doesn't carry a meaning beyond identifying the person, and it is indeclinable in Greek.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage there rests on a single passage.

definition: An exclamation expressing grief or denouncing impending judgment, like saying "woe!" or "alas!"
article: οὐαί is an interjection that cries out either in sorrow or in denunciation, most often rendered "Woe" and frequently followed by "for" when a reason is given (16 of 47 times). It can stand alone or take a person as its target—"woe to you"—and in the Septuagint it appears 60 times, translating the Hebrew lament-words הוֹי (29×) and אוֹי (14×). Strikingly, it is not found in classical Greek at all, yet Moulton-Milligan turned it up in an everyday Koine farce papyrus that piles it on: "Woe to thee wretched, hapless one! Woe to you, woe to me!"

definition: A time-marker meaning "when" or "at the time that," linking one event to another.
article: ὁπότε is a connecting word meaning "when" — it ties an action to the moment something else happened. In classical Greek it carried the sense of "whenever" (as in Homer), but in everyday Koine papyri it had softened to simply "when," and the New Testament follows this later usage in its single occurrence (Luke 6:3, where it introduces David's action when he was hungry). A nice papyrus parallel is P Oxy 243, dated A.D. 79, which uses ὁπότε περιῆν to mean "when she was alive."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: Zeus, the chief god of the Greek pantheon, identified with the Roman Jupiter.
article: Ζεύς is the name of the supreme deity of the Greeks, equated by the Romans with Jupiter. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 14:12-13, where the people of Lystra mistake Paul and Barnabas for gods and call Barnabas "Zeus." Notably, the name has an irregular grammar: in its oblique cases it borrows forms from a probably related, otherwise obsolete name (genitive Διός, dative Διΐ, accusative Δία).
caution: This is a rare proper name appearing only twice, so its range cannot be measured beyond these two passages.

definition: An older person, or a respected leader holding an office of authority within a community.
article: At its core πρεσβύτερος is the comparative "older," and it spans two related ideas: literally an older person (like the elder son in Luke 15:25) and, more often, someone holding a position of authority — the religious leaders or council members among the Jews, and later officers of Christian assemblies. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "elders" in 59 of 67 occurrences (95%), and it absorbs into surrounding phrasing 5 times. In the Septuagint it appears 165 times, usually translating the Hebrew זָקֵן ("old/elder," 120×), and everyday papyri confirm the ordinary sense — one Oxyrhynchus document even uses it of an elder brother, and another preserves a quirky double-comparative "our elder sister."

definition: A squad of four Roman soldiers assigned to guard a prisoner.
article: τετράδιον means a "group of four," built from the word for four (τέσσαρες), and in its single New Testament use (Acts 12:4) it refers to a squad of four Roman soldiers guarding the imprisoned Peter. The everyday Koine of the papyri shows the same core idea of "a set of four" applied to very different things: a heathen amulet uses it of days, and one document counts parchment in "twenty-five quaternions," or sets of four sheets. So while the soldier sense is fixed in Acts, the word's broader range is simply any group or set of four.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical sense rests on a single verse.

definition: To bring things together—words in conversation, thoughts in the mind, or people meeting, sometimes for hostile encounter.
article: The basic idea is 'throw together,' and from there the word fans out in several directions: turning thoughts over in your mind (Mary 'treasured' things in her heart), weighing a decision, or people putting their heads together to confer. It can even mean meeting someone, including in a hostile sense like going out to battle. The everyday papyri show the practical 'confer/arrange' use nicely—one document has a writer saying 'I arranged with Apollos and he appointed the eleventh for his coming down.'
caution: With only 6 occurrences and each measured sense appearing just once, the senses are thinly attested even though the lexicons agree on the broad range.

definition: A roll or scroll of a written document, originally a term for the little head or knob at the end of a papyrus roll.
article: In the New Testament κεφαλίς appears just once, in Hebrews 10:7, where the phrase "in the roll of the book" quotes Psalm 40:8 from the Septuagint. The word is literally a diminutive of κεφαλή ("head"), and lexicographers trace its meaning from a "little head" or the capital of a column, then to a scroll. Interestingly, while it's often said the term came from the knob at the end of the stick a papyrus was wound around, Moulton-Milligan notes that no actual example of that sense has ever been found.
caution: Evidence is thin (only one NT occurrence, all in a quotation), and the supposed link to the scroll's end-knob is unattested in the documents.

definition: Causing harm or injury; damaging to a person's well-being.
article: βλαβερός means "harmful" or "injurious," describing something that does damage. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:9, where Paul warns that the desire to be rich plunges people into "harmful" desires (rendered "ensnared" by the Majority Standard Bible). The word was at home in everyday Koine: a second-century medical papyrus uses it of ripe fruits warned against "as being very harmful," and a third-century B.C. inscription speaks of taking care that nothing harmful happen to the land. Its sole Septuagint use renders a Hebrew word at Proverbs 10:26.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range is very thin, and the lone NT rendering "ensnared" reads loosely against the basic sense "harmful."

definition: Nain, a village in Galilee where Jesus raised a widow's son.
article: Nain is a proper name—a small village in Galilee—and as a place name it doesn't really vary in meaning. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 7:11, where Jesus comes to the town and raises a widow's son. Abbott-Smith links the name to a Hebrew word (compare H4999), which fits its likely Semitic origin.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so the evidence base is very thin.

definition: To enlist or recruit someone as a soldier into an army.
article: This verb is built from the words for "army" (στρατός) and "to gather" (λέγω), and it means to recruit or muster troops. It appears only once in the New Testament (2 Timothy 2:4), where it refers to the one who enlisted a soldier. The Majority Standard Bible's translation "entangling" reflects the broader sentence about a soldier not getting tangled in civilian affairs rather than the bare meaning of the word, which everyday Koine papyri and writers like Josephus and Plutarch use plainly for enlisting soldiers.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range in Scripture cannot be measured.

definition: To spread or strew something out underneath, such as laying garments or bedding on the ground beneath someone or something.
article: This verb means to spread or strew something out beneath — like garments laid down to cover a road. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 19:36, where crowds spread their cloaks on the road before Jesus (the Majority Standard Bible's "rode" reflects the wider scene rather than the verb itself). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the same down-to-earth use: one document describes spreading out a clean linen cloth and olive branches, another spreading thorny bedding underneath someone.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (and none in the critical text) plus three Septuagint uses, the evidence base is thin.

definition: To melt or dissolve something, or in the passive, to melt away or waste away as under heat.
article: τήκω means to melt or liquefy, and in the passive to melt away or dissolve. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only once, at 2 Peter 3:12, where it describes the elements melting in heat — though the Majority Standard Bible renders that single occurrence as "hasten" rather than the expected "melt." The Septuagint uses it 35 times across 15 books, often for Hebrew מָסַס (6×) and מָקַק (5×), and the papyri attest a vivid sense of wasting away from fever, while Moulton-Milligan notes a related compound used of melting down lard.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the standard glosses ("melt") disagree with the single measured rendering ("hasten"), so its New Testament force is uncertain.

definition: Praise or commendation, especially praise offered to God.
article: In the New Testament αἶνος means praise, particularly praise directed toward God, appearing only twice (in Matthew 21:16 and Luke 18:43), where both occurrences are rendered simply "praise" or "ordained praise." Its range was once much wider: the classical lexica note it originally meant a tale or story (like μῦθος in Homer), and the everyday papyri and inscriptions show it used for an official decree, as in an Achaean council ruling. The Septuagint uses it six times, translating several different Hebrew words including those for "founding," "song," and even "conspiracy."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the lexica documenting a broad classical range (tale, decree, praise), confidence in the precise sense is low.

definition: A thin flake or scaly piece of material, such as a peeling of skin.
article: λεπίς refers to a scale or flake, derived from a verb meaning "to peel." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 9:18, where something like scales falls from Saul's eyes and he regains his sight; the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) consistently define it as a scale or scaly substance. Interestingly, the everyday papyri and inscriptions use the word for thin sheets of metal — one inscription from 279 B.C. mentions a censer fitted with a silver λεπίς — showing its ordinary sense was simply a thin flake or plate.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be confidently measured.

definition: Intense passion that can be positive zeal and devotion or negative jealousy and rivalry, depending on its object.
article: This word names a kind of burning intensity that points two directions: in the Byzantine New Testament it means jealousy 50% of the time (8×) and positive zeal 38% (6×). Its root sense is heat or boiling over (from ζέω, "to boil"), and the Septuagint uses it 30 times, most often (25×) for the Hebrew קִנְאָה. A revealing detail comes from an early erotic papyrus fragment where someone says "jealousy grips me and I am consumed with burning" — showing the word's core idea is fervor or burning passion rather than mere rivalry.
caution: Whether a given verse means "jealousy" or "zeal" depends heavily on context, and translators don't always agree on which sense fits.

definition: Those who came before in one's family line—ancestors or, when still living, parents.
article: πρόγονος literally means "born before," and in its plural form refers to the people who came before you in your family—either distant ancestors or living parents. It appears just twice in the New Testament: in 2 Timothy 1:3 it means "forefathers," while in 1 Timothy 5:4 it points to living parents, a usage also found in Plato. Moulton-Milligan notes that the exact phrase "from one's forefathers" (ἀπὸ προγόνων) was common in inscriptions, often describing someone respectable across generations.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and the MSB's odd "godliness" rendering at 1 Timothy 5:4 conflicting with the lexicons' "living parents," the measured data here is thin and partly unreliable.

definition: A fixed expression meaning "there is" or "there exists," used in the New Testament mostly to deny that something is present.
article: ἔνι is a compact, frozen form meaning "there is" or "there exists," functioning like the fuller phrase ἔνεστι. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 6 times across 4 books, almost always inside a negative statement denying that a distinction or thing exists—as in Galatians 3:28, where it three times declares "there is no" division between groups. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "nor" only twice; the other 4 times it dissolves into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this usage, where phrases like οὐκ ἔνι could even mean "it cannot be done."
caution: With only 6 occurrences and most absorbed into phrasing rather than rendered as a distinct word, the measured sense rests on thin direct evidence.

definition: To overstep proper limits and wrong someone, especially by taking advantage of them.
article: This word literally means "to step over," and that physical sense survives in everyday Koine papyri—one third-century BC document describes people who "all stepped over into my courtyard," while others use it for passing beyond a certain age. In the New Testament it appears only once, in 1 Thessalonians 4:6, where it is used figuratively for overstepping limits and wronging another person; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "violate." In the Septuagint it shows up 13 times across 7 books, sometimes translating the Hebrew for a heap or a threshold (something stepped over).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and lexicons disagree on whether it means "transgress" absolutely or "overreach/defraud" someone, so its precise force here is uncertain.

definition: Describing someone or something that is disgusting and deserving of strong moral rejection.
article: βδελυκτός means "detestable" or "abominable" — worthy of disgust and rejection. It appears just once in the New Testament (Titus 1:16), where it is woven into the phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. In the Septuagint it shows up only a handful of times; one notable point is the disagreement in the evidence over which Hebrew word it renders — the digest cites רָשַׁע ("wicked"), while Abbott-Smith links it to תּוֹעֵבָה ("abomination") in Proverbs 17:15.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament use and a few Septuagint occurrences, and the sources disagree about which Hebrew word it translates.

definition: To remind someone again of something they already know.
article: This verb means to bring something back to a person's memory, with the prefixes suggesting reminding "again" or in addition to what they already grasp. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 15:15, where Paul says he has written boldly to remind his readers. The Majority Standard Bible's wording there centers on Paul's boldness in writing, but the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) consistently define the word itself as "to remind again," so the act of reminding is the core meaning.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word, and the measured rendering ("bold") reflects the surrounding sentence rather than the verb's own meaning, which the lexicons give as "remind again."

definition: To please someone, or to act so as to win their favor — often by rendering willing service for their benefit.
senseLabels: to please or seek to please
article: At its core ἀρέσκω means to please someone, and that single sense covers all 17 New Testament occurrences, rendered "please" in 9 of them. But there's a richer shade behind the word: in everyday Koine it often carries the idea of actively serving others' interests rather than just pleasing oneself. Moulton-Milligan points to monumental inscriptions where ἀρέσκω describes citizens who "proved themselves of use to the commonwealth," which lines up with passages like Romans 15:1-3 and 1 Corinthians 10:33 where the focus is on benefiting others. In the Septuagint it appears 39 times, most often translating the Hebrew יָטַב ("to be good, go well").

definition: Hosea, the Old Testament prophet whose words Paul quotes.
article: Ὡσηέ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Hosea (הוֹשֵׁעַ), referring to the Old Testament prophet. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 9:25, where Paul cites the prophet's writing, and the name there is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. In the Septuagint it occurs 14 times across 4 books, usually rendering the Hebrew name Hosea (12 times), though twice it stands for an unrelated place-name element.
caution: This is a proper name with only one New Testament occurrence, so its range rests almost entirely on Septuagint and Hebrew evidence.

definition: Matthew, the personal name of one of Jesus' twelve apostles, also called Levi the tax collector.
article: Ματθαῖος is simply the proper name Matthew, borne by one of Jesus' twelve apostles, appearing 5 times across 4 books in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "Matthew" in all cases, with two occurrences (in lists of the apostles, Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13) tagged as "Matthew Zealot" — though this likely reflects list context rather than a separate meaning. Notably, the name is also attested in everyday Koine papyri, and scholars have debated its spelling: the double aspirate form Μαθθαῖος shows up in documents like a sixth-century papyrus from Florence.
caution: This is a personal name, so the two "measured senses" reflect translation context rather than genuinely different meanings.

definition: To go out or depart from a place; in some contexts the related participle marks the time or people involved in leaving.
article: This verb basically means to go forth or depart from a place. In all 4 of its New Testament occurrences (all in Acts), it appears as a participle, which is why translations render it variously — half the time it shades into a time marker ("the next" sabbath or day) and half the time it points to the people doing the departing ("those" who left). The everyday flavor shows up nicely in the papyri, where someone writes "as I was setting forth for Alexandria," exactly the sense of starting out on a journey.
caution: The measured "next" and "those" labels reflect how participles get smoothed into English rather than two distinct meanings, so the core sense "to go forth" is what to keep in mind.

definition: A room or chamber, used in the New Testament specifically for a prison cell.
article: At its root οἴκημα simply means a room or dwelling space, built on the verb οἰκέω ("to dwell"). The everyday papyri show this general sense—one petition from the third century B.C. complains about a neighbor who occupied two οἰκήματα in a shared courtyard. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 12:7), it is used euphemistically of a prison chamber, the room where Peter was held, and that is why both the Majority Standard Bible and BSB render it "cell" there. Interestingly, classical writers stretched the same euphemism even further, using it for a brothel.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its "cell" sense rests on a single verse, while the broader "dwelling" meaning comes from outside sources.

definition: An earnest plea or supplication made to someone in a position to grant a favor.
article: ἱκετηρία refers to a heartfelt petition or supplication addressed to someone with the power to help. It appears just once in the New Testament (Hebrews 5:7) and once in the Septuagint, where it translates the Hebrew word rak. According to the classical lexica, the word originally named the olive branch that a suppliant carried in his hand, which later came to stand for the act of pleading itself; everyday Koine papyri confirm this sense, as in a petition where a woman pleads with a governor on behalf of her orphaned daughter.
caution: Evidence is thin — the word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its range is hard to measure.

definition: Help or assistance given to others; in 1 Corinthians it names a role of practical support within the church.
article: ἀντίληψις means the act of helping or coming to someone's aid, and it appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 12:28, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "administration." The Septuagint uses it 6 times, mostly in the Psalms, often for the idea of strength or support. The richest evidence comes from everyday papyri, where it repeatedly shows up in petitions to the Ptolemaic rulers meaning "assistance" — as in one plea where the writers' "one hope" is the help that lies in the official's power.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so its precise sense there is hard to pin down and translations vary between "help" and "administration."

definition: A person who engages in sexual immorality, especially sex outside of marriage or with a prostitute.
article: πόρνος refers to a person who lives in sexual immorality, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sexually immoral" in 9 of its 10 New Testament uses, with the BSB agreeing 100%. The word literally meant a male prostitute (as in Xenophon and other classical writers), but in the New Testament it is generally understood in the broader sense of a fornicator. One striking detail: Deissmann compared the New Testament vice lists that include πόρνοι (as in 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:9) with the labels for vicious characters inscribed on the counters of a popular ancient game.

definition: To hold firmly to someone or something, staying loyal and committed to them.
article: In the New Testament ἀντέχομαι always appears in the middle voice meaning to hold fast or cling to someone or something—whether loyalty to a master (Matthew 6:24, Luke 16:13), supporting the weak (1 Thessalonians 5:14), or holding firmly to sound teaching (Titus 1:9). Though it literally comes from "hold against" and can mean to withstand, all 4 Byzantine uses carry the "cleave to" sense. The everyday papyri back this up beautifully: a document from 117 BC describes villagers "with one accord holding fast" to a patron's protection, showing the same warm sense of devoted attachment.
caution: All 4 NT uses were absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, so its force is felt only across whole clauses.

definition: A breaking that leaves complete destruction—either a literal fracture or, figuratively, ruin and calamity.
article: σύντριμμα comes from the verb συντρίβω ("to break in pieces") and names the result of such breaking: a fracture, a crushing, or by extension utter ruin. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Romans 3:16 ("ruin lies in their paths"), but turns up 31 times in the Septuagint, most often translating the Hebrew shever ("breaking," 17×). The everyday Koine papyri preserve the concrete sense nicely—a medical-magical text from the second or third century AD uses it for a literal "fracture" alongside a sprain, and Modern Greek still has συντρίμμια for "ruins."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the figurative "ruin" sense rests almost entirely on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than measured NT usage.

definition: To go down or set, used of the sun sinking below the horizon at the end of the day.
article: This verb describes the sun setting at day's end, built from ἐπί ("upon") and δύνω ("to sink"). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament — in Ephesians 4:26's warning not to let the sun go down on your anger — where the corpus shows it absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by its own English word. The Septuagint uses it just 3 times, and notably Abbott-Smith treats all three as translating Hebrew בּוֹא ("to come, go [down]"), even though the digest's raw counts list other Hebrew words alongside it.
caution: Evidence is very thin — one New Testament occurrence and three in the Septuagint — and the listed Hebrew counterparts disagree with Abbott-Smith's note, so the precise range is uncertain.

definition: Free from fault or blame; so upright that no one can rightly find anything to criticize.
article: ἄμεμπτος describes someone or something so beyond reproach that no fault can be found in it. The word is built from a negative prefix plus a form of μέμφομαι ("to blame"), so it literally means "unblameable." The four measured senses in the Byzantine New Testament are really one idea expressed in slightly different English phrases, and the BSB rendering matches independently every time. Everyday papyri put the word to vivid use: a marriage contract describes a wife conducting herself "blamelessly," and it shows up often on tombstones praising the dead alongside the word for "good" (χρηστός).
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences, each rendering rests on a single instance, so the apparent variety of senses is mostly one meaning in different wordings.

definition: To die or be destroyed together with others.
article: This verb combines "with" and "destroy," so it means being killed or wiped out alongside someone else. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament — at Hebrews 11:31, where Rahab did not perish with the disobedient — and seven times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew word sāphâ, meaning to be swept away. A papyrus from A.D. 131 uses it vividly when a man fears that, on top of losing his property, he might also "perish with hunger."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs just once in the New Testament and the digest reports it was absorbed into phrasing rather than translated as its own English word.

definition: Physical training or bodily exercise, like that of athletes preparing for the games.
article: γυμνασία refers to physical training or bodily exercise, the kind associated with athletes. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Timothy 4:8) and once in the Septuagint (4 Maccabees 11:20), so its biblical range is narrow. An inscription from Trajan's or Hadrian's era uses it for the formal exercises of athletic games overseen by judges, and Moulton-Milligan suggests that same ordinary sense fits 1 Timothy 4:8, where the value of bodily training is contrasted with spiritual training.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests on a single passage plus outside evidence.

definition: To come in alongside something, either as an addition that arrives later or as someone who slips in secretly.
senseLabels: to come in alongside, be added
article: This compound verb stacks "alongside" (παρά) onto "come in" (εἰσέρχομαι), and it carries two distinct shades. In Romans 5:20 it describes the law that "came in alongside" so that sin would increase — an addition entering the scene — while in Galatians 2:4 it describes false brothers who "slipped in" secretly, the sneaky sense. Moulton-Milligan note the everyday Koine flavor of related words: a papyrus from the third century AD uses a kindred form to say "you cannot creep in, for the woman has been in possession a long time."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences split evenly between two different senses, the evidence is thin and the meaning depends heavily on context.

definition: Being like the angels, especially in no longer being subject to death.
article: ἰσάγγελος combines the words for "equal/like" (ἴσος) and "angel" (ἄγγελος) to describe people who have become like the angels. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 20:36, where Jesus says those raised from the dead are "equal to the angels" and can no longer die. The word also turns up outside the Bible, including a Christian epitaph that speaks of someone's "angel-like fortune," and it follows a common Koine pattern of similar compounds like ἰσόθεος ("equal to a god") and ἰσοβασιλεύς ("equal to a king").
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from the biblical text alone.

definition: The form, shape, or outward appearance that expresses what something essentially is.
article: μορφή means the form or shape of something — its outward appearance, though classical and philosophical writers used it for the essential character that shows through that appearance. It is rare in the Byzantine New Testament, appearing only 3 times: twice rendered "form" (Mark 16:12, Philippians 2:6) and once as "form being made" (Philippians 2:7). A nice everyday touch comes from the Septuagint and papyri: in Tobit 1:13 God gives Tobit "grace and μορφήν," echoed in Greek papyri letters that ask the gods to grant someone favor and μορφήν before the king — here closer to "beauty" or pleasing appearance than abstract essence.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences — and lexicographers note the word carries a debated overlap between mere outward shape and essential, defining form.

definition: The ordinal number meaning sixth, as in the sixth in a sequence or the sixth hour of the day.
article: ἕκτος is simply the ordinal number "sixth," formed from the cardinal number ἕξ (six). Every one of its 14 occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament is rendered "sixth" (100%), and the BSB agrees fully, so its meaning is completely stable. It often marks the sixth hour of the day, as in the darkness at Jesus' crucifixion (Mark 15:33), and in the Septuagint it appears 33 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for "sixth" (29 of those uses).

definition: More boldly or freely, with greater confidence than one might otherwise use.
article: This is the comparative form of an adverb meaning "boldly" or "daringly," so it means writing or speaking with more confidence than usual. It appears only once in the New Testament (Romans 15:15), where Paul says he has written somewhat more boldly. The word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, where one third-century document uses the related adverb to describe acting "boldly."

definition: The future-tense form of the verb "to be," meaning "will be," "will exist," or "will happen."
article: This is simply the future tense of the common Greek verb εἰμί, "to be" — so it carries the same broad range, meaning "will be," "will exist," "will happen," or "will be present." Strong's lists it under "will be," and the KJV renders it with phrases like "shall be," "shall come to pass," and even "X live long" or "X sojourn," showing how flexibly a future "to be" stretches in English. The Abbott-Smith entry treats it under εἰμί, where the verb covers existing, occurring, and being present in a place.
caution: The digest records zero occurrences of this specific form in the Byzantine New Testament and the evidence is drawn from the parent verb εἰμί, so its independent range here is not measured.

definition: Red in color; in the New Testament always paired with "sea" to name the Red Sea.
article: ἐρυθρός simply means "red," but in both of its New Testament appearances (Acts 7:36 and Hebrews 11:29) it occurs in the phrase "the Red Sea" (ἡ ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα). The Septuagint uses it 25 times, most often (18×) to render the Hebrew סוּף in the name of that sea. Everyday Koine documents confirm the geographic usage: an inscription thanks the gods after a man sailed safely out of "the Red Sea," and officials are titled commanders "of the Red Sea," which ancient editors took to mean the Arabian Gulf.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both naming the Red Sea, there is no measured example of the plain color sense "red" used on its own.

definition: Literally "hard-necked," describing people who are stubborn and refuse to obey or listen.
article: σκληροτράχηλος combines the words for "hard" (σκληρός) and "neck" (τράχηλος) to picture someone stiff-necked and unwilling to turn—a vivid metaphor for stubbornness. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 7:51, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "uncircumcised" (though the word literally means stiff-necked, and KJV, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith all give "stiff-necked, obstinate"). The image comes straight from the Septuagint, which uses it six times in three books to translate the Hebrew phrase for a "stiff neck" (עֹרֶף), as in Exodus 33:3 when God calls Israel a stiff-necked people.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the lone measured rendering "uncircumcised" departs from the literal "stiff-necked" sense given by the lexicons, so treat the gloss with care.

definition: To lead or bring someone or something up or out, and—in sailing contexts—to put a ship out to sea.
article: At its core ἀνάγω means to lead or bring up, built from ἀνά ("up") and ἄγω ("lead"). In the New Testament its 23 uses split almost evenly between two streams: bringing or leading people somewhere (about 56% of renderings), and a specialized nautical sense of putting out to sea, which dominates the sea-voyage narratives of Acts ("sail" and "set sail" together account for 39%). The everyday Koine papyri add a vivid touch: the word was used for bringing back a runaway slave and even restoring land to use as a vineyard.
caution: The two main uses—leading/bringing versus sailing—are quite different, so the intended meaning depends heavily on context, especially in Acts.

definition: A formal charge or accusation brought against someone, often in a legal setting.
article: κατηγορία means an accusation or charge leveled against someone, frequently in a courtroom context. It appears 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the three measured 'senses' are really one consistent meaning—a formal charge—differing only in whether the accusation targets a person (John 18:29), is simply being sought (Luke 6:7), or concerns an elder (Titus 1:6). The everyday legal flavor shows up clearly in the papyri: an Oxyrhynchus document from A.D. 186 speaks of 'the proofs of his accusation' before entering a more serious lawsuit.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the three listed 'senses' all reflect the single meaning 'accusation,' so the divisions are contextual rather than truly distinct.

definition: To put or lay something aside or away, often used figuratively for renouncing sinful behavior like removing a garment.
article: In the New Testament this word always appears in the middle voice, meaning to put something off from yourself—either literally laying down a garment (as when the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of those stoning Stephen) or, more often, figuratively casting off sins and old ways of living. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "put" in 2 of its 8 occurrences, with other passages using phrasings like "put off" or "lay aside." The everyday papyri show a vivid secondary sense: "to stow away" or store goods, and one Egyptian document from 223 BC uses almost the exact phrasing of Matthew 14:3 about putting someone away in prison.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and translations spread thinly across several phrasings, the precise English rendering varies by context.

definition: To turn around, turn back, or return—physically reversing direction, or figuratively turning toward God.
article: This verb covers physical turning and returning, and at its core means to reverse direction. In the Byzantine NT it shows up 37 times, most often simply rendered "turn" (16×, 46%) or "turned" (8×, 23%), with the rest covering returning or going back. It's a workhorse word in the Septuagint, appearing 466 times and most often translating Hebrew שׁוּב (321×), the standard word for "return"—which is why it so naturally carries the figurative sense of turning back to God; the everyday papyri even use it with an ethical edge, as when someone "paid no attention" to an instruction.

definition: To become physically or mentally exhausted—to grow faint, weary, or to give out.
article: At its root ἐκλύω means to loosen or release, but in the New Testament it always appears in its figurative sense of being drained of strength. Across its 5 Byzantine occurrences it describes people fainting from hunger (40%) or growing weary in body and spirit, including losing heart under discipline. The literal meaning is vividly preserved outside the Bible: a papyrus from 113 BC uses it of someone "letting out" water onto his own land, while the Septuagint uses it 35 times, often rendering the Hebrew רָפָה ("to slacken or grow weak").
caution: The word is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, so its 5 occurrences reflect the Byzantine/Majority tradition rather than universally agreed readings.

definition: Describing someone easily angered or quick-tempered.
article: ὀργίλος describes a person who is easily provoked to anger — hot-tempered or irascible. It appears only once in the New Testament (Titus 1:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "quick"), but the Septuagint uses it 4 times, twice translating Hebrew words for wrath or fury (Proverbs 22:24; 29:22). A notable parallel comes from the Didache (iii.2), which warns "do not be ὀργίλος, for anger leads to murder," capturing exactly the sense found in the classical lexica.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax, so its precise range there rests on a single verse plus the broader Septuagint and Koine evidence.

definition: To rise above others—either by ranking higher in authority or by surpassing them in worth or excellence.
article: ὑπερέχω literally means to hold something above, and figuratively to rise above—either by outranking someone in authority or by surpassing them in value. Across its 5 New Testament uses the sense splits evenly: once of considering others above yourself (Philippians 2:3), once of something surpassing in worth (Philippians 3:8), and once of governing authority (1 Peter 2:13), with two more uses absorbed into surrounding phrasing. An everyday papyrus from 257 BC captures the flavor nicely, describing a boy trained for the games who 'in an exceedingly short time will far excel' the other competitors.
caution: Only 5 New Testament occurrences and two of them dissolve into phrasing, so each measured sense rests on a single example.

definition: Something that trips a person up—a snare or obstacle that causes them to stumble, sin, or take offense.
article: σκάνδαλον originally named the bait-stick of a trap—the trigger that springs a snare shut—and from there came to mean anything that trips someone up, whether literally or morally. In the Byzantine New Testament's 15 occurrences it most often appears as "stumbling block" (6×, 43%), with smaller groups rendered "cause sin" (2×) and "offense" (2×). In the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew מוֹקֵשׁ, a "snare" or "trap," which fits the word's trapping origins, and it even shows up in everyday papyri (8th-century documents pairing it with "pretext"), showing it was ordinary Koine, not just religious vocabulary.

definition: To be hungry, lacking food; figuratively, to deeply crave or long for something.
article: πεινάω simply means to be hungry or to feel hunger, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it that way in all 23 occurrences—about 70% rendered "hungry" and 22% "hunger." It can also be used figuratively for craving, as when Jesus speaks of those who "hunger and thirst for righteousness" (Matthew 5:6). In the Septuagint it appears 40 times, mostly translating Hebrew words for being hungry or weary, and Moulton-Milligan notes a vivid everyday papyrus from A.D. 85 describing someone going hungry during a famine.

definition: One who destroys or brings ruin; a destroying agent that kills.
article: ὀλοθρευτής means "destroyer" — one who brings ruin or death. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 10:10, and the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, KJV) consistently give "destroyer," with Strong's adding the special sense of a venomous serpent. Moulton-Milligan note that this is a New Testament hapax and discuss its unusual spelling, where an ε shifted to ο.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured-sense data oddly records it as "complain" (likely a tagging artifact from its verse context), which conflicts with the lexicons' unanimous "destroyer" — trust the lexical sense here.

definition: To fill up something that is lacking, supplying what is still needed, possibly on behalf of someone else.
article: This is a vivid triple-compound verb (from ἀντί plus ἀναπληρόω) that appears just once in the New Testament, at Colossians 1:24, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fill." The base idea is filling up what is still missing, and Dodson adds the nuance of doing so "in place of someone else," which fits the verse's sense of completing something on another's behalf. Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and point out that its opposite, ἀνταναιρέω ("subtract"), is extremely common in Ptolemaic land-surveys—over twenty instances in one Tebtunis papyrus alone.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force—especially whether it means filling up "in turn" or "in place of someone"—rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Describing someone as beautiful, fine, or attractive in appearance.
article: In the New Testament ἀστεῖος appears just twice, both times meaning "beautiful" — once of the infant Moses in Acts 7:20 and again of him in Hebrews 11:23. The word originally meant "belonging to the city" (from ἄστυ, a city), and like the Latin urbanus it could carry shades of "refined," "elegant," or "courteous," but that civic connection had faded in everyday Koine. A striking bit of evidence comes from the papyri, where a document from around 245 BC uses it of fine clothing — "let him wear as fine clothes as possible."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (low confidence tier), the fuller "refined/elegant" range survives only in the Septuagint, papyri, and classical sources, not in the measured biblical data.

definition: Isaiah, the Old Testament prophet whose writings the New Testament repeatedly quotes.
article: This is the Greek form of the name Isaiah, the Hebrew prophet, appearing 21 times across 6 Byzantine NT books and rendered "Isaiah" in 20 of them (95%). It is simply a proper name, so its meaning never varies; the New Testament cites him constantly as the author of quoted prophecies. In the Septuagint the name shows up 31 times and almost always stands for the Hebrew יְשַׁעְיָה (30 times), with one stray case translating חִזְקִיָּה.

definition: Hidden or concealed from sight; private, secret, or kept out in the open's view.
article: κρυπτός describes anything hidden, concealed, or done in private rather than out in the open — whether a secret act, an inner reality of the heart, or something not yet brought to light. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "secret" most often, and it appears 19 times across 8 books. It comes from the verb κρύπτω (to hide), and the everyday papyri show its practical edge: a sale document from A.D. 359 uses it for a slave's "hidden defect" (latens vitium) that the seller is liable for, showing how ordinary the word was for things concealed.
caution: In roughly 4 of 19 occurrences the word is absorbed into a phrase (such as "in secret") rather than translated by its own English word, so the rendering depends heavily on context.

definition: Describing something planted or rooted within a person, whether seen as naturally inborn or implanted from outside.
article: ἔμφυτος describes something rooted inside a person, built from the parts meaning "in" and "to grow." Its single New Testament appearance, in James 1:21, speaks of the implanted word, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "moral" there. There's a genuine debate about its exact force: Abbott-Smith lists both "innate" and "rooted, implanted," and the papyri (such as one referring to "your natural kindness") favor the sense "inborn, natural" — which is why scholars like Hort argued for that meaning over "implanted from without."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the evidence is thin, with sources genuinely divided over whether it means "inborn" or "implanted from outside."

definition: To strike someone on the head; in its only New Testament use, to wound on the head.
article: In the New Testament this verb appears just once, in Mark 12:4, where it describes servants striking a messenger on the head. The form is unusual: the word is built from the same root as κεφαλή (head), and elsewhere it naturally means 'to sum up' or 'state summarily' (as in Thucydides and the Septuagint at Sirach 32:8). Moulton-Milligan notes that the everyday Koine sense would be 'summed up,' yet the context of Mark 12:4 clearly demands 'struck on the head,' which is why some suspect Mark used a known word in an unfamiliar sense.
caution: This is essentially a one-off use whose 'wound on the head' meaning conflicts with the word's normal sense of 'sum up,' and scholars are genuinely uncertain how to explain it.

definition: To place oneself or someone else under a solemn curse, vowing destruction or binding an oath with the threat of God's judgment.
senseLabels: to curse or invoke a curse
article: This verb means to put yourself or others under a powerful curse — either by cursing outright or by swearing a binding oath that calls down destruction if it is broken. In the Byzantine New Testament its 4 uses split between Peter cursing as he denies Jesus (Mark 14:71) and a group of men who bound themselves with an oath to kill Paul (Acts 23). The Septuagint connection is telling: it renders the Hebrew חָרַם 12 of 13 times, the word for devoting something to total destruction, which explains the heavy sense of doom behind the term.
caution: The four New Testament uses are rendered with slightly different phrases, but they reflect a single underlying idea of cursing or oath-binding rather than truly distinct senses.

definition: To bring something forward against someone, such as a charge, accusation, or judgment, or simply to add or produce.
article: At its core ἐπιφέρω combines ἐπί ("upon, against") with φέρω ("carry"), meaning to bring or carry something toward a target — often in a legal or hostile sense like leveling an accusation or imposing a judgment. Across its 5 Byzantine New Testament occurrences each rendering appears just once: "brought," "speak," "highlights," and "charge," so no single sense dominates. The everyday papyri confirm this legal flavor: documents repeatedly use it for producing proofs or certificates in court, as in an Oxyrhynchus text where someone acts "in accordance with the proofs he produced."
caution: With only 5 occurrences spread evenly across four different renderings, the precise sense in any given verse depends heavily on context.

definition: A plan or decision reached by discussion, or the council of advisers that produces it.
article: συμβούλιον covers both the act of taking counsel together and the resulting decision—and by extension the advisory body itself. In the Byzantine New Testament's 8 occurrences it splits evenly: a quarter render it as plotting against someone (Matthew 12:14, Mark 3:6), a quarter as conferring (Matthew 27:7, Acts 25:12), and a quarter as a settled plan (Matthew 28:12, Mark 15:1). The papyri sharpen the 'council' sense beautifully: P Tebt II.286 describes a presiding judge who 'rose to confer with his council and deliberated,' matching the legal setting of Acts 25:12.
caution: With only 8 occurrences spread across overlapping meanings of 'counsel' and 'council,' the line between the act of deliberating and the resulting plan is not always sharp.

definition: An interrogative particle that signals a question, often one expecting the answer "no" or expressing uncertainty.
article: ἆρα is a question-marking particle that flags a sentence as an inquiry, frequently one anticipating a negative answer or carrying a note of anxiety or doubt. Because it works as a structural signal rather than a content word, it often dissolves into the phrasing of an English question — 6 of its 19 Byzantine occurrences carry no English word of their own, and translators most often supply "then" (4×, 31%) or "there" (2×, 15%). One vivid example from everyday Koine survives in a papyrus interview with a Roman emperor, where a condemned man demands, "Was it the senate, or you, the archpirate?" — showing the particle's natural conversational use.
caution: It appears 19 times in the Byzantine text but 0 times in the critical SBLGNT, so its presence is text-dependent, and grammarians note it is closely related to the similar particle ἄρα.

definition: The act of giving, or the gift that is given.
article: δόσις covers both the act of giving and the concrete gift that results, depending on context. It appears only twice in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible's rendering is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word (notably James 1:17, on every good gift coming from above). The papyri are especially telling here: Moulton-Milligan show the word was very common in everyday financial documents, where it meant an installment or payment, such as 'the second installment' in lease and loan records.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and no standalone English rendering measured, the evidence for its biblical range is thin.

definition: A threat — a hostile warning meant to frighten, intimidate, or pressure someone.
article: ἀπειλή means a threat: a hostile or intimidating warning aimed at someone. In all 3 measured New Testament occurrences (plus one where it was absorbed into the phrasing) the sense is consistent, and the Septuagint uses it 8 times, most often for the Hebrew גְּעָרָה ("rebuke"). The everyday Koine papyri show the same flavor vividly — one document describes a man being "driven away with a threat" (μετ᾽ ἀπιλῆς), confirming this was plain, ordinary language for menacing speech.

definition: To equip someone completely with weapons and armor for battle or defense.
article: καθοπλίζω means to arm someone thoroughly, head to toe, with weapons and armor. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:21, where it describes a strong man fully armed guarding his property — there it shows up in passive form. The word turns up in everyday Koine too: one papyrus describes a figure of Fear appearing fully armed, and the Letter of Aristeas uses it of selecting and arming the best men.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range in biblical Greek is very thin.

definition: An indefinite particle meaning "somewhere" or "anywhere," or, with numbers, "about" or "approximately."
article: πού is a small enclitic particle that points vaguely rather than precisely—it means "somewhere" or "anywhere," and when paired with a quantity it softens it to "about" or "roughly." The Byzantine New Testament has it only 6 times across 5 books (51 in the critical text), but its range is well attested: in Hebrews 2:6 and 4:4 someone has testified "somewhere," while in Romans 4:19 it means Abraham was "about" a hundred years old. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri, where third-century BC letters use it casually in phrases like "perhaps we too will be useful to you."
caution: With so few New Testament occurrences and some forms disputed in the manuscripts (note the variants μήπου and δήπου in Acts 27:29 and Hebrews 2:16), the precise sense in each verse can be hard to pin down.

definition: To act as a shepherd—tending and caring for a flock—and by extension to lead or rule over people.
senseLabels: to shepherd or tend a flock
article: ποιμαίνω means to act as a shepherd: to tend, feed, and care for a flock. The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "shepherd" in 7 of 11 New Testament occurrences (88%), with 3 more absorbed into surrounding phrasing; a rare rendering is "rule." The figurative reach toward governing is real—lexicons like Dodson note "I rule, govern"—but everyday Koine kept the literal sense alive, as papyri show people hired to ποιμαίνω, that is, to pasture someone's sheep. In the Septuagint it appears 52 times, overwhelmingly translating the Hebrew רָעָה ("to tend/graze," 34×).

definition: A person who shares in something with others — a partner, associate, or one who takes part alongside others.
article: κοινωνός describes someone who shares in something jointly with others, whether as a business partner, a companion, or a participant in some experience. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "partners" in 4 of 11 cases (44%) and "partaker" in 2 cases (22%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday Koine flavor comes through vividly in the papyri: a fishing contract from around A.D. 198–211 uses the word for a man taken on as a partner entitled to a one-sixth share in a lake's rent, showing it was the ordinary term for a business associate.

definition: The arm of a person, often used as a vivid image of someone's power or strength to act.
