article: βραχίων simply means the arm, and all 3 New Testament occurrences are rendered "arm" (100%), though in each case it pictures power in action—often God's. In the Septuagint it appears 108 times, most frequently translating the Hebrew word for arm (זְרוֹעַ, 67×), and the phrase "arm of the Lord" became a stock image for divine strength. One interesting detail: in an ancient inscription the word refers to a shoulder of meat given to a priest, showing its plain, physical roots in everyday Greek.
caution: This word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, so its measured range there is narrow even though the broader Greek evidence is rich.

definition: To go past or move by, and figuratively to pass away, perish, or come to an end.
article: παρέρχομαι covers the basic motion of going past someone or something, but in the New Testament it most often carries the figurative sense of passing away or perishing, used in 9 of its 29 occurrences for things that come to an end. It also describes time elapsing and people moving along a route, and a couple of times it shades into neglecting or disregarding something (as in Luke 11:42). The word is firmly rooted in everyday Koine: the papyri show it for ships passing by and for time that has gone by, and in the Septuagint it appears 133 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew עָבַר ("to cross over, pass") 95 times.

definition: Describing someone in a wretched, miserable state, worn down by hardship or distress.
article: This adjective describes a person who is miserable, distressed, and worn out by trouble. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament—Paul's anguished cry in Romans 7:24—and is rendered "wretched" every time. The everyday papyri show the same flavor: one second-century B.C. document pleads that officials "must spare the miserable populace," confirming that ordinary Greek-speakers used it for genuine human suffering, not mere poetic lament.
caution: Evidence is thin—just one Byzantine occurrence and three Septuagint uses—so the confidence tier is low, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: A high official commanding people—either a Roman city magistrate, a military leader, or the captain in charge of the temple guard.
article: στρατηγός is a title for someone in charge, and the New Testament uses it across a notable range. In Acts 16 it refers to the Roman city magistrates of Philippi (rendered "magistrates" 3× in the Byzantine text), while elsewhere it names the captain of the Levitical temple guard, a post the lexica describe as ranking just below the High Priest. The Septuagint reaches even wider, using the word 23× to translate several different Hebrew terms, including the Persian-era officials סְגָנִים (7×).
caution: Only the civic "magistrate" sense was measured here, so the temple-guard usage seen in Luke and elsewhere in Acts isn't reflected in the corpus rendering counts.

definition: Describing something as dark or filled with darkness, the opposite of full of light.
article: σκοτεινός simply means "dark" or "full of darkness," and it stands as the direct opposite of φωτεινός ("full of light"). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in Jesus' teaching about the eye as the lamp of the body (Matthew 6:23, Luke 11:34, 36). The word was part of ordinary Koine speech: a papyrus from 159 B.C. uses it for someone being put "into a dark place," and in the Septuagint it often renders Hebrew words for darkness, including the vivid term for deep shadow or "shadow of death."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, the three listed senses are really one meaning—"dark"—shaded by context rather than genuinely distinct senses.

definition: Of many kinds or sorts; varied or diverse in character, originally referring to something many-colored or variegated.
article: ποικίλος describes something that comes in many kinds or varieties, and in the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "various" or "kinds" in nearly every case, including the recurring use for people sick with "various diseases" (Matthew 4:24, Luke 4:40). The original concrete sense was "many-colored" or "variegated," which still shows up in the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew words like רִקְמָה (embroidered, multicolored cloth) and עָקֹד (streaked or spotted livestock). That literal coloring sense is vivid in the papyri, where an account of goats sorts them as black, red, and ποικίλαι (streaked).
caution: With only nine New Testament occurrences and a meaning that ranges from concrete "many-colored" to abstract "manifold," the exact shade depends heavily on context.

definition: Drusilla, a woman in the Herodian family who was the wife of the governor Felix.
article: Drusilla is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 24:24, where she is identified as the wife of Felix. The name comes from a feminine diminutive of the Roman name Drusus. Dodson adds that she was the daughter of Herod Agrippa I, born A.D. 39, placing her within the Herodian family.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its usage cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: Physical weakness or illness, especially the kind of bodily ailment that needs healing.
article: In the New Testament μαλακία always means bodily weakness or sickness, and it appears only 3 times, all in Matthew, always paired with νόσος ("disease") in describing the ailments Jesus healed. The Septuagint uses it the same way 15 times, most often rendering the Hebrew חֹלִי ("sickness," 9×). Interestingly, the classical lexicons note an older sense of "softness" or "effeminacy" (in Herodotus and Thucydides) that never surfaces in biblical use, and the word turns up on later Christian healing amulets begging God to "take away every disease and every sickness."
caution: With only 3 NT occurrences—all the same phrase in Matthew—the three measured senses are really one meaning, "sickness," distinguished only by surrounding wording.

definition: To disturb or trouble someone, especially by causing physical or mental distress.
article: ὀχλέω comes from ὄχλος ("crowd") and originally meant to mob or crowd around, then broadened to mean simply to trouble, vex, or disturb. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice (Luke 6:18, Acts 5:16), both times of people troubled by unclean spirits, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within phrases describing "those" who were afflicted. Everyday papyri show it had a thoroughly ordinary sense too — one letter pleads "don't worry the people of Sambas" — though some scholars detect a more technical, medical nuance in Acts 5:16.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and zero in the critical SBLGNT text, the evidence is thin and the sense is reconstructed largely from lexica and papyri rather than measured corpus range.

definition: A person who kills or violently strikes his own father.
article: This word names someone who murders or beats his own father, listed among grave offenders in 1 Timothy 1:9, its only New Testament appearance. Its range stretches between two shades: the strict sense "father-killer" (parricide) and the older, more literal "father-thrasher," since the second half of the word comes from a verb meaning "to smite." Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Deissmann compared its harsh tone to a stock insult hurled at a scoundrel in a Roman comedy.
caution: The single occurrence and the measured rendering "enacted" reflect a tagging artifact rather than the word's real meaning, so lean on the lexical evidence here.

definition: Describing someone who becomes invisible or vanishes from sight.
article: ἄφαντος literally means 'not made visible,' built from a negative prefix and the root of φαίνω ('to appear'). It occurs only once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:31, where the risen Jesus 'became ἄφαντος' from the two disciples at Emmaus — the word is absorbed into the phrase rather than translated as a single English word. Moulton-Milligan note it is a poetic term that resurfaced in later prose writers, and that Luke's addition of 'from them' (ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν) is unusual Greek, possibly a Hebraism imitating Septuagint phrasing.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range in biblical Greek cannot be measured from usage.

definition: Describing what is needed for a single day, especially food — the day's supply.
article: ἐφήμερος literally means "for a day" — built from ἐπί ("for") and ἡμέρα ("day"). In its single New Testament appearance (James 2:15), it describes the daily food a poor person lacks, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "daily" there 100% of the time, with the BSB agreeing fully. Moulton-Milligan note that everyday Koine papyri use the phrase to mean food for the day or the day's supply rather than simply "daily food," and Abbott-Smith adds an older sense, "lasting for a day," not seen in the NT.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament (a hapax), so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A settled condition or skill developed through repeated practice and experience.
article: ἕξις refers to a state or capacity that someone develops through steady, repeated use rather than something innate. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Hebrews 5:14, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the idea of "solid constant use" — the trained ability of mature believers to tell good from evil. The classical lexica (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) widen the range to include condition, state, and especially good condition of body or soul, but the single New Testament use measures only the "habit from practice" sense.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range here rests on a single occurrence plus broader lexical tradition.

definition: An earnest request to God arising from a sense of need, often translated as a prayer, petition, or supplication.
article: δέησις is an earnest appeal made out of genuine need, and in the New Testament it is always addressed to God. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "prayer" in half of its 19 occurrences and "petition" in another 28%, so the word blends both ideas of devotion and specific request. In the Septuagint it appears 58 times, most often translating the Hebrew תְּחִנָּה ("plea for favor," 14×), and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one Ptolemaic prisoner pleads "with supplication and entreaty" (μετὰ δεήσεως καὶ ἱκετείας). Lexicons note that unlike the broader word προσευχή (prayer in general), δέησις specifically stresses the sense of need behind the request.

definition: To smear or spread something onto a surface, such as putting a substance on a person's eyes.
article: This verb means to smear or spread a substance onto something, formed from the prefix ἐπί ("on") plus χρίω ("to anoint"). It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the account of Jesus healing the blind man by putting mud on his eyes (John 9:6, 11). A striking parallel comes from an inscription found at a temple of Asclepios in Rome (after A.D. 138), where a blind soldier is told by the god to mix ingredients and "smear them on the eyes" (ἐπιχρεῖσαι ἐπὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς) for three days, after which he regained his sight.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, both in the same healing story, the evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: The entrance area or vestibule leading from the street into a building's inner courtyard.
article: προαύλιον describes the entryway or porch that leads from the street into the inner court (αὐλή) of a building. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 14:68, where the Berean translations render it "gateway" 100% of the time. Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and one later Greek writer even used it figuratively in the plural to mean "preludes" or beginnings.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Brought in secretly or from the outside, like someone slipped in without proper authorization.
article: This word describes someone or something introduced surreptitiously, especially an outsider who doesn't truly belong to the group. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Galatians 2:4, where Paul speaks of false brothers who were smuggled in. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note from everyday Koine papyri that the term need not be sinister—it can simply mean someone 'alien' to the body they've slipped into, and the ancient lexicographer Suidas defines it plainly as 'foreign.'
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence with low confidence, and sources differ on whether it carries a hostile sense or just means 'outsider.'

definition: To shine brightly all around someone or something, surrounding them with light.
article: περιλάμπω means to shine all around, wrapping a person or place in light. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times describing a sudden glory of light: around the shepherds when the angel appeared (Luke 2:9) and around Paul on the road to Damascus (Acts 26:13). The word is built from περί ('around') and λάμπω ('to shine'), so its meaning is simply the sum of its parts — light blazing on every side.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, this is a thin sample, though the sources fully agree on its meaning.

definition: To make someone wise or instruct them; in some uses, to cleverly devise or invent something.
article: This verb is built from σοφός ("wise") and basically means to make someone wise or to instruct them, which is how both New Testament occurrences are rendered ("make," 2× — in 2 Timothy 3:15 the Scriptures make one wise for salvation). But the word has a second life: in the middle/passive voice it can mean to devise something cleverly, as in 2 Peter 1:16 ("cunningly devised fables"). The everyday Koine papyri show this sneakier edge too — one fourth-century text uses it for a person who "makes all manner of subtle excuses" before doing wrong. In the Septuagint it appears 11 times across 5 books, mostly translating the Hebrew word for "to be wise."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences (both rendered "make"), the corpus data is thin, and the lexicons show a real split between "instruct" and the cleverer sense "devise," so the measured data does not capture the word's full range.

definition: A person who joins others in a rebellion or riot, a fellow rebel.
article: This word describes someone who took part in an uprising alongside others — a fellow-insurgent or fellow-rioter. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Mark 15:7, where Barabbas is named together with those who had committed murder during an insurrection; notably the critical (SBLGNT) text does not include this form. The Majority text renders it loosely as "fellow," but Strong's, Dodson, and Abbott-Smith all agree the fuller sense is a partner in sedition, and Moulton-Milligan confirm the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This is a single occurrence resting on the Byzantine reading, since the critical text omits this form, so the evidence is thin.

definition: A hill in Athens, also the name of the high council or court that met there.
article: Ἄρειος Πάγος literally means the "hill of Ares" (the Greek god of war, which is why the KJV calls it "Mars' Hill"), an open space in Athens. By New Testament times the phrase had also come to mean the Council that met there—the supreme court of Athens—rather than just the rock itself. A notable detail: Moulton-Milligan cites Ramsay's evidence from inscriptions showing this colloquial shift, with one record reading "the Areopagus made speeches at Eleusis," clearly referring to the body of people, not the location.
caution: The measured "Paul" sense reflects a translation artifact where the phrase was absorbed into surrounding wording, not a genuine meaning of the term.

definition: Jonan, a man listed as one of Jesus' ancestors in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ἰωνάν is simply a personal name, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 3:30) as one ancestor in the line leading to Jesus. It carries no meaning beyond identifying this individual, and lexicons treat it purely as a proper name. Notably the spelling varies between manuscripts (Ἰωνάν and Ἰωνάμ), and the name probably stands as a form related to Iōannēs (G2491) or Iōnas (G2495).
caution: This name occurs only once and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, with manuscripts disagreeing on its spelling.

definition: Pleasure or the craving for it, especially the kind of self-indulgent enjoyment that pulls a person away from better things.
article: ἡδονή means pleasure, and in the New Testament it consistently carries a negative edge — the kind of indulgent enjoyment or craving that chokes growth or drives conflict. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "pleasures" in 4 of its 5 occurrences (80%), with the remaining case (James 4:1) rendered "among" simply because of how the phrase reads in English. Outside the Bible, the word was perfectly ordinary and even positive in everyday Koine: an inscription with a rescript of the emperor Septimius Severus speaks of "the pleasure you have in your achievements," showing the negative sense is a New Testament choice rather than the word's only meaning.
caution: The word appears only 5 times in the New Testament, and that second "measured sense" reflects an English phrasing in James 4:1 rather than a genuinely different meaning.

definition: The inner thoughts, reflections, or reasonings that go on in a person's mind.
article: This noun points to what goes on inside the mind — thoughts, reflections, and the inward pondering of the affections. Across its 4 New Testament occurrences it usually means "thoughts" (as when Jesus knew what people were thinking), and once in Acts 17:29 it shades toward a human notion or conception about God. Abbott-Smith notes a useful distinction: a related word ἔννοια is the work of the reason, while ἐνθύμησις leans more toward the affections, and the everyday papyri confirm the word was common Koine — it even shows up in a magic charm aiming to bind a person's mind and thoughts.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and one rendering (Acts 17:29) where the translation drifts from the simple "thoughts" sense, the precise range stays somewhat uncertain.

definition: A male personal name ( y three three different men in the New Testament book of Acts.
article: Ananias is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Chananyah, and it appears 11 times in Acts, always as a proper name. The book uses it for three distinct men: the husband of Sapphira who died after lying to the church, a disciple at Damascus who helped Paul, and the high priest in Jerusalem who opposed Paul. In the Septuagint the same name turns up 33 times across 6 books, where it mostly translates the Hebrew Chananyah (19 times) but occasionally stands in for other Hebrew names like Jeremiah and Mishael.

definition: Free from guilt or punishment; not held responsible for wrongdoing.
article: ἄθωος describes someone who is innocent and therefore not liable to punishment. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew 27, where Judas admits betraying "innocent" blood and Pilate declares himself free of responsibility for Jesus' death. In the Septuagint it shows up 48 times, most often translating the Hebrew נָקִי and נָקָה ("clean, acquitted"); everyday papyri use it in legal contexts, such as a Tebtunis document warning that an assailant should not "escape unpunished."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise shade — "innocent" versus "unpunished" — depends heavily on context.

definition: Done with one's own hands; describing an action performed personally rather than by someone else.
article: αὐτόχειρ literally combines "self" and "hand," describing something done by one's own hands. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 27:19, where the crew throws the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands. Interestingly, the Koine astrological writer Vettius Valens uses the word absolutely to mean "suicides" (those who die by their own hand), showing how the literal sense could specialize.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: A worthy achievement or successful reform, especially good public administration that sets things right.
article: This noun, built from κατά and a root meaning "upright," refers to something set right or successfully accomplished — classically a worthy deed or good public administration. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 24:2), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "prosecution," though that fits the trial setting more than the word's usual meaning of "beneficial deed." The everyday Koine flavor is captured in a papyrus praising a man named Aurelius Ploution for "accomplishing the greatest reforms (κατορθώματα) for his homeland," and an inscription honoring a benefactor who achieved many good things for his city.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine text and not at all in the critical text, and editors disagree over whether the original reading is κατόρθωμα or διόρθωμα, so the evidence is thin.

definition: To run down toward something or someone, as when rushing from a higher position to reach a place quickly.
article: This compound of κατά ("down") and τρέχω ("run") appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:32, where it is rendered "ran" 100% of the time, describing a commander rushing down with soldiers to the crowd. The Septuagint uses it 5 times across 5 books, sometimes for Hebrew words involving pursuit. Interestingly, the everyday Koine papyri show a more hostile edge: one document from 153 B.C. uses it for someone "running down" or attacking another person, and another for an official who "oppresses" farmers.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured, and the papyri suggest a more aggressive sense than the single NT use shows.

definition: Physical force or violence, especially the strength used to compel or overpower someone or something.
article: βία refers to physical force or violence—the kind of strength that compels, restrains, or overpowers. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and in most cases (2 of 3) it gets folded into English phrasing rather than translated as its own word; in Acts 21:35 the idea surfaces in how the crowd's violence forced Paul to be carried by soldiers. The everyday Koine papyri illustrate the word vividly, including a widow's complaint of being "subjected to unmitigated violence" and a man "forcibly detained," and the Septuagint uses it 14 times to render Hebrew words like פַּח and פָּרֶךְ (harsh, forced labor).
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences—and two absorbed into phrasing—the measured evidence is thin, though the classical lexica and papyri agree on the core meaning of force or violence.

definition: The act of rolling or wallowing, used in the New Testament for a washed pig returning to roll in the mud (its vomit/filth).
article: This word literally points to a rolling or wallowing, and by extension the filthy result of that rolling. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (2 Peter 2:22), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "vomit" 100% of the time, picturing a clean pig going back to wallow in mud. Interestingly, the form κύλισμα belongs to the Textus Receptus here; the best texts instead read κυλισμός, and Moulton-Milligan note that in Ezekiel 10:13 (Symmachus) κύλισμα keeps its proper sense of "something rolled round" rather than a wallowing-place.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word found only in the Textus Receptus reading of 2 Peter 2:22 (critical texts read κυλισμός), and the lexica disagree on whether it means a roll, a rolling, or a wallowing-place.

definition: Something seen, especially a supernatural sight or vision—often one granted in a dream or revelation.
article: ὅραμα is literally "that which is seen," and in the New Testament it nearly always refers to a vision—a supernatural sight, often granted in sleep or a trance. Of its 12 occurrences, 8 (73%) are rendered "vision," and the word clusters heavily in Acts, where figures like Cornelius and Paul receive divine messages this way. In the Septuagint it appears 41 times, frequently translating the Hebrew חָזוֹן ("vision"), and everyday Koine papyri use it the same way—one third-century BC letter and a temple inscription both speak of a ὅραμα as a vision experienced in sleep.

definition: To grow old or age, used of people becoming elderly and of things wearing out toward obsolescence.
article: γηράσκω means to grow old or age. In the New Testament it appears only twice: once literally of a person aging (John 21:18) and once figuratively of something becoming worn out and obsolete (Hebrews 8:13). In the Septuagint it shows up 14 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew root זָקֵן for being old, and Moulton-Milligan cite an everyday papyrus where an old man (γεγηρακότα) pleads for mercy.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the figurative 'obsolete' sense rests on a single verse.

definition: To be at or pass the middle point of a period of time, such as a festival being halfway through.
article: μεσόω means to be in the middle, especially of a stretch of time. Its single New Testament appearance (John 7:14) describes the feast being halfway over, and both the Majority Standard Bible and BSB render it that way 100% of the time. In the Septuagint it shows up 4 times across 3 books, including the memorable phrase "in the middle of the night" (Exodus 12:29), which captures the same time-midpoint sense.
caution: Appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Knowledge of a specific thing or person, often implying full recognition or accurate understanding.
article: ἐπίγνωσις means knowledge directed at a particular object—a recognition or accurate grasp of something or someone. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 20 times and is rendered "knowledge" in 15 of those (88%), with three more cases absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew דָּ֫עַת ("knowledge") four times, and an everyday papyrus from around 114 BC uses it of details being "accurately known," which fits the idea of full or precise discernment that some lexicons emphasize.

definition: A contracted form meaning "these same things" or "in the same way," pointing back to what was just mentioned.
article: This is a crasis — a fusion of the article and the pronoun αὐτός — that functions as an adverb meaning "thus" or "in the same way," essentially "the same things." The lexica (Strong's, Abbott-Smith) agree on this "in the same way" sense, with older glosses like "even thus" and "so." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament at all, so its profile here rests entirely on the dictionary derivation rather than measured biblical usage.
caution: This form has zero occurrences in the Byzantine NT, so the meaning rests on lexicon entries rather than measured corpus data.

definition: Someone who shares jointly with others in something, a co-participant or fellow partaker.
article: συμμέτοχος describes a person who takes part in something alongside others — a fellow sharer or joint participant. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both rendered "partakers" (100%), once with a genitive of the thing shared (Ephesians 3:6) and once with a genitive of the persons (Ephesians 5:7). Everyday Koine documents back this sense vividly: a London papyrus from A.D. 594 uses the word for the "joint-possessors" of a house.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though the consistent rendering and papyri usage agree.

definition: To give glory to someone, or in the passive, to be honored and recognized as glorious through someone.
article: This verb means to glorify or be glorified, built on the adjective ἔνδοξος (glorious). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both in 2 Thessalonians 1 (verses 10 and 12) and always in the passive—Christ being glorified in his people, and his name among them. It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it shows up 10 times and usually renders the Hebrew כָּבַד (to be heavy, honored, glorified), and a papyrus invocation to the Sun even uses it: 'because through you he was glorified.'
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin—only two passive occurrences, both in one passage—so its full range there rests largely on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: A weakness or shortcoming, especially the failings of those weaker in faith that stronger believers should bear with.
article: This noun appears just once in the New Testament, in Romans 15:1, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "shortcomings" — the weaknesses of others that stronger believers are called to bear. Older sources give a wider range: the KJV reads "infirmity," Dodson adds "weakness, doubt, hesitation," and Strong's even suggests "a scruple of conscience," though these go beyond the single measured use. It is built from the verb meaning to be weak, and Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and was already used by Aristotle, with Paul developing the sense in his own way.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range rests on a single passage, and the broader meanings offered by older lexica are not confirmed by the measured evidence.

definition: To come or gather together, as a crowd assembling around someone.
article: σύνειμι means to come together or assemble, built from σύν ('with') and a verb meaning 'to go.' It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 8:4, where a large crowd gathers around Jesus; the Majority Standard Bible renders it with 'while' in that context, describing the people coming together. Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri, though the surviving examples are all quite late (around A.D. 565–570).
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there cannot be measured from multiple uses.

definition: Fair, calm weather, especially a clear sky.
article: εὐδία refers to good, calm weather, the kind of clear sky people read to predict the day ahead. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 16:2, where it describes a red evening sky promising fair weather. Originally a poetic word, it shows up in everyday Koine: the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) uses it metaphorically for a peaceful, well-ordered state, and Herodas lists it among Egypt's glories alongside power and fame.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is actually rejected in the best critical texts of Matthew 16:2, so its New Testament attestation is genuinely disputed.

definition: Relating to horses or horsemen, and as a noun the cavalry — a body of mounted soldiers.
article: This is an adjective meaning "of a horse" or "of horsemen," and when used as a noun (with "force" understood) it means cavalry, a unit of mounted soldiers. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up just once in the critical text, plus twice in the Septuagint (1 Maccabees 15:33 and 3 Maccabees 1:1). The everyday papyri make its military flavor vivid: documents mention soldiers "of the first cavalry regiment," "cavalry barracks," and even a "horseman's holding" of land, and one note may use it for a stable.
caution: Evidence is very thin — absent from the Byzantine NT and attested only a handful of times in the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: To add more threats on top of those already made, threatening someone further.
article: This verb describes piling on additional threats — combining the prefix "pros-" (in addition) with the verb "apeileō" (to threaten). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 4:21, where the rulers threaten the apostles even more before letting them go; it is absent from the critical SBLGNT text. Beyond the New Testament, the lexicons note just a single Septuagint trace at Sirach 13:3.
caution: This word is a New Testament hapax with very thin attestation overall, so its precise force rests on only one or two passages.

definition: Emmaus, a village about 60 furlongs (roughly seven miles) from Jerusalem.
article: Emmaus is the name of a place in Palestine, appearing just once in the New Testament—in Luke 24:13, where two disciples walk there on the day of the resurrection. Abbott-Smith fixes its location at 60 furlongs (about seven miles) from Jerusalem. The name is probably of Hebrew origin, and every translation surveyed simply renders it "Emmaus."
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once, so its meaning is settled but its evidence base is necessarily thin.

definition: In clear, explicit terms; saying something plainly and in so many words.
article: This adverb means stating something explicitly, plainly, and in set terms. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 4:1, where the Spirit "expressly" says something. The everyday papyri back this up nicely: it shows up in official documents and letters to mean "explicitly" or "in so many words," and a related form, ἐπὶ τοῦ ῥητοῦ, meant "at the specified time."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "later" sits oddly against the classical lexicons, which all give "expressly" or "explicitly."

definition: Four times as much; multiplied by four.
article: τετραπλόος means "fourfold" — four times the original amount. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 19:8, where Zacchaeus promises to repay anyone he has cheated four times over; the Majority Standard Bible, BSB, and KJV all render it "fourfold." Moulton-Milligan note that this everyday word turns up in Koine papyri and inscriptions, often in the related form τετραπλάσιος, used in legal and commercial documents to specify quadruple payment.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so the evidence base is thin.

definition: An open courtyard, especially the enclosed space around which a house is built, or sometimes a sheepfold or palace.
article: αὐλή refers to an open, enclosed space—most often the courtyard around which a house was built, as in the scenes of Peter waiting outside while Jesus is questioned. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "courtyard" in 6 of its 12 New Testament occurrences (75%), with the other 4 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The word is extremely common in everyday Koine papyri: a Cairo document lists a man's house "and courtyard and another dwelling," showing the ordinary sense of the yard attached to a home. In the Septuagint it appears 170 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew חָצֵר.
caution: Lexicons stretch the range to "sheepfold" (as in John 10) and even "palace," but the measured New Testament data shows only the "courtyard" sense.

definition: A rope or cord, originally one made from twisted rushes, used for tying, hauling, or measuring.
article: σχοινίον is a small rope or cord, technically a diminutive of σχοῖνος (a rush), since such ropes were originally made from rush plants. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 27:32, where sailors cut the ropes of a lifeboat, and John 2:15), but turns up 25 times in the Septuagint, where it mostly renders the Hebrew חֵבֶל for a rope or cord. The everyday character of the word shows in the papyri, where one Oxyrhynchus document mentions a well-reel fitted with a new σχοινίον, and another records a man complaining of being suspended daily by ropes; in the Septuagint it could even shift into meaning a measuring-line.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of those absorbed into phrasing, the measured data is thin, though the basic meaning 'rope' is well supported across all sources.

definition: Persuasive or convincing, describing words designed to win someone over by appeal rather than by force or proof.
article: πειθός means "persuasive" or "enticing," and it comes straight from the verb πείθω, "to persuade." It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 2:4) and the Byzantine count is a single occurrence absorbed into a phrase, so it gets no English word of its own in translation. Strikingly, Abbott-Smith notes this exact adjective form is "not found elsewhere" — the standard classical word was πιθανός — and Moulton-Milligan treats it as a freshly minted adjective built directly from the verb-stem.
caution: This is essentially a one-off word with only a single New Testament occurrence and an unusual form not attested elsewhere, so confidence about its precise range is low.

definition: To fully supply or fill up a lack by adding what is needed.
article: This compound verb means to fill up a shortage by adding to it, supplying fully what is lacking. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians (9:12 and 11:9), where Paul speaks of meeting the needs of others; Moulton-Milligan note that it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Philo uses it the same way of supplying someone's want. In its only Septuagint occurrence (Wisdom 19:4), it carries the same idea of filling up.
caution: With only two New Testament uses and thin overall attestation, the confidence tier is low, so the precise shade of meaning rests on limited evidence.

definition: To hang upon someone's words, meaning to listen with rapt, close attention.
article: This rare middle-voice verb literally means "to hang from or upon" something, but figuratively it pictures listeners hanging on a speaker's every word in close attention. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 19:48, where the people "hung" on Jesus' teaching, and once in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew קָשַׁר ("to bind") in Genesis 44:30. Notably, the manuscripts differ on the exact form: the received text reads ἐξεκρέματο while WH read ἐξεκρέμετο, which would imply a present form ἐκκρέμομαι that is otherwise unknown.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a disputed verb form across manuscripts, the evidence here is thin.

definition: To tear or rip something apart, often clothing torn in grief or outrage, or nets bursting under strain.
article: This verb means to tear, rip, or burst something open, and the New Testament uses it in two main ways: tearing nets that break under a huge catch of fish, and tearing one's own garments as a dramatic show of grief or anger. Of its 5 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "tore" 75% of the time and "tore clothes" once. Notably, a papyrus from A.D. 389 uses the closely related form to describe people who "tore off" someone's outer garment and stole it, showing the word was at home in ordinary, even violent, everyday Koine.
caution: Abbott-Smith notes the Septuagint uses it chiefly for a Hebrew word for "tear" (קָרָע), but the digest's measured Septuagint example translates a different Hebrew word, so the Old Greek range is not fully pinned down here.

definition: To restore someone to health, or in its older general sense to serve and attend on someone.
article: In the Byzantine New Testament θεραπεύω overwhelmingly means to heal or cure, rendered "healed" or "heal" in 96% of its 44 occurrences, almost always describing Jesus restoring the sick. The older lexicons preserve a broader range, where the word first meant to serve, attend, or wait upon someone — a sense that survives in the New Testament at Acts 17:25. One careful detail from the papyri and inscriptions: as a medical term θεραπεύω strictly means to treat medically rather than to guarantee a cure, fitting Luke's reputation as a physician.
caution: The measured New Testament data centers almost entirely on "heal," but the lexicons add a service sense, so the word's full range is wider than the corpus counts suggest.

definition: An interrogative or exclamatory word asking or marveling at how great, how large, or how important something or someone is.
article: πηλίκος is a question word meaning "how great" or "how large," properly about magnitude (as πόσος is about quantity). It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Galatians 6:11 it marvels at how large the letters Paul wrote with his own hand, and in Hebrews 7:4 it points to how great a person Melchizedek was. In the Septuagint it shows up twice, including Zechariah 2:2, where it renders a Hebrew word asking "how much" or "how far." Notably, the measured "plunder" rendering at Hebrews 7:4 reflects the surrounding context (the spoils Abraham gave) rather than the word itself, which the lexicons consistently define as "how great."
caution: Very thin evidence (only 2 New Testament occurrences), and the measured "plunder" sense reflects context rather than the word's actual meaning of "how great."

definition: Describing someone who practices the same craft or trade as another person.
article: This adjective combines the ideas of "same" and "craft" to describe two people who share the same trade or occupation. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:3, where Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla because they shared his trade of tentmaking. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and that medical writers used it specifically of fellow physicians.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its full range in the biblical text cannot be measured from usage alone.

definition: A teacher who explains and instructs others in the (Jewish Mosaic) law.
article: This is a compound built straightforwardly from "law" (νόμος) and "teacher" (διδάσκαλος), meaning someone who teaches and interprets the Mosaic law. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament — in Luke 5:17, Acts 5:34 (describing Gamaliel), and 1 Timothy 1:7 — and the Majority Standard Bible renders every instance as "teacher of the law." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan and Abbott-Smith note that the word seems to be confined to the New Testament and later church writings, with the closest classical parallel being the related form νομοδιδάκτης used by Plutarch.
caution: Confidence is rated low: the word occurs only 3 times and appears almost exclusively in biblical and church writings, so its broader Greek usage is thinly attested.

definition: A Roman mile, a unit of distance equal to about 1,000 paces or eight stades—slightly less than a modern mile.
article: μίλιον is a measure of distance: the Roman mile, reckoned at 1,000 paces, eight stades, or roughly 1,478 meters. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jesus's words about going an extra mile (Matthew 5:41), and every translation surveyed renders it simply as "mile." The word is itself a borrowing from Latin (milia passuum), and the papyri confirm its everyday use—one document describes two villages as being "less than a mile apart."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured across varied contexts.

definition: A smell or scent, whether the pleasant fragrance of something or a mere odor.
article: ὀσμή simply means a smell — most often a pleasant one. Of its 6 New Testament uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fragrance" 3 times (75% of the rendered cases) and "odor" once, with two more uses absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 68 times, almost always (56×) translating the Hebrew רֵיחַ ("smell"), and everyday Koine papyri use it literally too, as in a writer instructing a friend to choose wine "by its smell."
caution: With only 6 occurrences and 2 absorbed into phrasing, the line between "fragrance" and plain "odor" rests on slim measured evidence.

definition: The act of being caught, captured, or taken—originally of prey or a city seized by force.
article: ἅλωσις refers to a taking or capture, the moment something is caught or seized. It appears just once in the New Testament (2 Peter 2:12), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "destroyed"—describing creatures born to be caught and killed. The classical and lexical sense leans toward "capture" or "being taken," and its single Septuagint appearance (Jeremiah 50:46) translates a Hebrew word meaning to seize or take.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and the translation "destroyed" stretches beyond the lexicons' core sense of "capture."

definition: To miss the target, and so to wander away from the truth or fail at what you were aiming for.
article: ἀστοχέω literally means to miss a target (built from a negative prefix plus a word for "aim"), and in the New Testament it always carries the figurative sense of straying from the truth. It is rare, appearing only 3 times across 2 books, all in the Pastoral letters, and in each case it is woven into the phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: a document from 163 B.C. speaks of people "failing of what is right" (P Par 35.26), closely paralleling 1 Timothy 1:6, and one ill-spelled letter even uses it for someone who "misses" and so causes lasting grief.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the Pastorals, so its full range rests largely on outside papyri and Sirach.

definition: Describing something or someone set apart for service or ministry, especially serving spirits.
article: λειτουργικός describes things or beings devoted to service or ministry. In its single New Testament appearance (Hebrews 1:14, 100%), it describes angels as "ministering" spirits, and the BSB agrees fully. The most interesting evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where the word names a "work-tax" or "liturgic" tax listed alongside police-tax and medical-tax in Egyptian taxation rolls, showing its ordinary civic sense of public service.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range rests on a single verse.

definition: To cause something to sink underwater, or to plunge it into ruin or destruction.
article: βυθίζω means to make something sink, literally pushing it down into water or, figuratively, into ruin. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Luke 5:7 the boats begin to sink under the weight of the catch, and in 1 Timothy 6:9 it describes desires that plunge people into destruction. Moulton-Milligan note the figurative use is matched in everyday Koine sources, including an inscription about a city sunk by constant wars and a writer describing sober judgment being drowned by passion.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured evidence is thin and confidence is low.

definition: A defeat, loss, or shortcoming — a falling short from what is full or complete.
article: This rare noun comes from the verb meaning "to be defeated," and carries the idea of falling short, suffering loss, or being beaten. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 11:12 and 1 Corinthians 6:7) and just once in the Septuagint, at Isaiah 31:8, where it renders the Hebrew word מַס. Scholars like Field argue that in both New Testament uses the underlying sense is simply "defeat," without any special moral or ethical coloring, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "means" while the BSB agrees only half the time.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences plus one in the Septuagint — and translators disagree on how to render it, so confidence is low.

definition: A curved blade used to cut grain or prune plants by hand during harvest.
article: A δρέπανον is a curved harvesting blade — what English calls a sickle or pruning-hook. Every one of its 8 New Testament occurrences was rendered "sickle" (4× measured, with the BSB independently agreeing 75% of the time), and it shows up mostly in Revelation 14's harvest imagery. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical sense vividly: one document from 218 B.C. lists "a sickle for reaping worth 2 drachmae," and two inscriptions from Phrygia even invoke "the sickle of the curse" in a written imprecation.

definition: A bottomless depth, used in the New Testament as the prison-place where demons and evil spirits are confined.
article: In its 9 New Testament occurrences this word names the Abyss, a bottomless depth understood as the abode of the dead and especially of demons and evil spirits. Originally an adjective meaning "bottomless" or "boundless," it became a noun for this place; the Septuagint uses it 37 times, most often (21×) translating the Hebrew תְּהוֹם, the watery "deep" of Genesis 1:2. A striking detail: Moulton-Milligan note it was a common term in the magic papyri, where phrases like "upon the Abyss" appear in third-century spells.

definition: Refusing to make peace; unwilling to be reconciled or bound by any truce.
article: The word literally points to someone "without a libation" — the drink-offering that once sealed a treaty — and so describes a person who will not be reconciled or bound by any peace agreement. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (in Romans 1:31 and 2 Timothy 3:3), rendered "faithless" and "without" in the Majority Standard Bible, where it sits among lists of hardened, broken character traits. The most telling outside evidence comes from Priene, where the phrase "asylei kai aspondei" turns up seven times meaning "without formal treaty"; Moulton-Milligan neatly captures the metaphor for 2 Timothy as "friends need no treaty, and implacable foes will not make one."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences, just 1 in the critical text), and the measured rendering "without" is incomplete, so the fuller sense "implacable" rests largely on the classical lexica and papyri.

definition: A group of people reclining together to eat, like a dinner party seated in companies for a meal.
article: This word literally describes a place or posture for reclining, and from there came to mean the people gathered to eat together. In its single New Testament appearance (Luke 9:14), the Majority Standard Bible renders it "down in groups" 100% of the time, describing how the crowd was arranged to be fed. The evidence shows a wide everyday range outside the NT: the papyri and inscriptions use it for a banquet couch, and Abbott-Smith even lists meanings like a hut or an easy chair, with 3 Maccabees 6:31 offering a parallel to Luke's sense of "companies."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and low-tier confidence, the dining-group sense rests on a single verse plus a few outside parallels.

definition: To shine through or break through with light, as when day dawns and brightness pierces the darkness.
article: διαυγάζω describes light shining or breaking through — the way dawn pierces the night. The Byzantine New Testament uses it twice, most clearly in 2 Peter 1:19, where the day is pictured as dawning; the lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree on this 'shine through, dawn' core. The everyday papyri back this up vividly: one document describes how, after a laugh, light appeared and 'shone through everything' (διηύγασεν τὰ πάντα), and the word is even used of pottery and a horoscope.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text) — and the two measured renderings ('confirmed' and 'consisting') don't reflect the word's actual 'shine through' meaning, so treat the corpus senses with care.

definition: A renewal or rebirth — either the spiritual renewal of a person or the future restoration of the world.
article: This word combines "again" and "birth" to mean a fresh start or renewal, and both New Testament uses are translated "renewal." It points in two directions: the personal spiritual renewal at conversion (Titus 3:5, the "washing of renewal") and the cosmic restoration of the world in the age to come (Matthew 19:28). Notably, the term shows up in everyday Koine papyri and was used by earlier writers like Philo for the world's renewal after the flood and by Josephus for the restoration of Judah, so its sense of large-scale restoration was already familiar.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise scope—personal versus cosmic—must be read from context in each verse.

definition: A connecting word marking the place at which something happens or exists — "where" or "in the place that."
article: ὅπου is a place-marking relative word, best translated "where." Across its 81 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "where" 54 times (83%) and "wherever" 8 times (12%), with the remaining instances absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. Everyday Koine papyri show the same plain usage — one second-century letter reads "where I live with my husband," and another describes a journey "to Libya, where Ammon sings oracles to all men."

definition: To strengthen or support someone further, especially to firmly establish people in their faith or resolve.
article: This verb means to make someone stronger or to firmly support and establish them, built from ἐπί ('upon') and στηρίζω ('to fix, make firm'). In the Byzantine New Testament all 4 occurrences cluster in Acts and describe the apostles strengthening the disciples in their faith. The Septuagint uses it 14 times across 6 books, where the lexicons note it can render a physical sense of propping up or holding fast (Abbott-Smith links it to Hebrew סָמַךְ, 'to support').
caution: The measured senses are all very similar (each just one occurrence), so the apparent variety reflects context rather than a genuinely broad range.

definition: To rob someone by stripping or plundering them of their property or resources.
article: συλάω means to rob or strip someone of what they have, often by force. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:8, where Paul says he "robbed" other churches by accepting their support to serve the Corinthians. The word was common in everyday Koine: papyri use it for real-life thefts, such as a man complaining that someone "robbed me of a number of tools" or another finding his house pillaged.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on outside evidence from papyri and lexicons rather than repeated biblical usage.

definition: A curse — a solemn pronouncement calling for harm or doom on someone, the opposite of a blessing.
article: κατάρα means a curse: a formal wish or declaration that harm should fall on a person, standing as the direct opposite of a blessing (εὐλογία). It appears 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament, always rendered "curse," and shows up 35 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew word qelalah. Everyday Koine documents preserve the same force vividly — a tomb inscription from Phrygia (A.D. 243) warns that anyone who opens the grave will have "the curses" fall on his sight, body, children, and life.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and the English word absorbed into surrounding phrasing in 4 of them, the measured sense rests on relatively thin direct evidence.

definition: To finish or fully complete a task or project that someone has begun.
article: ἐκτελέω means to bring something all the way to completion—not just to start it but to carry it through to the end. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Jesus' parable about counting the cost before building a tower (Luke 14:29-30), where a builder who cannot finish is mocked. Everyday Koine papyri attest the word too, often for carrying out religious duties, such as a Tebtunis document describing priests performing the services of the gods.
caution: Both New Testament occurrences come from a single passage, so the measured range is narrow; the two listed senses reflect the same idea of completing work rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: Describing words or things that cannot or may not be spoken, whether impossible to express or too sacred to repeat.
article: This word combines a negative prefix with the idea of "spoken," so it means something not uttered — either because it can't be put into words or because it's too sacred to say aloud. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 12:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "things" (the phrase "inexpressible words"). The most telling evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions, where Moulton-Milligan shows the word was tied to the secret "mysteries" of ancient religion — for instance a 61 BC inscription from Mantinea speaks of guarding the unspoken mysteries of a god — which fits Paul's sense of words too holy to repeat.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise force here — "impossible to express" versus "forbidden to speak" — rests heavily on outside inscriptional evidence.

definition: Refers to a different person or thing of the same kind — "other," "another," or "one" set apart from those already mentioned.
article: ἄλλος is a basic Koine word for distinguishing one individual or thing from another of the same kind. It's flexible: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "other" half the time (74×) and "another" in 28% of its 159 occurrences, with smaller uses like "one," "else," and "some" rounding it out. Lexicons note a contrast with the related word ἕτερος: ἄλλος usually marks simple numerical distinction (another of the same kind), while ἕτερος leans toward difference in kind. Everyday papyri even show it tacked onto repeated personal names — "Mary the other one" in Matthew 27:61 mirrors documents listing a second "Thaesis the other."

definition: To give birth to or bring forth, often pictured as the completion of pregnancy.
article: ἀποκυέω means to bring forth or give birth, used both literally and figuratively. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in James (1:15 and 1:18), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "birth" every time, and the BSB agrees fully. Originally noted as a medical term for the close of pregnancy, the everyday Koine papyri show it as an ordinary synonym of τίκτω ("to bear"), strengthened by the prefix ἀπό to imply a completed, safe delivery — as in a first-century papyrus where a mother prays that a woman "may give birth."

definition: One who pays back what is owed, used of God as the one who rewards those who seek him.
article: μισθαποδότης literally means someone who pays wages, built from the words for "wage" and "to pay back." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:6, where God is described as the rewarder of those who diligently seek him. Strikingly, a Byzantine-era Christian papyrus (P. Gen. I. 14) uses almost identical language, calling God "the rewarder," showing the word lived in everyday Koine and not just Scripture.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To give someone a name or title, or in the middle voice to call upon someone for help, worship, or formal appeal.
senseLabels: named or called by a name
article: This verb covers a surprising range, from naming someone (often rendered "surnamed") to calling on God in worship or prayer, to making a legal appeal—famously Paul appealing to Caesar in Acts. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 32 times, most often translated "called" (11×) or "call" (9×), with four occurrences as "appealed" in Acts. The Septuagint uses it heavily (140×), chiefly for the Hebrew קָרָא ("to call," 70×), and the everyday papyri confirm both the "surname" sense (a king "surnamed Alexander") and the plain "call" sense.
caution: Whether a given instance means "to name" or "to call upon/appeal to" depends entirely on context, so the boundaries between its senses are not always sharp.

definition: Showing no thanks or appreciation; ungrateful toward those who have given or done good.
article: This adjective describes someone who fails to show gratitude, formed from a negative prefix plus the root behind χαρίζομαι (to show favor). In both New Testament occurrences (Luke 6:35 and 2 Timothy 3:2), the Majority Standard Bible renders it "ungrateful" 100% of the time, and the BSB agrees. Interestingly, the related verb shows up in everyday Koine papyri, and one third-century papyrus even uses the word for a medical "antidote" described as "without favor," while Abbott-Smith notes a secondary sense "ungracious, unpleasing" not reflected in the New Testament usage.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 New Testament occurrences—and the lexica list a broader "ungracious/unpleasing" sense that the measured biblical data does not show.

definition: To feel angry, disgusted, or offended with someone, often to the point of loathing them.
article: This verb describes a strong negative reaction—being angry with, disgusted by, or loathing someone. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Hebrews 3 (verses 10 and 17), where it quotes the Septuagint about God's reaction to the wilderness generation. The Septuagint uses it 17 times across 7 books to render several Hebrew verbs meaning to abhor or be disgusted (such as גָּעַל), which deepens the sense beyond mere anger toward outright loathing.
caution: Evidence is thin: both NT uses are the same Septuagint quotation, and the lexicons split between "be angry" and the stronger "abhor/be disgusted."

definition: A bow — the weapon that shoots arrows.
article: τόξον means a bow, the weapon used to shoot arrows. The New Testament uses it only once, in Revelation 6:2, where the rider on the white horse holds a bow; in the Septuagint it appears far more often (71 times), almost always translating the Hebrew word for bow, qeshet. The everyday papyri confirm this plain military sense — one document lists "one bow, one quiver" together as standard equipment.
caution: In the New Testament this word appears only once, so its full range there cannot be measured from that single use.

definition: To touch something lightly, especially with a fingertip.
article: προσψαύω means to touch something lightly, even with just a finger. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:46, where Jesus criticizes experts who load people with heavy burdens but will not so much as touch those burdens with one finger. Abbott-Smith notes the word belongs to poetic and later writers, and Strong's specifically describes it as laying a finger on something.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured; the lexicons agree on a light touch, but the database label "weigh" seems to be a tagging artifact rather than the actual meaning.

definition: An adjective meaning very great or very much, describing something extremely large in amount or number.
article: πάμπολυς is a compound of "all" (πᾶς) and "much" (πολύς), meaning "very great" or "very much" — a strong way to describe a huge crowd or quantity. It is well known from classical Greek and everyday Koine papyri, where it describes things like "a great deal of wood" or events "a very long while afterwards." In the Bible it appears only in the Textus Receptus reading of Mark 8:1 (describing a very large crowd); modern critical editions read "again a large crowd" (πάλιν πολλοῦ) instead, so the word may not belong to the New Testament text at all.
caution: This word rests on a single disputed reading in Mark 8:1 that modern critical texts replace, so its New Testament status is uncertain; the measured "became" reflects surrounding phrasing rather than the word's actual meaning.

definition: The act of persuading someone, or the state of being persuaded into a belief or course of action.
article: This noun describes persuasion — either the act of talking someone into something or the condition of having been won over. It is built from the verb πείθω ("to persuade, win over"), and it appears only once in the entire New Testament, at Galatians 5:8. The most interesting point is that scholars cannot decide whether Paul means it actively ("this persuading") or passively ("this being persuaded"); Moulton-Milligan notes everyday Koine papyri attest both usages.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources themselves are split on whether it means the act of persuading or the state of being persuaded.

definition: To go around or move about from place to place, often as a wanderer or itinerant traveler.
article: περιέρχομαι combines "around" (περί) with "come/go" (ἔρχομαι), and means moving about from place to place — whether wandering as a homeless person, going house to house, or making a circuit. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, used both of restless wandering (Hebrews 11:37; 1 Timothy 5:13, going "from house to house") and of a ship tacking around (Acts 28:13). In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, most often translating the Hebrew סָבַב ("to go around"), and the everyday papyri show it for people "going about the city" or even for an inheritance "coming around" to someone.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the range rests on thin New Testament evidence, and one of those uses contributes no distinct English word.

definition: To be like a small child—innocent and inexperienced—especially in one's thinking.
article: This verb means to act or be like a baby or young child, used figuratively for innocence or inexperience. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 14:20, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "thinking"—Paul tells readers to be babes in regard to evil while being mature in understanding. Outside the Bible the word is rare: Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, but is otherwise cited only from Hippocrates, with Homer using the related form νηπιαχεύω.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax (one occurrence) with thin attestation overall, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: To cool something down or make it refreshingly cool, as by dipping in water.
article: καταψύχω means to cool something off, with the sense of bringing refreshment. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:24, where the rich man begs that a fingertip dipped in water might cool his tongue. The same verb shows up only once in the Septuagint (Genesis 18:4), translating a Hebrew word, and Moulton-Milligan note it in everyday Koine documents, including a use by Josephus where people 'did not let their zeal cool.'
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one in the Septuagint, the evidence for its full range is thin.

definition: An adverb meaning no longer, no more, or not any further—marking that something which once happened or was true has now stopped.
article: οὐκέτι is a negative adverb of time built from οὐ ("not") and ἔτι ("still, yet"), so it signals that a previous state or action has ceased—"no longer" or "no more." The Majority Standard Bible renders it "longer" 60% of the time, with smaller portions translated "again" (12%), "no" (12%), and "further" (10%), and in 6 of 48 occurrences it simply blends into the phrasing without its own English word. In the Septuagint it appears 96 times and most often stands for Hebrew עוֹד ("still, yet") used with a negative, and Moulton-Milligan find the same everyday sense in the papyri, as in a letter saying "we are no longer able to stay indoors."

definition: A cutting or mutilation of the body; Paul uses it as a biting pun for those who insist on circumcision.
article: κατατομή literally means a cutting or incision into something, and that plain sense shows up in everyday Koine: an inscription uses it for cutting, and a papyrus phrase describes cutting into the ground. Paul uses the word just once in the New Testament (Philippians 3:2), where he turns it into a sarcastic pun: instead of the true 'circumcision' (περιτομή), he labels his opponents the 'mutilation' (κατατομή). The wordplay is the whole point — two similar-sounding words set in pointed contrast.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical sense rests entirely on a single sarcastic play on words.

definition: Showing practical wisdom—being sensible, prudent, and discerning in how one thinks and acts.
article: φρόνιμος describes someone who is practically wise—sensible, thoughtful, and discerning—and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "wise" in half of its 14 New Testament occurrences. The word often appears as the opposite of being foolish (μωρός or ἄφρων), highlighting good judgment rather than book-learning. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word חָכָם ("wise," 8 times), and the papyri show it was common everyday Koine, even used as a personal name. One nuance worth noting: in phrases like "wise in your own conceit" (Romans 11:25; 12:16), the same word can carry a negative, self-satisfied sense.

definition: A sign, mark, or token that points to something beyond itself—often a miracle showing divine authority or a distinguishing identifier.
article: σημεῖον is something that signals or points to something else—a sign, mark, or token. In the New Testament it most often means a miracle viewed as a sign of divine authority, which is why "sign" accounts for 40 of its 77 occurrences (57%), with the rest mostly describing signs being performed. The Septuagint uses it 101 times, chiefly to render the Hebrew אוֹת (64×), the basic word for a sign or token; the everyday papyri show the same range, where σημεῖον could mean an unbroken seal on a document or a distinguishing physical mark on a camel or donkey being sold.

definition: A man's personal name, Epenetus, belonging to a Christian whom Paul greets in Rome.
article: Epenetus is a personal name, appearing just once in the New Testament when Paul greets him in Romans 16:5. The name comes from the verb meaning "to praise" and literally suggests "praised" or "praiseworthy." Moulton-Milligan show it was a real, everyday Koine name, found on an inscription from Corcyra and in a name-list from Hermopolis Magna, with a feminine form (Epainete) also attested.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage.

definition: A word marking a limit, meaning "until" in time or "as far as" in place — the point up to which something extends.
senseLabels: up to or as far as
article: ἄχρι is a small but useful word that marks a boundary, most often answering "until when?" but sometimes "how far?" In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 50 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "until" in 86% of cases, with the rest usually pointing to physical distance ("as far as"). It blends so smoothly into English phrasing that in 22 of 50 occurrences it gets absorbed and has no separate word of its own. The everyday papyri confirm this ordinary usage: legal documents like a will from A.D. 96 use ἄχρι οὗ ("until") for the point when a payment must be completed.
caution: Apparent senses like "gave" (2×) come from how the word folds into larger phrases, not from a distinct meaning of ἄχρι itself.

definition: A person who plays the trumpet, a trumpeter.
article: σαλπιστής means a trumpeter, someone who blows the trumpet, and it comes from the verb σαλπίζω, "to sound a trumpet." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:22, where the sound of trumpeters falls silent in fallen Babylon. This is a late Koine form of the older Attic σαλπιγκτής, and Moulton-Milligan shows it in everyday inscriptions, including one Roman-era text naming a trumpeter of a military cohort.
caution: The lexicons agree this means "trumpeter," but the corpus rendering data is garbled (listing the gloss "again"), and the word occurs only once in the New Testament.

definition: Someone who shares in or partners with others in something, whether a possession, experience, or relationship.
article: μέτοχος describes a person who shares in something or partners with others, ranging from sharing an experience to being a business associate. The word appears 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all in Hebrews and Luke, where it can mean partaking in something (Heb 3:1, 6:4) or being a partner (Luke 5:7). Moulton-Milligan note it was common in everyday papyri for business partners — one document from Augustus's time has three men declaring themselves "partners and joint-owners," each with a one-third share.
caution: The digest lists one occurrence rendered "therefore" (Heb 1:9), which does not match the word's normal partner/sharer range and likely reflects translation phrasing rather than a real distinct sense.

definition: To make a path straight or to steer something like a ship in the right direction.
article: This verb covers two closely related ideas: making a road straight (its direction, not its surface) and steering or guiding something toward a goal. It appears only twice in the New Testament, split evenly — once for John the Baptist's call to "make straight" the Lord's way (John 1:23, echoing the Septuagint) and once for the pilot who steers a ship (James 3:4). In everyday papyri the word took on a striking legal life: a magistrate who "called others to account," so that those being euthynomenoi were the culprits, even arraigned for murder.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the lexica spreading the meaning across straightening, steering, and even legal accountability, the precise range here rests on thin evidence.

definition: The accusative plural form of the first-person pronoun, meaning "us" — the people speaking, as the object of an action.
article: This is simply the word "us" — the object form of "we," used when the speakers are on the receiving end of an action. It doesn't appear in the Byzantine New Testament text in this digest, but it shows up 403 times across 27 books of the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew pronoun for "we" (24 times). Interestingly, it also frequently stands in for Hebrew words tied to deliverance (the verb "to save," 22 times) and phrases like "lest" (15 times), reflecting how translators recast Hebrew sentences around "us" as the object.
caution: This form has zero measured Byzantine New Testament occurrences in the digest, so its sense breakdown rests entirely on Septuagint usage and grammatical description.

definition: To nod off or grow drowsy, and by extension to be slack, negligent, or slow to act.
article: Νυστάζω literally pictures someone nodding off to sleep, and it carries a figurative sense of negligence or delay. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Matthew 25:5, where drowsy bridesmaids fall asleep (rendered as a delaying or slumbering action), and in 2 Peter 2:3, where the verb describes destruction that 'does not slumber' — meaning it is not idle. The Septuagint uses it 10 times, most often for the Hebrew נוּם ('to slumber'), as in Psalm 121:4 where God neither slumbers nor sleeps.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

definition: A connecting word meaning "and yet" or "although," introducing a fact that contrasts with or qualifies what was just said.
article: καίτοι is a concessive particle—a small joining word that means "and yet" or "although," used to introduce something that stands in tension with the preceding statement. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Hebrews 4:3, where it modifies a participle) and twice in the critical text, with Acts 14:17 as the other instance. It was common in everyday Koine, showing up in business and personal papyri from the third century BC onward—for example, a writer in BGU III.850 complains about someone's behavior "and yet I had asked you many times."
caution: The measured sense here is labeled "finished," which does not match this connecting word's actual meaning of "and yet/although"—the rendering data appears to reflect surrounding context rather than the particle itself, and evidence is thin with only one Byzantine occurrence.

definition: A bed or sleeping place, often the marriage bed, and by extension the act of sexual intercourse or conceiving.
article: At its core κοίτη names a bed or resting place, but it stretches naturally to cover the marriage bed and, by extension, sexual activity. The four New Testament uses spread evenly across this range: a literal bed (Luke 11:7), a woman conceiving (Rom 9:10, literally "having the marriage bed"), illicit intercourse in the plural (Rom 13:13), and the honored marriage bed (Heb 13:4). The Septuagint uses it 66 times, mostly for the Hebrew מִשְׁכָּב ("lying down/bed"), and everyday papyri confirm the plain sense — one sick woman writes she was "quite unable to rise from my bed."
caution: With only four NT occurrences each landing in a different sense, the word's range here rests on single examples rather than repeated patterns.

definition: To ask for something or make a request, whether to a person or to God.
article: αἰτέω means to ask for something or make a request, and the measured data is remarkably consistent: about 72% of its 71 New Testament occurrences are simply rendered "ask," with the rest being variations like "whatever you ask" that still center on requesting. In the Septuagint it appears 74 times and overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew שָׁאַל ("to ask"), 61 of those times. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the same plain meaning—one early first-century document uses it for asking a tanner to hand over a calf's hide—so this is ordinary, practical language, not specialized religious vocabulary.

definition: A person who tries to drive out evil spirits by reciting names, oaths, or spells.
article: This noun names someone who attempts to expel evil spirits, working through powerful names, oaths, or incantations. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:13, describing itinerant Jewish practitioners who tried using Jesus' name. The classical lexica note a broader earlier sense, "one who administers an oath," reflecting its root in ἐξορκίζω (to bind by oath), though the New Testament use is firmly the spirit-casting sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: Perga, a city in the region of Pamphylia in Asia Minor that Paul visited.
article: Πέργη is simply the proper name of Perga, a city of Pamphylia in Asia Minor, located on the river Cestrus according to Dodson. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, all in Acts (13:13, 13:14, and 14:25), where Paul passed through during his travels. Every translation surveyed renders it consistently as 'Perga,' with the one variation ('Perga where' in Acts 13:14) simply reflecting how the sentence continues, not a different meaning. Strong's notes the name may originally relate to a word meaning 'a tower,' but this is just a possible derivation, not a meaning the word carries in the text.
caution: This is a place name with very few occurrences (3 total), all in Acts, so the evidence is thin though the meaning is not in doubt.

definition: To regard or consider someone or something a certain way, or to lead and govern as an official ruler.
