article: This word carries two clear strands of meaning: a mental one, "to consider, regard, or deem" something to be a certain way, and a leadership one, "to lead, govern, or rule." In the Byzantine New Testament's 28 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "consider" half the time (8×), with the leadership sense showing up as participles meaning rulers or those "among" you (3×). The Septuagint heavily favors the leadership side, using it 102 times and most often translating the Hebrew נָגִיד ("ruler, leader," 24×), and the papyri preserve vivid everyday uses like a man who "scorned" official reports because of his superior local power.

definition: A repayment people have coming to them, whether a reward for good or a punishment for wrong.
article: μισθαποδοσία literally means "payment of wages" and refers to getting back exactly what one is owed. It appears only 3 times, all in Hebrews, and strikingly covers both directions of repayment: punishment (Heb 2:2), the reward held onto by faith (Heb 10:35), and the reward Moses looked toward (Heb 11:26). Abbott-Smith notes it stands in for the classical form μισθοδοσία and is used by metonymy for either reward or punishment, which is why Strong's sums it up as "requital, good or bad."
caution: Confidence is low: the word occurs only 3 times, so its range rests on very thin evidence, and one measured rendering ("away it holds") reflects surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself.

definition: Moral badness or wickedness, including the evil intentions and corrupt ways that come from a depraved heart.
article: πονηρία is a general word for moral wickedness — the badness in a person that shows up as evil intentions and corrupt behavior. It appears 7 times in the New Testament, most often simply rendered "wickedness," though it can sharpen to "evil intent" (as when Jesus perceives his questioners' motives in Matthew 22:18) or broaden to "wicked ways" (Acts 3:26). In the Septuagint it appears 48 times, usually translating the Hebrew word רַע ("evil"), and everyday papyri even use it for the "malignity" of diseases, showing how naturally it expressed something genuinely harmful or bad.

definition: To make oneself known to others, or to be recognized by them.
article: This rare verb means to make oneself known or to be recognized, used in the passive or middle voice. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, where it's absorbed into the phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word — in Acts 7:13, of Joseph making himself known to his brothers, though some critical texts (WH, SBLGNT) read a different verb, ἐγνωρίσθη, there instead. In the Septuagint it likewise occurs only once, at Genesis 45:1, the same Joseph scene, rendering a Hebrew form of the verb meaning 'to know' (the digest lists both אָפַק and יָדַע for that spot).
caution: Evidence is very thin: just one Byzantine and one Septuagint occurrence, the New Testament reading is disputed among critical texts, and the cited Hebrew counterpart is inconsistent.

definition: To set foot in or enter a place, used figuratively in the New Testament for intruding into or dwelling on things one has not actually seen.
article: This verb literally means to step in or onto something, and from there it stretches to ideas like frequenting, dwelling in, taking possession of, or invading. It appears only once in the New Testament (Colossians 2:18), where its precise sense is famously disputed — the Majority Standard Bible renders it as a "basis," while the KJV reads "intrude into." In the Septuagint it shows up twice in Joshua to translate Hebrew terms for inheriting or apportioning land, fitting the "enter into possession" sense, and it occurs several times in 1 Maccabees for invading territory.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the reading and meaning of that verse are heavily debated, so any single rendering is uncertain.

definition: Morally bad or evil, describing people, things, or actions that actively cause harm or wrongdoing.
article: πονηρός describes what is morally evil or wicked, and it shows up 78 times in the New Testament, rendered "evil" in about 63% of cases and "wicked" in another 19%. It can describe people, things, or actions, and in several places (about 9%) it refers as a title to "the evil one," Satan. In the Greek Old Testament it appears 305 times, almost always standing in for the Hebrew word רַע ("bad, evil"), and Strong's notes it stresses evil that is active in its effect or influence rather than merely in inner character. Everyday Koine papyri use it too, including a legal phrase warning against "evil intent" (δόλος πονηρός) in a will.

definition: To translate a word from one language into another, or to explain what a name or term means.
article: ἑρμηνεύω is about putting meaning across language barriers—either translating a word or explaining what a name signifies. In the Byzantine New Testament all 4 uses are John's habit of telling readers what foreign names and titles mean, like Siloam in John 9:7 or Melchizedek in Hebrews 7:2. The everyday Koine papyri show the same idea in a formal setting: a Roman legal official signs off a document with "I, Gaius Lucius Geminianus, Roman jurist, have translated the foregoing copy," certifying his rendering matched the authentic will.
caution: The evidence is thin—only 4 New Testament and 3 Septuagint occurrences—and a couple of these passages (Luke 24:27, John 1:39/43) are textually uncertain across editions.

definition: To be actively at work, producing real effects—whether someone works in a person or accomplishes something with power.
senseLabels: to work or be at work
article: This verb always carries the idea of effective, productive action rather than mere busyness, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it "work" in 12 of its 21 occurrences (71%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100%. Its range covers both being at work in or among people and actually accomplishing something, and in 4 of 21 cases it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word. The everyday Koine papyri confirm both uses: one second-century letter uses it intransitively ("you would do well to be active"), while later Greek even began letting it take a direct object, as in an Oxyrhynchus papyrus.

definition: To eat or consume food.
article: βιβρώσκω simply means "to eat," and it shows up only once in the New Testament, in John 6:13, where it describes those who had eaten before the leftovers were gathered into baskets. Don't be misled by the measured rendering "baskets"—that reflects how the surrounding phrase was translated, since the word here appears as a perfect participle ("those who had eaten") rather than the loaves or baskets themselves. The word is far more common in the Septuagint (38 times in 11 books), where it usually stands in for the Hebrew verb "to eat" (אָכַל), and the papyri preserve a vivid everyday example: a report that "mice have eaten up the crop."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the lone measured rendering ("baskets") reflects the wider sentence rather than the verb's own meaning of "eat."

definition: Trogyllium, a coastal promontory or town in Ionia, in Asia Minor just south of Ephesus, mentioned as a stopping point on Paul's journey.
article: Trogyllium is a proper name for a place along the coast of Ionia in Asia Minor, situated a little south of Ephesus, where Paul's ship stopped during his travels in Acts 20:15. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, and the major translations agree it is a place name. Notably, the critical text (SBLGNT) omits the word entirely, and the manuscripts spell it several different ways, so its very presence in the text is debated.
caution: This is a single-occurrence place name with uncertain derivation, variable spelling, and it is omitted altogether from the critical text, so the evidence is thin and disputed.

definition: To groan or moan together with others, sharing in a common distress or suffering.
article: Συστενάζω combines "with/together" (σύν) and "to groan" (στενάζω), describing the act of moaning alongside others as part of a shared calamity. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 8:22, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "pains" and the BSB independently agrees. Abbott-Smith notes it can take a dative of the person joined in the groaning, citing Euripides' Ion, which shows the word was already used in classical Greek for groaning together with someone.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be confirmed from biblical usage alone.

definition: To enroll or record someone in an official register or list, as in a census or tax record.
article: In the New Testament, ἀπογράφω always refers to official registration—enrolling people for a census or tax record, as in the famous account of Luke 2 where everyone went to be registered. It appears just 4 times in the Byzantine NT, all rendered as some form of "register." The everyday papyri confirm this exact use as a technical bureaucratic term: one document from the third century BC has a man stating "I have registered the site as subject to tax," showing how naturally the word fit the world of census and customs paperwork. The classical lexica add a broader, more basic meaning—"to write out" or "copy"—but that sense doesn't surface in the measured NT data.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 4 occurrences, both measured senses essentially the same act), and the lexicons note an additional "write out, copy" meaning not reflected in the NT renderings.

definition: A pillar or column that holds up a structure, often used figuratively for something that provides support or stability.
article: στῦλος means a pillar or column, valued especially as a structural support. All four New Testament occurrences are rendered "pillars," though several are figurative—people described as pillars of the church (Galatians 2:9) or the church itself as the pillar of the truth (1 Timothy 3:15). The word is well attested in everyday Koine papyri, where you find references to monolithic pillars and even a fifty-foot column being transported.

definition: A linking word that pairs alternatives, meaning "whether...or," used to list options or set up conditions.
article: εἴτε is a connecting particle, formed from εἰ ("if") and τέ ("and"), that strings together alternatives — most often as "whether...or." Across its 65 New Testament appearances it is rendered "or" 18 times (33%) and "whether" 10 times (19%), with the remaining cases blending into longer phrases; in fact 11 of the 65 occurrences contribute no separate English word at all, since the idea gets carried by surrounding wording. Paul is especially fond of it for stacking up paired options, as in 1 Corinthians 3:22 and Colossians 1:16, 20. Moulton-Milligan note that the related form was at home in everyday Koine, turning up in inscriptions and papyri.
caution: Because this particle so often dissolves into English phrasing rather than mapping to one word, its many "senses" are really translation artifacts of context, not distinct meanings.

definition: To physically lift someone or something up, or mentally to take up an idea by supposing or assuming it.
article: This verb literally means to take something up from below — to support or carry it upward — as when a cloud took Jesus up out of sight (Acts 1:9) or a Samaritan took up a wounded man (Luke 10:30). But it also shifted to a mental sense, "to suppose" or "assume," which is how it works in Luke 7:43 and Acts 2:15. Everyday Koine papyri show this same "assume, expect" usage richly, and the lexica add a further sense the New Testament barely shows — to "catch up" or pick up a thread in conversation, even to answer.
caution: Measured on only 4 Byzantine occurrences, and the lexica list extra senses (welcome, answer) that the New Testament data does not clearly confirm.

definition: Nahor, a personal name in the genealogy of Jesus, belonging to one of Abraham's ancestors.
article: Ναχώρ is the Greek spelling of the Hebrew personal name נָחוֹר (Nahor), an indeclinable proper noun. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 3:34, where it is part of the genealogy tracing Jesus' ancestry. The name is far more common in the Septuagint, occurring 19 times across 3 books, almost always rendering the same Hebrew name, though once it stands in for a different Hebrew word (בֵּרֹתִי).
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its identification rests entirely on the genealogical context and Hebrew background.

definition: The comparative form meaning "better," used for what is more advantageous, more useful, or more excellent than something else.
article: This is the neuter comparative "better," functioning as the comparative of "good" even though it is rooted in a word meaning "strong." In all 4 Byzantine New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "better" (100%), and the BSB agrees completely; the lexicons confirm two flavors of "better" — better in terms of advantage or usefulness, and better in terms of excellence. In the Septuagint it appears 7 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew word for "good," though it also stands behind several other Hebrew words including one meaning "strife."
caution: This spelling does not appear in the critical (SBLGNT) text, where the alternate form κρείττων is preferred, so the count depends on which Greek text you follow.

definition: A created thing—something that has been made or brought into being, whether a living creature or part of the wider creation.
article: κτίσμα refers to something that has been created, formed from the verb κτίζω ("to create"). In the New Testament's 4 occurrences it always carries this concrete sense—a created thing or creature—rendered as "creation" half the time and "creature(s)" in Revelation. Interestingly, the everyday papyri show a different, more physical meaning: documents use κτίσμα for a "foundation" or building work, as in a payment "for the building (κτίσμα) of the estate there."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the measured sense range is narrow, and the papyri "foundation/building" meaning shows a usage the biblical text never employs.

definition: The bringing of something to completion or fulfillment, whether a promise carried out or a goal reached.
article: τελείωσις names the act of completing or fulfilling something. The Byzantine NT uses it just twice, and the two occurrences pull in different directions: in Luke 1:45 it refers to the fulfillment of what God spoke, while Hebrews 7:11 uses it for the completeness (or lack thereof) that the priestly system could not deliver. The Septuagint most often uses it for Hebrew מִלֻּאּים (11×), tied to priestly consecration, and everyday papyri use it plainly for concluding a transaction—as in an Oxyrhynchus document where an agent is sent 'to conclude the transaction.'
caution: With only two NT occurrences pulling toward distinct senses, and a low computed confidence tier, the exact range here is hard to pin down.

definition: To raise someone to the very highest position, exalting them above all others.
article: This verb means to lift someone up to the supreme position, far above everyone else. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:9, where God exalts Jesus to the highest place. In the Septuagint it shows up 37 times across two books, often rendering the Hebrew word for being lifted high (rûm), and Abbott-Smith notes a related sense there: "to extol" or praise highly, as in the book of Daniel.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise range of this word rests largely on its Septuagint usage.

definition: Blastus, the personal name of the court official who served as chamberlain to King Herod Agrippa I.
article: Βλάστος (Blastus) is a proper name, not an ordinary word — it belongs to the chamberlain of King Herod Agrippa I, who appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 12:20). The lexicons agree completely that this is simply someone's name, and Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up as a personal name in everyday inscriptions, such as one from Cyzicus dating to the 2nd century BC. Note that the measured rendering 'furious' reflects the surrounding context of Acts 12:20 rather than the meaning of the name itself.
caution: This is a one-time proper name with thin evidence, and the measured sense 'furious' clearly comes from the verse's context, not from the name Blastus.

definition: In every way or entirely; an adverb describing something done completely or under all circumstances.
article: This adverb, built from πᾶς ("all"), means "in every way" or "entirely." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 24:3, where the Majority Standard Bible folds it into the sense of "acknowledge" within Tertullus's flattering speech to Felix. The everyday papyri are especially telling: it regularly pairs with πάντως in the phrase πάντῃ πάντως, meaning "under all circumstances" or "by all means," as in a 311 BC contract and a letter urging "be very sure to send Pindarus."
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one measured occurrence, so its range there rests almost entirely on outside evidence from the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: A preposition pointing to where something is headed—into, to, toward, or for a purpose or goal.
article: εἰς is one of the most common words in the New Testament, appearing 1,770 times, and it marks direction or destination—where something moves to, enters into, or aims at. Its core sense is overwhelmingly "to" (68%) or "into" (12%), but it stretches to cover location ("in"), purpose ("for"), and even result ("that" or "so"). It is so woven into Greek phrasing that 702 of its occurrences—nearly 40%—are absorbed into the surrounding wording with no separate English word at all. In the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew verb בּוֹא, "to come" or "go in" (1,035 times), which fits its strong association with motion toward a place.
caution: Its range is genuinely broad, so the exact shade—into, to, in, or for—often depends on context rather than the word itself.

definition: A tiny point of time, an instant or moment so brief it is over almost as soon as it begins.
article: στιγμή literally means a prick or point — the mark left by a sharp instrument — but in the New Testament it is used metaphorically of time, meaning a fleeting instant. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 4:5, where Jesus is shown all the kingdoms of the world "in a moment" (rendered "up an instant" in the measured data). The same image of a 'point of time' shows up in everyday Koine papyri and in classical writers like Plutarch, who calls life itself a στιγμὴ χρόνου, "a point of time"; in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew word for "suddenly" in Isaiah 29:5.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage.

definition: A large gate, gateway, or the porch and entrance passage of a house, palace, or walled city.
article: πυλών refers to a substantial gate or the entry structure attached to a building or city—either the porch and vestibule of a house or the gate-tower of a walled town. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 18 times, rendered "gates" in 14 of them (93%), with 3 occurrences absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too: one Tebtunis document (c. A.D. 131) describes attackers making a bold assault on someone's village house "at the gateway," showing the same ordinary architectural sense found in the New Testament.

definition: An adverb meaning "not yet" — pointing to something that has not happened up to a given moment.
article: μηδέπω is a simple adverb meaning "not yet," used to mark something that had not happened at a particular point in time. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:7, where it describes events not yet seen. The everyday papyri show the same plain usage: one document from Oxyrhynchus describes people who "had not yet even received the loan," and another mentions a slave "not yet thirty years old."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the listed measured sense "godly" is plainly a mismatch — all the lexical evidence agrees the word simply means "not yet."

definition: To counsel or correct someone gently, putting a concern in their mind so they change their behavior.
article: Νουθετέω literally means "to put in mind" (from noûs, mind, and títhēmi, to put), and it covers gentle but serious correction—admonishing, warning, or counseling a person. In the Byzantine New Testament its 8 occurrences split mainly between "admonish" (3×, 43%) and "warning" (2×, 29%), with the rest absorbed into surrounding phrasing. A nice everyday glimpse comes from a 6th–7th century papyrus where someone asks a bishop to "admonish" a presbyter into treating a letter-carrier justly—the same practical sense of applying pressure to make someone do right.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and a couple of stray renderings, the precise force—how gentle versus how firm—isn't pinned down tightly by the data.

definition: To choke something by smothering or crowding it out, or to suffocate a living thing, including by drowning.
senseLabels: to choke or crowd out plants
article: This verb means to stifle or choke—built from ἀπό plus πνίγω ("to choke")—and the New Testament uses it just 3 times across 2 books. In every measured rendering it describes thorns choking seedlings in Jesus' parable of the sower (Matthew 13:7, Luke 8:7), but Abbott-Smith notes it can also mean to drown, as in Luke 8:33 where it stands in for "caught up in the sea." A striking glimpse of everyday Koine comes from a manumission deed at Delphi that grimly granted an owner the right to "choke" (ἀποπνεῖξαι) a slave's child—showing how brutally literal the word could be.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into broader phrasing, the evidence is thin, so the full range (choking versus drowning) rests largely on the lexica rather than measured usage.

definition: Describing the part that is still left or remaining, such as the rest of one's life or time.
article: Ἐπίλοιπος describes whatever is left over or still remaining. It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Peter 4:2), where it modifies "time" — the rest of one's earthly life — though there it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a separate English word. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document speaks of caring for someone "for the rest of your life," and another of receiving "the remainder" of a dowry, showing this was plain, practical vocabulary.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 1 New Testament occurrence and a low confidence rating), so the sense rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri usage.

definition: To say, speak, or declare something — to put a message into words.
article: This entry covers ῥέω in the sense of speaking or saying, which the lexica treat together with λέγω — to say, speak, affirm, or declare. In practice it ranges from plain speech to commanding or even unspoken thought ("saying in oneself"), and it can introduce direct quotation, a "that" clause, or written words like "the Scripture says." Interestingly, in the Septuagint the related verb appears very frequently, chiefly rendering the Hebrew אמר ("to say"), and λέγει stands for the Hebrew נְאֻם, the prophetic "declares" formula.
caution: This form ῥέω has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, and the supplied evidence blends it with λέγω, so its independent range here is uncertain.

definition: To a great degree; greatly or very much.
article: This adverb, formed from the adjective μέγας ("great"), simply means "greatly" or "very much" and describes the intensity of an action or feeling. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Philippians 4:10, where Paul says he rejoiced greatly. The everyday papyri show the same flavor of strong emotion: one writer says "we rejoiced greatly," another complains "I blame you greatly," and a third is "greatly anxious about you."
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured-sense label "opportunity" appears to reflect surrounding Philippians 4:10 context rather than the word's actual meaning of "greatly," which the lexicons uniformly give.

definition: To bring people or things together into one place, or to be brought together as a group.
article: συνάγω means to bring things or people together — collecting items, gathering a crowd, or convening an assembly. In the New Testament it appears 61 times, and nearly every rendering is a variation on "gather" or "assemble," so its range is narrow and steady. In the Septuagint it occurs over 300 times, most often translating the Hebrew אָסַף (131×). One striking everyday touch: in the papyri the verb is used for adding up a total sum received by sale or purchase (compare Luke 15:13, where the prodigal "gathered" all he had — i.e. sold off everything).

definition: Michael, the archangel named in the Bible.
article: Μιχαήλ is the proper name of the archangel Michael, transliterated directly from the Hebrew מִיכָאֵל. It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament—Jude 9 and Revelation 12:7—and is always rendered "Michael"; the Septuagint uses it 13 times across 5 books, every time translating that same Hebrew name. Interestingly, the papyri and inscriptions show that worship of Michael was widespread in Asia Minor, with a major Church of St. Michael standing near the walls of Colossae.
caution: This is a proper name with only 2 New Testament occurrences, so its range is fixed rather than uncertain.

definition: To bring a boat to anchor or moor it at a place along the shore.
article: This nautical term means to anchor or tie up a boat at a landing spot, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Mark 6:53, where it describes Jesus and his disciples mooring their boat. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this maritime usage: a related verb shows up in documents about a boat coming to anchor at Memphis and loading goods. The word's range is narrow and consistent—it's simply about bringing a vessel to rest near land.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from the biblical text alone.

definition: A flat slab or tablet used as a writing surface, such as the stone tablets of the law.
article: πλάξ refers to anything flat and broad, but in the New Testament it always means a tablet for writing — both times rendered as "tablets" or "stone tablets" (2 Corinthians 3:3 and Hebrews 9:4). It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament but is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 33 times, always translating the Hebrew word lûaḥ. Interestingly, the papyri confirm this everyday meaning: an inscription granting a Jewish synagogue the right of asylum uses πλάξ for an inscribed stone tablet, showing the word was the late Koine replacement for the older στήλη.
caution: This word is rare in the New Testament with only 3 occurrences, and lexicons note its tablet sense belongs to later writers, so its full range rests on thin NT evidence.

definition: To stop or cease an action; in the middle voice, to leave off doing something or come to an end.
article: παύω is about bringing something to a halt or, more commonly in the New Testament, ceasing an activity yourself. In its 15 New Testament uses the Majority Standard Bible renders it "stopped" most often (6 times, 55%), and in nearly every case it appears in the middle voice meaning to leave off or cease—frequently paired with a participle ("did not cease teaching"). A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri: a second-century-BC letter warns, "if you do not cease your malpractices in the village, you will be sorry for it," showing the same plain sense of "stop it" in ordinary Koine.

definition: To fix your eyes on something or someone and look at them steadily and intently.
article: This verb describes a fixed, concentrated gaze — not a casual glance but staring intently at a person or thing. It's a favorite word of Luke, accounting for all 14 New Testament occurrences across 3 books, and it appears in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions as well. One vivid example outside the Bible describes Thecla's rapt attention to Paul's teaching, ἀτενίζουσα — gazing as if drinking it in — which captures the word's intensity well.
caution: The two measured senses ("stare" and "looked directly") are nearly identical in meaning, and 5 of 14 occurrences were absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single word.

definition: Epaphras, the personal name of a Colossian Christian and fellow worker of Paul.
article: Epaphras is a proper name, a shortened pet form of the longer name Epaphroditus, belonging to a Christian from Colossae who was imprisoned alongside Paul. It appears 3 times in the New Testament (Colossians 1:7; 4:12; Philemon 23), always referring to this same man. The three "senses" in the data are just translation artifacts — the name sits next to different surrounding words — not different meanings; it is simply a name throughout. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note this name was common in everyday inscriptions of the period.
caution: The name occurs only 3 times, and the apparent multiple senses are merely fragments of surrounding text, not real distinctions in meaning.

definition: Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of the Law mentioned in the book of Acts.
article: Γαμαλιήλ is a personal name transliterated from the Hebrew גַּמְלִיאֵל. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears twice, both times in Acts (5:34 and 22:3), where it refers to a prominent Pharisee and teacher of the Law described as the teacher of Saul (Paul). The same Hebrew name appears 5 times in the Septuagint, where it belongs to other individuals, showing the name was used more broadly than just for the figure in Acts.
caution: This entry rests on only two New Testament occurrences, so it is flagged as low-confidence evidence.

definition: To make something visible, known, or clear—to bring what was hidden into the open so it can be seen or understood.
article: φανερόω means to bring something out into the open—to make it visible, known, or plain. In its 49 New Testament appearances it leans heavily toward "revealed" (17×, 46%), with a related group of senses about appearing or coming into view, especially of Christ. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri: one writer says "I have made known both to the establishment of the praepositus and to his assistant," and a Christian prayer asks God, "reveal to me thy truth."
caution: Septuagint evidence is very thin (just 1 occurrence), and 12 of 49 New Testament uses are absorbed into phrasing without their own English word, so the precise sense in some passages is a translator's judgment call.

definition: In an orderly sequence, one after another; or, used as a noun, the time or people that follow.
article: καθεξῆς is an adverb meaning one thing following another in order, whether of events laid out in sequence or of time and people coming afterward. The measured renderings in the Majority Standard Bible only catch fragments of phrases ("having," "good," "whole sequence of events"), and in 2 of its 5 occurrences the word gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own — so the lexica (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) give a cleaner picture: "in order, successively" and "afterwards." The most interesting note comes from Moulton-Milligan, who cite Blass on Luke 1:3, where the word seems to describe the uninterrupted, connected flow of a carefully arranged narrative rather than mere chronological listing.
caution: Rare word (5 occurrences); the measured senses reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself, so lean on the lexica for its core meaning of orderly sequence.

definition: To destroy or kill, used of the agent who brings death or ruin.
article: This verb means to destroy or slay, and it derives from ὄλεθρος ("ruin, destruction"). It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:28, where it refers to the one who killed the firstborn at the first Passover. In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew words like כָּרַת ("cut off") and שָׁחַת ("destroy"), and Moulton-Milligan notes the word also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: The measured rendering "sprinkling" reflects the surrounding context of Hebrews 11:28 rather than the word itself, which the lexicons consistently define as "destroy"; with only one New Testament occurrence the evidence is thin.

definition: To swallow something down completely, or figuratively to consume, overwhelm, or destroy it entirely.
article: καταπίνω literally means to gulp something down whole, as when straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel (Matthew 23:24). It stretches naturally into figurative use — being overwhelmed or consumed, as when mortality is "swallowed up" in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). In the Greek Old Testament it appears 36 times, most often rendering the Hebrew בָּלַע ("swallow," 23×), and everyday papyri use it both literally (someone who "swallowed the snake") and dramatically (a sky that "was being swallowed up" by fire).
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences and 3 of them absorbed into phrasing without a distinct English word, the precise boundaries between its literal and figurative senses are somewhat blurred.

definition: A fixed boundary or appointed limit marking off where something ends, especially a set border in space.
article: ὁροθeσία combines the words for "boundary" and "to set," so it means a fixed border that has been deliberately appointed. It appears just once in the New Testament (Acts 17:26), where it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word, and the KJV simply translates it "bound." Long thought to be the only instance in Biblical or secular Greek, it has since turned up in an inscription from Priene (after 133 B.C.) referring to a Rhodian judgment and "delimitation," confirming that everyday Koine used it for marking off territory.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is rare in surviving Greek, so its range is known mainly from a single inscription.

definition: A common Greek preposition that shifts meaning with its context—signaling direction, place, standard, or opposition, often woven into the phrase rather than translated as a single word.
article: Κατά is one of the most flexible little words in the Greek New Testament, appearing 478 times across 26 books, and its sense bends to whatever it modifies—rendered "to," "in," "according to," "by," or "against" depending on context. Tellingly, in 194 of those 478 occurrences it carries no English word of its own at all, simply blending into the surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint, where it appears over 1,600 times, it most often stands in for the Hebrew word for "family" or "clan" (105×), reflecting its frequent use in expressions like "according to their families."
caution: Because its meaning depends so heavily on grammar and context—and nearly 40% of its uses are absorbed into phrasing—no single gloss captures it, so weigh each occurrence individually.

definition: A year, the basic unit for measuring spans of time or someone's age.
article: ἔτος simply means "a year," and it's used very consistently throughout the New Testament. In the Byzantine text it appears 49 times, rendered "years" in 44 cases (94%) and "years old" in just 2 cases when stating someone's age. The everyday papyri confirm this ordinary usage: one document speaks of coming "up to the metropolis at the New Year," and the phrase κατ᾽ ἔτος ("yearly") shows up in a contract requiring annual payments — the same expression found in Luke 2:41. In the Septuagint it occurs 613 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for "year" (שָׁנִים, 550×).

definition: To hunt or chase down prey, and by extension to try to catch or trap someone in their words.
article: θηρεύω literally means to hunt, ensnare, or catch an animal, and the everyday Koine papyri confirm this plain sense—one document is even a request for a permit to hunt and catch every bird in a particular mere. Its single New Testament appearance (in Luke 11:54) uses the word figuratively, of people trying to trap someone in something he might say. In the Septuagint it shows up 17 times across 7 books, most often rendering the Hebrew root צוּד, "to hunt," though once each it translates words for "lie" and "trouble."
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, where its meaning is figurative rather than literal, so its full range there rests on slim evidence.

definition: To follow closely after someone, staying right behind them.
article: κατακολουθέω means to follow closely behind a person, staying right on their heels. In the New Testament it appears just twice, always in this literal sense: the women who followed Joseph to see where Jesus' body was laid (Luke 23:55), and the slave girl who trailed after Paul (Acts 16:17). Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri use the word in a derived, figurative sense—'to comply with' or 'follow' written contracts, instructions, and established customs—a meaning the New Testament never employs.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences, the sense range here is narrow and the evidence thin.

definition: A cor, a large Hebrew dry measure used for grain, equal to about ten ephahs.
article: Kóros is a Hebrew measurement word borrowed into Greek, naming a cor—a large unit equal to ten ephahs (Dodson reckons it at roughly 120 gallons). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:7, where a debtor owes measures of wheat. The Septuagint uses it 13 times across 7 books, mostly translating the Hebrew כֹּר (7×), and Moulton-Milligan note it also shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This is a rare technical term with only one New Testament occurrence, so its English rendering rests on a single passage.

definition: Located beside the sea; coastal or along the seashore.
article: παράλιος describes a place lying alongside the sea — the seacoast or coastal region. In the Septuagint the noun form ἡ παραλία ("the coastland") appears 8 times in 5 books, most often translating the Hebrew חוֹף ("shore," 4×). One notable detail: in Attic inscriptions the related ἡ πάραλος could even name a ship, the seagoing vessel itself.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 6:17), and the Majority Standard Bible's rendering "level" does not match the standard "seacoast" sense given by the lexicons, so the measured data and the dictionaries disagree.

definition: To express gratitude, give thanks, or say grace—especially thanking God, often before a meal.
article: εὐχαριστέω means to express gratitude, and in the New Testament it overwhelmingly points to thanking God—appearing 40 times across 15 books, rendered "thank" (55%) or "giving thanks" (42%). It frequently describes saying grace before food, as when Jesus took bread and gave thanks (Matthew 15:36, Mark 8:6). Interestingly, the everyday papyri preserve an older, more practical meaning: "to do a good turn" or "oblige someone," as in a letter saying "by doing this you will oblige us"—a shade of meaning that had largely shifted to religious thanksgiving by New Testament times.

definition: The distance something can be thrown, used as a rough measure of how far apart two things are.
article: βολή comes from the verb βάλλω ("to throw") and literally means a throw or cast; in practice it measures distance, as in the phrase "a stone's throw." It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:41, where Jesus withdraws from his disciples about a stone's throw away. The Septuagint also uses it sparingly—including Genesis 21:16, where it renders a Hebrew word for the distance a bowshot reaches—confirming its role as a way of gauging a short, throwable distance.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and just a handful of times in the Septuagint, so its measured range is thin.

definition: Relating to a king — royal or kingly, used of high status, dignity, or a kingdom.
article: βασίλειος means "royal" or "kingly," describing things connected to a king. The measured New Testament renderings are tricky to read: in Matthew 11:8 and Luke 7:25 it appears in phrases about kings' houses (rendered as part of "fine" clothing or royal palaces), while in 1 Peter 2:9 it describes a "royal" priesthood — a quotation drawn from the Septuagint. In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew terms tied to a kingdom, and the papyri show it used flexibly, even standing in for βασιλικός ("royal") to describe a king's secretary.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences (just 1 in the critical text) — and the measured renderings reflect surrounding phrases rather than the word alone, so confidence is low.

definition: Physically disabled or maimed, having lost or being deprived of the full use of part of the body.
article: ἀνάπηρος describes someone who is crippled or maimed in body. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both in the same passage of Luke (14:13 and 14:21), where Jesus tells us to invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind to a banquet. Outside the New Testament it shows up only a couple of times in the Septuagint (Tobit 14:2 and 2 Maccabees 8:24), so the evidence base is quite thin.
caution: The word occurs only twice in the New Testament and rarely elsewhere, so its precise range is hard to pin down; the second measured 'sense' is a data artifact, not a real meaning.

definition: Describing someone who is deeply missed and greatly longed for.
article: This adjective describes a person who is dearly missed and earnestly wanted, built from the same root as the verb "to long for" (epipotheō). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Philippians 4:1, where Paul calls his readers his "longed for" brothers. In that single use it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word, and the lexicons agree it means "longed for" or "greatly desired."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range cannot be confirmed from usage alone.

definition: To speak or act with great boldness, making a daring venture without holding back.
article: This verb combines ἀπό with τολμάω ("to dare") to mean speaking out boldly or making a daring venture. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 10:20, where Isaiah is said to be "very bold" in his words. Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, though one inscription citation (Syll 803.94) is so damaged that the reading is only probable; the word is otherwise well attested in classical and Hellenistic literature.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: An emphatic form of "not" that means "not at all" or "by no means," often used in questions expecting the answer "yes."
article: οὐχί is a strengthened version of the ordinary Greek "no" (οὐ), adding emphasis—think "not at all" rather than a plain "not." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 56 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "not" in 68% of cases, though 16 of those 56 occurrences get absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of their own. Its most distinctive use, noted by Abbott-Smith, is in questions that expect a "yes" answer (like Latin nonne), as in "Do not even the tax collectors do the same?" The everyday Koine papyri confirm both this question-form and a plainer negative use.

definition: A thing done or being dealt with — a deed, action, matter, affair, or legal case.
article: πρᾶγμα is a broad word for a "thing" in the sense of something done or being handled — a deed, an action, a matter, or an affair, depending on context. It appears 11 times in the New Testament, and the measured renderings reflect this flexibility: the same word can be translated "before" (in legal phrasing), "anything," or "what" depending on the surrounding grammar. Interestingly, in 1 Corinthians 6:1 it carries the forensic sense of a "law-suit" — a usage well attested in everyday Koine papyri, and in the Septuagint it most often renders the Hebrew דָּבָר ("word" or "matter").
caution: The English renderings vary widely because the word's exact meaning depends heavily on its phrase, so any single translation undercounts its range.

definition: A turning or change, especially the regular shifting of the sun and other heavenly bodies through their cycles.
article: τροπή refers to a turning or shift, and in everyday Koine it was the standard word for the sun's solstice and the cyclical movement of heavenly bodies. The New Testament uses it just once, in James 1:17, where God the giver of lights is said to have no "variation" or "shadow of turning" — applying the astronomical sense figuratively to underscore his constancy. The papyri vividly confirm this range: the plural τροπάς appears for the turnings of irrigation water-wheels, while θερινή and χειμερινή τροπαί mark the summer and winter solstices.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its single measured sense rests on a single occurrence.

definition: The state of being ruined or lost, whether physical loss of something or eternal spiritual destruction.
article: ἀπώλεια covers a range from ordinary loss—like wasting money or property—to total ruin, and in the New Testament it often carries the heavy sense of eternal destruction set against salvation (σωτηρία). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "destruction" in 12 of 19 occurrences (80%), with the BSB independently agreeing 83% of the time. Tellingly, the everyday papyri show the milder edge of the word: one astrological fragment uses it of someone who will "spend and lose" his possessions, and Augustus-era nursing contracts use it for plain loss or damage of property.

definition: Subject to decay and destruction; something that will eventually break down, rot, or die rather than lasting forever.
article: φθαρτός describes anything liable to decay and destruction—a withering athlete's wreath, money that wears out, the human body that dies. The New Testament uses it 6 times, and translators render it "perishable" in 5 cases and "mortal" once (Rom 1:23), but these are really the same idea seen from two angles. Notably, it is built directly from φθείρω ("to destroy, corrupt") and is repeatedly set in deliberate contrast with its opposite ἄφθαρτος, the imperishable, as when it labels mortal humanity against the immortal God.
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and a single, somewhat different Septuagint use, the evidence base is fairly thin.

definition: Right away, on the spot, without any delay between one moment and the next.
article: ἐξαυτῆς is an adverb meaning "at once" or "immediately" — literally a shortened way of saying "from that very hour." It appears 6 times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "immediately" or a close equivalent in every case; two of those occurrences get folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single word. It was an ordinary, everyday Koine word, and Moulton-Milligan point to a papyrus letter from A.D. 40 where a writer urges, "please do well to send me the little [thing] at once."
caution: The measured sense labeled "immediately kind" almost certainly reflects a parsing quirk rather than a real distinct meaning, since all sources agree on the single sense "at once."

definition: To make empty, malicious accusations against someone, or more generally to talk nonsense.
article: φλυαρέω describes talking nonsense or babbling, and in its single New Testament appearance (3 John 10) it carries the sharper sense of making idle, malicious accusations against people. The word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, where it is absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by its own English word, so the measured data is thin. The everyday Koine papyri preserve its broader flavor nicely: a fourth-century Christian writer says he doesn't want to fill his letter with words and thereby 'prove myself an idle babbler.'
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the evidence for the precise force of this word is limited.

definition: Gomorrah, one of the cities near the Dead Sea destroyed by God, often paired with Sodom as an example of judgment.
article: Γόμοῤῥα is simply the place name Gomorrah, a city of the plain near the Dead Sea that was destroyed (Genesis 19). It almost always appears alongside Sodom and serves as a byword for divine judgment, occurring 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament and 20 times in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew עֲמֹרָה 17 of those times. A striking detail: Moulton-Milligan note that the words Sodoma and Gomorra were found scratched on a house wall in Pompeii, likely by a Jew or Christian aware of his surroundings.
caution: The two measured senses both refer to the same city; the second label ("leave Gomorrah") just reflects surrounding translation phrasing, not a distinct meaning.

definition: A particular place or location in space — a spot, region, or position something occupies.
article: τόπος is the ordinary Greek word for a place or location — a spot in space, limited by what occupies it. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "place" in 68 of 94 New Testament occurrences (94%), and another 22 times it gets absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own. In the Septuagint it appears 468 times and almost always stands in for the Hebrew מָקוֹם (358×), the standard Hebrew word for "place," and the everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — a stable's location, a safe spot to store something, even a seat in a theatre.

definition: A sickness, disease, or bodily ailment.
article: Νόσημα means a sickness or bodily ailment, the noun form built from the verb νοσέω, "to be sick." It is extremely rare, appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at John 5:4, and not at all in the critical SBLGNT text, which omits that verse. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agree it simply means "disease" or "sickness," so the meaning itself is not in doubt even though attestation is thin.
caution: This word is effectively a hapax tied to John 5:4, a verse absent from the critical text, and the measured rendering "stirred" reflects the wording of that passage rather than the word's actual sense of "disease."

definition: Describing someone who has been taught directly by God rather than by human instruction.
article: θεοδίδακτος is a compound adjective built from "God" (θεός) and "teach" (διδάσκω), meaning "taught by God." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 4:9, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "taught" (100% of its single occurrence). Abbott-Smith connects it with the phrase "taught of God" (διδακτοὶ θεοῦ) in John 6:45, and Moulton-Milligan note it sits alongside similarly formed words attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, such as the pagan parallel θεόγνωστος.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single example.

definition: At or toward the back of someone or something; coming up from behind.
article: ὄπισθεν marks position at the rear—either an action approaching from behind or a fixed location at someone's back. It works both as an adverb ("behind") and, with a genitive, as a preposition ("behind someone"), as in the woman who came up behind Jesus to touch his garment. In the Septuagint it appears 33 times across 15 books, most often rendering the Hebrew אַחַר (11×) and אָחוֹר (2×); a third-century magic papyrus even shows the same prepositional use, "standing behind him," set against "in front of him."

definition: A person captured in war or held as a prisoner.
article: αἰχμάλωτος refers to someone taken captive, especially a prisoner of war — the parts of the word literally combine "spear" with "being taken." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (in Luke 4:18, itself quoting the Septuagint), but the Septuagint uses it 19 times across 8 books, where it renders several Hebrew words for captivity such as שָׁבָה and שֶׁבִי. The word was also part of everyday Hellenistic life: papyri from after 241 B.C. mention allowances granted to actual prisoners, and it turns up in numerous inscriptions of the period.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence (absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word), the corpus-measured evidence is thin and rated low confidence.

definition: Moral wrongdoing or injustice — acting wickedly or unfairly, the opposite of righteousness and truth.
article: ἀδικία covers a broad span from concrete acts of injustice to a general state of moral wrongdoing, which is why the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it "wickedness" (9 of 26 times, 56%) and sometimes "unrighteousness" (2 times). It frequently appears in pointed contrasts — set against truth (1 Corinthians 13:6, 2 Thessalonians 2:12) and against righteousness — and in vivid phrases like "the wages of unrighteousness" and "the mammon of unrighteousness." The everyday Koine papyri are striking here: they repeatedly use the word for legal "hurt" or harm done against someone ("done by his father to our hurt"), a courtroom sense of injury that the New Testament hardly uses except in 1 Corinthians 13:6.
caution: In 10 of its 26 New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into a larger phrase rather than translated as a single English word, so individual renderings vary.

definition: A connective introducing the first of two alternatives, meaning "either"—the first "either" in an "either...or" pairing.
article: ἤτοι is a strengthened form of "either," built from ἤ ("or") and τοί, used to mark the first of two alternatives, as in "either...or." It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 6:16. The classical lexica trace it back to Homer and Herodotus, where it carries emphatic alternative force; Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured-sense label ("slaves") reflects a nearby word in Romans 6:16 rather than the meaning of ἤτοι itself, which the classical sources clearly define as "either."

definition: A small parchment case holding written portions of the Law, worn on the forehead or arm during prayer.
article: In its single New Testament appearance (Matthew 23:5), φυλακτήριον refers to the small parchment capsules, inscribed with portions of the Law, that were worn on the forehead or near the heart at prayer. The word literally means a guarded post or fortification, and classical sources also use it for a safeguard or protective amulet — the sense of protection is what gives the prayer-case its name. The Rosetta Stone (196 BC) interestingly uses the plural for the golden φυλακτήρια worn by the kings of Egypt, showing the broader 'protective ornament' range outside Jewish practice.
caution: The word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical meaning rests on that single verse alongside wider classical and documentary evidence.

definition: To turn away anger by becoming favorable—either to be merciful toward someone or to make atonement for sins.
article: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, splitting evenly between two senses: in Luke 18:13 the tax collector pleads for God to be merciful to him, and in Hebrews 2:17 Christ "makes propitiation" for sins. The word reaches back into everyday Greek—papyri and inscriptions use it for rendering a god favorable, as in an oracle promising things will go "better and finer" for those who honor and propitiate Zeus and Apollo. In the Septuagint it appears 12 times across 7 books, most often translating the Hebrew word for "forgive" (סָלַח, 5×), which leans the meaning toward mercy and pardon rather than mere appeasement.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a computed low-confidence tier, the split between "be merciful" and "make atonement" rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A forest or woodland, and by extension the wood or brushwood that fuels a fire.
article: ὕλη basically means a forest, woodland, or the wood and brushwood that comes from it; it can also mean fuel for a fire. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at James 3:5, where the imagery is of a small spark setting a great forest ablaze (the Majority Standard Bible renders the relevant phrase "great"). The classical lexicons add a striking range: from literal woodland to timber and fuel, and even to the philosophical sense of "matter" (Latin materia), as in the Wisdom of Solomon; a papyrus from 248–245 B.C. describes land "full of brushwood" (ὕλης μεστήν), fitting Hort's view that the word can mean rough, bushy hillside scrub.
caution: This is a single-occurrence word in the New Testament, so its exact force in James 3:5 rests on thin evidence and on debated lexical discussion.

definition: A preposition marking the means, channel, or reason something happens — "through," "by," or "because of."
article: διά is one of the busiest little words in the New Testament, appearing 671 times, and its job is to point at how or why something happens — the channel, instrument, or cause. With a genitive it usually means "through" or "by means of" (143 times rendered "through"), while with the accusative it leans toward "because of" or "for the sake of" (51 times "because"). It's so grammatically woven into sentences that in 230 of those 671 cases it gets absorbed into English phrasing without a word of its own, and in the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew כֵּן ("so, thus," 255 times). Tellingly, διά survived into Modern Greek as γιά, still meaning "for" — as in γιὰ τοῦτο, "therefore."
caution: Its meaning shifts heavily with case and context, so any single rendering is a rough guide, not a fixed equivalent.

definition: The basic verb "to be" — to exist, to be present, or to link a subject with what it is or does.
senseLabels: to be, exist, or be present
article: εἰμί is the ordinary Greek verb "to be," and it is everywhere — 2,495 times across all 27 books of the Byzantine New Testament. In the vast majority of cases (2,396 of them) it disappears into English phrasing as a linking word, the way "is" or "was" does, with only about 99 cases translated as a standalone word. It carries the full range of "to be": to exist, to happen, to be present in a place, or simply to connect a subject to a description. In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew הָיָה ("to be," 2,127×), and the papyri show its everyday forms — like the first-person past ἤμην — already well settled in common Koine letters centuries before the New Testament.

definition: The middle of the night, the point halfway between sunset and sunrise.
article: μεσονύκτιον is a compound of μέσος ("middle") and νύξ ("night"), and it simply means midnight—the midpoint of the night. All four New Testament occurrences refer to this same time of night, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "midnight" in three cases and "kept midnight" once (Acts 20:7, where Paul spoke until midnight). Interestingly, the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri too: a magical text directs an action "at midnight" (τὸ μεσανύκτιον), using the same accusative form found in Mark 13:35.
caution: The two listed senses are really the same meaning expressed differently, so this is effectively a single straightforward sense.

definition: A man's personal name, Asyncritus, used for a Christian greeted by Paul in Rome.
article: Asyncritus is a proper name, appearing only once in the New Testament when Paul greets him among the believers in Rome (Romans 16:14). The underlying word literally means "incomparable," formed from a negative prefix plus a derivative of synkrinō (to compare), but in this single occurrence it functions purely as someone's name. Moulton-Milligan note the name turns up in inscriptions beyond Rome — at Brundisium, Uria, and possibly Attica — and they also cite papyri using the related adjective in everyday Greek.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament as a personal name, so its sense here rests on that single verse.

definition: Suffering from dropsy, a medical condition in which the body swells with retained fluid.
article: This adjective describes a person suffering from dropsy, an old name for the painful swelling caused by fluid buildup in the body. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 14:2, where Jesus heals a man with this condition. The word was sometimes cited as evidence that Luke used medical vocabulary, but Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in the historian Polybius and in everyday Koine papyri, so it was not strictly a doctor's term.

definition: Pudens, the Latin name of a Christian man in Rome who sent greetings to Timothy.
article: Pudens is a personal name of Latin origin, belonging to a Christian in Rome who is named in only one place in the New Testament (2 Timothy 4:21). It functions purely as a proper name, so it has no meaning beyond identifying this individual. Interestingly, the name turns up in everyday Koine documents too: Moulton-Milligan cite an Egyptian papyrus (BGU II.455, first century A.D.) using the genitive form Πούδεντος, showing it was a real, ordinary name in circulation.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured data oddly labels it "Eubulus" though every source confirms the name is Pudens.

definition: A benefactor: someone who does good for others, often an official title for a generous patron or ruler.
article: εὐεργέτης names a benefactor, literally a "worker of good," built from the parts meaning "well" and "work." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 22:25, where Jesus notes that rulers who lord it over people are called "benefactors." The papyri show this was a real-world honorific: a petition from around AD 49–50 has a woman addressing the prefect as "my benefactor," and another text hails an official as "savior and benefactor of all," confirming it was a standard title of respect for patrons and rulers.
caution: The word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering ("themselves") appears to be a data artifact rather than a true sense of the word.

definition: The first-person pronoun "I" or "me," referring to the speaker, expressed in Greek mainly when emphasis is intended.
article: This is simply the Greek word for "I" — the first-person pronoun, appearing a massive 2659 times across all 27 New Testament books. Because Greek verbs already carry the subject, the standalone pronoun is usually added for emphasis, though Abbott-Smith notes it often carries no special stress. In the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew "I" words אָנִי and אָנֹכִי hundreds of times, and the phrase "behold, I" (ἰδοὺ ἐγώ) echoes the Hebrew הִנֵּנִי, "here I am." Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan points to inscriptions and magical texts where a solemn, repeated "I am" mirrors the style of statements in John's Gospel.
caution: The many "senses" here are just translation variations of one pronoun (case, number, possessive), not distinct meanings, so the labels reflect rendering patterns rather than separate definitions.

definition: Phoebe, the name of a Christian woman who served the church at Cenchreae.
article: Φοίβη is a personal name appearing only once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:1, where it names a woman associated with the church at Cenchreae and described by Abbott-Smith as a deaconess. The name was in ordinary use in Koine times: Moulton-Milligan find it as the name of a slave in a third-century papyrus and on inscriptions, including one honoring a woman named Claudia Phoebe for her excellence and goodwill. Strong's links it to the base of φῶς ("light"), suggesting an original meaning of "bright."
caution: This is a single-occurrence proper name, so its sense is fixed by that one verse rather than by a measurable range.

definition: Describes someone who is deeply and abundantly compassionate, full of tender mercy toward others.
article: This word literally combines "much" (πολύς) with "inward parts" (σπλάγχνον), the seat of emotion in Greek thought, to describe someone overflowing with compassion. It appears only once in the New Testament, at James 5:11, where it describes the Lord's character. Moulton-Milligan note it is the equivalent of the Septuagint's πολυέλεος ("full of mercy") in Psalm 103:8, and outside the Bible it is otherwise found only in the early Christian writing of Hermas.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is rare elsewhere, so its precise range cannot be measured.

definition: Beautiful or attractive, originally meaning ripe and in season, used of both people and things.
article: At its root ὡραῖος comes from ὥρα ("hour, season") and literally means "in season" or "ripe," which is exactly how it shows up in everyday Koine papyri — describing ripe fruits, preserved fish, and grape harvests. By extension it came to mean "blooming" and then simply "beautiful," which is how the New Testament uses it in all four occurrences, rendered "beautiful" 3 of 4 times. The one remaining case is the proper name of the temple's "Beautiful" Gate in Acts 3:10. In the Septuagint it appears 23 times across 13 books, translating several Hebrew words for beauty and pleasantness, including תֹּ֫אַר ("form, appearance") four times.
caution: The word appears only 4 times in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on thin biblical evidence, though papyri and the Septuagint confirm the seasonal-to-beautiful sense.

definition: A point or stretch of time — most often a specific hour, but also a season or the right moment for something.
article: ὥρα is the everyday Greek word for an "hour," and that is how it reads in 86% of its 105 New Testament appearances, with the Berean Study Bible agreeing 99% of the time. It also stretches to mean a broader "time" or "moment" (about 11% of cases), as in "the time is coming" — and older lexica note it could even mean a natural season. The everyday flavor shows up vividly in the papyri, where people timestamp documents and horoscopes "at the first hour," "at the third hour of the night," or "at 7 o'clock." In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew word עֵת, the general word for "time."

definition: An adverb meaning right now, at this very moment, marking the strictly present time in contrast to past or future.
article: ἄρτι pins down the immediate present — "just now," "at this very moment" — as opposed to what came before or what is yet to come. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "now" in 19 of its 36 New Testament appearances (63%), with a handful of cases where it shades into "still" or simply gets folded into the surrounding phrasing. The everyday papyri make its flavor vivid: one writer says he can't come to you "right now" (ἄρτι) because of a lawsuit, and a rescript of Hadrian uses it of a city that was "just" incorporated. Abbott-Smith notes it contrasts with both past and future time and stands close in meaning to νῦν.
caution: With only two Septuagint occurrences, the Old Greek evidence is thin, so its range there rests almost entirely on New Testament and papyri usage.

definition: A bitter rebellion or provocation, the angry defiance shown when people stir God to anger by their stubborn refusal to trust him.
article: παραπικρασμός describes a sharp, embittered rebellion against God — the act of provoking him through stubborn defiance. The Majority Standard Bible renders both of its two New Testament occurrences (Hebrews 3:8 and 3:15) as "rebellion," and the BSB agrees fully. Most striking is its Old Testament background: it appears once in the Septuagint, at Psalm 95:8, pointing back to the place name "Meribah" ("quarreling"), where Israel quarreled with God in the wilderness, which is why older glosses like "provocation" and "irritation" still cling to it.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament uses (both quoting one Psalm) and a single Septuagint occurrence — so the precise force ranges between "rebellion" and the older "provocation/irritation."

definition: The legal act of taking someone as one's own son or daughter, used to describe how God makes believers His children.
article: This word names the formal, legal process of adopting a son or daughter, and in the New Testament it always describes God establishing people as His own children. It appears 5 times across 3 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as some form of "adoption" in every case. A nice piece of background: Moulton-Milligan and Deissmann point out that the phrase "by adoption" (καθ᾽ υἱοθεσίαν) was common in everyday inscriptions, so Paul was borrowing a term ordinary people would have instantly recognized.

definition: To make something longer or larger; in its one New Testament use, to grow or lengthen as a plant does.
article: At its core μηκύνω means to lengthen or extend, and it comes from the noun μῆκος ("length"). Its single New Testament appearance (Mark 4:27) uses it of seed that "sprouts" and grows while the farmer sleeps, which is how the Majority Standard Bible renders it 100% of the time. The word's wider range is interesting: in the Septuagint it can describe causing plants to grow (Isaiah 44:14) but also stretching something out in time, and a papyrus example (Aristeas 8) uses it of dragging out an introduction too long.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence (and none in the critical text), so confidence in its measured sense is low.

definition: The distance something extends downward or inward, whether literal deep water or a figurative immensity like the riches of God.
article: βάθος names the measurable reach of something downward or inward — the deep part of a lake, the depth of soil, or the boundless extent of God's wisdom. In the New Testament it appears 8 times, rendered "depth" in half the cases and "deep" in a third, with two uses absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday roots of the word show up in the papyri, where it describes digging a trench "to a depth" and setting plants into garden furrows, and in the Septuagint it often translates Hebrew words for the lowest places or the ocean depths.
caution: The figurative senses (such as the "depth" of God's riches) sit alongside plain physical depth, so context decides which is meant.

definition: To win someone over by argument, or in its perfect tense, to be inwardly convinced, confident, or trusting.
article: At its core πείθω means to persuade — to bring someone around through argument or appeal — but in the New Testament it splits between two grammatical lives. In its ordinary form it means actively persuading people ("persuade," 7×), while its perfect tense carries a present sense of being settled and assured, hence "convinced" (10×), "confident" (5×), and "trust" (3×). Strikingly, the Septuagint uses this word 131 times mostly to render the Hebrew בָּטַח (47×), the language of "trusting" or relying on God, which colors the confidence shades of meaning. Everyday Koine papyri show the persuading sense vividly, as when a writer pleads with a friend to "persuade him to come."

definition: To share in someone's joy, rejoicing together with them, or to congratulate them.
article: This verb combines "with" (σύν) and "rejoice" (χαίρω) to mean sharing gladness alongside another person. Of its 7 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "rejoice" 4 times (67%), with single instances of "love takes pleasure" and "glad." Everyday Koine papyri show the same warmth: a mother writes to her son that she "rejoiced for you and for myself" upon learning he was studying Egyptian script. The classical lexica add a secondary sense, "to congratulate," which Abbott-Smith notes for Philippians.
caution: Evidence is moderate with only 7 occurrences, and lexicons add a "congratulate" sense not separately reflected in the measured renderings.

definition: To add or join something to what is already there, or to do something again or further.
article: προστίθημι means to place something alongside or in addition to what already exists — to add, join, or increase. In the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "added" in 7 of 18 occurrences (70%), while in 8 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. A striking feature comes from the Septuagint, where it translates Hebrew יָסַף 186 times; following that Hebrew idiom, the verb plus an infinitive can mean to repeat or continue an action ("he added to send" = "he sent again"), as in Luke 20:11 and Acts 12:3.

definition: Describing a woman who is married, that is, bound to and under the authority of a husband.
article: ὕπανδρος literally combines "under" and "man/husband" to describe a woman who is married. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 7:2, where it is folded into the phrasing about a married woman rather than getting its own English word. The same word shows up a couple of times in the Septuagint and in everyday Koine papyri, and writers like Polybius use it too, so it was ordinary vocabulary for a wife bound to her husband.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears only once in the New Testament and rarely elsewhere, so its range is hard to measure precisely.

definition: To have warm affection or fondness for someone or something, or to show such affection by kissing.
senseLabels: kiss as a sign of affection
article: φιλέω is the verb of warm personal affection — the love of friendship and feeling. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "love" in about 63% of its 24 Byzantine occurrences, but in two places it clearly means "kiss" (as in Judas's betrayal in Mark 14:44 and Luke 22:47), since a kiss was the physical expression of that affection. The Septuagint backing makes this vivid: of its 28 uses, 14 translate Hebrew נָשַׁק ("to kiss") and 6 translate אָהַב ("to love"). Everyday papyri use it the same warm way, as in a letter saying "you know how I esteem and love you."
caution: Strong's and Abbott-Smith distinguish φιλέω (affection, feeling) from ἀγαπάω (love of will and duty), but how sharply the New Testament keeps that line is debated.

definition: The chief or head shepherd who oversees the other shepherds.
article: ἀρχιποίμην combines the words for "chief" and "shepherd" to mean a head shepherd who stands over ordinary shepherds. It appears just once in the New Testament (1 Peter 5:4), where it describes Christ, and in that one place it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word. The most striking evidence is that this is no Christian coinage: it turns up on an Egyptian peasant's mummy label from the Roman period reading "Plenis, the younger, chief shepherd," and in a papyrus list of shepherds headed by an ἀρχιποιμήν, showing it was an ordinary occupational title in everyday Koine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage supported by scattered papyri and inscriptions.

definition: A person raised together with someone from childhood, such as a foster-brother, and by extension a close intimate companion of a ruler.
article: σύντροφος literally describes someone "nourished together" with another — a foster-brother or childhood companion. The word appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 13:1, where it describes Manaen as raised together with Herod the tetrarch. The Septuagint uses it 3 times, and in Hellenistic usage it became a court title for an intimate friend of a king; everyday papyri confirm the literal sense, as in a will leaving an inheritance to a daughter "and her foster-brother."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there — literal foster-brother versus honorary court title — cannot be settled from frequency alone.

definition: Apollos, a Jewish man from Alexandria known in the early church for his eloquent teaching.
article: Ἀπολλῶς is a personal name, that of a Jew from Alexandria who appears in Acts and several of Paul's letters, occurring 10 times across 3 books in the Byzantine New Testament. The name is probably a shortened form of Ἀπολλώνιος, a form that actually shows up in Codex Bezae at Acts 18:24. It was a real everyday name in the Greek-speaking world: Moulton-Milligan trace it through papyri and inscriptions, including one from the Serapeum at Memphis where it takes the genitive form Ἀπολλῶτος.

definition: To slaughter or kill someone off, completely putting them to death.
article: This is a strong, vivid verb meaning to slaughter or kill off completely \u2014 the prefix kata- intensifies the basic idea of slaying. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 19:27), where it's absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word, plus twice in the Septuagint. In Ezekiel 16:40 it translates a Hebrew word for cutting or hacking apart, and Moulton-Milligan note its only documentary parallel, an everyday papyrus from A.D. 117, where it apparently refers to victims falling as sacrifices.
caution: Evidence is thin: this word appears only once in the New Testament and twice in the Septuagint, so its precise force is hard to pin down.

definition: An accuser or slanderer; with the article, the Devil—the supreme accuser opposed to God.
article: In the New Testament this word overwhelmingly names the Devil: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "devil" in 31 of 38 occurrences (91%), and the BSB agrees 100% on those. But the root meaning is broader—it describes someone who accuses falsely or slanders, and the lexicons note this general sense applies to people in passages like 1 Timothy 3:11 and Titus 2:3. The Septuagint connection is telling: it translates the Hebrew שָׂטָן ("satan," the accuser/adversary) 17 of 20 times, which is exactly the courtroom-accuser idea behind "the Devil."

definition: The common people of a town gathered as a public body, especially a crowd or popular assembly.
article: δῆμος refers to the ordinary people of a city viewed as a public body, often a crowd or popular assembly. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in Acts, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "people" twice plus phrases tied to crowds and assemblies in the other two cases. Lexicographers distinguish it from related words: λαός tends to mean the people as a whole (often Israel), while δῆμος is the people as a body politic, and ὄχλος is an unorganized mob. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew מִשְׁפָּחָה ("clan, family") 136 times, and one scholar notes its New Testament uses suggest merely a rabble, since real Greek civic freedom had faded.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the measured senses rest on thin data, and the breakdown into separate "senses" partly reflects differing translation phrasing rather than clearly distinct meanings.
