definition: The specific section or passage of a written text that someone is reading or quoting.
article: περιοχή refers to a bounded portion of a text—the particular passage someone is reading—and appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 8:32, describing the section of Isaiah the Ethiopian official was reading. The word's literal meaning is "compass" or "circumference," something held around or enclosed, and in the Septuagint its 23 occurrences mostly translate Hebrew words for a fortress or stronghold (מְצוּדָה nine times, מָצוֹר five times). Everyday papyri use it concretely for the measured boundaries of a plot of land, which fits the underlying idea of an enclosed or circumscribed area.
caution: The single NT occurrence and the odd "eunuch" rendering in the measured data point to a quirk in how the verse was counted rather than the word's meaning, so treat the New Testament evidence as thin.

definition: Having a gloomy, downcast facial expression that shows sadness or sullenness.
article: σκυθρωpós describes someone whose face looks gloomy, sad, or sullen — it literally combines a word for "sullen" with the word for "face" or "appearance." It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Matthew 6:16, where hypocrites put on a somber look while fasting, and in Luke 24:17, describing the downcast faces of the disciples on the road to Emmaus. The word was at home in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite its use in papyri and even in the comic playwright Menander, where someone asks a gloomy-looking servant why he seems so troubled.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, though the lexica agree closely on its meaning.

definition: To leap up or spring up, often as a sudden burst of physical movement.
article: ἐξάλλομαι describes someone springing or leaping up, built from the parts "out of" and "to leap." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 3:8, where the healed man jumps to his feet — the Majority Standard and Berean Standard Bibles agree on "sprang" 100% of the time. In the Septuagint it shows up just 4 times, translating four different Hebrew words, and Moulton-Milligan note it was an everyday term in the papyri; some have even flagged it as a medical word favored by Luke.
caution: With only one New Testament use and scattered, varied Septuagint occurrences, the evidence base is thin and the precise range is hard to pin down.

definition: Producing no fruit or results, whether literally barren or figuratively useless and unproductive.
article: ἄκαρπος is built from a negative prefix plus the word for "fruit" (καρπός), so it literally means "without fruit." In all 7 New Testament uses it carries a figurative sense, describing people, works, or words that produce nothing of value — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "unfruitful" 4 times and "fruitless" once. An Oxyrhynchus papyrus from A.D. 316 uses it of a tree that had stayed barren and withered for many years, showing the same everyday image behind the biblical metaphor.
caution: Both measured senses ("unfruitful" and "fruitless") are essentially the same idea, and 2 of the 7 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing without a dedicated English word.

definition: To hold someone in a grip — either by harboring a hostile grudge against them or, in the passive, by being trapped or entangled in something.
article: ἐνέχω literally combines "in" and "hold," and its meaning splits along grammatical lines: in the active it describes holding a grudge against someone (as Herodias did against John in Mark 6:19), while in the passive it means being held fast or entangled in something, like the "yoke of slavery" in Galatians 5:1. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "held" once and "encumbered more" once, with one occurrence absorbed into broader phrasing. The everyday Koine evidence is striking: papyri use the passive form for people "guilty of" or "liable to" charges — an amnesty document excludes those "guilty of wilful murder or sacrilege" — showing the word could mean being caught in legal or moral entanglement.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a meaning that shifts between active "grudge" and passive "entangled," the precise sense depends heavily on grammar and context in each verse.

definition: A loan of money, or the debt that results from borrowing it.
article: δάνειον refers to a loan—money lent out, and by extension the debt the borrower owes. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Matthew 18:27, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "debt" (100%). The everyday business sense is well attested: the papyri show it used in actual loan contracts, such as a 239 B.C. document where Zenion must forfeit twice the amount of a 500-drachma loan to Theodote.
caution: This word occurs just once in the New Testament, so its full range there rests on a single passage.

definition: Noah, the patriarch who built the ark and survived the great flood.
article: Νῶε is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Noah (נֹחַ), used for the patriarch who built the ark. It appears 8 times in the New Testament across 5 books, always referring to him—often in phrases like "the days of Noah" that point to his era or household rather than just the man. The Septuagint uses the name 48 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew נֹחַ, though oddly it once stands in for נְקֵבָה ("female") and once for אוֹת ("sign"), likely scribal slips.

definition: To stay in one place, remain in a state or relationship, or continue and endure over time.
article: At its core μένω means to stay put — whether physically lodging somewhere, holding to a state or relationship, or lasting through time. The measured renderings cluster tightly around "remain," "stay," and "abide," with "remain" alone covering 44 of 121 occurrences (47%), and the BSB independently agrees with the lead sense 93% of the time, so the word's range is broad but consistent. Everyday Koine papyri show the same plain sense: one letter reads "I have no leisure to remain longer," and an oracle question simply asks "shall I stay in Bacchias?" — the same ordinary "stay here" the Gospels use, alongside the deeper "abide in me" language of John.

definition: A man's personal name, Artemas, a Christian companion mentioned once in the New Testament.
article: Artemas is a proper name appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Titus 3:12, where Paul plans to send him or Tychicus to Titus. As a name it doesn't translate into an ordinary English word and is simply rendered "Artemas." The name is a contracted form built from Ἄρτεμις (the goddess Artemis) and δῶρον (gift), so it originally carried the sense "gift of Artemis."
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so its evidence is very thin.

definition: A Syrian — a person from Syria, the region northeast of Israel.
article: Σύρος simply means a Syrian, someone native to the region of Syria. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 4:27, where it describes Naaman the Syrian, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders that single instance as "Naaman." In the Septuagint it shows up 32 times, mostly translating the Hebrew words for Aramean (אֲרַמִּי) and Aram (אֲרָם), reflecting the close link between Syria and the Aramean people. Everyday papyri confirm the word was common: one inscription even mentions a "village of Syrians" near Alexandria.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: A man who engages in same-sex sexual activity with another male.
senseLabels: a male engaging in same-sex acts
article: This rare word appears only twice in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10, and both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it "homosexual" every time. It is built from two parts, ἄρσην ("male") and κοίτη ("bed," used of sexual intercourse), so it literally points to a male who lies with a male. Moulton-Milligan note that the word first turns up among poets of the imperial period and that the related verb appears in the Sibylline Oracles in a list of things to avoid, alongside extortion and murder.
caution: This entry rests on only two occurrences and rare outside attestation, and the precise scope of the term is debated, so confidence is low.

definition: Sorrow, grief, or pain affecting the body or the mind.
article: λύπη is the standard Koine word for sorrow or grief, the inner pain that stands as the opposite of joy (χαρά). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "sorrow" in half of its 16 New Testament appearances, and the rest are mostly absorbed into phrasing like "made you sorrowful" rather than getting a separate English word. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew words for pain and grief, including the toil-and-pain word used in Genesis, and an everyday papyrus letter even uses it as a threat — that someone will "cause me lasting sorrow" if they fail.

definition: The north-west wind, and by extension the direction in the sky from which that wind blows.
article: χῶρος is a borrowed word, taken from the Latin caurus, naming the north-west wind and the quarter of the sky it comes from. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:12, where the harbor on Crete faces toward the south-west and north-west. The lexicons (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith, Moulton-Milligan) agree firmly on this 'north-west wind' meaning, and Moulton-Milligan confirms it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: It occurs only once in the New Testament, and the corpus-measured rendering 'unsuitable' reflects a translation choice in context rather than the word's actual meaning, which the lexicons consistently give as the north-west wind.

definition: The present participle of the verb "to be," meaning "being" or "existing" — describing who or what someone or something currently is.
article: This is simply the present participle form of εἰμί, "to be," so it carries the same broad range as the English verb: to exist, to be present, or to be a certain way. The Abbott-Smith lexicon notes its use in striking constructions like the description of God as "the one who is and who was" (ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν) in Revelation, and the phrase "the things that are not" (τὰ μὴ ὄντα) in Romans 4:17 and 1 Corinthians 1:28. Because it is a grammatical form rather than a distinct word, its precise meaning depends entirely on its sentence.
caution: This form has no measured senses in the digest (0 Byzantine occurrences listed), so its meaning rests on the general lexicon entry for εἰμί rather than counted data.

definition: Big or great—in size, intensity, volume, rank, or importance—across a very wide range of contexts.
article: μέγας is the all-purpose word for "big" in the broadest sense, covering physical size, intensity, loudness, and rank or importance. Of its 240 New Testament occurrences, 58% are rendered "great" and another 19% "loud" (as in a loud voice or cry), with the rest expressing comparison—"greater," "greater than," or "greatest." In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates Hebrew גָּדוֹל ("great," 396×). One striking detail: the papyri show μέγας was the standard epithet for pagan gods and goddesses ("great Isis," echoing "great is Artemis of the Ephesians" in Acts 19:28), yet the New Testament applies it to the true God only once, in Titus 2:13.

definition: To be accustomed or in the habit of doing something; the participle form describes what is customary or usual.
article: This verb means to be accustomed to something, and in the New Testament it almost always appears as a participle describing what was customary—Jesus going to the synagogue 'as was his custom' (Luke 4:16) or Paul reasoning from the Scriptures 'as was his custom' (Acts 17:2). It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament and is rendered 'custom' three of those times. The everyday papyri show the same flavor: one writer apologizes for sending little birds 'which I am not accustomed to eat,' confirming this was ordinary household language for habits and routines.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree closely on its meaning.

definition: A stream that flows in winter, swelling with rain but often dry in summer; a seasonal torrent or wadi.
article: χείμαῤῥος is built from the words for "winter" and "flow," describing a brook that runs full in the rainy season and can dry up otherwise. It appears just once in the New Testament, at John 18:1, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Valley" (the Kidron); the KJV calls it a "brook." In the Septuagint it usually stands for the Hebrew nachal (a wadi or seasonal riverbed), and the Letter of Aristeas (117) uses it of torrents that "flow down" into the plain.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: To bind or tie things together, or in the passive, to be bound alongside someone, as prisoners chained together.
article: συνδέω combines "with" (σύν) and "bind" (δέω) to mean tying things together, and in its single New Testament appearance (Hebrews 13:3) it describes being bound alongside others, like fellow prisoners in chains. It appears just once in the Byzantine text and seven times across five books of the Septuagint, where it renders several different Hebrew words. The everyday papyri show how concrete the word could be: one third-century letter uses it of a small letter "made up of different papyrus sheets fastened together."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word.

definition: The act of creating, or the thing created — whether a single creature or the whole created world.
article: In the New Testament κτίσις mostly means "creation," rendered that way in 13 of its 19 occurrences (81%), and the BSB agrees 100% of the time. The word spans both the act of creating and the result — anything from a single creature to the sum of all created things, as in the call to preach to "all creation." Interestingly, in everyday Koine inscriptions and in classical authors like Polybius, κτίσις was the standard term for the founding of a city, a sense not carried over into the New Testament's focus on divine creation.
caution: The standard lexicon (Abbott-Smith) splits κτίsis into several shades — the act of creating, an individual creature, and collective creation — that the single measured "creation" sense flattens together.

definition: The act of putting away, removing, or laying aside something.
article: ἀπόθεσις means the act of putting or laying something away, and it comes from the verb ἀποτίθημι ("to put off"). It appears only twice in the New Testament — at 1 Peter 3:21, where it describes the removal of dirt from the body, and at 2 Peter 1:14, where Peter speaks of the "putting off" of his body at death. Everyday Koine papyri use the same word for ordinary actions like the storing away of chaff, and one fourth-century inscription even applies it to the ceremony of resigning a priesthood.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured evidence is thin.

definition: To advance or make progress—growing in amount, maturing over time, or moving steadily toward a goal.
article: At its root προκόπτω pictures cutting a way forward, like a pioneer clearing brush, but in later Koine it became wholly intransitive—simply meaning to advance or make progress. It stretches across different kinds of progress: a person maturing (Luke 2:52 "grew in favor"), or time moving along (Romans 13:12 "the night is nearly over"). Everyday papyri show the same flavor: one ii/A.D. soldier writes home that he hopes "to be quickly promoted, if the gods will," while another letter wishes a friend health and continued advancement.
caution: With only 6 occurrences—4 of them dissolved into surrounding phrasing—the measured English range rests on a thin sample.

definition: A country, region, or stretch of land, sometimes the countryside as opposed to a town or city.
article: χώρα refers to an expanse of land—a country, a region, or sometimes the rural countryside set against the town. In the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "country" 7 times and "region" 7 times (each 39%), with the rest absorbed into broader phrasing, so the two main meanings are essentially the same idea at different scales. The Septuagint uses it 149 times, often translating the Hebrew מְדִינָה ("province"), and the everyday papyri show the same geographical sweep, including a phrase meaning "throughout the country or district."

definition: That which is produced or born — the crop a field yields, or the offspring of living creatures.
article: γέννημα refers to whatever is brought forth: the produce of the earth (crops, grain, the "fruit of the vine") or the offspring of people and animals. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times, rendered by the Majority Standard Bible twice as referring to the vine's fruit and twice as "store" of crops, with the remaining 5 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. A spelling worth noting: the best manuscripts and abundant papyri actually show the form γένημα for the earth's produce — Oxyrhynchus documents speak of πυροῦ γενήματος ("crop of wheat") and οἰνικοῦ γενήματος ("crop of wine"), confirming this was ordinary commercial vocabulary.
caution: Lexicons split the word: Abbott-Smith treats γέννημα as "offspring" (as in "brood of vipers") but notes the produce-of-the-earth sense belongs to the better-attested spelling γένημα, so the two forms and meanings are easily confused.

definition: To call someone in or invite them inside, especially into one's home.
article: This verb means to call someone in or invite them inside, and in the New Testament it appears only once, in Acts 10:23, where Peter invites his visitors into the house. The everyday papyri confirm this practical sense: a petition from 241 B.C. uses it to mean "summon" someone—asking an official to call the parties in to hear their case. So the word ranges from a friendly invitation indoors to a more formal summons, all built on the idea of calling someone into a place.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so its measured range rests on a single passage plus outside papyri evidence.

definition: A low muttering or grumbling complaint, whether secret whispering among people or open expressions of discontent.
article: γογγυσμός describes muttered discontent — the under-the-breath grumbling that spreads through a crowd or simmers in a community. The four New Testament uses cover a small range: it can mean quiet whispering about someone (John 7:12) or outright complaining (Philippians 2:14; 1 Peter 4:9). In the Septuagint it appears 8 times and most often (7×) translates the Hebrew word for the Israelites' "murmurings" against God in the wilderness, which colors its biblical flavor strongly toward rebellious grumbling.
caution: With only four New Testament occurrences spread evenly across distinct shades, the precise boundary between secret whispering and open complaint is hard to pin down.

definition: A high place or elevated thing, used both for literal height and for something raised up as a barrier or obstacle.
article: ὕψωμα refers to something lifted high — either a literal height or, figuratively, a raised-up thing that acts as a barrier. It appears only twice in the New Testament, split evenly between these two ideas: "height" in Romans 8:39 and a "barrier" raised against the knowledge of God in 2 Corinthians 10:5. Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri use the word in astrological horoscopes for the "exaltation" of a planet (the sun's ὕψωμα set against Saturn's low point), showing how naturally the word carried the sense of being elevated.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the full range of the word is hard to pin down.

definition: To wipe away, blot out, or erase completely, used for removing tears, canceling debts, or wiping out sins.
article: ἐξαλείφω means to wipe something out so it is gone—tears wiped from the eyes, a debt record canceled, or sins erased. Across its 5 New Testament uses it usually carries the idea of removal (rendered with "away" 75% of the time), and in the Septuagint it appears 39 times, most often translating the Hebrew מָחָה ("to wipe out," 19×). The most striking evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions, where the same word is used quite literally for striking a person's name off official lists—exactly the image behind Revelation 3:5's promise not to blot a name out of the book of life.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences, the sense range rests heavily on Septuagint and papyri evidence, and the lexica list a 'plaster/wash over' meaning not attested in the New Testament itself.

definition: The number thirty.
article: τριάκοντα is simply the cardinal number thirty, an indeclinable word formed from τρεῖς ("three"). It appears 10 times in the Byzantine New Testament and 169 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew word for thirty (146 times). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one document from A.D. 104 asks someone to "look out thirty fish."

definition: Zadok, a personal name in Jesus' genealogy, borne by an Israelite descendant in Matthew's record.
article: Σαδώκ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Zadok (צָדוֹק), an indeclinable proper name that appears twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both within Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. The Septuagint uses it 43 times across 6 books, almost always rendering the same Hebrew name (42 of 43 times). It is simply a personal name, with no meaning beyond identifying the man who bears it.
caution: The measured data lists a second rendering, "Achim," at the same verse, which likely reflects a tagging artifact rather than a genuine separate sense; evidence overall is thin.

definition: To step in between parties as a go-between, guaranteeing or confirming an agreement, oath, or arrangement.
article: μεσιτεύω means to act as a middleman who steps between two parties to mediate, vouch for, or guarantee a deal. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 6:17, where God 'guaranteed' his promise with an oath, which the Majority Standard Bible renders 'unchanging.' Notably, everyday Koine papyri use the word in ordinary business and legal contexts—people 'mediating and ceding property to others' (BGU III.906)—showing it was common commercial language, and inscriptions even speak of a city 'mediating' a treaty.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the biblical sense rests on a single verse plus outside evidence from papyri and classical sources.

definition: A person from Ethiopia (ancient Cush), the region south of Egypt in Africa.
article: Αἰθίοψ refers to an Ethiopian — someone from the African region the Greeks called Ethiopia and the Hebrews called Cush. The name itself comes from words meaning "to burn" and "face," describing dark or swarthy skin. In the Septuagint it appears 29 times across 11 books, most often translating the Hebrew כּוּשִׁי (Cushite), and it occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in the account of the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:27.
caution: The two New Testament occurrences are both in a single verse, so the word's range here rests on very limited evidence; the listed senses "started" and "court" reflect surrounding phrasing rather than the word itself.

definition: A rugged region south of Damascus, named in the New Testament when locating the rule of the tetrarch Philip.
article: Trachōnîtis is a place name for a rough, rocky district lying south of Damascus, mentioned just once in the New Testament. The name itself comes from the Greek word for "rough" or "rugged" (τραχύς), fittingly describing its rocky terrain. It appears in Luke 3:1, where it helps fix the political setting of John the Baptist's ministry by naming the territory governed by Philip the tetrarch.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond this single geographical use.

definition: To choose or appoint someone in advance, beforehand.
article: This verb means to select or appoint a person ahead of time, built from πρό ("before") plus χειροτονέω ("to choose or appoint"). In the New Testament it appears only once, in Acts 10:41, where it describes witnesses God had chosen beforehand. The same word turns up in an official report among the everyday Koine papyri (BGU IV.1191), used of someone "previously appointed," which shows it was ordinary administrative language.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: Eber, a personal name in the Old Testament genealogy, listed as an ancestor in Luke's family tree of Jesus.
article: Ἐβέρ is simply the Greek form of the Hebrew name Eber (עֵבֶר), a patriarch in the ancestral line. It appears just once in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Luke 3:35, where it functions as the name of an ancestor. The Septuagint uses it 8 times across 2 books, always rendering the same Hebrew name, and traditional sources identify him as the father of Peleg and son of Shelah.
caution: This is an indeclinable proper name attested only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single genealogical use.

definition: To formally inaugurate, dedicate, or set something new into effect, such as a covenant or a way.
article: ἐγκαινίζω means to officially open, dedicate, or set something into operation — to make it new and effective. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, both in Hebrews (9:18 and 10:20), once rendered "effect" and once absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it ten times across six books, mostly translating the Hebrew חָנַך ("to dedicate," 4×) and חָדַשׁ ("to renew," 2×), which fits its connection to ἐγκαίνια (dedication). A papyrus from 127 B.C. is especially telling: there the word means to "make no innovation," showing it was ordinary Koine and not just biblical language.
caution: Confidence is low: the word appears only twice in the New Testament, and the everyday papyrus sense ("innovate") differs from the inaugural sense seen in Hebrews.

definition: A place to lodge or shelter, specifically the nest or roosting spot where birds settle.
article: In the New Testament, κατασκήνωσις appears just twice, both times describing where birds settle—translated "dens" or "nests" in the famous saying that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20; Luke 9:58). The word's root meaning is broader: an encamping or taking up quarters, and the Septuagint uses it for a dwelling-place or tabernacle. A nice everyday parallel comes from an inscription where the people of Smyrna promised to provide shelter (κατασκήνωσιν) for migrants until they could build their own houses.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin Septuagint evidence, this is a low-confidence entry, and the lexicons note a broader range (encampment, dwelling) than the measured bird-nest sense.

definition: The eye, the body's organ of sight, often used figuratively for perception, attitude, or how one sees the world.
article: This common word means the eye and appears 102 times in the Byzantine New Testament, rendered "eyes" in 94 cases (99%). In the Septuagint it shows up 548 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for eye (עַ֫יִן). Beyond the literal organ, both the lexicons and Hebrew background extend it to moral attitudes—the "evil eye" (ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός) stands for envy or greed, echoing the Hebrew idiom in Proverbs, while Strong's even ties the figurative envy sense to the jealous side-glance.

definition: To hold back from harming, punishing, or burdening someone—to treat them gently or leave them unhurt.
article: φείδομαι means to spare someone—to refrain from harming, punishing, or imposing on them. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 10 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "spare" in 6 of those, usually with the person spared in the genitive (as in Acts 20:29 and Romans 8:32). The word was common in everyday Koine: one papyrus from 164 B.C. uses it to urge that the weak be spared, while a striking third-century A.D. text reads "as the gods have not spared me, so will I not spare the gods." In the Septuagint it appears 77 times, most often translating the Hebrew חָמַל ("have compassion, spare").

definition: To carry a dead body out, especially from a city to be buried.
article: This verb means to carry someone or something out, and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 7:12) it specifically describes carrying a dead body out of the city for burial. Built from ἐκ ('out') plus κομίζω ('to carry'), it appears in everyday Koine papyri both for burial and in broader senses — Moulton-Milligan cite documents where it means recovering a pawned garment, collecting wages, or receiving an allowance. The funeral sense fits the Luke scene well, where the only son of a widow is being carried out.
caution: It occurs only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word, so its precise force rests largely on outside evidence.

definition: To accept or welcome someone or something, whether agreeing to a request or receiving a person hospitably.
article: ἐπιδέχομαι is a compound of ἐπί and δέχομαι ("receive") and means to accept what is offered or to welcome someone in. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 3 John, where translators fold it into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendering it with a single English word. Everyday Koine papyri light up its range nicely: one document from 165 B.C. uses it for "cheerfully accepting what is proposed," while an Oxyrhynchus letter uses it of taking a destitute man into one's home — exactly the two shades (accepting terms versus receiving a guest) that appear in 3 John.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into phrasing and confined to a single short letter, the evidence here is thin.

definition: To pour out a liquid, usually wine, as a religious offering; figuratively, to give up one's life as a sacrifice.
article: σπένdω literally means to pour out wine or another liquid as an offering to a god, a libation. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, both times in the passive and figuratively—of a life being poured out like a drink-offering through the shedding of blood. The Septuagint uses it 17 times, mostly translating the Hebrew נָסַך ("pour out"), and the everyday papyri confirm its ordinary religious sense, as in a document describing children pouring out libations to the god Osorapis on behalf of their family.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the Byzantine NT (zero in the SBLGNT critical text), and both times its sense is carried by surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word.

definition: An adverb meaning late in the day, in the evening, or (with a following noun) late in or after something.
article: ὀψέ is a time-adverb that points to the late part of the day, the evening, in contrast to early morning. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just 3 times (4 in the critical text), all evening references, and the Septuagint uses it 4 times to render Hebrew words tied to dusk and lamp-lighting (Abbott-Smith cites Exodus 30:8, where the evening lamp is lit). The most interesting evidence comes from the papyri: a writer signs off saying he is writing 'very late,' and an old construction with the genitive (ὀψὲ τῆς ὥρας, 'late in the hour') lies behind the debated phrase in Matthew 28:1, which can mean either 'late on the sabbath' or 'after the sabbath.'
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 Byzantine occurrences) and sources disagree on whether the genitive construction means 'late in' or 'after,' which affects how Matthew 28:1 should be read.

definition: Heavily or with difficulty, used of ears that barely hear and so fail to understand.
article: βαρέως is an adverb from βαρύς ("heavy"), describing something done heavily or with difficulty. In both New Testament occurrences (Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27) it appears in the same phrase about hearing "heavily" — that is, dully or barely. The Septuagint shows a similar idiomatic range, using it both for hearing heavily (Isaiah 6:10, rendering a Hebrew word for being dull or hardened) and for the phrase "to take heavily" or be vexed (Genesis 31:35).
caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, and the digest's measured rendering label "people's" reflects the surrounding phrase rather than the word itself.

definition: An opening in rock, such as a cave, crevice, or hole from which water can flow.
senseLabels: a hole or opening in rock
article: ὀπή refers to a gap or opening in rock — a cave, crevice, or the hole from which a spring breaks out. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Hebrews 11:38, where the Majority Standard Bible's rendering gets absorbed into the broader phrasing about people wandering in deserts and caves, and in James 3:11, where it describes the opening of a spring. The Septuagint uses it six times, mostly for the Hebrew word חֹר (a hole), and Abbott-Smith links it to the cleft of rock where Moses was hidden in Exodus 33:22.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To recline at a table together with others, as people did while sharing a meal.
article: This verb describes lying down to eat alongside other people, the normal posture for dining in the ancient world rather than sitting in chairs. It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 3 books, often paired with a dative naming the people one dines with, and in half of those cases it gets folded into phrases about "guests" or "dining" rather than translated as its own word. Its single Septuagint appearance is in 3 Maccabees 5:39, and the parts that build it literally mean "to recline up together with."
caution: With only 8 New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence, the evidence base is fairly thin.

definition: A purple or violet semiprecious stone, a kind of quartz, used among the foundation gems of the New Jerusalem.
article: Amethyst is a purple variety of quartz; in the New Testament it appears just once, naming the twelfth foundation stone of the wall of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:20. The name itself comes from a negative prefix plus the verb 'to be drunk,' reflecting an old belief that the stone warded off intoxication, possibly because the best specimens were the color of unmixed wine. In the Septuagint the word shows up 3 times in 2 books, where it renders three different Hebrew gemstone terms, confirming it consistently denotes a specific precious stone.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range there cannot be measured; note that the measured-sense label 'twelfth' reflects its position in a list rather than the stone's meaning.

definition: To go, travel, or make one's way from one place to another, whether literally or in a figurative sense.
article: This is a common verb of motion that simply means to go, travel, or proceed on one's way, appearing 154 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The overwhelming majority of uses (92%) translate plainly as "go," with the rest being narrow variations like "go back," while a notable 39 times it disappears into English phrasing without a word of its own. In the Septuagint it shows up over a thousand times, mostly rendering the Hebrew verbs יָלַך and הָלַך, both ordinary words for walking and going; everyday papyri use it the same way, as when a writer reports "I have journeyed to Heracleopolis" about household business.
caution: Strong's and Dodson list a figurative sense "to die," but the measured New Testament data shows no such usage, so that meaning is not in view here.

definition: To be a financial burden to someone, weighing them down with the cost of one's support.
article: In Paul's usage this word means to weigh someone down financially — to be a burdensome expense to the people he ministered among. All 3 New Testament occurrences come from a single author in 2 Corinthians (11:9; 12:13-14), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "burden" two times and "burden way" once. Interestingly, its root literally means to grow numb or torpid (Abbott-Smith notes it relates to a Greek term meaning to grow numb), and it appears in the medical writer Hippocrates; Jerome even thought Paul picked it up as a regional expression from Cilicia.
caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 occurrences, all from one author in one book, so the measured "burden" sense rests on a very narrow base.

definition: A venomous snake, specifically the asp or cobra, often associated with deadly poison.
article: In the New Testament ἀσπίς refers to a venomous snake — the asp or cobra. It appears only once, in Romans 3:13, where the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering counts toward "graves" but the word itself names the snake whose poison is under deceitful lips. In the Septuagint it shows up 20 times across 8 books, most often translating the Hebrew פָּ֫תֶן (pethen, a venomous serpent). Interestingly, the same Greek word can also mean a round shield, and the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) uses ἀσπίς of the asp adorning the king's golden crowns.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse and on Septuagint evidence.

definition: A Hebrew word meaning "armies" or "hosts," used in the title "Lord of Hosts" as a name for God.
article: Σαβαώθ is a Hebrew word carried straight into Greek without translation, meaning "armies" or "hosts," and it appears in the New Testament only twice (Romans 9:29 and James 5:4), both within the title "Lord of Hosts." In the Septuagint it shows up 61 times and usually corresponds to the Hebrew צָבָא (44 times), though translators elsewhere often rendered the same idea with phrases like "Lord Almighty" instead of keeping the Hebrew word. Strikingly, σαβαώθ also turns up in everyday Koine magical papyri and amulets as a powerful name invoked over God, where scholars couldn't even tell whether the writer was Christian, Jewish, Greek, or Egyptian.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is thin, with only 2 occurrences, both essentially the same fixed title.

definition: A royal dwelling or palace, also used for a capital city or symbols of kingship.
article: βασίλειον is the neuter form of the adjective "royal," used as a noun for things connected to kings. In the New Testament it appears only once (Luke 7:25), where in the plural it means a palace, the place where richly clothed people live. The Septuagint uses it 15 times across 7 books, where it can also mean a capital city, and notably it sometimes translates Hebrew words for symbols of royalty such as נֵ֫זֶר (a crown or consecration band) and אֶצְעָדָה (an armlet).
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament, where the word occurs just once, so most of its range comes from the Septuagint.

definition: A lamb, a young sheep; in Revelation a recurring title for the slain yet living Christ.
article: Originally a diminutive of ἀρήν meaning "little lamb," though by Koine times that diminutive force had largely faded so the word simply meant "lamb." It is overwhelmingly a Revelation word: of its 30 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Lamb" 29 times, with one absorbed into phrasing. The everyday papyri confirm this plain sense, listing "yearling lambs" alongside other farm animals like goats and birds, showing that Revelation's author took a common vernacular word and made it an exclusive, frequent title.

definition: To hear, listen to, or perceive something with the ears, often implying attention or understanding.
article: This extremely common verb appears 436 times in the Byzantine New Testament and means to hear or perceive by hearing. In about 88% of cases it simply means "heard," while 11% lean toward active "listen" (paying attention rather than passively perceiving), and a handful are absorbed into time clauses translated "when [someone heard]." In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew שָׁמַע (714 times), and the papyri show a special use for a judicial hearing, as when an official endorses a petition with "it shall be heard."

definition: An interrogative adverb asking "where?" — pointing to a place or location in a question.
article: ποῦ is the question word "where?", asking about location either in direct questions ("Where is he?") or indirect ones ("they asked where the child was"). In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 44 times across 10 books, and roughly 80% of the time it is simply rendered "where," with the rest being minor variations of the same idea inside question phrasing. The Septuagint uses it 105 times to translate the Hebrew question words אַיֵּה, אָן, and אַי, and Moulton-Milligan finds it alive in everyday papyri — one letter literally asks "where did you put the notice of payment for the hay?"
caution: Lexicons note ποῦ sometimes drifts to mean "whither/where to" (as in John 7:35), so a few passages ask about direction rather than fixed location.

definition: From a distance; at or from a place far away.
article: μακρόθεν is an adverb meaning "from afar" or "at a distance," built from μακρός ("long, far"). It shows up 14 times in the Byzantine New Testament, almost always describing the literal physical distance from which someone stands or watches — like Peter following Jesus from afar (Matthew 26:58) or the women observing the crucifixion from a distance (Matthew 27:55). In the Septuagint it appears 31 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew רָחוֹק ("far"), and Moulton-Milligan note it as the everyday Koine replacement for the older πόρρωθεν, with the doubled-up phrase "from from-afar" (ἀπὸ μακρόθεν) being a common, slightly redundant idiom.

definition: A single seed or grain, the small kernel from which a plant grows.
article: κόκκος refers to a single small seed or grain, like the proverbial mustard seed of Jesus' teaching. In all 5 of its measured New Testament occurrences it is rendered "seed" (with another 2 of 7 absorbed into the surrounding phrasing). Everyday Koine documents back this up nicely: the papyri use κόκκος for counted grains and even pine-cones, and a related verb appears in a farming contract about clearing barley and darnel before planting.
caution: It appears only once in the Septuagint, so its broader Greek-Bible range rests almost entirely on the New Testament data.

definition: To unload a ship's cargo, discharging the freight it has been carrying.
article: This verb means to unload or discharge a ship's cargo, built from ἀπό ("off, away") and φορτίζω ("to load"). It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:3, where Paul's ship was set to unlade its cargo at Tyre. The measured rendering label reads "sighting," but the lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) consistently define it as unloading freight (τὸν γόμον), which is the verb's actual sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured sense label appears to mislabel a context word rather than the verb's own meaning, so rely on the lexicon definition of unloading cargo.

definition: A bold, shameless lack of restraint — pushing forward without embarrassment, especially in persistent or greedy asking.
article: ἀναίδεια describes shamelessness, particularly the kind of bold, unembarrassed insistence that keeps pressing for what it wants. The word appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 11:8), and there it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a single English word, so the corpus gives us little direct evidence of how translators handle it. The most telling material comes from the papyri: Moulton-Milligan cite an inscription pairing the related adjective with greed ('audaciously misusing their authority') and a document describing a man as shameless for forcibly levying contributions on his village — capturing its flavor of pushy, grasping boldness.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence (absorbed into phrasing) plus one Septuagint instance — so the precise shade of meaning leans heavily on the papyri.

definition: An opponent of Christ who falsely takes Christ's place or sets himself against him.
article: ἀντίχριστος combines the prefix ἀντί ("against" or "in place of") with Χριστός ("Christ"), naming someone who either opposes Christ or falsely poses as him. It appears only 5 times in the New Testament, all in John's letters (1 John and 2 John), and the Majority Standard Bible renders every instance as "antichrist." Notably, the word may have been coined by John himself, though the way he introduces it suggests his readers already knew the term well, and a probable model for its formation is the older word ἀντίθεος, "rival of God."
caution: The three listed "senses" all reflect the same meaning—the variations are just surrounding phrase fragments, not distinct senses—so this word effectively has one meaning.

definition: Uzziah, a king of Judah listed among the ancestors of Jesus.
article: Ὀζίας is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Uzziah, used as a personal name rather than a common word. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:8–9), where it is rendered "Uzziah" every time. The name shows up far more often in the Septuagint—21 times across 7 books—where it usually translates the Hebrew עֻזִּיָּה, though twice it stands in for a different Hebrew name (אֱלִיפְלֵהוּ). Dodson identifies him as the son of Joram and father of Jotham, king of Judah from about 785 to 746 B.C.
caution: This is a proper name with only two New Testament occurrences, so the evidence base is thin even though its meaning is not in doubt.

definition: A country town — a market village larger than an ordinary village but having only the standing of one.
article: κωμόπολις combines the words for "village" (κώμη) and "city" (πόλις), naming a settlement somewhere between the two: a large village or country town that functions like a town but ranks as a village. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 1:38, where Jesus speaks of going to the surrounding settlements to preach. Interestingly, the Majority Standard Bible renders the word here as "neighboring" (100% of its single occurrence), focusing on the nearby location, while the older lexicons (Dodson, Abbott-Smith) emphasize the settlement's status as a "country town" rather than its proximity.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise sense rests on very thin evidence, and the measured rendering ("neighboring") differs in emphasis from the lexicons' "country town."

definition: To bring something about through effort, producing a result or accomplishing what one sets out to do.
article: This is the emphatic, "perfective" form of the ordinary verb for working (ἐργάζομαι), and the prefix lays stress on the finished result rather than the process. Across its 24 New Testament appearances it consistently means to produce, bring about, or accomplish something — whether good outcomes or evil deeds. The everyday papyri are especially vivid here: the word was the standard term for cultivating a plot of farmland, as in a contract requiring someone "to cultivate at his own expense 10 arourae of land." Notably, the Septuagint uses it only 10 times, each rendering a different Hebrew word, so it never settled on one fixed counterpart there.
caution: In nearly half its occurrences (11 of 24) the verb is folded into the surrounding phrasing without its own English word, so its force often comes through the whole clause rather than a single rendering.

definition: Bethphage, a village near Jerusalem on the Mount of Olives, mentioned in connection with Jesus' approach to the city.
article: Bethphage is a place name—a small village on the Mount of Olives, close to Jerusalem and near Bethany. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, always in the account of Jesus approaching Jerusalem (Matthew 21:1, Mark 11:1, Luke 19:29). The name comes from Aramaic meaning "house of unripe figs," a vivid detail preserved in the lexical evidence.
caution: This is a proper place name with only 3 occurrences, all in the same narrative episode, so its meaning is fixed and its only interest is the Aramaic sense behind the name.

definition: To cause someone to stumble morally or spiritually—to trip them up into sin, doubt, or abandoning their faith—or to take such offense oneself.
senseLabels: to be better off avoiding offense
article: σκανδαλίζω always works figuratively in the New Testament, picturing someone being tripped up—led into sin, doubt, or turning away from faith. It appears 30 times and stays close to one core idea, though translators render it many ways depending on whether someone causes the stumbling (active, as in Mark 9:43 and 1 Corinthians 8:13) or suffers it (passive, as in Matthew 11:6 and Mark 14:27). Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note scholars who argue the underlying picture is setting a trap or enticement rather than simply placing an obstacle, which fits the related noun σκάνδαλον meaning a snare.
caution: The exact emphasis—trap and enticement versus mere stumbling-block—is debated, and the word is barely attested in the Septuagint, so its background relies heavily on New Testament usage itself.

definition: To pour out something until it overflows and spills over the edges.
article: This verb describes pouring something out so abundantly that it overflows and runs over. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 6:38, where the Majority Standard Bible renders the image as something "pressed" down and running over. The word is rare elsewhere—Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and as a variant reading in Joel 2:24, while Grimm-Thayer say it is otherwise not found at all.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical text, so its range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Canaanite — a person from the ancient land of Canaan, an old biblical term for the inhabitants of that region.
article: This adjective identifies someone as a Canaanite, a native of the ancient land of Canaan. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, describing the woman who approached Jesus in Matthew 15:22, where the Majority Standard Bible and Berean Standard Bible both render it "Canaanite." Notably, Matthew uses this old biblical name where Mark's parallel account (7:26) calls the same woman a Greek (Ἑλληνίς), suggesting Matthew deliberately chose the more archaic, scriptural term. In the Septuagint the word appears 85 times, usually translating the Hebrew kena'ani.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the SBL critical text, so confidence rests largely on its abundant Septuagint usage.

definition: A condition of lacking what one needs; poverty or want.
article: ὑστέρησις names the state of falling short of basic needs—poverty or want. It appears just 2 times in the New Testament, and both Mark 12:44 and Philippians 4:11 set it against the idea of abundance (in Mark, opposite "what was left over"). The word is rare enough that Abbott-Smith notes it as largely ecclesiastical, with one attestation in Aquila's Greek version at Job 30:3.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and thin attestation elsewhere, confidence in the full range is low.

definition: A law, rule, or established standard—especially the body of commands God gave Israel through Moses.
article: νόμος covers any binding rule or standard, but in the New Testament it overwhelmingly means "law," rendered that way in 188 of 196 occurrences (100% of the times it gets its own English word). It most often points to the law of Moses, though writers also stretch it to mean law in general or even a controlling "force" impelling action (as in Romans 7). In the Septuagint it appears 245 times, usually translating the Hebrew תּוֹרָה (146×), the word for divine instruction or teaching, which shows how naturally it carried the sense of God-given direction.

definition: The official who led and supervised worship in a synagogue, sometimes one of several and sometimes an honorary title.
article: This word names the person in charge of a synagogue—an administrative officer who oversaw the worship services. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "synagogue leader" in 44% of its 9 occurrences, with another 22% adding context about the leader arriving (as in the story of Jairus in Mark 5:38 and Luke 8:49); the two "measured senses" really reflect the same office plus surrounding narrative wording. Interestingly, papyri and inscriptions show the term wasn't exclusively Jewish: one inscription uses it for a profane civic or guild official, and Dodson notes the title was sometimes merely honorary.
caution: The two measured senses describe the same office, the difference being narrative context rather than meaning, so treat "synagogue leader" as the core sense.

definition: A respectful title meaning "my master," used to address Jewish teachers and, in the Gospels, often Jesus.
article: Rabbi is a borrowed Hebrew/Aramaic title (from rab, "master," with a possessive ending meaning "my master") used to address Jewish teachers respectfully, and the Gospels apply it especially to Jesus and once to John. It appears 17 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the translation is consistently "Rabbi" — rendered that way in 50% of cases and as "Rabbi" within address phrases another 31%. Interestingly, the lexica note a closely related form, ῥαββουνεί ("Rabboni"), which shows up in Mark 10:51 and John 20:16 as a slightly different, possibly more emphatic version of the same title.

definition: A skilled worker who makes things by hand, such as a metalworker, builder, or artisan.
article: A τεχνίτης is a skilled tradesperson who makes things by hand, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it this way in all four occurrences, rendered "craftsmen" wherever it gets its own English word. The Septuagint mostly uses it to translate the Hebrew חָרָשׁ (5 of 7 times), the general word for an artisan or engraver. The most striking development is figurative: in Alexandrian Jewish writing (Wisdom 13:1) and once in Hebrews 11:10, the word is applied to God as the "builder" or designer of a city — a sense the everyday papyri, which speak of goldsmiths and ordinary workmen, never reach.
caution: Only four New Testament occurrences, and the elevated sense of God as "craftsman" appears in Hebrews and Wisdom but not in the measured Byzantine renderings here.

definition: Not ready or prepared, especially when something expected has not been gotten ready in advance.
article: This word describes being caught unprepared, the negative form of the verb meaning to get ready (παρασκευάζω). It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:4, where Paul worries about being found unprepared. The standard lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) all agree on the plain sense "unprepared," though the Majority Standard Bible renders the verse loosely with "otherwise."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical evidence.

definition: Having four corners or sides; square in shape.
article: τετράγωνος describes something square or four-cornered, built from the roots for "four" and "corner." It appears only once in the New Testament (Revelation 21:16), where it describes the layout of the heavenly city, and 10 times in the Septuagint, six of which translate forms of the Hebrew רָבַע (to be four-sided). It was an ordinary everyday Koine word: the papyri use it for a square cushion or coverlet, a four-sided temple colonnade, and even a small square silver altar, showing it was plain construction vocabulary rather than anything technical.
caution: It occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on broader Septuagint and papyri usage rather than internal evidence.

definition: A winged creature, that is, a bird.
article: πτηνόν is an adjective meaning "winged," but it is used as a noun to mean "bird." It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 15:39, where Paul contrasts the different kinds of flesh, including that of birds. Moulton-Milligan note that the plural τὰ πτηνά for "birds" shows up in everyday Koine, as in the Letter of Aristeas.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range cannot be measured beyond that single verse.

definition: To put something forward, such as pushing a person to the front or, of trees, sending out leaves.
article: προβάλλω literally means to throw or push something forward. In the New Testament it appears only twice: once of trees putting forth their leaves (Luke 21:30) and once of people pushing a man to the front of a crowd (Acts 19:33). Everyday Koine papyri show the same range — one document uses it for a man "putting himself forward" for an office, and another for someone being appointed to public service.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the measured evidence is thin, so the lexica's broader range rests mainly on the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: Anna, a woman's name borne by a prophetess who saw the infant Jesus in the temple.
article: Ἄννα is a personal name, the Greek form of the Hebrew name Channah (חַנָּה). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 2:36, naming the elderly prophetess who recognized the infant Jesus in the temple. In the Septuagint it occurs 8 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew חַנָּה (7×), though one occurrence stands in for עֵלִי (Eli) — likely a textual quirk rather than a real meaning.
caution: This is a proper name with thin attestation (one New Testament occurrence) rather than a word with a definable range of meaning.

definition: The name of an Athenian woman who became a believer after hearing Paul speak in Athens.
article: Damaris is a proper name appearing just once in the New Testament, at Acts 17:34, where she is listed among the Athenians who believed after Paul's address. The name is otherwise unknown, though Moulton-Milligan note it surfaces in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Abbott-Smith links it to the poetic word δάμαρ, meaning 'a wife.' Interestingly, the scholar Renan suggested the name might actually be a variant of Δάμαλις, since Δάμαρις is so rare elsewhere.
caution: This is a personal name occurring only once in the New Testament, and scholars are uncertain whether the form is original or a variant of another name.

definition: A person who robs by force or violence, such as a bandit, brigand, or outlaw operating outside the law.
article: λῃστής refers to someone who takes by force—a bandit or brigand—rather than a sneak thief. In the New Testament it appears 15 times, rendered as "robbers" in 8 of those cases (57%) and as "outlaw" in 3 more (21%), the latter often describing those arrested or crucified as criminals. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this real-world sense vividly: a third-century BC document is literally headed "concerning an attack of robbers," showing the word named genuine criminal threats of the day. Lexicons note it stands in contrast to κλέπτης, the ordinary thief.

definition: To live or settle somewhere as one's permanent home, or to inhabit a place.
article: κατοικέω means to settle down and live somewhere permanently, whether describing where people reside or, figuratively, a divine presence dwelling within. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 44 times, rendered mostly as "dwell" (54%) or "living" (41%), with the two meanings differing little in substance. It appears a remarkable 627 times in the Septuagint, where it nearly always translates the common Hebrew verb יָשַׁב ("to sit, dwell"), and everyday Koine papyri use it plainly for the house someone lives in—as in a rental document for "the house at which she lives."

definition: To blow gently, used of a soft or light wind.
article: ὑποπνέω describes a wind that blows softly or gently. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:13, where the Byzantine text treats it as part of a phrase rather than translating it as a standalone word. Abbott-Smith notes an older sense found in Aristotle, "to blow underneath," but the New Testament use is simply the gentle-breeze meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A wreath, garland, or crown given as a victory prize, festive ornament, or mark of honor, sometimes also a royal crown.
article: Στέφανος is the encircling wreath or crown—awarded to victors in public games, worn as a festal ornament, or given to honor distinguished people. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 18 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders every single one as "crown." Although classical sources often distinguish στέφανος (a victor's wreath) from διάδημα (a royal crown), Moulton-Milligan warns this distinction shouldn't be pressed too hard, since στέφανος is not infrequently used for a king's crown too. In the Septuagint it appears 30 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew עֲטָרָה (23 times).
caution: Sources disagree on how sharply στέφανος (victory wreath) should be distinguished from διάδημα (royal crown); the boundary is not firm.

definition: To be encouraged or comforted together with others, sharing in mutual strengthening.
article: This word combines "with" (σύν) and "to encourage or comfort" (παρακαλέω), and it points to encouragement that flows in both directions between people. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Romans 1:12, where Paul describes being mutually encouraged together with his readers through their shared faith. Notably, it is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, and classical use (Plato) carries the more active sense of calling upon or exhorting together, while the New Testament occurrence is passive — being strengthened among one another.
caution: This is a single Byzantine occurrence absent from the critical text, so the evidence is very thin.

definition: To vote or count someone in, formally adding them to a group so they share a place among its members.
article: This verb describes formally adding someone to a group by vote or reckoning, so they are numbered together with the rest. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:26, where the lot adds Matthias to the eleven apostles, and the Majority and Berean Standard texts both render it that way 100% of the time. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note the word is barely attested elsewhere, but a similar compound form for 'numbered along with' shows up in an everyday papyrus document from around 27/26 B.C.; Abbott-Smith adds that Plutarch used a related sense meaning 'to condemn together.'
caution: This is a single-occurrence word with thin attestation, so its precise range is hard to pin down and the secondary 'condemn together' sense rests on one classical citation.

definition: A preposition meaning "for" or "on behalf of" someone, and also "above" or "beyond" when expressing measure.
article: At its core ὑπέρ means "for" or "on behalf of"—it shows who or what an action benefits, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it this way overwhelmingly, with "for" alone covering 82 of 159 occurrences (75%). The classical lexica note that its root sense is spatial, "over" or "above," and with the accusative it can mean "more than" or "beyond," though that physical sense barely surfaces in the measured New Testament data. Notably, in about 50 of the 159 cases it gets absorbed into English phrasing without its own word, and many of the small "senses" the digest lists ("I," "is") are just neighboring words swept into the count rather than separate meanings. In the Septuagint it renders a handful of different Hebrew words, most often טוֹב (good, 14×), reflecting how flexibly translators stretched it.
caution: Several of the measured "senses" ("I," "is," "I for") are artifacts of how surrounding words were counted, not genuine distinct meanings of the preposition.

definition: To kill someone by throwing stones at them.
article: καταλιθάζω means to stone someone to death—the prefix κατά intensifies the basic verb λιθάζω ("to stone"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 20:6, where the crowd is described as ready to stone anyone who denies that John's baptism was from heaven. Abbott-Smith notes it is the Koine equivalent of the classical καταλιθόω, and points to related stoning verbs in the Septuagint such as those at Exodus 17:4 and Numbers 14:10.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured from broader usage.

definition: A person's settled character, habits, or moral conduct—the customary ways of behaving that define someone.
article: ἦθος refers to a person's established character or customary way of behaving—the moral habits that make someone who they are. It's rare in the New Testament, appearing only twice in the Byzantine text (just once in the critical SBLGNT), and the famous instance is a quoted line believed to come from the playwright Menander: 'bad company corrupts good morals' (1 Corinthians 15:33). Everyday Koine papyri use it warmly of a person's true, noble character, as in one second-century letter praising someone's 'genuine, philosophical character.'
caution: Evidence is very thin—only two occurrences, one of them a borrowed quotation—so the word's full range in the New Testament cannot be firmly mapped.

definition: To sail across or through a stretch of open water from one place to another.
article: This verb describes sailing across a body of water, built from "through" (διά) and "sail" (πλέω). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, where it's absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word. Moulton-Milligan note a vivid detail from Acts 27:5: the verb "probably implies that at this point a favourable shift of wind" let the ship run straight across open sea (πέλαγος) instead of hugging the coast, and the same pairing with πέλαγος turns up in a third- or fourth-century inscription. Classical sources also record a figurative use, "to sail through life," though that sense does not appear in the biblical evidence.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured biblical range is too thin to confirm anything beyond its single literal use.

definition: Genuine and true, like a legitimate child born within marriage, hence authentic, real, and sincere.
article: γνήσιος describes something authentic and real, often applied to people who are true partners or genuine children in the faith. The New Testament uses it 4 times: three describe a "true" companion or child (Philippians 4:3, 1 Timothy 1:2, Titus 1:4), while in 2 Corinthians 8:8 the noun form means "sincerity." Its literal root sense is "born in wedlock" — the papyri preserve this, with the oldest dated Greek papyrus (311 BC) using it in a marriage contract for a "lawful wedded wife."
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the measured range is narrow, though the corpus renderings and the lexica agree closely.

definition: Describing the more inward or interior part of something, such as a deeper room or the space behind a barrier.
article: ἐσώτερος is the comparative form of ἔσω ("within"), meaning the inner or more interior part of something. In the New Testament it appears only twice, and both times it clearly means "inner" — the inner prison cell in Acts 16:24 and the area behind the temple curtain in Hebrews 6:19. The Septuagint uses it far more often (35 times), mostly to translate the Hebrew word for "inner" (פְּנִימִי, 22 times), and it even renders the word for the temple veil itself a few times.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured range is narrow, though the larger Septuagint sample and the lexicons agree on the meaning.

definition: To breathe out one's last breath, that is, to die.
article: This verb literally means "to breathe out," and in the New Testament it always describes the moment of death — to draw one's final breath. It appears only 3 times across 2 books, always in the Gospel accounts of Jesus' death (Mark 15:37, 39; Luke 23:46). Classical writers like Aeschylus spelled out what was being breathed out, adding words for "life" or "soul," but the New Testament uses the verb on its own to simply mean "expire."
caution: This word occurs only 3 times, all in the same death scene, so its range in the New Testament is very narrow.

definition: Egyptian — a person from Egypt, or the language and writing of Egypt.
article: Αἰγύπτιος simply means "Egyptian," describing either people who come from Egypt or, when paired with words for speech and writing, the Egyptian language itself. It appears 5 times in the New Testament, with 4 of those (80%) describing Egyptian people and 1 referring to Egyptian learning (Acts 7:22, where Moses is trained in it). The everyday papyri make this nicely concrete: in one second-century BC letter a mother congratulates her son for learning "Αἰγύπτια γράμματα," the demotic Egyptian script, the same kind of phrasing behind the "educated Egyptian" sense.

definition: Summer, the warm season of the year.
article: θέρος means summer, the warm part of the year. All three New Testament uses come in Jesus' parable of the fig tree, where tender branches and sprouting leaves signal that summer is near (Matthew 24:32, Mark 13:28, Luke 21:30). The word ties back to a root meaning 'to heat,' and in the Septuagint it usually renders the Hebrew קַיִץ; one interesting detail is that in everyday papyri θέρος could also mean the harvest or crop produced in that season.
caution: The New Testament evidence is thin—only three occurrences, all in the same parable—so the measured sense range is narrow.

definition: A person who shares citizenship with another, belonging to the same community or city.
article: συμπολίτης means a fellow citizen — someone who belongs to the same city or community as you. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 2:19, where believers are called fellow citizens of the saints, set in contrast to strangers and foreigners. The everyday papyri confirm the plain civic sense: documents from the second and third centuries A.D. use it for ordinary townspeople, as when 'our fellow-citizens have approached us in a petition.' Interestingly, the strict Atticist grammarians condemned the word as substandard, yet it was clearly common in real Koine usage.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured evidence is thin, though papyri usage points firmly to the same meaning.

definition: To cover something completely, especially to veil one's head or cover oneself.
article: κατακαλύπτω means to cover something fully, and in the New Testament it specifically describes veiling or covering the head. All 3 of its Byzantine occurrences are clustered in one passage (1 Corinthians 11:6-7), where it appears in the middle voice for covering or veiling oneself. In the Greek Old Testament it shows up 24 times, most often translating the Hebrew כָּסָה ("to cover," 13×), and an inscription from around 420 BC uses it to describe carrying a corpse "covered" in silence to the tomb.
caution: The flagged confidence is low: this word appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament (all in one passage) and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text.

definition: Something thrown around the body as a wrapping — a mantle, cloak, or covering.
article: περιβόλαιον is built from a verb meaning "to throw around," and it names whatever you drape over yourself — a mantle, cloak, or general covering. The Septuagint uses it 11 times, mostly for the Hebrew kĕsût ("covering"), and it shows up in Hebrews 1:12 picturing the heavens rolled up like a garment. In 1 Corinthians 11:15 it describes a woman's hair, and lexicographers split over whether it means a covering generally or specifically a "veil" — Moulton-Milligan favor the broader "clothing" sense, citing the everyday Greek of Aristeas 158.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and disagreement among sources over whether 1 Corinthians 11:15 means a general covering or a specific veil, the precise range is uncertain.

definition: To pour something onto or over a person or object, such as liquid applied to a wound.
article: This verb simply means to pour something over or onto something — the basic image is liquid spilling onto a surface. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:34, where the Good Samaritan pours oil and wine onto the injured man's wounds. The Septuagint uses it 21 times, most often (16×) for the Hebrew יָצַק, as when Jacob pours oil on the stone at Bethel (Genesis 28:18); everyday Koine papyri also use it concretely, including a warning not to keep pouring when a vessel is already full.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured New Testament range rests on a single verse.

definition: The greatness or majesty of God, used to describe his exalted divine grandeur.
article: μεγαλωσύνη means greatness or majesty, and in the New Testament it always points to God's divine grandeur — twice it stands plainly for "Majesty" (Hebrews 1:3 and 8:1), and once in Jude 25 it appears alongside terms for dominion. Built on μέγας ("great"), it shows up only 3 times in the New Testament but 14 times in the Septuagint, where it usually translates Hebrew words for greatness such as גְּדֻלָּה. A neat detail: it also turns up in everyday Koine documents, including the Letter of Aristeas, which speaks of "the greatness of His might," confirming this was real working vocabulary, not just a religious coinage.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 NT occurrences) and the rendering of Jude 25 is unsettled, so confidence is low.

definition: The outward form, appearance, or fashion that something or someone presents to the world.
article: σχῆμα refers to the external shape, appearance, or fashion that someone or something presents—its outward bearing rather than its inner essence. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 7:31 and Philippians 2:8), and in both the Byzantine text it is woven into the phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word; the KJV translates it "fashion." Greek writers used it to mark outward bearing in everyday documents, and the papyri attest expressions like "Egyptian fashion" (Αἰγυπτιακῷ σχήματι), highlighting visible style or manner. Lexicons note it contrasts with μορφή, which points to what is essential and permanent.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 2 New Testament uses and a single Septuagint occurrence—so confidence in its full range is low.

definition: A dangerous area of shifting sandbanks or shoals off the North African coast, feared by ancient sailors.
article: Σύρτις names the treacherous shallow sandbanks along the Libyan coast that sailors dreaded running aground on. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:17, where the crew fears being driven onto these shoals during a storm. The classical lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) identify it specifically as the Syrtis sandbanks off North Africa, and the word derives from σύρω, "to drag," reflecting sand dragged by the waves.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "hoisting" reflects a translation choice in the verse rather than the word's own meaning, which the lexicons agree is a sandbank.

definition: A group of people reclining together to share a meal, like guests gathered for a banquet.
article: At its root συμπόσιον means a drinking-party or banquet, and by extension the room where such a feast was held. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Mark 6:39, where Jesus has the crowd sit down in groups to be fed—so the word there points to clusters of dining guests rather than a literal party. Everyday Koine papyri confirm both senses: one document mentions paying rent for a small dining-room (συμπόσιον), showing how naturally the term shifted from the gathering to the place itself.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the measured senses listed oddly (splitting "Jesus" and "sit groups"), the data here is thin and confidence is low.

definition: To pay back in full what is owed, whether a debt, fine, or compensation.
article: This verb is a financial and legal term meaning to pay off or repay something owed, often a debt, fine, or compensation. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Philemon 1:19, where Paul promises to repay whatever Onesimus owes. In the Septuagint it shows up 29 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for repaying or making restitution (שָׁלַם, 25×), and the papyri use it constantly in contracts for paying penalties, frequently with an added "half as much again" surcharge.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the digest's measured rendering "mention" conflicts with the consistent "repay/pay in full" meaning shown by the glosses, Septuagint, and papyri.

definition: To call out to someone—whether to summon them, invite them to a meal or event, or give them a name.
senseLabels: invited to a meal or event
article: καλέω covers the everyday act of calling someone—summoning them, inviting them as a guest, or attaching a name to them. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 146 times, most often rendered "called" (86×), with "call" (17×) and "invited" (11×) filling out the range; about 32 times it simply blends into the phrasing without a separate English word. The everyday flavor is striking in the papyri: a fourth-century invitation from Oxyrhynchus reads "Theon, son of Origenes, invites you to the wedding of his sister tomorrow," using καλέω exactly as Matthew 22 does. In the Septuagint it almost always (372 of 420 times) translates the Hebrew קָרָא, "to call."

definition: To grasp something with the mind — to understand, perceive, or think carefully about it.
article: This verb, built from the noun νοῦς ("mind"), means to use your mind to perceive or comprehend something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 14 times across 8 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "understand" in 7 of those (64%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing 100% on that sense. A nice everyday detail from the papyri: the phrase "νοῶν καὶ φρονῶν" ("of sound mind and sober thought") was a stock formula in wills from Ptolemaic and Roman times, where a person certified they were sane when making the document.
caution: The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, KJV, Dodson) list a broader range including "think, consider, perceive," so the single measured sense of "understand" is narrower than the word's full attested usage.
