definition: To be like or resemble something or someone in appearance or character.
article: ὁμοιάζω means simply 'to be like' or 'to resemble,' built from the adjective ὅμοιος ('like, similar'). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Mark 14:70, where bystanders tell Peter his speech marks him as a Galilean. Abbott-Smith notes the word is essentially confined to the New Testament and shows up in only some manuscript traditions of Matthew 23:27 and 26:73, while a related compound παρομοιάζω carries the same idea.
caution: This word occurs just once and the evidence is thin, with the measured rendering 'more too speech' reflecting noisy data rather than a clear sense.

definition: To assert or claim something is true, often when the claim is doubtful or being challenged.
article: φάsko means to assert, allege, or profess that something is the case. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 2 books, and in 2 of those instances the Majority Standard Bible folds it into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it a separate English word. The everyday papyri are especially telling: φάσκω regularly introduces a claim being made in legal or disputed contexts—someone "asserting" weapons were in a place, or "professing" to be a creditor—which fits its New Testament use where people make assertions that are open to question.
caution: The evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences with just one rendered by a distinct English word—so the measured picture rests heavily on the papyri and lexica.

definition: Oil pressed from olives, used in cooking, lamps, anointing, and healing in the ancient world.
article: ἔλαιον means olive oil, the everyday product used for lamps, cooking, healing wounds, and anointing guests at feasts. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "oil" in 8 of 11 occurrences (73%), and the meaning is consistent across all its uses. In the Septuagint it appears 191 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word shemen (148×) and also yitshar (21×); everyday Koine papyri confirm the ordinary commercial sense, as in a 154 BC letter requesting a half-measure of oil be sent.

definition: An emphatic relative pronoun meaning "the very one who" or "who indeed," pointing back to a specific antecedent with added emphasis.
article: This is an emphasized form of the ordinary relative pronoun ὅς ("who, which"), built by attaching the particle -περ to sharpen the reference to "the very one who." It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Mark 15:6, in the phrase about the prisoner Pilate would release), and even there the critical text omits it. Though rare in the New Testament, Moulton-Milligan shows it was common in everyday Koine papyri, as in a deed noting "where he also had his domicile."
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is extremely thin: it occurs just once in the Byzantine text, is absent from the critical text, and even that single reading is a disputed textual variant.

definition: To wipe something off or dry, usually by rubbing it with the hands, hair, or a cloth.
article: ἐκμάσσω means to wipe something dry or clean, typically by rubbing. All five New Testament uses describe wiping with hair or a cloth—most memorably the women who wash Jesus' feet and wipe them with their hair (Luke 7:38, 44; John 11:2; 12:3). Strong's traces it from a root meaning "to knead out," and an everyday Koine inscription quoted by Moulton-Milligan uses it of a sculpted image, with Herodas rendering it "wipe dry."
caution: The single rendering "whose wipe" simply reflects an awkward relative-clause phrasing in one verse, not a distinct meaning.

definition: A means of gain or a way of making money or earning a living.
article: πορισμός means a source of profit or livelihood — a way of getting money. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Timothy 6:5-6, where the Berean Standard Bible renders both with "gain"; the second occurrence is grouped here as "course gain" because the surrounding phrase shapes the translation. Lexicons add a slightly broader first sense, "a providing" or "furnishing," and the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and the Septuagint (Wisdom 13:19; 14:2), where Moulton-Milligan note the related noun πόρος used the same way for someone's financial means.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same passage, so the measured "gain" versus "course gain" split reflects one verse each rather than a clear range.

definition: To buy back or ransom someone, like freeing a slave; figuratively, to make the most of available time.
article: This compound verb combines "out of" with "to buy," and in the New Testament it carries two related ideas. In Galatians it means to redeem or ransom—buying someone out of slavery—appearing in 3 of its 4 occurrences (75%), while in Ephesians and Colossians the middle voice means to buy up or make the most of the time. The Septuagint connection is striking: the word's single appearance there (Daniel 2:8) translates an Aramaic term and refers to gaining time, which lines up with the "act wisely" sense in Colossians 4:5.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and two distinct measured senses, the line between "ransom" and "make the most of time" depends on context, and some scholars read even the time-related passages as "buying back."

definition: To put something off to a later time, especially to postpone a legal hearing or decision.
article: This word literally means to "cast up" or "put off," and in legal settings it means to defer or adjourn a case. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 24:22, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "decide" — though the underlying sense is that Felix postponed the matter. The everyday papyri confirm this forensic use: a document from 112 BC uses it of referring a matter to an inspector, while elsewhere it can mean to cast something up or even set up a weaver's warp.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and just four in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, and the standard "defer/postpone" sense sits awkwardly against the measured rendering "decide."

definition: A written message or letter sent from one person to another.
article: ἐπιστολή means a letter—a written communication carried or dispatched from one party to another. The meaning is remarkably stable: in 22 of 24 New Testament occurrences (92%) it is simply rendered "letter," and the Septuagint uses it 24 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for a letter or dispatch (אִגֶּרֶת, 10×). It was an ordinary, everyday word in Koine: the papyri show official copies headed "copy of a letter" (ἀντίγραφον ἐπιστολῆς), confirming its plain administrative use, and lexicons also note specialized phrases like "letters of recommendation" (2 Cor 3:1).

definition: A sword or large knife—a bladed weapon used for fighting, killing, or, by extension, for war and violence.
article: μάχαιρα is the standard New Testament word for a sword, rendered exactly that way in 26 of its 29 occurrences (90%). Originally it could mean a large knife or dagger, distinct from the broader ῥομφαία or the thrusting ξίφος, and the Septuagint uses it 180 times, mostly for the Hebrew חֶרֶב. The everyday reality of the word shows up in the papyri: one Ptolemaic document from 157 BC describes a man who 'drew his sword and gashed my leg.' It can also be used figuratively for conflict, as in Matthew 10:34 where it stands opposite peace.

definition: Describing a young woman who is past the bloom of youth, beyond the prime age for marriage.
article: This rare word combines "over/beyond" with the idea of an "acme" or peak, describing a daughter who is past her prime marrying age. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 7:36, where the Majority Standard Bible's rendering folds it into the phrasing rather than translating it directly. Moulton-Milligan notes that everyday Koine papyri use related age-words like ὑπερετής for someone "aged over 60" and ὑπεργήρως for "exceedingly old," showing this family of words commonly marked people as past a certain age.
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with very thin evidence, and the lexicons agree only on a general sense while the precise meaning in 1 Corinthians 7:36 is disputed.

definition: To show or display something to others, sometimes to point out or prove a point.
article: This verb means to show or exhibit something to someone, whether physically presenting an object or demonstrating an idea. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "show" in 6 of those (75%), with the BSB agreeing 100% of the time. The everyday flavor of the word shows up nicely in the papyri: one document (P Fay 20) uses it for "making a much more conspicuous display of my magnanimity," capturing the sense of putting something on show.
caution: Lexicons note a secondary sense of "point out" or "prove" (e.g. Hebrews 6:17, Acts 18:28), but the measured data only registers a single "show" sense.

definition: Belonging to or coming from the city of Alexandria in Egypt.
article: This adjective simply means "Alexandrian" — relating to the great Egyptian port city of Alexandria. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Acts (27:6 and 28:11), and in both cases it describes a ship from Alexandria that carried Paul on his voyage toward Rome. The two "senses" measured here are really the same meaning: both rendering point to a ship of Alexandrian origin, so this is one consistent usage rather than a broad range.
caution: Confidence is low simply because the word occurs only twice, both describing the same kind of ship, so its range cannot be tested further.

definition: A trumpet, used in warfare and religious ceremonies, or the sound it makes.
article: A σάλπιγξ is a trumpet, and the word is remarkably consistent: all 11 New Testament occurrences are rendered "trumpet," with the Berean and Majority Standard translations agreeing 100%. The instrument shows up both in war and in religious settings, and the word can also stand for the trumpet's blast by extension, as in Matthew 24:31 ("a great trumpet") and 1 Corinthians 15:52 ("the last trumpet"). In the Septuagint it appears 78 times, most often translating the Hebrew shofar, the ram's-horn trumpet of Israel's worship and signaling.

definition: A made-up story or fable presented as if true, contrasted with reliable teaching.
article: In the New Testament μῦθος always means a fable or invented tale—the kind of fanciful story set against trustworthy teaching. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "myths" in every one of its 5 occurrences (one absorbed into surrounding phrasing), and the word appears only in the Pastoral letters and 2 Peter. The classical lexica note an older, broader range: Abbott-Smith lists earlier senses like "speech, conversation" and simply "a story or narrative" (Homer), and the papyri confirm this primary sense of "word, story" alongside the later "fable" meaning that dominates the NT.
caution: The word occurs only 5 times, all in a narrow set of books, so the measured "myth" sense reflects a small sample even though the lexica agree.

definition: It is advantageous or profitable; it serves one's purpose better than the alternative.
article: This impersonal verb means something is profitable or advantageous, and in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 17:2) the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render it 100% as "better than." The word's range is broader than that one verse suggests: Abbott-Smith notes a literal sense of paying expenses or indemnifying, fitting its build from λύσις and τέλος (loosely "settling the accounts"). Everyday Koine papyri confirm the impersonal usage—one third-century BC document reads "so it is more profitable to rent than to seek fodder," exactly the cost-benefit weighing the New Testament verse captures.
caution: Evidence is thin: the word appears just once in the New Testament and only a handful of times in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To shut someone or something out, keeping them excluded, cut off, or isolated from access or participation.
senseLabels: excluded as a matter of principle
article: This compound of ἐκ ("out") and κλείω ("to shut") literally means to shut out, and it covers both the abstract sense of ruling something out on principle (Rom 3:27, where boasting is "excluded") and the relational sense of cutting people off or isolating them (Gal 4:17). It appears only twice in the New Testament, split evenly between these two uses. An interesting witness comes from the everyday Koine documents: an early inscription (4th century BC) uses the verb for stripping citizens of their weapons and shutting them out of the city, showing its concrete "barred from access" force.
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a computed low-confidence tier, the full range of this word rests on thin evidence.

definition: To take a share of something, especially food, or to receive or obtain something for oneself.
article: μεταλαμβάνω means to get or have a share of something, most often used of partaking of food. With the genitive it means 'partake of' (as in Acts 2:46, where people shared their food), while with the accusative it shifts to 'obtain' or 'find' something, such as a time or opportunity (Acts 24:25). The everyday papyri confirm this range nicely: one document uses it of eating food, while another describes a man who 'succeeded to' an official post — showing the same verb covering both sharing in and acquiring something.
caution: It appears only 5 times in the Byzantine text and is rendered with its own English word just once, so its measured range rests on thin data.

definition: A connecting word meaning "yet," "nevertheless," or "even," signaling a contrast or exception to what was just said.
article: This little connecting word adds a sense of "yet" or "nevertheless," marking something that holds true despite what came before. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only 3 times across 3 books, and is well attested in everyday Koine papyri, where it often pairs with ἀλλ' to mean "but nevertheless" (as in John 12:42). Grammarians note that in two of its three NT uses (1 Corinthians 14:7 and Galatians 3:15) the word sits out of its expected position, which is why translations like "even" can feel awkward.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and an unusual word order in two of them, the precise force of ὅμως in some passages is debated among grammarians.

definition: To stay in a place for a while, spending time there.
article: In the New Testament, διατρίβω means to spend time or stay somewhere — to linger in a place rather than pass straight through. The Byzantine text uses it 10 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "spent" in 38% of cases, often as part of phrases like "spent time" or "spent some time," while twice it gets absorbed into the surrounding wording without an English word of its own. The everyday flavor of the word is confirmed by the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan shows it commonly meaning "live" or "sojourn" — for instance a complaint about people residing in a foreign city. The literal root sense is "to rub through" or "wear away," which Strong's links to the idea of wearing through time.
caution: With only 10 occurrences and most renderings clustered in loose time-phrases, the precise nuance in any single verse can be hard to pin down.

definition: A place to stay, whether a public lodging-place or a private guest room set aside for visitors.
article: κατάλυμα refers to a place where travelers could stay—sometimes a public inn or lodging-place, sometimes a private guest room offered to visitors. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, rendered "room" twice (the famous "no room" of Luke 2:7 and Mark 14:14) and "guest room" once in Luke 22:11. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri: one second-century BC document uses it for the lodging-place provided for residents of Arsinoë at the Serapeum.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 NT uses) and the lexica split on whether "inn" or "guest room" fits best in a given passage.

definition: Something to be grasped at, seized, or clung to — whether the act of seizing or the prize itself.
article: This rare word appears only once in the New Testament (Philippians 2:6), where modern translations render it in the phrase about Christ not regarding equality with God as something to cling to. It comes from the verb ἁρπάζω, "to seize," and the lexicons split on whether it means the active act of seizing ("robbery," as the KJV had it) or, passively, a thing seized — a prize or catch. Moulton-Milligan find it in an everyday astrological text where a marriage is described as a "great catch" or something gained by force, hinting at the "prize" sense most modern expositors prefer.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the lexicons openly disagree on whether it means "the act of seizing" or "a thing seized," so its precise force is genuinely uncertain.

definition: A member of a group called the Nicolaitans, mentioned in Revelation as people whose practices Christ opposed.
article: Νικολαΐτης names a specific group, the Nicolaitans, and appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Revelation (2:6 and 2:15), where their works or teaching are condemned. The name is built from the personal name Νικόλαος, and the lexicons identify these people as adherents of a Nicolaus, possibly described as a heretic at Ephesus. Beyond that, the text itself tells us nothing about who they were or what they believed; Moulton-Milligan simply cross-references the underlying name.
caution: This word is a proper-group name appearing only twice, and the connection to a particular Nicolaus is described as merely possible, so the identity of the group is genuinely uncertain.

definition: The plural form of "this," meaning "to, for, in, with, or by these" persons or things just mentioned.
article: τούτοις is simply a grammatical form of the common demonstrative pronoun οὗτος ("this"), specifically the dative plural — so it means "to/for/with/by these" people or things. As a demonstrative it points to something near at hand or already mentioned, much like English "this" and "these" (the lexicon compares it to Latin hic versus ille). In the Septuagint οὗτος most often translates the Hebrew demonstratives זֶה and זֹאת ("this").
caution: This particular dative-plural form has no measured occurrences or sense data in the digest, so the entry rests entirely on the general meaning of the parent word οὗτος.

definition: A preposition meaning located across from, in front of, or in someone's presence; sometimes against.
article: ἀπέναντι is a preposition (taking the genitive) that points to position: something standing across from, directly in front of, or in the presence of someone or something. Its range stretches from the physical "opposite" (as when two disciples sit facing a tomb in Matthew 27:61) to the figurative "in the presence of" and even "against" (Acts 17:7). It is common in everyday Koine — Moulton-Milligan cites a 126 B.C. papyrus using it for "opposite his door" — and it appears 79 times in the Septuagint, most often rendering the Hebrew word נֶ֫גֶד ("in front of").
caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences spread thinly across distinct uses, individual sense boundaries rest on very little data.

definition: To undergo or experience something, almost always painful—to suffer or endure hardship, pain, or mistreatment.
article: In the New Testament πάσχω overwhelmingly means to suffer or endure pain and hardship, appearing 42 times and rendered "suffered" or "suffer" in 93% of cases. Strictly the verb just means to be acted upon or to experience something—either good or bad—but in practice it nearly always points to misfortune, which is why it works without any qualifying word at all. The everyday Koine papyri show this neutral root sense vividly: "ἐάν τι πάσχω" ("if anything happens to me") was a common polite way of referring to one's own death in wills and contracts.
caution: The neutral "be acted upon" sense documented by the lexicons and papyri barely surfaces in the measured NT data, where nearly every use carries the painful meaning.

definition: To affirm something firmly and confidently, insisting on it despite doubt or contradiction.
article: This verb means to declare something with strong conviction, standing firm on your claim. It appears only twice in the New Testament: once when a man at Peter's denial insists that Peter was with Jesus (Luke 22:59), and once when servants keep insisting Peter is at the door (Acts 12:15). Built from 'through' (διά) and 'strong' (ἰσχυρός), it literally carries the idea of forcing something through by strength; Abbott-Smith notes an older sense 'to lean upon' alongside the confident-affirmation sense, though only the latter shows up in the New Testament examples.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the rendering driven by context, the precise force is thinly attested.

definition: A person who owes something—literally a debtor, or figuratively someone bound by an obligation or moral duty.
article: This word comes from the verb "to owe" (G3784) and ranges from a literal financial debtor to anyone under an obligation or duty. In the Byzantine New Testament's 7 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible most often renders it as being "obligated" (3×, 50%), with "debtors" twice (33%) and "obligation" once. A striking witness is a Christian amulet from around the sixth century A.D. that preserves the Lord's Prayer petition asking God to forgive us as we forgive "our debtors," showing how naturally this everyday word carried both monetary and spiritual weight.
caution: Several lexicons note a figurative sense of "sinner" against God (an Aramaism, e.g. Luke 13:4), but that sense does not appear in the measured Byzantine renderings here.

definition: To take hold of something, or to receive what comes to you, whether physically grasping it or getting it from another.
article: λαμβάνω is one of the most common verbs in the New Testament, appearing 263 times, and it covers a broad range from physically grabbing an object to passively receiving something offered. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "receive" about half the time (100×) and "took" or "take" about 41% (78×), with smaller groups for "accept" (8×) and counting "one" of a set (5×); notably, in 71 of those 263 cases it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing without its own English word. In the Septuagint it appears over 1,100 times, mostly translating Hebrew לָקַח ("take," 823×), and the everyday papyri confirm its plain commercial sense — letters say things like "I received your letter" and "the money which you received."

definition: A large mass of solid, living rock, such as bedrock, a cliff, or a hollow rocky cave.
article: πέτρα refers to a solid mass of rock fixed in place—bedrock, a cliff face, or even a hollow rock forming a cave—as opposed to a loose stone or boulder. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "rock" in 14 of 16 New Testament occurrences (88%), with a few cases pointing to "rocky" or "rocky ground." In the Septuagint it appears 94 times, mainly translating the Hebrew words סֶלַע (selaʿ) and צוּר (tsur), both meaning crag or rock. An interesting wrinkle from the papyri: in everyday documents πέτρα sometimes means "rocky ground," as in a note about garlic planted on the rock—much like the related word used for the rocky soil in Jesus's parable.
caution: Lexicographers distinguish πέτρα (bedrock) from πέτρος (a detached stone), but the evidence notes that in a few places (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8) the words overlap.

definition: The act of explaining or interpreting something, such as unlocking the meaning of a prophecy.
article: This noun describes the unraveling or solving of something — an explanation or interpretation. It appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:20, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it in a phrase about prophecy not being a matter of one's own interpretation. The everyday papyri are striking here: the word commonly meant the 'discharge' or settling of an account, while Abbott-Smith also lists a basic sense of 'release.'
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise meaning there rests on slim evidence and is debated.

definition: To live in an undisciplined, irresponsible way, neglecting your duties or proper conduct.
senseLabels: to behave in an undisciplined way
article: ἀτακτέω originally described soldiers who broke ranks or marched out of formation, and from there came to mean acting irregularly, neglecting one's duty, or being idle. The New Testament uses it just once, in 2 Thessalonians 3:7, where it is rendered "were undisciplined." The everyday Koine papyri preserve the word's earthier flavor: Moulton-Milligan cite inscriptions about rebellious peoples and ships' captains shirking orders, and even of an apprentice playing truant from work.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there leans heavily on outside evidence rather than internal usage.

definition: A stirring up or disturbance, whether physically (like agitated water) or socially (an uproar or riot).
article: ταραχή refers to something being stirred up or thrown into commotion, ranging from physically troubled water to social unrest. It comes from the verb ταράσσω ("to disturb"), and in the Septuagint it appears 16 times across 10 books, translating Hebrew words for terror, trembling, and strife. In everyday Koine papyri the word leans toward the political sense: a letter of the Emperor Claudius (A.D. 41) uses it for the "riot" against the Jews in Alexandria, pairing it with words for feud and even war.
caution: Confidence is low: the word appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a distinct word, and it is absent from the SBL critical text.

definition: The number fourteen.
article: δεκατέσσαρες simply means the number "fourteen," built from the words for "ten" (δέκα) and "four" (τέσσαρες). It appears 5 times in the New Testament, and every translation renders it the same way—the variations like "fourteen ago" (2 Corinthians 12:2) and "fourteen later" (Galatians 2:1) just reflect counting years in context. Abbott-Smith notes it is the later Greek form, more common than the older τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα, and Moulton-Milligan shows it counting everyday goods like measures of grain in the papyri.

definition: Ceremonial defilement or contamination, especially the kind that makes food unclean and unfit for use.
article: ἀλίσγεμα refers to ceremonial pollution or contamination, and the evidence points specifically toward defiled food. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 15:20, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "polluted" (100%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing fully. Abbott-Smith notes it comes from the late verb ἀλισγέω, "to pollute," and Dodson suggests it can mean "a polluted thing," especially of food.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the SBL critical text, so its precise range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To sit down or recline, especially settling onto the ground or at a table for a meal.
senseLabels: sat down to eat or rest
article: In the New Testament ἀναπίπτω means to sit down or recline, whether on the ground or at a meal, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sat down" in 40% of its 11 occurrences. Originally the word meant "to fall back," but later Koine writers used it for reclining to eat — the everyday papyri confirm this, including a 160 BC document that uses it for lying down on straw. The Septuagint uses it just once, translating a Hebrew word in Genesis 49:9 where a lion "crouched down" to rest.
caution: The shift from the classical "fall back" sense to the later "recline at a meal" sense means context, not the word alone, settles the exact posture meant.

definition: An official decree or ordinance issued by an authority, whether a ruler, the Jewish law, or the apostles.
article: δόγμα refers to a binding decision handed down by some recognized authority — a Roman ruler's edict (Luke 2:1), the regulations of the Jewish law (Eph 2:15; Col 2:14), or the rulings of the apostles (Acts 16:4). The Majority Standard Bible renders it "decree" or with phrases built around "decrees" in all 5 New Testament occurrences, so the range is narrow and consistent. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that in inscriptions δόγμα was the special term for a decree of the Roman Senate, carrying the sense of an order from a distant, unquestionable authority — and it could also label the settled teachings of philosophers.
caution: The MSB phrase-renderings split a single underlying sense into several labels, so the four measured "senses" really reflect one core meaning of an authoritative decree.

definition: Refers to every individual member of a group considered one by one, rather than the group as a whole.
article: ἕκαστος picks out every individual in a group, viewing them separately rather than as a collective whole. The range is narrow and stable: across 83 New Testament occurrences it is rendered "each" (64%), "each one" (22%), or simply "one" (7%), with all sources in close agreement. In the Septuagint it appears 270 times, most often translating the Hebrew word אִישׁ ("man," 146×), since "each" and "every man" overlap; and everyday papyri use it in stock phrases like "each day" — the same expression found in Hebrews 3:13.

definition: A title for God meaning "the one who is, and who was, and who is coming" — the eternal one spanning all time.
article: This isn't a single word but a fixed phrase used as a divine title, stitching together "the one being" (present participle of εἰμί), "the one who was" (its imperfect), and "the one coming" (present participle of ἔρχομαι). Strong's frames it as a name for the Eternal, applied as an epithet of Christ. The construction is striking because it freezes verb forms into noun-like titles, treating God's existence across past, present, and future as a name rather than a description.
caution: There are no measured occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament corpus, and the lexical evidence cited (Abbott-Smith) covers only the ordinary verb "to be," not this phrase as a whole, so its sense rests on the construction itself rather than corpus measurement.

definition: An empty, uninhabited place such as a desert or wilderness where no people live.
article: ἐρημία refers to a solitude — a desert or wilderness, a stretch of land where nobody lives. It appears only 4 times in the New Testament, and in the Majority Standard Bible the actual English word shows up just once (as "desolate" in Matthew 15:33), with the other three occurrences folded into the surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it to translate Hebrew words for ruin and devastation, and the papyri show it in ordinary life too — including a schoolboy's exercise about a murderer who fled into the desert (ἐρημίαν) to escape the law.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and just one given its own English word, the measured picture is thin even though the sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: A linking word meaning "and from there" or "and after that," pointing to the next place or time in a sequence.
article: This is a compound word, formed by squeezing together "and" (καί) with "from there" (ἐκεῖθεν), so it literally means "and from there." In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times, and most often (4×, 67%) translators render it as "After," since it carries the journey forward to the next stop or stage—fitting that it clusters in Acts travel narratives like Acts 20:15 and 21:1. Notably, in 3 of its 9 occurrences it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own, which shows how lightly this connector can sit in a sentence.
caution: The measured data leans toward a time sense ("after"), while the classical lexica list it strictly as a word of place ("and from there"), so the two sources emphasize different ranges.

definition: To fasten something to a surface; in its single New Testament use, to nail a person to a cross.
article: This verb means to fix or fasten one thing to another, built from πρός ('to') and πήγνυμι ('to fasten'). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 2:23, where it describes Jesus being nailed to the cross — and both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible render it 'nailing' there. The lexicons note that its general sense is 'to fasten to,' but in this lone biblical occurrence it carries the specific meaning of crucifixion.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be confirmed from biblical evidence alone.

definition: The part of the leg you stand on—the foot or, more specifically, the ankle area.
article: In the New Testament βάσις appears just once, in Acts 3:7, where the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB both render it "ankles"—the part of the lame man that was instantly strengthened. The word's range is wider than this single use suggests: it literally means a step or pace, and by extension the foot you stand on. The classical lexica add a vivid everyday sense documented in inscriptions and papyri, where βάσις regularly meant the "base" of a statue or pillar (as in OGIS 705, "he set up the statue with its base"). In the Septuagint it appears 67 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for a socket or pedestal.
caution: Evidence in the New Testament is extremely thin—a single occurrence—so confidence in the precise "ankles" sense is low, and the classical and documentary sources point more toward "foot" or "base."

definition: To seek something out earnestly, or—when blood or guilt is the object—to demand it back and call someone to account.
article: This compound of ἐκ ("out") and ζητέω ("seek") intensifies plain seeking into searching out, investigating, or craving—the Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times across 5 books. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "seek" 3 times (60%), often of seeking God (Acts 15:17, Heb 11:6), but in Luke 11:50–51 it shifts to a legal sense of demanding or requiring an accounting for shed blood. Its Septuagint footprint is huge—113 times—where it mostly translates Hebrew דָּרַשׁ (56×) and בָּקַשׁ (16×), and everyday papyri show the same flavor, as in a request to "search out the guilty persons."
caution: The "demand/require" sense rests on just 2 occurrences (Luke 11:50–51) where the verb's English is partly absorbed into surrounding phrasing, so its boundaries there are less crisp than the "seek" sense.

definition: Slow, dull, or sluggish — lacking energy and alertness, whether physically or in spiritual attentiveness.
article: Νωθρός describes someone who is slow, dull, or slack — lacking the energy and alertness to act. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews (5:11 and 6:12), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "sluggish"; in one of those two spots it gets absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than a single word. The everyday Koine papyri are revealing: a related noun shows up in a document (A.D. 184) describing someone who "neglected my rights" out of slackness, and Moulton-Milligan note the word is probably cognate with νόσος, the word for sickness.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences (both in Hebrews) and a single Septuagint use, so its full range is hard to pin down.

definition: To fall asleep, drifting off into slumber.
article: This verb appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 8:23, where it describes Jesus falling asleep in the boat before the storm—and translations agree 100% on rendering it "asleep." It's built from ἀπό plus ὕπνος ("sleep"), and Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. Interestingly, Abbott-Smith records a contrary classical sense, "to awake from sleep," so the word seems to have shifted from marking the end of sleeping to its beginning; Plummer calls the "fall asleep" usage medical and late.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources note real uncertainty about its history, since classically it could mean the opposite—"to awake from sleep."

definition: A seaport city in the region of Pamphylia where Paul and Barnabas stopped during their travels.
article: Attalia was a coastal city in Pamphylia, serving as the port for Perga. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 14:25, where Paul and Barnabas pass through it during their journey. According to the lexicons, the name traces back to a king of Pergamum, and the spelling varies slightly between editions (Ἀττάλεια and Ἀτταλία).
caution: This is a proper place name occurring only once, so the evidence is thin and limited to a single passage.

definition: To know, understand, or be well acquainted with something or someone.
article: ἐπίσταμαι means to know or understand something, often with the sense of being firmly acquainted with a fact, person, or skill. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 14 times and is rendered "know" in 10 of those (91%), with the remaining occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word. In the Septuagint it shows up 49 times and chiefly translates the Hebrew יָדַע ("to know") 23 times, and the everyday papyri use it just this way—one letter even says "since you know how I esteem and love you."

definition: To be silent, keeping quiet or holding one's peace, whether by choice or because one is unable to speak.
article: σιωπάω means to be silent or still—to hold one's peace. It covers both deliberate silence and the involuntary kind, as when Zechariah is struck mute in Luke 1:20, and it can even be addressed to the sea ("Be still!" in Mark 4:39). The Septuagint uses it 29 times across 13 books, most often for the Hebrew חָשָׁה ("to be silent"), and everyday Koine papyri show the same plain meaning, as in a document where a man simply "kept silent" after a petition was read.
caution: Strong's tries to distinguish this word as involuntary muteness versus the voluntary σιγή, but the dictionaries note the two terms are often used interchangeably, so don't lean hard on that contrast.

definition: Evidence or a statement given to confirm the truth of something, especially formal witness in a legal or public setting.
article: μαρτυρία is the testimony or evidence someone gives—the act or content of bearing witness. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 37 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "testimony" in 25 of those (69%), with closely related senses making up the rest. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this legal flavor: a second-century petition uses the phrase "to give evidence" (μαρτυρίαν ποιήσασθαι), and another asks that a document be registered "as evidence" (πρὸς μαρτυρίαν). In the Septuagint it most often stands behind the Hebrew word for "witness" (עֵד).

definition: An adult female, whether unmarried or married—context decides whether "woman" or "wife" is meant.
article: γυνή is the everyday Greek word for an adult female, and across its 220 New Testament appearances it splits between "woman" (126×, 65%) and "wife" (62×, 32%), with context alone deciding which. The Septuagint uses it more than 842 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew word for "woman/wife" (759×), so the same double meaning runs through both Testaments. Worth noting: in direct address the vocative "γύναι" ("woman") was a respectful, even tender term, not a rebuke, as when Jesus speaks to his mother and to others.
caution: Abbott-Smith lists a possible third sense, "deaconess" (1 Tim 3:11), but this is disputed and not reflected in the measured renderings.

definition: The heel of the foot, used in a figurative phrase about turning against someone.
article: πτέρνα means the heel of the foot. It appears just once in the New Testament, in John 13:18, where it shows up in the figurative expression "to lift one's heel against" someone — a quotation drawn from the Septuagint that describes turning on a companion. In the Septuagint it occurs 7 times across 4 books, where it translates several different Hebrew words, most often עָקֵב ("heel").
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and uncertain derivation, the evidence is thin and the word's figurative force rests on its Septuagint source.

definition: To raise up or produce offspring for someone, or (in some forms) to stand up and rise.
article: In the New Testament, this word appears only 3 times, and all 3 are rendered "up" — specifically about raising up children or offspring for a dead brother (Mark 12:19, Luke 20:28) and people rising up to speak (Acts 15:5). Lexicons split it into two grammatical patterns: in transitive forms it means "raise up" or "produce offspring," while in certain past-tense forms it means "rise up" oneself. Interestingly, everyday Koine papyri use the word in a legal sense — "to reject" judges, literally causing them to stand down from their seats.
caution: Confidence is low: with only 3 New Testament occurrences, the broader transitive/intransitive range comes mostly from lexicons and the Septuagint rather than measured New Testament data.

definition: A person's possessions, property, or goods — the things they own and have at hand.
article: As a noun, ὑπάρχοντα refers to the things a person owns — their property, goods, or belongings. It comes from the verb ὑπάρχω ("to exist, to be in hand") used as a substantive: literally "the things existing" for someone, hence what they possess. It appears 39 times in the Septuagint, where it most often renders the Hebrew רְכוּשׁ (9×), a word for movable property or accumulated wealth.
caution: This noun form does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament, so its New Testament range here is inferred from Septuagint usage and lexicons rather than measured NT data.

definition: The number nine.
article: ἐννέα is simply the cardinal number "nine," an indeclinable primary number. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, rendered "nine" in 4 of them and once as "all other nine" (Luke 17:17), where the lone healed leper returns and the remaining nine do not. In the Septuagint it occurs 36 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for nine (תֵּ֫שַׁע, 30 of 36 times), confirming its plain numeric meaning.

definition: To go up together with someone, especially traveling up to a place in another person's company.
article: συναναβαίνω is a compound of "with" (σύν) and "go up" (ἀναβαίνω), so it literally means to ascend or travel up in someone's company. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times describing people who had come up with someone to a place — the women who came up with Jesus (Mark 15:41) and those who accompanied him from Galilee to Jerusalem (Acts 13:31). The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the papyri, where one letter writer advises, "if he gives you trouble, go up with him," showing it was ordinary travel vocabulary in daily Koine.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the measured range rests on thin evidence, though the sources agree.

definition: Describing something that is bright, shining, or filled with light, the opposite of dark.
article: φωτεινός describes things that shine or are filled with light, standing as the direct opposite of "dark" (σκοτεινός), as seen in the eye that is either "full of light" or in darkness. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 5 times across 2 books, where translators render it "full" (of light) 3 times, "bright" once for the cloud at the Transfiguration, and "radiant" once. The word lived on in everyday Koine: a fourth-century papyrus letter even uses its superlative to address a person as "most enlightened," showing how naturally it stretched from physical brightness to a figurative compliment.
caution: With only 5 occurrences clustered in a couple of passages, the apparent senses mostly reflect translation choices for the single idea of being light-filled rather than truly distinct meanings.

definition: The radiance or brightness that streams out from a source of light, like a beam shining from something luminous.
article: ἀπαύγασμα refers to light beaming out from a luminous body — its radiance or effulgence. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 1:3, where the Majority Standard Bible captures the idea of the Son being the "exact" reflection of God's glory. Outside the New Testament it is found in the Septuagint only once, at Wisdom 7:26, so the word's whole biblical footprint is just two verses.
caution: This word is a New Testament hapax with only one further biblical occurrence, so its precise range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To dishonor someone or treat them with shameful indignity, often by violent or contemptuous mistreatment.
article: This verb means to dishonor or treat someone with indignity, functioning much like its close relative ἀτιμάζω (G818). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Mark 12:4, where the tenants shamefully mistreat a servant) and not at all in the critical SBLGNT, but it is well attested elsewhere: 13 times in the Septuagint across 6 books, where it usually translates the Hebrew בָּזָה ("to despise," 7×). A striking witness from the papyri comes from a decree after the 409/8 BC capture of Selymbria, where it carries the civic sense of stripping someone of their rights and privileges (disfranchisement).
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine NT and is absent from the critical text, so its New Testament range rests on thin and disputed manuscript evidence.

definition: The color white, or by extension something bright, brilliant, or gleaming, especially of clothing.
article: λευκός means "white" and shows almost no variation: the Majority Standard Bible renders all 24 translated occurrences as "white," and the BSB agrees 100%. The word also stretches toward "bright" or "gleaming," which is why lexicons like Dodson list "bright, brilliant" and why it describes radiant clothing as well as plain color. In the Septuagint it almost always renders the Hebrew word lāḇān ("white," 25 times), and everyday papyri use it both literally—"white wool," "the white dress"—and even as a nickname distinguishing a fair-haired soldier from a dark one.

definition: Describing a burden that is hard to carry or bear, especially heavy loads laid on people.
article: This word combines the prefix meaning "hard" with the verb "to carry," describing something difficult or oppressive to bear. In the New Testament it appears in just two passages (Matthew 23:4 and Luke 11:46), both picturing heavy burdens placed on people's shoulders, and Moulton-Milligan note it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. In its single Septuagint appearance (Proverbs 27:3) it renders the Hebrew word for "weight," describing the heaviness of stone and sand.
caution: The evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences (one omitted in some critical texts) and a single Septuagint use, so the picture of its range is limited.

definition: Describing the people or things that are left over after others are gone — the remnant or the rest.
article: κατάλοιπος means "left remaining" — the rest, the residue, what is still there after the majority has passed. Though it appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 15:17, in a quotation of the Old Testament where it refers to the "remnant of men"), it shows up 97 times in the Septuagint, most often translating the Hebrew word for "remnant" (30×). Everyday Koine papyri use it for plain accounting too — one document speaks of "the remainder paid over to Ptolemaeus" — so the word ranged easily from solemn prophecy to ordinary leftover sums.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament sense rests on a single quoted verse.

definition: To live or dwell somewhere, whether physically in a place or figuratively as something residing within a person.
article: οἰκέω means to live or dwell, and it works both literally—inhabiting a place or sharing a home in marriage—and figuratively, as when something "lives" inside a person. In the Byzantine New Testament's 9 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "living" 7 times (88%), often for things that dwell within someone, such as good, sin, or the Spirit of God (Romans 7:18, 7:20, 8:9). The word was common in everyday Koine: papyri use it for residing in a village or temple, and one Egyptian document even uses it in the sense of being deported to an island.

definition: To distribute or hand out something among people; in the passive, to spread or be circulated more widely.
article: At its core διανέμω means to portion out or distribute something among a group, and in the passive it shifts to the idea of something being spread around. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 4:17, where it is rendered "spreading" — there it describes news being circulated. Everyday Koine papyri use it concretely, as when officials "distribute" money or favors to citizens, and the Septuagint uses it once for the Hebrew chalaq, "to divide."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the measured evidence is very thin, though it agrees with the lexicons.

definition: An army, especially one camped or on the move, viewed as an organized military force.
article: στρατόπεδον combines the words for "army" and "plain," and its root meaning is a military camp—the ground where troops pitch their tents. By extension it came to mean the body of troops itself, and that is how it works in its single New Testament appearance (Luke 21:20), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "armies" in all instances. Notably, the everyday papyri preserve both senses: an inscription from A.D. 216 calls Julia Domna "mother of the unconquered armies," while a document from 128 B.C. uses it for an actual royal camp.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single occurrence even though wider Koine evidence is solid.

definition: To obey someone in authority, submitting to a ruler, magistrate, or other rightful command.
article: πειθαρχέω means to obey or submit to someone in authority, built from the ideas of being persuaded (πείθω) and rule (ἀρχή). It appears just 4 times in the New Testament, several times pointing to obeying God (Acts 5:29, 32) and once to being obedient to rulers and authorities (Titus 3:1). The everyday flavor comes through in the papyri, where marriage contracts use it for a wife "obeying her husband as is fitting," showing it described ordinary submission to recognized authority, not just religious obedience.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence base is thin, so the sense distinctions above largely reflect different objects of obedience rather than sharply different meanings.

definition: Describing something made of fine linen, a costly woven fabric used for luxurious or ceremonial clothing.
article: βύσσινος is an adjective meaning "made of fine linen," derived from the noun βύσσος. Its measured use is remarkably consistent: all 5 New Testament occurrences are rendered "fine linen" (100%), and it appears 16 times in the Septuagint translating several Hebrew terms for fine cloth. The papyri make this material vivid as a real industry: Moulton-Milligan note that fine linen manufacture was a government monopoly in Egypt, produced under priestly direction in temples that doubled as workshops.

definition: To send someone or something off to a destination or on an errand, dispatching them from where you are.
article: πέμπω means to send or dispatch a person or thing somewhere, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it that way nearly every time — rendered "sent" in 68 of 80 occurrences (88%). The remaining cases are simply participle forms ("the one who sent," "whoever sent"), mostly in John's Gospel describing God who sent Jesus, so the core meaning never really shifts. It was an utterly ordinary word in daily life: the papyri show people using it for everyday requests, like one letter from around 245 BC asking someone to "get the kid also from Aristion and send it to me." In the Septuagint it chiefly stands in for the Hebrew shalach, "to send."

definition: The first-person reflexive pronoun "myself," pointing the action or reference of a verb back to the speaker.
article: This is simply the Greek word for "myself" — a reflexive pronoun that loops a statement back onto the speaker, formed by combining "me" with "self." It appears 37 times in the New Testament, and nearly all of its renderings cluster around "I" and "I myself," with the various labels just reflecting how it fits into different sentences. Everyday papyri show the same ordinary usage, such as a third-century BC contract speaking of "my own wife" (τῆι ἐμαυτοῦ γυναικί) and another of someone being "master of my property."

definition: To hope or trust beforehand, ahead of others or before something is fully confirmed.
article: This is a compound of πρό ("before") and ἐλπίζω ("to hope"), so it means to place hope or trust ahead of time. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 1:12, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with the idea of being "first" to hope. The lexicons split the emphasis slightly: Strong's stresses hoping in advance of confirmation, while Dodson highlights being the first to hope — both senses sit comfortably in the single occurrence.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its exact shade of meaning rests on a single verse and cannot be confirmed by broader usage.

definition: A lamb, a young sheep, typically a male.
article: ἀρήν means a lamb or young sheep, and it appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 10:3, where it is consistently rendered "lambs" by every source. It is far more common in the Septuagint, occurring 27 times across 14 books, where it translates several Hebrew words for sheep and lambs, including כֶּ֫שֶׂב and טָלֶה. An interesting wrinkle: the nominative form ἀρήν had already dropped out of normal use by NT times, surviving only in early inscriptions, while the oblique cases (like ἄρνας in Luke 10:3) stayed alive in everyday Koine papyri.
caution: Evidence in the NT is thin (a single occurrence), and confidence is rated low.

definition: Severe torment or torture, the intense suffering inflicted as punishment.
article: This noun names torment or torture — intense, inflicted suffering — and appears only 6 times in the New Testament, all within Revelation. In 5 of those it plainly means "torment," with one occurrence (Rev 18:10) tied to a cry of torment. The word comes from the verb βασανίζω (to torture), and outside the New Testament it shows up in the Septuagint only in 4 Maccabees (9:6; 11:2), again describing physical torture.
caution: The evidence base is narrow — all New Testament uses are confined to Revelation, with only a couple of Septuagint parallels.

definition: To take hold of someone or something physically, especially to seize, capture, or officially arrest a person.
article: πιάζω means to grab or take hold of someone, ranging from simply laying hands on a person to formally arresting them. Across its 12 New Testament uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "arrest" 3 times and "laid" (hold) twice, with rarer renderings like "seized" and "caught," and 5 cases absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the seizing sense vividly — one fourth-century magic spell uses it of catching a thief, and another document mentions a "taker of malefactors." It is a Doric form of πιέζω (to squeeze) but in the NT always carries the meaning of seizing rather than pressing.
caution: With only one Septuagint occurrence and 5 of 12 NT uses absorbed into phrasing, the measured sense breakdown rests on relatively few clearly rendered instances.

definition: To teach a different doctrine than the true or accepted Christian teaching.
article: This verb combines the words for "other/different" and "teacher," so it literally means to teach something other than the sound message. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Timothy (1:3 and 6:3), where Paul warns against those who instruct people differently from the true teaching. The two occurrences are handled almost identically across translations, with the Majority Standard Bible and BSB rendering it in terms of teaching false or other "doctrine."
caution: With only two occurrences, both in a single book, the evidence base is thin and the confidence tier is low.

definition: A person who secretly spreads damaging gossip or slanders someone's character behind their back.
article: A ψιθυριστής is literally a 'whisperer,' but in the New Testament it describes someone who quietly attacks another person's reputation rather than confronting them openly. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Romans 1:29, listed among other vices. The word is well attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and Abbott-Smith notes it was even used as an epithet of the god Hermes, though the negative sense of 'secret slanderer' is what Paul intends — contrasted with κατάλαλος, the open detractor.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured sense label ('become') reflects a quirk of the verse rendering rather than the word's actual meaning, which is 'whisperer/secret slanderer.'

definition: To drink a liquid, whether taking an actual beverage or, figuratively, absorbing something.
article: πίνω simply means "to drink," and the New Testament uses it that way almost without exception — 73 of its 74 Byzantine occurrences are rendered "drink." It covers literal drinking, habitual use (as in Luke 1:15), and stretches metaphorically: Abbott-Smith notes it can describe the earth soaking up rain (Hebrews 6:7) or spiritual drinking of Christ's blood (John 6:53-56). In the Septuagint it appears 251 times and mostly translates the Hebrew verb שָׁתָה (192×), and a delightful papyrus shows a sulking schoolboy declaring "I won't eat, I won't drink!"

definition: Describing the higher-lying inland regions, as opposed to areas near the coast.
article: This adjective describes territory that lies higher up or further inland, away from the coast. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 19:1, where Paul travels through the "upper" or interior regions on his way to Ephesus. The word derives from ἀνώτερος ("higher, upper"), and the lexicons agree it carries the sense of more remote, higher-lying inland country.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire New Testament, so its precise range cannot be measured from broader usage.

definition: To make someone an outsider or stranger, cutting them off from a relationship or community they were excluded from.
article: ἀπαλλοτριόω means to estrange or alienate someone, making them a non-participant in something they're shut out from; in the New Testament it always appears in the passive — people being alienated from God or from spiritual life. All three Byzantine occurrences (Ephesians 2:12, 4:18, Colossians 1:21) carry this sense, and the Majority Standard and BSB renderings agree completely. The word was common in everyday legal documents: papyri and inscriptions use it for transferring or disposing of property, as in a third-century BC Olbia inscription where someone "alienated none of his possessions."
caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences, all in one sense and absent from the critical SBLGNT text — so confidence is rated low.

definition: A small flask or jar, often made of alabaster, used to hold perfume or scented ointment.
article: This word names a container for perfumed ointment, traditionally carved from alabaster stone but used loosely for any such flask. In the Byzantine NT it appears 4 times across 3 books, all in scenes where a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "alabaster jar" half the time and simply "jar" the other half. The everyday character of the word shows up in the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan find it paired with "perfume" (μύρου) and even preserved in the place-name Alabastropolis, "city of the alabasters."
caution: With only 4 NT occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and lexicons note the word could refer to a flask of any material, not strictly alabaster.

definition: Pleasing, agreeable, or worthy of affection — describing something that draws people's fondness or warm regard.
article: προσφιλής describes things or people that are pleasing, agreeable, and worthy of affection — literally something that invites fondness. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:8, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the list of "whatever" qualities to dwell on; the KJV captures the flavor with "lovely." The everyday papyri are especially telling: one writer says "I am pleasing to all who revere him," and Trajan's wife Plotina even calls the future emperor Hadrian "most dear to me in all respects," while the word also turns up commonly in epitaphs.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and just a few times in the Septuagint, so its range rests heavily on outside Koine evidence.

definition: An indivisible instant of time—a moment so brief it cannot be divided or split.
article: Built from a negative prefix and the root meaning "to cut" (G5114), ἄτομος literally means "uncuttable" or "indivisible," and is the source of our word "atom." In its single New Testament appearance (1 Corinthians 15:52), it describes time, naming an instant too small to divide—which the Majority Standard Bible renders "twinkling" 100% of the time, with the KJV using "moment." Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in Symmachus's version of Isaiah 54:8, "ἐν ἀτόμῳ ὀργῆς" (in a moment of wrath), suggesting Paul may have drawn the word from everyday Koine rather than directly from Plato or Aristotle.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: Courage, boldness, or confidence; the inner resolve that lets someone face difficulty without fear.
article: θάρσος means courage or boldness — the inner confidence to face something. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Forum" (Acts 28:15), but this reflects the place name "Forum of Appius" rather than the word's actual meaning, since the classical lexica uniformly point to "courage" or "boldness." The classical evidence is rich: it can mean courage to do a specific thing, the grounds or basis for confidence, and even, in a bad sense, audacity. In the Septuagint it appears 3 times and translates different Hebrew words including one meaning resolve or boldness.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured English rendering reflects a place name rather than the word's core meaning of courage attested in the lexica.

definition: A sacred song sung to musical accompaniment, or collectively the Old Testament book of Psalms.
article: In the New Testament ψαλμός is a sacred song meant to be sung, often with instruments, and it can also name the Old Testament collection known as the book of Psalms. It appears 7 times across 5 books, mostly rendered simply "Psalms" (5×, 71%), though one passage (1 Corinthians 14:26) pictures someone bringing a psalm to share in worship. In the Septuagint it shows up 81 times, chiefly translating the Hebrew מִזְמוֹר; an inscription from the second century AD even distinguishes ψαλμός (plucking the strings with the fingers) from κιθαρισμός (using a plectrum), preserving the word's musical roots.
caution: The senses labeled "Jesus Psalms" and "say psalm" reflect single occurrences in surrounding phrases rather than distinct meanings of the word itself.

definition: To slaughter or kill by violence, often referring to animals killed for sacrifice or people killed brutally.
article: σφάζω means to slaughter or kill by violence, a word used both for sacrificial animals and for the violent killing of people. In the New Testament it appears 10 times, rendered "slain" in 7 of 10 cases (88%), with the remaining two absorbed into surrounding phrasing; the imagery ranges from the slain Lamb in Revelation to Cain's murder of his brother in 1 John 3:12. The Septuagint uses it 81 times, overwhelmingly to translate the Hebrew שָׁחַט (67×), the standard verb for ritually slaughtering a sacrifice, which anchors its strong sacrificial flavor.

definition: To come together or assemble as a group, or to go along with someone as a companion.
article: This verb combines "with" (σύν) and "come/go" (ἔρχομαι), and its core idea is people coming together — whether assembling in one place or traveling along with someone. Across its 32 New Testament occurrences the renderings cluster around gathering ("come together," "together," "gathered") and companionship ("accompanied"), with the Septuagint using it for Hebrew words meaning to walk, come, or be gathered. Notably, the everyday Koine papyri show it as a standard term in marriage contracts ("to come together" as husband and wife), which fits its use in Matthew 1:18 of Mary and Joseph.

definition: The accusative masculine singular of the demonstrative "this," pointing to a specific man or thing as the object of a verb or preposition.
article: τοῦτον is simply the masculine accusative form of οὗτος, "this" — the case used when the word is the object of a verb or follows a preposition, so it typically means "this (man)" or "him." The lexica give it the basic range of "this, the same, that," the same meaning carried by all forms of οὗτος. Because it is a grammatical form of a very common demonstrative rather than a separate word, the digest records no measured senses of its own.
caution: The digest shows zero Byzantine occurrences and no measured senses, because this is one inflected form of οὗτος rather than an independent entry, so its meaning is borrowed entirely from the parent word.

definition: Plants or vegetation that grow from the ground, such as grass, herbs, or crops fit for grazing.
article: βοτάνη refers to vegetation that springs up from the soil—grass, herbs, and growing plants generally. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 6:7, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as what the land "produces." The word comes from βόσκω (to feed or graze), and it shows up 15 times in the Septuagint translating several Hebrew words for grass and herbage; interestingly, in everyday papyri it also turns up frequently in magical texts, where particular herbs were used for spells.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on one verse, so the corpus evidence here is thin.

definition: Caesar, the title of the Roman emperor, used as the name for whoever held imperial power.
article: Καῖσαρ is the Latin title "Caesar," used throughout the New Testament for the reigning Roman emperor. It appears 30 times in the Byzantine text and is rendered "Caesar" or "Caesar's" in nearly every case, with a few occurrences (like Matthew 22:21) contrasting what belongs to Caesar with what belongs to God. Notably, Moulton-Milligan points to the phrase "those of Caesar's household" in Philippians 4:22, which inscriptional evidence shows referred to a large group of slaves and freedmen serving the imperial palace.

definition: To keep, guard, or watch over something carefully — and so to observe, obey, or preserve it.
article: τηρέω means to keep careful watch over something — guarding it from loss or harm, preserving it, or, by extension, keeping a command or word by obeying it. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "keep" in about 75% of its 75 New Testament occurrences, and that single idea covers the whole range, from physically guarding a prisoner to observing the law or holding onto faith. Everyday Koine papyri show the same span: a worker paid for "keeping the wine," someone guarding a royal embankment, and a man saying he "kept" a friendship blameless — the very phrasing echoed in the New Testament.

definition: The possessive word meaning "my" or "mine," marking something as belonging to, coming from, or related to the speaker.
article: ἐμός is simply the emphatic way to say "my" or "mine" in Greek, an adjective form built from the personal pronoun "I." Nearly all of its 79 New Testament occurrences are rendered "my" or some close variant, and it appears most often in John's Gospel. Used by itself with the article (τὸ ἐμόν, "what is mine"), it can stand in for the noun entirely, as in "give me what is mine." One interesting detail: in everyday papyri the word was often unemphatic, simply meaning "my," and writers frequently used other reflexive forms in its place.
caution: The many measured "senses" mostly reflect surrounding pronouns and verbs in translation rather than distinct meanings—the word's core sense is consistently just "my/mine."

definition: Loving money; greedy for wealth and unwilling to part with it.
article: φιλάργυρος literally combines "loving" (φίλος) and "silver" (ἄργυρος), so it describes someone whose affection is set on money. It appears only twice in the New Testament, describing the Pharisees in Luke 16:14 and the greedy people of the last days in 2 Timothy 3:2, and the lexicons agree it means "money-loving" or "avaricious." The everyday character of the word shows in the papyri, where it even turns up as a personal name in a third-century AD document from Oxyrhynchus.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and one Septuagint use (4 Maccabees 2:8), the evidence is thin, though sources agree on the meaning.

definition: To hand out or distribute something to several people, dealing it out among them.
article: διαδίδωμι combines διά (through) with δίδωμι (to give), so it pictures giving something out across a group — dealing it out, sharing it around. It appears only 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it with an English word just once (as "distribution"), folding it into the surrounding phrasing the other 3 times. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one document from around A.D. 265 describes goods "distributed through the superintendents," and another speaks of bread "delivered and distributed," showing the word at home in official handouts of supplies.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and just one rendered as a standalone English word, the measured range is thin, though papyri and lexica agree on the core sense of distributing.

definition: An interrogative word asking what sort, kind, or quality something is.
article: ποταπός is a question word asking "what sort?" or "what kind?" — it appears 7 times in the New Testament, often expressing wonder, as in "What kind of man is this?" (Matthew 8:27). It can shade toward magnitude as well, since at Mark 13:1 the same word prompts renderings about magnificent buildings. Interestingly, this Hellenistic form replaced the older classical ποδαπός, which originally asked "from what country?" — and a papyrus mime fragment (P Oxy III.413) still uses it that way, though the New Testament never carries that local sense.
caution: The measured senses ("leaving," "magnificent") at Mark 13:1 reflect translation choices in context rather than separate meanings of the word, which fundamentally asks "what sort?"

definition: Methuselah, a man in the genealogy from Adam to Jesus, named in Luke as a distant ancestor.
article: Μαθουσάλα is simply the Greek spelling of the Hebrew name Methuselah, who appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:37) as one link in the chain of ancestors. It occurs only once in the New Testament, always as a personal name with no other meaning. In the Septuagint the same Greek form shows up 8 times, usually rendering the Hebrew name מְתוּשֶׁלַח (6×), but interestingly twice it stands in for a different name, עִירָד (Irad).
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured beyond identifying the person.

definition: A person from Nazareth, used as a description of Jesus identifying his hometown.
article: Ναζαρηνός simply means someone who comes from Nazareth, and in the New Testament it always describes Jesus. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "Nazarene" in every case it gets its own English word (2 times), though in 2 of its 4 Byzantine occurrences it gets folded into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word. The word is built directly from Ναζαρέθ (Nazareth), and Abbott-Smith notes the form is Semitic in origin.
caution: The Byzantine text has only 4 occurrences (6 in the critical text), so the evidence base is relatively thin.

definition: Relating to the Greek language or culture; describing something as Greek.
article: Ἑλληνικός is the adjective meaning "Greek," derived from Ἕλλην ("a Greek person"). In the New Testament it appears only twice and refers to the Greek language: in Luke 23:38 (in some manuscripts) for an inscription written in Greek, and in Revelation 9:11 for a name "in the Greek tongue." The Septuagint usage is a curiosity—its two appearances translate Hebrew words for "death" and "swiftness," which is unrelated to the adjective's normal meaning and points to translation difficulties rather than a real secondary sense.
caution: The evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences (one omitted in the critical text), and the Septuagint's odd Hebrew counterparts make its data unreliable for defining the word's range.

definition: To strive against or resist, opposing someone instead of yielding.
article: ἀντιπίπτω literally combines "against" and "fall," giving a picture of falling upon or pushing back against something. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Acts 7:51, where Stephen accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit (rendered "stiff-necked"). A nice everyday witness comes from a 2nd-century BC papyrus letter about the Serapeum Twins, where the related form means "without demur" — that is, complying without resistance.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament, so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To act with courage and strength, standing firm like a brave person facing difficulty.
article: This verb literally means "to make a man of" oneself, and in the middle voice it means to play the man—to act with courage and firmness. It appears only once in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 16:13), where it's woven into a string of commands and has no standalone English word of its own, but the Septuagint uses it 22 times across 10 books, most often (12×) translating the Hebrew אָמַץ, "be strong." A nice everyday parallel survives in a papyrus letter from around 233 BC that urges, "do not be faint-hearted, but be brave"—almost exactly Paul's wording.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise force here rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri parallels rather than direct New Testament evidence.

definition: Of time, to pass by or elapse; said of days or a period coming and going.
senseLabels: of time, to pass or elapse
article: This verb combines "through" (διά) with "to become" (γίνομαι) and in the New Testament always concerns time passing—days, a stretch of time, or the sabbath going by. It appears only 3 times across 2 books, and in two of those three the translators fold it into surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. The everyday Koine flavor shows up nicely in the papyri: a 3rd-century document (P Strass I.41) uses it in the phrase "much time has passed" (πολὺς χρόνος διαγέγονεν), exactly the sense seen in Acts.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 occurrences, two of which carry no distinct English rendering, so the confidence tier is low; older lexicons also note a broader sense ("to go through, to live") not reflected in the New Testament data.

definition: Forward movement or advancement, especially growth toward a goal—whether personal progress or the way events move things ahead.
article: προκοπή means progress or advancement, an image originally drawn from moving forward on a journey. In the New Testament it appears just 3 times, rendered as "progress" twice (Philippians 1:25; 1 Timothy 4:15) and as "circumstances" once (Philippians 1:12), where the sense is that events have moved things forward. Interestingly, the word is absent from classical Greek and was a technical term in Stoic philosophy for progress toward wisdom; Moulton-Milligan also shows its everyday use in a papyrus letter wishing someone "greater advancement."
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a thin record (the Atticists even condemned the word), this entry rests on limited evidence.

definition: The Greek name Dorcas, meaning "gazelle," belonging to a Christian woman in Joppa also called Tabitha.
article: Dorcas is a personal name, the Greek equivalent of the Aramaic name Tabitha, both of which mean "gazelle." In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Acts 9 (verses 36 and 39), where it names a Christian woman in Joppa known for her good works and charity. The name was common for women among both Greeks and Jews; one striking example is a Delphic inscription from the 2nd century BC where a manumitted slave named Dorcas is placed in someone's care.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only twice in the New Testament, so its full sense range cannot be measured from biblical usage.

definition: A loss, damage, or detriment — something that costs you, the opposite of profit or gain.
article: ζημία means loss or damage — the harm or cost something brings you, set explicitly against κέρδος (gain) in Philippians 3:7. In its 4 New Testament uses it is rendered either as the noun "loss" (twice, as in Acts 27:10, 21) or in the phrase "count as loss" (twice, in Philippians 3:7-8). It was an ordinary everyday word: Koine papyri use it of business losses, such as a vineyard lessee in a first-century petition pleading for a rent abatement because of the "losses" he had incurred on repairs.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences split evenly between the two measured renderings, the second sense reflects a Greek phrase rather than a distinct meaning of the word itself.

definition: The moon, the bright object that lights the night sky.
article: σελήνη simply means "the moon," and the meaning is remarkably consistent: in all 9 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "moon" 8 times (89%), with BSB independently agreeing 100%. In the Septuagint it appears 31 times across 14 books, most often translating the Hebrew word יָרֵחַ ("moon") 19 times, and sometimes לְבָנָה. One striking detail from everyday Koine papyri: astrologers reckoned days "according to the moon," and the word turns up repeatedly in ancient horoscopes, showing its place in calendar-keeping and star-gazing.

definition: Describing something that has been written down or inscribed.
article: γραπτός is a verbal adjective from γράφω ("to write"), meaning something that is written or inscribed.
