It appears only once in the New Testament, at Romans 2:15, where in translation it gets folded into the surrounding phrasing rather than standing as its own English word. Everyday Koine papyri show the practical sense vividly: in two letters from around A.D. 25–27, the phrase διὰ γραπτοῦ means "in writing" as opposed to by word of mouth. Abbott-Smith also notes a secondary sense "painted," though the New Testament use is clearly "written."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on very thin evidence.

definition: To rule together with someone as a co-regent, sharing in their kingship and royal authority.
article: Συμβασιλεύω combines "with" (σύν) and "reign" (βασιλεύω) to mean ruling alongside someone as a co-regent. It appears only twice in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 4:8 and 2 Timothy 2:12), and the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "reign" in one case while absorbing it into the surrounding phrasing in the other. The word shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including a reference to the συμβασιλισταί, apparently members of a royal military union.
caution: With only 2 occurrences this entry rests on thin evidence, so confidence is low; note also that the Abbott-Smith excerpt actually describes a different word (συμβουλεύω).

definition: To drag or pull someone away from where they should be, used figuratively of being lured toward wrongdoing.
article: This verb literally means to drag or pull something out or away, built from roots meaning "out of" and "to drag." It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (James 1:14), where it describes a person being lured away by their own desire, and five times in the Septuagint. A vivid piece of everyday evidence comes from a third-century BC inscription describing a healing, where the word is used literally of pulling a spear point out of a man's eye.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall data, the figurative "entice" sense rests mainly on a single passage.

definition: A dry measure of about a peck and a half (nearly three gallons), used for measuring quantities of flour.
article: σάτον is a unit of dry measure, equal to roughly a peck and a half, or nearly three English gallons. It comes into Greek from a Semitic measure (Hebrew סְאָה, Aramaic סָאתָא), and shows up only twice in the New Testament, both times in Jesus' parable of the leaven (Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it as "flour" in describing three measures of dough. The word also appears in the Septuagint at Haggai 2:17, and Moulton-Milligan note it turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, confirming it as a real working measurement term of the period.
caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament uses and two Septuagint uses — and the word's exact origin is disputed, with one scholar proposing a Coptic wine-measure source rather than the usual Aramaic derivation.

definition: To count or number people or things, tallying how many there are.
article: ἀριθμέω means to count or number something, whether the hairs on your head (Matthew 10:30, Luke 12:7) or a crowd too large to tally (Revelation 7:9). It appears only 3 times in the New Testament but 35 times in the Septuagint, where it usually renders the Hebrew סָפַר ('count,' 13×) and מָנָא ('number,' 7×). One striking detail: in everyday Koine papyri the verb very often means specifically counting out money for payment, as in receipts recording a price 'paid.'
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences, the range here is thin, so the prominent 'counting out money' sense seen in the papyri does not clearly appear in the biblical examples.

definition: A grave or tomb — the place where a dead body is buried.
article: τάφος means a grave or tomb, the place where someone is buried. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, rendered "tomb" in 5 of them, with one instance referring to the decorating of monuments (Matthew 23:29). The word is well attested in everyday Koine: papyri include a will (A.D. 138–161) leaving a bequest to be paid at the testator's tomb, and another document arranges a yearly feast to be held near the writer's tomb. In the Septuagint it occurs 45 times, mostly translating the Hebrew קֶבֶר (grave).
caution: The classical lexicon Abbott-Smith also lists an older sense "a burial" (the act), but no measured New Testament occurrence uses it that way.

definition: A bride or young married woman; also a daughter-in-law (a son's wife).
article: Νύμφη names either a bride/young married woman or a son's wife (daughter-in-law), with both senses appearing across its 8 New Testament occurrences. The Septuagint uses it 37 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word kallah (33×), which itself carries both 'bride' and 'daughter-in-law' meanings. The measured 'against' renderings reflect the family-strife passages (Matthew 10:35; Luke 12:53), where a daughter-in-law is set against her mother-in-law. One interesting detail: an inscription (Kaibel 570) uses the word of a little girl just five years old.
caution: The corpus tool's 'against' label is a quirk of phrasing in the family-conflict verses; the actual sense there is 'daughter-in-law,' and the two genuine senses are bride and daughter-in-law.

definition: To sail past or alongside a place without stopping there.
article: παραπλέω literally means to sail near or past something, and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 20:16) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "avoid" 100% of the time, since Paul chose to sail past Ephesus rather than stop. The BSB independently agrees on this rendering. Everyday Koine papyri use the same word for sailing past, and one early second-century document (P Oxy III.525) even uses the related noun for "the voyage past" a particular region.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: A Hebrew personal name, John, borne by several different men in the New Testament.
article: Ἰωάννης is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jochanan, and it appears 131 times in the Byzantine New Testament. The Majority Standard Bible renders it simply "John" in 88% of cases and as the possessive "John's" in 11% — the only difference is grammar, not meaning. The name belongs to several distinct men: John the Baptist, John the apostle (son of Zebedee), Peter's father, and John surnamed Mark, and Moulton-Milligan note the name was common enough to show up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: The Greek spelling of this Semitic name varies in the manuscripts (one or two n's), but its meaning and reference are not in doubt.

definition: To seize or arrest someone, or, of a woman, to conceive a child in the womb.
article: At its root this verb means to grab hold of, and that idea branches in two directions in the New Testament: physically seizing or arresting a person (about 46% of cases, rendered "seized" or "arrested"), and a woman conceiving a child (23%). The everyday papyri reinforce the "arrest" sense vividly — one document instructs that if you have arrested a runaway slave, you should hand him over. In the Septuagint it appears 89 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for becoming pregnant (23×) and the word for capturing or seizing (18×), neatly mirroring both NT meanings. The lexicons also note a further sense — to assist or take part with someone — used in Luke 5:7 and Philippians 4:3.
caution: The "assist/help" sense listed by the lexicons does not appear among the measured NT renderings here, so readers should watch context closely.

definition: An earthenware vessel such as a jar, jug, or pitcher used for carrying liquids like water or wine.
article: κεράμιον is an everyday earthenware container — a jar, jug, or pitcher. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, both times rendered "jug" (100%), in nearly identical scenes where a man carries a jar of water (Mark 14:13; Luke 22:10). The papyri make its ordinary, commercial life vivid: receipts and inventories list κεράμια of wine, sweet wine, and gum, and scholars note the jar held a quantity of liquid that could vary from 5 to 8 χόες rather than a single fixed measure.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and three in the Septuagint, the evidence base is thin, though sources agree on the basic meaning.

definition: Free from any charge or accusation that could be brought against you; not open to blame.
article: ἀνέγκλητος literally means "not to be called to account" — describing someone against whom no charge can be made to stick. The word comes from a negative prefix joined to a verb meaning "to bring a legal accusation," so its sense is rooted in the courtroom. In the Byzantine New Testament its 5 occurrences are rendered "blameless" 3 times (75%) and "above reproach" once (25%), with the two meanings being very close. A nice everyday parallel survives in a papyrus petition (P Oxy II.281), where a deserted wife insists she had "conducted herself blamelessly in all respects."
caution: With only 5 occurrences and a single LXX appearance, the evidence base is thin, though the sources agree closely on its meaning.

definition: To serve as a priest, carrying out the duties and rituals of the priestly office.
article: This verb means to function as a priest—performing the sacrifices and rites that came with the office. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:8, where Zechariah is serving in his priestly division, but it shows up 23 times in the Septuagint, mostly translating the Hebrew word כָּהַן ("to act as priest"). Interestingly, the word was already common in the pagan world: inscriptions like the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) use it for priests of various gods, so Luke and the LXX writers were simply applying a familiar term to Jewish worship.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range there rests mainly on Septuagint and inscription evidence.

definition: To long for or deeply yearn after someone or something with intense desire.
article: ἐπιποθέω means to long for or yearn deeply, and in the Byzantine New Testament's 9 occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "long" 6 times (86%), with the Berean Standard Bible agreeing every time. The word covers heartfelt longing for people (as in Philippians 1:8) as well as craving for things, and once shades toward "affection." In the Septuagint it appears 7 times and renders several different Hebrew verbs, including חוּס and דָּל twice each, showing the translators reached for it to cover a range of yearning and pity.
caution: Two of the nine occurrences are absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than getting their own English word, and older lexica list a wider range (even "lust") than the measured data shows.

definition: Hermogenes, the personal name of a man mentioned in the New Testament as having turned away from Paul.
article: Hermogenes is simply a man's name, appearing only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at 2 Timothy 1:15, where Paul notes that this man and others had deserted him. The name itself was common in everyday Koine, and Moulton-Milligan point to several papyri and inscriptions using it, including one striking inscription where a Hermogenes is punished by a god for slander over wine and then has to make amends. Strong's labels him an apostate Christian, but that characterization goes beyond what the single verse actually states.
caution: This name occurs only once in the New Testament, so the measured sense rests on a single verse.

definition: A supply, provision, or support that something or someone furnishes or contributes.
article: ἐπιχορηγία refers to a supply, provision, or support that is furnished to someone or something. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Ephesians 4:16 and Philippians 1:19), and the standard lexica (Abbott-Smith, Dodson) consistently gloss it as "a supply" or "support." The word was at home in everyday Koine: an inscription (Syll 378.9, A.D. 79-81) speaks of a supply drawn from temple revenues, showing its ordinary use for material provisioning.
caution: Evidence is thin (only 2 occurrences); the second measured sense rendered "distress" reflects translation context rather than the word's own meaning, since the lexica agree it simply means a supply.

definition: A noisy commotion or violent disturbance, especially the chaotic shouting of an agitated crowd.
article: θόρυβος names the loud, chaotic disturbance of an excited or angry crowd — the kind of commotion that can tip into violence. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times and splits evenly between two renderings: "riot" (3×) and "uproar" (3×), with one further occurrence absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday character of the word shows up in the papyri, where a Tebtunis document from 114 B.C. uses it for an actual village riot involving an attack on a local official, matching the stronger sense seen in passages like Mark 14:2 and Acts 20:1.
caution: The lexica list a milder range too (din, hubbub, confused noise), so the word can mean simple commotion as well as outright riot.

definition: A prolonged lack of food or going without eating, whether from circumstance or deliberate abstinence.
senseLabels: lack of food, going without eating
article: ἀσιτία describes the condition of being without food — fasting or abstinence from eating. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:21, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it with reference to "food"; the lexica define it more fully as the state of going hungry. A striking witness to its everyday use comes from a sixth-century papyrus (P Ryl I.10), part of a saint's discourse, where a man condemned to death by starvation says he was sentenced "to the ἀσιτία."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources frame it slightly differently — "food" versus "fasting/abstinence" — so its exact nuance rests on thin evidence.

definition: Enoch, an ancient figure listed before the Flood, known as the father of Methuselah.
article: Ἐνώχ is simply the Greek spelling of the personal name Enoch, transliterated from the Hebrew חֲנוֹך, which it renders all 17 times in the Septuagint. In the New Testament it appears 3 times, naming an early figure described as the son of Jared and father of Methuselah. The Majority Standard Bible renders one occurrence (Jude 1:14) as "Enoch also Behold," but this just reflects the surrounding phrase rather than a second meaning of the name itself.
caution: The apparent second sense ("Enoch also Behold") is an artifact of how the surrounding verse was rendered, not a genuinely distinct meaning of the name.

definition: To be fitting, proper, or appropriate for someone or some situation.
article: This verb describes when something is suitable, right, or appropriate—what fits a person or circumstance. It appears 7 times in the New Testament, and the various renderings ("proper," "fitting," "consistent") all circle the same idea of decency and appropriateness, often used impersonally as "it is fitting." Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way: one second-century document says the deified emperor Antoninus "deserved imperial power," capturing the sense of what suits or befits someone.
caution: The classical lexica list older senses like "to be clearly seen" or "to resemble" that don't appear in the measured New Testament data, where only the "fitting/proper" sense occurs.

definition: To blow or breathe, used in the New Testament of wind moving and gusting.
article: πνέω means to blow or breathe, and in all 7 New Testament occurrences it describes wind in motion — beating against a house (Matthew 7:25, 27), the unpredictable wind of John 3:8, or the breeze a ship catches (Acts 27:40). The Majority Standard Bible's four renderings ('blew,' 'wind blows,' 'wind,' and one garbled entry) all point to the same basic idea of air in movement. The everyday Koine papyri preserve a striking secondary use: an imprecatory tablet found in a grave prays that enemies' souls 'may not breathe,' showing the word's range extended from wind to living breath.
caution: The fourth measured sense ('back its would') appears to be a data error and should be read simply as wind blowing against something, as in Revelation 7:1.

definition: A person who breaks or violates a law, especially God's law; a transgressor.
article: παραβάτης means someone who steps across the line of the law — a lawbreaker or transgressor. All five New Testament uses point to this single idea, often paired with "of the law" (νόμου) in Romans and James, so the word's range is narrow and consistent. Interestingly, the older lexicon Abbott-Smith records a literal first sense — "one who stands beside," the warrior riding alongside the charioteer — but that physical meaning never appears in the New Testament, which uses only the moral "transgressor" sense.
caution: The word appears just 5 times, and the four measured renderings vary in wording, though they all converge on the same basic meaning of "lawbreaker."

definition: Shem, one of Noah's sons and an ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus.
article: Σήμ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Shem, a son of Noah. In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 3:36, where it sits within the genealogy tracing Jesus' ancestry. It shows up far more often in the Septuagint—16 times across 2 books—always rendering the Hebrew name שֵׁם. As a proper name borrowed straight from Hebrew, it doesn't change form (it's indeclinable) and carries no meaning beyond the person it names.
caution: This is a proper name appearing only once in the New Testament, so its range is limited to identifying the individual.

definition: To test someone thoroughly, putting them to the proof—often used of people improperly testing God.
article: ἐκπειράζω means to test or try someone thoroughly, an intensified form of the simpler verb πειράζω. In all four New Testament occurrences it describes putting God or Christ to the proof, as when Jesus says "You shall not put the Lord your God to the test" (Matthew 4:7, Luke 4:12). The Septuagint connection is telling: it renders the Hebrew נָסָה ("to test") in passages like Deuteronomy 6:16 and Psalm 78:18, the very texts Jesus draws on when refusing to test God.
caution: The measured senses "day test" and "killed" reflect surrounding wording in particular verses rather than separate meanings of the word itself, which consistently means "put to the test."

definition: To find out something precisely, learning the exact details by careful inquiry.
article: This verb means to ascertain something with precision—not just to learn, but to nail down the exact details. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew 2, where Herod carefully determines the exact time the star appeared from the magi. Despite Moulton-Milligan calling it fairly common in classical and Hellenistic Greek, they note it does not actually turn up in the papyri they surveyed, though a parallel in Vettius Valens carries exactly the same sense as Matthew 2:16.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and no papyri attestation, the evidence base is thin.

definition: Describing a penalty or judgment that is fair, just, and properly deserved.
article: ἔνδικος is a rare adjective meaning "just" or "deserved," used of a verdict or punishment that fairly fits the offense. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Romans 3:8 and Hebrews 2:2), and the lexicons agree on the core idea of "righteous, just, equitable." Tellingly, Moulton-Milligan note that the only other documented occurrences come from the ancient laws of Gortyna (fifth century BC), confirming its place in everyday legal language. Note that the measured renderings here—"slanderously" and "binding"—reflect how the surrounding sentence is translated rather than the word itself, which in both verses carries the sense of "just" or "deserved."
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the measured renderings reflecting context rather than the word's own meaning, treat the sense as based on thin evidence.

definition: A personal name, Onesimus, belonging to the slave of Philemon who became a Christian.
article: Onesimus is a proper name appearing 2 times in the New Testament, in Colossians 4:9 and Philemon 10, where it always refers to the same man—a slave of Philemon who became a Christian. The name comes from an adjective meaning "useful" or "profitable," which is why Paul makes a wordplay on it in Philemon. It was a very common name for slaves, and Moulton-Milligan shows it well attested in everyday papyri and inscriptions, including a first-century B.C. document.
caution: Evidence is thin, with only 2 occurrences, both referring to the same individual.

definition: Describing infants who were put outside and abandoned, left exposed to die.
article: ἔκθετος literally means "set outside" and describes babies who were abandoned to die from exposure—a real practice in the ancient world. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 7:19, where Stephen recounts how the Egyptians forced the Israelites to cast out their newborns; the Majority Standard Bible renders the phrase "exploited" there. An interesting twist comes from the papyri: in the astrologer Vettius Valens the word seems to mean "exiles" rather than abandoned infants, and the related noun ἔκθεσις commonly means a "list" or "schedule" in everyday documents.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range rests almost entirely on outside evidence, and the modern rendering "exploited" differs from the older glosses "cast out" and "exposed."

definition: A period of half an hour, a short stretch of time.
article: This word simply means "half an hour," formed from the parts for "half" and "hour," and it appears only once in the New Testament, at Revelation 8:1. Interestingly, the corpus measured the Majority Standard Bible rendering as "silence" 100% of the time — but that reflects the phrase "silence in heaven for about half an hour," not the word itself, which actually denotes the time span. Moulton-Milligan note the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including a second-century reference to "half a litra of purple," showing it was ordinary measurement language.
caution: This is a one-time word, and the measured "silence" sense is a quirk of how the surrounding phrase was counted; the word genuinely means "half an hour."

definition: To talk something through with others, whether by reasoning, discussing, arguing, or persuasive teaching.
article: This middle-voice verb means to converse, discuss, or reason something out with people, often in a back-and-forth that can shade into argument or persuasive teaching. The English translations cluster tightly around "reasoned," but five of the thirteen New Testament uses get absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single word, showing how naturally it blends into descriptions of conversation. The everyday Koine papyri confirm this ordinary range beautifully — one writer apologizes for leaving "without having talked with you about the pot," and another recalls how "I conversed with you about the sesame."
caution: With only one dominant measured rendering and many uses absorbed into phrasing, the precise force in any verse depends on context.

definition: The plain, factual word for "not" or "no," denying that something is true or real.
article: This is Greek's basic, absolute negative — the everyday way to say "not" or "no" about something real. It is overwhelmingly translated simply "not" (904 of 1,637 times, 73%), with the rest being grammatical variations like "did not," "do not," or a standalone "no." In the Septuagint it appears over 5,200 times, almost always rendering the Hebrew negative לֹא ("no/not"), and the papyri confirm it was the standard choice when stating a plain fact (the grammarians contrast it with μή, used for hypothetical or commanded negation).
caution: Roughly a quarter of its uses get absorbed into English phrasing and carry no word of their own, so its force is grammatical rather than easily pinned to a single gloss.

definition: The act of giving thanks or the inner attitude of gratitude, especially expressed toward God in worship.
article: εὐχαριστία covers both the inward feeling of gratitude and the outward act of giving thanks, and in the New Testament it leans heavily toward thanksgiving — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "thanksgiving" in 9 of 15 occurrences (75%) and "thank" in 2 more. Built from εὐχάριστος, it appears 15 times across 9 books, often in worship contexts directed to God. The everyday flavor of the word shows up in the inscriptions and papyri: Moulton-Milligan cite a letter from the Emperor Claudius to a sports club expressing his "gratitude" for games held in his honor, showing the word was at home in ordinary expressions of appreciation, not only religious ones.
caution: Septuagint evidence is thin (just one occurrence), and Abbott-Smith's two senses — gratitude versus the act of giving thanks — overlap closely enough that any single passage can be hard to pin down.

definition: Describing someone who is generous and willing to share what they have with others.
article: εὐμετάδοτος describes a person who freely gives and shares with others — built from "well" (εὖ) and "to impart" (μεταδίδωμι), so literally "good at sharing." It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:18, where it pairs with κοινωνικός ("willing to share"). The word turns up in everyday Koine documents too, including eight times in the astrologer Vettius Valens, where it sits among traits like "intelligent, sincere, generous, pleasant" — a snapshot of how ordinary people used it to praise a giving character.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise shade of meaning rests on a single verse plus scattered outside evidence.

definition: Joppa, a coastal town in Judea, northwest of Jerusalem.
article: Ἰόππη is simply the name of Joppa, a port town on the coast of Judea, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 10 times, all clustered in the story of Peter (the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Joppa" in 70% of cases, with the rest being phrases that happen to include the name). It comes straight from the Hebrew place name יָפוֹ, which the Septuagint translates three times. Interestingly, the spelling itself was debated in antiquity: ancient grammarians preferred the form Ἰόπη with one 'p', while the double-p spelling Ἰόππη of the New Testament manuscripts is supported by only a few coins.

definition: A confident expectation or hope, usually of something good and looked forward to with pleasure.
article: ἐλπίς means hope—not wishful thinking, but a confident expectation of good. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "hope" in 47 of 54 occurrences (92%), and the meaning is remarkably stable: in both the New Testament and classical Greek it nearly always points to something good rather than dreaded. In the Septuagint it stands behind several Hebrew words, most often תִּקְוָה ("hope," 17×) but also בֶּ֫טַח and related words meaning "trust" or "security" (over 20× combined), which is why glosses like "trust" and "confidence" appear. Everyday papyri use it the same way—one writer speaks of crops giving "the best hopes," and a disk simply reads "I have good hopes."

definition: To be amazed, marvel, or be surprised at something remarkable, unexpected, or hard to believe.
article: θαυμάζω covers the whole range of reacting to something striking — being amazed, marveling, or simply surprised — and the measured renderings cluster tightly around those ideas, with "amazed" alone covering 17 of 46 occurrences (41%). It can stand alone or take an object, including marveling at a person. A nice everyday touch comes from the papyri: one second-century letter uses it for the surprise (and disbelief) a writer expects to stir in his reader, and another writer says "I am much surprised at not receiving a letter from you," showing the same flavor of incredulous wonder found in passages like John 3:7.
caution: The senses shade into one another, so the line between "amazed," "marveled," and "surprised" is a translator's judgment rather than a sharp distinction in the Greek.

definition: To travel through or journey across a place, passing from one point to another.
article: διαπορεύομαι means to travel through or pass across a region, usually picturing someone moving from place to place. Built from διά ("through") and πορεύομαι ("to go"), it appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament — for instance, Jesus passing through the grainfields (Luke 6:1) or going through towns and villages teaching (Luke 13:22). It is far more common in the Septuagint (37 times in 16 books), where it usually renders the Hebrew עָבַר ("to pass over"), and the papyri even use a related participle for the "current" month, showing the word's everyday sense of something passing or running its course.
caution: The measured-sense labels here are garbled fragments of surrounding text rather than clean glosses, so they should be read as all pointing to the single, agreed meaning "to journey through."

definition: To announce something ahead of time, whether predicting a future event or promising something in advance.
article: This rare verb combines "before" (πρό) with "announce" (καταγγέλλω), giving the basic idea of declaring something ahead of time. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the sense splits: in Acts 3:18 and 7:52 it means to foretell or predict (as God did through the prophets), while in 2 Corinthians 9:5 it shifts toward a promise made in advance, rendered "gift." Moulton-Milligan note it is rare even in everyday Koine, citing a comparable form in Clement of Alexandria meaning "the previously announced land."
caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences with low confidence), and the prediction versus promise senses make its exact range hard to pin down.

definition: A preposition usually meaning "to" or "toward," marking direction, motion, or relationship between people or things.
article: πρός is one of the most common Greek prepositions in the New Testament, appearing 706 times, and the overwhelming majority of the time (88%) it simply means "to" or "toward," pointing at a person, place, or goal. It can also shade into "with" or "alongside" when describing being near or in someone's company. The classical lexica note it can pair with three grammatical cases, but in the New Testament it is almost entirely tied to the accusative (679 times) with only one genitive and seven dative uses. In the Septuagint it overwhelmingly translates the Hebrew word אֶל ("to, toward"), which fits its core directional meaning perfectly.

definition: Lasting for an age—eternal, without end, and sometimes without beginning, depending on context.
article: αἰώνιος describes what belongs to or lasts for an age, and in practice the New Testament uses it overwhelmingly to mean "eternal": the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way in 60 of its 70 appearances (91%). Built from αἰών ("age"), it can point to what has no end (eternal life, eternal fire), and the lexica note it can even describe what has no beginning. The most telling outside evidence is the papyri: it was a standard title for the emperor's "eternal" power and household, showing that everyday Greek never lost the sense of "perpetual." In the Septuagint it appears 115 times, almost always translating the Hebrew עוֹלָם ("forever, age")—91 of those cases.

definition: To fill something completely, or to bring something to completion—especially to make a prophecy or promise come true.
article: πληρόω carries two closely linked ideas: physically filling something up and bringing something to its intended completion. Most often in the New Testament it describes prophecy coming true—rendered "fulfilled" or "fulfill" in roughly half its 88 occurrences—but it also means literally filling a space or person, as when a sound "filled the house" (Acts 2:2). The Septuagint mostly uses it for the Hebrew מָלֵא ("to fill," 44 times), and everyday papyri show a striking commercial sense: "to pay" a debt in full, which survives in Modern Greek.

definition: Describing a person or thing that matches the divine standard of right—upright, fair, and doing what is proper.
article: δίκαιος describes someone or something that lines up with what is right—whether a person living rightly before God, an action that is fair, or a verdict that is just. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 81 times, and the standard rendering is overwhelmingly "righteous" (71%), with "right," "just," and "righteous man" filling out the rest. In the Septuagint it appears 308 times, most often translating Hebrew צַדִּיק ("righteous," 144×), and a vivid everyday detail survives in the papyri: the word was applied to a "just measure" and a "just rule," showing how naturally Greek speakers connected it with fairness and correctness.

definition: Describing someone or something that does not lie and is completely truthful.
article: ἀψευδής is built from the negative prefix and the word for falsehood (ψεῦδος), so it literally means "without lie" — truthful, free from deceit. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Titus 1:2, where it describes God as one who "cannot" lie, and only once in the Septuagint (Wisdom 7:17). Everyday Koine documents show the word and its adverb in active use; one inscription from Abydos pairs a closely related term with the idea of being "witnessed throughout the whole world," highlighting the sense of reliable truthfulness.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A blowing of air—either a gust of wind or the breath that gives a living being life.
article: πνοή covers the movement of air in two related ways: a rushing wind and the breath that animates a living person. It appears only twice in the New Testament, once for each sense—Acts 2:2 describes the sound of a violent wind at Pentecost, while Acts 17:25 speaks of God giving everyone life and breath. The breath sense dominates in the Septuagint, where the word renders the Hebrew נְשָׁמָה 13 times, including God breathing life into the first human in Genesis 2:7, and an ancient sundial inscription uses πνοή for the blowing of the west wind.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, confidence is low, though the Septuagint and classical evidence agree on the same two senses.

definition: The condition of being a slave; bondage or servitude, whether literal or used figuratively.
article: δουλεία means slavery or bondage — the state of being owned and subject to a master. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, almost always rendered "slavery" (4 of 5 occurrences); the one apparent exception ("itself" in Romans 8:21) just reflects English phrasing, not a different meaning. The Septuagint uses it 43 times, often translating the Hebrew word for forced labor or service (עֲבֹדָה, 14×), and several times it even stands for "Egypt" — the land where Israel was enslaved. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the same range, from the actual services of slaves to slavery as an abstract condition.
caution: The Romans 8:21 rendering "itself" is a translation artifact, not a separate sense, so the word effectively carries just one meaning.

definition: Made without yeast; in the plural it names the Jewish festival of unleavened bread tied to Passover.
article: ἄζυμος literally means "without yeast," built from a negative prefix plus the word for leaven (ζύμη). In practice the New Testament uses it mostly as a fixed name: the plural "the (Feast of) Unleavened Bread," which accounts for about two-thirds of its 9 occurrences, while the rest describe literal unleavened bread or matter. In the Septuagint it appears 54 times and almost always renders the Hebrew מַצָּה (matzah), the unleavened cakes eaten at Passover; Paul also stretches it figuratively in 1 Corinthians 5:7 to describe Christians as free from corruption.
caution: The figurative "uncorrupted/sincere" use noted by the lexica rests mainly on a single Pauline passage and is not counted among the measured senses.

definition: To try or attempt to do something, making an effort toward a goal.
article: This verb means to try, attempt, or make an effort. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and the Majority Standard Bible renders both visible occurrences simply as "tried" (for example, Acts 9:26 and Acts 26:21). It usually shows up in the middle or passive form (πειράομαι) even when the meaning is active, and Moulton-Milligan note it appears freely in everyday Koine papyri—one second-century BC letter uses it for people who "try to come home quickly" after escaping danger. In the Septuagint it stands in for the Hebrew נָסָה ("to test").
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 occurrences, with one absorbed into phrasing, so the sense range rests on a very small sample.

definition: A conflict between people, usually a quarrel or dispute carried on with words rather than physical fighting.
article: In the New Testament μάχη refers to strife, contention, or quarreling, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "conflicts" in both of the places it gives it a distinct English word (2 Corinthians 7:5 and James 4:1). Although the word can mean a literal battle, the weaker "verbal quarrel" sense is what shows up in the New Testament. In the Septuagint it appears 18 times, most often translating the Hebrew word רִיב ("dispute"), and Moulton-Milligan illustrate it from a quirky fortune-telling papyrus predicting that a twitching toe means a man "will have strife on account of a female."
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences—two of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing—the measured evidence is thin, though the lexicons agree on the "quarrel" sense.

definition: Something marvelous that astonishes you, or the feeling of amazement such a thing produces.
article: θαῦμα refers either to a wonder—a concrete marvelous thing—or to the abstract feeling of amazement it stirs up. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing just once in the Byzantine text (twice in the critical text), at 2 Corinthians 11:14 for the marvel itself and Revelation 17:6 for the amazement. The everyday flavor shows up in the papyri: one traveler named Antonius Theodoros boasts that he stayed a long time in imperial Rome and 'saw the wonders there'—using θαύματα for the sights of a great city.
caution: Evidence is thin: only one or two New Testament occurrences and a handful of Septuagint uses, so the precise split between concrete and abstract senses is not firmly fixed.

definition: The rudder or steering blade of a boat, used to control its direction.
article: Πηδάλιον is the steering rudder of a boat, and the New Testament uses it both literally and as an illustration. It appears just twice: the plural in Acts 27:40, where sailors loosen the rudders of Paul's ship, and the singular in James 3:4, comparing the tongue to a small rudder that steers a large vessel. Everyday Koine papyri confirm this nautical meaning vividly—one freight account from the first or second century lists a rudder priced at 14 drachmas and 4 obols, and another document describes a boat outfitted with two rudders.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences this word is thinly attested in the corpus, though papyri and lexica agree firmly on its meaning.

definition: The inhabited world — the populated earth and, in its narrower use, the Roman Empire and its peoples.
article: οἰκουμένη is literally "the land being inhabited," the populated world, and in the Byzantine NT it is rendered "world" 11 of 16 times (69%) and "earth" twice (13%). The range stretches from the whole inhabited earth down to a more pointed meaning: in everyday Koine it was a standard label for the Roman Empire. A papyrus announcing Nero's accession (P Oxy VII.1021, A.D. 54) calls him "the expectation and hope of the οἰκουμένη," showing how naturally the word stood for the Roman world. In the Septuagint it appears 45 times, most often translating the Hebrew tevel, "world."
caution: Classical and lexical sources note a narrower "Roman Empire" sense (and even "the inhabitants") that the broad renderings "world" and "earth" can obscure, so context decides the scope.

definition: A heifer, a young cow, especially one suitable for sacrifice.
article: Δάμαλις means a heifer, a young female cow. It appears just once in the New Testament (Hebrews 9:13), but turns up 39 times in the Septuagint, where it renders several Hebrew animal words including עֶגְלָה (calf/heifer) 11 times and פָּרָה (cow) 6 times. The word was at home in everyday Koine, showing up in inscriptions about sacrifices to the gods and even, interestingly, as a personal name for Athenian women.
caution: The single New Testament occurrence is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own word, so direct English evidence is thin.

definition: To let something hang loose, slacken, or weaken; or to pass over and disregard something.
senseLabels: to let droop or grow weak
article: In the New Testament παρίημι appears only once, in Hebrews 12:12, where it describes "limp" or drooping hands that need strengthening—the sense of being relaxed, slackened, or exhausted. The word has a wider range than this single use suggests: in the Septuagint it occurs 10 times across 9 books, rendering several Hebrew verbs like חָדַל and רָפָה ("to cease" or "slacken"), and lexicons note a second sense, "to pass by, neglect, disregard," seen in Luke 11:42 in critical texts. The everyday papyri are especially vivid here: one Oxyrhynchus document records a father's complaint that his son's name had been left off (παρεῖκεν) a list of young men, showing the "omit" sense in real bureaucratic life.
caution: With only one Byzantine NT occurrence and a low confidence tier, the measured data covers just the "slacken/weaken" sense, while the "disregard" sense rests on lexicons and the critical-text reading of Luke 11:42.

definition: Describing a person, body, or thing that is no longer alive; also used figuratively for what is lifeless or powerless.
article: νεκρός means "dead" in the plainest sense, and that is how it reads in 125 of its 131 Byzantine occurrences (98%). It works both as an adjective ("dead, lifeless") and as a noun ("the dead," a corpse), and the New Testament stretches it figuratively too — for people spiritually dead, or for things like faith and works that are powerless and inoperative. The everyday papyri reinforce its literal weight: documents list "expenses for the corpse" and note that a dead body was widely regarded as unclean, as in a Torino papyrus stating that certain goddesses abhor dead bodies.

definition: To seal something completely shut, fastening it securely with a seal so it cannot be opened.
article: This verb intensifies the ordinary word for sealing (σφραγίζω) by adding κατά, giving the sense of sealing thoroughly or all over. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 5:1, where the scroll is sealed with seven seals, and twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times rendering the Hebrew חָתַם. Everyday papyri confirm its practical use: one document describes a jar (σταμνός) being sealed up, and another mentions grain sealed away in a storage chest.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests mostly on Old Testament and papyri evidence.

definition: Greater in amount, degree, or measure than something else; more abundant or excessive.
article: This is the comparative form of περισσός (G4053), expressing something that is "more" — more abundant, greater in degree, or in excess. The lexicons agree on this range: it covers everything from a greater quantity to something superfluous or far more than needed. Notably, the word does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament text used here, though it shows up 15 times in the critical (SBLGNT) text, so its New Testament evidence depends on which Greek text you follow.
caution: There are no measured senses for this word, and it is absent from the Byzantine text (0 occurrences) while present 15 times in the critical text, so the evidence here is thin and text-dependent.

definition: To fold or roll up something, especially to close up a scroll after reading.
article: πτύσσω means to fold or roll up, and in the New Testament it appears just once, in Luke 4:20, where Jesus rolls up the scroll after reading. The word's range is narrow and physical: it describes the everyday act of furling a scroll back into its rolled form. The Byzantine NT and critical text agree it occurs only here, and the related noun πτυκτός shows up in the papyri meaning a folding writing-tablet, confirming this 'folding' sense in ordinary Koine.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its meaning rests on a single passage plus outside evidence; note also that the digest's measured 'attendant' rendering reflects surrounding context, not the verb's own meaning of rolling up.

definition: A state of being prepared and ready, or the firm footing that readiness provides.
article: This noun, built from the verb ἑτοιμάζω ("to prepare"), means readiness or preparation, and possibly a firm footing. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Ephesians 6:15, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "fitted readiness"; both BSB and Dodson agree with that sense. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times across 4 books, and everyday papyri use it for practical preparation — one document speaks of waiting "until the preparation is made" after sowing. Lexicons note a secondary possibility of "foundation" or "firm footing" (from Psalm 89:14), but this reading is debated.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one New Testament occurrence — and lexicographers disagree over whether it means "readiness" or "firm footing" in Ephesians 6:15.

definition: To believe or trust someone or something, especially to place religious faith in God or Christ.
article: πιστεύω overwhelmingly means "believe"—the Majority Standard Bible renders it that way 220 times (98%), and the Berean Standard Bible independently agrees at the same rate. Its range stretches from simply accepting that something is true to actively placing one's trust in a person, which is why it can also shade into "entrust" (as the passive "be entrusted with"). In the Septuagint it almost always stands in for the Hebrew אָמַן (36 of 48 times), the word behind ideas of firmness and faithfulness; the everyday papyri show the same construction "believe someone" used in ordinary documents.

definition: Poverty or destitution—the condition of having very little, even to the point of beggary.
article: Πτωχεία describes severe poverty or destitution, the state of someone who has next to nothing. The Majority Standard Bible renders all 3 New Testament occurrences as "poverty" (with one instance phrased "though poverty"), and the BSB agrees fully. In the Septuagint it appears 12 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew word for affliction or want (עֹנִי). A vivid glimpse of its everyday use comes from a Christian begging-letter on papyrus (P Gen I. 14) that pleads, "have pity on me in my poverty"; the word later even named poor-relief in Justinian's legal code.
caution: Evidence is thin—only 3 New Testament occurrences—but the few uses and the lexicons agree closely on "poverty."

definition: To give someone grace or favor, freely making them the object of special kindness.
article: χαριτόω means to endow someone with grace or favor — to make them the recipient of free, unearned kindness. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Ephesians 1:6 and Luke 1:28), and is built directly from χάρις, the word for grace or favor. One striking detail: the only comparable use Moulton-Milligan could find in everyday documents is a 4th-century charm (BGU IV.1026), which ends with the line "I will bestow favor upon thee" — and the word survives in Modern Greek as χαριτωμένος, meaning "charming."
caution: Evidence is thin: the word occurs only twice in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint (Sirach 18:17), and the lexica list overlapping shades — from "make graceful" to "cause to find favor" — so its exact force is somewhat uncertain.

definition: To unveil or uncover something, especially removing a covering that blocks clear perception or understanding.
senseLabels: a veil that stays in place
article: ἀνακαλύπτω literally means to take off a veil or covering, formed from καλύπτω (to cover) with the prefix ἀνά signaling reversal. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 3, where Paul uses it figuratively about removing the hindrance to perceiving spiritual things — though the two renderings here (
caution: - language captures it as a veil left unlifted or as beholding with unveiled face. In the Septuagint it shows up 19 times, mostly translating the Hebrew גָּלָה ("to uncover, reveal"), and Moulton-Milligan find it in ordinary papyri, including a healing inscription where a god "uncovers" a garment.",

definition: Eunice, the personal name of Timothy's Jewish mother mentioned once in the New Testament.
article: Eunice is a personal name appearing just once in the New Testament, at 2 Timothy 1:5, where she is identified as Timothy's mother. The name is built from the Greek elements meaning "well" and "victory," so it carries the sense of "victorious," and the lexica note she was Jewish. Interestingly, the measured rendering data here records "grandmother" for this single occurrence, which conflicts with the standard lexical identification of Eunice as Timothy's mother (his grandmother being Lois).
caution: This name occurs only once, and the measured "grandmother" rendering disagrees with the lexica, which consistently call Eunice Timothy's mother.

definition: A group of envoys or representatives sent to negotiate or deliver a message on behalf of someone.
article: In the New Testament, πρεσβεία means a delegation or embassy—a group of representatives sent to negotiate, used both times in Luke (14:32 and 19:34) where the Majority Standard Bible and Berean Standard Bible both render it "delegation" in all cases. The word literally springs from ideas of seniority and rank, and Abbott-Smith notes its older senses of "age" and "dignity," but in practice it points to the people sent on a mission. Moulton-Milligan observes that πρεσβεία was an everyday term in the diplomacy between Greek cities and kings, which sharpens its force in Jesus' parables; a later papyrus even uses it to mean "intercession."
caution: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its measured range here is narrow even though the lexica record broader senses like seniority and rank.

definition: A thought, purpose, or settled intention—the way of thinking that shapes a person's mind and aim.
article: ἔννοια refers to a thought, purpose, or settled frame of mind—what someone has decided to do or how they intend to think. It appears only twice in the New Testament (Hebrews 4:12 and 1 Peter 4:1), and the lexicons describe a range from "consideration, thinking" to a concrete "purpose" or "design." The Septuagint uses it twelve times, all in Proverbs, where it usually renders the Hebrew מְזִמָּה ("discretion" or "scheming"), and everyday papyri show the same flavor—one document speaks of people "having come to the same conclusion."
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences, and the measured rendering as "body" reflects the surrounding phrasing of 1 Peter 4:1 rather than the word's actual meaning of thought or intention.

definition: To make someone strong, giving them inner firmness and stability.
article: σθενόω means to strengthen or make firm, built on the noun σθένος ("strength, might"). It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Peter 5:10, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "secure" (the Berean Standard Bible agrees), describing God making believers firm after suffering. The word turns up in everyday Koine documents too: papyri use the related noun σθένος for sheer might, as in a petition asking that stolen cattle be sought "with all one's might."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense rests on a single verse plus the word's known root meaning.

definition: To wait for someone or something with eager, expectant longing.
article: This verb describes not just waiting but waiting with eager anticipation, used of expecting either a person or a thing to arrive. It appears 8 times across 6 New Testament books, and translators consistently render it as "eagerly await" or close variants like "wait eagerly." An interesting detail: Moulton-Milligan note this rare word also appears in the apocryphal Acts of Paul, describing Onesiphorus standing outside Lystra "waiting for" Paul to arrive—a vivid everyday picture of expectant watching.
caution: It is a rare word with relatively thin attestation outside the New Testament, though sources agree closely on its meaning.

definition: A personal name, Amos, borne by an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy.
article: Ἀμώς is an indeclinable proper name borrowed from Hebrew, appearing once in the Byzantine New Testament (the critical text has it 3 times) as one ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke 3:25. In the Septuagint it shows up 20 times across 5 books, where it stands in for three different Hebrew names: אָמוֹץ (the prophet Isaiah's father, 11×), עָמוֹס (the prophet Amos, 7×), and אָמוֹן (the king, 2×). Abbott-Smith notes the name's slipperiness, distinguishing the king Amon from the prophet Amos and observing that manuscripts and Josephus spell it variously.
caution: Evidence is thin and confidence is low: the name occurs just once in the Byzantine NT and the underlying Hebrew name behind it varies across the sources.

definition: Sosipater, the personal name of a man who was a relative of the apostle Paul.
article: Sosipater is a man's name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Romans 16:21), where Paul calls him one of his countrymen sending greetings. The name is a lengthened form of Sopater, and Moulton-Milligan suggests this Sosipater may be the same person as the Sopater of Acts 20:4. Both forms of the name were common in everyday life, well attested in Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once in the New Testament, so its identification with the Sopater of Acts 20:4 remains uncertain.

definition: To make something warm; in the middle voice, to warm oneself, as at a fire.
article: This verb means to heat or warm something, and in its middle form it means to warm oneself—most often beside a fire. In the New Testament it appears 6 times across 3 books, mostly describing people warming themselves at fires, like Peter in the courtyard during Jesus' trial (Mark 14:54, 67; John 18:18, 25). The Septuagint uses it 11 times, chiefly to translate the Hebrew verb חָמַם, also meaning to be or grow warm.
caution: The measured sense list separates "warming himself" and "himself," but these reflect translation phrasing rather than truly distinct meanings—the core sense is simply to warm or warm oneself.

definition: To make something firm, solid, or strong, whether physically or in a figurative sense like strengthening faith.
article: στερεόω means to make something firm or solid, and from there to strengthen. In the New Testament it appears only 3 times (all in Acts), and where it's translated it consistently means "made strong"—as when a lame man's feet and ankles are strengthened in Acts 3:7 and 16. The Greek Old Testament uses it far more often (29 times across 13 books), often rendering Hebrew words for spreading out or restraining, and a colorful medical-magical papyrus even uses it in a gout charm: "as the sun is made firm... so make firm this creature."
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and one of them absorbed into phrasing, the measured English evidence is thin even though the word's general meaning is well attested.

definition: The act of dividing something into parts, or of distributing or giving things out.
article: μερισμός covers two related ideas: dividing something into parts and distributing or handing things out. In its only two New Testament appearances it shows both senses — in Hebrews 2:4 it means a distribution (of gifts), while in Hebrews 4:12 it refers to a dividing or separation (of soul and spirit). Everyday Koine papyri confirm this practical range, using the word for the official division of grain measures and for securing one's allotted share.
caution: Only 2 New Testament occurrences, each rendered differently, so the word's full range rests on thin biblical evidence.

definition: A small emphasizing particle that adds urgency or precision to a command or statement, often like "now," "then," or "indeed."
article: δή is a tiny particle with no exact English equivalent; it adds emphasis or exactness to whatever word it attaches to, often rendered "now," "then," "indeed," or left untranslated. It is rare in the New Testament, appearing only 7 times across 6 books, and it frequently attaches to commands and exhortations (as in "Let us go now"). It is far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 274 times and overwhelmingly renders the Hebrew particle נָא (183×), a word that softens or urges a request. The everyday papyri show the same flavor, as in P Oxy 907's λέγω δὴ τῇ Διδύμῃ, "to wit, Didyme."
caution: The measured "senses" here are really fragments of surrounding translation rather than distinct meanings, since this particle rarely maps to a single English word and is sometimes absorbed into phrasing entirely.

definition: To approach someone with a request on another's behalf, or to bring a complaint against someone, to a person in authority.
article: At its core ἐντυγχάνω means to go to a person—often someone in authority—and make a petition, either for someone or against them. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, rendered "intercedes" twice (Romans 8:27, Hebrews 7:25) and "about" once where the appeal is against Israel (Romans 11:2); the remaining two are absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday Koine papyri make the basic sense vivid: Moulton-Milligan cite cases like the 13 village clerks who "appealed to the dioecetes," the standard verb for filing an official petition.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and 2 absorbed into phrasing, the measured "about" label simply reflects an appeal directed against someone (Romans 11:2).

definition: To say or declare something out loud, often introducing or quoting someone's spoken words in a conversation.
article: φημί is a common verb for speaking, used to report what someone says, declares, or asks. Its range is broad but tightly clustered around conversation: in the Byzantine New Testament it is rendered "said" 20 times (41%), with "declared," "replied," "answered," and "asked" filling out most of the rest, so the exact English word usually depends on the flow of dialogue. Tellingly, in 10 of 59 occurrences it gets absorbed into the phrasing with no English word of its own — it simply marks that someone is speaking. The everyday papyri confirm this plain usage, where ἔφη regularly means "he stated" or "he said" in contracts and reports.

definition: The seed-bearing head or ear of a cereal plant like wheat or barley, growing at the top of the stalk.
article: στάχυς refers to the ear or head of a grain plant — the cluster of seeds standing out at the top of the stalk. In the New Testament it appears 5 times, mostly describing disciples picking heads of grain (3 of 5 occurrences), though in Mark 4:28 it covers both the plant's head and its ripening grain. The Septuagint uses it 20 times, chiefly for the Hebrew word shibbolet (15×), and everyday Koine papyri such as a first-century farm account (A.D. 78–79) confirm it was the ordinary agricultural term.

definition: To unroll a scroll, opening it out so its writing can be read.
article: ἀναπτύσσω means to unroll or unfold something, especially a scroll. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 4:17, where Jesus unrolls the scroll of Isaiah to read it. In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times, where it usually translates the Hebrew פָּרַשׂ ('to spread out'), which fits the picture of unfurling something flat. Note that some critical editions of Luke 4:17 read ἀνοίξας ('having opened') instead of this word.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the manuscript tradition at Luke 4:17 is split between ἀναπτύσσω and ἀνοίξας.

definition: To turn something over in the mind—to ponder, plan, or busy oneself diligently with it.
article: μελετάω carries the idea of mentally working through something, whether pondering, planning, or practicing oneself in it. The Byzantine NT has it just 3 times, and in the one occurrence the Majority Standard Bible renders distinctly (Acts 4:25) it appears as "spoke," while the other two are absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The Septuagint uses it far more (31×), most often for Hebrew הָגָה (12×), as in Psalm 1:2, "in His law will he exercise himself"—and the ancient lexicographer Hesychius defines it as "exercise oneself, practice, train," suggesting an active, habitual sense beyond mere reflection.
caution: Evidence is thin and the rendering disputed—classical lexica favor "practice/exercise oneself" while the measured NT data shows only "spoke," so the precise range is uncertain.

definition: To be fitting, proper, or suitable; in the New Testament always used in the sense of what is right or appropriate.
article: καθήκω literally means "to come down" or "reach to," but in its 2 New Testament occurrences it always carries the figurative sense of being fitting or proper, rendered "fit" both times (Acts 22:22; Romans 1:28). The dictionaries note this same range: the original "come down, come to" meaning shades into "be fit, proper," often used impersonally. Moulton-Milligan points out that you don't need Stoic philosophy (where τὰ καθήκοντα was a technical term for "duties") to explain Paul's usage—the everyday papyri and inscriptions amply attest the plain sense of "is becoming, is fit," as in a soldier's "fitting allowance."
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a confidence tier marked low, this entry rests on thin biblical evidence, though the broader Koine sources agree on the meaning.

definition: Someone who joins with others in imitating a person or example, a fellow imitator.
article: This rare compound combines "with/together" (σύν) and "imitate" (μιμέομαι), so it means joining others in following someone's example. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Philippians 3:17, where Paul urges his readers to be "co-imitators" of him. Lightfoot suggested the force is "vie with each other in imitating me — one and all of you imitate me," and Moulton-Milligan note this is one of Paul's favorite compounds, also attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is otherwise unattested in biblical sources, so its precise nuance rests on a single verse.

definition: The state of being disgraced or dishonored, or a lowly, undistinguished use or function.
article: ἀτιμία describes dishonor, shame, or disgrace — the opposite of being held in honor. The same word can also shift toward something humbler: a vessel made "for common use" rather than for special, honored purposes (Romans 9:21; 2 Timothy 2:20). In the Septuagint it appears 34 times, most often standing in for the Hebrew קָלוֹן (15×) and כְּלִמָּה (8×), both words for shame and reproach; a papyrus edict of Caracalla (A.D. 212) even uses it for the official "mark of disgrace" attached to a person.
caution: With only 7 New Testament occurrences and 3 of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, the split between "disgrace" and "common use" rests on thin data.

definition: To make someone's way go well — literally to have a successful journey, or figuratively to prosper and succeed.
article: εὐοδόω is built from "well" (εὖ) and "road" (ὁδός), so its root idea is having a good journey, and from there it broadens to prospering and succeeding in general. It appears 4 times across 3 books in the Byzantine New Testament — covering both the literal travel sense (Paul hoping his way to Rome will go well) and the figurative one (the wish in 3 John 2 that the reader may prosper). The Septuagint uses it heavily, 50 times, most often (36×) for the Hebrew צָלַח, "to prosper or succeed," and the papyri confirm the everyday travel sense, as in a letter praying that God will speed the writer's journey to his sister.
caution: The New Testament evidence is thin (only 4 occurrences), and the literal-versus-figurative balance depends on context, though the lexicons and corpus data agree on the overall range.

definition: Words of comfort or encouragement that draw the mind away from worry and toward solace.
article: παραμύθιον refers to consoling or encouraging speech—the kind of words that ease a troubled mind. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:1, and just once in the Septuagint (Wisdom 3:18). One vivid example comes from a papyrus letter where a mother asks her son to write constantly about his health so she may have παραμύθιον, a comfort, regarding her own situation. The classical lexica note two shades—an exhortation or encouragement, and an assuagement or consolation—and Moule describes it as the converse that draws the mind aside from care.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and thin overall attestation, the precise emphasis (encouragement versus consolation) is hard to pin down.

definition: To fall down or collapse, whether a person dropping to the ground or a structure falling into ruin.
senseLabels: to fall down to the ground
article: καταπίπτω simply means to fall down or collapse, built from κατά ("down") and πίπτω ("fall"). In the Septuagint it can describe people who are bowed down being lifted up (Psalm 145:14), and the everyday papyri use it again and again for houses that have fallen into ruin, with one writer even using it figuratively for "bearing nobly the things that befall you." Note that the two MSB renderings shown here — "kick" and "minds" — reflect the surrounding phrasing of the verses, not the verb's own meaning, which the lexicons agree is "fall down."
caution: The evidence is thin (only 2 Byzantine occurrences) and the measured renderings reflect phrase context rather than the verb itself, so lean on the lexicon sense "to fall down."

definition: As an adverb, it means 'first'—first in time, order, place, or importance.
article: This is the adverb 'first,' the neuter of πρῶτος used to mark what comes first in time, sequence, rank, or importance. The range is narrow and stable: the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'first' in 53 of 59 cases (96%), with just 2 instances leaning toward 'begin'—as in 'First say, Peace to this house' (Luke 10:5). It appears 59 times across 17 books of the Byzantine New Testament, and 4 of those occurrences are absorbed into English phrasing without a word of their own.

definition: To carry, bear, or lead someone or something away from one place to another, sometimes by force.
article: ἀποφέρω combines ἀπό ("away from") with φέρω ("carry"), meaning to bear or lead something off to another place. In the Byzantine New Testament's 5 occurrences it ranges from a body being carried by angels (Luke 16:22) to Jesus being led away to Pilate (Mark 15:1), where the sense carries a hint of force. A charming bit of evidence comes from the papyri: a boy's letter complains, "So kind of you not to have taken me off with you to town!" — the same everyday verb at work.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences, the distinct senses here are really just one core meaning ('carry away') colored by different contexts.

definition: To imitate someone or something, following their example in behavior or character.
article: Μιμέομαι means to imitate or copy, taking another person or their conduct as your model. The New Testament's four uses split between imitating a person (as in 2 Thessalonians 3:7 and Hebrews 13:7) and imitating what is done (3 John 1:11, "imitate what is good"), but both are really the same basic idea of following an example. The word comes from μῖμος, an actor or mimic, and everyday Koine papyri show it in ordinary life—one letter urges a son to "imitate your father, the brave old man."
caution: With only four occurrences, the split into two "senses" reflects grammar (imitating a person versus a thing) rather than a real difference in meaning.

definition: A person who complains or mutters discontentedly, a grumbler.
article: γογγυστής means a grumbler — someone who mutters complaints rather than speaking openly. It appears just once in the New Testament (Jude 16), and in that lone instance it's woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than getting its own English word. The term comes from the verb γογγύζω (to murmur), and Symmachus and Theodotion used related forms in their Greek versions of Proverbs and Isaiah.
caution: This word is a New Testament hapax with only one occurrence, so its range cannot be measured from usage.

definition: To build something together with others, used in the New Testament for believers being built up jointly into one structure.
article: συνοικοδομέω combines "with" (σύν) and "build" (οἰκοδομέω), so its base meaning is to construct something jointly or build it up together. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Ephesians 2:22, where it is used figuratively of Christians being built together into a dwelling place for God; in that verse it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than carrying its own English word. The everyday literal sense is well attested outside the Bible: an Oxyrhynchus papyrus speaks of "dyeing-workshops constructed jointly," and Abbott-Smith notes it can mean either building with someone or building various materials up together.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a single Septuagint use (1 Esdras), the evidence base is thin and the confidence tier is low.

definition: Describing the late part of the day, used in the New Testament as a noun meaning evening or nightfall.
article: The basic idea of ὄψιος is 'late,' and in the New Testament it almost always appears as a noun (ἡ ὀψία) meaning 'evening.' All three measured senses point to the same time of day — the Majority Standard Bible renders it 'evening' or 'evening came' in every occurrence — so the apparent variety is really just sentence phrasing rather than different meanings. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the usage exactly: one document from A.D. 167-8 has the phrase 'when the hour was late' (ὀψίας τῆς ὥρας γενομένης), the same construction found in Mark 11:11.

definition: A helper—someone who comes to your aid or assists you, especially in time of need.
article: βοηθός means a helper or supporter, someone who comes to your aid. In the New Testament it appears just once, in Hebrews 13:6, where it is rendered "helper"—a quotation drawing on the Septuagint, which uses the word 49 times, most often to translate the Hebrew word for "help" (עֵזֶר). One striking detail comes from everyday papyri and ostraca, where βοηθός very commonly named the assistants of tax-gatherers, and even described a regional governor as "the helper of the district."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so the measured sense rests on a single passage.

definition: A person who makes peace—someone who brings about reconciliation rather than conflict.
article: εἰρηνοποιός describes someone who actively makes peace, built straightforwardly from the words for "peace" (εἰρήνη) and "do/make" (ποιέω). It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jesus' blessing on the "peacemakers" in Matthew 5:9, and every translation surveyed—the Majority Standard Bible, BSB, and KJV—renders it the same way. The lexicons add a slightly broader flavor, with Dodson noting senses like "pacific" or "loving peace," suggesting the word can describe a peaceable disposition as well as the act of making peace.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range cannot be measured from biblical usage alone.

definition: A personal name borne by a Christian woman in the church at Philippi.
article: Euodia is a woman's name, appearing just once in the New Testament (Philippians 4:2), where Paul urges her and Syntyche to agree with each other. Older translations like the KJV mistakenly rendered it as the masculine "Euodias," but the form is feminine, as Abbott-Smith and Dodson note. The name was common in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite it across inscriptions and papyri, including a B.C. 217 memorial tablet and a later receipt where a woman named Euodia handles two pounds of linen shirts.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only once, so there is no general meaning to define beyond the person it names.

definition: A connecting phrase meaning "which is" or "that is," used to explain or translate a preceding word.
article: This is a two-word phrase combining the relative pronoun ὅς ("which") with ἐστι, the third-person singular of the verb "to be" (εἰμί). Together they function as an explanatory connector—"which is," "that is to say"—often introducing a translation or clarification of a name or term. The Byzantine NT records zero occurrences of this as a tagged lemma, and the only substantial lexical material here concerns the verb "to be" on its own (its uses in Homer, Herodotus, and Thucydides for existing, being, or being true as opposed to merely appearing).
caution: The evidence is thin and mismatched: the phrase shows zero measured occurrences, and the lexicon excerpt describes the standalone verb "to be" rather than this explanatory phrase.

definition: A person's speech or way of talking, including the accent or dialect that reveals where someone is from.
article: λαλιά means speech or talk — the act of speaking and, often, the distinctive way a person talks. In the New Testament it appears only 4 times, and notably it can point to a telltale accent: Peter is recognized as a Galilean by his λαλιά (Matthew 26:73, Mark 14:70). The measured renderings here are fragmentary phrase-snippets rather than clean glosses, but the underlying idea is consistent: someone's speech or what they say. Interestingly, the classical lexica note this word originally carried a negative shade of "chatter" or "talkativeness," and Moulton-Milligan cites a Christian papyrus letter warning against much talking — yet in the New Testament the word has softened to plain "speech."
caution: The measured sense labels are mangled phrase fragments rather than reliable glosses, so lean on the lexica and context; also note that classical sources record a "chatter/loquacity" sense not clearly present in the New Testament.

definition: To roll or be rolled along the ground, often describing a body thrashing or wallowing back and forth.
article: κυλιόω means to roll or roll along, and in its single New Testament appearance (Mark 9:20) it describes a boy who fell and rolled around on the ground. The word is a late form of an older verb and shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, so it was ordinary, common-life vocabulary. In the Septuagint it occurs 10 times across 7 books, most often rendering the Hebrew גָּלַל ("to roll") three times, and Abbott-Smith notes that in Homer it could describe a person rolling about as a sign of grief.
caution: This word appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its New Testament range rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To count or include someone as part of a particular group or list.
article: καταριθμέω means to reckon someone in among a group — to count them as one of the number. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 1:17, where Judas was "numbered" among the apostles, and three times in the Septuagint. A papyrus from 164 B.C. uses it the same way, listing all men who are to be "counted in" as subject to the fish tax, the beer tax, and other charges, which nicely matches the New Testament sense of being included in a group.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single verse.

definition: The number four thousand, used to count people or things.
article: This word simply means "four thousand," built from the parts for "four" and "thousand." It appears 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament, mostly counting the crowd Jesus fed and a group of rebels in Acts. The measured data splits its renderings between "four thousand" (60%) and a shorter "four" (40%), but every occurrence still refers to the same figure—the difference is just how the surrounding phrase was translated. A 5th- or 6th-century papyrus uses it of four thousand artabas of grain that were sold, showing it was ordinary commercial vocabulary in everyday Koine.
caution: The "four" rendering in 2 of 5 cases reflects translation phrasing, not a separate meaning, since every source agrees the word always means four thousand.

definition: Describing sin as something that readily surrounds, entangles, or trips a person up, like an obstacle in every direction.
article: This word appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 12:1, where it describes sin as something that easily clings to or hinders us as we run our race. The compound packs in the idea of being "well-surrounded" on every side, and the Majority Standard Bible renders the single occurrence with the older phrase "let" (an archaic word for hindrance), matching the BSB. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan note that the related noun περίστασις turns up in everyday papyri (as in a B.C. 168 letter) meaning "distress" or "calamity," which supports an alternate reading: the sin "because of which one easily falls into distresses."
caution: This is a hapax with only one New Testament occurrence, and the early commentators (Westcott versus Theophylact) genuinely disagreed on whether it means "easily surrounding" or "easily leading into distress."

definition: Reverent devotion toward God that shapes how a person lives.
article: εὐσέβεια describes piety or devotion directed at God, expressing itself in a reverent way of life. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 15 times across 5 books and is rendered "godliness" in 13 of those (93%), with the rest absorbed into phrasing. The classical lexica note a broader range than the New Testament shows: Abbott-Smith records an earlier sense of reverence toward parents and others, and the everyday papyri use it for religious devotion and even "loyalty" — including a letter where the Emperor Claudius thanks an athletic group. In the Septuagint it usually stands behind the Hebrew word for "fear" (יִרְאָה), as in the fear of the LORD.

definition: To be a matter of concern to someone; to be something a person cares about or attends to.
senseLabels: it is a care or concern
article: This verb almost always shows up in the impersonal form "it matters" or "it concerns," usually paired with a person in the dative — as in "do you not care that we are perishing?" The Majority Standard Bible renders it as "care" in 4 of its 9 occurrences (80% of the times it gets its own English word), while the other 4 are absorbed into phrasing with no separate word.
