A nice everyday parallel survives in the papyri: a private letter from A.D. 84 reads "I know that you are concerned about me," using this very verb the same way the New Testament does.
caution: Classical lexica note a transitive sense "to care for," but Abbott-Smith says it appears in neither the Septuagint nor the New Testament, so the biblical range is narrower than the dictionaries' full entry suggests.

definition: Describing someone whose faith or trust is weak or insufficient.
article: ὀλιγόπιστος combines the words for "little" and "faith," describing a person whose trust falls short rather than someone who has no faith at all. It appears 5 times in the New Testament, almost always rendered "little faith" (4 of 5 times, 80%), with one instance (Matthew 16:8) shortened to "little." Notably, Moulton-Milligan reports the word is not found in non-biblical authors, suggesting it was a distinctively biblical and early Christian term, though it does appear later in the Acts of Thomas.
caution: The evidence is thin: this word occurs only 5 times, all in Jesus' words in Matthew and Luke, and is essentially absent from wider Greek literature.

definition: A large quantity of people or things; often the whole assembled group taken together.
article: πλῆθος names a large quantity — whether of people, fish, or even sins — and the various English renderings (number, multitude, crowd, large number) really capture shades of the same core idea. A distinct second use, marked by the definite article, refers to a whole assembled group, like a congregation or town population. It is very common in Scripture, appearing 32 times in the Byzantine NT and 185 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew רֹב ("abundance," 88×); everyday Koine papyri also use it concretely for "amounts" or "sums" of goods and money.

definition: Pharaoh, the title used for the kings of ancient Egypt.
article: Φαραώ is simply the title "Pharaoh," the general name for the kings of Egypt. It is an indeclinable word borrowed from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה, which the Septuagint renders some 249 times, and the New Testament uses it 5 times in references to Israel's history (Acts, Romans, and Hebrews). The slightly different renderings counted in the data—"Pharaoh," "Pharaoh's," and so on—are just grammatical variations of the same single meaning; in Acts 7:10 it even appears in the fuller phrase "Pharaoh king of Egypt."

definition: A person from Berea, a city in Macedonia.
article: This is an adjective meaning "belonging to Berea" or "a Berean," identifying someone as a native of that Macedonian city. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:4, describing Paul's companion Sopater. Note that the measured rendering as "province" disagrees with every lexicon (Strong's, Dodson, Abbott-Smith), which all define it straightforwardly as "Berean" — the lexical sources should be trusted here.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the measured "province" rendering conflicts with all the lexica, which agree it simply means "Berean."

definition: Something written — from individual letters of the alphabet to documents, bills, and the written law, or collectively, learning.
article: γράμμα covers anything written, ranging from single letters of the alphabet to bills, documents, and the written law. In the Byzantine New Testament the Majority Standard Bible renders it "letters" 4 times (40%) and "written code" twice (20%), the latter contrasting the external written law with the Spirit (as in Romans 2:27 and 7:6); 5 of 15 occurrences are absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. The most telling evidence comes from the papyri: hundreds of everyday documents describe an illiterate person with the phrase γράμματα μὴ εἰδότος, "not knowing letters," since someone else had to write on their behalf.

definition: To take hold of or grasp someone or something, whether to help, to arrest, or simply to take.
article: This verb means to lay hold of or grasp, and its tone depends entirely on context: it can be gentle help (Jesus taking a blind man by the hand) or hostile force (men seizing Paul to drag him off). Across its 19 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "took" 5 times, "took hold" 3 times, and "seized" 3 times, with the remaining 7 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it appears 44 times and most often translates the Hebrew חָזַק, "to be strong" or "to grasp firmly," which fits its sense of taking a firm hold.

definition: From heaven or from the sky; describing something coming down from above.
article: This adverb means "from heaven" or "from the sky" — the ending signals motion or origin from above. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 14:17 and Acts 26:13), and the Majority Standard Bible renders both as "heaven," with other translations agreeing. Beyond the New Testament it shows up once in the Septuagint (4 Maccabees 4:10), and Moulton-Milligan notes it was a real word in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, not just a literary form.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, the evidence base is thin, though all sources agree on the meaning.

definition: An adverb meaning "seven times," indicating how many times an action happens or is repeated.
article: This adverb, built from the number seven (ἑπτά), simply means "seven times" — the four measured renderings in the New Testament are all just variations of that single idea, each appearing once. It shows up only in Jesus's teaching on forgiveness (Matthew 18:21–22 and Luke 17:4). It's far more common in the Septuagint, where it appears 21 times across 6 books, often translating the Hebrew verb for sprinkling (נָזָה, 10 times) in ritual contexts where something is sprinkled seven times.

definition: The act of telling things apart by careful judgment, whether discerning good from evil or sorting out disputes.
article: διάκρισις is about the act of distinguishing or judging — separating one thing from another through careful evaluation. It appears only 3 times in the New Testament, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "distinguishing" twice (1 Corinthians 12:10; Hebrews 5:14) and "passing" judgment once (Romans 14:1). The everyday Koine papyri ground this nicely: one document from A.D. 233 uses διάκρισις for the official review or examination of tax-gatherers' books, and other papyri use it for inspecting priestly lists — so the word carried a practical sense of "examination" or "sorting out" in ordinary life.
caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, so its full range is hard to pin down.

definition: Pregnant; carrying an unborn child.
article: ἔγκυος simply means "pregnant" or "with child," and it has just this one meaning across its uses. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 2:5, describing Mary, and shows up only once in the Septuagint (Sirach 42:10). The word was thoroughly at home in everyday Koine: marriage and legal papyri use it matter-of-factly, as in an Oxyrhynchus document about a bride who is pregnant "at the time of the separation."
caution: This is a New Testament hapax with only one Septuagint use, so the corpus evidence is thin even though the meaning is clear and undisputed.

definition: A person from Tyre, the ancient Phoenician port city.
article: Τύριος is simply the adjective meaning "of Tyre" or "Tyrian," used to describe inhabitants of the Phoenician coastal city. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 12:20, where the Majority Standard Bible's rendering happens to fall on the word "king's" in context rather than a direct gloss of "Tyrian." In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times across 4 books, translating several different Hebrew words including צֹרִי (the Hebrew word for Tyre itself), which confirms its straightforward geographic meaning.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured sense rests on a single occurrence and should be read with that limited evidence in mind.

definition: A pointing word meaning "of this kind" or "such as the following," introducing something specific that is about to be described.
article: τοιόσδε is a demonstrative adjective meaning "such" or "of this kind," typically pointing forward to something specific that follows. In the New Testament it appears only once, in 2 Peter 1:17, where it introduces the words spoken by the divine voice at the Transfiguration. Classical authors like Homer used it both for quality ("such a minstrel as this") and for degree ("so great" or even "so bad"), and Moulton-Milligan also tracks its weaker relative τοῖος in everyday papyri, including a letter asking why someone came to talk "about such a woman."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise force of this word in biblical usage rests on a single verse plus its broader classical range.

definition: The accusative form of the first-person pronoun: "me," the speaker as the object of an action.
article: ἐμέ is simply the emphatic accusative of the Greek word for "I," meaning "me" when the speaker is on the receiving end of an action. It belongs to the pronoun ἐγώ, whose full forms (ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ) carry emphasis, while the lighter enclitic forms (μου, μοι, με) are used where no stress is intended. Interestingly, in the Septuagint this pronoun family renders Hebrew expressions like הִנֵּנִי ("here I am") and stands in for the simple "I am," and ἐγώ-related forms appear 235 times across 28 books.
caution: This form does not occur in the Byzantine New Testament text measured here, so its NT range cannot be assessed directly from those occurrences.

definition: An interrogative adverb asking about time, meaning "when?" or, in the phrase "how long?", asking how much time remains.
article: πότε is a question word about time, basically asking "when?" In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 19 times and splits fairly evenly between three uses: asking "how long" (often in the phrase "how long will I be with you?"), "when did" something happen, and "when will" something occur. It shows up in the Septuagint 43 times, most often translating the Hebrew מָתַי ("when?"), and the everyday papyri use it the same way—one third-century BC letter asks the recipient to clarify "when it will be convenient for you to send."

definition: Severity or sternness in dealing with someone, especially the harsh, decisive rigor of carrying something through to the full.
article: ἀποτομία describes severity or harshness—the literal sense of being "cut off" sharply, like the steepness of a rock face, applied figuratively to stern treatment. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only twice, both in Romans 11:22, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "severity" in contrast with God's kindness. The everyday papyri make the meaning vivid: a court document from A.D. 186 (P Oxy II. 237) speaks of "the severity of the law" being enforced rigidly, exacting a statute's provisions to the full rather than straining them.
caution: Both New Testament occurrences are in a single verse (Romans 11:22), so the measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Describing land that is mountainous or hilly; as a noun, the hill country, especially of Judea.
article: ὀρεινός is an adjective meaning "mountainous" or "hilly," built from ὄρος (mountain). In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Luke 1 (verses 39 and 65), where it functions as a noun for "the hill country" of Judea. The word was common in everyday Koine: the papyri regularly use it to describe canals along the edge of the desert, and in the Septuagint it occurs 17 times, often rendering the Hebrew שְׁפֵלָה (lowland).
caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a confidence tier of low, both uses are the same noun phrase, so the apparent two senses reflect translation wording rather than distinct meanings.

definition: Describing a ship marked with a figure-head or emblem identifying it.
article: παράσημος literally means "marked alongside" and in its single New Testament appearance describes a ship distinguished by a carved figure-head — in Acts 28:11, the twin gods Castor and Pollux (the Dioscuri). The word's range elsewhere is broader: classical writers used it for something marked amiss, counterfeit, or spurious, and later for notes marked in the margin of a text. The everyday papyri back up the New Testament use nicely; one document from A.D. 15 describes a ship whose figure-head is an ibis, confirming this was the standard nautical term for a vessel's emblem.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into the phrasing rather than rendered by its own English word, so its precise force rests on outside evidence.

definition: Water — the ordinary liquid used for drinking, washing, and baptizing, and also a figure for spiritual refreshment.
article: ὕδωρ is the everyday Greek word for water, and the corpus bears this out: in 77 of 79 Byzantine New Testament occurrences (99%) it simply means "water," whether for drinking, washing, or baptizing. Its range stretches naturally from the literal to the figurative — the lexicons note metaphorical uses like "living water" and "the water of life" for divine truth and spiritual refreshment. The Septuagint uses it 597 times, overwhelmingly for Hebrew מָ֫יִם (496×), and the everyday papyri show the same plain sense, as when a document records "we release the water" from an irrigation channel.

definition: To press something down firmly so that it is packed tightly together.
article: πιέζω means to press down or pack together, used just once in the New Testament at Luke 6:38, where a measure of grain is shaken and pressed down to fit more in. In the Septuagint it appears once, at Micah 6:15, describing the pressing of olives (translating a Hebrew word). The everyday papyri preserve this same root idea of pressing, and a related noun even points toward a crowbar or pressing-tool. Abbott-Smith notes a later sense, 'to seize,' which overlaps with the closely related word πιάζω (G4084), but that meaning is not seen in this word's New Testament use.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence is thin, and this word is easily confused with the related πιάζω.

definition: An opponent in a lawsuit—the person on the other side of a legal case, or by extension any adversary.
article: At its core ἀντίδικος is a legal term for the person on the opposing side of a lawsuit, and it's well attested in everyday Koine: Moulton-Milligan cite a vivid Egyptian papyrus court case about the identity of a child. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 5 times, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "adversary" or as part of phrases like "adversary hand" and "appealing against adversary," all matching the courtroom setting (Matthew 5:25, Luke 12:58, 18:3). In the Septuagint it appears 7 times, often translating Hebrew רִיב ("dispute"). Strong's also notes a special application to Satan as the arch-enemy, reflecting its use in 1 Peter 5:8.
caution: Several of the measured senses ("hand," "adversary hand") reflect how the word sits inside translated phrases rather than separate meanings, so the genuine sense is essentially just "legal opponent/adversary."

definition: A person who inherits jointly with others, sharing in the same inheritance.
article: Συγκληρονόμος combines "with" (σύν) and "heir" (κληρονόμος) to mean someone who inherits together with others — a co-heir. It appears 4 times in the New Testament, rendered "heirs" 3 times and "fellow heirs" once (1 Peter 3:7), where it takes a genitive object naming what is shared. Notably, this word was once thought absent from everyday Greek, but Deissmann found it in an Ephesian inscription naming someone a σ[υγ]κληρονό[μου], and it also turns up in Byzantine-era papyri, confirming it as ordinary Koine vocabulary.
caution: With only 4 occurrences, the evidence base is thin, though the meaning is consistent across all sources.

definition: Intense, overflowing joy — a jubilant gladness that bursts out in celebration.
article: ἀγαλλίασις means exuberant, exultant joy — not quiet contentment but gladness that overflows into celebration. Across its 5 New Testament occurrences the Majority Standard Bible renders it "joy" 2 times, while 2 more times it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing and once it appears within the Hebrews 1:9 expression about being anointed "above companions." In the Septuagint it shows up 17 times, mostly in the Psalms, where Abbott-Smith notes it is often paired with εὐφροσύνη ("gladness"), reinforcing its sense of paired, abounding rejoicing.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and nearly half absorbed into phrasing, the measured English picture is thin, and the listed Hebrew counterparts in the digest look mismatched to a word meaning "joy."

definition: Priscilla, a Christian woman married to Aquila, named several times in the New Testament.
article: Priscilla is the name of a Christian woman, the wife of Aquila, appearing 4 times in the Byzantine New Testament (3 in the critical text). The name is actually a diminutive — a more familiar, affectionate form — of the formal name Prisca; the book of Acts tends to use "Priscilla" while the letters use "Prisca." One striking note: the scholar Harnack suggested Priscilla may have authored the Epistle to the Hebrews, though this remains only a proposal.
caution: As a proper name it has a single sense, but the same person appears under both Priscilla and the formal Prisca, which sources treat as one woman.

definition: A small plant whose leafy stalks were tied into a bunch and used to sprinkle liquids in religious cleansing rituals.
article: Hyssop is a plant whose branches were bundled together and used for ritual sprinkling, appearing only twice in the New Testament (John 19:29 and Hebrews 9:19), always rendered "hyssop." In the Septuagint it shows up 10 times and almost always translates the Hebrew word אֵזוֹב (9 of 10 times), tying it firmly to Old Testament purification practices. One intriguing wrinkle: in John 19:29, where hyssop is offered to Jesus on the cross, some scholars suspect the original word was actually ὑσσῷ ("a javelin") rather than ὑσσώπῳ ("hyssop"), a possible copying error noted by both Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a documented suggestion that John 19:29 may originally have read "javelin" rather than "hyssop," the reading in that verse is genuinely disputed.

definition: The quality or state of being holy; moral and spiritual purity treated as an abstract attribute.
article: ἁγιότης names holiness as a state or quality, built from the adjective ἅγιος ("holy"). It is very rare, appearing just once in the Byzantine New Testament (twice in the SBLGNT critical text) and only once in the Septuagint, at 2 Maccabees 15:2. A striking detail from the papyri is that the word later served as a title of honor: a sixth-century letter addresses one bishop's "holiness" (τὴν σὴν ἁγιότητα), much as one might say "Your Holiness" today.
caution: Evidence is thin — only one Byzantine occurrence and a single Septuagint instance — so its range cannot be measured with confidence.

definition: To cut something off completely, such as severing a body part or cutting a rope loose.
article: ἀποκόπτω means to cut something off or sever it, used both for body parts (a hand or foot in Mark 9, the high priest's servant's ear in John 18) and for cutting ropes loose (Acts 27:32). Of its 6 New Testament occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "cut off" 4 times and "cut" once, with one instance absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The most striking detail comes from Galatians 5:12, where in the middle voice Paul uses the word for self-mutilation or castration — Moulton-Milligan notes this as the climax of his unusually blunt, vernacular language in that letter.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the harsher reflexive sense ("mutilate oneself") rests on a single disputed passage rather than measured frequency.

definition: To lead someone astray—either physically wandering off course or, more often, being deceived away from truth.
article: πλανάω literally means to cause something to roam or wander, but in the New Testament it overwhelmingly carries the figurative sense of deceiving people or leading them away from the truth—rendered "deceived" in 57% of its 40 Byzantine occurrences. The original wandering sense survives in passages like the lost sheep parable (Matthew 18:12-13), bridging the physical and moral meanings. In the Septuagint it usually translates Hebrew תָּעָה (40×), "to go astray." Everyday papyri confirm the deceptive sense vividly—one document from AD 123 complains of someone "injuring me much and ending by deceiving me."

definition: To rise or come up, especially of the sun, light, or clouds appearing in the sky; also to cause something to rise.
article: This verb mostly describes things coming up into view — above all the sun rising, but also light, clouds, and a star. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 6 books, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "rose" in 6 of those 9 (75%). The Septuagint uses it 55 times to translate several Hebrew words, most often צָמַח ("to sprout," 18×) and זָרַח ("to shine/rise," 14×), which adds a growing-or-springing-up flavor; everyday Koine papyri use the phrase "at the rising of the sun" to mean daybreak.
caution: Lexicons list both a transitive "cause to rise" sense (as in Matthew 5:45) and an intransitive "rise," but the measured renderings only capture the intransitive use.

definition: The supreme divine being, God; also, more generally, any god or deity worshiped as divine.
article: θεός is overwhelmingly the New Testament word for God, rendered "God" in all 1,216 measured occurrences (with the Majority Standard Bible at 100% and the BSB independently agreeing 97% of the time). Though the NT use is almost entirely about the one true God, the word's basic range is broader: classical lexica note it can mean any god or deity, as when crowds call Paul a god (Acts 28:6) or speak of pagan gods. In the Septuagint it appears over 3,200 times, mostly translating Hebrew אֱלֹהִים (2,187×) but also the divine name יְהֹוָה (230×); strikingly, everyday papyri and inscriptions even applied the title θεός to Ptolemaic kings, calling Ptolemy V "a god from a god and goddess."

definition: An adverb meaning "not yet," marking that something has not happened up to the present moment.
article: οὐδέπω is a negative time-adverb meaning "not yet" — it signals that an event or condition has not come about so far. The four measured renderings ("yet," "Jesus yet," "not," "something does not") all reflect this single "not yet" idea, just absorbed differently into English phrasing across its 5 New Testament occurrences. A nice everyday parallel comes from the papyri: an apprenticeship contract from A.D. 66 describes a boy as οὐδέπω ὄντα τῶν ἐτῶν, "not yet being of age" — that is, not yet old enough for the poll-tax.
caution: The word appears only 5 times in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so the sample is small even though sources agree on its meaning.

definition: An anointing—either the act of smearing with oil or the substance used—applied in the New Testament to a spiritual endowment from God.
article: χρῖσμα refers to an anointing, and scholars debate whether it means the act of anointing itself or the oil used to anoint—the digest notes commentators split on this point. All 3 New Testament occurrences cluster in 1 John (2:20, 2:27), and the Septuagint uses it 8 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word מִשְׁחָה for anointing oil. Interestingly, it also turns up in everyday Koine papyri, including a third-century document referring to a "lunar ointment."
caution: Confidence is low: the word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in 1 John, and sources genuinely disagree on whether it means the act of anointing or the substance used.

definition: A religious festival or feast, especially one of the recurring sacred celebrations in the Jewish calendar.
article: ἑορτή means a feast or festival — a sacred, often recurring celebration. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 27 times, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "feast" in 69% of cases, with the remaining occurrences usually naming a specific festival like the Passover. In the Septuagint it appears 97 times and most often translates Hebrew חָג ("feast," 59×), and the papyri show it was an everyday word — one letter from A.D. 84 mentions buying little pigeons "for the festival," while an apprenticeship contract grants a boy 20 holidays a year on account of festivals.

definition: To break apart or dissolve something, especially to scatter and disperse a gathered group of people.
article: At its core διαλύω means to break something completely apart or dissolve it. In its single New Testament appearance (Acts 5:36), it describes how the followers of the rebel Theudas were scattered and dispersed after his death. Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one document worries that a flock of sheep might be scattered (διαλυθῆναι), and an inscription forbids any proposal to break up a society or its sacrifices.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there is very narrow.

definition: A legion, a large unit of the Roman army, used to picture a very great number.
article: This is a Latin loanword (from legio) that Greek speakers borrowed for the Roman army's largest infantry unit, traditionally numbering several thousand soldiers. In the New Testament it appears 4 times, always rendered "Legion," sometimes literally and sometimes as a vivid way of saying "an enormous number." The everyday Koine papyri confirm the word's ordinary military use, with documents naming specific units like "the twenty-second legion."
caution: The word appears only 4 times in the Byzantine text and is absent from the SBLGNT critical text, so attestation in the New Testament itself is thin.

definition: To ask someone a question, or to make a request of them.
article: ἐρωτάω covers two related actions: asking a question to get information, and asking someone for something — that is, making a request. The questioning sense dominates the Byzantine New Testament, where renderings like "ask" and "asked" account for about 68% of the 58 occurrences, but the requesting sense shows up clearly too (for instance, asking on someone's behalf in Luke 4:38 and John 17:9). In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew שָׁאַל 52 of 64 times, and Moulton-Milligan note it is so well attested in everyday papyri — like a letter urging "I ask you by every means to send me the rest at once" — that there is no need to treat its requesting sense as a Hebrew influence.

definition: A preposition meaning "about" or "concerning" something, and sometimes "around" a place or "for" the sake of someone.
article: περί is one of the most common Greek prepositions, appearing 331 times in the Byzantine New Testament, and its core idea is "round about." In the New Testament it overwhelmingly means "about" or "concerning" (rendered "about" 136 times, 70%), though it also covers "for" or "on behalf of" (29 times) and occasionally "around" a place. One notable detail: in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew kāpar ("to atone") 101 times, reflecting its frequent use in sacrificial contexts where an offering is made "concerning" or "for" sin.
caution: Many fine-grained renderings (like "was," "that about," "about for") reflect translation phrasing rather than distinct meanings, and over a third of occurrences are absorbed into English without a separate word.

definition: To give an authoritative order or instruction, telling someone to do something, often by an official or person in charge.
article: προστάσσω means to give a command or instruction, and by extension to appoint or assign someone to a task or place. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across 4 books, mostly meaning to order or instruct, though Abbott-Smith notes a secondary sense of appointing (as in Acts 17:26). The papyri make its everyday legal flavor vivid: Moulton-Milligan cite documents from the 200s–100s BC where 'the sovereigns decree' (βασιλέων προσταξάντων) was a stock formula for official royal commands.
caution: In 2 of 8 New Testament occurrences the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a distinct English word, so its exact force can be hard to pin down in those cases.

definition: A wolf, the wild predator, often used figuratively for dangerous people who attack or exploit others.
senseLabels: wolf the hired hand abandons sheep to
article: λύκος is the ordinary Greek word for a wolf, and that literal sense covers most of its uses — the Majority Standard Bible renders it "wolves" in 4 of its 6 New Testament occurrences. The other two come from a single verse (John 10:12) describing the wolf that the hired hand abandons the sheep to and that pounces on the flock. In the Septuagint it appears 8 times and consistently translates the Hebrew זְאֵב (7×), and a 129 B.C. papyrus vividly records wolves mangling bodies after a door was left open. Beyond the literal animal, the word is regularly applied figuratively to predatory people, as in the warning about "wolves" in sheep's clothing.
caution: The two separate John 10:12 "senses" reflect different phrasings of one verse rather than genuinely distinct meanings.

definition: A common preposition marking movement, separation, or origin away from something — most often translated "from."
article: This is one of the most frequent prepositions in the Greek New Testament, appearing 654 times, and it overwhelmingly means "from" — separation or starting point — rendered that way in 99% of measured cases. It covers motion away from a place, a partitive sense ("some of"), and figurative separation from things like sin or death. Notably, in 249 of its 654 occurrences it gets absorbed into English phrasing without its own word, and in the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew preposition מִן (647 times), which carries the same "from" idea.

definition: To spit on or at someone, usually as an act of contempt or insult.
article: This verb means to spit upon someone, a deliberate gesture of scorn and humiliation. In all 6 New Testament occurrences it describes mockery, mostly aimed at Jesus during his trial and abuse. The Septuagint uses it twice for the Hebrew יָרַק, and a papyrus from 218 B.C. shows the same vivid phrase 'spit in the face,' confirming this was everyday Koine usage and not a specialized religious term. The single rendering 'kept spitting' (Mark 15:19) simply reflects the ongoing action in that scene; the basic meaning stays the same.

definition: The personal name Tertullus, a lawyer who prosecuted Paul before the governor at Caesarea.
article: Tertullus is a Roman personal name, appearing only twice in the New Testament (Acts 24:1-2), where he serves as the professional prosecutor brought against Paul before the governor at Caesarea. The two "measured senses" both simply render the name Tertullus, the second occurrence just falling near Paul's name in the text. Moulton-Milligan note it is a diminutive of Tertius and that it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, including as a name carried by a colleague of Pliny in the second century AD.
caution: This is a proper name occurring only twice, so there is no real range of meaning to analyze beyond identifying the person.

definition: To overcome, defeat, or prevail over an opponent, obstacle, or hostile power.
article: Νικάω means to conquer or prevail, and in the Byzantine New Testament it almost always carries this sense of overcoming—whether Christ overcoming the world, or believers overcoming evil and the enemy. The range is fairly tight: across 28 occurrences nearly half are rendered simply "overcome," with related phrasings like "one who overcomes" filling out most of the rest. Beyond Scripture, the everyday Koine papyri show a vivid spread of uses: it was a legal term for winning a lawsuit (as in Romans 3:4), an athletic term for winning a contest, and even a wish for an athlete to "always win."

definition: The Euphrates, a major river of western Asia that served as a boundary of the Roman province of Syria.
article: Εὐφράτης is simply the proper name of the Euphrates River. In the New Testament it appears only twice, both in Revelation (9:14 and 16:12), where it is named as a real geographic landmark. The name is far more common in the Septuagint, where it occurs 20 times across 9 books, almost always rendering the Hebrew פְּרָת.
caution: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its biblical range is too thin to say much beyond its identity as the river's name.

definition: Something owed to someone, whether a literal debt of money or a moral obligation that is rightfully due.
article: ὀφειλή covers what one person owes another, ranging from a concrete sum of money to a moral obligation. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears just twice, split evenly: once as a literal "summoned debt" (Matthew 18:32) and once as what is "due" to others (Romans 13:7). Tellingly, although older lexicons claimed the word was rare outside the New Testament, the papyri show it turning up frequently in everyday business documents in the plain sense of "debt"—including a loan record from 9 B.C.
caution: Evidence is thin, with only 2 Byzantine occurrences, so the sense range rests heavily on supporting papyri and lexicons.

definition: To fight against an enemy and win, overcoming or subduing them through struggle.
article: καταγωνίζομαι combines κατά with ἀγωνίζομαι ("to struggle") to mean struggling against someone and prevailing—conquering or subduing them. It appears just once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 11:33, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "conquered" (and the Berean Standard Bible agrees). The word shows up in everyday Koine outside the Bible too: an inscription (OGIS 553.7) uses it of someone "having conquered the adversaries," which fits the military sense lexicons give it.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range is judged from outside sources rather than measured biblical usage.

definition: To control something completely, like a master mastering a slave, bringing it firmly under one's command.
article: This vivid word literally means to make a slave of someone or drag them into bondage, but in its single New Testament appearance (1 Corinthians 9:27) Paul uses it figuratively of bringing his own body under control, which the Majority Standard Bible renders as 'discipline.' The image is forceful: not gentle training but a master subduing a slave. Everyday Koine papyri show both meanings—one Oxyrhynchus document from AD 49–50 uses the related noun for a man who tried to carry off a writer's young son into actual slavery, while the philosopher Epictetus uses the verb in the same moral sense Paul does.
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured meaning rests on a single verse.

definition: An adverb meaning "still" or "even now," pointing to a moment that continues up to the present.
article: ἀκμήν is an adverb meaning "still" or "even now," used to mark something that remains true right up to the present moment. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Matthew 15:16, where it is rendered "still" 100% of the time. The word is literally the accusative of a noun meaning "a point" (the source of English "acme"); in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions it could even carry the stronger sense of "greatly" or "by far," reflecting that original "point" meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range there rests on a single example.

definition: One who knows people's hearts — the inner thoughts, character, and motives hidden from others.
article: This compound word literally means "heart-knower," combining the words for "heart" and "to know." It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts (1:24 and 15:8), where it describes God as the one who knows the inner life of every person. Moulton-Milligan note it first surfaces in Acts and connects it to the thought in Jeremiah 17:10, where God is said to search hearts.
caution: With only two occurrences, both in Acts, the evidence is thin, and one source suggests the word arose from early Christian liturgical usage rather than wider Koine speech.

definition: A phrase meaning "if not," used to mark an exception — "except" or "unless" — to a preceding statement.
article: εἰ μή combines εἰ ("if") with μή ("not") to mean literally "if not," which in practice works as "except" or "unless." The KJV renders it variously as "but, except, save (only), saving," or "till," showing its main job is carving out an exception to whatever was just said. Note that this two-word phrase has no occurrences measured on its own in the Byzantine NT digest, since the evidence here describes the component particle εἰ rather than the full expression.
caution: The digest reports zero measured occurrences for this phrase and supplies lexical detail only for the single particle εἰ, so the range of εἰ μή itself is not directly attested in this evidence.

definition: To practice magic or sorcery, performing spells and occult arts.
article: This verb means to practice magic or sorcery, and it appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:9, describing Simon's activities. The classical lexica note it could also mean to be a Magus or skilled in Magian lore, though only the magic-practicing sense shows up in the biblical text. An interesting bit of evidence: the early Christian manual Didache pairs it with sorcery in an expanded Ten Commandments — "you shall not practice magic, you shall not practice sorcery" — and the word still survives in modern Greek meaning "bewitch."
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on very thin evidence.

definition: Something that binds people or things together — a tie, fastening, or uniting bond.
article: σύνδεσμος literally names something that fastens or binds, like the ligaments holding the body together (Colossians 2:19), and it extends naturally to the figurative idea of a bond that unites people — the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3) or love as the bond of unity (Colossians 3:14). Across its 4 New Testament uses the binding image stays constant whether literal or metaphorical. Everyday papyri use it concretely: Aristeas speaks of the great doorway and the 'fastenings' that held it to the door-posts, showing the plain physical sense behind the spiritual one.
caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences (2 of them absorbed into phrasing), the sense distinctions rest on thin data.

definition: To feel regret or change one's mind about something already done or said.
article: This verb covers the inner shift of regretting or rethinking something, whether that's a son changing his mind about working (Matthew 21:29), Judas filled with remorse (Matthew 27:3), or Paul reflecting on whether he regrets a painful letter (2 Corinthians 7:8). Its six New Testament uses spread fairly evenly across these shades, all of which the BSB renders independently the same way. In the Septuagint it most often stands in for the Hebrew נָחַם, and everyday Koine papyri show the same reflexive 'repent oneself' meaning, with a calendar inscription using the weaker sense of simply 'regret.'
caution: Lexicographers note the difficult-to-maintain distinction between this word and the related μετανοέω ('to change one's mind, repent'), and it does not appear in the SBL critical text.

definition: A written document such as a scroll or book, including a formal record like a divorce certificate.
article: βιβλίον is the everyday Koine word for a written document—a scroll, book, letter, or formal record. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 36 times, rendered "scroll" 15× (45%), "book" 12× (36%), and as "the Book" of life 4× (12%). Though it began as a diminutive of βίβλος, Moulton-Milligan note that it never actually meant a "little writing" but became the standard term for any book; in the Septuagint it occurs 161 times, usually translating the Hebrew סֵ֫פֶר (sēper, "book/scroll").

definition: Describing someone given to too much wine, and the drunken, quarrelsome behavior that comes with it.
article: πάροινος literally combines "beside" (παρά) and "wine" (οἶνος), picturing a person who stays close to the bottle. In its 2 New Testament appearances—both in lists of qualifications for church leaders (1 Timothy 3:3 and Titus 1:7)—the Majority Standard Bible renders it once as "dependent on wine" and once as "violent," capturing both the drinking habit and the aggressive conduct it produces. A vivid papyrus letter shows the related verb in action: a man named Artemidorus complains to Zeno that his companions got him drunk and led him astray, illustrating exactly the kind of behavior the word warns against.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a split rendering between "dependent on wine" and "violent," the precise emphasis—drinking versus the quarrelsomeness it causes—is hard to pin down.

definition: Lacking something necessary; in need, especially of basic resources like food or money.
article: ἐνδεής describes someone who lacks what they need — needy, poor, or in want. Although it appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 4:34), it shows up 22 times in the Septuagint, often translating Hebrew words for the poor or the lacking, and it's well attested in everyday Koine papyri. One papyrus poignantly records a family "being in want of 25 drachmas for the funeral of Philip," forced to sell his cuirass — capturing the word's ordinary sense of falling short of life's necessities.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there is narrow, though the Septuagint and papyri broaden the picture.

definition: A rainbow, or a halo of colored light encircling something.
article: In the New Testament ἶρις means a rainbow, and that is exactly how it is rendered in both of its two occurrences, both in Revelation (4:3 and 10:1), where the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible agree 100%. The word had a wider range outside the NT: lexicons note it could also name Iris, the messenger goddess of pagan myth, or the iris plant. That botanical sense is the one we see in everyday Koine: a 2nd-century papyrus has someone promising to send 'a cotyle of orris-root' (from the iris plant) for a daughter, and the single Septuagint use translates a Hebrew word for an aromatic spice.
caution: This word appears only twice in the NT, both in the symbolic visions of Revelation, so its 'rainbow' meaning rests on very limited biblical evidence.

definition: The act of choosing or selecting someone, used in the New Testament always of God's choice of people.
article: ἐκλογή means a choosing or selection, and across its 7 New Testament occurrences it always refers to God's choice—most often translated "election" (2×) or rendered through related phrases like "chosen instrument" (Acts 9:15) and "beloved chosen" (1 Thessalonians 1:4). In one passage (Romans 11:7) it stands by association for the chosen people themselves rather than the act of choosing. Outside the Bible the word was ordinary Koine: a papyrus ordinance from 118 BC uses it of officials picking out the best Crown land for themselves, and a marriage contract speaks of the "choice" resting with the bride.
caution: With only 7 occurrences and rendering split across five phrasings, the specific English wording varies even though the underlying meaning of divine choosing is consistent.

definition: Wool, the soft fiber from sheep used for making cloth.
article: ἔριον simply means wool—the fiber from sheep used in textiles. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: at Hebrews 9:19, where scarlet wool was used in a ritual, and at Revelation 1:14, where Christ's hair is described as white as wool. The everyday nature of the word shows up clearly in the papyri, where it turns up in inventories and shipping records measuring out quantities of wool by weight, and the Septuagint uses it 10 times, most often translating the Hebrew word for wool, צֶמֶר.
caution: The first listed "sense" ("proclaimed along wool") simply reflects the surrounding phrase at Hebrews 9:19, not a distinct meaning—both occurrences mean wool.

definition: To bear up under hardship and stay firm rather than give up, or simply to stay behind in a place.
article: ὑπομένω combines "under" and "remain," picturing someone who stays put under pressure rather than fleeing. In the New Testament it overwhelmingly means to endure or persevere through trials (about 81% of its 17 uses), with a smaller literal sense of simply remaining behind somewhere, as when the boy Jesus stayed in Jerusalem (Luke 2:43). In the Septuagint it leans toward a different shade—it most often translates Hebrew קָוָה, meaning to wait or hope (8×)—and the everyday papyri show the same range, with one writer vowing to "endure my ministry" after praying for healing.

definition: To get up or stand up, or to cause someone to rise — including rising or being raised from the dead.
article: At its core ἀνίστημι means to get up or stand up, but its range stretches both ways: intransitively a person rises from lying, sitting, or a place, and transitively someone or something is raised up — including raising the dead. The two most common renderings, "got up" (34×) and "rise" (24×), are everyday physical movement, but the word also carries the resurrection sense ("rise again," "raised"). One striking detail: in the Septuagint it renders Hebrew קוּם 354 times, and like that Hebrew word it often appears almost redundantly before verbs of going — "he rose up and went" — a usage the lexicons explicitly note. Everyday papyri also use the transitive form for setting up a statue or restoring walls.
caution: With 113 occurrences spread across many shades of meaning, the line between literal standing and figurative "rising" (especially resurrection) depends heavily on context rather than the word itself.

definition: Open conflict and quarreling between people—the strife, wrangling, and rivalry that breaks relationships apart.
article: This word covers the whole range of human conflict, from heated dissension to ongoing quarrels and rivalry, and the three measured senses really differ only in shade rather than substance. It appears 9 times in the Byzantine New Testament, almost always in lists of vices, and the Majority Standard Bible spreads it fairly evenly across "dissension," "quarrels," and "quarrels rivalry." Interestingly, while the New Testament treats it as a clear negative, the everyday Koine evidence is wider: a papyrus love-fragment uses it for "hate" taking hold of someone, yet an inscription uses it in a good sense, of beauty stirring up admiring rivalry in onlookers.
caution: The three measured senses overlap heavily and the MSB's "quarrels" and "rivalry" renderings have 0% independent agreement from BSB, so the boundaries between them are fuzzy.

definition: Nineveh, the ancient capital city of Assyria.
article: Νινευΐ is the place name Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian empire, taken directly from the Hebrew נִינְוֵה. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 11:32) and 17 times across 6 books of the Septuagint. Notably, this exact form is part of the Received Text reading; the critical SBLGNT does not carry it, and the single NT occurrence is absorbed into phrasing rather than rendered as its own English word.
caution: Evidence in the NT is thin: a single occurrence that is absent from the critical text, so the form's standing is disputed.

definition: A person who pretends to be something they are not, putting on a false outward show.
article: In the New Testament ὑποκριτής means a pretender — someone who acts out a false role, faking goodness or piety. The word literally meant a stage actor in ordinary Greek, and the evidence shows this clearly: inscriptions and papyri use it for performers in tragedies and even name a flour-account recipient who was an actor. The figurative "pretender" sense is the only one found in the Bible, appearing 20 times in the Byzantine text and matching the Hebrew word for "godless" or "profane" in its two Septuagint uses.

definition: Whole and complete, with nothing left out — perfect through and through.
article: ὁλοτελής means whole and complete, built from ὅλος ("whole") and τέλος ("end" or "goal"), so it describes something perfect with no part missing. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 1 Thessalonians 5:23, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "completely." Moulton-Milligan note it shows up in everyday Koine documents, including a 1st-century decree about Nero's grant of freedom to the Greeks, where it carries the same "in full, without exception" force. Lexicographers say it is nearly impossible to distinguish from the related word ὁλόκληρος, except that ὁλόκληρος draws more attention to each individual part.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: Something done or produced—an act, deed, or piece of work, whether by people or by God.
article: At its core ἔργον means anything done or made—a task, an act, or the result of working. The measured New Testament data shows a narrow, consistent range: "works" (61%), "deeds" (32%), and "action" (7%), with translators agreeing strongly on each. In the Septuagint it appears 428 times, most often rendering the Hebrew מְלָאכָה (120×, "work/labor") and מַעֲשֶׂה (113×, "deed/action"), and everyday papyri use it for ordinary jobs like farm work and postponed projects—confirming this was a common, down-to-earth word.

definition: To an extreme degree; far beyond the normal measure or limit.
article: This adverb means something happens to an extraordinary or excessive degree, far beyond what is ordinary. It appears only once in the New Testament, where Paul says he was beaten or imprisoned "beyond measure" (2 Corinthians 11:23), and just once in the Septuagint. An inscription from 139 B.C. uses it the same way, describing a rivalry that ran "excessively" high, showing the word was at home in everyday Koine.
caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament and once in the Septuagint, so its measured range rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A rising up out from among the dead; a resurrection.
article: This rare word means a rising up and out, used in the New Testament specifically of rising from among the dead. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Philippians 3:11, where Paul speaks of attaining the resurrection of the dead. Interestingly, while one source lists a Septuagint occurrence translating the Hebrew yeqûm, Moulton-Milligan notes the word is not found in the Septuagint at all; in everyday papyri it even shows up referring to a woman's ornament in a damaged document from A.D. 149.
caution: Evidence is thin (only one New Testament occurrence) and the sources disagree over whether it appears in the Septuagint at all.

definition: The flesh of an animal used as food; meat.
article: κρέας simply means animal flesh eaten as food — what we'd call meat. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul's discussions about whether eating certain meat might cause a fellow believer to stumble (Romans 14:21 and 1 Corinthians 8:13); the two "senses" the data lists are really the same word, just translated within those contexts. The everyday flavor of the word shows up vividly in the papyri: one document mentions a contract to supply a village with salted meat and cheese, and another father writes that he couldn't find meat to send his son, so he sent twenty eggs and vegetables instead. In the Greek Old Testament it occurs 84 times, usually rendering the Hebrew בָּשָׂר ("flesh").
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, both in the same kind of context, the measured range is very narrow.

definition: A sycamore-fig tree, a fruit-bearing tree mentioned once in the New Testament that a man climbed to see Jesus.
article: συκομωραία refers to the sycamore-fig tree, a name built from the words for "fig" and "mulberry," so it describes a kind of fig-mulberry distinct from the regular mulberry (συκάμινος). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Luke 19:4, where Zacchaeus climbs one to get a view of Jesus. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and one scholar suggested Luke's careful distinction between this tree and the mulberry may reflect his medical knowledge, since both were used medicinally.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and the spelling varies across manuscripts and lexicons (συκομωραία, συκομορέα, συκόμορος), so its exact form is uncertain.

definition: The number five.
article: πέντε is simply the cardinal number "five," and it behaves consistently: the Majority Standard Bible renders it "five" in all 36 of its 38 measured occurrences (the other 2 are absorbed into phrasing), with the BSB agreeing 100%. In the Septuagint it appears 252 times, almost always translating the Hebrew word for five, חָמֵשׁ (222×). One nice detail from the papyri: a 2nd-century BC document from Tebtunis uses it to count plots of farmland—"five arourae"—showing it was the ordinary everyday word for the number.

definition: A person who drinks wine to excess; a habitual heavy drinker.
article: οἰνοπότης literally combines the words for "wine" and "drinker," describing someone who drinks wine to excess. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Matthew 11:19 and Luke 7:34), both times as an accusation thrown at Jesus, and the lexicons agree it means a wine-bibber or heavy drinker. The everyday Koine papyri show the same sense: one document describes a man who, "being by nature a wine-drinker," took a holiday before starting work. Note that the Hebrew word it translates in the Septuagint (Proverbs 23:20) is סָבָא, meaning one who guzzles or is a drunkard.
caution: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, so its range rests on thin biblical evidence supplemented by papyri.

definition: To lead the way for others, especially by showing them honor and putting them first.
article: This word combines "before" and "to lead," and in everyday Koine papyri it means to give a lead or go first in something. It appears only once in the New Testament (Romans 12:10), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "devoted" and other versions read "preferring" one another in honor. Strikingly, Abbott-Smith notes this Romans sense — outdoing one another in showing honor — is found nowhere else, making the verse's exact meaning unusually hard to pin down. In its two Septuagint uses it carries the more ordinary idea of going before as a leader.
caution: This is a single New Testament occurrence whose precise sense in Romans 12:10 is, by the lexicons' own admission, otherwise unattested and therefore uncertain.

definition: To clean out thoroughly, especially to winnow grain by clearing away the chaff from the threshing floor.
article: This verb combines "through/thoroughly" with "cleanse," giving the sense of cleaning something out completely. In both of its New Testament appearances (Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17) it describes John the Baptist's image of thoroughly clearing the threshing floor, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it "winnowing" 100% of the time. A nice everyday parallel survives in a papyrus from about 250 B.C. that uses the related form for a man who "cleaned out" the water-channels in a tent, showing the word's plain practical sense of clearing something out.
caution: Evidence is thin — only 2 occurrences, and the lexica list slightly different forms (διακαθαρίζω in Matthew, διακαθαίρω in Luke), with critical editions favoring the latter spelling.

definition: To smash or knock something to the ground, or to flatten it level with the earth.
article: This verb describes violently bringing something down to ground level, whether by leveling a structure flat or dashing something down. Its single New Testament use is in Luke 19:44, where Jesus foretells that enemies will flatten Jerusalem to the ground. The lexicons split on the exact picture: Abbott-Smith notes both 'to beat level like a threshing floor' (from Theophrastus) and 'to dash to the ground,' and the Septuagint mostly uses it for the Hebrew רָטַשׁ in passages about dashing children to the ground (as in Psalm 137:9 and Hosea 14:1).
caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the sources differ over whether it means 'level flat' or 'dash down,' so its precise force here is uncertain.

definition: The food or sustenance needed to keep someone alive and supported.
article: διατροφή means the nourishment or provisions needed to sustain a person, built from τρέφω (to feed or support). It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 6:8, where Paul pairs it with covering or clothing as the basics worth being content with. Everyday papyri confirm this practical sense: an apprenticeship contract from A.D. 66 records five drachmas paid "on account of his keep," and a will arranges for a wife to supply a son's "sustenance and other expenses."
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse.

definition: A pleasant smell or fragrance, often used for the sweet aroma of a sacrifice offered to God.
article: εὐωδία means a sweet, pleasant smell, and in all three of its New Testament appearances it carries the imagery of a fragrant offering pleasing to God. The word's range is narrow: the Majority Standard Bible renders it as a fragrant sacrificial aroma once (Ephesians 5:2) and simply as fragrant once (Philippians 4:18), with one further occurrence absorbed into surrounding phrasing. Its background in the Septuagint is striking — there it appears 48 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for the soothing aroma of sacrifice (42 times), so the sacrificial overtone is deeply rooted. Everyday Koine papyri use it plainly too, advertising sweet-smelling jars of wine.
caution: With only three New Testament occurrences this entry rests on thin evidence, though the sources agree on its basic meaning.

definition: To kick out with the foot, especially in stubborn resistance against something pressing on you.
article: λακτίζω means literally to kick with the foot, and it appears just once in the New Testament, at Acts 26:14, in the proverbial phrase about kicking against the goads. The Majority Standard Bible renders this single occurrence with reference to "goads," and the BSB agrees fully. Everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain physical sense: one third-century BC document describes someone kicking at a door with their feet, and a related noun shows up alongside "fists and heels" in a description of a beating.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range here rests on that single verse plus outside Koine evidence.

definition: A female deity or goddess, the feminine counterpart of the word for god.
article: θeá simply means a goddess, the feminine form of θεός (god). It appears just twice in the Byzantine New Testament, both times in Acts 19 referring to the goddess Artemis worshiped at Ephesus. The papyri confirm this same form was the everyday Koine choice (rather than the Attic ἡ θεός), with one inscription even calling Isis "goddess of goddesses." Interestingly, in its two Septuagint appearances it translates Hebrew words that have nothing to do with deities, suggesting those are unrelated or difficult cases.
caution: Evidence is thin: only two New Testament occurrences, and the listed "senses" are really just fragments of the same single meaning, so confidence is rated low.

definition: A measuring rod or standard; figuratively, a rule to live by or a defined sphere of activity assigned to someone.
article: κανών starts as something concrete — a straight rod or measuring line used in building — and then stretches into the figurative ideas of a standard to measure by and a marked-out boundary or sphere of work. In the New Testament it appears only 5 times across 3 books, mostly clustered in 2 Corinthians 10 where Paul speaks of the limits or 'province' of his assigned ministry, plus Galatians 6:16 where it means a rule of conduct. A nice detail from the papyri: the word shows up in a temple-building inscription describing work done 'straight to a continuous rule,' which captures its literal origin perfectly, and it traces back to a Hebrew word for a reed.
caution: The evidence is thin, with only 5 New Testament occurrences and a single Septuagint use, and the measured renderings here are mostly fused into prepositional phrasing rather than standing alone.

definition: To act against the law; to break or violate it.
article: παρανομέω means to break or transgress the law, formed from παρά ("contrary to") and νόμος ("law"). It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, in Acts 23:3, where Paul accuses the high priest of acting unlawfully by ordering him struck. The word is well attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, where it describes lawbreakers facing punishment — for example, a sixth-century papyrus warns offenders that soldiers may be sent to punish their lawlessness.
caution: The measured NT sense here is rendered as "wall," which clearly reflects a data-tagging error rather than the word's actual meaning of acting unlawfully, so treat the occurrence count cautiously.

definition: To hide something inside or mix it into a larger mass so it disappears from sight.
article: ἐγκρύπτω means to conceal something by putting it inside or blending it into something else, so the parable of leaven "hidden" in flour captures the sense well. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (Matthew 13:33), where translators folded its meaning into the surrounding phrasing rather than giving it its own English word. In the Septuagint it shows up 6 times across 5 books, mostly rendering the Hebrew verbs טָמַן and צָפַן, both meaning to hide or bury — so the core idea of concealment runs consistently through the evidence.
caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and few Septuagint examples, this word's full range rests on thin evidence.

definition: To follow after something or someone, especially in the sense of imitating, obeying, or being guided by them.
article: ἐξακολουθέω means to follow closely or follow after, used figuratively for imitating or being guided by something. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, all in 2 Peter (1:16, 2:2, 2:15), where it's consistently rendered "follow" — for following cleverly devised myths or shameful ways. The most striking outside evidence comes from everyday Koine papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show the word often referring to penalties that "follow upon" or are incurred by wrongdoers, as in legal phrases about being released from the penalties one has merited.
caution: The evidence is thin — only 3 New Testament occurrences, all in 2 Peter, so the measured sense rests on a narrow base.

definition: To set someone free by paying a ransom, or more broadly to deliver and redeem.
article: λυτρόω means to free someone by paying a price—a ransom—and by extension simply to deliver or rescue. It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, all rendered "redeem" by the Majority Standard Bible, and it shows up 98 times in the Septuagint translating Hebrew words for redeeming, especially פָּדָה (31×) and גָּאַל (32×, the act of a kinsman buying back a relative or property). Strikingly, everyday Koine papyri use the word in plainly commercial settings—one document has a woman redeeming confiscated property, another covers a hundred drachmas paid to ransom someone's cloaks.
caution: Evidence is thin in the New Testament (only 3 occurrences, and none in the critical SBLGNT text), so confidence rests largely on the Septuagint and papyri.

definition: Describing something that comes at just the right time, well-timed, opportune, or suitable for the moment.
article: εὔκαιρος combines εὖ ("well") and καιρός ("time, season"), so at its core it means "well-timed" or "coming at the right moment." It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament: once describing a fitting day (Mark 6:21) and once of timely help (Hebrews 4:16). The everyday Koine sense shines through in the papyri, where one inscription (OGIS 762) uses the very phrase "let him help when timely" (βοηθείτω κατὰ τὸ εὔκαιρον), mirroring the "timely help" of Hebrews.
caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and the Majority Standard renderings ("opportunity," "help") differing from the BSB, the precise English wording is uncertain even though the underlying sense is clear.

definition: To eat something up completely, or figuratively to consume, destroy, or swallow up people and their possessions.
article: κατεσθίω is the intensified form of "eat" (ἐσθίω), carrying the force of eating something all the way down — devouring or consuming it entirely. In the New Testament it ranges from literal eating (birds eating seed) to vivid figures like fire consuming enemies or people "devouring" widows' houses, and the Septuagint uses it heavily (145 times), mostly for the Hebrew אָכַל ("to eat"). A nice everyday parallel comes from the papyri, where a complaint describes sheep that "overran, cropped, and utterly destroyed" a pasture — the same sense of eating something into ruin.
caution: In about a third of New Testament cases (4 of 10 measured) the word is absorbed into idioms like "make their houses," so the rendering "make" reflects English phrasing rather than a separate meaning.

definition: Hezron, an ancestor of Jesus listed in the genealogies, the son of Perez and father of Ram.
article: Ἐσρώμ is the Greek form of the Hebrew name חֶצְרוֹן (Hezron), a man who appears in the family line of Jesus as the son of Perez. It occurs only 3 times in the New Testament and is purely a personal name, not a word with meaning beyond its bearer. The translation breakdown looks scattered—rendered once each as "Perez," "Hezron," and "son"—but this simply reflects that the name sits inside genealogical sentences ("Perez the father of Hezron... the son of..."), so the surrounding words get counted alongside it.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a name that appears amid genealogical phrasing, the measured "senses" reflect neighboring words rather than distinct meanings of Ἐσρώμ itself.

definition: To sit down beside someone, settling in close to listen or stay near.
article: παρακαθίζω simply means to sit down next to someone. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 10:39, where Mary sits beside Jesus to listen, and the critical text doesn't use this exact form at all. Notably, the same word shows up in the Septuagint at Job 2:13, where Job's friends sit beside him, and Moulton-Milligan find the related forms in everyday papyri and inscriptions, including one phrase about "sitting in on the lectures."
caution: Evidence is thin: just one disputed New Testament occurrence (replaced by παρακαθέζομαι in critical texts) and one Septuagint use, so confidence is low.

definition: To listen to a request and respond favorably, especially when God hears and answers prayer.
article: In the New Testament εἰσακούω almost always means more than just hearing sound—it means God listening to and granting a prayer, used 4 times this way (as in Luke 1:13 and Acts 10:31). It is hugely common in the Greek Old Testament, appearing 222 times, where it usually renders the Hebrew שָׁמַע ('to hear'). Abbott-Smith notes a second shade, 'to obey' (as in 1 Corinthians 14:21), and a papyrus letter from around 250 BC uses it for someone refusing to 'listen to' a request, showing the same everyday sense of heeding.
caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences, the measured data captures just the 'answered prayer' sense; the 'obey' sense rests on the lexica and Septuagint rather than the NT count.

definition: To turn yourself away from someone or something — to avoid, shun, or keep your distance from them.
article: ἀποτρέπω means to turn oneself away from something, and in its single New Testament appearance (2 Timothy 3:5) it carries the sense of avoiding or shunning a certain kind of person. Though it occurs only once in the Byzantine text — and not at all in the SBLGNT critical text — the lexicons agree on a stable range: 'turn away,' 'avoid,' 'shun.' One nice detail: Moulton-Milligan note the word turning up in a woman's private letter among the papyri, showing that this verb, common in literature, was also ordinary everyday speech.
caution: This word appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament (and not at all in the critical text), so the measured sense rests on a single occurrence.

definition: To shine or gleam intensely, giving off a bright, flashing radiance.
article: στίλβω describes something that gleams or glistens with intense brightness. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Mark 9:3, where Jesus' clothing shone dazzlingly at the Transfiguration; the Majority Standard Bible's wording there ties the verb to a launderer's whiteness. The word is well attested in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, and a poetic example from Bacchylides pictures a 'fiery light flashing from his eyes,' showing how vivid the gleaming could be.
caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise force there rests on slim biblical evidence supplemented by outside Greek usage.

definition: The chief priest of the Jews, the leader of the temple worship, or in the plural the leading members of the priestly class.
article: In the New Testament ἀρχιερεύς points either to the single high priest who leads Israel's worship or, in the plural, to the broader group of "chief priests" — ex-high-priests and members of high-priestly families who held influence. The 122 occurrences split fairly evenly: about 51% are rendered "chief priests" and 44% "high priest," so context decides which is in view. Interestingly, the same title shows up in everyday Egyptian papyri, where an "ἀρχιερεύς of Alexandria and all Egypt" was actually a financial administrator, showing the word could name high-ranking officials well beyond the Jewish temple.

definition: To speak something out openly, especially to reveal or disclose information that was meant to be kept private.
article: This verb means to speak something out — to divulge or reveal what someone has told you. It appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:22, where the commander tells the young man not to disclose that he had reported a plot. The same word turns up in the Greek of Judith 11:9 and in everyday Koine papyri, so it was ordinary spoken vocabulary, not a specialized term.
caution: With only a single New Testament occurrence, the measured range here is very thin and rests mainly on outside evidence.
